## Volume front matter

### Series title page

*Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have survived from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, corrected with the utmost care; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the very extensive editions produced during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each individual volume or author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded with works both doubtful and apocryphal, and with works possessing some authority and influence in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes. The first is an index of subjects, by consulting which one may see at a glance whatever each Father has written on any given topic; the second is an index of Sacred Scripture, from which it is immediately evident to the reader which Fathers, and in which places of their works, have commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture. An edition of the utmost accuracy, and easily preferable to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently alike throughout the whole work, the smallness of the price, and above all this collection, which is unified, methodical, and chronological, of six hundred fragments and minor works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works concerning every age, place, language, and literary form.*

### First Series

The First Series, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of complete courses in the various branches of ecclesiastical learning.

The holy martyrs were raised onto a cross, with their heads lifted toward heaven. Sometimes they were hung with their arms bound behind their backs; weights were sometimes fastened to their feet by the ministers of the devil. They were also fastened to a cross with their heads turned toward the ground. Christian women were suspended by their hair.

A. A martyr was suspended by the feet, with a fire placed beneath him so that he would be suffocated.

B. A martyr was hung by a noose.

A. A martyr, hung with ropes tied around his body, had his shoulders loaded with clods of salt; a piece of wood was forced into his mouth to increase the torment.

C. A martyr was hung by both feet, while his head was battered with hammers.

D. The last was burdened with weights tied to his neck and feet.

A. Sometimes a slow fire was placed beneath suspended Christians so that the smoke rising from it would press upon their throats. These were people who could sing with the holy prophet David: “With fire, sweetest Jesus, you tested us, and no iniquity was found in us.”

## Dedication

“To the most holy Father and Lord, our Lord Pius VI, Supreme Pontiff, who, with exceptional and singular zeal for the cultivation, enlargement, and honor of ecclesiastical learning, most graciously permitted the title of the most sacred name to be prefixed to the Roman edition of the poems of Marcus Aurelius Clemens Prudentius: this second volume, in which the Catholic poet tramples underfoot the pollution of the nations, attacks the worship of idols, dedicates a poem to the martyrs, and praises the apostles, Faustino Arevalus, after the most humble kisses upon the feet of the blessed, has deservedly dedicated and presented.”

[Col. 0009]

## Preface

You have here, dear reader, a commentary on the poems of Prudentius that remained to be printed. It has appeared perhaps later than the opinion—or even the expectation—of many people would have wished, but much sooner than the work itself seemed able to bear, or than I had intended for it to emerge according to the judgment of my mind.

I had not been displeased when the earlier volume slipped from my hands and came into public circulation, because I had decided that this could be useful: made more learned by the advice and criticisms of others, I might either reconsider some things already said and improve them, or subject what remained to be said to a stricter standard of judgment. Whether this plan of mine would yield any fruit, I would willingly have left for others to decide, unless gratitude required me to acknowledge that it had done so.

But if any other kind of writing requires a long period of time for maturity, certainly a commentary on so learned a Christian poet does. For amid the almost infinite variety and abundance of topics, how many things are offered by time and circumstance—even while we are engaged in something else—that you would otherwise seek in vain, and that would scarcely prompt the thought of seeking them? Why should I mention the opinions and thoughts of learned men that arise in the very familiar and daily exchange of conversation? Rome in particular, where so many people both can and wish to help you in investigating sacred and secular antiquities, offers greater assistance than anywhere else for completing reflections of this kind.

Yet, lest I be accused of slowness and procrastination, or seem rather to have ceased working than to have wished to await a suitable opportunity until the work matured, I finally yielded to the advice of others and complied with their wishes.

This also encouraged me: many distinguished men made it plainly evident that they considered the industry I had devoted to the earlier volume not merely pleasing but also sound—distinguished men, I mean, removed from partisan zeal, outstanding for their sharp judgment, and, moreover, especially capable of expressing an independent opinion. For who would not judge me with complete freedom? I cannot, even if I wished, restrain the freer censures of any people, the prejudiced corrections of those who do not read, or the disdain of those who, although they might perhaps do better themselves, accomplish nothing, and prefer to pass judgments in the republic of letters rather than submit to them. Nor, if I could restrain them, would I particularly wish to do so. For this reason I owe the greater gratitude to those who have deserved well of me.

There was also this consideration: since I had decided to include the poems of Prudentius in two volumes, their bulk unexpectedly increased so much that I was forced to cut out several things and defer some others to another work. This is the principal point I wished to mention beforehand, lest my preface seem unnecessary.

For I had promised to place two dissertations before the commentary of this later volume: one on the destruction of the altar of Victory, the other on Prudentius’s confidence in reporting the acts of the holy martyrs. Since there is no opportunity for a fuller discussion of these subjects here, I have said in the commentaries what seemed necessary and ought to be sufficient for explaining the poet and defending his authority. I intend to include the additional material that could be added in treating both subjects more distinctly and fully in a separate work, so that, if it is added, it will not be superfluous to completing the interpretation of Prudentius, while, if it is absent, it will not be greatly missed.

Accordingly, I now publish Prudentius in much the same way as certain architects customarily complete their works: although they place a roof on buildings, however spacious, and apparently lacking nothing for their perfection and completion, they nevertheless leave on one side certain projections and foundations of walls, as traces of a continuation of the work, so that the building may, if the need arises, at some time be enlarged by themselves or by others and reduced to a more imposing form.

Farewell.

[Col. 0011]

# Psychomachia

## Preface to the *Psychomachia*

[Col. 0011A] **Note.**

*Psychomachia* is Greek; in Latin it is called “the battle of the soul,” because it depicts the battles in which the faithful soul fights against vices. But a preface drawn from the book of Genesis precedes the narrative of the poem, so that the divine authority may better commend the work that follows. —Iso.

Verse 1. Abraham is rightly called “the first,” as it is written: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness.” Therefore he is not only the father of circumcision, but also of all those who follow the path of his faith. —I.

2. “Blessed”: he became the late father of Christ’s blessed seed, so that desires might grow not only through delay, but also so that hearts might be prepared by many teachings to receive grace, and so that redemption, long awaited and finally arriving, might be received with greater gratitude. —I.

3. “Added”: the Hebrews say that God gave Abraham the letter *he* from his own name, which among them is the tetragrammaton, so that the man who had previously been called “exalted father” might afterward be called “father of many,” that is, of peoples or nations. —Iso.

5. “Aged”: the son who had been given to him in his old age; he offered the son who had been the pledge of his old age. —“Pledge”: children are called pledges because hope for future offspring is placed in them. —“Dedicated”: consecrated. —“Sacrifice”: for sacrifice. —Iso.

6. “To sacrifice”: to offer sacrifice. *Lito* is derived from *linio* and is a frequentative form, although it may seem to signify something else. —I.

[Col. 0011B] **Note.**

The title in the Marietti codex is: “Here begins, in Christ’s name, the preface to the *Psychomachia*.” In Vatican Codex C: “Here begins the book of Aurelius Prudentius, the *Psychomachia*.” In Alex., “Here begins Book IV of the *Psychomachia*”; but this may be an error, since at the end it says, “Here ends Book III of the *Psychomachia*,” unless it is called Book IV because it is fourth in the order of that volume, although it is the third work against heretics.

Verse 1. In the oldest Vatican codices A and B, the word *Psychomachia* is absent; it is present, however, in several others in which this work is contained separately. Since the poem contains much that is highly useful for directing the spiritual life, monks especially loved it and copied it frequently. In other codices, however, the *Psychomachia* is entirely omitted, because, as I think, the poem seemed already too widely known. Accordingly, it appears neither in the elegant Urbino codex nor in the Florentine one.

The codices of the *Psychomachia* written separately in the Vatican Library are those designated by the letters C, E, F, G, H, and L. The *Psychomachia* is found together with some other works of Prudentius in codices O and BB. For all of these, see the prolegomena, chapter 4; there you may also observe whether, and what, titles each codex contained. I discussed the codex of the *Psychomachia* in the Angelica Library in the same chapter. I gave other relevant material in the note to the preface of Prudentius, verse 39, and in the note to the title of the *Hamartigenia*.

In paragraph 216 of the prolegomena I noted that Bar-thius judged the division of the chapters to have been devised according to the ingenuity of the monks—or, as he puts it, “monkish.” On the Spanish translation of the *Psychomachia*, consult the prolegomena, paragraph 119; on the Greek translation, paragraphs 91 and 121.

Those who give the *Psychomachia* Latin titles such as “On the Battle of the Soul,” “On the Conflict of the Soul,” or “On the Contest of Virtues and Vices” do not do so improperly. Yet consider whether it could better be explained as “Spiritual Battle.” Under this title a celebrated book was published in Italian without the author’s name, reprinted many times, translated into several languages, and long ago restored to its true author, the Reverend Father Lorenzo Scupoli of the Theatine Congregation of Regular Clerics.

Two other Spanish books bearing the same title should nevertheless also be consulted. One is *Una Lucha y Combate del alma con sus afectos desordenados*—“A Struggle and Battle of the Soul with Its Disordered Affections”—Barcelona, 1610, by Ludovicus de Vera, a Carthusian. The other is *De la Perfección de la vida Christiana*, by Joannes de Castaniza, a Benedictine; this work appeared in Latin and Dutch under the title *Spiritual Battle*.

That Prudentius introduces virtues and vices as if they were persons in this poem is not new. See what J. C. Scaliger notes in Book III of the *Poetics*, chapter 3, concerning quasi-persons such as poverty, fame, and lust. But I do not recall that anyone before Prudentius had composed an entire poem out of such quasi-persons.

A small book by Emmanuel Martini deserves to be read: *On the Affections of the Soul*, in which he explains the Greek names of vices and virtues. It appears after his letters in the edition prepared by Petrus Wesselingius.

A treatise *On the Christian Contest* is found in volume VI of the works of St. Augustine, and another *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, which is more commonly attributed to St. Isidore. Others say that its author was St. Ambrose; others, St. Leo; the Maurists attribute it to Ambrose Autpertus, which is more probable.

In preparing to describe the contest between virtues and vices, Prudentius sets before us the example of the faithful old man Abraham as a model for conquering. Faith holds both the first and the last place in this triumph; hence the poet’s preface about Abraham is entirely appropriate. For just as Abraham, although old, conquered his enemies because he believed God, so we, although weak and feeble by nature, will nevertheless be able to overcome adversaries and vices when armed with the shield of faith.

In editions published before Heinsius—those of Aldus, Torn., Gis., and Weitzius—the reading was *prima credendi via est*, “the first way of believing is.” Heinsius removed *est*, citing his manuscripts. Bonon., Alex., and others support him. In Vatican Codex C the substantive verb *est* has been erased. Bede, in *On the Art of Meter*, copies the verse without *est*.

Nevertheless, *est* appears in Mar., Rat., Vienn., Prag., Vatt. G and L, and others. Gallandius deleted *est*, but does not recognize an explanatory construction. He thinks that all these words are governed by the verbs *suasit* and *dedit* in verse 10, which is more poetic and modeled on the manner of Pindar.

You have the whole history of Abraham in Genesis, chapter XI and following.

3. The place cited is chapter XVII, verse 9: “Your name shall no longer be called Abram, but you shall be called Abraham, because I have appointed you the father of many nations.”

4. Most printed editions and the best manuscripts have *parenti*, “for the father.” Aldus, together with Codex Angelicus and Vatican Codices O and BB, has *parente*, “by the father,” less satisfactorily.

[Col. 0012D] 5. *Dicare victimae* means “to dedicate in place of a victim.” Confirming this expression, Bar-thius, in Book XXIV of the *Adversaria*, chapter 5, testifies that Prudentius is a treasury of elegant expressions and observes that Catullus, Germanicus, Martial, and Claudian used similar expressions. Relevant here are the notes to Hymn 3 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 118: “Or given to smoking torches.”

6. Some derive *litare* from *luo*; others, more correctly, from Greek λιτή, λιτά, that is, “prayers” or “supplication.”

577. Faithful old man, the first way of believing,

Abram, late father of blessed offspring,

578. Whose name an added syllable enlarged,

Abram, called so for the father, Abraham for God.

[5] 579. The aged pledge whom he dedicated as a sacrifice,

Teaching that, when anyone wishes to sacrifice at the altar,

[Col. 0013A] **Note.**

[Col. 0013B] 7. He should believe that, just as Abraham offered his only-begotten son, whom he loved, so whatever is most precious in the heart must be offered to God. —“To the heart”: that is, *est*, “is.” —“Pious”: beloved. —I.

9. “Profane”: the profane nations are the passions of the soul, and the vices are the monsters of the heart; the soul’s passions are desire, joy, and grief. Hence Virgil also sang: “They desire, rejoice, and grieve.” —Iso.

10. “An example”: just as Abraham destroyed real kings, so he urged us to exterminate the vices by which we are subjected through the five senses. For Abraham signifies the warlike spirit; the five kings, the five bodily senses; Lot, faith captured by vices, which the warlike spirit releases; the 318 servants signify the faith established at the Council of Nicaea by 318 bishops. But the number may also refer to ten, for the Decalogue, and eight, for the eight beatitudes. Whoever lacks all these things will never attain the beatitudes mentioned above. —Iso.

11. “Offspring”: the fruit of a good work. —Iso.

12. “Brought forth”: produced, brought forth, created. —Iso.

[Col. 0013C] 13. “Slaughter”: killing. —“Warlike spirit”: reason, which exists in the soul and wages war against vices. When the warlike spirit has freed the heart from their service, it follows that offspring pleasing to God will be created from the mother, virtue—namely, the fruit of a good work. —I.

14. “Monsters”: prodigies, or vices. —Iso.

15. “Had captured”: whoever dwells with criminals is deservedly captured; indeed, he had chosen to dwell among them. Moses speaks against this: “Depart,” he says to the people, “from the tents of these wicked men.” There is no doubt that he means they should leave, lest they themselves become involved in the sins of those men. —Iso.

16. “Dwelling”: inhabiting. —Iso.

17. “Fostered”: inhabited, cultivated, loved. —Iso.

18. “Powerful”: growing, or shining, or abounding, as it is written: “God remembered Abraham and rescued Lot from the overthrow of the city.” —“In honor”: he was powerful because of the honor owed to his uncle Lot, as it is written, and so forth; or certainly because Abraham was regarded by all as a prophet of God. —“Cousin”: Abraham’s. —Iso.

19. “On the left”: contrary, adverse. The message from the left was an adverse report announcing the captivity of his nephew and that he had been captured and was serving barbarians. —“Roused”: disturbed. —Iso.

21. “Barbarians”: pagans. —Iso.

22. “Three times six”: eighteen. —Iso.

24. “Whom”: the abundance of rich treasure had made him slow to pursue the departing enemy. —Iso.

25. “Hindered”: *hostem* is used for *hostes*, the singular for the plural, as in the expression, “The most grievous fly came.” —“Resources”: riches. —Iso.

26. “Draws”: unsheathes. —“Full of God”: since he was full of God, he easily overcame the opposing ranks. —Iso.

27. “Mass”: greatness. —Iso.

28. “Drives away”: here we find the figure called *hypozeuxis*, namely, when different verbs are properly joined to each separate clause. —“Wounded”: injured. —Iso.

30. “Necklaces”: ornaments, standing for every kind of adornment. —Iso.

31. “Heifers”: cows, herds of cows, cattle. —Iso.

32. “Freed”: released, swift, or unbound. —Iso.

[Col. 0013C] **Note.**

7. In Vatican Codex D, contrary to the meter, the reading is *quod est dulce cordi*, “which is sweet to the heart.” Aldus, Gis., and other common editions have *quod dulce cordi est*, “which is sweet to the heart.” In the old manuscripts used by Heinsius, and in Mar., Rat., Weitz., Vatt., C, F, G, L, and most others, the substantive verb *est* is absent by explanatory construction, as in the first verse.

8. The scholiast on Persius, commenting on *Lusca sacerdos* in Satire 5, says: “Deformed women, or women lame in some part of the body, commonly devote themselves to the service of the gods.” Abraham taught by his own example that the opposite should be done.

10. Aldus, incorrectly, has *suasit* and *suum*.

12. Mar., Rat., Weitz., together with others, and Gis., have *parente*. All the manuscripts used by Heinsius, Alex., Vatican F and G, and most others have *placentem*. Fuldensis has the incorrect *placente*. Heinsius says that his manuscripts, together with Aldus, have *Deo placentem*; Teolius adds that all editions before Heinsius, except the Aldine, have *Deo parente*. But I find *Deo placentem* not only in the Aldine edition but also in other old editions, such as the Basel edition of 1540, the Cologne edition of 1594, and others.

Sichardus prefers *parente*, because *matre virtute* follows, just as Cicero boasted that he had labor as the parent of his nobility. Virtue is called a mother, as chastity is called a mother in Hymn 11 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 14.

14. Ald., Gis., Erfurt., Bong., and Angelicus, together with Vatican C, G, O, R, BB, and others, have *saevientis*, “raging.” Put., Oxon., Egm., Widm., Bonon., Alex., Mar., Rat. in its first hand, and others have *servientis*, “serving,” a word Prudentius often uses in a similar way.

Barthius, in Book XLIII of the *Adversaria*, chapter 7, had found *saevientis* in a certain manuscript and judged it excellent; but he admits that most codices have *servientis*, and explains it as meaning: unless the heart has reduced [the vices] to slavery and thus conquered its monsters, or its evil thoughts.

15. In Mar. there is the error *ceperit*, corrected above to *ceperant*. A similar error occurs in Vatican C, *ceparat*.

22. Pignorius, in *On Servants*, pages 22 and following, discusses the terms *verna* and *vernula*. The ancients called slaves born in the household by these names. Sometimes, however, *verna* was used in a broader sense for slaves of any kind, as Pignorius confirms with examples.

23. Mar. has *pergat*; above it has *pergant*, correctly.

24. Sichardus incorrectly has *triumphator* for *triumphus*. “Triumph” is called noble, as in Horace, Ode 1: “And noble victory.”

25. The Heinsian manuscripts, Alex., Vatican F, Ald., Bonon., Egm., and others have *captis tenebant*, “they held the captives.” Weitzius, Gis., Mar., Rat., Vatican C and F, and others have *captis tenebat*, “he held the captives.” The Viennese manuscript has *captum tenebat*, “he held the captive.”

26. Vienn. has *tunc ipse*, “then he himself”; others have *quin ipse*, “indeed he himself.” Erfurt., in its first hand, has *strinxit* for *stringit*.

31. Elmenhorstius, in his commentary on Arnobius, page 16, proves from ancient glosses, Virgil, and Aldhelm that *bucula*, for an ox, heifer, or cow, is so used. Aldus and Angelicus have *vestes*, “clothes”; others, *vestem*, “clothing.”

32. Mar. and Bonon., together with the Heinsian manuscripts, except Puteanus, have *expeditus vinculis*, “freed from bonds”; Heinsius did not follow them. Rat. has *expeditur vinculis*, “he is freed from bonds.” Most have *expeditus nexibus*, “freed from fetters.”

33. *Boiis*: *boia* is a chain fitted around the neck. He calls bonds *baccae* because of their roundness; smooth, rounded gems are also called *bacae*, as in: “And may he load the neck of the red shore with berries.” We also call the fruits of the olive or laurel *bacae*. *Baga* is said of the iron with which captive slaves are often driven, their necks and hands bound. —Iso. —*Bacis*: chains. Vatican T.

34. *Hostici*: hostile.

36. *Whom*: someone. —“Of blood”: of kinship. —“Lineage”: posterity, offspring; for it was unworthy that the leaders should possess the offspring of faithful blood. —Iso.

37. *Power*: authority. —Iso.

39. *Fercutis*: foods; metaphorically, provisions or tables. —Iso.

40. *Priest*: Melchizedek. —“Mighty”: very powerful. —Iso.

42. *Hidden*: Scripture, as the Apostle says: “Without father, without mother, without genealogy, having neither beginning of days nor end of life”; for Scripture reports none of these things about him. “Being made like the Son of God, he remains a priest forever” and bore the figure of God, who existed without beginning or origin. —Iso.

43. *Melchizedek* means “king of righteousness”: in Greek, *melchos* means “king,” and *salech* means “righteousness”; and rightly so, because he signifies Christ, who is the king of righteousness. —“From what ancestors”: born from which predecessors, that is, fathers. —Iso.

45. *Three-formed*: triple. —Iso.

46. *Magalia*: *mapalia* and *magalia* mean the same thing, namely, shepherds’ huts, which are also called a cottage or hut. —Iso.

47. *Quiet*: from childbirth, that is, barren. *Vieta* means curved; hence *vimina*, “withes,” from bending. —“Sarah”: for previously she was called Sarai, which means “my princess,” that is, the princess of the Jewish people. Later, after her name was changed, she was called Sarah, meaning simply “princess,” with “of all nations” understood. —Iso. —“Quiet,” that is, bloodless with respect to childbirth: for her womanly functions had ceased. Vatican T.

[Col. 0015B] **Note.**
33. Weitzius adopted Gruter’s conjecture *artita*, as though derived from *arto* or *arcto*. The ancients did indeed say *artita* for *artata* or *arctata*, *impetrita* for *impetrata*, and *dolita* for *dolata*. Some also take *artitus* to mean “instructed in the liberal arts.” But in this passage *attrita*, from *attero*, is correct and has been used similarly by several authors. Alcimus, Book I: “Shoulders oppressed by baskets, and necks worn raw,” to pass over Virgil, Ovid, and others. Egm. writes *adtrita*. The same should be said of Hymn 1 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 72: “And steel, worn against their necks, encircles them with heavy rings.”

There is great disagreement about *bacis*. Thus write Ang., Alex., Vatt. F, G, L, Egm., Pal., Aldus according to Weitzius (for he has *baccis*), Put., Teol., and the older editions of Heinsius. In Aldus, Vatt. D and BB have *baccis*, which is equivalent, although *bacis* is preferable orthographically. In the earlier Rottendorp manuscript there is a gloss: “*Bacae* properly means the fruits of the laurel, or clusters of ivy; but here the word is used for forms of chains. *Baccae*, with two *c*s, are the servants of Bacchus.” Gifanius, in his *Index to Lucretius*, under the word *vestis*, says that *bacis*, or, which is equivalent, *bagis*, should be read from the old books. Vatican O, together with Erfurt, has *bagis*. Fabricius, however, has either *baiis* or *boiis*. He prefers the word *baia*, from Borner’s manuscript, and interprets *baias* as “palm leaves,” on the authority of Jerome, or “branches of palms,” according to the ancient translator of John the Evangelist; from the shoots of these, he conjectures, the bonds were made by which prisoners’ necks were enclosed. Sich., Vienn., *bogis*; Mar., *boiis* or *bois*; Rat., *boiis*; Vat. R, *bois*; Thuan., *boigis*; Weitzius and Giselinus, *boiis*.

Giselinus observes that Jacobus Meyer, in the first hymn of the *Peristephanon*, after thoroughly purging it, restored this word to Prudentius; and rightly so. Giselinus rejects the reading *baccis* if it is understood to mean that the necks were worn raw by *baccae*, because they wore bead necklaces, or gem-studded ornaments, before they were captured. This is Nebrissa’s interpretation. Latinius likewise printed *boiis* for *baccis* in the *Bibliotheca selecta*. In Ducange’s *Glossary*, *boia* is a fetter or the collar of prisoners; from this it has been conjectured that executioners are called *boias* by the Italians, although others disagree. For the same thing are used *boga*, *bogia*, *baga*, and *bodia*. Jerome, Book V on Jeremiah, chapter 26, commenting on “Make for yourself bonds and chains,” says that those bonds and chains, or wooden forks placed around the neck, were called *boias* in the vulgar tongue. It should also be observed that Jeremiah is speaking of captives.

Mariettus undoubtedly says that *bogis* should be restored, because among the Insubrians the word *boghe* still survives for the yoke of oxen, by which their necks are rubbed raw. Isidore, Book V, chapter 27: “*Boia*,” he says, “is the collar of the condemned, like the yoke of oxen [or, according to another reading, ‘of an ox’]; it belongs to the class of bonds.” In that chapter he is discussing the punishments established by law. Some write *boya* in St. Isidore. Festus teaches that *boiae* were both wooden and iron, and were a kind of bond.

I think the same object was called by different names, as commonly happens, and Jerome hints as much concerning *bacis*. Therefore, whether one writes *boiis*, *bacis*, or in any other way, understand chains placed around the neck, both here and in Hymn 1 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 46: “The prison, bound with hard *boiae*, hampers their necks.” From this verse Mariettus suspected that one should read: “The free man raises his neck, formerly tightened, hindered, and bound by *boiae*.” Nothing should be changed, for *attrita* is more harmonious, as in the same Hymn 1 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 71: “And steel, worn against their necks, encircles them with heavy rings.”

It should also be noted that the verse cited by Iso, “And may he burden their necks with berries of the red shore,” is from Book III, meter 3, of Boethius’ *Consolation of Philosophy*, where the edition I use reads *baccis*, and the subject is gems.

34. Ald., *Abraham*; others, *Abram*.

36. Mar., in the first hand, Vatt. C, F, L, together with Ald., have *nequa*, a reading approved by Gifanius from an old book. The same reading occurs in Oxford. But Alex., Bonon., Vatican G, and others, as well as Heinsius, Weitzius, and Giselinus, have *nequam*. Weitzius wrote *prosapiem*. I do not approve this.

39. Bread and wine are called heavenly provisions because Melchizedek offered them, and the sacrament of the Eucharist was signified by them, as you will understand from the following glosses.

41. This verse and the following one are absent from Put.

43. Vienn., *Melchisech*. The meter requires *Melchisedech*. This name means “king of righteousness,” as Iso says, but from Hebrew origin, not Greek, as he thinks.

44. Bonon., contrary to the laws of verse, “known to God alone.”

45. The same Bonon. errs against meter and sense, reading *mox et informis* for *mox et triformis*. On this hospitality of the angels, see the title of *Dittochaeum*, 4.

46. Mar., Rat., all eleven Heinsian manuscripts, Weitz., *magalia*; Alex., Gis., and others, *mapalia*, together with Ald. and Bonon. Others write *mappalia*, such as Bong. and Vat. C. But the first vowel is short in Virgil and others. See Savaron on the huts of the Africans, *mapalia*, in Sidonius, p. 120, or, according to the correction, p. 111.

47. Ald., Gis. in the text of the first edition, Vat. F, and others:

“And now aged Sarah, fertile in the womb, the bloodless mother marvels at the gift of youth.”

That is, “and Sarah, the bloodless mother, marvels that the gift of fertile youth is now in an aged womb.” Heinsius says that, according to his manuscripts, one should write:

“And now Sarah, aged, marvels as a bloodless mother at the gift of youth, fertile in an aged womb.”

He explains this as meaning that Sarah is fertile in a womb already aged, as in the preface to *Arotheos*, verse 47, where certain manuscripts have *fertilis in herbam*. I think there is a great difference between the two expressions *fertilis in herbam* and *fertilis in alvum vietam*. I do not reject the former; I do not approve the latter.

There is great variation in the manuscripts. Vienn. has: “And now quiet Sarah, into a fertile womb, marvels as the gift comes, the bloodless mother.” Mar.: “And now quiet Sarah, into a womb, the fertile gift to come.” Rat.: “And now quiet Sarah, into a fertile womb, the gift to come,” which Weitzius printed. Alex.: “And now aged Sarah into a womb fertile with the gift of youth.” Benon.: “And now aged Sarah into a fertile womb,” but subsequently corruptly *majus juventae*. Fuld. likewise incorrectly has *Et jam fetam*. Palat. and Oxford agree with Alex. Thuan. has *quietam*; the remainder is as in Alexandrinus. Fabricius agrees with Aldus.

In the margin of certain editions is found: “And now quiet Sarah’s womb, the fertile gift coming.” Iso seems to have read *quietum* and *vietam*. “The gift of youth” means the power of giving birth, as in Paulinus’ poem on St. John the Baptist: “And youthful power came beneath an exhausted age.” Many write *Sarra*.

[Corrupt or uncertain text: *Attrita pons colla liber erigit*.]

Melchizedek, unknown in what lineage, from what ancestors,

48. “Bloodless,” as it is written: “Sarah’s periods had ceased,” Iso.

49. “Laughter”: Isaac was named from the father’s laughter, not the mother’s, because he had come from doubt, for which reason the woman too is reproved; but the father’s laughter arose from joy, Iso.

50. “Line”: shadow, figure, form, as painters first sketch future images with certain lines; thus everything happened to them in figure, but was written for us, and these things must certainly be fulfilled by us in straightforward paths.

51. “Which”: the line. “May retrace”: may renew. “With the foot”: by a path, in understanding, Iso.

52. “In arms”: that is, clothed in the arms of light, let us restrain from the service of foul lust the portion of our body represented by Lot, whose name means “he who turns aside,” joining our inward powers together, as in: “Whatever your hand finds to do, do it steadfastly, because neither work, nor reasoning, nor wisdom will exist in the underworld to which you hasten.” “Arms”: the virtues of the heart are the arms of the breast, Iso.

54. “Captured”: seized. “May it serve”: for *it was serving*, Iso.

55. “At home”: in you; our house is our mind. “Gathered together”: collected, assembled, Iso.

56. “Us”: that is, he teaches. “Abundantly”: plentifully. We are abundantly rich in household servants if we hold unwaveringly to the faith of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers. “Household servants”: good virtues, with virtues, I.

57. “Three hundred”: these three hundred signify a mystery, namely the cross. For the letter *tau*, which has the form of the holy cross, signifies three hundred. If you wish to know about the eighteen, consult arithmetic: you will count the smaller number within nine. It signifies that in the temple of Constantine three hundred and eighteen bishops defended the Church of God against the Arian heresy, I.

58. “Figure”: figuratively, Iso.

59. “Soon Christ himself”: therefore, after disturbances have been overcome through faith, and freedom has been granted to the bodily senses, with sin claiming nothing from us; then at last Christ, the true priest who offered himself immaculate to God, graciously meeting the victors, offers the bread of his body and the wine of his blood, I.

60. “From a parent”: as the prophet says: “Who has declared his generation?” Iso.

61. “Food”: eternal refreshment, Iso.

62. “Chaste”: the hospitable Trinity will deign to enter the humble mind of a chaste heart, according to: “I and the Father will come, and we will make our dwelling with him.” “Hut”: gentleness; examining the justice of each person’s heart, I.

63. “Hospitable”: if we wage war against vices, then the Trinity will enter our dwellings and make them fruitful with children of virtue. Among the ancients *hospita* was feminine; among us it belongs to the common gender, I.

[Note: [Col. 0017D]]

50. Nebrissa interprets *lineam* as a narrow path, which our life must retrace with a straight foot—that is, broaden by wearing it down. Compare Iso’s gloss. *Sculpere* is properly a term of the sculptor’s art. *Resculpo* means “to sculpt again,” or “to fashion,” and “to renew.” Tertullian, Augustine, and Rufinus used the word. See Rigaltius on chapter 5 of Tertullian’s *On Fasting*: “For the first people had retraced the crime of the first man.”

51. Fabr. has *rescalpit* for *resculpit*.

52. St. Prosper, near the end of the *Epigrams*: “There are never wars, never conflicts, lacking for the good; and the devout mind always has someone with whom it may contend.”

53. Egm., Widm., Pal., Mar., and Rat. have *pectoris*. Others, together with the printed editions, have *corporis*. Vienn. has: “And he teaches every portion of our body.” The verb *docet* is absent from other copies, and without it the meter cannot stand.

54. Ald. and Weitz. have *foede*, an adverb. Other printed editions have *foedae libidini*. In the manuscripts, some have a diphthong in the final syllable and others do not. But in many manuscripts diphthongs are entirely absent.

56. We explained this passage at length in chapter 20 of the *Prolegomena*. Among those who interpret the 318 as the Fathers of Nicaea in the vernacular Abrahamic tradition must be counted St. Mark the monk, fourth century, *Opusculum* 10, no. 8, volume VIII of Galland’s *Bibliotheca*. Barthius observes that his old book contains the error *non esse* for *nos esse*.

57. Vienn. corruptly has *trecentis*. In some vernacular copies, the addition “with these ninefold numbers” is incorrect. In a gloss, after the words “the figure of the holy cross,” supply *habet*, or something similar.

58. Barthius conjectures *prosint* for *possint*. But *possint* is excellent; or, if one wishes to change it, *possunt*, as in Virgil, Book IX of the *Aeneid*: “If my songs can accomplish anything.”

59. In Vat. C there is the awkward transposition “Soon Christ himself, who is the true priest.” We do not call these variations of readings, but errors of copyists.

60. Most copies, including Ald., Erfurt., Widm., Bong., Gifanius in the *Index to Lucretius*, under *de hiatu*, p. 437, Putean., Sich., Mar., Rat., Vienn., Vatt. D, F, L, O, and BB, have: “Born from a high and ineffable parent.” Alex. is preferable: “From an ineffable parent, and sprung from one,” together with Gis. and Pal. in the first hand. Vat. G and Fuld. have: “From an ineffable parent, and sprung from a high one.” Fabricius: “Born from a high and ineffable parent.” The first reading is sound, as Heinsius thinks, and the fourth foot is a tribrach, with elision excluded. Giselinus uses this diversity to argue that there were two editions of Prudentius’ works.

62. Ang., incorrectly, *pudici pectoris*.

584. The bloodless mother, now aged, marvels at the gift of youth,

rejoicing in her heir and repenting of her laughter.

[50] This line was prefixed as a figure,

which our life must carve anew with a straight foot;

we must keep watch in the arms of faithful hearts,

and every portion of our body

which, once captured, serves foul lust,

[55] must be freed at home by gathered strength.

[Col. 0018A] We are abundantly rich in household servants

if we understand what the three hundred,

with twice nine added, can signify in mystical figure.

Soon Christ himself, who is the true priest,

[60] sprung from an ineffable and one parent,

offers food to the blessed victors.

586. displaying the honor of the hospitable Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 0019A]]

64. “Soul,” which Sarah signifies. “Spirit”: by “spirit” he wishes Abraham to be understood, and by “soul,” Sarah, I.

65. “Married”: a syncopated form, that is, joined, as though married, from the verb *marito, -as*. “Offspring”: spiritual virtues. “Without”: unknown, I.

66. “Fertile”: fruitful with good works. “Seed”: if the seed is the word of God, consequently the children are also works, by whose reward we shall ultimately rule; not giving birth to a female, that is, something soft and relaxed, but to a boy, that is, something strong and solid, as in: “But when she has given birth to a boy,” etc., I.

67. “Dowry”: namely, virtues, a blessed life, or a righteous life; he allows those to enter whom he proves worthy. “Woman in childbirth”: giving birth to a boy, Iso.

68. “A worthy heir”: according to: “Your children are like olive shoots,” and elsewhere: “Direct their children”; and shortly afterward: “And direct the works of our hands upon us.” “Of the Father”: he is shown through divinity and humanity; although these are two, they are nevertheless not two, but Christ is one, Iso.

[Note: [Col. 0019A]]

64. Ald., Gis. in the text of the first edition, have *connexibus*; others, better, *complexibus*.

65. Aldus has *piae*, less correctly, for *pie*. Some vernacular copies have *expertam*; correct to *expertem*. Cauchius preferred *pie maritans* from a manuscript.

67. Ald., Nebr., and other vernacular copies have *Sarra*. Most printed editions and manuscripts have *sera*, as before verse 2, where Abraham is called a “late father.” In Vat. C, *sera* is in the first hand, with *Sarra* written above it.

68. Palat. has *implevit*; *implebit* is better.

Then the spirit, through its embraces,

will make the soul, long childless,

[65] piously joined in marriage, fertile forever from seed.

Then, late in life, the woman in childbirth, possessing her dowry,

will fill the house of the Father with a worthy heir.

## PSYCHOMACHIA

[Col. 0019]

[Note: [Col. 0019B]]

1. “Grievous”: great. “Having pitied”: a participle from *miseror, -aris*, which governs the accusative; hence he also says “pitying”: “Come to me, all you who labor,” Iso.

2. “Native”: paternal. Paternal virtue is Christ as substance, not an accident; nor is he the Father’s second quality, but his Son, because he did not beget himself from himself but from him. “You shine”: you grow, possess power. “One”: namely, one substance, I.

3. “In the threefold name”: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, I.

[Note: [Col. 0019B]]

1. In Rat. this is the title: “Here begins the book of the *Psychomachia* of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, concerning the battle of virtues and vices.” In Mar. it is “Invocation.” In other ancient manuscripts the titles are sometimes absent. More often, however, the book’s heading is found at the beginning of the preface rather than at its end. This first verse is fashioned in imitation of Virgil, Book VI of the *Aeneid*, verse 56: “Phoebus, who has always pitied Troy’s grievous sufferings.”

3. In the note on the preface to the *Apotheosis*, verse 31, I said that Prudentius and other Latin writers often use a superfluous expression; therefore *de nomine trino* (“by the threefold name”) is the same as *nomine trino* (“in the threefold name”). Heinsius, together with his manuscripts, Egm., Bonon., and Pal., read *de nomine utroque*, “by both names,” because, he says, the poet is speaking only of God the Father and the Son. Barthius, Book L of the *Adversaria*, chapter 11, found the same reading in an ancient parchment manuscript, but conjectures that one should read *te nomine trino*, “you in the threefold name,” or rather *te numine trino*, “you in the threefold divine power.”

“I do not consider it sufficiently pious,” he says, “to call the one God threefold in name only, nor is it consonant with what Augustine, Hilary, Athanasius, Cyril, Jerome, and countless others wrote at that time concerning the same mystery, none of whom speaks in this way.… But if any writer is cautious in the mysteries of faith, he is certainly our Prudentius, even though a poet—a class said to be granted greater license—and for this reason he deserves the commendation of all the more.”

Barthius is mistaken, however, in thinking that the other holy Fathers contemporary with Prudentius never spoke of God as threefold in name. I do not dispute his addition that it is not sufficiently pious to say that God is threefold in name only; but he supplied the adverb *only* from himself, and it is not found in Prudentius.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus, in his treatise *On Faith*, near the beginning, says: “We believe that there are three names and three persons of one essence, one majesty, and one power.” St. Paulinus, *Natalis* 9: “Thus, in the grace of the threefold name, he renews barren souls”; and again in the same work: “For he confessed one king under a threefold name.” And in Letter 12 to Severus: “Behold, as though under a threefold name, he worships one mind. Thus he consecrated the work as threefold in holy mass.”

In verses circulated under Claudian’s name, but which, as I have noted elsewhere, should be assigned to Merobaudes the Spanish Scholastic: “You alone are the companion of the Father and the guiltless Spirit, and, though so often threefold, simple in your threefold name.”

In a later period also a similar expression was in use. Drepanius Florus, a poet above the level of his age, in his poem on the Paschal candle: “The one divinity whom they celebrate under a threefold name,” where he seems to have imitated Prudentius. A charter of Ordoño III, from the year 955, in volume XXXIV of *Hispania sacra*, p. 459, begins: “In the triple, simple, divine name, I, Ordoño, by God’s will king,” and so forth.

I have cited other examples that could be brought here above, in the third hymn of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 20, and in the preface to the *Apotheosis*, verse 1, where I defended similar formulas of speech against Hincmar. Moreover, manuscripts Vatt. C, D, F, G, L, R, O, and BB have *de nomine trino*. In Vat. II, in both copies in the first hand, *trino* is written above the line. Alex. has *utroque*. Vienn., Mariet., Rat., Ald., Gis., Weitz., and the older printed editions have *trino*, which Chamillard preferred. Cellarius, influenced by Heinsius’ authority, printed *utroque*, as did Teolius.

Compare Peter Constantius’ *Vindications of the Confirmed Ancient Manuscripts*, which defends Gottescalc against Hincmar, and Lamius’ *On the Correct Faith of the Nicene Fathers*, chapter 33, no. 10. Lamius observes that in the missal edited by Cardinal Thomasius the expression *trina veritas*, “threefold truth,” is used in the questions addressed to the baptized, and he refutes Berninius, who in *History of the Eighth Century*, chapter 7, asserted that Gottescalc defended the expression *triplex deitas*, “triple deity.” For Lamius says that *trina deitas*, “threefold deity,” may be said, but rejects *triplex deitas*.

587. Christ, who has always pitied the grievous sufferings of humankind,

[Col. 0020B] who shine by paternal virtue and by your own, yet one—

(for we worship one God under a threefold name—

[Note: [Col. 0021A]]

4. Yet we must not believe in unity in God in such a way that we deny solitude. He is one, but not solitary, I.

5. “Declare”: show or speak. “With what soldier”: with what army to drive away vices, I.

6. “Armed”: the Apostle says, “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but powerful through God.” “May be able”: may be capable. “Cave”: in thought, Iso.

7. “Arises”: grows, or comes to pass. “When troubled”: gathered together, Iso.

8. “Sedition”: discord. “The flesh desires against the spirit,” and conversely. “Soul”: thought. “Diseases”: vices. “Strife”: contention. “Wearies”: afflicts, I.

9. “Defense”: aid. “For the sake of freedom”: which exists for protection. Far be it that Christ should have exposed believers to vices and left them deprived of strength, even if they are not endowed with the greatest virtues, since he says: “Do not fear, little flock”; and he blesses the little together with the great: “Stand firm, and do not again submit to the yoke of slavery”; otherwise, “the one who commits sin is sin’s slave.” “For the sake of freedom”: to do good, I.

10. “Battle line”: that is, it resists. “Furies”: vices or suggestions. “Heart”: the inward parts; the sound faculty of the mind, I.

[Col. 0021C] 11. “May resist”: may stand against. “With a better force”: with a heavenly host or virtue. “For not”: because. “Leader”: author or commander, I.

12. “Sinews”: virtues, strengths, I.

13. “Christ-worshipers”: Christians who worship Christ. “Ravaging”: laying waste. “You have set”: you have placed against, not removed, I.

[Col. 0022A] 14. “He himself”: “Put on,” he says, “the armor of God.” “Salvific”: marked or sealed. “Besieged”: the soul surrounded. “Companies”: virtues, I.

15. “To fight”: you command us to fight against vices. “You arm the mind with excellent arts”: you assist it with excellent virtues, I.

16. “Mind”: let the powerful mind conquer through Christ. Hence the Psalmist says: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory”; and likewise: “In God we shall perform mighty deeds.” “Mockeries”: for games; “uncleanness”: I.

17. “Powerful”: possessing heavenly help. “For you”: for your honor. “And for you”: for your praise. “May conquer”: then the flesh rejoices when it conquers vices, I.

18. “Present”: always ready for battle. “Hand to hand”: against, without interruption, close at hand; in the work that follows the vices are set against one another, and the opposing virtues against the vices they conquer. Hence it is conjectured that the whole poem was arranged by the author like painted historical scenes, I.

19. “Wrestling”: resisting, opposing, I.

20. “By strength”: by suggestions. “Monsters”: vices are rightly called monsters, for they do not exist according to nature but contrary to nature. “To mark”: to arrange, write, I.

[Col. 0022C] 21. “First”: it most rightly begins with faith, which, according to the Apostle, is both the beginning of good things and the foundation of virtues; otherwise whatever is not from faith is sin. “Attacks”: entered. “Field”: the field is the world, throughout whose boundaries the preachers’ sound has gone out; and the uncertain lot seemed to lie not among believers but among unbelievers. “Duel”: battle. *Duellum* is as though “the war of two men,” I.

[Note: [Col. 0021C]]

4. Isaiah 64:24: “I am the Lord, making all things, stretching out the heavens alone, establishing the earth, and there is none with me.” Prudentius says that God is one, yet not solitary: correctly so, because Isaiah there, attempting to turn the people away from the worship of idols, asserts the unity of the divine nature, which our poet acknowledges while at the same time asserting several persons.

8. Rat., Erfurt., Bong. have *animum*.

10. Vices are not improperly called furies. Lactantius, Book VI, chapter 21: “There are therefore three passions that drive human beings headlong into every crime: anger, greed, and lust. For this reason the poets said that there are three Furies who torment human minds: anger desires vengeance, greed wealth, and lust pleasures.” Seven principal or capital vices are now counted; formerly eight were customarily listed. On this, see Theodulf of Orléans, *Capitula to the Priests*, chapter 31.

13. Erfurt. has *spoliantibus*; the others, *populantibus*. By this reasoning Simonides’ error is overturned: he claimed that God had envied us because he allowed us to be subject to so many vices. For here he commands the salvific companies to fight in the besieged body.

15. Egm., Pal., and Barthius’ manuscript incorrectly have *armis* for *armas*. Barthius, whom I shall often cite now, discusses this manuscript and its corrections in Book L of the *Adversaria*, chapter 11; likewise in Book LI, chapter 9; Book LIV, chapter 12; and the same book, chapter 18. Barthius’ parchment manuscripts were extremely ancient and ornamented with paintings that reflected their antiquity.

19. Erfurt. incorrectly has *acies* for *facies*.

20. Vat. G has *infectis*; it has been correctly emended to *infestis*. After this verse a title is placed in many manuscripts, although Prudentius seems to have supplied no titles. Mar. and Rat. have “Faith.” Vienn. has “On the Battle of Faith and the Worship of the Gods.” Aldus has “The Battle of Faith and Idolatry”; he himself writes *idolatriae*. Chamillard has “Faith and Idolatry.” Weitzius and Giselinus follow Aldus.

21. The poet depicts virtues and vices vividly. Much could be drawn to illuminate this little book from Theophrastus’ *Characters*, with Casaubon’s commentaries, recently enlarged from Vatican manuscripts by the distinguished Johann Christoph Amadutius, and shortly before translated into Spanish by the distinguished Ignacio López de Ayala. The philosopher Seneca could also supply further material. For pagan philosophers sometimes discussed virtues and vices truthfully and cleverly. But Prudentius drew his teaching chiefly from Holy Scripture and the doctors of the Church. As I touch upon these sources, I am accustomed to praise the pagan philosophers and to marvel at them when they occasionally discover the truth, as one marvels at people blind in both eyes who, by labor and diligence, finally manage to walk correctly along some definite path without stumbling.

Faith is introduced first, uncertain beneath the lot of a duel. I do not think the poet looked only to the nature of war, in which fortune usually dominates, as Nebrissa, Weitzius, and Chamillard explain; rather, he looked to human free will, as Iso suggests. Sichardus says that faith is depicted as so eager that, at its first appearance, you would readily promise yourself victory.

Alcimus Avitus, *On the Praise of Virginity*, verse 365: “But you, virgin of God, whom holy conduct adorns, / modesty here, faith there, stronger in inward arms, / wage your battles.… These are the resources of virtue, these the consolations of war.… Thus Prudentius once sang with prudent voice.” Here he represents the subject of the *Psychomachia*.

Iso takes the Apostle’s words at Romans 14:23, “Whatever is not from faith is sin,” as referring to faith by which we believe in God; certain holy Fathers explain the same passage in this way. But these same Fathers understand “sin” here as an unprofitable work for attaining eternal life. Most others, however, more correctly interpret the Apostle as speaking of the faith, or conscience, by which we believe that some action is permitted to us, as is clear from the context itself. It is certain that not all the works of unbelievers are sins, nor are the virtues of philosophers vices.

588. Yet not solitary, since you, Christ, are God from the Father.)

[5] Declare, our king, with what soldier

the armed mind may drive faults from our heart’s cave.

Whenever, within our troubled senses,

sedition rises and the strife of diseases wearies the soul,

what defense then exists to preserve freedom,

[10] or what battle line, mingled with furies within the heart,

could resist with a better hand? For, good leader,

589. you have not exposed Christ-worshipers, powerless in great virtues

and lacking strength,

[Col. 0022A] to vices laying waste to them.

You yourself command the salvific companies

[15] to fight in the besieged body; you yourself arm the mind

with excellent arts, so that, powerful for attacking the heart’s

mockeries, it may fight for you and conquer for you.

The method of conquering is now at hand, if it is permitted

to mark face to face the very forms of the virtues

[20] and the monsters contending against them with hostile strength.

Faith is the first to enter the field, uncertain beneath the lot of the duel.

22. “Rustic”: for he chose not philosophers but fishermen for preaching. “Turbid”: angry, deformed, not warring according to the flesh. “Attire”: clothing, I.

23. “Bare”: ready for good works. “Shoulders”: having bare shoulders. “Unshorn”: uncultivated, not cultivated as virtue was. “Bared”: stripped for battle. “Although we walk in the flesh,” he says, “we do not fight according to the flesh.” “Upper arms”: arms, I.

24. “Sudden”: “and suddenly there came a sound from heaven,” Iso.

25. “Nor does she remember weapons”: for the holy preachers did not hurl Aristotelian syllogisms in the wisdom of speech, nor the twisted arguments of Chrysippus, I.

26. “Strong”: his breast was entirely strong, since he said: “Do you seek proof of the one who speaks in me, Christ?” “Limbs”: he had also uncovered his limbs: “We brought nothing,” he says, “into this world.” “Uncovered”: stripped bare, I.

27. “To be broken”: so that idolatry and the worship of the gods would no longer be practiced. “Of war”: of the age, I.

28. “Provoking”: challenging; idolatry first strikes faith when it pursues the preachers of faith. “Joined”: gathered together, I.

30. “That one”: faith. “Hostile”: it weakens the hostile head when kings or philosophers bow to the worship of religion. “Head”: idolatry. “Phalerate”: adorned, I.

31. “Faces”: those who look upon vanities are counted as nothing; for they also die while they contemplate them, in order to see, I.

33. “Crushed”: broken, I.

34. “Interchanges”: borrowed exchanges of breath; bands. “Tighten”: bind, I.

36. “Legion”: namely, of faith. “Gathered”: collected, Iso.

37. “Had stirred”: was urging, giving courage, I.

38. “Companions”: virtues. “Acquired”: a syncopated form, acquired, obtained, prepared; and it comes from the verb *parior*, I.

39. “Flowers”: flowers are the unfading freshness of eternal reward, because through the flood of their blood they earned eternal life; pleasures. “Burning”: he used the word for the ardor of love. “Purple”: purple clothing, I.

40. “Thereafter”: then. “Grassy”: covered with grass. “Field”: the exercise of continence is made joyful by continual greenness. “Ready to meet”: prepared to fight, I.

41. “Chastity”: chastity is rightly placed after faith, since just as integrity of faith is virginity of the mind, so purity of the flesh is the beginning of holy action; once this is destroyed, the whole structure of virtues collapses. “Splendid”: the weapons of light are splendid on both sides, as in: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning,” I.

[Note: [Col. 0023D]]

22. Fuld., not implausibly, has *vultu* for *cultu*. Iso interprets this poetic description of faith quite successfully. I will add Rupert of Tuitien’s interpretation, who in Book VI of *On the Work of the Holy Spirit*, chapter 16, says: “There were nevertheless very many who, not adorned with such garments of good works, ran to the confession of the holy name; and, still shining with recent baptism, wearing no ornaments of works, they clothed themselves in the glory of martyrdom. Of such faith someone sang: ‘Faith is the first to enter the field,’ and so forth.” At verse 24 he reads, contrary to the meter, *calor laudis*, “the heat of praise.”

23. We expose the upper arms, or bare the arms, when we wish to be especially free and intent for some work or labor. Giselinus observes that faith is strengthened by eagerness and steadfastness, while idolatry is adorned with phaleras: an apt observation.

24. Vienn. has *jamque*; others, *namque*. Put. has *labor*; the others, more correctly, *calor*. But Vat. F improperly transposed the words, giving *calor laudis* for *laudis calor*. See verse 22.

27. He says that dangers must be broken, as in Hymn 1 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 43: “when the situation of darkness has been broken.” One likewise says that audacity, plans, a judgment, or a disease is broken. After this verse Mar. and Rat. have the title “The Worship of the Gods.”

30. In both Mar. and Rat. *tympora* is written for *tempora*.

31. An imitation of Maro, who more than once in Books XI and XII has “rising higher.”

32. Some vernacular copies have *e pecudum*. The preposition *de* is often superfluous, as I noted at verse 3.

33. Weitzius, Gis., Mar., and Vat. R have *in mortem*. Most of the others, together with Heinsius and Aldus, have *in morte*; Heinsius confirms this because the poets say, “Eyes swimming in death.” He himself had printed *in mortem*.

34. In the Weitzian edition it is incorrectly noted in the margin as *ad oram arctans* for *arctant*.

37. Vienn. has *armarat*. Fuld. has *armabat*. Others, more correctly, have *animarat*. In a manuscript of excellent quality collated by Michael Piccart and held by Weitzius, the reading is *armarat*.

38. For *tunc*, Vienn., Mar., Rat., Bong., Torn., Gall., and others have *nunc*. Charles Paschal, *On Crowns*, p. 115, Book II, chapter 15, offers much evidence to show that poets sometimes use “flowers” for “crowns,” because crowns are made from flowers.

39. After this verse Aldus has the title “The Battle of Chastity.” Mar. and Rat. have “Chastity”; Vienn. has no title.

40. Fabr., Gis., and Vat. F and G have *gramineo campo* without *in*. Nebrissa reads *prona*; others, *prompt[a]*.

41. All virtues are called virgins, especially chastity. On faith, see the hymn to St. Romanus, verse 352: “And virgin Faith guards the first doors.” On justice, or Astraea, see Ovid and others. Mar. and Rat. place the title “Lust” after this verse.

590. Faith preparing to fight, turbid in rustic attire,

bare-shouldered, with uncombed hair, stripped for battle.

For suddenly the burning heat of praise, fervent for new

[25] battles, remembers neither weapons nor the protection of armor.

591. Rather, trusting in her powerful breast and uncovered limbs,

she challenges the dangers of savage war, which must be broken.

Behold, the ancient Worship of the Gods, provoking Faith,

dares, with joined forces, to strike first.

[30] Rising higher, she weakens that hostile head

and its temples adorned with ribbons; then she presses to the ground

the mouths, sated with the blood of cattle, and tramples beneath her foot

their crushed eyes in death; the interrupted passages of their severed throat

constrict their evil life,

[35] while long sighs weary its difficult death.

The victorious legion exults: Queen Faith had stirred against the enemy

the legion gathered from a thousand martyrs.

Then, for the victory won, she crowns her brave companions

592. with flowers and commands them to be clothed in blazing purple.

[40] Thereafter, prepared to meet in the grassy field,

the virgin Chastity gleams in splendid arms.

43. “And the pitch-bearing torch”: all adulterers, as though their hearts were a furnace, are kindled and stink inwardly with foul smoke, while they lack light. He calls it a pitch torch because in lust there are both burning and stench. “Pine”: a torch, I.

44. “Lights”: she desires to obscure the understanding of clear truth with unclean pleasures, I.

45. “She seeks”: she desired, I.

46. “The right hand”: with the firmness of steadfast purpose she swiftly drives impurities, which have been proposed through alluring persuasion, away from her sight, I.

47. “Harlot”: prostitute. “Undaunted”: she was a rock, Christ, I.

48. “With her mouth”: namely, her own, I.

49. **Disarmed**, without weapons. — **Throat**, breast, or neck, I.

50. **With a sword**: having therefore driven back impure thoughts, she uses the sword, which is the word of God; as in: “For God will judge fornicators and adulterers,” I.

51. **With blood**: what it cannot extort from the wakeful, it attempts upon sleepers, as though unwilling; nor is it allowed to proceed farther. — **Concreted**, mingled. — **Muddy**, foul, muddy. *Coenos* in Greek means mud, I.

53. **Cries out**: chastity, turning toward her own forces, says, I.

54. **This**, such; in this place. — **Always**, eternally, I.

58. **You**, I wonder, I.

59. **To grow warm again**, to revive, I.

42. **Mar.** has *Sodamita* for *Sodomita*. In *Rat.* an inept corrector, erasing the earlier reading, inserted *Sodomitis erimnis*, for thus he wrote it: as though Prudentius could not use *Sodomita* in the feminine gender, just as one says *femina sacerdos*, *testis*, and similar forms. They say it ought to be *Sodomitis*, *Sodomitidis*. Let them produce an ancient witness who asserts this and diminishes Prudentius’ authority; for I shall not put my faith in recent grammarians, who are no more reliable with the ancients when the writer himself is equally ancient and must be judged. Poets attribute torches to the Furies; but torches are more properly associated with lust, like the pine-torches mentioned below, and they are called “native” because she herself is called *Sodomita*. We discussed the conflagration of Sodom in the *Hamartigenia*.

44. Peveratus aptly notes from Chrysostom, *Homily 2 on the First Epistle to the Corinthians*, that lust invades the eyes and deprives them of the power of seeing.

47. Among the ancients, *lupa* means a prostitute, whence *lupanar*, “brothel.” Giselinus observes that the antithesis is especially apt: sulfurous torches as the weapons of lust, and a stone as the weapon of chastity. He proves by the authority of Galen, in the last book of *On Preserving Health*, that this is not foreign to medical doctrine. The gloss seems to have been transferred from the word *saxo* to *imperterrita*.

[Col. 0025D] 51. Barthius, book 36, chapter 7, thinks that *coenoso* here derives from *coena*, “dinner,” not from *coenum*, “mud”; he understands it as blood from the previous evening’s meal. But I think it more likely derives from *coenum*, since immediately afterward the spirit of lust is called filthy. As for Barthius’ collection of numerous names in *-osus*, which are considered obsolete and barbarous, and his view that their authors should not altogether be condemned, this hardly proves that *coenosus* ought here to be restored as deriving from *coena*, or that Prudentius used it in that sense. Barthius, moreover, produces many words which I do not know why he considers obsolete or barbarous: *ventosus*, *verbosus*, *gratiosus*, *luminosus*, *clamosus*, *aquosus*, *frondosus*. Scaliger, book 6 of the *Poetics*, chapter 7, collects the words in *-osus* used by Horace, who seems to have taken pleasure in them: *aestuosus*, *obliviosus*, *periculosus*, *libidinosus*, *otiosus*, *luctuosus*, *pretiosus*, *damnosus*, *vitiosus*, *sumptuosus*, *studiosus*, *speciosus*, *caliginosus*, *maculosus*, *belluosus*, *siticulosus*, *imperiosus*, *ulcerosus*, *generosus*, *cerebrosus*, *plagosus*, *laboriosus*, *injuriosus*, *formidolosus*, *dolosus*, *tumultuosus*, *fastidiosus*, *operosus*, *umbrosus*, *famosus*, *bellicosus*, *jocosus*, *animosus*, *fabulosus*, *ventosus*, *probrosus*. Heinsius conjectures *sanioso*, and thinks that *coenoso* arose from a badly prepared hand, since filthy lust is mentioned afterward. I do not approve the conjecture. Understand—or rather correct—Isō’s gloss as follows: Greek **κοινός** means “common,” and because things open to the promiscuous use of all commonly become contaminated and gather filth, it is therefore also taken to mean “impure”; the printed *impolluto* would ordinarily mean “unpolluted” and is contradictory here.

52. Weitzius, in support of *sordibus*, cites Giselinus. I understand him to mean the first edition, since in the second, corrected edition he has *sordidus*, as everyone else does.

53. **Alex., Vatt. G, H, O, BB, Heinsius’ copies, Erfurt., Palat., Mar., Rat.** have *Hoc habet, exclamat*. Thus Virgil, book 5: “He has it: this better victim is given to the great gods.” Terence, in the *Andria*, has *Captus est* (“He is caught; he has it”). It is a proverb from the gladiators’ arena, indicating that the defeated and wounded man has received a mortal wound. Others read differently. **Vienn., Gifanius, Vatt. F, L** have *Hoc habe, exclamat*, with hiatus. **Ang.** has *Haec habe, exclamat*. **Vat. D**, incorrectly, has *Hoc habeto, exclamat*. Aldus has *Hoc tibi habe, exclamat*, which Giselinus placed in the text, though uncertain whether he preferred *Hoc habe, exclamat*, adopted by Sich., Weitz., and other recent editors. Lipsius, book 2, chapter 21 of the *Saturnalian Conversations*, discusses the cry uttered at a wound, *Hoc habet*, and, citing Prudentius, says: “My Prudentius, in the *Psychomachia*, cries out, *Hoc habet, exclamat*.” Perhaps he is praising his own copy of Prudentius.

57. It is fortunate that we can listen to Giselinus, a physician of no mean reputation, as an interpreter of Prudentius, whose authority illuminates the poet’s doctrine. Giselinus teaches that, since the liver, like all the other viscera, owes its firmness to its fibers and is the source and origin of all the veins, it is rightly understood by metalepsis to signify every kind of lust and desire, and even the mind itself, both here and in innumerable other passages. Below, verse 761: “Because a divided will confounds the twofold mysteries in various fibers”; and verse 238: “Is the icy liver of chastity useful in battle?” Prudentius contrasts Christ’s lamp with the lamp of Venus, or Cupid, which is frequently mentioned among the poets.

60. **Weitz.**, together with *Erfurt.* and *Bong.*, has *cervixque*, less well, instead of *cervix*. **Mar., Rat., Vienn.** and others, following the Vulgate, have *Holofernis*; Heinsius’ copies have *Olofernis*; Aldus has *Olopherni*. Others have *Oloferni*. The story is found in the Book of Judith, chapter 13.]

Whom Sodomite Lust, girded about, attacks with her native torches,

And assails her modest eyes with flames,

[45] And attempts to suffuse them with hideous smoke.

But the fearless maiden strikes with a stone the right hand of blazing Fury

And the fiery darts of the dread she-wolf,

And drives from her sacred countenance the torches shaken loose.

Then, with a driven sword, she pierces the throat of the disarmed harlot:

[50] She vomits warm vapours thickened with muddy blood;

Then a foul spirit, breathing out,

Pollutes the surrounding air.

“She's got it!” cries the victorious queen; “here

Will be your final end: you will lie prostrate for ever.

62. **Bed**, couch. — **Of the adulterous man**, of an adulterer, a seducer, I.

64. **Trophy**, as she herself also prayed: “Strengthen me, almighty king of the ages,” I.

65. **From heaven**, divinely, I.

62. **Ald., Weitz., Gis., Vat. C, Mar., Rat., Vienn.** and others have *gemmatum* (“jeweled”). Heinsius preferred *gemmantem* (“gleaming with jewels”), with *Put.*, *Thuan.*, and the first *Rott.*, followed by *Alex.* and others. Prudentius uses the verb in both ways, as did other writers.

64. **Vienn.** has *ex hoste triumphum* (“a triumph from the enemy”).

65. Aldus had printed *mea vindex* (“my avenger”), then corrected it to *vindex mea* (the same words in reversed order). Nebrissa either failed to notice or disregarded Aldus’s correction.

68. **Ald., Thuan., Oxon., Rott.** and one *Vat.* cited by Teoli have *terreno in corpore fluxit* (“flowed in an earthly body”), from which Heinsius judged that the reading should be *terreno in corpore fulsit* (“shone in an earthly body”). But why is conjecture needed when most copies—*Mar., Vienn., Rat., Alex.* and others—have *terrena in corpora fluxit* (“flowed into earthly bodies”)?

70. **Vienn.** has *illum* (“that one”); others have *ullum* (“any one”).

72. **Ald., Fabr.** and Giselinus in the text of the second edition have *prisca propago* (“ancient stock”). Others have *pristina origo* (“former origin”); Cauchius has the difficult reading *naturam pristinam origo* (“origin … former nature”).

73. The first *Rott.* has *carnique novam vis ardua sevit*, that is, “the mighty force implanted a new nature in the flesh.” Nebrissa suspected *sumpsit* instead of *sevit*; and *sumpsit* is indeed found in *Vienn.*

74. When Prudentius asserts that an unmarried woman conceived, he does not mean merely that the Virgin conceived before she was betrothed, but rather that she conceived without the involvement of a man. *Nubere* is often used for sexual intercourse, as I noted at verse 571 of the *Apotheosis*.

75. Weitzius, with *Erfurt.* alone, has *mortalem de matre hominem* (“a mortal man from a mother”); this is not to be dismissed.

76. **Vienn.** has *unde*; others have *inde*. Chamillardus writes: “As I read this, a passage of St Jerome came plainly to mind, book 2 *Against Jovinianus*: ‘The Word was made flesh so that we might pass from flesh into the Word.’” The same passage had occurred to Weitzius, who copied it and also supplied another, still more similar, from Athanasius in Theodoret’s *Dialogue 2 Against the Heretics*: “Because the **Λόγος** assumed flesh, therefore **ἐθεοποιήθη ὁ ἄνθρωπος**”—“the human being was deified.” Cellarius reduces *divus* as an adjective meaning “holy” to Late Latin usage; he does not persuade me. The example he adduces from Prudentius is no less sound than those he approves: *diva mater*, “divine mother”; *diva Juno*, “divine Juno”; *divi penates*, “divine household gods.”

77. **Put., Egm., Palat., Alex.** have *consortis* (“of the sharer”); others have *consorti* (“to the sharer”). In *Vienn.* *sumpsit* (“took”) appears instead of *sumit* (“takes”), and this seems also to have been the reading in *Alex.*

79. **Put., the two copies of Rottendorph, Alex.** have *dum carnis glutinat usum* (“while he unites the nature of flesh”). Others have *carnis dum glutinat usum* (the same words reordered: “while he unites flesh’s nature”). The verb *glutino* was discussed above, hymn 11, verse 52. Chamillardus observes that the poet is arguing against the Photinians and Samosatenians, who asserted that Christ was merely human; refuting Carpocrates, Ebion, and Cerinthus, who taught that Jesus was born from the marriage of Joseph and Mary in the manner of other human beings; and attacking Tertullian and the Antidicomarianites, who believed that Mary was not a virgin after giving birth. Thus we rightly place the *Psychomachia* among those poems of which Prudentius says in the prologue: “Let it fight against heresies and examine the Catholic faith.”

82. Peveratus attributes to Christ a similar theological riddle: “I am what I was, yet I was not what I am, nor am I called both. My mother is human; my father is God without end.”]
