84. *Contulit*: “bestowed”—many good things, and his divinity. — *Mansit*: “remained,” namely, remained God. I.

85. *Ex nostris*: “from what is ours,” that is, from our members. — *Sua*: “his own”; he became a participant in our humanity so that he might make us participants in his divinity. I.

87. *Dona*: “gifts,” because no one can be continent unless God grants it. — *Lutulenta*: “muddy, polluted”; lust always delights in uncleanness and filth. I.

90. *Corpora*: “bodies,” according to the Apostle: “Other sins are outside the body,” but this sin stains and corrupts the bodies themselves. I.

91. *Abde*: “hide, conceal.” — *Frigida*: “cold,” that is, defeated. I.

92. *Claudere*: “be shut up.” I.

93. *Detrudere*: “be thrust down.” — *Fundum*: “the depth,” that is, Tartarus. I.

94. *Vada flammea*: “fiery pools”; deservedly is one tormented with sulfur and fire who here neglected to despise foul passions. I.

95. *Rotet*: “may it roll, whirl.” I.

97. *Suo*: “his own.” — *Regi*: “king,” namely Christ. I.

[Col. 0030B] 99. *Gladium*: “sword,” for the sword is the word of God, as the Apostle says. I.

100. *Abluit*: “washes,” while doing penance. — *Infectum*: “stained.” — *Sanies*: “gore”; it is impossible for fleshly frailty not to darken the human mind, but from that weakness it afterward rises more firmly to contemplation, because, remembering its infirmity, it is never puffed up by a good work. — *Rore rubenti*: “with red dew,” that is, with red blood. I.

101. *Nitidum*: “shining.” I.

102. *Expiat*: “cleanses.” — *Aciem*: “the blade”; she washes away the very stains of thought with tears of devout compunction. — *Lavacro*: “with a washing,” that is, baptism. I.

103. *Abolens*: “washing away.” I.

104. *Hostilis juguli*: “of the enemy throat,” that is, concupiscence. I.

105. *Condere*: “to conceal”; she does not wish the intention of her chaste purpose to be hidden. She does not wish it entrusted to herself but to God, so that it may shine and God, rather than she herself, may be glorified. I.]

[Note: [Col. 0029C]

87. The Heinsian manuscripts, Alex., Ang., Weitz., Vienn., Rat., Mar., Vatt. C, F, G, Sich., and others read *quod victa jaces* (“because you lie conquered”), the reading Barthius preferred from his parchments. Others have *queis victa jaces* (“by which things you lie conquered”) or *quis victa jaces* (“by which you lie conquered”). Vat. C has the error *luculenta* (“bright”) for *lutulenta* (“muddy”).

88. Ang. and Vat. C read *poteris* (“you will be able”), but the earlier letters in Vat. C were erased. Something was also erased in Vat. D. The true reading is *potis es* (“you are able”). Aldus has *perstringere* (“to graze or strike lightly”); others have *perfringere* (“to break through”).

89. Aldus, Nebrissa, and other old editions read *tu praeceps ad mortis iter* (“you, driving headlong onto the path of death”). Nebrissa explains *praeceps* actively as “casting headlong” or “driving precipitately.” Peveratus supports the same reading because lust and death are closely allied, as was signified by the ancient Roman custom of selling in the shrine of Venus Libitina the things required for burial; see Kirchmann, *On Funerals*, book I, chapter 9. The manuscripts consistently read *tu princeps* (“you are the leader”): so Alex., Ang., Vienn., Rat., Mar.—though Mar. corruptly has *princes*—and Vatt. D, F, G, H, and L, among others. [Col. 0029D] Barthius, at the cited place, and Becmanus, *Guide to the Latin Language*, chapter 6, defend the same reading from the Palatine manuscript; Becmanus also cites Cicero’s words in *On Friendship*: *Amor princeps est ad benevolentiam conjungendam* (“Love is foremost in joining goodwill”).

90. Both Rott. manuscripts read *commaculas* (“you stain”) rather than *commaculans* (“staining”).

91. Aldus reads *jam fervida* (“now burning”), which Nebrissa explains from the fiery nature of Venus. The others more correctly read *jam frigida* (“now cold”). I do not accept Chamillardus’s explanation that she is called cold because cold poison is crueler and acts more immediately. I prefer Iso’s gloss, “*frigida*: defeated,” or rather “extinguished.” Virgil, *Georgics* IV: “She was then already sailing, cold, in the Stygian boat.” Fracastoro imitates Prudentius in *Syphilis*: “Hide your head, Benacus, and conceal yourself beneath your stream.”

95. Vat. F corruptly reads *sulfinens* for *sulphureus* (“sulfurous”). Put. consistently writes *solporeus* and *vertex*, corrupt forms.

97. Bong. and Sich. read *Christo* (“for Christ”) in place of *regi* (“for the king”). In Erfurt *Christo* had stood as a gloss.

[Col. 0030C] 98. Bede cites this verse in *On Metre* and teaches that the ancients customarily pronounced *interefectae* so that a dactyl would stand in the fifth foot. I do not agree, for the older grammarians state expressly that a spondee is sometimes placed in the fifth foot of a hexameter.

100. Vat. C has the metrical error *cui sanies* (“to whom the gore”) for *sanies cui* (“the gore which”). Piccartus’s codex reads *sanies cui ore* (“the gore which on the face”), which Piccartus seems to defend on account of the hiatus; the sense, however, requires *cui rore* (“which with dew”), unless *cui* refers to Chastity. Why Chastity washed the sword in Jordan’s waters is clear from the following verses and from the note on verse 64 of hymn 2 of the *Cathemerinon*.

103. Ang. reads *ultricem* (“avenging”) for *victricem* (“victorious”); *ultricem* may perhaps be the true reading.

105. Aldus reads *vagina* (“sheath,” ablative); most others read *vaginae* (“of the sheath”). Giselinus’s second edition printed *vaginae*, but his corrections substituted *vagina*. The same Giselinus gives *ne sorde latenti / Occupet ablutum rubigo scabra nitorem* (“lest rough rust with hidden filth seize the washed brightness”). Heinsius does not understand by what authority this was done, since all his and Weitzius’s manuscripts consistently agree with Aldus in reading *ne tecta [Col. 0030D] rubigo / Occupet ablutum scabrosa sorde nitorem* (“lest concealed rust seize the washed brightness with rough filth”). Aldus punctuates badly: *ne tecta rubigo / Occupet. Ablutum scabrosa sorde nitorem / Catholico in templo divini fontis ad aram / Consecrat* (“lest concealed rust seize it. The brightness washed of rough filth she consecrates in the Catholic temple at the altar of the divine font”). Giselinus disliked this reading; because *rubigo* has a long first syllable elsewhere in Prudentius and other authors, he recast the verse until, he says, manuscripts should restore the true reading. All our manuscripts—Mar., Rat., Vienn., Alex., Vatt. C, D, F, G, H, and L, Bonon., and Ang.—read *ne tecta rubigo / Occupet ablutum scabrosa sorde nitorem*. Vat. O alone favors Giselinus, reading *ne sorde latenti / Occupet ablutum rubigo scabrosa nitorem*. There *scabrosa* may be an error for the damaged reading *sca…ra*, unless one prefers to shorten both *u* and *i* in *rubigo*. The common reading must nevertheless be retained. Why may the first syllable of *rubigo* not be common in quantity? Martial shortens it in book II, epigram 61, *Uteris ore aliter, nimiaque rubigine captus* (“You speak otherwise, seized by excessive rust”), and Ovid in *Metamorphoses* VIII.803, *Labra incana situ, scabraque rubigine dentes* (“lips gray with decay and teeth rough with rust”). I know that others read these passages differently, but the fact that they can be read this way gains some support from the word’s derivation from *rubeus*, whose first syllable is short. Barthius’s manuscript reads as the others do, except that it corruptly has *ablatum* (“removed”) for *ablutum* (“washed”); it also reads *vaginae*, not *vagina*.]

[Note: [Col. 0031A]

107. *Catholico*: “in the holy Church”; Chastity puts away her sword at her side. — *Divini*: “divine,” referring to the confession of divine baptism. I.

108. *Coruscet*: “may it flash,” shining in eternal proclamation. I.

109. *Ecce*: “behold.” Philosophers assert that the human soul has three parts: rational, irascible, and concupiscible. Therefore, after Faith, by which reason is ruled, and Chastity, by which concupiscence is restrained, Patience is placed, by whom anger is broken, so that a person may love God with the whole heart, soul, and strength. — *Gravi*: “grave, mature.” I.

111. *Vitalia*: “vital parts,” the inner chambers of hearts, namely human entrails. — *Pilis*: “with javelins,” weapons or darts. I.

112. *Spectabat*: “watched, looked upon.” — *Defixa*: “fixed downward, inclined.” — *Lenta*: “calm, untroubled.” I.

113. *Procul*: “from afar,” or “against.” I.

114. *Sanguinea*: “blood-red,” as the Psalmist says: “My eye is troubled by wrath,” for angry people commonly look with fierce eyes. — *Suffuso*: “poured beneath, suffused.” I.]

[Note: [Col. 0031B]

107. In Rat. a bold and inept corrector replaced *catholico* (“Catholic”) with *consecrat* (“she consecrates”) and erased the following verse so completely that no trace remains. The poet says that Chastity consecrated her sword in a temple, alluding to the custom by which victors or discharged soldiers hung their weapons in temples. Compare Horace, *Epistles* I, on Veianius hiding in the country after fixing his weapons to Hercules’ doorpost; Virgil, *Aeneid* XI, on dedicating Mezentius’s spoils as a trophy to the mighty god of war; and I Kings 21:9 on Goliath’s sword, with which David struck him, wrapped in a cloak behind the ephod. Prudentius calls the building a Catholic temple because in that period *templum* ordinarily meant an idol-shrine, as the Theodosian Code shows. Christians called their places of prayer churches, church assemblies, meeting places, oratories, the Lord’s houses, houses of prayer, and similar names. Once peace was restored to the Church and such sacred buildings became grander, the name “temple” was gradually adopted. The pagan charge that early Christians had neither temples nor altars proves only that Christians lacked temples and altars dedicated with pagan magnificence and ceremony. Rufinus’s version of Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII.14, records Maximian permitting Christians again to exist and to rebuild the meeting places where they prayed, provided they did nothing against public discipline. Who first applied “temple” to Christian churches is uncertain; some say St. Ambrose. A sermon on Psalm 126 attributed to St. Zeno of Verona—but really by St. Hilary—mentions a temple as a Christian church, unless the text is corrupt. See Gothofredus on the title concerning pagans in the Theodosian Code, Scipione Maffei on book I, tractate 5 of St. Zeno, and the commentary on verse 213 of hymn 3 of the *Peristephanon*. Christians adopted the name “basilica” more readily.

Chastity hangs the sword at the altar of the divine font, continuing the poet’s proclamation of baptismal grace, already signified by Jordan’s waters, river washing, baptism, and now the divine font. Barthius interprets the divine font as baptism and the altar as the baptistery, because there one who dies to the world is offered to God. One might read *ad aulam* (“at the hall”), a word often used by the ancients for sacred buildings. Paulinus, *Natal Poem* 10, uses it this way. If the manuscripts permitted it, the editor would say that Chastity’s sword was fixed in the hall or chapel of the baptistery; Fortunatus likewise calls a baptistery the “hall of baptism.” The inscription of Milan’s octagonal baptistery of St. Thecla says that the temple and font rose in an eight-sided form fitting the return of true salvation. Antonio Maria Lupi’s Italian dissertation, with notes and continuation by Francesco Antonio Zaccaria, treats the names for baptisteries—mostly terms also used for pagan baths: baptistery, bath, pool, washing, *colymbus*, nymphaeum, font, basin, lake, whirlpool, channel, and others, though “nymphaeum” is uncertain. Lupi especially documents “washing,” “font,” and “pool,” and discusses the symbolic name ΙΧΘΥΣ (“fish”) for Jesus Christ, formed from the initial Greek letters of “Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior.” Hence Christians were called little fishes, and marble fish still appear in Rome’s fonts of cleansing water. See also Anselmo Costadoni’s dissertation on the fish as a symbol of Christ among early Christians.

108. Erfurt and Widm. read *sub luce* (“under the light”), less well. Aldus and Fabricius read *nitescat* (“may it shine”); the others have *coruscet* (“may it flash”). After this verse Mar. and Rat. place the heading “Patience”; Aldus, “The Battle of Patience and Anger”; Weitzius, “The Conflict of Patience and Anger.”

109. Joseph of Exeter, who sang the Trojan War under Dares’s name, writes in book I concerning Patience: “Learn to endure hardships; Patience alone crushes the enemy, rules the Virtues, fights in innocent triumphs, and counsels honorable anger.” Barthius, book XXII, chapter 11, observes that this was drawn from Prudentius’s *Psychomachia*, which he calls a most divine poem. See Tertullian’s book *On Patience*.

110. Weitzius absurdly printed *tumultos*, found only in the Widmanstadt manuscript, as though that copyist could not mistakenly have written *o* for *u*; the reading means “tumults.”

112. Vincent of Beauvais, *Historical Mirror* XVII.102, reads: *Spectabat defixa oculos, et laeta manebat* (“She watched with eyes fixed downward and remained joyful”), while *lenta* (“calm”) is written in the margin as a variant. Printed books and manuscripts consistently have *lenta*, an epithet especially suited to Patience. Cicero, *On the Orator* II: “I am thought too patient and calm.” Chamillardus, from *Aeneid* VI, notes that keeping one’s eyes fixed is also a sign of constancy. After this verse Mar. and Rat. have the heading “Anger.” Descriptions of Anger occur everywhere in poets, sacred and secular orators, and historians. Walter of Châtillon appears to imitate Prudentius’s description in *Alexandreis* V.222. On the struggle with anger see Ambrose, *On Duties*, and Lactantius I.9.

114. Widm., against the meter, reads *sanguineaque involvens* (“and wrapping blood-red [things]”).]

By birth into better things: he enriched me, yet remained himself.

[85] Nor did God diminish what was his through what was ours;

Rather, by giving what was his to what was ours, he raised us to heavenly gifts.

These are the gifts: that you lie vanquished, filthy Lust,

And after Mary you are no longer able to break through my laws.

You lead the way to death; you are the gate of destruction,

[90] Staining bodies and plunging souls into Tartarus.

Hide your head in the gloomy abyss, now-frozen plague;

Die, brothel; seek the shades; be shut up in Avernus,

And be thrust down into the dark depths of night.

May fiery waters roll over you beneath, and black waters;

[95] May a sulfurous whirlpool revolve through resounding pools.

And no longer attempt the worshipers of Christ, greatest of the Furies,

So that their purified bodies may be kept for their own king.

She had said this, and Chastity rejoiced in the death

Of Lust, which she had killed; she washed her sword in the waters of the Jordan,

[100] To which foulness, with crimson dew,

Had clung and stained the shining iron with its wound.

Thus the victorious woman, taught by the river’s bath,

Purifies the victorious blade, erasing through baptism the stain

Of the enemy’s throat; nor is she now content merely to hide the cleansed sword

[105] In its sheath, lest concealed rust

Seize its polished brightness with rough filth.

She consecrates it in the Catholic temple, at the altar of the divine font,

Where it may shine and flash with eternal light.

Behold, modest Patience stood with a grave expression,

[110] Unshaken amid the battle-lines and their various tumult,

She watched, with fixed eyes, the wounds and vital organs pierced by rigid spears, and remained calm.

From afar, swelling Anger, hot with foaming jaws,

Wringing blood-red eyes suffused with bile,

[Col. 0033A] [Note: [Col. 0033B]

115. **As**, as if. — **Without a share**, without participation, I.

117. **Shaking**, stirring. — **Crests**, the upper part of the helmet, I.

118. **For you**, I give it; for your destruction. — **Mars**, war. — **Spectator**, Anger rebukes Patience, I.

119. **Receive**, this is the figure called sarcasm, that is, hostile mockery, I.

120. **Nor grieve**, irony. — **Shameful**, it is, I.

121. **Hissing pine**, he intends an arrow, I.

125. **Adamant**, Christ is the adamant. — **Triple-layered**, we may understand Christ as the triple stone, I.

126. **Breastplate**, a Greek accusative; a cuirass. The breastplate of faith is evidently triple, because of the confession of the Trinity, to which the unconquered adamant is compared, whenever it looks toward Jesus, the author of faith. — **Scaly**, shining or glittering, I.

127. **Had joined**, had surrounded, bound, or girded. — **Bands**, circles, I.

129. **Impenetrable**, the word is used in place of an adverb, that is, “impenetrably,” I.

131. **Waiting**, expecting, I.

132. **Untamed**, restless. — **Raging**, becoming angry, storming. — **Arms**, forearms, I.

133. **Had exhausted**, had wearied, I.

134. **Useless**, ineffective. — **Void**, obstructed or spoiled: obstructed because she had wounded it with no weapon, I.

136. **Spears**, weapons, I.

137. **Turns**, Anger strikes Patience with the sword, I.

138. **Blow**, wound; slaughter. — **Ear**, head, I.

139. **Strikes**, hits. — **Aimed**, measured, I.

140. **Helmet**, cuirass. — **Metal**, bronze is said to be more durable than other metals; hence it is also used to signify endurance, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0033C]

117. **Rat.** and **Vienn.** have *galeato vertice* (“with helmeted head”) without *in*. Weitzius reads *hirsuto* (“bristling”), but does not note the variant.

119. Aldus, Erfurt., and *Vat. II* in a second hand have *securo in pectore* (“in an untroubled breast”). The other copies omit *in* (“in”).

120. Aldus and Gifanius, under the word *vestis* in Lucretius’ index, have *gemuisse dolore* (“to have groaned in pain”); others have *dolorem* (“pain”), and *Vat. C*, in its first hand, *dolores* (“pains”). *Erfurt.* has *turpe tibi est* (“it is shameful for you”); the other copies omit the substantive verb, except *Angel.*, where the erroneous reading is *turpe tibi est genuisse dolorem* instead of *gemuisse*.

122. Nebrissa not implausibly conjectured *tenues* for *teneros*. But Chamillardus should not have inserted this noun into the text on the basis of conjecture alone. There is no reason why *tener* cannot be called a familiar word, just as *lenis* and *mitis* are.

123. **Rat.** has *recto* (“straight”); *rectoque* (“and straight”) is better.

124. Seneca, book 3 of *On Anger*, chapter 5: “As weapons rebound from a hard surface, and solid objects hurt the one who strikes them, so no injury diverts a great spirit from awareness of itself: the injury is more fragile than what it attacks.”

125. Virgil, book 5: “A cuirass joined with smooth hooks and triple-layered with gold.” The unconquered strength of Patience is displayed. Peveratus explains *provid[a] virtus* as prudence, as in Petronius *libera virtus* means freedom. This interpretation is not displeasing, provided that Providence is understood to have armed Patience.

126. For *thoraca*, *Vienn., Rat., Mar., Vat. C* write *thoracem* (the regular accusative “breastplate”). *Widm.* has the erroneous *thoracha*. *Bong.* has *humeros* (“shoulders,” accusative), not badly, instead of *humeris* (“on the shoulders,” ablative). Giselinus likewise has this. The first *Boher.* has *indurat* (“hardens”) instead of *induerat* (“had clothed”).

127. Some printed editions have *innumeros* instead of *intortos*. The “scaly fabric of iron” is the iron cuirass itself, woven from hooks in the shape of scales. At first such armor was made from leather straps, later from iron rings, between which bands were inserted for greater security, as Nebrissa infers from this passage.

129. Chrysostom, in *On the Priesthood*, dialogue 6, elegantly depicts the battle and the preparation for battle; there too occurs a rain of weapons.

130. **Vienn.** has *tacta est, et sine fine* (“she was touched, and without end”), a fragmentary reading.

134. *Supervacuam*, that is, “the right hand,” is preferable, with *Vienn., Rat., Mar., Vatt. G, H* and others, to *supervacua nube* (“with a useless cloud”). **Aug.** has *laxaverat* (“had loosened”), incorrectly, instead of *lassaverat* (“had wearied”).

136. The Heinsius copies and our copies—*Sich., Weitz.*—prefer *jactibus* (“throws”). Aldus, Giselinus in the text, Nebrissa, and *Vat. C, F, G, O* have *ictibus* (“blows”). *Vat. D* writes the erroneous *hictibus*. Piccartus’s manuscript has *ictibus et variis* (“with blows and varied [weapons]”).

137. **Vienn.** has *in capulum* (“toward the hilt”).

138. Our better copies have *connisa* (“braced”). Others write *conisa* (a spelling variant); others *connixa* (“having struggled”). Gifanius, in the Lucretian index under *nisus*, approves *connisa*. *Egm.* has *galeam* (“helmet”) instead of *plagam* (“blow”): thus Virgil, book 10, “He rises against the shield.” The expressions *conniti*, “to brace oneself,” *erigi in clypeum*, “to rise against the shield,” *in jaculum*, “against the spear,” and *assurgere*, “to rise up,” frequently express a military posture and exertion among the poets.

139. **Vienn.** has *vibrata* (“brandished”); others *librata* (“poised, aimed”). Gifanius, at the place cited, under *volgata*, reads *vibrata* from an old manuscript and thinks it more correct than the Vulgate reading *librata*: swords are brandished, missiles are poised. He thinks *vibrata* has active force, as in Lucretius’ *vulgata* and in an ancient poet cited by Cicero in a letter to Paetus: “A double bed used.” He does not persuade me. Here the hand, not the sword, is said to be *librata*, as Heinsius also observed. The expression *librata ab aure* occurs in Virgil.

140. In *Vat. G* *sed* (“but”) is missing after *aerea* (“bronze”); in *Vat. F*: *sed cocto formata cassis metallo* (“but the helmet formed from smelted metal”), which the meter rejects. Giselinus’ second edition, Weitzius, and others have *aerea sed cassis cocto formata* (“but the bronze helmet was formed by smelting”). Our better copies, with *Alex., Ald., Ang.* and others, have *aerea sed cocto cassis formata* (“but the bronze helmet was formed by smelting”). In *Put.* there is a metrical error: *aerea sed cocto cassis informata metallo* (“but the bronze helmet shaped from smelted metal”). From this Heinsius conjectures that Prudentius wrote *sed cassis cocto informata metallo* (“but the helmet shaped from smelted metal”), since *informare* occurs with the same meaning in Maro. I do not see, however, why an obvious error in the *Puteanus* manuscript should undermine the clear reading established by the authority of so many copies: *sed cocto cassis formata*, or *sed cassis cocto formata*. For *formare* is no less acceptable than *informare*.]

As though she were exempt from war, she challenges her with weapon and voice,

And, impatient of delay, attacks with a spear and rebukes her aloud,

Shaking the shaggy crests on her helmeted head.

“Here,” she says, “free spectator of our warfare, is something for you:

[120] Receive the deadly iron in your untroubled breast;

Nor grieve, for it is shameful for you to have groaned in pain.”

So she speaks, and the hissing pine follows the taunts,

Whistling through the gentle south winds, it is carried true

Against her very stomach and strikes with a direct blow;

But the breastplate rebounds, shaken off by the hard resistance.

[125] For provident strength had clothed her shoulders

In a triple-layered breastplate joined with adamant,

And had everywhere woven the scaly fabric of iron

Through twisted bands.

Then Patience remains calm, strong against every

[130] Shower of weapons, enduring as impenetrable;

Nor is she moved by the missile of the monster raging beyond measure,

Waiting for Anger to perish through her own strength:

For once the barbarian warrior had exhausted

Her untamed arms by raging, and with a cloud of javelins

Had wearied her useless right hand,

When her wind-borne weapons had fallen in their light flight

And her spears lay broken by empty throws,

The wicked hand turns to the hilt, and, braced for the blow,

The raised right hand is lifted high from the ear

And, aimed, strikes the middle of the brain.

[140] But the bronze helmet, fashioned from smelted metal,

[Col. 0035A] [Note: [Col. 0035B]

141. “It returns a ringing sound”: struck by insults, Patience returns a ringing sound, yet does not abandon the medicines of instruction.—“The edge,” namely, of the sword, I.

142. “Hard,” the helmet.—“Rebounding,” springing back or resisting.—“The vein,” the helmet, I.

143. “Struck,” beaten.—“Steel,” iron, I.

144. “Assaults,” blows or noise, I.

145. “Anger”: the sword of anger is broken on the head of Patience, I.

147. “Hilt”: the hilt remains without the weight of the iron; when words having no force are poured out in vain, I.

148. “Ivory,” the hilt: a metonymy, I.

149. “Faithless,” wicked weapons.—“Far,” greatly, I.

151. “Missile”: so called from *mittere*, “to send,” because it is discharged by the hand, I.

154. “Lung”: deservedly she pierces the lung, since she who did not hesitate to spare frivolity; nor was there a lack of an example in Saul, who, while pursuing the gentle David, was driven so far by his madness that, raging, he struck himself down with his own spear, I.

156. “Exulting vice,” rejoicing anger, I.

157. “Danger,” peril.—“This,” such a thing, I.

159. “Service”: as the Apostle says, “When I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful,” I.

162. “Cuts,” separates, I.

163. “Job”: just as different men shone forth through different virtues—Noah through perseverance, Abraham through obedience, Jacob through endurance—so holy Job was distinguished by patience, I.

165. “Funeral,” sickness, I.

167. “Sweated over,” labored over, I.

168. “Battles,” chastisements, wounds.—“Disgrace”: for Job was a disgrace to the enemy, that is, to the vices, because they were conquered by him, I.

169. “Him”: Patience speaks with Job, I.

171. “Perishing”: weeping over what had previously been lost (perhaps *fuere*), I.

172. “Masses,” armies, I.

173. “Wound-bearing,” bearing wounds.—“Untouched”: although the body is often injured, nevertheless she is in no way overcome in purpose.—“Showers,” by spears, I.

174. “Alone”: Patience, after the vices have been conquered, is joined to the virtues, I.

176. “Doubtful struggle,” uncertain battle, I.

177. “Is widowed”: the Lord shows that no one can be perfected without patience, when he says, “By patience possess your souls”; for without possession of the soul no virtue accomplishes anything, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0035C]

142. Vienna: “the vein was breaking,” not properly, for above it says “returns,” “blunts.”

143. The principal witnesses among ours—Mar., Rat., Vienna, with Weitz. and Sich.—read *cassis*: that is, the helmet itself, incapable of yielding, receives the assaults. Others read *cassos assultus*. Teolius incorrectly asserts that all witnesses except Weitz. and one Vatican manuscript have *cassos*. Chamillard hesitates, but printed *cassos* in the text. The meaning is clearer with *cassos*, while *vena* itself, that is, the helmet made from a vein of bronze or iron, is understood as incapable of yielding. In Aldus there is an error, *caedere* for *cedere*.

144. Vatican F has *assaltus*; the others, *assultus*: and *assaltus* is not Latin.

149. Aldus writes *abjicit*; the others more correctly have *abicit*. The same witness incorrectly has *munimentaque* for *monumentaque*, or *monimentaque*.

150. Gifanius, discussing the word *MOENERA, MUNERA*, observes that Prudentius was an exceptionally devoted student of antiquity, as the words *densere*, *vagare*, *clepere*, and here *spernere* for “to reject,” a usage belonging to Ennius, prove.

153. Vienna has *humo*; the others, *humi*.

165. Gis., Rat., Gal., and Vienna read *vulnere anhelus*. Heinsius had printed *vulnere*, but in the additions preferred *funere*, together with all his manuscripts. Teolius prefers *vulnere*, saying that it is found with all the Vatican editions except one. But Aldus, and most editions before Giselinus, consistently have *funere*, which also appears in the Marietti manuscript and in Ison’s gloss; nor should it have displeased Gallandius in Aldus.

166. Vienna has *vulnera*; read *ulcera*.

170. Aldus has *quae sunt*; the others, including the older editions, *quaeque*. Giselinus is agitated at this passage and suspects that *partis* should be read instead of *captis*. The meaning is that patience caused Job to multiply everything he had lost through the riches he had acquired, or possessed. You have the story in his book.

172. Weitz. has *illa* instead of *ipsa*. Fabr. and Bong. have *globum* instead of *globos*.

177. Thus Aldus, Gis., Weitz., Mar., Rat., Vienna, Alex. in the first hand, Ang., and Vatican manuscripts C, F, O. Albertus Eiib., or Eyb, likewise read this in the poetic edition of Marga, 1487. Heinsius, with Thuan., Put., and Vatican II, reads *Virtus: et vidua est, quam non patientia firmat* (“Virtue—and she is widowed whom patience does not strengthen”). In Vatican manuscripts L and BB there is the error: *Virtus namque vidua est, quam non patientia firmat* (“For virtue is widowed when patience does not strengthen her”). We may also punctuate differently: “No virtue undertakes a doubtful struggle without this one; for virtue is widowed whom patience does not strengthen.” After this verse Aldus has the title, “The Battle of Pride and Humility.” In Vienna: “On the duel of humility and pride”; in Rat. and Mar.: “Pride.” In others: “Pride and Humility.”]

603 Struck, Patience returns the ringing sound and blunts

The hard helmet blunts the rebounding blade; its resistant metal also breaks

The steel that has struck it, while, incapable of yielding, it receives

The futile assaults and safely resists the attacker.

[145] When Anger saw the fragments of the broken sword,

And the blade, far away, had burst into tiny pieces,

While the hand still held the hilt, now without the weight of iron,

Bereft of judgment, the wretched ivory, the treacherous tokens

Of shameful adornment, she casts away, and far off rejects

[150] The grim memorials, and rages toward her own death:

From the many missiles that she had scattered in vain,

She takes one from the dust of the field for its perverse purpose,

Sets the stripped shaft in the ground, turns the point toward herself,

Pierces herself, and drives it through her lung with a hot wound.

[155] 604 Then Patience, standing above her, said:

“We have conquered exulting vice through our customary virtue,

Without danger to blood or life. Our law prescribes this kind

Of warfare: by enduring, to extinguish furies

And all the raging force of evils.”

[160] Madness itself is its own enemy; raging,

Fiery Anger destroys itself and dies by its own weapons.

Having spoken, she cuts through the ranks unharmed,

Accompanied by a noble man: for nearby Job

Had remained amid the hard battles beside his unconquered mistress,

[165] Still stern of brow and gasping from the many deaths;

But now, smiling beneath his fierce expression,

He closes his sores and counts anew

The number of his scars—thousands of battles, his rewards,

The enemy’s disgrace.

The goddess finally orders him to rest

[170] From all the clash of arms, and to multiply whatever he had lost

Through the riches he had acquired, and no longer to recover things that were to perish.

She herself breaks through the masses of the legions and the converging

Lines, advancing untouched through showers bearing wounds;

[Col. 0036B] 605 Alone she is associated as companion with all the virtues,

And courageous Patience mingles her aid with theirs.

No virtue undertakes a doubtful struggle without her;

For virtue is widowed when Patience does not strengthen her.

[Col. 0037A] [Note: [Col. 0037B]

181. “By which,” that is, “upon which.” —“Supported,” raised high.—“Beastlike”: the beastlike appearance of pride, and likewise its feminine and equestrian appearance, is described, so that he might show that the proud have degenerated from human custom, that is, from reason, and are neither strong in virtue nor masters of themselves, I.

182. “Arrogance,” pride, I.

183. “Had piled up,” had raised, I.

185. “Lofty,” high, I.

186. “Linen,” white; *carbasum*, a kind of excellent linen.—“Highest,” full, I.

189. “Swollen,” sent in or hostile.—“Woven fabrics,” garments, I.

190. “No less”: pride rides.—“Hoof-clanging,” a horse, because it makes a sound with its feet, I.

191. “To be bridled,” to be restrained.—“Mouths”: when an accusative is joined to a passive verb, this is a figurative expression; one may supply either “having mouths” or the preposition *per*, “through the mouths.” —“Saw-toothed bits,” a bridle, I.

193. “Reins,” halters, I.

194. “This”: pride threatens the crowds, I.

195. “Between”: between humility and pride.—“Trapped-out,” adorned, properly said of a horse, I.

197. “Opposing”: placed against; contrary, and here an adjective: that is, pride sees the wedge of humility opposing itself.—“Watching,” looking around.—“Wedge,” people.—“Few,” small in number, I.

198. “Had gathered,” had collected, I.

199. “The humble mind”: humility without hope lacks steadfastness; and therefore it will not then be virtue, but vice, for it will be cowardice.—“Queen,” she was, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0037C]

178. Widm. and some copies of the Vulgate in the margin have *morte*; others, *forte*, which seems correct and more elegant.

179. Vienna has *effreno*; the others, *effreni*, which should be retained. Although certain words of this sort are pronounced in both ways, such as *inermus, inermis, hilarus, hilaris*, nothing novel should rashly be admitted. Giselinus added *effreno* in the margin.

180. Gis. has *ornaverat*, which Piccartus seems to approve from his own manuscript, citing Plautus, *Ornamenta Ajacis*. Pride is finely described sitting upon a horse: no animal is more exalted than a horse.

181. Vienna and Ang. have *jactantibus*. Others more correctly have *jactantius*.

183. Here one sees the ancient custom of arranging the hair, not unlike the practice of our own times. Heads and statues of women arranged in this form exist in museums. Ancient writers frequently mention it. Juvenal, *Satire* 6, verse 502, calls the steps by which the hair was raised into a high structure “ranks”:

“By so many ranks, by so many layers, she builds up

The lofty head; you will see Andromache from the front—

She is shorter behind.”

Ovid, speaking of a maidservant who dresses hair, *Amores* II, elegy 8:

“Set over hair arranged in a thousand fashions.”

Manilius, Horace, and others may also be consulted; among Christian writers, Gregory Nazianzen and Jerome in his letter to Demetrias, where he says that she builds a tower-like crown with other people’s hair; and Tertullian, *On the Dress of Women*, chapter 7:

“Moreover, you attach I know not what enormities of hairpieces, sometimes like a sheath and covering of the head, sometimes raised behind as a support for the nape. It is astonishing that one contends against the Lord’s commands. It has been declared that no one can add to one’s stature; but you add to your weight.”

Paulinus likewise speaks of a tower-like head. Compare Carlo Paschalio, *On Crowns*, book I, chapter 5, and the dissertation of Antonio M. Lupi, volume II, dissertation 13, on the inscription which he himself explains and reads as follows: “Gnome, the maidservant of Pierinus, a distinguished hairdresser, died on the fifth day before the Kalends of February, when Caesar was consul for the thirteenth time and Marcus Plautius Silvanus was consul.” Add Eugenio Guasco, *Tusculan Dissertation on an Ancient Funerary Inscription Belonging to a Hairdresser*. Rome, 1771, octavo.

187. Fuld. has *in pectore*.

188. Vienna has *limbi*, incorrectly, instead of *limbus*. Elmenhorst, in his commentary on Arnobius, p. 55, on Arnobius’ words “They would diminish foreheads with bands,” also cites Statius, *Achilleid*: “Or they bind the temples with jeweled bands.”

189. Gis., Mar., Rat., Weitz. have *ingestas*. Alex. has *infestas vel ingestas*, with the gloss “sent in.” Ang. has *infestas*, with the gloss “hostile.” Aldus, Widm. in the margin, and Vatican C, D, G, H have *infestas*, which Heinsius did not approve, although it was read in all his manuscripts. I do not find *infestas* especially objectionable, since the garments swell with hostile breezes. Sich. and Vienna likewise have *infestas*.

190. Vienna has *instabilis*.

192. In Rat. a clever corrector altered the text to *huc illucque fremens*, erasing the earlier reading.

193. In Vienna the *-que* in *pressisque* is missing.

194. He calls the virtues maidens, and pride a warrior-woman, which is something quite different; and the works of pride indeed fall more upon men than upon women.

196. After this verse Mar. and Rat. have the title “Humility.”

198. *Paupertinus* is a word found in Apuleius, Varro as cited by Nonius, Aulus Gellius, Symmachus, Ammianus, and Sidonius. Jonas, bishop of Orléans, followed Prudentius in book II of *On the Cult of Sacred Images*: “Despising his poverty-stricken weapons,” where some incorrectly read *pauperina* or *pauperrima*.

199. I do not find words of this kind, *humilis* and *humilitas*, used for a virtue in pagan authors. When Spartianus says in his life of Julian, chapter 9, “Pride was charged against him, although even in imperial power he was very humble,” he means the vice opposed to pride, not the virtue midway between the two.]

Perhaps Pride, swollen through her extended ranks,

Flew upon an unbridled horse, which she had covered

With a lion’s hide and burdened its powerful shoulders

[180] With shaggy hair;

That, supported by the beastly mane, she might carry herself

More boastfully, surveying the ranks with swollen arrogance.

She had piled her tower-like head high with twisted locks,

606 So that added heaps might enlarge the piled-up curls

[185] And her lofty brow might bear a raised summit.

A linen cloak, gathered from the shoulders at the top,

Came together in a rounded fold, tying a smooth knot at her breast.

A border flowing from her neck in a thin veil

Takes in hostile breezes through its swelling folds.

[190] [Col. 0038A] No less does the hoof-clanging horse display pride

In its unstable savagery, impatient to have its mouth bridled

With saw-toothed bits. Snorting, it turns its back

Here and there, while denied the freedom of flight,

And swells against the tightened reins.

607 Displaying herself in this boastful form,

The warrior-woman towers between the two battle lines,

Turns her richly adorned horse around, and threatens

By look and voice, watching the opposing wedge,

Which the humble mind had brought together for battle

With a small number of soldiers and poverty-stricken weapons:

A queen indeed, but lacking another’s

[200] Assistance, and not sufficiently confident in her own equipment,

[Col. 0039A] [Note: [Col. 0039B]

201. “Associate,” companion.—“Raised,” elevated.—“Whose,” of hope, I.

202. “Abundance”: the abundance of hope is suspended from the earth, because it is not promised from below but from above.—“With heavenly wealth,” I.

203. “Therefore”: pride again.—“Madly unsound,” deranged, I.

204. “With humble things”: because God chose foolish, lowly, and contemptible things through which to destroy all that is proud, I.

206. “Is she not ashamed,” ironically.—“Plebeian,” rustic, peasant, I.

207. “To attack,” to assail, I.

208. “Titles,” swords, I.

209. “Hills,” dominions, I.

211. “If it is permitted,” if it is possible, I.

212. “Behold,” said ironically, that is, “what sort.”—“To yield,” to happen, I.

213. “Scepters,” kingdoms.—“Who,” what sort, I.

214. “Stranger,” foreign. Those whom the king of pride—that is, the devil or tyrant—had invaded with the plow of preaching are cultivated more effectively by the preachers of humility, I.

215. “Hard,” namely, us.—“To drive out,” namely, they wish.—“By Mars,” by war, I.

216. “Ridiculous,” it is, Mar.

218. “Fosterlings,” children, I.

219. “Rough,” new, I.

221. “Dominions,” our empires, I.

223. “House,” family.—“We grew,” we increased, I.

224. “The created form,” Adam.—“Enclosure,” narrow, I.

225. “Boundary,” edge.—“Fled across,” went, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0039B]

202. Giselinus thinks that the poet alludes to the etymology of humility when he says that the abundance of hope is suspended from the earth; he does not approve the common interpretation, “hope produced by an abundance of all things and raised from the earth,” in the manner in which, among the Romans, newborn infants are first placed on the ground and then lifted up after the goddess Levana has been invoked. I do not dislike Bergius’ explanation, preserved by Weitz., that the passage means: “Blessed are the poor, because they will possess the kingdom of God.” The sense is this: hope alone is on earth, its abundance, and the rich kingdom in heaven. In the Cologne edition, Mariettius or someone else noted in the margin from a manuscript, “suspended from a hook”; the verse does not permit this, nor do I understand what “hook” would mean here.

204. Vienna and Vatican C and O have *extructam*; others, *instructam*.

205. Barthius, *Adversaria* XXIV, chapter 15, observes very correctly that the reading is as found in a manuscript cited by Boethius: “Alas, weak one! I am forced to enter mournful measures,” rather than “to begin mournful measures.” Aldus and Vatican C have *se fundit*; most have *se effundit*, as does Barthius. Cellarius has *se fundit*.

208. Sich., Weitz., and Bong. have *telis*. Others more correctly have *titulis*. Widm. above has *gladiis*.

209. Piccartus’ manuscript has *germine colles*.

210. Aldus, Weitz., Gis., and others have *nunc advena*. Gis.’s first edition prints it in the text, and an old manuscript in the margin of Weitz.’s edition, in the possession of the distinguished bishop Reggio, likewise has *advena*. This is not bad if the punctuation is altered.

212. An imitation of Virgil, *Eclogue* 1: “Behold the fields we have planted!” and *Aeneid* IX, verse 600: “Behold those who demand our marriage-rights for themselves by war!”

213. Aldus and Fabr. with some of our witnesses write *nostros* instead of *nostras*. Mar. and most others have *nostras*. Both forms are used. Compare Virgil’s cited eclogue, “cultivated fallow fields.”

215. Ang. and Vatican C have *duros expellere*.

216. Weitz., Mar., Vienna, and Rat. have *nempe hoc ridiculum*, with the gloss in Mar. “it is.” Others have *nempe, o ridiculum*. Vienna incorrectly has *non talibus horis*. Aldus and Erfurt have *natalibus oris*, I think because the ancients sometimes omitted aspiration. Pride boasts that a human being is in her power from the very day of birth.

217. Juvenal, *Satire* 7, verse 196: “Still red from his mother.”

219. Vienna incorrectly has *damnamur in ossibus*. Prudentius often uses *rudes* for “new,” although the bones of a newborn human being may properly be called rough or incomplete. Pride speaks of her soldiers, or vices belonging to that class, which she earlier called ancient kings.

221. Vienna has *ditioribus*, incorrectly.

222. Vienna, not improperly, has *nati cum luce sub una*. Ang. incorrectly has *natis sub luce*.

223. The house is the human being himself; the masters, previously called kings, are the various vices of pride or those closely related to it.

225. Vienna has *limine progrediens*. Weitz., with Piccartus’ manuscript alone, has *transfluxit* instead of *transfugit*. Vatican F incorrectly has *urbem* instead of *orbem*.

226. Rosweydus, in his notes on Paulinus, p. 871, on the words “clad in the hide of a great ox,” observes from this passage of Prudentius and from other passages of Jerome, Cicero, and Propertius that skins were the oldest clothing of the first patriarchs. I do not understand Weitz., who says that sacred Genesis, chapter III, and Cyprian and Basil offer us another reason. Unless everything greatly deceives me, in Genesis and the holy Fathers cited, pride was the reason Adam was ordered to depart from paradise. “The Lord God made garments of skin for Adam and his wife, and clothed them.” And he said: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil; now therefore, lest he stretch out his hand,” etc.; and above, verse 3, the serpent’s voice—which is precisely pride’s commandment—“You will be like gods.” Elmenhorst, in his commentary on Arnobius, p. 61, illustrates a similar passage of Arnobius, “They ceased to be clad in skins.”]

She had joined Hope to herself as a companion, whose abundance

Is elevated and suspended above the earth in a wealthy kingdom.

608 Therefore, when mad Pride saw the humble mind

Equipped with lowly weapons and no display,

[205] She poured herself forth in bitter words:

“Are you not ashamed, wretches, to attack illustrious commanders

With a plebeian soldier, and to challenge with steel a people

Distinguished by titles? A people whose martial virtue

Won riches in ancient times and gave them leave

[210] To tread prosperous hills beneath their empire?

Now a naked stranger strives, if it is permitted,

To drive out ancient kings.

Behold those who wish our scepters to yield as spoil

To their own hands! Behold those who seek to plow

Our fallow fields and cultivate the captured land

[215] With a foreign plow, and by war to drive out the hard colonists.

Surely, ridiculous rabble! From the hour of birth

609 We embrace the whole human being and his limbs still warm from his mother.

We scatter the force of our powers through the limbs

Of the new-born fosterling, and all of us rule over his undeveloped bones.

[220] What place was then being granted you in our seat,

When, born together, you were growing with kingdoms

And dominions of equal strength?

For born beneath the same light, house and masters

We grew up through equal years.

From the time when the new-created form,

[225] Advancing from the narrow boundary of paradise,

Fled out into the wide world,

Venerable Adam took on a garb of skin and bone [reading uncertain],

[Col. 0041A] [Note: [Col. 0041B]

228. “Of the mouth,” boundaries, I.

229. “Intrusive,” one who is close or suitable in nothing; he speaks of humility, I.

230. “Thus far,” up to this point.—“Exile,” one who is outside his native land, I.

231. “Are believed,” by them, I.

232. “Of the future”: he strives to empty the future, so that he may deceive the wretched through delight in the present, I.

234. “Idleness,” laziness.—“May soothe,” may temper, caress, I.

235. “Why not,” certainly; what else?—“Dust,” earth; in this age, I.

236. “Bellona,” the warrior goddess, goddess of war.—“Bronze,” a horn, I.

238. “In war,” for war, I.

239. “Piety,” chastity.—“Is sweated over,” is labored at, I.

240. “Mars,” the god of war.—“Virtue,” mine; “our army,” I.

241. “Trifles,” useless things, I.

245. “Shame,” blush, I.

246. “Covering,” of the shield, I.

247. “Prostrate,” bent down.—“Herself,” herself alone, I.

248. “Comes forth,” reveals, I.

249. “I shall make,” I do, I.

250. “Hand,” multitude, I.

252. “To stain,” to defile, I.

254. “Horn-footed,” a horse, because it has feet formed like horns, I.

255. “Desiring”: Pride strives to rush upon humility and hope.—“By the thrust,” by the horse’s chest, I.

257. “Into the pit”: Pride falls into the pit, I.

258. “Plain,” the earth; “field,” from equality, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0041C]

227. Aldus and Vatican C have *supra, nisi nostra*.

228. Mar. and Rat., with Weitz., have *horis*. Others have *oris*, which is correct. The ancients sometimes added aspiration where it was not needed, as *honus* for *onus*. Others did the reverse, as I noted at verse 216. Vatican C, O, and some others have *hostis nunc surgit*.

231. Giselinus’ first edition has *creduntur*; the second, *credentur*, which he again changed to *creduntur* in the *Observations and Corrections*. Many fail to notice such authorial corrections and second thoughts. Vatican C, Ang., Mar., Vienna, Aldus, and Weitz. have *creduntur*. Giselinus asserts that the poet uses an extraordinary, indeed unheard-of, irony in mocking the hope in which he had just before placed all the riches of humility as its companion. But now he expresses Pride’s thoughts; earlier he had explained his own true thoughts and those of others.

232. Aldus, Vienna, Alex., Vatican F, Pal., and Heinsius’ manuscripts have *jubet*. Mar., Rat., Weitz., Gis., and others have *jubent*.

233. Vienna has *spem fortasse bonam*, less well. Aldus, Fuld., Put., and Oxford have *lenta ut solatia*. Our better witnesses—Alex. in the first hand, Mar., Rat., Vienna, with Thuan. in the first hand, Weitz., Gis., and others—have *laeta*.

234. The more carefully corrected manuscripts of Heinsius and ours, Alex., Mar., and Rat. with Weitz., Gis., and others, have *meditamine*. Vatican C has *medicamine*; above, *meditamine*. Aldus, with some others, has *medicamine*.

238. See the note on verse 57, “The vein of the soul.”

242. Aldus has *cumque hanc virgineis dextram*. Someone might conjecture, “And to match this right hand with virginal dances.” Some copies of the Vulgate have *ac cum* instead of *et cum*.

243. Aldus has *justitia est nam semper egens*. Others have *justitia est ubi semper egens*. He calls justice needy and honesty poor, on the basis of what often happens.

244. Vienna, Ang., Vatican C in the second hand, and Rat. in a recent hand have *jejunaque*; others, *jejunia*.

248. Vienna has *prodet*. Vatican C, with the earlier reading erased, has *trepidatio prodit*. Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, verse 13: “Fear reveals ignoble spirits.”

249. Plautus, *Miles Gloriosus*, act I, scene 1: “Whose legions you have scattered with your breath, as wind scatters leaves or a painter’s brush.”

250. Aldus, Fabr., and Vatican C have *perstringere*, less correctly than *perfringere*. *Perstringere* also occurs in Mar., Rat., and others; but, as Giselinus observes, *perstringere* means “to touch lightly.” Here *perfringere*, “to break through with hard swords,” is more appropriate.

252. Aldus and Rat., from a recent and foolish correction, have *Imbuere et fragili vires foedare triumpho*. Cellarius copied the same error; at least that is what I read in his second edition, perhaps because he was deceived by an error in the notes to Heinsius’ second edition. Gallandius errs more seriously, saying that Chamillard printed *imbuere, fragilique viros* and himself reading, against the Muses, *imbuere, fragilique vires*.

253. Erfurt has *rabidum*; others, *rapidum*.

255. Aldus incorrectly has *impulsuum bonis equini*. Others likewise give the erroneous readings in Becmannus’ *Handbook of the Latin Language*: *impulsum bonis equini* or *impulsum bovis equini*. Nebrissa understands *equine boss* to mean a shield, or buckler, made from horse hide.

256. Alex. has *ruinis*; others, *ruinam*.]

Still naked, unless he had followed our commands.

Who now is this intrusive, unknown enemy rising from foreign shores,

610 Idle, wretched, degenerate, mad,

[230] Who, an exile until now, claims his rights so late?

Indeed, empty rumors are believed,

Which sometimes command the wretched to hope for some future good,

So that cheerful consolations may caress soft idleness

With sluggish meditation upon affairs.

[235] Why should idle hope not caress those whom Bellona,

In this dust, does not rouse as recruits with her grim bronze,

And whom enervated virtue dissolves, their souls unfit for battle?

Is the cold liver of Chastity useful in war?

Is the tender work of piety practiced in arms?

[240] How shameful, O Mars, and conscious Virtue,

[Col. 0041B] To stand against such a battle line, challenge trifles with steel,

And match this right hand against virginal dances!

611 Justice is always needy, and Honesty poor;

[Col. 0042A] Dry Sobriety, Fasting with a pale face,

[245] Shame scarcely suffused with thin blood,

Open Simplicity, exposed to every wound without a covering,

And the humble mind prostrate upon the ground,

Not free before its judge, whose trembling reveals its degeneracy.

I shall see to it that this feeble hand is trampled

[250] Underfoot like straw; for we do not deign

To break through it with hard swords, steeping iron in blood

And staining men with a feeble triumph.”

Shouting such words, she spurs her swift

Horn-footed horse and flies recklessly with loosened reins,

[255] Desiring, by the thrust of an equine-hide shield-boss,

[Col. 0042B] To lay low the humble enemy and trample upon the fallen body.

612 But she falls headlong into a pit which crafty Fraud

Had perhaps secretly dug across the level ground,

[Col. 0043A] [Note: [Col. 0043B]

260. “Crafty,” a skillful contriver, I.

261. “Pits,” trenches, I.

263. “Wedges,” armies.—“Ranks,” of the virtues, I.

264. “To discover,” to foresee, I.

265. “Cautious,” clear.—“Edges,” summits, I.

267. “Queen,” humility again, I.

270. “She,” namely, Pride, I.

271. “Gap,” pit, I.

274. “Levity,” instability, I.

276. “Face,” countenance.—“Sparingly,” moderately, I.

277. “Courteous,” honorable, serious, adorned, agreeable, I.

278. “Hesitating,” doubting, I.

280. “She”: humility cuts off Pride’s head, I.

284. “Extinguished,” extinguished pride, I.

287. “Brow,” pride, I.

288. “Loftily,” gloriously, I.

289. “Widely proclaimed,” greatly, I.

293. “Twisted,” threw, I.

294. “Pierced through,” through a passage, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0043C]

259. Aldus, Ang., and Vatican C in the first hand have *vitiorum pestibus* without *e*, which is certainly necessary. In Aldus there is a single one; the substantive verb is superfluous.

261. Heinsius prefers *vitiaverat* with Put. alone, and after Heinsius, Chamillard and others. But why should *violaverat*, found in the older printed editions and in our Mar., Rat., Vienna, Alex., Vatican C, F, G, O, and countless others, be rejected? You say that Prudentius sometimes used *vitiandi*; as though he had not used *violandi* more often. I prefer *violare planitiem scrobibus*, “to violate the plain with pits,” to *vitiare*. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* III, says *violare silvam*, “to violate the forest,” meaning to cut it with an axe.

264. Weitz. has *at ne*; others, *ac ne*. Some copies of the Vulgate have *possit*.

265. Aldus, Widm. in the margin, Vienna, Vatican C, L, BB, and Ang. have *clara acies*. Rat., Mar., and other excellent witnesses have *cauta*, which Gallandius preferred.

269. Vienna has *Venerat, ut foveae calcaret furta malignae*. In Vatican C, incorrectly and against the meter, *Venerat aut foveae nondum calcarat malignae*. In the margin, after *calcarat*, appears *furta*, but *nondum* is always superfluous.

270. Egm., Pal., and Barthius have *hinc eques*. Vienna has *huc eques*. Retain *hunc*.

271. In Vatican F the order of these verses is reversed: first comes *Prona*, then *Incidit*. “She fell into the deceit,” as at the beginning of Juvencus’ book II: “And now the day, descending with slanting light, had fallen upon the sea.”

272. Vienna has *una*; read *prona*. In Rat. an inept corrector, of the sort often mentioned, has *cervice rotata superque / Pectoris impressu quadripes provolvitur ipse*.

273. Fabr. has *vectoris pressu*. Giselinus printed this in his second edition, but later corrected it at the end to *pectoris impressu* from the manuscripts; some failed to notice this correction. In the first Rott. edition: *pectoris impulsu*. Vatican F has *inter dura*. The common reading is: “The four-footed beast, its neck bent forward, rolls beneath the pressure of its breast, broken between its legs.”

274. Bong. has *et virtus*; better, *at virtus*. *Moderamen* is used for *moderatio*; see *Apotheosis*, verse 47.

275. Vienna and Mar. have *conspicit obtritam*. Rat., Gis., and Weitz. have *perspicit obritam*. Fuld. has *prospicit obstrictam*. The best witnesses, with Aldus, have *prospicit obtritam*.

276. Fuld. has *parte*; read *parce*.

280. Vienna has *cruentatum*, less correctly.

281. Vienna has *contrahit*; better, *protrahit*.

282. Virgil, *Aeneid* X: “The neck bent back, cut off.”

283. Aldus and others have *et madido*.

Fraud, one of the detestable pests of the vices,

[260] Crafty artificer of deception, foreseeing the battle,

Had violated the level ground with treacherous pits,

Lurking on the hostile side, so that a ditch might receive

The rushing wedges and swallow the submerged ranks.

And so that the cautious battle line could not discover

[265] The deceitful pit, she had covered its edges with interwoven branches

And made the ground appear level by placing turf over it.

But the humble queen, although unaware, remained

Farther away and had not yet come to the hiding place of the deceit

Or trodden upon the wicked secrets of the pit.

[270] That horsewoman, while borne forward at headlong speed,

Falls into this trap and suddenly exposes the hidden gap:

613 She, headlong, is entangled in the neck of the plunging horse,

And, crushed beneath the pressure of its breast, is rolled between its legs.

But Virtue of calm restraint, when she sees the levity

[275] Of the monster crushed and lying in death,

Advances her step with moderation, raises her face sparingly,

And restrains her joy with a courteous expression.

To the hesitating woman faithful Hope, her companion, comes to her aid,

Offers her the avenging sword, and inspires love of glory.

[280] She seizes the bloodied enemy by the hair,

Drags her forward, and, with her left hand pulling back the face,

Turns it upward. Then she cuts off the head

Of the suppliant, whose neck she has bent,

And suspends the neck with its wet hair.

Extinguished Vice, Hope rebukes with holy lips:

[285] “Cease your grand talk: God breaks every proud thing.

Great things fall; inflated things crack; swollen things are crushed.

Learn to lay down your brow; learn to beware of the pit

Before your feet, whoever threatens from on high.”

614 The well-known saying of our Christ remains in force:

[290] “The humble climb to the heights, and the fierce return to the depths.”

[Col. 0044B] We saw Goliath, terrible in body and spirit,

Fall by a feeble hand: a boy’s right hand

Hurled a little stone with the whistling force of a sling,

And pierced his forehead through with a hollow wound.

310. Giselinus is quite ingenious here. He rejects the interpretation tentatively suggested by Nebrissa: that this should be understood of the world’s age inclining toward its decline, so that, as Giselinus says, he might free his Spain and Africa from this disgrace. He then considers it probable that the poet summoned the instruments of luxury from those regions, since they—and Spain above all—were remarkably famous for their abundance of gold, silver, wool, spices, and other things conducive to effeminate habits. “If these things,” he says, “had remained within their own boundaries, perhaps we Belgians would never have lost the praise bestowed upon us by Julius Caesar.” He is right to admit that the Belgians lost their ancient reputation; but as for assigning the cause to the Spaniards, he might perhaps now deny it, observing that the former Spanish masters are praised and missed by these peoples. I do agree with Giselinus, however, that the poet was referring rather to the whole West, insofar as that part of the world is distinguished from the East. For, as Sulpicius relates in the *Life of Saint Martin*, excessive luxury prevailed more in the West than in the East. Several writers teach that the word “West” signifies the devil. But since the Roman Empire was then divided and mention of both East and West was common, it is more probable that Prudentius means the Western Empire, and especially its capital, Rome, where luxury was then boiling over conspicuously, as Ammianus Marcellinus recounts at length. Among other things he says:

“Some, placing their highest distinction in carriages taller than usual and in ostentatious dress, sweat beneath the weight of their cloaks, and so forth. I pass over the gaping chasms of their tables and their various enticements to pleasure, lest I proceed too far. … Finally, a singer is summoned in place of a philosopher, and a teacher of frivolous arts in place of an orator; and, with libraries shut forever in the manner of tombs, they construct instruments such as water-organs, and so forth. At last matters came to such a degree of disgrace that, although foreigners were recently being driven headlong from the City because of the feared scarcity of provisions, and the very few followers of the liberal disciplines were expelled without any respite, the genuine devotees of mime—or those who temporarily pretended to be such—were retained; and three thousand dancing girls, together with their choruses, and just as many instructors, remained without even being questioned. And although, wherever you turn your eyes, you may see innumerable women with curled hair who, had they married, could by their age already have borne children three times over, stamping the pavements with their feet until one grows weary, whirling through revolving dances while they reproduce countless figures invented by theatrical fables.”

All these things correspond most fittingly to Prudentius’ description of luxury. I certainly would not deny that luxury was also unrestrained in the East at that very time, as is shown by the vices which Chrysostom reproves most severely and in the style of a preacher. But whether Antioch or Constantinople is compared with Rome, I do not doubt that license and moral corruption were far greater at Rome than in the other cities of the East.

311. Cornelius Tacitus, *Annals*, book XI: “Among the profligate, the final pleasure is disgrace.”

312. The second syllable of *delibuta* is lengthened here for metrical necessity. Gualterus imitated it in book V of the *Alexandreis*, verse 218: “With fresh gore besmeared her hair.” The earlier Rottendorf manuscript reads *oculos vaga, languida vocem*, “wandering in the eyes, languid in voice,” in the Greek manner, like *delibuta comas*. All our manuscripts, together with others, read *oculis vaga, languida voce*, except the Cauchian manuscript, which has the former reading. Heinsius printed *oculos … vocem*; Chamillard, Gallandius, and Teolius followed him. Barthius compares with Prudentius our Bacchiarius, who describes the eyes of fallen man as wandering, thereby indicating luxury and lust.

313. The Vienna manuscript has *edita*, “produced”; *perdita*, “ruined,” is better. The earlier Boher manuscript has *cura* for *causa*, less suitably. Virtues are commonly called the means of living. Juvenal, *Satire* 8, verse 84: “And for the sake of life to destroy the reasons for living.” By the contrary reasoning, pleasure is the means of life for the luxurious.

314. Persius, *Satire* 1, verse 104: “Utterly limp saliva.” The author of the dialogue *On the Orator* used *elumbis*, “without backbone.”

315. The usual verb when luxury is being discussed is *FRANGERE*, “to break.” See what Gothofredus notes on the words *FRACTA mollier plebe*, in the Theodosian Code, book VI, under the Julian law concerning adulterers, drawing on our poet and others.

316. Ratoldus, Mariettus, Weitz, and Alexandrianus have *ac tunc*, “and then.” Aldus has *et tunc*. The Vienna manuscript, Giselinus, and the Palatine manuscript have *at tunc*, “but then.” The Heinsian manuscripts agree with ours in reading *ac tunc*.

Heinsius conjectures *nervo impulsa fugit*, which Cellarius adopted. I would not alter the common reading *nervo pulsa fugit*, found in Alexandrianus, Vatican manuscripts C and D, G, L, O, BB, Mariettus, Ratoldus, Vienna, Aldus, and others. Other manuscripts, and the margin of Giselinus, have *frameam*. *Amenta*, according to Festus, are the cords by which javelins are bound so that they may be thrown. Hence *amentare* occurs in Lucan and Martianus Capella.

331. Aldus has *oblito*, less suitably, instead of *obliso*. Nor is the reading *choros* better, found in another Rottendorf manuscript and at Bologna instead of *toros*; I attach no importance to the fact that some manuscripts write *thoros*. Giselinus does not entirely reject *oblito*, as in Virgil, *Eclogue* 9: “Now forgotten to me are so many songs.” After this verse, the Vienna, Angers, Vatican C, L, and BB manuscripts contain these two verses:

Giselinus had found the same verses in a manuscript of Theodore Pulmannus and in another printed at Deventer, but rightly considered them fabricated. Giselinus, however, read *credita corda*, “entrusted hearts.”

343. The oldest Heinsian manuscripts, Vienna, Mariettus, Ratoldus, Weitz, Gallandius, and others have *ganearum*. Aldus, together with Tornesius and several others, has *ganeorum*, which I do not reject, since *ganeum* means a vaulted chamber. Giselinus says that some substitute *ganeonum* for *ganearum*. “Why?” he asks. “Are the laws the same for *ganea* and *ganeo*?” *Ganea* and *ganeum*, in their Greek origin, are written with eta, that is, long *e*. Becmanus, *On the Origins of the Latin Language*, under *GANEUM*, observes that the Latins often changed eta into *a*, and into short *e*, as in *gynaeceum* in Terence, with a short penultimate syllable; *cyclopeus* in Maro; and *conopeum* in Horace, *Ode* 9 of the *Epodes*. A *ganeo*, as Isidore says in book X, is a luxurious person, as though living in hidden and subterranean places, which the Greeks call *ganea*. After this verse, Mariettus and Ratoldus have the heading “Sobriety.”

347. Gretserus, book II, chapter 18, *On the Cross*, says that Prudentius is alluding to the practice of carrying an image of the cross before armies in battle; he confirms this practice with several examples at that place.]

350. The chief Heinsian manuscripts, together with Aldus and others, have *instimulans*. Our better manuscripts—Mariettus, Ratoldus, Alexandrianus, Giselinus, Weitz, and others—have *exstimulans*.

351. Barthius rejects *insanus* for *insanas*, although he found the former in his manuscript. The Egmond manuscript likewise has *insanus*.

353. The Vienna manuscript has *ah pudor!*; others have *aut* instead of *proh pudor!* The Vienna manuscript has *proferre lacertis*. Paschalius, *On Crowns*, book II, chapter 15, page 124, notes from this passage the mixing of flowers in crowns in imitation of nature. See Tertullian, *On the Military Crown*, who says that flowers were invented not to adorn the head but to delight the nostrils.

355. Iso and other early commentators interpret *ferrugineo* as “purple.” Mariettus, after noting from the gloss that *purpureo* was given instead of *ferrugineo*, added that it should be considered whether purple is associated with rust. Certainly, in Virgil, rust is darker than purple: *Georgics* I, “when he covered his shining head with dark rust,” and *Aeneid* IX, “bright with Iberian rust,” where Servius understands Pontic, not Spanish, rust; others take the opposite view.

357. Weitz and Erfurt have *ac rigidas*, “and stiff.”

359. Angers has, incorrectly, *cum bibat* instead of *combibat*. The Heinsian manuscripts and our better manuscripts have *infusum*. Vatican BB and another manuscript used by Teolius, the Cauchian manuscript, and Weitz have *infusam*. The Egmond manuscript has *relegamine* instead of *religamine*, incorrectly. The sacrament of confirmation is being described; see above, *Hymn of the Catholic Faith* 6, verse 128. See Baronius, volume I of the *Annals*, page 249, and John Laurence Bertius, book XXXII of *Theological Discourses*, chapter 10, on the form of anointing, besides others who explain the sacrament of confirmation through these verses of Prudentius. He also notes that Prudentius is criticizing the effeminate habits of men, who wore the *mitra*, a prostitute’s ornament, and wrapped their hair in a saffron-colored net. Juvenal, *Satire* 3: “Go, you to whom the painted foreign prostitute’s cap is pleasing.” *Satire* 6: “But with a yellow cap concealing his black hair.” *Satire* 2: “And they fill a golden net with their enormous hair.”

360. Weitz and Erfurt have *postquam*. So too does the second hand of the Widmann manuscript, but the first hand has *post quae*. Others have *per quae*.

362. The Vienna manuscript has *et tener*; *ut*, “so that,” is better. Luxury is indicated by the garment flowing all the way to the ground. Cyprian, or another author, *On Christian Fasting*: “Sweeping the pavements with ankle-length military cloaks.”

363. Giselinus explains *in fractis* as “in broken, soft, and effeminate [limbs],” so that, he says, there are two words. If one orders it to be written *infractis*, this is not necessary; for *infractus*, as a single word, can also mean “broken.” The verb *fluitare*, however, seems to require *in membris fractis*, “over broken limbs.” Most join the word as *infractis*. On the verb *frangere*, see verse 315.

364. Weitz, together with the Widmann manuscript alone, preferred to print *tonicam* and omit *tunicam*, which appears in all the others: absurdly. Angers has *dextro* instead of *docto*, less suitably. The subject is the grace of baptism, signified by the white stoles in which the newly baptized are clothed.

**[Col. 0050C]** 367. The Heinsian manuscripts, except Oxford, and our better manuscripts—Angers, Mariettus, Ratoldus, and Vatican H, together with Weitz—have *inde*. Many other Vatican manuscripts, C, F, G, L, O, and BB, together with Oxford, Aldus, and Giselinus, have *ite*, which Gifanius retained from an old book in his index to Lucretius. In Barthius’ manuscript, *inde* also occurs; in the following verse it has *dispuit* instead of *despuit*. *Inde* is more pleasing, and the question is then extended to verse 370: “are they watered?” Peveratus thinks this passage was taken from *Aeneid* VII, perhaps verses 146 and following.

369. Aldus has: “Upon the table, with dripping cups, an immense wave, where the couches are wet with abundant wine,” which Gifanius approves from an old book at the place cited, asserting that it is not inelegantly expressed by a learned poet, since he also calls wine “dew,” and in the *Dittochaeon*: “From where the ancient wine is poured, a fourfold wave,” panel 32, verse 128. Giselinus restored the reading: “Upon the table, with dripping cups, where the couches are wet with abundant wine,” and observes that in this poet several passages had been corrupted by the reckless and false joining of a preposition with its case. Certainly, in many ancient manuscripts words are sometimes joined together in such a way that keen judgment is needed to separate each one. Nevertheless, I would not deny that the reading of Aldus, Gifanius, and Fabricius is found in ancient parchment manuscripts, namely Vatican C, G, L, and BB, unless one prefers to read: “Upon the table, with dripping cups, a wave, where the couches are wet with abundant wine.” Angers has *unda*, incorrectly. Vatican H is completely corrupt: *stillantibus daubis multo Fulcra mero*. The Vienna manuscript has *cyathis stipulantibus*, which is useful to no one. Salvianus seems to have had this passage of Prudentius in mind in book IV *Against Avarice*: “The pavements of their dining rooms swim with wine; they make mud with noble Falernian; their tables and embossed vessels are continually drenched with unmixed wine, always wet.” From this, the reading *uda*, “wet,” is confirmed.

370. Sirmondus, commenting on Sidonius and praising these verses in letter 2 of book IX, advises that *toreumata* should be understood instead of *toralia*. Fabricius maintains that here too *toreumata* means works made and polished on a lathe, which the glosses also teach; but this is less satisfactory. Read again the words of Salvianus in the preceding note.]

> upon a table where the couches, beneath dripping cups,
>
> **[370]** are wet with abundant wine, and the embossed vessels are drenched with ancient dew?”

372. *Patribus*, “your [fathers],” I.

373. *Elicuit*, “drew out,” “brought forth,” I.

377. *Imbutos*, “led,” I.

378. *Lupanar*, “brothel,” I.

386. *Excitet*, “may stir you,” I.

389. *Attrectare* forbids touching with the hand. *Regem*, “Agag,” I.

**[Col. 0052B]** 390. *Incircumcisum*, “uncircumcised,” “corpulent,” I.

[Note: [Col. 0051B]

371. In Ratoldus, an obtuse corrector inserted: “Therefore the thirst of the wilderness fell from the thirsty souls; that Fountain given to the fathers in the wilderness,” evidently so that the second *in eremo* would not be shortened. You may read the sacred history in Exodus chapters XVI and XVII.

373. Aldus has *e vertice*. In the others, *e* is absent. Vatican F has *saliente*, and in some vulgate editions *scissis* is an error.

374. Some vulgate editions have *angelicusve*. The Cauchian manuscript has *patria in tentoria*. The Heinsian manuscripts, Mariettus, Ratoldus, Alexandrianus, and Vatican C, D, G, H, L, O, BB, Weitz, and others have *vestris*. Aldus, Giselinus, Vatican F, and the first hand of Angers have *nostris*. This also seems to have been the reading in the Vienna manuscript.

375. Ratoldus has *feliciter*, less suitably.

376. Erfurt has *de sanguine Christi*. Here you see a clear testimony to Catholic belief in the presence of Christ’s body in the Eucharist, since the similarity to the angelic food, manna, is often indicated by the holy Fathers. Among the works of Cyprian, in the sermon *On the Supper*: “This bread of angels, containing every delight through wondrous power, … fills and satisfies the appetites of those who eat more fully than that manna of the wilderness,” and so forth. Fabricius says that Prudentius’ expression “the evening people” is wonderfully chosen for those who will live in the final times, the form of speech being taken from the words, “Stay with us, because it is evening.” There is no doubt that the Christian people are meant; but this may also be understood in another way, because in sacred Scripture evening often signifies Christ, or his coming, and the seventh age of the world. See the Fathers who explain these allegories, listed by Lauretus in the *Allegorical Forest*. Peveratus thinks Prudentius calls the Christian people “evening” because after the ninth hour and in the evening, during the stations, they ate of Christ’s body. This does not seem to me to have been Prudentius’ intention.

379. Some have *viris*, incorrectly. In Ratoldus, a corrector ignorant of the usage of Prudentius’ age, after erasing the earlier reading, wrote *idolaque bello*. Aldus had correctly printed *non idola bello*; he foolishly changed it to *idolaque bello*. Giselinus observes that Aldus Manutius, if anywhere, was especially diligent in the second edition of this author, yet he transposed the middle syllables of this Greek-derived word. It is certain, however, that this did not originate with the author. I do not approve Giselinus’ suggestion that Prudentius lacked knowledge of Greek letters, since he simultaneously admits that Prudentius followed the usage of his own age, neglecting genuine quantity in consideration of Latin accent and other rules. Why could Prudentius not reserve knowledge for himself while granting usage to the people?

385. Aldus and the old editions have *natus homo*, “a man born,” instead of *esset homo*, “was a man.” Giselinus likewise has *natus homo* in the text, which pleased Gallandius more, although Gallandius printed *esset homo*.

388. See *First Book of Kings*, chapter XV.

390. The Vienna manuscript has *pariter*, incorrectly, instead of *patitur*. Fabricius has *neu praeda*; *ne praeda* is better. In the gloss, *crossus* is the same as *grossus*, “large.”

391. Ratoldus, Mariettus, the Heinsian manuscripts except the earlier Rottendorf manuscript, Giselinus, and Weitz have *recidiva*. Aldus, together with other printed editions, has *rediviva*.

393. Aldus has *nobis* instead of *vobis*; the latter is correct. The first hand of Angers had *notum est*, correctly corrected to *per votum est*.

394. Fulda has *contra legem matri, per siqua moveat*.

396. In Albertus Eyb’s *Poetic Miscellany*, canon of Bamberg, *si poenitet*, “if one regrets,” or *aut nocet error*, “or the error harms,” appears in place of *haud* or *haut*, according to an old writing practice of certain manuscripts.

397. See *First Book of Kings*, chapter XIV.

398. All the Heinsian manuscripts, the Palatine, Fulda, Widmann, Erfurt, Weitz, together with our manuscripts Mariettus, Ratoldus, Vienna, Alexandrianus, Vatican II, O, and Bologna, have *favo sceptri*, “with the honeycomb of the scepter.” In Mariettus the gloss says “that is, of the rod”; in Erfurt, the gloss says “honey received by means of the scepter.” Aldus, Tornesius, and Giselinus have *favo sumpto*, “having taken honey.” Gallandius says that the word *gustato*, “having tasted,” in the following verse may perhaps stand in the way of this reading, *favo sumpto*. Angers, Vatican L, BB, and some Heinsian manuscripts have, not improperly, *conviolasse favo, sumpti mellisque sapore*, “to have violated with honey, with the taste of honey taken.” Vatican D has, incorrectly, *favo cepit*. In Vatican C, this and the following verses are missing up to verse 450, since an entire leaf has been torn out.

399. In Vatican D, a metrical error has *mala voluptas*, “evil pleasure,” instead of *blanda*, “seductive.”

400. The Vienna manuscript has *jura resolvit*, “dissolves the oaths.” The final part of the gloss, “because he was not killed,” seems to refer to the following verse; nor is that the tearful fate.]

> which the mystical staff brought forth, springing from the split summit of the stone?

403. *Conspirare*, “to unite,” I.

404. *Viam*, “by providing,” I.

405. *Stipata*, “surrounded,” I.

406. *Pendat*, “pay,” I.

407. *Crucem*, Sobriety offers the Lord’s cross to Luxury’s chariot, I.

409. *Intentans*, “striking against,” I.

410. *Cornibus*, “of the cross,” that is, of the banner. *Fronte*, she offers the wood against its face, I.

415. *Axem*, an antiptosis, I.

**[Col. 0054B]** 417. *Addit*, Sobriety throws a stone and strikes Luxury’s mouth, I.

418. *Conjiciens*, “throwing,” “retaining,” I.

420. *Insigne*, “banner.” *Gerenti*, “ruling magnificently,” I.
