[Note: [Col. 0053B]

401. Vienna, Fulda, and the upper portion of Widmann, together with Barthius’ manuscript, have *ulla est*, “there is any.”

402. Aldus, Angers, Fabricius, and others have *tinxit*; others have *tingit*, or, as some write, *tinguit*.

408. Aldus, Angers, Gallandius, Weitz’s manuscripts except the Palatine, and our chief manuscripts together with Giselinus and others have *quadrigis*. More recent editions, together with Weitz, Putte, Rottendorf, and others, have *quadrijugis*, which Gallandius finds less satisfactory. Observe the power of the cross, which our poet often inculcates upon heretics despite their resistance.

410. All the Heinsian manuscripts, Mariettus, Ratoldus, Vienna, Vatican O, Weitz, have *oppansis* or *obpansis*. In Egmond, *obpannis* was corrected to *obpansis*. Vatican L, Barthius’ parchment manuscript, Giselinus with three manuscripts, and the Deventer edition—which he rightly regarded as equal to an excellent ancient source—have *oppassis*. Aldus, with other vulgate editions, has *expansis* or *expassis*, which is less convincing, especially since Prudentius favors compounds formed with the preposition *ob*, such as *oblidere*, *obbrutescere*, *obtrudere*, and *oppallesco*, as Giselinus had long ago observed. Aulus Gellius, book XV, chapter 13, insists that *passum* is always derived from *pando*; Gifanius disagrees in his index to Lucretius, under *DISPANSUS*, citing the authority of ancient manuscripts in this and other passages of Prudentius and other authors. Prudentius has used *pansus* more than once. In Erfurt, the following appears here together with the preceding verse: *quod ut expavere coruscum / Cornibus oppansis, et summa fronte renitens*, “when they saw the flashing thing, with horns spread wide and resisting with its forehead”; above *coruscum* is written *feroces*, and above *renitens*, *coruscum*. Indeed, *renitens* must be rejected on metrical grounds if it is taken to modify *coruscum*.

413. Aldus has *comasque madentes*; others have *comamque madentem*.

414. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VIII: “The father soils his gray hair and aged features with dust poured upon the ground.” Prudentius seems to have had this in mind. Most of our manuscripts—Mariettus, Ratoldus, Vienna, Vatican F and G, L, Aldus, Giselinus, and Weitz—do not recognize the Greek construction embraced by Heinsius and more recent editors, together with Putte, both Rottendorf manuscripts, Alexandrianus, the first hand of Vatican H, and Barthius. They read *pulvere foedatur* instead of *pulvere foedat humi*. Teolius also rejects the Greek construction, but should not have asserted that no trace of it exists in his manuscripts.

**[Col. 0054B]** 415. Aldus, together with several even ancient manuscripts, has *sub axe*, “beneath the axle.”

416. A *sufflamen* is a device placed beneath a wheel racing forward with excessive momentum, so that it may be restrained. Teolius not unreasonably understands this passage of Luxury’s own body entangled with the wheels.

418. The Vienna manuscript has *prima de parte*, incorrectly.

419. Most write *fors*; others *sors*. Choose whichever you prefer.

421. Barthius asserts that his parchment manuscripts clearly read *medii spiramen odoris*, “the breath of the middle odor,” which, he says, he would like to examine; “those who will treat our poet after us” will decide. I do not dare determine what others more skilled will judge. Nothing more certain occurs to me than that *spiramen odoris* is an error for *spiramen ut oris*, of the kind frequently found in very ancient manuscripts. In this very passage there is a clear error in Vatican D, G, and O, where *spiramen oris* is written without *ut*. Perhaps Barthius would approve the conjecture of reading: “The event drives the stone so that it might break the breath of the middle of the mouth,” so that the nose is understood to have been smashed by the stone. But what follows supports the common reading more strongly: the struggle is against the throat, not against the sense of smell.

422. Erfurt has *frangeret, atra cavo*. Alcimus Avitus, book I: “Thus the tongue in the hollow palate.”

**[Col. 0054D]** 423. It is not sufficiently clear why the throat is cut. Perhaps it would be better to read *lingua retectam dilaniata gulam*, “the tongue, lacerated, laid bare the throat.”

424. The first Giselinus edition has *frustis et sanguine complet*, “fills it with fragments and blood.”

428. Fulda and Erfurt have *pocula*, “cups,” instead of *fercula*, “dishes.” *Pocula* had occurred shortly before. On dishes, see *Cathemerinon* hymn 3, verse 16.

429. Aldus has *nimiis sub luxibus*, “beneath excessive luxuries,” which in the Widmann manuscript takes the place of a gloss. Others have *pro luxibus*, as in Piccart’s manuscript and several Vatican manuscripts, F, G, L, and BB, together with Angers and some Heinsian manuscripts. Barthius says, on the authority of his manuscript, that the true reading is *nimiis pro dulcibus aevi*, “excessive things instead of the sweet things of life.” The best of our manuscripts—Mariettus, Alexandrianus, Ratoldus, Vatican D and H—agree with him. The Vienna manuscript had *dolcibus*, which was perversely changed to *doloribus*. Putte, Thuanus, Cauchianus, Weitz, and Giselinus have likewise printed *dulcibus*. *Tristia* preceded it, that is, “bitter things.”]

> nor does the cruel sentence stain the ancestral axes,

> behold, I, Sobriety: if you are prepared to unite,

431. *Horrifico*, “with bitter drink,” I.

433. *Nugatrix*, “useless.” *Jocus*, the jester, throwing away the cymbals, flees, I.

435. *Sistro*, “trumpet,” a kind of musical instrument, I.

436. *Lita*, “anointed weapons,” I.

440. *Peplo*, “cloak,” I.

441. *Serta*, “headbands,” I.

447. *Agmen*, “army,” I.

448. *Redimicula*, “ornaments,” I.

**[Col. 0056B]** 449. *Fibula*, “virginal cloak,” I.

451. *Miles*, “army.” *Damnata*, “wicked,” I.

452. *Severos*, “grave,” I.

454. *Avaritia*, “love of money,” that is, Avarice, who searches for gold among the sands. *Gremio*, “lap,” I.

455. *Luxus*, “pleasure.” *Unca*, “greedy,” I.

456. *In ludibria*, “let it be a laughingstock to us Christians,” or “let the money be [for us] a laughingstock,” I.]

[Note: [Col. 0055B]

431. Fulda, Widmann above, and Oxford have *horrificos sapor ultimus asperet haustus*, “may the final taste make the horrific draughts harsh.” Most have *horrifico sapor ultimus asperet haustu*, “may the final taste make the horrific draught harsh.” But Vatican H, Aldus, Giselinus, Weitz, and others have *asperat*. The meaning is well known: the endings of pleasures are bitter.

433. In Angers, *locus* occurs; correct it to *jocus*. On trifles and the army of the jester, see *Catholic Hymn* 2, verse 32.

434. Some ancient manuscripts write *proiciunt*, as do Vienna, Mariettus, and others.

**[Col. 0055C]** 435. Erfurt and Fulda have *praelia*. Juvenal did indeed say *meditari praelia*, *Satire* 7, verse 128: “The one-eyed statue contemplates battles.” But in Prudentius, *bellum*, “war,” has already occurred. On the *sistrum*, see the commentary on verses 527 and 528 of book II *Against Symmachus*. Virgil, book VIII, concerning Cleopatra: “The queen summons her ranks amid the battle with her ancestral sistrum.”

437. Weitz, together with the Widmann manuscript alone, has *et lapsum humeris arcum*. But why should a hiatus be admitted here when all the other manuscripts disagree?

438. Erfurt has *liquit*, less suitably.

439. Rabanus Maurus, *On the Sacred Orders*, chapter 12: “The prophetic word shows that pomp, ambition, or boastfulness, and similar things, should be understood when it says: ‘Woe to you who are wealthy in Zion and trust in Mount Samaria: the leading men of the peoples enter the house of Israel pompously.’ But Clement and Prudentius, a most eloquent and Christian poet, used *pomp* in this sense in the book *Psychomachia*: ‘Pomp, display-loving,’ and so forth.” Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, had written these very words before Rabanus, in chapter 12 of *On the Order of Baptism*.

442. Fulda has *concordia dissona*, “discordant harmony.” The Heinsian manuscripts, our principal manuscripts, Alexandrianus, Vienna, Mariettus, and Vatican D have *turbat*; others, together with Aldus, have *turpat*.

443. Barthius reads *artitis pedibus* in his manuscript, explaining it as “with feet contracted because of the meaning of pain,” and confirms it with a similar reading in the preface to the *Psychomachia*, *artita colla*, “contracted necks,” instead of *attrita*, “worn.”]

444. Lucretius, Book VI, concerning those who are exercised in digging mines and condemned to that labor: “Whom great force restrains in such work.” Gifanius observes that Prudentius speaks in nearly the same way—“since greater force,” etc.—in his *Index Lucretianus*, under the word **VIS MAGNA**. He adds: “Since we have now, as I think, almost entirely rescued that Christian poet from innumerable errors, let us add also a few, so to speak, satchels.” Gifanius means the errors which he attempted to correct in the cited *Index*. Those who assert that Gifanius devoted further work to elucidating Prudentius were perhaps misled by this passage. What “greater force” means is explained by the legal scholars in *Ex conducto*, and in *Si merces*, § “Vis major,” *Digest*, *Locat.*; and in *De fluminibus*, § “Servius,” concerning defective construction. They understand it to be a divine force that occurs beyond all human precaution.

446. Ang., Ald., Gifanius, *Index Lucretianus*, Widm. in a second hand: **perdurat**; the others: **praedurat**. Gifanius argues under the word **PER** that in antiquity many words joined with this particle were later changed, whether into **prae** or otherwise. But the same could be said of the particle **prae**. See *Hymn to Saint Vincent*, verse 178, where the verb **praeduro** occurs.

447. Mar.: **gressibus** instead of **cursibus**.

448. Vienn., incorrectly: **crinialis**. Understand *damna* as “spoils.” Pignorius, *On Slaves*, p. 195, discusses the pin by which the hair was held and fastened, which Apuleius also calls a *crinalis acus* (“hairpin”) in Book VIII of the *Metamorphoses*. A *calamistrum* was a larger pin which, when heated, curled the hair.

452. Fuld.: **non fronte**; Weitz.: **ne fronte**. Neither reading is satisfactory.

453. Weitz reads **flectat**, because he previously printed **ne**. In Mar., **conibente** has been corrected to **conivente**. In Mar. and Rat. this verse is followed by the title “Avarice”; in Aldus, “The Contest of Avarice and Generosity”; in the others, “Avarice and Generosity.” Vienn. has no title here.

454. Rat.: **avarities**. The others correctly read **avaritia**, with the final syllable long.

456. Mar., Rat., Alex., Vatt. G, H, O: **pulchra in ludibria** (“beautiful things into mockeries”). I believe Vat. C intended this, and Piccart’s manuscript has **pulchra illudibria**, a word which Weitz thought deserved further investigation. Two manuscripts, Vatt. L and BB, read **pulchra et ludibria**. Aldus, with others, has **pulchra ad ludibria** (“beautiful things for mockery”).

457. Heinsius thinks the reading should be **aurique**, understanding *ramenta* as gold not yet refined. I do not approve this.

[Col. 0057A] **Note**

459. *Juvat*: delights. — *Crumenis*: purses; *crumenia* properly means fragments of gold. [I.]

460. *Fiscos*: bags, pouches. [I.]

461. *Laeva*: the left hand. [I.]

464. *Cura*: the multitude of vices which Avarice produces from black milk. [I.]

468. *Crimina*: sins. — *Grassantia*: ravaging. [I.]

469. *Creata*: that is, vices or faults. [I.]

470. *Fratris*: his own. — *Fulvis ceraunis*: red necklaces or little stones; *cerauna* is the proper name of a gem of yellowish colour, for in Greek it means “brightness.” [I.]

472. *Exerere*: to draw out or snatch forth. [I.]

[Col. 0058B] 475. *Bullis*: gems. [I.]

480. *Talia*: Avarice lays very many low; she lets others wander blind. [I.]

482. *Hunc*: a certain man. — *Adempto*: taken away. [I.]

485. *Baculo*: she did not permit him to carry a staff. [I.]

486. *Porro*: Avarice, while displaying something, wishes to strike with a dart; she ensnares. — *Intuitu*: she deceives by the sight of the eyes. [I.]

489. *Adactum*: driven in. [I.]

490. *Multos*: Avarice hurls many into the fire. [I.]

491. *Focos*: fires, or the Tartarean punishments of Styx. — *Aestuat*: boils. [I.]

[Col. 0057B] **Note**

459. Fuld. has *implicuisse sinus*, less well. For *infarcire*, others have *infercire*; for *crumenis*, some old copies have *cruminis*. The etymology of *crumena* is said to be from Greek κρεμάω, “to hang,” because it is pendent. The gloss is unsatisfactory.

460. Fuld. has *saccos* for *fiscos*.

461. Most old witnesses read *laterisque sinistri*. Heinsius printed *laterisque ministri*, but since he produces no variant reading, it is doubtful whether this fell out by chance. Chamillard followed Heinsius.

462. Barthius and Heinsius: *opermento*; Ang.: *adoperto*, the latter plainly corrupt. Most of ours have *oprimento*.

465. In the first Rott. manuscript: *insomnia, sortes*; others: *sordes*. Prudentius could excellently have said *sortes* if the game commonly called lotto had flourished at that time; to it these two little verses might not inaptly be adapted: “Corruption, deceit, contrivances, sleeplessness, lots, varied Eumenides, are borne along as the monster’s retinue.”

466. Ald.: *Eumenides furiae*; others: *Eumenides variae*, and in Mar. *furiae* is a gloss. For *variae*, Fabr. and Gis. have *varie*. Gallandius printed *variae*, but in his notes considers the repetition of *variae* corrupt, since they are separately enumerated earlier. But that is of no account: those Eumenides are called *variae*, that is, diverse from one another. The poet imitates Virgil, *Aeneid* XII.336: “The angers and ambushes are borne along as the god’s retinue.”

467. Boethius, perhaps imitating Prudentius, compared Avarice to a wolf in Book IV, prose 3.

468. In Ald. and in Mar. in its first hand, *crassantia* is an error, as *cessantia* is in Vat. C; read *grassantia*.

479. Whether one writes *pigneribus* or *pignoribus*, one follows ancient guides. I maintain the same concerning *fames* and *famis*. Vatt. C, F, G, L, O, and BB write *fames*. Do not object that the verse does not scan: Gifanius, who read *fames* in the *Index Lucretianus* from an old manuscript, infers that Prudentius often made short final syllables in *-es*. Heinsius prefers *famis*. Conversely Giselinus reproves Aldus for sometimes ending such nouns in *-is*, as in the *Hymn to Saint Hippolytus*, verse 190, *omnis adorat Pubis*, “all worship Pubis,” and *eunt, redeunt*. For Giselinus denies that Prudentius regarded the usage of the ancients, who sometimes pronounced such nominatives in *-es* and *-is*. For *impia*, Pal. has *improba*. Albertus Eyb, who included a passage from our poet in the *Margarita poetica*, reads *fames inopia*, an error contrary to the poem.

480. Vienn. has *generabat* for *edebat*, from some tasteless gloss.

481. In Rat. a recent hand changed *avaritia* to *avarities*, vainly.

484. Put. and Ang. have *offendicula*. Others, better, *offensacula*: as Heinsius observes, metrical rule rejects *offendicula*. His further belief that Prudentius was not very concerned about such matters, because he shortened the first syllable in *mitra* and in *rubigine*, is not sufficient reason to admit a reading contrary to rule when a better one remains; nor must the first syllable of *mitra* necessarily be lengthened. The Cauchian manuscript has *secum errare facit*, not *sinit*.

[Col. 0058D] 487. Mar. had *quod cum petit*.

491. Ang. incorrectly has *auram* for *aurum*.

492. Heinsius again attempts, from two very ancient witnesses, to defend *peculator* against the laws of metre, asserting that *speculator* scarcely has a place. But I do not see why Nebrissa’s interpretation should displease him: it means one who sees precious things perish in a fire. Riccioli, in the *Index of Syllabic Controversies*, had long ago observed that, according to Vossius’ testimony from manuscript codices, one should read *speculator*, not *peculator*. Aldus, Gis., Weitz, later editors, and all our manuscripts—Mar., Rat., Vienn., Alex., Ang., Vatt. C, D, F, G, H, L, O, BB—have *speculator*. Bonon. corruptly has *speculatum*.

[Col. 0059A] **Note**

493. *Mortalia*: human beings. [I.]

494. *Violentius*: more forcefully. Iso, Mar.

501. *Fors*: perhaps. Mar.

504. *Alumnos*: sons. [I.]

505. *Tuti*: safe, secure. — *Ope*: by aid, assistance. [I.]

507. *Paucos*: of the soldiers. Iso.

[Col. 0060A] 509. *Jugulis*: breasts, chests. [I.]

510. *Ingemit*: was stunned, or groaned. [I.]

515. *Formavit*: hardened. — *Rigor*: hardness. [I.]

517. *Ingenium*: of men. — *Tenera*: he refers to every age. [I.]

[Col. 0059B] **Note**

493. Vienn. incorrectly has *omnem hominem rapit* (“it seizes every human being”).

494. The vulgate has *neque enim est*. Heinsius had at one time proposed *neque ea violentius ullum*. Later, from the manuscripts, he recognized the hiatus. Giselinus has *neque enim est*, which is satisfactory. Aldus and Weitz, with the manuscripts, have *neque est*.

497. “If it is worthy of belief” is from Virgil, *Georgics* III.

498. Erfurt. has *fortes*, not unsuccessfully, instead of *forte*. I do not know why Nebrissa doubted which priests of the ancient law the poet was discussing; for it is perfectly clear that he is speaking of the priests of the new law, since the struggle of virtues and vices in the Christian soul is being described. Chamillard, however, more readily supposes that the ecclesiastical order is being mentioned, because Prudentius supposedly rebuked the pride of the Spaniards in the struggle against Luxury, since they did not obey the counsels of priests. For my part, I see nothing in that struggle from which it can be inferred that Prudentius rebuked Spanish pride, or that Spaniards failed to obey the counsels of priests—unless perhaps what was observed at verse 310. But it is one thing that, because of the fertility of the region, organs of Luxury could be placed in Spain, as Giselinus said; it is another that Prudentius particularly reproached the Spaniards with Luxury, which cannot be asserted except rashly. Chamillard, seeing that Spaniards were commonly charged with pride, interpreted Prudentius, when speaking of Luxury, as having had Spanish pride in mind. Yet the vice of pride, or arrogance, is not attacked by Prudentius in that passage, but Luxury and the vices arising from it: Jesting, Wantonness, and Lustful Love. No one, however, should imagine that these vices were or are peculiar to the Spaniards, since they rule equally in every land. Indeed, writers who provide geographical instruction, although they readily assign virtues and vices to each people according to their pleasure, nevertheless claim that the virtue opposed to Luxury and its vices belongs exclusively to no nation.

499. Widm. above: *primi ante aciem* (“first before the battle-line”). This reading is not objectionable.

501. After this verse Mar. and Rat. have the title “Reason.”

502. Weitz, following M. Bergius, observes that the poet may be alluding to the Mosaic *rationale*, which was on the breast of the high priest, dressed in its ornaments. I find nothing else here except that Prudentius took care of the reputation of ecclesiastics, even while charging them to some extent with the crime of Avarice. Certainly he could truthfully have said much about the intelligence and learning by which the priests of his time excelled, since at no other time had more learned men flourished in the Church. Those who in our own age rant everywhere and without restraint against the ecclesiastical order could learn moderation from Prudentius’ example when rebuking the vices of that order. Many, however, attribute Avarice to priests as though it were a vice especially characteristic of them, or at least attack them vehemently for it. Jerome rightly attacks the Avarice of ecclesiastics more sharply in Letter 52 to Nepotian, on the life of clergy and monks; it will be worthwhile to read it. As for Ammianus’ charge, in Book XXVII, that the Roman pontiffs of the fourth century displayed ostentation and greed, it is plainly fabricated by a pagan writer in order to diminish the authority possessed by the bishops of the eternal city, as he calls them in Book XV.

503. Erfurt. has *objectaret*; but the sense demands *objectasset*, and *texisset* follows.

506. Fuld. has *fortesque animo*; *animi* is more elegant.

507. The better Heinsian manuscripts, Barthius, Egm., Fuld., and Widm., with Rat., read *praestringens*, whose gloss is “slightly wounding”; Weitz and others have *perstringens*. Either form can be correctly used, and perhaps Prudentius wrote *praestringo* in one place and *perstringo* in another. I say nothing of even the oldest copyists, who often reformed their spelling at will.

508. Vienn. has *cassis*, an error for *castis*. On *lues* or *luis*, see verse 479 under *fames*.

510. Fuld. has *inquit*; the others *infit*.

511. Giselinus, with Aldus and the Daventrian edition, prefers *melius putat quam perfert* (“he considers it better than he bears it”). But Aldus tells Weitz, Heinsius, and me that he has *perfert*. This too is evidence of two Aldine editions. Weitz now presents the same reading as we do, though elsewhere he differs. It often happens that a reading is attributed to an author to whom it does not truly belong, the author’s name having been omitted when another should have been named. Weitz has *refert* with Widm. Fuld. has *profert*; Cauch. *praefert*. All the Heinsian manuscripts, Fabr., Widm. above, and most of our manuscripts have *perfert*, which fits the sense well.

515. Erfurt. and Vat. C in its first hand have *duravit*. In this Vat. C the form above is *formavit*. Giselinus writes *duravit* in the margin. Fuld. has *vigor aera*. Giselinus prefers *rigor* from most manuscripts, since hard things are said to *rigere* (“be rigid”), not *vigere* (“be vigorous”).

517. An imitation of Virgil, *Georgics* III: “And he gave the whole race to death, both of cattle and of wild beasts.” Horace embraces the same thought in Book II, Satire 3: “For every thing—virtue, fame, honor, divine and human—obeys beautiful riches.”

>
> in destruction. No vice among the lands
>
> is more violent, one that wraps the age of the world’s people
>
> in such disasters and condemns it to Gehenna.
>
> Yet she dared to attack with her hand the priests of the Lord themselves,
>
> if it is worthy of belief: those who perhaps led the battles
>
> [500] as commanders before the first line, in praise of Virtues,
>
> and filled the trumpets with a great blast.
>
> 631. And perhaps she would have stained her iron with innocent blood,
>
> had not all-powerful Reason, the ever-faithful companion
>
> of the tribe of Levi, set her shield in the way
>
> and covered the illustrious sons from the black enemy’s attack.
>
> [505] They stand safe by Reason’s aid, safe from every whirlwind,
>
> and brave in spirit; scarcely does Avarice’s spear,
>
> grazing the outermost skin with a slight wound,
>
> injure a few. The wicked plague was stunned
>
> to see her weapons driven far back from the chaste throats
>
> [510] of the heroes; she groans and begins, burning with furious words:
>
> 632. “We are defeated, alas! We are sluggish, and our power does not endure
>
> its accustomed force. The savage violence of inflicting harm grows weak,
>
> which once, with unconquered strength, used everywhere
>
> to break human hearts. For nature formed no man so iron-hard
>
> [515] that his rigidity could reject bronze,
>
> or that he might be impenetrable to our gold.
>
> Every human mind we have devoted to destruction—tender, rough, hard,
>
> [Col. 0061A] both learned and unlearned, brutish and wise,
>
> and chaste and unchaste breasts alike have lain open to my right hand.
>
> [520] I alone have seized whatever Styx hides
>
> in its greedy whirlpools; the richest Tartarus owes us
>
> the peoples whom it holds. Whatever the ages revolve is ours;
>
> whatever the world confuses in its mad business is ours.
>
> How does mighty Glory abandon her very powerful forces,
>
> while Fortune toys with useless arms?
>
> 633. Among Christ’s people the golden image of glittering coin is despised;
>
> the embossed figures of silver are despised, and every treasure
>

>

>

>
> and a guest of God, while deceiving one not at all ignorant of the covenant of the table,
>
> joins his right hand to the dish,
>
> 634. fell into our weapon, inflamed by desire,
>
> having bought the infamous field with the blood of his divine friend,
>
> destined to pay for the acres with his neck crushed.
>
> He had also seen at Jericho, amid its own slaughter, how much
>
> our hand could accomplish, when victorious Achan fell,
>
> renowned for slaughter and proud in the ruin of the wall;
>

>

[Col. 0061B] **Note**

518. *Bruta*: stupid. [I.]

519. *Incesta*: unclean. [I.]

520. *Styx*: Hell; he goes to Hell. [I.]

521. *Gurgitibus*: rivers. [I.]

523. *Quod miscet*: what the world of evil mixes and conducts. [I.]

524. *Vires*: its own powers. [I.]

525. *Cassos*: useless. — *Ludit*: is deceived. — *Fortuna*: our prosperity. [I.]

[Col. 0062B] 526. *Fulva*: red. [I.]

527. *Emblemata*: figures, or abundance. [I.]

528. *Nigrante*: despised. [I.]

532. *Haudquaquam*: in no way. [I.]

533. *Flammante*: burning. [I.]

534. *Infamem*: detestable. [I.]

535. *Numinis*: divine. [I.]

539. *Succubuit*: namely, to our prompting. [I.]

[Col. 0061B] **Note**

522. In Mar., *retinet*, skillfully corrected by a recent hand to *retinent*.

523. In Rat. *est* is missing, as in most printed editions and manuscripts. Aldus and Ang. have *nostrum est* in the same way as in the preceding verse.

524. In Rat. there was *quid fit*, but it has been changed to *qui fit*. In Mar., *qui*; in the margin, *vel quid est*. Sich. and some printed editions have *quid*, with Bong., where there is *quid sit*. Most have *qui fit*. Ang. and Vat. C have *quid fit*.

526. Ang. has *forma monetae* (“the form of the coin”); read *fulva*.

528. Weitz, from Piccart’s manuscript, has *migrante*; all the others have *nigrante*, which is the more correct reading.

529. Ang. has *fastigia*, not unreasonably, instead of *fastidia*. Nebrissa explains it as men who disdain treasures. It may be understood as “learned disdainfulnesses,” learned men—namely priests—who, elevated by pride through their learning, disdain with arrogance; or as men who disdain money. Ald., Alex., Vatt. E and O, Mar., Rat., Vienn., Weitz, the chief Heinsian manuscripts, and others have *nonne triumphum egimus ex Scharioth* (“did we not triumph over the Iscariot?”), from Schariot. In some manuscripts, *egimus e Scharioth*. Vat. G erroneously has *egimus Excarioth*, and Ang. *Ex Scharioth egimus*. Giselinus, I do not know on whose authority, prints *nonne triumpho egimus Ischarioth*. In the margin of the second edition, and in the text of the first, he has *nonne triumphum egimus e Scharioth*. Gifanius has *triumphos egimus ex Scariot*, claiming that the ancients spoke in this way. See the *Index of Lucretius*, under **VESTIS**.

530. Weitz, Vatt. C, G, O, and Pal. in a second hand have *summus*, as do Sich., Vienn., and Mar. in a recent second hand. The rest of our manuscripts and the better Heinsian manuscripts, with Aldus, Giselinus, and others, have *magnus*. The genitive construction with *magnus* is found also, as noted in *Hymn* 12, verse 77. Heinsius observes that Judas was not Christ’s chief disciple and therefore rejects the reading *summus* entirely. But since Avarice is speaking here, perhaps the poet wished to introduce her heaping false praises upon her distinguished pupil. I do not find Theolius’ claim that, according to Weitz’s opinion, which printed *summus*, the word was meant ironically.

531. Vienn., Fuld., Widm.: *foedera mensae* (“the covenants of the table”).

532. The older Heinsian manuscripts have this reading. In Put., *dextraque parapside jungit*; many write *parabside*. Our manuscripts—Mar., Rat., Alex., Vatt. C, D, G, O—also have *dextramque parapside jungit*. Vienn. has the same, but lacks the conjunction *-que* after *dextram*. Gifanius in his *Index Lucretianus* under **VESTIS**, and Weitz, agree with our reading. Aldus and Fabr. have *dextramque parapside tingit*; Giselinus, *dextramque paropside jungit*, with *tingit* in the margin. Heinsius says much about the spelling of *parapsis*, which he prefers to *paropsis*, although he admits that some distinguish them so that *paropsis* is a serving dish, while *parapsis* is Greek ἐμβάφιον (*embaphion*) or ὀξυβάφιον (*oxybaphion*). In old glossaries *parapsis* is a large cup or serving vessel, which some call a basin. In Saint Isidore, *Etymologies* XX.4, it is a quadrangular, four-sided vessel—“that is, with equal sides” (*paribus absidis*). Others write *absidibus*, and Paulinus was uncertain whether it should be called *absis* or *absida*. Barthius, from his manuscript, reads *paropside jungit* and denies that *tingit* can be read: Judas did not dip his hand in the dish but certainly joined it to the dish. Yet it might be cleverly said that Judas dipped the hand itself into the dish, so that the man’s filthiness might be marked.

534. He attributes to Judas the purchase of the field with the blood-money of his friend, because the chief priests and elders, after receiving the silver from him, purchased it. It should also be noted that Avarice is speaking; and it is not surprising if, from her mouth, events are narrated differently from the way they happened. Yet Prudentius may rather have had in mind the passage in Acts 1:18: “And this man indeed acquired a field from the reward of iniquity, and, having been hanged, burst open in the middle.” Judas is said figuratively to have possessed a field because, with the price given to him, the field was bought.

535. Aldus has *eliso*; the others *obliso*. See the note above on verse 331.

537. Rat. has *decidit*; the others *concidit*. For Achan or Achar, some have *Acham*.

538. Ang. has *murali strage* without *et*.

539. Read this history of Achar—or, as it is written in the Vulgate edition, Achan—in Joshua 7:1 and following.

540. There is great controversy over the word *anathema* and the quantity of its penultimate syllable. Some believe it should always be shortened, whether it signifies a sacred offering or excommunication. Others teach that it is shortened when it means excommunication, but lengthened when it signifies something consecrated to God; for in that sense it is written with eta in Greek, as in the cited chapter of Joshua and elsewhere in Sacred Scripture. Ricciolius, in his *Index of Metrical Controversies*, with Charles Estienne and Suidas, maintains that in either sense it may be both shortened and lengthened, since in either sense it may be written with eta or epsilon.

541. Vienn. has *festa*; the others *moesta*. *Festa* (“festive”) can not unreasonably describe the spoils taken from the anathema, etc.; *moesta* (“mournful”) follows from the result.

[Col. 0063B] **Note**

543. *Christo*: he means the coming of Christ. [I.]

544. *Nepote*: Christ. Iso.

545. *Generis*: of evil-doing. [I.]

546. *Exitii*: of destruction. — *Eadem*: one and the same. [I.]

549. *Fraude*: in the making of the calf. — *Impar*: that is, a Levite ought not to fight. [I.]

550. *Nil refert*: there is no distinction. [I.]

553. *Severa*: serious, severe. [I.]

554. *Parce vivere*: to live sparingly, or to preserve for one’s children. [I.]

556. *Artis*: of frugality. Iso.

557. *Coaptat*: joins, fits together. [I.]

[Col. 0064B] 560. *Obtegit*: resisting Avarice for a little while. — *Anguinos*: serpentine. — *Latentem*: hidden beneath the appearance of goodness. [I.]

561. *Rabiem*: form. [I.]

562. *Cleперe*: *cleps* means “a thief”; hence *clepere*, “to steal.” — *Parta*: things acquired. [I.]

565. *Imaginibus*: forms. — *Ferale*: mortal. Iso.

566. *Capit*: deceives. [I.]

568. *Attonitis*: the battle-line of the virtues hesitates, not fully recognizing Avarice. — *Ducibus*: virtues. — *Maniplis*: standard-bearers. [I.]

[Col. 0063C] **Note**

543. Fuld. has *propinquus*, less suitably. The annotator of the Cologne edition notes that *Juda* was corrected by Sichardus, but says it could not be read. In the Basel edition of 1527, where all corrections are attributed in the margin to Sichardus, I find *jura* in the margin instead of *Juda*.

545. Vienn. has *placet his quoque forma*. The sense more strongly demands *placeat quoque*.

548. Avarice calls the Christian priests “the people of Aaron,” by the same right by which deacons are called Levites. Compare what Generosity says against Avarice at verses 606 and following.

550. Vienn. has *nil distat*, a gloss in the Marietti manuscript. Avarice, unequal to the combats of Mars, turns to deceit. The sentence is Virgilian, from *Aeneid* II: “Deceit or valor—who would demand that of an enemy?” The deceit itself is sketched from the same passage of Virgil, where the Trojans exchanged their weapons for Greek weapons so that, mingled among the Greeks, they could more easily slaughter them. That vices often deceive under the appearance of virtues is too well known to require proof. In Vat. C correct the error *nil referet*.

553. In Mar. and Rat.: *cultuque, et veste severa*. Weitz, with Erf. and Widm., wants *vultuque, et voce severa*; but in Erf. and Widm. above the reading is *veste severa*. Heinsius thought Weitz had taken *et voce* from the Egmond manuscript and was mistaken, since Egm. has *vultuque, et veste*, with Aldus and the remaining Heinsian manuscripts, except the first Rott., which has *et voce*. But Heinsius is wrong in believing that the Erfurt manuscript, cited by Weitz as E, is the Egmond manuscript, which Weitz usually cites as Eg. Heinsius prefers *vultuque, et voce severa* because Prudentius likes to join these two, as in the *Hymn to Saint Romanus*, verse 720: “Thus he rebukes with face and stern words.” The example is not convincing, because the matter is very different; and Prudentius seems to have had Juvenal’s passage before his eyes, *Satire* 14: “For vice deceives under the appearance and shadow of virtue, though grim in bearing, face, and dress.” Since Weitz noticed this, I do not see why he himself read *vultuque, et voce severa*. Cellarius and Theolius depart from Heinsius. In the margin of the Cologne edition, from a manuscript, *voce* is given as a variant reading.

554. Rat. has *memোরent* (“they may remember”).

555. Juvenal, cited satire: “And the miser is doubtless praised as thrifty, as a sparing man and guardian of his possessions.”

556. Ang. erroneously has *ceu scedula*.

557. He calls Avarice Bellona, as though she were the goddess of this war; “deceitful,” because she has been made to look like virtue.

560. In some manuscripts you will find *anguineos*, in others *anguinos*.

561. Bong. and Erf. have *formam*; above, *rabiem*. Aldus: *intenta furori*.

562. Vienn. has *et rapere est*. In Greek, κλέπτης (*kleptēs*) means “thief,” from which come κλέπτειν (*kleptein*) and the Latin *clepere*.

563. Vienn., against the rules of the verse, has *jacit*. Aldus and Vat. C: *jactat*. Mar., Rat., Widm.: *lactet*; most have *jactet*.

565. Vienn., Ang., and Vat. C, with the meter opposed to it, have *monstrumque ferale*, which Weitz printed while following only Bong. and stating that the others have *monstrum ferale*.

566. In a similar passage, *Hamartigenia*, verse 427: “Under a false pact of friendship at first the sorrowful allied troops believe,” from Virgil, *Aeneid* II. In Aldus there is an error, *caput* instead of *capit*.

571. Aldus and Fabr. have *vocet*; the others *notet*. Vienn. has *notet laevum*, incorrectly. Nebrissa reads *in anceps notat*, that is, “it marks as uncertain.” Others, with Giselinus, punctuate differently: *ut lethum lubricet incertos visus* (“so that death may confuse uncertain eyes”).

> Neither his noble tribe nor Judah, ancestral father of the people,
>
> helped him, though noble through his later kinship with Christ,
>
> the patriarch made fortunate by such a grandson.
>
> [545] 635. Let those who approve an example of lineage approve also
>
> the form of his destruction; let the punishment be the same
>
> for those whose lineage too is one.
>
> Why should I linger over the fellow-countrymen of Judah, or the fellow-countrymen
>
> of the chief priest—for Aaron is said to be supreme—to deceive them
>
> by some trick, unequal to the encounters of Mars?
>
> [550] It makes no difference whether victory comes through arms or deceit.”
>

>
> she transformed herself into a respectable appearance.
>
> [Col. 0063B] She becomes virtue in appearance, with stern countenance and dress,
>
> which they call frugal: one whose heart is set on living sparingly
>
> [555] and preserving his own, as though she snatched nothing greedily;
>
> [Col. 0064A] she has earned praise for her simulated art, as though diligent.
>
> 636. In this appearance deceitful Bellona fits herself together,
>
> so that she may be thought not a greedy plague but frugal virtue.
>
> She also covers her serpentine locks with a tender veil of piety,
>
> [560] so that a white cloak may conceal her hidden rage,
>
> shrouded in dreadful fury, and so that she may boast that robbing,
>
> pilfering, and greedily hiding acquired goods
>
> are care for children under that sweet name.
>
> Mocking such too-credulous hearts of men,
>
> [565] she deceives them with these images; they follow the deadly monster,
>
> believing it a work of virtue. Impious Erinnys ensnares
>
> those readily consenting and binds them in tenacious shackles.
>
> While the leaders are stunned and the companies confused,
>
> [Col. 0064B] the battle-line of the virtues wavered, bewildered by the two-formed
>
> [570] portent, not knowing what in it to judge friendly
>
> and what hostile: death, changeable and twofold,
>
> [Col. 0065A] confounds uncertain eyes.

[Col. 0065B] **Note**

572. Fabr., Egm., and Bong. have *incertus*; then Nebrissa’s punctuation should be used, although Nebrissa himself understands it as “the battle-line confuses uncertain eyes.” After this verse Mar. and Rat. have the title “Generosity.”

573. Ald. has *dum subito*; Fuld. *tum subito*. In old printed editions, *miseratio* (“compassion”); in the manuscripts, *operatio* (“generosity,” literally “deed”). Sichardus restored this word before Giselinus. Alcimus Avitus uses the same word *operatio*, as do other earlier writers—Tertullian, Cyprian, Optatus of Milevis, and Paulinus. On this word, see Rosweyde’s note to Saint Paulinus, pp. 763 and following, under the words **FIDELIUM OPERATIO** (“the generosity of the faithful”). Hence the phrase “works of mercy,” and the title of Saint Cyprian’s book *On Works and Almsgiving*. Some think the word derives from Mark 14:6: “She has performed a good work.”

574. Weitz, with Bong. and Erf., has *capescit*. It should be written *capessit*, with the others.

575. In the older Boh. manuscript: *prima duello* (“first in the duel”), which Gallandius says in his notes he approves because it precedes the final phrase.

576. Fabr. has *tam triste*. Barthius, *Adversaria* XII.41, observes from this passage that Christians used *manum imponere* simply in the sense of “to absolve”: the ancients said *extremam manum imponere*, or *summam* or *supremam*.

577. Vienn. has *dejecerat*; *rejecerat* is better.

578. Ald., Fuld., and Vat. C have *exuviis* instead of *induviis*, whose gloss in Mar. is *indumentis* (“clothing”). Bong. and Vat. C have *multo se fasce levarat*. Vat. H incorrectly has *induviis, multo et fasce levarat*; Vat. G is no better: *induviis, et multo se fasce levarat*. This is an imitation of Virgil, *Eclogue* 9: “I shall relieve you of this burden.”

580. Ald., Widm. above, and Bong. have *miserendo*. In some vulgate copies, *inopes*.

581. Vienn. incorrectly has *prodiga*. The sense absolutely requires *bene prodiga* (“generous in a good cause”).

582. Put. and Thuan. have *ditata fidem*, a Greek construction which our chief manuscripts—Alex., Mar., Rat., and others—do not recognize; nor did others before Heinsius, who adopted it. In Erfurt., *aspectabat inanes*.

583. Rat. has *aeternam memorans*. Weitz, with only an old hand in Erfurt., has *reddendo*, less suitably. On the interest returning in heaven, see Matthew 19:21 and 29.

584. Aldus and the old editions have *fulmen inopsque*, which in Erfurt. is a gloss replacing *impos*. Vat. C and Sich. have *fulmen et inops*, which the meter rejects. Others have *impos*, whose gloss in Mar. is *impotens*.

585. In Rat. a corrector ineptly wrote *avara lues* instead of *avaritia*; he perhaps thought that the final *a* in *avaritia* interfered with the meter.

586. Erfurt. has *fraudi*, which does not displease Heinsius, who takes that reading from Egmond—unless he misunderstood Weitz, who cites only Erfurt as E. See the note on verses 555 and 593. Aldus, Gis., Bong., Ang., and Vat. C have *restat*. The Heinsian manuscripts, Mar., Rat., Alex., Weitz, and others have *restet*.

587. *Calcatrix* is formed like *amarix* and similar words. Calpurnius used *calcator*. In Weitz’s gloss there is an error, *speratio* instead of *operatio*.

590. Aldus: *eliso gutture* (“with throat crushed”). Weitz: *obliso robore*, with Widm., where above it is *gutture*. It is preferable to read *obliso gutture* with the others.

591. Erfurt. has: *compressa ligabat / Vincla lacertorum sub mentum faucibus arctis* (“with her throat compressed she bound the bonds of her arms beneath the chin with tightened jaws”). Bong. and Ang. have *compressa ligabant*.

593. Vienn. has *sanguine rupto*; Rat., the older Boher., and Widm. in a second hand have *rupta*. Weitz wished to write *rumpta* with Erfurt—not Egmond, as Heinsius thought—which is repugnant to usage. Egmond and the other Heinsian manuscripts have *rapta*, as do Mar., Ald., Gis., Vat. C, and others. Pal. and Barthius have *raptam*, as though the poet were saying “of such a kind,” in the manner in which Apuleius very often speaks.

594. Veu. Beda, in *On the Art of Meter*, asserts that the ancients lengthened *intercepto* so that a dactyl might occupy the fifth foot; this is unconvincing. See the note on verse 98.

596. Erf., Vienn., *genibus et calcibus* (“with knees and heels”).

[Col. 0066D] 598. Our better manuscripts. Alex., Mar., Rat., and others have *exstincto*, correctly. In Put., *exuncto*; in Erf., *exuto*, which Heinsius says occurs in Egm. He was perhaps misled by taking Egmondanus for Erfurtensis, the manuscript cited by Weitzius. Chamillardus is also mistaken when he claims that *exstincto* is read in the Paris royal manuscript, or Put. Heinsius thinks *exuto* should be read because Prudentius uses that word in a similar context, and Paulinus and Tertullian likewise employed it. But this argument is not sufficiently compelling, since comparable examples could be produced for *exstincto*. Barthius reads *exuncto*. Cellarius, following Heinsius’s conjecture, reads *exuto*. I suspect the ancient word was *exucto*, which I also read in Helpidius:

> Nor will old age furrow the curved face,  
> dried out though it is.

Perhaps the Spaniards therefore derive *enjuto*, meaning “dry,” as though “without sap,” from this word. Perhaps *exucto* is also equivalent to *exsucto*, from *exsugo* (“to suck dry”).

The uncertain vision slips beneath a doubtful appearance.

637 When suddenly, roaring, Operation leaps into the midst of the field,

springs to the aid of her allies, and takes up the battle,

[575] last in the army’s rank, yet alone about to lay hands upon her in single combat,

so that nothing grievous might now remain.

She had cast every burden from her shoulders and went stripped

of every covering; she had lightened herself by a great load:

once oppressed by riches and heavy talents,

[580] now free, pitying the poor, whom she had generously and kindly cherished,

lavishly pouring out her ancestral wealth.

Now, enriched by faith, she gazed upon her empty purses,

[Col. 0065B] counting the eternal sum of the interest that would return.

[Col. 0066A] Avarice, arrogant in mind, recoiled in horror from the thunderbolt of unconquered Virtue,

[585] 638 and clung there with her senses stupefied,

certain to die. For what avenue of fraud remained by which she herself,

the trampler of the world, might, defeated, collapse beneath worldly

seductions and once again entangle herself in gold?

Most valiant Virtue attacks the trembling creature with the hard

[590] knots of her arms and crushes her, throat bruised,

her bloodless, parched gullet. Her compressed bonds of arms

are tied beneath her chin, and with her throat constricted

they wrench out her breath. She throbs, her life

snatched away without any wound, and, the passage of breath cut off,

[595] suffers enclosed death in the prison of her veins.

As she struggles, Virtue presses upon her knees and heels,

pierces her ribs, and breaks her panting flanks.

[Col. 0066B] Soon she tears the spoils from the lifeless body, gold—

603. Thin, poor, I.

611. “May restore,” “sustains,” I.

615. “And let tomorrow not trouble you”: its evil is sufficient for the day, I.

599. Erf., Barthius’s codex, Palat., *recocta*, less well.

600. Put., *materiam*. The same manuscript and Egm. have *tiniis*, which Heinsius had elsewhere found written thus in the best copies. Puteanus also writes *marsuppia*. We follow the more usual spelling. Aldus, incorrectly, has *cinctis* for *tineis*. The same Ald., Gis., and Weitzius also have *etiam*, and Heinsius does not disagree. Perhaps the reading of Vienn. and others is more correct: *tineis et jam marsupia*. In old manuscripts words are often joined together, so that it is not always easy to determine whether there is one expression or two.

601. Fuld., Widm. above, *subducta aerugine* (“with the verdigris scraped away”).

604. Bong., Sich., *multum exsultante* (“greatly exulting”), makes no sense. From Fuld., Weitzius notes *tum* for *tunc*.

606. Rat., *justi discedite* without *sine*.

[Col. 0067D] 607. Barthius’s codex is corrupt here: *causa militanti*.

608. Mar., Sich., Bong., *illuvie*; more correctly, *ingluvie*.

609. Weitz., *supra quam*. Ald., Gis., Ang., and others, *postulat*. See Columbanus, poem against Avarice. The sentiment is golden, but commonplace, more often on people’s lips than visible in their lives.

610. Ald., *et simplex*. This is Paul’s injunction in the First Epistle to Timothy 6:8: “Having food,” etc. One garment is likewise prescribed in the evangelical counsel of Matthew 10:9–10.

612. In Fuld., *non trahat ultra*. In the Cologne edition I read in the margin *Ald. naturam*. It may be explained as “Let it not extend beyond nature.” But my Aldus has *naturae*. A second Aldine edition may perhaps be conjectured.

613. Erf., *non tollito*. Fuld., *nec tollito*, less well. The expression is taken directly from the Gospel: Matthew 10:9–10; Mark 6:8–9; Luke 9:3 and 22:35.

[Col. 0068C] 614. The Heinsian manuscripts and our principal copies have *ito*, with Sich., Weitz., and others. Ald. and Gis. have *esto* in the text; this is a gloss in Erfurt. Weitzius printed *tonicae* because he read it thus in Bong.; this is ridiculous.

615. Our Columbanus imitated this: “And let the abundance of things flowing around you not trouble you.” Albertus Eyb’s *ne te sollicitet* is incorrect, and in the following verse *deserit* is still worse for *defuerit*.

616. Egm., Erf., Palat., Barthius, *cum sole diurno* (“with the daily sun”).

619. Oxon., *non defore vitae*. See Matthew 6:26 and 10:29.

623. Three of the older Heinsian manuscripts, Pal., Weitz., Barthius, Vat. II, have *addubitas*. Ald., Gis., Ang., Vatt. C, F, G, O, and Albertus Eyb have *an dubitas*. Mar., Rat., Alex., Sich., Bong., Widm. have *at dubitas*. Fuld. has *ast dubitas*. Vienn. wrongly has *nec te* for *ne te*. The same manuscript has *deseret* for *deserat*.

624. Ald., Bong., *vitae dator est dator escae* (“the giver of life is the giver of food”). Eyb has the same in the *Margarita poetica*. Aldus is incorrectly punctuated: *vitae dator, est dator escae*. In Vat. C, *vitae dator* and *et dator escae* lack the substantive verb *est*.

625. Weitzius, with Widm. alone in its first hand, reads *quaerite lucifluum*. Ison’s gloss gives a different reading.

626. Erfurt., Ald., *alit*. Mar., Rat., Alex., Vat. H, Barthius, Put., Weitzius, Heinsius, and Widm. in its first hand have *invitiabilis*. Rott. has the earlier reading. Vienn. and Sich. have *insatiabilis*. Most Heinsian copies, Ald., Erfurt., Widm. above, Ang., Vat. G, Eybelius, and Torn. have *inviolabilis*. Vat. BB has *inviolabilis orbis*, with *supra aliter aevi*. The thought of these verses comes from Matthew 6:33: “Seek therefore first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you.”

630. The better Heinsian copies, Alex., Mar., Weitz., and others have *placitae*. Aldus, Gis., Vat. C, and others have *placidae*.

631. Fuld., *evertere solum*. *Vertere* should be read. Ison’s gloss has *pulverem* for *solum*. See what I noted on the third hymn of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 129.

632. Ald., Vat., C, Fabr., Bong. in a second hand have *discinditur*. Gifanius likewise read this in an old book: “But the following verse shows that *discingitur* is to be preferred.]

639 Filthy fragments of raw material not yet fired in the furnace,

[600] purses too gnawed by swarming moths,

and coins green with encrusted verdigris, long kept.

Victorious, she scatters them among the needy

and enriches the poor with gifts from the captured spoils.

Then, looking back at the crown surrounding her

[605] with an exultant face, she cries aloud, cheerful among the thousands:

“Lay down the battle array, righteous ones, and depart from arms:

the cause of so great an evil lies slain; since the greed

of the belly has perished, the saints may rest.

The highest rest is to desire nothing beyond what

[610] necessary use requires: so that simple food,

one garment, may cover the weak

640 and moderately restore their limbs,

[Col. 0067B] and may not extend beyond the limit appointed by nature.

When you set out on a journey, do not take a purse,

nor go provided with the possession of another tunic.

[615] And let tomorrow’s affairs not trouble you, lest food

[Col. 0068A] be lacking in your stomach: daily meals return with the sun.

Do you not see how none of the birds thinks about tomorrow

or, free from anxiety, trusts that it will be fed,

since God provides? Even lowly birds trust that food will not fail them,

[620] and sparrows, sold for a small coin,

have an unhesitating confidence that the mighty Lord cares for them,

so that they do not perish. You are God’s concern, and also the image of Christ.

Do you doubt that your Creator will ever abandon you?

Do not tremble, human beings: the giver of life is also the giver of food.

[625] Seek the light-bearing nourishment taught by heaven,

641 which, multiplying hope, may nourish the hope of an inviolable age,

while you are forgetful of the body: he who created it

is mindful to supply food and cherish needy limbs.”

[Col. 0068B] At these words care, fear, toil, violence,

[630] crime, and the fraud that corrupts approved faith

were driven away and turned the ground beneath them. Then kindly Peace, with

the enemies put to flight, drives war away, and all

633. For *exfibulare*, Forcellinus cites only Prudentius. Leisure is being indicated.

634. Weitzius, with Gifanius, reads *vestis et usque*, not *vestis ad usque*. Gifanius, under the verb *DISCINDO*, asserts that *usque* for *ad usque* is elegantly used; and under *VESTIS* he claims that the ancients used the expression in this way, ignorance of which produced the corruption in Prudentius. Heinsius dislikes this, and I too find it unconvincing.

635. Erfurt., *temperat et rabidum*.

637. Giselinus, *sedato pulvere* without *et*.

638. In Erf., *nuda*; in the margin, *suda*.

640. In some common editions, *agmina casta simul*, with Egm.

642. Revelation 3:21: “He who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, just as I conquered and sat with my Father on his throne.” Mar. and Alex., with three of the oldest Heinsian copies, have *arce*, which is pleasing: that is, “in the citadel of the ether.” I do not know why Heinsius conjectures *arces*, when most copies have *arcem*. Barthius, book 5, chapter 12, reads *arcem* and gives the gloss “that is, rule.”

643. Ald., Fabr., *portum* (“harbor”); Nebrissa interprets it as the heavenly kingdom, because the deeper a harbor, the safer it is. The true reading is *patrium profundum*, whose gloss in Mar. is “that is, sublimity.” See Gifanius, *Index to Lucretius*, under *PROFUNDUM*. After this verse Mar. has the heading “Concord.”

646. Aldus had printed *spes*; he correctly amended it to *species*. The same manuscript has *Deus ulli*. Ang. has *decus unquam*. The more correct reading is *nec par decus ulli*.

648. In Vat. II, corruptly: *Duceret hordinibus peditum stupere catervas*.

650. Giselinus warns that this verse should not be attached to the preceding sentence, as others ineptly did. The sacred history is found in Exodus, chapter 14.

651. In some common editions, *minantis*.

653. Erfurt., *callis*; above it, *calcis*.

654. Weitzius, with Erf. and Widm., has *repulso*; above it in both Erf. and Widm. is *relapso*. The others have *relapso*; Put. has *relaxo*.

655. Erf., *Niliacos*; the same, and Barthius, have *dependeret imo*.

656. Prudentius used *natatus* in the *Apotheosis*, verse 684. Statius likewise uses the noun in the *Silvae*, book 1, poems 3 and 5.

662. The matter was treated in the fifth hymn of the *Cathemerinon*, verses 65 and following.

664. Piccartus’s codex, *multimodis*.

665. Ang., *ad belli fauces castrensis*. From these poems Barthius infers that Prudentius was a soldier, or at least, he says, that Prudentius describes the camp gate skillfully because he had served in the army. Compare Prudentius’s life in the prolegomena. There were several gates in a camp; concerning them, see Turnebus, book 30 of the *Adversaria*, chapter 24, and Lipsius, *Roman Military Institutions*, book 5, dialogue 5. After this verse Mar. has the title “Discord,” with the epithet “heresy” in small type. Rat. likewise has this.

667. In some common editions, *hinc* for *hic*.

669. Ald., *vexavit*; others, *vexaret*. In Aldus and other copies the heading here is “The Battle of Concord and Discord.”

Terror ungirds its flanks when the belts have been torn away.

Her garment, descending all the way to her feet,

flows down to the lowest hem.

[635] Private modesty restrains her rapid step.

The curved bronze trumpets fall silent; the sword, now appeased,

fills its sheath. With the dust of the battlefield settled,

a serene face returns, under a clear, cloudless day;

you would see the purple light of heaven grow bright.

[640] 642 The chaste ranks, their battle driven away, felt the face of the Thunderer

smile cheerfully upon them,

and Christ rejoice in his victorious people in the citadel

of the ether, and open the ancestral deep to his servants.

Concord gives the favorable signal: to return the victorious

[645] eagles to the camp and gather them into the tents.

Never had any force of Malice displayed so great a spectacle,

[Col. 0069B] nor had any equal glory, when, with the ranks

drawn up in formation, the divided companies led on

the infantry, whose troop sang psalms,

while on the other side the cavalry resounded with hymns.

[650] Thus once before Israel sang, looking back upon the gaping

rage of the threatening sea behind them,

when, advancing now, he trod the farther shores

with dry feet, while the mountain of hanging water

fell roaring along its outer edge,

[Col. 0070A] and, as the black whirlpool flowed back,

[655] seized the Nile-dwellers in its deepest bottom,

643 and the wave, its hollow receding, now gave the swimmer back

to the fishes and, rushing onward, covered the bare sands.

God’s throng struck resonant drums with a ringing plectrum,

celebrating the wondrous deed of the Almighty,

memorable throughout the ages: amid liquid straits,

[660] between banks cut apart by waves,

with the storm held in place, the waters could rise

and suspended masses of water remain poised.

So, when the people of vices had been conquered,

the mystical songs of virtues resound in sweet-toned psalms.

[665] They had come to the throat of the camp gate, where the narrow

entrance of the threshold is formed by doors on a double hinge.

Here an unexpected, tearful storm of evil

arises through cunning, an envious disturber of tranquil Peace,

which would assail such a triumph with sudden ruin.

[670] While Concord was bravely moving her foot amid the packed

wedges, already surrounded by secure walls,

she receives a hidden blow from the attack of lurking vice—

673. In Rat., a corrector ignorant of poetry placed *latere in laevo* for *laevo in latere*, failing to notice that the final *e* in *latere* can correctly be lengthened because of the two consonants in the following word, a practice familiar to Prudentius.

674. Some have *subtegmine*; others, *subtemine*. See writers on orthography or lexicographers.

675. In Erf., the error *ambierent*.

679. In the Cologne edition, in the margin, *Ald. conjunctura*. My Aldus has *commissura*.

681. Mar., in a second hand, *intulit huc vulnus*; in the first hand, *hoc vulnus*.

683. Fabr., *laetos*; our manuscripts have the better reading. Gifanius agrees with Fabricius in his *Index to Lucretius*.

684. Prudentius hints that Discord sometimes secretly slips in under the pretense of friendship. Weitzius observes that the poet also touches upon military custom, whereby different soldiers wore different clothing; this poem, he notes, sets out several other military practices.

685. Virgil, *Aeneid* 8.702:

> And rejoicing Discord goes with torn cloak,  
> followed by Bellona with her bloody whip.

Petronius, in the *Satyricon*: “And mourning Concord with torn cloak.” The Heinsian manuscripts, Alex., Vatt. G and O, Ald., and Rat. in its first hand have *structum et serpente*, as though formed from *struo*. He also used the expression in the hymn to Saint Laurence, verse 176: “ranks formed with talents.” Mar., Rat. in a second hand, Ang., Weitz., have *strictum et serpente*. Vat. C, *palla structum serpente*. Vat. BB, *et structum serpente*. Gifanius, as cited by Heinsius, has *et structum*.

686. Mar., *medio*, incorrectly. The older Heinsian copies, Alex., Vienn., Rat., Mar., Gis., Weitz., and others have *jacebant*. Aldus, Fuld., Vat. C have *jacebat*.

687. Widm., *oleo*; above it, *olea*. The olive is the emblem of Peace, with which Discord girds herself while falsely assuming her companion’s appearance. The second syllable in *redimitos* is lengthened, rarely, and perhaps in this one example alone. One might read *coronatos*, since elsewhere Prudentius often shortens the second syllable of *redimire*. But nothing should be changed.

688. Ald., Fabr., Widm., Ang., *respondit*.

690. Ald., *tanto in numero*. Mar., *tanto ex numero*. Rat., *et solam tanto e numero*. Vienn., *te solam e tanto numero*. Most copies, *te solam tanto e numero*.

695. Giselinus found *prospera nostra* in all the old copies he saw. The Heinsian and our copies agree. Aldus and other common editions have *pectora*. Barthius also reads *prospera nostra vulnerat* and observes that *vulnerare* may be applied even to inanimate things, as in Eutropius, book 10, concerning Julian: “There were some who inflicted wounds upon his glory,” and in Symmachus, book 2, letter 30: “The Sicilian affair was wounded.” Anyone can find similar examples.

697. Mar. has *ferro sedasse*, perhaps better than *bello*. I nevertheless understand *ferro sedasse* and *bello sedasse* to mean the same thing; otherwise *bello* is acceptable, especially since *pace* follows.

[Col. 0072D] 699. Widm. above, *castos* for *maestos*. Arator, book 2:

> But the fiercer enemy will be within,  
> and Discord carries the heavier evil,  
> which creates a wound beneath peace.

704. Vienn., *et deprensa fuit*. Ald., Gis., Weiz., Ang., Vat. C, Rat., *et deprensia tremit*. Mar., Ang., with three of the older Heinsian copies, *et deprensa tremunt*. The more recent copies retain this.

708. Ald., *et jussu*. In Vat. C one word has been erased, whether *jussu* or rather *missu*, which appears in all the others. Ang., *venerat ipsa*; Mar., Rat. in the first hand, *venerat illa*. The others, *venerit illa*.

709. Vienn., incorrectly, *discordia discors*.

710. In Rat., the familiar corrector wrote *a Styge duco genus*, after erasing the earlier words, evidently so that the first syllable of *heresis* would not be shortened, although our author shortens it so often.]

—a blade struck into her left side, although glistening

644 fabric woven with interlaced iron threads

the blade, nor did the tough threads allow the weapon,

driven in by rigid knots, to penetrate her vitals.

Yet a rare opening allowed the steel to pass through a thin point:

a joint where the outer edge of the polished
