and, cheerful, responded to the festive dances:

645 but beneath her garment she concealed a dagger, seeking you,

greatest Virtue—you alone, Concord, among so great a number—

[690] with grim deceit. Yet she was not permitted to pierce

the vital parts of the sacred body: only the outermost surface

was injured only by a superficial touch; the wounded skin

traced a thin stream of blood.

Virtue, suddenly disturbed, cries out: “What is this?

[695] What hostile hand is hiding here? Who wounds

our prosperity and brandishes iron amid such great rejoicing?

What good is it to have subdued untamed furies in war,

and, with vices destroyed, to have recovered everything sacred,

if Virtue falls beneath Peace?” The trembling companies

[700] turned their sad eyes. Blood, the sign of the wound,

dripped from the iron garment. Soon fear also revealed

the enemy standing close by: the pallor on her face,

conscious of the daring deed, gave signs of guilt,

and, once she was detected, her feeble hand and pallid complexion trembled.

[705] The entire legion of Virtues quickly surrounded her

[Col. 0072B] with drawn blades, asking amid heated tumult

both her race and name, her homeland and sect, and the God

646 whom she worshipped, and by whose command, from what nation,

she had come. She, bloodless and shaken by fear, said:

“I am called Discord,

[710] by the additional name Heresy. My God is multiform,” she said.

[Col. 0073A] [Note: [Col. 0073A]

711. Now, sometimes. — *Modo*, sometimes, Iso.

717. A spear, a pointed blade, Iso.

718. A point, a spear, I.

722. Mud. — Exhaling, stinking. — Sewers: ditches, pools, or latrines; a pool receiving filth in the middle of a city is called a sewer, Iso.

726. Favorable, prosperous, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0073B]

712. Vat. L and Fuld., *complacet*, incorrectly; Vat. D is no better: *Cum placet*, which is more elevated, and concerns a phantom-like appearance.

713. Vienn., Fuld., *haut innata*; others, *aut innata*. In Heinsius’s Thuan., second hand, *animam*, which makes no sense; Rott., *haut innata*. Mar., Rat. in the first hand, *nomen*, less well. Discord cleverly says that her God is a *numen*—that is, the true God—whenever she wishes to jest, not when she is speaking seriously. Some punctuate *ludere numen*.

714. Mar., Barthius, Put., and Thuan., together with three of Weitzius’s manuscripts, Egm., Erfurt., and Widm., which Weitzius follows, agree with the printed reading *Praeceptor Belia mihi, domus, et plaga mundus* (“Belia is my teacher; the world is my home and region”). Aldus, Ang., and Vatt. C, G, and L read *Praeceptor Belial mihi est, domus est plaga mundi* (“Belial is my teacher; my home is a region of the world”). The first Rott. reads *Praeceptor Belial mihi sit, domus, et plaga mundus* (“May Belial be my teacher; the world [is] my home and region”). The second reads *Praeceptor Belial mihi adest, domus, et plaga mundi* (“Belial is present as my teacher; [my] home and a region of the world”). Vat. D agrees with the first Rott. Vatt. F and O read *Praeceptor Belial mihi, domus, et plaga mundus* (“Belial [is] my teacher; the world [is] my home and region”). Some common editions read *Praeceptor Belial mihi fit, domus est plaga mundi* (“Belial becomes my teacher; my home is a region of the world”); others read *Est mihi praeceptor Belial, domus est plaga mundi* (“I have Belial as teacher; my home is a region of the world”). Against the meter, Chamillardus printed *Praeceptor Belial mihi, domus et plaga mundus* (“Belial [is] my teacher; the world [is] my home and region”). Gallandius copied this, although he preferred Aldus’s closing phrase for the verse, *Praeceptor Belial mihi est: domus est plaga mundi* (“Belial is my teacher: my home is a region of the world”). Yet the metrical fault lies at the beginning of the verse as Chamillardus printed it. In Rat., an unscrupulous corrector wrote *Est mihi praeceptor Belial* (“I have Belial as teacher”) after erasing the earlier words; then *domus et plaga mundus* (“the world [is] my home and region”) is in the old hand. In his second edition Giselinus first printed *Est mihi praeceptor Belial, domus est plaga mundi* (“I have Belial as teacher; my home is a region of the world”); later, among his corrections and on the authority of a single manuscript, he judged *Praeceptor mihi Belial, domus et plaga mundi* best (“Belial [is] my teacher; [my] home and a region of the world”).
715. Fabr., *blasphemica monstri*. Certainly *blasphemia* is plural; the noun must therefore be formed as *blasphemium*. Commodianus likewise used *blasphemium*, *ignominium*, and *infamium*.

716. You will find excellent praises of faith throughout chapter 12 of Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews. Nevertheless, understand that charity is greater.

719. Weitzius, with Fuld. alone, has *furialis bestia* (“frenzied beast”). Weitzius was altogether inclined, as often, to choose an inferior reading taken from a single manuscript.

721. Aldus, *corvisque edacibus*. Others, better, *corvis quod educibus*. Barthius has *ultor* for *ultro*; this is unconvincing.

723. Mar. and Widm., *quod trudat*; in Mar., above in smaller writing, *tradat*. Put. and the other Heinsian copies have *trudat*, except Thuan., where *tradat* occurs and is retained in most manuscripts and printed editions, unless Teolius cites four Vatican manuscripts for *trudat*.

724. Vienn., against the meter, *discissum feris*; Rat. has the same, but a recent hand has added *-que*. Weitzius rashly adopted *discissum feris*, omitting our reading, or the other acceptable form *discissumque feris*, with Mar., Rott., and Ang. Vat. C has the metrical error *discissumque foedis*.

725. Aldus printed *ruptis haeresis perit horrida membris*, correctly, except that he wrote *haeresis* with the diphthong. In a second revision he incorrectly changed it to *ruptis perit haeresi horrida membris*. This correction escaped Gallandius and others, who insist that Aldus read *heresis perit*. In Rat. the same correction, made by a recent hand, was used by Giselinus to defend the poet against Nebrissa, who had accused him of making the same syllable long in one place and short in another, since Nebrissa, with Aldus, had read *perit haeresis*. I agree with Giselinus, on the basis of the manuscripts, that the word order is reversed, though not for the reason he gives—that the nominative case should precede its verb. After this verse Mar. and Rat. have the title “On Faith and Concord.”

726. Among so many variant readings here, it is difficult to determine which is truest. The reading printed in the text is retained by Heinsius, Giselinus, Chamillardus, and other common editions, and the old manuscripts agree with it in large part.

Aldus reads:

> *Compositis igitur rerum, morumque secundis*  
> *In commune bonis tranquillae plebis ad unum*  
> *Contigit hac statione frui, valloque foveri*  
> *Pacificos sensus, et in otia solvere curas.*  
> *Exstruitur.*

That is, fragmentarily: “Thus, with affairs settled and conduct favorable; for the common good of the peaceful people, [brought] into unity; it befell [them] to enjoy this station and be sheltered by the rampart, and to release peaceful minds and cares into repose. It is built.”

Vienn. agrees with Aldus, except that it has *postquam intra tuta morari* (“after [they began] to dwell within safety”) in place of *tranquillae plebis ad unum* (“of the peaceful people, into unity”).

Mar. and Ang. read:

> *Compositis . . . . . in commune bonis tranquillae plebis ad unum*  
> *Sensibus in tuta valli statione locatis,*  
> *Contigit hac statione frui, valloque foveri,*  
> *Exstruitur.*

That is, fragmentarily: “With [affairs] settled … for the common good of the peaceful people, [brought] into unity, with minds placed in the safe station of the rampart, it befell [them] to enjoy this station and be sheltered by the rampart. It is built.”

The Ratisbon manuscript has *Composito tandem postquam requiesse tumultu* (“when at last, the tumult settled, [they came] to rest”), written by an inept corrector after the earlier words had been erased, although enough remains to show that *compositis* had stood there; no trace of the other words remains. The line *In commune bonis postquam intra tuta morari* (“for the common good, after [they began] to dwell within safety”) was struck through by the corrector, not erased. In *Contigit ac statione frui, valloque teneri* (“it befell [them] to enjoy the station and be held by the rampart”), the whole line is by the old scribe except *teneri*, which is in a recent hand. The lines *Pacificas virtutum acies, quas pestis iniqua / Turbarat meditata dolos, et solvere curas / In commune datum tranquillae plebis ad unum* (“the peaceful ranks of the virtues, which the wicked pest had disturbed while plotting deceits, and [the ability] to release cares was given in common to the peaceful people, into unity”) are all by the inept corrector after earlier writing was erased, apart from the surviving beginning *pacific…* of the first word. Mariettus records nothing else from Rat.; in the editor’s judgment *exstruitur*, etc., follows there.

Put. and Rott. read *In commune bonis tranquillae plebis ad unum / Sensibus in tuta valli statione locatis, / Exstruitur* (“For the common good of the peaceful people, [brought] into unity, with minds placed in the safe station of the rampart, it is built”). Egmondanus agrees with Giselinus, but in an interpolating hand; its margin then says, “Another book has *In commune bonis*, etc.,” as in Put.

Thuan. and Oxon., with Giselinus, add after *solvere curas* (“to release cares”) the line *Sensibus in tuta valli statione locatis* (“with minds placed in the safe station of the rampart”). Weitzius follows Giselinus but gives *valloque fovere* (“and to shelter by the rampart”) for *valloque foveri* (“and to be sheltered by the rampart”). Heinsius approves the Greek construction *valloque foveri pacificos sensus* (“for peaceful minds to be sheltered by the rampart”).

Widm. reads *Compositis . . . . . In commune bonis tranquillae plebis ad unum / In commune bonis, postquam intra tuta morari / Contigit, ac statione frui, valloque fovere / Pacificos sensus, et in otia solvere curas / Sensibus in tuta valli statione locatis, / Exstruitur* (“With [affairs] settled … for the common good of the peaceful people, [brought] into unity; for the common good, after [they began] to dwell within safety, it befell [them] to enjoy the station and to shelter peaceful minds by the rampart and release cares into repose, with minds placed in the safe station of the rampart. It is built”). The line beginning *Sensibus in tuta* is written in the margin of Fuld.

Erfurth. reads *In commune bonis postquam intra tuta morari / Contigit, ac statione frui, valloque fovere / Pacificos sensus, et in otia solvere curas, / Compositis igitur rerum, morumque secundis, / Exstruitur* (“For the common good, after [they began] to dwell within safety, it befell [them] to enjoy the station and to shelter peaceful minds by the rampart and release cares into repose; thus, with affairs settled and conduct favorable, it is built”).

Piccartus’s codex reads *In commune bonis tranquilla et pace solutis / Sensibus ut tuta valli statione locari / Contigit, ac statione frui, valloque foveri, / Exstruitur* (“For the common good, with minds released in tranquillity and peace, so that it befell [them] to be placed in the safe station of the rampart, to enjoy the station, and to be sheltered by the rampart, it is built”).

Vat. C reads *In commune bonis tranquillae plebis ad unum / Sensibus in tuta valli statione locatis / In commune bonis postquam intra tuta morari* (“For the common good of the peaceful people, [brought] into unity, with minds placed in the safe station of the rampart; for the common good, after [they began] to dwell within safety”). The rest is as in Giselinus.

In Vat. D, *In commune bonis tranquillae plebis ad unum* (“for the common good of the peaceful people, [brought] into unity”) is in a second hand. The first hand continues: *Contigit, ac statione frui, valloque foveri / Pacificos sensus, et in omnia solvere curas / Sensibus locatis valli in tuta statione / Exstruitur* (“It befell [them] to enjoy the station and be sheltered by the rampart, and to release peaceful minds and cares into everything, with minds placed in the rampart’s safe station. It is built”). This word order is inverted and contrary to the meter.

Vat. F reads *Compositis . . . . . In commune bonis tranquillae plebis ad unum / Sensibus in tuta valli statione locatis / Contigit, ac statione frui, valloque foveri / Pacifico sensus, et in otia solvere curas, / Exstruitur* (“With [affairs] settled … for the common good of the peaceful people, [brought] into unity, with minds placed in the safe station of the rampart, it befell [them] to enjoy the station and be sheltered by the rampart, and to release the mind into peaceful repose. It is built”).

Vat. G agrees with Aldus but inserts *Sensibus in tuta valli statione locatis* (“with minds placed in the safe station of the rampart”) between the lines beginning *Pacificos* and *Exstruitur*. Vat. L is like Vat. F but has *hac statione* (“this station”), *curam* (“care”) for *curas* (“cares”), and the corrupt *sensus in otia* (“the mind into repose”). Vat. BB is like Vat. F but has *curam* for *curas*. Vat. O agrees with Giselinus and adds the line beginning *Sensibus* before *Exstruitur*.

Bonon. reads *In commune bonis tranquillae plebis ad unum / Sensibus in tota vallis statione locatis, / Exstruitur*, that is, fragmentarily: “For the common good of the peaceful people, [brought] into unity, with minds placed in the entire station of the rampart, it is built,” etc.

Who would believe such variety among the manuscripts? From this passage Heinsius suspects that Prudentius produced two editions of his works.]

Now lesser, now greater; sometimes double, sometimes single. At pleasure he is more aerial, a vision produced from a phantasm; or, whenever I wish to play, the divinity is innate in the soul. Belia is my teacher; the world is my home and region.”

[715] Faith, queen of the Virtues, could no longer endure

the blasphemy of the captive monster. She interrupts

the speaker’s words and closes the passages of her voice

with a spear, piercing the polluted tongue

647 with a rigid point.

[Col. 0074A] The savage beast is torn apart by countless hands;

[720] each person snatches a piece to scatter into the air,

to give to dogs, to offer to greedy ravens,

to consign to foul-smelling, muddy sewers,

to give sea monsters to possess.

The whole corpse, torn among hideous creatures,

[725] is divided; with its limbs burst apart, dreadful Heresy perishes.

When, therefore, matters and morals had been settled favorably,

[Col. 0075A] [Note: [Col. 0075B]

727. “For all together,” “into unity,” I.

731. Higher, loftier, or more elevated, I.

732. Raises, exalts, I.

744. Canvas coverings, cloaks, I.

745. Snoring, sleeping, Iso.

746. “With ears”: Charity addresses the ranks of the virtues. — Assembly, gathering. — “What,” “why,” Iso.

753. Barbarism, paganism, I.

754. Oppressed: anger and lust, I.

755. Private, particular. — In countryside and forum, in villages and cities, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0075D]

727. The gloss refers to another reading.

730. Fuld., *construito media*, incorrectly. The custom of the Romans is represented: constructing in the camp an earthen tribunal for the commander. Concerning this, see Lipsius, *Roman Military Institutions*, and Tacitus, *Annals* 1: “At the same time they pile up clods and build the tribunal.” Others call it an embankment, as our poet does below, verse 738. Pal. has *camporum* rather than *castrorum*, less well.

731. Vienn., *quod*, that is, “the tribunal”; others, *quem locum* (“which place”).

732. Mar., Angel., *in speculum*, which I do not approve. Both have *inde omnia* (“from there, everything”), not badly.

733. Heinsius approves *circuminspicit* from Put. I follow the others, who correctly give *circumspicit*, with Alex., Vat. C, Prag., Rat., Vienn. Teolius says that the manuscripts have *circuminspicit*, but does not explain which manuscripts, or whether all have it.

[Col. 0076B] 734. Put. and Egm. have *huc*; Oxon., *hinc*; neither pleased Heinsius. Barthius also read *huc* in his manuscript but considered *hunc* more genuine; our copies, with Aldus and others, support *hunc*. Erfurt. has *tunc*.

737. Cham., incorrectly, *per sanctum*.

738. See the note on verse 730 concerning the embankment and the earthen tribunal. Montfaucon, *Antiquities*, volume 4, page 103, illustrates such tribunals; he thinks that on occasion the tribunal may have been a stone.

739. In Vat. O, *que* is missing from *populosque*. In Fuld., *conspicuaeque jubent populos*, which pleased Weitzius.

740. Rat., *alacres e castris omnibus*.

743. Weitzius, following one Fuld. manuscript, *degenerem*.

746. Heinsius, with Put. and Thuan., preferred *exspectant*, saying that he had restored many such forms in ancient authors with the help of manuscripts. But since both forms are correct, and all our copies—Mar., Rat., Vienn., Alex., Ang., Vatt. C, F, G—with other manuscripts and printed editions before Heinsius have *exspectat*, nothing should be changed.

748. Vienn., *victoribus addere*.

749. Vienn., *erupit*; Ald. and Fabr., *primam in vocem*. Ang., *prima se voce*, against the meter and with unusual phrasing.

750. In the earlier Boher., *sat gloria*; others, *jam gloria*.

[Col. 0076D] 752. Heinsius criticizes Weitzius for bringing back *hoc habet* prematurely in place of *contigit*; see the note on verse 53. But apart from Widm. in its first hand, which he cites, Weitzius finds Mar., Vienn., and Rat. agreeing with him among our manuscripts. Gifanius, *Index to Lucretius*, page 436, reads from an old book, with respect to division or separation: *Contigit exstincta multo certamine saeva*. Vat. C agrees with Gifanius. This is unconvincing.

753. In the Aldine edition that I use, there is, I think, a note by Marietti observing that the holy city seems here to mean Rome, from which the poet says that all barbarism, or paganism, was driven out. Compare the beginning of book 2 *Against Symmachus*, “I believed that by vices,” etc., and the prolegomena, sections 69 and following.

755. Fuld., *publica jam requies*. An excellent sentiment, and evangelical, from Matthew 12:25: “Every kingdom divided against itself will be desolated, and every city or house divided against itself will not stand.”]

648 With goods held in common, after they had managed to dwell within safety,

and to enjoy their station, and to have their peaceful dispositions sheltered by the rampart,

and to release their cares into leisure:

[730] a tribunal is built in the middle of the camp,

649 in a higher place: a mound whose pointed summit

rises into a watchtower, from which the free eye

looks out widely upon everything beneath it through unobstructed air.

Faith, sincere, and Concord, her sister,

[735] sworn by a sacred covenant beneath the love of Christ,

climb to the summit. Soon the lofty tribunal

rises above them, a holy pair, dear to each other,

equal in the right of authority. They take their stand

at the top of the embankment, conspicuous,

[Col. 0075B] and command the assembled crowds to stand before them.

[740] Everyone rushes eagerly from every camp;

[Col. 0076A] no inactive part of the mind lies hidden, covered

by some recess of the body, to conceal itself

in sluggish degeneracy. All the tents stand open

with their canvases spread; the coverings are unfastened,

so that no inhabitant may languish sleeping in darkness.

[745] With ears intent, the assembly awaits what
May Concordia, the leader, call the victors after the wars—her whom Faith too wishes to add to the virtues as a law.

Concordia is the first to break into speech with this address:

[750] “Already, indeed, abundant glory has come to you,

O most faithful pledges of the Father, O of Christ the Lord;

the savage barbarism that had surrounded the natives

of the holy city, and oppressed its men with sword and flame,

[Col. 0076B] has been destroyed through much struggle.

[755] But public repose consists in private friendships, in countryside and forum:

[Col. 0077A] [Note: [Col. 0077B]

756. Domestic, civil, I.

757. The state, the condition, I.

759. Foreign, deadly. — With roofs, covered, I.

760. Split, divided or separated, I.

761. Secret, hidden. — Two-formed, divided. — With fibers, with sinews, with thoughts, I.

763. May agree, may confirm, I.

773. Approves, pleases, I.

776. Preserving, holding something against a brother. — Vow, will, [Col. 0078B] Iso.

777. With slanting bile, with hidden gall, I.

778. To have expended, to give, I.

781. Gives, dismisses, I.

782. Desires to precede, hastens to forestall, I.

788. Hands down, taught. — Doves, Christians, I.

789. The serpent, the devil, I.

790. Innocent ones, virtues, or doves, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0077C]

759. Aldus and Giselinus read *in vestris*, “in your [homes].” Heinsius, our text, and the Weitzian manuscripts read *in nostris*, “in our [homes].” In Mariettus, *nec secta*; others, *ne secta*. The word *exotica* is Plautine and has been restored by others.

760. Alexandrinus, Mariettus, the Vatican manuscripts F and G, Giselinus in the margin, and Heinsius read *fissa*, except the Thuaneus, which has *fusa* from the first hand, and the earlier Rottendorf manuscript, where it is *fixa*. Barthius and Weitz likewise have *fissa*. Vatican C has *scisa*. Erfurtensis, Angelicanus, Aldus, and Giselinus from the first hand have *scissa*. *Fissum* was the name given to the liver of a slaughtered victim, to which the word *fibris* perhaps refers.

761. Widmannstetter, in the margin, has *infundit variis*, less suitably.

762. Weitz, with only Erfurtensis, reads *conjunctet*. Why not rather, with the others, *conjungat*?

764. Aldus has *medium intervenit*. One should read *medius intervenit*. A ridiculous corrector of the Ratianus manuscript made it *genus intervenit*, since he supposed that the poem could not scan in any other way. Fuldensis has *atque homini, atque Deo medius*: this is not displeasing. From such a formula of speech and idea arose the word *mediator* for Christ. See *Cath. hymn.* 11, line 16.

765. The poet also uses the word *carneus* in the *Apotheosis*.

[Col. 0077D] 771. Boethius seems to have imitated Prudentius, book IV, meter 6: ‘If you wish with pure and skillful mind to behold the laws of the lofty Thunderer, look upon the heights of the highest heaven. There, by a just covenant, the stars preserve the ancient peace of things … This harmony regulates the elements by balanced measures,’ etc.

773. Matthew is witness to this matter, chapter V, verse 23. Most read *probat*, “approves.” Heinsius, with the Thuaneus, more correctly thinks—and maintains—that it should be *probet*, “may approve.”

775. Aldus has *flammivomis*. *Flammicomis* is better, in agreement with the manuscripts. Thus Marius Victor, book II on Genesis: ‘Extending far and wide fire-bearing hair’; and Juvencus, book IV: ‘and the fire-haired stars will rush,’ and shortly afterward: ‘girded with the adornment of flame-haired torches.’ In the Parma edition there is the error *flammicolis*, which is repeated in the note.

777. Slanting bile is treacherous, deceitful, like “slanting” speech. Consult the lexicons. See the thought in Paul, First Corinthians XIII, 3. In Aldus, Fabricius, and the Ratianus, by an incompetent corrector, *prosit Iesu*, “may it benefit Jesus.” In the note to verse 764 I observed the audacity of the Ratisbon corrector, who introduced *genus* in place of *medius*, so that *Iesus* would be trisyllabic.

779. The poet continues to express the Apostle’s teaching from the same chapter.

781. The Egmondanus and Palatinus have *contra offensacula*. Barthius, who found this in his manuscripts, says: “I do not think *CONTRA* was invented by scribes.”

782. Here again one sees an exposition of the Apostle, from Ephesians IV, verse 26.

783. Fuldensis has *concitus*; *conscius* is more correct.

784. Giselinus remarks here that he himself inserted the particle *quisqui*, as he writes, for easier understanding, although he thinks Prudentius left *quisque* in his text. It would certainly have been better not to alter what Giselinus admits Prudentius wrote; and to me, at least, *quisqui* seems more difficult to understand than *quisque*. See the note to *Cathemerinon* hymn VII, verse 216.

786. In the first edition Giselinus had *facta ad donaria* in the margin; in the second edition’s Commentaries he explains that *donaria* are either gifts consecrated to God or places intended for such gifts. Places may be called holy, he says, but gifts cannot, since they must be commended by the integrity and innocence of the person offering them; thus, in this sense, one may read *facta ad donaria*. I am not moved by this distinction: gifts too can be called holy, not in themselves, but because they have been dedicated to God.

787. Puteanus has *puro* instead of *liquido*.

789. Gifanius, in his index to Lucretius, under the word *VESTIS*, observes that Lucretius said *vestis araneae*, “the spider’s garment,” and *vestis anguis*, “the serpent’s garment,” just as Virgil, with marvelous beauty, has *exuviae anguis*, “the serpent’s cast skin,” and Prudentius here, with no less elegance, *vestis plumarum*, “a garment of feathers,” which he attributes to the dragon, or winged serpent—that is, to the demon.

790. This is also drawn from Matthew VII, 15: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves.” See also chapter X, 16: “Behold, I send you as sheep among wolves,” etc. As for the reading *ovibus* rather than *avibus* in the Palatinus, it is mistaken: the latter belongs to the preceding thought concerning innocent birds and the dragon.]

Constancy in friendships: domestic division disturbs

the state of the people and makes it totter abroad, because it disagrees within.

Therefore beware, men, lest discordant judgment exist

in our thoughts, lest a foreign faction arise within our homes,

[760] forged from hatreds; for a divided will

confounds secret, twofold things in various fibers.

651 May love join together what we understand; may what we live

agree in a single purpose: nothing divided is secure.

And as a mediator intervened between man and God, Jesus,

[765] who joins mortal humanity to the Father, lest things of flesh be distant

from the eternal Spirit, and so that the one God may be both:

so may the one Spirit weave together by uniform bonds

whatever we do, both in mind and in bodily action.

Peace is the complete work of virtue, peace the consummation of labors,

[770] peace is the reward of completed war, and the reward of danger.

The stars thrive in peace; earthly things stand firm in peace:

[Col. 0078A] nothing is pleasing to God without peace—not even a gift which you desire to offer

at the altar—if your troubled mind, in the hidden chamber of a peaceless heart,

hates your brother.

[775] Nor, if as a martyr for Christ’s name you leap into flame-haired fires,

while preserving an unloving resolve beneath crooked bile,

will it profit Jesus that you have offered your precious life:

652 for peace is the consummation of merit.

It is not swollen with pride, does not envy a rival brother,

endures everything patiently, and believes everything.

[780] It never grieves at injury; it forgives every offense.

Anxious to forestall the setting of the light with pardon,

it hastens lest the sun, conscious of anger, leave behind lasting resentment.

Whoever wishes to sacrifice burnt offerings to God,

let him offer peace first: no sacrifice is sweeter to Christ.

[785] [Col. 0078B] By this gift alone, turning its face toward holy offerings,

it delights in the clear fragrance.

Yet God himself also teaches the snowy doves

to distinguish with discerning skill the feathered serpent,

clothed in a tender garment of plumage,

[790] mixed among innocent birds: and the wolf, with bloody mouth, lies hidden

[Col. 0079A] [Note: [Col. 0079B]

795. They reveal, they display, I.

796. Fresh, produced by discord, I.

797. Stealthy, hidden; he said this because discord was secretly wounding it, I.

798. By chance, of concord, I.

799. Favorable, prosperous, I.

800. May cease, now, I.

[Col. 0080B] 802. Its own, proper, I.

804. Work, house. — Remains, must be done by us, I.

805. Leaders, virtues. — At last, formerly, I.

806. Warlike, David, I.

807. Established, in a carnal sense. — Progenitor, David, I.

808. Of kings, of the gentiles, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0079B]

793. The Viennese has *anguineos*; the Angelicanus, from the first hand, *anguinos*. One should read *agninos*, “lamb-like,” from *agnus*, a word used by Horace, Plautus, and others. Barthius observes that *funera* means killings, robberies, and pestilence in L. Septimius’ *On the Trojan War*. Lactantius, or another writer, in *On the Lord’s Passion*: “I became man and suffered dreadful funerals.”

794. In the Ratianus: *sese ostentant*, “they display themselves.” Marietto did not dislike this reading, since above, in verse 688, there is also *ostentans* concerning discord, although it was hiding itself. These remarks are subtler than they are true, unless I am mistaken. Discord displayed its hair crowned with an olive-bearing branch, although it had assumed a false appearance of virtue. Arius and Photinus concealed their savagery by this device.

798. Virgil, book V, verse 700: “Shaken by bitter chance,” and verse 869: “and shaken in spirit by the misfortune of his friend.” But I think the poet had read Jerome’s words in the *Dialogue against Lucifer*, no. 19: “The whole world groaned and was amazed to find itself Arian.” Prudentius skillfully uses *populus*, “the people,” for any multitude. See examples in the lexicons.

799. The Viennese, with *generosa*; Aldus, *tunc* with the others. Some have *tum*.

801. Of the Heinsian manuscripts only the Thuaneus has *sed defensa fide*; the others have *fides*. I do not understand why modern editors, Chamillard and others, adopted the common reading *fide*: the sentence is more harmonious as “Concord has been wounded, but faith defended”; indeed, “and Concord, unharmed, accompanying her sister Faith, laughs at her wounds.” *Fides* is read in Mariettus, Alexandrinus, Weitz with his manuscripts, Sichardus, the Ratianus, although not very clearly, and others. In Vatican C and G there is *fide*, as also in Vatican F from the second hand. Giselinus, following Aldus and Nebrissensis, reads *fide*, although others had *sed defensa fides*, because, he says, faith was already victorious through its defense and did not here require defense. Teolius likewise adopted this reasoning, thinking the more reliable Vatican manuscripts had *fide*. But this proves nothing: the assertion is that faith, though Concord has been wounded, has been defended from every wound; hence what follows: “and Concord,” etc.

803. He imitated Maro, book IX, verse 262: “Nothing sad after his recovery.”

804. The better Heinsian manuscripts, the Ratianus from the first hand, Fabricius, Vatican G, Piccolomini, and Alexandrinus have *egregio*, together with Giselinus and others; the Ratianus above, Mariettus, the Viennese, Aldus, Weitz, Vatican C and F, and others have *egregium*. Either may be retained, whether one understands “an excellent work” or “for excellent labor.”

805. The Viennese has *tantum*; *tandem* is better.

806. The Viennese has *belliger*, incorrectly. The subject is Solomon, the peace-bearing heir of the kingdom under David, the warlike one. In the two oldest Heinsian manuscripts, the Egmondanus, and the Palatinus, followed by Weitz, the reading is *inermus*. The same appears in Vatican F and L and in Alexandrinus, where it is written *inhermus*, and in Barthius’ manuscript, who says *inermus* is more elegant than *inermis*. I willingly accept *inermus*, as in Virgil *vulgus* and *pectus inermum*; nevertheless I would not reject *inermis*, found in Aldus, Mariettus, the Ratianus, the Viennese, many Heinsian manuscripts, Giselinus, and Vatican C and BB.

807. In some common editions, in the margin: *instruxit Salomon*, “Solomon built.”

809. Erfurtensis has *jam terso*, “now cleansed.” Vatican C transposed the words and overturned the meter: *fundatur templum, et ara*, “the temple is founded, and the altar.”

811. Some write *Jerusales*, others *Jerusalem*, others *Hierusalem* or *Hierusales*. Cauchius had noted *Jerusale* from his manuscript, which seemed acceptable; Aldus has *tunc hic Jerusalem*. Giselinus has *tunc et Jerusalem*. The best and most manuscripts omit both *et* and *hic*. Aldus has *lustrata* instead of *illustrata*; Alexandrinus, Vatican O, Mariettus, the Ratianus, the Heinsian manuscripts, and Weitz with Giselinus have *quietum*. Others have *quieto*. In the first edition Giselinus, and in the margin of the second, reads *Hierusalem templo tunc illustrata quieto*. I do not discuss the quantity of the syllables in *Jerusalem*. Barthius reports a singular reading from his manuscripts: “Then Jerusalem, illuminated by the quiet temple, already received the goddess.” Fridericus Besselius, *Miscellanea*, treatise, p. 31, reads *quietum* and rightly explains it of the ark, which Solomon first brought into the temple so that it might establish its seat there, First Kings, chapter 4, verse 7: “The Philistines were afraid, saying: ‘God has come into the camp.’” Most interpreters assert that the ark buried by Jeremiah has not yet been found, that it was not in the second temple, and that Titus did not carry it in his triumph. Some interpreters of Prudentius, in the note to *Apotheosis*, verse 538, have taught that it is represented within Titus’ arch, as have many writers on Roman antiquities, to pass over the others. But the most careful Villalpandus, after examining the matter more closely, discovered that the ark is not shown on Titus’ arch: those who wrote otherwise were deceived either by false accounts of others or because, seeing the arch themselves, they thought that the table represented there was the ark. Some place the ark not on the side where the table is, but on the opposite side. Nevertheless I agree with Villalpandus, for in more recent images of Titus’ arch the ark is nowhere represented. See Ribera on Haggai, chapter 1, no. 15 and following, who himself was at times deceived when he saw the arch.]

653 Having fashioned a milk-white sheep beneath a soft fleece,

while exercising raw slaughter with lamb-like jaws,

Photinus and Arius conceal themselves by this art,

[795] savage wolves in their ferocity: the signs disclose

our condition, and recent blood, even though from the surface of the body,

shows what a stealthy hand can do. The whole people of the virtues

gave a groan, shaken by bitter chance.

Then noble Faith added these words: “Rather, amid prosperity

[800] let the groan cease: Concord has been wounded,

[Col. 0080A] but Faith has been defended; indeed, Concord, unharmed,

accompanying her sister Faith, laughs at her wounds.

654 This alone is my salvation: with it received, nothing is sad for me.

One excellent work remains after the wars, an arduous task,

[805] O leaders: the peace-bearing heir of the kingdom at last,

the unarmed successor of the warlike king and armed court,

Solomon established it, since the panting right hand of his progenitor

had smoked with the hot blood of kings.

For when the blood has been cleansed, the temple is founded, and the altar

[810] is set up—the lofty house of Christ beneath gilded roofs.

Then Jerusalem, illuminated by the temple, the divine city received the peaceful God

[Col. 0081A] [Note: [Col. 0081B]

812. Goddess, divine, I.

813. Ark, which signifies Christ’s flesh, I.

815. Whose, of the temple. — Holy, holy souls, I.

816. Phalanxes, vices, multitudes, I.

817. Son, Christ, I.

818. Purified, in baptism, I.

819. Needy, lacking, I.

820. It was fought, it was struggled over. — At close quarters, nearby, I.

821. Duties, hymns, services of the house. — May perform, may do. — Silent, peaceful, I.

822. Sacred things, those of Christ. — May hasten, may accelerate. — Ungirded, from war, I.

823. Queen, faith. — Proud, glorious, or beautiful, I.

824. Leapt down, from the throne, I.

[Col. 0082B] 825. Foundation, “no one can lay another foundation,” etc., I.

826. Level surface, the temple’s plain, I.

827. Fronts, the four corners, I.

828. Joints, conjunctions. — Separated, with unequal measurements, I.

829. Ingenious, subtle, narrow. — May mutilate, may corrupt. — *Semetra*, half-measure; a hanging little stone, I. — Discordant, dissonant. — *Semetra*, measurements, Vatican T.

830. Dawn, the east signifies boys, the south young men, the west maturity, the north extreme old age, I.

831. South wind, the south, I.

835. Solid, solidity. — High, aloft. — Carving, a hole, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0081C]

815. After this verse, Erfurtensis places verse 820, “Thus far with alternating …,” and afterward “For what benefit the earth-born …”

816. The Ratianus from the first hand, the Egmondanus, has *nunquid*. Giselinus had published *nunquid*, but in the *Emendations* restored *nam quid*, which Heinsius seems not to have noticed. Most old manuscripts have *phalangas*. Nevertheless I read *phalanges* in Alexandrinus, Vatican C and F, and others. Fuldensis has *phalanga*.

818. The Viennese has the erroneous *illapsum*.

819. The Ratianus has *intrat*; others, *intret*. Lactantius, *Epitome of the Divine Institutes*, chapter 8: “Let the breast be emptied of every stain, so that it may be able to be God’s temple, which is illumined not by the splendor of gold or ivory but by the radiance of faith and chastity.” Compare the hymn of Saint Romanus, verse 341. Heretics abuse passages of this kind to reject the adornment of temples: most foolishly, for because the adornment of the heart is better than that of the temple, it does not follow that the adornment of the temple must be rejected—a form of adornment our Prudentius often praises.

820. Some common manuscripts have *hactenus alterius*, “thus far of another.”

821. Gifanius, in his index to Lucretius, p. 362, under *MOENERA*, asserts that Prudentius was exceedingly devoted to antiquity and, from an old book, reads *moenia nunc agitet* instead of *munia*, just as in Lucretius there is *moenera* for *munera*. Others have the better *munia*. Vatican F has *menia nunc agitet*. The Egmondanus has *munia nunc agit en*, which Barthius, finding it in his manuscript, thought excellent.

822. Aldus, Alexandrinus, Mariettus, the Ratianus, the Viennese, Vatican F, Angelicanus, Widmannstetter, and the two oldest Heinsian manuscripts have *atque sacris sedem*. Sichardus has *adque sacri sedem*. The Palatinus has *adque sacris sedem*. The Oxford manuscript has *atque sacri sedem*. Giselinus has *atque sacris aedem*, and Giselinus asserts that it had previously read *adque sacri sedem*. “Ridiculous,” he says. “For the seat had not yet been selected; so where would they be hastening?” For *discincta*, many old manuscripts cited by Heinsius have the less suitable *distincta*. Barthius reads *properat discincta juventus*. Prudentius, he says, alludes to the happiness of his own times and indicates … he himself, by every name, time, place, and devotion, worthy of commendation. Understand the happiness mentioned again in *Against Symmachus* I, verses 545 and following. After this verse, Mariettus and the Ratianus have the heading “The Building of Faith and Concord”; see the *Prolegomena*, no. 65. Weitz added the same inscription.

824. The Heinsian manuscripts, Aldus, Gifanius in his index to Lucretius under *DISSILUIT*, Mariettus, and Weitz have *desiluit* or *dissiluit*. Giselinus, the Ratianus, Cellarius, and Teolius have *desiliit*. Mariettus has *concors* instead of *consors*, but the latter is more truthful.

825. The Viennese has the bad reading *meditatura novum*. The Ratianus is no better with *metitura*. The Thuaneus has *laeto* instead of *jacto*. I do not like this reading; Heinsius conjectures *lato fundamine*. How much better is *jacto*, which appears in all the others? See Revelation, chapter XII.

827. Vatican D, by a ridiculous transposition, has *frontes undique*.

829. The Viennese and Ratianus have *mutilet argutam*. The meter better supports *argutam mutilet*. Giselinus and Aldus have *symmetra*, which Gallandius preferred to follow and Fabricius explains as “having equal distances.” The more faithful Heinsian manuscripts have *semetra*; as Heinsius observes, the poet seems to make *semetra* contrary to *symmetra*. The word is half Latin, like *primoplastus*. Fuldensis has *semeta*; the Ratianus, *semitra*; the Angelicanus, *argutam normam mutilet per dissona*, where something is missing. Mariettus, Alexandrinus, Vatican C from the second hand, and Vatican D, F, L, O, and BB have *argutam mutilet per dissona semetra normam*. Nebrissensis teaches that *norma* is *el cartabon* in Spanish, not *carbaton*, as it has been incorrectly printed in some places.

832. In the Ratianus, a completely unskilled corrector replaced *occiduis* with *qua sol occidit*, “where the sun sets.”

833. Fabricius has *totidemque aquilonis*, “and as many of the north.”

834. In the Egmondanus, *strictile saxum*, which I believe is an error. The Thuaneus has no *hic*, with hiatus.

835. Chamillard asserts that the noun *dolatus* is unheard-of among the ancients. But has he himself heard all the ancients? Has he read everything they wrote? Apuleius used *dolamen* with the same meaning. In Erfurtensis, *dolata foratu* occurs instead of *forata dolatu*. In Vatican G from the second hand, *forata dolatu*, with the earlier reading erased.]

655 after the wandering ark had settled, established upon marble altars.

“Let a venerable temple also rise in our camp,

[815] whose Almighty One may revisit the holy places of the saints.

For what benefit is it to have driven earth-born phalanxes away with the sword,

if the Son of Man, having descended from the citadel of heaven,

enters the city of a purified body, unadorned,

poor in the splendor of the temple?

[820] Thus far we have fought at close quarters with alternating weapons:

now let the white toga of silent peace perform its duties,

and let youth, released from war, hasten to provide a seat for sacred things.”

656 When the queen had spoken these words, she leapt down by the proud steps,

[Col. 0082A] and Concord, her companion in so great a work,

[825] was about to measure out a new temple upon the cast foundation.

A golden measuring rod runs across the level surface,

having measured the spaces so that the four fronts may form a square on every side,

lest an unequal angle, at the separated joints,

mutilate the ingenious design through discordant half-measures.

[830] On the side of dawn, a bright region is opened with three gates;

toward the south, the number of doors is three;

the triple entrance offers doors to the western regions,

657 and three times the lofty house opens toward the northern axis.

There is no hewn stone there;

[835] but the solid mass is hollow and pierced by much carving,

[Col. 0083A] [Note: [Col. 0083A]

836. Threshold, entrance. — Arch, vault, I.

839. Senate, by the names of the apostles; through whose preaching the Holy Spirit embraces the secrets of the heart, Iso.

840. Inscriptions, the names of the apostles. — Hidden things, the hidden things of human beings, I.

[Col. 0083B] 841. Encompasses, surrounds, enters. — Innermost parts, in the soul, I.

842. Nature, of the human being, I.

843. Fourfold, the four elements that animate a human being—fire, air, earth, and water—and the four regions of the world. — Power of the soul, the state of life. — Threefold, the Holy Trinity, or of the threefold nature, namely rational, appetitive, and spirited. — Altar, seat. Iso.

[Col. 0084A] 845. May lead, may nourish: those who are in childhood. — *Ephebes*, young men, those who are in youth, I.

846. Of age, those who are in old age, I.

849. Meets, each of these. — Divinity, the triune God, through the four sides of the house, I.

850. Arranges, ordered. — In twelves, whom he placed in a square circuit, [Col. 0084B] I.

851. Emblems, ornaments, I.

852. And souls, splendors that represent souls. — Of colors, various, I.

853. Pours forth, sent forth, Iso.

855. From here, from one side, I.

856. Honors, sapphires and beryls, I.

857. Dull, into brightness, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0083B]

836. Mariettus has *lumen*, “light”; above it, in smaller letters, *limen*, “threshold.” Revelation XXI, 11, says: “Its light was like a precious stone, like a jasper stone, clear as crystal.” Giselinus says that the poet seems to have read: “And its threshold was like the most precious stone, like jasper, crystallizing”; otherwise, he says, the poet invented the description of the gate himself. Giselinus had prefaced this by saying that scarcely anyone had adapted this allegory more correctly and elegantly. For *arcu*, Puteanus has *actu*. *Relucenti actu* is not pleasing; *arcu* is found in Mariettus, the Ratianus, the Viennese, Alexandrinus, Vatican C, D, and F, and elsewhere, apart from the old editions. The subject is the twelve gates of heavenly Jerusalem in Revelation XXI, 21: “The twelve gates are twelve pearls, each several gate being of one pearl.” Thus each gate consisted of a single enormous pearl, and the perforated pearls provided an entrance. Prudentius referred to this, not to verse 11, as Giselinus thought. See Ludovicus ab Alcazar’s commentary.

838. Some common manuscripts have *summus*; one should read *summis*.

840. This passage is understood from Paul’s words in Ephesians II, 18 and following: “For through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father. Therefore you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone. In him the whole structure, joined together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord. In him you also are built together into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit.”

[Col. 0083D] 841. The earlier Boehmer manuscript has *intrat, et electos*, “enters, and the chosen.”

842. Erfurtensis has *qua hominis*. Weitz, with Mariettus and the Ratianus, has *qua corpore*, “insofar as the body.”

843. Mariettus and the Ratianus have *vis animae*, “the power of the soul”; Weitz likewise, and therefore reads *qua corpore toto*, “insofar as the whole body.” Then the fourfold power of the soul approaches the altar of the heart. Nebrissensis interprets this fourfold power as the four ages of a human being.

845. The Egmondanus has the erroneous *seu pueros sub primus agat*.

847. Erfurtensis from the first hand has *lux alta*, “high light,” not implausibly. The two older Heinsian manuscripts, Alexandrinus from the first hand, Aldus, Mariettus, and Weitz have *borrae*; Giselinus has nearly the same, *borrhae*, and Vatican L and Angelicanus have *borreae*. Others have *boreae*, including Erfurtensis, Fabricius, the Egmondanus, and three Heinsian manuscripts. Vatican C, F, and others likewise. Widmannstetter has *borrae et boreae*; Vatican D, *borae*; the Viennese and Ratianus, *boreae*; Mariettus, *algidae borrae*. Gronovius rightly corrected the earlier reading to *algida* and orders some manuscript to be lamented, from which the displayed reading is *boreae algida sive*. The Greeks use both βόρρης and βορέας, “Boreas.” In Teolius I think *seu* is an error for *sive algida borrae*. Teolius also seems to have thought that *borreae* appeared in none of the Vatican manuscripts, which is false. *Borrae* better suits the poem, and it is also read by Paulinus in his ode to Nicetas: “The whole region of Boreas calls you father.”

848. The Viennese has *fovet* instead of *vocet*.

[Col. 0084C] 849. The better Heinsian manuscripts, with Aldus, Vatican F and L, and Vatican G from the first hand, have *nomen*. Giselinus, Weitz, Mariettus, the Ratianus, the Viennese, Alexandrinus, and Vatican C have *numen*, which Iso adopts. Heinsius thinks *nomen* more correct, and I agree. Vatican O has: “The triune divinity meets at the fourfold crossroads.”

852. A new and remarkable expression: “living souls of colors” instead of “living colors.”

853. Gifanius, in his index to Lucretius, says that Prudentius undoubtedly imitated a passage of Virgil, *Georgics* II: “If the lofty house with proud doors does not pour forth at dawn a great flood of welcoming visitors through all its rooms.” Thus light pours forth.

854. Weitz writes *chrisolitus*, because he found it in Widmannstetter. But would it not have been better to write *chrysolithus*, as in the others?

855. An exceedingly bold corrector in the Ratianus, after erasing the earlier reading, substituted *et beryllum*, so that the first syllable of *beryllum* would not be shortened. Fortunatus shortened it, as did Fridegodus in *The Life of Saint Wilfrid*, no. 46: “Immediately, after admission, a phrase shone with beryl.”

856. Fuldensis and the Palatinus have *variarat* instead of *variabat*. Heinsius printed *variarat* but, as is his habit when departing from the old editions, did not record the variant readings. Chamillard and Teolius followed Heinsius; Cellarius and Gallandius restored *variabat*.

857. The Ratisbon corrector mentioned recently again displays his ignorance: *Chalcedon hebes hinc perfunditur*. Weitz, the Heinsian manuscripts, the Palatinus, and Alexandrinus have *hic chalcedon*. Aldus, Giselinus, Mariettus, the Ratianus, the Viennese, Vatican F, Gallandius, and others have *hinc chalcedon*. See the interpreters concerning these gems.]

A gem set in a shining arch encloses the threshold,

and one stone forms the passable vestibule.

On the highest doorposts, inscribed in gold,

the names of the apostolic senate shine, twice six.

[810] Through these inscriptions the Spirit encompasses the hidden things of the mind

and calls the chosen senses into the innermost heart.

And wherever human nature flourishes, which a fourfold power

658 animates throughout the body, it approaches the altar

of the heart through three entrances and worships its sanctuary with pure vows:

[845] whether the first sun leads on boys, or excessive heat

[Col. 0084A] inflames young men, or the full light of mature age

completes men, or the cold age of Boreas

calls decrepit old age to holy rites;

the triune Name meets it at the fourfold crossroads,

[850] which the King suitably arranges for the twelve disciples.

Moreover, just as many jeweled emblems gleam, set into the walls,

and deep light pours forth living souls of colors

from its clear depths.

659 A great chrysolite, inlaid with native gold,

[855] had joined a sapphire to itself on one side, and a beryl on the other;

the intervening radiance varied their contrasting splendors.

Here a dull chalcedony is suffused by the color of hyacinth,

[Col. 0085A] [Note: [Col. 0085A]

858. Beside, near the blue pool in which this stone is found, I.

859. Pools, waters. — Stone, hyacinth. — Holding together, coagulating. — With purple, for it has a purple color, [Col. 0085B] I.

862. Appearance, colors. — Emerald-like, emeralds are green, I.

863. Has willed, makes. — Waves, splendors, I.

[Col. 0086A] 864. Structure, of stones, I.

866. Rope-hung, hanging from a rope. — Machine, house, I.

867. Heights, toward heaven: for they drew the built house toward heaven, [Col. 0086B] I.

869. Cut away, cut, I.

870. Of which, of the columns. — Pebble, crown, I.

871. Heads, summits, I.

873. Pearl, stone, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0085B]

861. The Egmondanus, Palatinus, Alexandrinus, and Puteanus have *Sardium*, which Heinsius declares can scarcely be tolerated here; he prefers *Sardoum* with the Thuaneus, since the stone is called *sardous* from Sardinia and the herb *Sardoa*. Teolius says that Heinsius printed *Sardoum* from the Royal manuscript; but it should be noted that by “Royal manuscript” Heinsius means the Puteanus, where the reading is *Sardium*. Angelicanus has *Sordonium*. Aldus and Giselinus, with Weitz, Mariettus, the Ratianus, the Viennese, and others, have *Sardonium*. In the other Rottendorf manuscript, *Sardon* is placed there. Giselinus and Fabricius have *appositus* instead of *appositum*. Gifanius defends *topazion* from an old book, through contraction; I do not deny that this could stand, but I do not agree that *topazon* is wrongly read elsewhere. Venantius Fortunatus, book I on the Virgin’s birth: “When white topaz is set in the pavements.” Perhaps Prudentius used *topazus* or *topazos* in the masculine gender.

862. Here too Weitz wished to retain the singular reading of the one Egmondanus manuscript, namely *zmaragdina*.

863. Angelicanus has *vomitque vagos*, “and pours forth wandering [waves].” The meter rejects this; *vomit* is correct. *Herbidus*, “herb-like,” is used for a grassy or green color by Ovid, Columella, Pliny, Plautus, Sidonius, Paulinus, and others.

865. The Palatinus, Vatican C, and some of the older Heinsian manuscripts have *saxis stillantibus*, “stones dripping,” but Heinsius warns that they should not be followed. Others write *chrisoprase* or *crysoprase*. Venantius Fortunatus, book III of *The Life of Saint Martin*, says: “A mantle from the shoulders, mixed with chryso-prase-beryls.” In Cangius’ *Glossary*, enlarged and illustrated by the Maurists, there is doubt whether this means “mixed with gold,” that is, with gold and prase-beryls, or whether *chrysoprasoberyllis* is a single word. In the manuscript of Saint-Germain at Paris it is read: “A mantle from the shoulders, mixed with chrysophara-beryls,” which makes the verse more obscure. I think Venantius is speaking of *chrysoprase*, but inflecting it as *chrysoprasis, -is*; accordingly the words should be divided: “mixed with chrysoprase and beryls.” Prudentius and Fortunatus differ in the quantity of the syllables, which is hardly surprising in such Greek names. In the latest Roman edition of Fortunatus it is read: “mixed with chrysoprase and beryl.” But who would believe that Venantius shortened the *o* in the ablative? 

866. After this verse there is nothing more in the copy of the Viennese library with which Mariettus compared the preceding material. He says that this fragment of the *Psychomachia* is quite corrupt and carelessly written, and that no other poems of Prudentius are found in that manuscript.

868. Virgil, *Aeneid* I, verse 641: “But the inner house,” etc. Proverbs IX, 1: “Wisdom built herself a house; she hewed out seven pillars.”

869. Weitz absurdly printed *cristalli*, as usual, relying on the authority of Widmannstetter alone, although the other manuscripts write *crystalli*. Mariettus, the Ratianus, the Palatinus, and Widmannstetter have *albentis* above. Aldus and others have *algentis*, which is preferable, since in the immediately following verse there is *calculus albens*. “Crystalline” is cold because it is said to congeal from ice. See *Cathemerinon* hymn 2, note to verse 71.

870. Heinsius, with the Egmondanus and Palatinus, has *quadrum* instead of *quarum*, namely “a square [stone] into a cone”; Heinsius also says that Barthius read this in an old manuscript. I cannot find Barthius’ passage; and although Heinsius cites from Paschasius Radbertus “under the square hinge of heaven,” and from Hericus of Auxerre, book II on the *Life of Saint Germanus*, “a square piece of wood, a square world,” I nevertheless follow all the best Heinsian manuscripts, Mariettus, the Ratianus, Alexandrinus, Vatican C, F, and G, Aldus, Giselinus, Weitz, and others, which have *quarum tegit*, etc. The sense is excellent: “the white pebble covers the raised heads of these [columns], cut into a cone.” Iso agrees with us: “*QUARUM*, of the columns.” The more recent editors—Chamillard, Cellarius, and Teolius—followed Heinsius. Gallandius, however, thought *quadrum* in Chamillard was an error.

871. The Palatinus writes *in quonum*. A cone is a summit, or one may prefer to call it a capital, since several lines rise from the circumference to a single point. Aldus and Vatican C have *sinuamina*.

872. Aldus has the error *margaritarum* instead of *margaritum*. Burmann proves from Servius, Varro, a fragment of a letter of Augustus, and others that *margaritum* is correctly used in the neuter gender. Saint Jerome often spoke in this way. From two copies of Pulmannus, Giselinus restored *opibusque, et censibus hastae addictis*, and does not think another reading in his own manuscript should be rejected: *opibusque, et viribus arcae adductis*. Heinsius approves the former with the Puteanus and Egmondanus. In the others he found *opibusque, et viribus hastae*, or *arte*, or *haustae*; hence Cauchius conjectured *opibusque, et jure sub hastae addictis*, rightly rejected by Heinsius. Weitz reads *hasta*, not *hastae*, in the Egmondanus. Fuldensis and Widmannstetter have *viribus haustae*; Erfurtensis likewise has *hausta* above, as does the Palatinus. Fabricius has *arte adductis*. Aldus has *opibus et viribus arte adductis*. In some manuscripts cited by Weitz, *arcae adductis*. Mariettus and the Ratianus have *opibusque, et viribus hauste addictis*. Alexandrinus has *opibusque, et juribus hastae addictis*, with the gloss: “*JURIBUS*, that is, of war or victory; *HASTAE*, that is, to sale or seizure.” Vatican C has *opibusque, et viribus arte adductis*; the same appears indistinctly in Vatican D. It should be noted that in old manuscripts it is often difficult to distinguish whether one should read *juribus* or *viribus*. Vatican F has *opibusque, et juribus arte additis*; likewise Vatican G from the first hand. Vatican L and BB have *opibusque, et viribus arte additis*. Of all these, *additis* must certainly be rejected, since it conflicts with the meter. Gifanius prefers, from an old book, *opibusque et viribus hastae addictis*, and says that *censibus* seems to be a gloss. Heinsius, on the contrary, thinks *censibus* very beautiful. I do not dislike *juribus*. I further think that *hastae* must unquestionably be read: in the Angelicanus there was *viribus … additis*, and the word *hastae* was missing. In the Bononiensis: *viribus astu et addictis*. On the verb *addicere*, “to sell,” see the commentary on verse 77 of hymn 2, *Peristephanon*.]

874. Salmasius, who in Julius Capitolinus, p. 90, also reads in the Puttean manuscript *opibusque, et censibus hastae addictis*, then explains what “courageous faith” means: namely, faith that spares no expense and is not at all afraid of outlay, as *animose* (“courageously”) is used of a man in the Codex Theodosianus, and *animose comparare* (“to acquire courageously”) in Suetonius. Weitz, Marolles, and Ratramnus read *parabat* (“was preparing”). Prudentius touches on the parable in Matthew 13:45–46: “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls. When he had found one precious pearl, he went away, sold everything he possessed, and bought it.” Hence it is understood what is meant by “with wealth and resources sold at auction,” namely, that the man courageous in faith sold everything he possessed and bought that pearl, that is, the kingdom of heaven.

878. The Angers manuscript has *nec arte* (“nor by art”); read *non arte*. Paschalius, *De Coronis*, book III, chapter 8, notes that lilies, roses, or both were customarily placed on sceptres.

879. Thus the Heinsian, Erfurt, Widmannstetter, Weitz, Alexandrian, Vatican O, Marolles, Ratramnus, and Bologna manuscripts. In Aldus, Giselinus, Vatican C and L: *Sed lignum vivum est, viridi quod stirpe recisum* (“But it is living wood, cut from a green stock”); Gallandius rejects this reading because verse 881 says *Fronde tamen viret incolumi* (“Yet it is green with undamaged foliage”). Fulda, Palatine: *Sed lignum vivum, viridi est quod stirpe recisum*. Vatican C: *Sed lignum vivum viride est, quod stirpe recisum*. Vatican F: *Sed lignum vivum viridi de stirpe recisum*. Angers: *Sed lignum vivum, viridi quod stirpe recisum est*. Puttean incorrectly has *recisos*; the Thuanus and Oxford manuscripts read *Sed lignum vivum viridi est, quod stirpe reciso*. Salmasius, according to Heinsius, had written in the Puttean manuscript the following passage from an old grammarian, which he thinks alluded to these lines: “*Stirps*, when it means a shoot, is feminine; but when it signifies material, it is masculine, as in *stirpem recisum*.” I do not think so. Quintilian, book I, chapter 6, says that poets may plead metrical necessity, unless they vary where nothing prevents either form from fitting the rhythm, as in the example: “Indeed, cut from the stock.” The passage is indicated as Virgil, book XII, verse 208: “Once cut in the woods from the very root.” Prudentius imitates Virgil, who also speaks of a sceptre.

881. Aldus has *tunc sanguine* (“then with blood”); the others have *tum*. Vatican C incorrectly has *te* (“you”).

882. In Widmannstetter’s manuscript above the line is *intertexta*, as in the others; in the text it is *intertecta*, which I do not know why Weitz accepted.

884. Saint Augustine compares the Lord’s cross—for this is the sceptre described up to this point—with Aaron’s rod, *Sermon* 31 in the appendix: “Therefore all the princes of the tribes must have their rods; but there is one alone, as Scripture says, the true high priest, of whom the priest Aaron bore the figure. His rod, therefore, blossomed. For just as Aaron’s rod blossomed among the Jewish people, so Christ’s cross flowered among the Gentile people.” Augustine, or rather Origen, says much else excellently on the same subject. On Aaron’s rod, see Numbers, chapter XXII. Many say that the first two syllables of *Aaron* are shortened according to the Hebrew idiom. Ricciolius believes that the second is lengthened by Prudentius because in Hebrew it is less short than the first: the second is *patach*, or a short *a*, while the first is *chatef patach*, that is, a very short *a*. More fully on this in the *Prolegomena*.

On the twelve stones: “In the jasper, therefore, the greenness of faith; in the sapphire, the height of heavenly hope; in the chalcedony, the flame of inward charity is represented. In the emerald, the strong confession of that same faith amid adversity; in the sardonyx, the humility of the saints amid virtues; in the sardius, the revered blood of the martyrs is expressed. ## THE DITTOCHAEUM. (C)

### THE OLD TESTAMENT.

665 1. Adam and Eve.

[Col. 0089C]

[Note: [Col. 0089C]

1. *Eva columba*—“Eve, a dove”; these are four-line stanzas. *Tum, primo*—“then, first,” I.]

[Note: [Col. 0089C]

1 and 2. Aldus calls this work the *Dittochaeum*, and I do not see why others have altered the title and devised a new one. In the Prague manuscript the inscription is *Dicta Prudentii Aurelii* (“Sayings of Aurelius Prudentius”); all the verses run continuously without any title. In Marolles: *Incipiunt tituli historiarum per Adam et Adam* (“Here begin the titles of the stories through Adam and Adam”; one should read “through Adam and Eve”). In Vatican A there is no title, and everything is written extremely carelessly. In Vatican B: *Tituli historiarum per Adam et Evam* (“Titles of the stories through Adam and Eve”); likewise in Ratramnus. In the Alexandrian: *Incipiunt tituli historiarum* (“Here begin the titles of the stories”); in an old but smaller character in the margin: *Iste liber Dirocheum vocatur, id est duplex refectio* (“This book is called the *Dirochaeum*, that is, double refreshment”). In the Urbinate manuscript: *Incipit liber Ditrocheus, qui continetur in titulis historiarum* (“Here begins the book *Ditrocheus*, which is contained in the titles of the stories”). In Vatican I: *Incipient tituli historiarum per Adam et Eva* (“Here begin the titles of the stories through Adam and Eve”). In Vatican Q the titles are missing. See further in the *Prolegomena*, chapters 3, 4, and 5, where Prudentius’ works are discussed. In Marolles the *Dittochaeum* is placed after the ode *Immolat Deo Patri* (“He offers sacrifice to God the Father”), which is the epilogue in Aldus and in our edition. In Vatican B it is placed after the book of the *Peristephanon*.

Chamillardus, along with others, gives it the title *Enchiridion*, and adds that some, with Fabricius, attribute this little poem to a certain unknown Amoenus, an ancient poet; others, with Sichardus, to Sedulius, because this poem is more polished than Prudentius’ other verses. Before Chamillardus, Philippus Labbeus had asserted that this poem surpassed Prudentius’ others and was therefore denied to Prudentius by many. Bailletus says the same in his *Judgments of the Learned on Prudentius*. Aldus, in the *Life of Prudentius*, testifies to the contrary: *Dittochaeum*, “double food,” from Greek *διττὸς* (*dittos*), “double,” and *ὀχή* (*ochē*), “food.” For these are the titles of stories from the Old and New Testaments, and hence I think Prudentius called this book the *Dittochaeum*, that is, “double food.” But since this book is not so cultivated and elaborated as the others composed by the poet, some say that it is not Prudentius’. I, however, have not dared to separate it from the others, both because Gennadius, who wrote after Saint Jerome concerning illustrious men, says that the *Dittochaeum* was composed by Prudentius, and also because this little book was inserted among Prudentius’ other works in a very ancient manuscript. In that manuscript the title was *DIRROCHAEUM*, through scribal error; I infer this readily because it was interpreted there in the most ancient characters as *DUPLEX REFECTIO* (“double refreshment”) instead of *DUPLEX CIBUS* (“double food”). On this ancient title in the manuscripts and its interpretation, see the *Prolegomena*, especially the whole of chapter 4.

Heinsius notes from his manuscripts: In the Oxford gloss, *Iste liber proprie Dirochaeum vocatur* (“This book is properly called the *Dirochaeum*”); in another Oxford manuscript, *Incipient tituli historiarum Aurelii Prudentii Hispaniensis, quod Dirocheum de utroque Testamento vocatur* (“Here begin the titles of the stories of Aurelius Prudentius of Spain, which is called the *Dirochaeum* from both Testaments”). In the Thuanus manuscript it is cited under the title *Historiarum* (“of the stories”) at the beginning of the work, where an index of Prudentian poems is presented. At the end of this poem: *Explicit Tituli historiarum* (“Here end the Titles of the stories”). In Cauchian: *Tetrasticha de Veteri et Novo Testamento* (“Four-line stanzas on the Old and New Testament”).

Heinsius titles it *Diptychon*, following Gifanius’ conjecture, and denies that it is Prudentius’ work; but when he says that Aldus held the same view, he is mistaken, as Aldus’ words show. From the Thuanus manuscript Heinsius extracted the headings of the four-line stanzas, since he had seen no older copy. Sichardus says that he changed the commonly received inscription of the book on the basis of old exemplars, which do not have *Dittochaeum* but *Enchiridion*. He admits that the oldest exemplars agree remarkably in assigning this work to Prudentius, but suspects that it is by Sedulius or by some Amoenus, whose name he had seen prefixed in an old manuscript at Strasbourg. He reports in the preface to all the works that this manuscript belonged to Werner Wolflin of Strasbourg. Fabricius incorrectly says that Sichardus held the view that the work was Sedulius’; Sichardus is uncertain.

But Fabricius’ opinion that, in this uncertainty, one should follow what an old book would prove, and thus assign the poem to Amoenus, is not sufficiently consistent, since he often cites verses of the *Dittochaeum* under the name of Sedulius, while on the other hand Sichardus admits that all the oldest exemplars attribute it to Prudentius. Our old exemplars, however, differ from Sichardus’ exemplars, for they have *Dittochaeum*, not *Enchiridion*. I also think that the name Amoenus became attached to Prudentius from the work itself, because someone had called it *amoenum* (“pleasant”).

Weitz, apparently from Goldastus’ manuscript, adorned the *Dittochaeum* with this inscription and ancient verses: *Prudentii Amoeni Diptychon, sive Tituli historiarum Veteris et Novi Testamenti. Incipiunt Tituli libri manualis amoeni* (“The *Diptychon* of Prudentius Amoenus, or Titles of the stories of the Old and New Testament. Here begin the Titles of the pleasant manual book”). The remaining verses are found in the *Prolegomena*, no. 244. I have no doubt that the ancient author of these verses called it *Manuale amoenum*, or “the pleasant manual book.” Someone understood this as “the manual of Amoenus,” just as a certain poet is now called *Facetus*, because the word *facetus* (“witty” or “elegant”) occurs at the beginning of an anonymous poem.

The encomium was indeed drawn from Gennadius, as can be seen in the *Prolegomena*, chapter 3, where the same words, *Exceptis personis* (“apart from the persons”), occur. In nearly the same way the designation *Enchiridion* was fabricated, because the book could easily be carried in the hand, or was a manual; and because it contains headings, or titles, of the stories, it was called *Tituli historiarum* (“Titles of the stories”). The term “four-line stanzas” is less surprising, since it is taken from the type of poem: in ancient manuscripts the metrical genre is often attached to each poem of Prudentius.

In the Ratramnus manuscript Gennadius’ encomium of Prudentius is reported; and because in Gennadius most read *Dittochaeum*, while some read *Dirocheum*, Ratramnus has *χειροχαῖον* (*chirochaion*), with the gloss *i.e. manualem librum* (“that is, a manual book”). Thus I hesitated for some time whether I should believe that *Chirochaeum* had been written by Prudentius; but I decided that *Dittochaeum* should not be changed.

This little work was often published separately, and also in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* among Prudentius’ works and under the name of Amoenus, where Heinsius warned that the poems had been interpolated. I have never found in manuscripts written by an ancient hand the title *Diptychon*, or *Diptychion*, although Gifanius suspected that it should be restored in his *Index to Lucretius*, p. 359, under the word *MARE MAGNUM*, because the law makes frequent mention of *diptychon* and *diptychion*—not because he had found this reading, or a trace of it, in ancient parchment, as Cellarius asserted. For Gifanius says that in the old book and in Gennadius’ *Life of Prudentius* the forms are *Dittocheum, Dirocheum,* and *Chirocheum*.

Giselinus likewise acknowledged that some called it *Chirocheum*, which they translated as “manual”; but on the authority of his own manuscript and another belonging to Buslidius he preferred the title *Tetrasticha de Veteri et Novo Testamento* (“Four-line stanzas on the Old and New Testament”), whose parallels are found in Ausonius and others.

I have taken the glosses of this little work from the *Biblical Manual of Holy Scripture*, published in 1610; see the *Prolegomena*, chapter 4. Although Joannes Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina vetus*, book III, chapter 2, no. 20, asserts that these glosses are found in Weitz’ Prudentius, that is false. Weitz, unaware of the glosses that had already been published, took a few from a manuscript, as becomes clear to anyone who compares the two sets. Labbeus, in *Nova Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*, p. 64, praises a manuscript of this Prudentian work that was more accurately corrected than Goldastus’ *Tetrasticha* in the *Biblical Manual*.

You can observe that several painted images of the things Prudentius describes survive on the tombs of ancient Christians in volume III of the *Christian Antiquities* of the most learned Father Thomas Maria Mamachi, pp. 30 and following, where he supplies explanations and interpretations. Barthius, chapter 12 of book VIII of the *Adversaria*, argues from many similar passages that Prudentius is the author of the *Dittochaeum*; from him we shall derive benefit by adding several further points.

Eve is first called a white dove and then a black one, as in the *Psychomachia*, verse 787: “God himself gives them to the snowy doves.” For what Barthius says—that elsewhere Prudentius said of Paul, “to change ravens into doves”—appears in the *Dittochaeum* itself, verse 192. See Genesis, chapter 2.

Many write *anguinum* in verse 2, others *anguineum*. Prudentius used this word more than once. For *malesuada*, the Vatican manuscripts N, Y, Z, AA, BB, and CC have *malesuasa*, which I shall certainly not follow.]

Eve was a dove, first white, then black,

[Col. 0090C] 666 Made so by the venom of the serpent’s evil counsel,

4. Teolius found in one Vatican manuscript: *Mox draco dat nudis ficulnea tegmina victor* (“Then the victorious dragon gives the naked ones fig-leaf coverings”). In the Vallicellian manuscript: *dat nudis ficulnea mox draco tegmina victor*. Barthius observes that this is not from the sacred text but from a Jewish interpretation, according to which the dragon, or Satan, wove fig-leaf coverings for Adam and Eve. But on behalf of our poet it may be answered that his words are *dat victor draco tegmina* (“the victorious dragon gives coverings”), not because he himself wove them, but because he was the cause of sin, from which the fig-leaf coverings followed.

Title 2 is absent from Vatican B. In Vatican A, D, and Alexandrian: *Abel et Cain* (“Abel and Cain”). In Marolles, Ratramnus, and Vatican I: *Cain et Abel* (“Cain and Abel”). Aldus and Thuanus: *De Abel et Cain* (“On Abel and Cain”). In the Vallicellian manuscript no titles are prefixed to the four-line stanzas. See Genesis IV.

6. Goldastus has *occipiens* (“beginning”), which I think is an error for *accipiens* (“receiving”). On this story Prudentius speaks in the preface to the *Hamartigenia*, where verse 5 reads: “Here one serves the terrifying things, the other the living.” In the hymn *On Funerals*, the flesh is called earthly and the spirit living; in the *Hamartigenia*, the flesh is represented and explained by the example of Cain.

Title 3 in Vatican B and I, Marolles, Ratramnus, and Thuanus: *Arca Noe* (“Noah’s Ark”). In Vatican A and Aldus, with Alexandrian: *De Noe et diluvio* (“On Noah and the Flood”). In Vatican D: *De arca Noe et diluvio* (“On Noah’s Ark and the Flood”). See Genesis, chapter VIII.]

[5] God, by discriminating authority, assesses the sacred offerings

Of the two brothers, accepting what is living and rejecting what is earthly.

The form of the soul is represented; our flesh is in Cain’s offering.
