12. Heinsius, *Adversaria posthuma*, book I, chapter 6, wishes *ratae* to be corrected to *datae*. No correction is necessary. Teolius, commenting on the word *haeserat* (“had clung”), notes that Prudentius read according to the Septuagint: “which [the raven] went out and did not return.” But why not according to the Vulgate, which reads the same way?

Title 4 in Giselinus and Thuanus: *Hex Mambre*. Vatican B and I, Ratramnus, Marolles, and Weitz: *Ad ilicem Mambre* (“At the oak of Mamre”). Alexandrian: *De Abraham et hospitio ejus* (“On Abraham and his hospitality”). Vatican D: *De hospitio Sarae* (“On Sarah’s hospitality”). Aldus: *De Abraham et hospitio* (“On Abraham and his hospitality”). See Genesis, chapter XVIII.

13. Vatican A incorrectly has *haec* (“this [feminine]”) instead of *hoc* (“this”). Teolius notes that *hoc* is missing in one Vatican manuscript, and it is likewise absent from the Vallicellian. Several interpreters think that Abraham received the Lord himself, not angels, as a guest, and recognize here the mystery of the Holy Trinity. Prudentius holds the same view in the *Apotheosis*, verses 28 and following, where Abraham is called Christ’s host, that is, the host of the Word.

14. Vatican A incorrectly has *armentalis enim* (“for herding”); Ratramnus, Weitz, and Goldastus in Weitz’ edition above have *praetexit* (“covered over”). Prague: *praetexit*. Marolles: *pertexit* (“wove over”). Aldus, Giselinus, Urbinate: *protexit* (“protected”). Goldastus in the *Biblical Manual*: *pertexit*, which Weitz also reported in the text from that same Goldastus. Alexandrian likewise has *pertexit*, to omit the others. *Culmen* (“roof” or “summit”) is sometimes used for a poor cottage, as in Virgil, *Eclogue* 1: “the roof of the poor hut piled up with turf.” Compare the note on hymn 1 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 14, “standing beneath that roof.”

15. In the Vallicellian, *gaudia tarda* (“late joys”), and, as a variant reading, *sera* (“late”).

Title 5. Most of the best manuscripts have *Monumentum Sarae* (“Sarah’s Monument”) as title 5, although some write *Sarrae*. Vatican D: *De Abraam et agro empto* (“On Abraham and the purchased field”). Aldus: *Abraham agrum emisse* (“Abraham bought a field”). Genesis XXIII.

17. Weitz and Giselinus, with the Palatine and Goldastus in Weitz’ edition, have *mercatur* (“buys”). Nearly all manuscripts have *mercatus* (“having bought”), but in some the substantive verb *est* is incorrectly added, since *mercatus agrum* (“having bought the field”) is by epexegesis. Against the metre I reject *mercatus est agrum*, which Teolius found in one Vatican manuscript. Heinsius, with Thuanus, Egmond, and some others, has *cui conderet* (“in which he might bury”), as Aldus printed. Most of ours have *quo* (“where”), as Marolles, Ratramnus, Prague, Vallicellian, and Vatican I and Y. Vatican D has *in quo* (“in which”). Other manuscripts nevertheless have *cui*, such as Alexandrian and Vatican A. In some of our manuscripts *mercatur* is also found in a second hand, namely Marolles and Ratramnus. Teolius printed *quo*, but in his notes on this verse and on verse 105 of the *Psychomachia* he seems to prefer *cui*.

[Col. 0094B] 18. Vatican A and Palatine incorrectly have *moratus* (“having delayed”).

19. In one Vatican manuscript, according to Teolius: *hoc illi millibus emptum* (“this, bought by him for thousands”).

20. The Vallicellian, against the metre, has *sepulcrum* (“tomb”) instead of *spelaeum* (“cave”). *Favilla* (“ashes”) is elsewhere also used by the poet for the remains of the dead, whose bodies are not burned. See the *Cathemerinon* hymn *Omni ora*, verse 100, and the hymn *On Funerals*, verse 142.

Title 6 is *Somnium Pharaonis* (“Pharaoh’s Dream”) in most manuscripts. Aldus: *Pharao somnium vidisse* (“Pharaoh saw a dream”). Vatican D: *De somno Pharaonis* (“On Pharaoh’s dream”). Consult Genesis, chapter XLI, and *Cathemerinon* hymn 6, verse 57.

21. Ratramnus, Prague, Goldastus in Weitz, and one Vatican manuscript reported by Teolius have *spicae et vaccae* (“ears of grain and cows”), which Weitz retained. In the others: *spicae, vaccae* (“ears of grain, cows”). Vallicellian: *spicae et totidem vaccae* (“ears of grain and just as many cows”).

22. Giselinus in the margin has *portendunt visae per somnum* (“the things seen in sleep signify”). Sichardus reads likewise.

23. In the Bongarsian and Vatican I, *tum* (“then”) instead of *duo* (“two”). In Marolles also *dum* or *tum* appears above *duo*. For *uberis*, Vatican A has the erroneous *verberis*.

24. This is also very frequently used by Prudentius, who puts Christ for God and for the divine Word. See *Cathemerinon* hymn 4, verse 68.

The heading of title 7 in most manuscripts is *A fratribus agnitus Joseph* (“Joseph recognized by his brothers”), or *Joseph a fratribus agnitus* (“Joseph recognized by his brothers”); the latter form is found in Vatican B and I, Alexandrian, Marolles, Ratramnus. In Vatican D: *De Josephi venditione a fratribus* (“On Joseph’s sale by his brothers”). Consult Genesis, chapter XXXVII.

25. Vatican B has *venditur* (“is sold”).

26. Vatican A incorrectly has *in terris sacco* (“in an earthly sack”). Fabricius and the Palatine: *Cratera in fratris sacro* (“the cup in the brother’s sacred [thing]”). Weitz retains *crateram* (“cup”) with the Urbinate. Giselinus, with Goldastus in the *Biblical Manual* and many old manuscripts, has *cratera*. Aldus also has *cratera*, and Weitz cites it as *pro fratris sacco* (“for the brother’s sack”); in my copy it reads *in farris sacco* (“in a sack of grain”). The more recent Vatican manuscripts, such as D, N, AA, and others, have *in fratris sacco* (“in the brother’s sack”). Others have *farris sacco*, such as I and Q. In Vatican D and the Vallicellian: *in sacco fratris* (“in the brother’s sack”). Vatican B, Marolles, Ratramnus, and Prague: *Crateram in farris sacco* (“the cup in a sack of grain”).

[Col. 0094D] 27. The Heinsian manuscripts, Marolles in the first hand, Urbinate, Alexandrian, Vatican A and I, Weitz, Giselinus in the margin, and the Vallicellian have *auctio fallax* (“a deceptive sale”), a reading supported by the words of the following verse, *veniaque pudescunt* (“and they are ashamed of the pardon”), namely, pardon granted by Joseph for the sale or auction of himself, which was then disclosed and revealed. Vatican B, D, N, and Q, Marolles in the second hand, Ratramnus, Prague, Widmannstetter, and others read *actio fallax* (“a deceptive action”), understanding an action by which Joseph for some time deceived his brothers, who were unaware of what had happened.]

33. *Tutus agit*—“acts protected.” *Vel per mare, vel etiam*—“either across the sea, or also,” I.

37. *Montis apex*—“the summit of Sinai,” I.

38. *Saxorum pagina*—“the tablets,” I.

28. Giselinus in the margin has *veniaque pudescunt*, with most manuscripts; in the text, *vanique pudescunt*. Prudentius used this verb in *Cathemerinon* hymn 2, verse 26, and in the *Apotheosis*, verse 776. Teolius notes from one Vatican manuscript *veniamque petiscunt* instead of *petissunt* or *petessunt*, with the gloss *poscunt* (“they ask”). In the Vallicellian, incorrectly, *veniamque poscunt* (“and they ask for pardon”), whose gloss *petunt cum pudore* (“they seek with shame”) seems to have been made for *pudescunt*.

[Col. 0095C] Title 8 in nearly all manuscripts: *Ignis in rubo* (“Fire in the bush”). Aldus: *Mosem rubum vidisse ardentem* (“Moses saw the bush burning”). The event is narrated in Exodus, chapters III and IV.

29. *Deus igneus* (“fiery God”) is a Prudentian expression, as in the *Cathemerinon* hymn *Circa exsequias*: “Fiery God, source of souls,” and often elsewhere. Compare the note on verse 1 of that hymn. Our poet treated this same story in *Cathemerinon* hymn 5, verses 31 and following, where similar phrases occur. See also the *Apotheosis*, verses 55 and following: “Yet I shall feel,” and so forth.

Title 9, *Iter per mare* (“Journey across the sea”), in the manuscripts and printed editions. Aldus: *Pharaonem in mari submersum* (“Pharaoh drowned in the sea”). One may read Exodus, chapter XIV.

33. The same poet has in *Cathemerinon* hymn 4, verse 46: “O ever-secure piety and faith.” Cyprian, in the final part of his letter to Donatus, praises a mind steadfast toward God and secure faith; Gronovius needlessly troubles this passage in *Ecclesiastical Observations*, chapter 3, for *fides tuta* (“secure faith”) is said quite correctly. *Mare magnum* (“great sea”) occurs frequently among poets, borrowed from Greek; on it see Gifanius, *Index to Lucretius*, under *MARE MAGNUM*. This is the celebrated title of a certain ancient bull, and now of a recent Italian poem in Rome. The Vallicellian reads *vel per mare Rubrum* (“either across the Red Sea”), which is a gloss.

34. Vatican A incorrectly has *scissum* instead of *scissim*. Bongarsian has *sensim* (“gradually”). In the hymn of Saint Vincent, verse 842: “The Red Sea to open wide.”

35. Aldus, Prague, Alexandrian, and Vallicellian have *rapidos* (“swift”); the others *rabidos* (“raging”).

In title 10 the heading is *Moses accepit legem* (“Moses received the law”) in Alexandrian, Vatican B and I, Marolles, Ratramnus, and Weitz; in Giselinus and others, *accipit* (“receives”). Aldus: *Mosi legem datam* (“The law given to Moses”). Reread Exodus, chapters XIX and XX, and *Cathemerinon* hymn 7, verses 36 and following.

37. The Vallicellian has *Montis fumat apex* (“the summit of the mountain smokes”).

39. An error in Vatican A: *rejussit* instead of *revisit* (“he revisited”).

40. Egmond and Vatican A incorrectly have *vitulis* (“calves”), since the form of a calf was God for the Hebrews.

Title 11: *Manna et coturnices* (“Manna and quails”). Aldus: *Manna in deserto datum* (“Manna given in the desert”). The story is found in Exodus, chapter XVI, and in the *Psychomachia*, verse 374, where nearly the same words, “angelic food” and “tents,” occur.

44. The Tornesian manuscript has *conjecta coturnix* (“a quail having been cast”). Many of these titles are included in *Cathemerinon* hymn 5. In that hymn, verses 101 and following, he speaks of the cloud of quails, which he recounts here again.

[Col. 0096C] The heading of title 12: *Serpens aeneus in eremo* (“The bronze serpent in the wilderness”). Others have *aereus* (“of bronze”). So in Ratramnus, but in a recent hand, the earlier writing having been erased. Aldus should be corrected from *in remo* to *in eremo*. Consult Numbers, chapter XXI.

45. Aldus has *Aspide sicca malo via defervebat eremi*; Ratramnus, in a recent hand with the earlier writing erased, has exactly the same. Such emendations are owed to those foolish correctors who boldly correct what they do not understand. They did not wish the second syllable of *eremi* to be shortened, and for that reason introduced a new verse. In the recent hand of Vatican B, *acris* was made from *atris*, and the verse is punctuated: *Fervebat via sicca eremi serpentibus; acris, Jamque venenati* (“The dry way of the wilderness was burning with serpents; fierce, and now poisonous”).

46. In the Urbinate, Palatine, and some others: *per vulnera livida* (“through livid wounds”).

48. Vatican A has *virus qui temperet* (“the poison which he may restrain”). Vatican B has *qui verus*, but this was made from *qui virus*. Vatican I and Weitz: *virus ut temperet* (“so that he may restrain the poison”). The more common reading is *qui virus temperet* (“which may restrain the poison”).

Title 13: *Lacus myrrhae in eremo* (“The pool of myrrh in the wilderness”) in Vatican B, Marolles, Ratramnus, Weitz, and Thuanus. Some write *heremo*, as in Vatican I. Giselinus has *Lacus deserti amarus* (“The bitter pool of the wilderness”). Aldus: *Moses aquas amaras per lignum in dulcedinem vertit* (“Moses turned bitter waters into sweetness through wood”). Alexandrian: *Lacus amara in eremo* (“The bitter pool in the wilderness”).

See Exodus, chapter XV, and *Cathemerinon* hymn 5, *On the New Light*, verse 93. In the cited passage of Exodus, verse 23, it says: “And they came to Marah, and they could not drink the waters of Marah, because they were bitter; therefore he gave the place an appropriate name, calling it Marah, that is, bitterness.” Hence the Alexandrian inscription: *Lacus amara*, perhaps *Lacus Mara*; in others, *myrrha*, because myrrh is bitter.

Saint Paulinus, letter 27 to Victricius: “By which letters, our mind, bitter from sins, like that myrrh in Moses’ hand through the wood of mystery, etc.” And in *Natalis* 8: “By the image of the cross he changed the sad myrrh, with the sweetness of the sacred wood, into a drink for the people”; and shortly afterward: “As the sad things of myrrh, the poet changes the human being.” Prudentius uses *tristificos* (“saddening”), *contristare* (“to make sorrowful”), both here and elsewhere, to signify “bitter.” See Rosweidus’ note on Paulinus, p. 869.]

54. *Vitreo*—“clear,” Iso.

55. *Septenas decies*—“seventy,” Iso.

56. *Pinxit*—“figures,” I.

[Col. 0098B] 62. *Meretrix*—elsewhere *meritrix*. *Tanta fidei vis*—“such is, or was, the power of faith,” I.

51. A Vatican manuscript used by Teolius has *gurgite in isto* (“in this whirlpool”), which is also found in the Vallicellian.

52. Most ancient manuscripts write *conicite*, not *conjicite*; the latter is now the more common spelling. Vatican I has *concite*, and above it *et*, making *concite, et in dulcem*. Bongarsian: *Concite, et in dulces vertentur amara sapores* (“Pour them together, and the bitter things will be turned into sweet flavors”). One should read *conjicite*. Fabricius: *Conjicite, in dulces vertentur amara sapores* (“Throw them in; the bitter things will be turned into sweet flavors”).

Title 14 in Vatican B: *Helim locus in eremo* (“Elim, a place in the wilderness”). So also Alexandrian, Marolles, and Vatican I, with Weitz and others. Ratramnus and Thuanus: *Helim lucus in eremo* (“Elim, a grove in the wilderness”). Aldus: *De XII fontibus et LXXX palmis* (“On the twelve springs and eighty palms”; one should read LXX, seventy). Giselinus: *Fontes duodecim, et palmae septuaginta* (“Twelve springs and seventy palms”). See Exodus, chapter XV.

53. Aldus has *Mosi duce* (“with Moses as leader”); others *Mose duce* or *Moyse duce*. Teolius has *Moysi duce*, whether deliberately I do not know.]

55. Aldus had printed *qui mysticus aelim* (“which mystical Elim”); he corrected it to *qui mysticus olim* (“which was formerly mystical”), though it would have been better not to emend it. It should indeed be written *Helim*; but Egm. has *aelim*, and others *Elim*, which I accept with the Vulgate edition of Holy Scripture.

[Col. 0097C] 56. Egm. has *locus* (“place”). The meter requires *lucus* (“grove”). The apostolic number is signified by the twelve springs; the number of the disciples, which may in some sense be called apostolic, by the seventy palms. In the Vulgate it is indeed read that there were seventy-two disciples; but the Greek text has only ἑβδομήκοντα, “seventy.” On this controversy see Brugensis on Luke 10:1 and the sacred critics. We prefer the Vulgate reading and defend the neglect of the smaller number by Prudentius and others. Saint Ildefonsus, chapter 9, *On the Journey through the Desert*, in volume I of the Toledan Fathers, p. 236:

> From there one comes to twelve springs of sweet waters and seventy palms, which show us the twelve apostles and the seventy disciples, etc.

Ildefonsus has other material that could illuminate the *Dittochaeum*. Compare Isidore, *Questions on Exodus*, chapter 21, and what Saint Martin of León copies from him in sermon 2, *On the Nativity of the Lord*, §20, pp. 297 ff., volume I of his works, [Col. 0097D] which, illustrated with notes from the autograph, was published at Segovia in 1782 by the most eminent Lord Don Francisco Antonio de Lorenzana, archbishop of Toledo, primate of Spain, who had rendered the greatest services to the Church through his own published writings and those of others, and who, as we publish this, has now deservedly and amid the highest acclaim of all been admitted into the sacred college of cardinals.

In title 15, *Twelve stones in the Jordan*, which appears in Vatt. B and I, Alex., Mar., Rat., Thuan., and others, Giselinus has *Twelve stones in the Jordan*. Aldus: *The sons of Israel cross the Jordan and collect stones from it*. See Joshua, chapter 4, and *Cath. hymn* 12, verse 177, where the river is said to flow backward, and *Hamartig.* verse 482: “If the banks of the receding Jordan.”

58. Wid. has *populus* (“people”), incorrectly, instead of *populis* (“peoples”). Vat. B, Rat., Mar., Prag., Weitz., Urb., and Vat. I have *reliquit* (“left”). [Col. 0098B] Aldus, Alex., Gis., and others have *relinquit* (“leaves”).

60. Sich., Gisel. in the margin, Fabr., Egm., and Bong. above have *ad formam* (“in the form”); Vall. has *in forma* (“in form”).

Title 16: *The house of Rahab the prostitute*; Thuan. has *Rahab the prostitute*. Giselinus: *The house of Rahab*. Aldus: *Rahab received the spies at Jericho*. Joshua, chapter 2.

61. Ald., Fabr., and Gisel. in the margin have *sola astant* (“the halls alone stand”); the others, more correctly, *sola stant*. Giselinus considers this similar to the poetic license in *via sicca eremi* above, verse 45, but he is mistaken; because of the *st* of the following word, the preceding short vowel is often lengthened.

62. Some ancient copies write *meritrix*. Giselinus thinks that this verse may be inverted, against the authority of all the manuscripts, as follows: *vis tanta fidei est* (“so great is the power of faith”), although Prudentius always shortened the second syllable elsewhere. The manuscripts consistently read *tanta est fidei vis* (“so great is the power of faith”), except Goldastus, who in his *Biblical Manual* reads *tanta fidei vis*. Paulinus lengthened the second syllable more than once, and in a closely parallel passage [Col. 0098C] in the poem *On Saint John the Baptist* has:

> *Auscultat nato genitrix* (“The mother listens to her son”) *(vis tanta fidei)*.

I would read it thus in Prudentius if he had ever lengthened the *e* in *fidei*, or if the manuscripts permitted it. Carolus Cangius notes that in the *Office of Cicero* he praises the hemistich *levisque fidei* (“and of light faith”) and criticizes the pedants who dared to change *fidei quoque plenus* (“also full of faith”). No such hemistich appears in the surviving works of Prudentius. Parrhasius, at verse 428 of the *Passion of Romanus*, reads:

> *Aliter precabor, quam fidei ut militent* (“I shall pray otherwise, that they may serve faith”);

but the manuscripts and other printed editions that I have seen have *fidele* (“faithful”). Iso, in Goldastus’s glosses, reads *tanta fidei vis* or *vis tanta fidei*, for he adds *est, vel erat* (“is, or was”) as a gloss.

63. Weitz., Ald., Gis., Vall., and many others commonly have *incolumi secura domo* (“with the house safe and secure”), together with Alex. in its first hand. Goldastus, cited by Weitz., Vat. B, Urb., Rat., and Mar. in its first hand have *incolumis secura domus* (“the safe, secure house”), and in Vat. B there is a gloss explaining that *domus* is a genitive: either that Rahab is “safe because of the uninjured house,” or that the uninjured house was to be preserved. In Prag. there is *Incolumis, secura domo*, which Mar. has in its second hand. The poet calls the scarlet cord, by which the spies were lowered from the window, “conspicuous crimson”; see the cited chapter of Joshua.

Title 17. Ald., Vat. B, Mar., Rat.: *Samson*. In Thuan.: *Samson kills the lion*. Gis. and Weitz.: *The lion of Samson*. In Vat. A this quatrain is missing, as also in Vat. I. It was likewise absent from Alex., but is supplied at the bottom of the page. Barthius considers it attributable to Prudentius, although he did not find it in his own manuscript. It is also absent from Egm. and from the Palatine manuscript cited by Weitz. The history is set out in Judges, chapters 14 and 15.

67. Ald., Weitz., Heins., Teol. have *asinae* (“of the she-ass”); others have *asini* (“of the ass”), which is more correct, for in this passage sacred Scripture often calls it an ass, not a she-ass.]

Moses the holy says: “Give wood; into this flood

throw it: bitter things will be turned into sweet flavor.”

The men came, under Moses’ leadership, where six springs

and perhaps six others watered seventy palms with glassy dew.

in its books.

With its current flowing backward, the Jordan left dry for God’s peoples the fords to be trodden.

[Col. 0098A] Twice six stones bear witness, which the fathers

set up in the very river, in the form of the disciples.

The prostitute who welcomed the holy men—so great is the power of faith—

[65] Samson, unconquered in the strength of his hair, attacks

the lion and breaks it; he kills the beast, but from the lion’s mouth

honey flows; the ass’s jaw freely pours forth a spring.

70. *Pone faces* (“place torches”), *post* (“behind”), *juxta* (“beside”), I.

71. *Vulpis* (“of a fox”) instead of *vulpes* (“foxes”), I.

68. It is well known that stupidity is signified by the ass.

The title of quatrain 18 is also *Samson* in Vat. B, Mar., and Rat. Aldus: *On Samson*. Giselinus: *Samson’s foxes*. Thuan.: *Samson catches foxes*. Alex.: *Samson*. Read Judges, chapter 15.

[Col. 0099C] 69. Egm. has, incorrectly, *trecentum* (“three hundred”).

71. Prudentius uses the word *allophylus* in *Hamartig.* verse 500. See the notes. Here it stands for the Philistines. Aldus, so that the first syllable of *heresis* would not be short, altered these verses:

> “He burns the foreigner and the crops; now heresy,  
> the cunning fox, scatters the fires of vices  
> into the fields.”

The manuscripts and Prudentius’ usage protest against this: he always shortens the first syllable of *heresis*. For *vulpes*, some have *vulpis*, as has often been said. Fabr. has *quae callida vulpes* (“which cunning fox”).

Title 19. *David* in Rat., Mar., Vatt. B and I, Weitz. and others. Aldus: *David, shepherd of sheep, rises to be king*. Thuan.: *David fells Goliath*. Giselinus: *David the shepherd*. Read 1 Samuel, chapters 16 and 17.

73. Vat. A has *Jessem*; *Jesse* is better.

74. Weitz. notes from Egm. this variant reading, *olive*; I call it an error for *ovile* (“sheepfold”).

Quatrain 20. *The kingdom of David* in Mar., Rat., Vatt. B and I, Weitz. and others. Aldus: *David is anointed king*. Thuan.: *On the kingdom of David*. Giselinus: *David the king*. In Alex. this title and several others following are missing.

B and Q, Mar., Prag., Rat., Urb., Vall., together with Ald., Weitz., Giselinus, and many others. The latter reading could therefore be retained, although I do not deny that the poet sometimes used *mitificus*. Paschalius, *On Crowns*, p. 47, book I, chapter 15, praises these verses.

78. Mar. and Vat. I have *oleum, et cornu* (“oil, and horn”); others have *oleum, cornu*, without *et*.

Title 21 is *The building of the temple* in Vatt. B and I, [Col. 0100C] Mar., Rat., Gis., Thuan., and Weitz. Aldus: *Solomon builds the temple, and the queen of the South brings gifts*. See 1 Kings, chapters 6 and 10.

83. Egm. has *sub tempore Christum* (“Christ beneath time”). Vat. A has *sub pectore Christum* (“Christ beneath the breast”). The correct reading is *sub pectore Christus* (“Christ beneath the breast”).

Aldus, Gis. in the text, Palatine, Alex. have *quod Graia colant, quod barbara ditent* (“which Greeks may worship, which barbarians may enrich”), and in Alex. there is the gloss *GRAIA*, that is, “Greek.” From the Egmond manuscript Weitz. cites *quod la*, perhaps *quod dia*, for in Vat. A there is *quo dia colant, quo barbara ditent*, whose meaning I do not understand. In Vat. N: *Quo Gaza colat, quo barbara ditent*, with the gloss *Quo*, that is, “in which temple.” Urb., Vatt. B, I, Q, Iso, and others, together with Weitz., have *Quod Gaza colat, quod barbara ditent* (“which Gaza may worship, which barbarians may enrich”). Mar. and Rat. agree. In Prag.: *quod Gaza colit, quod barbara ditent*. Gis. in the margin and Goldastus in the *Biblical Manual*: *quod Gaza colentum barbara ditet*. Weitz. reports that this very reading occurs in Aldus; it does not, however, appear thus in my edition. Sichardus has *quod Gaza colant, quod barbara ditent*. In Vall.: *quod Gaza colat, quo [Col. 0100D] barbara dicet*, with the gloss *sanctificet* (“may sanctify”). But *dicet*, from *dico, dicas*, is incompatible with the poem. Gallandius thought *Gaza* was an error.

89. This word too, *peccamen* (“sin”), has the flavor of Prudentius.

90. Teolius observed *ad arces* (“toward the citadels”) in one Vatican manuscript. But *ad amnes* (“by the rivers”) is correct, from the psalm cited. On this hemistich, “by the rivers of dreadful Babylon,” see the prolegomena, no. 74, in the note.

Vat. I has the same. Others distinguish the passage better: *praecepta recusat, Organaque* (“he refuses the commands, and the instruments”).]

[Col. 0101C] Title 24. Weitz., Mar., Vatt. B and I: *The house of Hezekiah*. Giselinus: *The house of King Hezekiah*. Aldus: *On King Hezekiah*. Thuan.: *On King Hezekiah*. In Rat. there is no title. 95. Aldus, Alex., Egm., and Gisel. have *quod gradibus, quos vespera texerat umbra* (“which he showed by the steps that evening had covered with shadow”). Giselinus observes that it had previously been read *tot gradibus quot* (“as many steps as”), as though he himself had first restored the reading that Aldus had already printed. Vatt. B and N, Urb., Mar., Prag., Rat., and others have *tot gradibus quot*. Alex. agrees with Giselinus. Heins. has *umbram* (“shadow”); others followed him.

After this quatrain, Vat. B and Mar. have: *Here begins [the section] on the New Testament*. Vat. I, Weitz., and Rat.: *The Old Testament ends. The New Testament begins. Mary and the angel Gabriel*. In Aldus only: *This is the Advent of the Lord*. In Thuan.: *The New Testament. The Annunciation of the Lord*. Giselinus: *The New Testament. Gabriel to Mary*. Others differ. What follows, up to title 39, is expounded in *Cath. hymns* 9, 11, and 12, and *Apoth.* verses 650 ff. I shall indicate only the Gospel chapters. The Annunciation of the Lord is related in Luke, chapter 1.

100. Prudentius also used this same quantity for *Maria* (“Mary”) in *Apoth.* verse 643 and *Psych.* verse 88. In Rat., by a different and recent hand, after the earlier text was erased, there is the extremely inept reading *O Maria, implebit*. Prudentius seems in the words of Luke to take the Holy Spirit for the Word, as I shall explain more fully at verse 266 of book II of the *Symmachus*.

Aldus had correctly printed *Sancta Bethlem caput est orbis, quae protulit Iesum* (“Holy Bethlehem is the head of the world, which brought forth Jesus”); in a second revision he incorrectly changed it to *quae protulit ipsum* (“which brought forth him”). Prudentius more than once made the first two syllables of *Iesus* into one long syllable. Some write *Bethlehem* instead of *Bethlem*, which I do not criticize, since synizesis may occur.

110. Ald., Pal., and others have *de virgine* (“from the Virgin”); Mar., Rat., Vat. I, Weitz., and others have *ex virgine* (“from the Virgin”). Giselinus has *e virgine*.

The title of quatrain 29 is *Infants are killed in Bethlehem*. So Rat., Ald., Alex., and Thuan. In Vat. I and Goldastus’s *Biblical Manual*: *Infants are killed in Bethlehem*. Giselinus: *The slaughter of infants in Bethlehem*. Vat. B and Mar.: *The killing of infants in Bethlehem*. Weitz.: *Children are killed in Bethlehem*. You have the history in Matthew, chapter 2.

113. In Thuan. there is *caedibus noctis* (“by the slaughter of the night”), emended to *actis* (“deeds”). Others have *hostis* (“enemy”). Herod is also called an impious enemy by Sedulius in the alphabetic hymn *A solis ortus cardine*: *Hostis Herodes impie* (“Impious enemy Herod”), for which we now recite *Crudelis Herodes, Deum Regem venire quid times?* (“Cruel Herod, why do you fear God the King’s coming?”), so that the meter may scan. But, as I noted elsewhere in the *Hymnodia Hispanica*, it could more sweetly be restored as *Herodes hostis impie* (“Herod, impious enemy”); perhaps Sedulius wrote it so. Fabricius certainly printed it so in the Christian poets, but, I think, on Erasmus’s conjecture, not on the authority of the manuscripts.]

117. *Perfudit fluvio* (“he drenched in the river”), understand “the people,” I.

121. *Pinna* (“pinnacle”), “the holy Church,” or *penna* (“wing”), as in Maximus, who gives the example *qui ambulas super pennas* (“who walk upon wings”), I.

[Col. 0104A] 122. *Angulus* (“corner”), “the spiritual sense”; the Church itself, because Golgotha is in the Church, or rather Christ, I.

125. *Auspice*, “under a favorable sign,” I.]

115. Prudentius often uses the word *lacteolus* (“milky”); in a similar passage, verse 699 of the *Passion of Romanus*:

> “And let the tender back be cut by hard blows,  
> so that more milk than blood may flow from it.”

Juvenal, satire 11, has of a kid: “which has more milk than blood.” Ausonius, *On Oysters*, letter 7: “the flesh indicates milky blood.” Hartmann of Saint Gall, in his feast of the Holy Innocents, imitated our poet: “Hail, feast adorned with milky blood.”

116. Prag. has *udis* (“wet”) instead of *calidis* (“hot”).

Title 30, *Christ is baptized*, from Vatt. B and I, Mar., Rat., and Alex. In Aldus: *Christ is baptized in the Jordan*. The same in Giselinus. Thuan.: *Christ is baptized*. Read Matthew, chapter 3.

117. Mar., Rat., Vallic., Vat. I, Alex. in its first hand, and Thuan. have *perfudit* (“drenched”), which Weitz. adopted from his manuscripts. Others have *perfundit* (“drenches”). Barthius observes that Prudentius imitated both the syllable and the subject from the hymn *Of Those Who Fast*, in the words *pastus Baptista locustis* (“the Baptist fed on locusts”). Certainly; but why should he have pronounced *locustis* with a different quantity? Juvencus likewise has in book I: *Arvis qui solitus ruralibus esse locustas* (“who was accustomed to be [among] locusts in rural fields”). In the *Copa* of the unknown author, or of Virgil, it was read: *Nunc vero in gelida sede locusta sedet* (“But now the locust sits in a cold seat”). Burmannus, volume I of the *Anthology*, p. 716, together with others, wants *lacerta* (“lizard”) to be read, but gives no reason why the *o* in *locusta* should be long. Fabricius, in his *Commentary on the Christian Poets*, says that those who think *locustae* were the Spanish *ragustae* have not yet proved it. Fabricius perhaps meant to say *langostas*, for among Spaniards there is no such word as *ragustas*.

118. Goldastus, in the *Biblical Manual*, has *silvarum favis* (“with the honeycombs of the forests”), without the conjunction *que*, which the meter requires. Aldus is also wrong with *amictu* (“with the clothing”) instead of *amictus* (“clothed”), and Vat. A ridiculously has *camilli* instead of *cameli* (“camels”).

119. Teolius reported *tinxit* (“he dipped”) instead of *tin[x]erat* (“he had dipped”) from one Vatican manuscript. But the meter does not allow *tinxit*.

120. One Vatican manuscript cited by Teolius has *qui cunctis* (“who for all”), which I find in Vallic.

Title 31, *The pinnacle of the temple*, with the broad agreement of the manuscripts and printed editions. Compare Matthew, chapter 21, and Psalm 117, verse 22:

> “The stone that the builders rejected—this has become the cornerstone.”

131. In some commonly circulated copies, *prima* (“first”) occurs as an error instead of *pinna* (“pinnacle”). Barthius gives an extensive account of the ancient common tradition concerning the pinnacle of the temple. Christians kept aside a certain stone that had once been the temple’s pinnacle, treating it as that cornerstone whose likeness the Lord used when he said that he himself had been made the cornerstone from a stone set aside. Hence, whether religious practice or superstition, a certain conspicuous corner-stone was displayed as a kind of testimony to the saying. Barthius gathers this from the present passage of Prudentius and from the very ancient Bordeaux Itinerary published by Pierre Pithou, where one may read:

> “There also is the great cornerstone of which it was said: ‘The stone that the builders rejected.’ Also, at the corner and beneath the pinnacle of that very tower are many chambers, where Solomon had his palace.”

[Col. 0104B] Fragments of this same stone, which they said had been rolled away, were venerated with equal devotion alongside the holy relics, as reported by the monk Gunther in Canisius, volume V of the *Antiquities*. This tradition lasted into more recent times, as is clear from Pietro Bellonio, *Observations*, book II, chapter 83. I readily concede to Barthius that the words of sacred Scripture in which Christ is called the cornerstone are to be understood of Christ himself, just as “ornament of the house,” “living stone,” and similar expressions are used figuratively. Prudentius indeed seems to explain the sacred testimonies about Christ in this way, while acknowledging that tradition. Nevertheless, nothing would otherwise prevent the Lord from having said, in Matthew 21:42, with reference to the likeness of that stone which ancient Christians displayed:

> “The stone that the builders rejected—this has become the cornerstone”;

and in verse 44:

> “Whoever falls upon that stone will be broken; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him.”

The memory of this event may have been handed down to later generations. Nevertheless, if anyone prefers to assert that in this verse Prudentius in no way acknowledges that common tradition concerning the surviving cornerstone, he may assert it without offending me, nor will he easily be refuted.

123. Some commonly circulated copies, and Vatt. N, Y, Z, AA, have *spernunt* (“reject”); the older copies have *sprerunt*. Giselinus in the margin of the second edition: “which the Jews rejected.” The manuscripts otherwise differ.

124. Sich., Ald., Rat., Prag. in its second hand, Mar., Alex., Vatt. A, B, I, and Q, and Weitz. with his manuscripts have *et lapidum compago novorum* (“and the joining of new stones”). In Prag. in its first hand: *et lapidum compago priorum* (“and the joining of former stones”). Gisel. in the text: *et laterum compago duorum* (“and the joining of two bricks”). The Heinsian manuscripts and Gis. in the margin: *et lapidum compago duorum* (“and the joining of two stones”), which occurs in Vall. and Vatt. N, Y, Z, AA, and BB. Barthius prefers *laterum compago duorum*. “For,” he says, “it makes a projecting corner more prominent by two pieces joined together; hence it is also called a stone of stumbling.” But *lapidum compago novorum* proceeds correctly, for Christ is the head of the new temple, the Church, and the joining of the new stones from which this temple rises, as from living and chosen stones. Ephesians 2:19 ff.:

> “You are fellow citizens with the saints and members of God’s household, built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone.”

Title 32, *Water into wine*, in Alex., Thuan., Ald., and Weitz. In Rat. and Vat. I: *Water into wine*. Vat. B and Mar.: *Water changed into wine*. Giselinus: *Wine made from water*. See John, chapter 2. Angelus M. Bandini published at Florence in 1746 *Observations on an Ancient Ivory Tablet Exhibiting Certain Sacred Mysteries of Our Lord Jesus Christ in Relief*. The front face of this tablet depicts the miracle by which Christ changed the water contained in six jars into wine.

D and N have *saltatrix sparsis*; Vall. has *salta*, and above it *saltria*. I prefer *psaltria*. Macrobius, book II of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 1:

> “There were also those who asked that a female harpist be admitted, so that a girl, intentionally softer than nature, might exercise her allurements over the philosophers through melodious sweetness and the slippery art of dancing.”

Livius and Quintilian likewise use the term. See Bulengerus, *On Banquets*.

140. Gifanius, in his index to Lucretius under *MARE MAGNUM* (“great sea”), reads *mergitat* (“repeatedly plunges”), not *mergit, at* (“plunges, but”). Giselinus has *mersitat*. In Egm. there is *plantas mergitur* (“the soles are plunged”), an elegant Graecism, as Heinsius thinks. In Oxon.: *plantis mergitur*. In Weitz., one of the Goldastus manuscripts has *mergitat*; the Palatine has *mergitur*. Aldus, [Col. 0106C] Weitz., Mar., Rat., Prag., Alex., and many Vatican manuscripts have *mergit, at*. Aldus has *manum tegit* (“covers the hand”); others have *manum regit* (“guides the hand”); some have *manu regit* (“guides with the hand”), as do Vatt. D, Z, AA, and Rott., which Heinsius does not dare condemn. For in a similar verse of Virgil, *Aeneid* 3, *Trunca manum pinus regit, et vestigia firmat* (“The mutilated pine guides the hand and steadies the steps”), he had found *manu* in not a few very old copies; and Prudentius imitated Virgil.

In the Parma edition the punctuation is incorrect:

> *Infelix collum laqueo, pro crimine tanto*,  
> “Unhappy Judas constricts his neck from afar with a noose, for so great a crime,”

instead of the correct reading:

> *Juda eminus arctat*  
> *Infelix collum laqueo*,  
> “Unhappy Judas constricts his neck from afar with a noose,”

which is preserved by Alex. (where *laqueus* appears above), Mar., Rat., Prag., Vatt. B, I, and Z, Urb., Gis., Weitz., Vall., and others. Heinsius’s conjecture, *Judae manus arctat / Infelix collum laqueo* (“Judas’s unhappy hand constricts his neck with a noose”), is pointless. Gifanius’s opinion that Prudentius could not have used *Juda* in this way is also pointless: just as he says *Helia*, *Belia*, and similar forms, he could say *Juda*. *Eminus* (“at a distance”) is elegantly placed to signify that Judas died by hanging. In the *Passion of Romanus*, verse 109:

> *Eviscerandum corpus eculeo eminus*  
> *Pendere*  
> “The disemboweled body hanging at a distance on the rack.”

In *Cathem.* hymn 9, verse 109:

> *Hunc eminus aere ab alto*  
> “Him from afar, from the high air.”

Mariettus suspected *munus* (“gift,” that is, “price”) instead of *eminus*. But the meter is against it.

Quatrain 41. Giselinus: *The column to which Christ was tied and scourged*. Others have the wording that I placed in the text. See Mark 15.]

161. Vatt. B, D, I, Prag., Rat., Mar., and Weitz. read *atque columnis* (“and to the columns”). Alex., Urb., Gis., Ald., Pal., and others read *columnae* (“of the column”), which is preferable, since below we have *veneranda columna* (“the venerable column”).

162. Vat., I, and Rat. in the first hand, Mar. in the first hand, and Weitz. read *annexum tergum* (“his back attached”). In Mar. *servire* (“to serve”) stood in place of *servile* [Col. 0108B], with the gloss *scilicet potuisset* (“namely, it could have stood”); afterward it was changed to *servile*.

163. Concerning the Temple of the Venerable Column, I read in St. Jerome, *Letter* 27, “On the Places of Jerusalem”: “There the column supporting the portico of the church was shown, stained with the Lord’s blood; to it he is said to have been bound and scourged.” From this you understand what is meant by “and it supports the temple.” Bede testifies that in his own time it stood in the middle of the church. Gregory of Tours also mentions this column and its miracles in his book *On the Glory of the Martyrs* [Col. 0108C]. See Lipsius, *On the Cross*, book II, chapter 4, where he proves that people were accustomed to be scourged at a column. That sacred column now stands in Rome, in the church of St. Praxedes. For this memory could—and ought to—have been preserved among devout Christians down to our own time.

164. Egm. reads *immuneres*, incorrectly, instead of *immunes*.

The title of tetrastichon 42 is the same in all the copies I have seen: “The Passion of the Savior.”

165. In some copies, *transjectus*; in others, *trajectus*. The conjecture of certain scholars—that one should read *Trajectusque latus dextrum* (“and the right side was pierced”), so that both sides would not be said to have been pierced—has been rejected in the note on *Cathemerinon* hymn 9, line 86, where we examined this unusual interpretation. From this tetrastichon alone it may be asserted that Prudentius is the author of the *Dittochaeon*, consistently maintaining his own usage everywhere. In the Cologne edition, *laticemque cruorem* (“the liquid and blood”) is noted in the margin from an old book as a variant reading; but *laticem atque cruorem* is the genuine reading. Gaspar Sagittarius published a dissertation on the spear by which the side of Jesus Christ was pierced; I discussed it in the commentary on the passage cited [Col. 0108D]. Some call him Carolus Sagittarius, because his name is usually represented only by the initial C. But that letter stands for Caspar, whom we more commonly call Gaspar.

166. In Gold. the gloss reads *AGIT, fudit* (“he pours out”). Aldus has *victoria sanguis* (“blood is victory”); most others have *sanguis victoria* (“blood, victory”). In Aldus the substantive verb *est* is missing after *lavacrum*. Many say that through the blood flowing from the Savior’s side martyrdom is signified, and through the water baptism. Orientius, in Martene, vol. V of the *Anecdota*: “The blood claims martyrdom for itself, the water the washing.”

Tetrastichon 43 is absent from Aldus, Torn., and many manuscript codices. See Matthew 28, and, concerning the resurrection of the saints who had fallen asleep, chapter 27, verse 53. These verses do not appear to be by Prudentius; nevertheless, it is established from ancient monuments that the tomb and the resurrection were once customarily painted and sculpted. An example is an ancient coin with the Greek inscription *Anastasis*, that is, “resurrection,” showing the tomb, terrified soldiers, and so forth. Through the kindness of the most eminent Stefano Borgia—who was exceptionally devoted to and learned in all antiquities, and at this very time had been enrolled in the Sacred College of Cardinals—I present here a drawing of it, so that judgment may more readily be formed [Col. 0109B]. John Tristanus of Saint-Amant and Jacobus Sirmondus long disputed over a similar coin. Franciscus Vavassorius examined it in chapter 2 of *On the Form of Christ*, and the distinguished Victorius exhibited a somewhat inaccurately drawn version from his own collection in his commentary *On the Bronze Coin*, where he discusses ancient representations of Christ. There he calls the round building a temple, whereas we have called it Christ’s tomb. Sirmondus, indeed, thinks that it is the temple called *Anastasis* by the ancients, erected at the site of the resurrection.

The title of tetrastichon 44 is “The Mount of Olives.” In Aldus, “Mount Olivet.” Read Acts of the Apostles, chapter 1.

173. Egm. and Gis. have *ad oram oliveti* (“at the edge of the olive grove”) instead of *oliviferi* (“olive-bearing”). Latinius correctly placed *oliviferi* in place of *oliferi*, which he found in Torn.

174. Heins. and Gif. punctuate the passage from an old book as follows: “signaling the footprints of peace with everlasting foliage: rich moisture melts.” This is not satisfactory, for the poet seems to understand the footprints that Christ, ascending to the Father, is said to have left imprinted. He calls them footprints of peace, alluding to the olive-bearing mountain and considering the effect of the Ascension. He then says that moisture flowed from olive branches, signifying the gift of chrism. He calls the olive branches “everlasting,” as Virgil does in *Georgics* II: “the grove rejoices in the vigorous olive of Pallas,” leaving aside the mystical sense. Likewise, in *Peristephanon* hymn 12, line 34: “the enduring foliage of the olive, fruitful in chrism,” which is better than the reading of others, “the spring.” Many testimonies of the Fathers exist concerning the footprints impressed on the summit of the Mount of Olives—those of Augustine, Paulinus, Sulpicius Severus, Optatus, and Bede. Calmet indicates the passages in his *Biblical Dictionary*.

175. In Rat. in the first hand, *linquitur* (“is left”), correctly emended to *liquitur* (“melts”).

I much prefer *miranda* (“wondrous”), with Ald., Gis., Alex., Prag., and others. He calls Stephen the first crown-bearer, the protomartyr, elegantly alluding to his name. Bembus falsely says in his hymn to St. Stephen that lesser writers made the name Stephen derive from the crown of martyrdom; Stephen was called that before his martyrdom.

B, I, Q, AA, Urb., Mar., Prag., Rat. in the first hand, Thuan., Weitz., Torn. in the margin, Heinsius, and others have *damnatos* (“condemned”). In Vat. I the gloss is *debiles* (“weak”). Compare Ison’s gloss. Heinsius conjectures *luxatos* (“dislocated”) from *laxatos*, and in Egm. from *laxatus*, although he thinks it possible to say elegantly and poetically *damnatos gressus* (“condemned steps”), as in *Hamartigenia*, line 650: “Condemn my ears, merciful Father.”

The lemma of title 47 is “Peter’s Vision.” In Mar. and Rat., “Peter’s Dream.” Read Acts of the Apostles, chapter 10.

[Col. 0110D] 185. Mystics commonly call even a clear vision, infused by God during an ecstasy of the mind, a dream. Prudentius, always consistent with himself, says of the Apocalypse of John the Evangelist in *Cathemerinon* hymn 6, line 113: “In such sleep the righteous hero relaxes his mind.” Since visions generally occur in ecstasy, or alienation of the mind from the bodily senses, visions are appropriately called dreams by analogy. They explain the dream of the philosopher Epimenides of Crete—said by some to have lasted fifty-seven years, by others fifty—as well as the dream of a certain boy mentioned by Pliny in book VII, chapter 57, said to have lasted fifty-seven years, as mental ecstasies, according to those who believe these stories. Likewise they speak of the seven holy Sleepers, who, they maintain, having fallen asleep in a cave, truly slept for nearly two hundred years; the distinguished Joseph Simonius Assemanius attempted to establish this by many arguments in volume I of the *Oriental Library*, pages 335 and following [Col. 0111A]. See the note on line 56 of *Cathemerinon* hymn 10. St. Bernard explains the bride’s sleep in the *Song of Songs* as the sublime contemplation of the soul, as I said in the commentary on line 77 of *Cathemerinon* hymn 6.

189. Prag. and Rat. read *vestitus* (“clothed”). Nouns and adverbs indicating location, such as “here,” “in these rooms,” and the like, show that these titles were composed for pictures customarily displayed in churches, as was said in section 66 of the prolegomena. St. Paulinus says of such a picture in *Poem* 9: “What is represented above by titles, so that the letters may show what the hand has depicted.” From Paulinus it is also clear why the picture of the two Testaments, as a twofold food, may be called a *Dittochaeon*: “Whoever sees these things, recognizing truths in empty figures, may feed his faithful mind with an image that is not empty.”

# AGAINST SYMMACHUS (C)

## Preface to Book One of *Against Symmachus*

[Col. 0111C] [Note: [Col. 0111C]

1. *Paulus*: because overcoming the viper-like tongue of so great an orator is a weighty task, he first sets before us the example of the Apostle Paul, whom a viper bit but did not injure; he himself likewise invokes divine aid against the viper’s teaching [Col. 0112C], Prag.

2. *Stylo*: “by preaching”; Iso.

4. *Immanes*: “savage” or “cruel.” — *Seminans*: “teaching”; I.]

[Note: [Col. 0111C]

I have supplied the inscription found in Mar. In Vat. A there is no title. In Alex.: “Here begins Book I against the speech of Symmachus.” Ald.: “Book I against Symmachus.” Egm.: “Against Symmachus.” Boher. the elder: “Against the speech of Symmachus.” In Vat. T, which contains glosses: “Book I against Symmachus.” Now concerning the preface. In some places this book is called *Paulus* from its first word. See also chapter 4 of the prolegomena. Juretus and Grangaeus have illuminated these books with special commentaries. Ausaldus translated them into Italian; we have spoken of this in chapter 3 of the prolegomena. Juretus calls these books exceptionally elegant and says that Symmachus’ arguments are accurately refuted and overthrown in them [Col. 0111D]. He used a very ancient codex, from whose collation he presents the scriptural variants.

V. 1. The name “herald of God” was attributed to the apostles from the earliest centuries of the Church, as can be seen in the *Life of St. Peter*, which is commonly attributed to St. Clement. In the fourth century there seems to have been in some churches a herald who summoned the faithful to church. Blessed Eusebius, bishop of Alexandria, says in a sermon on the Lord’s Day: “The herald calls to church (ὁ κῆρυξ), but everyone pleads sleep and illness.” Prudentius calls Paul the herald of God [Col. 0112C], but in the preface to book II he calls Peter “the supreme disciple of God,” thereby implying that he is the Church’s sole head.

4. Oxon. reads *placito dogmate* (“by an agreeable doctrine”).

5. Egm. has *et*, incorrectly, instead of *ut*. Ald. and Teol. write *caerimonias*; *ceremonias*, or *cerimonias*, is better for the sake of the meter. Heinsius does not object to *jam mansueta* in the earlier Rott. *Immansueta* may also be taken for *mansueta*, just as *infractus* may stand for *fractus*. Giselinus says that in printed editions the two words *in mansueta* occur, and he attempts to defend this manner of writing against what he considers the faulty, harsh practice of writing *inmansueta, inlustris, inludo, inradio*, appealing to the authority of Virgil, Cicero, M. Scaurus, Priscian, and Servius [Col. 0112D]. Most people now think otherwise and willingly write *adpellare* and other harsher forms; I do not willingly write them merely in rivalry.

6. Mar. has *mens pagana* (“pagan mind”). *Gens* (“nation”) is better, for the subject is the Apostle of the Gentiles. Christian writers use *paganus* for an ethnic or Gentile person, that is, a worshiper of idols. Orosius, book I, chapter 1: “You had instructed me to proceed against the empty-headed depravity of those who, being strangers to the citizenship of God, are called *pagani*, or Gentiles, from the crossroads and villages of rural places,” and so forth. Others investigate and report other explanations of this meaning [Col. 0113C]. See the commentary on line 448 of this book I, and Gothofredus on the title of the Theodosian Code, *On Pagans*. What Prudentius says about God being recognized perhaps refers to the “Unknown God” of the Athenians, concerning whom we read in Acts of the Apostles.]

Driven by the blackest whirlwinds, he had already endured

The stormy sea in a frail vessel

And the force of the shipwrecking south wind.

[10] But when the Lord’s right hand ordered the battles

Of the blue-green waters to cease,

The drifting boat glides back to the harbor

And sets the rowers, contracted by the rainy cold,

On the wet shore.

[15] Then from the shore’s hedges, chilled,

They quickly carry the dry branches of vines,

To build swift fires from them.

Each gathers his own bundle onto the flames,

Awaiting the abundance of the warm pyre.

[20] While Paul strives to gather the fragile twigs

691 [Col. 0113B] And compress the heap of fuel,

He thrusts his unwary hand into the piles,

Where a sluggish viper lay numb with ice,

Entwining the loops of its body around the branches.

[25] When it grew warm from the smoky fire,

It loosened its fierce, stiff neck,

[Col. 0114A] And now easily bent, it brought back toward the hand,

Its head vibrating, the points of its teeth,

Clinging fast by its bite to the finger’s wound.

[30] Carrying it hanging there, Paul shuddered.

The others cried out, thinking that deadly poison

Was spreading through his livid skin.

But the apostle was not terrified

By the sad appearance of so sudden a danger.

[35] Raising his eyes, he gazes upon the stars,

Murmuring Christ beneath his silent breast,

692 And shakes off the asp far away.

The cast-down serpent lashes the air

And releases the points of its gaping mouth.

[40] Soon all discharge and pain leave

The torn right hand, as though it had suffered no wound,

[Col. 0114B] And the viper’s fluid dries up and vanishes,

While the rush of its impulse whirls the plunging water-snake

Into the midst of the fires that will consume it.

[45] Thus now, after winter and the violence of the harsh sea,

By which the vessel of wisdom was then tossed,

52. Prudentius says that the Christian faith was tossed about and terrified under pagan emperors, and after that storm endured a wound-bearing bite. Although the hidden poison of idolatry concealed itself under Christian rulers, it nevertheless burst out again, namely in Symmachus’ speech. In Rat., after the earlier words had been erased, this and the following verse read *se prius abdita / Viro nec nec gravidum protulerat caput*, which is wholly inept.

84. Heinsius printed *si potis est*, but *si potis es* seems more probable to him, since he saw it in another Rott. and it also occurs in Vat. A. But most copies have *si potis est*, which Gifanius defends in his *Index to Lucretius*, under *viridans*. It can be understood as “if Symmachus can be relieved,” or “if he can obtain mercy.” Gifanius explains *si potis est* as in Terence and the ancient writers, meaning “if it is possible,” “if it can happen.” Heinsius thinks one should then say *si pote est*, not *si potis est*. But Forcellinus demonstrates in his *Dictionary* that *si potis est* can also be said for “if it is possible.”]

89. He returns to line 44, “that will burn,” and so forth. In Mar.: “The preface ends.” Concerning the reason why Prudentius wrote these two books against Symmachus, although I intend at some future time to discuss it more fully, I shall now say a few things. After the battle of Actium, Augustus built the Julian Senate House in honor of Julius Caesar, and placed in it a statue and altar of Victory, so that senators assembling there might offer prayers with incense and unmixed wine. Constantius, the son of Constantine the Great, was the first to destroy the altar. Not long afterward Julian the Apostate restored it, and the Christian emperors Jovian and Valentinian the Elder did not remove it. Gratian, son of Valentinian the Elder, not only destroyed such an altar but also refused the payments customarily made to the Roman pagan priests and Vestal Virgins. In 382 Symmachus, on behalf of the pagan senators, asked Gratian to restore the altar of Victory and the priests’ subsidies. But Pope Damasus of Rome sent Ambrose, bishop of Milan, a petition from several Christian senators who declared that they had authorized nothing of the kind. Thus, through Ambrose’s intervention, Symmachus was not even heard [Col. 0117B]. After Gratian’s death, however, Symmachus presented his *Report* to Valentinian the Younger, Gratian’s brother, requesting the restoration of the altar of Victory and the privileges of the priests. Ambrose, remembering the embassy that Damasus had entrusted to him two years earlier, refuted it in two petitions. Valentinian followed Ambrose’s advice, and Theodosius certainly did the same when a similar embassy of the Senate was later brought to his attention, as can be gathered from Ambrose’s words: it was the same *Report* of Symmachus, or the same principal arguments on which it rested. An embassy was sent again to Valentinian in Gaul, but it could obtain nothing, even in Ambrose’s absence [Col. 0118A]. Later, however, the tyrant Eugenius, although he had once and again resisted the pagan petition, granted it on the third request. After Theodosius defeated Eugenius in 394, he annulled Eugenius’ acts in favor of pagan superstition. At the beginning of the fifth century, when the Goths invaded Italy, Symmachus seized the opportunity and began to pursue the restoration of the altar of Victory, using the same arguments as before. Prudentius completely suppressed his effort. From Prudentius it may be inferred that the statue of Victory, as an ornament of the City, remained for a longer time; Claudian confirms this in his *Panegyric on the Sixth Consulship of Honorius*.]

695 Into the sheer pit of the falling man.

Not carry him burning into the midst of the flames.

15. He persists in the same metaphor of disease and medicine, which authors of that period frequently employed.

18. Egm., Pal.: *medico*, contrary to the metre, though supported by *medico*. He praises Theodosius because he endeavored to eradicate idolatry from its roots.

21. Vat. A: *posset ab*; Rat.: *servare veterno*. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XII, chapter 8, compares this passage of Prudentius with a similar passage of Claudian, *Against Eutropius*, book II: “Ulcers deeply suffused through the possessed marrow,” etc.

22. Chamillard interprets the tyrants as Constantius, Julian, Valens, and Valentinian the Elder, a supporter of the ancient rites. Teolius adds Magnentius. But it is more probable that Prudentius is speaking only of the tyrants whom Theodosius defeated, Maximus and Eugenius, whom he again calls tyrants at verses 410 and 463. Indeed, several severe laws of Constantius are preserved in the Theodosian Code, concerning the pagans and directed against the sacrifices, temples, and worship of images of the heathen. I would more readily believe that Magnentius is here called a tyrant together with Eugenius and Maximus [Col. 0119D].

23. Egm., Pal.: *quis status*.

25. Vat. A: *ceu male*; *heu* is better.

27. Capella, book V: “And the lesser crowd of heavenly beings trembles.”

28. He seems to be speaking of eternal life. Prag. has *praetendit*, less suitably.

30. A very celebrated saying of Plato; on it, see Barthius, book XX, chapter 18. But Prudentius speaks cautiously of those who cultivated the doctrine of heavenly wisdom.

31. After this verse, one page is missing in Prag., continuing to verse 116.

34. Vat. A: *aetheria*, less suitably.

35. Sich. and Gis., first edition, in the margin: *est operae pretium* instead of *contigit ecce hominum*.

36. He calls Rome “ours” because it was the common fatherland. But this may be intended to evade the arguments of those who dispute whether Prudentius’ homeland was Caesaraugusta or Calagurris [Col. 0120C].

37. Rat. has *fid et*, but *fiet* seems to have been intended. A later hand has *viget*.

38. Bong., first hand, Rat.: *teterrimus*. Aldus and other editors and manuscripts, including three of Gifanius’ codices and one of Juretus, have *deterrimus*, which Gifanius rightly considers preferable. Gis., second edition, also has *deterrimus*, but in the second edition he changed it to *teterrimus*, a reading reproduced by Fabr. and Heins., although the latter recorded nothing from the manuscripts. Idolatry is called “the most detestable superstition” in law 20 of the Theodosian Code, *On the Pagans*.

39. Vat. A: *atque superstitio*. Ison’s gloss is not satisfactory. I say that the ancestors are the ancient Romans, or Italians, worshipers of idols. Below, at verse 180: “These ancestors brought in the Italians.”

41. After this verse there is an inscription in Mar., Rat., and others: “On Saturn.” It is absent from Vat. A. Others note in the margin *Saturnus*, or *On Saturn*, and the same occurs in the following titles.

42. Egm.: *avus* for *avos*. On this myth and the others which Prudentius recounts and casts up to the heathen, one may consult, besides the poets and commentators on the poets, the ancient mythographers Hyginus, Palaephatus, Fulgentius Placiades, Phornutus, Albricus the philosopher, Aratus, and Apollodorus. Among more recent writers, Lilius Gyraldus, Natalis Comes, Joannes Seldenus, Joannes Gerardus Vossius, Banier—in a work published in French at Paris in 1738—and countless others have labored on this subject. Ison’s explanations are by no means to be despised. Authors often disagree in explaining the same myth; this should not seem surprising, since the same thing frequently happens in historical narratives. Few representations of Saturn survive. Montfaucon, *Antiquities*, book I, volume II, page 30, presents a complete image of him. On consular coins he is also shown with an aged head and a sickle placed behind him.

45. Vat. A: *cum Deus*, incorrectly.

697. “[Fragment:] would consecrate [it] to the All-begetter, in accordance with [his] supreme majesty?”

He alone was concerned that the public wound in morals,

[15] once lightly closed over by a superficial scar,

should not conceal a deeply impressed hiding-place

of the festering wound, eaten through to the core

by putrid corruption, while the joined surface,

deceiving the physician, nursed it.

But he took pains that the nobler part of man within

[20] might live, and that the soul, cleansed from deadly plague,

might know itself protected from inward poison.

That had been the medicine of tyrants: to see

what condition would suit present and perishable affairs

before their eyes, and to give no thought to the future.

[25] Alas, they deserved ill of the people and fawned

ill upon the fathers themselves! They allowed them

to plunge headlong into Tartarus with Jupiter

and with the many gods of the common people.

But this ruler extended his power farther into the age to come,

698 desiring to establish the salvation of his descendants.

[Col. 0119B]

[Col. 0120A]

Surely a certain most learned man spoke beautifully:

“The commonwealth,” he says,

“would then be sufficiently fortunate if

either kings were wise or wise men ruled.”

Is he one of the few who, having received the diadem,

cultivated the doctrine of heavenly wisdom?

[35] Behold, it happened to the human race and to the toga-clad nation

that a wise leader came; under the reign of justice

our Roman commonwealth flourishes happily:

obey the master who governs the scepters.

He admonishes that the most detestable error,

and the superstition of our ancient ancestors,

should be far removed,

[40] and that no one should think a god exists except him

who stands supreme above all things

and created the immeasurable expanse of the great universe.

Was Saturn, who instructed the rustic minds

and barbarous hearts of men with such decrees,

699 believed to have ruled the Latin ancestors better?

[Col. 0120B]

[45] “I am a god; I come as a fugitive.

Provide hiding-places; conceal the old man,

cast down from his throne by the savagery of his son.

I, this fugitive and exile, desire

to lie hidden; I shall give the people and the place the name Latium.

[Col. 0121A]

[Col. 0121A]

49. *Putandis*: “to be cut off,” Ison.  
50. *Procudam*: “I shall forge,” “fashion”; “a sickle.” *Chalybem*: “a little sickle for cutting vines”—I.  
52. *Nemus*: “my grove,” namely, Ison.  
53. *Coelo genitus*: “son of heaven,” Ison.  
55. *Minores*: “descendants,” Vat. A.  
56. *Profugus*: he speaks of Saturn. *Equina libido*: Saturn had intercourse with the nymph Philyra. When Ops came upon them, he changed himself into a horse so that he would not be discovered; hence he is said “to neigh at Tuscan girls”—Ison.  
59. *Olympi*: Olympus, as though from *ololampus*, “entirely aflame”—Ison.  
60. *Spurcavit*: “defiled,” “violated.” *Lacaenas*: Greek women. Laconia is a region of Greece, from which Leda came. Jupiter, changed into a swan, violated Leda, the mother of Helen, who laid an egg from which Pollux, Castor, and Helen were born—Ison.  
61. *Nunc bove*: Jupiter wished to have intercourse with Europa; therefore he changed himself into a beautiful bull and in this form violated her. *Subvectam*: Europa, who was the wife of Phoenix. *Crimen*: “sexual violation,” Ison.

[Col. 0121B]

48. Virgil, book VIII, recounts the whole story: “And he preferred that it be called Latium, because he had safely lain hidden in those shores.” Minucius, in the *Octavius*: “Therefore he preferred that his hiding-place, because he had lain hidden there safely, be called Latium, and the city Saturnia after his own name.” Arnobius, book IV, Lactantius, book I, chapter 14, and Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 10, reproach the heathen with this very matter.

49. Egm., Pal.: *male, cura potandis*.

51. Oxon., incorrectly: *Saturnia nobis*.

53. Vat. A: *tum quia*; read *sum quia*. Gallandius notes that *quianam* is used interrogatively among the ancients [Col. 0121C]. This is indeed usually the case; but without an interrogation *quia nam* is correctly used pleonastically. Thus Plautus, *Amphitryon*, act II, scene 2, verse 34: “For indeed we arrived late.” Saturn was thought to be the son of Heaven and Earth. Hence the ancients said that those who appeared unexpectedly had descended from heaven, and they called unknown men “sons of Earth.” Minucius is the authority: “For he was the son of Earth and Heaven, because among the Italians he had been exposed with unknown parents; just as even today we call those unexpectedly seen to have been sent from heaven, and men of low and unknown birth sons of Earth.” See Muretus, book XIII of the *Various Readings*, chapter 7; Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 10, with Heraldus’ notes; and Lactantius, book I, chapter 2.

54. Heinsius says that *patria spectata sepulcra* is preferable, and that others have interpolated the text improperly; nor is Cauchius right in reading *in patria*. In his book Juretus found *quorum patrias, peccata, sepulcra*, and defends this as the true reading, because Prudentius argues that those are ridiculous gods whose fatherland or origin, wicked life, and death or tombs are known—an argument also made by Lactantius, book I of the *Divine Institutes*. Weitzius reads *quorum patrias spectare sepulcra*. Mar.: *patrias, spectata sepulcra*. Rat.: *patriam, spectata sepulcra*. Urb.: *patria spectare sepulcra*, which seems to have been the reading in Egm. and Palat. In Widm. and Bong. there is *patrias*, but Weitzius does not explain whether *spectare* follows or whether something else does. The reading of Juretus’ codex seems preferable to me. Vat. A has *unde* instead of *inde*. The origin of the gods in Italy is traced back to Saturn. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 10: “Before Saturn, no god existed among you; from him is reckoned the whole or the chief or the better-known divinity.”

55. In the margin of Juretus’ codex, instead of the variant reading, there is *minore*, which is faulty. Lucretius, Pliny, and others use *minores* for descendants. In our matter Arnobius, book V: “Ancient time brought forth the sickle-bearer and transmitted him to the age of his descendants.” Juretus discusses at length the use of bronze in statues, drawing on Pliny, Isidore, Cassiodorus, and others. Add Bulengerus, *On Painting and Statuary*, book II, chapter 11, “On statues cast in bronze.”

56. Barthius, Turnebus, and other critics observe that *equinam libidinem* and *adhinnire* are used of excessive lust [Col. 0122B]. But Prudentius also alludes to the myth, which Ison and Hyginus, *Fables* 138, describe: “Saturn, in Thrace, changed himself into a horse and had intercourse with Philyra, daughter of Ocean; she bore him Chiron the centaur.” Virgil comes closer to Prudentius, *Georgics* III: “Thus Saturn himself, swift at his wife’s arrival, poured out a mane upon his horse-like neck and, fleeing, filled high Pelion with a sharp neigh.” Valerius Flaccus, book V, verse 152: “And the shores called by Philyra’s name, which Saturn struck with his equine horn.”

58. Egm. has, less suitably, *simulato nomine moechus*. What is recounted about Saturn seems contrary to what Juvenal says, *Satire* 6: “I believe that chastity, under Saturn’s reign, remained on earth and was seen for a long time.” Certainly the poets are not very consistent with themselves in describing the happiness of the golden age. Ovid, *Fasti* I: “Hardly anyone, I think, did I see under Saturn’s reign whose heart did not cherish sweet thefts.” After this verse, Rat., Mar., and others have the title “On Jupiter.”

59. Heinsius says that Weitzius set Becmanus’ conjecture *sinuosi* into the text by a very bad example, in place of *silvosi*, which is correctly said of Olympus, like “leafy” and “shady.” Those who sometimes adopted Heinsius’ conjectures without any reason ought to have followed this warning. From Ison’s gloss, Isidore, book XIV, chapter 8, can be emended: “Olympus is so called, as though *ololampus*, that is, as though ‘heaven.’” The gloss is better understood as “entirely aflame,” or rather “luminous” or “splendid.” Isidore quotes from Virgil, “Olympus rises above the clouds,” which Grialius notes is not found in Virgil. I find this half-line in Lucan, book II. History teaches that Jupiter lived on Mount Olympus; hence the myth of Jupiter reigning in heaven. See Lactantius, book I of the *Divine Institutes*, chapter 11 [Col. 0122D].

60. Heinsius, in Gis., disapproves of *incestas*, because the better manuscripts have *incesta*. Ald. and Urb.: *incestas*. Rat.: *incesta*, but the gloss has *pollutas*. In the gloss, for “Laconia is a city of Greece,” read or understand “Lacedaemon,” or, as this city is named in some dictionaries, “Lacon,” since a *Lacaena* is a Spartan woman. Leda, Helen, and Hermione, women of Lacedaemon, were disgraced by a reputation for unchastity.

61. Vat. A has *tunc* for *nunc*. For *bove*, Rat., Mar., first hand, and Widm., first hand, write *boe*. Weitzius also printed *boe*, because Colerius, in his notes on Valerius Maximus, page 568, says that it is so written in his manuscripts. Observe that these are the same manuscripts which we cite under the name Mar. For *subvectam*, Widm., Bong., Mar., Rat., and Gis., first edition, in the margin, have *subjectam*. In the Parma edition there is the error *ad crinem* for *ad crimen*. Montfaucon, *Antiquities*, book II, volume I, displays images of Jupiter in which this and other myths are represented [Col. 0123C].

“I shall hide, and I shall give the people and the place

the name Latium.

For pruning the vines, if that is any concern,

I shall forge curved steel;

[50] and I shall establish for you Saturnia,

the walls of your river on its bank.

You shall celebrate me with a grove,

and with altars consecrated beneath my honor—

‘for I am born of heaven.’

Then, of the gods whose fatherlands, crimes,

[55] [Col. 0122A] and tombs we know,

they fashioned dull images in bronze,

the descendants of the fugitive stranger,

whom lust in the form of a horse

brought into Italy. For he was the first

[60] to neigh at Tuscan girls,

an adulterer under a pretended divinity.

Soon Jupiter, worse than his father,

the inhabitant of wooded Olympus,

701 defiled the Spartan women with incestuous pollution.

Now, carrying off in the form of a bull

the woman he loved, he turns love into a crime.”

[Col. 0123A]

[Col. 0123B]

62. *Tenera*: “swans’,” Ison.  
63. *Immorientis*: the swan, while dying, gives forth sweet sounds; or “perpetual and immortal,” because it is a star in heaven—I.  
64. *Capta*: “deceived.” *Quibus*: “with which whispers.” *Virguncula*: Leda, the wife of Theseus—I.  
65. *Surdis*: “closed.” *Pessulus*: “a bolt,” “bar”—I.  
66. *Dives amator*: Jupiter—I.  
67. *Imbricibus*: “with the roof tiles,” Ison.  
68. *Amicae*: Danaë, the wife of Acrisius—I.  
69. *Modo*: “now,” Ison.  
70. *Miserum*: “violated.” *Afficiens*: “oppressing.” *Catamitum*: Ganymede; *catamitus* and *succuba* mean the same thing—I.  
71. *Pellice*: “concubine.” *Indignante sorore*: Juno, Jupiter’s sister, was indignant that her sister Hebe had been removed from service and Ganymede received in her place—I.  
73. *Hospite*: Saturn. *Crudus*: “uncultivated,” “raw,” “new,” “undigested.” *Stupor*: “stupidity.” *Finxit*: the golden ages existed under Saturn because there was the best of peace—I.  
76. *Pellem*: by transferring his own. *Faciemque*: his own—I.  
77. *Esse bovem*: when he violated Europa. *Praedari*: when he carried off Ganymede. *Concumbere*: with Alcmena. *Cygnum*: “through a swan,” I.  
78. *Et nummos*: he calls the golden rain “coins,” or the money he gave to the guards—I.  
81. *Dedere*: “to hand over voluntarily.” *Diae*: “divine”; *dia*, “noble,” and *eugenes* mean the same thing—I.  
82. *Nebulonis*: “of the deceiver,” Ison.

[Col. 0123C]

62. Heinsius, with his manuscripts, as well as Juretus’ codex, Egm., and Palat., have *nunc tener, ac pluma levior*. Ald., Mar., Rat., Gis., Weitz., Fabr., and others have *nunc tenera pluma levior*. Vat. A has *tunc tener, ac*. Arnobius, book IV: “Is not Jupiter himself, king of the universe, infamous among you for having gone through countless forms and concealed the flames of wanton love beneath servile disguises? Was any account ever written by us of his completing his lustful thefts—now changed into gold, now into a playful satyr, a dragon, a bird, a bull?” See Elmenhorstius’ notes on Arnobius, page 91. Tertullian, in the *Apology*, calls Jupiter a “feathered lover,” because he changed into a swan for love of Leda and into an eagle to carry off Ganymede. Chamillard has another interpretation: he prefers this verse to refer to Jupiter changed into a cuckoo in order to possess Juno, or into an eagle in order to violate Asteria. What most authors recount of Leda, others relate of Nemesis. Some say that after her death Leda took the name Nemesis [Col. 0123D].

64. Vat. A has, less suitably, *rapta* for *capta*. Fabr.: *volucrum*, rightly rejected by Heinsius. Gronovius conjectured *volucrem amantem*. Gis., second edition: *volucrum*, but corrected it to *volucrem* from the single swan, as he explains.

65. Vat. A has, incorrectly: *Tunc foribus surdis sura quas ve*.

66. Thuan., Vat. A, and Juretus’ codex support *firmarant*, which Heinsius retained. Aldus and our other witnesses have *firmarat*. Tertullian, in the *Apology*, also touches on this myth. Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*: “If someone delights in adultery, he looks to Jupiter and derives from him the fuel for his desire; he approves, imitates, and praises the fact that his god deceives in the form of a swan, carries off in the form of a bull, plays in the form of a satyr, and, so that he may become accustomed to being generous in wickedness, corrupts a confined woman with gold flowing abundantly.” Hence the myth arose. Because the poets imagined that Danaë’s guards had been corrupted by gold, they invented Jupiter changed into a shower of gold.

69. Egm., Pal., Vat. A: *causante rapinam*. It is well known that Jupiter’s armor-bearer was an eagle.

[Col. 0124C]

70. Rat., Vat. A, Mar., and the better Heinsian witnesses, Sich., Gis., Fabr., Widm., Pal., and Bong. have *afficiens*; Ald. and Gis., in the text of the first edition, have *cupiens*. Gifanius, under the verb *affigere* or *adfigere*, on the basis of an excellent old book, has *affigens*, which pleased Weitzius. Vat. A writes *Catamintum*; the same name in Julius Firmicus was corruptly read as *Cantamitus*. Ald.: *Catamytum*; most have *Catamitum*; some *Catamithum*. Cicero, *Philippics* II: “That I might display you as a catamite,” etc. Barthius, book XXIII of the *Adversaria*, chapter 7, discusses catamites, or effeminate men, at greater length.

71. Vat. A has, incorrectly, *quam puero*. Rat. writes *pelice* with one *l*.

74. In Cellarius’ second edition, *illam* is an error.

75. Vat. A, Weitz., *concumbere*. Heinsius, with more recent witnesses, has the same, but does not state on whose manuscript authority. Gis., Fabr., Mar., Colerus at the cited passage, and Rat. have *concingere*. Rat.’s gloss adds, “for *concinere* because of the metre,” which is absurd; above, the variant reading is *concumbere*. Mariettus thinks *concingere* should be retained, meaning “to embrace as with wings.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VI: “He made Leda recline beneath swanlike wings.” Aldus is cited by Weitzius in support of *concingere*; but in Aldus, Gis., first edition, and other common editions, I find *confingere*, which is not an unworthy reading [Col. 0124D].

78. Mar., in Heinsius, another Rottendorf manuscript, Rat., first hand, Weitz., and Gifanius, under the verb *ninguere*, on the basis of three old books, have *serere*, which Gifanius calls an extremely elegant expression. I prefer *fieri*, with the others.

79. Rat., incorrectly: *rusticitans*.

80. Heinsius, with Thuan., has *ritusque*, and says that Gifanius improperly changed it to *rictus*. Juretus likewise found *ritus* in his codex. Nevertheless, *rictus* occurs in Mar., Rat., Urb., and apparently in Alex., second hand; it also appeared in the printed editions before Gifanius. Indeed, when Gifanius quotes this verse, he says: “*pecudes inter rictusque*”—adding that in the second edition he read *ritusque*.

81. Gifanius, under *diva*, reads *degere* and *divae*. Ald., Mar., Weitz., Torn., and others have *divae rationis*. Juretus’ codex has *diae* as the variant reading, which most editors retain.

82. Vat. A, Pal.: *callida struxit*, ineptly.

Now lighter than a tender feather, and repeating sweet whispers

in the manner of the sweetly dying swan:

by these the deceived maiden might bear a bird’s love.

[65] Now, with deaf doors—

doors which a bar, or bolt,

had firmly fastened with wedges—

the wealthy lover, breaking through the roof tiles,

702 poured down a rain of streaming gold

into the lap of his waiting beloved.

Now, by means of his armor-bearer, contriving a sordid abduction,

[70] he violated the wretched catamite with filthy intercourse,

while his sister was now more indignant at the boy as a concubine.

[Col. 0124A]

This is the cause and origin of evil:

that, while the ancient guest ruled,

a savage stupidity fashioned the golden ages,

and that crafty Jupiter, with his novel ingenuity,

[75] wove manifold devices and various deceits,

so that, whenever he wished to change his skin and face,

they would think him a bull, the eagle plundering,

the swan copulating,

703 and coins becoming [golden rain] and entering a girl’s lap.

For what would the rustic simplicity

of untamed men not believe—

men accustomed, among cattle,

to surrender their minds to customs of beasts,

destitute of divine reason?

The unhappy race readily lent its ear to whatever belief

the cunning of the deceiver drew it into.

[Col. 0125A]

A more corrupt age succeeded Jupiter’s rule:

[85] it taught rigid countrymen to serve vices,

men inexperienced in theft.

Mercury, born of Maia, imbued them with this art.

Now he is held to be a great god,

the one whose experience produced thieves.

And that man, most learned in Thessalian magic,

[90] is said to have recalled extinguished souls

to the light by the power of an assumed wand,

to have annulled the laws of death in Cocytus,

while the shades flew upward.

But he also condemned others to death

and plunged them into deeply hidden chaos:

he was skilled in both,

[95] and armed life with a twofold crime—

for magic art knows how, by a spell,

to call forth delicate figures

and skillfully enchant sepulchral ashes,

and likewise to strip others of life.

A simple-minded antiquity, marveling at the criminal craftsman,

[100] worshiped him above mankind,

pretending that he was carried through the clouds

and sped lightly on winged feet through the winds.

705 Behold, a Greek man, fashioned and cast in bronze,

stands numbered among the gods,

and shines in the lofty citadel of Numa.

A certain vigorous man was master of a cultivated field,
