[105] and famous for the wealth of his gardens;

yet this same man was an excessive fornicator,

accustomed to harass little rustic prostitutes

among the willow thickets.

[Col. 0126B]

[Col. 0127A]

110. *Otia*: “security,” Ison.  
111. *Hic*: “such a one”; he speaks ironically. *Hellesponto*: Hellespont is a city on the island of Lampsacus—I.  
113. *Sinum*: a vessel in which milk is drawn. *Quotannis*: “each year,” Ison.  
114. *Vineta*: from *vinea*, “vineyard”; *viteta*, from *vitis*, “vine”; *dumeta*, from *dumus*, “thorn-bush.” *Sabini*: Italians; a town of Italy, Ison.  
115. *Turpiter*: for he carries a branch in his hand, from which he seems to guard the vineyards and the gardens entrusted to him. *Pudeat*: “let each person be ashamed,” I.  
116. *Mollis*: “violated,” I.  
117. *Ardor*: “love,” “passion.” *Jactata*: “wearied by tossing,” namely in a shipwreck. *Efferbuit*: “burned.” *Argo*: the ship, I.  
118. *Maris*: masculine. *Nemea sub pelle*: the Colchian woman; for Nemea was the daughter of the king of the Colchians, whom she gave to Hercules. Hercules had intercourse with Pallantea, daughter of Evander, beneath the lion’s skin—the lion having been captured in the Nemean forest—Ison.  
119. *Hylan*: “Hylas”; “nor did that celibate man blush,” that is, one leading a heavenly—or perhaps *caelibem*, “celibate”—life. *Caelebs*: “abstinent,” I.  
120. *Saliis*: “with dances”; the Salii are said to be those who, dancing, circle the altar of Hercules; consult the story in Virgil. They are so called from leaping. *Domus*: “family.” *Pinaria*: Pinarius and Potitius were priests of Hercules—I. *Saliis*: “with dances,” Rat.  
121. *Aventini*: a mountain said to have been named from the arrival of birds; for, rising from the river Tiber, they seek the mountain’s summit—I.  
122. *Thebanus juvenis*: Liber Pater, I.  
123. *Successu*: “with success,” “prosperity.” *Lascivit*: “he acted wantonly,” I.  
125. *Diffluit*: “dissolves into luxury.” *Semiviro*: “castrated”; for he had with him a certain castrated, effeminate, and enervated companion, I.

[Col. 0127C]

108. Saint Paul seems to call a brothel or place of fornication simply “beds” in Romans 13:13: “Not in beds and immoralities,” etc.

109. Since the sense proceeds correctly, I do not know why Heinsius wished to disturb the manuscript reading by conjecturing *indomito intendens animo, semperque parato*. Gronovius preferred to replace *animum* with *nervum*.

111. Sich., Mar., Weitz., and others have *et patrio*. Lampsacus is a city situated opposite Callipolis in the Thracian Chersonese [Col. 0127D], beside the strait of the Hellespont, by which the Chersonese is separated from Asia. The gloss is plainly corrupt, as is generally the case in the other geographical descriptions.

112. Vat. A, first hand: *sacros*. Juretus’ codex, Egm., Pal., and Vat. A have *cultoribus* for *cum turpibus*; the latter should be retained. The “shameful rites” are the *Priapeia*, concerning which see Meursius, book V, *On the Festivals of the Greeks*, and Montfaucon, book I of the *Antiquities*, volume I, part 2.

113. Weitzius writes *quodannis*, because he found it in Egm. Why not *quotannis*, since others write it so? This verse is from Virgil, *Eclogue* 7: “A bowl of milk, and these cakes, Priapus, it is enough for you to await each year; you are the guardian of a poor garden.”

114. I understand Horace’s Sabine estate.

115. Egm., Pal., incorrectly have *puderat* for *pudeat*. Grangaeus and Heinsius understand the branch as the obscene part. Ison explains it as the branch he carries in his hand. Horace, *Satires* I.8, on the Priapus of his estate: “For with his right hand he restrains thieves … but with a reed fixed upon his head he frightens away the troublesome birds.” Virgil, *Georgics* IV: “And guardian of thieves and birds, with a willow sickle.” In Rat. and Mar. the title “On Hercules” follows this verse [Col. 0128B].

116. Barthius, *Adversaria* XXI.15, says that Prudentius elegantly gave Hercules’ Greek name a Latin form, just as Horace used *Ulysseus* and Virgil *Achilleus*. But here *Herculeus* must be an adjective, namely “Herculean love,” unless *arsit* is read instead of *ardor*. The sense is: “Herculean love was famous for the love of a soft boy.” Horace, *Odes* I.3, has “Herculean labor.”

117. Thuan.: *jactata ferbuit Argo*. Vat. A: *jacta*, incorrectly, and *efferbuit Argo*. Mar., Prag., and Rat., first hand: *jactata efferbuit Argo*. Others have *jactatae efferbuit* or *ferbuit Argo*. Heinsius thinks *jactatae efferbuit Argus* should be read; Barthius maintains that *jactatae efferbuit Argo* should be read, with *Argo* left undeclined. Urb. has, incorrectly, *ardor in transtris*. In the gloss I do not know what *minna* means, unless perhaps *migma* or *mimax* is intended—that is, a fiery mixture so violent that it burned even beneath water. See Macer’s *Sacred Lexicon*.

118. Vat. A, corruptly: *nec mea suppelle*. Aldus and the common editions: *Nemaea pelle*. Mar.: *Nemaea sub pelle*. Rat., Prag., and Juretus’ codex: *Nemea sub pelle*, as Gifanius and Heinsius corrected it. Thus, in *Aeneid* VIII, *Nemea sub rupe* is found in corrected manuscripts. In Vat. A, a metrical error has *efferbuit* for *erubuit*.

119. Some write *Hilan* and *coeleps*. Arnobius, book IV: “I do not know who loves Hylas.” See Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*; Valerius Flaccus, *Argonautica* III; and Hyginus, *Fables* 207.

120. The Salii were priests of Hercules and Mars. Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII: “Then the Salii, with singing, attend the burning altars, their temples bound with poplar branches.” On the house of the Pinarii, the same Virgil writes: “And the Pin arian house, guardian of Hercules’ sacred rite.” See Macrobius, Servius, and others.

121. After this verse, Mar. and Rat. have the inscription “On Liber, who is also Bacchus.” It is absent from Aldus and several others.

125. Rat.: *defluit*. Juretus’ codex: *in lusum*, according to an old manner of writing. Lactantius, book I, chapter 10: “For, having been carried to Crete with an effeminate retinue, he encountered an unchaste woman on the shore.” This imitates Virgil, *Aeneid* IV: “But now that Paris with his effeminate retinue …”

And to enter dense hedges and obscene couches,

706 directing his untamed mind,

always ready for crime,

[110] he never granted repose to his fevered passions.

This god, most nobly born in his native Hellespont,

came all the way to Italian gardens

with his shameful rites.

He receives a bowl of milk

and these sacrificial cakes of vows each year,

and guards the vineyards of the Sabine countryside,

[115] shamefully fixed with a branch

which anyone would be ashamed to look upon.

Herculean love, famous for its passion

for a soft boy,

[Col. 0128A] burned fiercely on the benches of the Argo,

tossed upon the waves.

707 Nor did he blush to harbor intercourse

with Nemea beneath a lion’s skin,

nor, as a celibate, to seek Hylas

as he perished.

[120] Now, with the Salii and their song,

he throngs the temple of the Pin arian house

in the vaulted seat of Aventine Hill.

The Theban youth becomes a god

after conquering India;

while exulting in victorious success,

he revels and carries back the gold

of the captive nation,

and, proud of his spoils,

[125] dissolves into luxury with his effeminate retinue.”

[Col. 0129A]

127. *Musto*: “new [wine].” *Falerno*: a mountain productive of excellent wine—Ison.

128. *Perfundens*: he splashed wine upon the horses. *Ferarum*: for tigers are said to be in his chariot—Ison.

129. *Caper*: because it is hostile to vines—Ison.

130. *Discindunt*: “they bite.” *Chelydros*: serpents—Ison.

131. *Bromium*: Bromius was Liber’s attendant. Bromius—that is, Bacchus—from *bromus*, that is, “cellar”; or from *bruma*, the season in which much is eaten. A goat is also sacrificed to him because it greatly harms vineyards—Ison.

132. *Satyrorum*: satyrs are rustic beings, because they cannot be sated with lust; or poets, because they are never sated with wisdom—Ison.

134. *Maenadas*: women, also Bacchae, that is, frenzied women. *Rotatas*: “hurled headlong”—Ison.

135. *Temulentus*: from *temetum*, that is, old wine—Ison.

[Col. 0130A] 136. “Shore,” in greenery; the pleasantness of the beaches; “shore,” sandy or pleasant places—for the Greeks call the shore *aktē* (ἀκτή). I. “With pleasantness,” Rat.

[Col. 0130B] 137. “Harlot”: Neaera, I.; Ariadne, daughter of Minos, whom Theseus had abandoned, Vat. A.

138. “In incestuous intercourse”: illicitly, or in pollution, Iso.

139. “Neaera”: a mistress or concubine, I. He called her Neaera, as though she were a common lover, Rat.

142. “Ariadnean”: Ariadne, daughter of Minos, king of Crete, was received by Liber the Father in marriage; on her account she was placed among the stars, or she was Liber’s wife. When he had taken her, Vulcan brought a crown containing seven jewels; Liber placed it in the sky out of love for Ariadne. This is the crown they now call [the Crown].—“Fire”: love, *minna*, I.

143. “With honor”: on account of honor, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0129C]

126. Vat. A, in the first hand, has *hastum*, corruptly.

127. Becmanus, in *Manuductio ad linguam Latinam*, chapter 6, corrected *paterae* for *patere*, which appeared in some copies of the Vulgate. Ald., Bong., Torn., Widm., and other older witnesses have *multo*. But *musto* seems more correct to Heinsius, together with Egm. and Cauch., because *multo haustu* had preceded. In Alex. and Juretus’s manuscript there is also *musto*, and in Widm. above *novo*, so that *musto* corresponds to it. I do not dislike *multo*, for Prudentius often makes use of such repetitions. Compare Virgil, book I: “He eagerly drained the foaming cup and bathed himself in the full gold.”

128. Rat., in the first hand, incorrectly has *injugum* for *bijugum*. Tigresses and lynxes are commonly assigned to Bacchus’s chariot.

130. Prag. has, less correctly, *creditur* for *caeditur*. Prag., Widm. above, and Rat., in the second hand, have *chelindros*. Bong. and Widm. have *celindros*. Rat., in the first hand, has *chelidris*. It should be read, with the others, *chelydros*. Mar. likewise has *chelydros*, but above it has *chelyndros*, with the gloss “hairs.” Martinus Roa, book II of the *Singularia*, part 2, chapter 10, demonstrates the similarity between wine and a serpent and explains the passage in Proverbs, “Wine will bite like a serpent.” Hence the dragon was dedicated to Bacchus; but the goat was slaughtered for him because it harms the vines. Virgil, *Georgics* II: “For no other fault is the goat slaughtered at every altar to Bacchus, and the ancient games enter upon the stage.” Arnobius, book V: “Let us also pass over the monstrous Bacchanalia, whose Greek name is *omophagia*—in which, with feigned frenzy and the mind’s sanity set aside, you entwine yourselves with serpents and, to demonstrate that you are filled with the god’s divine power and majesty, you tear apart with bloody mouths the entrails of bleating goats.” See also St. Augustine, *City of God* VII, chapter 21, and Julius Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*. Prudentius relates this particular detail: that the Maenads were crowned not only with serpents but also crushed them with their mouths. This is the meaning of *discindunt*, or, as Juretus’s manuscript reads, *descindunt*, as though they were tearing serpents apart with their teeth. Barthius, book XI of the *Adversaria*, chapter 15, thinks that Arnobius should read *ophiophagiis*, as also in Clement of Alexandria, whose words Arnobius translated. Thus Prudentius correctly says *ore discindunt*, for *ophiophagia* signifies the tearing apart or devouring of serpents—such things, too, as we still see performed in considerable number by conjurers today. Although *chelydri* are also said of green grape-clusters hanging in the form of serpents, Prudentius’s words point to something else.

131. Mar., in the first hand, and likewise Rat., in the first hand, have *placere*; *placare* has rightly been emended, as meter and Latin usage require.

134. Some write *menadas*. Pal., erroneously, has *rotatus*. On these matters see Catullus’s poem, *The Marriage of Peleus and Thetis*.

135. Prag. has *hic* for *hoc*. Ricciolius, in the *Index Syllabarum Controversarum*, proves at length that the first and second syllables of *temulentus* are common. Barthius, in the passage cited, insists that *merulentus* should be read, but he has not convinced me.

136. Juretus rejects *arca* for *acta*, though I do not know where he found *arca*. He notes that *acta* means a secluded and pleasant shore, and that brothels were formerly established on the shores; from this, it may be seen, the French word *bordeau* may have developed.

[Col. 0130D] 137. Vat. A has, incorrectly, *cortum et illis* for *scortum et illic*. This young man, Theseus, was faithless.

138. Egm. has *liquerat ingesto*.

139. Vat. A has, incorrectly, *Neaerem*. Bong., incorrectly, *Neaetram*. Antonius Delrius, in his commentary on Seneca’s *Hercules Oetaeus*, observes that Prudentius calls Ariadne Neaera here because well-kept and plump prostitutes, whom the Athenians called *pugiles* and the Romans *Neaerae*, were so named. Tibullus, Horace, and others commonly apply this name to prostitutes or to their own lovers.

142. Rat. writes *Ariadneus*; Prag. *ariagneus*. Hyginus, *Poetical Astronomy* II, chapter 5, gives fuller and varied accounts of Ariadne’s crown. Paschalius, *On Crowns* I, chapter 9, discusses at length this very crown of Ariadne, added to the stars. For the word *minna* in the gloss, see the commentary on verse 117.

143. Heinsius conjectures *honorae*, namely “of the night”; Gronovius, “this honor” by explanatory expansion, that is, “he pays this honor, the price of the night.” To me the reading of the manuscripts seems clearer: “with this honor he pays the price of the night.”]

And greedy for wine, he drenched himself with a great draught,

Foaming from a jeweled cup, and with Falernian must

708 Sprinkled the dewy backs of the two-yoked wild beasts.

For these services a goat is now slaughtered to Bacchus at every altar,

[130] And green serpents are torn apart with their mouths

By those who wish to appease Bromius; this is what the drunken madness

Of the satyrs already did then before the king’s eyes,

And I think the Maenads themselves did it, driven by frenzied goads,

Whom unmixed wine inflamed and whirled into every crime.

[135] [Col. 0130A] 709 While this chorus danced around him, the drunken adulterer

Found, exposed upon the secluded shore, a woman of outstanding beauty,

A harlot whom the faithless young man had abandoned there,

Sated with incestuous desire.

After the wine, in his passion, he orders Neaera,

[140] Once taken up, to stand with him amid the delights of his floating triumph

And to wear the royal ornament, a crown, upon her head.

Soon the Ariadnean fire is added to the heavenly stars;

With this honor he pays the price of the night.

[Col. 0131A] [Note: [Col. 0131B]

146. “He led”: he considered, I. “Folly”: stupidity, I.

149. “Royal”: palace, I.

154. “The ancestral custom”: it existed when they said, “Our fathers worshiped these gods, and therefore we do likewise,” I.

155. “Clouded”: deceitful, I.

157. “Of light”: of life, I.

158. “Yielded”: came to pass, I. “Urns”: tombs, I., Rat.

159. “Mockeries”: they were so called because, when the girls heard that he had acted in this way, they mocked him and were further aroused to lust, I.

160. “Secret”: adultery. “Marital”: matrimonial or lawful, I.

163. “To remember”: namely, she is accustomed to, Iso.

166. “I shall briefly recall”: I shall commemorate. “Gradivus”: Mars. “Cytherean”: Venus, I.

167. “He”: Mars. “The priestess”: Rhea Silvia, priestess of Pallas, by whom Remus and Romulus were born. “She”: Venus, I.

168. “Phrygian”: of Anchises, I. Of the Trojan Anchises, Vat. A, I.

169. “The goddess”: Venus, I.

170. “Heaven-dwelling”: Mars, I.

172. “August”: noble. “Blood”: of Jupiter, I.

173. “A private”: poor, Anchises, I.

175. “Sedge”: a plant, I.

176. “I would believe”: I, Prudentius. “Noble”: of noble birth, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0131B]

144. Prag., not incorrectly, has *arcem* for *axem*.

145. Thuan. has *illo sed tempore*.

146. Prag. has *dicebat ineptia*; Palat. has *fatuique docebat*. Both readings can be defended. Muretus, book XVIII of the *Various Readings*, chapter 9, praises *ineptia*—*ineptiae* from Terence and Prudentius—against grammarians who prohibit *ineptiam* being used in this way and prescribe *ineptias*.

147. *Induperator* for *imperator* occurs in Ennius, Lucretius, Juvenal, and others.

148. Rat. has *possit*; *posset* is better.

151. Urb. has *thura*; Egm., Widm. above, *tura*; elsewhere *turae*, and *cura et ducibus*, incorrectly. Egm., Pal., Widm. above, and the earlier Rott. have *parvusque*. Heinsius conjectures *parilisque*. Juretus’s manuscript has *thura, et ducibus parvusque*.

152. In some copies of the Vulgate, incorrectly, *imperitus honor*. Vat. A and Juretus’s manuscript have, less well, *aut honor* for *aut amor*.

156. Ald., Bong., Gis., Heins., and later witnesses have *tum quia*. Weitzius, with most of his witnesses, Mar. in the second hand, and Rat. have *tum quoque*. Prag. intended this very reading in *tu quoque*. The sense *tum quoque* seems more correct. The thought is from Lactantius, book I, chapter 15.

[Col. 0131D] 159. Gronovius wanted *pignora, raptas*, which, as Heinsius says, can be joined so that *raptas* is in the accusative. Prudentius means the sons and offspring of unmarried girls. In many old manuscripts *pignera* is written when children and affections are meant; Juretus confirms this with the words of Agraetius: *Pignora rerum, pignera liberorum et affectionum*—“pledges of things, pledges of children and affections.”

160. Gronovius conjectured *defensa jugalis*. But *deprensa* is better. Others write *deprehensa*.

162. Barthius, book LVI, chapter 9, says that Prudentius uses *fervere vitiis* with great elegance, though most people pay little attention to it because it is used so frequently. Propertius, Valerius Flaccus, Petronius, and others use *fervo*. The distinction established between *fervit* and *fervet* is that *fervit* refers to what is now boiling, whereas *fervet* refers to what retains its heat for a long time. Lucilius, cited by Quintilian, book I, chapter 6, section 10: “The water *fervit* and *fervet*: *fervit* now, *fervet* for a year.”

163. In Rat., Mar., and others, this verse is preceded by the title “On Mars, Venus, Juno, and Cybele,” or *Cybelle*, as some write it.

164. Mar., in the first hand, has *ut Romanos*; correctly emended to *ut, Roma, tuos*.

165. Weitz., Widm. above, and Gifanius, in the passage cited under the word *AUCTUS*, emend from an old manuscript to *auctam* for *ortam*.

166. Ald., Gis., Alex., Urb., and others have *perstringam*. Weitz., Heins. with his witnesses, Juretus’s manuscript, and Mar. have *praestringam*, which Heinsius considers characteristic of Prudentius. Some write *Cytheream*, others *Cytherean*, and others *Citheream*.

168. Ald., Gis., Widm. above, Bong., Mar., and others have *succumbit*.

169. Two Rottendorph manuscripts, Widm. above, Bong. in the second hand, Juretus’s manuscript, and others have *mortalis obire*, which Heinsius retained because “earthly” and “mortal” mean the same thing. Cham., Cell., and Teol. agree with Heinsius. Gis. and some copies of the Vulgate have *mortalis inire*. Ald., Sich., Weitz. [Col. 0132D] with his witnesses, Fabr., Urb., Mar., Thuan., and other followers of Heinsius and our own witnesses have *mortale subire*. Gifanius, in the passage cited under *EPITHETA GEMINATA*, reads *mortale subire* from an old manuscript and criticizes Servius and other grammarians for teaching that it is faulty in verse to attribute two epithets to one noun, since Virgil and Lucretius often did so, and Ennius and the very oldest poets did so very frequently. This, however, should not be accepted. He himself assembles examples; others may be seen in Vulpius’s commentary on Catullus, preface to verse 1, among others.

171. Mar. and Prag. have *furtitove igne*.

174. Prag. has, incorrectly, *Citherea sacram*.

175. Widm. above, incorrectly, has *nisa* for *lusa*. Vat. A, less well, has *misit*, and in the first hand *in ulvam*.]

Liber, so that the harlot might illuminate the heavenly vault.

[145] At that time the untaught folly of the foolish populace reckoned

710 That all kings had such power that the emperor

Could pass, with all his filth, into the eternal kingdom

Above the heights of heaven.

At that time every royal power of majesty, and every power,

[150] However small, believed itself to retain command of heaven;

Honor was bestowed even with incense upon rulers and with a small shrine.

While fear, love, or hope heaped it up,

The ancestral custom continued for a long age among the wretched.

The image of false piety began

[155] To proceed through the ignorant descendants in clouded error.

Then, too, the veneration previously accorded to living kings

Passed, when they had fulfilled their office of life, to the dead,

And transferred its altars to the black urns.

From this came the mockeries of girls, the pledges, the offspring,

[160] The secret love of young men, and the detected corruption

[Col. 0132A] 711 of the marriage bed; for the royal palace

Was then accustomed to boil with vices, and the offspring of the gods,

Ruined by luxury, no longer remembered holy modesty.

And, Rome, that I may briefly touch upon your heavenly ancestors,

[165] Whom you boast were the authors of your half-divine origin—

Gradivus and Cytherea—

He violates a priestess; she, in return, submitted to a Phrygian man.

For both, the union was unequal.

Neither was it fitting for a terrestrial goddess to enter into a mortal

[170] Marriage, nor for a heaven-dwelling youth to descend to a virgin’s disgrace

And burn with secret fire.

712 But Venus, a woman from august blood, clung, in forbidden disgrace,

To a lowly and private man.

And if Rhea, through the wanton love of Mars,

[175] [Col. 0132B] Lost her sacred chastity in river sedge,

I would believe that some man of noble stock, but that same man—

[Col. 0133A] [Note: [Col. 0133A]

180. “Led them in”: deceived them, I.

181. “Martian”: the Campus Martius at Rome. “Sacred rites”: sacrifices, I.

[Col. 0133B] 182. “Capitolia”: temples. “Founded”: constructed, Iso.

183. “By a title”: in memory. “Pelasgian”: Greek, of the Greeks. The Pelasgians are called Greeks, named after Pelasgus, a Greek leader, I.

184. “Of Pallas”: of Minerva. “Libyan”: African, I.

185. “Kindred”: the relatives of Mars. “Naked”: conspicuous or pure, because Venus was depicted naked, I.

186. “They might summon”: they might call. “Erycine”: Mount Eryx. “From the summit”: from the summit, I.

187. “Mother”: Ops, who was worshiped on Mount Ida, I.

188. “Green”: because it is green with olives or vines. “Rites”: sacrifices. “Naxos”: a mountain or island where Bacchus was worshiped, I.

191. “Manes”: gods of the underworld, I.

193. “Ancus, etc.”: these were Roman rulers, I.

195. “Thus Vesta”: such was Vesta. “Thus the Palladium”: such is Minerva’s temple, I.

196. “Terror”: a divinity. “Asylum”: a house of refuge, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0133B]

180. Tertullian, chapter 4 of *On Idolatry*: “Human error therefore worships everything except the creator of all.” Minucius likewise relates that the Romans worshiped all the false gods of all peoples. Elmenhorstius, Ouzelius, Wowerus, and Rigaltius discuss this passage at greater length. The Roman belief was that all gods ought to be worshiped by a wise person; for this reason they rejected the true God and the Christian religion, because this worship was contrary to the worship of the false gods. From this you will understand that the argument of certain people who think the Roman persecutions against Christians have been exaggerated is weak, because Roman religion admitted all religions. Other peoples, indeed, venerated their own gods without denying that others ought to be worshiped. Christian religion, by contrast, declared war on all idols. There was also the implacable hatred of the Jews toward Christians, by which they are often found to have incited the pagans.

181. These sacred rites were called *equiria*. They were games in honor of Mars, celebrated in the Campus Martius through horse-racing. See Ovid, *Fasti* III.

182. Cellarius and Teolius note that the Palatine Hill is distinct from the Capitoline, and therefore the word *Capitolia* may be taken loosely for any Roman hill. That *Capitolia* may refer to Capitoline Jupiter was observed at verse 444 of the *Apotheosis*. Chamillardus says that *Capitolia* may mean any lofty and distinguished temple, especially one dedicated to Jupiter. But he correctly adds that the temple of Capitoline Jupiter could be said to have been founded with Palatine stones, because it was built from the stones of the Palatine Hill. In the Capitoline temple there were three shrines: Jupiter’s in the middle, Minerva’s on the right, and Juno’s on the left, as Donatus confirms in *On the City of Rome* II, chapter 4.

[Col. 0133D] 183. Jupiter was Mars’s father and therefore the Romans’ great-grandfather. Chamillardus says that he is called their great-grandfather because he was Venus’s parent. But the passage concerns gods related to Mars, as in verse 185.

184. Juno was especially worshiped by the Carthaginians. See Virgil, *Aeneid* I.

185. Heinsius dislikes that Barthius, in his second set of notes on Claudian, wished to emend *cognatos* to *det Sparta deos*. Giselinus explains it as “gods touching one another,” because, having been conquered in war, they had likewise been transferred to Rome. But he suspects that *cognatos de matre deos* should be read—that is, Castor and Pollux, born from the same egg which Leda, embraced by Jupiter, laid. This conjecture greatly pleases Chamillardus. I think Prudentius clearly calls Jupiter, Pallas, and Juno the Roman gods related to Mars—that is, on Mars’s side.

186. The most famous temple of Venus was on Mount Eryx in Sicily.

187. See Ovid, book IV of the *Fasti*.

188. The earlier Rott. has *Bacchia*. Vat. A, incorrectly, *Bacchida*. Naxos is an island dedicated to Bacchus.

189. St. Leo, in sermon 1 on Saints Peter and Paul: “With the most diligent superstition, everything that had anywhere been established by vain errors was collected and preserved at Rome.”

190. Weitz., with his witnesses, Thuan., the earlier Rott., Prag., Rat., Gif., and Gifanius under *AUCTUS*, read from an old manuscript *quot in orbe sepulcra*, which Heinsius says is entirely correct. Ald., [Col. 0134C] Gis., Mar., Vat. A, Urb., Teol., and others have *in urbe*. Juretus approves *in urbe sepulcra Heroum*. But he falsely thinks that all printed and old books have this reading, except a certain inferior witness in which he read *quot in urbe sepultos Heroes*. He observes that pagan temples were originally tombs, as Clement of Alexandria, St. Cyril of Alexandria, Julius Firmicus, Arnobius, and others teach. Kirchmannus, book II, chapter 16 of *On Roman Funerals*, confirms from this that many tombs formerly existed within the City, especially those of distinguished men and Vestal Virgins. Eutropius perhaps speaks of emperors’ tombs when he says of Trajan: “He alone of all was buried within the City. His bones, placed in a golden urn, are situated in the forum he built, beneath the column.” Some hold the empty opinion that this golden urn was placed above the column; nor do I doubt that it is still beneath the column. For the rest, I much prefer *in orbe*. The poet is charging the Romans with worshiping as gods all the heroes whose tombs existed throughout the world.

[Col. 0134D] 191. In Prag. the reading appears to be *inanes* for *manes*; Egm. has *manens*; read *manes*. I conjecture *quot fabula manes*: the sentence thus proceeds that the Romans worshiped as many dead people as legend had ennobled. Horace, book I, Ode 4: “Now night and the Manes of legend will press upon you.”

192. Prudentius calls the Roman people “our people,” although he was not born at Rome. This is therefore not sufficient evidence for considering him a native of Caesaraugusta or Calagurris.

193. Vat. has, corruptly, *Tellus* for *Tullus*.

194. Prag. has, incorrectly, *fugierunt*.

195. On the Palladium, see verse 544 of book II; on the Penates, verse 965 of the same book II of the *Against Symmachus*.

196. Ald. and several others have *terra asservavit asylum*. Heinsius at one time thought *reseravit terror*; Cronovius, *sacravat terror*. The common reading, *antiquum servavit terror asylum*, should not be disturbed; Oxon. has *antiquam*, less correctly. Virgil, book VIII: “From here Romulus the fierce brought back the great grove that served as an asylum.” After this verse Mar., Rat., and others give as a title: “From this error prevailed.”]

Infamous in character, after forcing a virgin by violence,

He said that he was a god, so that no one might dare

To reproach the shameful, wretched girl with a god’s violation.

[180] This story, or this error, induced the Italian forefathers

To celebrate the rites of Mars in Romulus’ field,

And to designate the Capitolia, built with Palatine stones,

By the title of their great-grandfather Jupiter and Pelasgian

713 Pallas, and to summon Juno from the Libyan citadel,

The gods related through Mars; and that the nobles should summon

Venus’ naked image from the Erycine summit.

And that the Phrygian Mother of the gods should be conveyed from Ida,

[Col. 0134A] And Bacchic rites should be sought from green Naxos:

Rome was made the sole home of earthly majesty,

[190] And Rome had as many temples of gods as there are tombs

714 Of heroes throughout the world, if one may count them: those whom legend

Ennobles as Manes, our people worships and adores.

Ancus, Numitor, Numa, and Tullus held these as gods.

Such deities fled the Pergamean flames.

[195] Such is Vesta, such the Palladium, such the shade of the Penates;

Such terror preserved the ancient asylum.

[Col. 0135A] [Note: [Col. 0135B]

203. “Molae”: *mola*, a kind of sacrifice made from spelt and salt. “Smeared”: polished, I.

204. “With ointment”: with oil. “Lares”: fires, I.

205. “Of Fortune”: of the goddess. “With a rich horn”: that is, a golden one. Fortune is said to hold in her right hand a horn which the nymphs filled with every good thing, I.

208. “Trampled”: kissed, Rat.

211. “Convinced”: certain, hoped for, I.

213. “Senseless”: foolish, imprudent, I.

[Col. 0136B] 214. “Private”: poor, I.

216. “Capitolia”: temples, I.

218. “Sacred Way”: the Sacred Way is in Rome, as is the Latin Way; on that road the Sabines and Romans were reconciled. “Lowings”: namely, of oxen or sheep. “Before”: in his presence, I.

219. “Shrine”: the temple of Venus and the goddess Rome rose to equal height. “She too”: irony, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0135B]

198. Vat. A and Prag. have *una superstitio*.

199. Juretus notes that the best writers often join horror and veneration.

[Col. 0135C] 201. Rat. has *monstrarent*. Ald., Weitz., Palat., Gis., Heins., and others have *primo*. Mar., Prag., Rat., and other Weitzian witnesses have *prima*.

204. Mar. writes *ungento*. I shall discuss the custom of the ancients of anointing boundaries, or stones that served as boundaries, in book II. In this same sense *saxa illita ceris* in the preceding verse can be explained, as I have shown elsewhere, although it may also be understood that the statues themselves were painted with multicolored wax, a practice common among the ancients. Janus Rutgersius, *Various Readings* V, chapter 4, adduces much evidence to suggest that waxing the knees of the gods meant nothing other than attaching votive offerings with wax to the thigh, citing Apuleius and Juvenal, satire 9: “When shall I attach something?” The words of Lucian in *The Lover of Lies* concerning a certain statue are sufficiently clear on this point: “Many obols lay before its feet, as well as other coins, some silver pieces fastened with wax to its leg; and silver plates, the vows of someone.” This passage may therefore be explained in that way, especially since vows were often added to vows. [Col. 0135D] Lucretius, book VI: “Nor join vows to vows.” Olearius, in his notes to Philostratus’s *Heroica*, chapter 2, note 13, page 673, explains this passage of Prudentius and distinguishes those who anointed the gods for honor’s sake from those who waxed the gods’ knees, or smeared stones with wax—that is, attached with wax a tablet containing votive offerings. Philostratus’s words concerning a statue are these: “By rubbing it, both time and those who, by Jupiter, are accustomed either to anoint it or attach vows with wax, have altered its appearance.”

205. Arnobius, book VI, frequently uses this expression concerning the form of statues: “Mulciber with a craftsman’s form,” or “Fortune with a horn full of apples, figs, or autumnal fruits.”

206. Arnobius, Minucius, and Livy take *lapidem* to mean a statue. Many think that in the earliest times stones and stakes were regarded as images of the gods. But stakes, stones, and columns that were worshiped as gods, as I believe, generally displayed some rough outlines of human form.

[Col. 0136B] 209. Egm., Pal., Vat. A, and Juretus’s manuscript have *impressit*, a reading that can be defended by a similar passage in Propertius, book I, elegy 16: “And I gave kisses, leaning upon pressed knees.” For the other reading, see St. Jerome, letter 3 to Rufinus: “How I would fix with pressed lips that mouth which once either erred with me or had good sense.” Compare the notes of Wowerus, Elmenhorstius, Heraldus, Rigaltius, and Ouzelius on these words of Minucius: “Bringing his hand to his mouth, he pressed a kiss to his lips.”

[Col. 0136C] 210. Heinsius conjectured *caesa* for *caeca*. Cellarius followed this conjecture. Teolius likewise printed *caesa* and confirmed that both forms occur in the Vatican manuscripts. Mariettus saw only *caeca* in his witnesses, and I prefer that reading, since images are commonly called both blind and deaf. Rat. and Weitz., with their witnesses, have *opemque*, not incorrectly.

211. Fabr. and Bong. have *quid quis*. Prudentius admirably proves that the pagans began to worship gods through error, from prejudices and preconceived opinions instilled from early childhood, and persisted in the same worship. Certain impious people attempt by similar reasoning to weaken the truth of the Christian religion, but most foolishly. Prudentius first shows that the worship of the gods began in open falsehood and error; then he adds in the following verses that the gentiles never subjected the grounds of their worship to examination, but persisted in superstition solely through use and custom. The Christian religion, however, immediately revealed what it was, and was not strengthened by the growth of errors. Though it taught many obscure things and imposed difficult commands, adults nourished in other religions embraced it. Now, of course, most people are born and raised in it; nevertheless, the arguments by which its truth is demonstrated are everywhere available and powerful enough to dispel all doubt.

212. Ald. and Torn., incorrectly, have *non qui* for *nunquam*. Egm., Palat., Vat. A, and Juretus’s manuscript have *animamque*.

215. Mar., in the first hand, has *namque domo*.

216. Virgil, Cassiodorus, and others have *Capitolia celsa*. Compare the glosses.

217. Rat., in the second hand, has *lanigeros*. Retain *laurigeros*.

218. Ald. has *at Sacram*; others, *ac Sacram*. In Mar. and Rat., after this verse appears the lemma “On the statue of Rome and various statues.” Others have only “On the statue of Rome.”

219. The Smyrnaeans were the first to establish a temple of the city Rome as a goddess. The Alabandians followed their example and added annual games. Hadrian built a temple in the City itself to Venus and Rome. See Lipsius, book III of *On the Grandeur of the Roman Empire*, chapter 6, and Patinus, *Roman Emperors*, coins, page 3, where he displays coins inscribed ΘΕΑ ΡΩΜΗ and adds much about the worship accorded to Rome by the Synnadans, Temenothuritans, Amorians, and Ancyreans. Prudentius speaks of the temple that Hadrian erected to Venus, the mother of the Aeneads, and to Rome, as though to her offspring. Donatus, *On the City of Rome* III, chapter 5, thinks it was one temple with two shrines. Teolius, with Ciampini, maintains that they were two distinct but adjoining temples, later converted into the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian. Claudian, elsewhere in book II of *On Stilicho*, seems to place the temple of Rome on the Palatine: “They gather at the goddess’s roof, which shines white on the Palatine Hill.” The reference is to the temple of Rome. In the gardens of Santa Maria Nuova, or of the monastery of Saint Frances of Rome, the walls of two temples that had been joined together still exist. Some have thought them temples of Isis and Serapis, others of the Sun and Moon. Famianus Nardinus, book III, chapter 12 of *Ancient Rome*, held with certainty that these were the temples of Venus and Rome. The distinguished Carlo Fea, who held the same opinion, showed me the site and fully convinced me that this was so. As is still apparent, these two temples rose to equal height and remain joined at the rear, so that in the very middle wall joining them there is a large arched doorway; perhaps a common altar had been erected in this doorway, where incense was burned simultaneously to both goddesses. These two temples stood on the Palatine, with a view toward the Sacred Way. The Sacred Way did not pass between the Arch of Titus, as some think, but ran approximately where the church of Santa Maria Nuova now stands. That site was once much lower and more depressed; it now appears elevated because the ruins of buildings have accumulated there. It is therefore clear why Prudentius says: “The Sacred Way resounding with lowings before the shrine of Rome.” The words of Xiphilinus, drawn from Cassius Dio’s account of Hadrian, strongly support this interpretation. He says that Hadrian sent Apollodorus the architect a model of the temple of Venus that he had built at Rome, to show that a great work could be made without his assistance; then he asked whether the temple seemed well and rationally constructed. Apollodorus replied that it ought to have been built much higher and wider, so that its height would make it more prominent on the Sacred Way and its breadth would accommodate machines that could be assembled secretly inside it and suddenly brought into the theater. He also said that the statues were too large for the proportions of the temple’s height and breadth: “For if the goddesses should wish to rise and come out, they would be unable to do so.” Compare the commentary on verse 765 of book II. On the coins of several emperors one may see a temple with six columns and the inscription *Romae Aeternae*. Juretus discusses this title at length in his commentary on book II of *Against Symmachus*, letter 55. Ammianus Marcellinus, Spartianus, Tacitus, Cassiodorus, and Xiphilinus may also be consulted concerning the temple of Rome.]

Once vain superstition had occupied the pagan hearts of their forefathers,

It ran on uninterrupted through a thousand stages of the ages. The tender heir feared

[200] And worshiped whatever his hoary ancestors had shown him to be venerable.

The infancy of children first drank error with its milk; amid

Cries it had tasted the sacrificial meal of spelt; it had seen stones smeared with wax

And black Lares made moist with ointment.

[205] 715 As a little boy, he had seen the fashioned image of Fortune with her rich horn,

And the consecrated stone standing in the house,

And his mother growing pale there in prayer.

Soon, placed upon his nurse’s shoulders, he too rubbed

[Col. 0136A] The stone with lips pressed upon it, offered childish vows,

[210] And sought riches for himself from the blind rock;

And he was convinced that whatever one wished must be sought from it.

716 Never raising his eyes and mind to the citadel of reason,

He turned them back; but, credulous, he retained the senseless custom,

Honoring private gods with the blood of lambs.

[215] And now, leaving home, when he marveled at public festivals,

Holy days, and games, and saw the lofty Capitolia,

And the laurel-bearing ministers of the gods standing at the temples,

And the Sacred Way resounding with lowings before

The shrine of Rome (for she too is worshiped with blood

[Col. 0137A] [Note: [Col. 0137A]

222. “To the goddesses”: to Rome and Venus, I.

223. “Thinking it true”: the infancy of children, or every pagan, I. Namely, the boy mentioned above, Vat. A.

226. “There”: in the temple of Rome. “Alcides”: Hercules, from his father Alcaeus. “At Gades”: Gades are islands near Britain, which Hercules plundered, and there he killed Geryon. “Guest”: of Evander, I.

227. “Stands rigid”: stands there. “The twins”: Castor and Pollux, namely, they stand there, I.

[Col. 0138A] 228. “Corrupted”: ignoble. “Ledaean”: an explanatory expression, “the sons of Leda,” I.

229. “Nocturnal”: because they shine at night and because they were horse-tamers. “Horsemen”: perhaps because they were still alive and rode at night; or he says this on account of the two stars which, when they move, seem to be riding, I, Vat. T.

230. “They hang”: namely, bent over. “Holding back”: namely, the course they used, Vat. T. “Holding the spear”: that is, an arrow, Vat. S.]

[Note: [Col. 0138B]

223. Ald., Torn., and Gall. have *Vera ratus quaecunque senatu auctore probentur*. Vat. A likewise has this, but *probantur*, not *probentur*. Alex., Egm., Pal., Widm. above, and Juretus’s manuscript agree with Vat. A. Heinsius says that Thuan. and others, both his own witnesses and Weitzian witnesses, have *quaecunque senatu auctore probentur*. But Weitzius has *probantur*, although he asserts that Ald. printed *probentur*, the only form I find there. Weitzius likewise suggests that Widm., in the first hand, has *quaecunque fiant auctore senatu*; in the margin, *fuant*. Colerus also found *fuant*, Cauch. *cluant*, and thinks it should be emended whenever *fiat* occurs in Prudentius with its first syllable shortened. Prag., Mar., the one Rott., Weitz., Gis., and other later witnesses have *quaecunque fiant auctore senatu*. Rat., in a later hand, has *fiant quaecunque*, with the earlier words erased. In Mar. there is the error *sanatu*. It is well known that the Roman Senate judged matters of religion. Tertullian, chapter 5 of the *Apology*: “There was an ancient decree that no god should be consecrated by the emperor unless approved by the Senate.”

224. In Vat. A, *putabit* is an error.

226. Vat. A, Rat. in the first hand, Mar. in the first hand, and Urb. incorrectly have *spoliatis gradibus*. Grangaeus thinks that Prudentius is speaking of the forum Augustus built, in one portico of which stood statues of Latin kings and in the other statues of Roman kings. Hercules was called Alcides from his grandfather Alcaeus, not from his father, as Iso says; Iso also wrongly explains Gades.

227. Ald., Weitz., Widm., and Bong. write *Archadiae*. Rat. and Mar. have *Arcadia*. Prag. has *Archadio*. To Heinsius, the expression *hospes Arcadiae*—“guest of Arcadia”—for *hospes Arcadis*, that is, “guest of Evander,” seems harsh and unusual. Gronovius thought *Arcadii* should be read; Heinsius, *Arcadis* from *fulvo*. Perhaps Prudentius means that the statue of Alcides was made of bronze from Arcadia, as though it had once been erected by Evander. Thus: “He stands rigid in the bronze of Arcadia.”

228. Prag., instead of *nothi*, has *riget*, and above it the gloss [Col. 0138D] “in golden statues.” He imitates the expression “bastards begotten from a mother’s bed” in book VII of the *Aeneid*.

229. Vat. A has, corruptly, *avo* for *duo*. Lactantius, book II, chapter 8: “Then there is the story that Castor and Pollux were seen during the Latin War at the Lake of Juturna washing the sweat from their horses, when their temple, which adjoined the spring, had spontaneously opened; and that during the Macedonian War, mounted on white horses, they appeared to Publius Vatinius as he was approaching Rome by night, announcing that King Perseus had been defeated and captured that day.” Iso explains *nocturni equites* differently.]

230. Fabr., Gis., Weitz. with his copies, Mar., Rat., Prag., the second Rott., and the vulgate retain *retinentque veru*; Prag. adds the gloss *hastam* (“spear”), a reading and explanation approved by Mariettus. Ald., Vat. A, and Juretus’s manuscript have *impendent retinente solo* (“they hang, being held only by the base”); one Rott. has *dependent retinente solo*. Thuan., Oxon., Alex., Urb., Heins., and later editions read *impendent retinente veru* (“they hang, being held by a spear”). But Chamillardus and Heinsius think that *veru* means a spear or military instrument, as *veru sabellum* in Virgil; Ansaldus accordingly translates it in Italian verse: “They lean upon their spears, and, made / Of cast lead, arrest their steps.” Holstenius, in his letter on the *fulcra* or *veruba* of the Ephesian Diana, reports from a first-rate Latin glossary, found in three Vatican manuscripts, that *verua* are rods or iron rods. He explains Prudentius as referring to such elongated iron supports by which statues are usually held upright, and thinks that he is pointing out the popular error of those who admired the statues as hanging and on the point of falling. By this reading, which Holstenius had seen in the Urbinate manuscript, he defends a similar reading in the first Roman edition of Minucius: “Diana meanwhile is a huntress, girt high; and the Ephesian goddess, built up with many breasts and *veruba*; and Trivia, dreadful with three heads and many hands.” Evidently the whole mass of breasts was supported by *veruba*, for that image, like Egyptian statues, stood with its feet tightly compressed. Holstenius maintains that Georgius Fabricius, having consistently found *retinente veru* in his copies, improperly corrected it to *retinentque veru*. I do not know where Fabricius acknowledged this, unless it was in his *Commentary on the Christian Poets*, under the words *GEMINI FRATRES*, where he states that the reading had hitherto been corrupted; yet it is clear that the old editions and manuscripts had various readings. I greatly approve Holstenius’s reading and explanation, though another interpretation can also be defended. For even if one reads *retinente veru*, it can still be understood as “the spear itself holding them,” upon which they lean.

717. *More deae, nomenque loci, ceu numen, habetur,*

And the custom of the goddess is observed, and the name of the place is held as a divinity,

*Atque Urbis, Venerisque pari se culmine tollunt*

while temples of the City and of Venus alike raise themselves to equal height:

*Templa: simul geminis adolentur thura deabus),*

incense is burned at the same time for the two goddesses—

*Vera ratus, quaecunque fiant auctore senatu,*

believing to be true whatever is done on the authority of the senate,

*Contulit ad simulacra fidem, dominosque putavit*

he transferred his faith to the images and thought them masters

[225] [Col. 0138A] *Aetheris, horrifico qui stant ex ordine vultu.*

of heaven, standing in a terrifying row with their dreadful faces.

*Illic Alcides, spoliatis Gadibus, hospes*

There Hercules, after the sack of Gades, a guest

*Arcadiae fulvo aere riget: gemini quoque fratres*

of Arcadia, stiffens in tawny bronze; the twin brothers also,

*Corrupta de matre nothi, Ledeia proles,*

bastards born from a corrupted mother, the offspring of Leda,

*Nocturnique equites, celsae duo numina Romae,*

and the nocturnal horsemen, two divinities of lofty Rome,

[230] 718. *Impendent, retinente veru, magnique triumphi*

hang there, held by an iron support, announcing a great triumph.

[Col. 0139A] [Note: [Col. 0139A]

232. *Insignia*: statues. I.

234. *Picus*, son of Saturn, concerning whom Virgil says: “Circe made him into a bird and sprinkled color over his wings.” I.

235. *Epotum*: contraction for *epotatum* (“drunk up”); [the poison] given by his wife. *Sparsus*: having it spread over his limbs. I.

237. *Mense*: in January. I.

238. *Auspiciis*: by omens, portents, auguries. Iso.

239. *Agitant*: frequent, celebrate. I.

[Col. 0140A] 240. *Calendarum*: of the convocations. I.

243. *Catenam*: the evil practice that binds a person. I.

246. *Mense*: because the eighth month was named in his honor. *Adytis*: temples, sacrifices. *Flamine*: priest. I.

247. *Augustum*: Octavian. I.]

[Note: [Col. 0139C]

231. Vat. A has the corrupt reading *suffusa* (“poured over”); Egm. and Pal. have *suffosso* (“having been poured beneath”). It was an ancient practice to pour lead into the base so that statues would adhere more firmly. Christian writers consequently took the opportunity to ridicule the divinities of the pagans. Arnobius, book VI: “You would have seen those gods long ago … held back from collapse and disintegration by props and chains, hooks and rings; and lead poured throughout all the cavities and joints, providing the images with a salutary delay against the passage of time.” And later: “If they suffer the necessity of remaining in place, what could be more wretched or more unfortunate than this: that hooks hold them in their bases and leaden applications?” Juretus proves from many sources that pagans sometimes used to fasten bonds to statues lest the gods flee. He also censures the ignorance of a certain little scholar who had added in the margin of his copy that Prudentius’s words referred to cast and leaden statues. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 12, mentions lead in statues: “Before the application of lead, glue, and bolts, your gods are headless.”

233. Gis., Rat., Egm., Cauch., and Widm. above have *Tros Italus*; Oxon. likewise prefers *Dros Italus*, and Vat. A has, corruptly, *Ros Italus*, perhaps because the initial letters of verses are sometimes missing in Vat. A. Mar. and Widm. again above have *dux Salius*. Others have *dux Italus*. Heinsius reads and punctuates *Tros, Italus*, so that *Tros* signifies Aeneas. On Italus, Sabinus, Janus, and Saturn, see Virgil, book VII, to which Prudentius seems to be referring. I therefore agree with Gifanius under *strata viarum*, who reads from book V *dux Italus*, whom the poet calls a leader because he was the original founder of the name “Italy.”

236. Rat., by correction from some little scholar, has the poor reading *sua sordida cuique*. Ald., Mar. in a second hand, Gis., and others have *sua cuique vetusta* (“to each his own ancient [altar]”). Vat. A has *sua cuique vetusto*. Egm. and Palat. have *sua cuique vetustas*. [The phrase] *Agna Jano etiam* also occurs. Prag., Mar. in the first hand, Oxon., Widm., and Fabr. have *sua cuique sordens*, so that the word *cuique* forms a dactyl, as I have already explained. Molinaeus, in his treatise *On Altars*, thinks that the multitude of altars which Prudentius reproaches the pagans for having was borrowed by Catholics from the pagans—but this is shameless. The poet mocks little altars soiled with blood, consecrated everywhere before the feet of men and monsters. What has this to do with Catholic altars?

237. Vat. A, incorrectly in the first hand, has *de mense ligatur*. The January Kalends were extremely famous; a sermon of Saint Maximus is directed against them. See Bingham, *Christian Antiquities*, volume IX, book XX, chapter 1, section 3. He teaches that these festivals continued under Christian emperors without idolatrous rites, but in such a way that councils and the Fathers spoke against them.

240. Ald. incorrectly reads and punctuates *gaudia ducunt*. The observance of the Kalends festivals increased. In the *Collection of Canons of Saint Martin of Braga*, chapter 73, it reads: “It is not permitted to practice the wicked observances of the Kalends and devote oneself to pagan leisure, nor to encircle houses with laurel or the greenness of trees. All this observance belongs to paganism.”

244. In Mar., Rat., and others, the heading *On the Image of Augustus* follows this verse.

246. Prag., Pal., and some others have *mensa* (“table”), a reading approved by Cauchius because sacrificial tables served in place of altars. Heinsius says that the older copies have *mensa*; yet he himself must have written *mense*, since he printed it in the text, and most copies read it so. Here the reference is to the month Sextilis, which was called August in honor of Augustus. Writers frequently discuss the honors paid to Augustus while he was still alive. See Horace, book II, epistle 1. His head is seen on coins crowned with rays. It is also established that women served as his *flamines*, or priestesses.]

*Nuntia suffuso figunt vestigia plumbo.*

They fix their footsteps with lead poured beneath them.

*Assistunt etiam priscorum insignia regum,*

There also stand the insignia of ancient kings,

719. *Dux Italus, Janusque bifrons, genitorque Sabinus,*

the Italian leader, and two-faced Janus, and Sabine father,

*Saturnusque senex, maculoso et corpore Picus,*

and aged Saturn, and Picus with his spotted body,

[235] *Conjugis epotum sparsus per membra venenum.*

with poison given by his wife and drunk, spread through his limbs.

*Omnibus ante pedes posita est sua cuique sordens*

Before the feet of all is placed for each his own filthy

*Arula. Jano etiam celebri de mense litatur*

little altar. Janus too is worshiped in the famous month,

*Auspiciis, epulisque sacris, quas inveterato,*

with omens and sacred banquets, which, under an established—

*Heu! miseri sub honore agitant, et gaudia ducunt*

alas, wretched!—honor they celebrate and take delight in,

[240] [Col. 0140A] *Festa Calendarum. Sic observatio crevit.*

the festivals of the Kalends. Thus the observance grew.

*Ex atavis quondam male coepta: deinde secutis*

Once badly begun by our forefathers, then handed down

*Tradita temporibus, serisque nepotibus aucta.*

through succeeding ages and increased by late descendants.

*Traxerunt longam corda inconsulta catenam,*

Unreflecting hearts dragged along a long chain,

720. *Mosque tenebrosus vitiosa in saecula fluxit.*

and the dark custom flowed on through corrupt generations.

[245] *Hunc morem veterum docili jam aetate secuta*

Posterity, now following this ancestral custom at a teachable age,

*Posteritas, mense, atque adytis, et flamine, et aris*

worshiped Augustus with month, shrines, priesthood, and altars;

*Augustum coluit, vitulo placavit, et agno.*

they appeased him with a calf and a lamb.

[Col. 0141A] [Note: [Col. 0141B]

248. *Strata*: posterity. *Pulvinar*: the couch of the gods; a ceremonial couch and altar. I.

249. *Tituli*: inscriptions, honors. I.

250. *Caesareum*: Octavian’s. I.

251. *Quo*: so that. *Livia*: the wife of Octavian. I.

255. *Viri*: of a man other than Octavian. Iso.

256. *Geniale*: nuptial. I.

257. *Sponsus*: still, as yet. I.

[Col. 0142B] 258. *Pactam*: joined, betrothed, a bride. Iso.

259. *Ort um*: birth. I.

261. *Fescennina*: nuptial songs, so called from the town of Fescennium, or because they drive away witchcraft. The god Fescenninus is also called the god of marriage. Iso. “Nuptial songs,” Mar.

262. *Deum sortes*: the responses of the gods. I.

263. *Taedas*: marriage. I.

266. *Floras*: hence *floralia*. *Creasti*: appointed, assigned. I.]

[Note: [Col. 0141B]

250. Tacitus, *Annals*, book I: “After the burial had been completed according to custom, a temple and divine honors were decreed.” By the poet’s phrase “in the likeness of Jupiter,” I understand a temple decreed for Augustus, just as temples were customarily erected for Jupiter. Chamillardus and others reasonably think that the image of Augustus was displayed in the form of Jupiter. After this verse, Mar., Rat., and others have the heading *On the Image of Livia, the Wife of Augustus*.

251. Aid. incorrectly has *adjacere*. Ouzelius, commenting on Minucius’s words “and the other deified kings who are consecrated,” discusses at length the apotheosis of Livia, which he concludes from these verses to have been consecrated in the form and under the name of Juno. Chamillardus agrees. I do not find this clear. For the poet’s words seem only to imply that Livia was made a goddess according to pagan custom and received the honors attributed to Juno. While still alive, Livia was also called Juno by flattery, just as Augustus was called Jupiter. Grangaeus states that old books have *quo Julia Juno*, and this is correct if one considers the adoption. Livia was adopted by her husband Augustus and consequently acquired the name Julia. Coins exist on which she is called “the divine Julia, daughter of Augustus.” But I do not know which old books he means. Giselinus conjectured that *Julia* should be read instead of *Livia*, because Augustus imposed his daughter Julia on Agrippa, having, as was suspected, corrupted her himself. But there is no doubt that Livia is meant.

254. Suetonius, *Life of Augustus*, chapter 62: “He took Livia Drusilla away from her marriage to Tiberius Nero, and indeed when she was pregnant.”

256. Ald. reads and punctuates: *gerebat, Pronuba jam gravidae fulcrum, et geniale parantur*. Mariettus also seems to have read this in his copies, except in Prag., where it is *paratur*. Weitzius agrees, with his copies, but in Bong. *et* is absent after *fulcrum*. In Oxon., Alex., and Urb. it is *fulcrum et geniale parantur*. The reading of Giselinus and others seems correct: *gerebat Pronuba: jam gravidae fulcrum geniale paratur* (“the matron of marriage carried [the child]: now the bridal couch is prepared for the pregnant woman”). Thus *lectus genialis* in Horace; and in book II of the *Symposium*, verse 615, *genialia fulcra*; verse 1083, *fulcra jugalia*. Instead of *jam*, Widm. has *tam*, less well. Colerus, page 568, commenting on chapter 1 of book VI of Valerius Maximus, thinks that Prudentius is attacking the bridal bed, concerning which Valerius says: “the most sacred bridal couch of Julia.” Lipsius taught that Livia is meant here. At this passage Colerus praises his own manuscript of Prudentius, which we cite under Marietti’s name; he himself calls Prudentius an ardent poet, full of the most devout zeal.

257. Juvenal, satire 6, verse 599: “and to distress the womb with children leaping within it.”

259. Augustus was a stepfather and Drusus a stepson, because Livia was the wife of Augustus and the mother of Drusus.

261. Livia gave birth before the third month; hence, in a certain sense, amid the nuptial songs. Giselinus objects that Livia conceived by adultery with Augustus and cites Suetonius as witness. But Suetonius merely says that this was suspected. It is said that nuptial verses, full of obscenity, were brought to Rome from Fescennium, a town of Etruria. Hence Horace’s phrase “Fescennine license.” *Fescennia* is less correctly found in some copies.

[Col. 0142C] 262. Gifanius, under the word *FAC*, argues that the reading should be *Utque deum sortes, sic Apollinis antra dederunt*, from old books, although these had *atque deum*, and one, with erasure, *idque deum*. Heinsius dislikes Gifanius’s attempt to emend it in this way, in the worst possible example, with no regard for the metrical rule. Yet Heinsius himself often errs in this manner. Weitz., apparently with his copies, Thuan., the second Rott., Mar., Prag., Rat., and Alex. have *id Apollinis*. Ald., Gis., and Urb. have *et Apollinis*. Balthus, *On the Silence of Oracles*, part 2, chapter 5, understands these verses as referring to the responses of haruspices, not to oracles, which had already ceased; but he denies that the verses prove that the ancient oracles were merely impostures of priests, even if they are understood as referring to oracles. In fact Dio reports that the pontiffs, not Apollo, were consulted. This nevertheless does not prevent some oracle of Apollo, whether genuine or fabricated, from having been circulated. Juvenal, satire 6, verse 553: “Whatever the astrologer shall say, they will believe it reported from the face of Ammon, since at Delphi the oracles have ceased, and darkness condemns the human race to uncertainty about the future.” Van Dale, *Dissertation 2 on Oracles*, argues from this whole passage of Prudentius that Augustus, after his death, gave oracles—obviously fabricated—and that while he lived oracles were spread among the people, either by himself or by the flatterers of himself and Tiberius.

263. Ald. incorrectly has *cederet aedes*. Pal. and Vat. A have *credere thedas*. Mar. and Prag. have *caedere tedas*. Egm. and Widm. above have *credere taedas*. Others correctly have *cedere taedas*.

264. Mar. and Widm. above have *nupta vocatur*. Mar., in another hand, has *jugatur*.

266. Ald. and Mar. have *flores inter, Veneresque*, less well; Prag. has *Veneremque*. The Circus and the temple of Flora are situated between the Quirinal and Pincian hills.

267. *Sapiens* is missing in Vat. A. Prag., contrary to the meter, has *nec mirum, si quis enim sapiens*. Cauch., Urb., the two Rotts., and Heinsius retained *dubitaverit*.]

*Strata ad pulvinar jacuit, responsa poposcit.*

She lay stretched upon the sacred couch and demanded responses.

*Testantur tituli, produnt consulta senatus,*

The inscriptions bear witness, and the decrees of the senate declare it,

[250] *Caesareum Jovis ad speciem statuentia templum.*

which established a Caesarean temple in the likeness of Jupiter.

*Adjecere sacrum, fieret quo Livia Juno,*

They added a sacred rite by which Livia was to become Juno,

*Non minus infamis thalami sortita cubile,*

having received a bridal chamber no less infamous

*Quam cum fraterno caluit Saturnia lecto.*

than when the Saturnian goddess grew warm in a brother’s bed.

*Nondum maternam partu vacuaverat alvum,*

She had not yet emptied her maternal womb by childbirth,

[255] 721. *Conceptamque viri sobolem paritura gerebat*

but was carrying, to give birth, offspring conceived by another man,

*Pronuba; jam gravidae fulcrum geniale paratur,*

the matron of marriage; now the bridal couch is prepared for the pregnant woman,

*Jam sponsus, saliente utero nubentis, amicos*

now the bridegroom, while the bride’s womb leaps,

*Advocat, haud sterilem certus fore jam sibi pactam.*

calls his friends, certain that his betrothed will not remain barren.

[Col. 0142A] *Vitricus antevenit tardum praefervidus ortum*

The stepfather, burning with impatience, anticipates the slow birth

[260] *Privigni nondum geniti; mox editur inter*

of the stepson not yet born; soon, amid

*Fescennina novo proles aliena marito.*

the Fescennine songs, a child not his own is born to the new husband.

*Idque deum sortes, id Apollinis antra dederunt*

The lots of the gods and the cave of Apollo gave this

*Consilium: nunquam melius nam cedere taedas*

counsel: never was it more fittingly answered that the marriage torches should be set aside

722. *Responsum est, quam cum praegnans nova nupta jugatur.*

than when a pregnant new bride is joined in marriage.

[265] *Hanc tibi, Roma, deam titulis, et honore sacratam*

This goddess, consecrated for you, Rome, by titles and honor,

*Perpetuo Floras inter, Veneresque creasti.*

you established forever among the Floras and Venuses.

*Nec mirum: quis enim sapiens dubitaverat, illas*

Nor is this surprising: for what wise person would have doubted that women

[Col. 0143A]

*Mortali de stirpe satas vixisse, et easdem*

born from mortal stock had lived, and that they,

*Laude venustatis claras, in amoribus usque*

famous for the praise of their beauty, had persisted in their loves

[270] *Ad famae excidium formae nituisse decore?*

until the destruction of their reputation, shining in the splendor of their appearance?

*Quid loquar Antinoum coelesti in sede locatum?*

What shall I say of Antinous, placed in a celestial seat—

*Illum delicias nunc divi principis, illum*

him, once the darling of the divine emperor, him,

723. *Purpureo in gremio spoliatum sorte virili,*

stripped of his manly condition and reclining in the purple lap,

*Hadrianique dei Ganymedem, non cyathos diis*

the Ganymede of the god Hadrian, not offering cups

[275] *Porgere: sed medio recubantem cum Jove fulcro,*

to the gods, but reclining on the central couch with Jupiter,

*Nectaris ambrosii sacrum potare lyaeum,*

drinking the sacred wine of ambrosial nectar,

*Cumque suo in templis vota exaudire marito?*

and hearing prayers in temples together with his husband?

*Ergo his auspicibus, Trajanus, Nerva, Severus,*

Thus, under these auspices, Trajan, Nerva, and Severus,

*Et Titus, et fortes gesserunt bella Nerones:*

and Titus and the vigorous Neros waged wars—

[280] [Col. 0144A] *Quos terrena viros illustres gloria fecit,*

men whom earthly glory made illustrious,

*Et virtus fragilis provexit in ardua famae*

and whom frail virtue raised to the heights of fame,

*Ascita e terris sub relligione jacentes.*

though they lay beneath a religion imported from foreign lands.

724. *Quam pudet, hoc illis persuasum, talibus ut se,*

How shameful that they were persuaded of this, that by such means they

*Romanasque acies censerent Martis amore*

could govern themselves and the Roman battle lines

[285] *Posse regi, dum se Paphiae male blandus adulter*

through love of Mars, while the deceitfully seductive adulterer of Paphian Venus

*Venditat, Aeneadasque suos successibus auget?*

advertises himself and increases his own Aeneads by successes.

*Felices, si cuncta Deo sua prospera Christo*

Happy would they have been if they had known that all their prosperity had been arranged

*Principe disposita scissent, qui currere regna*

by God under Christ the prince, who willed kingdoms to run

*Certis ducta modis, Romanorumque triumphos*

according to fixed designs, and the triumphs of the Romans

[290] *Crescere, et impletis voluit se infundere saeclis.*

to grow, and himself to pour into the ages when they had been fulfilled.

[Col. 0145A] [Note: [Col. 0145B]

291. *Luce*: wisdom. I.

292. *Adytis*: temples. I.

293. *Junonum*: of Juno and Livia. I.

295. *Crassis*: foolish. I.

298. *Id duxere*: the Romans adopted it into their religion. I.

299. *Figuras*: of the gods. I.

301. *Statuis*: images or columns. *Neptunum*: the god of the sea. I.

302. *Cyaneas*: watery. I, Vat. A.

303. *Dryadas*: goddesses of the woods. *Napaeas*: goddesses of the mountains. I.

305. *Perhibetur*: is called. I.

307. *Regnare*: to rule, dominate. I.

[Col. 0146B] 308. *Aeoliae*: the eight islands of Sicily, assigned to Vulcan because of their emission of fire. *Aetnae*: of Mount Etna in Sicily, which is always burning. I.

309. *Conspicuis*: bright, clear, shining. *Superos*: heavenly gods. I.

311. *Conditio*: law. *Vigilem*: continuous. I.

312. *Orbe*: circuit, circumference. I.

313. *Praecipitem*: swift. *Per inane*: because neither the sun nor the other seven planets are fixed in the firmament; rather, they travel through empty space. I.

315. *Area*: the extent of a field. I.

316. *Diffusius*: more broadly, more widely. I. Mar. has *latius* (“more widely”).

317. *Emicat*: leaps, springs. I.]

[Note: [Col. 0145C]

292. Vat. A incorrectly has *angustique adytis*.

293. Giselinus understands the second Juno to be Proserpina. Others understand Livia; this supports the conjecture that Livia was consecrated in the form of Juno, just as other emperors and their wives were represented in the form of gods and goddesses.

294. Prag. incorrectly has *barathri*.

295. Ald. corruptly has *orbem*.

296. Mar. has *haeserat*, believing it to have been corrected by the same hand. The same Mar. has *immersoque*. Evidently *haeserat* and *immersoque* arose from *esse rati, mersoque*. After this verse, Rat. and Mar. have the heading *On the Worship of the Elements under the Appearance of Certain Beings Who Are Not Gods but Demons*.

297. Ald., Gis. in the text, and some vulgate copies have: *Quidquid humus, pelagus, coelum mirabile gignunt* (“Whatever the earth, sea, and wondrous heaven produce”). Others have: *Quidquid humus, quidquid pelagus mirabile gignit* (“Whatever the earth, whatever the sea wondrously produces”). Juretus’s codex has *gignunt*, as do Widm. above, Pal., Bong., and Alex. in the first hand. Gallandius rejects Ald.’s reading because the poet is discussing the worship of the elements, and no one would say that heaven produces; moreover, the following verses begin to speak of the sun and moon. I think that in Ald.’s reading *coelum* can correctly be understood as “air.”

298. Weitz. with his copies, the second Rott., Ox., Prag., Rat., and Colerus, page 568, on Valerius Maximus, have *induxere deos* (“introduced gods”). Vat. A and Mar. have *adduxere deos* (“brought in gods”). The earlier Rott. has *id dixere deos* (“they called this gods”). The readings preferred by Heinsius have *id duxere deos* (“they took this for gods”). Heinsius suspects *induxere deo* or *deis*. Cassiodorus, book X of the *Tripartite History*, chapter 30, calls this “deifying the elements.” Saint Athanasius, in his *Oration against the Gentiles*, and Lactantius, book II, chapters 5–6, attack this madness.

299. Ald., Juretus’s codex, Pal., Egm., and Widm. above have *formant elementa* (“they form the elements”).

302. Cyane is represented by the poets as having been transformed into a river.

303. Ald. has *silvam*. Some write *Napheas*, others *Napeas*, and others *Napaeas*.

305. Ald. has *perhibetur qui virtute*. Pal. has *qui in virtute*.

306. Heinsius conjectures *deis et nomine, et ore Assimulatus*, and this appears in some editions. Alex. has *deus nomine*, but correctly above *et nomine*.

307. Prag., Mar., Bong., Gis., and Heins. have *assim ulatus*. Ald., Weitz., Teol., and others have *assimilatus*. Weitz., Prag. in the first hand, and Rat. in an old hand have *nec jam regnare*. *Necnon* is better.

308. The heading *On the Worship of the Sun, Whom They Think to Be Apollo* is placed under this verse.

309. Vat. A has, less well, *conspicuus*. This verse and the next two are read in book IV of Hyginus’s *Astronomy of the Poets*, chapter 13, “On the Sun,” at the end. They were inserted by some shameless little scholar, a fact many failed to notice, despite Delrio’s warning in his *Commentary on Seneca’s Medea*, pages 72–73. Delrio notes that the first two verses are cited by Calpurnius Bassus in his commentary on Germanicus’s *Phenomena* with a similar act of dishonesty—unless this Bassus was some obscure person much later than Prudentius, or unless those who attribute the commentary to him are imposing upon us. See below the notes on verse 365. The Romans worshiped the sun with exceptional honor. A temple of the Sun and Moon stood near the amphitheater. Augustus dedicated a sundial obelisk in the Campus Martius; through the generosity of Pius VI, it now stands before the Innocentian Curia. Angelo Bandini wrote an entire book about this obelisk.

315. Heinsius suspects *procurrit*.

317. Prag. incorrectly has *hic volucri*.

318. Heins., with Thuan., Mar., Prag., Weitz., and Gis. in the text, has *breviorem*. Others have *breviore*. Everyone now agrees that the earth should be called smaller in circumference than the sun. In ancient times the Stoics, Lucretius, Lactantius, and others disagreed.]

*Sed caligantes animas, et luce carentes,*

But they plunged darkened souls, deprived of light,

*In Jovis, Augustique adytis, templisque duarum*

in the shrines of Jupiter and Augustus, and in the temples of the two

*Junonum, Martisque etiam, Venerisque sacellis*

Junoes, and also in the little sanctuaries of Mars and Venus,

*Mactatas, tetro lethi immersere barathro,*

sacrificed, into the dreadful abyss of death,

[295] *Supremum regimen crassis in partibus orbis*

thinking that the supreme government lay in the dense regions of the world

*Esse rati, mersoque poli consistere fundo.*

and that it stood fixed in the sunken depth of heaven.

*Quidquid humus, quidquid pelagus mirabile gignit,*

Whatever the earth produces, whatever the sea wondrously brings forth,

725. *Id duxere deos: colles, freta, flumine, flammas,*

they took for gods: hills, straits, rivers, flames—

*Haec sibi per varias formata elementa figuras*

the fathers fashioned these elements for themselves in various forms,

[300] *Constituere patres, hominumque vocabula mutis*

and wrote human names

*Scripserunt statuis, vel Neptunum vocitantes*

on mute statues, calling the sea Neptune,

[Col. 0145B] *Oceanum, vel Cyaneas cava flumina nymphas,*

or the hollow rivers Cyanean nymphs,

*Vel silvas Dryadas, vel devia rura Napaeas.*

or the woods Dryads, or the remote fields Napaeas.

*Ipse ignis, nostrum factus qui servit ad usum,*

Fire itself, made to serve our use,

[305] [Col. 0146A] *Vulcanus perhibetur, et in virtute superna*

is called Vulcan, and is imagined in a heavenly power;

*Fingitur, ac delubra deus et nomine, et ore*

as a god, in name and appearance,

*Assimulatus habet, necnon regnare caminis*

he is given sanctuaries, and is said to rule over furnaces

*Fertur, et Aeoliae summus faber esse, vel Aetnae.*

and to be the chief smith of Aeolia or Etna.

*Est, qui conspicuis superos quaesivit in astris,*

There is one who sought the gods above in conspicuous stars,

[310] *Ausus habere deum solem: cui tramite certo*

and dared to regard the sun as a god; to it, on a fixed course,

726. *Conditio imposita est, vigilem tolerare laborem,*

the condition was imposed that it endure unceasing labor,

*Visibus objectum mortalibus, orbe rotundo*

exposed to mortal eyes, with rounded disk,

*Praecipitem, teretique globo per inane volantem,*

plunging headlong and flying through empty space on a smooth sphere,

*Et quod nemo negat, mundo, coeloque minorem.*

and, as no one denies, smaller than the universe and the sky.

[315] *Area major enim, quam qui percurrit in illa,*

For the space in which it runs is greater than it is,

*Et longe campi spatium diffusius, in quo*

and the extent of the plain is far wider in which

[Col. 0146B] *Emicat, ac volucri fervens rota volvitur axe.*

it flashes forth and its burning wheel revolves on its swift axis.

*Quamvis nonnullis placeat, terram breviorem*

Although some prefer to say that the earth is smaller

*Dicere circuitu, quam sit pulcherrimus ille*

in circumference than that most beautiful

[320] *Circulus, et flammas immensi sideris ultra*

circle and the flames of the immense star, extending beyond

*Telluris normam porrecto extendere gyro.*

the measure of the earth in an outstretched circuit.

*Numne etiam coeli minor, et contractior orbis,*

Is the sun’s orbit also smaller than heaven and more constricted,

*Cujus planitiem longo transmittere tractu*

whose surface the circling instrument struggles to traverse

*Circinus excurrens meta interiore laborat?*

along its long course to an inner limit?

[325] *Ille Deus verus, quo non est grandior ulla*

That is the true God, than whom no substance is greater,

*Materies, qui fine caret, qui praesidet omni*

who has no limit, who presides over all

*Naturae, qui cuncta simul concludit, et implet.*

nature, who simultaneously contains and fills all things.

*Solem certa tenet regio, plaga certa coercet.*

A fixed region holds the sun; a fixed zone confines it.

727. *Temporibus variis distinguitur: aut subit ortu,*

At varying times it is marked off: it either rises at dawn,

[330] *Aut ruit occasu, latet aut sub nocte recurrens:*

falls at sunset, or hides, returning beneath night;

*Nec torquere facem potis est ad signa trionum,*

nor can it turn its torch toward the signs of the Septentrions,

*Orbe nec obliquo portas aquilonis adire,*

nor approach the gates of the north on an oblique orbit,

*Nec solitum conversus iter revocare retrorsum.*

nor, turning back, retrace its accustomed path in reverse.

[Col. 0147B] *Hic erit ergo Deus, praescriptis lege sub una*

Will he, then, be a god subject to duties prescribed

[335] *Deditus officiis? Libertas laxior ipsi*

by a single law? A freer liberty

*Concessa est homini: formam cui flectere vitae,*

is granted to man: he may bend the course of his life

*Atque voluntatis licitum est, seu tramite dextro*

and his will, whether it pleases him to climb

*Scandere, seu laevo malit decurrere campo,*

by the right-hand path or run down the left-hand field,

[Col. 0148A] *Sumere seu requiem, seu continuare laborem,*

whether to take rest or continue his labor,

[340] *Seu parere Deo, sive in contraria verti.*

whether to obey God or turn toward the opposite.

*Ista ministranti regimen solemne dierum*

To the sun, which performs this customary governance of days,

*Haudquaquam Soli datur a factore potestas:*

the Creator grants no such authority at all;

*Sed famulus subjectus agit, quodcunque necesse est.*

rather, as a servant subject to command, it does whatever is necessary.

*Hoc sidus currum, rapidasque agitare quadrigas*

They imagined that this star drives a chariot and swift four-horse team,

[345] *Commenti, et radios capitis, et verbera dextrae,*

with rays upon its head and a whip in its right hand,

728. *Et frenos, phalerasque, et equorum pectora anhela*

and reins and trappings, and the panting breasts of horses,

*Aeris inaurati, vel marmoris, aut orichalci,*

made of gilded bronze, marble, or *orichalcum*,

*Jusserunt nitido fulgere polita metallo.*

and ordered them to shine, polished with gleaming metal.

*Post trabeas, et eburnam aquilam, sellamque curulem*

After the *trabeae*, the ivory eagle, and the curule chair,

[350] *Cernuat ora senex barbatus, et oscula figit*

an old bearded man bows his face and plants kisses

[Col. 0148B] *Cruribus aenipedum, si fas est credere, equorum:*

on the bronze-footed legs of horses, if it is permissible to believe it;

*Immotasque rotas, et flecti nescia lora*

and he either adorns the unmoving wheels and the reins

*Aut ornat redimita rosis, aut thure vaporat.*

that cannot bend with roses, or makes them smoke with incense.

*Hoc tamen utcunque est tolerabile, quid, quod et ipsae—*

This, at any rate, is tolerable; but what of the fact that even they themselves—

356. *Eumenidum*: of the Furies. *Stygio*: infernal. *Exerit*: raises, lifts up. I.

358. *Adire*: to approach with an answer. *Quirites*: Romans. I.

364. *Spargere*: because she was a huntress. I.

365. *Sublustri*: somewhat bright, faintly shining. I.

366. *Calamos*: arrows. *Latonia*: from her mother Latona. Lucina or Luna in heaven, Diana or Latonia on earth, Proserpina or Hecate among the dead—that is, a goddess of a hundred powers. I.

367. *Solio*: abyss. I.

[Col. 0150B] 368. *Megaerae*: of that Fury; the name of a Fury. I.

369. *Triviae*: of Trivia, “of the three roads.” I.

373. *Subigit*: compels, Mar. The demon himself compels. I.

379. *Sacraria*: temples. *Ditis*: of Pluto. I.
