381. Purified, cleansed.—Phlegethontian, infernal.—At Rome, human beings were sacrificed to the infernal gods. I.]

[Note: [Col. 0149B]

356. In the Rat., after the earlier words had been erased, an inept replacement was inserted: “Mistress of the Eumenides, Stygian,” by some ignoramus who, unaware of metrical rules, wished to repair the meter. Concerning Proserpina and her worship, see Minucius Felix: “Meanwhile Diana is a huntress, girt high,” etc. Here the commentators illuminate the whole subject from Prudentius and others.

359. Virgil, Book VI: “And a barren heifer for you, Proserpina.”

360. The same Virgil: “Calling Hecate aloud, powerful in heaven and Erebus.”

361. Gis. now has “two-horse chariots.” Others consistently read “two-horse chariots.” Ausonius and Claudian assign young bulls and heifers to the moon. Ovid, the ancient Capitol anaglypha, and the Pio-Clementine Museum assign horses; Festus, mules. Here too he imitates Virgil, Book VI: “He summons the fierce bands of sisters.”

362. Oxon. has “upon these,” so that he may designate oxen maddened by the gadfly, which Columella calls “goaded.” Heinsius notes this. The common reading is uniquely correct.

365. Egm. has “shines.” This verse and the following two were inserted by some inept ignoramus into Book IV of Hyginus’s *Astronomy*, in the chapter on the Moon; for that reason they have been omitted from recent editions of Hyginus. Delrius observed this long ago. See above, the commentary on verse 309. In the commentaries on Aratus’s *Phenomena*, under the name of Caesar Germanicus, this verse and the following one are inserted among the prognostics concerning the Moon. The Moon is called Diana and also Proserpina—that is, celestial, terrestrial, and infernal. Concerning her, someone writes: “Finally,” etc. In the following verse, “she lies upon her arrows” is faulty. Meursius, Book IV, chapter 3 of his *Critical Notes on Arnobius*, suspects that a scribe in haste omitted, at verse 367, “When she sits leaning upon her throne,” etc.

366. Pal. wrongly has “upon her arrows.” One may still see Diana’s legs tightly girded in ancient statues. For this reason Aeneas, when Venus appeared before him “naked to the knee, her flowing robe gathered up in a knot,” hesitated whether she was “Phoebus’s sister or one of the blood of the Nymphs.” Virgil, Book I of the *Aeneid*.

367. Prag. has “while leaning upon it.” Ald. and others write “wife.” After this verse Weitz., Widm., Bong., Mar. in the first hand, Prag., Rat., Urb., and others insert this additional line: “When she is carried away, she is a Fury and the wife of grim Pluto.” In Prag.: “While she is carried away.” It is absent from Alex., the best Heinsian manuscripts, and others. Heinsius says that elsewhere too Prudentius shortens the second syllable in *Plutonis*. I think this false. For I find in Prudentius neither *Plutonis* nor any other oblique case of *Pluto*, except below at verse 398, “the fierce vows of his Pluto,” where the second syllable is long. The *o* in *Plutonia* is likewise pronounced long. As for verse 99 of Hymn 5 of the *Peristephanon*, where Weitzius reads “those Plutos of the guilty,” I shall show at that passage that it must be read otherwise. The verse is plainly superfluous; yet, to suit the meter, it could be read: “When she is carried away, she is a Fury and also the wife of grim Pluto.”

369. Mar., Weitz. with its associates, and Prag. have “you may seek.”

373. Egm. has “and error.”

375. Prag. has “with a fatal funeral,” less well.

376. Mar. in the old hand has “those caught”; Prag. has “the prostrate women,” incorrectly.

377. Prag. has “may overwhelm.”

378. In Mar. and Rat. this verse is followed by the heading: “What was worshiped at the spectacles.”

379. Lipsius, *Saturnalia*, Book I, chapter 3, shows that gladiators were dedicated rather to Mars or Saturn; he says that these words of Prudentius may be understood of Saturn, so that the poet has put Dis for Saturn, or even that gladiators were sacred to Dis because they were given to appease the Manes. Tertullian and Salvian assert that gladiatorial spectacles were sacred to Mars; Lactantius, Ausonius, and Plutarch, to Saturn. Prudentius may be explained as calling these spectacles “the sanctuaries of Dis,” because human beings perish in them and are thrust down to the underworld. The same difficulty recurs at verse 397 and following: “At Pluto’s altar.”]

Do the shadows of the infernal abyss give you gods, Rome?

The mistress of the Eumenides thrusts her head from the Stygian cavern,

729 Proserpina, carried off to the bridal chamber of the king of Tartarus,

And, whenever she deigns to approach her own Romans,

She is appeased by the severed neck of a barren cow,

[560] And is thought at once to rule heaven and Erebus:

Now to rein oxen in a two-horse chariot, now to send the savage bands of her sisters

Against the gods above with a serpent-bearing whip,

Now also to scatter winged arrows upon the backs of deer,

And three times to vary her own forms in the same person.

[365] Finally, when she is the Moon, she shines in a somewhat dim garment;

When, as the Latonian virgin, she casts her arrows, she is Diana;

When, seated and leaning upon her throne, she is the Plutonian wife,

[Col. 0149B] 730 She rules the Furies and dictates laws to Megaera.

If you seek the truth: under the name of Trivia a Tartarean demon

[370] [Col. 0150A] Is worshiped—the one who now snatches you up to the ether

And persuades you to venerate a god in a starry constellation;

Now compels you to wander through the forests of the deadly world,

To follow errors and suppose her to be the goddess of the groves—

She who pierces the trembling hearts of human beings,

[375] And destroys wild minds with a deadly wound;

Now, beneath the earth, she overwhelms the senses, cast down by fear,

So that they implore deities deprived of light

And entrust themselves to the power of hidden night.

Look upon the guilty sanctuaries of dread Dis,

[380] To whom the ill-fated gladiator falls, poured out in the arena,

The Phlegethontian victim of Rome, so poorly purified.

731 For what purpose does the impious art of the mad spectacle exist?

[Col. 0150B] What purpose do the deaths of young men serve? What purpose does pleasure fed on blood?

[Col. 0151A] [Note: [Col. 0151B]

385. *Amphitheatralis*: a circle; or, lavishly, an amphitheater, a place enclosed by a wall belonging to a theater. A theater is a spectacle wherever it is set up, Iso.

386. *Charon*: the devil, I.

387. *Inferias*: funeral rites for the dead.—*Sacro*: accursed, as in “the accursed hunger for gold”; or, according to those who thought so, sacred, I.

388. *Jovis infernalis*: of Orcus, I.

389. *Arbiter*: an assessor, judge, Iso.

390. *Regem*: ruling, I.

391. *Censere*: to construct.—*Litanda*: sacrifices, I.

392. *Relligionis*: of divinity.—*Subternis*: subterranean, infernal, [Col. 0152B] I.

393. *Ministrum*: the devil, I.

395. *Taurica sacra*: the Tauric region, in which foreigners were sacrificed to Juno, a practice the Romans condemned; yet they themselves eventually did the same, I.

396. *Latiari*: Roman, from Latium, I.

398. *Quid sanctius*: ironically, I, Vat. A.

399. *Egestum*: poured out, I.

401. *Rimeris*: you investigate, I.

402. *Inficiaris*: you deny, I.

403. *Manibus*: infernal deities, I.

404. *Marmora secta*: inscribed marble, Vat. A. On these was written *Dis Manibus*.—*Lego*: I read, I see.—*Latina*: the road, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0151C]

387. The earlier Rott. has *pro div. script.*, Cauch. has “with sacred payment,” alluding to the arena’s prizes. Vat. A has “with sacred blood.”

389. Ald. and the earlier Rott. have “peacefully he rests in obscure Avernus.” Ald. also punctuates: “In these things, the judge.” I do not approve.

390. Gifanius observed in an old book the expression “the people, king,” where the common text previously read “king for the peoples.” The sense cannot apply to the emperor or emperors whom Prudentius addresses in this work. It imitates Virgil, *Aeneid* I: “Hence, king over a wide people, proud in war.” *Populum* also appears in Thuan., Urb., and Alex. in the first hand. Understand “the Roman people.”

392. Weitz. has “beneath the earth” instead of the common reading. See the commentary on verse 922 of the *Hamartigenia* and verse 443 of this book.

394. Vat. A, Cauch., and Jureti’s codex have “may grant funerals,” together with Egm. and Pal.

[Col. 0151D] 395. Prag. corruptly has *manutaurica* for *jam Taurica*. Mar. in the old hand has *jam turica*, incorrectly. Some who cite this verse transpose the words as follows: “We now customarily condemn the Tauric rites in vain.” It should be read, with the manuscripts: “In vain to condemn now.” The final *e* in *arguere* is lengthened by reason of the caesura. Colerus, in his commentary on Valerius Maximus, p. 568, understands the Tauric rites to be *suovetaurilia*. Weitzius explains them as sacrifices made to Pluto with bulls and a black animal. There is no room for doubt that the subject is the sacrifices of the island of Taurica—or, as we more commonly and accurately say, the peninsula. Hyginus, *Fabula* 120: “It was the custom among the Taurians that whoever came within their territory as a stranger should be sacrificed in the temple of Diana.” Tertullian, Athanasius, Augustine, Lactantius, Cassiodorus, and Eusebius of Caesarea, among many pagan authors whom I omit, discuss Tauric Diana and the human victims slaughtered to her. In the gloss I would more readily read “to Diana” instead of “to Juno.”

[Col. 0152B] 396. Ald. has *Latiali*; Vat. A, *Laciari*; most have *Latiari*. Prag. has: “Human blood is poured out in the Latiarian offering.” Prudentius is speaking of the gladiatorial spectacle in honor of Jupiter Latiaris. Lipsius, in *On the Amphitheater*, notes that *Latiari* is in the dative case, namely “to Jupiter Latiaris.” From this and similar passages some argue that human victims were customarily sacrificed to Jupiter Latiaris. But the meaning is that Jupiter was worshiped with the human blood of those who were either killed in gladiatorial combat or condemned to the beasts. Tertullian, chapter 9 of the *Apology*: “I leave the Tauric stories to their theaters. Behold, in that most religious city of the pious descendants of Aeneas there is a certain Jupiter whom they drench with human blood in their games. ‘But they are beast-fighters,’ you say. That, I suppose, is less than being human.” See the notes of Pamelius, Minucius, Julius Firmicus, Lactantius, Tatian, and others, who reproached the Romans for such savagery. We count its eventual abolition by the Christian religion among the greatest benefits conferred upon humanity by Christ.

397. An inept corrector in Rat., after erasing the earlier text, substituted: “And that assembly of spectators.” Pal. has “and the assembly.” Egm. in the first hand has “and the seated spectators,” incorrectly. In the second edition of Cell. I think the error is *that assembly there*. Concerning the assembly in the amphitheater, see the commentary on verse 372 of the *Hamartigenia*.

404. Mar. in the first hand and Weitz. with its associates have *quaecunque*. *Quacunque* is much better. The Romans once placed tombs along public roads, and apparently the Jews did so as well. Genesis 35:19: “Rachel died, therefore, and was buried on the road leading to Ephrath.” Concerning the Latin Road, Juvenal, Satire 1: “Whose ashes the Flaminian and Latin Roads cover”; and Satire 5: “While you ride past the monuments of the sloping Latin Road.” On the Salarian Road stood a monument of costly workmanship belonging to Licinius, Augustus’s barber and freedman, as Cornutus relates in his commentary on Persius, Satire 2. Other roads famous for tombs were the Appian, Aurelian, Lavican, Laurentian, Ostian, Praenestine, and Tiburtine. The distinguished jurist Vincentius Bartoluccius published at Rome in 1786 a dissertation on public roads. Whether the letters *D. M.* or *D. MA.*, which sometimes appear on Christian tombs, mean *Dis Manibus* or something else was disputed between Fabretti and Mabillon: the former insisted that the inscription was always pagan, while the latter denied this. [Col. 0153C] Lupius, in his dissertation on baptisteries, nos. 158–159, cites an inscription that he considers Christian, with *Dis Manibus* placed by some ignorant neophyte and overlooked by the priest in charge of the cemetery; that this sometimes happened is sufficiently probable. The inscription is as follows:

“TO THE INFERNAL DEITIES OF PRINCIPIUS, HIS SWEETEST SON, HE PLACED THIS, WHO LIVED SIX YEARS, TWENTY-SEVEN DAYS, IN PEACE.”

A learned dissertation by the distinguished Cajetanus Migliore on the *Dis Manibus* is found again on p. 1172.]

[385] Sad spectacles of the amphitheater’s pomp?

These are the delights of infernal Jupiter; amid these things

[390] Are you not ashamed, a people who are king and powerful with scepters,

To judge such things sacrifices to be offered for the safety of your country?

To seek the aid of religion from subterranean caverns?

to whom Death may pay splendid human deaths as tribute.

[395] [Col. 0152A] 732 In vain we now condemn the Tauric rites:

[400] Or is your faith in doubt, that beneath blind darkness

Behold, why do you deny that the Manes are regarded as gods?

733 I read carved marble dedicated “To the Infernal Deities,” wherever the Latin

405. Cornutus, in his commentary on Persius, says that *salarium* properly means a day’s food, in which salt is especially included. Iso’s explanation is less satisfactory. After this verse Rat. and Mar. append the heading “He addresses Rome.”

406. Prag. has “here, to whom you write this inscription.” Ald. has “say, to whom you write this inscription here.” Vat. A and some Heinsian manuscripts have “say, to whom you inscribe this title.” Most have “say, to whom you write this inscription here.”

407. Vat. A corruptly has *verito ceu*.

410. Pal. and Vat. A have “twice victorious from the slaughter of the twin victor.” Egm. incorrectly has “twice victorious by slaughter”; in the second hand, “twice victorious from slaughter,” or “twice the conqueror by slaughter.” Weitzius does not clearly explain this reading of Egm. and Pal. It is certain that this prince is Theodosius. Understand by the tyrants Maximus and Eugenius. Grangaeus objects to Prudentius that, in narrating this history, he departs somewhat from the truth: for Theodosius, after defeating Maximus, celebrated a triumph in 389 and did not return to Rome until many years after defeating Eugenius. But even if I granted that the order of the narrative had been somewhat disturbed, the poet could not therefore be accused of falsehood, since he does not explicitly say that Theodosius triumphed after conquering two tyrants. Moreover, in the speech that follows, mention is again made of the two tyrants conquered by Theodosius.

413. Ald. has “of shadowed night.”

414. Vat. A corruptly has *arcebit*. Concerning this manner of expression—“clear sky,” “upper sky,” and similar phrases—see Dausqueius’s commentary on Silius, Book XII, verse 4.

417. Egm. and Jureti’s parchment have *clues*. Mar. in the first hand has *superbum*.

421. Heins., Cham., and Teol. incorrectly have *ab ora*. Egm. writes *hebitat*. Prag. has *obumbrat* instead of *ob ora*. Rutilius, Book I of the *Journey*, verse 193, praising the purity of the Roman sky, says: “Nor is that place known to me by the sign of smoke.”

423. Prag. has “I see you darkened.” Widm. and Bong. in the first hand write *circumferier*.

424. Ald. has “and black idols fly”; Rat., after erasing the earlier reading, has “and black idols fly.” Neither comes from the author’s hand. Grangaeus followed Ald.

430. Contemporary writers of Prudentius commonly call Rome “queen.”

432. Rat. has *superstes*; read *superstas*.

433. He calls the worship of idols and the old wives’ tales invented by Numa “nonsense.” Some say that the idols themselves are called “nonsense,” as *naenias* is elsewhere.

434. Prudentius more than once calls the monsters and prodigies of the pagans gods. Minucius: “There are as many monstrosities of Jupiter as there are names.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VIII: “Monsters of every kind of god, and the barking Anubis.”

435. In the Theodosian Code, title “On Pagans,” law 12, enacted by Theodosius in 392: “But if anyone venerates with incense images made by human workmanship and destined to endure through the ages,” etc.

436. In Rat. *gypsum* is made from *gypsus*. Prag. has *gypsea*, incorrectly. Arnobius, Book VI, Firmicus, and Capitolinus in the life of Gordian discuss the plaster images of the ancients. Plaster images were sometimes covered with sheets of metal. Compare the Italian version of Johann Winckelmann’s *History of the Arts of Design*, with the learned notes of Carlo Fea, Book VII, chapter 1.]

It guards the ashes and the tombs crowded along the Salarian Road.

Say to whom you write this inscription—unless it is that you worship

The dominion of savage Orcus as though it were true majesty?

Behold the palace of supreme power, defiled by these things,

He saw the City beset by blackening clouds,

By the darkness of shadowed night. Turbulent air

Drove away the clear sky from the sevenfold citadel.

[415] He groaned in pity and spoke thus: “Lay aside your sad appearance,

Faithful mother. Certainly you shine, adorned in magnificent dress,

And lift your head high, distinguished by splendid spoils,

And abound in much gold around you.

But the summit of your lofty head, beset by clouds flying about it,

[420] [Col. 0153B] bristles; even the gems themselves

[Col. 0154A] Spread before your face blunt the radiant diadem of your brow.

By a slight blow. If soft plaster, a sheet of metal

I think the reference is to chapter 19 of Book XIX: “*Taratrum*, as though *teratrum*. *Scofina* is so called because, by clinging, it makes a groove; perhaps one should read ‘because it makes one by rubbing.’”

444. Prag. and Widm. in the first hand have *inferni*, less well.

445. Aldus had printed: “Nor is God the powers of human beings or of souls.” He emended it to: “Nor is God the powers either of human beings or of souls.” Others have: “Nor are the powers of human beings God, or of souls.” Prag. has “or of darkness.” The meaning is that God is neither the powers of human beings, such as chastity and faith, nor the wandering forms of souls and spirits, such as demons and angels, beneath a tenuous image.

446. Ald. corruptly has *vagi*. Virgil, Book VI: “And unless my learned companion warned me that insubstantial lives without bodies were flying beneath a hollow image of form.”

[Col. 0156B] 447. Juretus notes that elsewhere it is read: “May there be for you a grove, and its presiding spirit,” and that this reading can be defended, since pagans attributed the greatest religious significance to groves. Prudentius often calls idols “shadows”; thus above, at verse 195: “the shadow of the household gods.”

449. Several explanations are commonly offered for why idolaters were called *pagani*, from *pagi*, as I indicated at verse 6 of this book’s preface. See also below, at verse 621. To me the explanation drawn from these verses appears true: superstition flourished especially in the villages, and thus all those who, after the Christian religion had been spread everywhere, clung superstitiously to the worship of idols were rightly called *pagani*. Heraldus, in his commentary on Arnobius, p. 4, understands idolaters to have been called *pagani* because they no longer occupied the whole world but had been confined into a narrow space, as though enclosed in certain villages. He thinks that the origin of the term was obscure even in antiquity, just as we still do not know clearly where the Huguenots got their name. Gothofredus, in his commentary on law 13 “On Pagans” of the Theodosian Code, asserts that the name *pagani* began under the Christian emperors; its earliest occurrence known to him is in law 18 “On Bishops,” from the year 365: “The Gentiles, whom they commonly call pagans.” He thinks that the Christian populace, who had once been called by various insults by the Gentiles, returned the name *pagani* to the Gentiles, as if calling them simple, rustic, and country-dwelling.

451. Mar. in the first hand, against meter and sense, has “honorable men whom.”

463. See Demsterus, p. 66, on Corippus’s verse: “And the most powerful kingdoms shall come beneath your feet.” Prudentius is speaking poetically; for Theodosius did not triumph or come to Rome after defeating Eugenius.

464. Prag. has *agnoscat*. Retain *agnoscas*.

465. Muretus, Book XIII of the *Various Readings*, chapter 8, admirably refutes Petrus Crinitus, who did not hesitate to attribute this impious law to Theodosius in Book IX of *On Honorable Discipline*, chapter 9: “Since we are diligently concerned in all things to preserve the religion of the heavenly deity, we permit no one to fashion, carve, or paint the sign of Christ the Savior in colors, stone, or any other material. Whatever is found, we order removed, imposing the severest penalty on those who attempt anything contrary to our decrees and authority.” The words of the law in the Justinian Code, Book I, title 8, are: “We specially order that no one may carve or paint the sign of Christ the Savior either in the ground, or in flint, or on marble slabs placed upon the ground; whatever is found must be removed, and the person who attempts anything contrary to our statutes must be punished with the severest penalty.” In Prudentius’s verses, a jeweled cross may be understood on the purple of the standards, woven with gems and made of solid gold at the tops of the spears. Compare Baronius under the year 312, and the many others who celebrate the triumphs of the cross.

466. After this verse Ald., Mar., Rat., and others have the heading “On the power of the cross.” Urb. has “On the praises of the cross and its power.” Headings of this sort are absent from many manuscripts.

467. Vat. A corruptly has *vinctus* for *invictus*. Ald., Egm., and Pal. have *ultro*, less well, for *ultor*. Theodosius cites Constantine as an example to persuade the Romans of the power of the cross. Constantine is therefore not speaking, as Chamillardus and some recent writers with him maintain. For the person who speaks at verse 422 says: “I see dark shadows,” and afterward: “I advise”; “I shall not permit”; “with me as your guide”; “we shall establish.” After Constantine’s example has been presented: “Therefore beware, noble head of the world … I would have you lay aside your festivals,” etc. Constantine’s victory is narrated as an already ancient event: “You yourself know … the illustrious senate remembers, which at that time,” etc. Eusebius narrates the history in his *Life of Constantine*.

468. Egm. has “he released the wondrous thing.” I do not approve.

469. Prag. incorrectly has *pestiferam*.

[Col. 0158B] 471. Vat. A corruptly has *ut sis*.

472. Mar. writes *dyroque*. Gallandius preferred *raptae*, so that it might refer to *pactae*. But *rapta* is correct: that is, the agreements were seized and carried off.

473. Heins., with Thuan., has “he mourned amid chains”; later writers followed him. Prag. has “he groaned amid chains.” Mar. has “he grieved,” against the meter. Most have “he consumed amid chains.” The construction is: “The bridegroom, plunged in darkness and harsh chains, was paying the price for the interrupted agreements of his bride, carried off by a cruel guard.” But “to pay the price for interrupted agreements” is not sufficiently elegant, and the bridegroom is better described as groaning over the interrupted agreements.

475. Mar. in the first hand has *domino*, incorrectly.

Mar., Weitz., Prag., Rat., Colerus in his commentary on Valerius Maximus, p. 568, and Widm. have “vaulted over the minds.” The better Heinsian manuscripts, Ald., Gis., and Heinsius have “confessed too greatly.” Alex., with a published gloss, agrees. Others have “joined in their minds.” Heinsius thinks that “confessed their minds” means “drew out sighs.”

481. This verse is absent from Egm., Boherius’s very old manuscript, the earlier Rott., Vat. A, and Pal. It is present in the others. Aldus has *nimiam* for *nimiae* and punctuates after *traxit*. The force of the passage is better understood as “sighs that confessed the force of excessive freedom and paternal grief.” Gallandius approves *nimiam* with Aldus, not *nimia* with Chamillardus. In Chamillardus I read *nimiae*, namely “of excessive freedom,” which is better.

482. Vat. A in the first hand has *Christicolis*, incorrectly. Constantine is not speaking, as Iso maintains, but Theodosius. He imitates Horace, Book IV, Ode 4: “The Metaurus River bears witness, and Hasdrubal, defeated.”

483. Heinsius insists that one should read *Mulvius*, not *Molvius* or *Milvius*. Others also write *Mylvius*, others *Molbius*. Aldus had printed *Mulvius* and corrected it to *Milvius*, as Gallandius also observed, so that one may understand that Aldus had no Aldine edition at hand other than the one I use and believe to be unique. The bridge is now called Ponte Molle. Maxentius is simply called “the tyrant” three times in Nazarius’s panegyric to Constantine and in other ancient monuments and writers.]

486. Mar. in the first hand incorrectly has *radiarit*. Prag. has *radiarunt*.

488. Egm. and Pal. incorrectly have *lavacrum* for *labarum*. Turnebus, *Adversaria*, no. 459, attests that an old glossary gives *laborum* for *labarum*. Gyraldus, Dialogue 25, boasts that he was the first to explain this verse of Prudentius, and explains *labarum* as an exceedingly precious military standard, which Constantine converted into the sign of the cross. Tertullian, Ambrose, and others use the word *labarum*. Rabanus Maurus, in his poem *On the Cross*, altered its quantity: “Hence these sacred *labara* mark the triumph of the cherubim.” Some assert that the name was invented only under Constantine, and read *cantabra* in Tertullian, as also in Minucius: “For the standards themselves, the *cantabra*, and the military banners.” Rigaltius, in his note on this passage, says that *cantabra* were a kind of banners inscribed with verses, signifying something agreeable and pleasant to the soldiers. Some derive the origin from Cantabria, though I do not know whether with better justification. Bulengerus, *On the Roman Empire*, Book V, chapter 5, has more on the *labarum*. Countless critics and other authors quote these verses of Prudentius. See a description of the *labarum* in Aringhus, *Subterranean Rome*, Book VI, chapter 23.

489. Saint Jerome, Letter 107 to Laeta: “The military standards are the emblems of the cross. The purple garments of kings and the burning gems of their diadems are adorned by the image of the saving cross.” Saint Augustine, on Psalm 36: “The cross ended in punishment; it remains in glory. From the places of punishment it made its way to the foreheads of emperors.”

491. He is speaking of hair bound together, according to the custom of Roman criminals. The same usage occurs in Hymn 11 of the *Peristephanon*: “He had ordered the ranks, with prison filth in their hair, to stand opposite.”

495. Earlier he said “avenger,” “vindicator”; now he says “of the avenging army.” This is precisely expressed by the inscription of Constantine’s triumphal arch.]

IMP. CAES. FL. CONSTANTINO. MAXIMO. P. F. AVGVSTO. S. P. Q. R. [Col. 0159D] QVOD. INSTINCTV. DIVINITATIS. MENTIS. MAGNITVDINE. CVM. EXERCITV. SVO TAM. DE. TYRANNO. QVAM. DE. OMNI. EIVS FACTIONE. VNO. TEMPORE. IVSTIS REMPVBLICAM. VLTVS. EST. ARMIS ARCVM. TRIVMPHIS. INSIGNEM. DICAVIT

**The emperor Caesar Flavius Constantine, the greatest, pious and fortunate Augustus, the Senate and People of Rome dedicated this arch to him because, through the inspiration of the divine power and the greatness of his mind, he avenged the Republic with just arms, at one and the same time, both upon the tyrant and upon his entire faction.**

The inscription was copied from the original itself, for the published copies vary somewhat. Inside the larger arch, on the sides, one reads:

**TO THE FOUNDER OF PEACE, TO THE LIBERATOR OF THE CITY**

Above the smaller arches on either side:

**FOR VOWS OF TEN YEARS; FOR VOWS OF TWENTY YEARS**

And on the reverse side, above the same smaller arches:

**THUS FOR TEN YEARS; THUS FOR TWENTY YEARS**

It is clear from Prudentius that not only the cross was represented on the labarum, but also the name of Christ—namely, the monogram of Christ, consisting of the two Greek letters of Christ’s name, Χ and Ρ. They do not signify “for Christ,” as many think, believing them to be a sign of martyrdom. Since, therefore, Christ’s name had been impressed upon the labarum, and it was customary for the labarum to be worshiped by the soldiers, because it always preceded the emperor, Prudentius rightly says that the senate worshiped the name of Christ, which shone brightly upon the arms.

**497.** Ald., Gis., Heins., *posthac* (“hereafter”); Weitzianus and most of our manuscripts, *post haec* (“after these things”).

**498.** Heinsius rejects Weitzius because he read: *Prodigia esse deos stolido tibi fingere cultu* (“that, in foolish worship, you imagine prodigies to be gods”). Yet this is the reading of Rat., Mar., Prag., Urb., and others. Ald. and Tornaes., *solito* for *stolido*; Thuan., *olido*. Others, with Vat. A and Gis., approved by Heinsius, read: *Prodigia, et larvas solito tibi fingere cultu* (“to fashion prodigies and phantoms for yourself with accustomed worship”). In Weitzius’s edition, Ald., Gis., and Palat. read: *Prodigia, et larvas stolido confingere cultu*. But Ald. and Gis. read as I have just explained.

**500.** Egm., *vitiose* (“faultily”), or *in puerilia* (“into childish things”).

**502.** Ald., Egm., Palat., *lavare* (“to wash”); *lavate* (“wash”) is better. According to Festus, wine was called *respersum* (“sprinkled”) because, during the nine-day funeral rites, the tomb of the dead was sprinkled with wine. But Prudentius is more likely speaking of the gore and blood of the victims with which the images of the gods were spattered. The learned Fea, volume III of his works on Winckelmann, page 279, aptly refutes Randini, who had wanted this passage to be understood of statues of distinguished men, not of gods.

**503.** In book XVI, title 10, *On Pagans*, of the Theodosian Code, images are permitted as works of art, to be judged by their artistic value rather than as divinities, as is gathered from law 8 together with Gothofredus’s commentaries. That law 5 was issued by Theodosius the Great in the year 382. [Col. 0160D] Later, in 399, Honorius issued law 15 of the same title: “Just as we prohibit sacrifices, so we wish the ornaments of public works to be preserved.” Here, and therefore also in Prudentius, *ornaments* means images of the gods attached to public works, such as baths, the forum, streets, crossroads, and porticoes; Tertullian discusses these in chapter 8 of *On the Spectacles*, and Ambrose in *Against Symmachus*. These same public ornaments were prohibited by Honorius in Africa in 399 by law 18, and throughout the empire in 408 and 415 by laws 19 and 20: “So that they may not provide a temptation to those who are in error.”

**504.** Mar., Rat., Prag., *pulcherrima* (“most beautiful”); I would prefer *pulcherrima*, which is acceptable, although all editions have *pulcherrima nostrae*. Heinsius, with Thuan., reads *hae* for *haec* and refers it to the statues. More recent editors follow Heinsius. Most of the older witnesses have *haec ornamenta* (“these ornaments”), which is equally sound.]

He may have preferred them, with whatever emblem the spears might gleam.

Christ, woven in purple upon glittering gold,

740 marked the labarum; Christ had inscribed the emblems of the shields;

A cross added to the very crests blazed above.

[490] He himself recalls the most illustrious order of senators:

Those who then came forward with matted hair,

Filthy in prison chains, or bound by massive fetters,

And embracing the victor’s feet, weeping, toward the renowned

Standards they fell prostrate; then that senate

[495] Adored the title of the avenging army, and the revered

[Col. 0160A] 741 name of Christ, which shone upon the arms.

Therefore beware, illustrious head of the world, hereafter

Of fashioning empty prodigies and phantoms for yourself with foolish worship,

And of despising the proven power of the true God.

[500] I would have you now lay aside your festive childish things,

Your ridiculous rites, your shrines unworthy of so great a realm.

Wash, senators, the marbles stained with decaying gore;

Let it be permitted for statues to stand pure—

Works of great artists, these most beautiful ornaments, as I would prefer—

**505.** The Codex Jureti, Ald., Mar., Rat., Weitz., Widm. above, Egm., Coleri’s codex, and others read *fuant*, which does not displease Gallandius. Vat. A, Prag., Widm. again in the second hand, Thuan., Cauch., and Urb. read *fiant*. Bong., Gis., and Widm. read *cluant*, a reading approved by Heinsius and more recent editors. In Egm., the gloss on the verb *fuant* is *erunt* (“they will be”). All these readings can be admitted, but not *fugant* in Ox., nor *fluant* in the earlier Rott. In Alex., *fiant* is in the first hand and *fuant* in the second.

**506.** Gis., in the margin, *arcis* (“of the citadel”), less well. The true reading is *artis* (“of art”). From this final part of the speech I gather that, after the altar of Victory had been overthrown, a statue of that same goddess still remained in the Julian senate-house, but without any worship and solely as an ornament. I understand Claudian to refer to this statue in the sixth consulship of Honorius:

“By right the senate-house, now clad for war, serves the palace hall.  
Winged Victory herself was present at her own temples,  
Guardian of the Roman toga, who with rich wing  
Fosters the venerable shrines of the patrician assembly.”

See the commentary on verses 28 and 29 of book II.

**508.** Many writers, including ancient and reliable ones, write *vigeto* instead of *vieto*. The gloss of Vat. A seems to take *vieto* as *vegeto*. But here *vietus* means languid, shriveled; nor is the passage about Constantine, but about Theodosius and his decrees, issued long before and confirmed and expanded after Maximus had been defeated. Prudentius does not deny that, before Theodosius’s decrees, many Roman senators were devoted to the Christian religion; he merely asserts that, through Theodosius’s example and persuasion, Rome was transferred wholly to the faith of Christ in love, as he says in verse 524. It should also be noted that in verse 41 Prudentius calls an “edict” the speech by which Saturn persuaded the ancient Latins to idolatry.

**510.** Ald. and most manuscripts, *vocante* (“calling”); Bong. in the first hand and some printed editions, *vocantem* (“him who calls”).

**511.** In Ald. I think *magnanimo doctore* (“with the great-hearted teacher”) is an error; *ductore* (“leader”) should be read.

**512.** Aldus’s error: *primam* for *primum*.

**514.** Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XL, chapter 7, compares with these verses the words of Lucretius: “Whereas, on the contrary, religion has often in former times given birth to criminal and impious deeds.”

**515.** In Mar. the reading was: *Mox ubi contiguit fossis muralibus, agros*, etc., which is certainly corrupt.

**517.** This passage should be noted against those who boast that the number of martyrs was small.

**518.** Vat. A, corruptly, *magne poenitet*, and likewise the edition.

**520.** Vat. A, incorrectly, *vulnere* (“wound”).

**521.** Vat. A and Egm., *petendae*, incorrectly; nor is Alex. better, *venia quae petenda*.

**523.** Egm. in Weitzius, *solvit* (“he absolved”) instead of *quaerit* (“he seeks”). Heinsius found nothing of the sort in Egm., but says it was copied by Gis. from his own manuscripts. In Giselinus’s first edition *solvit* does indeed appear, but in the second the reading is clearly *quaerit*.

**524.** Mar., *veri transfertur amore* (“is transferred by love of truth”); above, instead of *div.*, the manuscript has *pleno transfertur amore* (“is transferred with full love”). Marietti prefers the first reading: the sense is “is transferred into the faith of Christ by love of truth,” which is confirmed by the marginal gloss in Ratisbon: *id est, pro veritatis* (“that is, instead of *veritatis*”), for the latter is certainly attached to *veri*, not to *pleno*.

**528.** Ald., *contigit*; correct to *contulit*. In Rat. there is a most absurd gloss: “Cethegus, a certain king.”

**530.** Ald. and the first edition of Gis. in the text, *praescripsit* (“prescribed”) instead of *prospexit* (“provided for”). The passage concerns Theodosius, not Constantine, who died in 337. Hence it follows that, in that speech concerning Theodosius, Prudentius includes all his actions against paganism, even if they belong to different periods.

**533.** Prag., *Internaque hominum strage tormenta parantes*, with the gloss that, according to some, *ge* should be extended in the ablative. Mar. in the second hand and Weitz., *Internoque hominum stravit*: that is, “he struck down those preparing torments within men.” Mar. in the first hand, *internaque hominum stravit*. Rat. in the second hand, *internaque hominum statui*: here *interna* refers to the torments. The more common reading is: *Internoque hominum statui tormenta parantes*.]

742 Let them become ornaments of the fatherland, and let no debased use

Pollute monuments of art turned toward vice.

Informed by such decrees, the City recoiled from

Its ancient errors, and shook off the murky clouds

From its withered mouth, now prepared in nobility

[510] To attempt eternal ways and follow Christ who calls,

Under a great-hearted leader, and to send its hope into the ages.

Then for the first time Rome, made teachable by old age, blushed

At its own long era: it is ashamed of the time that has passed,

And hates the years gone by with their foul religions.

[515] 743 Soon, when it remembers that the fields adjoining the city ditches

Were soaked with the innocent blood of the righteous,

And sees around it the hateful thousands of tombs,

[Col. 0161B] It is more deeply sorry for its judgment and its uncontrolled rule,

And for its excessive anger on behalf of shameful rites.

[520] [Col. 0162A] It wishes to compensate the most dreadful wounds of injured

Justice by late obedience and by seeking pardon,

Lest, under so great an empire, the crime of cruelty remain after piety has been rejected; it seeks the prescribed expiations,

And is transferred wholly into the faith of Christ through love.

[525] The laurel of victorious Marius was less useful to the City,

When he dragged the Numidian Jugurtha amid the people’s applause,

[530] Provided and bestowed good things: he drove many Catilines

744 from their home—men preparing, not savage fires for roofs

[Col. 0162B] or daggers for senators, but black Tartarus for souls

[Col. 0163B] **540.** *Tropaea*: victory. — *Quirini*: Roman, I.

**535.** Above, verse 216: “the lofty Capitoline.”

**536.** Egm. in the second hand, *quin conjuratas*. The same manuscript has *vitalia, plebes*, incorrectly.

**539.** Mar., Rat., *latitante*. Egm., *cogator*, above *negator*; correct to *togatus*. *Triumphator* is a word frequent in Apuleius, Cyprian, and inscriptions of the later age.

**540.** Egm. above, *resque Quirini*.

**541.** *Assuescit pollere*: compare hymn 9 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 95, *redire insuesceret mortuos* (“he would grow accustomed to bringing back the dead”).

**542.** From Virgil, *Aeneid* I: “I set neither bounds nor periods to their dominion; I have given them empire without end.” I do not know why Heinsius, contrary to the authority of the manuscripts, wishes to conjecture: *Denique nec metas statui, nec tempora poni* (“Finally, I set neither bounds nor periods”). He immediately adds: “It teaches, clearly, what follows.” Chamillard understands Heinsius’s conjecture so that *statui* and *poni* refer to *docet*. The manuscript reading is clear and should not be disturbed.

**544.** After this verse Rat. and Mar. have the heading “On the conversion of the senate,” which appears in Alex. in the margin. Urb. has “On the conversion of the senate.” Aldus has “The Roman senate converted to Christ.”

**545.** On such encomia of the Roman senate, Juretus supplies abundant testimony from the ancients in his note on Symmachus, letter 46, book I: “The better part of the human race, the senate.”

**547.** Another Rott. has *candidiora togae* (“the brighter garments of the toga”), which seemed not inelegant to Heinsius. I see here nothing but an error, *candidiora* for *candidiore*. Countless critics and antiquarians discuss the white toga and these very verses of Prudentius. Here is the substance. The toga of the Romans was always white; but since on feast days they wore new, clean clothing, they were then called and were, in a particular sense, “whitened.” Moreover, candidates made their togas whiter with chalk; hence the name *candidates* remained attached to them. Prudentius therefore means that the Romans assumed a brighter toga as though on a festival day. So in hymn 11 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 203: “No less does a shining line of troops unfold itself at the Alban gates and extend in long ranks.” But Prudentius also seems here to indicate a mystical meaning, namely the brightness of piety and innocence. Nor do I dislike what Dominicus Macer says in the *Hierolexicon*, under the word *BAPTISMUS*: that Prudentius alludes to the white garments of the newly baptized.

**549.** Ald., *in rupe retectis* (“revealed on the rock”); I understand it as “lying hidden” or “covered.”

**550.** In the Codex Jureti this verse was interpolated as follows: *penetralia noxa reorum* (“the inner chambers, the guilt of criminals”), without sense or with an opposite sense. In Egm. it was *noxa virorum* (“the guilt of men”), from which *noxa reorum* arose.

**552.** Fabr., Widm., Bong. in the second hand, Mar., and Rat. have *Aeneadum*, incorrectly. Vat. A and Prag. have *Amniadum*. In this verse two families are mentioned that later merged into one, those of Annius and Probus. A third, that of the Anicii, is added in the following verse. The gloss *electorum* (“chosen men”) is inept.

**553.** Someone might correctly conjecture that we should read *orbis Illustrasse caput* (“to have illumined the head of the world”). Compare above, verse 497: “Therefore beware, illustrious head of the world.” But perhaps Prudentius calls the senate the head of the City. This Anicius was a descendant of the Annii and the Probi. Some seek these names under Constantine. But Prudentius clearly speaks of those who, after Theodosius’s decrees, or at least under his rule, renounced pagan superstition and embraced the Catholic faith. Baronius therefore should not be followed when he supposes that this Anicius was Anicius Julianus, consul with Petronius Probianus in A.D. 322. Chamillard believes him to be Sextus Petronius Probus, prefect of the praetorium under the emperor Valentinian and consul with Gratian in 371. He is certainly called “the summit of the Anician house” in an inscription on a monument dedicated by his son, Anicius Hermogenianus Olybrius, ordinary consul, and Anicia Juliana. I, however, see no reason why the son of Sextus Petronius Probus, who is called Anicius Hermogenianus in that inscription, should not rather be the Anicius who first gave his name to Christ after the laws concerning the Christian religion and the overthrow of idols had been promulgated by Theodosius. Claudian, Marcellinus, Zosimus, Ausonius, and others may be consulted concerning these families and their nobility. St. Jerome, in his letter to Demetrias, says: “Surely I do not need to recall the famous names of the Probi and Olybrii, and the illustrious lineage of Anician blood . . . Or should Olybrius, the father of our virgin, be brought forward, whom Rome lamented when untimely death took him away?” In the notes this Olybrius is said to have held the consulship in 305; perhaps 395 should be read. In the consular fasti I find the following men who may belong to these families: in 322, Petronius Probianus and Anicius Julianus; in 341, Probinus with Marcellinus; in 371, Sextus Anicius Probus with Gratian; in 379, Hermogenianus Olybrius with Ausonius; in 395, Sextus Anicius Olybrius and Sextus Anicius Probinus; in 406, Sextus Anicius Petronius Probus with Arcadius; in 408, Anicius Bassus with Philippus.]
