**556.** *Fastis*: in books, because he made the books into authorities. — *Palmata*: victorious, I.

**557.** *Martyris*: of any martyr. — *Fasces*: the dignities that Brutus held as consul, Iso.

**558.** *Ambit*: desires. — *Ausoniam*: Italian. — *Christo*: on account of Christ. — *Securim*: authority, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0165B]

**555.** Weitzius, in the *Various Readings*, says that Pal. has *numinis* and *nominis*; but in the text he printed *nominis*, which is certainly correct. Becmanus seems to have read *numinis haeres* (“heir of the divinity”) in some printed edition, for he corrects it from his own manuscript to *nominis* (“heir of the name”). In Prudentius’s time there were two highly distinguished men named Olybrius: one was prefect of the City under the second consulship of Valentinian and Valens; the other was his son Olybrius, who held the consulship with his brother Probinus. I more willingly understand Prudentius to mean the son, who is certainly heir of the Olybrian family and of its name. Olybrius the father had married Proba, daughter of Sextus Petronius Probus, whom I discussed shortly above. Gothofredus provides further information about these Roman nobles in his notes on the Theodosian Code.

**556.** Sich., Widm., Bong., Weitz., Rat., and Mar. have *ab aula*; Prag., *ab olla*, which amounts to the same thing, since *au* was often exchanged with *o*. Ald. and Gis. have *abolla*; Heinsius copied this, and later editors followed him, without indicating the variety of readings. Yet the first reading could be defended. The consuls’ garments were called *palmatae* without anything else being added. Cassiodorus, book VI, letter 1: “We bear the labors of the consuls, and you the joys of office; for your *palmatae* are proved to be our victories . . . Paint the broad shoulders of the *palmata* in varied color.” Olybrius, therefore, having been entered in the consular fasti and distinguished by the *palmata*, desired, as I think, to lower the consular fasces before the doors of the martyr, the prince of the apostles. Grangaeus likewise interprets *martyr* in this way. Fabricius proves that *abolla* is correctly read in the Aldine copy, because the *abolla* was the senators’ garment, as the toga was that of the knights; and both were called *palmatae*. The *abolla* of emperors may perhaps have been called *palmata* from *palma*, or victory. The *abolla* of consuls and the *palmata* toga of knights seem to have been called so from the breadth of the stripe, that is, from a palm’s breadth. Teolius, together with Hugh Menard, notes that the name *palmata* was transferred to an ecclesiastical garment. For in a Mass published by Illyricus mention is made of a garment called *palmatica*, and in letter 66 of book I of St. Gregory the Great, *palmatianae* garments are mentioned. I wish Teolius had confirmed with clearer evidence his claim that Christians of that age, as soon as they had obtained the praetorship and consulship, customarily hurried to the apostles’ shrines and distributed money and clothing to the poor. For the passage that, in Teolius’s view, shows that the same practice had previously been performed by pagans is Ammianus’s account in book XXVII of Symmachus, the father whom Prudentius attacks: “He had enriched with great gifts certain needy persons summoned from the Vatican.” It is not clear that this should be understood of the apostles’ shrines or of Christian paupers. Ammianus reports this not of Symmachus but of Lampadius: “When he was giving magnificent praetorian games and distributing with great generosity, unable to endure the uproar of the people, who often pressed him to give many things to the undeserving so that he might display himself as generous and as one who despised the crowd, he enriched with great gifts certain needy people summoned from the Vatican.” Valesius, who had expressed Teolius’s opinion in his note on this passage, offers some remarks in the same direction, but they are less clear than Prudentius’s words. Ammianus means poor people who lived in the Vatican. As Olaus Borrichius proves in chapter 16 of his *Brief Dissertation on the Ancient Appearance of the City*, the Vatican was once despised by the Quirites because of its harsher climate, stagnant and idle waters, foul vapors, and stench from corpses. I understand Prudentius more simply: Olybrius, as consul, subjected himself, and therefore his dignity as well, to Christ. Nevertheless, I would not object if someone added that a rite had already been introduced by which a Christian consul lowered the fasces and inclined the axe when entering a church—like the signs of reverence that can be seen in soldiers standing at sacred ceremonies.

**558.** To Heinsius, *securim* seems more characteristic of Prudentius than *securem*.

**559.** St. Paulinus, bishop of Nola, is praised here; Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, and other contemporaries provide much information about his conversion and holy conduct. His life is narrated by Sacchini, Le Brun, and Muratori. He was born in Aquitania of a most noble Roman family, advanced to the highest honors, including the consulship, and went to Spain, where he married Therasia, apparently a Spanish woman. By her he had a son at Complutum, where the child died and was buried beside the tomb of the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor. He was baptized by Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux, and ordained priest by Lampius, bishop of Barcelona; as he himself says, he was dedicated to the priesthood solely of the Lord, not also to a particular church. Paulinus’s conversion is assigned to approximately the year 380. Whether the Bassus mentioned here was Junius Bassus, who died as prefect of the City and a neophyte in 358, as is clear from an inscription published by Sirmondus in his notes on Ennodius, may be questioned. Most affirm this, and Philippus Laurentius Dionysius follows them in *Monuments of the Vatican Basilica*, plate LXXXI. But since Prudentius seems to be listing only those nobles who embraced the faith of Christ under Theodosius, I understand him to mean another man. I believe Bassula belonged to this family of the Bassi, a pious woman who was the mother-in-law of Severus Sulpicius and is mentioned in the letters of Paulinus and Severus. Anicius Bassus held the consulship in 408, as I said shortly above. Some deny that Bassus was a family name. This matters little to us, nor do they prove what they assert. In volume I of the Pio-Clementine Museum there is an old inscription, reproduced from the preface of the learned Pietro Francesco Foggini to the Roman *Fasti* of Verrius Flaccus, which concerns this Anicius Bassus and therefore should not be omitted here.]

**TO BASSUS ANICIUS AUCHENIUS BASSUS, VIR CLARISSIMUS, PROCONSUL OF CAMPANIA, OVERSEER OF THAT PROVINCE, RESTORER OF THE ANICIAN LINEAGE: ON ACCOUNT OF HIS DISTINGUISHED MERITS, THE COUNCIL AND PEOPLE OF THE CITY OF PRAENESTE SET THIS UP BY DECREE.**

This inscription was discovered at Praeneste around 1779. Foggini says that from it one may infer why Bassus was called by the name of Anicius; I wish he had explained the matter more fully.]

**746.** *Illustrasse caput*: thus illustrious Rome boasts of itself.

[555] Moreover, heir both of the Olybrian family and of its name,

Entered in the consular fasti, distinguished by the palmata abolla,

[Col. 0166A] 747 He desires to lower the fasces of Brutus before the martyr’s doors,

And to bow the Italian axe before Christ.

The ready faith of the Paulini and the Bassi did not hesitate

[560] [Col. 0167A] [Note: [Col. 0167B]

**560.** *Superbam*: noble, I.

**561.** *Patriciae*: the consuls were patricians who governed the people according to the custom of their fathers, I.

**562.** *Plebicolas*: lovers of the plebs, I.

**564.** *Praecipuos*: leaders, I, Vat. A.

**565.** *Lictoribus*: attendants or soldiers, I.

**567.** *Domos*: families, I.

**568.** *Placet*: it is permitted, I.

**569.** *Idolii*: paganism. An *idolium* is a place in which sacrifices were offered to idols; an *idolothyte* is the sacrifice; an idol is the object to which the sacrifice is offered. — *Emersisse*: to have emerged, I.

**570.** *Si persona*: that is, if temporal dignity has any value before God, I.

**571.** *Formam*: beauty, I.

**573.** *Potiores*: more excellent, better, I.

**574.** *Cellam*: a church, a temple, where the Roman nobles assembled, I. The church of St. Peter, Rat.

**576.** *Obtritos*: worn out, destroyed. — *Aegre*: with difficulty, I.

**577.** *Exactas*: past, Iso.

**578.** *Solem*: Christ, I.

**579.** *Quota*: how great, I.

**580.** *Infectam*: polluted. — *Sanie*: putrefaction, I.

**581.** *Coenacula*: the Capitoline temples, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0167B]

**562.** The Codex Jureti has, incorrectly, *Graecos* for *Gracchos*, or, as some prefer to write it, *Graccos*. In the margin of the same codex some foolish schoolmaster had written, for purposes of interpretation, *Graecos*: “as being closer to the Romans, they were accustomed to be joined to pledges of marriage and offices.” In some printed editions there is *poplicolas*, which Weitzius not improperly preferred on the authority of Egm.; yet in Egm. Heinsius found *plebicolas*. He calls the Gracchi *plebicolas* because their ancestors, Gaius and Tiberius Gracchus, supported the plebs in promoting the agrarian law. The Gracchus whom Prudentius has in mind was a relative of Laeta, whom St. Jerome praises in letter 107: “A few years ago, did not your kinsman Gracchus, whose name sounded of patrician nobility, while he was prefect of the City, overthrow, break, and burn the cave of Mithras and all the monstrous images into which the raven, nymph, soldier, lion, Persian, sun, and Bromius the Father (or Dromus the Father) are initiated, and, having first sent these forward as hostages, obtain the baptism of Christ?” Baronius says this occurred in A.D. 383; Gothofredus and Pagius place it in 376; more plausibly, Philippus a Turre, in the final chapter of his work on Mithras, thinks that Gracchus did not enter the prefecture of the City before 378. In the cave of Mithras the symbols of the stars and planets were worshiped, some of which Jerome lists. See Vallarsius’s notes.

**564.** Bong. in the first hand, *jussisse repelli* (“to have ordered them to be driven away”).

**566.** Ald., Egm., Palat., *se congregasse* (“to have gathered”), contrary to the meter.

**567.** Mar., Prag., Rat., *domus* (“houses”).

**568.** The gloss should be read in the opposite way: *LICET*, “it is permitted,” unless *placet* is a different reading in Isone.

**569.** Ald., *idoli*, contrary to Prudentius’s usage, who shortens the second syllable. Vat. A and Egm. have *profano* for *profundo*; the latter should be retained. Prag. reads, incorrectly, *mersisse*.

**572.** Prag. always writes *hii* for *hi*. Another Rott. has *juncta quoties*, which Heinsius thinks was produced according to Prudentius’s usage.

**574.** In Mar. *est* was missing. The glosses explain *cellam* as “church”; I would prefer *curiam*. Above he called the senators “the lights of the world.” The senate customarily assembled in temples or other consecrated places; and in temples there were various *cellae*, or small chapels and shrines. Prudentius therefore means the *cella* in which the senate was held. The learned Antoninus Valsecchius of the Dominican order, highly esteemed for his writings in defense of the Christian religion, rendered these verses of Prudentius, as well as others elsewhere, into Italian verse in his work *The Victorious Religion*, part 2, chapter 2, against the empty and sophistical philosophy of Fréret. Fréret, influenced by Symmachus’s words, which he had not reproduced with sufficient accuracy, argues in his *Critical Examination* that the more illustrious part of the senate agreed with Symmachus. Valsecchius refutes him by the authority of Ambrose and Prudentius. The poet, he adds cleverly, “is well worthy of being heard and appreciated even by a perpetual secretary of the Royal Academy of Inscriptions and Belles-Lettres.”

**576.** The Jureti parchment has *obstrictos* (“bound”), together with Ald. and Gis. in the margin. Most witnesses, including Gifanius and Colerus in their notes on Valerius Maximus, have *obtritos*, that is, rejected and utterly despised.

**578.** Aldus, *nec cernere*; others, *non cernere*, taken from a proverb. After this verse Mar. and Rat. have the heading “On the credulity of the people,” which also appears in Urb. and Alex. in the margin. Aldus has “The Roman people’s belief in Christ.”

**579.** Ald. and the first edition of Gis. in the text: *quis in Urbe est, Qui* (“who in the City is there, who”); others: *quota pars est, Quae* (“what proportion is there that”). In Vat. A, *est* is missing.

**580.** Egm., Thuan., and Pal. have the corrupt reading *disputat*; Weitz., *dispuit*; Rat. and Gis., *despuit*; most, *despuat*. Tertullian, book *On Idolatry*, chapter 11: “With what face will a Christian incense-bearer, if he passes through temples, spit upon and blow away the smoking altars, for which he himself had once taken thought?” And chapter 13 of *On the Spectacles*: “We spit upon temples no less than upon tombs.” Minucius in the *Octavius*: “They regard temples as tombs, spit upon the gods, and laugh at sacred rites,” and so forth. See what Heraldus, Elmenhorstius, Wowerus, and Ouzelius note on this passage. Origen, book VIII *Against Celsus*, seems to disapprove of this in Christians. “Who among us,” he says, “is so foolish as to say such things, and not see that nothing of this kind is effective in removing belief in the gods?” The periods must be distinguished. Under pagan emperors this could not be done publicly without some special impulse inspired by God, except imprudently; under Christian emperors it was now permitted. Compare the commentary on verse 128 of the hymn of St. Eulalia.

**581.** Prag., *celso*; read *celsa*. Heinsius thinks that *vulgus* entered from a gloss, for the common people are plainly designated by this circumlocution, and he conjectures that Prudentius’s own reading was either *Omnis qui celsa scandit coenacula scalis* (“Everyone who climbs the lofty upper rooms by ladders”) or *Omnis qui scandit coenacula celsa domorum* (“Everyone who climbs the lofty upper rooms of houses”). It does not seem to me that *vulgus* is superfluous. The common people are named, and at the same time their condition is poetically described, which is by no means inelegant. The poor lived in upper rooms, as is shown by Juvenal, Martial, and others.]

748 Ready faith gives itself to Christ, and raises the proud stock

Of the patrician race for the age to come.

Now why should I run through in song the plebeian-loving Gracchi,

Supported by the authority of office, and foremost in the senate’s citadel,

Who ordered the images of the gods to be torn down,

[565] And, together with their lictors, humbly consecrated themselves

749 To almighty Christ, to be governed by him?

It is permitted to count six hundred houses of ancient blood,

Noble families converted to the standards of Christ,

Having emerged from the vast depths of foul idolatry.

[570] If personal dignity has any significance, or if the condition of the City is represented in these men,

[Col. 0168A] If the more excellent order gives shape to the fatherland,

They accomplish this, whenever the judgment of the people is joined with theirs,

And the greater number think as one with the more distinguished.

Look to the illustrious chamber, where the public light is found:

[575] You will find only very few minds overgrown with pagan trifles,

With difficulty retaining worn-out rites,

And pleased to preserve the darkness that has passed,

750 And not to see the sun shining in the middle of the day.

Then turn your eyes to the people: what proportion is there

[580] That does not spit upon Jupiter’s altar, polluted with filth?

All the common people who climb the lofty upper rooms,

[Col. 0169A] [Note: [Col. 0169B]

**582.** *Terit*: foot soldiers, I.

**583.** *Et quem*: the poor. — *Dispensus*: distributed, I.

**584.** *Vaticano*: where the body of St. Peter rests. — *Tumulum*: tomb, Iso.

**585.** *Quo*: where. — *Genitoris*: of Peter. — *Obses*: one who is given in place of peace is called a hostage; blessed Peter was a hostage to the Romans, bringing them peace, I.

**586.** *Lateranas*: to the basilica of St. John the Baptist, where there is a church in honor of the twelve apostles, I.

**591.** *Extendere*: to prolong, I.

[Col. 0170B] **593.** *Luce*: the light of the Gospel, I.

**594.** *Meritis*: the virtues of warfare. — *Sanguine*: lineage, nobility, I.

**595.** *Titulis*: inscriptions, I.

**596.** *Fastorum*: the books of the years, I.

**598.** *Veteres*: leaders. — *Cera*: because the most distinguished men of ancient times made wax and bronze statues. — *Aere*: on bronze tablets, I.

**599.** *Caterva*: multitude, I.

**604.** *Si consulta*: if it was not otherwise permitted to preserve the faith of Christ than as the Fathers ordained it—the faith ordained by the three hundred bishops, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0169C]

**582.** Ald., Egm., *variis discussibus*. Roman flint is black in color. Juvenal, satire 6: “Nor is she better who wears away the black flint with her feet.” In 1784 an Italian dissertation entitled *On Roman Flint* was published at Rome by Giovanni Gerolamo Lapi. He denies that Roman flint was formed from a mass melted by ancient fires in the mountains and subsequently cooled into stone, contrary to what many suppose.

**583.** Gifanius, under the word *VERTERE*, observes that the ancients very often used simple forms of words rather than compounds, as *vertere* for *evertere*. Such, he says, is Prudentius’s truly remarkable *DISPENSUS* for *DISPENSATUS*. The title of book XLV of the Theodosian Code is *On Civic Grain Rations and Graded Bread*. Bread used to be distributed to citizens from steps, so that those distributing it would not be crushed by the crowd. Hence it was called *gradilis*. Others say that bread was customarily distributed on steps. In book II *Against Symmachus*, verse 498: “What district endures dreadful hunger with its steps empty?” Lipsius, in *Selectae*, book I, chapter 8, infers from Prudentius that steps may have been erected in each district of the City where this distribution took place.

**584.** St. Jerome, letter 107 to Laeta, written in 403: “The gilded Capitol is grimy. All the temples of Rome are covered with soot and spiders’ webs. The City is moved from its foundations, and the surging people rush before the half-ruined shrines to the tombs of the martyrs [lacuna] Paganism suffers desolation even in the City.”

586. Ald., Gis., Egm., Pal., Alex., Urb., “hurries to the Lateran.” Vat. A, “hurries to the great Lateran.” Most of the best manuscripts, “hurries with great throngs to the Lateran buildings.” Some confirm by these verses that, already in Prudentius’ time, there existed in the Lateran buildings a baptistery, evidently constructed by Constantine.

587. Vat. A, “royal.”

588. An imitation of Virgil, Book VI: “And do we still hesitate to extend our courage through our deeds?”

593. Oxon., “does not open his lofty eyes in the light.” Teolius also printed it this way and implies that Heinsius had done so. But Heinsius printed *sub luce oculos* in the text and merely reports in the notes the variant reading in the Oxford manuscript, adding several similar examples.

594. Ald., “however distinguished.”

596. The *Fasti* were marked by the names of the consuls, as is well known.

597. Rat., “they might mark,” less well.

598. Widm. above, “paper”; read “wax.”

600. Rat., “nor does the senate-house unite,” incorrectly.

601. Ald., Mar. in the first hand, Thuan., Egm., Ox., Pal., Alex. in the first hand, Urb., “foster.” The punctuation should then be: “and whatever private inclination of study they foster (those few), this now rare [interest] possesses;”

602. Ald., “and public.” In others, “but public.” Prag., Mar. in the margin, Rat., “this now rare [interest] possesses.” Others, “and now.” If *fovet* is read, then “this now rare [interest] possesses” is better.

604. Ald., Weitz., Heins., “thus the decrees of the Fathers.” The more recent manuscripts agree with Heinsius. But Heinsius departed from Giselinus’ reading *contra morem* without indicating the variant. Gis., Rat., Prag., Mar., and others, “if the decrees”—which I prefer.

606. Prag., “then one hundred”; read “three hundred.”

608. Rat., “of the number, and divided in part”; above, “and in a small part.” Retain “and in a small part.” Symmachus could raise no objection to this argument: for in Book IV, Letter 27, he says, “The law of our senate makes the authority of the larger number prevail with me.” Hence this formula was used in the senate: “Count the senate.” After this verse, the lemma in Mar., Rat., and Alex. addresses Symmachus. In Urb., “Concerning the reliability of the senate” follows.

And whoever wears down the black flint in his various rounds,

and he whom bread, distributed from the lofty steps, sustains,

[585] or frequents the tomb beneath the Vatican hill,

where that ash lies hidden—the beloved pledge of his father—

or hurries with great throngs to the Lateran buildings,

from which he may bring back the sacred sign with royal chrism:

And do we still doubt that Rome, dedicated to you, Christ,

has passed over into your laws, and that, willing with all

[590] the people and with the highest citizens, she now stretches

an earthly kingdom above the stars of the great heaven?

Nor am I moved by the fact that the rarest part of humanity

[Col. 0169B] does not open its closed eyes in the light and wanders in its steps.

[Col. 0170A] However distinguished in merits and illustrious in blood,

[595] though they have brought back the lofty rewards of virtues,

increased by titles and honors, and have attained the citadel of the *Fasti*,

and marked the annalistic tablets with their own name,

and are counted among the ancients in wax and bronze,

[600] nevertheless, when the company has now dwindled to a few,

the person of the fatherland is no longer present,

nor does the senate stand firm;

and whatever private inclination of study fosters,

this now rare [interest] possesses: but public votes cry out,

with celebrated dissent condemning the trembling murmur.

If the decrees of the enrolled Fathers are to stand,

[605] it was permitted in former times in no other way than if

three hundred elders were found to have held one opinion:

[Col. 0170B] “Let us preserve the ancestral laws: let the weaker

voice of the smaller number yield, and be silent in the small part.”

[Col. 0171A] **Notes**

609. *Subsellia*: tribunals, Iso.

610. *Infame*: detestable. — *Pulvinar*: a temple; from *pulvinaria*, that is, the couches which they set up in the temples of the gods, where they received responses from the gods, I.

612. *Principis*: of Theodosius, I.

613. *Frequentia*: multitude, I.

614. *Terret*: “he terrifies,” so that he might compel belief in Christ; each person believed in Christ of his own accord, I.

616. *Ratione*: by preaching, I.

618. *Sacricolis*: pagans, I.

620. *Pago*: paganism, Vat. A.

[Col. 0172B] 622. *Obstant*: “they hinder,” by compelling, I.

623. *Ipse*: God, the emperor, I. — *Tibi*: “to you, O Symmachus,” Vat. A.

626. *Assertor*: “O Symmachus,” I.

628. *Furores*: madnesses (*minna*), I.

629. *Iliacae*: of Ops. — *Megalesia*: solemn sacrifices. — *Bacchica*: rites of Liber Pater. — *Nisi*: from the city of Nysa, where Liber was worshiped, I.

631. *Mimica*: foolish, buffoonish. — *Calvis*: deceivers, I.

**Notes**

609. Mar. in the first hand, *plena*, incorrectly. I noted in the prolegomena, no. 70, note c (Col. 615, Patrologia, vol. LIX, n. a), Fabricius’ error: from these verses he had inferred that there were many pagan senators when Prudentius wrote this. Paulinus agrees with Prudentius in *Natale* 11: “All Rome is reckoned under the pious name of Christ.” Nevertheless, some leading men still retained paganism at Rome, as is plainly evident from that same Paulinus’ poem to Licentius:

> “Nor should the nobility seem free to you,  
> whom now you see carried in majesty  
> through the astonished City; whom you see  
> imagining such liberty for themselves  
> that they disdain to bend their hearts to God.”

610. Ald., Egm., Pal., *discernant*; *decernant* is far better.

611. Ald., Rat., incorrectly, *idolum* for *idolium*; worse, Vat. A, *furandum* for *fugandum*.

612. Prag., Rat. in the second hand, *quo vocat*. Vat. A, incorrectly, *qui vocat*. Here the gloss concerning the emperor Theodosius proceeds correctly, but it is not consistent with other passages, where it understands Constantine instead of Theodosius.

613. Vat. A, corruptly, *libera compedibus*. Ald., Teol., *tum pedibus*; others, *cum pedibus*. Freretus, in his *Critical Examination*—as he himself calls it—of authors who wrote apologies for the Christian religion, shamelessly asserts that the Christian religion was propagated through the violence of Christian emperors. These verses of Prudentius, and the very fact that he recounts, refute that slander. And who does not know that the Christian religion grew through the blood of the martyrs?

615. Ald., *cunctique probatu*, not *non jussu*.

616. In Rat. there seems to be *capiti ratione*, which is an error, as in Palat., *capitis ratione*.

617. Rat., *promeritis*, and Gifanius always orders this to be read in Prudentius under the word *PROMERITA*, because Prudentius, although later, readily imitates the ancients. He thinks the passage should be punctuated as follows: “Finally, the good leader, repaying earthly merits with equal gifts, bestows the highest honors upon the pagan priests and permits them to vie with the renown of his own people.” Others punctuated it: “gifts to the pagan priests, the highest honors,” and so on.

620. Vat. A, incorrectly, *nec pago illicitos*. Barthius, Book XVII, chapter 1, notes that *pagus* in Prudentius, both in the *Romanus* and here, means idolatry, because the more stupid people who lived in villages worshiped cruder gods and unworked pieces of wood. Sulpicius Severus calls pagans “rustics,” and Aldhelm, in *On the Praise of the Virgin*, says, “Changing rural bands (*ruricolas phalanges*) into the kingdoms of heaven.” See above, on verse 449.

[Col. 0172B] 626. Ald., incorrectly, *assertor regum*. In the *Romanus*, verse 1: “O Roman, strong champion of Christ God.” Egm., *solis* for *solus*. I do not dislike this reading, although *Phoebi furor* follows: for the poet seems to be noting the adultery of Venus and Mars, which the Sun revealed and Vulcan avenged.

627. Virgil, *Georgics* IV: “the deceits of Vulcan and Mars, and their sweet thefts.”

[Col. 0172C] 628. Egm., *Fybique furores*. When Saturn wished to eat his son Jupiter, his wife Ops substituted a stone for Jupiter, which he immediately swallowed, believing it to be his son. “Phoebus’ madnesses” indicate the insanity by which Apollo’s prophets were driven while they were foretelling something. Virgil, Book VI, on the Sibyl:

> “Apollo shakes the reins  
> for the raging woman and turns the goads beneath her breast.  
> As soon as the frenzy subsided and her rabid mouth grew quiet…”

Iso explains it as *minna*; concerning this word, see above in the commentary on verse 117.

629. The other Rott., *Bacchia Nisi*. Heinsius, Book I of the *Posthumous Adversaria*, chapter 19, thinks *Nisei* or *Nisae* should be read, not *Nisi*. *Niseus* is Bacchus; others write *Nyseus*. Nisus was the nurse of Bacchus. Thus, by any of these forms, the festivals of Bacchus are understood. Prag. has *Magalesia* instead of *Megalesia*. The Megalesia are games in honor of Cybele, who is called Iliac because of Ilium, where she was especially worshiped. Concerning these, see Livy, Book II, and Ovid, *Fasti* IV: “At once, when the Berecynthian flute had begun with its horn…” Add what Fogginius notes in Verrius Flaccus’ *Fasti*, pp. 42 and following. But we shall discuss these games again in the *Romanus*.

630. Mar. writes *Osirin*. Minucius says of these rites:

> “Isis mourns, laments, and searches for her lost son with her Cynocephalus and bald priests; and the wretched Isiac worshipers beat their breasts and imitate the grief of the most unhappy mother. Soon, when the little one has been found, Isis rejoices, the priests exult, and the discovering Cynocephalus boasts. Yet every year they do not cease either to lose what they find or to find what they lose. Is it not ridiculous either to mourn what you worship or to worship what you mourn?”

Lactantius, Book I, chapter 21; Athanasius, *Against the Pagans*; Firmicus, *On the Error of Profane Religions*; Origen; Cyprian; Eusebius; Augustine; Paulinus; and other Christian writers repeat much the same, to say nothing of the pagans.

631. Gis. and some common manuscripts, *mimicaque et ridenda suis*. Rat. likewise, but with the earlier letters erased. The manuscript copies, Ald., Weitz., and others, *mimica, ridendaque suis*, correctly. In *ridenda*, the *a* is lengthened, not for the reason Gifanius gives under A—namely, that among the ancients *a* is often lengthened contrary to the common rules of grammar—but rather because of the enclitic *-que*: this enclitic causes the accent to fall on the *a*. See the prolegomena, where we explained this kind of rule.

Look how our benches, filled with a full senate,

[610] decree that the infamous couch of Jupiter,

and every idol, long purified from the City, must be driven away.

Wherever the judgment of the excellent prince summons,

there the multitude, free both in feet and in heart, hastens.

There is no place for envy; no harsh power terrifies anyone.

[615] Before our eyes it is evident that this is desired,

and all follow what has been approved, not what has been commanded,

captured by reason alone.

Finally, repaying earthly merits with equal gifts,

the good leader bestows the highest honors upon the pagan priests

and permits them to compete with the fame of his own people:

[620] [Col. 0172A] nor does he prevent men entangled in paganism

from proceeding through the appointed heights of the world,

since heavenly things never obstruct those who walk

along the accustomed earthly path.

He himself conferred upon you the office of consul;

he himself bestowed the tribunal and gave your toga

its golden covering—

[625] [Col. 0172A] you, O champion of dying gods, to whom his religion is displeasing: you alone proclaim the restoration

of Vulcan’s, Mars’ and Venus’ deceits,

of old Saturn’s stones, and of Phoebus’ madnesses;

the Megalesian rites of the Iliac mother,

the Bacchic rites of Nysa,

[630] the rites of Isis, who forever mourns her lost Osiris,

and the theatrical, laughable solemnities of her bald priests.

[Col. 0173A] **Notes**

638. *Liquidam*: bright, clear, beautiful, Iso.

643. *Pretiosa acies*: the splendor of gold. — *Acies*: sharpness, I.

646. *Frivola*: trifles, Iso.

[Col. 0174B] 648. *Indocilis*: myself. — *Lacessere*: to provoke, I.

649. *Liber*: Symmachus, I.

650. *Partam*: prepared. — *Fulmine*: with thunder, Iso.

**Notes**

636. If Symmachus’ works had not come down to us, then from the praises which Prudentius, Ambrose, Ausonius, Prosper of Aquitaine, Macrobius, and other ancients bestowed upon him, one would have to judge that the man flourished with a kind of divine eloquence. Now, since another style of expression is preferred, his letters are almost despised.

638. Prag., *liquido*; *liquidam* is better.

639. Vat. A, incorrectly, *ut aliter*. Ald., *quam cum rastris quis tentat*. So also four older manuscripts cited by Heinsius, Alex., and Urb. Heinsius prefers *quam si rastris quis tentet*. But in Book I of the *Posthumous Adversaria* he conjectured *rustris* for *rastris*, because a *rustrum* is a kind of mattock. Yet *rastra* are listed among agricultural implements by Isidore, Book XX, chapter 14; he says that they are so called either from scraping the earth or from the sparseness of their teeth. I shall also take the word as a digging implement at verse 283 of Book II. Clement of Alexandria, as Chamillardus notes, said something similar: “No one makes a silver mattock or a golden sickle; for in agriculture one must use suitable material, not wealth.” Tertullian likewise says in *On the Apparel of Women*: “Certainly no field is prepared with gold-work, nor is a ship constructed with the strength of silver. No two-pronged tool of gold is plunged into the earth.” Among proverbs are counted: “To turn the soil with ivory rakes,” “to dig the earth with golden mattocks,” and “to fish with a golden hook,” used of misusing something for an extraordinary and splendid purpose. The Jews, when under Julian the Apostate they wished to restore the temple, made mattocks, spades, and baskets out of silver. See Theodoret, Book III of the *History*, chapter 20.

640. Egm., corruptly, *verrare solum*.

642. It could also be written *scrobes*, like *lues*, *fames*, and *Joannes*, with the final syllable shortened.

646. Aldus punctuates: “I remember myself enough, and I know my trifles,”. Symphosius: “But having spoken many trifles.” Ausonius: “And so I sent you trifles more foolish than Sicilian nonsense.” Juvenal, *Satire* 3: “Now Ucalegon carries away trifles.” Sidonius, Book IV, Letter 3, seems to imitate Prudentius.

649. The error of Aldus is *manet* for *maneat*.

655. Ald., *cur mi fas*. Cicero, *Against Catiline*: “How many of your attacks, directed in such a way that they could not possibly be avoided, have I escaped by a slight sidestep and, as they say, by moving my body aside?” Catullus, poem 114: “I avoid those missiles of yours by turning aside.” See Vulpianus’ commentary.

656. Lipsius, *Saturnalia* II, chapter 20, conjectures *sarissas* for *sagittas*, because spears are thrown, not arrows. Heinsius does not approve this conjecture. “Windy arrows” are so called on account of windy eloquence, as in the preface to Book II: “He swells with the winds of eloquence.” Petronius used the phrase “windy loquacity.”

657. An imitation of Virgil, *Eclogue* 1: “And now far off the summit”; and *Georgics* II: “And now it is time to release the horses’ smoking necks.”

658. Ald., “The first book against Symmachus ends.” Alex., “The first book against Symmachus ends.” Urb., “Book I against Symmachus ends.”

And whatever masks are accustomed to close the Capitoline temples,

O tongue flowing with an astonishing fountain of words,

[635] glory of Roman eloquence, before which even Tully himself

must yield—your rich eloquence pours forth these gems!

A mouth worthy to shine, dyed with eternal gold,

if only it had preferred to praise God: to whom it preferred

filthy monsters and defiled its clear voice with sin.

It is just as if someone should try with ivory rakes

[640] to turn over a muddy field,

and, if it happened, cultivate marsh plants dripping with mud

with little golden mattocks:

the dark trench soils the splendor of a shining tooth,

and the precious blade grows foul in the filthy field.

I do not fear that anyone will accuse me of excessive confidence

[645] or think that I am entering into a contest of talent.

[Col. 0174A] I remember myself, and I know my own trifles well:

I would not dare to match my foot against his,

nor, untrained in speech, to provoke with missiles a tongue so mighty in utterance.

Let the book remain unharmed, and let the excellent volume

[650] retain the fame it has won through the thunderbolt of eloquence;

but let me be permitted to protect my breast from attack

and to ward off the flying dart with an opposing shield.

For if our faith, already secure in a peaceful age,

has been assailed by hostile forces and hostile art,

[655] why should it not be permitted me, bending aside

with a curve of the flank, to mock the windy arrows

that perish in their flight?

But now it is time to restrain the journey of the long little book,

lest the poem, drawn out without end, bring weariness.

At the possible departure of the light,

when saffron evening glows,

[5] he had torn away the curved anchor,

catching the winds in his sails

and wishing to cross the strait.

Night stirs up an opposing wind,

which mingles the sea from its depths

[10] and shakes the battered vessel.

The sailor’s cry, lamenting and howling,

strikes the heavens together with the shriek of the ropes.

No hope remained for the shipwrecked,

who were nearly drowning,

[15] when, from far away, the pallid crowd,

terrified by danger, sees Christ

walking on the sea with his feet,

as though he were walking around

on dry ground along a solid road.

[20] The other frightened passengers

gaze in astonishment at these miracles.

Peter alone, unafraid,

recognizes the Lord of heaven,

of earth, and of the pathless sea—

[25] he whose omnipotence

can subject the waters beneath his feet.

He stretches out his hands in supplication

and asks for the familiar aid.

[30] [Col. 0176A] But Christ, calmly nodding,

commands him to leap down from the stern.

Peter obeys the command,

but had begun to dip his footsteps

into the tops of the waves.

[35] As his step faltered, he began

to plunge his slippery feet into the depths.

God rebukes the mortal man,

because he has no steadfast faith,

and cannot tread the flowing waters,

[40] nor follow Christ.

Then with his right hand he raises the servant,

sets him upright, and teaches him to walk

across the swollen back of the strait.

So I, having emerged from secure silence,

[45] [Col. 0176B] my loquacious tongue carries

into doubtful dangers—not like the disciple Peter,

confident and rightly so in his faith,

but like one whom frequent guilt,

light-minded, tosses shipwrecked across the seas.

I am indeed utterly presumptuous,

who, conscious of the night that I spend

[Col. 0177A] in the darkness of life,

am not afraid to entrust my vessel to the waves

against so great a man, than whom none is now more eloquent.

## Against Symmachus, Book Two

[Col. 0177]

[Col. 0177B] **Notes**

1. *Cunabula*: beginnings, Iso, Vat. A.

2. *Hebes*: foolish, I.

4. *Objecta*: the charges brought against me by Symmachus. — *Legam*: I shall gather, I.

5. *Unde*: I shall say, Vat. A. — *Coepisse*: to have begun to cultivate this heresy. — *Quibus*: by what causes. — *Orsum*: begun, I. “Namely, to be,” Vat. A.

[Col. 0178B] 6. *Quo*: so that. — *Illice*: by persuasive, deceptive art, I.

7. *Armorum*: of wars. — *Dominos*: Romans, I.

8. *Patris*: of the fathers. — *Genitos*: born, raised. — *Imagine filio*: in the image of the son, who is the image of the father. — *Avita*: ancient, ancestral, I.

9. *Exempla*: by examples. — *Congesta*: heaped up, accumulated, I.

**Notes**

In Rat. the title is: “Against Symmachus, Book II begins.” In Mar.: “Of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens,” with nothing further. The other manuscripts have no inscription.

3. Juretus’ manuscript, *cedere Christo*, “to yield to Christ,” which I do not know why Cellarius prefers as more worthy of the poet.

5. Widm. in the margin, *inde*; *unde* is better.

6. Vat. A writes *inlice*. After this verse, many manuscripts insert the following words from Symmachus’ report:

> “Who is so familiar with barbarians that he does not demand the altar of Victory? Let us be cautious for the future and avoid such omens of affairs. Let at least the honor denied to the divinity be restored to her name. Your eternity owes much to Victory and will owe still more. Let those who gained nothing turn away from this power. Do not abandon the patronage of your triumphs. This power is desired by all. Let no one deny that she should be worshiped whom he professes to wish for.”

There are several variant readings in the manuscripts. In Vat. A, *arma Victoriae* for *aram Victoriae*. In Aldus, *non quaerat* for *non requirat*. Vat. A, incorrectly, *aut in posterum* for *cauti in posterum*. Most, including Heinsius, have *sumus*, and afterward *vitamus*; I prefer, with Aldus, *simus, vitemus*. Vat. A, *ostentavimus*; Mar. in the first hand, *ostentamus*; Prag., *ostenta videmus*; others correctly, *ostenta vitemus* or *vitamus*. In Mar., with the earlier letters erased, *dignitas vestra*. Rat. in the first hand also has *dignitas* for *aeternitas*. Mar., *arceant hanc*. Prag., corruptly, *nociva* for *votiva*, whose gloss in Vat. A is *chara*. Some manuscripts write *Symmachus* before Symmachus’ words and *Prudentius* after them.

7. In Prag. and Ald. there is the error *venerantes* for *vernantes*; Heinsius would prefer *vernantis*. Becmanus, in his *Handbook of the Latin Language*, also corrected this error, *venerantes*, and restored *vernantes* from his manuscript. Some thought that “these lords of arms” were the sons of Constantine; others, Valentinian II and Arcadius, who are later called brothers, since Theodosius stood to Valentinian in the place of a father. But there is no doubt that Prudentius is speaking of Arcadius and Honorius. What he says at verse 10, “The skilled orator incites,” may be understood either because Symmachus had perhaps presented his report to these emperors, or because, from that report addressed to other emperors, the minds of the young emperors could be stirred by others unless it were refuted by a strong reply.

8. Mar., *patres*, in the first hand; Prag., *patrum*: *patris* should be read. Vat. A, Prag., and Rat. in the second hand have *vitae* incorrectly for *avita*. Marietto says that here one should ask which wives followed their husbands into the army camps and bore children there. I think that “among the father’s camps” can be understood while the father was serving, without implying that they were born in the camps themselves. See also the gloss, where the different reading *patrum* is found, though it is not good.

9. Vat. A and Weitz with his manuscripts, *edoctos*; but above in Bong. was *eductos*, which the others also have, correctly, for “raised,” as in Plautus, Terence, Juvenal, and others. Mar., Alex., Urb., Weitz., Sich., Ox., [Col. 0179B] Cauch., and Thuan. in the first hand, Rat. in the second hand, Torn. in the margin, *calentes*. Pal., Widm. above, Prag., Rat. in the first hand, Ald., Torn. in the text, and Gis., *tenentes*. Gis. in the margin, *colentes*. Heinsius and the more recent editions have *calentes*, which Heinsius considers Prudentian, since Prudentius likes to join words with the accusative, such as *aestuare*, “to be hot”; *sudare*, “to sweat”; *flere*, “to weep”; *vivere*, “to live”; *anhelare*, “to pant”; *arietare*, “to butt”; *currere*, “to run”; *suspirare*, “to sigh”; *credere*, “to believe”; *sitire*, “to thirst”; *spirare*, “to breathe”; *pluere*, “to rain”; *prurire*, “to itch”; *ludere*, “to play”; *mendicare*, “to beg”; *glorificare*, “to glorify”; *resultare*, “to rebound”; *ruere*, “to rush”; *spumare*, “to foam”; *sufflare*, “to blow”; *susurrare*, “to whisper”; *sapere*, “to have taste”; *tumere*, “to swell”; *triumphare*, “to triumph”; *strepere*, “to make a noise”; *cogitare*, “to think”; *ardere*, “to burn.”

of the ancient gods,

and of the causes by which foolish error was fashioned in the world;

and Rome now believes in our Christ.

Now I shall read the objections; now I shall refute words with words.

[762] born amid their father’s military camps,

raised in the image of their ancestor,

heated by examples accumulated at home,

10. Egm. above, *ortator catus*, that is, *hortator*. Retain *orator*.

13. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book I, speaking of the Palatine Hill: “At the summit of the hill, having built a shrine of Victory, the Arcadians established the practice of performing a sacred rite to her in alternate years, as the Romans also do in our time.” Cicero, Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*, chapter 61, and Livy, Book XXIX, testify that there was a temple of the same goddess on the Palatine. Dio, Book XLV, mentions a temple of Victory in which there was a shrine or small chapel of Capitoline Jupiter. P. Victor, in his description of the City, lists a temple of Victory in the eighth region. Livy, Book XXXV, chapter 9: “During those same days Marcus Porcius Cato dedicated a shrine of Victory Virgo near the temple of Victory.”

14. Fabr., Gis., *ecquis*; others, *et quis*. Ald., *et quis magnus*; *et quis amicus* is better.

15. Vat. A, *hanc vestro sancto*. Ald. and others, *hanc sancte vestro*. Prag., *neget*. This is precisely what Caecina said in Book VI of Cicero’s *Letters to Friends*: “There is no one among us, I think, who has not offered vows to his own Victory; no one who, even when sacrificing for another matter, did not nevertheless at that very moment wish that Caesar might be defeated as soon as possible.”

[Col. 0179D] 16. Vat. A, *quid*; *quod* should be read.

17. Ald., Gis. in the margin, first edition, *haec ubi dicta dedit*, which Grangaeus observes is used frequently by Virgil. He likewise notes that *reddunt*, “they give back,” is correctly used for *respondent*, “they answer,” since *dare* sometimes means “to speak.”

18. Mar. in the first hand, *victoria ducis*, incorrectly.

19. Ald., *fortibus Ausoniae, vir facundissime lingua*, less well.

22. Teolius, in his note on verse 8, infers from this verse 22 that the grandfather of Arcadius and Honorius was devoted to the Christian religion. I do not think this is clearly established: for the method of preparing victory that follows also applies among pagans. It is certain from Orosius that their grandfather wished to be baptized before he was killed. After this verse, the remainder is missing from the Prague manuscript.

23. Ald., *non farre sale*. Read *non farre molae*. From a paper manuscript, written in an old and excellent hand, Barthius records various readings for this and the following verses in Book XX, chapter 8. The verse there read: “Not with altars, not with grain and meal, does swift Victory…” *Arris* is an error. But Barthius rightly thinks that *farre, mola* should be separated, so that the poet’s eloquence may have greater abundance. He does not dislike *velox*: for who would not regard Victory as winged?

24. In Barthius’ manuscript: *labor, impigra et aspera virtus*, a reading he neglects.

25. Teolius says that nearly all the Vatican manuscripts and most of Heinsius’ manuscripts have *violentia, cura*; but in his notes Heinsius prefers *vigilantia, curae*, a reading Chamillardus approves exclusively. I do not know which manuscripts have *vigilantia, curae*. Regarding *violentia, cura*, Heinsius merely notes: “Thus the manuscripts; nevertheless, *vigilantia* seems to require correction.” Chamillardus adds nothing else; he printed *violentia, cura* and merely says in a note: “Thus, says Heinsius, the manuscripts; nevertheless, *vigilantia* seems to require correction.” Heinsius may have taken the conjecture from Barthius, whose manuscript reads: “The excellent strength of spirit, ardent violence, cares,” and who thinks *curae* preferable; he then believes *violentia* should be changed to *vigilantia*. But since the manuscript copies disagree, nothing should be changed, because *violentia* here can also mean boldness, or can have the sense in which Scripture says that “the violent seize the kingdom of God.” Catullus says in the wedding poem: “Victory loves care.”

26. In Barthius’ manuscript one reads: “This they attribute, hard and in arms a strength for handling.” But Barthius prefers *durum tractandis robur in armis* without *et*, so that these words constitute a kind of definition of victory: nothing other than unconquerable strength, unacquainted with yielding in arms. I do not approve this: rather, I take *durum robur* in the nominative, so that *robur* too may be understood as attributing victory. The whole thought is expressed in Sallust’s *Catiline* and in Arnobius, Book VII, as Chamillardus noted.

28. Turnebus, *Adversaria* no. 390, explains “Victory unfolds her shining wings” by Cicero’s words in Book III of *On the Nature of the Gods*, where he mentions golden Victories, evidently because they were accustomed to make them from gold. Claudian, in the panegyric on the sixth consulship of Honorius, speaks of Victory in the Julian Senate-house: “Guardian of the Roman toga, which with her rich wing protects the venerable shrines of the senators.” Among the Romans, Victory was usually represented as a winged figure; nevertheless, on a certain coin of Titus she is shown without wings. The Lacedaemonians and Athenians also represented Victory as winged, as though she would always remain among them.

29. Ald., Tornaes. in the text, Galland., Gis. in the text of the first edition and in the margin of the second, *formata metallis*. In Iso, *metallis* seems to be a different reading, not a gloss. Prudentius seems chiefly to be speaking of the Victory that stood in the Julian Senate-house, truly formed from many talents of metal. Dio, Book LI, on Augustus after the victory at Actium: “After these things had been completed, he dedicated the temple of Minerva and the building called the Chalcidicum, and then the Julian Senate-house, constructed in honor of his father; and in it he placed an image of Victory, which still exists today, once brought from Tarentum to Rome, then placed by Caesar in the Senate-house and adorned with Egyptian spoils. By this Caesar clearly showed that he had obtained his rule through Victory.” In the old Roman calendar of the Maffeis, the Altar of Victory in the Senate-house is recorded as having been dedicated on the fifth day before the Kalends of September. Concerning this golden Victory, weighing 320 pounds, sent by Hiero, see Livy, Book XII, chapter 37, who reports that it was placed on the Capitol and in the temple of Jupiter. Ammianus, Book XXVIII, discusses the golden images of Victories presented to Valentinian by the people of Tripolitania.

The shrewd orator incites them, as though the war-trumpets

were sounding, and sharpens their spirits, proclaiming words such as these:

“If victory already won, men, is dear to you,

or victory yet to be won hereafter,

let the temple consecrated to the virgin goddess

remain in your possession while you reign.

And what friend of the enemies denies that she must be worshiped

[15] in a holy manner by your empire,

she who is always present and fills it with praise?”

When the envoy had spoken, the most peaceful faces

of the brothers and rulers replied:

“We know, most eloquent man of Ausonian speech,

how sweet victory is to the brave;

[20] but by what means it is obtained,

and by what method it must be sought,

we know. With this art the father first imbued his sons;

the boy himself learned it from his father as teacher.”

Neither by altars nor by sacrificial meal does fortunate victory come when entreated: tireless labor, harsh courage,

[25] strength of spirit, surpassing ardor, force, and vigilance: they attribute it to hardiness in handling weapons. If these are lacking to warriors, even though in a marble temple golden Victory should unfurl her gleaming wings

and rise, fashioned from many talents of gold,

30. *Versis*: when men are turned to flight.

32. *Formae*: of the goddess Victory, who has the form of a woman.

34. *Anhelantum*: sweating in battle.

36. *Pexo*: adorned. — *Virago*: a strong woman, Victory.

[Col. 0182A] 37. *Suspensa*: raised aloft. — *Strophio*: a girdle.

38. *Tumidas*: through “swollen.”

40. *Jure*: because this is the law of poets.

41. *Lepida*: open, eloquent, beautiful. — *Sacello*: temple.

42. *Notis*: figures, colors.]

[Note: [Col. 0181B]

30. *Pal.* has wrongly *non aderint*. Juretus reports that in some manuscripts *alis* is read instead of *hastis*, and says that both are entirely appropriate: for Victory is represented as winged, and she turns the spears when she redirects all her force elsewhere. He therefore thinks one should not rashly depart from the old and accepted reading, which has its own elegance.

31. Aldus, Palatinus, Mariettus in his first hand, Heinsius’s manuscripts except the other Rottendorfian manuscript, and most of ours have *aptas*, with the gloss in Alexander, “that is, you associate.” Juretus likewise considers *aptas* more harmonious; it stood in his manuscript. Urb., Weitz., and Gis. have *optas*. Barthius asserts that his manuscript read and punctuated the passage as follows: “Why, soldier, distrustful of your own strength, do you seek / useless solace for yourself in a woman’s beauty?”—so that the abrupt thought seems to express Victory’s indignation.

34. Aldus and Mariettus in his first hand have *Vidit anhelantem, regeret quae tela virorum*, “She saw one panting, who would direct the weapons of men,” which is inferior.

35. Aldus, Mariettus, Weitz., and Gis. have *sua dextera cuique est*. Vat. A, Egm., Juretus’s manuscript, Pal., and Widm. above have *sua dextera forti est*, which Juretus prefers because it is not the achievement of just anyone, but of brave men, to obtain victory; this also appears in Alexander as a variant reading. Fabr., Gifan., in the short *e*; Thuan., Urb., and Alex. have *sua cuique dextra est*, which pleases Heinsius because the preceding lines sufficiently establish that the matter concerns brave men. For this reading Heinsius cites the Palatine manuscript, which Weitz had cited for another reading, as we have seen. Compare the commentary on verse 105 of the *Hamartigenia*, *sua cuique jura*. Barthius reads *sua dextera cuique est* and wishes this verse to confirm that victory is “strength hard for the handling of weapons,” as in verse 26, but he is not convincing: there the reference was to victory as already attained, whereas here it is to the very cause of victory, which the ancients imagined as a goddess. Arnobius, book IV: “By what reasoning, by what path, can Victory, peace, equity, and the other things mentioned above be understood to be gods and to belong to the council of the higher gods? For we neither think nor perceive that any of these possesses divine power, nor that they are contained in any particular form of their own, but that they are the virtue of a man, the safety of one who is safe, and the victory of a victor.”

36. Schulz, in his dissertation on the Altar of Victory, concludes from this description and from Greek and Latin monuments that the statue of Victory can be recognized by these features: a standing female figure, more rarely seated; her head bare or covered; her hair bound with a fillet; a woman’s tunic falling to the ankles, either more tightly fastened or looser and flowing; standing barefoot upon the earth, a globe, a helmet, or a ship’s prow; bearing two wings attached to her shoulders, sometimes hanging down toward the ground, sometimes spread out to either side, and sometimes raised upward; holding in her right hand a crown made of olive, oak, or laurel, and in her left a palm branch or trophy; more often suspending weapons from a trophy with both hands, or inscribing letters upon a shield.

37. Ald., Rat. in his first hand, Mar., Vat. A, Bong., Alex., Urb., Gis., Cell., Teol., and Galland with Tornaesius have *recincta*. Heinsius, with Cauchy, Weitz, and most of the Weitzian manuscripts, has *revincta*, which Heinsius says is preferable because *recin­gi* signifies something else; Cauchy confirms that on ancient coins Victory is represented with her fillet bound around her. Cellarius, however, says that Prudentius likewise has *recincta veste* in *Romanus*, verse 236, from Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, verse 518. Perhaps *strophio recincta* can be understood as equivalent to “crowned” or “with her head encircled by a fillet.” In another sense *recin­gi* means to loosen one’s girdle. *Revincio* likewise has two contrary meanings. Victory was sometimes represented suspended by one foot, to indicate her instability.

38. Bong. and Widm. have *fluitantes investita* above *fluitante sinu investita*, which Weitz retained. Others have *fluitante sinu vestita*. In the Pio-Clementine Museum there is a marble statue of Victory in which the nipples are shown entirely bare. Perhaps, if *investita* is read, the word has a negative force. In Tertullian, *investis* means naked, *On the Pallium*, chapter 3: “Naked and unclothed, Adam stands before his potter.” Beardless boys were also called *investes*.

39. Aldus and Mariettus in his first hand have *at vos*. Aldus and Weitz have *assimilatis*, which Heinsius does not approve in place of *assim­ulatis*.

40. Egm., Pal., and Bong. above have *nomen* instead of *numen*, less suitably. Weitz, Mar., Widm. in his first hand, and Bong. in his first hand have *numen imponere*. In Barthius’s manuscript: *manus, assimilatis Jure poetarum monstris, componere numen*.

41. Barthius’s manuscript in its first hand has *ex vestro prompsit*. Giselinus thinks that Prudentius ironically calls the books of the poets a chapel or shrine of the pagans. I understand *sacellum* as a sanctuary, temple, and pagan superstition, which the art of painting has enhanced together with the poem. For, as is clear from the whole sequence of the speech, Prudentius affirms that poetry, painting, and superstition each played a part in fashioning the appearance of Victory. On painting there is an excellent passage in Wisdom 15:4: “For neither has the evil invention of human art led us into error, nor the shadow of a picture, a labor without profit, an image sculpted in varied colors.”

42. The ancients used to paint with wax and to burn the painting into the liquid wax, as Pliny teaches in book XXXV, chapter 11, and book XXI, chapter 14. For that reason ancient writers, both secular and ecclesiastical, whenever they speak of painting, frequently mention wax at the same time. Saint Paulinus, letter 8 to Severus: “He painted not on perishable tablets, nor with liquid wax, but on the fleshly tablets of your heart.” See Fronton Ducæus’s note on these words of Paulinus. To pass over others who have written about the ancient method of painting, Joannes de Fonseca and Figueroa left a manuscript book *On Ancient Painting*, praised by Nicolas Antonius. The learned Requeno, not many years ago, successfully rediscovered—or devised anew a similar method—the ancient manner of painting and of using wax in place of oil, which had long since been lost; Petrus García de la Huerta advanced the matter successfully through many experiments and learned observations, which he plans to publish for the general public. I wished to mention this at an appropriate point so that the words of the learned Stefano Antonio Morcelli in his elegant commentary on the *Constantinopolitan Calendar*, vol. I, p. 116, may be better understood: “Panels painted in encaustic are not damaged by water, as painters in the City recently discovered by a most certain experiment when encaustic painting was rediscovered.” Morcelli rightly demonstrates from the Second Council of Nicaea that even in the eighth century this method of painting was familiar to painters: “Not honoring a panel covered with wax, but the king . . . although an image is nothing other than wood, and colors mixed and tempered with wax.” In the Roman *Ephemerides* for 1781, p. 119, an English booklet by Mr. R. E. Raspe, published in London in 1780, is discussed. It argues that among the Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans the practice of painting with oil probably existed, or that ancient painters came very close to it; he asserts that the practice certainly existed in the tenth or eleventh century. He includes two treatises from approximately the tenth century, one by the priest Theophilus and the other by Heraclius, *On Colors and the Arts of the Romans*. A Spanish poem *On Painting*, published at Segovia with notes by Don Diego Antonio Rejón de Silva, is highly commended in the same *Roman Ephemerides* in 1786, issue 47; we know that he is devoting himself admirably to publishing new books for the illumination of the liberal arts.]

45. Heinsius with the other Rottendorfian manuscript, Fabr., Widm., Bong., Teol., Cham., Gis. in the margin, Sich., Vat. A, Rat., Torn. at the edge, and Mar. have *sic cassa figuris*. Urb. has *sic segnia rerum*. Alexander in his first hand, Weitz, Widm. at the edge, Bongars at the edge, Gifanius from three old books, Oxford, Thuan., and Egm. have *sic inania rerum*. Gifanius maintains that it can be shortened in such a way as to make *fac* scan. Heinsius objects, and incorrectly cites Aldus for *sic inania*: Aldus did print it that way, but corrected it to *et inania rerum*, the reading I approve, which appears in Alexander as a variant and is adopted in Giselinus’s text. Galland says that Tornaesius has *inania rerum* with Aldus in the text, but does not explain whether it is *et inania* or *sic inania*. It often happens that inept correctors have corrupted the true reading in Prudentius because they did not know that he frequently lengthened a short syllable for metrical reasons at the caesura.

46. Gifanius, who struggles to explain this entire passage through the word *fac*, observes that *acrem* has the sound of “clever.” In Vat. A the reading *acer Apellas* is an error. Poetry is indicated by Homer, painting by Apelles, and superstition by Numa.

47. Aldus, Gifanius in the passage cited, Weitz, Widm. above, Alex., Urb., Gis. at the edge, Thuan., and the older Boher have *cognatumque volunt*. Vat. A, Juretus’s manuscript, and Thuan. in its second hand have *cognatumque vocant*. Mar., Rat., the other Rottendorfian manuscript, Oxford, Fabr., Gis., Bong., Widm., Heins., and Teol. have *cognatumque malum* by way of explanation, so that painting, poetry, and idols are “the kindred evil.” In place of *pigmenta*, Bong. and Widm. in their first hand have another reading. Gifanius has *figmenta*. Retain *pigmenta* and understand painting. Heinsius further writes—and says it should be written—*camoenas*, despite the manuscripts; Teolius silently followed him. I do not dislike Heinsius’s reading, and it had occurred to me earlier as well; but it must be considered whether the manuscript reading can be defended. Gifanius reads *cognatumque volunt figmenta camoenae* and explains *acri cognatum volunt*, that is, “they regard the creations of Egeria the Muse as identical.” He supposes that Egeria is called a Muse because she was pleasing to the Muses, as Ovid says in book III of the *Fasti*. Thus, he says, Numa’s fiction concerning Egeria belongs to the same category. This explanation does not satisfy me. I therefore think one should read: *cognatumque malum, pigmenta, camoenae, idola, convaluit fallendi trina potestas*: “the kindred evil grew strong—painting, poetry, and idols”; that evil is the threefold power of deception. This reading is supported by the fact that in some copies there is a comma after *idola*. See the following verse.

48. In Rat. a clever corrector had inserted *spectraque* for *idola*. Aldus, after printing *Idola conflavit fallendi trina potestas*, ineptly attempted to correct it to *Trinaque conflavit fallendi idola potestas*, lest the *o* in *idolum* be shortened. Aldus, Gis., and Heinsius have *conflavit*. Most manuscripts, including Vat. A, Mar., Rat., Urb., the manuscripts of Gifanius and Juretus, and Weitz with his copies, have *convaluit*. Alexander in his first hand has *conflarunt*, in the second *conflavit*. Heinsius rejected *docta potestas*, which, he says, had previously circulated. But even before Heinsius, Aldus and Weitz had printed *trina potestas*, and *docta potestas* should not be dismissed, since it appears in Mar., Rat., Bong., Gifanius’s manuscript, Fabr., and Gis. Barthius likewise reads *docta potestas* in book VI, chapter 26 of the *Adversaria*, and thinks it refers to the eloquence of those who introduced idols. There he notes that Prudentius used the same expression found in Varro’s satire *Know Yourself*, which Nonius explains: “What are the Muses? Your poetry, which you have led by art.” He reads those words as *Nihil sunt musae policis vestrae quas aerifice duxti* (“Are the Muses of your thumb nothing, which you, bronze-worker, led?”; the corrupt wording is uncertain); Janus Rutgersius and Lipsius emend them differently. The meaning would then be: “The kindred evil forged idols”; and this kindred evil consists of painting—Apelles; poetry—the Muses and Homer; and the learned power of deception—superstition and Numa. It is better, however, to retain *trina potestas*, so that painting, poetry, and superstition are included. There is no reason to doubt that poetry and painting have a certain kinship and similarity. This is peculiar to Prudentius: he ingeniously joined superstition to these arts of invention. Heinsius’s explanation is that the threefold power of deception forged—so he reads—painting, poetry, and idols, which are the kindred evil. Our interpretation is closer to the manuscripts and to Prudentius’s thought: the kindred evil—the threefold power of deception, namely painting, poetry, and idols—grew strong, that is, gained strength and mutual force through cooperation. This is what Prudentius argues.

49. “If the pagans deny this,” says Prudentius, “let them answer and explain why they themselves derive sacred practices from paintings and poetic myths.” For example, why do the priests of Cybele castrate themselves, unless because poetic myth represents Attis as emasculated or castrated, and painting also displays this? The same applies to other sacred practices, because horses are kept away from Diana’s temple. What do these things imply, I ask, except that the worship of idols has grown out of poetry and painting?]

50. Vat. A has erroneously *ex fabulis*. Rat., Weitz, Widm., and Bong. have *praestet*; others have *praestat*, as later with *perdit*.

51. Mariettus in his second hand has *perdat*. Prudentius imitates Minucius in the *Octavius*: “It is shameful to speak of Cybele’s Dindyma, who, because she could not entice her adulterer—unfortunately pleasing to her, although she herself was deformed and old, like the mother of many gods—to intercourse, cut him up, so as to make the god a eunuch. Because of this story the Galli worship her, and the punishment of their half-man body.” Catullus and Arnobius say that Attis cut off his own genitals. Anyone wishing to know more may read the commentators on Minucius, leaving aside the mythographers.

52. Aldus and Gis. have *cum pulcher sese castraverit Attis*. Most and better copies have *cum pulchrum poesis castraverit Attin*. Teolius says that Heinsius restored the previously corrupt passage in this way. But Weitz, with all his manuscripts, had already printed *cum pulchrum poesis castraverit Attin*; Sich. and Gifanius had restored it earlier in the same way; Juretus had read it in his manuscript; and Galland confirms that it appears in the margin of old editions. Galland also found *cur pulchrum*, but others consistently have *cum*. Gifanius notes that the use of *cum* should be observed: “Why do the Galli cut themselves, since it is known from poetic myths that Attis was castrated?” That is, why do they cut themselves unless because this is known, and so forth. “Why are horses kept away from Diana’s temple, unless because the Muse, or poetry, makes Hippolytus carried away?” Some write *Atys*, but here *Attis* is preferable, so that the first syllable is long; it is usually short in *Atys*.

53. From Virgil, book VII: “Hence horn-footed horses are kept away from Trivia’s temple and sacred groves.”

54. Aldus, Widm. above, Pal., Vat. A, Gis., Alexander in his second hand, and the old editions cited by Galland have *cum Phaedra pudicum*. Juretus’s manuscript has *cur Phaedra*. Grangaeus interprets Phaedra as the reason Hippolytus was carried away, as Hyginus relates in fable 47. In Egm. *pudicam* is an error. The more accurate and common reading is *cum musa pudicum*, concerning which see Gronovius in the *Diatribe Statiana*, whom Heinsius recommends consulting.

55. Gifanius and Gis. at the edge have *littora cursu*.

58. Rat. has *similatis*, less correctly, instead of *simulatis*. Cudworth, *System of Intellectual Philosophy*, chapter 4, observes that Prudentius, imitating the Greeks, calls incorporeal things “affections of things,” and events such as victory. From verse 236 of this book and verse 191 of the *Apotheosis* he concludes that Symmachus and other pagans believed many ancient divinities to be perfections of one God, clothed in the names of persons, and that the goddess Victory was nothing other than one virtue among many of the one God. Cudworth labors in vain: although it is certain that the pagans were not consistent enough in explaining the power and authority of their divinities, from the verses of Prudentius soon to be cited it follows only that Symmachus divided divinity into various parts. Prudentius therefore reproves him because, although God is one and cannot be divided, he wished to introduce a thousand divinities. See the commentary on verse 236. Valsecchi seems to approach Cudworth’s interpretation: from the passage cited in the *Apotheosis* he concludes, in book I of *On the Foundations of Religion*, chapter 9, that idolaters believed in one God, while the various divinities were either perfections of that one God or virtues superior to human beings but servants of God.

59. Aldus and others incorrectly punctuate *plumis obducere frustra*. Heinsius noted that it should be punctuated *obducere: frustra / Fertur avis*.

60. Mar. has *ab his*; above, in the same hand, *avis* with the rest. Mariettus approves the first reading of his manuscript and says that *avis* is a gloss incompetently transferred from the word *vultur* to the words *ab his*. He explains the passage thus: “The same Victory is carried by these feathers while she is imagined to fly, and is both a woman and a great vulture”; that is, “you make her a ridiculous monster by making her at once both woman and bird.” Heinsius thought *magicusque* might be read, since he had demonstrated through several examples from Ovid that this word often degenerates into *magnus* because of the similarity of the letters, although even with this reading he found the verse suspect in relation to the preceding one. Iso interprets it as referring to a myth in which a woman is said to have been changed into a bird, for example into a vulture. Chamillard says that Victory is called a great vulture either because, winged in the manner of vultures, she flies over the army, or because every large bird may be called a vulture. Grangaeus notes that the Egyptians represented the mother and the sky—which they regarded as female—in the form of a vulture, and also represented Pallas and Juno, because they believed there were no males among vultures, which were said to conceive by the wind. He adds that Isis may perhaps be intended here by the vulture. Baronius, volume III of the *Annals*, in the life of Julian, mentions a coin whose obverse shows the god Serapis with Julian’s face engraved upon it, while the reverse shows two Isises with crowns of asps on their heads, swords in their hands, and vulture wings on their backs. Thus that bird-woman-vulture is a bird sacred to the goddess Isis. When consulted on this matter by Grangaeus, Federicus Morellus replied as follows. This can be confirmed because Aelian, book X *On Animals*, chapter 22, reports that the Egyptians adorned a statue of Isis with vulture feathers, and many believe that the Egyptians worshiped vultures. But, to speak frankly, I prefer Chamillard’s interpretation: Victory is falsely imagined as a woman, goddess, and vulture, or as equipped with great wings like a vulture. This may be connected with the fact that vultures were sacred to Mars, and that ancient commanders carefully observed toward which side of the battle vultures looked, hoping thereby for victory or defeat. On these matters see Rhodiginus, *Ancient Readings*, book VIII, chapter 18. It is reported in the literature that the Egyptians, Persians, and Greeks represented Victory for themselves in the image of a hawk. The Egyptians seem to have worshiped the hawk and eagle as divinities from whom they prayed for victory. Perhaps this is why Victory is painted as a bird.]
