116. Weitz, with some others, thinks *Deus quid* should be emended.

117. Vat. A has *praestet*; others have *praestat*.

118. Fabr. has *summoque*. Gis.’s first edition has *et summo*, the second *summoque*. The better manuscripts have *infirmus et summo*, for it is characteristic of Prudentius to lengthen a short syllable at the caesura. See Gifanius under *incisio*.

119. Alexander in his first hand, Urb., Mar., and *et inanis*—not unacceptably. Rat. has *nominis umbra est*, less suitably.

121. The same thought appears in nearly the same words in *Catholic Hymn* 4, verse 13.

125. Mar., Rat., Weitz with his copies, Sich., Gis., and the other Rottendorfian manuscript have *subjecta polo*. Most of Heinsius’s manuscripts, Gis.’s first edition in the text, Aldus, Urb., Alex., and Vat. A have *subjecta situ*. Teolius printed it thus but incorrectly cites Aldus for *polo*: Aldus gives *situ*, as do Weitz, Heinsius, and I; Heinsius retained it. The thought is taken from Isaiah 55:9: “For as the heavens are exalted above the earth, so are my ways exalted above your ways, and my thoughts above your thoughts.”

126. Lucretius, book IV: “As far as the lofty expanse of heaven extends above the earth.”

131. Widm. above and Mar. have *quae sunt*.

132. Heinsius, with his better copies, has *cuncta equidem, et continet ipsa*; Aldus, Vat. A, and Alexander in his second hand have this as well. Most of our other manuscripts and editions have *cuncta quidem, et continet, ipse Principio institui*. Teolius follows Heinsius but does not punctuate correctly: *quae continet, ipsa Principio institui*, unless perhaps Teolius understands “all the things which the earth itself contains.” Heinsius understands “which the earth itself contains.” Others understand “I myself established all things at the beginning.”]

773 We strive to conceive in our minds the one who had no beginning or will have no end,

who existed before chaos and created the world.

The power of human understanding is small,

and too narrow for so great a task:

for if nature should attempt to direct its vision

[100] more sharply and penetrate the secrets of the supreme God,

who would doubt that, overcome, its frail sight would grow weary,

and that the power of the exhausted mind, within its small breast,

would be thrown into confusion and yield to feeble cares?

But the way of faith readily urges us

[105] to believe in the Omnipotent, who not only grants present goods

but also promises those to come, throughout endless ages,

so that, wholly dissolved into emptiness,

I may not perish into nothingness after my brief enjoyment of the light.

Weigh the authors of the gift by the gift itself:

[110] the eternal one bestows eternal things; the mortal one confers

774 mortal things; God, divine things; the perishable one, things destined to fall.

All things that time accomplishes and dissolution removes

are worthless because of their brevity and unworthy of the eternal

giver, whose proper wealth is never to cease,

[115] and to give humanity what will never cease.

For if God grants something corruptible or destined to be corrupted,

and possesses nothing more precious than these things,

he is poor, weak, unworthy of the highest honor,

not omnipotent, but the empty shadow of a divinity.

[120] By this reasoning faith wisely concludes—indeed,

it does not doubt—that God truly exists: the one who commands us

to hope that what we are and what we live will always remain unharmed,

if we prove worthy. “If it pleases you,” he says, “to climb

to heavenly things, drive earthly cares from your mind.

[125] For as far as the earth lies beneath the pole

[Col. 0190B] and the realm of the vaulted heavens is separated from the ground,

so far do your worldly things differ from my future things—

the harsh from the good, the sinful from the devout, the darkness from the serene.

775 Whatever can pass away, I advise you to flee; whatever

[130] by nature’s law admits corruption and grows old,

regard as nothing, since it returns to nothing.”

All things indeed that the earth produces and contains, it itself—

[Col. 0191A] [Col. 0191B]

### Notes

135. “With restrained habits”: with frugality. I.

137. “Fleeting”: that which passes quickly. I.

138. “Not, not for that reason”: he does not distribute. Iso.

139. “Would lead”: would regard, estimate. I.

143. “Enervated”: weakened. “Of the wrestling-school”: of contest, struggle, or wrestling. I.

144. “Enticing”: illicit. “Of these”: of these pleasures. I.

147. “Steadfastness”: bound by the devil. Iso.

[Col. 0192B] 148. “Flexible”: pliable. I.

149. “Bitter”: punishments. I.

153. “Ears”: popular favor. I.

154. “Let him display”: let him boast, vaunt himself. “And swollen with beauty”: as it appears to human beings. I.

156. “Let him extend”: let him enlarge, draw toward himself. I.

157. “Let him assign”: let him grant. I.

158. “What is useful to the just man”: usefulness to justice, or earthly advantage. I.

[Col. 0191B]

134. Some vulgar editions read incorrectly, “and broad seeds.”

135. Vat. A has, incorrectly, “and frugal.” In Heinsius, the corrupted manner of writing creates difficulty: he reads *volvi* for *valui*. Chamillard likewise printed *volvi*.

136. Aldus has *aegri*; *aeger* is better. In Alexander, by the first hand, incorrectly *ager*.

138. Giselinus found *captus humo* in a certain manuscript. Thuanus has *inaniter usus*.

140. Giselinus and Bongarsius in the text, and Mariettus by the first hand, read *et species tenues*. The Juretus manuscript, Sichardus, Alexander, Vat. A, Weitzius with most of his copies, Thuanus, Egmondanus, Boherius, and the earlier Rott editions have *et specie tenui*. The Urbinas reads and punctuates *et specie, tenui quas currere tempore jussi*.

When Gifanius, under the entry **VIS MAGNA**, had cited another passage of Prudentius, he said: “Since we have now, as I believe, almost entirely freed that Christian poet from innumerable errors, let us add a few, so to speak, bundles, and especially this one from Book II *Against Symmachus*.” He then transcribes and explains these verses. But I should opportunely warn the reader that those who claim that Gifanius left manuscript notes on Prudentius may perhaps have been misled by these words. Gifanius says here nothing other than that he had freed almost the whole of Prudentius from errors in that very index of Lucretius. His explanation, however, rests upon the words *et tenui specie*: “He forbids us to place all good in pleasure, which is derived from things and from their delicate appearance or brilliance.” He thinks that *et species tenues* makes no sense.

Giselinus, together with his manuscript, insists that one should read *et species tenues*, because it refers back to *speciosaque semina finxi*, which are to be used sparingly and in due measure. Mariettus also approves this reading and confirms it from verse 733, *Exiguas rerum species*. The sense would then be: “He would regard all good as placed in the sweetness of things, and would regard as good the delicate appearances that I ordered to pass with time.” Another reading seems to me more correct and clearer; it is also that of Aldus, Heinsius, and the more recent editors.

143. After this verse Fabritius, Bongarsius, and the other Rott edition insert two further verses:

“Could weaken his strength through corrupted leisure  
And lie sluggish, inactive in every contest.”

Others omit this verse, “Enervated strength,” and put those two in its place—for example, the Juretus manuscript, the earlier Rott edition, Oxford, Vat. A, the earlier Boherius, and Egmondanus, as Heinsius claims to have read them, although Weitzius denies it. Others recognize only the verse “Enervated strength,” such as Widmanstetter and Mariettus. In the Ratianus, this seems to have been the only verse; the other two were added by a recent hand and were rightly omitted by Giselinus and others.

The Urbinas and Alexander contain the two verses, but as an alternative reading, not so that all three should be accepted together. Weitzius thought that Aldus had given the place to all three verses, and so indeed he had; but afterward he advised deleting the first verse, “Enervated strength should bear, without the praise of the wrestling-school.” It is clear that the other two verses were added by someone who did not want the first *e* in *enervatum* to be shortened; I have said enough about this at verse 64 of Hymn 8 *Cathemerinon*. Alexander writes *inervatum*, as does Thuanus.

146. Lactantius, Book VI, chapter 22: “These pleasures must therefore be avoided as snares and traps, lest, caught by the softness of delights, we be brought under the dominion of death together with the body to which we enslave ourselves.” Lactantius is speaking of the pleasures of taste and smell.

147. *Elaqueare*, “to free from snares,” occurs in Sidonius; *elaqueatus* occurs in Ammianus.

149. Aldus, Giselinus, the Juretus manuscript, Oxford, Egmondanus, and Vat. A read *nitendum summis*. Heinsius preferred this reading in the brief list of errors or passages requiring alteration, as I shall say at verse 719 in the *Romanus*; in the text he printed *luctandum*, and so forth. Teolius imputes *nitendum* to Heinsius, but Heinsius clearly printed *luctandum* with most of his own and our copies. In his notes he observes only that Oxford, Egmondanus, and Aldus have *nitendum*.

151. Aldus and Palatinus have *ne congerat*. Giselinus reads and punctuates *amet nimium: ne congerat aurum*; this is how it stands in the text, but in the list mentioned shortly before: *amet; nimium ne congerat aurum*. Most have *amet, nimium nec congerat aurum*. Mariettus incorrectly has *nec congeret*. Fabricius has *ne congerere aurum*, that is, “lest he should wish to heap up gold,” which follows shortly afterward.

153. Virgil, Book VI: “Even now rejoicing too greatly in popular applause.” On “popular applause,” see the commentary on verse 22 of Hymn 1 *Cathemerinon*.

154. Mariettus, by the first hand, incorrectly has *tumescit*.

156. Salvianus, Book I *To the Catholic Church against Avarice*: “You see what wealth God commands parents to prepare for their children—not treasuries of money . . . not immeasurable estates exceeding the knowledge of their owner, which deem it unworthy to tolerate partners and regard a neighboring property as an injury.” The same thought is repeatedly expressed even by pagan writers, by Horace, Juvenal, and others.

At the beginning I established all things, bestowed their distinguishing ornaments upon the shining world, and fashioned beautiful seeds.

[135] Yet I wished there to be a limit, and allowed them to be enjoyed with restrained habits, so far as the mortal, sickly use of body and fleeting life required.

Not so that a man captivated by desires and burning vainly should suppose that all good lies in the sweetness of things

[140] and in their delicate appearance, which I commanded to run its course in time.

776 I also appointed an age in which I might test noble hearts, lest sluggish and unexercised virtue should bear enervated strength without the glory of the wrestling-school.

For the taste of those things which, as they pass, hold minds entangled and bound in wondrous delight is enticing and destructive.

[145] Pleasure must be conquered, and steadfastness of mind freed from snares, lest, tied and captive in soft and pliant bonds, it be crushed.

One must struggle with utmost efforts; amid bitter trials the path of virtue must be pursued, lest one love the pleasures of a frail condition and heap up too much gold,

777 or, ambitious, desire greedily to look upon the varied colours of gems; nor let one display oneself before popular favour and swell, puffed up with fair honour.

[155] Let one not extend one’s native soil or acres of ancestral land, nor spread one’s mind into foreign fields;

and let one not assign everything one wills or does to bodily senses, nor prefer expediency to justice.

Let him establish all his hope in me, never destined to perish,

[160] Which I shall give, and my gifts are to endure through a long age.

Since God makes this promise, who, possessing strength and vigor,

and able to exercise virtue, would prefer anything brief in himself

to things everlasting? Or what wise man would consider the pleasures

of the limbs better than the rewards of the living mind?

[165] Is it not one thing alone that separates a human being from a beast:

that the goods of four-footed creatures are placed before their eyes?

I, on the contrary, hope for what is preserved beyond the range of sight

for a long age.

For if my whole life perishes together with the body,

and nothing of mine can survive after death,

[170] [Col. 0193B] who is my ruler of heaven? Who is the creator of the world?

Who is God? Or what power, now deservedly to be feared, exists?

[Col. 0194A] I shall go through impure pleasures in burning lust;

I shall defile legitimate marriage-beds; I shall trample sacred modesty;

I shall deny that I hold some deposit entrusted by a kinsman,

when there is no witness;

[175] I shall greedily plunder my poor dependants.

I shall kill my aged mother by a magical incantation.

The old woman delays her second master by postponing her death.

Nor do I fear wrongdoing: public laws are deceived.

Armed law sits in judgment, but does not know the hidden crime,

[180] or, if the matter comes to light, the judge is corrupted by gold.

Rarely does a just penalty strike the guilty with the executioner’s axe.

But why do I rehearse these things? Behold, God recalls me,

threatening in severe majesty. He denies that the moments of my deeds

will perish through death: “The inward man who breathes will not die,” he says.

[185] [Col. 0194B] “He will pay everlasting punishment for having badly ruled

the limbs placed under his command.

Nor is it difficult for me to surround the liquid nature with flames—”

[Col. 0193C]

159. Aldus, Mariettus, Palatinus, Widmanstetter, Gifanius from an old book, Alexander, Heinsius with most of his copies, Weitzius, Sichardus, and others read *spemque in me omnem statuat*, admitting a hiatus that Heinsius considers characteristic of Prudentius. Compare Gifanius under **HIATUS**. Some manuscripts avoid this hiatus both here and elsewhere. The other Rott edition and the Urbinas have *spemque in me statuat omnem*. Vat. A and Giselinus in the text have *spemque suam in me omnem statuat*; in the margin, *spemque in me omnem*. Fabricius has *omnem spemque in me statuat*. The first edition of Giselinus has *in me spemque omnem statuat*.

160. Aldus and the first edition of Giselinus have *sunt: aeternum mea dona manebunt*. Most others have *longoque die mea dona trahenda*. Fabricius and the second edition of Giselinus have *longoque die mea dona manebunt*.

161. Egmondanus has *qui fortis*. Mariettus has *et acris*; above it, *acer*.

162. The Ratianus has *breve quidve*.

168. See the Apostle, 1 Corinthians 15:19 and 32. Cicero, Book I *On the Laws*: “For what will that man do in darkness who fears nothing except a witness and a judge?” See what Valsecchius argues against Bayle in Book III *On the Foundations of Religion*, Part I, chapter 3, where he renders these verses of Prudentius in Italian verse.

172. Mariettus has *fluxus*; Alexander, by the first hand, *luxos*; read *luxus*.

174. Egmondanus has *habens aliquid*.

175. The Ratianus has *avidis*, by an old hand, incorrectly.

178. Weitzius and, after him, Chamillard cite Bernard as somewhere discussing in a similar way the corrupt use of the courts in his own time: “Let the laws be engraved on the Twelve Tables, and let rights be prescribed on publicly displayed bronze: among the laws themselves there is wrongdoing,” and so forth. I could not find this passage when I searched for it. Later I came upon these very words—not in Bernard, but in Cyprian, Letter 1 *To Donatus*, where he says: “Let the laws be engraved on the Twelve Tables, and let rights be prescribed on bronze publicly set up: wrongdoing is committed among the very laws, sin is committed among rights.” Weitzius called Cyprian “Bernard” through an error that happened to him more than once. Chamillard habitually follows Weitzius without examination in copying such authorities; this was one reason, among others that I now omit, why I judged it inappropriate to reprint the edition for the use of the Dauphin.

179. Barthius, Book II *Adversaria*, chapter 17, notes in explanation of this verse that Trebellius Pollio said in his preface: “Imperial majesty ought to be armed not only with weapons but also with laws.” Juretus, in his notes on Letter 13 of Book II of Symmachus, gathers many passages to the same effect, since laws are often said to threaten, as though they could be moved by emotion. Hence “the terrors of the laws,” and in Prudentius, *Romanus*, verse 203, “entangled in the snares of threatening Julia.” Constantine, in Law 31 *On the Julian Law concerning Adultery*, wrote that laws rise up and rights are armed with an avenging sword; Marius Victorinus refers to the same idea in Book II of his Commentary on Genesis: “Laws armed with swords, and with avenging steel.”

184. The Ratianus, Mariettus, Weitzius, Giselinus, and others have *monimenta* or *monumenta*, which Gallandius judged uniquely correct because it was found in the Tornesianus. Alexander, Urbinas, Egmondanus, Palatinus, Thuanus, the earlier Boherius, Aldus, and Heinsius have *momenta*. Aldus, Weitzius, Mariettus, the Ratianus, and Vat. A have *occidit*. Giselinus and most of Heinsius’s copies have *occidet*.

185. Aldus and Vat. A, by the first hand, incorrectly have *qui sperat*. Mariettus, by the first hand, has *luat*, correctly corrected to *luet*. See Matthew 3 and 5.

187. Why the soul is called “liquid,” and in what sense, has been explained sufficiently in the prolegomena, chapter 15, against Bayle’s “singing inanities.”

Nature, although that fluid substance is carried along

like the south wind, I shall nevertheless seize it and apply torments:

[190] I myself, incorporeal, the one creator of spirits.

Indeed, I shall decree equal fellowship of punishment for bodies,

since I can renew the ashes into their former shape;

nor is the power to be despaired of:

I who was able to form him at first will restore him when dead.

[195] 780 There are examples of my power: in the very seeds

nature teaches that all things revive after death.

For they dry up when the vigor by which they formerly lived perishes;

then, dry and dead, consigned to furrows or pits,

they lie hidden, buried as in a tomb,

[200] [Col. 0195B] and from the burial-mounds they rise with a life-giving shoot.

Can you know, or conjecture, what skillful craftsman builds this,

or what power acts within it?

Let not the doctrines of the natural philosophers deceive you, wretched men.

Behold, I am master of generation and of restoring

[205] what has perished and passed away; I bring every withered thing

back into its former shapes, whether through flower or leaf.

[Col. 0196A] And this same thing I shall one day do for man,

so that he may rise from the empty ashes and stand in his former structure,

which, according to its merits, may either pay me back through punishments

[210] its crimes or shine in the citadel of supreme virtue,

never thereafter to perish, whatever its lot may be.

Meanwhile, while the substance mixed together remains vigorous as one,

let it remember its own creator, revere and pray to

781 its Maker with submissive devotion. One did not create

[215] the figure of the breathing soul, and another that of the body.

Nor do many gods govern the various goods of the present life.

It is not one god who supplies crops and grain-bearing ears,

[Col. 0196B] and another who gives must from the clusters

and pours purple juice from the heavy vine-shoot.

[220] I myself am he who makes green olive trees grow fat with berries,

those which you imagine to have sprung from Greek Pallas,

and I who grant the hours of light to those being born.

By my law, through reciprocal bonds, the twofold sex

loves to beget offspring and rejoices in the propagation of its race.

[225] [Col. 0197A]

[Col. 0195C]

188. In one place *perstabilis* occurs incorrectly instead of *perflabilis*.

189. In the Ratianus, *adhibentur* seems to have stood; a recent hand altered it to *adhibebo*.

190. Thuanus has *spirituus*, which Heinsius claims is for *spiritibus*. I think it is an error for *spirituum*.

191. Aldus has *parili consortia poena*.

192. Mariettus observes that *favillae* is used for ash in which small particles commonly lie mixed, since the poet below says, “let him rise from the ash.” We have noted elsewhere that *cinis* and *favilla* may refer to any fine powder into which the bodies of the dead are reduced, even when they have not been burned.

193. Mariettus writes *disperanda*.

194. Aldus punctuates incorrectly: “I who was able to form what was new, I shall restore what has perished.” Others have expressed similar thoughts about the resurrection. Lactantius, Book VII, chapter 23: “If at the beginning God fashioned man in some ineffable manner, let us believe that he can be restored by the same one who made him anew.” Minucius in the *Octavius*: “For who is so foolish or brutish as to dare deny that man, just as he was first able to be fashioned by God, can likewise be fashioned anew; that after death there is nothing, and before death there was nothing? Just as it was possible to be born from nothing, so it is possible to be restored from nothing.” Minucius also adduces the example of seeds, which revive only after they have decayed. Innumerable others develop the same argument. See Hymn 10 *Cathemerinon*, verse 121.

203. Aldus and Alexander have *ne vos*. Others have *nil vos*. Egmondanus and Palatinus have *ad vos*; Heinsius thinks *at vos*. Teolius punctuates it as follows: “Let not the doctrines of the natural philosophers deceive you, wretched men,” unless the printer has erred, which I readily believe. Barthius, Book XI *Adversaria*, chapter 21, observes that Prudentius calls natural philosophers *physici*, those versed in the science of natural things; physicians were eventually called by this name.

205. Aldus and the first edition of Giselinus, together with Gallandius and the old editions, have *siccissima quaeque*.

206. Aldus has *aut flores*, against the meter.

209. Gifanius under **PROMERITA**, as I have already said, and Alexander and the Urbinas have *promeritis* joined together. Egmondanus corruptly has *reprendat*.

213. Sichardus transposes the words in this and the following verse: “Let him remember his own Maker, revere him, and pray to his Author with submissive devotion.”

216. Mariettus, by the first hand, incorrectly has *gubernat*.

218. Mariettus has *ast*; so does the Ratianus, but as a variant spelling for *aut*. Weitzius also has *ast*, as do Alexander and the Urbinas; but in Alexander *aut* seems also to occur. Giselinus, Heinsius, and the more recent editions have *aut*. Aldus, the Tornesianus, and other printed editions have *haud*, which is the only reading Gallandius approves.

220. Hosea 2:8: “And she did not know that I gave her grain, wine, and oil,” and so forth.

[Col. 0196D] 222. Juno was called Lucina because she was believed to preside over childbirth, from the vital light. Diana was likewise called Lucina for a similar reason. Turnebus, *Adversaria*, no. 390, says that it is remarkable and notable for its novelty that Prudentius calls the hours of light and life *lucinae*. Salmasius, page 66 on Aelius Spartianus, says that *lucinae* is used in the same way as *colossum* for *colosseum*, *aurus* for *aureus*, *electrum* for *electreum*, and similar forms. Just as it is not Pallas but God who supplies oil to human beings, so it is God himself, not Juno, who grants the hours of light to those being born.

224. The Ratianus, Mariettus by the first hand, Widmanstetter by the first hand, Bongarsius by the second hand, and Weitzius have *gignere habet*. Aldus, Giselinus, Heinsius’s editions, Alexander, the Urbinas, and Vat. A have *gignere amat*.

225. On the glossed word *minna*, see verse 117 of Book I.

227. Alexander, Egmondanus, Widmanstetter, Bongarsius, Weitzius’s Heinsian manuscripts, Sichardus, Vat. A, Mariettus, and the Ratianus have *Unus ego elementa*. The first edition of Giselinus, the Urbinas, and Cauchus have *Unus ego haec elementa*. In the text of the second edition of Giselinus and in Fabricius: *unus ego ipse elementa*. Weitzius incorrectly cites Aldus in support of his reading: Aldus had indeed printed *unus ego elementa*, but corrected it to *unus ego haec elementa*. I do not like admitting a hiatus as often as Heinsius and the more recent editors do.

228. The vulgar editions have *aut miser*, incorrectly.

229. The Juretus manuscript, Aldus, Egmondanus, Palatinus, and the manuscripts cited by Heinsius, except the other Rott edition, as well as Alexander, the Urbinas, and Vat. A, have *et non resolubilis aetas*. Mariettus, the Ratianus, Giselinus, and Weitzius have *nec morte solubilis aetas*.

231. *Ministeria* means the ministers themselves.

234. Oxford has *et quam natura creatis*.

235. Vat. A has *servatur ad usus*.

236. The Juretus manuscript has *nomina mille*, less well. I do not approve Iso’s interpretation. Prudentius says that Symmachus passes over the one true God and invents a thousand gods, into which he divides God’s powers, thereby diminishing God himself into various parts. Symmachus therefore was not saying that those many gods were subject to one God, or that they were the powers of one simple God, as Cudworth seems to think; see above at verse 58.

Rather, Prudentius argues that all those invented gods are not truly gods but are powers of the one God, who is simple and cannot be divided into various parts. The powers of God are not in reality multiple; to speak with the theologians, they are distinguished from one another only virtually or formally.

The substance of the argument is this: Divinity is one, simple, and indivisible. Therefore there are not multiple gods divided from one another; consequently, those powers whom the pagans call goddesses ought not to be worshiped as different gods, but the one God should be worshiped, since he is the head and source of all powers.

Petavius, Volume I, Book II, chapter 2, explains the error of the pagans somewhat differently, establishing from this passage the simplicity of the divine nature. Prudentius, he says, has seasoned this theological argument with poetic charm in the second book *Against Symmachus*, where he reproves the ignorance of the pagans who worshiped God’s powers separately and piecemeal, as though they were parts of him: “You, passing me by,” and so forth.

237. Widmanstetter has above *simulas*. Here *parere* does not mean “to obey” or “to be subject,” which is the second meaning of the verb *pareo*. Iso says it means “to shine,” but properly it means “to be present,” “to exist,” or “to stand ready”; from this first meaning of *pareo* the other meaning, “to obey,” arose. Symmachus therefore pretended or imagined that distinct gods were present in the divine powers, although those powers are not truly distinct, or that a divided divinity inhered in them. But, as I said, the theology of the pagans varied.

242. The Ratianus incorrectly has *valeat*, by the first hand.

243. In the Ratianus, this verse and the following three were written by a recent hand.

245. The Juretus manuscript has *caementa remitte*.

246. Egmondanus and the Juretus manuscript have *rupis*, according to the ancient usage, as elsewhere *famis* and *luis*. On the ancient luxury displayed in marbles, see Savaron on Sidonius, page 109.

Prudentius lists five kinds of marble: white Parian, yellow Punic, Synnadic marked with spots, green Lacedaemonian, and Egyptian purple, which he poetically calls “the natural purple of the cliff.” By this he means porphyry, whose name derives from its redness like purple, as Isidore says in Book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 5. Consult him, and also Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapters 5 through 8. Statius frequently describes different kinds of marble in the *Silvae*. Fabricius observed long ago that the same kinds of marble still exist in the ornamentation of churches at Rome and Siena, and foreigners admire them.

247. Aldus, so that the final syllable of *Lacedaemon* would not be pronounced short, freely altered the verse: “Which spotted Synna possesses, and green Lacedaemon.” In the Urbinas: “And which green Lacedaemon possesses,” with *et* redundantly added. The Ratianus has *quae viridis Lacedaemon habes*. Some write *Synna*, others *Sinna*. Heinsius says that one must write *Synnas*, as Thuanus has, with Cauchus, as a variant spelling. Martial and Juvenal indeed say *Synnas*, but I do not see why both forms could not be used, as happens with other proper names, especially those taken from Greek. Iso says that Lacedaemon is a mountain; why not rather the city of the Peloponnese, the seat of Menelaus?

248. Vat. A has, corruptly, *decidet ostrum*.

249. Heretics eagerly seize on these and similar words to declaim against the ornamentation and adornment of churches. But how foolishly! For from Prudentius it is rather inferred that these two things fit together well: that God especially loves the temple of the mind, and that nevertheless it is honorable and holy to adorn temples with marble and gold, since Prudentius himself repeatedly mentions with praise the marble and wealth by which Christian churches shone, as may be seen in the hymns of Saint Eulalia, Saint Hippolytus, and the holy Apostles Peter and Paul.

Whom you violate with wanton passions,

and whose adulteries you conceal beneath the shadow of the goddess Venus.

I alone govern these elements; nor, [p. 782] like some wretched,

weak, or fragile being, am I wearied by the burden of labor.

For me there is immeasurable light and an age that cannot be dissolved,

an eternity unknown to your senses.

[230] Therefore I need no ministers for so many administrations of the world,

nor do I require participants or associates.

Moreover, it belongs to me to know the angelic legions

that my right hand made, and what nature subsists in created things,

and what kinds of things are preserved for my uses.

[235] You, passing me by, devise a thousand gods,

which you pretend to be present in my powers,

so that you may diminish me into various parts:

for no part of me can be cut away or shaped,

because I am a simple substance

[240] and cannot be a part. Division belongs only to composed

and fashioned things. No one created me,

so that I could be split apart: I alone am the Creator of all.

Believe that what I formed from nothing is not a part of me.

Therefore come, mortal: build a temple for me alone,

[245] revere me as the one God. I waive the cement,

and the stones that Paros cuts, and those that the Punic rock supplies,

and those that green Lacedaemon possesses, and spotted Synna.

Let no one dedicate to me the natural purple of the cliff.

I love a temple of the mind, not of marble; in it, golden— [inherited source break]

252. Aldus incorrectly punctuates: “Justice: inwardly it spreads: alone painted in ruddy—” Gifanius reads the short *e* and punctuates: “Inwardly it spreads, alone painted in the ruddy flower of chastity: nourishing modesty guards the chambers,” from an excellent old manuscript, which he calls most elegant. Alexander indeed has *pudicitia*, and Prudentius often lengthens a short vowel because of the caesura. Most others read and punctuate: “Inwardly it spreads, alone painted in the ruddy flower of chastity; nourishing modesty guards the chambers.” Gifanius’s and Alexander’s reading is more harmonious. Many punctuate *justitia: interius*.

257. Aldus and Fabricius have *ut lux*; *ut lux* is better.

258. Aldus, Vat. A, Mariettus, apparently by a second hand, Alexander, and others have *et*, “and preparing the body.” Vat. A, Egmondanus, and Widmanstetter in the margin have *dubitabile*, less well, instead of *habitabile*.

259. The Ratianus, by the first hand, incorrectly has *poscit*. The same manuscript above, Alexander, and the Urbinas have *possit*, which Weitzius, Heinsius, and other recent editors retained. Others, including Giselinus, have *posset*, and Heinsius did not note the orthographical difference. I think Teolius’s printing of *placido* instead of *placito* is an error, not a variant reading.

260. Apart from Ovid and Juvenal, Minucius expresses the same thought in the *Octavius*.

261. Weitzius, together with Widmanstetter in the margin, Giselinus, and Fabricius, has *viribus* instead of *sensibus*, less well. The gloss is rather a different reading.

262. Widmanstetter above has *sublime tuendum*.

263. Fabricius has *respexit humum*. Others have *despexit* or *dispexit*, as Egmondanus, Palatinus, and Oxford write. This is as far as Mariettus’s copy extends; he himself says that it is “the best and most correct of all that I have seen up to this point.”

265. He is speaking of man, for whose restoration the Son of God was sent.

[Col. 0200B] 266. He expresses the angel’s words to Mary in Luke 1:35: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.” Iso explains *informavit* as “taught.” But here the speech concerns the limbs fashioned from clay, or the body assumed by the Son of God; alternatively, Prudentius may use the expression for the words, “the power of the Most High will overshadow you.”

We have noted elsewhere that the Word of God is sometimes called “Spirit” by Prudentius and others, because it proceeds from the Father. Many ancient writers give an explanation of Luke’s words similar to Prudentius’s, including Justin Martyr, Tertullian, Ambrose, and Hilary, followed by some more recent writers. They say that the words “the power of the Most High will overshadow you” repeat what precedes, and that both expressions signify that the Spirit, the Son of God, descended upon the Virgin and overshadowed her. Consult Calmet’s Commentary. Prudentius says similarly in the *Dittochaeon*, verse 99: “The Holy Spirit will fill you, Mary; you will bear Christ, holy virgin.”

268. We have defended the expression “assumed man” elsewhere.

270. In Vat. A the word *Patris* is missing.

272. Aldus and Alexander have *veterum tantum morem*, “only the custom of the ancients.” Earlier, at verse 69, a similar variation occurs: *Allegat morem veterum* or *veterem*. Bongarsius and Widmanstetter, by the first hand, have *tantummodo rem*, less well, instead of *tantum morem*. In the Basel edition of 1540 I also read *tantummodo rem, neque*. Sichardus placed another reading in the margin, as he usually does. Becmanus, chapter 6 of the *Manuductio ad linguam Latinam*, does not appear to have observed another reading in the printed editions, for from his manuscript he says that it should more correctly be emended to *an veterem tantum morem*.

273. Heinsius, together with Thuanus, omits *et* and says that it should be omitted after *dici*. It does not seem to me superfluous in *dici id patitur*, although more recent editors follow Heinsius.

276. After this verse, Symmachus’s words are usually inserted:

“Each person has his own custom; each person has his own rite. Now, if long antiquity gives authority to religious practices, the faith preserved through so many centuries must be maintained, and we must follow our ancestors, who successfully followed their own.”

Vat. A begins with “Now, if long antiquity.” The Ratianus has: “Each person has his own custom; each person has his own right.” Sichardus likewise. Vat. A has: “our ancestors are happily followed by us.” The Ratianus has: “our ancestors are followed.”

On firm foundations faith remains; a structure, shining with

snow-white piety, rises upward; the lofty summit is covered

with inward justice; the floor spreads painted red with

the flower of chastity; nourishing modesty guards the chambers.

This house is suitable for me; this most beautiful dwelling

[255] receives me, worthy of an eternal and heavenly guest.

Nor is this place new: my glory flowed into the limbs,

and the true light of God; God illumined the nurturing material,
and the parent himself made the material into an inhabitable body

for himself, so that he might rest in a temple pleasing to him.

[260] I had created perfect man and commanded him to behold heavenly things,

turned toward me with all his senses,

[Col. 0199B] upright in bearing, lofty in posture, and looking upward:

but he looked down upon the earth, bent himself toward the riches

785 of the world, and drove my divinity from his breast.

[265] He had to be restored to me. My own Spirit descended

in submission upon him and fashioned the limbs formed from clay

with divine powers.

And now the supreme God transferred the assumed man into divinity

and taught him to grow warm again through our worship.

[270] I should like to know with what ears you receive these commands

of the Father, you most learned censor of the Italian people.

Do you choose merely the ancient custom, abandoning reason,

and does your intellectual acuity and the talent of a wise man

allow this to be called wisdom? To me the former custom is preferable

[275] to the way of justice, piety to what has been revealed from heaven,

and faith in truth to the rule of the right sect.

[Col. 0200B] 786 If whatever custom the newly born world possessed

in the untutored years must be reverently honored and preserved—

279. “Footprints”: one by one. I.

280. “To condemn”: to abandon. “Step by step”: in order, gradually. Iso.

281. “Later”: afterward. “Found”: up to this point. I.

282. “They subdued”: they dug, plowed. I.

284. “Of holm-oak”: of oak, from *ilex*. I.

286. “A forging”: a mass of hot iron. I.

287. “May drip again”: may be left behind. I.

288. “Induviae”: garments. “Slaughtered cattle”: skins. I.

292. “Sadly”: an adverb. “Wild”: because at that time they lived individually like wild beasts. I.

293. “Ancient”: works. I.

294. “Scythian”: Scythia is a region in which sons hurled their fathers from hills or high bridges into the sea, anticipating their death, supposedly thinking this an act of piety; or they even ate them, providing them with such pious burials. “Vietum”: each old man deprived of strength. I.

295. “Votive”: because it was the father’s will. I.

[Col. 0201B]

279. From Virgil, *Georgics* II, verse 402: “And the year rolls back upon its own tracks.”

281. Cicero, Book I *Academica*: “The most recent things are the most corrected and amended.” Virgil, *Georgics* II, verse 22: “Practice itself found a way for itself.”

282. Likewise from Virgil, *Georgics* I: “Before Jupiter, no farmers subdued the fields.” He calls the world “new,” as at verses 338 and following, “recent lands,” an “empty world.”

283. Chamillard observes that poets use the word *rastrum* for a digging instrument, as do Pliny and others. Suetonius likewise, in *Nero*: “He first dug the earth with a rake.” See the commentary on verse 639 of Book I.

[Col. 0201C] 284. Acorns are called *quernae* from *quercus*, “oak,” and *ilignae* from *ilex*, “holm-oak.” On oak acorns, see Virgil; on holm-oak acorns, Horace, Satire 4 of Book I: “The Umbrian, nourished on holm-oak acorns.” Ancient writers frequently report that the first human beings were accustomed to eat acorns.

285. This too comes from Virgil, *Georgics* I: “For the first men split the cleavable wood with wedges.” Prudentius refutes Symmachus by introducing an account of an ancient custom such as the pagans themselves described, although it was evident that human beings had wisely abandoned it.

286. Virgil, Book VIII: “Forgings of steel.” See the glosses. Vaticanus A and Juretus’s codex have *securim* (“axe”) instead of *secures* (“axes”).

288. Egmondanus has *indubias*; correct to *induvias*. These lines are repeated from Lucretius, Book V, and Juvenal, Satire 6. Lucretius:

> Thus hatred of acorns arose; thus, once they were abandoned,  
> their beds were spread and enlarged with grasses and leaves.  
> The hide too fell away; the wild beast’s garment was despised.

Juvenal:

> When the cold cave offered them small dwellings.

Arnobius used the same argument against the pagans, Book II:

> For what if we should wish in this way to bring blame upon those earlier and most ancient ages, because, once grain had been discovered, they despised acorns and rejected the fruit of the arbutus; because, after woven clothing had been devised—more compact through use and convenience—they ceased to cover and wrap themselves in skins; or because, after houses had been built and more elegant dwellings established, they did not cherish the old huts, nor prefer, like beasts, to remain beneath rocks and in caverns?

See Elmenhorst on this passage, page 61.

290. Bongars has *hirsutis* (“shaggy”), but the erasure shows that another reading stood there. Vaticanus A has *hircos* for *hirtos*, incorrectly.

293. Vaticanus A has, corruptly, *immemores redeant* (“let them return forgetful”).

294. Juretus observes that the reading of a certain manuscript, *Scythica juvenis feritate*, is inferior: for “piety” is used here ironically, just as at the end of the *Book of the Vestals* occurs “kindly modesty, free from bloodshed.” Vaticanus A writes *Scythyca*, Rat. *Scithica*. The same Rat. has *vigetum* for *vietum*, as do Bongars and Widmann; on this matter see elsewhere.

The cruelty of the Scythians is notorious: they scarcely, or rather scarcely at all, abstained from their parents; certainly they devoured them once they were dead. Two questions may be raised here: whether the Scythians really used to hurl their fathers from a bridge, and whether this custom ever prevailed among the Romans.

Fortunatianus affirms the former in Book II of his *Art of Rhetoric*:

> It was the custom among the Scythians, he says, for men of sixty to be sent over a bridge. A Scythian at Athens threw his sixty-year-old father from a bridge; he is accused of parricide. For he says that he acted according to the custom of his people.

Among the Romans there was the proverbial expression, “to throw sixty-year-olds from the bridge.” Festus reports from Manilius that in former times sixty-year-olds were thrown from the bridge because the Aborigines, who first inhabited Rome, had been accustomed each year to sacrifice a sixty-year-old man to Father Dis; later it was instituted that reed images of human beings should be thrown from the bridge into the Tiber.

He adds, on the authority of others, that after Rome had been captured by the Gauls, because of a shortage of food, men sixty years old began to be cast into the Tiber. But, he says, the most certain explanation is this: when voting in the assemblies first began to take place over a bridge, the younger men shouted that the sixty-year-olds—who by then held no public office—should be thrown down, so that they themselves might choose a commander rather than those old men. Sinnius Capito also held this view. Afranius confirmed the mistaken belief about the Tiber bridge in his *Repudiatus*.

Festus seems to deny that sixty-year-olds were actually thrown from the bridge into the river; this is confirmed by others who cite Varro in Nonius Marcellus. Prudentius hints that the sixty-year-olds were thrown from the bridge on which votes were cast—for ecclesiastical writers call votes *vota*, whence *pons votivus*, “votive bridge”—into the river, and he had in mind Ovid, *Fasti* V:

> Some think that, so that the young alone might cast the votes,  
> the feeble old men were hurled from the bridges.

Ovid reports and follows another opinion.

296. On the infants who were sacrificed to Saturn because of Jupiter’s hatred, Lactantius, Book I, chapter 21, Tertullian in the *Apology*, and others should be consulted. Arnobius, Book II:

> Before Hercules’ arrival in Italy, when, at Apollo’s command, human heads were offered in supplication to Father Dis and to Saturn, did you not likewise change this custom through a crafty deception and an ambiguity of names?

Many report that this sacrifice was customarily performed in certain parts of Africa, especially Minucius, whose commentators collect much material about it.

The idol Moloch, frequently mentioned in the sacred writings, to whom the Ammonites burned their sons and daughters, is the same as Saturn, if Saturn is the sun, as Servius and Macrobius teach; although some maintain that infants were not burned in Moloch’s honor, but merely led through fire.

> Let us turn the whole age back along its own tracks  
> [280] to the beginning: let us gradually condemn  
> whatever succeeding, later usage discovered.  
> In the new world no farmers were subduing the fields.  
> What need was there for ploughs? What use for the superfluous care of the rake?  
> The belly is better filled with acorns from the holm oak.  
> [285] The first men split cleavable wood with wedges:  
> let the axe-heads boil down again into a mass,  
> and let the metal vein drip back into its own substance.  
> Let us put on the skins of slaughtered beasts, and let the cold cave  
> [787] offer small dwellings: let us return to the caverns;  
> [290] let us take shaggy coverings of sewn skins.  
> Let huge peoples, once tamed after being savage,  
> now roar mournfully, return again  
> to beastly ways, and resort to their former customs.  
> Let the Scythian youth, with Scythian filial “piety,” hurl his aged father  
> [295] from the votive bridge: such was the custom in former times.  
> Let the Saturnian rites smoke with the slaughter of infants.

[Col. 0203B]

299. The earlier Rott. has *habuisse Remum* (“that Remus had”), and Heinsius notes that *habuisse* occurs instead of *habitasse* (“had inhabited”). It may also be understood as: “Thus they report that Remus had a hut.” Remus is used for Romulus, as in Propertius, Book II, Elegy 1:

> By what steps did that house of Remus once rise?  
> One hearth, the greatest possession of the brothers, was all there was.

Certainly among poets Remus is not rarely used for Romulus, and other writers of prose call it not Remus’s hut but Romulus’s hut.

The ancients often mention this hut of Romulus. Valerius Maximus, Book IV, chapter 4:

> By the hut of Romulus, by the low roofs of the ancient Capitol, and by the eternal hearths of Vesta, still content even with earthen vessels, I swear, and so forth.

In the *Controversies* attributed to Seneca the Elder, Book I, Controversy 6:

> Amid such widely extended walls, nothing is more renowned than a humble hut.

Gothofredus thinks that *Romuli casa* (“Romulus’s hut”) should be read as *nobilius* (“more renowned”). The same hut is mentioned by Ovid, Book III of the *Fasti*; Vitruvius, Book II; Seneca the Younger, *Consolation to Helvia*, chapter 9; Macrobius, Book I of the *Saturnalia*; and Martial, Book VIII.

Barthius, Book XXII of the *Adversaria*, chapter 4, confirms that Prudentius alluded to Romulus’s hut, and quotes Saint Jerome’s words from the preface to Didymus’s books *On the Holy Spirit*:

> Immediately, as though by a restoration of rights, I returned to Jerusalem and, after the hut of Romulus and the Lupercal games, I saw Mary’s lodging and the Savior’s cave.

The same Barthius cites Tacitus, *Annals* XV, concerning the same hut:

> and the royal house of Numa, and the shrine of Vesta, with the household gods of the Roman people, were burned.

But I would ask Barthius how Romulus’s hut could have been seen in Saint Jerome’s time if it had been destroyed in Nero’s fire, since he explains the household gods of the Roman people as Romulus’s hut. I therefore think it more likely that Tacitus means the temple of the household gods, whom they say Aeneas once brought into Italy, unless one prefers to understand the household gods themselves, preserved in the temple of Vesta.

Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Book I, speaks of Romulus’s hut as follows:

> Their life, however, was pastoral and laborious. They often erected huts for themselves in the mountains from wood and reeds and covered themselves with them. One of these still remained in my own time, in a corner where the palace turned toward the Circus, and was called the HUT OF ROMULUS. Those charged with its care still preserve it as sacred, adding nothing more magnificent to it; but if some part suffers either from winter or from age, they strengthen what remains, and, where anything has collapsed, restore as far as they can structures similar to the earlier ones.

300. Widmann writes *Lybistridis*, Egmondanus *Libytidis*, and Bongars *Lybistidis*. Virgil, Book VIII:

> and laid him down upon leaves spread beneath him,  
> with the hide of a Libyan bear;

and Book V:

> Terrible with his spears and with the hide of a Libyan bear.

Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 36, denies that bears are produced in Africa. Many, including ancient writers, affirm it, but some think that what the Romans called Libyan and Numidian bears were lions. See Ruaeus on Virgil, Book V, line 37.

301. Aldus and Palatinus have *villosam* (“shaggy”); Egmondanus *vestent*, Palatinus *vestant*, incorrectly, instead of *gestent* (“wear”).

302. Rat. and Gis. have *habebat* (“he had”); most have *habebant* (“they had”). Cellarius suspects that this Tuscan was Tyrrhenus, the brother of Lydus, mentioned by Velleius, chapter 1. Iso more appropriately understands Evander: for Prudentius seems to have wished to encompass the two lines of Virgil, one referring to Evander and the other to Acestes.

Cellarius says that Evander founded Pallanteum on this side of the Tiber. That is indeed true; but Tuscia, or Etruria, extended immediately across the Tiber, and the Tiber itself is often called Tuscan and Tyrrhenian.

Virgil, Book X, speaking of the troops Evander gave to Aeneas, says:

> Meanwhile, let a force from the Tuscan shores accompany  
> Aeneas and arm the ships, and so forth.

Among other things, Evander shows Aeneas the Janiculum in Book VIII:

> This city Father Janus founded; Saturn founded that one:  
> the one was called Janiculum, the other Saturnia.

The Janiculum hill, however, already stands in ancient Etruria.

Because of ignorance of this matter, the learned writers of Spanish literary history, the Mohedano brothers, did not explain very successfully a difficulty that they themselves had created in the *Life of Columella*. In Volume VIII, which is wholly about Columella, pages 40 and following, they ask why Columella owned the Ceretan estate in Etruria, where the town of Cerveteri now stands, since he himself prescribes that estates should be nearby. They answer that Columella could have traveled to the Ceretan territory in two or three days.

They evidently thought that Etruria had formerly been contained within the same boundaries as the present domain of the Grand Duke of Etruria. Otherwise Caere—whether it is Cerveteri or Cervetri, or, as I think more likely, Ceri, for I believe Cervetri to have been Agylla—is indeed situated in ancient Etruria, but lies only about twenty-five miles from Rome.

303. The earlier Rott. has *Roma sibi antiqua* (“ancient Rome for itself”); Heinsius suspects *Roma sibi antiquum non constat versa per aevum* (“ancient Rome does not remain the same after being transformed through the ages”). Arnobius, Book II:

> For if changing one’s opinion is any fault or crime, and moving from ancient institutions to other new arrangements and wishes is blameworthy, that accusation also applies to you, who have changed your life and customs so often, who, by condemning earlier practices, have passed into ever different customs and rites.

307. Vaticanus A has *more[m] servare* (“to preserve the custom”), incorrectly.

311. Rat., Weitz., Gis. in the margin of the first edition and in the text of the second, and Sich. have *in tabulis*, which Heinsius followed without noting any variant reading. The more recent editions agree with Heinsius.

But Juretus’s codex, Alexandrinus, Urbinas, Aldus, and others have *instabilis placiti* (“of unstable judgment”), which Juretus favors. For this expresses the inconsistency of the Roman Senate and people in revising laws and customs.

Tertullian uses a similar expression in the *Apology*, chapter 4:

> Do you not also, by daily experiments that illuminate the darkness of antiquity, cut down and hack away that entire ancient and squalid forest of laws with the new axes of imperial rescripts and edicts?

See Theodosius’s *Novella* 2, *On Invaders*, and Aulus Gellius, final book, chapter 1.

In Egmondanus and Palatinus there is *novarat* instead of *novarit*; in Alexandrinus, in the first hand, incorrectly, *noverit*.

> The altars resound with savage cries of lamentation.  
> Let the Romulan people themselves weave huts  
> with fragile thatch: thus they report that Remus lived.  
> Let them spread regal couches with hay,  
> [300] [789] or wear a cloak made from the hide of a Libyan bear,  
> shaggy with its hairy body.  
> Such things were possessed by the Sicilian leader or by the Tuscan.  
> Ancient Rome does not remain the same after being transformed through the ages,  
> changed in sacred rites, dress, laws, and arms;  
> [305] it worships many things that it did not worship under King Quirinus:  
> [790] it established some practices more wisely, avoided others,  
> and did not cease to vary its own custom; what laws  
> it had formerly founded, it turned into their opposites.  
> Why do you object to me, Roman senator,  
> [310] with your customary rites, when the decree of the fathers  
> and the people’s frequently changing judgment has revised them?

313. Juretus seems not to have noticed Giselinus’s correction. Giselinus had printed *damnare retenti* (“to condemn what has been retained”), but in his additions corrected it to *damnare recenti* (“to condemn with what is recent”). Heinsius made the same error, printing *retenti* without correcting it.

316. Elmenhorst, in his work on Arnobius, page 45, discusses these matters more fully in connection with Arnobius’s words *pauperrimae necessitatis inventa* (“discoveries of the poorest necessity”), drawing on Columella, Virgil, and Lucretius.

318. Prudentius seems to have borrowed all this from Lucretius, Book III, lines 446 and following.

322. The earlier Rott. has *consilii melior* (“better in judgment”), which Heinsius calls elegantly expressed, as Silius Italicus often uses it. To me *consiliis melior, sed viribus aegra* (“better in judgment, but weak in strength”) seems more elegant.

324. Rat. and Gis. in the margin, Weitz., have *fluxit* (“flowed”). Alexandrinus, Urbinas, Vaticanus A, and most others have *duxit*, namely, “led the age.”

325. This is the reading of Alexandrinus, Urbinas, Widmann, Weitz., Gis., both Boher editions, Heinsius, and others. Aldus, Vaticanus A, Bongars in the first hand, Fabricius, Rat. in a recent hand—with the earlier readings erased—have:

> thus, foolish among the beginnings, sunk into the ground, he stumbled,  
> and, like a four-footed child, dragged his milk-filled limbs.

Aldus has *versumque* instead of *mersumque*. Teolius says that Heinsius cut these lines as superfluous; but Giselinus had cut them earlier, and Weitz after Giselinus. Giselinus, however, noted that the longer reading was found in the printed editions, not entirely without merit. Weitz claims that the Egmondanus supports our reading; Heinsius denies this, having inspected it more carefully.

326. He alludes to the riddle of the Sphinx, solved by Oedipus. See Hyginus, *Fable* 77, and Palaephatus, Book I, chapter “On the Sphinx.” The riddle was: what animal is four-footed in the morning, two-footed at midday, and three-footed in the evening? Oedipus interpreted it as a human being.

327. Aldus has, incorrectly, *artibus aptus* (“suited to the arts”).

330. Virgil, *Aeneid* II:

> and his powers stand firm in their own strength.

334. Sich., Gis. in the margin of both editions, Widmann in the first hand, Bongars, Weitz, Alexandrinus, Urbinas, Heinsius with most of his copies have *si tantus amor est* (“if such great love exists”). It seems to have been taken from Virgil, *Aeneid* II:

> But if such great love exists to know our misfortunes.

Aldus, Tornesius, the first Boher edition, the earlier Rott., Egmondanus, have *si tantum studium est* (“if there is only so much eagerness”), which is Iso’s gloss.

Gronovius, chapter 5 of the *Ecclesiastical Observations* on manuscripts, admits that *quanquam si tantus amor est* (“although if such great love exists”) is what he read, but suspects that *si tibi tantus amor* (“if such love for you exists”) should be read, because otherwise there is an inexcusable metrical defect, which could never have come from Prudentius. But I have already observed that it is common among other poets to lengthen a short syllable because of the caesura, and that this practice is particularly familiar to Prudentius. Gronovius ought not to have been unaware of this.

335. Thuanus has *ut a prisco* (“as from the ancient”), incorrectly.

339. Virgil, *Georgics* I, line 62:

> Deucalion cast stones over the empty world.

340. Aldus has *nostrae ducit* (“leads our”).

341. In Rat., in the first hand, *indigae*; but the gloss *inde genitae* (“born from there”) shows that this is an error.

343. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 25:

> For although superstitious curiosity originated with Numa, divine worship among the Romans had not yet been established either in images or in temples. Religion was frugal, its rites poor, and there were no Capitols competing with heaven, but only altars hastily formed from turf, and Samian vessels still, and the smell rising from them—and the god himself nowhere. For at that time the ingenuity of the Greeks and Etruscans had not yet flooded the city with the making of images.

Add Saint Augustine, *City of God*, Book III, chapter 12, and Book IV, chapter 31.

345. Rat. has *concentum* (“harmony”); correctly above, *contentum* (“content”). Gis. in the margin has *paucis* (“with few”). Chamillardus observes, from Melanthius and Apollonius, that the ancients were accustomed to build temples for their deities, especially Jupiter, in elevated places. The temple of Jupiter Latiaris was situated on the Alban Mount; we saw its ruins.

Mazochius, Volume I of the *Spicilegium*, page 67, says that idols are called *excelsa* (“lofty”) in the sacred writings because of their tall stature and elevated location, and traces the origin of the term to the Tower of Babel.

346. Aldus has *post inde* (“after that”). Minucius:

> Thus throughout all empires, provinces, and towns we see individual peoples possessing their own pagan rites and worshipping local gods: the Eleusinians worship Ceres, the Phrygians Mars, the Epidaurians Aesculapius, the Chaldaeans Belus, the Syrians Astarte, the Taurians Diana, the Gauls Mercury, and the Romans all of them.

Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 10:

> Nor will I run through them one by one: so many and so great are they—new, ancient, barbarian, Greek, Roman, foreign, captive, adopted, native; common, male, female, rustic, urban, nautical, military.

See Book I, lines 180 and following, and Sirmondus on Sidonius, page 138, concerning those who compile catalogues of municipal gods.

> Now too, whenever it benefits us to depart from accustomed things  
> and condemn former practices by recent observance,  
> we rejoice that something has been discovered and at last revealed  
> [315] which lay hidden. Human life, always increased by gradual stages,  
> grows and advances through long experience.  
> Such is the changeable order of mortal time;  
> such are nature’s alternating transformations. Infancy crawls;  
> the weak child’s steps and mind alike stumble;  
> [320] warm blood makes vigorous youth burn;  
> soon comes the age of mature strength, now firmly established;  
> [791] at last, better in judgment but weak in strength,  
> old age, with its purified mind, yields in body.  
> Through such divergent stages changeable time has led  
> [325] the human race: thus, foolish at the beginning,  
> [Col. 0205B] sunk into the ground, it proceeded like a four-footed creature.  
> Soon, tender but gifted with a teachable mind, and now suited  
> to learning the arts, it was refined by the changing novelty of things.  
> [Col. 0206A] Then, swelling with vices, it grew into vigorous years,  
> [330] until, its strength perfected, it consolidated its powers.  
> The time arrives when it may now understand divine things  
> through the counsel of a serene mind, more keenly and shrewdly seek  
> hidden realities, and at last devote itself to eternal salvation.  
> Although, if such great love and concern for ancient custom exists,  
> [335] [792] and if it pleases you not to depart from the ancient rite,  
> there stands in the ancient books a noble example:  
> even then, in the time of the Flood—or earlier—  
> one God had joined the people to himself  
> who first inhabited the newly formed lands  
> and dwelt in an empty world.  
> [340] From there our extended offspring derives its descent,  
> and restores the ordinances of native piety.  
> But since we are speaking to Romans about religious worship,  
> I show that the people of Hector’s blood, for a long time,  
> worshipped not many gods, and, content with few shrines,  
> [345] placed only a few altars upon the hills.  
> Later, after their strength had subdued others, countless gods—

### Notes

[Col. 0207A]

351. *Signum*, “image,” “statue.” — *Bimaris*, “between two seas,” because Corinth is surrounded by two seas. — *De strage*, “from the destruction,” as Mummius did, I.

352. *Athenis*, “from the Greeks,” I.

353. *Canini*, “of Anubis, of Mercury.” Mercury is portrayed with a dog’s head because of the shrewdness of speech, and nothing is more sagacious than a dog, I.

354. *Ammonis*, “of Jupiter,” I.

355. *Syrtica*, “sandy.” — *Cornutas*, “horned,” on account of Jupiter, who was horned, I.

[Col. 0207B]

347. Egmondanus and Widmann above have *viribus* (“by strengths”), incorrectly, instead of *urbibus* (“by cities”). Aldus, Egmondanus, Widmann above, Gis., and Rat. have *ex claris* (“from illustrious [things]”); *et claris* (“and illustrious”) is better.

351. Horace, Ovid, Sidonius, and others call Corinth “two-sea Corinth,” because it lies between the Ionian and Aegean seas. This epithet seems to have been created from a similar Greek expression by Muretus in his *Various Readings*.

L. Mummius destroyed Corinth. Florus, Book II, chapter 26, describes that destruction and reports that Corinthian bronze was carried away from there and received its name:

> Because, when many statues and images had been mingled together in the fire, the veins of bronze, gold, and silver flowed together into one mass.

Isidore, Book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 20, says that this happened when Hannibal captured Corinth; but this is a *mnemonic error* (*μνημονικὸν ἁμάρτημα*), that is, he put Hannibal in place of L. Mummius. In the gloss, *Numenius* is an error for *Mummius*.

352. Sulla conquered Athens, from which he brought columns of the temple of Olympian Jupiter to the Capitol buildings. See Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 6, and Plutarch in his *Life of Sulla*.

355. Chamillardus wishes this to be understood of the Nasamones, a Syrtic people. Curtius, Book IV, section 29, says of them:

> The inhabitants of the grove, whom they call Ammonians, live in scattered huts.

358. These new deities seem to be the *dii novensiles*, according to Cincius’s opinion reported by Arnobius, Book III:

> Piso believes that the *Novensiles* are nine gods among the Sabines [lacuna] Cincius declares that foreign deities were called *Novensiles* “from novelty itself.” For the Romans were accustomed to distribute all the gods of conquered cities partly privately among families and partly to consecrate them publicly; and, so that nothing might be omitted through the multitude or ignorance of the gods, they invoked them all together under the single name *Novensiles*, for the sake of brevity and economy.

Arnobius reports and ridicules other opinions of others about the *Novensiles*. Tertullian, cited above at line 346, also mentions new gods. Cicero, Book II *On the Laws*, says:

> Let no one possess gods separately, nor new gods; and let no one privately worship foreign gods unless they have been publicly adopted.

359. Saint Augustine, *City of God* III.12 and IV.31, uses this same argument to show the impotence of the pagan gods.

364. Mariettus notes here—and we must not omit it—that in Rat. *relligione* is always written with a double *l*. Some think this is not properly done, even when the syllable would otherwise have to be lengthened. I, however, think that ancient poets often doubled the following consonant in order to lengthen a short syllable, and pronounced and wrote *repperit*, *reccidit*, *relligio*, and similar forms.

365. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 6:

> Where is religion? Where is the reverence owed by you to your ancestors? In dress, food, equipment, understanding, and finally in speech itself, you have renounced your forefathers. You are always praising antiquity, yet each day you live in a new manner.

366. Vaticanus A, the earlier Rott., Cauchus, Gis. in the margin, and Urbinas have *externumque migrans devenit in orbem* (“and, migrating outward, it came into a foreign world”). From this Heinsius conjectures *externamque migrans devenit in urbem* (“and, migrating outward, it came into a foreign city”), although he does not dislike *externum orbem*, since *urbem* occurs shortly afterward.

He adds: “You could also read *emigrans venit*” (“it came as an exile”). Certainly in the Egmondanus we find *exsultat, externumque micam venit in urbem*, in which clear traces of the true reading appear. I do not sufficiently understand this. Weitz cites the Egmondanus for *externumque migrans devenit in orbem*.

Heinsius, with most of his copies, and Weitz, Widmann, Bongars, Alexandrinus, and Rat. have *externumque inimicam venit in urbem* (“and it came into the city as an external enemy”). Weitz cites Giselinus in support of this reading; yet Giselinus reads *aeternumque inimicam venit in urbem* (“and it came into the city as an eternal enemy”).

Gifanius, in the word *vestire* (“to clothe”), says that the old book should be read as *externumque* instead of *externorum*. Perhaps Fabricius, by a similar figure, printed *externamque inimicum venit in urbem*, that is, *inimicum* (“enemy”) for *inimicorum* (“enemies”).

Gallandius follows Heinsius’s more common reading, but in Aldus and Tornesius he praises *aeternumque inimicam* as sufficiently appropriate to Prudentius’s meaning, since he borrowed all these ideas from Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 25:

> Thus there are as many sacrileges of the Romans as trophies; as many triumphs over gods as over nations; as many spoils as there remain images of captive gods. They endure being worshipped by their own enemies, and they have granted endless empire to those whose injuries rather than flatteries they ought to have requited. But since they feel nothing, they are harmed with as much impunity as they are worshipped in vain.

Verrius Flaccus reports that in sieges the Roman priests were accustomed first of all to summon the god to whose protection the city had been entrusted, promising that god the same or a greater place among the Romans, as appears in his fragments preserved by Pliny, Book XXVIII, chapter 2.

369. Aldus, Egmondanus, Palatinus, Widmann above, Juretus’s codex, and Rat. have *sed solers* (“but skillful”). Others have *at solers* (“but the skillful one”). Heinsius printed *sed solers*, without making any observation, although he had departed from Giselinus.

> [793] Rome, having subdued cities by her might and won illustrious triumphs,  
> amid the smoking ruins of temples,  
> with the victor’s right hand seized hostile images,  
> [350] and carried the captives home, venerating them as gods.  
> This image she seized from the destruction of two-sea Corinth;  
> that one she took as booty from Athens, once it had been burned.  
> Conquered Cleopatra gave her some images  
> with dogs’ heads; others, after the sands of Ammon had been subdued,  
> [355] furnished trophies with horned faces from Syrtis.  
> Whenever Rome received the famous chariot of a triumphing commander  
> with applause, she added as many altars of the gods  
> and made new deities for herself from the spoils:  
> [Col. 0208A] [794] deities which, torn from their ancestral walls,  
> [360] could offer no protection to their own shrines.  
> Do you see how the traces of ancient custom are always proved to have stumbled,  
> wavering variously with uncertain steps,  
> by adopting gods unknown to their ancestors  
> and devoting themselves to a foreign religion,  
> [365] and not preserving their own rites? Whatever belongs to sacred worship  
> is exiled, and an external enemy has come into the City.  
> [795] In vain, therefore, you cling to customary things, perverse observance.  
> The ancestral custom you cherish is no ancestral custom, wicked observance; it is not.  
> But the skilled orator says that the City, allotted by fate,  
> [370] lives out its appointed span under whichever genius governs it.

### Notes

[Col. 0209B]

367. *Solitis*, “customs,” “things,” I.

370. *Sortitam*, “receiving,” I.

375. *Competat*, “agrees with,” I.

376. *Spiritus*, whether it exists or not, I.

377. *Munera*, “duties,” I.

379. *His*, “souls,” I.

[Col. 0209C]

381. *Vegetet*, “strengthens,” “supports,” “fortifies,” I.

382. *Succendat*, “kindles” with heat, “warms.” — *Riget*, “infuses with movement.” — *Relaxet*, “softens,” I.

384. *Componere*, “to govern,” “to arrange,” I.

387. *Tutacula*, “protections.” — *Nudis*, “limbs”: we call a thing *nudum* (“bare”) when it needs counsel in every respect, I.

389. *Agitetur*, “is moved,” I.

390. *Consultet*, “provides,” I.

395. *Gemellos*: a well-known story about the vultures which the two brothers Remus and Romulus saw flying from Mount Aventine at the beginning, when they began to reign. The poet imagines that a spirit came together with them. He says, mockingly, “I suppose that the spirit first entered little Rome when the she-wolf nourished Remus and Romulus in the wooded valley; then too the spirit was nourished together with them,” I.

[Col. 0210C]

398. *Penetralia*, “inner chambers,” “dwellings,” I.

399. *Forensia*, “civil,” “public,” I.

400. *Acres*, “strong,” I.

401. *Urget*, “compels the Romans,” I.

402. *Digna*, “to be worthy,” I.

403. *Fingamus*, “let us compose,” I.

405. *Hauserit*, “has drawn,” “has received,” “has taken.” — *Animetur*, “may be strengthened,” or “may be given life.” — *Medullis*, “in the innermost parts,” I.

[Col. 0209C]

373. In many manuscripts, after this line, Symmachus’s words are inserted:

> The divine mind distributes various guardians among cities. As spirits are assigned to those being born, so fated genii are assigned to peoples.

Vaticanus A has: “The divine mind distributes various guardians among cities.” Aldus has *induntur* (“are put on”) instead of *dividuntur* (“are distributed”).

374. Vaticanus A: “what the genius may be.”

375. Aldus has *et possit* (“and may be able”). Gis. printed this, but I do not know whether he corrected it; Heinsius seems not to have noticed it.

376. Aldus has *formane, an ulla* (“is it a form, or any…”). Gis. and Weitz have *formave, an ulla* (“or a form, or any…”). Vaticanus A, Rat., Alexandrinus, Urbinas, Juretus’s codex, and Heinsius with his copies have *formave, et ulla sit species* (“or a form, and whether there is any appearance”).

Gallandius judges this less correct and, with Aldus, prefers *formane, an ulla*. But the more common manuscript reading should be retained, with this sense: “I do not know even whether it is a form, and whether there is any appearance.” Elmenhorst, commenting on Arnobius’s words *civitatumque genios* (“the genii of cities”), explains the matter through these lines.

377. Vaticanus A has *munere* (“office”), less correctly.

378. Vaticanus A has *inde pererratis* (“then, having wandered through”); *unde* (“from which”) is better. Aldus incorrectly has *viget* for *vegetet* (“strengthens”).

384. Vaticanus A: *mens ficto quam tu componere tentas* (“a mind which you try to compose with fiction”).

385. Alexandrinus, Aldus, Gis., and others have *membrorum* (“of limbs”). Most have *murorum* (“of walls”), which seems genuine to Heinsius. Nevertheless, at line 446 we find *perque omnia membra Urbis* (“through all the limbs of the City”).

386. Vaticanus A has *qui nec corporibus* (“which does not [belong] even to bodies”), incorrectly.

387. Bongars and Widmann have *consilium fit* (“counsel is made”), or *tutacula*, which is obscure.

390. Widmann, Bongars, Rat., and Sich. have *consulet et cui* (“it will consult, and for whom”). Weitz cites Aldus for *consulte cui se* (“deliberately for whom itself”), and therefore did not notice Aldus’s correction, *consultet cui se*.

391. Aldus has *quem putat* (“whom it thinks”). He and Thuanus, in the first hand, have *quae rerum summa sequatur* (“what summation of affairs it should follow”).

396. Vaticanus A writes *innota* (“unknown”). Romulus and Remus are said to have taken an omen concerning the founding of the city. Remus saw six vultures on Mount Aventine, while Romulus saw twelve on the Palatine. Ovidius says:

> Romulus holds the decision and the rule of the city.

He tells the story in Book IV of the *Fasti*, among other writers. On ancient coins Rome is sometimes represented with vultures.

397. Thuanus, the earlier Boher, and the later Rott. have *repentina de nube* (“suddenly from a cloud”). Egmondanus has *repentini* (“of the sudden one”), incorrectly. Other manuscripts and editions have *repentinam* (“a sudden [form]”).

398. Alexandrinus, Aldus, and Heinsius’s preferred copies have *servat* (“guards”), which is pleasing. Rat., Tornesius, Gallandius, and Weitz have *servans* (“guarding”). Gis. has *servat* and in the margin *servans*, and, instead of the divided reading, *curans* (“caring for”).

401. The earlier Rott. and Cauchus have *lituo ciet* (“calls with the augur’s staff”). Egmondanus, Oxoniensis, and Juretus’s codex have *lituos ciet* (“calls the augur’s staffs”). Most have *lituis ciet* (“calls with trumpets”).

405. Gis. in the margin has *et calidas animet curata medullas* (“and, cared for, may give life to the warm marrow”).

406. Rat. and Weitz with their copies, except Bongars, have *de religione tenenda* (“concerning the religion to be maintained”).

> For, he says, whether a destiny or a genius is placed in every people or city,  
> it is placed according to the custom of our souls,  
> which enter new bodies under unequal lots.  
> First, what the genius is, or what condition  
> [375] belongs to it, I do not know: what it can do, and from where it arises,  
> whether the bodiless spirit is formless or has a form,  
> whether it has any appearance, what it knows, or what duties it performs.  
> But I understand the souls of human beings as diffused within  
> their vital veins, so that from them the blood receives  
> [380] gentle movement and tender warmth.  
> From there, having wandered through the limbs, it invigorates the heart,  
> kindles the cold, gives motion to the dry, and relaxes the hard.  
> [796] Thus the living mind regulates and governs human life for itself.  
> You try to construct it from a fictitious genius of the limbs,  
> [385] which exists nowhere and has never existed.  
> Indeed, the living mind that governs bodies exercises  
> supreme counsel, so that it may provide faithful protections  
> for the bare and helpless limbs, avoid threatening dangers,  
> foresee what is useful, be moved toward various arts,  
> [390] deliberate for which master it should submit itself,  
> and whom it should think the author of the world and the one whom the sum of things follows.  
> But your genius of the City—tell me, I wish to know—when  
> did it first begin to enter little Rome?  
> Did it flow from the she-wolf’s breasts in the wooded valley  
> [395] and nourish the twin infants while it itself was being born?  
> Or, flying with the vultures unknown through the air,  
> did it draw a sudden shape from a cloud?  
> Does it sit upon the highest summits, or guard the inner chambers,  
> [797] establish customs, and formulate civil laws?  
> [400] Does it also enter the trenches of the camp? Does it drive  
> strong men to arms, call them with trumpets, and press them against the enemy?  
> Who would not see that such notions deserve the laughter of the wise?  
> Yet let us imagine that there is something which cares for such matters,  
> a shadow or a soul, through which the republic has drawn  
> [405] its destiny and the whole body is animated with warm marrow.  
> Why does this same being not also—concerning the religion to be worshipped—

[Col. 0211B]

407. *Consultat*, “foresees,” “inquires,” I.

409. *Fingit*, “composes,” I.

410. *Licet*, “it is permitted,” Iso.

412. *Erravit*, “almost erred,” I.

413. *Lubrica*, “unstable,” I.

414. *Aequa*, “just,” I.

416. *Grandaevis*, “senators,” “consuls,” I.

417. *Proceres*, “younger men and grandsons,” Iso.

419. *Collatas*, “joined together,” I.

421. *Consule*, “under a consul,” I.

426. *Fastos*, “books,” I.

428. *Fluctibus*, “errors,” “instabilities,” I.

430. *Augustum*, “noble.” — *Diademate*, “crown,” I.
