436. *Aegre*, “with difficulty,” “scarcely,” I.

437. *Probet*, “approves,” “praises,” I.

[Col. 0211C]

407. Aldus, Giselinus in the text, and Juretus’s codex have *prospectat*. Widmann, Bongars, and Giselinus in the margin have *aspectat*. Most others, including Giselinus in the margin under “different reading,” and the codices of Gifanius and Becman, have *suspectat*. Virgil, *Georgics* I, line 375:

> The heifer, looking up at the sky, caught the breezes with her wide nostrils.

408. Aldus has *cur tibi*; the others, *cur sibi*.

409. Juvenal, *Satire* 14, line 246:

> Your nativity is known to astrologers.

410. Aldus and Giselinus have *cur jam*. Most have *cui jam*, and Widmann’s marginal gloss is: “to which genius it is permitted to be unwilling.” Tertullian, *Apology* chapter 6:

> Let those who are now the most religious guardians and avengers of the laws and paternal institutions, if they have departed from none of them, answer, I should like, concerning their fidelity, honour, and obedience toward the ordinances of their ancestors.

412. Florus counts seven hundred years from King Romulus to Caesar Augustus; others reckon about seven hundred and eight years.

414. Aldus, Giselinus, and Weitz have *imperii et quae*. The word *et* is absent from Heinsius’s manuscripts and from ours.

[Column 0211D]

416. Aldus incorrectly has *curatum in parte* (“managed in part”). Concerning these changes in the Roman government, consult Florus and the notes of John of Camerino, who briefly indicates other historians, whether agreeing or disagreeing.

417. The kings were expelled in the 245th or 254th year from the founding of the City, and consuls were then created.

418. In the year 387 a law was passed that one consul should be elected from the plebs, as had been proposed in the year 309. Grangaeus understands this of the first consul, the *novus homo* L. Sextius; Chamillardus understands it of the tribunes of the plebs created in the year 259 because of the plebeian secession, which is more likely, as is clear from what follows: “This arrangement suddenly becomes displeasing,” etc.

421. This verse is rejected by Vat. A, Egm., Oxon., and Rottend. and placed after the verse “The public state.” Aldus incorrectly divides the words as *plebs, fisa*.

422. In approximately the 301st year from the founding of the City, the decemvirs were created in place of the consuls for the purpose of enacting laws; they are the “twice five summits,” etc. Concerning the insignia, fasces, and axes, Livy, Book III, chapter 36, writes: “When the earlier decemvirs had maintained the arrangement that one man should bear the fasces, and that this royal emblem should pass in turn through the whole group to each man in succession, suddenly they all appeared with twelve fasces apiece. One hundred and twenty lictors had filled the Forum, carrying axes bound into the fasces.”

425. Egm. corruptly has *doctoris* (“of the teacher”) for *ductoribus* (“leaders”). In the year 304 from the founding of the City, authority was again entrusted to two consuls.

426. Some place verse 421, “The nobility under a consul,” after this verse.

427. The triumvirate of Caesar, Lepidus, and Antony, whose cruelty contains nothing less than the number one hundred and forty senators (the proscribed). Its conclusion was disgraceful, savage, pitiable, and so forth. See Florus, Book IV, chapter 5.

429. The earlier Rott. has *reprendere rectum* (“to correct the right [course]”).

430. Gis. in the margin has *diademate texit* (“covered with a diadem”). Giselinus likewise arranged the catalogue of these changes as follows:

“First kings ruled. After them consuls began in the year 245 from the founding of the City. Consuls and senators together with tribunes of the plebs in 261. The decemvirs alone in 303. Consuls also from the plebs in 306. The triumvirs after Caesar’s death in 712. Octavius alone in 723.”

He concludes that the verse “The nobility under a consul” is correctly placed where we have inserted it.

431. Suetonius, chapter 58, on Augustus: “The Senate, in agreement with the Roman people, hails you as Father of the Fatherland.”

433. Because of his great achievements Augustus was called perpetual dictator and Father of the Fatherland. It was even debated in the Senate whether, since he had founded the empire, he should be called Romulus. But the name Augustus seemed more sacred and reverent, so that, while he was still governing the world, he might by that very name and title be consecrated. See Florus at the end of his history.

436. Aldus has *aegrae* (“with difficulty” in the feminine); read *aegre* (“with difficulty”).

Does she deliberate? Why does she not recognize that heaven is free?

Why does she think that an unchangeable fate has been prescribed for her,

as for a captive? Why does astrology invent chains?

[410] To whom it is now permitted to refuse what then it was permitted to will,

And to abolish his errors and bend his inclinations?

Thus for approximately seven hundred years it wandered,

Uncertain and ever hesitating which form of government might please,

Which power of ruling might be equitable.

[415] 798 The City had then arisen under royal rule,

not without assigning aged men a share in its cares.

Soon we see the nobles, sprung from an ancient stock,

Handling the helm of policy; thereafter plebeian troops,

[Column 0211B] Mixed with the patricians under equal authority,

Ruled for a long time, directing affairs in war and peace.

Under a consul the nobility flourished; the plebs trusted a tribune.

This arrangement suddenly becomes displeasing, and twice five

Summits of the highest nobles are created; twelve fasces

[Column 0212A] Surround each of them, and an axe as well.

[425] Again the whole commonwealth returns to two leaders

And permits the consuls to compile the fasti.

At last a bloody triumvir disturbed the generations.

Amid these disturbances fate, or a genius, or the spirit

799 Of the commonwealth wandered; at length, having learned the right path,

[430] It crowned the august head with a diadem,

Calling him Father of the Fatherland, of the people, and of the Senate,

The ruler who should be commander in war and also

Dictator, censor, and good teacher of morals,

Guardian of wealth, avenger of crimes, giver of honors.

[435] [Column 0212B] But if, through so many stages of affairs, so many times changed

By differing policies, it finally arrived with difficulty at that

Which it approved and which public reverence preserves

Under a sacred covenant, why does it hesitate to acknowledge divine laws?

[Column 0213A]

[Note: [Column 0213B]

440. *Gratemur* (“let us give thanks”), in place of *gratulemur* (“let us congratulate”), I.

445. *Thermis* (“baths”), *balneis* (“bathing places”).—*Tabulis* (“shops”), *tabernis* (“shops”), places for keeping tablets, I.

446. *Membra* (“limbs”), *moenia* (“walls”), I.

452. *Acceperit* (“received”), that is, “when it was born,” Iso.

453. Lachesis, Clotho, and Atropos are the names of the Fates: one holds the distaff, another draws out the thread, and the third breaks it, I.

[Column 0214B] 457. *Eruta* (“dug out”), *diruta* (“destroyed”), I.

460. *Constituunt* (“they establish”), *docent* (“they teach”), Iso.

461. *Rubrica*: the name of a law; a law; the line used by masons to see whether the wall itself is straight or not. But it is used for “law” or “judgment,” I.

462. *Ferrea* (“iron”), *dura* (“hard”), I.

463. *Inevitabile* (“inevitable”), namely punishment, I.]

[Note: [Column 0213B]

441. The ancients often joined these two words, “Christ God,” and the expression occurs frequently in our author. The military oath of Christians is reported by Vegetius, Book II, chapter 5: “They swear by God, by Christ, and by the Holy Spirit, and by the imperial majesty, which, after God, ought to be loved and honored by the human race.” Some incorrectly render these words as “by God Christ and the Holy Spirit,” so as to adapt them to Prudentius’ words. This same argument for the divinity of Christ against the Arian heresy is also found in ancient inscriptions. Lupius, in his *Epitaphs*, produces from the Kircherian Museum a Greek inscription of Saint Severa in which one reads: “in God the Lord Christ.” See also Gaspare Aloysius Odericus, *Sylloge Inscriptionum*, p. 263 and following, although he incorrectly applies here this title from the cemetery of Saint Saturninus: “PRIMA. VIVIS. IN. GLORIA. DEI. ET. IN. PACE. DOMINI. NOSTRI.” For here Christ is not joined with God. More relevant are other inscriptions in Georgius, *On the Monogram of Christ the Lord*, chapter 4: “OLYMPIODORE, MAY YOU LIVE IN GOD”; “HILARI, MAY YOU LIVE IN GOD”; “HERE LIES PERPETUUS IN CHRIST HIS GOD.”

444. Many have written about the *genii* of the ancients. On this subject Emmanuel Martin praises a book published by Emmanuel Navarro in Book IV, Letter 10. Elmenhorst, in his notes on Arnobius, p. 14; Heraldus, in his notes on Arnobius, p. 40; Lactantius, Book II, chapter 15; and his interpreters contain much about *genii*. Barthius, *Adversaria*, Book LII, chapter 12, discusses at length the *genii* of the ancients, their religious devotion, worship, and superstition in honoring them; the etymology, abundance, and characteristics of *genii*; and the *genii* of cities, places, houses, regions, people, and other things. He declares that no one has refuted more skillfully the pagan opinion that such demons inhabit every place and undertaking than Prudentius in this brilliant poem. Petavius, volume III, Book II, chapter 6, discusses theologically the guardianship and protection undertaken by angels, both publicly for all and privately for individuals—what the pagans commonly asserted concerning their *genii*. The *genius* of Rome is often called on coins the *genius populi Romani*, and in Ammianus the *genius publicus*. Martial, Book VI, epigram 41, aptly says: “A book destined to survive ought to have a genius”; we may now say “a guardian angel.” See Censorinus, *On the Birthday*.

445. Rat. and Iso less correctly have *tabulis soleatis* (“with shod tablets”).

446. Ammianus also called the parts of the City its “limbs,” Book XVI: “Then, surveying the limbs of the city placed within the summits of the seven hills, along its slopes and level ground, etc.” They are not walls, as Iso says, but parts of the City.

447. Mariettus observes here that in Rat. *milia* is always written with one *l*, which is the correct spelling and is preferred by many to *millia*.

449. Aldus incorrectly has *similis clementia* (“similar clemency”).

452. Pal. writes *oris* (“of the mouth”) for *horis* (“hours”).

453. In the gloss I find a hexameter if the words are correctly read and transposed: “One retains the distaff, another draws it out, the third breaks it.”

454. Aldus has incorrectly *rectorumque trabes* (“and beams of the righteous”).

455. *Tigillum*, from *tego* (“I cover”) and *tignum* (“beam”), is a beam upon which a roof is placed.

456. Vat. A has corruptly *cujus stille* (“whose drop”). Ald., Alex., have *hortu*; it should be written *ortu* (“rising”).

458. Petavius, *On the Work of the Six Days*, Book III, chapter 7, says that Prudentius has expressed excellently in these verses the conflict between the necessity of fate and the freedom of the human will, even though fate compels the will to will. For the pagans asserted that the will is compelled to will by necessity.

461. Many have already observed that laws are called *rubricae*, even from this verse of Prudentius. Persius, satire 5, verse 90: “Unless the rubric of Masurius has marked something.” Juvenal, satire 14, verse 191: “Read through the red laws of our ancestors.” Laws were written in red because *rubrica* is a plant resembling minium. Hence the name *rubrics* in ritual books. Hermanus Hugo, *On the First Origin of Writing*, p. 103, chapter 12, teaches that writing in encaustic was very familiar to emperors, and that for this reason almost all sections of the law were colored with red pigment. This was done both for majesty and for terror, so that laws marked with red ocher or cinnabar and threatening something bloody and bloodstained might acquire greater majesty—a point Prudentius suggests in these verses. For why a law is said to threaten, see the commentary on verse 179, “The armed law sits.” On the sanction by which punishment is imposed, see Antoninus Augustinus, *On Laws*.

463. Vat. A and Gis. have *ad facinus cogunt* (“they compel to crime”). The Heinsian manuscripts and ours, together with Weitzius and Aldus, have *cogunt ad facinus* (“they compel to crime”).]

Unknown before to itself, and at last revealed?

[440] Let us give thanks: it no longer doubts, for, subjected to Christ,

Rome serves God, abhorring her former worship.

800 I speak of the men of Rome, whom we believe to be the mind of the City,

Not its genius, whose image is falsely represented.

But why do you invent one genius for Rome,

[445] When you customarily assign their own genii to gates,

Houses, baths, and stables? And throughout all the limbs

Of the City, and throughout all places, you invent many thousands

Of genii, so that no corner may be empty of its own shadow?

It remains that similar madness should also impose fate

[450] On every building: that each wall, founded and built

[Column 0214A] Under its own star, should have received at the first hours of its birth

The lot by which it would remain, and when it would fall.

They falsely assign Lachesis’ mighty threads to the stones,

And believe that the beams of houses depend upon spun wheels,

[455] And attribute decrees even to the little beams themselves:

As though it mattered at the rising of which star an ash tree was uprooted,

though it might tower and climb to the highest summit.

Finally, there is no human matter, no action in the world,

Upon which they do not say that a fated lot rests.

[460] Since they establish this, let them say why the law of the Twelve Tables

Was founded, or why the red law threatens,

Which forbids the guilty to sin, although iron fates

Compel them to crime and plunge them into inescapable punishment.

[Column 0215A]

[Note: [Column 0215B]

464. *Adigunt*, *cogunt*, *compellunt*: “they drive,” “they compel,” “they force.” *Insinuantia*: “showing,” I.

467. *Plectentia*: “punishing,” I.

472. *Alterutrum*: either the good or the evil. *Suum*: “one’s own,” I.

476. *Sciat*: “let him know,” namely, that he believes only in the Lord and that no fates do harm, I.

477. *Vetitum*: namely, “to be forbidden,” I.

478. *Mathesis*: the course of the stars. *Praescripto*: prescribed, fixed, an impediment. *Repelli*: namely, “to be able to be driven back,” Iso.

[Column 0216B] 479. *Effert*: “draws forth,” “brings out,” “raises,” Iso.

481. *Momenta*: recollections. *Premit*: he despises in his thoughts, I.

482. *Sortem*: “fate,” I.

484. *Lux*: Christ, I.

485. *Secta*: “doctrine,” I.

488. *Donata*: “adorned,” I.

489. *Age*: the word of one praying. *Bellatrix*: Rome. *Ede*: “tell,” as elsewhere: *Ede Martialem*, that is, “recite” or “sing,” I.]

[Note: [Column 0215B]

466. Heinsius would prefer *gladiumque recondite* (“and hide the sword”). But *retundite* (“blunt it”) better suits the poet’s thought. He means that the sword of justice should be wholly blunted, as already superfluous, if human beings do not sin freely. Thus later he does not say that the prison should be closed, but dissolved.

468. A prison chamber is the inner confinement of a prison; the Spanish call it a *calabozo*. Prudentius describes it in the hymn of Saint Vincent, where I shall say more, and Sallustius describes it in *The War against Catiline*: “There is a place in the prison called the Tullianum. If you descend a little to the left, it is sunk about twenty feet below ground; walls fortify it on every side, and above it a chamber joined by stone vaults. It is neglected, foul with darkness and odor, and its appearance is terrifying.” If the Mamertine prison at the foot of the Capitoline Hill, where the acts report that the holy apostles Peter and Paul were detained, is not the same place called the Tullianum, it is certainly very similar to it. The distinguished Cancellieri strongly confirms on many grounds that the Tullian and Mamertine prisons were one and the same in his work *Information about the Tullian Prison, Later Called the Mamertine*, etc., Rome, 1788.

473. Alex., Urb., Ald., Widm. above, Pal., Ox., and Egm., in a second hand, with the old writing completely erased, have *sed fit reus ipse suapte Arbitrio* (“but he himself becomes guilty by his own choice”). Rat., Widm. in the first hand, Bong., Fabr., Gis. in the margin, and Cauch. have *sed fit reus ipse per amplum Ingenium* (“but he himself becomes guilty through broad ingenuity”). Gis. in the text and Jureti’s manuscript have *suopte Arbitrio* (“by his own choice”). Thuan. has *suopte Ingenio* (“by his own nature/genius”). The earlier Rott. has *suapte Ingenio*; the other, *suopte Ingenium*. Heinsius printed *suopte Arbitrio*. But he says that it ought to be written *sed fit reus ipse suapte. Ingenitum placitumque nefas* (“but he himself becomes guilty by his own [choice]. Innate and willingly chosen wickedness”). *Suapte* means “of his own accord.” He understands innate wickedness as original sin, as in verse 913 of the *Apotheosis*: “And infancy at birth retains the innate stains of the first man upon souls.” Heinsius is not displeased by *suopte ingenio* either. Thus *ingenium* may sometimes mean the innate power of the soul or nature, as in Apuleius. It seems to me that *suopte* or *suapte arbitrio* is correct, so that man is understood to sin by his own choice and of his own accord.

475. Aldus has *suppliciis et merito* (“with punishments and deservedly”), but *et* is inserted against the meter. Urb. has *ne sorte*; read *non sorte* (“not by lot”).

476. Most manuscripts have *quisque putat fato esse locum* (“whoever thinks there is a place for fate”). Urb. has *putet*. Aldus has *quis putat esse locum fato* (“who thinks there is a place for fate”), namely in the corrected editions; for, against the meter, he had printed *quis putat esse fato locum*. *Quisque* is used for *quisquis*, concerning which something has already been said; Burmannus may be consulted in the *Anthology*. Aldus less correctly has *omn ipatentem*.

477. Aldus, two Bohers, Thuan., Egm., Oxon., Pal., Gis. in the text, have *nosse Deum* (“to know God”), which is also found in Alex. Others, with Rat., Urb., Weitz., the other Rott., and Heinsius, have *esse deum* (“that there is a god”). The earlier Rott. has *posse Deum* (“that God is able”). Then all the Heinsian manuscripts, Jureti’s manuscript, Aldus, Gis. in the margin, Fabr., Bong., Pal., Rat., Alex., and Urb. have *fatalibus* (“fated”); some have *fallacibus* (“deceptive”). In Rat. what appears to be *veritum* is incorrect for *vetitum*. The meaning is that neither good nor evil actions are performed necessarily.

478. Aldus and Rat., in a recent hand with the earlier writing completely erased, have *Nec praescripto aliquo pellit pia vota mathesis* (“Nor does astrology drive away pious vows by any prescription”). The recent correctors wanted *mathesis* to be pronounced with its second syllable long by nature, because they themselves pronounced it so. Egm. has *perscripto* for *praescripto*. In antiquity astrology was especially understood by the name *mathesis*.

482. Rat., Widm., Bong., Alex. in the first hand, Thuan., both Rott., Gis. in the margin, and Sich. have *fingere* (“to fashion”). Others have *figere* (“to fix”), which Heinsius adopted because it is a technical astrological verb.

483. *Huc ades* (“come here”), a manner of speech very common in Virgil and others.

484. Rat. has *vacat* (“is empty”); above, *vocat* (“calls”).

486. After this verse are Symmachus’ words: “There is also usefulness, which above all asserts the gods to man. For since every reason lies concealed, from where can knowledge of the divine powers come more correctly than from the memory and evidence of favorable events?” Rat. has *deos esse asserit* (“asserts that there are gods”). Aldus has *quam memoria* (“than memory”).

487. Rat. has *si multi duxere dei* (“if many gods led [Rome]”). Alex. has *sed multi* (“but many”). Urb. has *sed multa duxere dii* (“but many gods led [her]”), which Aldus approved, and I do not dislike it. *Prospera multa* (“many successes”) is correct, for the subject is the usefulness that Symmachus claimed the gods had brought.

489. Rat. has *subjecerat* (“had subjected”), in a recent hand; it is not correct. On this superstition of the Romans, who boasted that they had subjected the world with the help of the gods, Minucius and Tertullian, chapter 25 of the *Apology*, may also be consulted. Iso cites verse 144 of Hymn 4, *Peristephanon*, on the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza, which reads: “Tell of Successus, sing of Martial.” *Ede* is used for “tell.” Juvenal, satire 3, verse 296: “Tell me where you are staying.”]

Indeed they compel even the willing, insinuating a wicked desire,

[465] 802 So that the wretched may not be permitted to refuse to commit what is forbidden.

Give way, if you have any shame, and blunt your sword,

Your harsh laws that punish those deserving nothing:

Dissolve the prison chamber beneath which

You hold the bodies of an innocent host guilty through fate.

[470] No one is guilty, if fate governs what is lived and done;

Rather, he is guilty who willingly dares what is not permitted.

Since to will either one belongs to oneself, and fates do not

Impose guilt upon man, he himself becomes guilty by his own

Choice and willingly chosen wickedness; he pays for impious deeds

[475] with punishments, deservedly, not cut down by fate.

[Column 0215B] Whoever thinks that there is a place for fate should know

[Column 0216A] That God, the Father of all, exists; no one is forbidden by the fated stars,

Nor are pious vows driven back by any prescription of astrology.

For the spirit breathes greater things, raises itself higher

[480] Than the stars, crosses their paths, and tramples beneath its feet

The clouds of fate and the moments that are thought

To fix the allotted destiny at the time of birth.

Come here, every race of human beings; come here, cities, gather:

The immense light calls; recognize your Creator.

[485] The free doctrine lies open: nothing is fated; or, if

There are any fated things, they vanish as powerless before Christ.

But many gods led Rome through prosperity,

Whom she worships because of their merit, adorned with great triumphs.

804 Come then, warrior Rome: tell what power subjected Europe and Libya to you,

[490] [Column 0217A]

[Note: [Column 0217B]

491. *Cretae*: of Crete, an island. *Pallas*: Minerva. *Argis*: Argos, among the Greeks, I.

492. *Cynthius*: Apollo, from Mount Cynthus, where he was raised. *Delphis*: Delphi, the place where Apollo’s altar stood, I.

493. *Isis*: the goddess of Egypt. *Nilicolas*: Egyptians. *Rhodios*: the peoples of Rhodes. *Cytherea*: Venus, I.

494. *Venatrix*: Diana. *Ephesum*: the city. *Dedidit*: gave freely. *Hebrum*: the river of Thrace, I.

495. *Destituit*: abandoned. *Thebas*: the people. *Bromius*: Bacchus, I.

496. *Phrygiis*: Trojans, Romans, I.

497. *Dominam*: Africa, the city of Carthage, I.

498. *Fovetque*: in spirit, I.

499. *Romuleis*: under Romulus’ [rule]. *Addictam*: the nation. *Frenis*: laws, I.

501. *Prodentibus*: yielding, handing over, betraying, I.

[Column 0218B] 502. *Alumnos*: nourished dependents, servants, I.

504. *Transfugio*: desertion, I.

506. *Infestas*: troubling, disturbing, I.

507. *Obnixa*: set against, resisting, struggling. *Globis*: armies. *Illam*: that religion, I.

508. *Virtus*: Roman [valor], I.

509. *Est*: as I said. *Indiga*: lacking, needing. *Veri*: truth, I.

510. *Superstitio*: religion, empty worship, I.

511. *Genti*: of the Romans, I.

512. *Procinctus*: for military preparations, for a military expedition, I.

514. *Nunc*: at some time, or “then this happened.” *Dictaeis*: Cretan. *Corybantibus*: those peoples, I.

515. *Samnitis*: a leader from the province of Samnium. The Samnites and Marsi were peoples of Beneventum, I.]

[Note: [Column 0217C]

491. This Argive Pallas is the one worshiped at Argos and called Σάλπιγξ, “trumpet,” concerning whom see Eustathius, Book VI of the *Iliad*. See the *Priapea*: “Dodona is sacred to you, Jupiter,” etc.

493. Latinius seems to have found *Nicolas* in Tornaes. He correctly emends it to *Nilicolas*. Aldus and Nebr. have *Venus alma* (“nourishing Venus”); others have *Cytherea*. Urb. corruptly has *Citharea*.

494. Urb. and Alex. in the first hand have *dedit* (“gave”). The law of the meter requires *dedidit*. In Alex. *Effesum* is incorrectly written for *Ephesum*.

496. Vat. A has *suis*; correct it to *suos*.

497. Virgil, *Aeneid* I: “This kingdom the goddess already aimed to make belong to the nations, if the fates should allow it, and she fostered it.” Tertullian, chapter 25 of the *Apology*, makes this very point against the Romans, as I shall say at verse 510.

500. Heinsius, with Cauchius, thinks that *indigetum* should be read, without manuscript authority. But the manuscript reading *indigenum* can be defended, as in “the monsters of every kind of god,” and above, verse 341, “he reforms the laws of native piety.” The meaning is the same.

501. Rat. has *distructaeque jacent* (“and lie destroyed”).

502. Virgil VI: “Alas for piety, alas for ancient faith!”

504. Alex., the Heinsian manuscripts, and Gilanius from an old book have *transfugio*. It is clear where *quae* arose: it follows *numinibus*, and the copyists did not understand this figure, which is called a change of gender. The sense and meaning of *dei* agree with *numinibus*; therefore the gender changes from the neuter gender of *numina* to the masculine gender of *dei*. Examples may be seen under Gifanius’ entry *generis mutatio* and in his additions. Ludovicus Cavallus, in his manuscript work against the corrections of the Roman Breviary hymns under Urban VIII, which I discussed in the prolegomena, chapter 23, criticizes the corrector of that hymn for passing from the neuter gender to the masculine: “The heavenly Word proceeding from the bosom of the eternal Father, who, born for the world, comes to its aid,” etc. Yet that hymn can be defended by this change of gender, which the ancients often employed: *Verbum* is used for the Son of God.

507. Virgil, Livy, Nepos, and others use *globus* for a mass gathered together.

508. Heinsius has *fregit.* with a period; it is better with a question mark: *fregit?* (“did it break?”).

509. Gis. has *imo ita id est* (“rather, this is how it is”). The manuscripts, with the hiatus of which we have often spoken, have *imo ita est* (“rather, so it is”).

510. Vat. A, against meter and sense, has *gloria fugat* (“glory drives away”). Egm. has *fugat*; above, *inanis gloria fugit* (“empty glory flees”). Tertullian, chapter 25 of the *Apology*: “Would Juno have wished the Punic city, preferred to her beloved Samos and beloved, certainly, by the race of Aeneas, to be destroyed? As far as I know, here were her arms, here her chariot; the goddess was already striving and fostering that this kingdom should belong to the nations, if the fates allowed it. That wretched wife and sister of Jupiter could not prevail against the fates.” Clearly Jupiter himself stands subject to fate.

512. Rat. has *latae procinctus*, and the gloss above says that *procinctus* is plural. Weitzius printed *late procinctus*, but in the variant readings writes *nate procinctus* with Widm. and Bong. I think *nate* has fallen out in place of *late*. The other Rott. also has *late procinctus*. In Thuan., both Bohers, Egm., Aldus, Oxon., Alex., Jureti’s and Gifanius’ manuscripts, there is *natae ad procinctus*. The earlier Rott., Cauch., Urb., Vat. A, and Teol. have *natae ad procinctum*, which seems more harmonious to Heinsius, although he printed *natae ad procinctus*. Heinsius and Juretus do not seem to have noticed that Giselinus’ error *natae procinctus* had been corrected by Giselinus himself to *natae ad procinctus*. Mariettus thinks the reading of the Regensburg manuscript, *latae procinctus*, is genuine, with *procinctus* as the accusative of *latae*, meaning “having extensive forces.” The better reading is *genti natae ad procinctus*, or *procinctum*, that is, “born for war.”

514. Vat. A corruptly has *nunc cum dicta eis*. Aldus, Widm. above, Pal., Teol., Jureti’s manuscript, and Urb. have *tunc* or *tum cum Dictaeis*. Rat., Weitz., Gis., and others have *nunc cum Dictaeis*. Dicte is a mountain of Crete where Jupiter was raised.

515. Vat. A and Urb. have *Samnites*. Vat. A, Urb., Alex., Rat., and others have *gerebat* (“was waging”); Aldus has *gerebant* (“were waging”). Egmond., with some words omitted, has *levi sudoris oleoque et gymnadis arte*, which is corrupt. It was easy for the Roman army, says Prudentius, which consisted of Marsi, Samnites, and Etruscans, to defeat in war the Phrygians in Asia—whom he ironically calls Corybants or Galli, that is, priests of Cybele—and even the Lacedaemonians, dripping with oil like boxers and *mastigophori*, or attendants of boxers. Giselinus explains it approximately this way. He observes that *Samnitis* is used for *Samnis*, as in the hymn of Saint Hippolytus, and that the first syllable of *pugil* is lengthened, whereas it is shortened in *pugillaris*, hymn 9 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 15, although, as he adds, some derive the former from *pugnus* (“fist”) and the latter from *pungere* (“to prick”). In *pugilibus* the first syllable may be lengthened because of the necessity they mention when three or four short syllables occur together, as in *catholicus*, *strigilibus*, and similar words. In *pugillar* I do not know why some say that the first syllable is necessarily long. As for Giselinus’ statement that the Dictaean Corybants are called Phrygians, it may perhaps be better explained of the Cretans, for in Crete the Corybants were properly Dictaean, so that they are different from the Corybants mentioned at verse 522.]

Europe and Libya to you: name the gods.

Jupiter, so that you might rule Crete; Pallas, so that you might rule Argos;

Cynthius, so that you might rule Delphi—granted them to you under a favorable omen.

Isis left the Egyptians; Cytherea left the Rhodians.

The virgin huntress gave Ephesus, Mars gave the Hebrus.

[495] Bromius abandoned Thebes, and Juno herself granted

Her Africans to serve the Phrygian descendants.

And the goddess, if the fates should permit it, already aimed and fostered

That she should be mistress of subject nations,

And ordered her to live subjected to Romulean reins.

[500] Was it through the treachery of native gods that so many cities fell?

And do the altars lie destroyed, with the gods themselves betraying them?

805 O piety, O sacred faith! Faithless majesty led

[Column 0218A] Its dependents elsewhere, and people believe in those

Divine powers who deserved consecration by desertion?

[505] Or did religion wish to preserve her own, and, after struggling greatly,

Attempt to drive back the hostile troops,

Resisting them with Roman armies, but did stronger

Valor crush her in the mournful dust of the battlefield?

Rather, so it is: lacking truth in arms and strength,

[510] Superstition was defeated, and empty glory fled.

Nor was victory difficult or especially arduous for a people

Born for military expeditions, to break the inert

806 Necks of every kind of god and bend them down.

Now the Samnite and Marsian were waging harsh war

[515] With the Dictaean Corybants with little exertion.

[Column 0219A]

[Note: [Column 0219A]

516. *Marrucophoris*: peoples of Asia. *Gymnadis*: of exercise, Iso.

517. *Pugilibus*: with swords, short weapons. *Hetruscus*: Latin, Italian, I.

518. *Petaso*: *petasus*, the footwear of Mercury, with which he used to fly; we also speak of a flying *petasus*. *Petasus* is said to derive from *peto* (“I seek upward”), namely Mercury’s winged sandals and spurs, Iso.

[Column 0219B] 519. *Palaestras*: wrestling exercises, or their games, I.

516. Ald., Weitz., Gis., Jureti’s manuscript, and others have *mastigophoris*, to which Alex.’s *mastigoforis* refers; the word means “whip-bearers.” Rat., Sich., Widm., Bong., the other Rott., have *marrucophoris* or *marrucoforis*; Urb. has *masucoforis*. Both seem to stand for *mastrucophoris*, which, Heinsius says, occurred in the margin of one Weitzian manuscript as a variant reading. To prevent Heinsius from misleading anyone, it should be noted that Heinsius often seems to take the editions cited by Weitzius for Weitzian manuscript codices; thus here G. in the margin means Giselinus’ marginal edition. The *mastrucophori* could then be understood as those who fought with boxing gloves, for *mastruca* or *mastruga* is a leather garment, as will be said shortly. I have no doubt that *mastigophoris* is correct, a word found in the final book of the *Arcadian*, section 1, *On Offices and Honors*: “The *mastigophori* also, who accompany the judges of the games in contests and serve as scribes in the personal office of the magistrate.” Who were called by this name is not agreed by all. Some interpret them as gymnasiarchs, who presided over boxers and, following the example of Mercury, the god of the wrestling grounds, held a rod in their hands with which they restrained the unruly gestures and dissolved the holds of wrestlers; others as whip-bearers for dispersing the crowd; others as the gladiators themselves, because they were accustomed to be beaten; others as those who went before the judges or presidents of the games. Savaro may be consulted, p. 109, on Sidonius.

518. Pal. above has *pegaso*; read *petaso*. The glosses explaining this word depart from the truth, as they do in the case of *pugiles*. *Petasus* comes from the Greek πετάζω, “I stretch out,” and is a hat spread out so as to protect against the sun. Apuleius calls it the shade of a hat, and the Spaniards call it *sombrero*, from “shade.” See Becmanus, *On Origins*.

519. Arnobius, Book III: “Mercury presides over boxing and wrestling with the *ceroma*.”

520. Rat. has *Appenninicolem*, less correctly.

[Column 0220B] 521. Chamillardus does not refer this to Asia, the third part of the world, but to the Trojan region, which was called Asia after the philosopher Asius; for Cybele was not worshiped with special honor throughout all Asia. Maeonia, or Lydia, was also called Asia, whence the Asian marsh. Troy was situated in Asia Minor, and not far away was Mount Ida, where Cybele was especially worshiped.

522. The priests of Cybele were called Galli, and their chief was the Archigallus, either from the river Gallus in Phrygia or from a certain man named Gallus, who perhaps was Cybele’s first priest. Jerome, in his commentary on Hosea, chapter 4, gives another explanation: “These are the men whom today at Rome they call Galli, servants not of the mother of the gods but of demons, because, having been mutilated by lust, the Romans enslaved men of this nation as priests in honor of Attis, whom the prostitute goddess had made a eunuch. They emasculate men of the Gallic nation for this reason, so that those who captured the city of Rome might be struck by this disgrace.” This history seems false to me and ridiculous to others as well. Nor is there lacking someone who suspects that these words were stitched onto the works of Saint Jerome.

523. Understand *Idalias* not as deriving from Mount Ida, as the gloss explains, but from Mount Idalium and its grove in Cyprus. The subject is Venus. Nor do poets derive *Idalius* from Ida, but *Idaeus*, as Prudentius himself says elsewhere. Moreover, it is more appropriate to attribute roses to Idalium and Venus than to Ida and Cybele, or to Ephesus and Diana. In Apollo’s laurel, Delos and Delphi may be understood; in Diana’s bow, Delos and Ephesus.

526. Urb. and Gis. have *difficilisque operis fuit* (“and it was a difficult task”). The old and best manuscripts, including Jureti’s and Gifanius’ manuscripts together with Weitzius, have *difficilis operis*. Gifanius, under the word *INCISIO*, cites many similar passages, which are generally corrupted in widely circulated books because correctors often failed to consider the force of the incision, or caesura, and the poets’ customary practice.

527. Vat. A writes *Acciacis*. Propertius and Virgil say that Antony and Cleopatra used the sistrum in the Actian war. Prudentius calls it a *symphonia*, which is a certain kind of musical instrument; Iso incorrectly calls it a trumpet. Isidore, *Etymologies* III, chapter 22: “A *symphonia* is commonly called a hollow piece of wood with stretched hide on both sides, which musicians strike from either side with rods. From the agreement of low and high it produces the sweetest song.” Jerome, Letter 21, elsewhere 146, to Damasus, says that some Latins wrongly think a *symphonia* is a type of organ, since the word signifies harmonious singing in praise of God: “For *symphonia*,” he says, “is rendered in Latin as consonance.” Yet although this is the first and proper meaning of *symphonia*, custom prevailed so that it came to be understood as a kind of musical instrument. I think this is the sense in which it should be explained in Daniel 3:10: “Whoever hears the sound of the trumpet, pipe, lyre, sambuca, psaltery, symphonia, and every kind of music.” Isidore distinguishes the sistrum from the *symphonia*, although he does not explain what kind of musical instrument the sistrum is. One may consult the dissertation of Francesco Blanchini of Verona, *On Three Kinds of Instruments in the Musical Art of the Ancients*, Rome, 1742, where chapter 3 discusses the class of percussion instruments, to which the *symphonia* and sistrum belong. Plate VIII, figure 12, describes a bronze four-stringed rattle, which is a type of sistrum. Figure 7 of plate VII depicts a military drum, which seems to be Isidore’s *symphonia*. Compare the special dissertation of Benedict Bacchini, *On Sistra and Their Forms and Their Difference*, together with the short treatise and notes added by Jacob Tollius. Mazochius, volume I of the *Specimen Bibliothecae*, pp. 308 and following, discusses at length the *symphonia* mentioned in the book of Daniel and argues that it is a pipe or flute, also called an *ambubaja*. It is probable that the same name denoted different instruments at different times and in different places.]

529. Ald., Widm. in the margin, Jureti’s manuscript, Egm., Oxon., Urb., and the earlier Rott. have: “The slender boats and fragile skiffs stood in line,” which Heinsius considers correct because Prudentius ironically compares the Egyptian boats with the Roman Liburnians. ### 530

Liburnian ships, or liburnae, were a type of very swift vessel, deriving their name from the Liburnians, peoples of Illyria. Horace, Propertius, and Suetonius relate that Augustus used liburnian ships against Antony. Dio and Florus record that Antony’s ships were much larger than Augustus’s. But why does Prudentius call the liburnians “towered”? Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XII, chapter 14, asks whether, in Horace’s verses (*Epodes* 1: “You shall sail among the high bulwarks of the liburnian ships, Maecenas”), Maecenas was to proceed among the bulwarks and towers of the high ships, or among the high bulwarks and towered masses of the liburnians themselves. He answers that Horace’s words admit the former interpretation, on the basis of Dio and Florus, who celebrate the size of Antony’s ships; but the latter is supported by this verse of Prudentius and by another passage of Propertius, book III, elegy 9:

> She dared to set barking Anubis against our Jupiter,  
> and to compel the Tiber to bear the threats of the Nile;  
> to drive back the Roman trumpet with the rattling sistrum,  
> and to make the Liburnian prows follow barides and poles.

Grangaeus, however, recognizes a hypallage in Prudentius’ verse, as though Prudentius wished to say that the towered Egyptian ships, when compared with Augustus’s liburnians, were like a *phaselus*, or some extremely light skiff. He interprets Propertius in the same way, as though all Antony’s equipment had been like the poles of some small skiff. I think that there were two kinds of liburnians, one of small size and the other large, both valued for their speed. In Horace I understand the high bulwarks to be those of the liburnians themselves, and in Prudentius I understand those same liburnians to have been towered. Antony’s ships were not therefore small; rather, Prudentius compares them with slender, fragile *phaseli*, and Propertius with barides—that is, Egyptian little boats—because they were defeated with the greatest ease by Augustus’s fleet. Indeed, I readily agree with Dio and Florus that Antony’s ships were larger. Virgil calls the ships of both Augustus and Antony towered in book VIII:

> You might think the Cyclades had been torn loose and were floating on the sea,  
> or mountains were colliding with other mountains:  
> with such mass the men press upon towered sterns.

Yet I will conceal nothing: Prudentius seems to assert that Augustus’s liburnians were larger than Antony’s Egyptian ships, for he asks why Augustus conquered Antony without the aid of the gods. See Scheffer, *On the Varieties of Ships*, and Vossius, *On Triremes and Liburnians and Their Construction*.

### 531

See Propertius, quoted above; Virgil, at the passage indicated; and Saint Augustine, *Confessions* VIII.2:

> The monsters of gods of every kind, and barking Anubis, which had once borne arms against Neptune, Venus, and Minerva, and which Rome, now conquered by them, was already imploring, etc.

Augustine is speaking there of the rhetorician Victorinus, converted to the faith in old age, who had previously defended those monsters together with almost the whole Roman nobility.

### 532

Urb., Sich., and some others read *ductor exercitus* (“leader of the army”). Heinsius conjectures *ductorem exercitus ardens* (“the fiery leader of the army”), which I do not approve.

### 533

Alex. reads *miserat Alcidus*. For this reading Weitzius cites Aldus, since he evidently did not notice that in the corrected edition Aldus substituted *Algidus*. Heinsius says that Aldus has *gelido quam miserat Alcidus axe*; I find in Aldus *quem miserat Algidus*. Cauchius found in his books *gelido quem miserat arctos ab axe*, and took it to refer to the tyrant Maximus, who unsuccessfully undertook an expedition from the West against Theodosius. Yet everyone sees that the discussion still concerns the battle of Actium. The later Rottendorfian edition has *boreae quem miserat algidus axis*, which Heinsius followed, since talk of Mount Algidus is nonsense. Sichardus perhaps has the same reference in *gelido quem miserat algidus axis*. Chamillardus, Cellarius, and Teolius follow Heinsius. But Rat., Urb., Ald., Weitz., Gis., and others read *gelido quem miserat Algidus axe*, so that Mount Algidus, twenty miles from Rome, is understood. Grangaeus adds the conjecture that Augustus’s liburnians were built from the timber of this mountain, for Horace says in book III, ode 23:

> For the oak that feeds on snowy Algidus  
> is devoted among oaks and ilexes.

The same Horace says in book I, ode 21:

> And whatever woodland foliage  
> rises above cold Algidus.

Gronovius, chapter 5 of the *Ecclesiastical Observations*, prefers the reading of the Rottendorfian edition, *boreae quem miserat algidus axis*, because Italy, lying opposite Egypt, faces north. I prefer the more common reading of the manuscripts, *gelido quem miserat Algidus axe*. Just as above he named the Samnites and Marsi, so now he names Algidus, a snowy and cold mountain, in order to signify a hardy people whom he opposes to Antony’s effeminate army.

### Editorial notes

540. Rat. and Fabr. read *cultu celebris* (“celebrated in worship”).

544. The Juretus manuscript, Ald., Vat. A, Alex., Urb., Cauch., most of Heinsius’s manuscripts, and Pal. read *custodibus arcis* (“the guardians of the citadel”). Rat. reads *custodibus ultro*. Gis., Weitz., the other Rottendorfian manuscript, and Boher. read *caesis custodibus, ultro legit* (“having slain the guards, he chose it”). The first reading is confirmed by the passage and by the verse of Virgil that Prudentius imitates, *Aeneid* II:

> The Palladium, after the guardians of the lofty citadel had been slain.

545. Ald., Fab., Thuanus, Heinsius’s older editions, Alex., Urb., and Vat. A read *legit, ubi*. Sich., Gis. in the margin of the first edition, Rat., and Weitz. with his manuscripts read *legit, ut*. Vat. A has the erroneous *sugillo* for *sigillo*. Prudentius elsewhere also uses *sigillum* for a statue; here, however, he uses it strictly for the Palladium, about which Apollodorus writes in *Bibliotheca* III. It had fallen from heaven and had been given to King Ilus. It was three cubits high, in the form of a person advancing; in its right hand it held a raised spear, and in its left a distaff and spindle. Apollodorus recounts its history at length. Prudentius is referring to the Virgilian passage cited above:

> Scarcely had the image been placed in the camp when flashing flames blazed from its uplifted eyes, and salty sweat ran through its limbs.

546. Vat. A reads *altus*, incorrectly, for *altos*. The older Heinsian manuscripts, together with Oxon. and the earlier Rottendorfian manuscript, read *ductor Macetum*, which later editions retain—not improperly, since *Macedo* and *Maceta* designate the same people.

547. Sich., Gis. in the margin of the first edition, Fabr., Bong., and Cauch. read *cumulavit ab Indis* (“he piled up from the Indians”). Heinsius conjectured *Aphidnis*, which belonged to Lacedaemonian territory, for the passage concerns the war Alexander the Great waged against the Lacedaemonians. He later recognized that *Amyclis* also fits the passage. In fact, most read it thus; just as Lacedaemon is a city and the royal seat of Menelaus in the Peloponnese, Amyclae is likewise a city in the Peloponnese, the royal seat of Tyndareus and the birthplace of Castor and Pollux. *Aphidnae* is a less familiar name in ancient writers.

548. Egm. reads *dominis*, which is not very satisfactory.

549. Fabr. and Gis. in the margin read *Assyriaque vehi Babylonis ab arce*. Bong. reads *Assyriaeque vehi Babylonis ab arce*. *Ad arcem* is better. Alexander died at Babylon.

550. On the phrase *sudataque bella*, see *Hymn* 2 *Catholicorum*, verse 76.

553. Some write *deminuit*, others *diminuit*. Someone might ask whether those who attribute everything bravely accomplished by Christian soldiers to the special assistance of God diminish the rewards in the same way. But Christians, who freely confess that they possess nothing they have not received from God, attribute with even greater willingness to that same benevolence whatever is shown to have been accomplished by his special assistance. Human good works, freely performed by human beings themselves, do not therefore lack glory or reward.

554. What he says about Venus should also be understood of the other gods, although a temple of Venus Victrix was dedicated at Rome by Pompey, and emperors commonly attributed their victories to Venus Victrix, as is remembered on ancient coins.

555. Rat., the other Rottendorfian manuscript, and Weitz. read *summa miramur in arce* (“we marvel at the summit in the citadel”). Most read *summo miramur in arcu* (“we marvel at the top of the arch”). The Juretus manuscript has *mirantur*. Heinsius says that *arx* may refer to the Capitol, while *arcus* designates triumphal arches. See also what I noted about *arcus* and *arx* at verse 523 of the *Apotheosis*.

556. Pal. and Egm. have *quadrijugo*, erroneously. Juvenal, *Satire* 8.3:

> And the Aemilian figures standing in chariots.

558. Triumphal statues were represented with enemies lying and prostrate at their feet, as may still be seen. Statius, in *The Great Horse*:

> Instead of empty turf, beneath the bronze hoof  
> the captive Rhine grinds his hair.

Propertius, book IV, final elegy:

> Beneath whose inscriptions, Africa, shorn, you lie.

The *tituli* are the inscriptions on the bases.

559. The Juretus manuscript reads *depressis*, less appropriately.

560. Properly speaking, trophies were headless bodies bearing spoils, such as still exist at Rome before the Capitol and are said to have been erected by Marius. The ancients also used towers, altars, and columns as trophies; indeed, even rough tree trunks on which they hung spoils. These matters are explained at length in Ouzelius’s notes on Minucius, p. 229, where he explains Minucius’s words:

> As many spoils from the gods as from nations, and trophies.

562. Vat. A reads *Flora, Ceres, Matuta*; others, *Flora, Matuta, Ceres*. Egm. and Alex. in its first hand read *Larentina*, which seems to Heinsius better than *Laurentina*. Weitzius attributes *Larventina* to the Egmond manuscript; Heinsius has more correctly read *Larentina*. She was the wife of Faustulus and nurse of Remus and Romulus; the Larentalia were instituted in her honor. Matuta is the goddess presiding over the morning. Hence the reading of Vat. A better accords with the meter and should therefore be preferred.

> But you say that the gods had chosen [the places] where the more sacred observance  
> of temples would endure without end in celebrated worship,  
> and that, out of love for King Numa, they voluntarily followed  
> the victorious standards of the men descended from Aeneas, without compulsion.  
>   
> Did Pallas likewise willingly choose the tents of Diomedes  
> and the camp of fierce Ulysses, after the citadel’s guards had been slain,  
> when the mournful image sweated in the damp?  
>   
> Or how often did the mightiest leader of the Macedonians  
> heap up the ashes of temples upon conquered Amyclae?  
> Did their masters wish the captive divine powers to be mingled with the spoils  
> and to be carried to the citadel of Assyrian Babylon?  
>   
> I cannot endure, Roman name, that your hard-won wars  
> and honors acquired with so much blood should be censured.  
> He detracts from the unconquered legions and diminishes Rome’s rewards  
> who attributes everything bravely accomplished to Venus;  
> he takes the palm from the victors.  
>   
> In vain, therefore, do we admire on the summit of the arch  
> the four-horse chariots and the commanders standing on lofty chariots:  
> Fabricii, Curii, then Drusi, and Camilli;  
> and beneath the commanders’ feet, captives with bent knees,  
> pressed down beneath the yokes, their hands twisted behind their backs,  
> and fragments of weapons hung upon a heavy trunk—  
> if Brennus, Antiochus, Perseus, Pyrrhus, and Mithridates  
> subdued Flora, Ceres, Matuta, and Larentina.

### Editorial notes

564. Meursius found *omnia* in some ordinary editions and correctly observed in his notes on Arnobius that it should be corrected to *omina*. Aldus had anticipated this, and Weitzius followed him. The reading *omina* is confirmed by our better manuscripts, by the better Heinsian manuscripts, and by the Juretus manuscript.

566. Livy, book VII, chapter 25, tells this story. The raven, fighting on behalf of Marcus Valerius, harassed the Gallic enemy with its beak, claws, and wings. Why Prudentius says *gutture* (“with its throat”) may be explained by the raven’s song and prophetic cry, as though it had leapt upon the Gaul croaking. Virgil, *Georgics* I.410:

> Three times the ravens repeat their voices from their constricted throats,

and verse 423:

> The ravens rejoicing in their throats.

568. *Funera* is sometimes used for the bodies of the dead.

569. Florus, book II, chapter 6, on this slaughter:

> Paulus was ashamed; Varro did not despair.

570. Rat., Urb., Widm., and Bong. read *partha*; Fabr. reads *parta*. Latinius also seems to have found *parta* in the Tornesian edition, and substituted *parra*, as most write it. Some have *parrha*, which amounts to the same thing. The call of the *parra* is extremely unpleasant. Horace, book III, ode 27:

> May the omen of the croaking *parra* pursue the impious.

Birds are called *oscines* when they give omens by their mouths, just as *alites* give them by their wings. The gloss says that Cremera was a town; most say that it was a river in Etruria, and perhaps there was both a river and a town of that name. Some count the Fabii who perished as three hundred and six; but a round number is often given even by those who know that some variation exists. Ovidius at one point says three hundred, at another three hundred and six. Poets enjoy greater license in these matters, since they serve their meters. Juvenal joins these two disasters, *Satires* II:

> What of the legion destroyed at Cremera, and the youth consumed at Cannae?

In Rome in 1784 there appeared a *Letter on the Killing of the 306 Fabii*. Its anonymous author proves by conjecture that not all belonged to the Fabian family, but that most were connected with it through blood relationship, clientship, or some other bond.

571. The Juretus manuscript reads *novit*; Vat. A, *juvit*: read *monuit*. None of the gods warned that three hundred would perish through the *cornix* or *parra* as an omen-bird. Aldus incorrectly punctuates *parra*. *Nemo deum* is a noteworthy expression: *nemo* is ordinarily said of a human being, meaning “no man.” Prudentius also says *nemo dies* in the *Romanus*, verse 744, a usage I do not find elsewhere. Virgil, book IX:

> Turnus, which no one of the gods would dare promise to one who wished it.

573. Alex. writes *Carrhis*; Urb. and Ald., *Carris*; Rat., *Charris*. Crassus was scattered and routed by the Parthians at Carrhae; histories of that disaster are readily available. Carrhae, however, is not a people, as the gloss says, but a Mesopotamian city named from the neighboring river. Some say that Carrhae was a city of Arabia.

576. Ald. and Urb. have *lembum*, which Grangaeus interprets as “belt.” Cauchius explains it as Venus’s girdle; he had found *libum* in his manuscripts. Fabr. reads *nimbum*, meaning “splendor,” which, as Servius says, is always associated with divinities. Our older manuscripts and the Heinsian manuscripts have *limbum*. Rat. writes *lymbum*. In place of *Persica*, *Parthica* may perhaps be read, although at that time the Parthians controlled the Persian empire.

578. Urb. and Weitz. read *dices*; Rat., *dicens*; Alex. and other editions and manuscripts, *dicis*.

579. Rat., in a recent hand with the earlier text erased, has *cuncta* for *quaeque*. The same manuscript has *retexit*; above, *retexis*.

581. *Fercula* ordinarily means courses of meat; sometimes it means frameworks on which spoils are carried in a triumphal procession. Pliny uses *fercula* in this same sense in the *Panegyric on Trajan*, where he vividly describes a triumph.

583. Ald., Alex., Gis., and others read *fortibus*. Rat., Urb., Widm., the other Rottendorfian manuscript, and two Boher manuscripts read *fotibus*, a reading later followed by Weitzius and others in their editions. Iso recognizes both readings. Rittershusius added *fontibus* in the margin of his book; someone later conjectured that *fotibus* arose from *fontibus*. On the phrase *in tantum*, see the note on verse 153 of the *Hamartigenia*.

> Yet by these auspices success was granted by a favorable right hand:  
> auspices bringing joy, and a fortunate bird was present.  
>   
> What does valor mean, what glory, if the raven of Apollo  
> helped Corvinus by wing or throat?  
>   
> Yet why was this raven absent on that fatal day,  
> when corpses covered ill-fated Cannae,  
> and the consul would die upon the piled-up corpses?  
>   
> Why, on the fields of Cremera, did no god warn  
> by a crow or prophetic *parra* that three hundred Fabii  
> would perish in adverse battle, scarcely one branch of the stock surviving?  
>   
> Did no mournful owl of Tritonia, flying to Carrhae,  
> announce to Crassus that the goddess was present?  
> Or did the snowy doves carry the Paphian goddess,  
> at whose gilded hem the Persian people would tremble?  
>   
> But I see what examples of ancient valor move you:  
> you say that the world was subdued by land and sea;  
> you recount joyful circumstances and every success;  
> you recall, in order, a thousand triumphal processions,  
> and the frames bearing spoils drawn through the heart of Rome.  
>   
> Do you wish me to say what cause raised your labors, O Roman,  
> to such a height, by what supports your glory was increased?

### Editorial notes

584. Rat. has *sic cluet*; Bong. and Widm., *quis valet*; above, *cluat*. Sich. reads *sic valet*.

591. Arator, book I of the *History of the Apostles*:

> You see that one heart resides in so many distinguished ranks,  
> and that the people acquire one soul.

Prudentius advances the same idea in the hymn to Saint Lawrence, and I do not see what could be devised better for persuading people of the unity of religion under one head.

593. Vat. A has the erroneous *placidissimum*.

594. Widm. above, Gis. in the margin of the first edition, and Urb. read *seminis humani*, which is not very good. The Juretus manuscript, Vat. A, Egm., and Pal. read *orbem*. Others have *orbi*.

597. Rat., in a recent hand with the earlier text erased, has *in terris, occasu quas vagus ambit*. Alex., Oxon., Thuan., and the earlier Boher manuscript read *quas distinet occidualis*. Ald., Vat. A, Rat., Urb., and the older editions read *quas continet occidualis*. Heinsius and later editors read *destinet*.

598. In Vat. A the conjunction *que* after *roseo* is missing.

600. Alex., Vat. A, Ald., Weitz. with most of his manuscripts read *armabatque*. Bong., Gis., Urb., and Fabr. read *armoratque*. Heinsius followed Giselinus but did not report the variant. Rat. has *armaratque ferens*; above, *feras*. Marietto preferred *ferens*, which stands there without any erasure, rather than *feras*, which was written above by another hand.

604. Iso takes *Tagus* as a river of Thrace. Perhaps *Lusitaniae* should be read. Everyone agrees that the gold-bearing Tagus is a river of Spain, and I have heard nothing of another river named Tagus.

605. Rat. corruptly has *coniger Hesperidum*. In the same manuscript a recent scholar, after erasing the earlier text, added from his own resources:

> The ruler of the waters of the Hesperides,  
> between whose rivers he flows; and the seven mouths of the warm Nile bathe  
> [him]. The Ganges also nourishes him, alone stretching toward the rising sun,  
> spreading through uncertain springs into a broad river.

Widm. wrongly has *et quas* for *et quos*. The Tiber seems to be indicated; Virgil, book VIII, says:

> The horn-bearing river of the Hesperides, ruler of the waters.

Rivers are called horn-bearing by poets. In Virgil, Lucretius, Ovid, and others, the horns of rivers are their bends and winding courses. Others explain the expression differently; some think that the force of the waters is represented by horns, as power is represented in Sacred Scripture.

606. Alex. writes *Ganges*; others have *Gangis*, like *Joannis* and *famis*. Gis. in the second edition has *trepidique*; more correctly in the first edition, together with other editions and manuscripts, *tepidique*. The Nile is indeed called warm by Juvenal, Propertius, and others, because, when the snow melts through heat, it floods Egypt.

611. Gis. in the text has *concilientur*; in the margin, with the manuscripts, *conciliemur*. Egm. has *conciliamur*. Rome is called the common fatherland by Cicero, Seneca the Philosopher, Claudian, Symmachus, and others. It is also so called in Digest 50.1.33 and 26.7.4. This explains why Ulpian writes in Digest 48.22.7 that a person forbidden his fatherland was also required to stay away from Rome. Claudian, *On the Consulship of Stilicho* III, develops several ideas agreeing with these verses.

615. Nuptial beds prepared for girls who were marrying were properly called *geniales lecti*.

616. Juretus had found in a certain sheet *aeterni ad jus connubii* (“of the eternal right of marriage”), a reading he rightly rejects. Ulpian, book of the *Rules*, title 5, writes that Roman citizens had the right of marriage with Roman citizens, but with Latins and foreigners only if it had been granted. The ancient custom is likewise evident from Seneca, *On Benefits* IV.35:

> I promised you my daughter in marriage; afterward you appeared to be a foreigner. I have no right of marriage with a stranger. The same law protects me that forbids it.

There are, however, records of the right of marriage being granted to Roman citizens with barbarians and foreigners; today such a grant would be called a dispensation. From Prudentius’s words interpreters infer—and Juretus states this regarding the passage—that in Prudentius’s time the ancient custom by which foreigners were excluded from the Roman right of marriage had fallen into disuse. A distinction is nevertheless necessary. Macrobius, writing in the same age, states that foreigners had no customary marriage relationship with Romans. Moreover, in the Theodosian Code III.14 there is a constitution of Valentinian stating that no provincial, whatever his rank or place, should have a marriage with a barbarian wife, nor should any barbarian marry a provincial woman; if such marriages occurred, it threatened capital punishment. This is the sole law of that title, enacted in the year 370. Here *gentiles* does not mean unbelievers or pagans, but barbarians, specifically those who had come from various peoples into the Roman Empire. Gothofred rejects the opinion of those who think that, under the famous constitution of Antoninus mentioned in Digest 1.5.17, *De statu hominum*, all barbarians admitted into the Roman armies were to be counted among Roman citizens. Prudentius mentions the right of marriage with foreigners as something new and as a fruit of the received Gospel. After Valentinian, such marriages began to be requested and granted by imperial rescript; and because Valentinian’s law had been abolished, Tribonian omitted it.

> Thus one offspring is woven from peoples joined in turn.  
>   
> This was accomplished through the great successes and triumphs  
> of the Roman Empire. Believe me: for Christ, already then approaching,  
> the way had been prepared, which the public friendship of our peace  
> had long since built under Rome’s governance.  
>   
> For what place could there be for God in a savage world,  
> with human hearts at odds and each defending its own laws  
> according to a different order, as it once was?  
>   
> Thus, when the feelings in the human breast were disordered  
> and the parts of the soul separated by a troubled bond,  
> neither clear wisdom visited them nor did God enter.  
>   
> But if the summit of the mind, having obtained the right to rule,  
> restrains the impulses of the combative stomach and rebellious fibers,  
> and governs the whole liver by a single rational principle,  
> the condition of life becomes stable, and the settled judgment  
> draws God into the heart and is subjected to one master.  
>   
> Behold, Almighty, enter and flow into lands made harmonious:  
> now the world contains you, O Christ, which peace and Rome  
> hold together in a gathered bond. You command these to be  
> the heads and summits of affairs, and Rome is not approved by you without peace.  
>   
> Rome’s excellence makes peace pleasing:  
> she restrains diverse movements at once by her rule  
> and suppresses them by terror. For she has not grown old, stripped  
> of her former strength; she has not felt the passage of the ages;  
> nor, when wars summon her, does she grasp arms with trembling muscles;  
> nor does she plead with so degenerate a mouth before venerable rulers  
> as that famous senator, skilled in the art of entreaty  
> and trained in cunningly feigning  
> the weight of a solemn mask,  
> as a tragic actor covers his face with hollowed wood  
> so that some great crime may breathe through its opening.

### Editorial notes

621. In the Parma edition, *paci* is a mistake for *pacis*, contrary to the meter.

622. Heinsius printed *possit*; but since other editions and manuscripts have *posset*, and that reading better suits the sense, I think *possit* arose by omission for *posset*. Chamillardus followed Heinsius and printed *possit*.

623. Aldus printed *rectoribusque hominum*. Since this conflicted with the meter, he corrected it to *principibusque*. The true reading is *pectoribusque*.

627. Wisdom of Solomon 1:4:

> For wisdom will not enter a malevolent soul, nor dwell in a body subjected to sins.

628. Egm. and Vat. A in their original hands read *ut si*.

633. Ald. has *una ades*; others, *en ades*.

635. Rat. has *pax, et Roma tenet*.

641. Florus, book I, chapter 1, concerning Rome:

> Through the inactivity of the Caesars she had, as it were, grown old and withered, except that under the emperor Trajan she moved her limbs.

646. Vat. A erroneously has *ora caveto*. Virgil, *Georgics* II:

> And they put dreadful faces on with hollowed bark.

See Bulengerus, *On the Theater* I.45. The tragic singer is a tragic actor; *singer* is used for *actor*, as some think, by Horace in the *Art of Poetry*:

> Until the singer says, “You applaud.”

Aeschylus first introduced a mask into the theater, or a false face made from hollowed wood, through whose opening the words could be heard. See Ficoroni, *On Theatrical Masks*.

647. *Hiatus* is used of tragic actors by Juvenal, Persius, and others, properly of the opening of the mask. Juvenal, *Satire* 3:

> The rustic child fears, in his mother’s lap,  
> the opening of the pale mask.

Lucian describes masks and the other theatrical decorations in *On Dancing*. Grangaeus says that some manuscripts have *carmen anhelet* (“let him breathe out a song”), but that *crimen* (“crime”) is better, since in the tragedies of the pagans there are as many crimes as songs, so that Prudentius elegantly says that tragic actors breathed out not songs but crimes. I would gladly adopt *carmen* if I had suitable authorities; Juvenal supports it in a similar passage, *Satire* 6.635:

> We revel in a great song through Sophoclean opening.

The old scholiast interprets this as “we write tragedy.” You see the words *carmen*, *grande*, and *hiatu*, which seem to have been transferred into Prudentius’s verse; for *anhelet* is correctly placed in place of *bacchamur*. Nor do I see why all the songs of pagan tragedies should be called crimes. Rather, retaining the common reading, I take *crimen* not of the song but of the subject matter itself of tragedy, which generally concerns some great crime.

After this verse come Symmachus’s words:

> Let us now imagine Rome standing before us and addressing you in these words: “Excellent emperors, fathers of your country, respect my years, into which pious custom has brought me. I shall use the ceremonies of my ancestors; I do not regret it. I shall live according to my own custom, because I am free. This worship brought the world under my laws. These rites drove Hannibal from the walls and the Senones from the Capitol. [Was I preserved for this, to be censured in my old age? Shall I see what is thought necessary to establish? Yet the correction of old age, coming late, is insulting.] Therefore we ask peace from our ancestral gods, the gods who dwell within.”

The words enclosed in brackets are absent from Aldus and others, but are found in Giselinus and Heinsius. Vat. A is extremely corrupt in these and other words of Symmachus. It reads *reverimini* for *reveremini* and omits *me* after *in quos*. The other Rottendorfian manuscript has *reverimini canos meos* (“revere my gray hairs”).
