### Editorial notes

651. Jupiter gave his aegis, his shield, to Pallas, who placed upon it the head of Medusa. Here understand Jupiter and Pallas, or rather all the gods.

653. Vat. A and Rat. in their first hand read *fatetur*. Cauch. has *profetur*; read *profatur*.

655. The person praised here is Theodosius the Great, not Constantine, for Honorius and Arcadius were not Constantine’s sons. This also shows that the emperor addressing Rome in book I was Theodosius.

658. Rat. reads *aliud parat aevum* (“he prepares another age”).

659. Vat. A has *quae videndo*; a recent hand correctly changed this to *vivendo*.

[Note: [Col. 0231C]]

**661.** Saint Leo, *Sermon 1 on the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul*: “Having been made the head of the world through the sacred see of blessed Peter, you preside more widely through divine religion than through earthly dominion.” Prosper, *Poem on the Ungrateful*, at the beginning: “The see of Peter, Rome, made the head of the world in pastoral honor, holds by religion whatever it does not contain by arms.”

**665.** Rat.: *persuaserit*, “he will have persuaded”; incorrectly.

**667.** Ald.: *belli*. Vat. A: *scelerare*. Pal.: *sceleraret*. Alex., first hand: *fenere*; second hand: *funere*. Ald., Gis. in the margin: *in funere*. It should be read: *bellis scelerarem funere*. *In funere et belli* can be tolerated.

**670.** Perhaps Prudentius is alluding to Nero’s fire.

**[Col. 0232C] 671.** Weitzius cites Aldus for *post haec* (“after these things”); perhaps he intended to indicate another edition, for in Aldus I read *post hunc* (“after him”). Decius initiated the seventh persecution, as it is commonly counted, but one plainly cruel and very similar to Nero’s. The distinguished Franciscus Maria Luchinius discussed the persecutions of Christians under pagan emperors with acute judgment and extensive learning in the preface to his Italian translation of Ruinart’s *Acts of the Martyrs*. He distinguishes and explains eleven persecutions: the first under Nero, the second under Domitian, the third under Trajan, the fourth under Marcus Aurelius, the fifth under Severus, the sixth under Maximinus, the seventh under Decius, the eighth **[Col. 0232D]** under Valerian, the ninth under Aurelian, the tenth under Diocletian, and the eleventh under Julian the Apostate.

**672.** Ald.: *mox haec sitis*, “soon this thirst.”

**674.** Egm., Gis. in the margin: *et trahere*, “and to drag.” Giselinus says in his notes that *extrahere* (“to draw out”) can be tolerated, although he prefers the reading of his manuscript and of the Daventrian edition, so that *per vulnera tristia animas trahere* (“to drag souls through grievous wounds”) should mean the same as *ludere poenis* (“to sport with punishments”). Vat. A has the erroneous *extraxere*. “To sport with punishments” aptly corresponds to the various tortures inflicted upon Christians. Tacitus, *Annals* XV.44: “And mockeries were added to those dying, so that, covered with the skins of wild beasts, they might perish by the tearing of dogs, or, fastened to crosses, or set alight, and, when daylight failed, be burned for use as nocturnal illumination.”

**675.** Alex., with others: *defundere*. Urb. and others: *diffundere*. Virgil, *Aeneid* X, at the end: “And he pours out his life-blood in a flood upon the weapons.” This is also the place to observe the audacity of those who deny that the number of the holy martyrs was great.

---

**819.** “If I may imitate a voice—namely, this voice is more fitting for Rome than the one I shall now utter in her name.

**[650]** She, because she thinks it shameful to lament the rejection of temples,

to say that the aegis fought on her behalf in doubtful dangers,

and to admit that she is bowed by advancing old age,

having embraced her leaders, thus speaks joyfully:

‘Hail, illustrious leaders, noble offspring

**[655]** of the unconquered prince, under whom all my old age was renewed,

I laid aside my senescence and saw my gray hair

become golden again. For although old age diminishes

all mortal things,

**820** long time gives me another age.

**[Col. 0231B]** Through long life I have learned to despise death.

**[660]** Now, now, the proper reverence is due to my years;

now I am rightly called venerable and the head of the world,

as I shake my helmet beneath an olive branch and my red crests,

**[Col. 0232A]** veiling my warlike belts with a green garland,

and, armed, worship God without the guilt of slaughter.

**[665]** For, alas, savage Jupiter had persuaded me

to stain the sword accustomed to wars with the sacred blood of the righteous in a criminal slaughter.

At his instigation Nero was first: after killing his mother,

he drank apostolic blood and polluted me

**[670]** with the slaughter of the godly; in his savagery he forced his own crime upon me.

After him Decius, raging amid exposed throats,

fed his insane fury. Soon a thirst also burned,

**821** similar to that of many others, blazing through grievous wounds,

**[Col. 0232B]** to drag out illustrious souls and sport with punishments,

**[675]** to pour deaths in floods into my lap

and cut innocent necks under the law of the court.

Your age has now cleansed me of this stain.’”

---

[Note: [Col. 0233B]]

**680.** *Tradidit*: “he taught,” “he instructed.”

**681.** *Inolescere*: “to grow”; *dies festos*: “festive days.”

**685.** *Libyn*: “the African.”

**688.** *Saxo*: “on the Capitoline.”

**690.** *Inculcant*: “they charge against me,” “they impute.”

**695.** *Geticus*: Radagaisus or Alaric.

**696.** *Istro*: the Danube.

**698.** *Mastrugis*: *mastruga*, as though “a monstrous garment,” made from skins; we also call *mastrugae* *renones*, which in rustic language are called *crotinae*.

**699.** *Venetos*: Venice.

**700.** *Ligurum*: Liguria, a maritime and pleasant region.

**701.** *Victo amne*: having crossed the Tiber.

**704.** *Cruda*: strong. *Congredientum*: of those fighting.

[Note: [Col. 0233B]]

**678.** Vat. A, Pal., and Egm. erroneously have *vobis aucta mihi impia* (“impious things increased for me by you”).

**682.** Vat. A: *saevit*; read *saeviit* (“he raged”).

**683.** Ald.: *qui vobis* (“who for you”). This was an old complaint of the pagans against Christians. Arnobius, Book I: “For when you are accustomed to cast up against us the frequency of wars, their causes, the devastations of cities, and the incursions of Germans and Scythians—and I say this with your peace and kind permission—what is the character of this statement you make? You do not see it, through a lust for slander.” Even when they had no hope left of recovering the ancient worship of idols, they renewed complaints of this kind. To blunt them, Saint Augustine wrote his books *On the City of God*, and he prompted Orosius to compose books of history and to record individually the disasters that had occurred before Christianity.

**686.** Prudentius refutes the words of Symmachus. It was reported that Hannibal was deterred by thunderbolts when he was attacking Rome. “Whether heaven thunders, or Rome,” says Claudianus in *On the Gothic War*.

**688.** Urb., Egm., Widm., and Bong. write *ecelso*, which Weitzius printed. Heinsius says that the manuscripts have *e celso*. But Alex., Rat., and Ald., Gis., and others have *excelso*, and I think this is itself *ecelso*, although it could also be divided as *e celso*. Virgil, *Aeneid* IX: “While the immovable Capitoline rock borders the house of Aeneas.”

**691.** Vat. A: *nullis*; correct to *nullus*.

**692.** Virgil and Juvenal speak of the bars of gates, as do Catullus, Ovid, and Seneca in nearly the same way. Savaro interprets this passage in his notes on Sidonius, *Letter* 2, Book I, concerning the Goths. Grangaeus says that it must certainly be understood of the Gauls, who differed from the Romans in weapons, clothing, and hair: “No barbarian enemy, like Hannibal, shakes my gates with his spear; no stranger in weapons, clothing, and hair, like the soldier of Brennus and the army of the Senones, wanders at large through the captured city.” I approve this interpretation more.

**695.** The “Getic tyrant” is Alaric. The Goths were called Getae. The title of Claudian’s poem is *On the Getic War*, or *On the Pollentian War*.

**696.** Although the Goths had come from the north, they had long been settled beside the Hister; hence he calls it their ancestral Hister. He also alludes to the barbarian custom of swearing by rivers. Claudianus, likewise concerning Alaric, in *On the Getic War*: “He had sworn by the divinity of his ancestral Hister.” The Romans and Greeks too relate in their myths that rivers possess some divinity.

**698.** Alex.: *astrucis*; above, *mastrucis*. Rat.: *mastrugis*, the reading retained by Weitzius; others write *mastrucis* or *mastrycis*. A *mastruca* was a garment made from the skins of wild beasts, which Cicero attributes to the Sardinians. Quintilian, Book I, chapter 5: “Cicero deliberately mocked *mastruca*, a Sardinian word.” Isidore preserved Cicero’s words. Jerome, *Dialogue 1 against the Luciferians*: “He defended, not without reason, that Christ had died, and that the Son of God had descended not merely because of a Sardinian *mastruca*.” The Goths wore garments of this kind and are therefore called “skin-clad” by Rutilius and Saint Jerome. Turnebus, *Adversaria* no. 312, says that a *mastruga* was a leather garment, extremely heavy and foul-smelling. The gloss may be connected here with *crotina*. In the same gloss, *renones* are a garment peculiar to the Germans, as is clear from Saint Isidore, *Etymologies* XIX.23. Although a *mastruca* is said to be the characteristic garment of the Sardinians and *rhenones* or *renones* that of the Germans, since both are made of skins, Prudentius correctly uses *mastruca* here. In Saint Isidore some read, “*Mastruca*, a German garment”; but there is no doubt that “a Sardinian garment” must be read, as is demonstrated by the words of Cicero that follow and by chapter 1 of the cited book. To clarify Isidore’s gloss, I add his etymology of *mastruca*: “It is called *mastruca*, as though *monstruosa*, ‘monstrous.’” Concerning garments of skins, Saint Paulinus, *Poem on the Return of Nicetas*: “Both the Getae run, and each Dacian: he who inhabits the middle of the earth, and that neighbor of the rich bank, clothed in the hide of many an ox.” Rosweyd, in his notes, supplies much information about this most ancient clothing of primitive peoples.

**699.** Rat., Weitz., Bong., and Widm.: *prostraverat* (“had overthrown”). Others, including Widm. above: *protriverat* (“had crushed”).

**701.** Isidore understands the river to be the Tiber. Whether correctly, see the commentary on verse 719.

**702.** Ald. has the incorrect *hos equitum nimbus*. Others have *hos nimbos equitum*. Claudianus, *First Consulship of Stilicho*, verse 352: “But he learned … not to withstand with Italian spears the rain poured forth by frequent javelins, nor the showers of horsemen.” Nearly all Roman poets and historians discuss the vigilant goose whose cackling awakened the Romans and caused them to throw down the Gauls as they approached by night.

**704.** Ald., the manuscripts of Heinsius, Alex., Urb., Egm., **[Col. 0235A]** Palat., Widm., and Bong.: *perfractaque*. Fabr. and Gis.: *praefractaque*. Rat.: *perfectaque*. *Praefractaque* seems preferable, for Virgil has the same word in *Aeneid* XI: “And the broken chests of the galloping four-footed creatures crash against chests.”

---

“I live in piety, with you as my authors, though formerly, I confess, impious

through Jupiter’s art. For what did he not hand over stained with blood,

**[680]** or what mild or peaceful thing did he demand for himself?

While he feared beforehand that the worship of Christ

might grow, he raged and defiled the wretched age with blood.

And there are those who do not hesitate to reproach us

for disastrous wars, after we rejected the altars of the temples,

**[685]** and assert that the African Hannibal was driven back from the threshold of the Collina Gate by Jupiter’s and Mars’s command,

**822** and that the victorious Senones were driven from the citadel of the Capitol,

when the gods were fighting upon the lofty rock.

Let those who repeat to me the former disaster and ancient sufferings

**[690]** see that, in your age, I now endure nothing of the kind:

no barbarian enemy shakes my gates with a spear;

**[Col. 0234A]** no stranger in weapons, clothing, and hair

wanders at large through the captured city,

carrying my population beyond the Alps into bondage.

**[695]** Recently the Getic tyrant attempted to destroy Italy,

coming from the ancestral Hister, bound by an oath,

to level these citadels with the ground,

to dissolve the golden roofs in flames,

and to clothe senators who wore the toga in skins.

**823** Already rushing onward, he had crushed the Venetian fields with his troops,

**[700]** ravaged the wealth of the Ligurians and the pleasant country

of deep-soiled Po, and, after crossing the river, was pressing the Tuscan land.

It was not the vigilant goose that drove away these showers of horsemen,

the betrayer of hidden danger in the dark night,

**[Col. 0234B]** but the fierce strength of men and the steadfast breasts of those who fought,

**[705]** **[Col. 0235A]** and a spirit unafraid to submit to death

for their country and to seek beautiful glory through wounds.”

---

[Note: [Col. 0235A]]

**708.** *Dux*: Constantine.

**709.** *Christipotens*: Theodosius, son of Arcadius, consul and father-in-law of Honorius. *Juvenis*: one who was still young.

**[Col. 0236A] 710.** *Utrique*: Constantine and Stilicho.

**712.** *Draconis*: the cross. That Roman standard had a dragon’s head.

[Note: [Col. 0235B]]

**706.** Rat., first hand: *quaerere mortem* (“to seek death”). Virgil, *Aeneid* IX: “And let him hasten toward beautiful death through wounds”; and XI: “And they seek beautiful death through wounds.”

**708.** The glosses concerning Constantine, Theodosius son of Arcadius, and the father-in-law of Honorius are full of anachronisms and errors. Honorius is called leader of the army and of the empire, not because he himself was present at the battle of Pollentia, but because the battle was conducted by Stilicho—or rather, as I shall say in the note on verse 719, by the general Saul—under his auspices and authority. Nor was Honorius far away, since he was residing at Ravenna.

**709.** Stilicho is called the companion of Honorius not so much because of that dignity which in the Middle Ages was called the *comitatus*, as because of his office as Honorius’s guardian, which Theodosius, when near death, entrusted to Stilicho; and because Stilicho gave in marriage to Honorius two daughters born to him by Serena, the sister of Theodosius: first Maria, and then, after her death, Thermantia. For the same reasons he is called a parent. Saint Ambrose, *Funeral Oration for Theodosius*: “For he had nothing new to provide concerning his sons, to whom he had given everything, except to commend them to their present parent.” Claudianus, *Third Consulship of Honorius*, sings that Theodosius, near death, said to Stilicho:

“Come, since heavenly glory summons me;

take my cares upon yourself; alone cherish

my pledges; with your right hand protect

my twin sons … put on a father’s mind.”

From this passage Giselinus conjectures that Prudentius did not live until Stilicho’s treachery and death, which occurred around the year 413, as he says, or rather in 408, as history establishes. Otherwise, he would have introduced Stilicho’s name into his work, just as Virgil substituted “the region of Nola” for Nola itself, because he was angry with the people of Nola. Yet Stilicho’s name could not be erased from all monuments, and it is much more difficult to introduce or alter anything in a written work already published. **[Col. 0235D]** Virgil had not yet published the *Aeneid* when he died, and therefore he was able to erase from the manuscripts whatever he disliked. Teolius disrupts the chronology: “From this,” he says, “it is plainly evident that the poet composed these verses before the year 405, when Stilicho’s downfall occurred.” He adduces a false account of the actual matter, for Stilicho’s downfall did not occur before 408. That I said Stilicho’s name was not erased from all monuments is shown by this inscription:

“TO FLAVIUS STILICHO, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, MASTER OF THE CAVALRY AND INFANTRY, COUNT OF THE DOMESTIC GUARD, PRAETORIAN TRIBUNE, AND, FROM HIS EARLIEST AGE, RAISED THROUGH THE RANKS OF THE MOST DISTINGUISHED MILITARY SERVICE TO THE HEIGHT OF EVERLASTING GLORY AND ROYAL KINSHIP; SON-IN-LAW OF THE DIVINE THEODOSIUS; COMPANION OF THE DIVINE THEODOSIUS AUGUSTUS IN ALL HIS WARS AND VICTORIES, ADMITTED BY HIM INTO ROYAL KINSHIP, AND ALSO FATHER-IN-LAW OF OUR LORD HONORIUS AUGUSTUS. AFRICA WAS FREED THROUGH HIS COUNSELS AND FORESIGHT, BY DECREE OF THE SENATE.”

This inscription exists at Rome in the courtyard of the rear palace of De la Valle. Smetius and Manutius saw it, and Gruterus reports it on page 412. Smetius writes *progeneri*, Gruterus *progenero*, as it truly appears on the marble that I saw and compared. The first line is now missing; it may once have stood at the top of the base. I corrected some details against the original; several things have been erased and can scarcely be read. An inscription mentioned by Gruterus on page 1053 also seems to belong to the same Stilicho. It begins: “In the second consulship of M. F. Stilicho, the boy was laid to rest.” Stilicho indeed professed the Christian name; but his son Eucherius, whom his father attempted to install in the imperial office, had from childhood, while still a private citizen, been planning a persecution of Christians. For other inscriptions in which Stilicho is mentioned, see Guasco, volume III of *Capitoline Inscriptions*, nos. 1246–1247, where his name is written sometimes *Stilico*, sometimes *Stilicho*, and sometimes *Stiliko*. So difficult is it to restore the true spelling from stones.

**712.** Rat. and Weitz.: *draconis*; likewise Fabr., whom Weitzius incorrectly says has *dracones*. Most have *dracones*, and Giselinus wrongly says that some have the singular *draconis*. For the first standard is understood to be the imperial *labarum*, on which Christ’s monogram appeared, and no one will believe that Christ’s emblem was joined with the figure of a dragon. Grangaeus, however, defends and explains the reading *draconis*, since the custom of carrying representations of dragons in the army was retained under the Christians, but in such a way that Christ’s monogram stood above the dragons. Therefore Prudentius adds that it “raises Christ’s emblem higher.” Both explanations are plausible. I do not approve Giselinus’s argument: why could Christ’s emblem not have been placed above standards on which a dragon was painted? Isidore’s gloss could perhaps be corrected as follows: “Roman standards have the head of a dragon.” Concerning the dragon-bearers, see *Peristephanon* hymn 1. **[Col. 0236D]** These verses provide a splendid indication of the piety of ancient Christian soldiers: they not only worshipped at altars—that is, God before the altars—but also marked their foreheads with the cross before entering battle. Saint Augustine, on Psalm 63: “Why are you afraid for your forehead, which you have armed with the sign of the cross?” Perhaps Sedulius had the same thing in mind in Book I: “You will receive the golden rewards of eternal life, weapons borne with all the strength of the Lord; fixed upon my forehead is glory—I bear glory and weapons—and I remain the final part of your warfare, good king.” It is well known to everyone, and we have explained it elsewhere, that Christians from the very beginning of the nascent Church were accustomed to protect their mouths, breasts, and especially their foreheads frequently with the sign of the cross. Tertullian said admirably in *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 3: “We mark our forehead with the sign of the cross,” indicating its frequent use. Sagittarius, chapter 16 of *On the Cross*, understands this passage either as the sign of the cross, at least one made with a finger in the air, or as the sign of the cross that ancient Christians carried inscribed on their foreheads; he gathers much evidence from every side to confirm both practices. It is useful to add the words of Orosius, Book VII, chapter 35, where he describes Theodosius’s battle against Eugenius: “Knowing that he was to be protected not only by the sign of the cross but also to obtain victory, Theodosius, fortifying himself with the sign of the cross, gave the sign of victory; and with the sign of the cross he gave the signal for battle; and he entered the war, destined to be victorious even if no one followed him.”

---

“**826.** which rises before it, raising Christ’s emblem higher.”

There the destructive people of Pannonia, for thirty years,

**[715]** at last paid the penalty, utterly destroyed.

Bodies once enriched by infamous plunder

lie heaped together in mounds. You will marvel, posterity,

through the ages, at the unburied corpses spread far and wide,

which covered the fields of Pollentia with bones.

**[720]** **[Col. 0238A] 827.** If, when Camillus returned,

I was able to raise my head, cut off by Gallic hands,

from the squalor of the ashes;

if I received the standards with a smiling brow;

if I was able to crown my wretched ruins with garlands

and bind my badly hanging towers with laurel—

**[725]** with what embrace shall I receive you, bravest prince?

What flowers shall I scatter, with what crowns shall I adorn

my halls, and what purple hangings shall I suspend from the gates?”

---

[Note: [Col. 0237A]]

**713.** *Effert*: raises, elevates.

**715.** *Pependit*: paid in full.

**717.** *Mirabere*: an apostrophe.

**718.** *Inhumata*: scattered, unburied.

**720.** *Manibus*: “from the hands.” *Excisa*: destroyed, cut down.

**721.** *Redeunte*: Rome.

**[Col. 0238A] 722.** *Fumans*: still, yet.

**723.** *Redimire*: to adorn.

**724.** *Lauro*: with laurel, a sign of victory.

**725.** *Princeps*: Theodosius, or Stilicho, or Constantine.

**726.** *Insertabo*: I shall adorn.

[Note: [Col. 0237B]]

**713.** Gis., in the margin: *sublimior offert*; in the margin: *sublimiter effert*. Others: *sublimior effert*.

**714.** Claudianus, *On the Getic War*: “And in a single day Rome paid back whatever we had lost in thirty years of battle.” The Goths were defeated by Stilicho in the year 403, after they had invaded the Roman Empire thirty years earlier. Cassiodorus, in his *Chronicle*, incorrectly assigned the battle of Pollentia to the fifth consulship of Arcadius and Honorius, which fell in the year 402.

**715.** In Rat. this verse is placed after the following verse, *Corpora*. The sense requires a different order. The people of Pannonia are meant. There were two Pannonias: one Upper Pannonia, where the eastern part of Austria is now located; and the other Lower Pannonia, where much of lower Hungary and part of Slavonia now lie. Cassiodorus calls Pannonia Sirmiensis the seat of the Goths in Book III of the *Variarum*, in the letter concerning the Colosseum.

**716.** Rat.: *dicata rapinis*, contrary to the meter.

**717.** Gis., in the margin: *conjecta jacent* (“lie cast together”).

**719.** Claudianus, in the passage cited: “O Pollentia, to be celebrated by me through all ages.” Pollentia was a city of Liguria, now Potenzo near the Tanarus. Many write *Polentia*. There is another Pollentia in Picenum, now Monte Melone. I omit yet another Pollentia in Majorca, now Pollenza. The battle of Pollentia refers to Pollentia in Liguria. Claudianus, in *On the Getic War*, reports that Alaric was routed in the upper region of Liguria. But why did Prudentius say in verse 701, “and was pressing the Tuscan land after crossing the river”? I think Alaric reached Tuscany and the Tiber, and after withdrawing from there was defeated at Pollentia. See the commentary on verse 729. Cassiodorus and Jordanes report that Stilicho, with the Roman army, was defeated and put to flight by the Goths at Pollentia. But greater faith should be given to writers contemporary with Prudentius—Claudianus and Orosius. Orosius was writing after Stilicho’s crime and death, and although he does not praise what was done at Pollentia, he does concede that the Romans won. Thus he writes in Book VII, chapter 37, concerning Rufinus and Stilicho: “The one let in the barbarian nations; the other fostered them. I say nothing of King Alaric with his Goths, often defeated, often hemmed in, and always released. I say nothing of those unfortunate events at Pollentia, when the entire conduct of the war was entrusted to a barbarian and pagan commander, that is, Saul; through his wickedness the revered days and holy Easter were violated, and the enemy who was retreating on account of religion was compelled to fight. Although, when God’s judgment was soon revealed, showing both what his favor could accomplish and what his vengeance demanded, we defeated them while fighting, and, though victors, were defeated. I say nothing of the barbarians’ own mutual tearing apart, when two Gothic wedges, and then the Alans and Huns, ravaged one another in various slaughters.” He proceeds to narrate the destruction of Rhadagaisus and his army. I think that by the words “though victors, we were defeated,” Orosius means that the Romans, while Stilicho favored the Goths, were defeated by Alaric himself when he besieged and entered the City. Unless one prefers to understand it as referring to some minor victory which the Goths, though defeated by the Romans, obtained against the Roman victors after the battle of Pollentia, when they had been negligent—a reading wholly inconsistent with Claudianus’s account. For Claudianus, in the *Panegyric on the Sixth Consulship of Honorius*, mentions another victory won by Stilicho near Verona after the battle of Pollentia: “When Rome was now far from danger, and the Po flowed between as arbiter of the war.” Cassiodorus and Jordanes—perhaps deceived because they did not understand Orosius correctly—may have been mistaken. Certainly these verses of Prudentius plainly show that the Goths were so scattered at Pollentia that Rome was now considered secure. From Orosius it may also be inferred that Stilicho himself was not present at the battle of Pollentia, but the general Saul, to whom the entire conduct of the war had been entrusted.

**721.** Aldus inserts *et* after *caput*, but the law of the verse rejects it. Camillus drove the Gauls, who were besieging the Capitol, away.

**722.** Ald. and Fab.: *signa renitenti*; this violates the meter. *Renidenti* means “smiling.”

**723.** Egm.: *misera*; Vat. A: *miserans*; others: *miseras*.

**724.** Thuan.: *lauru* for *lauro*.

**725.** This passage correctly establishes that Prudentius wrote these verses before Honorius celebrated his triumph, and therefore between the victory at Pollentia and Honorius’s triumph, which occurred toward the end of 403, according to Tillemont. Grangaeus, from Claudianus’s *Sixth Consulship of Honorius*, argues that it was the year 404, when Honorius and Aristenaetus held the consulship.

**727.** Prudentius gathers together all the things customarily done by the people in celebrating a triumph: crowning the walls with garlands, girding the towers with laurel, scattering flowers, decorating the halls with crowns, and hanging purple cloths from the gates. Many sources could confirm all this, but the matter is certain, and its traces remain especially clear and conspicuous at Rome. Victorius, in his *Philological Dissertation*, proves that silk-and-gold hangings were formerly used for the ornament, adornment, and embellishment of a sacred building, arranged with arches and friezes in the manner of an *encarpus*; Prudentius refers to these here. Yet Prudentius is not now discussing the decoration of temples. Paulinus indicates more than once that the custom was preserved in churches; on this one may consult Ciampini, in his work *On Sacred Buildings*, and Buonarroti, in his *Observations on Sacred Diptychs*. Grangaeus doubts whether the hangings were suspended only from the triumphal gate or from the other gates of the City as well. He nevertheless conjectures that “gates” here means doors, which seems clear to me. This custom too still persists: on more solemn days, the doors and windows of churches and houses are decorated with tapestries and hangings.

---

[Note: [Col. 0239B]]

**728.** Vat. A, corruptly: *accestante sub armis*.

**729.** Rat., Egm., Widm., first hand, and Gis.: *Alpe tenus* (“as far as the Alps”). Ald., Alex., Urb., Vat. A, Weitz., Thuan., the better manuscripts of Heinsius, and the codex of Juretus: *aure tenus* (“only as far as the ears”), which is much better. Vat. A has *tumultos*; correct to *tumultus*. From this verse it may be inferred that Alaric was not far from the City, as also from verse 701: “and was pressing the Tuscan land after crossing the river.” Claudianus reports that the walls of Rome were repaired upon hearing the rumor, *Sixth Consulship of Honorius*: “They gave the new walls a handsome appearance, completed recently upon hearing the rumor of the Goths.” Jordanes, *On Gothic Affairs*, actually relates that Alaric approached the bridge of Condinianus, three miles from Ravenna, where Honorius was then residing. When Alaric had secured Gaul and Spain for himself and his army, he left Italy and was forced to fight in the Cottian Alps near Pollentia. This seems to confirm the passage of Orosius cited in the note on verse 719. Perhaps “Tuscan land” is correctly understood as the Tuscan region around the Po, so that Alaric did not touch Etruria or the Tiber at all, and Rome experienced the Gothic disturbances only “as far as the ears,” because Alaric had approached the bridge of Condinianus but proceeded no farther.

**730.** Rat. and Weitz.: *spoliisque repertis* (“and the spoils recovered”).

**731.** Gis. and others in the vulgate: *data vincula demam* (“I shall remove the chains once given”). Aldus, together with the manuscripts, had already printed *date* (“give”), and Gifanius noted that, with the verb *vestire*, the expression *date, vincula demam* (“give them; I shall remove the chains”) is elegant. Virgil, *Aeneid* IV: “Give [me] the wounds; I shall wash them with water.” Prudentius himself, *Apotheosis* verse 594: “Give [me] the book; open it.”

**733.** Egm., first hand: *caterva* (“crowd”).

**736.** Vat. A incorrectly has *ingenium se nosse*. From Virgil, *Aeneid* XI: “Let all fear be absent.” Juvencus also imitated this in Book III: “Then Christ speaks to the frightened: let all fear be absent.”

**739.** Aldus’s error is *postquam pertulerat*. Earlier Prudentius said *claustra*, which now means the gate-bars.

**[Col. 0240B] 742.** Heinsius, with his manuscripts, Rat., Weitz., and Gis. in the margin: *congressus*. Ald., Vat. A, Urb., Alex., and others: *congressum*. *Congressus* is better. Although Stilicho was not present at the battle of Pollentia, he is nevertheless said to have engaged “at close quarters,” because everything was carried out through his counsels and foresight; and he seems to have been present at the other battle beyond the Po.

**743.** Gis. in the text: *virum*; in the margin: *virûm*. Claudianus, *Sixth Consulship of Honorius*: “When he saw horsemen clad in steel and their hoofed horses hidden in bronze, he asked: ‘From what people have these armored men come?’” If one reads *congressum* in the preceding verse, the construction will be: “He forced the man who had engaged at close quarters to turn his armored back from the very battle line.” I cannot understand what sense Giselinus’s marginal *virûm*, or *virorum* in other editions, produces.

**744.** Gis., second edition: *et mea virtus* (“and my strength”). The first edition, together with the manuscripts and other editions, has the better reading *et mera virtus* (“and sheer strength”). There is no need to discuss the word *mera* again.

**747.** Rat., Alex., Urb., and others: *juvit amoena* (“pleasant Tarentum helped”), with Alex.’s gloss, “that is, it.” Ald. and Weitz.: *vicit*, “he conquered,” namely Hannibal. *Juvit*, retained by Heinsius, is better, although he did not notice the disagreement among the manuscripts. Fabius is the famous Cunctator, “the one man who by delaying restored our cause.”

**[Col. 0240D] 749.** I have often noted that Gifanius reads *promeritis*, and this is indeed found in Alex. and Urb.

**750.** Vat. A: *statui*; read *statuis*.

**751.** Vat. A: *nil tale decet* (“nothing of this kind is fitting”).

**752.** Heinsius says that the manuscripts have *eripit*, not * eruit*. I do not know who printed *eruit*.

**753.** Vat. A, first hand: *defluit usus*.

**756.** Ald. and Gis., together with Alex., Urb., and others: *secuto*. Heinsius retained this, although he gave no information from the manuscripts. Weitzius, with his manuscripts, and Rat.: *secutum*. *Secuto* is better.

**759.** Vat. A: *rhetoris oris*. Alex.: *ore*. Others, better: *rhetoris, oro* (“I beg you, orator”). Mariettus argues from this that this was a new embassy of Symmachus to Honorius, in response to which Prudentius wrote these books to Honorius.

---

**828.** “Free from so great a war, and with you standing armed,

free, and having experienced the Gothic disturbances only as far as the ears?

**[730]** Mount the triumphal chariot, and, with the spoils recovered,

come here with Christ accompanying you. Give [them to me]; I shall remove the chains

from the captive herds. Lay aside the manacles,

worn away by long servitude, crowds of mothers and young men.

Let the old man unlearn slavery, an exile from his ancestral home;

**[735]** let the boy, when his mother has returned to the ancestral threshold,

learn to know himself as freeborn. Let all fear be absent.

We have conquered; I rejoice. What such thing happened

when the former commander of the Carthaginians was repulsed?

After he had battered the trembling bars of the gate he sought,

**[740]** **[Col. 0239B]** released by the Baian waters, he abandoned the hardest strength

of his body to luxury,

**829** and broke iron through lust.

But our Stilicho, engaging at close quarters,

forced the armored men to turn their backs from the very battle line.

**[Col. 0240A]** Here Christ our God was present for us, and sheer strength;

**[745]** there, fertile Campania, your pleasures overcame

the wanton enemy. Jupiter did not protect the brave Fabius;

but pleasant Tarentum helped,

which gave the tyrant, subdued by its allurements, to be trampled underfoot.

For these merits, what worthy rewards can I render?

**[750]** I have none. To fashion his limbs in statues is worthless.

Nothing worthless befits virtue; for what time removes is worthless:

bronzes fall, or bright gold runs away,

or the whiteness of silver perishes if use has failed,

and the vein, darkened by neglect, corrupts its color.

**[755]** Living glory is owed to you, prince: to one who follows virtue, a living reward—

immortal honor.

**[Col. 0240B] 830.** You will be joined forever with Christ, ruler of the world,

under whose leadership you draw my kingdom toward the heavens.

Let not the voice of the great orator move you, I beg,

**[760]** who, under the guise of an embassy, laments the dead sacred things,

**[Col. 0241A]** **[Note: [Col. 0241A]**

**769.** *Non admittenda*: not to be admitted, not to be received.

**770.** *Ab haruspice*: from the haruspex; from Apollo; from the magicians.

**[Col. 0242A] 771.** *Patria*: Rome.

[Note: [Col. 0241A]]

**765.** *Palatia* were called splendid and spacious houses, such as were first built on Rome’s Palatine Hill. The hill itself was also called the Palatium. I think Prudentius is alluding to the temple of the goddess Roma, which I discussed at verse 219 of Book I; from Claudianus it may be inferred that this temple stood on the Palatine Hill. I understand the words soon to be read, “Let my palace serve,” as referring to the same temple, for I have shown more fully elsewhere that *aula* may mean “temple.” Nevertheless, nothing prevents the passage from being understood of Rome as a whole and its buildings.

**768.** Rat. and Gis.: *sic effata*. *Affata*, with the others, is more harmonious.

**771.** Aldus incorrectly separates *a patria patriae, nam*. Oxon.: *patriae sua gloria*. Prudentius denies that Symmachus was sent as an envoy by his country, because most of the Roman nobility had already converted to the faith when he was answering Symmachus, and because even earlier, when Symmachus presented his report to Valentinian II, many Christian senators had dissented. Otherwise, it is established from his *Report* and from Ambrose’s *Responses* that Symmachus really did serve on such embassies, sent by the Senate, to restore the Altar of Victory. At this point we must inquire and consider whether an old inscription that is in circulation belongs to him. Weitzius and Chamiliardus publish it and attribute it to this Symmachus, without noticing any reason for doubt, although Juretus long ago argued that the inscription did not concern this Symmachus, the letter-writer. Most scholars certainly understand the following words of Ammianus, Book XXVII, as referring to the father of the letter-writer Symmachus:

“Long before this happened, Symmachus succeeded Apronianus in the prefecture of the City. He deserves to be named among the foremost examples of learning and modesty. While he was in office, the most sacred City enjoyed leisure and abundance more generously than usual, and rejoiced in an ambitious bridge, as well as in the very strong bridge that he himself built and dedicated amid great joy among the citizens—an event whose outcome proved them ungrateful, since after several years they burned his beautiful house in the Trastevere district.”

The inscription, however, is as follows:”

PHOSPHORII [Col. 0241D]

To L. Aurelius Avianius Symmachus, clarissimus man, urban prefect, consul, prefect of the praetorium in the City of Rome and the neighboring provinces, prefect of the grain supply of the City of Rome, chief pontiff, quindecemvir of the Sacred Rites, who, having undertaken many embassies on behalf of the wishes of the most distinguished order before the divine emperors, was accustomed to be the first in the Senate to be asked for his opinion and, through authority, prudence, and eloquence, filled the greatness of his position in a manner worthy of so great an order. The most distinguished Senate, by frequent decrees, obtained from our lords and Augusti an illustrious golden statue; and our emperors, having triumphed, ordered that it be set up, with an address appended that should contain the order and sequence of his achievements. Their enduring judgment added this also to so great an honor: that a second statue, of equal splendor, should be placed at Constantinople.

[Col. 0242B] When I wished to compare this inscription, I did not find it. Gruterus reports it on page CCCLXX, no. 3, from Smetius and Boissardus. In describing it, I followed Smetius rather than Boissardus, since Smetius states that he saw it on a base beneath the Capitol, but does not specify the exact location. Boissardus, *Antiquitates et monumenta*, part 5, p. 53, asserts that the inscription exists at the house of Franciscus Lisca. On the right side of the base one read:

DEDICATED ON THE THIRD DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF MAY, IN THE CONSULSHIP OF OUR LORD GRATIANUS FOR THE FOURTH TIME AND MEROBAUDES.

Gratianus and Merobaudes were consuls in the year 377. From this comes Juretus’s argument: Symmachus, the author of the letters, did not hold the consulship before the year 391; moreover, the Symmachus praised in that inscription is called Lucius, whereas Symmachus the letter-writer bears the praenomen Quintus in the old manuscripts and in Macrobius and Sidonius. Nevertheless, since all the praises of the inscription fit Symmachus the letter-writer extremely well; since no other Symmachus is known to have flourished at that time with such renown; and since in the consular fasti the praenomen Lucius is assigned to Symmachus the letter-writer, I judge it highly probable that the inscription belongs to this same Symmachus. The praenomen Quintus may perhaps have clung to him in the manuscripts because his son Quintus published the letters after his father’s death. Nor is it sufficiently clear whether Macrobius names the father or the son.

If the title “consul” expressed in the inscription is to be understood of an ordinary consulship, no Symmachus appears in the consular fasti to whom the statue could be assigned—unless perhaps it was that Symmachus who was consul with Gallicanus in the year 330, that is, forty-seven years before the statue was dedicated. But what prevents Symmachus the letter-writer from having been suffect consul before the year 377? Indeed, I find unmistakable traces of that dignity in Letter 1 of Book I, where he says of himself:

> Among these, a youthful glory, yet exalted by senatorial honor,  
> You shine, Symmachus, raised six times by the fasces.

Juretus understands this of Symmachus’s ordinary consulship in the year 391 and from it argues that Symmachus was appointed consul while still a young man. But the chronology scarcely fits. It is established that already in the year 382 Symmachus had been the Senate’s envoy to Gratianus, seeking the restoration of the altar of Victory. Moreover, when Symmachus assumed the urban prefecture, he gave these thanks to the younger Valentinian in Letter 15 of Book X:

> Though I was at peace and had long since withdrawn from the pursuit of offices, you freely bestowed upon me the prefecture which many desired;

and to Theodosius in the following letter:

> You wished to appoint me, a man who had once been proconsular and had long since yielded to the ways of the powerful, to office before I had expected it.

It is therefore wholly inconsistent to say that this Symmachus was still a young man in the year 391. I even suspect that this same man was praised by Marcellinus in the words quoted above. A greater difficulty is created by another inscription, which I shall present and examine at verse 909, where I shall discuss Symmachus’s pontificate.

> He dares, with the weapons of his intellect and the powers of speech,  
> Alas, to test our faith: he does not see that you and I,  
> Augustus, are devoted to God—God for whom  
> We have closed the filthy temples and cast down the altars dripping with gore.
>
> [765] Let one Christ rule and preserve our palaces,  
> So that no demon may now know the citadels of Rome;  
> But let my palace serve the Lord of peace alone.
>
> Thus Rome addressed and entreated her pious children  
> To reject the envoy, who sought what must not be admitted:
>
> [770] The envoy of Jupiter, sent from the shrine by the seer—  
> But not from the fatherland: for Christ is the fatherland’s glory.

[Col. 0243A] [Note: [Col. 0243B]

772. “To journey,” toward the truth, I.

775. “Crossroads”: *compitum* is said of a place where many roads “meet,” that is, join. “By the same route,” I.

779. “They sacrifice,” they perform sacrifices, I.

780. “For all,” to be, I.

783. “By the vault,” by the sky, I.

784. “Unclean,” polluted, I.

785. “With the mouth,” from the mouth—“of the gladiator”: of the clown. A *mirmillo* was a gladiator and is used for any murderer, I.

[Col. 0244B] 787. “Spring,” springlike, I.

790. “For pirates,” for maritime robbers, I.

793. “Of either kind,” of good and evil, I.

797. “It preserves,” on the day of judgment, I.

802. “And ready,” because it serves everyone, Iso.

804. “Capital,” by which the defendant must be punished with death, I.

808. “Garamans,” peoples of Sicily.—“Galaulas,” peoples in the East, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0243C]

772 and 773. Vaticanus A has *esse vocandi*, “to be called,” less well. Prudentius seems to acknowledge that Symmachus professes one God. But this is not so: Symmachus’s argument rests on the claim that there are many ways of seeking divinity, since those who assert one god seek it just as much as those who assert several gods. See verse 879.

774. Aldine, Alexandrian, Urbinate, Weitzian: *seorsum*; Heinsius, Giselinus, Ratoldus: *seorsim*.

775. Alexandrian and Ratoldus: *anfractos*. Others: *anfractus*. Vaticanus A, Ratoldus, and Widmanstetter write *competa*. Weitzius, who cites the Aldine edition for *competa*, had not seen its correction to *compita*. See the commentary on verse 7 of the preface to Book 2 of the *Apotheosis*, where I said more about the spelling of *compitum*.

779. The words of Symmachus are appended to this verse:

> It is fair that whatever all worship should be regarded as one. We look upon the same stars; the sky is common to us; the same world surrounds us. What does it matter by what wisdom each person seeks the truth? One road cannot lead to so great a secret.

780. The Aldine edition incorrectly has “the same thing common to all living beings.” In the Tornesian edition, too, *ipsum* appeared; Latinius corrected it.

786. The Egmond manuscript and Vaticanus A: *hausto*. Alexandrian: *austu*; above, *haustu*, which is correct.

787. Vaticanus A has *nubis*, in the ancient manner.

789. *Aestiva* are shady places where, during summer, cattle avoid the heat of the sun, according to Servius on *Georgics* III, where he adds from Statius: “And the shady summer shelters of Lycaeus stood open.” Prudentius calls the pool “summer” not so much because it might be shady as because during summer the heat is avoided by its water.

[Col. 0244C] 790. Vaticanus A has “the sea boils”; the others more correctly have *servit*. Ratoldus, in the first hand, has *servat*; above, *servit*. Seneca, *On Benefits* IV.26: “If you imitate the gods, give benefits even to the ungrateful. The sun rises for criminals, and the seas lie open to pirates.”

791. These words, “nor does the wave less obey the enemy,” are missing in Vaticanus A. The Egmond manuscript has the erroneous *sedius* for *secius*.

792. Aldine, Tornesian, Gallandian, and Giselinian editions in the text: *dominae*. Ratoldus, Weitzius, Widmanstetter, the Heinsian manuscripts, and more recent editions: *licitae*.

800. Heinsius would prefer *impluit imber*.

804. Arnobius, Book IV: “God supplies equally to all the sun’s generative heat, the seasons of night, winds, rains, and crops—to good and bad, unjust and servants, poor and rich.” Matthew 5:45: “So that you may be sons of your Father, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the bad, and rains upon the just and the unjust.”

807. Urbinate, Widmanstetter, Ratoldus: *Dana*; Vaticanus A: *Deba*; Aldine, Heinsius, Weitzius, Egmondanus, Alexandrian: *Daha*; Giselinus: *Daa*; Fabrus: *Dea*. Ratoldus writes *Wandalus*, Fabrus *Vandulus*, others *Vandalus*. Alexandrian has *unus*; correct to *Hunnus*.

808. Heinsian manuscripts and others: *Garamans* and *Alamannus*; Heinsius nevertheless printed *Garamas, Alamanus*. The gloss ineptly calls the Garamantes peoples of Sicily, just as it calls the Galaulas peoples in the East. Some write *Alemannus*. Ratoldus and Thuaneus: *Galaula*; perhaps *Galaules*. Orosius, Book I, chapter 2, in his description of Africa: “To the south are the peoples of the Aulolum [elsewhere Autolum], whom they now call Gaulales, extending as far as the western ocean. This is the boundary of all Africa.” Lucan, Book IV, calls the Autoles or Autololes *Autololes*; they are peoples neighboring the Numidians and Gaetulians. Grangaeus says that he has not read in the geographers who this people is, and doubts whether *Galaulas* may have arisen by transposition for *Gaulalas*, the people mentioned by Orosius. He also suspects that *Galaudas* should be read, since in Aethicus’s *Cosmography* he had found: “To the south are the peoples of the Aulolum, whom they now call Galaudas, extending as far as the western ocean.” But these are Orosius’s exact words, except that *Galaudas* is written for *Gaulalas*. Such proper names are easily corrupted by copyists, and it is not difficult for different authors to pronounce them in different ways. In any case, some editions of Orosius actually read *Galaules*.]

831 Yet he persists in asserting that the way of journeying

832 Is many-branched and varied when the one God is sought.

From here some hasten, from there others, separately,

[775] Each along its own winding paths; but the roads converge at the same

833 End, constrained and meeting together as one.

Indeed, sky and earth, winds, sea, and clouds

Are given in common to all—to those who worship you,

Christ, and to those who sacrifice rotting entrails upon carved stones.

[780] I do not deny the common use, for all living beings,

Of air, stars, sea, earth, and rain.

Rather, unjust and just alike dwell beneath one

[Col. 0243B] vault: the impious and the pious breathe the same air;

The chaste and the unchaste; prostitute and married woman; nor does the breath

[785] Drawn from the priest’s mouth differ from that of the gladiator,

As it is the airy draught that sustains life.

The spring cloud rains when driven by the west wind; yet equally

It makes fertile the fields of the thief and the innocent farmer.

The traveler approaches the clear waters

[790] Of the summer pool just as the weary robber does; the sea serves pirates

[Col. 0244A] no less than the merchant:

834 Nor does the wave obey the enemy less than when it carries the benches of a lawful ship.

Therefore nature, capable of either condition,

Offers herself for the creation of peoples, and does not distinguish the differing

[795] Merit of living beings whom she has merely been commanded to nourish.

For the world serves; it does not judge. The highest lord of nature

Reserves this for the appointed times.

Now the gifts granted to humanity are present under the same laws,

Under which they were once granted: the spring melts, the river overflows,

[800] The sail-bearing sea is cleft by ships, rain pours in,

[Col. 0244B] The gentle breeze flies, the mobile air is invigorated,

And nature’s gift becomes public and available to all,

While the elements, serving, maintain their appointed course.

Thus the upright person and the one guilty of a capital crime

[805] Enjoy the same stars and the easy favor of the sky.

Living is common to all; earning merit is not common.

Finally: Roman, Daha, Sarmatian, Vandal, Hun,

Gaetulian, Garamantian, Alamannian, Saxon, Galaulan—

812. “Wild asses”: *onos* means “ass”; hence *onager*, “wild ass,” I.

813. “Its own,” nominative. “Our water,” in which we swim, I.

814. “Wild,” strong, I.

815. “Roman,” both Roman and barbarian, Christian and pagan, I.

816. “Two-footed,” human, I.

[Col. 0246B] 819. “To be maintained,” which must be preserved, I.

822. “It makes no difference,” it is different, or matters; there is no distinction, I.

823. “Earth,” from the earth, Iso.

825. “Distinction,” discrimination, I.

826. “Into the midst,” into common use, I.

827. “Would become foul,” would sin, I.

838. “More,” I shall say. “They will be,” a vain matter, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0245C]

812. Giselinus in the margin, Widmanstetter, and Ratoldus in the first hand have *in agris* for *onagris*. Widmanstetter’s gloss also has *stat* for *onagris*, and in Ratoldus it is written by another hand as *onagris*. The Urbinate writes *honagris*.

813. Aldine; Ratoldus by another hand; Egmondanus; Widmanstetter above; Fabrus; Giselinus in the margin: *sordida sus*. Giselinus in the text: *spurcaque sus*. Urbinate, Ratoldus in the first hand, Widmanstetter in the first hand, and two Boher manuscripts: *spurca suis*. Heinsius, Alexandrian, and Thuaneus: *spurca sues*. The nominative *sues* or *suis* is correct, as with *plebs, plebes, plebis*, also in the nominative in the ancient manner. Thuaneus has “and the same air [animates] dogs.” Heinsius observes that poets commonly use *canes* in the feminine gender.

[Col. 0245D] 816. Ratoldus, by a recent hand after erasing the earlier text, has: “The quadruped is separated from the two-footed; then, in the ancient copyist’s hand, follows *lipedi* or *muta loquenti*.” Aldine, Fabrus, Tornesian, and the Egmond and Oxford manuscripts: “Quadrupeds are separated from the two-footed, or the mute from the speaking,” so that no one should think this a recent correction. Heinsius seems not to have noticed that in the second edition of Giselinus a typographical error, *adjuncta*, had been corrected to *abjuncta*. Giselinus himself remarks in his notes that numerical symmetry should be preserved from the manuscripts: *quadrupes*, not *quadrupedes*. Gifanius also reads from an old book: “The quadruped is separated,” and so forth. In Hymn 2 of the *Peristephanon*: “the separated wounds.” As above they are distant, so now *abjuncta est* has the same sense. Avitus has *abjunctae partes*, “separated parts,” and *abjuncta elementa*, “separated elements.” Hericus of Auxerre has *abjuncto corpore*, “with the body separated.”

[Col. 0246B] 817. Aldine, Alexandrian, Giselinian, Heinsian, and more recent editions: *quantum etiam*. Ratoldus, Weitzius with his manuscripts, and the Urbinate: *tantum etiam*.

818. Heinsius corruptly has *errotibus absunt*.

819. Vaticanus A incorrectly has *nos facit*. Ratoldus: *in religione tuenda*. Heinsius printed this, following Weitzius, whereas Giselinus and most others have *in religione tenenda*.

821. Aldine, Heinsius with his manuscripts, Weitzius, and Widmanstetter above: *recidivaque*. Giselinus, Fabrus, Widmanstetter in the first hand, and Ratoldus: *redivivaque*. *Recidivaque* is preferable; it is also found in the Alexandrian, Urbinate, Juretus’s manuscript, and Gifanius’s old book at the word *victus*.

826. Barthius, *Adversaria* LX.15, observes that *in medium venire* is said of what is given for everyone’s use, on the basis of this verse of Prudentius and Virgil, *Georgics* I: “They sought in common, and the earth itself bore everything more freely, with no one demanding.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XV: “He gave them things to be learned in common.”

828. Ratoldus: *ac se*; others: *aut se*.

830. Latinius, Urbinate, Alexandrian in the first hand, Giselinus, and Weitzius: *colluminat*. Aldine, Ratoldus, Tornesian, and Vaticanus A: *cum luminat*. *Colluminat* better suits the meaning. Otherwise, the verb is Prudentius’s *luminat*.

[Col. 0246D] 832. Tertullian, *On the Spectacles*, chapter XX: “The sun, indeed God himself, looks down from heaven and is not polluted. Certainly the sun carries its rays even into a sewer and is not defiled.”

833. Vaticanus A corruptly has *Capitoli ut lara*. There were two Capitols at Rome and others elsewhere. Prudentius means magnificent temples.

835. Aldine, Egmondanus, Alexandrian, and Tornesian corruptly have *redolent in fornice*. Urbinate, Ratoldus, the better Heinsian manuscripts, and Weitzius: *redolenti fornice*. Giselinus in the margin: *redolenti in fornice*.

836. Giselinus noted in his corrected text that *quod* is a referring particle, as below also in *quod sunt qui summum*.

838. In the gloss I would read *una res*, “one thing.”

840. Ratoldus and Tornesian: *quot sunt*, less well. The same manuscripts have *qui celsi dominum venerantur Olympi*, but the two words *celsi dominum* were written by a recent hand after the earlier text had been erased; the remainder is in the same ancient copyist’s hand.]

835 All advance upon the same earth; the sky is one for all.

One ocean also, which contains our world.

I add another point: animals drink from our springs.

The same dew that is grain for me is grass for wild asses;

The filthy sow swims in our river and enters it, and our

Air also enters dogs and gives life to animal bodies with its light breath.

But Roman and barbarian differ as much as

A quadruped is separated from a two-footed creature, or a mute from one who speaks;

As much, too, as those who rightly follow God’s commands

Are distant from foolish rites and their errors.

The sharing of air and sky therefore does not make people equal

[Col. 0245B] in maintaining religious observance: it merely

Creates, nourishes, restores bodies, and preserves returning seeds;

Nor does it matter of what kind, what shape,

Or what merit they are, provided they are bodies produced

[Col. 0246A] from the earth, whose strength comes from earthly elements,

[825] Because the work of the Father, the Artisan, flows into common use

Without distinction and does not run as a miserly gift,

Given before the first man Adam became foul.

Nor does it fail because of the fault of those who use it, nor restrict itself,

Nor withdraw from the unworthy, nor avoid what is foul or shameful.

[830] In no other way does the sun’s ray illuminate everyone,

With its radiance spread over every place: it strikes golden roofs,

But it also strikes dark summits soiled with black smoke.

It enters the bright Capitols with their marble; but it also enters

The cracks of the prison and the foul openings of the closed

[835] Dung-house, and the filthy cell smelling in its vaulted chamber.

But those dark workhouses will not be what

837 The royal ceilings gilded with jeweled metal are.

Indeed, they will not be what those are who seek the divine power

In urns and tombs and appease ghosts with blood.

[840] What those are who worship the highest lord of heaven are,

841. Argument of Symmachus.

844. Vaticanus A, incorrectly: *obita calles*. Giselinus and Fabrus: *tramitibus si centenos*. Heinsius in his notes corrected this to *tramitibus si centenis*, from his better manuscripts, by reading *tramitibus et centenis*. I think a mistake has dropped out, and that his notes should read *TRAMITIBUS SI CENTENOS*, “by paths, if a hundred,” rather than *tramitibus et centenos*. For he printed *tramitibus et centenos*, as do the other editors and the manuscripts, together with Juretus’s manuscript.

845. Ratoldus: *latenter*; others: *latentem*.

846. Heinsius and Chamillardus incorrectly have *multa ambage*. This very argument of Prudentius can be brought against those heretics who claim that eternal salvation exists in every sect. Johannes Hessels handled this excellently, using these verses, in *On the Duty of the Pious and Truly Peace-Loving Christian Man amid a Rising or Prevailing Heresy*, chapter 34.

847. Ratoldus: *anfractos*; above, correctly, *anfractus*.

848. From Proverbs 10:9: “Whoever walks simply walks confidently.”

849. The better Heinsian manuscripts: *in deverticulum*, “into a side road”; hence the Alexandrian manuscript’s *indeverticulum*.

850. Egmondanus and Widmanstetter in the margin: *infiteus*, from which Weitzius suspects *infiteor*.

[Col. 0247D] 851. Lactantius, Book VI, chapter 3: “All this discussion of the two roads therefore concerns frugality and luxury. For they say that the course of human life resembles the letter Y: when each person first reaches the threshold of adolescence and comes to the place where the road divides in two, he remains hesitating and wavering, not knowing toward which side he should rather incline.” On this fork of virtue and vice, see the commentary on verse 789 of the *Hamartigenia*.

853. Ratoldus: *multifidi*; above, correctly, *multifida*. Weitzius with his manuscripts, Giselinus in the margin, and Heinsius with the second Rott manuscript: *altera et unum Una Deum*, which seems more harmonious to Heinsius than *altera et una*, found in most others. I prefer *et una*, since *una* occurs again in the following verse and has the same simple sense.

854. It is clear from this that Symmachus asserts several gods, not one god to whom several powers are subordinate.

[Col. 0248B] 860. Ratoldus: *tinnitos*, incorrectly. Minucius: “The cymbals of the Corybantes produce a ringing, so that the father may not hear the cries.” Ovid, *Fasti* IV: “For a long time Ida has resounded with ringing, so that the child may cry out safely with an infant’s voice.” The Corybantes, as Lucretius says, struck bronze against bronze.

861. These rods of the Luperci were goatskins; their blows were called *catomus*, as may be gathered from the scholiast on Juvenal, Satire 2.142: “It does no good to offer your palms to the agile Lupercus.” The Luperci are mentioned again in Laurentius, verse 518, and in Romanus, verse 162. On the word *catomus*, see the commentary on verse 697 of the *Romanus*.

862. Ratoldus: *magalesius*; others: *megalesius*. Note the transferred expression *discursus nudi* for “the running about of naked young men.”

863. Oracles were called responses, as in “the responses of the Sibyl” and “the responses of the gods.”

865. Ratoldus writes *holuscula*. Juvenal, Satire 15: “O holy peoples, for whom such divinities are born in gardens.” In the same passage Juvenal says more about the ridiculous superstition of the Egyptians—for example, that it is sacrilege to violate leeks and onions or break them with a bite.

867. Vaticanus A and the better Heinsian manuscripts have *Serapen*, not *Serapin*. Ratoldus also has *Serapen*, insofar as it could be inferred from the traces of the old writing: an inept corrector erased the text and shaped the verse as follows: “And to place Serapis above the stars of heaven,” and after this verse, also erasing the preceding text: “And the ibis fed to snakes.” But these all come back to the same thing. Then in the margin: “This is it—Serapis, for he is the husband of Isis, and the great-tailed monkey.” He clearly wanted the second syllable of *Serapis* to be long. Understand the verse added in the margin as connected with the preceding verse in this sense: “But these return to the same thing.” Martial lengthened the second syllable of *Serapis*, although Martianus Capella, Book II, shortened it: “The Nile worships you as Serapis, Memphis as Osiris.” In proper names, especially foreign ones, poets are permitted this license, pronouncing them with varying quantities. It should be noted that Serapis was the husband of Isis; this is suggested by the gloss, where perhaps after “husband” the name “of Isis” has fallen out.

868. Vaticanus A corruptly has *et grandissima cauda*. Juvenal, in the passage cited: “The golden image of the sacred *cercopithecus* shines.” Martial, Book XIV, epigram 202, on the *cercopithecus*: “A clever monkey to evade the spears thrown at it; if I had a tail, I would be a cercopithecus.”]

They perform sacrifice to Justice as well and adorn the temple of their heart.

Yet the great secret concealed by reason cannot be sought otherwise

Than if, with the roads scattered into many paths,

The track wears down a hundred routes,

[845] Seeking God, who lies hidden through varied investigation.

The truth is far otherwise: the many tangled roads

Have uncertain windings and wander more perplexedly.

Only the simple road is free from error, incapable of turning

Into a side path and not wavering among multiple forks.

[850] Yet I do not deny that a double road always confronts us,

That mortals travel in two directions,

838 Since ignorance hesitates over where to guide its steps.

One is many-branched; the other is simple and one.

[Col. 0247B] One follows God; the other worships many gods,

[855] [Col. 0248A] And its divergences are as numerous as the images of temples,

As the phantoms that flit through the air in monstrous shapes.

One road carries some to the Dionysian festivals of thyrsus-bearing Bacchus;

Another lures others to the Saturnalian celebrations;

Another teaches what secret rites Diespiter, the infant,

[860] Demands be performed for him amid the ringing of bronze.

Now the Lupercal rods and the running about of naked young men are sought.

From another direction the Megalesian eunuch, inflamed

With dreadful madness, is summoned to blind responses.

There are those prepared to travel by shorter four-way paths,

[865] 839 Who dare to place cheap garden vegetables from the Nile among the gods:

Leeks and onions, daring to raise them as gods to the clouds,

And garlic, and Serapis, to set him above the stars of heaven.

[Col. 0248B] For Isis, Serapis, and a monkey with a great tail.

873. “They tread,” they walk, I.

874. “Of heaven,” of truth, I.

875. “Savage,” under the devil, I.

878. “Distinction,” discrimination, I.

[Col. 0250B] 881. “One,” road, I.

883. “Slope,” truth, I.

884. “First,” the one that leads to life. “Appearance,” quality. “Sad,” in the present, I.

887. “To repay,” to recompense, I.

888. “Many-branched,” namely, of the road; he speaks of the left-hand road, I.

890. “Bearded,” strong, I.

891. “It lures,” that is, it deceives them, I.
