869. Widmanstetter writes *crocodrillus*, Alexandrian *crocodillus*, others *crocodilus*. Oxford has *idem est*. Thuaneus and nearly all the Heinsian manuscripts, Alexandrian and Urbinate with the Aldine, have *idem, quod*. Weitzius with his manuscripts, Giselinus, and Ratoldus have *id est, quod*. The Aldine edition corruptly has *Lavena*. Becmanus, *Manuductio ad linguam Latinam*, I do not know where he found *Laurena*, which he correctly emends to *Laverna*, or *Laberna*, the goddess of thieves.

870. Aldine and Giselinus: “These gods you, Nile, worship, and you, Tiber, adore.” Ratoldus: “These you, Tiber, worship; those the Nile adores.” But the words *Tibri, deos colis, illos Nilus* were introduced by an audacious corrector after the earlier text had been erased. Gifanius correctly reads from an old book: “These gods you, Nile, worship; those you, Tiber, adore.” Weitzius followed this, as did his manuscripts, and it agrees with our text and the Heinsian manuscripts. The final syllable of *colis* is lengthened by the rule of the caesura, something frequently found in Prudentius, as we have often noted.

871. Juretus observes that the correct reading is *una superstitio*, “one superstition in all,” not *vana superstitio*, “a vain superstition.” Honorius and Theodosius spoke in nearly the same way in Law 60, *On Heretics*, Code of Theodosius XVI: “Their sects weary the most pious sanction, for although all have different names, they share one treachery.”

874. Aldine, Fabrus, Alexandrian, Ratoldus, and Vaticanus A: “Whatever lies hidden in the forests is covered, ignorant of heaven.” Urbinate: *latet*. Giselinus, Weitzius with Widmanstetter’s first hand: “Whatever lies hidden in the forests is covered, ignorant of heaven.” Heinsius recognized no variant, following Giselinus. Perhaps the reading should be: “Whatever lies hidden in the forests is covered; the mind of men, ignorant of heaven, lives captive under a savage tyrant.” Heinsius added a mark of exclamation to *tyranno* in the following verse. Thus: “Whatever lies hidden in the forests is covered: the mind of men, ignorant of heaven, lives captive under a savage tyrant!”

880. “Monsters,” as elsewhere “monsters of the gods.” Here too Prudentius confirms that pagans acknowledge many divinities in which supreme divinity resides.

[Col. 0250C] 883. Aldine: *celsam*, less well; nor is Teolius’s *sublime dextro celsam ad fastigia clivo* better. Read *sublimen* and *celsa*.

888. Aldine and Fabrus: *multiplici daemon sed adest*. Giselinus: *multiplicis dux daemon at est*. Ratoldus: *multiplicis daemon dux est*; but the three words *daemon dux est* were introduced by an extremely bold corrector after erasing the preceding text. Widmanstetter and Weitzius: *multiplicis dux daemon adest*. Palatine, Juretus’s manuscripts, Gifanius at *vestis*, Heinsius with the first Rott manuscript, and Oxford: *multiplici dux daemon adest*. Weitzius cites the Egmond manuscript for *multiplicis*, Heinsius for *multiplici*. Alexandrian and Urbinate agree with Heinsius, although the Alexandrian writes *demon*, not *daemon*. It is possible to say *dux alicui* and *dux alicujus*. Aldine and Fabrus: *morte sinister*; others: *parte sinistra*.

890. Juvenal, Satire 14.12: “Though you bring a thousand bearded teachers from there.” Vaticanus A incorrectly has *barbatus*.

891. Gifanius, at *mare*, reads from an excellent old book *inlicitat volucrum linguis*. Mariettus does not approve this, because Prudentius means the songs of birds, or augury and haruspicy, by which many were deceived. Heinsius rejects the same reading because *illicitat* is poor Latin; *illectat* should be used. Mariettus may perhaps have been refuting with that argument the form *haruspide*, which he read in Gifanius and which really does occur there. But I think *haruspide* is an error for *haruspice*.

892. Weitzius with Widmanstetter’s first hand: *bacchatus*. Others: *bacchantis*. Vaticanus A incorrectly has *sibyllae*.

893. Aldine, Ratoldus by an ignorant corrector after the preceding text was erased, Fabrus, and the old editions apud Gallandus: “He draws into magical arts and involves in astrology.” This was done by those who knew that the second syllable of *mathesi* was long and were unaware of the contrary old practice.

897. Aldine, Alexandrian, Urbinate, Fabrus, and Egmondanus: *monstrat*. Vaticanus A, Ratoldus, Weitzius, Giselinus, and Heinsius: *monstret*.

899. Vaticanus A: *tristitia et subita praeceps*. Urbinate: *tristis, et in subitam*, which is not objectionable. Some write *Charybdim*, others *Charybdem*. The thought is taken from Matthew 7, Luke 8, and Ecclesiasticus 16.]

And the crocodile is the same as Juno, Laverna, and Priapus.

[870] These gods you, Nile, worship; those you, Tiber, adore.

There is one superstition, though the error is not of the same color.

840 From here another path arises, covered with dark thickets,

A path which cattle and mute animals tread,

And whatever lies hidden in the forests; the mind of men, ignorant of heaven, is covered over,

[875] Living captive under a savage tyrant.

It thinks that there is no god, for everything is turned

By chance, and the ages revolve under no protector.

This road is not at all far removed from

Those paths which you tread, who consider many divinities

[880] [Col. 0249B] And monsters to be the supreme God, in great number.

Therefore God is the guide of the simple road: he commands

Mortal humanity to travel by one road, which he himself directs,

High toward the lofty summit along a steep right-hand slope.

[Col. 0250A] The first appearance of the road is uncultivated, somewhat rough, sad,

[885] Difficult; but at its end it is most beautiful,

Endowed with broad riches and abundant in perpetual light,

And able to repay the labors already endured.

A demon is present as guide for the many-branched road;

On the left side he confuses the road into a hundred paths

[890] 841 And draws from there bearded men powerful through wealth or honor.

He lures them by the tongues of birds and deceives them through the seer;

He incites the raving old woman by the winding utterance of the Sibyl;

He entangles them in astrology and drives them into magical arts;

He troubles them with omens, captures them through augury, and terrifies them through entrails.

[895] Do you see how there is one road wandering through many windings,

After suffering such a guide, who does not allow it to go toward

The Lord of salvation, but points out the road of death through byways?

[Col. 0250B] Byways painted with brief advantages, but at their very end

Sad and plunging headlong into sudden Charybdis.

[900] [Col. 0251A] [Note: [Col. 0251A]

903. “Perplexed,” difficult, Iso.

[Col. 0252A] 909. “Last,” at the very end, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0251A]

903. Ratoldus: *praevius infelix*, “the unhappy guide.”

904. Here he again indicates that the pagans assert a multitude of gods.

905. Ratoldus: *lux est iter*, “the road is light”; this does not fit the meter.

906. Juretus’s manuscript: *spem sequimur, gradimurque fides*. But Juretus says that this is not entirely correct. Indeed, I think *gradimurque fides* cannot correctly be said. Paulinus also used *spe sequimur* in writing to Ausonius. Minucius, in the *Octavius*: “We are encouraged by hope of future happiness and by faith in his present majesty.” Elmenhorstius, commenting on this passage, praises this verse of Prudentius along with several other Church Fathers and reads: “We follow hope and proceed by faith.”

908. After this verse the following words of Symmachus’s speech are usually appended:

> How much benefit has been withdrawn from your treasury by the privilege of the Vestal Virgins? Under the most generous emperors, what the most frugal supplied is denied. In that stipend of chastity there is only honor. Just as their ribbons provide adornment for their heads, so it is considered an insignia of priesthood to be free from public burdens. Let no one think that I am defending only the cause of religion. From such acts all the troubles of the Roman people have arisen. The law of our ancestors had honored the Vestal Virgins and the ministers of the gods with modest maintenance and just privileges. The integrity of this endowment stood until the degenerate money-changers who converted the provisions of sacred chastity into the payment of cheap porters. A public famine followed, and a poor harvest disappointed the hopes of all the provinces. These are not faults of the earth. Let us not blame the southern winds. Neither rust harmed the crops nor did oats kill the grain. The year withered through sacrilege. For everything that was denied to religion had to perish for all. What comparable thing did the provinces suffer when public honor supported the ministers of religion? (For the produce of the earth supplied the sustenance of the priests, and it was a remedy rather than generosity. Is it doubtful that what was given from the abundance of all has now been exacted by the want of all?)

Heinsius reads *sacri aerarii*, “of the sacred treasury.” The Aldine edition printed *praerogativa detracta est, sub largissimis*; he corrected this to *detracta, sub*. The Ratisbon edition has *in illud velut stipendium*. Aldine and Ratoldus: *ex ejusmodi facinoribus orta sunt cuncta humani generis*. The Aldine has *privilegiis stetit* without a punctuation mark. The same edition has *trapezetas*. It also has *falimenta*, incorrectly, for *alimenta*. Heinsius: *austris*; Ratoldus: *astris*. The Aldine printed *imputemus austris* and corrected it to *astris*. Ratoldus: *fruges necuit*. The first Rott manuscript and Egmondanus with the Aldine have *quid tale proavi pertulerunt*. The old manuscripts, as Heinsius himself admits, are defective after the words *publicus pasceret*. Therefore the words enclosed in parentheses are taken from Heinsius.

909. Vaticanus A has *deleta dolore*, incorrectly. The fields that Numa had assigned to the Vestals and priests had also been increased by private persons; under Valentinian and Theodosius, in the year 383, the treasury seized them. In that year a public famine followed. Hence, in his *Relation* of the year 384, Symmachus reproaches the Christians that the year had withered through sacrilege. From this final complaint of Symmachus it is argued that he was a pontiff, a conclusion also gathered from his letters, where he speaks of the Vestals as though their cause belonged to him.

In the inscription which I cited at verse 771 and judged possibly applicable to this Symmachus, L. Aurelius Avianius Symmachus is called chief pontiff. In the Caelian gardens of the Casalii, near what is called Santo Stefano Rotondo, there are two stones dedicated by Q. Fabius Memmius Symmachus; it is useful to present their inscriptions. The first stands on the right for one reading from the front, the second on the left.

I.

[Col. 0252A]

TO EUSEBIUS Q. AURELIUS SYMMACHUS, CLARISSIMUS MAN, QUAESTOR, PRAETOR, CHIEF PONTIFF, CORRECTOR OF LUCANIA AND BRUTTIUM, COUNT OF THE THIRD ORDER, PROCONSUL OF AFRICA, URBAN PREFECT, ORDINARY CONSUL, MOST ELOQUENT ORATOR. Q. FABIUS MEMMIUS SYMMACHUS, CLARISSIMUS MAN, TO HIS EXCELLENT FATHER.

II.

To Virio Nicomachus Flavianus, of clarissimus rank, quaestor, praetor, chief pontiff, consular governor of Sicily, quaestor of Africa, twice praetorian prefect within the palace, ordinary consul, a most eloquent historian: Q. Fabius Memmius Symmachus, of clarissimus rank, [dedicates this] to his excellent grandfather-in-law.

Corsinius published both of these inscriptions in *On the Prefects of Rome*, the first from Sponius and the second from Reinesius. I have corrected them against the original. Q. Fabius Memmius Symmachus is believed to have been the son of Symmachus the letter-writer; consequently, his father was Q. Aurelius Symmachus, the very man whom Prudentius attacks. L. Aurelius Avianius Symmachus, therefore, concerning whom I spoke at verse 771, seems to have been a different man, if the epitaph reproduced there from the marble was accurately transcribed.

Sirmond, in the preface to his notes on Sidonius and in his note on the first letter, observes that after the fall of the republic there was great variation in names and praenomina, and that one and the same man was often called by five names. In ancient inscriptions these two names are not rarely joined together, Lucius Quintus or Quintus Lucius. Thus there is still room for doubt whether the same Symmachus is praised in both inscriptions—namely, one who was called Q. Lucius Aurelius Avianius Symmachus.

Corsinius infers from the Theodosian Code that Q. Aurelius Symmachus was corrector of Lucania and Bruttium in 368, and proconsul of Africa in 370 or 373. The second inscription, which we have cited here, is also relevant to us, not only because the monument was erected by Memmius Symmachus, whose grandfather-in-law was Nicomachus, but because this same Nicomachus worked with the greatest determination to restore the worship of idols and for that reason was the instigator of Eugenius’ seizure of imperial power.

Nicephorus, book XII, chapter 30, calls him a man distinguished in learning; the inscription calls him consular governor of Sicily and a most eloquent historian. There is therefore no doubt that the subscriptions found in many manuscript copies of Livy must be referred to this Nicomachus; several of them were collected from the Vatican manuscripts by the distinguished Giovenazzi and shown to me.

But there were two Nicomachi: one was Nicomachus Dexter, who corrected Livy’s manuscript according to the copy of his ancestor Clementianus; the other was Nicomachus Flavianus, whose subscription appears at the end of book VII in Vatican Codex 1840:

> “I, Nicomachus Flavianus, corrected Livy. Having been prefect of the City three times, at Henna I was correcting the text for the lords Symmachus. The seventh book ends.”

Subscriptions of this kind have been written out by Sirmond in his notes on Sidonius, by the younger Pieter Burman in his notes on Valesius’ *Critique*, and by other very learned men in such a way that the correction is understood to have been made “from the foundation of the City.” They do not themselves mark the distinction, nor explain that it should be marked for others. They write approximately as follows:

> “I, Nicomachus Flavianus, corrected it from the foundation of the City. Victorianus, of clarissimus rank, was correcting it for the lords Symmachus.”

But those ancient correctors inserted their subscriptions between the lines of the manuscript; later copyists continued all the words they found in a single uninterrupted sequence, as has happened in the subscription before us. It should nevertheless be read and punctuated as follows:

> “Livy’s *History from the Foundation of the City*: the seventh book ends.”

Then, as though written above and between the lines:

> “I, Nicomachus Flavianus, prefect of the City for the second time, at Henna, corrected it. Victorianus, of clarissimus rank, was correcting it for the lords Symmachus.”

He is understood to have been prefect for a second time, since *ter* is corrupt for *iter* or *iterum*. Henna was a Sicilian city, where Nicomachus held the rank of consular governor. Corsinius could have illuminated the urban prefecture of Nicomachus from the subscriptions found in the Livian manuscripts.

Away, nations! You have no fellowship of roads  
with the people of God. Depart far away,  
and pierce your own chaos, where that guide  
calls you through the tangled paths of infernal night.

842 But for us who seek the Lord of life, there is one  
[905] [Col. 0252A] road: light, clear day, and simple grace.  
We follow in hope, walk by faith, and enjoy what is to come—  
things toward which the joys of the present life do not reach,  
nor do pleasures already possessed and yet to be possessed run together.

The final complaint of the envoy is lamented in grief:

[Col. 0253A] [Note]

910. *Palladiis*: offerings to Minerva.

913. *Rarius*: less frequently.

917. *Triptolemi*: the discoverer of agriculture. *Cereris*: the goddess of grain.

918. *Penu*: provision, alms.

920. *Pharios*: Egyptian.

921. *Stagnare*: to irrigate. *Canopi*: an Egyptian town.

922. *Affert*: announces, reports.

923. *Memphim*: Egypt, a city of Egypt.

[Note]

910 and 911. Aldus and the old Heinsian manuscripts have *stipis*, together with the Alexandrian, Urban, Ratian, and other copies. Weitz, with Widmann, has *stipes*. Either form can be used in the nominative according to ancient usage. Later usage requires *stips*. In the immediately following verse, Ratian, Vatican A, Juretus’ manuscript, Weitz, Widmann, Egmond, the Palatine, the old Heinsian manuscripts, and Giselinus in the margin have *castisque choris*. Aldus, Giselinus, and the common editions have *castisque toris*, which is not objectionable. Nevertheless, Gifanius says that *choris* is preferable on the basis of the word *vestis* in his old book.

913. The Alexandrian manuscript, Juretus’ manuscript, Aldus, Egmond, Fabricius, and the Heinsian manuscripts, except the second Rottendorf manuscript, have *rarius agros*. Ratian, Urban, Weitz, and Giselinus have *parcius agros*. Tertullian also used *frugescere*. On words ending in *-escere*, see Hispaniolus in the *Apology*, where he says that Furius Antias delighted in such words as *lapidescere*, *serescere*, *diescere*, *noctescere*, *caulescere*, *virescere*—for *vires assumere*, “to acquire strength”—*opulescere*, and *lutescere*.

914. Aldus, the Alexandrian and Urban manuscripts, Ratian, Juretus’ manuscript, and all the Heinsian manuscripts have *saevire famem*, “famine rages.” Giselinus and the common editions have the erroneous *servire famem*.

917. Aldus had omitted this verse and added it in his corrected edition: “the hateful famine, by which [the wrath] of Triptolemus and Ceres …” The other copies have: “famine, which … of Triptolemus”; some write *famis*. Vatican A, against the meter, has *Treptolemique, Cererisque*. Virgil calls Triptolemus in book I of the *Georgics* “the boy who showed the curved plow.” He learned from Ceres to sow grain.

918. The Thuanean manuscript has *peno* instead of *penu*.

919. There is mention of the famine that occurred in 383 in Ammianus, whose words I cited at verse 310 of the *Psychomachia*, and in St. Ambrose, book III of *On Duties*, chapter 7. He seems to be speaking of this famine:

> “How much more useful was this than what recently happened at Rome, that those who had already spent a lifetime there were expelled from that vast city? … And certainly the fertility of the year had smiled upon us; only the City itself was in need of imported grain,” and so forth.

Symmachus, book II, letter 7, to his brother Flavianus, says:

> “Gods, show favor concerning the neglected sacrifices. Drive away the wretched famine.”

Why, then, does Prudentius deny such a famine? It may be answered that Prudentius expressly speaks of the time at which he was writing, of the present time. But since Symmachus’ speech was delivered in 384, what is gained by answering that there was no famine when Prudentius wrote, if Symmachus affirms that there had been one?

Some say that Prudentius forgot that several years had already passed since that famine. It may also be added that Prudentius was probably far from Rome at the time of the famine, and therefore it is not surprising that he knew nothing about it.

Indeed, St. Ambrose, who admits that there was a famine in 383, adds in his *Reply*:

> “And yet even in the previous year we know that most provinces overflowed with produce. What should I say of Gaul, richer than usual?”

Moreover, I believe that the same speech of Symmachus, which he delivered to Valentinian in 384, was handed over either by Symmachus himself or by some of his pagan friends to Honorius, so that he might read it. For many things cited by Prudentius suggest some new attempt of the pagans; and since Prudentius refutes an old speech, I think that the same speech, eagerly preserved by the pagans, was again released to the public and presented to the emperor. Thus Prudentius rightly tears apart Symmachus’ arguments from what he saw occurring in his own time.

Symmachus himself once admitted that these arguments were empty. This is how I interpret his letter 82 to Rufinus in book III:

> “I merely watch from the bank of the Tiber—for the river flows through my estates—ships heavily laden, no longer anxious, as before, about the famine of the citizens. For public fear arising from scarcity has been turned into joy, after the revered father of his country balanced Africa’s losses with Macedonian supplies; now everyone loves him as the god who nourishes the human race. For he did not permit the defiant south winds to do anything against Rome. In the report he says, ‘Let us attribute nothing to the south winds.’”

920. Widmann has *varios* above, *Pharios*, or, as some write, *Farios*.

922. Giselinus had found *aut veniat sicco* and conjecturally corrected it to *haud venit a sicco*, which he later saw confirmed by the Buslidian manuscript. Heinsius adopted this, noticing nothing particular from his own manuscripts; later editors followed Heinsius. Weitz, with Egmond, Widmann, Gifanius, had read *aut veniat sicco*. But when Weitz cites Aldus in his support, he is mistaken: Aldus had indeed printed *aut veniat*, but corrected it to *haud veniat*, a fact Fabricius did not overlook. He certainly printed *haut veniat sicco*. Nevertheless, I retain Weitz’s reading, confirmed by Ratian, Vatican A, the Alexandrian and Urban manuscripts, and explained by Gifanius under the word *vestis*. From the old book, without controversy, one should read *aut veniat sicco*, and so forth. That is: if I report falsely, let someone appear and say that, with the Nile now dry, Egypt is perishing from famine.

923. Ratian and Weitz with his manuscripts have *sitis*; Aldus, the Alexandrian and Urban manuscripts, Giselinus, and others have *siti*.

843 Since the offerings of meal are denied to Palladian hearths,  
or since food is denied to the priestesses themselves  
and to the chaste choirs,  
the Vestal fires are deprived of their customary provisions.

Hence, he says, sterile fields produce grain less often,

845 and grim famine rages, and throughout the whole world  
[915] mortals grow pale in poverty, lacking bread.

[Col. 0254A] I do not remember any famine so great  
in the present time, or so hateful,  
that it could have stirred the anger of Triptolemus and Ceres,  
avenging the virgin’s deprivation of provisions,  
nor does rumor whisper of anything of the kind.

[920] 846 I hear that the Nile is flowing through the Pharian fields  
in its customary manner, and that the green crops of Canopus  
are being irrigated.

Or let him come who reports that, with the river dry,  
Memphis lies barren beneath the dust,  
wasted by thirst and fasting.

[Col. 0255A] [Note]

924. *Pelusiacae*: Pelusium, a promontory of Egypt.

925. *Fons*: the Nile.

927. *Nostras*: our own.

935. *Aequor*: fields.

936. *Libyci*: African.

938. *Acervos*: heaps, piles.

939. *Leontini*: Sicilian. *Sulcator*: plowman.

940. *Lilybaeo*: a promontory of Sicily, where grain is especially abundant.

941. *Rumpat*: break apart, because of the abundance of grain.

942. *Sardorum*: peoples.

943. *Ergo*: ironically.

944. *Poenus*: African.

945. *Remi*: Roman.

946. *Suppeditat*: supplies.

947. *Circi*: the theater.

948. *Regio*: district, part. *Gradibus*: the tiers of the theater.

949. *Sustinet*: endures, suffers. *Janiculi*: the Janiculum is a hill where the temple of Janus stood and many mills had been built. *Muta*: formerly “silent.”

[Note]

924. On Pelusium, Ammianus should be consulted rather than Isidore, book XXII, chapter 16:

> “In Augustamnica there is the famous town of Pelusium, which is said to have been founded by Peleus, the father of Achilles, who, on the gods’ command, was ordered to be purified in a lake washing the walls of that same city.”

925. The source of the Nile, formerly unknown, was discovered long ago in the Moon Mountains of the kingdom of Goyam in Abyssinia.

926. Arnobius, book I: “For we have learned that mighty rivers have dried up, their mud having been parched.” Virgil, *Eclogue* 7: “You might see dry rivers; the field is parched.” Elmenhorst gives further material in his notes on Arnobius.

927. The better Heinsian manuscripts and our own read *praestringere*, not *perstringere*.

928. Egmond has *exustus*; *exustos* is better.

930. Ratian and Urban have *obsorbentur*.

931. Vatican A, the first hand of the Alexandrian manuscript, and Urban have *nec sulcos*; *ne sulcos* is better.

933. Vatican A has *ad pingue solum*.

934. “The crop waves” is a poetic expression drawn from Virgil and others. Fields are “haired” like the foliage of trees. Salvianus, book VII of *On the Government of God*, calls Aquitania “surrounded by harvests.”

935. Gifanius says under the word *vestis* that this is wonderfully expressed. Lucretius: “that the plain clothe itself with ears of grain.” Columella likewise spoke of “banks clothed with grass,” and Virgil, book VIII: “Then youth first clothed my cheeks with its flower,” as Gifanius read it from book V; others read *juventus*. Cicero, book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*: “the earth clothed with flowers”; Ovid, book IV of the *Fasti*: “fields clothed with harvests”; Propertius, book III: “waves clothed with foliage.”

936. Horace, Seneca in the *Thyestes*, Claudian, Lucan, Petronius, Apollinaris, Juvenal, Rutilius, and others everywhere confirm that Rome’s grain supply was brought chiefly from Africa.

937. Grangaeus notes that this concerns history: Egypt sent its grain to Constantinople, Africa to Rome. Claudian, *On the Gildonic War*, verse 62:

> “The Egyptian fields have yielded to a new destination; our only hope remained, Libya.”

Grain from Africa and other regions arrived at Rome through the mouths of the Tiber. Symmachus, book X, letter 22, to Theodosius and Arcadius, mentions Egyptian grain:

> “You will also send the imperial fleet, which may increase the nourishment of the devoted populace with grain supplies. The senate, mingled with the people, will therefore receive it at the mouths of the Tiber. They will venerate as sacred the ships that have brought the fortunate cargoes of Egyptian grain.”

939. The fields of Leontini are praised in matters of grain by Cicero, Pliny, Apollinaris, and others. They were so called from Leontium, a city of Sicily. See Ferrari’s *Lexicon*.

940. Egmond has *frugigeras*; others have *frugiferas*.

941. Ratian has *horrea frangat*; the others have *rumpat*. Virgil, *Georgics* I: “The immense harvests have burst his granaries.” Sidonius, book I, letter 6:

> “Granted that your must will foam through vineyards multiplied for you, granaries too, burst by the countless heaps of grain you have stored, will provide you with innumerable piles.”

Teolius thinks that, unless this is hyperbole, it must refer to granaries suspended above the ground. I refer it more readily to hyperbole.

942. Ratian has *Sardonum*; read *Sardorum*. Grain was also brought to Rome from Sardinia, according to Strabo, Horace, Florus, Valesius, Salvianus, Symmachus, and others. Gothofredus indicates the passages in his notes on book IX of the Theodosian Code, title 40, law 3.

944. Virgil, *Aeneid* III, verse 649:

> “They give an unhappy sustenance, berries and stony cornel cherries; the branches, and the uprooted herbs, provide food.”

St. Ambrose, replying to Symmachus, has similar passages.

945. In the Ratian manuscript an inept recent corrector erased the earlier reading and substituted *quernas*, along with another word that Marietto could not even read. He had erased *quernas Sardinia*, so that *secunda* would not be lengthened in *Sardinia*, where it is usually shortened. But in such proper names ancient poets used greater freedom, and we may not condemn their practice.

946. The first Rottendorf and the Heinsian manuscripts have *cibos*, so that these words depend on what precedes. Virgil, *Georgics* II: “the stony cornel cherries redden.”

948. On bread distributed by tiers, see the commentary on verse 583 of book I.

949. Aldus, Giselinus, and Fabricius have *Janiculo mola nota*. Aldus had printed *mota*, but in his corrected edition placed *nota*. Ratian, Urban, Vatican A, Weitz, and most of the Heinsian manuscripts have *Janiculi mola mota*. Heinsius, with the earlier Rottendorf manuscript and both Boherian manuscripts, thinks *Janiculi mola muta* correct; the Alexandrian manuscript supports him. Procopius, book I of *The Gothic War*, reports that all the mills had been built at the foot of the Janiculum. See Lipsius, *Electa*, book I, chapter 8, where he explains this passage. Procopius’ words are:

> “At the foot of the Janiculum, and in the Tiber itself, all the city’s mills had formerly been constructed, because there the immense force of the waters is first compressed into a narrow channel and then led down precipitously through a conduit, so that it is carried along in a violently descending current.”

Nor does the Pelusian marsh sweat out its mud.

[925] Has the spring, hidden beneath nature’s secret covering,  
dried up, barely letting a thin trickle of water flow?

Does the river, turning away, refuse to touch our banks,  
and divert its course toward the parched Indians?

Does the thirsty riverbed, halfway along its course, swallow the water,

[930] and are the pools suddenly absorbed in a gaping chasm,  
so that the waters cannot cover the furrows,  
nor be drawn across the dry plains of Egypt  
to soften the rigid clods with streams poured onto rich soil,  
from which the crop might wave broadly across the fields,

[935] 847 and the plain might clothe itself more thickly with heavy ears?

Consider whether the plowman of the Libyan countryside  
has ceased to load ships with grain  
[Col. 0255B] and send to the mouths of the Tiber  
[Col. 0256A] heaps of wheat as food for the people;

whether the plowman of Leontine fields  
has ceased to dispatch grain-bearing boats

[940] from the Lilybaean shore;

whether the fleet, carrying Sardinian granaries,  
no longer sets sail across the straits  
or bursts the Roman storehouses.

Is it therefore the case that the African plowman fills tables  
with wild pears, and the Sicilian feeds on uprooted herbs?

[945] 848 And now Sardinia supplies the Roman people  
with acorns from oaks, and the stony cornel cherry is food for the Quirites?

Who comes hungry to the spectacles of the great Circus?

What district endures dreadful fasting

In Egmond, *si* is omitted, although it is necessary for the meter. Urban has: “with new grain, and the green harvest, but mature.” I think the passage should be punctuated:

965. Most punctuate: “Vesta, the Penates.” The poet also joined the Palladium, Vesta, and the Penates in verse 195 of book I:

> “Thus Vesta is, thus the Palladium, thus the shade of the Penates.”

In the Roman Forum, near the temple of Vesta, stood the temple of the Penates. As the Halicarnassian reports in book I, there were two youthful male figures there, seated, armed with spears, and sculpted in the ancient manner. These were the Penates, whom Aeneas is said to have brought with him. The same Halicarnassian reports that in ancient temples there were other statues of these same gods, all represented in military dress. Some think that the great gods—Jupiter, Neptune, Pluto, Vesta, Apollo, and others—occupied the place of the household spirits, Lares, and Penates.

966. Virgil, *Aeneid* V, verse 743:

969. Giselinus says that some manuscripts have *quonam*, others *quomodo*, both foolishly. Aldus has *quonam*. The true reading is *quoniam*. Lipsius, in *Syntagma on Vesta and the Vestals*, chapter 2, says that fire was indeed worshiped at Athens, but that the more certain origin of the Vestal fire should be sought among the Trojans and at Alba, where the sacred fire remained. Pallas is called Ἀθήνη (“Athena”) in Greek; Athens was therefore both founded and named after her.

970. Chamillard debates whether Vesta derives her force and origin from the earth, from the power of standing, or from fire. Both explanations seem to be gathered from ancient writers and coins. Consult Lipsius, chapter 1 of *On Vesta*, and Ovid, book VI of the *Fasti*. Some also thought that Vesta had no image, because, as Ovid says in book VI of the *Fasti*:

> “The undying fire is hidden in that temple; Vesta has no image, nor does the fire.”

But this must be understood of an image in the temple of Vesta, where there was only an altar for sacrifice. The image of Vesta is frequently represented on coins and in statues, as may be seen in Lipsius’ work on Vesta.

971. Lipsius, in the passage cited, reads *sacravitque*.

974. Vatican A has *alias*; read *alios*. He calls the tendency of nature a “law,” an expression sufficiently familiar to philosophers. Minucius in the *Octavius*: “The sea is enclosed by the law of the shore.”

Servius says: “Rust is a kind of disease by which the stalks perish … It usually arises from mist.”

1003. Egmond has *statuta* for *stata*; but Weitz does not explain whether he omits *dona*, or reads *vestris statuta negantur*, or *vestris statuta dona negantur*. Both possibilities violate the rules of meter. Urban has *vestris haec dona*.

1005. Most critics use these verses of Prudentius to explain Terminus and the rites by which the pagans worshiped him. Petrus Pithoeus may be consulted in part II of his *Miscellaneous Adversaria*, chapter 14.

Siculus Flaccus explains the rites observed when boundary markers were established in his book *On the Establishment of Fields*:

> “When they set out boundary markers, they placed the stones themselves upright in solid ground, close to the places where they intended to fix them after digging pits, and they anointed them and crowned them with coverings and garlands. In the pits where they were going to place them, after performing a sacrifice and slaughtering an unblemished victim, they threw burning torches into the pit; when it had been covered—or, according to another reading, adorned—they let the blood drip into it, and threw incense and grain upon it. They also added honeycombs, wine, and other things that custom made sacred to boundary markers. When all the offerings had been consumed by fire, they placed the stones over the hot remains and thus secured them with careful attention; they also added fragments of stone and stamped them down around the markers, so that they would stand more firmly.”

This, and more, is found in Siculus Flaccus.

In ancient times, however, Numa had forbidden anything living to be sacrificed to Terminus, the guardian of peace and protector of friendship. From this passage of Prudentius it is inferred that not only when a boundary marker was first fixed, but also on other days—and perhaps every year on a fixed day—the festival of the Terminalia was celebrated. I understand Horace’s words in *Epode* 1 in this sense: “the ewe slaughtered at the Terminalia festival.”

A boundary marker was a stone, a stake, or a tree. Ovid, *Fasti* II:

> “Terminus, whether you are a stone or a stake abandoned in the fields, you too have been a divinity since ancient times.”

Here *desertus* means something like planted or fixed in the ground. Others read *defossus*, “buried,” and some *desectus*, “cut down,” since boundary markers, whether stones or stakes, were usually shaped into images. Minucius in the *Octavius*:

> “Do you allow him to dash against stones on so bright a day—stones, indeed, fashioned into images, anointed, and crowned?”

Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* I, verse 381: “To pray to a stake stripped by the axe.”

Apuleius in the *Florida*: “A trunk shaped by the axe.”

I think that trees themselves sometimes served in place of boundary markers. Paulus, book V of the *Opinions Received*, title 22, speaks of “boundary trees.” Likewise, in law 1, paragraph 3, of the *Digest* on boundary markers, trees and stones are indiscriminately called boundary markers.

At times heaps of stones also served as boundary markers. These were called “heaps of Mercury,” and perhaps they are the very heaps mentioned in Proverbs 26:8:

> “Like one who casts a stone onto the heap of Mercury is one who gives honor to a fool.”

I remember seeing some trace of this superstition in Spain.

That the custom of celebrating the Terminalia varied is clear from Siculus Flaccus himself:

> “They also added honeycombs, wine, and other things that custom made sacred to boundary markers.”

Prudentius alone, so far as I know, mentions a chicken’s lung, by which Terminus was watered or anointed; for at verse 1007 I think *rigare*, “to water,” should be read, not *rogare*, “to ask.”

That Terminus and all the other ancient gods were decorated with garlands and crowns is well known to everyone. Perhaps this is relevant to Lucretius, book V:

> “There is no piety in being often seen to turn toward a veiled stone.”

Compare Paschalius, *On Crowns*, book IV, chapter 4.

1007. Aldus, the Alexandrian and Thuanean manuscripts, and the Oxford manuscript have *fasceolis*; others have *fasciolis*. Gifanius, under the word *lapis*, thinks that *rigare* should be read, and Juretus states that some people attest that *rigare* is found in their old parchment manuscripts. Weitz, with most of his manuscripts, apparently also has *rigare*. I strongly approve this reading, and it corresponds to the following verse; nor is the boundary marker violated by any entrails: that is, “it is anointed with no entrails,” as pagans were accustomed to do, as is clear from Siculus Flaccus and Minucius. To them add Arnobius, book I:

> “If ever I had seen a slippery stone smeared and soiled with olive oil.”

Apuleius, book I of the *Florida*:

> “For neither an altar crowned with flowers, nor a cave shaded with foliage, nor an oak burdened with horns, nor a beech crowned with skins, nor even a hill consecrated by a hedge, nor a trunk shaped by the axe, nor a turf moistened with a libation, nor a stone drenched with oil would justly impose a religious delay upon a traveler.”

I do not agree with Teolius, who thinks that *rogare* with a chicken’s lung signifies the customary rite of taking auspices by inspecting the entrails of birds and cattle. It is well established that the intestines of victims were customarily offered in pagan sacrifice. Persius, satire 2:

> “Or what is it, at what price do you buy the ears of the gods? With anointed lungs and entrails?”

[Col. 0261D] **1009.** Lipsius, *Electorum*, book I, chapter 3, observes from this passage that the ancients used to hang lamps on sacred trees, since a lamp was evidently a sacred object; hence little sacrificers and prophets carried a lamp and laurel, according to Seneca, *On the Happy Life*, chapter 27. Prudentius calls the tree “wreathed,” because, as we saw shortly before, trees too were crowned. On this subject see hymn 10 of the *Peristephanon*, line 302, and Winkelmann’s remarks in volume I of the work cited, page 57, based on Philostratus, Statius, and Aelian. There he explains an ancient monument standing in the villa of the exceptionally distinguished Albanian family at Rome, including the tree decorated with ribbons represented on it. I think that in each estate there was some ancient and notable tree which the owners worshiped, such as the oak described by Lucan and compared with Pompey in book I:

> It stands, the shadow of a great name. Like a lofty oak in a fertile field,  
> bearing the ancient spoils of the people and the sacred gifts of commanders,  
> no longer clinging to its stout roots, but fixed by its own weight;  
> spreading bare branches through the air, it makes shade with its trunk, not its foliage.  
> Though at first it nods, ready to fall beneath the east wind,  
> while so many surrounding woods raise themselves with sturdy timber,  
> it alone is worshiped.

Virgil, book VII:

> There was a laurel . . . sacred in its foliage and preserved for many years out of fear.

The custom of hanging lamps on trees may also be related to Martial, book X, epigram 6:

> When will that day come when the Campus, the tree, and every window  
> adorned by the Latin bride will shine?

Prudentius expresses the tree’s ribbons or bands, which he elsewhere calls “variegated wool.” Statius, book II of the *Thebaid*:

> From the chaste tree they weave purple ribbons with snowy contrast.

Arnobius, book V:

> Why are the branches of the tree adorned with violet crowns and wreathed?

In the Theodosian Code, title “On Pagans,” law 12, *a tree wreathed with ribbons*, Gothofredus proves that this superstition continued for a long time.

**1010.** Widm. has *servebat*: read *servabat*.

**1013.** Ald., Weitz., Gis. have *temperat*. The manuscript of Heinsius, Rat., Alex., Urb., and others have *temperet*. Ald., Heins., and Gis. print *aut pluvius*; Alex., Rat., and Fabr. likewise, more correctly than Weitz. and Gis. in the margin, who have *aut pluviis*.

**1014.** Widm. has *venientibus*; correctly placed in the margin is *viventibus*.

**1015.** Gronovius, chapter 5 of the *Ecclesiastical Observations*, conjectured *censu* for *sensu*. This conjecture is sufficiently confirmed by the correction of another passage of Saint Cyprian from the book *On Discipline*. Cauchius too preferred *censu*, which Heinsius adopted from the earlier Bohersian edition, followed by more recent editors. Gallandius adds that in the old editions *sensu* is mistakenly printed for *censu*. I do not dislike the reading of the manuscripts, *sensu*: just as in the following verse the poet says that Christians do not exult through avaricious zeal in profit, so here he affirms that they are not released into rejoicing by abundant feeling. I will not, however, conceal that the epithet *amplo* (“ample”) fits *censu* better than *sensui*.

[Col. 0262D] **1021.** Giselinus recognizes a change of number in *quales, quos*, as in that passage of Terence’s *Phormio*, act V, scene 11:

> Who, when the matter comes to wives, then become old men for me.

The parable of Christ indicated here occurs in Matthew 13.

**1023.** Virgil, *Georgics* I, line 223:

> Which you entrust to the furrows as their destined seed.

[Col. 0263C] **1030.** Vat. A, contrary to meter and sense, has *robur arctat*.

**1031.** Public roads were protected by embankments so that rainwater might run off. Hence *agger* is sometimes used for a road. An embankment is frequently called an *agger viae*. Virgil, *Aeneid* V:

> Like a snake often caught on the road’s embankment.

**1034.** Meursius, book I, chapter 10 of his *Critical Observations on Arnobius*, would prefer *conformat* to *confirmat*.

**1035.** Thuan. understands *non surda* as “with no deaf ear.” But Prudentius’ *summa aure* means “with only the outer ear,” just as *summum corpus* and *summus tactus* occur in the *Psychomachia*, lines 796 and 692; Cicero likewise used *summam aquam* for the surface of the water.

**1039.** Rat. and another Rott. have *exstirpemus*. Widm. and Rat. have *nostro de pectore*. Others read *sentos*, that is, “thorns.” Prudentius has more than once used *sentus* for “thorny,” imitating Terence.

**1041.** The holy Fathers and interpreters everywhere splendidly transfer this parable to the vices of the soul, which are signified by thorns, having learned this from Christ himself. Prudentius himself treats the same subject in the *Apotheosis*, lines 59 and following, where several similar expressions occur. He is everywhere consistent with himself.

**1042.** Ald., Urb., Thuan., Gis., the earlier Rott., and Heins. have *sentis*. Alex., after erasing the earlier reading, has *sentix*. Rat., Egm., Widm., and Weitz. do likewise. Gifanius, under the word *LATERAMINA*, says that Prudentius remarkably used *sentix* for *sentis*, since three old books plainly had *sentix*, with a marginal note that this was the rarer word. Thus Plautus and Persius used *junix* for *juvenca*; likewise the ancients perhaps used *pistrix* and *pistris*; similarly *curax*, and Calus the jurist used *vigilax*. Mariettus, who had seen a copy of Lucretius annotated by Gifanius’s manuscript notes, asserts that Gifanius wrote in the margin of this passage that he preferred *sentis*, which he had found in a better old book. Gifanius observes that Lucretius favored words of this kind: *lateramen, augmen, momen, vocamen, conamen, glomeramen, duramen*; and that Prudentius has *peccamen* in this verse.

[Col. 0264B] **1043.** Virgil, *Georgics* II, line 212:

> For indeed the gravel of the sloping countryside is barren,

where Servius explains *jejunam* as dry and sterile soil; hence, at verse 1024, *macies lapillorum*.

**1045.** Ald. has *affectis*; others, *effetis*. He lengthened the first syllable of *charisma* also in the preface to book I of the *Apotheosis*, line 11.

**1048.** Ald., Urb., and Alex. have *supra*; it should be printed.

**1050.** See hymn 7 of the *Cathemerinon*, line 220:

> And enriches the fruit-bearing field with a hundredfold return.

**1051.** Ald. and Urb. have *rediget*. Rat., Alex., the manuscript of Heinsius, and Weitz. have *redigit*; Fab. and Gis., *reddit*; Widm., in the margin, *redit*. *Redigit* seems more correct, as at verse 1059, “the fruits are brought into the barns.” Weitz. has *acriter*, but Ald., Gis., and our manuscripts have *acrius*.

**1052.** He used *acervum* simply for a heap of grain also in *Cathemerinon* 5, line 68:

> Taking care to guard the closed heaps.

Virgil, *Georgics* I:

> And the weevil ravages the great heap of grain.

**1054.** From the parable of the hundredfold fruit he passes to Christian virgins, for whom this reward was promised, as verse 1059 expresses: “Hence ten times ten.” This is a most lucid testimony from antiquity concerning the perpetual chastity and most holy life of our virgins, whom Prudentius compares with and greatly prefers to the Vestal virgins. Those virgins of ours were called “devoted to God,” and virginity promised to God was likewise called “devoted.” Ausonius, although not a Christian—or perhaps a Christian who had again become a pagan—and certainly not very devout, as his writings show, nevertheless praises virgins devoted to God. Thus, in *Parentalia* 6, the title reads: “Aemilia Hilaria, maternal aunt, a virgin devoted to God.” Then comes this epigram:

> Hatred of the female sex was always yours, and from it  
> grew the love of devoted virginity,  
> which you cultivated for nine times seven years;  
> the end of life was also the end of chastity.

Prudentius says the same shortly afterward:

> And the law of chastity, completed together with the end of life.

Ausonius again, concerning his aunt Julia Cataphronia:

> Unmarried, she cherished the love  
> of devoted virginity, and, though an old woman, remained sparing.

From these passages it is clear that perpetual virginity was once promised to God even at an age not yet fully mature. Indeed, Prudentius’ argument against the Vestals sufficiently proves that Christian virgins were consecrated to God in youth:

> At last Vesta grows weary of virginal old age.

If Christian virgins had been able to vow virginity only when approaching old age, one could answer Prudentius: “Vesta grows weary of virginal old age, but your religion grows weary of virginal youth.” Observe also that Aemilia, whom Ausonius praises, cultivated devoted virginity for nine times seven years.

Who, however, could sufficiently marvel at the intolerable impudence of Pawius, an irreligious man, who adapted Prudentius’ forthcoming declamation against the Vestals to our nuns, as though Prudentius had blamed the Vestals for preserving their virginity? Here are his words from *Philosophical Researches on the Americans*, by M. de Paw, volume II, Berlin, 1777, page 95:

> “Prudence wrote a Christian satire against the Vestals, who still existed at Rome in his time, and he made it a crime for them to have preserved their virginity. If this pious declaimer could then have foreseen that Christianity would one day be burdened with nuns, he would have kept silent.”

If Pawius had foreseen that these words would one day be appended to the praise with which Prudentius celebrates Christian perpetual virginity, and to that very declamation in which he condemns only the forced, temporary, and vice-exposed virginity of the Vestals, I do not know whether he would have laid violent hands upon himself; but certainly, if he had possessed any sense of shame, he ought to have fled from human sight. For how could Prudentius have regarded preserved virginity as a crime, when from “the law of chastity, completed with the end of life,” he concludes, “Hence ten times ten fruits are brought into the barns”? But we shall return to Pawius shortly.

What is sown: first, because the luxuriant shoot,

abounding in sap, grows strongly; then, when its moisture fails beneath the heat

of the fiery sun, it is scorched by thirst and dries up.

And lest the seeds fall among thorny brambles:

for rough bonds weave themselves around the rising crop,

[1030] and the bramble constricts the fragile stalks with sharp knots.

And lest the scattered grains lie along the road’s embankment:

because they lie exposed to birds and are devoured everywhere,

and lie filthy, as a disgraceful plaything for unclean crows.

By these laws God confirms the farmer; but he does not understand

[1035] the Father’s heavenly law with the highest part of his ear.

Yet he arranges both the crop of the heart and that of the field,

so that the inner breast may shine no less with cultivation,

[Col. 0263B] **856** than when joyful acres display their harvests.

For we uproot the thorny brambles from the breast,

[1040] [Col. 0264A] lest vicious scourges destroy the life-giving shoot,

lest the thorn of sins, through repeated wrongdoing,

hinder the fruit and crop of the soul.

Lest thin gravel dry with barren sands

the faith languishing beneath the heart, lest the heat of the breast

[1045] blaze and burn the gifts through exhausted veins.

Finally, lest a worthless concern for God leave him

in the worn-out part of the liver, and abandon the hope

on which we inwardly feed, handing it over to obscene birds to eat,

and lest faith, cast away, become prey to the enemy bird.

[1050] Such is the diligence of our people: it brings back the hundredfold

**857** fruits of the fields, applies itself to them more keenly,

[Col. 0264B] and does not fear that the weevil will ravage the gathered heap,

nor that the black ant will store it away in its hollow.

There are also most beautiful rewards for our virgins,

**1055.** *Pudor*: modesty, chastity.

**1057.** *Tenues*: lowly, worthless, or small.

**1059.** *Hinc*: after this. *Decies*: he is speaking here of widows: ten times six make sixty, and the sixtyfold number pertains to widows, according to Iso.

**1060.** *Horrea*: that is what I mean.

**1064.** *Pudoris*: chastity.

[Col. 0265C] **Notes**

**1055.** Tertullian, especially in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 16, proves that Scripture established a law requiring a woman’s head to be veiled; nature bears witness to it, and custom demands it, especially in the case of a virgin who has married Christ. Cyprian agrees with Tertullian in his book *On the Discipline and Conduct of Virgins*.

[Col. 0265D] **1059.** Ald., Alex., and Juretus’s manuscript have *decies seni*. Rat., Urb., Gis., Weitz., and Heins. have *decies deni*, which I prefer, since Prudentius seems again to mention the hundredfold fruits, although the first reading is not displeasing. See the commentary on verse 121 of the hymn to Saint Agnes. Various interpretations are offered of the thirtieth, sixtieth, and hundredfold fruit; and different judgments are made according to the different states of life being compared. Theodulf of Orléans, book VI, poem 7:

> Thirtyfold shines in marriage, sixtyfold among widows.  
> The third order of goodness surpasses these two,  
> and the glory of a hundredfold fruit is given to virgins;  
> this number is sacred and fitting for martyrdom.

The gloss is not satisfactory.

**1060.** Alex. incorrectly has *nonnunquam*. Urb. has: “The barns are never at any time exposed to the nocturnal thief.”

**1065.** Let Pawius learn from this what Prudentius criticizes in the virginity of the Vestals. First, that they are taken in tender years, even unwilling and resisting. Then, that they sigh over a hidden wound and lost marriage torches—not only because they are forced to enter that community before the free exercise of their own will has condemned the lawful bonds of marriage between the sexes, but also because hope does not wholly kill the fire, since at the appointed time they may rekindle their dormant flames. Moreover, he reproaches the Vestals for attending public spectacles, even the bloodstained gladiatorial games, and for not merely witnessing the slaughter of human beings but also ordering it and taking pleasure in it. These matters are clear in Prudentius; Pawius, however, fabricates the claim that he “made it a crime for the Vestals to have preserved their virginity.”

Juretus says that the reading should certainly be *capiuntur*, not *rapiuntur*, according to an old manuscript and better printed editions. Yet the latter can also be defended with some plausibility, since young virgins were for the most part assigned to the sacred service through force and against their will. Properly speaking, however, the Vestals were said to be “taken.” Ulpian, book of the *Rules*, title 10:

> Those who are inaugurated as flamines diales cease to be under the authority of their parents, as do those who are taken as Vestals.

Aulus Gellius, book I, chapter 12:

> Those who wrote about the taking of a Vestal virgin denied that it was lawful to take one younger than six or older than ten.

Suetonius, chapter 31, in his life of Augustus:

> He increased the number, dignity, and privileges of the priests, especially those of the Vestal virgins. When another had to be taken in place of one who had died, and many people sought to avoid giving their daughters for the lot, he swore that if the age of any of his granddaughters were suitable, he would offer her.

Tacitus, book XV of the *Annals*:

> When the Vestal virgin Laelia died, Cornelia, of the family of the Cossi, was taken in her place.

Saint Ambrose speaks in the same way in his response to Symmachus. Aulus Gellius, in the passage cited, gives the reason for this expression:

> A virgin is therefore said to be “taken,” because she is seized by the hand of the chief pontiff and led away from the parent under whose authority she is, as though captured in war.

Shortly afterward Prudentius says:

> Captive modesty is assigned to unwilling altars.

The chief pontiff used this formula:

> “I take you, Amata, as a Vestal priestess, to perform the sacred rites which it is right for a Vestal priestess to perform for the Roman people and the Quirites, according to the best law.”

In these words some, with Aulus Gellius, book I, chapter 12, think that the virgin is called “Amata” because the first Vestal virgin was named Amata. Others add that Virgil gave this name to Lavinia’s mother for the same reason. I think it more likely that *amatam* here means “chosen.”

I have explained these matters at length so that the distinction between our nuns and the Vestal virgins may be more evident. I strongly disagree with Teolius, who claims that these verses rightly establish that in those days our virgins were accustomed to be consecrated to God only at a mature age. For what was accepted among us, he says, our own poet would never have condemned among the pagans. And indeed, in the same age as Prudentius, Saint Leo the Great decreed that virgins were not to be consecrated by receiving the veil before the age of forty.

I disagree, that is, if he means that Christian virgins did not vow their virginity to God until mature age. The veil of consecration was something else: it was then bestowed as a reward for proven virginity. Prudentius condemns among the pagans the practice of taking girls before the age of ten—or no older than that—as though captured in war, without allowing them even at that age the freedom to decide whether to reject marriage.

Therefore it is not correctly inferred that our virgins were accustomed to be consecrated to God only at mature age, unless by “mature age” you mean the age at which virgins were capable of choosing or rejecting the bond of marriage. Saint Damasus, concerning his sister Irene:

> She had vowed herself to Christ while life remained,  
> so that holy modesty might prove the merit of a virgin;  
> she had not yet completed twice ten winters.

Most understand this to mean that Irene died in her twentieth year; others that she vowed virginity in that year.

There was formerly diverse discipline regarding reception of the veil. The Second Council of Carthage, canon 4:

> It was decreed that before the age of twenty-five neither deacons should be ordained nor virgins consecrated.

The Council of Agde, canon 19:

> Nuns, however approved their life and conduct may be, are not to receive the veil before their fortieth year.

The Council of Zaragoza, in the year 380, canon 8:

> Likewise it has been read that virgins who have vowed themselves to God are not to be veiled unless their age of forty years has been tested and approved by the priest.

Basil, *Canonical Epistles*, canon 18, requires that a virgin be more than sixteen or seventeen years old before she is enrolled in the register of sacred virgins.

and private honor, neither notorious nor publicly displayed,

and rare, meager meals, and a mind always sober,

and the law of chastity completed together with the end of life.

Hence ten times ten fruits are brought into the barns,

[1060] [Col. 0266A] the barns never at any time exposed to the nocturnal thief.

For no thief enters heaven; heavenly things are never unsealed

by fraud; fraud rolls about in the lowest regions of earth.

What is now the honor of Vestal virginity,

I shall examine, by what law it governs every form of modesty.

[1065] First, they are taken while still small, in tender years,

**1070.** *Contempta*: despised. *Perit*: willingly.

**1072.** *Caecum*: hidden.

**1074.** *Ignem*: love; *minna*.

**1075.** *Resides*: sluggish. *Faces*: torches of love. *Adolere*: to kindle.

[Col. 0267C] **Notes**

**1068.** Ald., Fabr., Urb., and Alex. in their first hand have *condemnat*; Gis., in the margin, *contemnat*; Rat., *contemnet*; Weitz., *condemnet*, which Heinsius adopted from Giselinus, although he noted nothing from his own manuscripts. *Condemnat* seems more harmonious with the others, as in Virgil, *Aeneid* II:

> First, modesty, before I violate you or undo your laws.

Many have already advised that this should be read not *violem, resolvam* but *violem, resolvam* in the subjunctive sense; likewise, “before I say these things.” Corradus, book VI of *On the Latin Language*, takes a different view and applies the appropriate distinction.

**1070.** Ald. has *contenta*: read *contempta*.

**1071.** Indeed, not even their eyes were untouched, for Pliny, book XXVIII, chapter 4, says concerning the evil eye:

> The god whom the Vestals worship among the Roman sacred rites.

**1076.** Understand *flammeum* as the veil with which newly married women were covered, although Iso thinks otherwise.

[Col. 0267D] **1079.** Ald., Heinsius’s manuscript, Widm. in the margin, Alex., Urb., Rat., and others have *dum thalamis*. Bong., Fabr., and Gis. have *tum*; Weitz., *cum*. Aldus incorrectly has *timuit vigor*.

**1081.** Some difficulty arises here: why does Prudentius call a veteran old woman a Vestal, when, having completed her service, she married? Pawius magnifies this difficulty with falsehoods in the note cited:

> “After twenty-three years of service, she was considered emerita and acquired the freedom to marry, as one may convince oneself by reading in Prudentius’ poems the satire just cited. It is rather surprising that this writer says in his little book that the former Vestals who entered the marriage bed brought into it not a single spark of the fire of love, since desire and old age had extinguished it in their worn-out hearts. A former Vestal who married at thirty certainly did not incur this reproach.”

What could one expect from this writer, when he speaks about American affairs, since he so shamelessly presents a fabricated history of the Vestals and cites Prudentius’ poems on the same subject? He says that the Vestals were considered emeritae after twenty-three years of service and could marry, so that in their thirtieth year of life they were permitted to contract marriage. But where did Prudentius teach this? Indeed, who has transmitted that the matter stood thus?

Dionysius, book I, explicitly says:

> They must remain chaste and free from marriage for thirty years, performing the sacred rites according to custom. During that period they must spend ten years learning, ten years performing the sacred rites, and ten years teaching.

You see that thirty years were assigned to the priesthood of the Vestals, after which they could marry—that is, in their thirty-seventh year of life or afterward, not before.

Nor is it true that Prudentius says the fire of love in the Vestals had been completely extinguished in the year when they were permitted to marry. For he adds:

> Even the newly married woman learns to grow warm in the cold bed.

Moreover, if the Vestals could be joined in marriage at about the age of forty, it may rightly be asked why a married Vestal is called a veteran old woman. I think Prudentius said this to indicate that the Vestals were excluded from marriage in youth, or in the better part of youth, when they were more suitable for marriage, and that it was finally granted to them in old age or at an age close to old age. No one will deny that a woman of about forty is already less suited to contracting marriage.

Certainly Statius, book II, calls a Vestal priestess long-lived:

> The long-lived priestess will tend the ever-watchful fire on the hearth.

Others think that Prudentius had in mind the Alban Vestals, who served for fifty years, as Dionysius teaches in book I. Some had incorrectly read *πενταετεῖς* (“five-year”) in place of *πεντηκονταετεῖς* (“fifty-year”), that is, five years instead of fifty, as Lipsius observed in his *Syntagma on Vesta and the Vestals*.

In any case, there is no greater difficulty in Prudentius’ words than in those of Ambrose, book I, chapter 4 of *On Virgins*:

> Who holds up to me the virgins of Vesta and the priestesses of Pallas? What kind of chastity is this—not of morals but of years—which is prescribed not by perpetuity but by age? Such integrity is overly wanton, whose corruption is reserved for later age. They themselves teach that their virgins ought not—and cannot—persevere, since they have put an end to virginity. What kind of religion is that in which chaste young women are ordered to become unchaste old women?

**1082.** Alex., Egm., Fabr., one Rott., Heins., and Gis. in the text have *juventas*. Weitz., Thuan., and the other Rott. have *juventa*. Heinsius cites the earlier Rottendorphius for *juventas*, and again the earlier Rottendorphius for *juventa*. Perhaps he meant to say the other or later one, but I cannot distinguish the matter sufficiently. Heinsius and Weitz. also cite Aldus for *juventas*, and therefore did not notice that Aldus had changed *juventas* to *juventus* in his corrected editions. Gis. in the margin, Widm., Bong. above, and Urb. read *juventus*. Gifanius, under the word *INVALIDUS*, thinks *juventa* should be read, that is, “in youth,” when she was a girl. In the old manuscripts, however, he generally found *juventus*, and in others *juventas*: “I do not know,” he says, “what it means.” Yet the same Gifanius, under the word *VESTIRE*, reads in Virgil, book VIII:

> Then youth first clothed my cheeks with its flower.

*Juventas* and *juventus* are the same; and even if one reads *juventa*, I do not understand, with Gifanius and Juretus, “in youth,” but rather that youth itself had served the hearths.

burning with praise of chastity and love of the gods,

condemns the lawful bonds of marriage between the sexes.

[1070] nor does pleasure perish, despised by the wretched, but the pleasure

of an untouched body is taken away; nor is the mind kept untouched,

nor is any rest granted to the marriage beds. For the unmarried woman sighs

and to cover the gray hairs of the aged with wedding flames.

[Col. 0269A] **Notes**

**1083.** *Emeritas*: veterans, full of old age. Soldiers are called *emeriti* because they cease to earn, that is, to serve in the army.

**1086.** *Adolet*: kindles, sets on fire.

[Col. 0270A] **1088.** *Pilento*: the *pilentum*, the *essedum*, and the *petorritum* are kinds of vehicles and perhaps one and the same thing.

**1089.** *Attonitae*: astonished. *Exspectabilis*: desirable.

[Col. 0269B] **Notes**

**1084.** Gifanius, under the word *INVALIDUS*, says that in an old manuscript he found *ingelido* for *valde gelido*, just as *indurus* means “very hard,” and in Lucretius *invalidus* means “very strong.” I discussed the word *indocilis* with the same meaning in the note on hymn 3 of the *Cathemerinon*, line 111. In another old manuscript Gifanius found *in gelido*, which, he says, may perhaps be more correct; and it certainly is more correct, although *ingelido* also occurs in Urb. and Alex. In old manuscripts, however, and especially in Alex., words are often joined together through the error of copyists. Juretus too read *ingelido* joined together in his manuscript, but I cannot grasp the interpretation: “that is, very cold and warm.” For that particle increases the force of the expression. Thus Penelope to Ulysses:

> I would not have lain cold in the deserted bed.

Perhaps in Juretus one should read “very cold and icy.”

**1085.** In describing the dress of the Vestals, Prudentius mentions the *infula*, ribbons, narrow bands, and cords added to the hair. All these terms are often used for the same object, but they were nevertheless distinguished from one another. On the *infula*, which properly belonged to priests, see book V of the commentary on verse 5 of hymn 9 of the *Cathemerinon*. A *vitta* was a more general headband, and there were specifically virginal ribbons, used by virgins and distinguished from the ribbons of married women.

Fabrettus, *On Trajan’s Column*, chapter 6, thinks that the ribbons were distinguished from the *infula* in such a way that the ribbons hung down while the *infula* encircled the head. He demonstrates this from two images of Vestal virgins, in which the ribbons relate to the *infulae* as streamers relate to wreaths. Festus says of these:

> Streamers, that is, colored little bands hanging down from crowns.

Iso below says that the *taeniolae* were the upper edge of the *vitta*. Saint Ambrose mentions both ribbons and the *infula* in his response to Symmachus:

> The ribbons of the banded headgear, the points of purple garments.

Dionysius mentions ribbons rather than the *infula*:

> They may marry after completing the required years, but only after laying aside the ribbons and the other insignia of the priesthood.

Ovid, wishing to indicate that Ilia, having lost her virginity, was no longer worthy of priestly insignia, says in book III of the *Fasti*:

> I stood beside the Trojan fires when the woolen ribbon  
> slipped from her hair and fell before the sacred hearths.

By contrast, Juvenal, to indicate more plainly the crime of a Vestal, says in satire 4:

> With the man beside whom the ribboned priestess had recently lain,  
> she who, while her blood was still warm, was destined to go beneath the earth.

For a Vestal convicted of incest was, according to the institution of Numa, to be buried alive.

**1086.** The Romans believed that when Vesta’s fire was extinguished, some disaster was foretold for the empire. Livy, book XXVI, chapter 27.

**1087.** Vat. A has *ut publica pompa sacerdos*. Correct *pompa plateas*. Barthius, book XLII, chapter 17, thinks that Prudentius referred to the custom of leading little women to a brothel with musicians, a crowd, and a procession. Barthius, however, explains it better in book XXXV, chapter 14, as the procession in which statues of the gods were carried around. Thus Plautus, in *The Soldier*:

> So that today I might lead you past there like a procession,

that is, as though you were a god, equipped with your attendants and all your finery. Horace, *Satires* I.3:

> Often, as though he were carrying the rites of Juno.

The words of Isidore, to be cited in the following verse, bear on this:

> To carry sacred objects and lead sacred objects, as Virgil says, means to carry the equipment necessary for sacrifices.

**1088.** Lipsius, *Syntagma on Vesta*, chapter 12, teaches that the Vestals were accustomed to be carried in a litter, and even in a *pilentum*, on the basis of this passage of Prudentius and Tacitus, *Annals* XII. Prudentius expressed Virgil’s statement in book VIII:

> Chaste mothers carried the sacred objects through the city  
> in soft *pilenta*.

Servius interprets *molle pilentum* as “hanging,” perhaps because *pilentum* derives from *πῖλος*, felted wool, which was used to make their seats softer.

Chamillardus improperly says that Saint Ambrose and Prudentius were mistaken: one wrote that the Vestals traveled in a litter, the other in a *pilentum*, whereas Tacitus, book XII, clearly says that they used a carriage:

> Agrippina also raised her dignity higher by entering the Capitol in a carriage;  
> this custom, anciently granted to priests and sacred rites, increased the woman’s veneration.

Yet Virgil’s verse makes clear that the sacred objects were also carried in *pilenta*. Moreover, although priests were permitted to enter the Capitol in a carriage, this does not prevent the Vestals from being transported through the streets in a litter or *pilentum*. Lipsius concludes from the same book of Tacitus that the Vestals used a *pilentum*.

Isidore, book XX, chapter 12, defines a *carpentum* as a ceremonial kind of vehicle, almost a processional cart. Thus a *pilentum*, decorated and equipped for a procession, can be called a *carpentum*. Pyrrhus Ligorius, *On Vehicles*, chapter 23, teaches that *pilentum*, *carpentum*, and *vehiculum* can be used interchangeably, because matrons used all these for promenades and sacrifices. Joannes Schefferus, in his notes, says that careful authors distinguish them; but in *On Vehicles*, chapter 25, he proves that the *pilentum* was more honorable than the *carpentum*, and that matrons were accustomed to be carried in a *pilentum* to games and sacrifices, as were the Vestals, to whom all the rights proper to matrons had been granted.

Livy, book V, chapter 25, concerning the gold contributed by the matrons to the treasury, says:

> This matter was especially welcome, and in recognition of their generosity the matrons were honored by being permitted to use the *pilentum* for sacred rites and games.

**1089.** Barthius, book XLII, chapter 17, reads *spectabilis* and says that critics act without sufficient judgment when they restore *exspectabilis*. Ald., Gis., and the common text with Heinsius also read *spectabilis*. Alex. and Urb., however, agree with Weitz. and Rat. in restoring *exspectabilis*, which also stood in Sich. and in the first edition of Gis. in the margin.

For *imputat*, Giselinus placed *implicat* in the margin from Pulmannus’s manuscript, but he did not approve it. For how does the Vestal entangle or intermingle herself with the city if she sits in a soft *pilentum*, if she is conspicuous like a public procession, and if she sits in the better part of the theater? Giselinus therefore explains *imputat* as “casts up” or “exhibits,” and shows her disgracefully, as though by that very act accusing the city of excessive expenditure. Suetonius uses the verb *imputare* in the same sense in his life of Tiberius, chapter 53.

Teolius, from codices Vat. and Alex., adds the gloss *imputat, exprobrat*: “she reproaches the state that it owes its safety to her and to her virginity.” Perhaps Prudentius meant nothing more than that the Vestal displays herself conspicuously with her face uncovered. Earlier he had praised our virgins for having their faces covered with a sacred veil, and it is evident from ancient coins that the Vestals did not use a head covering.

Although the *pilentum* was covered above and constructed like a chamber, this verse nevertheless shows that it was open at the sides, where the Vestals presented themselves to be seen. Aldus, without any regard to sense, placed a question mark after this verse.

She transfers the wrinkles of her years of service to the marriage-bed supports,

[1085] meanwhile, while the twisted *infula* binds her wandering hair,

It is carried through the middle of the streets, like a public procession,

863 seated in a soft pilentum, and, with her face uncovered,

the conspicuous virgin, her face uncovered, displays herself to the astonished City.
