1090. Heraldus, on Arnobius, p. 274, and Elmenhorstius, on the same author, p. 54, illustrate these verses. Cyprian, Letter 2 to Donatus: “A gladiatorial show is prepared, so that blood may delight the lust of cruel eyes. The body is filled with stronger foods, and its robust mass grows fat with layers of lard, so that, fattened for punishment, a man may die at greater cost. A man is killed for the pleasure of a man, and skill is cultivated so that one may be able to kill; crime is not merely committed but taught. What could be called more inhuman, what more bitter? … What of that, I ask you, where men expose to wild beasts those whom no one has condemned?”

1092. Gladiators practiced their art so that they might be fed; hence he calls wounds “sold for food.” Propertius, elegy 8 of Book IV: “Who will give the fates of the unclean to the fattening-ground for sale?” See Vulpius’s notes.

1093. Aldus and Tornaesius have *sed et*; read *sedet*. The verb *sedet* seems especially appropriate for expressing the woman’s arrogance. Thus Juvenal, Satire 10: “She sits in her prepared flame-colored veil.”

1094. On the ribbons, see above. Lipsius, Book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 15, treats Prudentius as some kind of crude man of our age, or a schoolboy, and comes close to ordering him to be flogged. “*Lanista*,” he says, “designates an executioner,” according to Isidore. Prudentius uses it for gladiators: “not quite properly, indeed incompetently.” First, I should ask Lipsius why he does not prefer Prudentius to Isidore, if perhaps they disagree among themselves about the meaning of a word. Moreover, in Isidore, Book X of the *Etymologies*, under the letter L, I read as follows: “*Lanista* means gladiator, that is, an executioner, so called in the Tuscan language, evidently from *laniando*, ‘tearing bodies to pieces.’” Donatus, in the *Eunuchus*, Act II, Scene 2, says that *lanii* are those who tear animals to pieces, and that hence *lanistae* are called those who are in charge of tearing gladiators apart. Janus Gruterus, in his notes on Seneca, Book VI *On Benefits*, chapter 12, explains at length who the *lanistae* were. Some teach that they were the teachers and instructors of gladiators. Juvenal, Satire 3, verse 157: “Here let the son of the polished herald applaud among the well-dressed youths, and the youths of the *lanista*.” Some explain this as the sons of the chief of the gladiators, who trained gladiators; others as the sons of the gladiators’ instructor, who taught the art of handling weapons. Prudentius adheres to the word’s primary sense, *laniare*, “to tear apart.”

1095. In the Parma edition, incorrectly, *adictus*, written as one word.

1097. Rat. has *agit esse* with the gloss *aestimat*, “he judges.”

1098. Juretus testifies that in certain manuscripts one reads *virgo molesta*, an easy scribal error. *Modesta*, ironically, is the true reading, just as earlier *pudor almus* and *expers sanguinis*. The ancients turned their thumbs when they denied favor, and at spectacles when they ordered death. Juvenal, Satire 3, verse 36: “With the crowd’s turned thumb, they kill anyone indiscriminately.” Conversely, when we favor someone, we are even proverbially instructed to press down our thumbs, as Pliny says in Book XXVIII, chapter 2. Angelus Politianus illustrates this custom in *Miscellanea*, collection, chapter 42. The Romans generally ordered those gladiators who sought to win their lives in combat to be killed, and favored those who were willing to die or who thrust their sword fiercely into an opponent’s throat. Testimony to this is found in Seneca, Book I *On the Tranquility of Life*, chapter 11, and Book I *On Anger*, chapter 2. Our writers reproached the pagans for this cruelty, as Tertullian does in *On Spectacles*, and Lactantius in Book VI, chapter 20: “I ask now whether men who are pious and just can be those who not only allow men placed beneath the stroke of death and begging for mercy to be killed, but demand it, and cast cruel and inhuman votes for death—who are neither satisfied with wounds nor content with blood. They even order those who have been struck down and are lying there to be attacked again, and the corpses to be torn apart by blows, lest anyone deceive them by pretending to be dead.” It is well known that Christians always shrank from such bloody spectacles, and even more so those who served the sacred ministry among Christians.

[Col. 0272C] 1100. On the *secutor*, Isidore says the following in Book XVIII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 55: “The *secutor* is so called from pursuing the *retiarius*. For he carried a point and a leaden weight, which impeded his opponent’s missile, so that before the latter could strike with his net, he might rush out against him. This armor was sacred to Vulcan, for fire always pursues water; and therefore he was matched with the *retiarius*, since fire and water are always enemies to one another.” On the *retiarius*, the same Isidore says in the preceding chapter: “The *retiarius*, from the type of armor, secretly carried in the gladiatorial game a net against another fighter; this net is called a *jaculum*, ‘a missile,’ so that he might cover the opponent while pursuing him with his spear, and, once entangled, overcome him by force. This armor fought for Neptune because of the trident.”

1102. Vat. A has the corrupt reading *alatii* for *latii*. Aldus has, less satisfactorily, *palatii*. I understand *palatium* to mean Rome itself, as *palatia* does earlier, at verse 765; or perhaps the pledge of the empire, of which Livy says in Book XXVI, chapter 27: “the temple of Vesta was sought, together with the eternal fires and the fatal pledge of Roman power stored in the innermost sanctuary.” Some think that this pledge was the Palladium.

1103. The Vestals were said to redeem the life of the people, either because they performed sacred rites on its behalf, or because, as Plutarch relates in *Numa*, if they happened by chance to meet someone being led to execution, he was released from punishment. It was necessary, however, to swear that the meeting had occurred by chance and not by design. Rualdus, in his *Observations*, sets against this the praetor’s words from the perpetual edict, quoted by Aulus Gellius in Book X, chapter 15: “I shall not compel a Vestal priestess or the *flamen Dialis* to swear within my entire jurisdiction.”

1104. Iso seems to have read *bene vel male*, “well or badly”; but the true reading is *bene vel bene*, “well or well.” Pliny, Book XVI, chapter 44, writes as follows: “That one is older—the lotus—but its age is uncertain; it is called the hair-bearing one because the hair of the Vestal virgins is brought to it.” Fabrettus, *On Trajan’s Column*, chapter 6, maintains that the Vestals wore their hair cut and bound. Lipsius distinguishes the matter better and reports that they were shorn once, at their entry into the priesthood, and afterward allowed their hair to grow. This passage of Prudentius clearly proves that the hair was spread even down to their necks, and thus confirms Montfaucon, volume III of the *Antiquities*, p. 217, against Fabrettus. For according to Festus, brides adorned their heads with sixfold locks, and the Vestals used the same arrangement. Ovid, Book III of the *Fasti*, concerning the Vestal Silvia, mother of Remus and Romulus: “Weary, she sat down upon the ground, received the winds upon her open breast, and restored her disordered hair”; and shortly afterward: “When the woolen ribbon slipped from her hair and fell before the sacred hearths.”]

to behold with consecrated eyes men’s bloody contests, deaths, and wounds sold for sustenance.

There she sits, distinguished by the venerable ornaments of her fillets, and delights in gladiators.

and whenever the victor thrusts his sword into the throat,

orders the breast of the fallen man to be torn open by a turned thumb,

865 so that no part of the soul may remain hidden in the deepest organs,

for the majesty of the Latian palace,

Is it because they bathe their necks well with their hair, or bind

1105. Aldus writes *litia*. In the gloss I would gladly read “for the whole ribbon,” not “for the whole garment.”

1106. Fabr. and Gis., in the margin, have *tristibus umbris*, “with gloomy shades.” Urb. has the incorrect *tectibus umbris*. They performed sacred rites beneath the earth for Vesta, because they believed her to be the earth. Perhaps for that reason Prudentius says *testibus umbris*, “with witnessing shades”; or, as Chamillard thinks, because the ancients believed that the spirits of the dead were present at altars and hearths.

1107. Prudentius often uses *murmur* for the subdued voice of those praying. See the preface to Book I, verse 36.

1108. Suetonius, chapter 44, in his *Augustus*: “He assigned the Vestal virgins a separate place in the theater, opposite the praetor’s tribunal.” Juvenal also mentions the podium in Satire 2: “with everyone looking toward the podium.” The *podium* in an amphitheater was the gallery above the belt of the wall surrounding the arena; it served both as an ornament and as a place for seating, and was somewhat more spacious than the other tiers. Senators and other persons distinguished by rank sat in the podium. Jos. Emmanuel Miniana, a highly respected man, asks in his dialogue *On the Theater at Saguntum* how the podium could have been at the front of the stage in a theater, when it is clear from Suetonius and Prudentius that the Vestals were given a place in the podium opposite the praetor’s tribunal. When he consulted Emmanuel Martinus on this matter, the latter could resolve the difficulty only by emending Suetonius, so that one should read “in the amphitheater” instead of “in the theater,” or “beside the praetor’s tribunal” instead of “opposite the praetor’s tribunal.” But, as I think, the podium in the theater was indeed opposite the stage, yet formed a semicircle in such a way that the place assigned to the Vestals could have been opposite the praetor’s tribunal—if, that is, the semicircle began at that tribunal on one side and ended at the Vestals’ seats on the other. Miniana shrewdly observes that Prudentius rightly said “in the better part of the podium,” because Tiberius decreed that whenever Augusta entered the theater, her seat should be among the Vestals, as Tacitus relates in Book IV of the *Annals*. Perhaps greater light may be shed on the matter by the words of Bulenger, Book I *On the Theater*, chapter 9: “That the theater did not consist solely of a semicircle is shown by the shape of the theater at Rome, that of Marcellus. For since they used lines bent back beyond the semicircle, removing a quarter from the complete circumference of the circle, they assigned what remained to the theater.” Arnobius likewise, in Book IV, objects to the pagans that priests and Vestals sat at public spectacles: “The colleges of all the priests and magistrates sit at public spectacles—the chief pontiffs and chief curiones; the fifteen priests crowned with laurel, and the *flamines Diales* with their caps; the augurs, interpreters of the divine mind and will; and also the chaste virgins, perpetual nourishers and preservers of the fire.” I observe that by Prudentius’ time the athletic games seem already to have ceased. For Nero, as Suetonius reports in his *Life*, chapter 12, invited even the Vestals to an athletic spectacle, because at Olympia the priestesses of Ceres were also permitted to watch. If in Prudentius’ time the Vestals had attended athletic contests, Prudentius would not have omitted to draw from this an argument against their chastity.

1109. Ald. and Gis. have *tridente*; others, *tridenti*. Aldus incorrectly punctuates: “they watch the bronze face?” The *mirmillo* covered his face with iron. This is the *secutor*, whom I discussed above, who fought against the *retiarius*. The *retiarius* was armed with a trident, or fork, and a net.

1110. Widm. has *quatiunt*, “they shake.” Aldus incorrectly divides *hastilia saucius*, and *quam*.

1111. Vat. A incorrectly has *arenis*. Urb. and Alex. write *harenis*.

1112. Rat. has *quando*, whereas above it correctly has *quanto*. From these verses of Prudentius it can be inferred that the Vestals had not yet been abolished in his time. Lipsius asks when they ceased to exist and answers that this occurred under the elder Theodosius; many others say the same. But the only established fact is that Theodosius and other earlier Christian emperors deprived the Vestals of their revenues and privileges. Nevertheless, the women themselves remained even after such edicts, and either retained certain privileges or, with the magistrates’ connivance, arrogated them to themselves again. Thus throughout the East the privileges of the priests were completely abolished by Arcadius in the year 396, by Law 14 of the Theodosian Code, *On Pagans*: “Let them not congratulate themselves on being protected by privilege, whose profession is known by law to have been condemned.” Yet Gothofredus observes that some privileges remained—for example, the privilege of the *alytarch* of Antioch, namely, that of cutting down one cypress from the grove of Daphne, which was finally abolished by Justinian. Thus, after their revenues were withdrawn and their privileges diminished or abolished, the Vestal virgins gradually disappeared, as may reasonably be conjectured. Perhaps Symmachus’ Letter 99, Book IX, addressed to a Vestal virgin, refers to this: “You are said to wish to withdraw from the Vestal seclusion before the years fixed by law. I do not yet believe the report, but I await the assurance of your own voice.” In the inscriptions that I wrote out at verse 909, Symmachus and Nicomachus are called chief pontiffs long after the privileges of the Vestals had been abolished.

[Col. 0274D] 1114. There can be no doubt that Honorius is meant, whatever the glosses say; they contradict one another and in no respect reach the truth. Lipsius, Book I of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 12, reports approximately the following about gladiatorial games: Nerva reduced the expense and number of gladiators but did not abolish them entirely, contrary to Zonaras’ false claim. Constantine prohibited these games, according to Sozomen, Eusebius, and Callistus, Book VII. Under Constantius the games broke out again, as may be gathered from the Theodosian Code, Augustine, and Prudentius. Constantine’s law is found in Book XI, title 43, of the Justinian Code: “Bloody spectacles are not pleasing amid civic leisure and domestic peace; therefore we altogether prohibit gladiators.” It was enacted during the consulship of Paulinus and Julianus, in the year of Christ 325. Guillelmus Pyrrho, in his notes for the use of the Dauphin on Claudian’s *Panegyric of Mallius Theodorus*, says that Claudian does not list gladiatorial games among the other games because they had been abolished by Constantine. He should more correctly have said, “by Honorius.”]

1115. Lipsius, in the place cited, rightly observes that the game is called sacred because the gladiatorial contest was sacred to the infernal gods, who were to be appeased. The weapons themselves were sacred to the gods. See the commentary on verse 1100. Isidore, *On Spectacles*, Book XVIII, chapter 16: “Thus in Etruria, among the other rites of their superstitions, the Lydians also established spectacles in the name of religion. From there the Romans borrowed artists who had been summoned.”

1118. Aldus incorrectly has *servabit pietas*, “piety will preserve.”

1122. Fabr., Bong., Gis., and Alex. in the first hand have *patris*, “of the father.” Others have *patri*, “for the father,” which is better.

1125. Ancient writers commonly call spectacles *voluptates*, “pleasures.” Isidore, in the passage cited, says: “Spectacles, as I think, are generally called pleasures—things which do not defile by themselves, but through what is done there.” Symmachus, writing to Theodosius and Arcadius in Letter 19, Book X, about the Roman people, says: “Therefore it asks your Clemency that, after those subsidies which your generosity will provide for our sustenance, you also supply the circus and Pompey’s theater with the pleasures of the curule and theatrical shows.” Cassiodorus several times mentions a *tribune of pleasures*.

1128. *Homicidia ludat*, “may play at homicides,” is correct, because, as Grangaeus notes, the art of gladiators itself is called a game.

1131. Ald., Urb., Weitz., Gis., and others have *belli*, “of war.” Oxon., the earlier Rott., Heins., Alex. in the first hand, later witnesses, and Gallandius have *bellis*, “wars.” Heinsius additionally cites some Weitzian manuscripts in favor of *bellis*; but Weitzius printed *belli* and recorded no differing reading. Certainly *bellis sequatur*, “let him follow in wars,” is more harmonious and appropriate, so that *pietate sequatur*, “let him follow in piety,” may immediately follow it.

Aldus adds after the final verse: “It ends against Symmachus.” Rat. has: “Here ends Book II.” Vat. A has nothing. Mariettus noted at this point that this manuscript is extremely corrupt in the second book against Symmachus, and not very good in the first either.]

Look closely: is not this place of paternal merit vacant,

which God and the piety friendly to your father

have preserved for you to fill? Shall he alone possess

the rewards of such great virtue? “A share I reserve for you,

[1120] my son,” he said, and left the honor whole and untouched.

Seize the fame prolonged into your own age, O leader,

and, as successor to his praise, possess what remains for your father.

[Col. 0276A] He forbade the City to be stained with the blood of bulls;

## THE BOOK *PERISTEPHANON*. [Note: [Col. 0275C]

For the Book *Peristephanon*, most people place the ode “He Sacrifices to God the Father” as a preface; on the authority of the best manuscripts, we relegate it to the end of the works. In nearly all manuscripts the title is *The Book Peristephanon*, or *Here Begins the Book Peristephanon*, as in Vat. A and Egm. In Vat. S. the title is *On the Crowned Ones*. Better is the testimony of St. Gregory of Tours, Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 93: “Aurelius Clemens offers testimony of this matter in the book *On Crowns*, saying in these verses: ‘That hidden praise is not unknown,’ etc.” For the book *Peristephanon* ought to be titled in Latin *On Crowns*, namely, of the holy martyrs. Although this book needs no commendation, it is nevertheless worthwhile to hear Petrus Crinitus, Book V *On Latin Poets*: “He achieved particular praise, in the judgment of the more learned, from that poem in which he celebrates the integrity and steadfastness of those who devoted themselves for the Christian religion.” Giselinus observes that the praises chiefly celebrated are those of the holy martyrs who suffered death in the kingdom of Spain—both so that later generations might have examples whose footsteps they could firmly follow and pursue, and so that they might at the same time know to whom they owed that supreme good, the faith. With a similar aim, in 1749 at Madrid, Io. Ignatius de Larralde, S.J., published in octavo a work entitled *The Holy Year Poetically Arranged*. I had previously sought it in order to mention it in my *Hispanic Hymnody*; afterward the distinguished Raymundus Diosdado reported that he had discovered it while diligently assembling, from every source, materials for the Hispanic library that we hope someday to publish.]

(C)

870 I. HYMN IN HONOR OF THE HOLY MARTYRS HEMETERIUS AND CELEDONIUS. The names of the two martyrs are written in heaven.

[Col. 0277A] [Note: [Col. 0277A]

Verse 3. “With marks”: with characters; Iso.

4. “Shines”: sparkles. “Iberian”: Spanish; I.

8. “Sands”: tombs; I.

[Col. 0278A] 10. “Of the outer world”: of a foreign province; I.

12. “They surround”: they desire; I.

13. “Heaped together”: accumulated; Iso.]

[Note: [Col. 0277C]

Verse 1. Aldus gives the title of the first hymn as “Hymn of the Holy Martyrs Hemeterius and Celedonius of Calagurris.” He corrected it in this way, having previously printed “of Emeterius and Chaledonius.” Heinsius did not notice the correction and claims that Aldus wrote “of Emeterius and Chaledonius.” The Ambrosian manuscript has: “Here begins the hymn of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens in praise of the holy martyrs Emeterius and Chelidonius of Calagurris.” In this manuscript, as in Aldus, the hymn immediately follows the martyrdom of Romanus, which is contained in a separate book in many manuscripts. Thuan. writes “of Ematerius and Cheledonius of Caleguerris.” Rot. has “The Passion of Hemeterius and Celedonius.” The meter is trochaic. Alt. has “Hymn in honor of the holy martyrs Hemiterius, etc.” Egm. has “Hymn of the holy martyrs Emeterius and Celedonius of Calagurris.” Heinsius, with Put., has “Hymn in honor of the holy martyrs Emeterius and Chelidonius of Calagurris.” Vat. A has “Hymn of the holy martyrs Emetrius and Chelidonius of Caesaraugusta”—read “of Calagurris.” Vat. B has “Hymn in honor of the martyrs …” [the page is torn at this point] “and of Celedonius of Calagurris.” Alex. has “Hymn in honor of the holy Emiterius and Chelidonius,” with “in honor” added by a second hand. Other manuscripts have no title. I write these names amid such great variation in the ancient manuscripts as I find them in our breviaries, although “Chelidonius” appears to preserve greater antiquity. Lesleus, in his notes on the Mozarabic Missal, observes that the very ancient Acts of these martyrs, once read in Spain, agree entirely with the Mozarabic Missal and with Prudentius’ hymn. Whether these two martyrs were Calagurritans, I shall discuss at the end of the hymn. In the heading they are called Calagurritan martyrs because they suffered at Calagurris; it is not certain that Prudentius himself wrote the words in that form. In Marietti’s manuscript these verses are divided into groups of three by large red letters. Aldus ignored this division. Others divide them into individual verses in the following way: “The names of the two martyrs are written in heaven.” Giselinus, in his commentary on the *Cathemerinon* hymn, insists that these verses and the whole hymn ought to be written as complete trochaics, and praises Jacobus Meyerus for restoring this hymn and the first *Peristephanon* most elegantly by changing their metrical form, since previously they had been broken into Alcmanic and Euripidean cola. In fact, the Alcmanic and Euripidean forms together make a complete catalectic tetrameter verse. Yet complete trochaic verses of these hymns are found not only in many ancient parchments but also in editions printed before Meyerus. The beginning of this hymn is most elegantly drawn from Luke 10:20: “But rejoice that your names are written in heaven.” Prudentius speaks more than once in this book about the book of life. Paulinus also uses *caelo* for “in heaven,” in *Natales* 11.

2. Egm. has the inferior reading *aureisque*, “and with golden [letters].”

3. Gis. and also the Bollandists printed *notis et eadem*; I do not know whether they took this from their own manuscripts or found it in Giselinus. Giselinus wished to accommodate the meter; but the manuscripts have *eadem*, and at that time it was customary for the accusative and nominative plural to lengthen the second syllable in both forms, *eadem*. The Mozarabic breviary also reads *eadem*. This hymn occurs in that breviary on March 3, from which I shall record the variant readings. Becmanus, in his *Introduction to the Latin Language*, chapter 11, asserts that in this hymn, as it was then commonly printed, the sentence hung suspended twenty times or more and was intricately entangled because the divisions by commas, cola, and periods were either omitted or placed in the wrong position. He emended and punctuated the beginning of the same hymn from the Palatine manuscript. He reads this verse as follows: “He delivered to the earth the same names written with the marks of blood.” This is correct with respect to the meter, but, as I think, not on the authority of the ancient manuscripts. Weitzius, who, in my opinion, had consulted this very Palatine manuscript, did not report this variant. In Urb. I find *notis eorum*, “with the marks of them.” Just as Prudentius says that the names were recorded in heaven in letters of gold, so he says that the same names were written on earth in the marks of blood poured out through martyrdom. For the marks are like abbreviations of letters, as we shall explain in the hymn of St. Cassianus.

4. Here “the Iberian land” is more suitably understood as the particular region called Iberia in Spain than as Spain as a whole. Barthius, Book XL of the *Adversaria*, chapter 7, notes that *stemma* among writers of the declining age means “crown.” Ennodius liked to use the word, but Sirmondus and Schottus, who in the same year became Ennodius’ defenders, changed *stemmata* into *schamata*. Barthius dislikes this, since later ages used *stemmata* for ornaments in a thousand places. I think Prudentius was referring to the title of his own book: he entitled the book *Peristephanon*, and immediately sings that Iberian land possesses this crown. Anyone who knows Greek will easily recognize that *stemma* and *stephanos* have the same origin and meaning. Hericus of Auxerre reproduced the words of this verse in Book II: “The blessed one will shine entirely with a maidenly crown.” Paulinus also seems to take it as “crown” in *On the Death of Celsus*: “But those whom piety has raised through heavenly action will bear crowns shared with God the King.” See the commentary on verse 81 of Hymn 7 of the *Cathemerinon*. Gifanius, under the word *POLLERE*, marvels that this verb, once so familiar to ancient people, even to Cicero, in the sense “to be strong,” is scarcely known today.

7. Egm. has the erroneous *hicalentes* for *hic calentes*. The Mozarabic breviary corruptly has *hauxit undas caedit ictu*.

8. Vat. A incorrectly has *arenae*. Gretzerus, *On Sacred Pilgrimage*, Book I, chapter 18, aptly cites these verses to support his subject. Baronius, in the Roman Martyrology under March 3, praises the same verses to demonstrate the pious devotion of the faithful. Peveratus wisely observes with what veneration the first Christians treated the blood of the holy martyrs, since they crowded around sands stained with blood, beseeching them. From this point onward I shall use, in their proper places, the notes of a most learned man on the manuscripts, which I possess, having had them copied and sent from Ferrara by the distinguished Antonio Polop with exceptional care and diligence.

10. The Mozarabic breviary has, corruptly, “The foreigner, and also of the city, arrives here as a colonist,” which requires correction. It should be noted that not only Spaniards but also peoples of other nations came to the martyrs’ tombs. Hospinianus, *On the Origin of Christian Festivals*, pp. 12–13, while discussing memorials of the martyrs, suggests that pilgrimages to martyrs’ tombs began only after St. Augustine. This is refuted not only by the poems of Prudentius but also by innumerable passages in Augustine.

11. Fabr., Gis., Ald., and the Mozarabic breviary have *praecucurrit*, “ran ahead.” Most, including the Bollandists, have *percucurrit*, “ran through.” Gifanius, in *PER*, reads *percucurrit* from an old book and asserts that among ancient writers there were many words joined to the particle *per* that today have been changed either into *prae* or into some other form, as *perdurat teneras* in the *Psychomachia*. Petavius, volume IV, Book XIV, chapter 11, observes from this and other passages of Prudentius that, in describing the triumphs of the martyrs in elegant verse, he often commemorates their relics and tombs, and the honor paid to them there as well as the benefits received from them. Petavius adduces Latin and Greek Fathers in agreement with this.

12. The Mozarabic breviary has *ambiunt*, “they surround.” Cellarius, an otherwise not unsuccessful grammarian, plays the theologian unsuccessfully here: “PATRONS OF THE WORLD. But,” he says, “there is only one Christ.” Let the shoemaker not go beyond his last. With the permission not only of heterodox grammarians but of all Reformed theologians, let Prudentius—and let us—call the holy martyrs “patrons of the world” in the phrase and sense that, already in Prudentius’ age, the report spreading through all lands proclaimed: “Here are the patrons of the world, whom people surround with prayers.” St. Augustine more than once called the martyrs patrons and spoke of the patronage of the martyrs, especially in his book *On Care for the Dead*.

13. Cellarius says that the final syllable in *frustra* has been shortened improperly. I have no doubt that the final syllable in *frustra* is normally short, although it is often found lengthened. Avienus shortened it in the *Aratea*.]

871 With golden letters Christ recorded them there;

with marks of blood he handed the same names down in writing on earth.

Happy Iberian land shines throughout the world with this crown.

a chaste dwelling for the bodies of the blessed.

Here, stained with the blood of twofold slaughter,

it drank the warm waters.

[Col. 0278A] Now the inhabitants throng the sands

stained with holy blood, beseeching with their voices,

their prayers, and their gifts.

[10] The foreigner, and also the colonist from the outer world,

comes here, for the revealing report has run through all lands:

that here are the patrons of the world, whom people surround with prayers.

873 No one has gathered pure prayers here in vain:

17. “Murmur”: prayer; I.

21. “Witnesses”: martyrs, for martyrs are interpreted as “witnesses”; I.

23. “At a loss”: “in a loss”; I.

[Col. 0280B] 25. “Honest”: approved, good; and *probus* is said as though “approved by integrity,” or goodness; I.

27. “Hostile”: *hosticus* and *hostilis* are the same; I.

30. “In the red fountain”: of blood; I.]

[Note: [Col. 0279B]

15. Egm. incorrectly has *justum est poposcit*, “he demanded what was just.”

16. Ald. and the Mozarabic breviary have *suffragantum*; read *suffragantium*.

17. Ald., Gis., Noms., Rott., and the Bollandists have *sinant*; others, *sinunt*. Nebrissensis reads *sinant* and says that the order is: “They hear, and immediately carry their prayers to God, so that they may not allow empty murmuring—which, supply, someone has poured forth with his voice.” The construction is certainly obscure. Read *non sinunt*, “they do not allow,” and the sense proceeds clearly. Cham. incorrectly has *murmure* for *murmur*. On this word, see the preface to Book I against Symmachus, verse 36, where it does not seem to displease Chamillard. Here again Cellarius adds an impious note: “THEY DO NOT ALLOW … THEY HEAR: this is the mystery of iniquity, then beginning to operate.” What could be more foolish? Prudentius solemnly affirms that this persuasion and practice had spread through all lands, while Cellarius wants to teach us that it is the mystery of iniquity, and that this mystery had already begun at that time. More truly we may say that religion and piety—the reverence and invocation of the saints—flourished in the first centuries of the Church and are now growing cold. See the prologue, chapter 7.

18. See here not the mystery of iniquity but the catholic doctrine concerning the invocation of the saints: “They carry [their prayers] to the ear of the eternal King.” From there abundant gifts flow from him to the earth like a fountain. God, therefore, is the source of all good things, and he sends gifts to the earth through the intercession of the saints; consequently it is right to ask and venerate them.

19. Gis., in the margin, has *unde larga*, “whence abundant.” The Mozarabic breviary corruptly has *inde largo fonte abyssi*, “from there, from the deep fountain.” Our author very often professes that God is the fountain of all good things.

20. Vat. A incorrectly has *supplicium*, “punishment.” Nebrissensis shrewdly observes that the causes here are illnesses; hence sick persons are called *causarii*, and *causaria missio* is release from military service on account of illness. Giselinus does not seem to have found this meaning in his books—that is, in the medical writers—for he explains it as: “They cause those who came for whatever reason to depart as successful petitioners.” Prudentius uses a term belonging to jurists and soldiers to indicate illnesses, although the jurists, in the Digest, Book XLIX, title 16, law 13, define *causaria missio* as occurring when someone, being less fit for military service because of a defect of mind or body, is discharged. With a similar meaning, the Italians call someone in poor health *cagionevole*, and the Spaniards *achacoso*. Although the Spanish Academy Dictionary says that the primary meaning of *achaque* is poor health, from which it later comes to mean a pretext or excuse, it ought nevertheless to be investigated more carefully whether the matter does not stand the other way around.

21. Hailsbr. and Widm. above have *suis bonis*, “with his good things.” *Bonus*, “good,” is better. In Latin, martyrs are *testes*, “witnesses”; hence “with his witnesses.”

22. The Mozarabic breviary, against the meter, has *isti sunt, quos*, “these are they whom.” Rat. and the Mozarabic breviary not badly have *quos nec talena dura nec mors terruit*, “whom neither the hard chain nor death terrified.” Others have *quos nec catenae dura nec mors terruit*, “whom neither chains, hard [things], nor death terrified.” For *dura*, many have *dira*, “dreadful,” with the Bollandists, Ald., Weitz., Gis., and Vat. A and B. Gifanius, however, insists that *dura* must be read, together with the old book: the subject is the horror of death, and therefore he says *dura*, “hard,” not the kind of death, which would require *dira*, “dreadful.” *Dura* is found in Alex., Put., Thuan., two Torrentian manuscripts, Heinsius, and others. Prudentius often mentions the chains in which martyrs were accustomed to be bound, as shortly afterward in this hymn, and in the hymns on Fructuosus and Cyprian. Augustine, on Psalm 136: “The wicked man rejoices in pomp; the martyr rejoices in chains.” Gallonius, chapter 3 *On the Torments of the Holy Martyrs*, and Gaspar Sagittarius, in his work on the same subject, chapter 2, produce further examples from Tertullian, Lactantius, Cyprian, Jerome, and the Acts of the martyrs.

23. Aldus incorrectly divides *fateri, sanguinis dispendio / Sanguinis sed*. Nor does Teolius correctly divide *sanguinis dispendio: / Sanguinis*; but such...

24. Gis., in the margin of both editions, has *rependit largior*, “he repays more abundantly,” which is not bad; the others have *longior*, “more prolonged.”

25. In Vat. A, Egm., Palat., Alt., Rott., and Noms., *est* is omitted after *decorum*. It is better to add it, lest we make such hiatus more familiar to Prudentius than Prudentius himself intended. Cauch. found *probum* in an old manuscript instead of *probis*, from which he conjectured *probrum*, “reproach,” which Heinsius thinks is not inelegant.

26. Vat. A has *membra mortis*, “limbs of death”; correct to *morbis*, “diseases.” Likewise, in the Mozarabic breviary, *exedenda* should be read instead of *excidenda*. Here too bodily limbs are called *texta*, “woven structures,” as in the hymn *On Burial*: “and I weave again the dissonant structures.” Elsewhere the body is called “a clay latticework.”]

27. Egm. incorrectly has *histico* for *hostico*. Vat. B, Prag., Rat., Weitz., Gis., and the Bollandists read *domare*. Ald., Alex., and the manuscripts of Heinsius have *donare*, which Heinsius considers more elegant [Col. 0280D]; it is also the reading in the Mozarabic Breviary. When Teolius says that the Vatican manuscripts have no other reading, I think he does not mean all of them. Weitz., Egm., and Widm. have *mortem, et hostem*. Burmannus testifies in the *Anthologia* that this is the reading in Egm., although this variant escaped Heinsius’s notice. The manuscripts of Heinsius, together with the Mozarabic Breviary and the Bollandists, read *morte et hostem vincere*. But Alex., Vat. A and B, and Rat. have *mortem, et hostem*. I prefer another reading.

28. The Mozarabic Breviary, contrary to both meter and sense, has *patitur*. Arnobius, book I *Against the Nations*: “No innocent person ever unjustly killed is disgraced, nor is anyone stained by any mark of shame who suffers not severe punishment deservedly, but the cruelty of the torturer.”

29. Hymn 10 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 90: “The arduous road that is opened to the righteous through the tortures of death.”

30. The Mozarabic Breviary has, corruptly, *rubrosi decoris* for *rubro sede cordis*. Martyrdom is called the baptism of blood, and the baptistery is called a fountain. Hence the pagans mocked Saint Pudens, drenched in blood: “Washed safe, washed safe,” as is read in the Acts of Saint Perpetua. Consult Ruinart.]

32. *Perenne*: soldiers used a belt. — *Cingulum*: a crown, I.

33. *Sueta*: accustomed, formerly, once. — *Militat*: now it serves in the warfare of the spirit. — *Sacrariis*: the temples of Christ, I.]

31. Ald. has *ante viam*, contrary to the meter.

32. Ald. had correctly printed *Milites, quos ad perenne cingulum Christus vocat*. I do not know why he later incorrectly changed this to *Milites, quos ad perenne cinguli Christus vocat*. Iso explains *cingulum* as “crown”; he would have done better to say “military service,” through which an everlasting crown is acquired.

33. The Mozarabic Breviary corruptly has *bello ense armis militat sacratis*. In Put. the reading is *nunc fidei militat* instead of *militat sacrariis*. The second syllable of *fidei* would then have to be lengthened, as it is in fact lengthened by Lucretius and often by Paulinus. But since Prudentius very often shortens it, I do not accept the reading of Puteanus. See the commentary on verse 62 of the *Dittochaeon*. Someone might wonder from these words, *militant sacrariis*, whether these holy martyrs, after abandoning Caesar’s army, served among the clergy. The words mentioned below, *orarium* and *annulus*, could also be brought into this connection, since they were ornaments associated with the clergy. *Sacrarium* was usually understood to mean an altar. See the hymn of Saint Vincent, verse 517, “For it was placed beneath the altar,” and the hymn of Saint Laurence, verse 51, “The talents beneath the altars.” Nevertheless, since Prudentius did not speak clearly about their being counted among the clergy, it is understood only that they embraced Christian warfare, as is clear from the following verse.

34. The Mozarabic Breviary transposes the words and corrupts the meter: *signum crucis eligunt*. Christians sometimes abandoned Caesar’s military service because, as Ruinart says concerning the martyr Maximilian, under pagan emperors—who often ordered soldiers to sacrifice to the gods—soldiers had frequent occasions for sin. Thus, when Dion asked, “Those who serve in the army—what evil do they do?” Maximilian replied, “You know what they do.” See the Acts of Maximilian and Saint Marcellus.

35. Vat. A has *draconem*, incorrectly. Fabr. has *quod gerebant*, also incorrectly. One may conjecture *quae gerebant*. Lipsius, in *De militia Romana*, book IV, dialogue 5, discusses at length the dragons, military standards, and whether they were painted on a cloth or woven with needlework, or whether the entire body was solid and made of fabric. He thinks that Prudentius is introducing the first view. Grangaeus, in his commentary on book II of Symmachus, verse 713, believes that Prudentius referred in these two verses to the image of Constantine, which was painted on a panel before the entrance of the palace. In it a dragon was shown pierced through the middle of its belly by a cross, as Eusebius teaches in *The Life of Constantine*, book III, chapter 3. Hear Eusebius’s words:

“Moreover, on a certain lofty panel set before the entrance of the palace, he displayed for all to see the saving sign placed above his head; beneath it, however, that enemy and adversary who, through the agency of impious tyrants, had attacked the Church of God, was shown falling headlong in the form of a dragon . . . Therefore the emperor wished the dragon, pierced through the middle of its belly by darts and cast into the deep whirlpools of the sea, to be painted in wax softened by fire beneath the feet of himself and his children, and displayed before everyone.”

Here the method of painting with wax softened by fire—*διὰ τῆς κηροχύτου γραφῆς*, “by encaustic painting”—should be noted. This panel was represented on many coins; Baronius gives an image of them in volume III of the *Annals*, under the year 325, no. 206. Prudentius says that these two martyrs, although formerly they had been dragon-bearers, preferred the cross that subdued the dragon—either because he referred to Constantine’s image, as Grangaeus reasonably suspects, or because the dragon, that is, the devil, was truly subdued by the power of the cross.

Ammianus gives a vivid description of the standards on which the dragon was displayed, book XVI: “Around the steps of the other imperial power, many dragons woven from purple cloth encircled them, fastened to the golden and jeweled tips of spears; open-mouthed and blown through, they therefore hissed as though stirred by anger, while their coils of tails were left to the wind.”

As for Chamillardus’s interpretation, together with Nebrissensis, of *ventosa pallia* as “vain and proud cloaks” rather than cloaks agitated or swollen by the wind, I do not agree. Peveratus explains *ventosis* as meaning dragons woven so round and hollow that they would swell with the wind admitted through their throats. But afterward, in connection with the word *palliis*, he concludes from Prudentius’s meaning that the dragons were merely painted or embroidered with a needle on a veil, and did not hiss because the wind was taken in through their throats, as some infer from Claudian’s verses.

I think that the cloaks are called *ventosa* because they swell when stirred by the wind, and that the dragons hissed in the same sense, because cloaks driven by the wind produce a sound resembling a hiss. Claudian’s verses are from his third consulship of Honorius:

“These carry the flying eagles; these raise the painted  
Necks of dragons, and a great serpent swells through the clouds,  
Angry as the south wind spurs it; it lives by the blasts  
It has received, and counterfeits hissing with its winding course.”

Dragons were carried into battle by the *draconarii*, generally one for each cohort; eagles were carried by the legions. Thus the eagle was the chief military standard.

36. Thuan. has *in signo lignum*, incorrectly. Heinsius suspected *insigne ligni*.

37. The Mozarabic Breviary has *spiculum*. Vegetius, book I: “What of the dragon-bearers and standard-bearers themselves, who control the spears with their left hand?” Chamillardus notes these words, which occur in chapter 20 of his book I. But why does Prudentius say “with their right hands”? I think it is because Prudentius is enumerating nearly everything soldiers are accustomed to do, including the dragon-bearers when circumstances require it, while the standards have meanwhile been laid aside.

38. The Mozarabic Breviary has *castra forte*, probably incorrectly.

39. In Vat. A the word *manus* was added above in smaller letters.

40. He calls Christians the “second offspring of Israel,” because, after the first Israelites were rejected, they succeeded them.

41. The Mozarabic Breviary has, less well, *auctor aulae*.

42. The Mozarabic Breviary and Fabr. have *refugas*, not as well as *defugas*. Latinius has *perfugas*. Alex. has *defugas*, but the *g* seems to have been supplied by a later hand. The word *defuga* also occurs in book XII of the Theodosian Code, title and final law: “defuga of a curia or college.” Barthius, book XLI of the *Adversaria*, chapter 15, asserted that *refugas* was an error and that *transfugas* was read in the old manuscripts and editions; I have nowhere seen this. Barthius nevertheless thinks that both forms are corrupt and that the original word was *apostatas*, which is not at all convincing.

Nebrissensis says that *litare* improperly means “to sacrifice,” since properly it means “to obtain something through sacrifice.” Giselinus denies that this distinction is perpetual and consistent and maintains that *litare* is sometimes used for “to sacrifice.” He does not, however, prove that this is its proper use. In any case, the usage of others in this sense supports Prudentius, whether that usage is called proper or improper. I do not know why Giselinus confidently asserts that the authority of our reading *portae* is worthless. As for his addition, “especially since critics unanimously condemned it,” one must ask who these critics are and why they condemn it.]

They had not previously led a rough life of harsh labor,

Soldiers whom Christ calls to an everlasting belt,

Their accustomed valor in war and arms now serves in the sanctuaries.

876 They prefer the wooden emblem that subdued the dragon.

[Col. 0282A] They consider it worthless to carry spears in ready right hands,

To strike walls with engines, to surround camps with trenches,

[40] 877 Perhaps then the savage commander of the universal palace

Had ordered the second offspring of Israel to go to the altar,

To sacrifice to black idols, to be apostates from Christ.

The plague, girded with a sword, was pressing upon their free faith:

44. *Illa*: that faith. — *Ungulas*: a kind of torture by which the skin was stripped from martyrs, I.

45. *Expetebat*: desired, longed for, I.

[Col. 0284A] 46. *Boiis*: *boia* and *baga* are the same; in the plural, *bucae* means chains, I. — *Bagis*: that is, *bouga*, Vat. S.]

[Note: [Col. 0283B]

44. The Mozarabic Breviary incorrectly writes *bissulcas*. The holy martyrs were sometimes struck with an axe, but more often with a sword; that death by the sword involved greater disgrace is proved by Gallonius in the final chapter of *On the Tortures of the Holy Martyrs*. He also confirms that those destined to be struck with the sword were accustomed first to be beaten with rods. Saint Ambrose writes beautifully on the axe, class 1, letter 25: “I know that many of the pagans were accustomed to boast that they had brought back an unstained axe from the administration of a province.”

Aringhus wonders whether the axe carved on two sepulchral stones, which he reproduces in volume II of *Subterranean Rome*, book VI, chapter 50, was an emblem of a craft or of martyrdom. In the image of the Seven Holy Sleepers, which I reproduced from an ancient monument in volume I, page 356, one can see two axes: one near Saint Malchus, the other near Saint Martinianus. These are instruments of their martyrdom, just as the knotted clubs near Maximianus and John, the nails near Constantine and Danesius, the burning torch near Sarapion, and the hook at the feet of the same Sarapion are instruments of martyrdom. With the hook, the bodies of dead martyrs were accustomed to be dragged to the Gemonian stairs, the public sewers, or the rivers.

There was another kind of hook with which the bodies of martyrs were torn apart; I shall discuss it at verse 173 of the hymn of Saint Vincent. The *ungulae* were iron pincers with which the bodies of martyrs were torn and furrowed. Saint Jerome, Saint Augustine, and others relate that their bodies were furrowed with *ungulae*. Prudentius calls them *bisulcae* here and elsewhere because they made double furrows; this will be clear to anyone examining plate 13, letter A, of the *Tortures of the Holy Martyrs*.

Gallonius described them from examples preserved in the Vatican basilica and discovered under Paul III; some incorrectly thought that these were scorpions. The scorpions are depicted on plate 9, letter D. They are included under the name of rods. They were knotted and pointed rods called scorpions because they inflicted an arched wound upon the body, as Isidore says. The rods were made either of elm, birch—a Gallic tree—oak, ash, willow, or vine. Rods that were not knotted were called smooth. Other rods were made of iron, which was sometimes applied to the body while glowing, or of lead. For the methods by which the holy martyrs were beaten, see plates 10 and 11.

The form of the scorpions reproduced by Sagittarius in chapter 17 resembles Gallonius’s image. The impression of the double-forked *ungula* that Sagittarius gives in the same place differs more from Gallonius’s impression: in Sagittarius’s impression only three iron points are attached to the head; in Gallonius’s, these three and three others are attached to the middle. Perhaps for this reason they are called *bisulcae*: the two points of the head made one furrow, and similarly the points in the middle made another.

Sagittarius is mistaken when he says that the *ungulae* described by Gallonius owe their form more to the ingenuity of the author than to ancient monuments. For genuine *ungulae* of the kind Gallonius describes exist in the Vatican basilica, as Aringhus also reports in several places and reproduces more than once in an engraving. Another kind resembles an iron glove with three fingers; it was discovered in the cemetery of Calepodius. See plate 26 and Aringhus, volume II, page 687.

Whether the *fidiculae* are the same as the *ungulae* has been debated among learned men. Some thought that they were cords of sinew by which the limbs of defendants were fastened to the rack; most affirm that they were iron *ungulae*, a view clearly supported by Isidore and Prudentius in the hymn *Romanus*. They were called *fidiculae* from *findere*, “to split,” or *fodicare*, “to pierce,” as some prefer; the *ungulae*, however, were so called because they imitated the claws of wild beasts. For this reason they are explicitly called in the Theodosian Code, book IX, title 12, law 1, “the tracks of beasts, the claws of beasts.” See verse 481 in *Romanus*.]

That faith, fearless through love of Christ, willingly and bravely desired

[45] 878 Rods, axes, and double-forked claws.

The prison hinders necks bound in harsh *boiae* (iron neck-rings),

[Col. 0284A] [Note: [Col. 0284A]

48. *Plectitur*: he is punished, penalized, condemned, Iso.

50. *Ingesta*: placed upon the face, I.

51. *Dulce*: it was a sweet thing, I.

53. *Sodalitas*: companions are called *sodales*, as though “eating together,” that is, “sharing a meal,” I, Vat. A.

[Col. 0286A] 56. *Catastas*: a kind of torture, namely iron beds on which the martyrs were placed, with fire set beneath them, I.

58. *Mammonae*: the demon, or worldly wealth, I.

60. *Coelestis ignis*: the soul, I.

61. *Chirographo*: a written military oath, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0285B]

47. Weitz. has *barbarus*, recognizing only that *barbaras* occurs above in Vulg. and Widm. Most nevertheless read *barbaras*. It should be noted from the Acts of the Martyrs that such butcheries were usually carried out in the forum. Sometimes, however, they took place outside the city; Kirchmannus proves that the executioners themselves lived outside the city, *On Roman Funerals*, book II, chapter 24. Some trace of this custom remains at Rome.

49. Gis. has *perculit solum* (“struck the ground”) in the margin. The martyr struck with a sword is shown in plate 21, letter D.

50. For the various ways in which martyrs were delivered to the fire, see plates 16 and 17.

51. In Thuan. and the first Boher., both very old manuscripts, the reading is *jussit* for *justis*. Heinsius conjectures *jus fit*. The common reading is better: “Then it is sweet for the righteous to be burned”; and in Heinsius’s notes one should read *dulce tunc*, not *dulce nunc*.

52. Ald., Fabr., Weitz., and the Bollandists have *convalescunt* for *concalescunt*, which is more characteristic of Prudentius. Gifanius is cited by Weitz and Heinsius for *convalescunt*. Vat. A and Rat. have *corpora*, which Weitz found in some place. Retain *pectora*.

53. Prag. has *vinxerat sodalitas*.

55. A *bipennis* is an axe, so called from its two blades or wings—that is, its two projecting edges—which were sharpened on both sides. Peveratus, following Baronius in the Roman Martyrology for the ninth day before the Kalends of April, wonders whether an axe was in use at that time. Yet although it is credible that most Christians were struck with the sword rather than the axe, as I recently stated from Gallonius, there can be no doubt that some were killed with an axe, as Prudentius alone demonstrates, and Sagittarius confirms more fully in chapter 7 of *On the Tortures*.

Savaro, in his notes on Sidonius, page 88, observes the expression “to offer the neck,” from Apollinaris and Ado of Trier: “Thus they willingly gave their necks to the axes.” That martyrs willingly offered their necks to the executioner to be cut is established by six hundred examples in their acts and martyrologies.

56. Vat. A has *crepantem*, less well. Nebrissensis conjectured *ligneas* for *igneas*; Sagittarius, chapter 10, did not dislike this conjecture. He adds that *catastas igneas* could metaphorically refer to the higher platform on which the pyre was kindled, namely, one radiant with much fire. Nevertheless, he observes that in Iso and another old glossary *catasta* is read as an iron bed.

Giselinus found *ligneas* in the Daventrian edition; but, as he himself observes, since in the hymn of Saint Laurence, verse 399, an iron grating that had already been heated is called a *catasta*, there is no reason to change *igneas* into *ligneas*. Among Christian writers *catasta* often signifies an elevated place where punishment was inflicted upon defendants. Some think that the Spanish *cadahalso* and Italian *catafalco* derive from it.

57. The pagans’ common cry was “Christians to the lion,” as Tertullian, Cyprian, and others report. Sometimes it was “Christians to the beasts.” Jerome combines both expressions in book VII of his commentary on Isaiah, chapter 18. Eusebius, book I of his *History*, chapter 16, mentions leopards, to whose tearing apart Christians were exposed. In the martyrdom of Saint Ignatius, some mention leopards instead of lions.

[Col. 0286C] 58. From Matthew 6:24: “You cannot serve God and Mammon.” Barthius, book LV, chapter 4 of the *Adversaria*, says that Iso should not have separated “the devil” from “worldly wealth.” For Mammon is no more an idol of riches and wealth than Mars is the god of war. Another glossator cited by the same Barthius explains *mammoneam fidem* as “money-loving, worldly, greedy.” Barthius discusses the matter further there and in the following chapter, treating *Mammon* as a demon, greed, and wealth. He wrote this verse: “Shall we, begotten for Christ, serve Mammon?” I think this was an error of memory.

59. Cauchius preferred *serviemus idolo*, “shall we serve an idol?” Heinsius says that this is unnecessary.

60. Aldus had correctly printed *absit ut*. I do not understand what he intended when, against the meter, he changed it to *absit ne*. He rightly emended *igni* to *ignis*. The thought is taken from 2 Corinthians 6:14: “What fellowship has light with darkness?”

61. Ald. has the error *capra* for *capta*. Nebrissensis suspects *coepta*. It is unnecessary to point out that the *chirographum* is the military oath. From Ambrosius Morales, Peveratus noted that the church of Toledo possesses a very ancient manuscript containing the life of the martyrs, in which the words quoted by Eulogius concerning these martyrs occur, as though spoken by Celedonius while exhorting Hemeterius. He adds that it is especially important to note how ancient this history is, since it was written in Eulogius’s time. Yet Prudentius is much earlier than Eulogius.

Eulogius, book I of the *Memorial of the Martyrs*, writes as follows: “Thus indeed, when the blessed martyrs Hemeterius and Celedonius longed to give their souls for the Lord, they urged one another onward to suffering by addressing each other with this exhortation: ‘May the confession brandish its weapons everywhere against the enemy, and let us seek out the enemy of faith wherever he may be concealed.’”

The most eminent archbishop of Toledo, Francisco Lorenzana, in his highly learned notes in volume II of the *Holy Fathers of Toledo*, says that in the Acts of the Martyrs first published by Juan Tamayo de Salazar, later by the Antwerp editors under 3 March, and finally by Manuel Risco in volume XXXIII of *Hispania Sacra*, appendix 2, the words “May the confession brandish its weapons everywhere against the enemy” appear to belong to one of the two martyrs, and, according to several manuscripts, to Hemeterius; the remainder belongs to the other, namely Celedonius.]

[Col. 0286A] Whether the neck must be offered to the public double axe,

64. *Tribuni*: over a thousand. — *Absistite*: depart, withdraw, I.

65. *Torques*: collars, rings. — *Sauciorum*: of the wounded, infirm. — *Praemia*: the rewards that are, I.

68. *Infames*: without good repute, inglorious.

[Col. 0288A] 71. *Rigor*: harshness, hardness, I.

72. *Chalybs*: iron; *chalybs* is Greek *sideros*, I.

62. Matthew 22:21: “Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”

63. Rat. and two manuscripts of Heinsius have *quidquid proprium est Dei*, contrary to the metrical rule. Vat. B, Weitz., Cauch., and Widm. in its first hand have *quidquid est suum Dei*. Others correctly have *quidquid est proprium Dei*.

64. The Mozarabic Breviary has *adsistite*, incorrectly. The Bollandists have *assistite*. The manuscripts of Heinsius, Ald., Weitz., our copies, and others have *et vos*. Giselinus omitted *et*. The reference is to military tribunes, or commanders of legions, not to tribunes of the plebs. Compare Iso’s gloss.

65. Aldus had printed *aureos auferte torquens*; in the corrected edition he introduced a new error, *aureos auferre torques*. Vat. A has *afferte*, correctly emended above to *auferte*. The same manuscript has *aureas*; others have *aureos*. The Mozarabic Breviary incorrectly has *aureos offerte*. Vegetius, book II, chapter 7: “Double-pay torquarii and single-pay torquarii, for whom a golden collar was the reward of steadfast valor.” Stewechius says in his commentary that auxiliary soldiers were presented with golden collars by the Romans, while citizens received only silver ones. Iso explains *sauciorum* as “the infirm”; it is better understood as referring to those who had received wounds in war.

66. The Mozarabic Breviary has, incorrectly, *clara vox angelorum vocant stipendia*.

67. The army of the martyrs is called “the white-robed army” in the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*. See the commentary on verse 157 of hymn 3 of the *Cathemerinon*.

69. The Mozarabic Breviary has, not badly, *Quaeque deridenda nobis monstra divos fingitis*.

71. *Rigor* is used for hardness, as *rigor ferri* in Virgil, *Georgics* I, and *rigor auri* in Lucretius; see the material noted by Gifanius in the index under *RIGOR auri*. Paulinus, *Natalis* 4: “Iron stands upon their hands and neck.”

72. Ald. had correctly printed *circulis*, which he improperly changed to *cyclis*. See what I discussed in the notes on this same verse in the *Hymnodia Hispanica* for 3 March; you will understand that, contrary to the meter, the reading is *gravis ambit circulis*, as Weitz printed it with Hailsbr. and Widm. Vat. Q is no better with *gravis ambit circulus*. Vat. P also incorrectly has *circuit* for *circulis*.

Weitz, with Hailsbr., writes *calyps*; Alex. and Widm. have *calips*. Gruterus preferred *artita*, and Weitz followed him. Hailsbr. has *atrita*. Widm. in the margin, and Vat. A and B, Prag., and Rat. have *astricta*; others have *attrita*, which Heinsius uniquely supports from his manuscripts. Compare the preface to the *Psychomachia*, verse 33: “The neck, freed from worn chains, raises itself.” In the Mozarabic Breviary the variant is *colla duriter ambit* for *gravibus*.

73. Arnobius, book IV, near the end: “But if any indignation on behalf of your religions had possessed you, you ought rather to have burned these writings and these books, to have destroyed them . . . For why should our writings have deserved condemnation by fire? Why should our meeting places be demolished?”

Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 2, mentions the edict by which Diocletian ordered the sacred books of the Christian religion to be burned and the churches to be demolished to their foundations. The same matter is mentioned by Optatus, Saint Augustine, and many Acts of the Holy Martyrs. This occurred around the year 303. Saint Jerome, book II of his commentary on Zechariah, chapter 8: “We saw these things carried out in the Church of Christ during the persecution, when the savagery of the persecutors was aroused to such madness that they even destroyed our meeting places and gave the divine books to the flames.” Consult Ruinart’s preface to the *Acts of the Martyrs*.

Regarding this custom of burning writings, and its origin among the Romans, Tacitus and the author of the *Controversiae* and *Suasoriae* under the name of Seneca the Elder do not entirely agree. The latter, speaking of Labienus in the preface to book V of the *Controversiae*, says:

“A new punishment was first devised against him. Through his enemies it was brought about that all his books were burned. It was a new and unusual thing to take punishment from literary studies. By Hercules, after Cicero this ingenious cruelty was invented for the public good . . . The writings of the man who had pronounced this sentence against Labienus’s writings were afterward burned while he was still alive—not now as a bad precedent, since it was his own precedent . . . A witty saying of Cassius Severus, a man very close to Labienus, was widely repeated. At the time when Labienus’s books were being burned by decree of the senate, he said: ‘Now I ought to be burned alive, since I have learned them by heart.’”

Now hear Tacitus, *Annals* IV, chapter 5, where he explains in the senate the case of Cremutius Cordus, in the year 778 from the founding of the City and the tenth year of Tiberius’s reign:

“With Cornelius Cossus and Asinius Agrippa as consuls, Cremutius Cordus was prosecuted on a new charge, one then heard for the first time: that in his published annals he had praised Marcus Brutus and called Gaius Cassius the last of the Romans . . . Cremutius, resolved to end his life, began in this manner: ‘My words, Conscript Fathers, are accused, while I am innocent of deeds . . .’”

“The letters of Antony, the speeches of Brutus, and the poems of Bibaculus and Catullus, filled with insults against the Caesars [perhaps: Caesar], though indeed false concerning Augustus, are read; but the divine Julius himself and the divine Augustus both endured such things and left them unpunished.”

Tacitus adds other details from which one may conclude that books were first burned by decree of the senate at that time. For my part, I agree more with Tacitus; perhaps I shall untie this knot at another time.

77. Many recent scholars assert that these holy martyrs suffered martyrdom at the beginning of the fourth century or shortly before. But it is better, with Prudentius and the author of the Acts preserved by the Bollandists, to admit that the time of their passion is unknown.]

881 Having discharged Caesar’s service, it has paid every debt.

It is time to repay to God whatever belongs properly to God.

Go, masters of the standards; and you, tribunes, withdraw.

[65] Take away the golden collars, rewards of the wounded:

Reigning from on high upon his throne, he condemns the infamous gods,

And you, who fashion for yourselves laughable monsters as gods.

[Col. 0288A] While they speak thus, the martyrs are overwhelmed by a thousand punishments:

Harshness binds both hands, wrapping them in twisted bonds,

And worn iron encircles their necks with heavy rings.

882 O obsolete oblivion of a silent antiquity!

These things are begrudged us, and even their fame is extinguished.

[75] For once the blasphemous guard removed the documents,

So that learned ages might not discover from tenacious books

The order, time, and manner of the passion that had been recorded,

85. *Annulus*: a ring that signifies and represents faith without end, I.

86. *Orarium*: from *os, oris*, that is, a cloth for wiping the mouth, I.

87. *Intimum*: secret, hidden, I.

[Col. 0290B] 88. *Liquentis*: liquid or clear, I.

89. *Visum*: of men, I.

92. *Haerens*: doubting, hesitating, I.

96. *In*: for *ad*. — *Spiritus*: souls, I.]

80. The Mozarabic Breviary has the corrupt reading *catenis ad capillum tracti*, “dragged by chains by the hair.” Nebrissensis notes: “It is not established by what kind of death they were afflicted; whether they died in chains and grew long hair and a beard. We have restored the order of the verses, which had been confused and disturbed the sense.” He arranges them as follows: *Dulcibus, Quo viros, Jugibus, Hoc tamen, Illa laus*. But the order preferred by the manuscripts produces a correct sense. Among the Romans, prisoners grew their hair; therefore the continuous chains, or the long duration of imprisonment, could be recognized from the long hair. See verse 53 of hymn 11 of the *Peristephanon*, where the martyrs detained in prison are called “hairy bands.”

81. Hailsbr., Widm. above, the Mozarabic Breviary, and Gis. in the margin, together with Vat. A, P, and Q, have *quave pompa*, which Heinsius approves, as though victims were being discussed. Gallandius thought that the context rejected *pompa* and, in support of *poena*, cited the excellent Aldine edition of 1501, namely the very edition we use. Thuan. and Alex. have *quaeve pompa*. Vat. B, Urb., Weitz., the Bollandists, and others have *quave poena*. I do not dislike this, since *dolore tortor* precedes; but instead of *ornaverit* I would prefer *affecerit*, or another word of similar meaning. Nevertheless, the expression is poetically and figuratively sound.

85. Aldus has the error *nubae*. Although Teolius admits that everything we know about these two martyrs is owed to Prudentius, he nevertheless asserts, following Chamillardus, that the ring belonged to Hemeterius and the *orarium* to Celedonius. I do not find this distinction in Prudentius. Teolius does rightly infer from this passage that ancient Christians commonly wore rings, some of which are preserved in the Vatican museum and were illustrated by the distinguished knight Victorius.

If someone asks why the ring represents faith, I would answer that a ring is also given by a bridegroom to a bride as a sign of marital fidelity. Thus Innocent III, granting a ring to Fulk, abbot of Corbie, wrote these words: “Among the other ornaments granted to prelates of the Churches is the ring, which is the seal of faith, according to the command that the father give a ring into the hand of his returning son, so that the prelate may guard the Church entrusted to him with unsullied faith, and may be continually admonished by its visible form to observe that faith faithfully.” See Macer in the *Hierolexicon*, under the word *annulus*, where he explains Innocent’s words.

86. In ecclesiastical usage *orarium* was formerly understood to mean a stole, as is well known. This designation appears to have been partly preserved in the corrupt Latin of a tenth-century deed of donation, found in volume XXXIV of *Hispania Sacra*, page 455. There Bishop Ovecus of León, around the year 951, among other gifts, donated “ten white garments with their amices, ten *orales*,” which the scribes say are stoles. I do not think that *orarium* is used here in this sense.

Ambrose and others used *orarium* for a cloth with which the mouth is wiped; and in the glossary I read that it derives “from wiping the sweat of the mouth” or “from wiping the mouth.” Chamillardus thinks that *orarium*, from *os, oris*, may mean a covering for the head, which the ancients used while invoking God; in this sense the *orarium* would be a sign of Celedonius’s piety. But he gives no witness for that meaning. I therefore adhere to the gloss.

I have explained the special etymology of *orarium*, from *aurarii* and *auris*, in hymn 1 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 22. It should also be observed that sometimes the eyes of martyrs who were to be struck with the sword were bound with a linen cloth or *orarium*. Ado, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June: “Thus, after taking an *orarium*, Saint Julius bound his eyes and received the palm of martyrdom while the sword struck him.” And on the sixth day before the Kalends of December:

“Blessed Alexander, as he was being led away, met a certain widow, whom the blessed martyr addressed, saying: ‘Lend me your *orarium.’ She gave it to him. The officials then said to the woman: ‘You have lost your *orarium.’ After making the sign of the cross, the blessed martyr stripped off his tunic, and, standing in his undergarment, covered his eyes with the *orarium*. Then, kneeling, he received the sword.”

88. In Prag. *per* is missing before *poli*.

89. Vat. A in the first hand has *visus*; in the second hand, *visu*. Read *visum*.

92. Vat. A has *et manus*. Gis. in the margin has *palluit*, and as an alternative reading, *expalluit*. Vatt. P, Q, and Urb. write *obpalluit*; Alex., *oppalluit*.

93. Nebrissensis explains *peregit ictum* as “he struck and cut down the martyrs,” but adds that this contradicts what he had said above. It does not seem contradictory to me, not only if the tortures short of death are taken into account, as Nebrissensis interprets them, but also if the manner of death is kept before one’s eyes. Prudentius previously said that the attendant had taken away the tablets, so that posterity would not know the manner, sequence, or time of the passion, and that it would remain unknown by what punishment they had been afflicted. Now he says that the executioner completed the blow, so that neither the manner of the passion nor the punishment is clearly discerned. This device, lest the glory should perish, is also used by others in recounting the passions of the martyrs. Thomas Hurtado, in his work *On True Martyrdom*, resolution 35, excursus 2, where he discusses at length certain instruments with which tyrants tortured martyrs, section 10 asks why martyrs almost always yielded to the sword, whereas the sword rarely yielded to martyrs; rejecting other explanations, he answers with Delrio that the reason is that the sword is the principal, most legitimate, and ordinary instrument of avenging justice. I think it may be added that the martyrs yielded to the gentlest kind of death, while at times they survived other forms of torment in which incredible sufferings and pains had to be endured, so that their steadfastness might be attributed solely to divine power.

95. Rat. has *immolaret*. Brev. Moz. has *heroum* instead of *pro*, incorrectly.

96. Brev. Moz. has *relatum hostiarum spiritum*.

102. *Quaestione*: “examination,” Iso.

105. *Crescit*: “swells,” “becomes enlarged,” I.

113. *Algidus*: “fever,” I.

[Col. 0292B] 117. *Iberus*: a river of Spain. *Alluit*: “washes,” I.

118. *Hymnite*: “sing,” I. *Hymnizantes*: “singing hymns,” Vat. A.]

97. Ald., Vat. B, Alex., Urb., the Bollandists: *domantur*. Vatt. A, P, and most editors: *domentur*. Vat. Q, incorrectly: *domuntur*. It is unnecessary to speak of the miracles performed at the martyrs’ tombs, for the Acts of the holy martyrs are full of them.

98. Vatt. A, B, P, Alex., in a second hand, Hailsbr., Widm. above, and the Bollandists: *rictu*. Vat. Q, Urb., and most editors: *ritu*. For *devorant*, the Mozarabic Breviary incorrectly has *deformant*.

[Col. 0291C] 99. Vat. A, corruptly, has *stragulant*.

100. Gis. in the margin has *nunc suo nam*. Fabricius says of the word *poenae*: “Punishments dreadful in the sight of God are often inflicted upon the persecutors of Christians by divine judgment, as Prudentius writes of a certain Spaniard under Stephen I: driven mad and beaten with lashes by Satan, he was bound and hung.” Fabricius did not understand Prudentius: for Prudentius does not here call the man tortured by the demon a persecutor of Christians.

101. Breviar. Mozarab. has *spumans*, contrary to the meter.

102. Nebrissa does not interpret *non suorum criminum* as referring to “his own crimes,” because that crime belongs not to the man but to the demon. Chamillardus says that innocent people may be tormented by a demon, and adds that the possessed do not sin when they utter words or commit shameful deeds unwillingly. Teolius agrees entirely with Chamillardus. I think Prudentius used the phrase *non suorum criminum* as a formula of exorcism, already in use at that time; it may be seen to be described to some extent in *Apotheosis*, verse 406: “Flee, crafty serpent,” and so forth. There are many things there, both in Prudentius and in my notes, that may illuminate this entire passage concerning the possessed and exorcisms.

103. The Breviary Mozarabic corruptly presents this verse: “Hearing these things, the torturer is present with mournful lamentation.” Teolius published *nec tortor instat*. I do not know whether he was moved by the authority of his manuscripts, or because he had read in Heinsius’s notes that *instat* occurs in Noms’s copy and in Cauchy’s papers, while *astat* had already appeared above. Cellarius, also prompted by this note of Heinsius, published *instat*. Heinsius, however, placed *astat* in the text, and his statement that *astat* had already appeared above is false, unless he meant *astans*, which is found at verse 91. Some write *hejulatus*.

105. Brev. Moz. incorrectly has *latentibus est*.

106. Cellarius restores this in his notes: “Divine power torments the devil.” He seems to disapprove of the phrase “the martyrs’ power.” Yet the holy Fathers spoke in this way, and our theologians aptly distinguish between the proper power to perform miracles, which belongs to God alone, and the power or capacity to perform those same miracles, communicated by God, concerning which Matthew 10:8 says: “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons.”

107. Vat. A incorrectly has *cohercit*. The Marietti manuscript begins with this verse.

108. Brev. Moz. not ineptly has *e medullis exilit*.

109. This imitates Virgil, *Aeneid* II: “and the abandoned cubs wait with parched jaws.” Nebrissa says that the translation is taken from wolves who leave their prey bloodless and depart with parched jaws. But Virgil is speaking of the cubs who wait; for he had prefaced this concerning the wolves: “Wolves, like plunderers in the black mist, whom the wicked madness of their bellies drove blindly onward, and the abandoned cubs,” and so forth.

110. When he says *ungue ab imo*, he sufficiently indicates the toenail.

111. Brev. Moz. has *nec gehennae*, which could be defended to some extent.

113. Ald., Mar., Weitz., the older manuscripts of Heinsius: *decoloros*. For this reading Heinsius cites Weitz’s Egmond manuscript, which seems to me to have been cited by Weitz for *decolores*. Vatt. B, P, Q, Urb., Alex. in a second hand, and Brev. Moz. also have *decoloros*. Prag., Vat. A, the Bollandists, and others have *decolores*. Giselinus prefers *decolores* because Prudentius elsewhere used *decolor*; Chamillardus also finds this reasoning acceptable. Yet words of this kind—*unicolor*, *multicolor*, *decolor*—can also be inflected according to the second declension. Prudentius himself elsewhere wrote *multicolor fucus*, and elsewhere *multicolora prata*; in both places the meter requires the form used there. In other passages the discrepancy makes no difference, whether one says *decolores* or *decoloros*. He calls the horror *algidus*, meaning either bristling horror or the chill that precedes a fever.

114. Egm. and Vatt. A, Q: *reliquit*; others: *relinquit*. Widm. above has *color versus*. Brev. Moz. has: “Here swelling … here color.”

116. Brev. Moz. has *quod membra*.

117. Mar. has *sospitansque*, and in the margin, as a different reading, *sospitantque*. Alex. has *sospitantque*; *sospitant quae* is better.

118. Vat. B incorrectly has *martyres* instead of *matres*. Rat., Vatt. B, Q, Mar., Prag., Weitz., the better manuscripts of Heinsius, Alex., Urb., the Bollandists, and others have *hymnite*. Ald., Nebr., Fabr., Sich., Egm., Gis. in the margin, Gall., *hymnistae*; Pal. and, apparently, Vat. Q, *hymnitae*. Cauchy conjectured *Clara nunc hymnistriarum* instead of the received *pro receptis parvulis*. Brev. Moz. has *invictae matres*. The true reading is *hymnite*, from the Greek ὑμνεῖτε, “sing hymns.” Vossius, in *On the Vices of Latin Speech*, book III, chapter 14, argues that *hymnistae* should be read because, as he says, in Prudentius’ age *ae* sounded like *e*; yet he offers no similar example from Prudentius. Indeed, he himself maintains that *hymnista* is masculine only, and that a man who sings hymns should properly be called not *hymnista* but *hymnetes*. Why, then, does he reject the reading *hymnite* found in the best manuscripts? Moreover, in his old manuscript of the glossary the same Vossius found *imnio* for *hymnum cano*, as he reports in book IV, chapter 10. Nor does Teolius rightly assert that the verb *hymnio* is peculiar to Prudentius and is found in no other Latin writer. In an old hymn of St. Aemilianus in the Mozarabic office for November 12 we read: “Sing hymns with me in harmonious song.” See what I observed concerning March 3 in *Hispanic Hymnody*.

Why, however, does Prudentius say *state*—“stand”—and can it be inferred from this that hymns were customarily sung standing? Someone may reasonably ask this. I think Prudentius was referring to the term *statio*, the vigil held on Saturdays, Sundays, and the anniversaries of the martyrs’ solemn celebrations. Chrysostom, *Homily 1 on the Words of Isaiah*, at the beginning: “From where do I see that the discourses are advancing toward their purpose? Surely from this gathering … from this unbroken night-long vigil, from the fact that, imitating the station of the angelic ranks, you offer praises and hymns to the Creator without ceasing.” I discussed the *stationes* at *Hymn* 8 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 9.]

See how openly the savage demons are subdued here:

Those who devour the innermost parts, seized in a wolfish maw,

Strangle the minds themselves and mingle with the senses.

[100] Then the raging man, already filled with his enemy,

Blows out foaming saliva and rolls his fierce eyes,

To be purged by an examination—not of his own crimes.

You hear it, though no torturer is standing there, mournful wailings:

The body is torn by lashes, though no whip is seen,

[105] 886 And, suspended by hidden bonds, he himself grows larger.

In these ways the martyrs’ power shakes the filthy robber;

[Col. 0291B] It restrains, torments, and burns him; it shakes his chains;

The tormented robber strips himself out of the marrow he has left behind.

[Col. 0292A] He leaves the plunder unharmed and flees with parched jaws:

[110] From the very base of the nail to the hair, he restores everything intact,

Confessing that he is burning, for he is an inhabitant of hell.
