When a chilly horror shakes the discolored limbs,

The swelling leaves the face; here the true color returns.

[115] The Savior himself granted this blessing for us to enjoy,

When he consecrated the martyrs’ limbs to our city:

887 They now protect the inhabitants whom the Ebro washes.

[Col. 0292B] Stand now and sing hymns, mothers, for your children who have been received back:

[Note: [Col. 0293A]

Verse 1. *Fanorum*: “of temples,” “of idols.” Temples are called *fana* from *fano*, that is, “voice,” namely from oracles. *Parens*: “mother,” I.]

[Note: [Col. 0293B]

119. Ald., Mar. in the first hand, Gis. in the text, Weitz., Alex., the Bollandists, and Heinsius: *maritarum*. Prag., Rat., Widm., and others: *maritorum*. Ald., Fabr., Sich., and Gis. in the first edition: *strepet*. Gis. in the margin of both editions: *crepet*. *Strepat* is better.

120. Brev. Moz. not badly has *sit sacrata gaudiis*. After this hymn, in Vatt. A, B, and Mar., follows the passion of St. Vincent the martyr; in Aldus and others, the hymn of St. Lawrence. Learned writers disagree concerning the homeland of these martyrs. From this hymn of Prudentius it can only be inferred that they suffered martyrdom in a town of the Vascones washed by the Ebro. From another hymn, concerning the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza, it is argued that this town was Calagurris: “Our Calagurris will bear both, whom it venerates.” There is no doubt that both hymns concern Saints Hemeterius and Celedonius, although their names are not expressed. The title of this hymn explicitly states that it is in praise of these martyrs, who in many very ancient manuscripts are called Calagurritani. Yet it is not established whether this designation came from Prudentius’ own hand, or whether it merely indicates that the martyrs suffered at Calagurris.

Tradition and common opinion hold that they came from the city of Legio in Spain and were sons of St. Marcellus the centurion, whose twelve sons are listed as martyrs. Risco, volume XXXIV of *Hispania Sacra*, page 315, reports that in a manuscript of the church of León there was a note added by Aria, a learned man, in the year 1069, in which they are called the sons of St. Marcellus of León: “These are the names of the saints found in the Toledo archive. The church of Calahorra received Emeterius and Celedonius,” and so forth. The same may also be seen in volume XXXIII, page 276.

Nebrissa wishes to confirm that these same holy martyrs were Calagurritani from the hymn concerning the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza; he thinks they were said to come from Legio because they were legionary soldiers, that is, from some imperial legion. But he does not persuade me. Teolius nevertheless confidently asserts that they were Calagurritani. Against this stand the ancient Acts printed by the Bollandists under March 3, as well as the Roman Martyrology, Usuard’s martyrology, and most others, in which these martyrs are called Legionenses, and more clearly are said to have come from the city of Legio in Spain.

From the ancient Acts some infer only that they served as soldiers in this city of Legio; but it seems clear to me that they are called Legionarii because they were born there. We may nevertheless observe that Prudentius did not state their homeland, as we now begin to clarify the reasoning of the distinguished Perezius de Bayer, who, in his dissertation *On the Spanish Claim to and Vindication of St. Lawrence*, denies that Prudentius was accustomed to designate the homeland of the holy martyrs.

Teolius confidently replies that this is to abuse the readers’ credulity excessively, since, of the fourteen hymns of the holy martyrs that make up this book of the *Peristephanon*, if three or four are excepted, all the rest explicitly reveal—and indeed proclaim—the martyrs’ homeland. In this first hymn, however, we have seen that neither Calagurris, which Teolius believes to have been the homeland of these martyrs, nor Legio, which was more truly their homeland, is revealed or proclaimed as their homeland.

The passage concerns Calagurris of the Vascones, now called Calahorra, not another ancient Calagurris near Osca, where Loharre now stands. Formerly most people thought that the Calagurris which still exists and is called Calahorra had been called by the Romans Fibularia or Fibularensis, while the other Calagurris was called Nassica and lay near Osca. The distinguished Risco, volume XXXIII of *Hispania Sacra*, treatise 69, chapter 3, learnedly confirms the opinion of Marca, Cellarius, and Wesseling that Calagurris of the Vascones is Julia Nassica itself, for which Florez provides several ancient coins in his work *On the Ancient Coins of Spain*; whereas the other Calagurris, near Osca, was Fibularia. I shall show this opinion to be sufficiently probable at *Hymn* 4, verse 13.

Bartholomaeus Leonardus de Argensola, in a letter to Juan de Mariana, which I cited in chapter 2 of the *Prolegomena*, also doubts whether the holy martyrs suffered martyrdom at Calagurris, Tudela, the town of Tauste, or some other place nearer Zaragoza. But this doubt is adequately refuted by the ancient and constant tradition, and by the most certain monuments, which altogether confirm that Prudentius is to be understood as referring to Calagurris.

As for his objection that Calagurris was a most distinguished colony, while the town in question was inferior to a city or municipality, and that the statement could not appropriately be made of Calagurris, I shall demonstrate at verse 333 of the hymn of St. Vincent, “Throughout the whole town,” that this is entirely false. I shall note in passing another error of the same Bartholomaeus: that Aldus published the works of Prudentius at Rome.

Verse 1. I copied the title from Vat. B, where this hymn is placed after the hymn of St. Vincent, as it is also in the Marietti manuscript. In Vat. A it is entitled “The Passion of the Most Blessed Lawrence,” and is placed after the hymn of St. Agnes. This should be noted, lest anyone think that a firm argument can be constructed from the order of the hymns for claiming and vindicating a Spanish origin for St. Lawrence. The manuscripts vary in establishing this order, and the sequence observed by Prudentius cannot easily be demonstrated.

Alex., Thuan.: “Here begins the passion of the most blessed Lawrence.” Ald., Put., Ox.: “A hymn in honor of the passion of the most blessed martyr Lawrence.” Janus Parrhasius: “The passion of the most blessed martyr Lawrence.” I shall now begin using this edition of Parrhasius, previously unknown to me and not indicated by others. It is an octavo volume, entitled as follows: *Sedulius’ Paschal Poem. The Poems of Aurelius Prudentius*. After Sedulius’ *Paschal Poem* is completed, there follows an encomium of Prudentius written by Gennadius, falsely attributed to St. Jerome: “The Divine Jerome on Illustrious Men.” One peculiar reading should be noted there: *agnoscitur palatinus* appears instead of *miles fuisse*. After the encomium comes Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, the Christian poet’s *περὶ στεφάνων*, that is, *The Book of Crowns*.

This little volume contains only the hymns of St. Romanus, of Saints Peter and Paul, of St. Lawrence, of St. Hippolytus, of St. Cassianus, of St. Agnes, of the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza, and of Saints Fructuosus and his companions, together with two hymns from the *Cathemerinon*: “The Hymn of the Divine Prudentius after Eating,” as it is entitled, and “The Hymn of the Divine Prudentius after Fasting.”

After the hymns there is a letter of Janus Parrhasius to Francisco Medulla of Atella, the Milanese vicar, in which he illustrates and explains Sedulius and Prudentius in many places and adds several emendations. At the end: “Printed at Milan, at the expense of Janus and Catellianus Cotta, through the skill of the brothers Guillaume le Signerre.” The year of publication is gathered from the privilege of Louis, king of the Franks and duke of Milan, dated July 1, 1501. From it we learn that Sedulius and Prudentius, “the most excellent poets of our religion,” had recently been brought into the light through Janus’ expense and industry; Janus is there also called a benefactor of the true worship of God.

Argelatus seems to have been unaware of this edition. In his attempt to catalogue the Milanese library’s editions produced before 1501, he mentioned other undated early editions and an edition of Claudian prepared by Parrhasius in 1501, but entirely omitted this edition of Sedulius and Prudentius.

When I had begun using this exceedingly rare edition, found by chance, I received a letter written to me by the very courteous Jacopo Morelli, keeper of the outstanding Library of St. Mark in Venice, informing me that the Library of St. Mark had recently acquired the same edition. Parrhasius seems to have found an old manuscript containing only Sedulius’ poem and these few hymns of Prudentius; nevertheless, it has quite a few variant readings that are by no means unworthy of notice and are strongly commended by the reputation of the famous editor. I shall record them accurately as readings from an old manuscript.

One of Blanchini’s celebrated arguments for a Roman birthplace of St. Lawrence is that Rome is called by Prudentius in the first verse “the mother of temples.” Let him himself assess the force of the conclusion. Had he not found that ancient copy of his Sacramentary in the archive of the Chapter of Verona, where this novel opinion had lain buried for as many centuries as he himself may wish, I think even this method of argument would have perished. Certainly Rupert of Deutz was not so perceptive: in book VI of *On the Work of the Holy Spirit*, chapter 18, he copied the beginning of this hymn and drew the conclusion that I shall shortly report.

In the Mozarabic Breviary, the feast of St. Lawrence is celebrated with a few strophes taken from this hymn; for that reason we shall cite it less frequently.]

With joy at the safety of their husbands, let the happy voice of wives resound:

[120] Let this day be festive for us; let it be hallowed joy.

14. Roman historians speak everywhere of these commanders and their victories. In the Marietti manuscript a different reading is added above in small letters, but it is inept: *Classica millia ut Caesaris* (“a thousand martial trumpets, like Caesar’s”). Merenda, section 3 of *On the Works of Damasus*, says that it can clearly be inferred from this that Lawrence was born at Rome no less than Cossus, Camillus, and Caesar.

Against this Rupert of Deutz, in the passage cited, after quoting these very verses, says: “Indeed, this could have been said of all the martyrs of the holy Roman Church, because through those commanders Rome triumphed over barbarian rites; but here the principal commander of that triumph is the one whose unusual, or unprecedented, death, like the loudest trumpet of the whole war, was heard throughout the entire world and continues to resound.” Rupert, however, has a metrical error in *Camilli atque Caesaris*.

22. Some write *Xistus*, others *Xystus*, others *Sixtus*. Nebrissa says that *Xistus* should be written, not *Sixtus*, as the common people write it with the letters transposed. Perhaps some people pronounced the name *Sixtus*, others *Xystus*, or the same name was pronounced in both ways. In Greek, *xystus* is a portico in which athletes exercised during the winter.

Sichardus and others thought that this Xystus was Xystus I, who succeeded Alexander in the time of the emperor Hadrian, in the year 116. But the Xystus discussed in this hymn is Xystus II, who held the pontificate after Stephen I in the year 257, under the emperor Valerian. Most assert that Xystus was beheaded. Cyprian, letter 82, elsewhere numbered 80, says that he was put to death in the cemetery, not by the sword, as many claim, although the sword is mentioned in the martyrologies where the death of St. Xystus is announced.

Pamelius, in his notes on Cyprian, explains this passage of Prudentius as referring to the cross in general, meaning any torture or punishment of whatever kind; the Prague gloss explains it in the same way. Mariettus approves this interpretation because, in the hymn of St. Vincent, Prudentius calls Vincent “a companion of Christ’s own cross,” although it is established that Vincent was not crucified. Verse 254 of the same hymn of Vincent also supports it: “Skilled craftsman of the cross.” Gallonius, *On the Torments of the Holy Martyrs*, pages 65–66, proves that the rack and other instruments of torture were once called crosses.

Moreover, although interpreters unanimously report that Prudentius alone narrated that Xystus was crucified, in the Venetian Hymnary of Thomasio there is a hymn in honor of St. Lawrence, without the author’s name, in which I read: “The bishop Xystus warned the minister, fixed upon the wood of the cross: You will carry this out for me quickly.” In the same Hymnary there is another hymn in honor of St. Lawrence under the name of St. Ambrose, and another composed from this hymn of Prudentius. The Bollandists do not dare to brand with rashness anyone who, following Prudentius, restricts Cyprian’s *animadversum* to death on the cross.]

65. *Orgia*, in its specific sense, refers to those rites in which mysteries and sacraments were performed. For this reason the nocturnal rites of Christians are compared by pagans to *orgia*, since pagans often initiated people into shameful deeds in their own *orgia*. If the pagans had gained some suspicion concerning the wine that is changed into Christ’s blood, they may perhaps have called the nocturnal rites of Christians *orgia* for this reason, as though they were the rites of Bacchus or Liber.

But when *orgia* is understood simply as any ceremonies, as Servius states in his note on *Aeneid* IV, the word is also appropriate here in that sense. Some derive the etymology from ἀπὸ τῆς ὀργῆς, “from fury or anger”; others from ἀπὸ τῶν ὀρῶν, “from the mountains,” because the rites took place in the mountains. Virgil, book IV, verse 302: “When the Bacchic rites have been heard, they stir him, and Cithaeron calls by its nightly cry.” Others derive it from ἀπὸ τῶν ὀργάδων, that is, from places consecrated to some god.

68. In the Mar. manuscript *ut* is absent, correctly supplied above. It seems sufficiently certain that in some churches chalices were occasionally wooden, glass, marble, or horn, either because of their poverty, the negligence of their ministers, or because Christians wished to avoid the greed and avarice of the pagans. [Col. 0300B] That such sacred vessels were generally made of gold and silver, however, may be gathered clearly enough from this passage; St. Ambrose confirms it, *On Duties*, Book II, chapter 28:

> Was it ever said to St. Lawrence: “You ought not to have distributed the treasures of the Church or sold the vessels of the sacraments”? … In these three classes it is permitted to break up, melt down, and sell even vessels consecrated to the Church.

What the faithful believed concerning this matter in St. Augustine’s time is clearly demonstrated by a few words of his, quoted for another purpose, *Letter* 26:

> If you had found a golden chalice on the ground, you would give it to the Church of God.

Compare the *Prolegomena*, chapter 13.

70. Vat. A has *libare sacrum* (“to pour out the sacrifice”). The prefect alludes to the story related by Minucius in the *Octavius*:

> The story about initiating novices is already well known, and as detestable as it is familiar. An infant, covered with meal so as to deceive the unsuspecting, is placed before the person who is to be initiated. The novice, having been provoked by the surface of the meal—as though invited to harmless blows—kills the infant with blind and hidden wounds. Shameful to relate, they thirstily lick its blood; eagerly they divide its limbs among themselves. By this victim they enter into a compact, and by the consciousness of crime they pledge one another to mutual silence.

Simon Magus, Menander, Carpocrates, the Nicolaitans, and the Gnostics are said to have provided an occasion for this slander, since they perpetrated similarly criminal acts in their rites. Heraldus, in his notes on Minucius, says that this slander was refuted by all the Christian apologies, and that no one has been found who has stained any sect of heretics with even the slightest suspicion of such savagery. [Col. 0300D] Accordingly, he thinks that everything subsequently reported by Epiphanius and certain others about the Gnostics and Quintilians is false and fabricated. Compare also Elmenhorstius’s notes on the same Minucius. Gis. says that, according to St. Augustine, certain pagans maliciously fastened upon Christians the worship of Ceres and Bacchus. Perhaps the prefect means by “to make the sacred blood smoke” wine converted into blood. In Giselinus, *teste August.* should be explained as *teste Augustino* (“according to Augustine”). Chamillardus wrote *teste Augusto*.

Weitzius most ineptly printed *Tum summa est cura fratribus* (“Then the greatest concern is for the brothers”), although he noted that Bong. has *Tum summa cura est fratribus*, which both the meter requires and the other witnesses support. For although Aldus printed *Tum summa est cura*, he corrected it in the revised editions. It should be noted that formerly all Christians were commonly called *brothers*, as is also clear from the sacred Scriptures. Hence the pagans mocked this expression of ours. Minucius says:

> And indiscriminately they call one another brothers and sisters.

It should be observed that these sacred names were regarded by the pagans as lascivious and amorous terms. Thus, in Minucius, the pagans wished by their slander to insinuate this meaning.

75. According to the discipline of the early Church, Acts 4:34–35:

> For as many as were owners of lands or houses sold them, brought the proceeds of what they had sold, and laid them at the apostles’ feet.

Those who in our age commonly boast of the poverty of the ancient Church would, if they were recalled to this practice, rather praise our customs, by which ecclesiastical ministers are offered not so many new gifts as old ones are taken away.

76. *Sestertius* was so called as though *semistertius*, because it was worth three *asses* less a half. *Sestertium*, in the neuter gender, was worth one thousand *sestertii*. In old books *sestertius* is written *IIS* or *IIS*, because the two strokes mark two asses each, while *S* marks a half. Vossius, in his *Etymological Dictionary*, says that *sestertium* in the masculine gender is a silver coin worth four asses, or a quarter of a *denarius*, which was worth sixteen asses. Prudentius uses the specific term for the generic.

77. Rat. has *addita* (“added”) in the first hand, incorrectly, for *addicta*. Among jurists, *addicta* is used for “sold under condition”; and there is a title in the *Digest*, *On Conditional Sale*, where Paulus writes:

> A conditional sale is made in this way: “Let that estate be purchased by you for one hundred, unless someone before the next Kalends of January offers better terms, in which case the property shall pass from the owner.”

Weitzius, following Rudolphus Fornerius, *On Daily Matters*, Book V, chapter 23, observes that legal authorities did not readily believe that anyone should be compelled to surrender ancestral estates, household shrines, or tombs. Hence it was always considered less honorable to alienate paternal or ancestral estates, and honorable to recover those that had been sold. This, however, must be understood with the qualification that alienation is praiseworthy especially when an honorable religious purpose is involved, since such property ought not to be retained by any law or transmitted to posterity. It is a slander, however, that Christian parents customarily disinherited their children, as the prefect alleges.

78. In the gloss it is not sufficiently clear whether *quibus* or another reading should be adopted.

80. Vat. A and Prag. have *satis*; read *sanctis*. The prefect speaks ironically and uses the Christians’ own designation as a reproach against them. They were called *saints*, as is clear from St. Paul’s letters: “Beloved of God, called to be saints.”

86. Weitzius, Widm., Parrhasius, Put., and several others write *praestrigiis*. See the commentary on verse 140 of Hymn 4, *Cath.* There is also a spelling variation in *praestringere*: some prefer to write *praestinguere*.

87. Vat. A has *exaggerandos*, less correctly.

90. Nebrissa correctly distinguishes the terms, so that *fiscus* is the emperor’s treasury, while *aerarium* is the treasury of the state.

91. Heinsius, with Put., has *didita*, as though Torrentius had indicated that Cauchius restored it. Cauchius’s manuscript notes and Parrhasius have *debita*. Others have *dedita*. Vat. Q erroneously has *suspendiis* for *stipendiis*.

94. Hailsbr. above has *reddite*.

96. Aldus, Weitz., and the other editors and manuscripts consistently have *nomisma*, except that Alex. writes *numisma*, Parrhasius’s edition has *nummisma*, Vat. Q seems to have *nommisma*, and certain Vulgate manuscripts have *numisma*. Heinsius says that Wowerus should not be followed when he emended Minucius to *aenigma nummis inditum* (“a riddle impressed on coins”), although John Gerard Vossius agreed with him. Wowerus does say that *aenigma* may perhaps be more correct. But, he adds, *νόμισμα* (*nomisma*), *χάραγμα* (*charagma*), and *nummus* all denote a coin. On *nomisma*, see the commentary above on verse 50 and Ducange’s *Glossary*.

97. Matthew 22:19 and following:

> Show me the coin of the tribute. And they offered him a denarius. And Jesus said to them, “Whose image and inscription is this?” They said to him, “Caesar’s.” Then he said to them, “Therefore give back to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”

98. Parrhas., *Da. Nempe justum postulo?* (“Give it. Surely I ask only what is just?”)

99. Hailsbr. has *aut*, following the writing practice of certain old manuscripts, for *haud* or *haut*, as Weitz. reports. Ruinartius printed *aut*.]

100. Tertullian, chapter 10 of the *Apology*: “Saturn himself was the first to mark the tablet and the coin with an image.” Minucius attributes to Janus the teaching of the Italians to mark coins. Lampridius says the same of Alexander Severus, that he caused coins to be figured. Ducange and others think that Justinian, around the year 685 after Christ, first stamped coins with a sign. These verses of Prudentius may indeed prove that in the time of St. Lawrence there were no coins marked with the image or name of Christ; they cannot properly be cited to prove that this did not happen in Prudentius’s own age. For Prudentius speaks in the person of the prefect, adapting his words to the prefect’s time.

102. Egm., Hailsbronn., and Vat. P incorrectly have *Philippus*. Vat. A and Uro. have *Philippeos*, Alex. *Filippos*; read *Philippos*, so called from King Philip. Horace writes *regale numisma Philippos*. The glosses explain them as Byzantine coins or *mancosi*. The gloss concerning *Mancuosa*, “the city of Philippi,” is corrupt, inept, or both.

104. Parrhasius writes *marsyppio*.

106. Ald., Vat. A in the first hand, Oxon., Gis. in the text, and Vat. Q. Ura. have *quae vos*, that is, “which you profess”; most have *quam*, namely “faith.” Put. and Alex. have *qua*; above, however, read *quae* with Vat. P and others.

113. Gis. in the margin: *Praedives, inquit* (“‘Very rich,’ he says”).

115. Gis. in the margin: *opesque et auri* (“and wealth and gold”).

116. Ald., Mar. in the first hand, and Bong. omit *est* after *orbe*. [Col. 0303D]

118. Nebrissa says that *emblematum* should be read and understands vessels decorated with emblematic designs. Parrhasius in fact read it this way, and Weitzius testifies that some copies have *emblematum*. Nevertheless, the true reading is *aenigmatum*. Giselinus, following Hubertus Golzius, observed that the inscriptions on the reverse of coins, which displayed the offices and honors of distinguished men and often their personal emblems by means of particular signs, were commonly true riddles to foreigners and posterity. The hieroglyphic writings of Giovanni Pierio, composed for this purpose, are evidence of it. In Latin-barbarian glossaries, *aenigma* is said of a coin. Gothofredus, *Theodosian Code*, Book IX, title 22, law 1, thinks that Prudentius calls coins struck with the images of the Caesars “riddles,” and confirms that an old glossary explains *aenigma* as “coin.” He adds that the Arabs call the coins of Christians bearing a human head *methalia*, a word that properly means *εἰκόνες* (“images”). Hence the Spaniards and Italians call them *medullas* and *medaglie*, or rather forms derived from *metallum*.

[Col. 0304B] 119. Iso ridiculously explains *Augustum* as “Octavian.” All emperors were called Augusti. I suspected that the reading might be *Augustus, arcam possidens, Cui nummus omnis scribitur* (“Augustus, possessing the treasury, for whom every coin is inscribed”). It is no objection that *Locupletis arcam Numinis* occurs shortly afterward, since Prudentius often repeats the same word within a short passage, [Col. 0304C] and here it is elegant to compare the treasury of the wealthy God with the treasury for which every coin is inscribed, or in which coins are piled up everywhere. The ancients sometimes used *arca fisci*, *arca publica*, or *arca populi* for the state treasury, as is clear from old inscriptions. There were also the chests of pontiffs, colleges, and private persons; hence those who administered them were called *arcarii*. There were moreover wine chests, oil chests, grain chests, and quaestors’ chests; on these see Gothofredus, *Theodosian Code*, Book XII, title 6, law 14, and Salmasius’s notes on Aelius Lampridius; on church treasuries, see Ducange. If *arcem* is read, *arx* is simply used for imperial power, as Barthius noted, *Adversaria*, Book V, chapter 12, from an old gloss in an ancient manuscript on Prudentius’s verse in the *Psychomachia*: “And Christ rejoices in the citadel of his victorious followers.”

120. Nebrissa and others interpret the line as saying that Augustus’s image is inscribed on every coin. Juvenal used the expression similarly, *Satire* 6, verse 204: “Germanicus shines in written gold.” It may also be understood as “for Augustus,” or “for the citadel” or “treasury,” every coin is inscribed or deposited. To “write coins for someone” is said of a person who guarantees to a creditor by a written obligation that he will pay them on a fixed day. See Plautus, *Asinaria* 2.4.34, and Horace, *Satires* II.3.69.

122. Vat. B, Prag., and Mar. in the first hand have *minis*, incorrectly, for *numinis*. Tertullian and Augustine also call it an *arca*; Paulinus calls it a *mensa*; Cyprian, a *corbona*; others call it a *gazophylacium*, *secretarium*, or *sacrarium*—the place where the Church’s wealth was kept. Before verse 42 Prudentius has *coelestis arcanum domus* (“the heavenly secret treasury of the house”). See Rosweydus on Paulinus’s Letter 34 and Bingham, vol. I, p. 333, Book II, chapter 21, where he proves that the archdeacon was called the guardian of the treasury. Paulinus of Petricordia, *Life of St. Martin*, Book IV:

> Immediately to the deacon standing nearby, whom the bishop, following the custom of earlier times, had appointed guardian of the holy treasury.

123. Prag. writes *volgabo*.

124. Ald. has *quae Christi*, less correctly.

126. Nebrissa correctly notes the word *induciarum* (“truce” or “delay”), since Lawrence was to wage battle with the prefect after three days.]

Peveratus had also read *spe devorat* and cited a similar phrase from Cicero, *Pro Flacco*: “For what had been devoured in hope has been lost beyond hope.” The ancients read and punctuated *ac spem devorat, aurum* (“and he devours hope—gold…”).

159. This was formerly a praiseworthy custom: the Church’s treasury fed the poor. It flourished especially in the Roman Church, the mother and teacher of all the Churches, although every Church may rightly be called the mother of those brought up in it. The poor stood before the church doors to receive alms. See verse 178.

160. All the old editions, including Parrhasius, printed *ipse primus* (“he himself first”). Heinsius restored *promus* from Put., finding it confirmed in the very old Boher manuscript. Teolius found *promus* in one Vatican manuscript, perhaps Alex., where it seems to be given as a variant reading. Vat. P has *primos*. All recent editors adopt *promus* without hesitation. And indeed *promus* is appropriate, since *penu* precedes it and the deacons presided over the Church’s treasury, as Heinsius notes. I add an inscription from St. Paulinus’s Letter 12 to Severus, on the right side of the apse:

> This is the place, the venerable treasury where the nourishing splendor of the sacred ministry is stored and brought forth.

Thus the first deacon, who governed the treasury with entrusted keys, as Prudentius had earlier said—for “this treasury is the heavenly secret of the house”—may properly be called *promus* and *promus condus*. Nevertheless, I do not entirely reject the common reading *primus*, found in so many manuscripts and also present in a very ancient eighth- or ninth-century manuscript of the Bollandists. For Lawrence may be understood to have known the poor because he was first among the seven men, or deacons, as verse 37 explicitly states; and care of the poor belonged to the first deacon, as is clear from verse 44, “distributing the entrusted wealth,” and from the Council of Carthage IV, canon 17:

> The bishop shall administer the care of widows, orphans, and strangers not personally, but through the archpresbyter or archdeacon.

Jerome says in his commentary on Ezekiel, chapter 48:

> He who is first among the ministers, because he preaches to the people individually and does not depart from the bishop’s side, considers it an insult if he is ordained a presbyter.]

163. Teolius attacks Ignatius Comus, who claimed that in describing these circumstances Prudentius had narrated matters somewhat differently from the Acts, either abusing poetic license or, being far removed from Rome by two Alps, failing to learn the facts accurately. Although poetic descriptions ought to be more attractive than historical narratives, if there is any discrepancy in the facts themselves, Prudentius should be trusted rather than the anonymous Acts. For what Comus says—that Prudentius composed this hymn when he was a young man, before he had come to Rome and before he had been appointed a court poet—is nonsense advanced without any suitable authority.

164. Here he says “before the church”; later, verse 173, “a vast atrium”; verse 175, “through spacious porticoes”; verse 178, “the sacred door.” All these expressions prove that at Rome there was a large house to which Christians gathered in the time of St. Lawrence and which was at least then known to the prefect of the City. The early Christians did not call such sacred buildings *templum*, since that word suggested some form of pagan consecration. The matter is entirely certain. To the first century belongs what the author of the *Recognitions* reports at the end of his work: “Theophilus, who was higher than all the powerful men in the city, consecrated the great basilica of his house in the name of the Church.” Eusebius, Book VIII, chapter 1, relates that the number of Christians grew so greatly during the persecution between Valerian and Diocletian that, no longer content with their old buildings, they constructed spacious churches from their foundations in every city. Optatus of Milevis, Book I, testifies that before Diocletian’s persecution there were many basilicas which were taken from the Christians and later restored. Arnobius, Lactantius, Eusebius, Jerome, Augustine, Theodoret, Gildas, and others frequently speak of churches leveled to the ground in the final persecution under Diocletian.

170. Ald., Sich., Mar., and some others, together with Gis. and Weitz., have *dispostas*. The more accurate Heinsian manuscripts and Alex. have *dispositas*, [Col. 0308B] which the meter does not at all reject. Parrhasius printed *dispositas* but replaced it in his corrections with *dispostas*, which is more pleasing to the ear.

172. Lawrence uses the ambiguous word *sanctis*, by which the Church’s shrines and secretaries, or the treasury, or even the church itself might be understood; at the same time Christian poor people are signified. For, as was established at verse 80, the designation “saints” was applied to all Christians. *Sanctum* meaning “temple” is not a word restricted to the Latin of inscriptions, as some have thought. Persius used *sanctum* for a temple, *Satire* 2, verse 69: “Tell me, priests, what is gold doing in the sanctuary?”

200. Lucan, Book III, verse 118:

> So entirely does the love of gold know neither fear of steel nor fear of death; laws perish without distinction when they are lost.

Virgil, Book VI, verse 632:

> He fixed laws by price, and by price overturned them.

But concerning avarice, the root of all evils, sayings of this kind are everywhere encountered.

201. Nebrissa explains that gold is the poison of glory, either because true glory perishes through it or because, in Christian usage, glory is understood as eternal life. The first interpretation is preferable: thus modesty is dissolved by gold, integrity is violated by gold, and so forth.

204. Teolius thinks that the verse may be explained as follows: “If you seek gold, carried away by its splendor, know that the human race is light and that the poor are children or participants of light.” Nebrissa’s interpretation is truer and simpler: Christ, who is the light of the world, and human beings redeemed by him. Hence he adds: “These are children of the light,” concerning which light John bears witness in chapter 1. Certainly Lawrence, taking the opportunity presented by the gold desired by the prefect, aptly preached Christ to him as the true gold and light. Toletus, on John 1:

> John deliberately used both expressions in the present passage. He said, “In him was life,” where “life” means that which the Word produces and gives us. Then he added, “And the life was the light,” where “life” refers to the Word itself, which is the cause of life.

[Col. 0309D]

209. Concerning the verb *disjicit*, or *dissice*, as most manuscripts write it, or *disicit* with one *s*, as Rat. has, the matter was already discussed in Hymn 1, *Cath.*, verse 97. Ald., Fabr., and Gis. in the text have *dissecat* (“cuts apart”). Parrhasius, Gis. in the margin, Sich., and others have *dissicit*. Gifanius, in *Proicere*, says that he found *dissicit* in manuscripts of Ovid and Prudentius, and *disicit* in one old Prudentian manuscript; and that in an old manuscript of Virgil *dissice* was consistently written, as Pierius had noted. He adds:

> To speak frankly about what I think, I confess that these passages are not clear to me, but I dislike alterations … Further investigation is therefore necessary.

Weitzius and Heinsius adopted *dissicit*.

236. Aldus, Bongarsius: “of my poor people,” without *est*.

237. Teolius, from Mazochius, *Biblical Specimens*, vol. I, dissertation 8, part 2, relates the etymology of silk to the tree *sorek*, mentioned in Genesis 49:11. Becmanus had already discussed the same origin in *On the Origin of the Latin Language*, under *ser*, following Buxtorf and Kimchi, who nevertheless interpret *sorek* properly as “shoot” or “twig.” *Sorek* is generally taken to mean “vine.” The common opinion, including that of the most ancient writers, derives the etymology from the Seres, the name of the animals that spin the thread, or raw silk, and of the peoples where these animals are raised. Some think that silk is produced from trees without the labor of silkworms; but it seems more likely that the ancient writers mention trees because the Seres-worms weave their wool, or silk, upon trees. On comparisons between bodily illnesses and faults of the mind, see Chrysostom, Basil, and other holy Fathers, who frequently explain them. Giselinus, since he practiced medicine, illustrates these verses more carefully and skillfully, so far as concerns medical matters; it is useful to reproduce his explanation. Prudentius makes the haughty and proud like sufferers from dropsy, whose abundance of crude humors, poured upon their corrupted blood, has made their skin excessively swollen. He compares the ambitious and honor-seekers to those suffering from fever (*καύσῳ*); for when the disease arises in them from cares, sleeplessness, and intense thought, there are generally present perpetual thirst for cold water, broad and frequent breathing, vomiting of bile, and immense, biting heat throughout the body. He compares the avaricious, and the “sharp-handed” (*ὀξύχειρες*), because their hands are grasping and ready to seize, to sufferers from gout in the hands: to avoid increasing the pain caused by malignant humor driven into the ligaments and joints of the fingers, such people neither draw their hands together nor spread them out, but keep them in an intermediate position, which is both most free from pain and most in accord with nature. Thus also he compares malicious slanderers to those afflicted in the liver or spleen: perhaps because, although all their limbs are dry and consumed by starvation, they nevertheless loathe food, bile bursts forth in vomiting, and finally they cannot keep their nails from scratching; all this could be transferred to slanderers without impropriety. He further compares the envious to those with scrofula, or “swollen glands” (*χοιραδώδεσι*), and not without reason, since this kind of disease eats away the fat surrounding the flesh and even the skin itself, making the ulcer more malignant each day as it spreads farther. Finally, he says that idolaters resemble those suffering from the royal disease: just as such patients must be soothed by softer beds, games, and sensual pleasures if they are to recover their health, so the wretched worshipers of demons, since religion is for them a game and a scarecrow for the empty-headed common people, are carried into such blindness by almost impotent softness, insolence, and dissolution. God’s language to them is crude and uncultivated. They are said to attribute to the immortal gods their own destinies, the courses of the heavens, and the spirits of the celestial spheres, and to do so for amusement; otherwise they are atheists, far from dreaming of immortality. As for the revelers who abase themselves to embrace the most putrid whores, he makes them equal not to sick people but to men of the lowest station who sweep out brothels, latrines, and sewers.

Aldus, all the Heinsian manuscripts, Fabricius, Weitz, and our manuscripts have *lucido* (“shining”), and Nebrissa notes Horace’s “the glassy bile swells” and Persius’ “shining bile”; Heinsius, however, cites Horace’s “watery languor in a pale body.” Giselinus, in the margin, has *lurido* (“sallow”), which did not displease Heinsius. Parrhasius has *livido* (“livid”). Teolius says that all manuscripts have *lucido*, while editions have *lurido*. But most editions clearly prefer *lucido*.

Gronovius, chapter 5 of *Ecclesiastical Observations*, reads from Widman’s manuscript, “Hands curved into a palm,” and since the Vulgate has “Hands curved, and the palm,” he himself wishes to restore “Hands curved into a palm, and folding.” Heinsius follows the Vulgate, as does Teolius, who asserts that the better Vatican manuscripts support Heinsius. Cellarius followed the Widman manuscript, which is in fact supported by Vat. B, Mar., Rat., and Prag. It is correctly said that “to draw curved hands into a palm,” as in verse 156, “he draws the sinews into the arm.” On the avaricious, *Psychomachia*, verse 463: “And he exercises his bronze nails upon his spoils.”

B: namely, “folding and with hooked claws,” not “folding with hooked claws,” as it has hitherto been printed. Egm., Pal., and Widman have less correctly *ungulis* (“hooves”) instead of *unguibus* (“nails”). *Ungula* is ordinarily used of animals that do not have fingers. In Iso, *ungulis* may perhaps be a different reading.

276. Weitz explains that golden crowns are given to martyrs after the likeness of soldiers. But here the speech concerns poor Christians who, if they have lived rightly, will shine in the Father’s citadel, whether they have been martyrs or not. Therefore all who attain eternal life will be given golden crowns, which Prudentius calls “gleaming” in verse 926 of *Hamartigenia*. Paschasius, *On Crowns*, book VIII, chapter 5, shows from Prudentius that Christ’s martyrs are marked with golden crowns after the likeness of soldiers, as triumphers over tyrannical impiety.

286. In place of *aut*, Mar., Rat., and Vat. P have *ac*. Egm., Hailsbronner, Palatine, Vat. A, and the better Heinsian manuscripts have *putidum* (“foul”); Aldus, the old editions, Parrhasius, Vat. P and Q, Alex., Urb., Mar., Rat., and many others have *putridum* (“rotten”). I do not see why Teolius should have cited nearly all the Vatican manuscripts in support of *putidum*. Heinsius indeed reads *putidum*, moved by two arguments: because *putri* (“rotten”) has already preceded, and because Prudentius is accustomed to shorten the first syllable of *putris*. I would not have Heinsius say this. What preceded was *putris*, not *putridus*, and the sense is somewhat different. As for Prudentius’ supposed habit of shortening the first syllable of *putris*, what prevents his sometimes lengthening a syllable that is naturally common, whether in *putris* or *putridus*? Indeed, he lengthens it in *putris*, *Hymn* 7 of the *Catholic Hymns*, verse 9: “Nor, sweating out the putrid excess of gluttony.”

Virgil, *Aeneid* VI: “Above it no winged creatures could spread their course unharmed upon their wings; such a breath, pouring itself forth from black jaws, bore itself upward to the vaulted heavens. Hence the Greeks called the place by the name Avernus.” Hence, “the jaws of foul-smelling Avernus.”

289. Writers of a later age often spoke in this way, and they generally placed the participle first, *versa vice*, not *vice versa*: Prudentius has *inversa vice* for metrical reasons. There seems to be an error lurking in the gloss *vacat* (“is idle”). Prudentius says that to the souls whom bodily beauty once delighted, a corrupted form is inflicted in reverse fashion. Nebrissa explains this in Aristotle’s words, *Ethics* III: “Some punishments are medicinal, such as those that must be inflicted by contraries, so that those who, while alive, were devoted to adornment may be deformed in death.”]

295. Hailsbronner has *quod nec* (“which neither”). From Luke 12:33: “Make for yourselves purses that do not grow old, an unfailing treasure in heaven, where no thief approaches and no moth destroys.”

299. Aldus and Giselinus in the first edition have *numinis* (“of the divinity”) in the text; the other witnesses more correctly have *luminis* (“of light”). So in verse 205: “These are nurselings of light,” although here the splendor of the gems may be understood.

300. This is a singular point worth noting: the relative pronoun *quibus* completes the construction of the phrase, a rare instance of transposition.

301. Mar. in the first hand, Prag., Widman, have *cerne* (“see”); Hailsbronner has *cernes* (“you will see”). Others have *cernis* (“you see”).

302. Bongarsius, Fabricius, Palatine, and Giselinus in the first edition have *mireris* (“you may wonder”); others have *miraris* (“you wonder”). Nebrissa and Chamillard understand *intactas anus* to mean widows untouched by the second fire after the loss of the first marriage-bed, although elsewhere Virgil calls an untouched maiden *intacta*. I think that here too the consecrated virgins themselves are called *intactae anus*, “untouched old women,” because they preserved their virginity into old age; then there are added those who are widows and have not known a second fire. That is, some are untouched, others have not known a second fire. Aldus and Parrhasius distinguish the passage in such a way that they place a question mark after *intactas anus*, while Iso places the gloss *viduas* after *nescias*. Gothofredus, in book IX, title 25, law 2 of the Theodosian Code, suspects that *inviras* should be read, as though *univiras*, or that *viduas* should be read for *vel invitas*, because here and elsewhere Prudentius and the Fathers join widows and virgins and equate their abduction. The words of that law, issued by Jovian in the year 364, are as follows: “If anyone should dare, I will not say to abduct, but even to attempt, for the purpose of contracting marriage, consecrated virgins, or unwilling women, let him be punished by capital sentence.” He further conjectures that *vel non invitas* (“or even those not unwilling”) may be read. But it seems to me that the sense of the law proceeds correctly: it forbids attempting, for the purpose of contracting marriage, consecrated virgins even if they are not unwilling, and other non-consecrated women if they are unwilling. I could confirm this at greater length, but there is no time.

305. This praise of virgins and widows may be added to countless other praises by which Christian chastity is rightly celebrated. Saint Cyprian, in his book *On the Discipline and Conduct of Virgins*: “That is the flower of the ecclesiastical shoot, the honor and ornament of spiritual grace, a joyful disposition, a work of praise and honor, whole and uncorrupted, the image of God corresponding to the holiness of the Lord, the more illustrious portion of Christ’s flock. Through them and in them the glorious fertility of the mother Church rejoices and flourishes abundantly; and the more plentiful virginity adds to her number, the more the joy of the mother increases.”

307. The Church is compared to a bride adorned for her husband in Revelation, chapter 21. In the hymn for the dedication of a church at Vespers: “And you are girded in the manner of a bride … endowed with the glory of the Father.”

317. I do not understand Iso’s gloss. It is well known that a *furcifer* was a slave who, for the sake of disgrace more than punishment, was compelled to carry a fork through the neighborhood or through the city. On the old and new fork, see Lipsius, book III, *On the Cross*.

318. Thuanus has *capillo* (“with hair”), incorrectly. Heinsius noted that in Sedulius, book V, *circumferri labellis* is wrongly circulated as *circumferri favillis*, in place of *cavillis*: “And now a thousand falsehoods fly, fabricated against the Lord by the empty mockeries of men.” A *mimus* is so called from imitation of things, expressions, and persons; hence *pantomimus*, an imitator of everything. Mimes used to mingle jokes and sayings in their representations, and the sayings of Publius the Mime are famous. Lactantius, book VII, chapter 12: “The maxim of a madman was more suited to a mime than to a school,” which he seems to have taken from Minucius: “That saying seemed worthy not of philosophical study but of the vice of a mime.” Others read *mimico officio* (“with mimic service”) or *mimi convicio* (“with a mime’s abuse”). Heraldus suspects that *mimi cavillo*, *cavillitio*, or *mimico cavillitio* should be read, because mockery is characteristic of mimes.

319. One correctly says *strophas nectere* (“to weave tricks”). Ammianus, book XV: “Paul was given the surname Catenarius because he was indissoluble in linking together chains of calumnies.”

320. Stories and songs too will be danced, that is, represented through dancing; see further the note on the Roman poem. Ovid, *Tristia* V.7: “Because our songs are danced in the crowded theater.”

You think, fork-bearer, that you may safely

Have woven such tricks

With clownish mockery,

[320] While you, a clown, dance a story?

Is it a neat kind of urbanity

915 To treat us with entertainments?”

325. “Is it really so?”: is it not so? I. “Severity”: strictness, Mar. “Strictness”: harshness, I.

326. “With the fasces”: with honors, I.

327. “Is it really to such an extent?”: so greatly, I.

329. “I shall die”: I shall perish. *Oppetere* is as though “to seek the earth,” for brave men, while dying, seek the earth so that their voice may not be heard, I.

330. “Votive”: desirable, I. “Dear”: Mar.

333. “I shall grant”: I shall allow, Mar.

[Col. 0318B] 335. “Abbreviated”: brief, more difficult, I.

339. “Inextricable”: endless, or insoluble, indissoluble, I. “Endless”: indissoluble, Mar.

344. “Hidden”: concealed, secret, I.

345. “Growing old”: failing, I.

347. “Gradually”: gently.

348. “Half-scorched”: half-burned; *semustulatus* and *semiustus* mean the same, I.

352. “Should”: that is, others, I.]

323. Parrhasius, Heinsius with Ambrosius, and Ruinartius have *ergon’ cachinnis* (“was I then sold with laughter?”); Hailsbronner has *ego* (“I”); others, including the Bollandist manuscript, have *egon’ cachinnis*. Bongarsius incorrectly has *chachinnus*.

324. Vat. A and Parrhasius have *ac Romae festivum* (“and a festive thing at Rome”), against meter and sense. The Heinsian manuscripts, Aldus, Vat. B, Mar., have *acroma*; others have *acroama*, which can be defended. *Acroama*, or, if one prefers, *acroma*, in Latin means “a hearing,” but it is used for a festive and pleasant narrative and sometimes for the person who recites it. Prudentius may have imitated Cicero, *Against Verres* VI: “Here, as though a festive entertainment, so that he might not depart without a garland”; and *For Sextius*: “That very performer, not only a spectator but also an actor and entertainment.” Ruinartius thinks that the hearing, or even the hearer, of such a narrative may sometimes be designated by the name *acroama*; I judge this doubtful concerning the hearer.

325. Parrhasius has *adeo nulla* (“so entirely none”); Aldus, *adeone ulla* (“is there really any?”). Both are wrong.

326. Heinsius does not agree with Salmasius, who here understands *censura* as dignity: thus, he says, *censura oris* (“the dignity of the face”), and *vir censorius* (“a censorial man”), are used for a handsome man. Chamillard favors Salmasius. It is better, however, to understand *censura* as severity, to which leniency presently responds. The fact that *austeritas* (“severity”) has already preceded is no obstacle; the same thought is intensified.

327. Mar. has *adeone securim* (“does softness blunt the axe so completely?”), which I would not dare condemn. He calls it the public axe, as in the preceding hymn, verse 55, “the public double axe.” Parrhasius writes *securem*.

328. Aldus and Parrhasius have *retudit* (“has blunted”), incorrectly.

329. I do not accept the etymology in the gloss. One is said *oppetere* when he seeks something contrary to himself; thus *oppetere mortem* (“to seek death”), and simply *oppetere* is said of a brave man who seeks death, although this is contrary to nature.

332. The pagans considered it vain and foolish that Christians should wish to die in hope of a future life. Minucius: “Oh, wondrous folly and incredible boldness! They despise present tortures while fearing uncertain future things; and while they fear dying after death, meanwhile they do not fear to die.” Lactantius, book VII, chapter 5: “Thus it is necessary that the wise man be regarded as a fool, who, while seeking goods that are not seen, lets go from his hands the things that are visible … This happens to us when we refuse neither torture nor death for the sake of the faith.” Note the word *persuasio*, which was ordinarily used for a vain and foolish opinion, and was also called *praesumptio* (“presumption”). Minucius: “I hear that they worship, through some foolish persuasion, the consecrated head of a most shameful beast, an ass.” Ammianus, although a pagan, seems to praise this steadfastness in Christians, book XXII: “Those who were compelled to depart from their religion endured torturous punishments, advancing with unshaken faith even to a glorious death, and now they are called martyrs.”

333. Parrhasius incorrectly has *sed jam* (“but now”).

336. Arnobius, book II, at the end: “Likewise you too subject our bodies to flames, exiles, tortures, and wild beasts, by which you tear and long torment them.” Others read it somewhat differently.

337. Saint Augustine, tractate 27 on John, concerning Saint Lawrence: “For he was not killed quickly, but tortured in the fire. He was permitted to live for a long time; rather, he was not permitted to live long, but was compelled to die slowly.” Saint Cyprian, *To Demetrianus*: “Nor are you even content with the brevity of our sufferings and the simple, swift shortness of punishment; you apply prolonged tortures to bodies being torn apart, and multiply numerous penalties for mangled entrails.”

338. Peter Faber, book III of *Semestria*, chapter 8, would prefer *moratam* (“prolonged”). But, as Heinsius advises, there is no need.

339. Prag. and Mar., apparently in the first hand, have *ut mors* (“so that death”); others have *et mors* (“and death”). *Inextricable death* means a slow death, one unable to find an end, as Mariettus noted.

340. Mar., Prag., Rat., and Widman above have *protrahat* (“may prolong”); this is better, so that the sense is “which may prolong.” Others have *protrahet* (“will prolong”).

345. *Vapor* (“vapor”) is often used for heat by the best writers, Lucretius, Virgil, Horace, and others. Virgil, book V: “And the slow vapor of the ships.” See Gifanius under *vapor*, index to Lucretius.

348. Aldus and the Bollandist manuscript have *semustulati*; Parrhasius and others, *semiustulati*.

350. *Mysteriarches* is so called because he was first and chief among the deacons, whose duty was to instruct the faithful concerning the mysteries of the faith. See the commentary on verse 160.

352. Weitz and Giselinus in the margin have *quod mox* (“which presently”); Mar. and Prag. likewise.]

Was I sold amid laughter,

Was I a festive entertainment?

[325] Is there really no severity,

No strictness in the fasces?

Does softness so completely blunt

The public axe?

You say: “I shall gladly die:

[330] Death is a martyr’s desire.”

This is, as we know,

Your vain persuasion.

916 But I shall not grant the willing man

That he be given the brief

[335] And abbreviated exit of a swift death:

I shall not let him perish quickly.

I shall hold on to his life,

And prolong it with continuous

[Col. 0318A] Punishments of delay;

[340] And inextricable death

Will prolong the long sufferings.

Spread out the warm embers,

Lest the fiery heat

Seize the insolent mouth too strongly,

And enter the hidden places of the heart.

[345] 917 Let the aging vapor grow weak,

Which, spread out by a gentle breath,

May gradually temper the torments

Of the half-scorched body.

It is well that, out of them all, the master of mysteries himself
[350] Has fallen into punishment:

He alone will provide an example

359. “To strip”: to deprive, I.

360. “To bind”: to tie, I.

361. “Face”: countenance, I.

363. “Lawgiver”: Moses, I.

368. “Impatient”: not enduring, I.

371. “Through the rain”: through the density, I.

374. “Recent”: newly. “Cleansed”: baptized, I.

379. “Blackening”: black, I.

380. “Bright”: brightness, I.

384. “Clear”: serene. We call *sudum* that serenity which follows rains, as though “beneath the damp,” I.

353. Giselinus in the margin and Weitz with most of his manuscripts have *constructum*. *Constratum* (“spread out”) is better, as above: “Spread out the warm embers.”

354. Gallonius, chapter 7, plate 17, describes the iron grid on which Saint Lawrence was roasted; it is reverently preserved partly in the church of Saint Lawrence in Lucina and partly in San Lorenzo in Panisperna. Sagittarius casts Gallonius’ description into doubt in chapter 10, since, as he says, we cannot safely place confidence in the remains of the Laurentine grid preserved at Rome. Yet besides its venerable antiquity, we may place greater faith in these relics because that grid consists of three ribs. Ado describes the little bed, or iron grid, as follows: “A bed with three ribs was brought, and Lawrence was stripped of his garments and stretched out upon an iron grid; and fire-pans with embers were brought and placed beneath the iron grid. When he was pressed down from above with iron forks, he said, etc.” From *batulus*, an iron shovel, comes the diminutive *batillus*, Spanish *badil*. Gallonius distinguishes the iron grid from the iron bed, since the iron bed was like an actual bed, while the grid was made with several ribs running lengthwise and separated from one another. See plate 17. Sagittarius doubts this distinction. In this passage, the little bed is used for the iron grid. On the veneration with which Saint Lawrence’s grid was honored from the time of the emperor Justinian and Saint Gregory the Great, see the Bollandists.

355. Rat., Vat. B, Mar., and Prag. have *tunc si licebit* (“then, if it will be permitted”). Others have *libebit* (“it will please”).

356. Prag. writes *Volcanum*. It refers both to the god and to fire. Was Lawrence mocking the gods? Compare verse 403: “And test what your burning Vulcan has accomplished.”

358. Hailsbronner incorrectly has *torrentes parant* (“they prepare torrents”).

359. Mar., Parrhasius, and Rat. have *amictum* (“the garment”); *amictu* (“of the garment”) is better.

360. Alex. in the first hand has *vincere* (“to conquer”); Vat. A has *vinciri* (“to be bound”). Both require correction.

363. See Exodus 32 and 34.

[Col. 0320B] 366. Some editions incorrectly have *et die color*; read *et decolor* (“and discolored”).

369. See Acts of the Apostles 6 and 7.

372. Lucretius used *coeli* (“heavens”) in the plural; scarcely any other pagan writer did. Among Christians it is extremely common, drawn from Sacred Scripture and Hebrew style.

373. Nebrissa suspected that the text should be read differently, but explains *illuminatum* (“illuminated”) as referring to the radiance seen by the baptized and not by the pagans. He remains uncertain whether the speech concerns the radiance of Stephen or of Lawrence, since Lawrence’s face too shone with beauty. Giselinus declares the Egyptians more blind than the blind, who think there is an error in the text, and says that they are blinking in broad daylight; yet he has not explained to others what is clear to him. Cellarius says that the sense is that all the Christians who were present saw heaven opened, but not the pagans, who were unworthy of so great a light. Thus he seems to understand it as referring to the opened heaven while Stephen was being overwhelmed by stones. Yet I am certain that Prudentius is speaking of the radiance of Saint Lawrence; concerning its fragrance he goes on to narrate a similar miracle in verse 385: “Indeed, the very quality of the odor.”

375. Heinsius, book I of *Adversaria*, chapter 6, conjectures *baptisma ratum* (“a confirmed baptism”). There is no need to change the text. These seem to be the Fathers who are praised later, in verse 490.

[Col. 0320D] 379. *Catholic Hymns*, hymn 7, verse 154: “He covers his face with a blackening veil.”

386. Virgil, book XII: “And the burned flesh gave forth a stench.” See Elmenhorst on Arnobius, book VII, page 116.

387. Rat. has *diverse* (“differently”), not badly.

388. On the stench, see the commentary on verse 759 of *Apotheosis*. *Nectar* is used for the odor flowing from nectar. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV: “He sprinkles his body and the place with fragrant nectar.” Lucretius, book II: “And the flowers of nard, whose nectar breathes upon the nostrils.” Prudentius, *Hymn of Saint Vincent*, verse 280: “Nectar in the fragrant prison.” Gifanius observes that metaphors are commonly transferred from one sense to another, and therefore *nectar* is used for an exceedingly sweet odor. But he would have spoken more accurately had he said that the cause is used for the effect, as when someone uses “wine” for the very sweet smell of wine.]

390. Aldus varies the reading; *variatus* (“varied”) is better.

392. Rupert of Tuy, book VIII, *On Divine Offices*, chapter 10, concerning Saint Lawrence: “Whose roasting gives forth a sweet fragrance throughout the whole Church of Christ.”

393. On why God is called fire, see *Hamartigenia*, verse 71.

396. Egm. and Palatine have *uret* (“will burn”); others have *urit* (“burns”).

399. Parrhasius writes *cathasta*. Josephus, in the book concerning the Maccabees, mentions frying platforms and says that the martyr was cast into the fire upon a platform. I suspect that here Prudentius uses *catasta* for the iron grid. See the commentary on verse 56 of hymn 1 of *The Crowns of the Martyrs*. Sagittarius, chapter 10, says that the passage may be explained as referring to a higher scaffold, upon which it is likely that Lawrence was tortured.

400. Hailsbronner has *affectu brevi* (“with brief affection”); above, *affatu* (“with speech”), correctly.

407. Bongarsius has *experimento* (“experiment”), not so well. The antepenultimate syllable in *experimentum* is ordinarily marked short; Prudentius lengthens it by diastole, or because of the meter.

408. Hailsbronner has *sic crudum*; read *sit* (“let it be raw”).

409. Someone might ask whether this jest ought to be praised in the martyr Lawrence. The holy Fathers who praised it resolve the question. Augustine, sermon 303, formerly 123 *On Various Subjects*: “What more need be said? The grid was brought, and he was roasted. And when one side had been burned, he is said to have endured those torments with such tranquility that what we have just heard in the Gospel was fulfilled in him: ‘In your patience you will possess your souls.’ Finally, burned by the flame but tranquil through patience, he said: ‘It is cooked now; what remains, turn me over and eat.’ Such was the course of his martyrdom; with such glory was he crowned.”

413. Put. and Ambrosian have *nomen unicum* (“the unique name”), a reading Heinsius attempts to support because in verse 139 of the following hymn we read: “And the sacred name itself speaks through the purple of the blood drawn forth.” But it is very different for blood, in a certain sense, to speak the name of Christ, and for Christ to be called “the unique name” while he is invoked. Perhaps an allusion to “the name above every name” would be better.]

414. In the Roman [manuscript], verse 468 reads, “Christ, the splendor of the Father’s glory.” Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 1, verse 3: “Who, being the splendor of his glory and the likeness of his substance.”

419. Mar. incorrectly has *et mundum* (“and the world”).

421. See the Prolegomena, chapter 8.

423. Saint Augustine, *City of God*, book 19, chapter 7: “Indeed, care was taken that the imperial city should impose upon conquered peoples not only its yoke but also its language through the peace of its alliance; thus there would be no lack—indeed, there would be an abundance—of interpreters.”

428. Ald. has *ad ipsum* (“to that very one”); *id ipsum* (“that very thing”) is better.

429. Ald., Weitz., Parrhasius, and others have *quo magis* (“the more”); some have *quod* (“which”).

431. Gis. in the margin has *ad oram*; Rat. in a second hand has *quocunque*; Oxon. has *quacunque*; the better witnesses have *quodcunque*.

[Col. 0322D] 432. Bong., Fabr., Rat., Gis. in the margin, and Teol. in the margin have *illigares* (“you might bind”).

434. Ald. incorrectly has *Christiani* (“of the Christians”).

437. Ald., Parrhasius, Put., Oxon., Heins. have *confoederantur* (“are joined in alliance”), followed later by *mansuescit* (“grows gentle”). Celarius likewise adopts this reading and cites manuscript codices in its favor; Teolius also adduces better witnesses for it. Nevertheless, *confoederentur* (“may be joined in alliance”) is found in Vat. A, Mar., Prag., Rat., the Weitzian manuscripts, most of the Heinsian manuscripts, the Bollandist codex, and others. Gallandius preferred *confoederentur, et mansuescat* (“may be joined in alliance, and may grow gentle”), together with the extremely carefully corrected Tornesian edition. Saint Leo the Great, Sermon 88, not only expressed this thought but seems also to have taken Prudentius’s very words:

“For since the work divinely ordained was being arranged, it was especially fitting that many kingdoms should be joined in alliance under one empire, and that universal preaching should soon have peoples accessible to it—peoples whom the rule of a single state would hold together.”

Jerome, in his commentary on Isaiah; Eusebius, book 1, chapter 4 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*; Origen, book 2 *Against Celsus*; and Ambrose, on Psalm 45, argue in the same vein. Jerome, Orosius, and Tertullian use the verb *confoederare* (“to join in alliance”), although others read *ad conferendam* (“for bringing together”) in Tertullian’s *Apology*, chapter 2.

439. *Mansuescat*: may he become gentle, become mild, I.

438. Ald. has *hic ide membra*, corruptly.

439. Vat. A has *mansuescat et orbi*, which is not satisfactory. The Marietti codex has *mansuescit*, although at verse 437 it has *confoederentur*.

440. In the Roman [manuscript], verse 167, Rome is called “the supreme head of the world”; Orosius, book 2, chapter 12, calls it “the head of the nations.”

441. Most of the Heinsian manuscripts, Ald., Mar., Parrhasius, Sich., Weitz., Gis. in the margin, Vat. Q, and others have *abjunctas*, a reading approved from an old book by Gifanius under *INCEDERE*. Vat. A, B, P, Fabr., Egm., Pal., Hailsbr., Bong., and Widm. in a second hand have *adjunctas*, which is less satisfactory. On the verb *abjunctus* meaning “separated” or “divided,” see book 2 against Symmachus, verse 816.

443. Parrhasius has *fiatque fidelis* (“and may he become faithful”), which can be defended.

445. Trojan Aeneas brought his gods into Latium, as Virgil says at the beginning of the *Aeneid*.

446. Book 1 against Symmachus, verse 546: “And the council of elders rejoicing in the Catos.” Two Catos in particular were regarded as wise men at Rome. Juvenal, satire 2, verse 40: “A third Cato fell from heaven.” See Ruaeus on verse 841 of book 6 of the *Aeneid*.

447. Vat. B, P, Mar., Bong., and Parrhasius have *veneratur* (“he worships”); most have *veneratus* (“having worshiped”). The subject is the fire of Vesta, which burned in hidden places. Virgil, *Aeneid* 2, verse 296: “Thus he spoke; and from the innermost sanctuary he carried forth in his hands the fillets, mighty Vesta, and the eternal fire.”

448. Weitzius preferred to write *Frigum* (“of the Phrygians”), with Widm. and Bong., rather than *Phrygum*, found in the other excellent codices. It is well known from Virgil that Aeneas brought the exiled household gods with him. I discussed their temple in my commentary on verse 965 of book 2 against Symmachus.

449. Iso does not seem to have recognized the god Sterculus, whether he was Saturn himself, as Macrobius explains, or some son of Faunus, a king of Italy and inventor of manuring. Pliny calls him Stercutius; others call him Sterculius. Lactantius, book 1, chapter 10, and Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 25, ridicule him.

451. In Teolius, Vat. has *unus, referens* (“one, referring”), which is less satisfactory than *dicere* (“to say”). What has already been said in the books against Symmachus concerns the monsters and portents of the gods of the pagans, as well as the Saturnalia.

452. Ruinartius has *lenis* (“gentle”); the Bollandists have the same with Ruinartius, but note in the margin that their manuscript reads *senis* (“of the old man”). They might have added that *lenis* is metrically impossible and does not suit Saturn.

454. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book 8, chapter 12, says that Prudentius, consistent with himself, followed the same quantity of syllables in *Gabriel* here and at verse 98 of the *Dittochaeon*, where he writes: “Gabriel from the Father’s throne, and suddenly the seat.” But the second syllable in that verse of the *Dittochaeon* must necessarily be long in *Gabriel*; here, however, it could be short, with an iamb in the third foot.

456. Ald., Parrhasius, Palat., most of our manuscripts and the Heinsian manuscripts, Gis. in the text, and one manuscript he saw have *Iuli*. Gis.’s first edition, one Rott., and Bong. have *Iulica*, incorrectly; Weitz., with Widm., has *Iulia*, no better. Gis. in the margin, from his manuscript, and one Rott. have *Iula*, a reading approved by Cauchius. In Vat. P., *Iulii* amounts to *Iuli*. Virgil, *Aeneid* 1: “Julius, a name descended from great Iulus.” Widm. above has *civitas* (“state”) instead of *caecitas* (“blindness”).

460. I discussed these verses in the Prolegomena.

463. Whether *primus* or *primam* is read, the meaning concerning the primacy of the apostle Peter is the same, with the error of the two-headed Church rejected. The following are the variant readings. Ald., Widm. above, Put., Thuan., Oxon., Rott., Noms., Gis. in the text, Fabr., Rat. in a first hand, Vat. B in a second hand, and Mar. in a first hand and clearly in the margin have *primam*. Weitz., the Bollandist codex, three Tornesian manuscripts, Palat., Hailsbr., Parrhasius, and Sich. have *primus*. Ambr. seems to have *primas*, and in the same manuscript *creditus*.

465. Baronius, volume 1 of the *Annals*, under the year 69, explains by these verses of Prudentius certain oracles and prodigies that foretold the approaching end of the Roman empire as referring to the change of religion for the better.

466. Juno was the sister and wife of Jupiter.

468. Some punctuate: “And the people, now Christ’s: flee.”]

[440] may the supreme head also grow gentle.

May it perceive the separated regions

923 coming together in a single grace.

May Romulus become faithful,

and may Numa himself now believe.

[445] Trojan error confounds

the senate-house of the Catos still,

having worshiped in hidden hearths

the exiled household gods of the Phrygians.

The senate worships two-faced Janus

[450] and Sterculus—I shudder

to name so many monsters of the ancestors—

and the festivals of aged Saturn.

[Col. 0323B] Wipe away, Christ, this disgrace.

[Col. 0324A] 924 Send forth your Gabriel,

[455] so that the erring blindness of Iulus

may recognize the true God.

And now we possess hostages

most trustworthy for this hope:

for here two leaders of the apostles

[460] already reign.

One, the caller of the nations;

the other, possessing the first chair,

opens the doors of eternity

entrusted to him.

[465] Depart, adulterous Jupiter,

forgetful of the outrage against your sister;

leave Rome free,

471. In Vat. B, *ex armaveras* was changed into *amaveras*, which is less satisfactory.

472. Tertullian, chapter 50 of the *Apology*: “Yet none of your more refined cruelty accomplishes anything; it is rather an inducement to our sect. We become more numerous whenever we are mown down by you. The blood of Christians is seed . . . . . Hence it is that, in that very matter, we give thanks to your judgments, since there is a rivalry between the divine and the human cause.”

473. All interpreters, both ancient and recent, assert that this prince is Constantine. For my part, I am more inclined to believe that Prudentius is praising his own, or rather our, Theodosius. For Theodosius truly was the man who forbade Rome to serve idols, closed the temples with bars, and caused the bronze images once regarded as idols to remain harmless, while allowing statues to remain as works of artistic value, not to be measured by divinity. See book 1 against Symmachus, verse 503. Orosius writes of this same Theodosius after Prudentius, book 7, chapter 34:

“When Gratianus saw the state of the republic afflicted and almost collapsed, with the same foresight by which Nerva had once selected the Spaniard Trajan, through whom the republic was restored, he too selected Theodosius, likewise a Spaniard, and, compelled by the necessity of restoring the republic, clothed him in the purple at Sirmium and placed him at the head of the Eastern and Thracian empire. His judgment was the more excellent because, although Theodosius equaled Trajan in all the virtues of human life, he surpassed him without comparison in the confession of faith and the practice of religion: the one was a persecutor, the other a propagator of the Church.”

It should be observed that, until the reign of Theodosius, the leading Roman nobility was devoted to the worship of idols. Augustine, *Confessions*, book 8, chapter 2, speaking of Victorinus, says: “He had deserved and received a statue in the Roman forum; until that time he had been a worshiper of sacred idols and a participant in sacrilegious rites, with which nearly the whole Roman nobility then breathed.”

474. Ald., Mar. above in another hand, and some common editions have *servos* (“slaves”). Read *servus* (“a slave”). The same Theodosius is called “a good prince” in hymn 12 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 47.

477. Here *templa* (“temples”) means shrines of idols, which the early Christians specifically called temples. Jerome, Letter 109, elsewhere 53, to Riparius, concerning Vigilantius: “And with Julian the persecutor of the saints, either he destroyed the basilicas or turned them into temples.” Zeno of Verona, sermon on continence, book 1, tract 5: “For you the church, for him the temples must be entered.” Above, however, at verse 164, Prudentius called a Christian basilica or meeting-place—what Arnobius, Lactantius, Orosius, and Ammianus call a temple. See verse 107 of the *Psychomachia*.

Theodosius issued a law in the year 391, *Codex Theodosianus*, “On Pagans,” book 11: “Let no one be granted the power to sacrifice; let no one visit temples; let no one approach shrines. Let the profane recognize that access has been closed to them by the barrier of our law.” He confirmed this still more fully in the following year and law.

479. Ald., Parrhasius, Pal., all the Heinsian manuscripts, and some others have *nefasta* (“accursed”); Vat. B, Marietti, Rat., Prag., Weitz., Gis., and others have *nefanda* (“abominable”).

480. Gis.’s second edition has *aeno* (“bronze”); his first edition has *aenos*, as do the others except Parrhasius, who has *aenis pessulis* (“bronze bars”). Some write *ahenos*, others *aenos*. Alex. has the corrupt form *aaenos*.

483. Ald. has *Stabunt et vera innoxia*; Parrhasius, *Et stabunt aera innoxia*; both are metrically defective. Alt., Noms., and Rott. have *Stabunt ut aera innoxia*. The true reading is *stabunt et aera innoxia* (“and the harmless bronzes will stand”). Theodosius addresses the Romans in book 1 against Symmachus:

“Wash, O senators, the marbles stained with crumbling spray; let pure statues be permitted to stand—the works of great artists.”

[Col. 0326C] 486. Sich. has *et finis item* (“and likewise the end”), which conflicts with the rule of meter. In Ald., read *vinculi* instead of *vincula*.

487. Gallandius, with Ruinartius, emended the text to *volans* (“flying”) instead of *volens* (“willing”). But *volens* is correct, supported by the manuscript evidence and fitting well here; compare verse 329: “You say, ‘I will gladly meet death.’” See the commentary on verse 22 of the preface to the poems. Nevertheless, *volans* should not be rejected; Latinius also read it.

489. From the place of martyrdom—namely, the Viminal Hill, according to tradition, where the church of Saint Lawrence in Panisperna now stands—the body was carried to another place, namely, the estate of Cyriaca in the Veran field, on the Tiburtine Way, where another church of Saint Lawrence stands. Montfaucon describes it at length in the *Italian Journal*, and Ciampini in *On Buildings*.

490. In the commonly circulated Acts of Saint Lawrence and in Ado, the fathers who carried Saint Lawrence’s body are called Justin and Hippolytus. Yet these men had long since been Christians, and Prudentius calls them “fathers,” a name that seems to designate senators newly converted to the faith because of the martyr’s admirable freedom and steadfastness. Therefore, besides Hippolytus and Justin, who are mentioned by Ado, others gathered to carry the body. Teolius rebuked Comus for asserting that Prudentius’s “fathers” could appropriately be understood as Justin and Hippolytus; the Bollandists likewise thought that Justin and Hippolytus were intended. Perhaps Prudentius’s later statement, “I desire Christ,” can be explained as a desire for martyrdom. But the following verses and verse 375 suggest otherwise.

493. Ambr., three Tornesian manuscripts, Rottendorphius, and Canchianus have *replens* (“filling”), which also occurs in Parrhasius, where *indole* is corrupt; Cellarius approved *replens*. Most read *repens*, that is, “sudden disposition,” which Giselinus explains as “a free and noble generosity.” *Repens* could also be understood adverbially as *repente* (“suddenly”), as in *Eulalia*, verse 161: “From there a dove suddenly flashes forth.”]

496. *Nugas*: idols, I.

497. *Retrixit*: froze, I.

499. *Sacellis*: temples of the gods, I.

500. *Tribunal*: to the church, I.

511. *Vesta*: goddess of fire, I.—*Lares*: fires, I, Mat.]
