496. The “former follies” are old wives’ tales about the worship of the gods. Some think that *nugas*, “follies,” may also be understood as *naenias*, “dirges,” and thus refer to ghosts and idols. The matter comes to the same thing whether one understands idols or the fabulous doctrine concerning idols. See the commentary on verse 34 of hymn 11 of the *Catholic Hymns*: “Worshiping empty dirges.”

497. What I said at verse 164 concerning the growing multitude of Christians before the persecution under Diocletian is relevant here. Pliny, even before Saint Lawrence’s martyrdom, complained in Letter 97 of book 10 that the temples had almost been deserted because many people of every rank were becoming Christians. Cicero used the word in a similar sense in Letter 1 of book 1 to Atticus: “When the Forum at Rome has grown cold from the courts.” Vulpius, commenting on Catullus’s poem 62, thinks that Prudentius imitated this, since, as he says, Prudentius was an especially devoted student of the elegance of the ancients, and he understands Catullus’s words *tepida limina* (“warm thresholds”) in the same sense.

500. Cauchy conjectured *cursitat* (“he hastens repeatedly”), but *curritur* (“people hasten”) is correct. Latinius reads these two verses in this way, having found in the Tornesian edition: “The people hasten to Christ’s tribunal; they are fewer in the shrines.” Cauchy likewise notes that the poet is referring to the tribunals of the basilicas. Concerning this tribunal, Prudentius writes in hymn 11 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 225: “Before the facing front, a lofty tribunal is raised on steps, from which the bishop proclaims God.” Father Franciscus a Puteo wished to explain the matter according to our current manner of speaking: namely, that the reference is to the sacred baptisteries and to the tribunals of churches, in which Christian priests sit to cleanse and absolve the guilty of their sins, according to rites instituted by Christ and the power divinely conferred upon them. He seems to understand what we now call confessionals, which are commonly called tribunals of penance. I fear that heretics may ridicule this.

505. In Mar. there seems to be *tum demum* (“then at last”), incorrectly.

[Col. 0327D] 511. Vat. A has *Palladis*; Egm., *Pallidios*; Vat. B, *Palladeos*; Weitz., *Palidios*. The correct form is *Palladios*. But what is meant by “Palladian household gods”? Nebrissa says that it means the temple where the Palladium was kept. Chamillardus understands household gods, or domestic deities. They were called Palladian because of the Palladium, namely, the statue of Pallas that was said to make the city in which it was located impregnable. Yet in his interpretation he says that neither Vesta nor the Palladium was now worshiped by the Romans. Cellarius, drawing on Herodian, book 1, chapter 14, notes that the Palladium was kept in the temple of Vesta. The Marietti Gloss, with Iso, interprets *lares* as “fires,” something recent interpreters do not seem to have noticed.

I do not approve the interpretations of the others; I do not know whether mine will please others. The subject here is the fire of the Vestals, mentioned at verse 447: “Having worshiped in hidden hearths the exiled household gods of the Phrygians.” He later tells how the Vestals were converted to Christ, at verse 527: “The Vestal Claudia enters.” He says that the Vestal fire could safely be abandoned because the Vestal virgins were to be beaten with scourges if through their negligence that fire should be extinguished.

The fire of Vesta is called Palladian both because the Palladium was preserved among the Vestals and because, in Athens—the city founded by Pallas—this fire either had its origin or was honored with particular reverence. Prudentius, book 2 against Symmachus, verses 164 and following:

“If I am not mistaken, this land, corrupted by such vices, had already lain beneath them before the Palladium, before Vesta and the household gods preserved the fire beneath the Pergamene hearth; before Priam’s father built the walls with hired workmen; before Pallas, a virgin, founded her Athens. For tradition tells that the origin of the Vestal flame lay in those cities.”

Although Prudentius says “then Vesta,” he is speaking of his own time, as the following verses clearly show.

Finally, the glosses of Iso and Marietti teach that the *Lares* were fires, or were understood as such. The sacred fire belonged to the Lares; and, as I think, the very iron instruments used to feed and preserve the fire and for activities around the hearth were decorated with little images, which were worshiped as the household gods, the Lares. I understand the following passage of Horace’s *Epode* 2 as referring to these Lares—whether gods or instruments fashioned in the form of gods: “And the household Lares shining around, placed there, the retinue of the house of Dis”; and verse 204 of book 2 against Symmachus: “And for the black Lares to be moistened with perfume.”

Prudentius, who ridicules the Lares, calls them black because of kitchen smoke. Horace calls them shining, either to signify the care taken to polish them, or—if one prefers—to explain “shining” as gleaming with the oil with which they were anointed.

Indeed, what Isidore says in book 20 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 2—that *lardum* (“bacon”) is so called because it is kept *in laribus*, that is, in houses—does not seem as plausible as the derivation of *lardum* from *Larbus*, from which it hung, near which it was kept, or with which the Lares were anointed for religious purposes.

The Spaniards call *llares* the iron chain from which cauldrons hang over the fire. It may not be true that this word derives from the Lares, but it is certainly plausible; I see that it also pleased our Couarrubias. Barthius is right, I think, when he says of the Spanish language, which is called Romance, in book 47 of the *Adversaria*, chapter 13:

“Even today the Spaniards claim for themselves the title of the Roman language; and certainly I think that no idiom is closer to it, nor has any preserved the words more completely. Thus the modern Castilian language has given us great delight.”

This could be confirmed especially by the fact that in the Spanish language there are so many words at once Latin and Spanish that, both in prose and in Spanish meter, several little works exist composed in Hispano-Latin words by Juan de Mena, Fernando Pérez de Oliva, Ambrosio Morales, Ludovico González, Francisco de Castilla, Juan de Guzmán, Maestro Martínez, Diego de Aguiar, Juan Rodríguez de León, Juana Agnes de la Cruz, and many others.

But, to return to the Lares, one must not omit that mention of the Lares, as also of the Penates, frequently occurs in descriptions of the Vestal fire. Virgil, book 5, verse 744: “The Pergamean household god and the inner sanctuary of gray Vesta.” We have already seen passages from Prudentius in this same hymn and in book 2 against Symmachus. Nor is this surprising, since Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book 3, chapter 4, lists Vesta herself among the household gods, or at least as one of their companions.]

and had compelled them, through love of the exalted God,

the people were fewer in the shrines;

928 Thus Lawrence fought;

[505] Then the demon challenged

God’s unconquered witness to battle;

Then Vesta’s Palladian household gods

516. *Resultat*: praises, I.

517. *Lumina*: leaders, principal figures, I.

518. *Luperci*: idols. They are called priests of Pan because they keep wolves away from sheep. They are truly shepherds. The Lupercal is the temple of Pan, so called because solemn games are celebrated there; hence brothels are called *lupercalia*.—*Flamines*: priests of the gods. *Flamen* is said to derive from *filamen*, because the ancients bound their heads with a thread, I.

512. Hailsbronn. has *deleri* (“to be destroyed”); correct to *deseri* (“to be abandoned”).

514. Put., Noms., two Tornesian manuscripts, Oxon. in a second hand, Thuan., Widm., Weitz., Vat. A in a second hand, Vat. Q, Alex. in a first hand, Rat., Mar. in a first hand, and Prag. have *Orare simpuvium Numae* (“to pray to Numa’s simpuvium”). Ruinartius, Gallandius with the manuscript of Saint Michael in *Periculo maris*, Hailsbr. above, Egm. in the margin, and Gifanius under *MOENERA*, from an old book, have *Ornare simpuvium Numae* (“to adorn Numa’s simpuvium”). Ald., Torn., Fabr., and Sich. have *Ornare res vanas Numae* (“to adorn Numa’s empty things”). Vat. A in a first hand, Hailsbr. in a first hand, Egm. in a first hand, Oxon. in a first hand, Alex. in the margin as a variant, and Vat. P have *Ornare res impias Numae* (“to adorn Numa’s impious things”); Teolius unjustly attributes this reading to Aldus. Urb. has *Ornare res Numae impias*. Gis. from a manuscript, and Hailsbr. in the margin, have *Ornare naenias Numae* (“to adorn Numa’s dirges”), a reading Giselinus confirms from verse 34 of hymn 11 of the *Catholic Hymns*: “Worshiping empty dirges.” Giselinus asserts that other manuscripts have *ornare res sacras Numae* (“to adorn Numa’s sacred things”).

Parrhasius reads *Orare in pulvinar Numae* (“to pray at Numa’s sacred couch”), but the meter does not permit it. *Ornare pulvinar Numae* (“to adorn Numa’s sacred couch”) could be defended. Thus Horace, book 1, ode 37: “To adorn the sacred couch of the gods.”

Yet Weitzius and other recent editors of Prudentius rightly prefer *Orare simpuvium Numae*, which Cauchy also approved. Some write *simpuvium*, others *sinpuvium*, others *simpubium*, others *simpulum*, and others *simpullum*. It was a vessel suitable for sacrifices, because all the priests drank from it together, whether the word was derived from *sumere* (“to take”) or had some other origin. Numa’s *simpuvium* was held by later generations in the highest honor.

Cicero, *Paradoxes* 1: “What then? Was Numa Pompilius? Do we really think that the simple vessels and little clay urns of the immortal gods were less welcome than the elaborate cups of others?” Persius, satire 2: “Gold, Numa’s vessels.” Apuleius, *Apology* 1, refers to the same thing: “Poverty established the Roman people’s empire from the beginning, and for that reason, to this day, it sacrifices to the immortal gods with a *simpulum* and a bowl.” Juvenal, satire 6: “To laugh at Numa’s *simpuvium* and black bowl.”

Prudentius expressed this. He says *orare simpuvium* (“to pray to the simpuvium”) because the pagans worshiped it and prayed to it. Marietti noted that this interpretation is confirmed by book 1 against Symmachus, but he did not identify the passage. See Meursius on book 4 of Arnobius, chapter 9, for more on the *simpuvium*.

516. Some common editions have *martyrum* (“of the martyrs”), which may perhaps be more correct.

517. Cicero, Lactantius, and others repeatedly call senators “the lights of the senate” and of the senate-house.

518. Ald., Torn., Gall., and Parrhasius have *aut flamines* (“or flamines”). The same reading occurs in many manuscripts. But Heinsius changed it to *et flamines* (“and flamines”), following Geselino. There were three colleges of Luperci at Rome: the two most ancient, those of the Fabians and Quintilians, and a third, that of the Julians, added by Gaius Julius Caesar.

519. Parrhasius has *aut martyrum* (“or of the martyrs”).

520. There is a historical investigation entitled *On the Thresholds of the Apostles*, delivered by Pietro Salomoni at Rome in 1777. The author of the dissertation is Pietro Lazzeri, who died recently at Rome after flourishing for a long time with a great reputation for exceptional learning. He proves that these thresholds were in the Vatican basilica—not the thresholds of the outer enclosure, but those of the confessio, as it is called, which is the platform or place where the bodies of the holy apostles Peter and Paul are buried.

Even if this is true, the rite of kissing the thresholds at the very doors of churches seems to be indicated here. Certainly the rite is extremely ancient. Saint Paulinus, *Natale* 6:

“Having entered the sacred hall with great weeping, he lies prostrate before the doors and plants kisses on the doorposts; he waters the whole ground with tears, stretched upon the earth before the holy threshold.”

Chrysostom, homily 30 on the Second Epistle to the Corinthians:

“We are the temple of Christ. Therefore we kiss the vestibules and entrance of the temple, just as we kiss one another. Do you not see how many people even fix a kiss upon the vestibules of this temple, some with bowed head, some holding them with the hand and bringing the hand to the mouth? Through these gates and doors Christ entered, and he enters into us when we receive communion.”

Even today this pious custom is religiously observed by many. See more concerning this rite in Rosweid’s notes on Paulinus’s poems 18 and 21, and in Muratori’s notes on *Natale* 12. There he less appropriately doubts whether Chrysostom’s words about the mystical temple of God, which we are, may be interpreted in this way; for it is certain that Chrysostom draws his argument from the reverence shown to the vestibules of churches. Martin Kempius’s work *On Kisses*, where he discusses Christian kisses, requires much correction.

521. Parrhasius has *illustres domo* (“illustrious by birth”).

523. Paulinus confirms the custom of offering children to God in *Natale* 13, verse 64:

“And at the same time Eunomia, a virgin already betrothed to the eternal bridal chambers in heaven, whom Christ, snatched from her mother’s breast, consecrated to himself, having quickly made her pleasing through love.”

And verse 261, concerning Asterius:

“Whom his parents, united in true devotion, established as sacred to Christ while still an infant.”

Muratori, in his notes on this verse, rightly rebukes the heterodox for attacking monasticism and the vows of religious people, since ancient Christians consecrated their children to God from their very beginnings. See the commentary on verse 154 of book 2 against Symmachus.

524. Latinius reads *Clarissimorum* (“of the most distinguished men”), which seems entirely preferable, especially if the manuscripts support it.

526. Vat. A writes *asscitur*. I do not know why Giselinus remarks that *adscitur* occurs in manuscripts written by hand, since it is also found in Aldus and other printed books, although others write *ascitur*. Gis. reasonably thinks that the metaphor is drawn from those who are admitted into a college or society. Chamillardus printed *accitur*.]

527, 528. Mar. [reads] “And the same to Laurentius”: not well, though it could be defended in some fashion.

He names Claudia for any Vestal Virgin, because the Claudian family was exceedingly noble; Suetonius discusses it at length in *Tiberius*, chapter 1. From that family came the Vestal Virgin who followed her brother, triumphing contrary to the people’s orders, after mounting the same chariot, all the way to the Capitol, so that no tribune might have the right either to forbid or to interpose. A Claudia of the same family was also the woman who dragged away the ship laden with the sacred image of the Mother of the Gods, which had become stuck in a ford of the Tiber, openly praying that it should follow her only if her chastity were sound.

Montfaucon, in *Antiquities Explained*, vol. I, book II, presents images of the Vestals Bellicia, Modesta, Neratia, and Tuccia. Valerius Maximus discusses Tuccia in book VIII, chapter 2. Lipsius transcribes several inscriptions concerning the Vestals from ancient records in his *Syntagma de Vestalibus*. From this passage Victorius conjectures that Prudentius is speaking of the church of St. Lawrence called *in Palisperna*, or *Panisperna*, now held by Franciscan nuns.

This argument, however, is of little strength. For the fact that the Vestals entered the church of St. Lawrence proves only that they had become Christians from among the Vestals, as Prudentius says earlier that former senators, Luperci, or flamines kiss the thresholds of the apostles. But not even the slightest argument can be drawn from this verse—“The Vestal Claudia enters”—to show that, in Prudentius’ time, that church was attached to a monastery of nuns.

A stronger conjecture in favor of the church of St. Lawrence in Palisperna may be drawn from the custom that still continues: every year the Conservators of the Roman people offer St. Lawrence, at his church in Palisperna, a silver chalice and a silver paten together with four funeral candles. The offering of a wax taper at the altar of St. Lawrence is represented on an ancient lead tablet of Victorius, of which the following is a facsimile:

*Philological Dissertation, in which several monuments of sacred antiquity taken from the Victorius Museum are published, engraved on copper, examined, and illustrated.* Rome, 1751, 4to, Palladis Press. The author is Victorius himself.

As far as St. Lawrence is concerned, he explains a gem of ring size on which St. Lawrence is seen upon a gridiron. We shall present this gem at verse 563, together with five other ancient monuments that illustrate the ancient worship given to St. Lawrence at Rome.

Victorius then explains the ancient round lead tablet mentioned above. It was, as is reasonably believed, carried by some Christian, hung around the neck like a sacred amulet, in order to obtain the martyr’s intercession with God. Victorius says much there about such sacred amulets. On one side of the tablet or medallion, behind the martyr, a woman seems to stand, either raised somewhat into the air or looking heavenward from an elevated place; she is girded beneath the breasts and has her hands raised and spread in the manner of one praying. Perhaps she represents Lawrence’s soul. Among the pagans, too, souls were customarily represented in female form. Concerning Lawrence’s soul Prudentius says at verse 487: “The spirit burst forth, following Heaven.”

On the other side of the medallion an altar is engraved, with four rounded columns. Its ancient name is a *confessio*. In the *Ceremonial of Bishops*, book I, chapter 12, section 4, we read:

“The place that in most churches is beneath the principal altar, where the bodies of the holy martyrs rest, is called a martyrion or confession.”

Anastasius the Librarian, in his life of Sixtus III, speaks of a confession, a screen, and an altar of St. Lawrence, apparently in the basilica in the Veran field; he then speaks of another basilica of St. Lawrence, which is probably the church of St. Lawrence in Lucina.

Victorius adds further information about the churches of St. Lawrence that exist at Rome and about the worship of that martyr. Ignatius Como, in his work on St. Lawrence, where he discusses the martyr’s posthumous glory, enumerates the ten principal churches of his that exist at Rome as follows:

1. The basilica in the Veran field, which he places first and in which the body of the holy martyr lies; Prudentius, he thinks, was speaking of this church.
2. The church of St. Lawrence in Lucina.
3. St. Lawrence in Damaso.
4. St. Lawrence in Panisperna.
5. St. Lawrence at the fountain beneath the roots of the Esquiline Hill.
6. The parish church reached when one ascends toward the Capitoline Hill from the eastern side.
7. St. Lawrence in Miranda, near the ancient Roman Forum.
8. St. Lawrence in the Borgo, otherwise called *in Piscibus*.
9. Saints Benedict and Lawrence in *Piscinula*.
10. The Lateran papal oratory, or the Holy of Holies.

Concerning this papal chapel I have seen an learned booklet, *On the Oratory of St. Lawrence in the Lateran, Now Called the Holy of Holies: A Discourse by Benedetto Millino*. Rome, 1666.

The Bollandists discuss the other most famous churches of St. Lawrence, especially those at Florence and the Escorial, in section 4, “On the Posthumous Glory of St. Lawrence.” Ignatius Como does likewise. In chapter 3 he repeats a story a hundred times imported from abroad and a thousand times rejected by the Spaniards—namely, that the construction of the building was owed to Fox, a Parisian architect.

The most certain monuments establish that the first architect was Giovanni Battista de Toledo, while his disciple Giovanni Herrera completed a large part of the work. Concerning the other churches of St. Lawrence that once existed at Rome, Martinelli may be consulted. For, excepting the Mother of God, no saint seems to have had so many churches consecrated to him at Rome.

929. He felt himself abandoned with impunity.

Whatever the Quirites had been accustomed to pray for with Numa’s *simpulum*, frequently visiting the halls of Christ, resounds in hymns to the martyr.

The very lights of the Senate, once Luperci or flamines, kiss the thresholds of the apostles and martyrs.

931. We see noble houses, distinguished in both sexes, offering to the vows the pledges of their most illustrious children.

A pontiff once wearing the fillet is summoned to the sign of the cross, and the Vestal Claudia enters your church, Lawrence.

528. “Vestal”: one who was sacred in her clothing. “Claudia”: a virgin of Vesta. A certain servant of Vesta, the daughter of Claudius, belonged to the Claudian family.

529. Fabr., Gis., “four times and, O, seven times.” Virgil, *Aeneid* I: “O three and four times blessed.” Prudentius’ hymns are full of such invocations, as are also the poems of Damasus, Paulinus, and others. Nor should these be treated as insignificant merely because they are spoken by poets; rather, they ought to be brought forward as evidence that such words were customarily sung in the public gatherings of the churches.

How foolish and shameless the heretics’ response is may be gathered from Sagittarius’ words in *On the Birthdays of the Martyrs*, chapter 5, no. 42. He is not ashamed to assert that in those centuries there was no one with sufficient authority to correct or restrain those superstitious and erroneous invocations. As though the many most holy and learned men who flourished in the fourth century had lacked either authority or willingness to correct superstitions and errors! Indeed, they themselves encouraged such corruptions.

932. The Vestal Claudia enters.

933. O three, four, and seven times.

530. “Inhabitant”: Roman citizens.

531. “Near at hand”: nearby.

532. “The seat of the bones”: the tomb.

533. “Because of”: beside. “To roll oneself upon”: to prostrate oneself.

534. “Sprinkles with tears”: weeps.

536. “With murmuring”: with prayer, with whispering.

537. “Iberus”: a Spanish river.

538. “Alps”: mountains.

539. “Of the Cottian Alps.” There are two Alpine ranges, the Cottian and the Pyrenean. “Of the Cottians”: of the Scots [a mistaken gloss].

540. “Snow-laden”: from snow.

543. “Urban”: civic.

547. “Before”: in person, openly.

548. “Heaven”: toward God. “We look upon”: we draw near through our works. “From afar”: at a distance.

550. “Passion”: the day of the Passion.

554. “Admitted”: chosen, summoned. “Fellow citizen”: a tax-collector official, or a citizen.

556. “Civic”: angelic, or domestic; of the citizens of heaven; heavenly.

531. Vat. A in the first hand, Egm., Pal. in the first hand, and the Bollandist manuscript read *qui te praesentem*, against the meter.

532. Egm., the older manuscripts of Heinsius, Vat. A, Bong., and Hailsb. read *ossuum*, which Heinsius approves; and certainly *ossua* for *ossa* often occurs in ancient inscriptions. Hailsb. has the incorrect reading *sede*.

533. It was an ancient custom to embrace the tombs of those whom one held dear. Leo, *Novella* 53: “It is a great consolation for their grief and bereavement if they can embrace the tomb of their friends and pour out tears upon it.” Christians, however, prostrated themselves before the tombs of martyrs for religious devotion and veneration. Prudentius is witness to this in many places, as are other ecclesiastical writers.

534. Hailsbr. reads *spargat*, less correctly.

535. Vat. A reads *aspectus*; above, *qui pectus*, which must be retained.

536. In Put. *murmurae*, incorrectly. Heinsius, contrary to the evidence of the manuscripts, reads *murmura*. So above, as he says, “and dispenses the vowed gifts,” which they also wrongly altered there. I do not know who altered verse 44, except that everyone there reads *Votasque dispensans opes*; in this note Heinsius has *Votasque dispensat opes* through a typographical error.

Teolius followed Heinsius and adds that some editions read *murmure*, but that here it is *murmura vota*, that is, “votive murmurs,” or vows made to St. Lawrence. Gallandius agreed with Chamillardus. Before Heinsius, however, all editions had *murmure*, and no manuscript is cited in favor of *murmura*. I therefore make no alteration. Indeed, even if the manuscripts differed among themselves, I would prefer *murmure*. For Prudentius says that vows are poured forth in a subdued voice, which he often explains by this word *murmure*. Iso interprets it in the same way.

If an alteration were necessary, I would rather write: “Who pours forth murmurs with his voice,” for Prudentius uses a similar phrase in hymn 1, verse 17: “May he pour forth a murmur with his voice.”

537. Alt., the Vulgate in some copies, and Cauchus by conjecture read *Iberos*: *Iberus*, or *Hiberus*, is better. This is the river called the Vasco because it washes the Vascones, not because it rises in Vasconia, as Nebrissensis asserted. See the *Prolegomena*, nos. 35 and 36, and compare Wesseling on the *Ancient Roman Itinerary*, p. 393.

Teolius explains: “The river Iber separates us Spaniards.” But Iber does not separate all Spaniards from Rome, only those who live beyond the river. Virgil, *Eclogue* 1: “The Britons divided from the whole world.” Ovid, *Ex Ponto* I.9: “And you, by all the world divided from your shores.”

538. In Teolius’ edition the meter is faulty: *Nos binis remotos Alpibus*. Delete *nos*. Nebrissensis noted that these two Alpine ranges are the Cottian and the Pyrenean.

Gellius, speaking of Cato, says: “When he was writing about the Alpine Spaniards who dwell around the Iberus.” Ausonius, writing to Paulinus in Spain, says: “Now for you beyond the Alps and marble Pyrene.” Scaliger, in book II of his *Readings on Ausonius*, chapter 16, understands this of the Pyrenean mountains, which may be called Alps.

Isidore, *Etymologies* XIV.8: “In the language of the Gauls, high mountains are called Alps.” Concerning the Cottian Alps, see the note on verse 216 of the *Apotheosis*. Aldus writes *Cotianorum*. The gloss *Scottorum* is written incorrectly or incompetently.

540. Some vernacular editions print *ningidos*. The Bollandists and Franciscus a Puteo, following Ruinart, added *nividos* for a different reading or as a marginal gloss. This is neither Latin nor compatible with the meter. *Ninguidus* derives from the ancient *ninguis*, from which comes *ninguere* as well. Ausonius uses *ninguidus* in letter 22: “Barcino, the snowy ridge of double-peaked Pyrene.”

541. I shall speak of the multitude of the holy martyrs in the note on verse 1 of the hymn to St. Hippolytus.

544. Servius says that Ennius, Lucretius, and Virgil used the verb “to flourish” in entirely different applications. Lucretius wrote: “The rivers flourish with flames; the cities flourish with children; the sea flourishes with ships.” But this expression of Prudentius is exceedingly elegant: “The civic soil flourishes with the tombs of martyrs.” Isidore openly imitated it in book XV of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1: “Caesaraugusta … flourishing with the burials of holy martyrs.” Perhaps Isidore wrote *sepulcris*, “with tombs,” since he took the phrase from Prudentius.

545. Parrhasius reads *sed quia*, “but because,” incorrectly.

546. From this passage alone one may learn that the blood of the holy martyrs was carefully preserved in vessels, linen cloths, and sponges. Compare the note on Hippolytus, verses 140 and following.

548. Parrhasius reads *coelum tuemur*, “we behold heaven.”

551. Bayerius, in his dissertation on the homeland of St. Lawrence, chapter 4, ingeniously conjectured that Prudentius expressed this thought from Cicero, who, speaking of Marcus Porcius Cato, born at Tusculum, says at the beginning of book II of *On the Laws*: “I firmly believe that both he and all municipal citizens have two homelands, one of nature and the other of citizenship.”

554. Concerning the heavenly Jerusalem, see Revelation, chapter XXI.

555. Weitz. together with Egm., Hailsbr., and Widm. reads *aeterne*; others read *aeternae*, correctly.

556. Weitz. and Egm. read *gestis* for *gestas*. Mariettus adds a gloss, whether his own or someone else’s: “Civic—of citizens,” because Lawrence freed citizens from idols. A civic crown was given to one who had freed a citizen.

Teolius wishes *civicam* to be understood because Lawrence freed his fellow citizens, thereby anticipating his opinion that Rome was the birthplace of St. Lawrence. But who has ever dreamed that a person awarded the civic crown must be understood to have been born at Rome?

Aulus Gellius, book V, chapter 6: “The civic crown is called the crown that a citizen gives to the citizen by whom he was saved in battle, as a token of life and safety received. It is made from oak leaves. In the Senate, the former censor L. Gellius judged that the consul Cicero should be awarded this civic crown by the state.”

Paschalius, *On Crowns* VII.8, thinks that Prudentius chose the civic crown from among all crowns with which to honor Lawrence, who dwells in heaven, solely because of the dignity of this reward.

The blessed inhabitant of the City is he who celebrates you and, close at hand, the resting place of your bones.

934. He beside whom one may prostrate oneself, who sprinkles the place with tears, who presses his breast upon the earth, who pours forth vows with murmuring.

The Iberus of the Vascones divides us, separated by two Alpine ranges, beyond the ridges of the Cottian Alps and beyond the snowy Pyrenees.

935. Scarcely is it known, in our hidden regions, how full of saints Rome is, how richly the civic soil flourishes with sacred tombs.

But we who lack these blessings, and cannot see the traces of the blood in person, gaze from afar upon heaven.

Thus, holy Lawrence, we seek your Passion. For you have a double hall: here, one of the body; in heaven, one of the soul.

There, admitted as a citizen of the ineffable city, you receive an everlasting consulship in the citadel of the eternal senate and wear the civic crown.

557. “I seem to see”: it appears to me that I behold.

558. “The man”: Lawrence.

559. “The heavenly Rome”: Jerusalem.

560. “Chose”: selected.

561. “Entrusted”: namely, entrusted to him.

562. “Given”: namely, given to him.

563. “Quirites”: soldiers.

564. “You assent”: you come to their aid, or agree, or help.

565. “Asks”: prays.

568. “Anyone”: namely, any human being.

557. From this passage of Prudentius, Vulpius conjectures that Catullus 60 should read *Flammeum videor videre*, “I seem to see the flame,” rather than *venire*, “to come.”

561. At this passage Weitzius cites Lessius, *On Justice and Law* II.36, and Chemnitius, *Examination*, part 3, p. 352. But just as we embrace Lessius’ doctrine concerning the veneration of the saints with both arms, so we abhor the heresies of Chemnitius and the other innovators, supported by the authority of Prudentius and the unanimous testimony of the holy Fathers.

563. St. Augustine, sermon 304, otherwise *On Various Matters* 37: “For all Rome bears witness to how glorious and how richly adorned with a multitude of virtues, like a variety of flowers, is the crown of the martyr Lawrence.”

Indeed, apart from what I cited at verse 528, numerous very ancient monuments make clear with what singular devotion the Romans honored St. Lawrence. On the attached bronze tablet are displayed four such monuments, discovered in Roman cemeteries and distinguished by the first four numbers. All of them seem to have preceded the age of Constantine, as may be gathered from Buonarroti’s preface to his work on cemetery glasses.

The six monuments that we reproduce are also collected together in the anonymous booklet of the devout and learned Franciscus a Puteo: *Memories of the Life, Martyrdom, Miracles, Worship, etc., of St. Lawrence*. Rome, 1766.

Under number 1 is shown a fragment of glass preserved in the Vallicellian Museum, previously published by Aringhus and Victorius. The name of Lawrence is inscribed in gold letters. A monogram of Christ appears on the head, and on one side the omega, to which, as is correctly inferred, the alpha corresponded on the other. Around these only the fragment ANE VIVAS IN CR remains (“… may you live in Chr[ist]”).

The cross rising above St. Lawrence’s back indicates either that the holy martyr carried the Lord’s cross even to his martyrdom, or that he was a deacon, whose particular duty was to carry the cross during sacred services. This may perhaps be why St. Lawrence is represented in the most ancient mosaic paintings carrying a cross in his hand.

On the second glass, number 2, St. Lawrence is depicted between the holy apostles Peter and Paul, as though he had been placed by them upon the heavenly throne. Lawrence holds the Gospel in his left hand, since reading the Gospel belongs to the office of the deacon. Several other ancient images of Lawrence of the same kind are preserved in Aringhus, Ciampini, and the Bollandists, *Propylaeum*, p. 918.

On glass number 3, St. Lawrence displays a somewhat unfolded volume of the Gospel. Around it is inscribed in gold letters: “Victor, may you live in the name of Lauretius.” In *the name of Lawrence*, the letter *n* is omitted according to the ancient usage of the Greeks and Latins, or perhaps through the ignorance or carelessness of the craftsman.

On glass number 4, Christ crowns two unnamed saints. Around them are represented Peter, Paul, Lawrence, Sustus—that is, Sixtus—Ciprianus—that is, Cyprian—and Epolitus—that is, Hippolytus.

On number 5 of the same tablet, St. Lawrence is tortured upon a gridiron with fire placed beneath it. Two executioners bring the fire near with poles; a third appears to carry coals in a sack in order to increase the fire.

On number 6, the martyrdom of St. Lawrence is likewise depicted on glass, with living flames beneath him. On St. Lawrence one may observe a heavenly halo and the clerical tonsure proper to the clergy. This last monument was preserved at Palermo in the Martinian Museum.

John Fell, in his note on Cyprian’s letter 80, says that, to establish the Passion of Lawrence, an author more worthy of belief than the commonly circulated martyrologies ought to be desired. He had read little: he was ignorant of so many very ancient monuments and of the countless testimonies of the earliest Fathers confirming the same martyrdom, or else he regarded them as later than the martyrologies.

567. Most of Heinsius’ manuscripts, including Ambr. and three Torrent. manuscripts, as well as Parrhasius, Bong., Vat. B, Alex., Prag., Rat., and Sich., read *poscunt, jocantur*—“they ask, they rejoice”—and Heinsius did not dare oppose them. Giselinus likewise printed this reading in the margin, although in the text he published *litantur* with Aldus.

Nebrissensis retained *litantur*, explaining it as equivalent to *litant*, “they obtain what they ask.” Vat. A, Alt., Egm., and Palat. read *laetantur*, “they rejoice,” against the meter. Widm. reads *jocanter*; above, *laetantur*. Hailsbr. has *latenter*, “secretly,” which is not absurd, since hidden murmurs and vows may be indicated; above, *laetanter*.

Weitzius wrote *licenter*, following Fabricius, who has *licentur*. Giselinus likewise placed *licentur* in the margin as a variant reading. Heinsius thought that Weitzius was citing the Fulda manuscript, having been misled by the letter F—a mistake that also deceived me once or twice in the first hymns of the *Cathemerinon*. It is certain, however, that this letter indicates Fabricius, whom Weitzius cites. Weitzius used the Fulda manuscript only in the *Psychomachia* and usually calls it “Fuld.”

Chamillardus confidently followed Weitzius’ conjecture: “Who does not see that neither *litantur* nor *jocantur* should be read?” Gallandius likewise adopted this opinion. But if it is permissible to depart from the manuscript codices, I would restore: “They ask, they sacrifice, and they indicate.”

I seem to see a man gleaming with brilliant jewels, whom heavenly Rome has chosen for herself as her perpetual consul.

What authority has been entrusted to him, and how great a gift has been granted, the joy of the Quirites proves—those whose requests he answers.

Whatever each suppliant asks, he successfully obtains. They ask, they make offering, they indicate it, and no sorrowful person returns.

569. “May you be present”: for *adsis*.

570. “Foster children”: sons.

569. Aldus writes *assies*; Vat. A *adsias*; others *adsies*, which is also used by Terence for *adsis*. For *ceu* I suspect that the reading should be *tu praesto*, “you are present.”

570. Just as Rome is antonomastically called “the City,” so Romans are called *Urbici*, “City-folk.” Ambrose uses the same expression in his letter to Valentinian against Symmachus: “the expenses of the priests of the City,” meaning the pagan Roman priests. Pope Siricius was called *Urbicus* by Paulinus in letter 1 to Severus.

Because Lawrence favors the Romans as their patron, they are called his foster children. Thus one finds in ancient inscriptions: “The patron placed this for his foster child.”

No one would misunderstand the meaning of these verses unless carried away by partisan zeal. “You, Lawrence, embracing the Romans, who are your foster children, in your nursing bosom, nourish them like a father, or with a father’s love.” Who would dare object?

But since there has now arisen such a desire to gather arguments from every direction in order to persuade people that St. Lawrence was born at Rome, certain recent Italian writers try to confirm this opinion from these verses as well.

I could immediately frustrate their efforts if, together with the excellent Alexandrian manuscript, I read *orbicos*: then all who throughout the whole world implore and experience Lawrence’s help would be understood. I could bring forward in the same connection verse 573: “Among these, O glory of Christ, hear also the rustic poet.” But let us read *urbicos*.

St. Leo, sermon 2 on the nativity of the holy apostles, calls the Romans the foster children of St. Peter. Teolius interprets *tuos* in Prudentius as “your fellow citizens”—“whom else but the Romans?”

I shall say only this: those who still maintain that the holy levite should be counted among the Spaniards have nothing to answer the argument drawn from Prudentius’ silence. To reply, as Father Perez and the recent author on the holiness of St. Lawrence do, that Prudentius was not accustomed to identify the homeland of martyrs is simply to abuse the credulity of readers. For, apart from three or four of the fourteen hymns of martyrs that make up this book of the *Peristephanon*, all the rest explicitly reveal—and even proclaim—the martyr’s homeland.

Who this Father Perez is, whom Teolius appears to portray as some obscure friar or monk, I explained in chapter 5 of the *Prolegomena*, no. 106, in a note.

What Prudentius’ hymn proves is explained by Pinius in his preliminary commentary, section 4: “Concerning the homeland and parents of St. Lawrence, no new information has been handed down in memory by the Fathers, nor by Prudentius in the hymn that he composed about the saint.” And again: “As for the city of Rome, the opinion that Prudentius drew his birth from it seems so entirely devoid of every appearance of probability that it deserves not even to be proposed, much less refuted.”

Nor did Prudentius’ silence prevent the Bollandists from assigning Prudentius to the Spaniards.

I shall now briefly set out the arguments of the most learned and highly esteemed Perezius de Bayer, prefect of the Royal Spanish Library, against Teolius.

Perezius says that Prudentius was not accustomed to identify the homeland of martyrs. This is entirely true, and it becomes clearer if a proper distinction is made and explained.

Just as there are two births of martyrs—one by which they are born on earth, the other by which they are born into heaven—so there are two homelands corresponding to this double birth: one where they are born into mortal life, and the other where they are born into eternal life.

Similarly, just as in the case of martyrs and other saints it is chiefly the birth by which they attain eternal life that is celebrated, so it is not usually their homeland in which they first came forth into this miserable light that is proclaimed, but rather that place—whether one calls it a second homeland or refuses to give it that name—from which they flew to heaven and where their ashes are preserved.

Prudentius followed this custom. He often praises the cities in which martyrs were crowned and in which their bones rest; in most hymns he shows no concern for the place where they were born. See verse 176 of hymn 4 of the *Peristephanon*.

Let the hymn before us serve as an example. Nowhere does it say that Lawrence was born at Rome, or that Rome could glory in him as a foster child and offspring. What does it say that the Romans celebrate?

“The blessed inhabitant of the City, who celebrates you and, near at hand, the resting place of your bones.”

This was the place to indicate that Lawrence had also first seen the light of day at Rome. What, then, is the basis for Teolius’ assertion that in most of Prudentius’ hymns the martyrs’ homeland is explicitly revealed and even proclaimed?

In the first hymn the homeland of the holy martyrs is not revealed at all. Teolius thought that they were Calagurritans, whereas they were more probably Legionenses.

In the hymn to Eulalia I readily grant that Emerita is proclaimed as her homeland, although some doubt it. See the commentary on verse 4.

Concerning the eighteen martyrs of Caesaraugusta, see verses 15, 107, and 113 of hymn 4.

Nor was Paul, who in that hymn is assigned to Narbo, necessarily a native of Narbo; nor is it established concerning the other saints praised there that they were born in the cities that glory in their relics or patronage.

Next comes hymn 5, on St. Vincent, in which his homeland is not mentioned at all, as I shall say in the note on the title of that hymn.

Likewise, in the note on the title of hymn 6, I shall observe that the homeland of St. Fructuosus and his companions cannot be established from Prudentius’ hymn.

Then follows hymn 7, on St. Quirinus. At verse 5 I shall say that it is doubtful whether the words “They cherish him in a fatherland’s embrace” indicate that Siscia was his homeland.

In hymn 8, verses are spoken for the adornment of some baptistery, but it cannot be discovered where that baptistery stood or who the two holy martyrs were who are said to have suffered in that place.

Nor does hymn 9 establish that St. Cassian, who is praised there, was born at Forum Cornelii, as I shall note in the title of that hymn.

In hymn 10 there is nothing from which one can argue that St. Romanus was by birth a Palestinian. See the commentary on the hymn’s inscription.

Prudentius did not indicate the homeland of St. Hippolytus in hymn 11, nor is it clearly established for us from any other source.

In hymn 12 the homeland of the holy apostles Peter and Paul is not mentioned at all, much less proclaimed.

From hymn 13 we know that Punic soil produced St. Cyprian; nothing more certain can be extracted from it.

Hymn 14 explicitly declares that the tomb of St. Agnes is at Rome; it expresses nothing about the virgin’s birthplace.

With what right, then, does Teolius infer that, with three or four of these fourteen hymns excepted, all the rest explicitly reveal and even proclaim the martyr’s homeland?

Bayerius splendidly refutes Blanchini’s arguments, especially by providing a suitable explanation of the words drawn from the ancient Sacramentary under the name of St. Leo. Certainly, if that sentence is not corrupt, it is obscure. It reads as follows:

“For although, through your propagation, Lord, the glory of your saints is renowned throughout the whole world, nevertheless Rome rejoices more particularly than the others in the solemnity of the blessed Lawrence, whose birth made him a citizen, whose sacred ministry made him a servant, and whose dedication to your name made him your special gift.”

“May you always be present.”

571. “Nursing”: satisfying.

583. “To the body”: to sin.

1. “Offspring”: generation. “Eulalia” means “good-speaking” or “eloquent.” “Blessed Eulalia”: good-speaking. “Eusebia”: good worship or culture. “Theosebia”: worship or culture of God.

571. Vat. A, B, P, Q, Alex., Mar. for a variant reading, Prag. for a variant reading, Parrhasius, Rat., Gis., Weitz., and Heins. read *lactante*, and Weitzius and Heinsius note no disagreement among the manuscripts.

Aldus and Prag. in the first hand read *jactante*, which Gallandius preferred because *jactare* can mean to incline oneself bodily toward someone. I greatly doubt this meaning, however, unless *jactor* is passive or *jactare se* is intended.

Mar. in the first hand reads *laxante*. Alex. in the first hand reads *lactente*. Prag., instead of *complexus*, incorrectly has *complexos*, together with Mar. in the first hand.

573. Father Franciscus a Puteo confirms with many other testimonies this most illuminating testimony, as he calls it, of a learned and especially orthodox author of the fourth century concerning the invocation of the saints. We have discussed the matter more fully in chapter 7 of the *Prolegomena*.

Weitzius refers the reader to Camerarius’ book on pious prayers. But let the heterodox finally understand that we use Camerarius as an authority for explaining Plautus, not for explaining the doctrine of the Christian faith.

574. Aldus, Weitz., Parrhasius, Heins., and others read *audi poetam*, “hear the poet.” Mar., Prag., Rat., and Bong. read *audi et poetam*, “hear the poet also.”

579. Heinsius, Parrhasius, Alex., and others read *martyras*. Aldus and others read *martyres*. Prudentius often calls martyrs “patrons,” a usage that it is useful to repeat here, despite the heretics.

Ambrose, letter 22, class 1, concerning Saints Gervasius and Protasius: “We had patrons, and we did not know it.”

580. Vat. A, B, Mar., Rat., and Prag. read *medela*. *Medelam* is better.

582. A person is called “guilty of Christ,” just as, in Cicero, Clodius is called “guilty in the case of Milo,” because he was accused by Milo.

584. *Ablue* is an error of Aldus, corrected by Aldus himself, which Becmanus does not seem to have noticed in chapter 6 of his *Manuductio*. He corrected it to *absolve* from the Palatine manuscript.

Among ecclesiastical writers, *saeculum* means the world and worldly affairs. Thus Jerome, letter 22, speaks of “secular books.” In Vat. B, the hymn to St. Hippolytus follows this hymn, as it also does in Parrhasius.

1. Vat. B has this title: “Hymn of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, Illustrious Man, in Honor of the Martyr Eulalia.” Mar. likewise has this title but adds: “Here begins the hymn in honor of blessed Eulalia,” and so forth. Rat. has: “Here begins the hymn in honor of Eulalia, the blessed martyr.” Vat. A: “Hymn in honor of the Passion of the most blessed virgin Eulalia.” Aldus: “Ode in praise of the martyr Eulalia.” Heinsius, who follows Put. and Oxon. in recording the titles of the hymns of this book, has: “In honor of the Passion of the most blessed martyr Eulalia.”

Our manuscripts here, and often elsewhere, write *in honore*, not *in honorem*, as though they were speaking of a festival.

Osiander, *Epitome of Ecclesiastical History*, century 4, book I, chapter 9, observes that Eulalia’s martyrdom was elegantly described by Prudentius.

Ruinart rightly preferred this hymn of Prudentius to the other published acts and judged that the martyrdom of St. Eulalia should be assigned to the year 304.

I have discussed at greater length in the *Hymnodia Hispanica*, under December 9, the defense of Prudentius’ credibility in his account of this martyrdom.

Some have thought that Prudentius mistakenly transferred the acts of St. Eulalia of Barcelona to St. Eulalia of Emerita.

In any case, since Prudentius lived in the same century in which Eulalia of Emerita suffered martyrdom; since he wrote in the province of Tarraconensis, where he could more readily have learned and proclaimed the praises of Eulalia of Barcelona than those of Eulalia of Emerita; and since clear testimonies concerning Eulalia of Emerita are offered by Idatius, Isidore, the author of the seventh-century life of St. Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, the more-than-thousand-year-old Veronese manuscript of the Gothic office edited by Joseph Blanchini, Gregory of Tours, Fortunatus, and other ancients—whereas among the ancient writers the first certain author clearly to mention her was Eulogius in the ninth century, if we set aside the doubtful hymn of Quiricus and the anonymous acts, which certainly have no greater weight than the acts of Eulalia of Emerita—in view, I say, of all these facts, I may rightly repeat here the words of Lucius Andreas Resendius from his letter to Bartholomaeus Quevedo:

“Concerning the woman of Emerita, both acts and that holy Prudentius exist. Let the citizens of Barcelona look into the other woman and investigate more diligently.”

In the martyrology of the German Church, which had lain hidden for seven hundred years and was published from the library of Fridericus Beckius in 1687, Eulalia the virgin is mentioned on December 10, with Pope Melchiades. In February no Eulalia is named.

Recently this controversy was being debated in Spain with great fervor, as you may infer even from the title of this work: *A Just Rebuttal of the Argument from Silence and of the Errors on Which the Reverend Father Master Fray Agustín Sala Based the Defense of His Censure, Published in Order to Attack Certain Facts Concerning the Martyrdom of the Illustrious Virgin and Protomartyr St. Eulalia of Barcelona*. By Don Josef Pedros y Riera. 4to, 256 pages. Madrid, Hilario Santos Alonso, 1787.

I saw certain booklets that had preceded it, both by Boria and by Sala. The latter strives to defend his opinions by weakening Prudentius’ credibility; the former strives to strengthen it.

Sala went so far as to assert that Prudentius himself was aware of his own errors, since he admitted that the acts of the martyrdoms of Saints Hemeterius and Celedonius had perished. I do not at all perceive the force of this argument.

As for his additional claim that Prudentius was mistaken about Romanus, Hippolytus, and Cyprian, we shall see in the appropriate places what sort of claim that is.

Nor, if Prudentius has at some time appeared to a learned man to have made an error, may Sala therefore judge in the same way, moved by considerations of such slight weight.

Still less may he assert that in the fourth century, when Christian doctrine and religion flourished most fully, an exact method of judgment was lacking.

I wish he had omitted these words:

“Prudentius often erred in historical matters concerning the saints, because in those so troubled times the records and acts of the martyrs were very rare and scarce, criticism was not very exact, and credulity was excessive.”

Let the acts of Eulalia of Barcelona be defended in whatever manner one wishes; for my part, I ask only that Prudentius and his contemporaries retain their credibility.

939. Embracing your Roman foster children in a nursing bosom,

940. Nourish them with fatherly love.

Among these, O glory of Christ,

hear also the rustic poet,

[575] confessing the sins of his heart

and revealing his own deeds.

I acknowledge and know myself unworthy—

one whom Christ himself might hear—

but through the martyr-patrons

[580] [Col. 0340A] may obtain a remedy.

Hear, in your kindness, the suppliant,

Prudentius, guilty before Christ;

and release him, serving the body,

from the bonds of this world.

2. *Indoles* is ordinarily called the expectation of future virtue in children which we infer from their appearance, and by the Greeks it is called χαρακτήρ, “character.” Here, therefore, it is taken for character, or for the manner of death. Nebrissensis explains it as “virtue,” so that the effect is put for the cause, since *indoles* precedes virtue. Heinsius observes that the manuscripts have *mortis et*, not *mortis at*, or *mentis et* in place of *mortis et*. Gis. and Weitz. had printed *mortis at*. Cauchius conjectured *moris at*; but Heinsius, from Statius, observes: “A cruel disposition toward death.” In the *Romanus*, verse 665: “The character of a nursing mouth.” *Cat.* 12.68: “O boy for whom the Father predestined a threefold character.”

4. I have no doubt that Emerita is here declared to be the homeland of Saint Eulalia. Riscus, in volume XXX of *Hispania Sacra*, chapter 10, modestly rejects the very distinguished Spaniard who had asserted that Prudentius never identified the homeland of the martyrs whom he celebrated. Certainly Bayerius, in his dissertation on Saint Lawrence, openly admits that Prudentius said Eulalia had been brought into the light at Emerita, although only in passing. I do not see how “she who was born from its breast” can be understood unless we say that Saint Eulalia arose from Emerita.

Nevertheless, speaking of this Eulalia of ours, Giselinus says that a girl was catechized in the city of Barcelona by the priest Donatus; this agrees poorly with Prudentius’ account. Florezius, in volume XIII of *Hispania Sacra*, treatise 61, chapter 6, examines several other opinions about Saint Eulalia’s homeland and rightly rejects them, relying on Prudentius’ authority. Yet it must also be noted that here Prudentius turns this chiefly to the praise of Emerita: namely, that it became renowned through Saint Eulalia’s martyrdom and tomb, as I observed at the end of the preceding hymn, and as is still more clearly evident from verses 186 and following of this hymn. I shall comment somewhat on Emerita at those verses. For now I shall merely warn that Schelstratus, in the appendix to his *Ancient Ecclesiastical Geography*, rather rashly asserted that nothing now remains of the city of Emerita except ruins.

5. The Mozarabic Breviary inserts this entire hymn into the office of Saint Eulalia. From it I shall record the variant readings. Here it incorrectly reads *amoreque colit*.

6. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book V, chapter 21, illustrates several verses from a manuscript sheet on which the hymn of Eulalia had been written out, and records differing readings. He says that *occiduum*, without the addition of the word “sun,” designates the western region, as in Calpurnius: “The Baetis is said to drive on western sands.” Ovid, Claudian, and others may also be added or preferred. What is peculiar to Prudentius, however, is that he uses *occiduum* without *sun*, *world*, *water*, or some similar substantive, in place of “western.”

7. Prag. has *qui attulit*, “which brought.” Barthius’ sheet has: “Which bore this outstanding glory.” From this verse also it is clear that Eulalia was born at Emerita. For the same place which bore Eulalia is said to have become more illustrious through her martyrdom and tomb.

8. The Mozarabic Breviary incorrectly has *urbs potens*, “a powerful city.” The same source writes, less well, *locuplex*, “wealthy.” Chamillardus, both in the text and in the note, reads *orbe potens*, “powerful in the world.” I do not know whether he did so intentionally; he does not say that he is departing from all other witnesses. If the manuscript reading had to be abandoned, I would more willingly read *arce potens*, “powerful in its citadel.” Thus Ausonius writes in an epigram, which I shall soon examine: “Neither Cordoba nor Tarragona, powerful in its citadel, contends with you.”

9. Prag. has *martyris*, “of the martyr,” against the metre.

10. *Titulus* means a tomb, as Prudentius often uses it, although here a basilica together with the tomb may also be understood.

11. The age of twelve years is expressed in these two verses. Barthius pointed this out so that no one might understand twenty-four years. For afterward she is called a little girl, almost at the threshold of the bridal chamber.

13. Soon, at verse 156: “The crackling flame flies into her face.” Virgil, *Georgics* I.85: “To burn with crackling flames.”

14. Nebrissa and Teolius explain *aspera* as “harsh toward herself.” I prefer the gloss “strong.” The words “she terrified the trembling men” also suggest in some sense that she was harsh—or terrifying—to the executioners. Add the martyr’s speech to the tyrant, verses 127 and following: “He roars, and spits into the tyrant’s eyes.”

15. The Mozarabic Breviary incorrectly has *subit* for *sibi*.

18. The Mozarabic Breviary has *et sua*: read *nec sua*. Prag. has *dicare toro*.

19. Most of our manuscripts write *repulerat* with a single *p*; but since the first syllable is long, it should correctly be written *reppulerat* here.

20. The Mozarabic Breviary has *pusilla*: correct to *pusiola*.

21. Some manuscripts write *sucina* with one *c*. Sich., Weitz., Bong., and Iso have *flare*, which Salmasius approved and Heinsius judged correct in his notes, ultimately adopting it. Cellarius too printed *flare* and supported it by the authority of Suetonius, *Caligula* 38: “He blew away the diplomas of Julius and Augustus as old and obsolete.” Among ecclesiastical writers, *exsufflare* is commonly used as an indication of contempt; so also *insufflare* in the *Romanus*, verse 920: “He blows upon them as though he saw demons.” Ambrosian and Oxford manuscripts have *flore rosas*, which pleased Chamillardus, that is, “roses blooming in flower.” The Mozarabic Breviary reads *succina flores rosas*, but this conflicts with the metre.

Chamillardus’ surprise that no one had dared to remove the corruption in this passage, and his opinion that *flare* or *flore* should be read, show that he had read Heinsius rather carelessly; from Heinsius he could have learned that Weitz had printed *flare* from the Bongarsian manuscript, besides Sichardus, who wrote the same in the margin. Our manuscripts, however, and most of Heinsius’ manuscripts read *flere rosas*, which Nebrissensis explains as “to cast away with a breath.” Gallandius also considered *flere* more appropriate to the context, namely, *flere*, “to despise, reject.” I think *flare* more likely and more suitable to the context, since *flare* and *respuere* indicate contempt in almost the same way. The editor of the latest Paris edition of the Fathers reached the same judgment as Chamillardus.]

64. The Mozarabic Breviary has *tribunalia*. The metre demands *tribunal*. *Superbus* is more often taken in a bad sense, though sometimes in a good one, as here and elsewhere in Prudentius. In my censure of Santolius Victorinus’ hymns, I wrote that I did not like Saint Barbara to be called proud because Christ was her spouse. This example from Prudentius could be cited. I would answer that the epithet is less inappropriate for Saint Eulalia, who was to fight the tyrant with a strong and fearless spirit, than for Saint Barbara, who appears to be called proud only because she had Christ as her bridegroom.

Sala, in his booklet on Saint Eulalia of Barcelona, says on page 129 that Saint Eulogius, in book I of the *Memoriale Sanctorum*, denies that the Emeritan Eulalia presented herself unbidden to the judge. But Eulogius does not deny this; and even if he did, he would not deserve greater credence than Prudentius, who was nearly contemporary with Eulalia. Perhaps the opinion had already arisen at that time that the Saint Eulalia of Barcelona and the Saint Eulalia of Emerita were the same.

It is certain from Eulogius’ works that there was then a very great scarcity of ecclesiastical books at Cordoba, as Ambrosius Morales also observed. Certainly, if Eulogius had read Prudentius’ *Peristephanon*, he would have used his authority in the *Memoriale Martyrum*.

65. Lictors carried the fasces and the axe before magistrates: the fasces were used for certain lighter punishments, the axe for inflicting death.

This passage could support the reading of some manuscripts at verse 210 of book I against Symmachus: “Cut from the rock, he asked for it.”

Anyone can readily read *pretium* and *tolerare*, after which the metre proceeds correctly.

After this verse, Aldus introduced two other verses, which are verses 110 and 111 in their proper order: “Near in endowments and in the bridal chamber. The golden pomp of the marriage bed does not move me.” Aldus again inserts them in their proper place.

Cellarius understands Maximianus Herculeus, who was emperor in the year 303, although Galerius Maximianus was then Caesar and the instigator of the persecution. Ruinartius holds the same opinion, because it is certain that in 304 Datianus raged in Spain, which obeyed Maximianus Herculeus. He rightly gives Prudentius’ authority preference over the Acts, which report that Eulalia suffered under the governor Calpurnianus.

Elsewhere too Prudentius lengthens the *a* in *utraque* when it is nominative.]

P and Q, Weitz., Egm., and Widm. have *si potis est*, which seems to occur in Alex. and is defended from an old book by Gifanius in *Viridans*, who considers it elegantly said, as in Terence and the ancients, *si potest*, *si poterit*. This does not please Heinsius, because, in imitation of the ancients, one should say *si pote est*, not *si potis est*. See the commentary on verse 84 of the preface to book I against Symmachus. Although Gifanius calls this poem on Saint Eulalia most elegant, he says that Prudentius expressed *revocare nequitiam* rather crudely. Perhaps this is what Giselinus wished to avoid, for in his text he printed: *Si potis es, revocare viam / Torva puellula, nequitiae* (“If you are able, grim little girl, to turn back from the path of wickedness”); Fabricius printed virtually the same at about the same time. The manuscripts oppose this. Ovid likewise said, in a similar sense, *Metamorphoses* IX: “If it were permitted me to undo my deeds”; and Seneca, *On Benefits* IV, “to revoke a promise.” Cicero likewise uses *revocare se* for changing one’s opinion.

Peveratus notes that *gladio feriatur* (“let him be struck with the sword”) was a formula by which defendants were sometimes condemned, so that capital punishment by the sword was inflicted on them. Pontius the deacon, in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*: “The sentence was read from the tablet in these words: ‘Let Cyprian be struck with the sword.’” Sagittarius, chapter 7 of *De Cruciat.*, adds much else about this formula—*feriatur*, *gladio feriatur*, *securi feriatur*—from civil law, the Fathers, and martyrologies. 117. This may be understood of crucifixion, in which the condemned were left to be torn by dogs and birds of prey; Horace refers to it: “You will not feed ravens on a cross.” See Lipsius, *De Cruce* III.11, and plates I and II, where martyrs led to the cross are depicted. Gifanius, however, thinks that *feros* may mean horses, as in the hymn of Saint Hippolytus, who was torn apart by horses.

118. Barthius maintains that this is most elegantly said, where people commonly would say, “kindled for use as a torch.” Catullus: “And you will not be handed over to the mill and the ass”—that is, to the mill in place of an ass. See the commentary on the preface to the *Psychomachia*, verse 5. Tacitus mentions this kind of punishment of Christians in *Annals* XV: “To their deaths were added mockeries: covered with the skins of beasts, they died by the tearing of dogs, or fastened to crosses, or destined for the flames; and when daylight had failed, they were burned for use as nighttime illumination.” Sulpicius narrates this in nearly the same words in *Sacred History* II. See plate XVII. Cellarius understands only ordinary burning. Sagittarius, chapter 10, considers it credible that Prudentius looked to the kind of punishment with which Nero afflicted Christians, but that it may also be explained of the torches by which martyrs were sometimes burned. The garment in which martyrs to be burned were wrapped was called the troublesome and burning tunic. Seneca, *Letters* 14: “Think here of prison, crosses, racks, the hook, the stake driven through a man’s middle and emerging through his mouth, limbs torn in different directions by chariots driven apart, that tunic smeared and woven with fuel for fires, and whatever else cruelty has devised besides these.” Barthius reads *Aut facibus data funificis*; I do not know whether this comes from his sheet, or whether *funificis* has slipped in for *fumificis*, since *fumificis* occurs in the others.]

121. The judge seems to answer Saint Eulalia’s words at verse 66, “I ask, what madness is this?”, and other similar words.

122. Ald. wrongly separates *e minulis*. *Digitis eminulis* means “with the very tips of the fingers,” as though projecting or prominent. Lactantius, I.20: “For they worship with incense and with the tips of their fingers things at which they ought to shudder with their inmost senses.” And V.19: “I have shown, I think, why our people are thought foolish by fools. For to prefer being tortured and killed to throwing onto hearths incense held in three fingers seems as absurd as, when one’s life is in danger, to care more for another’s soul than one’s own. For they do not know how great a crime it is to worship anything other than God.” Jerome, letter to Heliodorus: “There is not merely servitude to an idol if someone casts upon an altar’s pyre incense compressed in two little fingers.” Hence the “crumb of incense” in Ovid, Columella, and Pliny. Compare Brissonius, *De Formulis* I, and verse 82 of the hymn of Saint Cyprian. Varro and Apuleius use the word *eminulus*. Peveratus observes that wealthy persons were accustomed to heap piles of incense on hearths, while the poor threw on a few grains with their fingertips. Salt is mentioned because of the salted meal, discussed shortly afterward. Teolius plausibly judges that the use of salt in sacrifices passed from the Hebrews to the pagans. Calmet, however, on Leviticus II.13, states that in heroic times salt was not used in sacrifices at all. Later Greeks and Romans, on the contrary, performed no sacrifices without salted meal.

125. The Mozarabic Breviary corruptly has *poenam gravem procul aufugeris*. Urb., Vat. P, Aldus, and others have *abfuerit*, which is preferable to *affuerit*, with Vat. Q; or *afuerit*, as Alex., Weitz., Egm., Hailsbr., Bong., and Heinsius write. In favour of this reading Heinsius cites two very ancient manuscripts and says that it is so read in Virgil, Gellius, and commonly in the oldest copies. Teolius follows Heinsius, although he admits that *afuerit* occurs in only one Vatican manuscript and *abfuerit* in the rest. Vat. Q, as I have said, must be excepted.

126. Baronius, *Annals* II, p. 734, for the year 303, thinks that this moved the Fathers of the Council of Elvira to decree that one who had broken idols and been killed there should not be admitted to the number of martyrs. Gabriel Vasquez, however, vol. I, in the third part, question 25, article 3, disputation 105, chapter 2, does not consider this probable, because everyone ought not merely praise but imitate Eulalia when Christians of that period were being compelled to sacrifice to idols: on that occasion, trampling idols was not only permitted but glorious. He nevertheless condemns the rashness of some who offered themselves untimely to martyrdom.

128. Pope Benedict XIV, book III of *De Beatific.*, chapters 16 and 17, discusses at length whether it is lawful voluntarily to offer oneself for martyrdom, provoke a tyrant to inflict death, spit upon and break idols when death is certain to follow. The sum of all is that such actions are often not lawful unless performed under a special impulse of the Holy Spirit. See the commentary on verse 580 of book I against Symmachus. That Eulalia had this impulse is plainly inferred from her constancy in enduring tortures and from the miracles which followed. I thought that *inque tyranni oculis* could be read, as though she spat upon idols before the tyrant. Certainly I have not read a similar example, although the Acts of the martyrs contain many others concerning those who spat upon idols or scorned images with their breath. Yet I understand Eulalia to have done nothing else but show this contempt by blowing or spitting lightly. See the cited passage of Gabriel Vasquez.

130. The Mozarabic Breviary has *pede prosiluit*. The correct reading is *prosubigit*, drawn from *Georgics* III: “and he treads the earth with his foot.”

132. The Mozarabic Breviary has, corruptly, *lancea* for *juncea*. Boria, in his booklet on Saint Eulalia of Barcelona, was deceived into thinking that *juncea* was ablative and meant the instrument by which the breasts were torn; he explains it in Spanish as *con juncos*, “with rushes.” Prudentius calls the breasts *juncea*. Terence, *Eunuchus* II.3, of a slender woman: “Food makes them, though their nature is good, reed-like.” Prudentius looked to this. Catullus similarly used the metaphor *laneum latusculum* for a soft little side; he and Lucretius, in the opposite sense, call women with dry and sapless bodies wooden. Chamillardus’ opinion—that Prudentius means limbs beautifully drawn and arranged, like things made of rushes—does not persuade me, though he seems to have followed Nebrissensis, who explains *pectora juncea* as beautifully drawn and arranged. I prefer Iso’s gloss. Donatus explains Terence’s words thus: *BONA*, full, large, and fat; *JUNCEAS*, thin and pale.

151. The Mozarabic Breviary has, incorrectly, *Crinis et odor ut in jugulos* (“The hair and fragrance as into the throats”). Aldus, Puteanus, Thuaneus, Altinatus, and Rottendorf have *Crinis odorus ut in jugulos* (“Fragrant hair as into the throats”); Heinsius says that this should not have been altered. Nevertheless, Vatican B, Marietti, Ratoldus, Prague, Weitz, and others read *et in jugulos* (“and into the throats”). Giselinus likewise has *et*, but in his notes he observes that most books read *ut* for *et*, and that the sentence should be suspended until the second quinion or stanza.

He calls the hair fragrant because, through a divine miracle, it gave off a sweet scent, as Virgil says (*Aeneid* I.403): “And the ambrosial locks breathed a divine fragrance from her head.” Nebrissa cites this verse of Virgil, but explains *odorus* not as meaning fragrant at that moment, but as referring to hair that was habitually perfumed. Other interpreters rightly reject this view. I suspected *crinis honorus* (“honored hair”). I think, however, that the hair is called fragrant because, when the flame spread through the locks—as he later relates—the hair ought to have emitted a stench, but instead gave off a sweet odor. A similar miracle in the fragrance that emanated from the body of Saint Laurence was explained at verse 385 and following. Add that *odorus* may be understood of something smelling either pleasantly or unpleasantly.

161. In the margin of the Marietti manuscript, as a variant reading, is *columba recens* (“a fresh dove”). The Mozarabic Breviary has *replens* (“filling”). Latinius, by conjecture—I think ingeniously—reads *columba tepens* (“a warm dove”).

Peter Lazzeri, in his dissertation on the rules of criticism, §6, asserts that in the Acts of Saint Polycarp the words “A dove came forth” signify only that the soul departed. For, as is clear from Aringhus and others, a dove is frequently found on the Christian catacomb monuments and certainly on their funerary inscriptions, to indicate the souls of the just.

He lists other stories in which a dove is said to have come forth: this story of Saint Eulalia in Prudentius and in the Mozarabic Missal concerning both Eulalias, the Emeritan and the Barcelonan; and the stories of Saint Potitus, Saint Quintinus, Saint Reparata, Saint Devota, Saint Spes the abbot, Saint Felix of Trier, Saint Meningus the fuller, Saint Blaise the farmer, Saints Vitus, Modestus, and Crescentia, Saint Oliva, Saint Amator, and Saint Scholastica.

Lazzeri suspects that some people embellished a miracle from the simple phrase “A dove came forth.” Whatever may be the case with the other stories, Prudentius most clearly relates that a dove, whiter than snow, appeared to leave the martyr’s mouth and follow the stars; he interprets it as Eulalia’s spirit. See below, verse 171. On doves and their significance, compare the commentary on *Cathemerinon* hymn 3, verse 165.

186. Prague has *hunc locum* (“this place”), erroneously. Vatican P has *non locus* (“not a place”), also incorrectly. Aldus, Heinsius, the Marietti manuscript in the second hand, Alexandrian, Vatican Q, Urbinas, Weitz, and others have *nunc locus* (“now the place”). Ratoldus, Widmanstadius, and others have *hic locus* (“this place”).

Florezius, *Hispania sacra*, volume XIII, treatise 41, chapter 6, thought that the word *tumulo* (“tomb”) indicated the elevated place where Emerita is situated. It is clear to me—and I believe to others as well—that the subject is Eulalia’s tomb, which Prudentius says existed at Emerita in his own time. Where the remains of this holy virgin are now located, Florezius explains learnedly.

187. Lucan, book IV, uses an *o* in *Vettones*, or *Vectones*: “the light-footed Vettones, fugitives from the ancient race of Gauls.” The older manuscripts of Heinsius and our own write *Vettonia*, not *Vectonia*; yet the Alexandrian manuscript has *Vectoniae*, and Vatican Q *Vetoniae*. Prudentius shortens the second syllable in *Vettonia*, taking advantage of a liberty very common in proper names.

Ruinart, Chamillard, and Teolius place the Vettones between the Douro and Tagus. But then Emerita would lie outside Vettonia, since it is not situated between the Douro and Tagus; rather, the Ana flows past and bathes its walls. Cellarius places Vettonia between the Douro and the Ana, especially in the later period, and cites an ancient inscription from Gruterus, p. 383:

> *PROC. PROVINCIAE LUSITAN. ET VETTONIAE* — “Procurator of the province of Lusitania and Vettonia.”

Gruterus says that this inscription survives in New Hispalis, from Fabricius and Morales. He cites a similar inscription from Resendius, p. 591, which was seen at Emerita in the house of Peter Mexia.

In the following hymn, verse 37, Prudentius calls Emerita “the chief of the cities of Lusitania”; therefore Vettonia seems to belong to Lusitania. It is not sufficiently clear, then, why the ancient inscription distinguishes Lusitania and Vettonia—unless one says that Emerita was a colony of Vettonia and at the same time the capital of Lusitania, which does not fit ordinary usage very well. Nebrissa likewise thinks that the Vettones were a people of Lusitania.

To resolve the question, Florezius, in the place cited, observes that Prudentius places Emerita in Vettonia, Strabo among the Turduli, Mela, Dio Cassius, and Aggenus in Lusitania, and Hyginus in Baeturia. He explains this by supposing that some authors understood a province and others understood regions: Emerita was the capital of the province of Lusitania, stood in the region of the Turduli, and lay on the borders of the Vettones and Baeturia.

Scaliger, in *Lectures on Ausonius*, chapter 30, infers from Prudentius’ words that Emerita is called “Emerita Augusta of Vectonica,” where *Vectonica* must be understood as “of the state,” since the Vectones were a people of Lusitania; among them Emerita was the chief city and mother-city of the whole province of Lusitania. But since Prudentius says that Emerita is the distinguished colony of Vettonia, it seems more consistent to judge that Vettonia is the region of the Vettone peoples rather than another name for Emerita Augusta.

Scaliger also maintains that Ausonius’ epigram 8 on cities fits Emerita, as the common reading had it, not Hispalis, whose name is found in the old manuscripts. It was once read as follows:

> Henceforth you shall rightly be remembered by me, Iberian name,
>
> where the sea-touched river flows past Hispalis.
>
> To you all Spain submits her fasces;
>
> neither Corduba nor Tarraco, powerful in its citadel, competes with you,
>
> nor wealthy Bracara, which displays itself in the sea’s gulf.

Scaliger reads *Emerita* instead of *Hispalis*, because a sea-touched river does not flow past Hispalis but does flow past Emerita, and he adduces Prudentius as a witness. For the river Ana bathes this city, a fact which, he says, Prudentius explains most explicitly in these verses.

I, on the contrary, think that the sea-touched river flows past Hispalis, not Emerita. Scaliger explains that rivers are called *aequorei* (“marine” or “sea-touched”) because their mouths, where they discharge into the Ocean, undergo the Ocean’s tides. I add that a sea-touched river which bathes a city is understood to be one that flows past the city where it experiences the Ocean’s tides; otherwise the term could indiscriminately be applied to all rivers that discharge into the Ocean.

Now the Baetis flows past Hispalis, and where it bathes the city the sea’s tides are felt. Emerita, however, is situated beside the Ana so far inland that it is far removed from the sea’s tides.

Moreover, the Iberian name mentioned by Ausonius is properly applied to Hispalis and less properly to Emerita, whose name is rather Latin or Italian, as Ausonius says of his own name in letter 16:

> Ausonius has sent you tales from the very boundary of the Rhine—
>
> Ausonius, an Italian by name, teacher of your Augustus.

Hispalis was indeed at that time a very famous city, called Colonia Romula in Florezius, plate 29, and on ancient coins.

After I had thought through these matters concerning the restoration of Ausonius’ passage, I later came upon the commentaries of Gothofredus on the *Theodosian Code*, law 5, title *On Betrothals*. There he explains a law of Constantine addressed to Tiberianus, vicar of the Spains, and received at Hispalis in the year 336. Gothofredus says that this law shows that the seat of the vicar of the Spains was Hispalis, and that Ausonius’ epigram reads *Hispalis* in an old book; he also says that the praises Ausonius bestows there suit Hispalis.

He adds that Ausonius’ words, “To you all Spain submits her fasces,” do not imply that the tribunal of a proconsul stood in that city—for at that time there was no such tribunal—but that it was the first city of all Spain.

188. Teolius writes *Anas*, while most have *Ana*; either form is permissible. The Marietti manuscript joins the words and writes *Amnisana*. Aldus had printed this form exactly, but corrected it to *amnis Ana*. Nor is *Amnisana* without justification, since certain cities are named by combining a common civic name with another distinctive name.

The river is now called Guadiana, a compound name from *guad*, the Arabic word for “river,” and *Ana*, the ancient Latin name of the river. Other similar names in Spain are derived from Arabic: Guadalquivir (*Baetis*) and Guadalupe (*Aquae Lupiae*).

Heinsius, on the authority of the Vossian manuscript, says that in Ausonius’ letter to Paulinus beginning “We shake out,” etc., the verse

> *Emeritaeque amnes, lataeque fluenta Garumnae* — “the rivers of Emerita and the broad streams of the Garonne”

should be corrected and read:

> *Emeritensis Anae, lataeque fluenta Garumnae* — “of the Ana of Emerita and the broad streams of the Garonne.”
