189. He calls the pool of the Ana green because of the trees, says Nebrissa, or because of the neighboring grasses, which are characteristic of that river. The grasses in the meadows of the Ana are particularly abundant; cattle are driven from the mountains of the Astures to graze on them in winter, despite the very long journey.

What Nebrissa says about the Ana dividing Baetica from Lusitania must be explained according to the modern arrangement: the Ana flows through Extremadura and then, at the extreme Algarve, separates Portugal from Baetica.

> “The nourishing halls shine, traveler,”

and so forth.

These and the following verses should be noted for their description of the decoration and adornment of churches; see the prologue, chapter 13.

198. Nebrissa testifies that pavements in Emerita, ornamented with cut marble in mosaic designs, can still be seen in the churches. The same is well known of the oldest Roman temples.

199. The Mozarabic Breviary has *rorulenta* (“dewy”); read *rosulenta*, from the roses and flowers represented on the pavement. He uses *rosulenta* by analogy with *rorulenta* in hymn 7, verse 168. *Rosatus* and *rosulatus* are words of a later age, according to Ducange.

[Col. 0355D] 201. The flowers with which tombs were customarily decorated were discussed in the prologue, chapter 14.

202. Ratoldus has *sanguineos* (“blood-red”); in a later hand, *sanguineosque*, which the meter requires.

203. The Mozarabic Breviary has *gemellis* (“twin”), which should be corrected to *genialis*. In Virgil, *Georgics* I.302: “Kindly winter invites.” Prudentius says that flowers grow at Emerita because of the mildness of the climate; or he may also suggest that spring flowers before its time, so that Eulalia’s tomb may be adorned. Paulinus, *Natale* 3:

> “Let purple spring breathe in winter; let the year be flower-filled
>
> before its time; let nature yield to the holy day.
>
> Earth, you owe garlands at the martyr’s tomb.”

204. Prague, in the first hand, has *aura lepens* (“a gentle breeze”), which I do not dislike, if *glacies* (“ice”) is taken as a plural accusative. The Mozarabic Breviary has, incorrectly, *laxat et arctat tepens glacies* (“the warm ice loosens and tightens”).

208. The Mozarabic Breviary has, erroneously, *choro et in medio* (“in the choir and in the middle”). Poets commonly call their own poems garlands and crowns with which, they say, the head of the person they praise is adorned.

[Col. 0356B] 209. He indicates the meter used by the poem, namely the dactylic meter, as often elsewhere. I noted in the prologue, no. 217, that Blanchinus incorrectly corrected this to *dactylo* (“in a dactyl”) instead of *dactylico* (“dactylic”).

211. The Mozarabic Breviary has *venerari* (“to venerate”), contrary to the meter, instead of *venerarier*, as in the following verse; and *altare* (“altar”) instead of *altar*. See verse 80 of the *Dittochaeon*.

212. This was an ancient custom: the bones of martyrs were reburied beneath an altar—or rather, altars were built above the places where the bodies of martyrs lay buried. Prudentius teaches the same thing again in the following hymn, verse 189:

> “Placed beneath the everlasting altar,”

and in the Passion of Vincent, verse 517:

> “For it is placed beneath the shrine,”

and in *Hippolytus*, verse 169:

> “Beneath such coverings Hippolytus’ body is committed,
>
> beside which an altar dedicated to God has been placed.”

Even now this custom is observed at many altars, so that the body of some saint is placed beneath the altar. Since in former times altars were not usually erected unless the saints’ relics were placed beneath them, a priest still approaching the altar prays to the saints whose relics, he says, are here.

It should nevertheless be observed that the modern custom differs little from the ancient one. It is no longer permitted to place upon an altar the chest in which the body of a saint has been deposited and expose it to the veneration of the faithful, although some portions of the body may be placed above the altar in suitable reliquaries. See the prologue, chapter 2, no. 27.

Cardinal Baronius rightly infers this from the words of Eunapius, which he quotes there. Eunapius was a fierce enemy of the Christian religion under Julian the Apostate; Baronius discusses him under the year 389, no. 82:

> “The ancient observance must also be noted from Eunapius’ words: not only were the relics of martyrs enclosed beneath altars, but their principal limbs were also left outside, visible to all and to be worshiped on appointed days.”

213. Prudentius says that Eulalia was placed beneath God’s feet because above her stood the sacrament of the Eucharist or the sacrifice of the Mass was celebrated, as he explains more clearly in *Hippolytus*, at the place cited.

Saint Felix, the Roman pontiff who died in 274, is said by Anastasius the Librarian to have established that Masses should be celebrated above the tombs of martyrs. Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*, volume II of his works, p. 395:

> “The Roman bishop therefore acts wrongly who offers sacrifices to the Lord over the venerable bones of the dead Peter and Paul—which according to us are venerable bones, but according to you mere worthless dust—and considers their tombs the altars of Christ. And not only the bishops of one city but of the whole world are in error,”

and so forth.

Ambrose, letter 22, volume II of his works, concerning the relics of Saints Gervasius and Protasius:

> “Let the triumphant victims take their place where Christ is the victim: he upon the altar, who suffered for all; they beneath the altar, who were redeemed by his suffering.”

Some think that when pagans asked why Christians had no altars or temples, Minucius, Origen, Clement of Alexandria, Arnobius, and Lactantius answered that no altar could be dedicated to God more pleasing than the soul of a just person, because the slabs or covers beneath which the bodies of martyrs were buried served as altars for the earliest Christians.

I consider this more subtly devised than true. The pagans were asking about altars and temples such as they themselves possessed; Christians denied that they had such things, although they did have churches and perform sacred rites. They added that no temple was holier than a pure soul and no altar more pleasing, thereby indicating that inward religion was chiefly to be praised.

Whether the bodies of saints were formerly placed not only beneath an altar but also beneath an *ara*, since some distinguish between *ara* and *altare*, I shall discuss in the passage cited from the hymn of Saint Hippolytus.

Another question also arises: did Prudentius think that the souls of martyrs and saints rested beneath the altar, awaiting the blessed hope of the resurrection? Prudentius certainly did not hold that opinion, for at verse 169 he expressly stated:

> “His breath, rejoicing, claps its wings in the air.”

And in the poem on Vincent, after speaking of bones placed beneath a shrine, he says at verse 521:

> “Thus the body; but the very seat of God receives and contains it.”

Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca sancta*, book VI, cites the opinions of several Fathers who seem to interpret the words of Revelation 6, “I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been slain,” as denying that the souls of the saints enjoy the glory of the divine vision before the resurrection of the body. He also lists Prudentius, as though in the following hymn, “Placed beneath the everlasting altar,” he had placed the souls of martyrs beneath the altar.

But, to say nothing of the others, Prudentius does allude to the words of Revelation, yet in such a way that he repeatedly expresses the Catholic belief that the souls of the just are received into heaven before the resurrection of the body. He means only that the ashes of the saints are beneath the earthly altar, and that the custom of burying the bones of martyrs beneath the altar arose from the words of Revelation—a view held by many and not without probability. He also looks to God’s throne in heaven, beneath which the holy souls are found.]

215. *Propitiata*: appeased, I. — *Fovet*: cherishes, nourishes, I.

3. *Caesaraugustam*: one city named by Caesar Augustus, its founder, I.

4. *Res cui*, namely, “a matter entrusted to it,” I.]

[Note: [Col. 0357C]

215. The Mozarabic Breviary has, incorrectly, *Carmine propitio tali foveat* (“may it cherish with such an appeasing song”). Ruinart likewise has the erroneous *propitiata foret* (“would have been appeased”). After this hymn, Vatican B and Marietti place the hymn of Bishop Fructuosus, etc. Vatican A has *The Book of the Blessed Martyr Romanus*. The Alexandrian manuscript follows with the hymn of Saint Vincent, and after that the hymn of the eighteen martyrs. Weitz follows Vatican B and Marietti; the other printed editions, together with Aldus, retain the order we follow here. I find no sufficiently adequate reason for the great diversity among the manuscripts in the placement of the hymns of *The Crowns*.

1. I have given the inscription found in Vatican A, except that in it, as in most others, *in honore* (“in honor”) is read, as I said in the note on the preceding hymn.

Vatican B: “Here begins the hymn in honor of the Saragossan martyrs.”

Marietti: “Here begins the hymn in honor of the twenty-three Saragossan martyrs.”

Ratoldus: “Here begins the hymn in honor of the eighteen Saragossan martyrs.”

Aldus: “A song in praise of the eighteen holy Saragossan martyrs.”

Heinsius: “Hymn in honor of the eighteen holy Saragossan martyrs.”

In Vatican A it is placed after the Passion of Saint Vincent; in Vatican B and Marietti, after the Passion of the holy apostles Peter and Paul.

The title “In honor of the eighteen Saragossan martyrs” seems more accurate. The other martyrs who are mentioned appear to be introduced here as an episode: Vincent, Encratis, Caius, and Crementius. Together with the eighteen they make twenty-two; therefore I do not know why the Marietti manuscript has “In honor of the twenty-three.”

Of the eighteen Saragossan martyrs, the Roman Martyrology, on April 16, says:

> “At Saragossa in Spain, the birthday of the eighteen holy martyrs: Optatus, Lupersus, Successus, Martialis, Urbanus, Julia, Quinctilianus, Publius, Fronto, Felix, Caecilianus, Eventius, Primitivus, Apodemius, and four others, who are reported to have been called Saturnini. All of them were punished and put to death together under Dacian, governor of the Spains; their illustrious martyrdom Prudentius adorned in verse.”

The order of the names was taken from Prudentius, not from other older Acts. Prudentius had to arrange them in this way to accommodate the meter; nor could anyone easily claim that they happened by chance to be arranged in the same order in the older Acts.

The martyrdom of these holy martyrs occurred around the year 304, during the persecution of Maximian under the governor Dacian. Some assign their feast to April 15, others to April 16. Ruinart prints Prudentius’ hymn among the *Sincere Acts*, p. 516 of the Paris edition of 1689. The Bollandists had likewise copied it under April 16.

2. Rodriguez de Castro, in the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, says that Prudentius perhaps included all the tombs of the holy martyrs existing in the Saragossan district under the name of a single tomb, since Prudentius’ purpose was also to speak of other martyrs who were not buried at Saragossa. Thus Lucretius called the earth a common tomb.

I, however, think that Prudentius plainly speaks of one tomb existing at Saragossa, since he adds, “We call it the city of Saragossa, a place to which such greatness belongs.” I understand these eighteen martyrs to have been buried beneath one altar, which Prudentius rightly calls a tomb, as others call it a confession, a martyrial shrine, or a memorial of the martyrs. Compare verse 189 and following:

> “Placed beneath the everlasting altar.”

It should also be observed that Prudentius often uses *servare* (“to preserve”) of the relics of martyrs, as in the preceding hymn:

> “The venerable earth preserves in its lap,”

and again in this hymn, verse 191:

> “The crowd whom the creative mother of purple-clad men preserves.”

In *Hippolytus*, verse 173:

> “The tomb preserves the bones for the hope of the eternal Judge.”

The beginning and end of the hymn clearly show that Prudentius’ purpose is to praise the eighteen Saragossan martyrs, although, in praising Saragossa on an occasion drawn from this great number, he adds other martyrs as well.

4. Latinius has *res ubi* (“a place where”); *res cui* (“a matter to which”) is good and correct. Parrhasius says that Prudentius may be forgiven, but that it cannot be tolerated that *cui* should be made disyllabic and its final consonant changed into a vowel. What I said about this word in the prologue, nos. 209 and 212, note, applies here: Martial pronounced *cui* as a disyllable in precisely the same way.

6. Chamillard infers from this and other passages of Prudentius that our poet believed the earth would be utterly destroyed at the end of the world. To me it does not seem so clear that Prudentius held this view. His words, like other similar passages of sacred Scripture, can suitably be understood of a great transformation of the world.

Moreover, many think that after the resurrection heaven and earth, and the elements generally, will be established as wholly different from those that now exist. Most defend the view that the world will not be reduced entirely to nothingness but transformed into something better. See Calmet’s dissertation on the end and condition of the world after the judgment, before the Epistle of Paul to the Galatians.]

961 She looks upon these things and, having been appeased by song,

[215] cherishes her peoples.

IV. HYMN IN HONOR OF THE EIGHTEEN SARAGOSSAN MARTYRS

Our people preserves in a single tomb

[Col. 0358A] 962 the ashes of twice nine martyrs.

We call it the city of Saragossa,

a city to which such greatness belongs.

[5] The house, full of mighty angels,

does not fear the ruin of the fragile world.

[Col. 0359A] [Note: [Col. 0359A]

7. *Gestans*: while it bears, I.

9. *Cum*: when, I.

10. *Nube*: in a cloud, for we believe that he will come to judgment in the cloud in which he ascended to heaven. — *Rubente*: fiery, I., Marietti.

13. *Excitata*: raised up, lifting its head, I. — *Caput*: through the head, Marietti.

[Col. 0360A] 14. *Properanter*: swiftly, I.

16. *Canistris*: sarcophagi, I., Marietti.

17. *Afra*: African, I.

20. *Tresque coronas*: namely, of other martyrs. *Tres martyres*: that is, Faustus, Januarius, and Martialis, I. — *Tres martyres*, Marietti.]

[Note: [Col. 0359B]

9. The Mozarabic Breviary has, corruptly, *quem Dei dextram* (“whom the right hand of God”).

10. The Mozarabic Breviary has, erroneously, *rubentem* (“reddening”). See hymn 11 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 101 and following, with the commentary.

11. The Mozarabic Breviary has *posituros* (“about to place”), incorrectly. The description of God weighing good works in one pan and evil works in the other on the day of the final judgment may derive from Job 6:2: “Would that my sins, by which I have deserved wrath, and the calamity that I suffer, were weighed in the balance”; and from Daniel 5:27: “You have been weighed in the balance and found wanting.” See Mazochius, *Spicilegium Biblicum*, volume II, p. 285.

Furthermore, to indicate that justice is weighed out to each person with an equal balance, the Greeks use the old proverbial expression “to hold the scales,” mentioned by Eustathius in his commentary on book VII of the *Iliad*: “More upright toward justice than the balance.” Consult the notes of Elmenhorstius and Heraldus on Minucius’ words: “So that you may hold the balance of the most equitable judge and not lean inclined to either side.” Virgil imitated Homer in book XII, verse 723:

> “Jupiter himself holds two scales with balanced beam.”

13. In the Alexandrian manuscript this entire stanza was omitted; it was added in the margin by an old hand. It was also absent from the Thuaneus manuscript. Prudentius says that the head of the cities was raised up, or that their head was raised up, as in the hymn of Fructuosus on Tarraco:

> “It lifts its head, flashing with fires,”

and:

> “Where the head of our city is raised.”

15. Aldus, Tornesius, and some vulgate copies have *civitas omnis* (“every city”), which Gifanius says is not sufficiently Latin, in his discussion of the long *e*. The manuscripts have *civitas quaeque* (“each city”), so that the final *e* is long because of the following word beginning with *pr*; this is familiar in Prudentius and not at all objectionable. The Mozarabic Breviary has *civitas quoque* (“the city also”), incorrectly.

Teolius explains “precious gifts” as the native martyrs whom Saragossa will offer to Christ—eighteen of them. Teolius is still thinking of the homeland of Saint Laurence. Prudentius certainly means here the martyrs who are buried in the individual cities, especially those who are patrons of those cities, whether native to them or not. Nor is it clear that all eighteen Saragossan martyrs, individually and collectively, were born at Saragossa. On the contrary, it is certain that Felix, whom he assigns to Gerunda, and Cucufas, whom he assigns to Barcelona, were not born in Spain.

16. The glosses explain *canistris* as *sarcophagis* (“sarcophagi”). Prudentius may have had this in mind because gifts are commonly carried in baskets and some marble sarcophagi are carved in the shape of baskets.

17. Weitz, with Widmanstadius, writes *Kartago*, and notes *Chartago* from Hailsbrunner. He calls it African Carthage to distinguish it from New Carthage, which is also called Spartaria and is now Cartagena in Spain; another, more recent city of that name was founded in America.

Nebrissa says that Prudentius places only African Carthage among foreign cities, since all the others are in Spain. I do not see how Arelate and Narbo can be said to be in Spain at the time when Prudentius wrote, nor how Narbonese Gaul had yet been occupied by the Goths.

18. A hymn on Saint Cyprian is the thirteenth in this book; there Prudentius calls him “our love,” that is, a Spaniard. In Vatican B these verses are read as follows:

> “African Carthage will bring forth your bones,
>
> Cyprian, teacher with eloquent speech.”

19. Vatican A and Ratoldus have *Acisdum*. Prague has *Ascisclum*. Widmanstadius has *Asclisclum*. Egmondanus and Palatinus have *Aclisdum*. Others, with Aldus and several martyrologies, have *Acisclum*. The older manuscripts of Heinsius have *Aclisclum* or *Aclisdum*, except that Puteanus has *Aciscum*. In the Oxonian manuscript is *Ascisdum* for *Ascisclum*, as in the martyrology of Ado.

To Heinsius, *Acisclus* seems to be the genuine name of the martyr. *Acisclus* is formed from *Acisculus* by contraction, and some members of the Valerian family were called *Acisculi*, from a stonecutter’s tool. Philip of Torre, in *Ancient Monuments of Antium*, chapter 2, discusses at length the cognomen *Acisculus* of the Valerian family from the coins of that family, and suggests that our martyr may be assigned to the Valerian family. Mazochius confirms that this cannot at all be inferred from the title *Dedication beneath the ax*.

For *Zoellum*, Vatican A has *Zoelum*, and above it, in smaller letters, *Zolutum*. Ratoldus has *Zoelum*. The Marietti manuscript in the first hand and Vatican A have *Encellum*. Prague has *Enetellum*.

On Acisclus, the Roman Martyrology, November 17, says; on Zoelus or Zoilus, the same martyrology, June 27: “At Corduba, the holy martyrs Zoilus and eighteen others.” Saint Eulogius, in *Memorials of the Saints*, book II, chapter 6, mentions a church named after him. In the Mozarabic Breviary, on November 17, the office of Saint Acisclus and his companions is celebrated. In the prayers they are usually called Acisclus and Victoria, and sometimes Acisclus and his companions.

In the same Breviary, on June 27, the office of Saint Zoilus is celebrated with a proper hymn, composed here and there from verses taken from Prudentius’ present hymn and badly stitched together.

That Acisclus’ tomb existed at Corduba is also clear from Saint Isidore’s *Chronicle*, under the Spanish era 587, where he writes of Agila:

> “When he made war against the city of Corduba, and, in contempt of the Catholic religion, inflicted injury upon the most blessed martyr Acisclus, polluting the holy place of his tomb as a profaner with the blood of enemies and beasts of burden, he entered into battle against the citizens of Corduba and deserved fitting punishments, inflicted by the saints.”

[Col. 0360D] 20. Chamillard asks why Prudentius speaks of three crowns, since the Roman Martyrology makes it clear that nineteen others besides Zoilus were granted the palm of martyrdom.

He replies that in Surius’ Life of Saint Anastasia, the body of the martyr Chrysogonus was carried by the waves to the seashore, where Zoilus, a pious man and priest, was staying with Agape, Chionia, and Irene, sisters. Chrysogonus appeared to him in a dream and foretold that he would soon end his life for Christ, and likewise those three handmaids of Christ. Chamillard therefore concludes that these are the three crowns indicated by Prudentius.

The Bollandists, however, think that by the three crowns Victoria is meant: she saw as many crowns descend from heaven, and therefore joined herself as a third to those two. Iso says more accurately that the three martyrs are Faustus, Januarius, and Martialis.

Their feast is celebrated in the Mozarabic office on October 13. Gallandius, with Ruinart, understands Prudentius to mean these three, since they suffered at Corduba; Ruinart notes that in a manuscript of the Royal Library eight hundred years old the gloss is *martyres* (“martyrs”).

A Mass for these three Corduban martyrs is found in Leslie’s Mozarabic Missal, p. 387, on the fourth day before the Kalends of October. Ruinart published their Acts from four manuscript copies. The martyrologies disagree in assigning the date of their feast.]

25. *Strophio*: with an ornament or belt; *strophium* is a belt, from *stropha*, meaning “to turn,” I.

26. *Gemelli*: the two deacons, I., Marietti.

[Col. 0362A] 31. *Ambos*: the two, I.

32. *Quos veneramur*: namely, the martyrs mentioned above, Hemeterius and Celedonius, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0361A]

21. Weitzius thinks that Prudentius is alluding to a custom common in that age, by which virgins wore their names woven into necklaces; concerning this, see Aristenaetus, Book I, Letter 1, and Meursius, *Exercitationes criticae*, Part 2, Book II, chapter 16. Paschalius, *De coronis*, Book IX, chapter 11, observes that Prudentius recognized three gems in the diadem, not because only those gems were there, but because they first strike the eyes. He understands them to be the gems described by Capella: “For there were three gems at the forehead—lychnis, astrites, and ceraunus”—which I do not think Prudentius had in mind. Saint Leo the Great appears to have imitated Prudentius quite clearly in this passage, among other places, in Sermon 1 on Saints Peter and Paul: “The Church is not diminished by persecutions, but increased; and the Lord’s field is always clothed with a richer harvest, while the grains that fall singly are born again in multiplied abundance. Thus these two distinguished shoots of divine seed, Saints Peter and Paul, have grown into so vast a progeny that thousands of blessed martyrs bear witness to it. They surrounded our city, the place of the apostles’ triumphs, with purple and far-shining multitudes, and, as though by the honor of many gems joined together in a single diadem, crowned it.”

23. Ptolemy and the ancient monuments place Tarraco among the Cosetani, on the shore of the Mediterranean Sea. See Cellarius, *Geographia antiqua*, Book II, chapter 1. Chamillardus observes that Tarraconian wines were formerly highly valued, according to Martial, Book XIII: “Tarraco yielding only to Campanian wine.” Pliny and Silius Italicus confirm the same. It may also be added that those wines are still valued today—except that Spain now has so many wines of different kinds, held in the highest esteem everywhere, that many others must be preferred to those of Tarraco. One is prompted to wonder why the Romans either formerly ignored or despised those wines, or—or what I am more inclined to believe—why the Spaniards did not take greater care in cultivating their vineyards. For among the ancients Spanish wine is not mentioned nearly as often as other wines. Yet I see that Ovid prescribes its use for deceiving, soothing, or putting guards to sleep:

“Many a guard is deceived by abundant wine;  
let her be a grape gathered from a Spanish vine.”

Concerning Fructuosus and his companions, we have Hymn 6 of this book.

24. Paschalius says that *sutile vinclum* is a gem sewn onto a metal plate, by which the diadem is closed and fastened, just as by a clasp. In Virgil this is a golden clasp:

“A golden clasp fastens the purple garment.”

For Prudentius it is a jeweled clasp in the diadem, or a sewn fastening. Prudentius calls the stones “sewn” in *Cathemerinon* 7, verse 158, and calls the hyacinths “sewn” in *Hamartigenia*, verse 268: they are sewn into a crown or attached to a diadem.

25. Aldus, against the meter, has *hoc nomen gemmae*. Aldus, Weitzius, Giselinus, and the older editions read *illigatum est*, as do most of our manuscripts, Thuan., Noms., Ambr., Put., and Parrhasius. *Illigatae* is found in the more recent witnesses, and Heinsius rightly prefers it. Yet Saint Isidore had already read *illigatum est* in Book XIX, chapter 33 of the *Etymologies*. A *strophium* is a golden belt adorned with gems, as Cinna says: “Her nursing breasts girded with a *strophium*.” Prudentius likewise says:

“This name of the gem is fastened to the *strophium*.”

The first hemistich is from Catullus’ *Marriage of Peleus and Thetis*, but it may have been shared by him with Cinna, as Isidore’s annotator observes. Paschalius suspected the reading *Nomine hoc gemma est strophio illigata*. Nebrissensis conjectured *Hoc novae gemmae strophio illigatum est*. Yet the reading of the manuscripts proceeds correctly, whether one follows Heinsius or, as we have done, retains the older reading together with Saint Isidore.

27. Theolius: “the splendor burns”; the meter is corrupt because *et* has been omitted.

29. The Roman Martyrology, 1 August: “At Gerunda in Spain, the feast of Saint Felix the martyr, who, after various kinds of torture, was ordered by Datianus to be torn apart until he gave back to Christ his unconquered spirit.” In the Mozarabic Breviary his feast is celebrated on 1 August, and there is a trochaic hymn which I would readily attribute to Prudentius, were it not that some verses appear corrupted by the violence of time and the carelessness of copyists, as is known to have happened in other hymns inserted in the same breviary that certainly belong to Prudentius. I make the same judgment concerning several other hymns of the Mozarabic Breviary; perhaps someday I shall restore them to their proper author and original purity from manuscripts and conjectures.

The hymn of Saint Felix begins:

“God, fountain of everlasting life,  
light, origin of light,  
look upon the people singing  
the feast of the great martyr.”

You see the Prudentian style and the exact law of the meter. The latter is disturbed in the following verse:

“Receive the prayers of those who pray,  
accept the songs of praise,”

although this can be defended on the basis of the caesura. The author perhaps wrote: “Receive the prayers of those who pray to you; accept the songs of praise.”

Felix, a native of Caesarea in Mauretania, went as far as Gerunda, eager for martyrdom, as may be gathered from the hymn just cited and from Saint Eulogius, Book I of the *Memorial of the Martyrs*:

“For thus also the most blessed Felix, when he learned through trustworthy report of the persecution of the Catholics then taking place at Gerunda, a city of Spain bordering on Gaul, and learned that the Church of God there was being cruelly harassed by pagans, immediately abandoned the study of liberal letters, which he had been cultivating while residing at Caesarea in Mauretania. Crossing the sea with swift passage, he went to the aforesaid town, and there, as a devoted soldier of Christ, triumphantly completed the martyrdom that his homeland lacked.”

Concerning this Saint Felix, see Saint Gregory of Tours, Book I, chapter 92. Ruinartius had seen the acts of Saint Felix in several manuscripts, but thought them somewhat corrupted.

30. Gerunda, now Girona, is said to be a city in the territory of the Ausetani, formerly belonging to the Tarraconensian jurisdiction.

31. Vatican A and Mar. write *Galagurris*; Gis. in the text, and Cellarius, have *praestabit*. Our manuscripts and those of Heinsius, together with Aldus, read *gestabit*. Weitzius seems to have read *praestabit* in some of his copies. Gregory of Tours, Book I of *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 93: “The city of Calagurris in Spain bears the martyrs Hemeterius and Celedonius,” and so forth. He alludes to these verses of Prudentius, from whom he takes the eulogy of those martyrs. Parrhasius writes *Calaguris*, and the same form is found in other monuments, such as the fragment of Livy published first from rewritten, as they are called, very ancient parchment manuscripts of the Vatican Library and illustrated with notes by the distinguished Vitus M. Giovenazzius.

Livy’s words contribute greatly to determining the location of Calagurris:

“Having set out from there, through the territories of the Bursaones, Cascantini—so it should be read—and Graccuritani, after devastating everything and trampling down the crops, he came to Calagurris Nasica, a city allied with him. After crossing a river near the city by means of a bridge, he established his camp.”

From this passage Giovenazzius splendidly confirmed the view that Calagurris of the Vascones was the same city as Nasica, or Nassica, as others write. For since Livy says that Sertorius came from the territory of the Graccuritani to Calagurris and then crossed, by means of a bridge, a river near the city, it certainly follows that Calagurris surnamed Nasica was situated beyond the Ebro. Therefore, what remains except that the city on this side of the river was both Fibulariensis and so called? Graccuris is also a city of Vasconia according to Ptolemy.

32. I have found *veneratur* in one place. But most manuscripts and printed editions read *veneramur*.

You, mother of the pious, will offer Christ  
a beautiful diadem of three gems.

Tarraco: Fructuosus  
wove for it a sewn fastening.

[25] “This name of the gem is fastened to the *strophium*:”

Twin stones shine beside one another,  
and the equal splendor of the two burns  
with flashing fire.

The little city of Felix will display its glory,  
[30] rich in holy limbs, Gerunda,  
and our Calagurris will bear both,  
whom we venerate.

[Note: [Col. 0363A]

33. *Barcinon*, a city. *Cucufate*, a martyr. *Freta*, having trusted, I.

34. *Narbo*, a city, I.

35. *Arelas*, a city, I.

37. *Lusitanorum*: Lusitania is a region of India, said to have been named from the spindles (*fusi*) of fauns and satyrs, who came dancing to meet Father Liber, Vatican A. — From the homeland, Lusitania, a province. — *Caput*: which is the capital, I.

42. *Ferculum*: a sarcophagus, Mar.

43. *Complutum*: a city, a town. — *Juvabit*: it delights to bear, I.

44. *Duorum*: of two martyrs, I.

45. *Tingis*: a city of Cotia. — *Sua*: its own, I.

46. *Monumenta*: remembrances, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0363B]

33. Vatican B, Mar., Prag., Weitz., Widm., Hailsbr., Bong., and Sich. read *Barcilon*; Rat. and *Parcilon*; Fabr., *Barcinon*. The older manuscripts of Heinsius, together with Aldus, have *Barchinon*. One manuscript of Torrent. has *foeta* instead of *freta*. In the Mozarabic Breviary, on 30 July, the hymn begins: “Barchinon, flourishing in joyful Cucufas.” The body of Saint Cucufas was formerly preserved at Barcelona, or not far away in the monastery of Saint Cucufas, Sant Cugat del Vallès; it is now said to be kept in the Parisian monastery of Saint-Denis. Baronius, in the *Roman Martyrology*, page 309, under 25 July, prefers the hymn sung in the Toledan Breviary to the other published acts of this martyr. I think he means the hymn of the Mozarabic Breviary, where it is related that he came to Spain from the city of Scillium. The Bollandists say more about him under 25 July.

34. *Narbo* is also commonly used in the masculine gender. Concerning Saint Paul, the Roman Martyrology, 22 March, says: “At Narbonne in Gaul, the feast of Saint Paul, bishop and disciple of the apostles, who is said to have been Sergius Paulus the proconsul. Having been baptized by the blessed Apostle Paul, and being left at Narbonne as he was going to Spain, he was there endowed with episcopal dignity. Having diligently fulfilled the office of preaching, he departed to heaven, distinguished by miracles.” Compare the Bollandists.

35. Arelas, for us Arles, is a city situated in Narbonensian Gaul.

36. This Genesius is different from another of the same name, a mime and later a martyr. See Baronius on the Roman Martyrology, 8 Kalends of September, and Rosweydus in the notes to the homily on the martyrdom of Genesius of Arles, published under the name of Paulinus of Nola.

37. The gloss of Vatican A is not to be trusted.

38. Aldus: “The city of the worshiped and the ashes of the maiden”; Widm.: “The worshiped city and the ashes of the pious”; Urb.: “Worship the city, and the ashes of the maiden”; Vatican Q and Rat.: “The worshiped city, the ashes of the maiden”; Mar.: “The worshiped ashes of the maiden”; a later hand has *adoratos*, which is not objectionable. The more correct reading is that of Vatican A, B, Rat., Parrhasius, Alex., Gis., Weitz., Heinsius, and others: “The city worships the ashes of the maiden.” The subject is Eulalia, whom Emerita, the capital of Lusitania, honored, as we saw in Hymn 3.

39. Heinsius conjectures *obvia Christo*. Rat. and Mar. in the first hand have *radians*. *Rapiens* is better.

40. Prag. has *porrigit*, which is not as good.

41. The feast of Saints Justus and Pastor, the martyrs of Complutum, is celebrated on 6 August in the Mozarabic Office, with a hymn that I discussed in *Hymnodia Hispanica*. They say it was composed by Asturius, bishop of Toledo, who discovered their bodies. In his panegyric on the death of Celsus, Paulinus of Nola understands Justus and Pastor when, speaking of his little son, he says:

“We entrusted him to the city of Complutum,  
joined by the bond of a tomb to neighboring martyrs,  
so that from the nearby blood of the saints he might draw  
that with which he could cleanse our souls in the fire.”

43. Nebrissensis says that Complutum was a city of Tarraconensian Spain, perhaps Alcalá, for everyone thinks so. Cellarius, in *Geographia antiqua*, says that no one doubts Complutum was Alcalá de Henares. Nevertheless, several serious writers deny this; their arguments may be seen in *History of the Town of Guadalajara*, chapters 5 and 6, by Alfonso Núñez de Castro. I do not know whether anything opposes the common opinion that Complutum was Alcalá de Henares.

45. Prag. has *ingerit*; *ingeret* is better. Iso calls Tingis a city of Cotia, perhaps because in Mauretania, where Tingis—Tangier—is situated, there is a mountain called by that name. See the commentary on verse 216 of the *Apotheosis*. This Cassianus is different from the Cassianus whom Prudentius praises in a separate hymn of Book IX. The Roman Martyrology says: “At Tingis in Mauretania, the passion of Saint Cassianus the martyr, who, having long exercised the office of registrar, was finally inspired from heaven and judged it abhorrent to serve in the killing of Christians. Therefore, renouncing that office under Christian confession, he deserved to obtain the triumph of martyrdom, on the third day before the Nones of December, in the year of Christ 303.” Ruinartius publishes his genuine acts. Ado, under 3 December, calls Tingis a metropolis.

46. Weitzius writes *Massilum*, Hailsbr. *Massellum*, and above *Masilum*. Others have *Massylum*, that is, for *Massylorum*. Virgil speaks of these people in Book IV: “And the Massylian horsemen rush upon them.” There is no universal agreement about where this people was located. Some place them near the Barcaeans, others among the Gaetuli, and others to the west in Numidia. Prudentius favors the last view. Papebrochius, volume II, April, 16th day, page 409, conjectures that *Fessa*, or Fezza, should be read instead of *festa*, and understands Fez, the most renowned city of Tingitanian Mauretania. Wesselingius, in his notes on the *Ancient Roman Itinerary*, page 58, says that *festa* is best: “And who,” he asks, “among the ancients remembers Fessa, or rather Feza?” Bernardus Aldrete, Book III of *Spanish Antiquities*, chapters 7 and 8, shows that the city was first founded by the Saracens.

The meaning here could be: “Tingis will offer its Cassianus, who is the festive monument of the Massylian kings, because his memory is celebrated in Massylia”—to which Theolius alludes. Or, with Chamillardus: “Tingis, where the Massylian kings are committed to burial, will offer its Cassianus, who is now ashes but formerly compelled conquered peoples to the yoke of Christ.” Ruinartius says that it is uncertain what should be understood by the name *Massylum*, and that in the manuscript of Saint Michael it is read *Maxillum*. The passage is somewhat obscure to me, but the poet’s meaning is sufficiently clear.]

Barcelona, relying on its illustrious Cucufas,  
will rise, and beautiful through Paul, Narbo;  
and powerful Arles will possess you,  
holy Genesius.

The capital of the towns of Lusitania,  
seizing the ashes of the worshiped maiden,  
will carry her to meet Christ  
and [40] present her herself at the altar.

Complutum will gladly bear in its bosom  
the blood of Justus, to whom Pastor clings,  
a double offering and twin gift,  
the limbs of two martyrs.

[45] Tingis will offer its Cassianus,  
the festive monument of the Massylian kings:

48. *Juga*: faith, I.

49. *Paucae*: few cities, I. — That is, cities, Mar.

52. *Functae*: having used, I.

53. *Revehes*: you will bring back, I.

57. *Numerosiores*: more numerous, I.

61. *Parens orbis*: Carthage, Vatican A. — Carthage, mother. — *Poeni*: Africans, I.

69. *Umbrarum*: of demons, I.

77. *Inde*: namely, from Caesaraugusta, I.

78. *Clerus*: a body of clergy, that is, Caesaraugusta, I.

79. *Infulata*: adorned, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0365C]

49. Of the cities Prudentius has mentioned, Calagurris offers two martyrs, Tarraco three, and Corduba five. He says that Caesaraugusta is to be preferred for the number of its martyrs.

51. Vatican B has *Christo*; the others have *Christi*, which should be retained. Prudentius often uses *testes* for martyrs. Paulinus, *Natale* 13, verses 85–86: “Hence, whether to holy confessors, or to witnesses consecrated by suffering.” Muratorius reads this incorrectly as “or to consecrated witnesses.”

53. Rat. and Widm. have *revehis*.

54. Vatican A, Pal., Put., Oxon., Alt., and three manuscripts of Torrent. have *Christo*.

55. Aldus has *vertice*; *verticem* is better. Caesaraugusta is described as having its head crowned with yellow olive branches because it abounds in olives, which are a sign and honor of peace. See the epigram of Nebrissensis on his edition of Prudentius, preface, no. 107, in the note.

56. Heinsius, following the manuscripts, printed *honore*, but suspects that *honorae* should be read. Theolius has *honorae* in the text, but in the note says: “Thus Heinsius; almost all our copies have HONORE”; nor does Ruinartius read otherwise.

57. These more numerous troops of martyrs are understood to be the countless martyrs of Caesaraugusta, whose feast is celebrated on 3 November. The Mozarabic Breviary does not mention them. Someone might doubt whether Prudentius calls the eighteen martyrs of Caesaraugusta “more numerous troops” than the martyrs whom other cities were to offer to Christ. But what follows clearly distinguishes the matter and sufficiently demonstrates that the martyrs were countless. The Roman Martyrology, and those of Florus, Usuard, and Galesinius, celebrate them under the name “the countless martyrs.” Many confirm that they were called the “white mass” because their ashes, distinguished from those of others by their whiteness, were found gathered together. Ruinartius says that this miracle is absent from the older manuscripts.

61. The Mozarabic Breviary has *Penis* incorrectly instead of *Poeni*. Some have regarded the word *populosus* with suspicion. Apuleius, Solinus, Ammianus, Vegetius, and others used it; their passages are listed in the dictionaries.

66. Mar. has *excludit*, apparently.

68. Mar. has *orbe piato*, but above has *orbe glosso*, that is, *urbe*. Someone also corrected it there to *urbe piata*.

69. Parrhasius has the erroneous and metrically impossible *latetinctus horror*.

72. Mar. omits *est*; it was added by a later hand.

73. Nebrissensis rightly explains it as “the homeland of the martyrs,” where martyrs spring forth in excessive abundance.

75. He calls the martyrs “candidates” because of their white robes, concerning which see Revelation 7. I understand “the noble order clothed in the toga” in the same sense, rather than taking it to mean “the toga-clad people,” that is, the Romans. Below, at verse 191, he calls the same martyrs “purple nobles” because of their shed blood.

77. Riscus, volume XXX of *Hispania sacra*, infers from this that Vincentius was from Caesaraugusta, and rightly refutes Dodwell in Dissertation 19 on Cyprian and John Morinus, Book IX, chapter 19, *On the Administration of the Sacrament of Penance*, who deny that the persecution of Diocletian and Maximian reached the Spaniards. Some think that Vincentius was first crowned with martyrdom, then the eighteen martyrs, and finally the countless ones. But Prudentius’ verse 105 contradicts them: “He knew the famous palms won eightfold and tenfold in this temple.”

78. Vatican A, Fabr., Bong., and Gis. have *clerus hinc*, and in the following verse the same witnesses have *sacerdotum hinc*. Heinsius departed from Giselinus and printed *hic* in both places, yet did not notice the variation in the readings. Theolius agrees with Heinsius, although, on the authority of the two Vatican manuscripts, *hinc* may perhaps be better. Most copies, including Parrhasius, have *hic*.

79. Prag. has *sic sacerdotum*. Peveratus thinks that the Valerius who was bishop of Caesaraugusta, attended the Council of Elvira, and had Saint Vincent as his deacon was one and the same person, although Prudentius names several Valerii in the plural. Baronius held this view under the year 305. Chamillardus says at this passage: “Because the Church of Caesaraugusta recognizes only one bishop named Valerius, I follow this opinion, although Prudentius seems to indicate otherwise.” But since the Church of Caesaraugusta does not possess an exact and continuous catalogue of its bishops, there may have been two or more bishops named Valerius whom it does not now recognize. Thus this argument is too weak for us to abandon Prudentius’ opinion—or indeed the historical account. Whether it can certainly be argued from Prudentius’ words that he acknowledged several bishops named Valerius, I would not dare assert; but he certainly suggests that several bishops flourished in the Valerian family. See the preface, nos. 31, 32, and 58, and Baronius on the Roman Martyrology, 28 January.

It may be questioned whether Prudentius calls the house of the Valerii “adorned with the bishop’s fillet” also because in that family there was often a *flamen* among the Romans. On the coins of this family one sees the distinctive priestly cap in the excellent collection of Roman republican coins belonging to the distinguished Baron Alminusa Alexander Recuperus of Catania, who will soon publish a new system concerning the Roman *as*.]

Who compelled conquered peoples  
to the yokes of Christ.

To each city, a few, three, or two,  
perhaps some will be pleasing in groups of five,  
as witnesses of Christ, formerly having fulfilled  
their pledge by sacrifice.

[50] You, Caesaraugusta, bring back ten saints and eighteen,  
devoted to Christ,  
your summit bound with golden olive branches  
in honor of peace.

You alone prepared to meet the Lord  
more numerous troops of martyrs;  
you alone, rich in abundant devotion,  
enjoy the light.

Scarcely does populous Carthage,  
parent of the world, surpass you in this gift;  
scarcely does Rome herself, seated upon her throne,  
deserve to surpass you, our glory.

[65] At every gate, the sacred blood that was sacrificed  
drove out the hateful race of demons  
and repelled the black darkness  
from the purified city.

No terror of shadows remains hidden within:  
for the plague, driven out, flees the people.  
Christ dwells in every street;  
Christ is everywhere.

You would think it the homeland of martyrs,  
entitled to sacred crowns, from which a choir rises  
and stretches toward heaven, clothed in snow-white robes,  
the nobility of the toga.

From there, Vincentius, your palm arose;  
this clergy alone produced such a triumph.  
Here the bishop-adorned house of the Valerii

80. *Valeriorum*: they were bishops, I.

85. *Nostrum*: for *nostrorum*, I.

88. *Grandine*: persecution, I.

89. *Peregre*: in a foreign land, I.

91. *Futuri*: of the future, I.

99. *Prope littus*: a promontory of the sea, I.

100. *Sagunti*: of a city of Spain, a city faithful to the Romans, and feminine in gender, I.

101. *Palaestra*: wrestling, I. *Certamine*: contest, Mar.]

80. Parrhasius writes *Valleriorum*. In Florez, many Caesaraugustan and Calagurritan coins bearing the name Valerii appear on plate 4 and plate 9. The Bollandists, under 23 January, quote these words from the 1572 edition of the Breviary of Caesaraugusta: “Valerius, distinguished both for piety and learning, born at Caesaraugusta from the consular company of the Valerii, according to Prudentius.”

83. Nebrissensis understands *templum* to mean Christians, who are the temple of God. It is better understood as the church, or the city of Caesaraugusta, as below at verse 105: “He knew the famous palms won in this temple.”

85. Henschenius had read “Nor did any of our fury depart without praise”; but later, in the appendix to volume II of the April series, he corrected it to “Nor did any fury depart without praise of ours.” The meaning is that in all the persecutions at Caesaraugusta very many suffered martyrdom.

87. It is certain that the number of Christians increased as more were crowned with martyrdom, and most interpreters affirm that Prudentius intended this. But perhaps Prudentius only suggests here that at Caesaraugusta the number of martyrs in each persecution was always greater, and that more suffered in the final persecution than in the preceding ones.

88. Barthius, Book IV of the *Adversaria*, chapter 9, noted that *hail* is used for adverse fortune, as in Ovid: “When God has thundered.”

89. Aldus, Vatican P, Urb., and Gis. have *necatus* at the margin; others have *necandus*. Alex., Vatican P, Urb., Aldus, Gis., other editors, and the manuscripts have *peregre*. Gifanius restored *peregri* from an old book in the index to Lucretius under the word *colli*; Heinsius adopted it from his manuscripts, as did Theolius after Heinsius. Nevertheless, he cites all the Vatican manuscripts in support of *peregre*. I found *peregri* in Vatican Q and in the first hand of Alex. The verse proceeds correctly with *peregre* as well. Parrhasius has the distinctive reading *peregrine*.

90. Nebrissensis notes concerning the words “with a thin dew of blood”: “Perhaps he says this because there he learned how he ought to be a martyr when he saw his fellow citizens suffering martyrdom.” Chamillardus interprets it as follows: “Did you not, Vincentius, who were destined to die in another region, mark here, by the slight outpouring of your blood, what sufferings you would endure patiently when death approached?”

I shall relate a matter that may perhaps seem insignificant, but for which I have a very weighty authority, Saint Eugenius, bishop of Toledo. Before Saint Vincentius was led from Caesaraugusta to martyrdom, blood flowed from his nostrils, and this blood was reverently preserved at Caesaraugusta. Prudentius referred to this. Hear the epigram of Eugenius, *On the Basilica of Saint Vincentius at Caesaraugusta*, in volume I of the *Works of the Toledan Fathers*, page 23:

“Rejoice, your own glory, Vincentius, martyr and foster-son,  
our only hope, rejoice, your own glory.  
By your purple blood you earned the snow-white heaven,  
and purple you follow the snow-white Lamb.  
Holy suffering raised your name to the heavens;  
may holy suffering preserve your people.  
Here lies that blood which you give as a pledge for your body;  
here lies that blood of yours, flowing from your nostril.  
Here now is your tunic, which accomplishes what Christ’s fringe does;  
for by touch your tunic now saves.  
Here may vows obtain forgiveness of guilt and favor;  
may the one who seeks forgiveness here receive the highest joys.”

I am uncertain whether that blood flowed spontaneously, or whether it was drawn out by Vincentius himself or by someone striking him.

91. Bayerius, in his dissertation on Saint Lawrence, astutely suspected that *specimen futuri* should be read. It is easy to conjecture that this specimen was the stole of Saint Vincentius preserved at Caesaraugusta, a portion of which King Childebert of Gaul carried to Paris. See Ado in his *Chronicle* under the year 527, Gregory of Tours, Book III of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 29, and others.

93. Nebrissensis says that one may read *hunc colunt cives*. He explains it as meaning that Vincentius was born and instructed in the faith at Caesaraugusta. To me this seems to be the specimen of which I spoke shortly before: the blood poured from his nostrils, caught either in a tunic, a stole, or a small linen cloth. Ruinartius incorrectly reads *velut ipso*.

94. The Mozarabic Breviary, in the feast of Saint Zoilus, reads *suos et paternos* against the meter.

98. Gis. in the text, and Fabr. and Bong. in the first hand, have *sepulcro*.

99. Vatican A has *gloria*; read *gloriam*.

100. Vatican A has *Sagonti*; Egm., *Saginti*. Saguntus, now Morviedro, was founded, as is said, by people from Zacynthus, and perhaps in this sense it is called “high” or “ancient.” It is not far from Valentia, where Vincentius suffered. Perhaps it is called “on the shore” because its citizens resisted Hannibal fiercely, by whom the city was eventually destroyed. I do not approve the opinion of someone who thinks *forte* is an adverb, as though Prudentius were uncertain about the place of martyrdom. Prudentius calls Valentia a city unknown to Vincentius himself, that is, a foreign city. Livy wrote that Saguntum was about one thousand paces from the sea, Pliny three thousand; now it is farther away, which indicates that the sea has receded. See Florez, volume VIII of *Hispania sacra*, treatise 25, chapter 4.

101. Petrus Mantuanus interprets “in our wrestling ground” as referring to Valentia near Saguntum; many have already observed that this is absurd. Here *palaestra* means the Christian religion or warfare, as Nebrissensis explains, or the place of combat, as the gloss suggests. The following hymn, verse 213: “We have come to the wrestling ground of glory; hope and cruelty contend.” The word *our* clearly means that this wrestling ground is Caesaraugustan. In the Mozarabic Breviary this stanza is also applied to Saint Zoilus.]

Valeriorum.

Whenever a savage whirlwind  
shook the world battered by ancient storms,  
the rage grew more grievous  
and turned its wrath against this temple.

[85] No fury ever withdrew without praise of ours,  
nor without being empty of glorious blood.  
The number of martyrs always increased  
under every storm.

the sign of what was to come

This is what the citizens honor, as though their own soil

near the shore of lofty, perhaps ancient,  
Saguntum.

He is ours, and as a boy in our wrestling ground

[Note: [Col. 0369A]

105. *Templo*: namely, of Vincentius, I.

106. *Partas*: syncope. — *Palmas*: martyrs, Iso.

107. *Laureis*: crowns, Iso.

108. *Cucurrit*: he was crowned, I.

109. *Encrate*: a woman’s proper name. *Encrates* means “self-controlled” or “abstinent” in Greek. Hence the heretics called Encratites, who condemn God’s creatures. They say that it is not good to eat flesh or drink wine, I. — *Encrates* means “abstinent” in Latin. Hence the heretics called Encratites, who abstained from the foods created by God, Vatican A. — *Encrate* is a Greek name placed in the vocative, as *Socrate* is found in some places, Prag.

110. *Ossa virtutum*: that is, strong deeds; for she was alive when these words were written. — *Quibus efferati*: savage through the bones, I.

112. *Dedecorasti*: you cast down—perhaps “you disfigured”—I.

115. *Tu morti*: you alone remained alive after martyrdom, I.

117. *Seriem*: order, I.

118. *Carnis et caesae*: with the flesh cut away; it is mangled, I.

121. *Barbarus*: harsh, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0369B]

102. These three verses and the following one are absent from the Put. manuscript. In the Mozarabic Breviary, at the feast of Saint Zoilus, *fidei collybo* is corruptly read instead of *fideique olivo*. Since the poet had mentioned a wrestling ground, he appropriately adds “the olive oil of faith”: the oil of chrism is suggested, and the custom of athletes is indicated, since they were rubbed with oil. Peveratus observes that from this use of the word *oil* comes the sense of expenditure or expense incurred in fully learning some science or art, whence arose the proverb, “I have lost both oil and labor,” the metaphor being taken from athletes whom the trainers and instructors used to anoint.

103. Pal. incorrectly has *vinctus* instead of *unctus*. The Mozarabic Breviary, at the feast of Saint Zoilus, has *cunctis*, against the meter.

107. Aldus, Weitz., Egm., and Oxon. have *doctas*, which Heinsius does not dare condemn; that is, “he ran through learned palms.” Compare the commentary on verse 53 of Hymn 12. From the words “the native crowns” and from verse 191, “the throng which the creative mother of purple nobles preserves,” Riscus argues that these eighteen martyrs were natives of Caesaraugusta, and with considerable probability. The Bollandists likewise think so and therefore reject the opinion assigning those eighteen martyrs to Lusitania. Nevertheless, I shall not for that reason confidently affirm that every one of the eighteen martyrs, or of the countless martyrs, was born at Caesaraugusta. For Prudentius is satisfied that most of them originated in that city and that the rest lived there and obtained the palm of martyrdom there. Accordingly, at verse 175 and following, he says that the eighteen martyrs hold the rule of a single city by right of their tomb. This very effort by which he persuades us through many arguments that Vincentius ought to be counted among the people of Caesaraugusta proves that, in other cities, Prudentius chiefly praises the glory of the tomb and of martyrdom.

109. Aldus printed *Encrati*; he emended it to *Encratis*, which Heinsius did not notice, although he cites Put. and Ambr. together with Aldus in support of *Encrati*. Mar., Rat., Prag., Rot., Weitz., and others have *Encrate*; Gis., *Encrates*; Parrhasius, *Eucrate*; Oxon., *Encratia*; the Mozarabic Breviary, *Engrati*. Today this holy virgin is called Engracia in Spanish. Heinsius and the more recent editors have *Encrati*, which is also found in the Alex. manuscript. The Roman Martyrology, 16 Kalends of May: “At the same place, Caesaraugusta, the feast of Saint Encratis, virgin and martyr, who, with her body torn, her breast cut off, and her liver ripped out, nevertheless survived and was shut up in prison until her ulcerated body rotted.” This appears to have been taken from Prudentius’ hymn.

110. I do not agree with Iso, who says that Encratis was alive when these words were written. Compare the commentary on verse 137.

111. The Mozarabic Breviary has *spiritu*; read *spiritum*. Hailsbr. has *violata*; above, correctly, *violenta*. It appears to be taken from the words of the Gospel, Matthew 11:12: “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.”

113. The Mozarabic Breviary has *remeante vita*, and the same is also read there at the feast of Saint Zoilus, to whom this stanza is sung. From this and the following verse, the distinguished Bayerius proves that the eighteen martyrs were not natives of Caesaraugusta, as though none of the martyrs had lived at Caesaraugusta while alive. Riscus disagrees, because Prudentius only reports that Saint Encratis, surviving her tortures, lived at Caesaraugusta, something that did not happen with the other Caesaraugustan martyrs. I entirely agree with this.

115. The Mozarabic Breviary reads *solus* and *subprestes* incorrectly. At the feast of Saint Zoilus it likewise has *solus*, but *superstes*; and with regard to Saint Zoilus, *solus* is grammatically correct, though not metrically, whereas with regard to Saint Encratis it is correct neither metrically nor grammatically.

116. The Mozarabic Breviary has *Vivis in orbem*. Vatican A has *Vivis in urbe*, which is not objectionable.

117. Properly, *retexere* means to weave something again, to restore something undone. Thus Prudentius, in Hymn 10 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 16: “And I have rewoven the discordant fabrics.” Elsewhere it means “to recount,” as here and in Hymn 5 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 81: “What tongue could finally recount your praises, Christ?”

118. Aldus has *recentans*, which Nebrissensis interprets as “renewing,” and as though reopening a wound that had already closed into a scar. Others have *retentans*. The Mozarabic Breviary writes *retemtans*. I do not dislike *recentans*, for *recento* means “I make fresh,” as may be observed in Nonius and Aulus Gellius. It may perhaps also be derived from *cano*, as though *recanto* or *recino*. Iso’s gloss seems corrupt. Perhaps one should read *frustata est*, from *frusto*, “I cut into pieces,” a verb attributed by some to Florus.

119. The Mozarabic Breviary reads incorrectly: “The earth, telling what bitter furrows it has.”

Artfully trained in virtue and anointed  
with the olive oil of faith,  
he learned to subdue the dreadful enemy  
by his strength.

[105] He knew the famous palms won in this temple,  
eightfold and tenfold; taught by the native crowns,  
he ran the same course  
with the same glory.

Here, too, Encratis, lie  
the bones of your virtues,  
by which, a violent virgin,  
you cast down the savage spirit of the world.

No other martyr, with life remaining,  
was granted to inhabit our lands;  
you alone, surviving your own death,  
live in the world.

You live, and recount the sequence of your punishment,  
retaining the remnant of your mutilated flesh;  
you tell how dreadful wounds  
have deep and bitter furrows.

A savage torturer carved your entire side,

[Note: [Col. 0371A]

122. *Impensus*: it has been poured out, given, I.

125. *Minus*: that is, not, I.

126. *Abolens*: erasing, I.

128. *So*: I beg, sleep-inducing, I.

129. *Cruda*: fresh. — *Longum*: for a long time, long, I.

140. *Viva*: while living, Mar.

141. *Titulum*: this glory. — *Fruendum*: to be possessed, Iso.

143. *Juge*: for a long time, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0371B]

### 122

Gifanius teaches that *impensus* in earlier writers has the same meaning as “great” or “huge,” a usage he confirms by the authority of Lucretius and Caesar, and he adduces this verse of Prudentius. But here *sanguis impensus* means “blood poured out”; and because *impensus* can mean “poured out” or “lavished,” it sometimes has the force of “great” or “huge,” as in *impensa libido* (“excessive desire”) and *impensum pretium* (“a high price”).

### 123

Some write *abscissa* with double *s*, while older witnesses have *abscisa* with one. The Roman Martyrology perhaps took its wording from Prudentius: “Mamilla cut off, and the liver torn away.” In the basilica of the eighteen martyrs there was preserved a severed breast, as is clear from an epigram of Saint Eugenius, which I shall transcribe at verse 145.

### 125

Aldus, Oxford, Urbino: *peractae* without *est*. Ambrose, the older Heinsian manuscripts, Mariettus, Ratoldus, Prague, Bongarsius: *peractae est*. Vatican manuscripts A, B, P, Q, and Widmanstetter’s first hand: *peractum est*. In the Alexandrian manuscript there is *pa*, with the rest obscure. Weitzius cites Fabricius for *per ictum*, but he must have intended someone else, since Fabricius reads *peractum est*. The Mozarabic Breviary has the erroneous *peracta est*. Nebrissensis explains it as “not to be highly valued,” for *pretium* sometimes means “punishment.” Certainly it does not have that meaning here, since Prudentius says that the martyrs who died appear worthy of lesser praise than Encratis, who survived her martyrdom.

### 127

The Mozarabic Breviary has the faulty reading *concita membra* (“excited limbs”).

### 128

Aldus and the Mozarabic Breviary: *fine supremo* (“at the final end”). Most manuscripts, including the older ones: *soporo* (“sleep”). Both readings are recognized by Gis., Prague, the Palatine manuscript, Widmanstetter, Sichardus, and others.

### 129

Hailsbrunner: *te longe* (“you for a long time”). In some copies *tenuat* appears incorrectly in place of *tenuit*.

### 131

Vatican B, Ratoldus above, and Weitzius: *tenuit*; *tenuat* is better.

### 133

Saint Cyprian, Letter 53, concerning those overcome by torture:

> When those who desired to die were not permitted to be killed, but torture tore their exhausted bodies apart for as long as it could not overcome their faith, which is unconquerable, but could only weary their flesh, which is weak.

### 134

Egm., Hailsbrunner, and Vatican A in a later hand: *negaret* (“denied”). Vatican A in its first hand: *necaret* (“killed”); Prague: *necarit*. Both are wrong.

### 135

The Mozarabic Breviary incorrectly has *perempta* (“destroyed”).

### 137

For this reason some have perhaps thought that Prudentius was present at Encratis’s martyrdom. But Prudentius was not old enough to have seen it. Lupercius Leonardus, in a letter to Mariana, attacks Ambrosius Morales for having inferred from this verse that Prudentius claimed to have seen part of Encratis’s liver. Lupercius replies that Prudentius is speaking poetically, as though he had been present at the martyrdom. Bartholomaeus Leonardus, in another letter to Mariana, confirms the same argument; yet there seems to be an error, since Encratis suffered at least three years before Prudentius was born.

Nebrissensis interprets the passage roughly as follows: “We could have seen it, had we been present.” Moreover, in hymns of this kind Prudentius often speaks from the standpoint of a city or people that was, or might have been, present—as though these praises had been sung by the people not long after the martyr’s death.

I think that this part of the liver had been preserved in Prudentius’s time, and that his meaning is that the part of the liver which had long lain there could be seen and displayed. Compare the epigram of Saint Eugenius below, at verse 145.

### 138

Vatican A, as a variant reading: *late jacuisse* (“to have lain widely”). The Mozarabic Breviary, contrary to sense and meter, has *jacuisset* (“had lain”). Nebrissensis explains *pressis* as “pressed into the very inner recesses of the ribs,” so that the simple verb *premo* must be understood as the compound *imprimo*. In this way poets use *verto* for *everto* (“overturn”).

### 139

The Mozarabic Breviary, Sichardus, and some other vulgar copies have *pellens* (“driving away”). We should read *pallens* (“pale”), the proper epithet of death: “pale death” occurs everywhere. Interpreters take *tuorum* as an ellipsis for *tuorum membrorum* (“of your limbs”). But *tuorum* may be taken as neuter, standing substantivally, for “your things.” The meaning is that part of the liver torn away had died while Encratis herself still survived.

### 140

Mariettus also noted that the word seems to mean “still to be seen.”

### 141

Since the tombs of martyrs were called *tituli* from the epitaphs inscribed upon them—*titulus* meaning an inscription—the poet cleverly says that Christ gave Caesaraugusta this new *titulus*: it was to be a dedicated house, almost a shrine, and the martyrdom of the still-living martyr Encratis.

### 143

Aldus, Parrhasius, Ratoldus, Weitzius, all the Heinsian manuscripts, and most others: *juge viventis* (“of one continually living”). Gis., first edition, has the same; but in the second edition, in the text, he has *tumba*, along with Fabricius and Bongarsius above, Vatican B, Sichardus, and the obscure reading of Mariettus. Vatican A has *jure*; Vatican B, as a variant spelling, has *luge*. The true reading is *juge*.

Bivarius maintained that bishops formerly sometimes consecrated churches in honor of martyrs who were still alive after their torments. He adduces verse 113, “Of the martyrs none,” and this stanza. Riscus rightly refutes him, since Prudentius’s verses should not be understood in that way and there is no trace anywhere in antiquity of so absurd a practice.

In the spurious Marcus Maximus there is this verse concerning Saint Encratis:

> She saw temples dedicated to her while she still lived in the body.

But everyone can see that such a verse was fabricated by some recent impostor to strengthen the faulty interpretation of Prudentius’s verses.

Just as above Prudentius called Caesaraugusta a house full of angels and a temple, so here he calls it a house dedicated to the martyr who continually lives. Nevertheless, I shall not strongly object if someone infers from the epigram of Saint Eugenius, which will shortly be presented, that relics of Saint Encratis while she was still alive—namely, a cloak reddened with blood and a nipple severed with its fibers—were preserved in some basilica, or even that after Encratis’s death her house was consecrated as a church.

---

Poured-out blood, mangled limbs;

her breast, her nipple cut away, lay open

beside the very heart.

**[125]** Now the lesser price of death has been paid:

she, abolishing the venomous pains,

granted her limbs a swift

rest in final sleep.

A raw scar held you for a long time,

**[130]** and burning pain lingered long in your veins,

while a wasting fluid thinned

your rotting marrow.

**[Col. 0372A]** Although the jealous sword

of the persecutor denied

your final death,

**[135]** yet punishment crowns you, martyr,

as though you had been destroyed.

We saw part of the liver torn away,

lying far off beneath the pressure

of the claws;

pale death still possesses something

**[140]** of you, though you live.

Christ himself gave our Caesaraugusta this new title to enjoy:

that the house of one who lives continually

should be dedicated as a martyr-shrine.

---

### Notes

#### [Col. 0373A]

145. *Sacra*: “the city.” *Candidatis*: “made martyrs.”

147. *Conscriptum*: “appointed.”

148. *Pangere*: “to praise.”

149. *Ede*: “bring forth, compose, or sing.”

150. *Tibi*: “by you.” *Concinatur*: “may be sung.”

155. *Tulerit*: “may have endured.”

157. *Bella*: namely, the martyrs’ battles.

158. *Quantus tua*: namely, “how great the blood of your battles.”

161. *Posthinc*: “afterward.”

162. *Renuente*: “rejecting, refusing.”

163. *Saturninos*: because they were barbarian names; for that reason they could not be placed in the meter.

#### [Col. 0375B]

145. The eighteen martyrs are “three times six made martyrs,” whom above, at verse 74, he called “the snowy choir of toga-clad nobility.” Their names, says Teolius, he lists individually, except for the four Saturnini, whom he joins together because, as verse 162 says, the meter rejected them, since their first syllable is long.

I do not sufficiently understand whether, in Teolius’s view, the first syllable in the names omitted by Prudentius is long, and why the meter rejects them, or whether Teolius says that it is long in the name *Saturninos*. If this alone is intended, then Prudentius eventually named the Saturnini despite the meter’s refusal. The reason must therefore be explained why he passed over the particular names of the four Saturnini, if they had other names.

Some have denied that the four Saturnini were individually distinguished by their proper names. Yet they did have their own names, and Saint Eugenius gives them in his epigram concerning the Basilica of the Eighteen Saints, in volume I of the works of the Fathers of Toledo, page 22. I shall present it here:

> This temple is inhabited by a blessed crowd of the devout,  
> whose blessed lot has earned the heavenly realm.  
> Here one urn contains three times six men,  
> lofty in the summit of their sacred virtues.  
> They abandoned the smoky pleasures of the corrupt world  
> and gave their limbs to death for the faith of the Lord.  
> Here also lies the martyr Encratis, equal to them in merit,  
> separated from them by the lot of burial.  
> Her inexhaustible triumph the holy relics attest:  
> a cloak reddened with blood, a nipple severed with its fibers.  
> If you wish to know the names of the holy men,  
> the following list will quickly declare them to you.  
> But since the meter cannot contain them all together,  
> receive them arranged in different meters.  
> Quintilian is here, and Eventius, and Cassianus,  
> Felix, Lupercus, Januarius, and Julius,  
> Urbanus, Apodemius, then Primitivus,  
> Optatus, Publius, and Caecilianus.  
> Here are Successus and Matutinus.  
> Here are Faustus, Fronto, and afterward Martialis.  
> May this powerful crowd grant you prosperity, reader,  
> and may this powerful crowd grant you pardon.

In the margin these variant readings are indicated: *magnorum* (“of the great”) for *sanctorum* (“of the saints”), and *Evotius* for *Eventius*. The names of the Saturnini omitted by Prudentius are Cassianus, Januarius, Matutinus, and Faustus. Of these, Faustus is a highly suitable name for the Sapphic meter; Cassianus can be fitted into it no less than Martialis and Primitivus. Januarius and Matutinus are less easy, but can nevertheless be made to sound in the same poetic form.

146. Aldus writes *optato et luperco*, as though these were not proper names. The error is clear in the gloss of Mariettus: *luperco, sacerdote* (“Lupercus, a priest”). Ambrose writes *et Taepecco*; the Palatine manuscript, *Obtato*; Parrhasius and Nepaeus. The name Lupercus is mentioned more than once on the coins of Caesaraugusta in Florez. Peveratus notes, on the authority of Baronius, that Lupercus suffered martyrdom in Novempopulania, and, on the authority of Scaliger, that he suffered under Decius. Scaliger cites certain old lives of the martyrs of Aquitania. But that Lupercus must be different from ours is proved by the Bollandists under 28 June.

147. Earlier, at verse 75, he called the martyrs of Caesaraugusta “toga-clad nobility”; now he calls them the “enrolled senate.” In his hymn to Laurence, at verse 560, he likewise called Laurence “the perpetual consul.”

151. In editions and most manuscripts, including the Roman Martyrologies, *Juliam* is also read; but *Julium* must be restored from very ancient local monuments, namely the epigram of Eugenius, the Acts attributed to Saint Braulio, and the Mozarabic Breviary. Usuard, Ado, a manuscript of Saint Michael preserved by Ruinart, and one Vatican manuscript cited by Teoli agree. Widmanstetter has *resonat* instead of *resonet*.

152. Prague: *Quintilianam*.

153. Prague, the Mozarabic Breviary, Fabricius, Gis., Vatican A and B, and others have *pangat* (“may strike up”); Heinsius, following three manuscripts and Aldus, has *pandat* (“may unfold”), as in Valerius Flaccus at the beginning of his work:

> May your offspring, Idume, unfold the story—  
> for it can—of the brother blackened with Solymian dust.

Mariettus too, and Ratoldus in his old hand, have *pandat*.

157. The Mozarabic Breviary, Ratoldus, Vatican B, Widmanstetter’s first hand, Mariettus, Thuanus, and Noms.: *Euvoti*; Vatican A and Prague: *Evanti*; Put.: *Evovoti*; Alt., Weitzius, and the manuscript of Saint Michael preserved by Ruinart: *Euvanti*; Ambrose: *Eunoti*; Bongarsius and Sichardus: *Heuvanti*. Aldus, most martyrologies, and many manuscripts: *Eventi*. Parrhasius: *Eugori*. Rottus and one Torrentian manuscript: *Evoti*.

Heinsius vigorously defends *Evoti* as preferable to the others, adducing evidence from a very old copy of Usuard’s Martyrology, closer in date to Usuard’s own age, which was preserved in Paris at Saint-Germain. There the names of the eighteen martyrs are listed in the same manner in which we said that Eugenius describes them, except that it gives the name Evotus, not Eventius.

He also cites the oldest Martyrology of Ado in the same library, Ado’s Martyrology edited by Rosweyde, Usuard’s Martyrology written in a very old hand in the Bigotian Library, and an edition of Usuard prepared in Paris by Jean Chapelle, cantor of the College of Navarre, in 1490. On the basis of these witnesses, Heinsius orders Eventius henceforth to be expelled from the martyrologies. I do not yet accept this judgment, since so many very ancient monuments stand against it. More recent scholars, including Gallandius together with Ruinart and Papebrochius, give *Evoti*.

159. Aldus, Sichardus, and some vulgar copies: *cum tuos* (“with your own”).

163. I explained in the prolegomena, no. 211, why the name *Saturnini* is rejected by the Sapphic meter. Iso likewise thought that these were barbarian names, which is shown to be false by the epigram of Saint Eugenius above, at verse 145, and by the Acts bearing the name of Saint Braulio.

In the Spanish work of the most learned Florez, *On Coins*, the name Saturninus appears among the coins of Calagurris. It should be noted that the Roman Martyrology reports this from Prudentius: “and four others who are said to have been called Saturnini.” Usuard seems to have taken the four proper names from Eugenius or Braulio.

Nevertheless, I ask why Prudentius should summon ancient antiquity as a witness for the common name Saturnini, if these martyrs received their crowns at the beginning of the fourth century. Elsewhere too he speaks in much the same way: he calls a time that has already passed, although not very distant, “antiquity.”

---

The martyr’s name would have been.

**[145]** Therefore, three times six sacred martyrs,

rich in Optatus and likewise in Lupercus,

go on, and with psalms compose

the enrolled senate appointed for yourself.

Bring forth Successus; sing of Martialis;

**[150]** let Urbanus’s death be sung for you;

let song resound for Julius,

and likewise for Quintilianus.

Let the choir strike up Publius,

and recount what kind of trophy

**[155]** belonged to Fronto,

what good Felix endured,

what fierce Caecilianus endured.

How great was the blood, Eventius,

that stained your battles;

how great the blood, Primitivus,

**[160]** that stained yours;

and may praise, Apodemius,

still living, recall your triumphs.

Four men remain thereafter,

whose name must be exalted,

though the meter refuses it:

those whom it records as having been called

**[Col. 0375A] Saturnini.

---
