#### [Col. 0376B]

166. *Parvi facit*: “makes little of, despises.”

168. *Rudis*: “new.” *Indocta*: “unlearned.”

171. *Explicandus*: “to be declared, pronounced.”

173. *Recolet*: “may count.”

176. *Jure*: “by law.”

177. *Ad antiquum numerum*: “to the ancient number,” seventeen—or perhaps eighteen.

178. *Specimen puellae*: “the beauty of the girl,” Encratis.

179. *Sanguis*: “lineage.”

180. *Fons*: “origin.”

181. *Silendi*: namely, “you must be silent.”

183. *Secundo*: “prosperous.”

184. *Agone*: “contest, struggle.”

189. *Sub altari*: “beneath the hidden place of God.”

191. *Creatrix*: “mother, parent.”

#### [Col. 0375B]

165. It is clear from this that Prudentius omitted none of the martyrs’ names because the name conflicted with the meter. Rather, the word *Saturninos* was placed contrary to the laws of the poem. He calls the names “golden,” as at the beginning of Hymn 1 of the *Peristephanon*: “the golden letters that Christ inscribed there.”

167. Aldus has *otiosa* (“idle”). Sichardus restored *vitiosa* (“faulty”), supported by the manuscripts and by the rules of the poem; Parrhasius had already printed this reading.

168. Aldus: *haec rudis* (“this unlearned”); read *nec rudis* (“nor unlearned”).

169. Egmondanus: *modus adnotator*.

171. Mariettus, Prague, Ratoldus, and Heinsius with his witnesses, except Oxford, Sichardus, and Gis.: *explicandus*. Parrhasius and others: *explicandus*. Aldus, Oxford, and some other manuscripts: *explicandas*. Egmondanus and Hailsbrunner: *explicandos* in Weitzius.

For this book of life, see the Apocalypse of John, chapters 3, 20, and 21. Fortunatus, book VIII, poem 4:

> Happy are those whose fixed names, through Christ’s love,  
> are granted to live forever in the book.

174. Prudentius is speaking of the final day of judgment and of the angels who will separate the wicked from among the righteous. Chamillardus understands the angel to be the guardian angel of the church of Caesaraugusta, for the holy Fathers teach that angels are present not only with peoples and nations, but much more with churches and oratories where Christian worship is celebrated. I do not object; and perhaps for this reason Prudentius said at verse 5 that Caesaraugusta was “a house full of mighty angels.”

176. Prudentius clearly gives the martyrs’ right to burial precedence over the right of their fatherland.

177. Aldus, Parrhasius, Vatican B, Mariettus, and Weitzius: *trahentur* (“will be drawn”). Vatican A in a later hand: *tracentur*, incorrectly. Giselinus printed *trahetur* (“will be drawn,” singular), and Heinsius followed him without noting the manuscript variants. More recent scholars usually copy Heinsius without examination.

Riscus argues from this verse that Saint Encratis’s martyrdom occurred later than that of the eighteen martyrs of Caesaraugusta. But since Prudentius joins Vincentius to them, whose martyrdom is narrated earlier than Encratis’s in the Acts of Braulio, the argument drawn from this hymn is indeed probable, but not altogether certain. Let others judge how much confidence the Acts attributed to Braulio deserve.

179. Put. and Oxford, as a variant reading: *Tuque, Vincenti*. Vatican P has the erroneous *morse Vincenti*.

180. Parrhasius: *Pons et honoris* (“the bridge and honor”); in the corrected variant apparatus: *fons* (“source”).

181. Aldus writes *Gagio*; Weitzius and Ratoldus, *Gaio*; most have *Caio*. The following eight verses are absent from Put. Salmasius likewise testified that they were absent from the Tilian manuscript.

The Roman Martyrology, on 16 April, clearly derives the following from these verses of Prudentius: “Caius and Crementius, having confessed a second time and persevering in the faith, tasted the cup of martyrdom on 16 April in the year 303.” The Bollandists suspect that the first contest occurred under the governor Rufinus and the second under Datianus.

182. Some vulgar copies, contrary to meter and sense, have *quibus incrementum* (“for whom increase”).

183. That is what the Roman Martyrology means by “having confessed a second time.” I wonder, however, whether Prudentius may not rather call the second contest of praise a confession, since the first and principal contest is martyrdom. Caius and Crementius received an unbloody distinction through confession, which was a second and less glorious contest, or struggle, of praise.

185. In former times *confessors* were called those who confessed Christ before tyrants but did not obtain the martyr’s palm. Saint Paulinus, *Natale* 13, on Saint Felix, verse 94:

> Having already fought the battles of confession,  
> but consecrated by an unbloody end.

187. Aldus: *leniter* (“gently”); the meter requires *leviter* (“lightly”). Riscus thinks that these verses do not exclude martyrdom but indicate that the death was less bitter. I do not judge so. The expressions “unbloody distinction” and “both confessed” signify confessors, not martyrs. In my opinion, the same applies to the second contest of praise.

189. There is frequent mention of the bodies of martyrs buried beneath an altar. Here, however, the gloss of Mariettus should be noted. The altar is called “everlasting,” as in Saint Paulinus, Letter 12 to Severus: “The holy bones rest beneath eternal altars.” This is because Christ is priest forever, and our altars will never fail.

190. The Mozarabic Breviary has the erroneous *lapsisque nostris* (“and for our fallen ones”). Ambrose and Parrhasius: *precantur* (“they pray”).

191. Whether it can be certainly inferred from this passage that Caesaraugusta alone was the birthplace of all eighteen martyrs, see the commentary on verse 107.

---

Ancient antiquity.

**[165]** Love of golden names

makes little of the laws of the poem,

and concern for expression regarding the saints

is never faulty or unlearned.

The method is full of art:

to recite before Christ the forms

of the names inscribed in heaven’s book,

which must be opened at the proper time.

Then an angel will recall eight and ten saints

before the Father and the Son—

those who by right of burial

possess the governance of a single city.

Indeed, to the ancient number will be drawn

the girl still alive after the trial of punishment,

and the death of Vincentius,

whose blood is hence a source of honor.

Add Caius—he must not be passed over—

and you, Crementius:

for them it happened to bear

an unbloody distinction from a second contest of praise.

Both confessed the Lord;

they stood firmly against the roar of the tyrants.

Both lightly tasted

the savor of martyrdom.

This crowd, placed beneath an everlasting altar,

prays for pardon for our lapses—

the crowd which the mother of the nobles preserves.

193. *Date*: “allow, permit.”

194. *Sulcos*: “letters.” *Epitaphia*: “epitaphs.”

197. *Generosa*: “noble.”

1. *Prospera*: “bring prosperity.”

193. The Palatine manuscript has *hos pio*. On the verb *date*, consult the commentary on verse 594 of the *Apotheosis*. It means the same as *age* (“do, perform”).

194. Nebrissensis and Cellarius interpret the passage as meaning that the hope of resurrection lies hidden in the ashes. It is clearer—and this also seemed right to Teoli—that Prudentius hoped for forgiveness of sins through the intercession of the martyrs whose ashes were covered by those marble slabs.

195. The Mozarabic Breviary and Parrhasius have *ut absolvat* (“so that it may release”), with *spes* understood; this is less satisfactory.

196. Alexandria, first hand: *vincla eorum* (“their bonds”), incorrectly.

197. The Mozarabic Breviary wrongly has *te toga* (“you, robe”). Parrhasius corruptly reads:

199. The Mozarabic Breviary: *resurgentis* (“of the one rising”); read *resurgentes animas* (“the souls rising again”).

200. Instead of this verse, Prague has the following words:

> If you seek all these things,

Mariettus comments: “I do not know what this means.” Nor do I think it is anything other than the error of a careless or incompetent copyist.

In Vatican A, after this hymn follows “A Hymn in Honor of the Most Blessed Martyrs Fructuosus the Bishop, Augurius, and Eulogius.” In Vatican B and Mariettus, “The Passion of Saint Agnes.”

Most manuscripts agree on this title. In some of them this hymn is placed after Hymn 1, as I said at its conclusion. Fabricius has “Hymn V, to the Divine Vincentius, Martyr of Caesaraugusta.” Aldus: “An Ode in Praise of Saint Vincentius the Martyr.”

In a very old manuscript of the church of Velletri, mentioned in the note to Prolegomena no. 212, there is a hymn concerning Saint Vincentius. Since I believe it has not yet been published, I shall not hesitate to transcribe it here:

> A lofty day, bright to all the faithful,  
> is honored throughout the ages,  
> duly dedicated to the martyr of Christ, Vincentius;  
> on whose birthday we today offer our deserved praises.  
> Once you shone conspicuously, Levite,  
> flourishing beneath Valerius with a twofold doctrine.  
> Burning with divine love, you boldly trampled  
> the slippery pleasures of the world, a steadfast athlete.  
> You despised the savage kinds of punishment;  
> with serene heart you laughed at chains,  
> blows, rages, torches, fetters, claws,  
> and the grate.  
> The black prison did not frighten you,  
> nor any cruelty of the torturer,  
> nor the blazing machine of iron . . . . .  
> You fearlessly endured the rough fragments  
> of fired clay thrust into the flames.  
> Soon enclosed by heavenly wedges,  
> you happily sang mystical songs.  
> Wonderful organs sounded,  
> resounding together with measured voices.  
> Having conquered your enemies as victor, you saw  
> the Victor close at hand;  
> you sang with the choir of angels  
> in a ringing voice . . . . .  
> Hail, unconquered soldier!  
> Having laid aside your perishable burden,  
> may you bind us to the flowering citadel of heaven.  
> After the many punishments of torment  
> had been happily completed and overcome,  
> you entered the starry heavens.  
> Crowned with a shining robe,  
> following the Lamb among gleaming lilies,  
> you, the combatant, now dance in triumph.  
> Now, now, holy soul, pour forth pious prayers  
> for our foul crime with diligent prayer.  
> Cherish, O martyr, your undeserving servants,  
> driving away guilt and granting every blessing.  
> May we rejoice with you in coeternal glory,  
> singing Alleluia.

Where the dots appear, the manuscript records, as variant readings, *primo loco teterrima trusus pelea* and, in the second place, *ter collega*; I do not understand either of these. In other places it is easier to recognize that an error lies beneath the text than to discover the true reading; nor is it worth the effort to investigate it.

I presented Saint Eugenius’s epigram concerning the Basilica of Saint Vincentius in the hymn above, at verse 90. In Prudentius’s hymn there is no mention of Saint Vincentius’s homeland, nor is the town in which he suffered named, although at verse 556 he speaks, as often elsewhere, in the name of the people: “We kiss the little bed,” and at verse 563, “If we lie prostrate amid the joy of your footprints.”

At verse 333 he calls the place where Vincentius suffered a town: “The whole town gathers.” From the Acts preserved by Ruinart and the Bollandists, it is clear that this was Valentia near the coast of Saguntum.

That this hymn was composed to be sung on Saint Vincentius’s death day is clearly shown by the first and second stanzas. Ruinart believes that Prudentius composed most of the hymn from ancient Acts that he himself publishes. This is quite plausible, since Prudentius’s hymn sometimes agrees even in wording with the Acts, and the Acts seem to be older, perhaps composed immediately after the persecution of Diocletian. That they were read in churches is evident from the sermons of Saint Augustine.

Nevertheless, there are certain conjectures that lead us to believe that the Acts now extant were composed after Prudentius. Ruinart has more concerning the cult of Saint Vincentius, especially in Gaul, and we too made some observations in the notes to the *Hispanic Hymnody*. See also volume V of the *Acts of the Saints* of the Benedictine order, and Florez, volume VIII of *Sacred Spain*, treatise 25, chapter 7.

Nicolaus Antonius, *Bibliotheca Hispana*, volume II, page 109, praises an unpublished dissertation by Michael John Vimbodinus and Queralt concerning the translation of the sacred body of Vincentius, the Spanish Levite and martyr.

In Boldetti, book I, chapter 39, of the *Observations*, there is an ancient monument copied from the cemetery of Callixtus, in which the holy martyrs Vincentius, Agnes, and Poltus—Hippolytus—are represented in glass.

4. The sentence is taken from 2 Timothy 2:5: “For one who competes in the contest will not be crowned unless he has competed lawfully.” Although the poet perhaps did not intend this, it should be noted that *tibi vincenti* can mean both “to you who conquer” and “to you, Vincentius.” I have no doubt that Prudentius deliberately applied Vincentius’s name to the crown given to the one who conquers. Paschalius, *On Crowns*, book I, chapter 6, page 19, discusses at length the crown that is the reward of martyrdom.

10. Aldus, Weitzius with his witnesses, most of the Heinsian manuscripts, and all the Vatican manuscripts except Alexandria: *colluces* or *conluces*. Put., Alexandria in its first hand, the Cauch manuscript, and the Graevian papers: *collucis*. Gifanius reads *colluces* and says that Prudentius often shortens *e*, as in *fames*. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book IV, chapter 9, thinks that *colluces* is too gross an error to be allowed to the poet, and therefore conjecturally corrects it to *Luces coinsigni stola*. Giselinus likewise, to avoid the same difficulty, printed *Luces in insigni stola*. Why Barthius did not notice this, although he had elsewhere worked through Giselinus’s commentaries, is unclear.

But since many distinguished manuscripts have *collucis*, and there are many verbs of this kind belonging to the second and third conjugations, of which Priscian treats in book X, and since Prudentius observed the same usage in *percenseo* and *extorqueo*, *collucis* must unquestionably be read.

Purple-clad.

With pious tears may we, allow us,

wash the furrows of the marble slabs

beneath which is covered

the hope that will release

the bonds of my restraints.

Spread yourself wholly, noble city,

with me over the holy tombs;

then, when the souls and limbs

rise again,

may you follow them all.

## V. Hymn: The Passion of Saint Vincentius the Martyr

**[Col. 0378A]**

Blessed martyr, make prosperous

your triumphal day,

on which the reward of blood,

a crown, is given to you,

Vincentius.

**[5]** This day lifted you from the darkness of the world

to heaven,

with the torturer defeated

and the judge defeated,

and restored you rejoicing

to Christ.

Now, as a companion of the angels,

you shine in a distinguished robe.

25. Put.: *Nazoreni*. For *assistite* one might conjecture *absistite*, as though meaning “abandon your religion.” Thus *absistere bello* (“to desist from war”), *absistere incoepto* (“to desist from an undertaking”), and simply in Virgil, *Aeneid* I, 196: “nor does he desist beforehand.”

Christians were formerly called *Nazaraei* or *Nazareni* insultingly by pagans and Jews. On this name, see the many writers on Christian antiquities, Mamachi, Bingham, and others.

In the gloss, read *Antiochiam*, not *Alexandriam*. Perhaps *receptum* should also be read instead of *repertum*, since the writing is ambiguous. But *repertum* is satisfactory. In the other words, understand *factus est* (“was made”), or correct it to *fuit* (“was”).

26. Vatican B corruptly has *rudumque*.

27. Giselinus admits that all printed books have *haec saxa* (“these stones”); he says nothing about the manuscripts, in which the same reading is found. Nevertheless, he reads *haec sacra* (“these sacred rites”), as below at verses 105 and following:

> Let the rites of Tarpeia be trampled by you alone, stubborn one?

For, he adds, Datianus would not admit that he worshipped stones instead of the divinities represented by the stones.

Yet the true reading is *saxa*, stones in which the pagans thought divinity dwelt, as can be inferred from Vincentius’s reply and as I have shown more fully in the commentary on Hymn 11 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 35. Nor would it be appropriate to say that sacred rites are appeased by smoke and sacrifice. The pagans worshipped stones because they believed spirits lived within them. See verse 77.

30. Saint Isidore, *Etymologies* VII, chapter 12, is relevant:

> Levites were named from their founder: for the Levites arose from Levi, and through them the ministries of the mystical sacrament were fulfilled in the temple of God. In Greek they are called *diakoni*, in Latin *ministri*, “ministers,” because just as consecration belongs to the priest, so the administration of the mystery belongs to the deacon.

32. Among the Spaniards the same practice seems to have prevailed as in the Roman Church concerning the number of seven deacons, which the apostles established when they chose deacons in Acts, chapter 6.

As to why they are called “milk-white columns,” Iso recalls the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; Chamillardus, the innocence and chastity with which they ought to have been endowed, and the fact that they then supported the Church as though they were its columns.

I think Prudentius alludes to the robe mentioned above and to the custom of standing before the altar. Canon 4 of the Council of Barcelona says: “Let a deacon not sit in the company of a priest.” Chapter 60 of Martin of Braga’s collection says: “A deacon may not sit before a priest unless by the priest’s command.” See verse 38 of the hymn to Saint Laurence: “Those who stand close beside the altar.”

35. The Acts read:

> For those whom you order us to acknowledge as gods are wooden and stone idols. You are their witness, and may you, as pontiff of the dead, become dead among the dead.

Here the agreement between the Acts and Prudentius is clearly visible.

37. In the prolegomena, chapter 22, I set out the conjecture of the distinguished Giovenazzi: the reading should be:

> We shall confess, Datianus,  
> the Father, author of light,  
> who alone is the true God,  
> and Christ his Son.

He preserves this conjecture, supported by many weighty arguments drawn from theology and ecclesiastical antiquity, in his manuscript commentary on Saint Hilary’s hymn, “The throng of brothers dedicates a hymn,” which he has long owed to the wishes and benefit of learned readers.

39. Ratoldus: *qui est solus* (“who alone is”).

In the Acts:

> We profess that we are worshipers of the Christian religion, and servants and witnesses of the one true God who endures forever.

40. Ratoldus: *fatebimur* (“we shall confess”), contrary to the meter. The memory of this Datianus appears in a Spanish inscription in Gruter, page 199. Datianus, governor of the Spanish provinces, evidently ordered a stone to be placed as a boundary between the Eborenses and the Pacenses under the emperors Diocletian and Maximian Herculius, as is explained more fully at the beginning of the inscription. It then reads:

> BOUNDARY BETWEEN THE PACENSES AND THE EBORENSES,  
> UNDER THE CARE OF P. DATIANUS,  
> VIR PERFECTISSIMUS, GOVERNOR. H. H.

had washed in streams of blood.

When the attendant of the idol,

girded with dark laws,

**[15]** compelled you by sword and chains

to sacrifice to the gods of the nations,

he had first poured forth

soft words, gently persuading you:

**[20]** it intends to snatch away,

but first plays with it.

has decreed that all must serve

the minister of God’s altar,

one of its seven milk-white columns:

**[35]** May you, dead among the dead,

### 50.

Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XXV, chapter 7, reads these verses as follows:

> Now an altar of turf, to be entreated with incense,  
> must now be entreated by you;  
> or delay must be paid for with blood.

He understands an altar made of turf. Burmann, in the *Anthology*, vol. I, p. 734, dislikes this emendation, which Sagittarius, *On Torture*, chapter 10, not only adopted but also affirmed that this passage is commonly read with insufficient correction. Barthius added the following to his emendation:

> We have observed many such things in the divine poet: from whose poetic spirit the remaining Christian poets are also far removed.

Ausonius likewise uses *pregor* in the *Ephemeris*: “I must pray to God and to the Son of the supreme God.”

On the turf altar, which Virgil calls grassy, see Petrus Berthaldus, *On the Altar*, edition of 1636, octavo, pp. 57–58, chapter 6. The ancients not only built turf altars hastily and in military camps, but often also used turf to construct other altars, or used turf upon an altar already constructed for sacrifice. Why Prudentius joins incense with turf may perhaps become clear from Horace, book III, ode 8:

> What the flowers mean, and the censer  
> full of incense, and the coal placed  
> upon the living turf, you wonder;

and book I, ode 19:

> Here, boys, place living turf for me,  
> here the vervain, and incense.

Ausonius in the *Ephemeris* is also relevant:

> Nor do I leave cakes of honeyed crust  
> and a little fire of living turf  
> to empty altars.

Teolius observes that Mazochius, *Biblical Specimens*, vol. II, dissertation 3, concerning the Mosaic turf altar, has more on this matter and censures later writers because they spell *caespes* with a diphthong. Cellarius, following Festus and others, maintains that *caespes* derives from *caedere* (“to cut”) and should be written with a diphthong. In controversies of this sort concerning orthography, almost nothing firm can be established, since the ancients themselves generally disagree among one another.

In the cited passage Barthius distinguishes *cavis recocta* and *follibus*, understanding *cavis* as “the hollow furnace.” But *cavis* seems to be an epithet meaning “vented,” or “hollow,” and receptive of air, although it is certain that *cavum* can also be used substantivally.

### 77.

Put. has *at sunt* instead of *adsunt*. Heinsius says that this is confirmed by other manuscripts, in which the following verse also has *sunt*; but “they are the teachers of crimes” seems to answer the first half of this verse. Heinsius adopted this reading, and most recent editors followed him, including Ruinartius. Gallandius retained the older reading and shows that he approves no other. The meaning is the same: demons lurk in the statues of idols, gods who cannot be gods, since they are teachers of the crimes to which they incite people by teaching an impure religion. Prudentius alludes to the gods of the pagans, who were themselves demons; and when they were expelled from statues or from the bodies of the possessed, they asserted that they bore the names under which they were worshiped in temples. See the commentary on verse 402 of the *Apotheosis*. Those gods were also demons, as verse 92 says, and by their own example they were teachers of crimes.

### 78.

Gis. has *sed sunt*; most copies have *sunt sed*.

### 79.

Rat., Vatican B, Mar., Prag., Alex. in its second hand, and Gis. have *aucupes*. Alex. in its first hand and the older manuscripts of Heinsius have *aucipes*. Ald., Fabr., Egm. have *auspices*. Hailsbr. has *aucupes* above and *auspices* below; later it has *capaces*, which suits neither meter nor sense.

### 80.

Minucius, speaking of the oracles of the pagans, says:

> They are insincere, wandering spirits, weighed down from heavenly strength into earthly filth and desires.

These spirits, therefore, after losing the simplicity of their substance, burdened and immersed in vices, do not cease—ruined as they are—for the consolation of their misery, and so forth.

Chamillardus says that from what Prudentius wrote about demons it can easily be inferred that he considered them pure spirits, without bodies. Chamillardus adds that they could nevertheless possess ethereal and subtle bodies, which would not prevent them from being called spirits. I do not know whether he derives this from Prudentius’ view, from which nothing of the sort can certainly be inferred. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book IV, chapter 9, observes that among Christians *sordidus* (“filthy”) is a distinctive epithet of the devil.

### 81.

Vatican A incorrectly has *latentes* (“hiding”). *Incitus* means “driven on,” “stirred up.” Catullus, in the *Gall iambus*, or poem on Attis, has: “Drive some on, driven forward; drive others mad.”

### 82.

Vatican A has *compellant*, and instead of *div.* [the abbreviated reading] *compellunt*.

*Perfidus* is used for *infidelis* (“faithless”), a word employed by Christian writers.

Concerning these cries of demons, see the note on verse 413 of the *Apotheosis*. This stanza was absent from the manuscript of Saint Michael.

Vatican A, Q, and Hailsbr. have *pulsi ex*. Put. and Oxford, instead of *corporum*, have *viscerum*, not unsuccessfully. Heinsius printed this reading.

### 95.

Nebrissa forgot what the meter required when he declared *obstruite* a purer reading than *obtrudite*, or, as Weitzius writes with Widmann, *obstrudite*. *Obtrudite* is nevertheless better.

### 99.

Egm. and Widm. in the margin, and Put., have:

Heinsius had this reading before his eyes at verse 362 of book I *Against Symmachus*, as we said there. Cellarius observes that executioners profit from the punishments of the accused, and are generally muscular, as though fed on flesh.

### 103.

Heinsius, following Put., reads:

Heinsius thinks that this repetition adds considerable force to the speech. Recent editors follow Heinsius, except Gallandius.

### 107.

### 109.

The torture of the *eculeus* is described here. See plate IX and Gallonius, *On the Tortures of the Holy Martyrs*, chapter 3; also Sagittarius, who in chapter 17 presents a similar depiction of the *eculeus*. He defines it as a wooden machine made in the likeness of a horse, onto which men were raised and bound, then stretched upward and downward and tortured in various ways. Hence the expressions “to be raised on the *eculeus*” and “to be suspended on the *eculeus*.”

Sagittarius corrects a passage in book V, chapter 27 of Isidore’s *Etymologies*: “The *eculeus* is so called because it is stretched.” He thinks it may be supplemented thus: “The *eculeus* is so called because the accused is placed upon it like a horse and stretched.” In the latest Madrid edition, however, it reads: “The *eculeus* is so called because it stretches,” with *quod extendatur* given as a variant.

Saint Jerome, letter to Innocent I, elsewhere numbered 49, writes:

> But the woman … when the *eculeus* stretched her body and the fetid hands of the prison restrained her hands behind her back with bonds, lifted to heaven those eyes which the torturer alone could not bind.

See also the note on verse 110 in the *Romanus*, where I will explain another opinion of Barthius concerning the *eculeus*. The body was stretched on the *eculeus* while the machine itself was extended by screws. Moreover, those lying on the *eculeus* were tortured with hooks or cords, as Prudentius explains in the following stanza, and sometimes also with burning lamps.

Saint Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*, says:

> Now the *eculeus* would stretch him, now the hook would tear him open, now the flame would scorch him.

*Nubilo*: darkness, gloom.

#### [129]

*Proh pudor!*: “O shame!”—I speak with shame.

#### [131]

*Renidet*: shines with joy; from *nitor*, “to shine.”

#### [137]

*Alumni*: servants, attendants.

#### [138]

*Par*: partnership, fellowship, companionship.

### 110.

The stretching of the body is attributed to the *eculeus* as though it were the characteristic power of this torture. Cyprian, *Letter 1 to Donatus*, says:

> And the executioner is at hand: the hook tears open, the *eculeus* stretches, the fire burns.

This description can also suit the torture in which the body was repeatedly raised by pulleys, called by the Spaniards *trato de cuerda* and similarly by the Italians *tratto di corda*. Concerning this punishment Victor of Vita, book III *On the Vandal Persecution*, writes:

> After innumerable blows, raised by repeated pulleys, while he hung over the entire city, now the swift blow lifted him upward, now, when the ropes were released again, the weight of his body fell upon the paving stones, and he collapsed like stone upon stone. He was pulled up again and again, rubbed against the sharpest stones, and, with the skins separated from the flesh, you could see the body’s hides hanging from his sides, back, and belly.

See plate VIII and Nicolaus Agnellus, *On the Punishment of the Rope, or On the Cruelty of the Rope-Blows*, Ferrara, 1786. It should nevertheless be noted that the *Acts of Saint Vincent* mention the *eculeus*, and most interpreters explain Prudentius in this way.

### 111.

Most old books have *ossuum* (“of bones”).

### 113.

Alex. has *iulcis ictibus*, which Teolius printed in the text; I do not know whether deliberately, since in his notes he has *hiulcis*. Oxford has *bisulcis* (“split in two”), not unsuccessfully, since the subject is the hooks, which he called *bisulca* in verse 44 of hymn 1 of the *Peristephanon*. Concerning the same hooks, see verse 452 of the *Romanus*: “With gaping blade,” as many interpret it.

### 115.

Put. and Oxford have *latebras vulnerum* (“the hidden places of wounds”). In the *Apotheosis*, verse 221, he likewise used *lacunas* (“gaps”) when speaking of the wounds of Jesus Christ.

### 117.

Prag. has *ridebat hic* (“he was laughing here”), less well.

### 119.

Rat. has *quo*; a later hand has *quod*.

### 121.

Vatican A has *sic jam*. In Giselinus’ first edition, reprinted at Cologne, the margin has *satellitum*, as though it were a gloss on *fortium*.

### 123.

Aldus has *anhelos*; read *anhelus*. Nearly all these details occur similarly in the *Acts*:

> The hands of the executioners grew tired, while the defeated hand hung over the holy man’s sides; exhausted, their strength failed … the vigor of the strong withered … the weary breast trembled with panting … Let the sharper hook probe the innermost ribs … Then Vincentius, smiling again, said, and so forth.

### 126.

“Gloom of sorrow” and “the mind’s clouds” occur frequently in Sidonius, Cassiodorus, and other writers of the same period. “Cloudy times” occurs in Ovid and others. Ovid himself used *nubes* (“cloud”) for sadness in the *Tristia*, elegy 5:

> Let the rest of life remain free from a sorrowful cloud;

and elsewhere often.

### 127.

Fabr., Gis., and Widm. above have *illuminat*. Heinsius says that his manuscripts consistently and correctly have *luminat*, because he used the same form in the hymn of Saint Eulalia, verse 192:

> Splendor brightens the gracious halls.

Chamillardus went further and added that Fabricius and Giselinus, together with Weitzius—he should have said “with one of Weitzius’ manuscripts,” as Heinsius said, meaning Widmann’s codex—have *illuminat*, but this is wrong. I prefer *luminat*, but I would not dare condemn *illuminat*, which occurs in the very old manuscripts Vatican B, Rat., and Mar. Prudentius also used *illuminat* more often than *luminat*. Vossius, in his notes on Velleius Paterculus, book II, chapter 35, confirms that *In altissimo luminavit* should be read in Velleius because he had read *luminat* here in his copy of Prudentius. He would have done better to cite the verse mentioned from the hymn of Saint Eulalia, for there the meter requires *luminat* and the manuscripts do not vary. Here too *illuminat* can stand. Caelius Aurelianus often used the verb *lumino*. Prudentius speaks of a serene forehead in order to set it against gloom.

### 131.

Hailsbronn incorrectly has *gaudet, renitet* (“rejoices, shines”). *Renidere* means “to smile,” as in Catullus and others; above Prudentius says *ridebat* (“he was smiling”).

### 132.

Aldus has *Tortor, et tortus*; Vatican A, *Tortorem tortor*. Both are corrupt. Saint Cyprian, letter 8, says:

> The tortured stood stronger than those who tortured them.

And in *On the Praise of Martyrdom*:

> For although, as the drops persist, the returning hook leaps back into the wound, and when the scourges withdraw, the thong returns carrying away a piece of the body, yet he stands unmoved, stronger than his punishments, and so forth.

That work is included among those attributed to Cyprian.

### 134.

Prag. has *noxiarum*; read *noxiorum*.

### 138.

Vatican Q, Ald., and Sich. have:

> The invincible part is always mine.

Urb. and Widm. in the margin have:

> The invincible part is always mine.

Fabr. has:

> The part is always mine; keep your invincible right hand back for a while.

Giselinus perhaps first restored the true reading.

### 139.

In the *Acts*:

> But hold back your right hands for a little while; recover your strength, so that the renewed soldier may restrain the wicked enemy more harshly for punishment.

### Notes

#### [142]

Here the Putean manuscript breaks off.

#### [144]

The notes of Noms. and the Graevian papers have *diluet*. Vatican A has *diruat*; others have *diruet*.

#### [146]

Aldus and Weitzius have *suam tuorum*, which seemed insufficiently Latin to Becmanus. Cauchius conjectured *satin’ tuorum*. Most manuscripts, including the Palatine cited by Becmanus, have *si jam*, for which Weitzius improperly cites Aldus. For *perspicis*, Vatican A has *praespicis*.

#### [147]

Paulinus, *Natale* 5, concerning the attendants questioning Saint Felix:

> While the Lord mocked them, he frustrated the gaping dogs.

Barthius, *Adversaria*, book VIII, chapter 14, notes that the attendants are called “dogs” here, an insult that remains extremely severe today among the Turks, Hungarians, Poles, and others. I add specifically the Spaniards, Italians, and, as is clear from the Old Testament, the Hebrews. Aeschylus, in *Prometheus Bound*, calls the eagle of Jupiter, which was ready to carry out his commands, a dog. Among Homer and Quintus of Smyrna this insult is very common. Barthius likewise reports from Aeschylus and Hyginus that the Furies and Harpies were also called dogs. Again, in book XLI, chapter 9, he observes that *Cane pejor* (“worse than a dog”) is a proverb, and at verse 216 of the *Apotheosis* cites: “The half-beast Goth thinks him worse than a dog-soldier.” Thus he reads and concludes that the Goths led dogs into battle. I think it was peculiar to call the attendants “dogs,” as may be inferred from this verse of Prudentius and from the passage of Paulinus cited above; Cicero’s *Against Verres* I agrees remarkably with them:

> Verres used to say that he must also take account of his own needs: he needed much for himself and much for his dogs, whom he kept around him.

### 149.

Vatican A has *ostendo* (“I show”), which is not as good.

### 153.

Giselinus and others after him consider *sumere poenam meam* (“to exact my punishment”) for *de me* (“from me”) harsh and entirely unusual. But what can one do, Giselinus adds, when what is in one’s hands belongs to another and not to oneself? I do not understand what this is intended to mean. Hailsbr. reads *si novam* for *si meam*. Chamillardus was mistaken when he asserted that all manuscripts without exception have *si meam*, and Weitzius had already cited the Hailsbronn manuscript. The possessive *meus* has the same force as *de me* or *a me*; its usage is remarkably varied.

### 154.

Widm. has *vitam* (“life”) instead of *poenam*. Latinius correctly emended *terere* to *te rere* in Torn.

### 156.

Seneca uses *lancino* in the same sense. Arnobius, book II: “You tear apart and long torment our bodies.” Catullus said *bona lancinata* (“goods torn apart”), and Pliny used *lancinare aures* (“to tear the ears”) metaphorically.

### 157.

Vatican B, Mar., Prag., Rat., Weitz., Gis., and others have:

> There is another, there is an inner one.

The first edition of Gis. has:

> There is another one here within.

Fabr. has:

> Another man is within.

Ald., Torn., and Gallandius have:

> There is another man within.

Cellarius preferred this and charged Prudentius with a metrical fault because *homo* has a long first syllable. See what I argued against this in the prolegomena, number 208, note. Heinsius followed Giselinus and recorded no manuscript variation. Prudentius is referring to the Apostle, 2 Corinthians 4:16:

> For this reason we do not lose heart; but although our outward man is being corrupted, yet our inward man is renewed day by day.

### 159.

Vatican A has *laetus* (“joyful”) instead of *liber* (“free”).

### 160.

Rat. has *expers* (“without a share”), and indeed without erasure; above, as a variant, it has *exsors*.

### 163.

The Apostle calls the body a vessel. See the commentary on verse 190 of hymn 7 of the *Cathemerinon*.

### 164.

The Apostle, in the passage cited, verse 7:

> We have this treasure in earthen vessels.

### 169.

Widm. has *hunc lacesse*. Weitzius improperly attributes this reading to Aldus; Aldus emended it to *hunc tu lacesse*. Others have *hunc, hunc lacesse*.

### 170.

Ald., Weitz., and Vatican P have *Invictum, insuperabilem* (“invincible, unsurpassable”), which could be defended despite the hiatus. Thus the error is not as obvious as Chamillardus claims, since he elsewhere acknowledges hiatus in Prudentius. Heinsius too, though he often testifies that hiatus is familiar in Prudentius, now unjustly declares that the verse limps in this form.

Thuan., the three Torr. manuscripts, Alex., and Urb. have *Invictum inexsuperabilem*. Heinsius therefore orders that *Invictum, inexsuprabilem* be read, saying that Prudentius likes such contractions of letters. Teolius agrees with Heinsius. But why should we admit this sort of contraction—one scarcely found elsewhere in Prudentius—against the testimony of the manuscripts? The verse stands firmly with *Invictum, et insuperabilem*, with an anapest in the third foot, which is both permissible and customary in Prudentius. Chamillardus rightly rejected Heinsius’ reading *inexsuprabilem*—not *inexsuperabilem*, as Gallandius says. Chamillardus himself reads *Invictum, et insuperabilem*, as found in Fabricius. Giselinus has this in the text, but in the margin *Invictum, et inexpugnabilem*.

### 173.

Egm. has *et tridentibus* (“and with tridents”), which is not displeasing if the hooks were tridents, as appears from the ancient monument of the Seven Sleepers reproduced in volume I, p. 356; I also discussed it at verse 44 of hymn 1 of the *Peristephanon*. Other hooks with which the bodies of martyrs were torn apart were curved nails, as represented in plate XIII of Gallonius and in plate XXVI added by us, where a hook once found in the cemetery of Saint Agnes is shown, fixed to the head of a martyr. Sagittarius, chapter 17, number 18, gives its shape, which resembles the hook in plate XIII of Gallonius, letter B. The learned Mamachius, in *The Customs of the Primitive Christians*, chapter 6, p. 306, represents the same hook in a somewhat different form. Aringhus, *Subterranean Rome*, vol. II, final book, chapter 1, drew the hook found in the cemetery of Saint Agnes as it is reproduced by us in plate XXVI. Hooks were suitable both for suspending and for dragging, tearing apart, and lacerating. Horace, book I, ode 35:

> Nor is the harsh hook absent, nor the liquid lead.

Ammianus, book VII:

> The *eculei* were stretched out, and the executioner prepared hooks.

Elmenhorst, in his notes on book I of Arnobius, p. 38, discusses the executioners’ hooks. See verse 63 of *Peristephanon* 11.

### 176.

Soon, at verse 197, the prefect is called a serpent. Here *anguina verba* (“serpentine words”) is rightly said to hiss.

### 177.

This metaphor of callus transferred to the mind was used by Cicero and others.

Arnobius, book VII *Against the Pagans*:

> It will be Ceres’ lectisternium on the coming Ides; for the gods have couches, and so that they may lie upon softer coverings, the pressure of pillows is raised and made prominent.

### 180.

Mar. writes *abhomineris*.

### 181.

Rat. has *saltim* (“at least”). That the pagans carefully sought out the books of Christians in order to consign them to fire is related in hymn 1 of the *Peristephanon*. During the persecution of Diocletian this madness was especially prevalent, and hence the name *traditores* became attached to those who handed over the books. See Optatus, book I. Elmenhorst, in his notes on Arnobius, book III, p. 69, has more on the custom in well-ordered states of burning by fire books that undermined the religions. The *Acts of Saint Vincent* contain no mention of this matter.

Mar., Rat., Widm., and Weitz. have *minaris* instead of *minitaris*.

### 189.

Alex. and Hailsbr. write *romfea*; Weitz. and Heins. *rhomphea*; others *rhompaea*. Gis., in the margin, has *jam* instead of *nam*.

### 195.

Vatican B, Widm. in its first hand, Rat., and Mar. in an older hand have *Sodomae nec*. Vatican Q has *Sodomite*. Sichardus has *Sodomus*. Latinius has *Sodomius*. *Sodomita cinis* (“Sodomite ash”) is correct: just as a citizen of Sodom is called *Sodomita*, why could the ash of Sodom not also be called that? In the *Psychomachia* he likewise said *Sodomita libido* (“Sodomite lust”). Here *Sodomita* can also be understood as “turned into ash in the manner of Sodom.” In the hymn of the eighteen martyrs, concerning Saint Cassianus, he says:

> By whose ashes he compelled conquered nations  
> to the yokes of Christ.

### 197.

Egm., Palat., and Hailsbr. in their first hand have *semper* instead of *serpens*; the latter is a good reading. See above, verse 176: “He hisses serpentine words.”

### 198.

Weitz. has *sulphoris* and cites Aldus for this reading; in Aldus I find *sulphuris*.

### 202.

Elmenhorst, in his notes on Arnobius, book I, p. 9, illustrates similar words of Arnobius:

> Let the flames burn fiercely; let the panting breast cast breath from its mouth;

and in book V:

> He burns … foams, pants, and boils over.

### 204.

Egmond, in Burmann, vol. I of the *Anthology*, p. 736, gives *digerit* as a variant instead of *egerit*, but Burmann does not approve it. This variation in the Egmond manuscript, noted by Burmann, had escaped Weitzius and Heinsius.

### 205.

Heraldus, in his notes on Arnobius, book I, p. 37, observes that Arnobius correctly counted fire as the final torture: “You torture, tear apart, burn,” as may also be observed in these verses of Prudentius. Seneca, *On Anger*, book I, chapter 19:

> He had tortured him with everything that is most grievous in nature: with cords, boards, the *eculeus*, fire, and his own face.

Apuleius, *Metamorphoses*, book X:

> Nor were the wheel or the *eculeus*, prepared for his tortures in the Greek manner, now absent.

“But hardened by extraordinary presumption, he yielded neither to any blows nor even to the fire itself.” After fire, the final contest followed: wild beasts or the sword.

### 206.

Pal. has *discernit*; it should be read *decernit*. I have punctuated it accordingly. Others have: “He decrees all the final punishments: fire,” and so on.

### 207.

Fabr. has *ignis grabato*. Oxford has *igni ut grabato*. Rott. has *ligno, grabato*. Gifanius, in *vemens* for *vehemens*, prefers *lamminis* and says that this is how the word is written in the old book whenever Prudentius uses it. Other manuscripts have *laminis*.

Whether an iron bed was distinct from an iron grating was debated between Gallonius and Sagittarius; I discussed it at verse 354 of the *Laurentianus*. The Roman Martyrology records that Saint Vincent was burned on an iron grating. Prudentius, Ado, and Bede call the iron instrument both a bed and a *grabatus*. I think the grating was often called a bed because the martyrs reclined upon it, but that there were nevertheless iron beds that did not resemble a grating; for the distinction is often clearly expressed in the martyrologies. Bede, under 18 April:

> Eleutherius first overcame an iron bed, then a grating and the fire placed beneath it, and afterward a frying pan boiling with pitch and fat.

See also the Roman Martyrology under 18 April.

Mar. has *torrem*. *Cauter* and *cauterium* are so called because they burn; the term is sometimes used for a mark, sometimes for a treatment, so that the force of a disease may be dried out by the heat of fire. *Cauteriata caro* means flesh burned with a cautery. Hence Paul: “Having a cauterized conscience,” that is, a corrupted one; for just as flesh is corrupted by a cautery, so the mind is corrupted by wicked doctrine.

Alex. and Widm. have *poene*; read *poenae*.

In the gloss in Laurentianus there was an error: *in Laurentio* instead of *in Vincentio*.

### 216.

Aldus has *hic martyr*; read *hinc*.

### 217.

Nebrissa says that *lamina* might more conveniently have been used than *regula*, as in Virgil, *Georgics* I, verse 143:

> The sharp-edged plate of the saw.

The *Acts* have:

> For the savage minister had already ordered a bed with iron ribs to be brought forth, and, after a heap of coals had been placed beneath it, ordered the martyr of God to be laid upon it to be burned.

### 218.

Aldus and Weitzius, together with Vatican Q, Urb., and most other manuscripts, have *dente infrequenti* (“with an infrequent tooth”), which Nebrissa explains as “very frequent,” since *in-* often intensifies a word. Giselinus testifies that some copies have *dente frequenti*, adopted by Cauchius, Salmasius, Heinsius, and later editors, with the final syllable of *dente* lengthened before the mute and liquid of the following word; this can indeed be defended. Giselinus printed *dente in frequenti*, which I found clearly confirmed in Vatican P and sufficiently clearly in Alex.

Errors of this kind often occur in Prudentius through the joining of different words, as below at verse 537, where most read *obis* for *o bis*.

### 224.

Peveratus thinks Prudentius alludes to the ancient custom by which victors themselves assumed crowns, but only after the judgment of the *hellanodikai*, to whose tribunal the athletes came after completing the contest. Paschalius, *On Crowns*, book VI, chapter 22, shows that the crown was customarily placed by the judges’ own hands upon the head of the person whom the herald had proclaimed the victor.

### 226.

Mariettus notes from his manuscript the variant *excussio*, which I think is a gloss, both in that manuscript and in Rat. Heinsius took *salis* as a nominative. Chamillardus dislikes this and conjectures *excussum sale* (“shaken-out salt”), using the nominative as Ennius did. Gallandius conjectures:

> a pyre scattered with a sprinkling of salt,

with *rogus* understood from verse 221. The addition “and boiling with sharp crackling points” indicates that shaken-out salt is meant. Nebrissa is correct, along with the authors of the glosses, in treating *excussus* as a substantive meaning “shaking out.” Thus in hymn 5 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 7, Giselinus, following the Daventer edition, printed *excussus cinis* (“shaken-out ash”) and judged another reading inept.

The *Acts* explain it thus:

> The crackling grains of salt scattered upon the fire leap apart throughout the limbs.

In a sermon formerly attributed to Saint Augustine and Saint Leo, but more correctly to Saint Leander, as Florezius proves in volume VIII of *Hispania Sacra*, appendix 1, we read:

> The injection of salt hissing within the exposed entrails.

I find no distinct mention of this torture in Gallonius or Sagittarius.

### 227.

Mariettus explains *puncta* as “drops of salt,” apparently from an old gloss.

Cauchius conjectured *frigitur* (“is fried”), but *figitur* (“is fixed”) is better—namely, the salt.

The first edition of Gis. has *post haec*; others have *posthinc*.

Widm. writes *chauterem*.

235. Virgil, *Aeneid* II: “Stretching his blazing eyes vainly toward heaven—for bonds restrained his tender hands.” St. Jerome: “With his eyes—which alone the torturer could not bind—he looked up to heaven.” See other examples in the commentary on verse 109.

247. Hailsbr. has *horrendos*. Corcinus says this so that the prison may be understood to have its own underworld beneath the earth—that is, a deeper and more secure confinement. In the *Acts of Saints Chrysanthus and Daria*: “There was a lowest confinement in the Tullian prison, from which a horrible stench rose, because the refuse of the houses, carried through the channels of the sewers, continually flowed down there. And in this runoff channel was a low, muddy, and dark confinement, so that the air, completely deprived of light, showed there neither any sign of day nor any trace of light.” In the martyrdom of St. Ignatius: “Take him, put iron chains on him, fasten his feet in the stocks, and guard him in the lowest part of the prison, and let no one see him even through a hole.” See the commentary on verse 468 of Book II against Symmachus.

[Col. 0393C] 251. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.1, on this punishment: “When they had been thrown into prison and were lying in places covered with dreadful darkness and full of hardships, and their feet were held fast after being placed in thick stocks, and were stretched apart as far as the fifth hole, with a long interval between them.” St. Paulinus, *Natalis* 4: “And their feet grow stiff as the stock draws them apart.” Rufinus also called this wooden fetter a *nervus* (“sinew”); I think the name was taken from the sinews by which the feet, inserted into the holes like greaves, were tightened. But *nervus* is also used for any bond by which feet or necks are tied. In the *Acts of the Holy Martyrs* that wooden fetter is often called a *cippus* (“stock”), and the name has remained among the Spaniards as *cepo*. In Acts XVI.24 it is called *lignum* (“wood”): “He put them into the inner prison and fastened their feet in the stocks.” The Greeks also call the stocks, κατ’ ἐξοχήν (“pre-eminently”), *xylon* (ξύλον, “wood”). Henricus Valesius describes it in his note on the cited passage of Eusebius: “It was a wooden trunk, hollowed out with five holes on each side, divided from one another by a fixed interval. The feet of the condemned were inserted into these holes, as into a kind of greaves, and were fastened with bonds or sinews.” See more in Sagittarius, chapter 2.

252. In the *Acts*: “Moreover, spread his legs apart and stretched them out, and fasten his feet in the wood.”

256. *Fando* may be understood either passively or actively. Virgil, *Aeneid* II: “If by chance, through hearsay, anything has reached your ears.” The same author in the cited book: “Who could tell such things in speech?” Someone might ask whether others before St. Vincent had been tortured by having fragments of pottery placed beneath them. St. Paulinus records this very thing of St. Felix, *Natalis* 4: “Pottery fragments are spread out, so that a punitive bed may keep sleep away by its sharpness.” Eustratius suffered a similar punishment according to Nicephorus VII.14, although Nicephorus rather suggests that Eustratius’ body was rubbed with pottery fragments. St. Damasus, on the martyr Eutychius: “They prepare fragments of pottery, lest sleep should approach.” St. Damasus also called it a new punishment: “A new punishment throughout the limbs follows the filth of the prison.” Prudentius perhaps means only that this punishment was new and unheard-of in the town or province where Vincent was being tortured. Sagittarius, chapter 2, examines this torture and shows that this rolling over pottery fragments and other sharp objects took place not only in prison but also outside it. Moreover, Eusebius of Caesarea, Socrates, and the Martyrologies establish that torturers rubbed the martyrs’ bodies with such pottery fragments.

259. *Acuminare* is a verb used by Pliny and Lactantius.

Cellarius says that interpreters have not reached the meaning of this passage because something is discordant in the sentence, unless perhaps we should read, “Anxious pains arm the entire bed with spikes.” But Prudentius seems, using metonymy, to put “anxious pains” for the fragments of pottery themselves, by which anxious pains are produced.

268. Weitz. preferred to write *comenta*, with Hailsbr. The gloss is far from correct, for *commentus* is the past tense of *comminiscor*. Moreover, *commentor* forms *commentatus*.

269. *Carceralis* and *carcereus* are words scarcely used by the ancients before Prudentius.

270. Ald., Vat. A in the first hand, Weitz., Hailsbr., Widm., and Gifanius from an old book read *fulgorat* instead of *fulgere*.

271. The “bites” of the stocks are not the holes in the wood, as though the wood were biting the feet, but the bite by which the two pieces of the stocks are locked together. Ducange shows that in writers of the later period, especially, *puncta* are called the marks drawn at the beginning and end of individual lines, or pierced with an awl, within which the strokes of the lines themselves are inscribed—the strokes called *sulci*. This is especially observed in codices made of parchment. Ducange confirms this with the words of Iso’s gloss.]

Giselinus found in his manuscript and in the Daventria edition *ruptis catenis* (“with the chains broken”), and understands the iron bonds by which the pieces of wood, hollowed out ἡμικυκλικῶς (“semicircularly”) at fixed points, were joined and tightly fastened. 301. This is absent from Rat. and Mar., though it must be added. Gifanius observes that *vas* (“vessel”) used for the body is an unusual and novel expression in Lucretius, and most elegant here in Prudentius; we have said more about it elsewhere. Prudentius, at the conclusion of his works, verse 26: “Christ fits an obsolete little vessel to perishable uses.”

329. Two Heinsian manuscripts, together with Thuan., Vat. Q, and the later Alex., have *exemptus carceri* (“released from prison”); the others have *carcere* (“from prison”).

333. Cellarius interprets *oppidum* as Saguntum. But it is certain from the *Acts* that it was Valentia. In Hymn 1 *Peristephanon*, Calagurris is called an *oppidum*, and any city may properly be called an *oppidum*. The Theodosian Code, Book XVI, Law 2, *On Monks*, uses *civitas* and *oppidum* for the same thing. Deacons seem especially to have been appointed to visit martyrs detained in prisons. But there is no doubt that other Christian men and women also did so, as is clear from the histories and Acts of the martyrs.

335. Gis. has *perfultum*; the others, *praefultum*. Giselinus and Chamillardus explain the couch as hard and rough, as couches ordinarily are when stretched and stuffed; I strongly disagree with them. Since *fulcrum* means a bed, because a bed is raised and supported by supports, and *fulcrum* is derived from *fultum*, Prudentius here calls the couch *praefultum* from the supports themselves, as though it were well raised and supported. In the sermon of St. Leander mentioned above: “The jealous mind orders the supports of a softer bed to be substituted.”

337. The furrows are called “double” because the martyr had been flayed with double-clawed instruments. See Hymn 1 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 44.

338. The custom of the ancient Christians is noteworthy: they reverently kissed the chains and wounds of the martyrs. Tertullian, *To His Wife* II: “What pagan would permit a Christian wife to crawl forward to kiss a martyr’s bonds?” Compare the Martyrology of Ado, June 5, September 8, and the Roman Martyrology, June 23. Theodoret, I.2, reports that Constantine put his lips to the scars of those who had confessed Christ and endured torments. Optatus, *Against Parmenianus* I, seems to refer to this custom: “It was said that one kissed the mouth of some martyr, if indeed he was a martyr”—which he says of Lucilla, the patroness of the Donatists.

[Col. 0397D] 341. Ald. and Gis. have *lineam*; the better witnesses, *linteam*. The zeal of the ancient Christians in preserving the martyrs’ relics was extraordinary, especially in collecting blood; no one describes it more clearly than Prudentius, whose account is openly echoed by the *Acts*: “You would see the crowd of bystanders eagerly kissing the holy footprints, touching with pious curiosity the wounds of the entire lacerated body, and catching the blood in linen cloths, to benefit posterity through sacred veneration.” I wish the heretics who attack the veneration of sacred relics would notice that these very *Acts* were customarily read in the Church in the time of St. Augustine and were often praised by St. Augustine.

[Col. 0398C] 345. Chamillardus understands *manceps* as the prefect of the prison, just as the Theodosian Code says *manceps thermarum* (“superintendent of the baths”) and *manceps salinarum* (“superintendent of the saltworks”); he does not think it necessary that the *manceps carceris* be assigned to the service, as Nebrissa wants. Properly, however, a *manceps* is one who takes with the hand. Turnebus, *Adversaria* I.13, explains *manceps* in Prudentius as the prison guard, whom Ambrose, he observes, calls the *option* of the prison.

347. Here too Prudentius calls antiquity “conscious,” as in the Hymn of the Eighteen Martyrs, verse 164, *priscam vetustatem* (“ancient antiquity”). Yet this event occurred in the fourth century.

348. Prag. has *Christo*. Alex. has *reddidit*; above, *credidit*, which should be retained.

350. Rat. and Vat. B in the first hand have *densum*. Mar. has *densae*, but *sae* was produced by erasing the preceding letters.

354. Mar. has *contulit*; in the margin, with the others, *contigit*. Nebrissa explains *quietem* as referring to the fact that he slept briefly. The *Acts* say: “For the martyr of God, having been carried to a little bed and placed in the softness of the bedding by the pious hands of the saints, soon, released into a precious death, gave back his spirit to heaven.”

356. Gis., first edition, has *est mortis*; second edition, *et mortis*, but he corrected it to *est mortis*, which is not displeasing. Most others have *et*, so that the sentence is suspended until verse 367. “And then the victorious spirit” is an apposition, as though Vincent—that is, his victorious spirit—were said to take possession of heaven.

357. Ald., Weitz., and Gis. in the text have *hujusmodi*. Most have *ejusmodi*.

358. St. Fulgentius, in his sermon on St. Stephen: “Today the soldier has gone forth from the prison of the flesh.” Since an *ergastulum* is a place of punishment where prisoners work, Chamillardus aptly observes that the word suits the body, though he considers *corporalis* barbarous and unusual. But Seneca, Letters 58 and 78, uses it more than once, even in the compound *incorporalis*.]

363. Ald., Tornaes., Gis., and some of the common editions have *inclytam*. Egm., Pal., Ambr., Thuan., Altin., Oxon., Rott., have *elutam*, as do the more recent editions, including Ruinartius with Heinsius; Gallandius favored this because of the word *lavacris*, although he printed *inclytam*. *Elutam* also occurs in Vatt. A, P, and Alex., where the gloss is *ablutam* (“washed clean”), and in Urb. *ablutam* occurs in the text. Weitz., with some of his witnesses, Vatt. B and Q, Mar., Prag., and Rat., has *erutam*, and in Mar. above *lavacris*, in a later hand, in place of the variant reading, *periclis*. Since so many very old codices support *erutam*, and the law of the meter also seems to require it, I prefer *erutam*, for *inclytam* is not found in the manuscripts and Heinsius rightly thinks it arose from Aldus’ conjecture. If *elutam* is read, the second syllable must then be shortened; I would maintain that this can be done on the authority of Prudentius alone. One might conjecture *elitam*, from *elino*, “I cleanse,” a verb attributed to Lucilius.

365. Aldus had printed *recline*, properly; he corrected it to *reclive*, though there was no need to change it. See the commentary on verse 150 of Hymn 4 of the *Cathemerinon*: “May he lie reclining.”

366. Rat. and Mar. in the old hand have *redegit*; *rejecit* is better. In the gloss I would read *redegit*.

370. Vat. A has *servatur*; read *reseratur*.

371. Prag. has *caesus ab impio*, which is not bad.

375. Vat. A, Vat. B in the second hand, Mar. in the margin, Pal., all the Heinsian witnesses, and others have *missum*. Ald., Weitz., and Gis., with many manuscripts, have *missus*, which pleases me more. Cellarius and Teolius say that the manuscripts have *missum*, not *missus*. But the manuscripts vary, and the old editions agree with us.

383. Ald. incorrectly punctuates: *exsultans ait Rebellis*.

390. The Romans deprived criminals put to death of the honor of burial; they either dragged their bodies with a hook into the Tiber or left them to be torn apart by birds and dogs. They inflicted this disgrace on Christians so that the faithful would not flock to their graves. Lactantius writes elegantly, Book V, chapter 11, on the cruelty shown toward Christians: “No one can adequately describe the savagery of this enormous beast, which, though lying in one place, rages throughout the whole world with iron teeth; it not only scatters human limbs but even crushes the bones themselves and rages against the ashes, so that no place of burial may remain. As though those who worship God sought this—that people should come to their graves—and not rather that they themselves should come to God!” Gallonius and Sagittarius provide many further examples gathered from histories and Martyrologies.

391. *Gregalis* is customarily said of fellow-members or companions, especially low-status persons, almost as a term of contempt.

392. Vatt. A, P, Alex., Oxon., Alt., Thuan., two Torrentian manuscripts, and the manuscripts of Cauchy, together with Heinsius, have *fingat*; Ald., Vatt. B and Q, Mar., Weitz., and Gis. have *figat*, which is preferable. The subject is the epitaph of a tomb, which was called a *titulus*; and from the title or inscription the tomb itself was called a *titulus*. Chamillardus asserts that Nebrissa did not understand this passage because he explained it as an epitaph, and refers to verse 45 of Hymn 12 of the *Peristephanon*: “On the other side, the title of Paul guards the Ostian road.” But in this very passage, what prevents us from understanding a tomb inscription, poetically used for the tomb itself? Moreover, as I have said, the tomb was called a *titulus* from its inscription, and here *titulus* may mean an epitaph, elsewhere a tomb. Martinus Roa, *On the Sacred and Secular Birthday*, chapter 21, discusses titles learnedly. He says that veils were formerly placed before altars, sometimes plain and sometimes painted, and that these were called *tituli*; Ambrose, writing to Marcellina, called them royal curtains. He adds that *titulus* is also understood as a church, because at the place where a church was to be erected a cross was placed as a *titulus*, and he explains Prudentius’ verse, “And let him erect the martyr’s title,” to mean that he should set up a title in the form of a cross, so that a sacred place might designate the intended church. But he returns again to the veils: when these bore painted images of martyrs or merely an inscription of their names, they were called the titles of the martyrs. He also conjectures, from Paulinus and from a Roman custom still current, that such titles were customarily placed before the doors of churches. For even today at Rome a festive ornament is used, namely garlands of branches and foliage, which are called festoons. In these, circles or squares are left at intervals, within which titles or veils containing painted images of the saints are enclosed. Paulinus: “And let them cover the holy thresholds with plates affixed before them.” Roa understands these titles in Prudentius, *Hippolytus*, verse 183: “The little shrine, which holds within it those bodily remains of the soul, gleams with solid silver.” But, to return the matter to its beginnings, the name *titulus*, as I was saying, was transferred from the title or epitaph of a tomb to the tomb itself, to a memorial, a confession, and a basilica of martyrs—and, if you wish, to those veils about which Roa speaks, and to which, as I conjecture, the images now placed on altars owe their origin. The custom of erecting a cross as a title is very ancient, as may be seen in Baronius’ notes on the Roman Martyrology and in Sagittarius’ book *On the Birthdays of the Martyrs*, chapter 3. It should also be noted that the expression “to fix a cross” occurs frequently, as in Prudentius, “And let him erect the martyr’s title”; it is therefore probable that Prudentius is alluding to that custom. In the Roman Church, the designation *tituli* has, by antonomasia, remained attached to those churches granted to cardinals as their titular churches. It is also likely that the title required for any priest being ordained derived its name from this, because formerly men were generally not admitted to holy orders unless they were attached to some title—that is, to a basilica or church. As for what Roa and others say, that whenever a church was formerly to be erected a cross was raised as its title, I think this arose because, since churches in the earliest times were accustomed to be built where there was a title or tomb of a martyr, afterward they were also built where no such tomb existed, and a cross was raised to serve as the title. Mazochius traces the origin to Genesis XXVIII.18: “Then Jacob rose early, took the stone that he had placed under his head, and set it up as a title,” etc. Mazochius says that a title is any stone, even a mute one, provided that it can transmit a memorial.]

401. Chomillardus refers this only to the eagle, because *clangere* properly belongs to eagles. But since the *Acts* say, “When the other birds approached, he drove them away from a distance with a certain rush of his swift wings, making them fearful,” and eagles are not named, there is nothing to prevent *clangens*, if it refers to any bird, from being understood generally. Nor can a *clangor* be referred less properly to cranes and other birds than to eagles, although the author of the poem attributes a cry to eagles in the *Philomela*. For *clango* is a verb formed to imitate a sound. Thus the ancients attribute *clangor* to the coot, hawk, goose, cranes, sparrow, phoenix, and hens. Lexicographers provide examples. A dog’s barking is also called *clangor*.

437. Ammianus, Book XXII, on George and his companions under Julian: “The savage multitude, not satisfied with this, carried the mangled bodies of those who had been killed, loaded on camels, to the lakes; then, having suddenly burned them with the same fire, it scattered the ashes into the sea, fearing, as it shouted, that if the remains were collected, buildings might be erected for them, as for the others who, compelled to depart from the religion, endured torturous punishments and proceeded with unshaken faith even to a glorious death, and are now called martyrs.” Rittershusius, in his commentary on Pliny’s letter about the Christians, reads *vexit ad litus* (“carried to the shore”) and *subdito igne* (“after fire had been placed beneath them”). Epiphanius, heresy 76, relates that George’s ashes were scattered to the winds; but he denies that George should be counted among the martyrs, because he was killed by pagans not for professing the Christian name but because of the violence with which he oppressed the city and its people. George was an intruded Arian bishop, after Athanasius had been expelled.
