### Apparatus variants: lines 244–271

- **244.** Vat. A reads *strangulant, claudant*: “they choke, they shut in.”
- **246.** I glosses *diurni sideris* as *solis*: “of the daytime star,” that is, “of the sun.”
- **247.** Hailsbr. reads *horrendos*: “terrible, dreadful”; the note connects this with the deep or innermost prison.
- **249.** I explains *barathrum* as the name of an immense depth or abyss.
- **252.** I glosses *divaricatis* as “with the legs spread apart,” also “separated, parted, or forced apart.”
- **254.** I glosses *crucis* as *supplicii*: “of punishment/torture.”
- **257.** Vat. A has the corrupt spelling *fracmenta*; Mar. improperly prints *testarum* for the abbreviated variant.
- **258.** Hailsbr. has *herta* (a damaged or erroneous form); Mar. has *ungulis* (“with claws”), while a later hand gives *angulis* (“with corners/angles”), identified by the note as the true reading.
- **260.** Tornaes. and some Weitzian witnesses read *jacenti* (“lying down”); Rott. and a marginal hand of Gis. have *sternere* (“to spread/lay out”). Heinsius conjectures the damaged form *jacentis sternier*; the received reading is retained.
- **263.** Prag. incorrectly has *insomno* (“sleepless”); Widm. above the line and Prag. below have *subtus latus* (“beneath the side”).
- **265.** I glosses *vafra* as *callida*: “cunning, crafty.”
- **266.** Vat. B, Rat., Mar. supra, and Weitz. have *meditator* (“a planner/contriver”); the preferred form is *meditatus* (“having devised/planned”).
- **267.** Weitz. has *cum* (“with”); Egm. and Hailsbr. have *Beelzibulis*, Widm. *Beelzeb*, and Alex. first hand *Belzebolis*: variant spellings/forms of the Beelzebub name, retained without forcing a normalization.
- **268.** *Commenta* is explained from *commentor/commiscor*, “to devise”: *commentum* is a work devised by a learned author; Iso gives the perfect *commentus sum*, not *commentatus*. Weitz. preferred *comenta* with Hailsbr., but the note rejects that gloss.
- **269.** *Carceralis* and *carcereus* both mean “prison-related/prison-like”; the note says such vocabulary was scarcely used before Prudentius.
- **270.** Ald., Vat. A first hand, Weitz., Hailsbr., Widm., and Gifanius read *fulgorat* for *fulgurat*: “flashes/shines.”
- **271.** *Morsus* denotes the joining “bites” or notches of the wooden stocks, not holes in the wood biting the feet; I’s *punctos* means the marked or pierced points/holes (*foramina*) of the fastening.

### Apparatus variants: lines 272–330

- **272.** Giselinus’s manuscript and Daventry edition read *ruptis catenis* (“with chains broken”); the margin also gives *catenis*. Most witnesses have *cavernis* (“cavities/holes”), understood as the openings of the stocks.
- **273.** Rat. has *tunc* (“then”) against the metre; I gives *hic* (“here”).
- **279.** Widm. has *vestiri* (“to be clothed/covered”), judged erroneous.
- **280.** *Nectar* is explained as “every sweetness”; Nebrissa takes it for ambrosia. The damaged printed *Peristephanωn* preserves the Greek omega and is not expanded beyond the recoverable title reference.
- **282.** I glosses *cominus* as *prope*: “near, at close quarters.”
- **283.** I glosses *augustior* as *excellentior, nobilior*: “more distinguished, nobler.”
- **284.** Egm. and Hailsbr. read *hic* (“here”); the note directs *lege his*, “read *his* (‘with these words’).”
- **289.** Ald. incorrectly has *decussa jam*; the form is retained as an erroneous witness reading.
- **294.** Ald., Torn., Gall., and Rat. corrected hand give *Fortissimisque fortior* (“braver than the bravest”); the true reading is *Fortissimorum fortior* (“braver than [one] of the very bravest”). Rat.’s correction *Et fortium fortissime* means “and most bravely of the brave.”
- **298.** I glosses *compensat* as *retributionem reddit*: “renders recompense”; *intermino* means “unbounded, endless,” from *interminatus/infinite*.
- **299.** *Collegam* is “a colleague,” from one who shares an embassy; here *collega crucis* is “a companion of the cross.” Ald. has *proprieque*, less correctly. The damaged gloss is conservatively read as *collega crucis, socius crucis*: “companion of the cross.”
- **301.** I glosses *pone* as *pro depone*: “put down/lay aside.” Rat. and Mar. omit *hoc*; the note says it must be supplied.
- **304.** The note states that Prudentius again confesses that souls pure from every stain go straight to heaven after death.
- **305.** I glosses *haec ille* as “the angel was saying these things.”
- **308.** Hailsbr. has *proditor* (“betrayer”); the preferred reading is *proditur* (“is revealed/shown forth”).
- **309.** I identifies *hoc* as *lumen*: “this light.”
- **310.** I glosses *obsessor* as *custos*: “guard, keeper.” Rat. seems to have *luminis* (“of light”), but *liminis* (“threshold”) is correct.
- **312.** I glosses *feralem* as *asperam*: “grim, harsh.”
- **313.** The note records that martyrs often sang sacred psalms and hymns amid tortures.
- **314.** I glosses *praedulce* as *valde dulce*: “very sweet.”
- **315.** *Aemulae* is glossed as *imitatricis*: “imitating”; *instar* functions in place of a noun.
- **316.** I explains that the echoing *aemula vox* is an imitative voice; *conclave* means an inner room or chamber.
- **318.** I glosses *admota* as *adjuncta*: “brought near/applied.” Heumann’s *admonita* is rejected; Gallandius notes that *admota* was already read.
- **321.** Chamillardus glosses *vernare* as “to shine”; the note prefers its proper sense, “to gleam and put forth as in new spring.”
- **327.** I glosses *volvit* as *cogitat*: “turns over in his mind, thinks.”
- **329.** Two Heinsian witnesses with Thuan., Vat. Q, and later Alex. have *exemptus carceri* (“released from prison”); others read *carcere* (“from prison”).
- **330.** I glosses *benignis fotibus* as *blandis, mitibus nutrimentis*: “kind, gentle restoratives/nourishment.”

### Apparatus variants: lines 335–385

- **335.** Gis. reads *perfultum*; others *praefultum*. Both point to a bed “propped/supported.” The note prefers *praefultum*, from the bed’s *fulcra* (supports), not the gloss “stuffed and rough.”
- **336.** I glosses *siccare* as *tergere*: “to dry, wipe.”
- **337.** *Duplices sulci* are “double furrows,” because the martyr had been torn by two-pronged claws.
- **338.** The note records the Christian custom of reverently kissing martyrs’ chains and wounds.
- **341.** Ald. and Gis. read *lineam*; stronger witnesses read *linteam*: “a linen cloth,” used for preserving relics.
- **343.** I glosses *tutamen* as *firmamentum, protectionem*: “safeguard, protection.”
- **345.** *Manceps* is “one who takes by hand,” hence a keeper/contractor; here it is explained as the prison guard. It can denote one who enslaves or is enslaved, while *emancipatus* is freed from servitude.
- **348.** Prag. has *Christo*; Alex. has *reddidit*, with *credidit* written above and retained: “he believed.”
- **350.** Rat. and Vat. B first hand read *densum* (“dense/thick”); Mar. has *densae*, apparently altered after erasure.
- **354.** Mar. has *contulit* (“brought/conferred”); its margin has *contigit* (“came to/passively befell”), with other witnesses. The note explains the line as rest or a brief sleep and cites the Acta’s account of the martyr’s death.
- **356.** Gis. first edition has *est mortis*, its second *et mortis*, then corrected back to *est mortis*; many others have *et*, making the syntax continue to line 367.
- **357.** Ald., Weitz., and Gis. in the text have *hujusmodi* (“of this kind”); most witnesses have *ejusmodi* (“of that kind”).
- **358.** *Ergastulum* is a penal workhouse/prison; the note applies it aptly to the body, while recording Chamillardus’s objection to *corporalis* as unusual.
- **363.** Ald., Tornaes., Gis., and some printed witnesses have *inclytam* (“renowned”); Egm., Pal., Ambr., Thuan., Altin., Oxon., and Rott. have *elutam* (“washed out/cleansed”), supported by newer editors; Vatt. A/P/Alex. have that reading with *ablutam* (“washed”) as gloss, Urb. *ablutam* in text. Weitz., several of his witnesses, Vatt. B/Q, Mar., Prag., and Rat. read *erutam* (“drawn out”), preferred because old witnesses and metre support it. Mar.’s marginal *periclis* is retained as a variant, not expanded.
- **365.** Ald first printed *recline*, then corrected it to *reclive*; the note says no change was needed and retains the adverbial “reclining.”
- **366.** Rat. and Mar. first hand have *redegit* (“drove back/reduced”); *rejecit* (“cast back/rejected”) is preferred. The gloss should read *redegit*.
- **370.** Vat. A has *servatur* (“is preserved”); read *reseratur* (“is opened/unbarred”).
- **371.** Prag. reads *caesus ab impio* (“slain by the impious man”), judged acceptable.
- **375.** Vat. A, Vat. B second hand, Mar. margin, Pal., all Heinsian witnesses, and others have *missum* (“sent,” neuter/accusative); Ald., Weitz., Gis., and many manuscripts have *missus* (“sent,” masculine/nominative), which the editor prefers.
- **383.** Ald. punctuates wrongly: *exsultans ait Rebellis*; the faulty division is retained as a punctuation variant.

### Apparatus variants: lines 391–471

- **391.** *Gregalis* means “of a group/companions,” especially low-status associates; *plebs* is rustic common people, and *gregales/gregarii* are those who accompany cavalry troops.
- **392.** *Titulum* means an epitaph, memorial, or inscription; *figat* means “may set up/write.” Vat. A/P/Alex./Oxon./Alt./Thuan. and other witnesses read *fingat* (“may fashion”), while Ald., Vat. B/Q, Mar., Weitz., and Gis. read *figat* (“may fix/set up”), preferred.
- **393.** Widm. has *frendet* (“gnashes/rages”); above it is *frendit* (“he gnashes/rages”).
- **394.** Vat. A has the corrupt *addirum*; Vat. B *ac dirum*; Mar. and Rat. *a dirum*; Alex. *adirum*. The true reading is *ah! dirum*: “ah, dreadful!”
- **397.** Ambr., Thuan., and Vat. A have *famis* (“of hunger”); other, including old, witnesses have *fames* (“hunger”).
- **400.** Hailsbr. has *tractu* (“by a drawing/dragging”); read *tactu* (“by touch”).
- **401.** *Clangere* is properly said of eagles, but the note permits the cry of any bird here; *clangor* is an onomatopoeic cry, also used of cranes, geese, hawks, and even dogs.
- **402.** Alex., Ambr., and Thuan. have *circumvolarat* (“had flown around”), preferred by Heinsius; most have *circumvolaret* (“might/would fly around”).
- **404.** Hailsbr. has *fuga* (“flight”); read *fugam* (“flight,” accusative).
- **407.** Most Heinsian witnesses, Vat. A, Hailsbr. first hand, Alex., and others have *sedule* (“diligently,” less usual); Ald., Mar., Weitz., and others have *sedulo* (“diligently”); Egm. incorrectly *sedulae*.
- **410.** Iso may have read *infessus* (“unwearied”) or explained *non festus* (“not joyous/not festive”); the ambiguity is retained.
- **413.** Ecclesiastical writers use *perfidi* for “unbelievers/faithless persons.”
- **416.** Vat. A has the corrupt *cessisce*; no unrecorded expansion is supplied.
- **421.** Ald. incorrectly reads *audiendi* (“of hearing”); the note cites Vergil’s *cernenti* (“seeing/beholding”).
- **432.** Weitz with his witnesses and Rat. read *frangit* (“breaks”).
- **437.** The Ammianus/Epiphanius note preserves the historical discussion of scattered ashes and its qualifications; Rittershusius reads *vexit ad litus* (“carried to the shore”) for *vexit ad lacus* (“carried to the lakes”), with *subdito igne* (“a fire having been applied”).
- **439.** I glosses *ignoscit* as *mitescit, parcit*: “softens, spares/forgives.”
- **441.** Hailsbr. reads *mobile* (“movable”), a defensible variant.
- **446.** *Scabri* means “rough, savage”; *murices* are “sharp rock-peaks,” though *murex* can elsewhere mean purple.
- **447.** *Recessus* means “retreats/secluded places”; *scrupeos* means “rough, stony.”
- **450.** I glosses *cymham* as *navis*: “ship.”
- **455.** *Lembulo* refers to a *lembus*, a small pirate boat, or to the edge of a gilded garment.
- **457.** *Sparteus* derives from *spartus*, a thorny or rush-like plant; the damaged *junrus* is retained without expansion. The note explains the Roman punishment of parricides in a sewn *culleus* with animals.
- **458.** *Culleus* can mean an inner sewn strip, a garment/sack of spartus, a wicker basket, or a leather bag in which condemned persons were cast into the sea; Mar. gives the basket/leather-bag alternatives.
- **461.** I glosses *emices* as *vadas, exilias*: “you may emerge/go forth/leap out.”
- **462.** *Praepes* means “swift”; *palmula* means “oar.”
- **466.** *Nomen* means “the name—namely, whose [name].”
- **467.** *Barbarus* is glossed *rusticus*: “foreign/barbarous, rustic.”
- **469.** *Funale* is glossed *funerale*: “funeral.”
- **471.** *Emensus* is glossed *navigans*: “having traversed, sailing.”

442. Concerning motion in water, Virgil, *Georgics* I, verse 369: “Or swimming at the surface of the water to play with their wings.” The same Virgil, concerning the agitation of winds, *Aeneid* VI: “Do not entrust songs to the leaves, lest, tossed about, they fly as toys of the swift winds.” Horace, concerning the ship, *Odes* I.14: “You are destined to be the sport of the winds.”

443. Aldus, Tornaesius, and several copies of the *Vulgate* read *Austris feretur flatibus*, “it will be borne by southern winds,” from which Cauchius conjectured *Austris feretur flantibus*, “it will be borne while the south winds blow,” or *Austri feretur flatibus*, “it will be borne by the blasts of the south wind.” Most read *Vagis feretur flatibus*, “it will be borne by wandering blasts,” except that in Thuan., Gis. at the margin, and Fabr. there is *fluctibus*, “waves,” instead of *flatibus*, “blasts.”

445. Widmann printed incorrectly *aut suffragosis*.

447. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI: “There was a lofty cavern, craggy, with a vast and monstrous opening.”

449. Aldus, Mar. in the first hand, Weitz., and some others: *et quis*. The same variation occurs elsewhere.

450. Mar. reads *paratus*, “prepared,” and, in place of the gloss, *peritus*, “skilled.” Most write *cumbam*. I do not know in what manner Prudentius wrote it, and *cymba* is the more common spelling.

453. Widm. and Mar. read *palustri cespite*, “from the marshy sod.”

458. In Spain, after strangulation, uxoricides are enclosed in a wooden vessel with a cock, snake, dog, and cat and thrown into the river; in Spanish this is called *encubar*. Compare Hurtado, *De Martyrum rebus*, 35, dissertation 2, who reports the matter in this way. But, as I hear, the cock, snake, dog, and cat are not enclosed alive with the body of the condemned person; rather, they are merely depicted above the sack or barrel, both for the sake of humanity and of infamy. Perhaps the practice varied according to time and place. In the *Acts*: “He is sewn up,” he says, “the folded corpse in the parricide’s sack.”

459. Weitz., together with Widm. and Hailsbr., wished to write *conexus*, “bound together.”

461. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI: “The hand of the youths flashes forth burning.”

462. Giselinus indicates *rotante* as a different reading instead of *rorante*. Vat. A has *praepes* for *praeceps* as a divergent spelling. Heinsius preferred *praepes*, with Ambr., Thuan., Rott., and three Torr. manuscripts, especially since *praeceps* had occurred shortly before. Certainly *praepes* fits the sense better.

469. Mar. has *fanale*, correctly emended above to *funale*. Ison’s gloss is ridiculous, as though *funalis* derived from *funus*, “funeral,” rather than from *funis*, “rope.” For examples of the substantive *funale*, see Gifanius, and the commentary on verse 16 of hymn 10 of the *Cathemerinon*.

470. Vat. A has *suto*, with others, but above, as a divergent reading, *sancto*. Prag. has *scuto*, incorrectly.

It grows mild, and clemency tames

the ravenous ravens;

I shall plunge the corpse into the waves.

The frenzied wave never forgives

shipwrecked men, and the foaming deep

[440] knows not how to spare.

Or, forever in motion there,

amid uncertain mockeries,

it will be borne by wandering blasts,

feeding the scaly shoals;

[445] or beneath the rugged rocks

the rough bosses of the stones

will tear apart the entrails

among the craggy recesses.

Is there any man among us, resolute,

[450] [Col. 0403B] skilled in driving a boat

with oar, rope, and canvas,

who could cut across the sea?

Could you snatch from the marshy sod

the body lying untouched,

[455] [Col. 0404A] and, carried in a light skiff,

bear it away across the broad waters?

But let a wicker sack

enclose the folded corpse.

Let a stone bound by a rope

[460] plunge it headlong into the depths.

Yet you flash through the waves,

swift with your dripping oar,

until the greater distance

hides the abandoned land from view.

[465] A certain soldier, charged with this order

(his name was Eumorphius),

violent, bold, barbarous,

seething with fury, seized it.

He fastens together a woven rope (*funale*)

and fills it with the sewn-up body.

[470] [Col. 0404B]

Having traversed much of the sea,

amid the storms he casts it out.

O almighty power of God,

creative power of all things,

475. Matthew relates this in chapter 14.

478. Virgil at the end of *Aeneid* VII: “Nor should the swift feet touch the water.”

483. Ald., Sich., and others, contrary to the meter, have *dum profundo aridum*. Vat. A and Hailsbr. in the first hand have *dum fundo arido*, which is not displeasing. Hamartig., verse 474: “The mud in the middle of the whirlpool dried up and thirsted.” See the commentary on this verse.

484. Ald., Tornaes., Galland., and Sich. have *Secura plebs incesserit*. Mar. in the first hand, Rat. in the first hand, Vat. B, Alex., several of Heinsius’s copies, Weitz., and Hailsbr. above have *iter terit*, which Giselinus also found in a very carefully written manuscript of the canons of St. Catherine of Nijmegen. He himself prefers *iter legit*, with his own manuscript and another from Buslidius, as softer and more poetic. Thuan. reads *Secunda plebs iter legit*. One Torr. has *Secura plebs iter terat*; Rat. has *iter gerat*. Mar. in the second hand, Egm., Pal., and Vat. A have *iter gerit*. Rat. in another hand has *iter tulit*. Most recent editions, with Giselinus, read *iter legit*.

485. Vat. A has *et ipse* as a divergent spelling. The same is mentioned almost identically concerning St. Quirinus in his hymn.

487. Prag., Vat. Q, and Urb. have *passibus*. Alex., with others, has *lapsibus*; above, *cursibus*.

490. Vat. A has *spuma cadens*, incorrectly.

494. Virgil, *Aeneid* II: “And having crossed the sea.” For *mari*, “sea,” Virgil and others frequently have *marmor*, “marble.”

496. Here *aestus maris*, “the sea’s tide,” may be understood as agitation produced by the wind, not as the tide itself, since here it is opposed to the ebb. Nebrissensis takes it as the tide, which, as I think, Teolius intended, although he wrote *Undarum refluxu sequente, et vento*, “with the ebb of the waves following, and with the wind.” Chamillardus reports the opinion of a very learned man and, as he says, easily the foremost of mathematicians, who thought that in the depths of the sea a fermentation of some substance occurred in the same manner as in the bodies of fever patients; through this fermentation the sea swelled, just as a mass swells while fermenting. He added that the periods of the tides are no more beyond our understanding than the periods of tertian or quartan fever.

501. Vat. A has *delatos*: correct to *relatos*.

506. Mar. in the first hand has *successus*, but the reading adopted by most is *secessus*. Aldus and several copies of the *Vulgate* have *recessus*.

509. Widm., Mar., and Victorius, *Dissertationes philologicae*, p. 16, demonstrate from this the difficulty of burying the bodies of the holy martyrs during the persecutions. He also cites these words from the epitaph of St. Alexander the martyr under Antoninus Pius: “O unhappy times, in which, amid sacred rites and prayers, we cannot be preserved even in caves. What is more wretched than life? But what is more wretched in death, when they cannot be buried by friends and relatives?” See Aringhus, *Roma subterranea* I.3 and following, where you will find more reliable monuments confirming this difficulty; for some have labored in vain to persuade others that the inscription of St. Alexander is fabricated. The Christians’ devotion in burying the bodies of the dead, even those who were not martyrs, was remarkable, as is clear from the hymn *Exsequiarum*; nor was it unknown to the pagans. Julian the Apostate praises it even while calling the Christian religion impious, in letter 49 to Arsacius the high priest: “Let us turn our eyes to the things by which the impious religion of the Christians grew—that is, to their kindness toward strangers, to the care they showed in burying the dead, and to the sanctity of life that they pretend to possess.”

512. Horace, *Odes* III.30, spoke of “future praise.” Nebrissensis understands “future life” as the day of judgment, quite suitably; this can be confirmed by the hymn of St. Fructuosus, verse 136: “But that the remains are to be raised again,” and shortly afterward, “to be with the Lord together,” and so forth, “when they divide the places by separate tombs.” But perhaps Prudentius means that St. Vincent’s body had been preserved by the faithful for later generations, or for the benefit of those to come. Thus, above verse 343, concerning the same martyr’s blood: “So that they may preserve the sacred protection for their own descendants.”

513. Stephen Anthony Morcellus, in his elegant and highly learned commentaries on the calendar of the Church of Constantinople, I, p. 134 and following, attempts to confirm by these verses that an ancient custom existed whereby Christians formerly began the solemn veneration of martyrs chiefly with the translation of their bodies. For he thinks that among our people “to raise the bodies of martyrs” meant precisely the same as “to decree heavenly honors for martyrs.” He observes that Prudentius mentions both burials in such a way that, once the first burial had been completed, the second clearly indicates that the martyr received the highest honor. I have willingly presented this interpretation, so that those who find it convincing may retain it; for it has been ingeniously devised. But, I think, Prudentius means nothing more than that an honorable altar could not be erected for St. Vincent during the persecution, but was erected once peace had been restored. Meanwhile the Christians regarded and venerated him as a martyr, and preserved his relics, even while he was alive, so that they might be a protection for those who came after them. This is clearly expressed in the *Acts*: “Therefore, because they could not, owing to the fury of the pagans, bury him with the fitting honor of veneration, they carried him to a certain small basilica to be buried. At last, when the cruelty of the faithless had ceased and the devotion of the faithful was increasing, the most blessed martyr was raised from there for an honorable burial and transported with due reverence, and was placed beneath the sacred altar outside the walls of that same city of Valencia, there to rest.” In the *Acts of St. Saturninus*: “At that time he received a makeshift burial”—or, according to another reading, “a tumultuous burial”—namely, because of the fury of the pagans. The official readings of the Spanish rite report that St. Valerius, who died not long after St. Vincent, arranged for a church dedicated to St. Vincent his deacon to be erected in the little town of Anet; this is not confirmed by ancient monuments.]

The same power had commanded it,

the power that once, as Christ walked,

had subdued the swelling sea,

so that, treading upon the ocean’s back,

he might proceed with dry footsteps

without wetting his feet in the waves,

[480] the vast traveler of the whirlpool.

That very power now commands

the Red Sea to split open,

while, with the bottom exposed and dry,

the secure people make their way.

[485] And now it commands the sea also

to serve the holy body,

with the calm movements of its waters

bending submissively toward the curved shores.

A rock of millstone weight,

[490] [Col. 0405B] floating like gleaming foam,

a little basket, guardian of so great

a pledge, is carried by the waves.

The sailors watch in amazement

as it is borne across the marble sea.

[495] [Col. 0406A] It glides gently backward

with the favorable tide and wind.

They too strive, speeding onward,

to cleave the sea with a small vessel;

but the limbs fly far ahead

[500] toward earth’s tender embrace.

At last the quiet soil receives

the body brought back,

before the ship, driven with all its strength,

could touch the harbor.

[505] Happy is that retreat

of the pleasant shore, which, cherishing

the sacred entrails in its sands,

provided the place of a tomb,

while the pious care of the saints,

[510] [Col. 0406B] lamenting, adorns the mound

and entrusts the body to the tomb,

preserving it for the life to come.

But soon, when the enemies had been subdued,

515. *Altar*: “an altar,” “a recess,” I.

517. *Subjecta*: “the limbs,” I.

519. *Auram*: “grace,” I.

520. *Perfusa*, namely, “steeped in heavenly grace,” I.

521. *Corpus*: “the place,” I.

[Col. 0407B] 525. *Illis*: “the Maccabees,” I.

[Col. 0408A] 527. *Malorum*: “of hardships,” I.

528. *Supremus*: “last,” “final,” I.

529. *Sector*: “Isaiah,” I.

531. *Segmenta*: “pieces”; strictly speaking, these are women’s garments, but not in this passage, I., Vat. A.]

515. Rat. has *quietam*, but it was corrected to *quietem*. Ald. has *debitum*, namely, “the altar owed.” Giselinus had printed it thus, but corrected it to *debitam*, which is found in our older manuscripts and in those of Heinsius.

517. Chamillardus says that Prudentius uses *sacrarium* for *pastophorium* or *secretary*, namely, that part of the temple where sacred objects are stored and where the holy of holies is located. But since *sacrarium* also means “altar,” I understand it rather of the altar, concerning which Prudentius spoke shortly before and beneath which the bones of the holy martyrs were placed, as he testifies at the end of *Eulalia* and of the hymn on the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza.

[Col. 0407D] 518. Vatt. A and B, Mar., Rat., and Prag. have *jam jamque ad aram*, “already, already at the altar.” *Imamque ad aram*, “and deep beneath the altar,” is better. Alex. in the first hand has *imamque ad oram*, “and deep beneath the edge,” less suitably. Prudentius seems to indicate a distinction between *ara* and *altare*: the bodies of the saints were buried beneath the altar, not beneath the sacrificial platform, but beneath the ground beside the altar. See the commentary on verse 170 of the *Passion of Hippolytus*.

519. Nebrissensis, Chamillardus, and Cellarius explain the words as meaning that the martyrs’ bones remain intact, preserved by divine favor. Teolius understands them much better as referring to the Eucharistic sacrament, which was celebrated at the altar and over the martyrs’ bones. See the commentary on verse 213 of the hymn of St. Eulalia. I also think Prudentius alludes to the opening or openings made in the upper part of the tombs of the holy martyrs, through which cloths, nard, and oil were inserted, so that, through contact with the tomb, the power of miracles might be made more manifest—as though Prudentius wished that power, arising from a heavenly gift or from the Eucharist, to flow outward like a breath. St. Paulinus, in fragment 9 of an uncertain *Natalis*: “And although hidden from ancient time in the tombs, yet, living by God’s reviving power and surviving in their limbs, the grace that breathes divinity in the martyr’s bones brightens them for the people, while the buried man lives by his merit”; and in *Natalis* 13, concerning the tomb of St. Felix: “This surface of the tablet opens with a double mouth, offering beneath it openings for the nard poured in; the sacred dust, coming from its resting place, sanctifies, healing with the hidden breath of the spirit.” In the hymn of St. Hippolytus, concerning his tomb: “They pour forth balsams, and moisten their faces with tears.”

520. Ald. and Gis. have *subter*. Weitz., with most manuscripts, has *subtus*. Cellarius, under the word *PERFUSA*, cites verse 131 of Fructuosus: “And the bones are said to be drenched with wine,” as Barthius had already indicated in *Adversaria* LXI.9. But in that hymn the subject is bones not yet buried; here it is bones placed beneath the sanctuary.

523. The history in 2 Maccabees, chapter 7, describes the death of the seven brothers called Maccabees, because that book contains the account of their tortures and death. Compare *Romanus*, verses 751 and following.

524. Alex. writes *Esaiae*, with Weitz. and others. Ald., Giselinus in his first edition, and Fabr. have *secto* without *-que*. The tradition that the prophet Isaiah was cut apart with a wooden saw is exceedingly constant among the Jews and is confirmed by numerous authorities, including Justin, Origen, Lactantius, Basil, Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, and other Fathers. Consult the interpreters on verse 37 of chapter 11 of the Apostle’s Epistle to the Hebrews: “They were stoned, they were sawn apart,” and so forth. This marks the distinction between *proximus* and *vicinus*: *proximus* denotes one than whom no one is nearer, whereas *vicinus* need not be the nearest if someone else is nearer. Plautus, Terence, Cicero, and others elegantly join *vicinus proximus*, “the nearest neighbor”; for someone can be *proximus*, “nearest,” without being *vicinus*, “neighbor,” as in Virgil, *Aeneid* V: “Next to him, but next at a long interval.” Sometimes this distinction is not observed, and *proximus* is used for *vicinus proximus*, “the nearest neighbor.”

525. Aldus has, incorrectly, *contingit*.

532. Giselinus says that the received reading is *aut vinclis dedit*, but not without a serious error. Perhaps this was the reading in the Daventrian edition, which we have not seen; it is certainly found in Sich. and Fabr., but in Aldus *aut undis dedit* is clearly printed.

533. Ald. and Giselinus in the first edition have *nam* instead of *num*. Weitz. cites Fabricius for *nam*, but Fabricius in fact reads *num*. That alone is correct.

535. Widm. above and Gis. at the margin have *ruptamve*. *Raptamve* is better. Properly speaking, a skin is *rapta* when it is stripped from a living creature, as in Seneca, “fiber torn from living breasts,” and in Virgil, “he tore out the entrails from the living.” See Brissonius, *De Formulis*, p. 23, who gives several ancient examples and notes that entrails were therefore torn out so that, while still breathing and throbbing, they could be consulted.]

[Note: [Col. 0409B]

538. *Brabii*: “of the prize or reward,” I.

540. *Laureas*: “crowns” or “victories”; for the laurel is used for a crown, I.

541. *Victor*: namely, “you,” I.

552. *Stipitem*: “a block,” by means of a strap or sinew, I.

553. *Testeum*: for potsherds were broken beneath the martyr, so that he might lie more harshly, I.

554. *Parta*: syncopated form, I.

561. *Diem*: “his own day,” I.

562. *Ore et pectore*: “with mouth and heart,” “with praise and vow,” I.

566. *Favorem*: “aid,” I.

572. *Perfunctam*: “service completed,” I.

573. *Quae*: “the flesh,” I.

[Note: [Col. 0409B]

537. In several common editions the error *obis* has crept in for *o bis*; Aldus gave occasion for it, either because he printed it so or because he did not divide it clearly enough. Nebrissensis already read *o bis*, and others had read it before Barthius, who, unaware of this correction, attempted another in *Adversaria* LXI.9. He therefore read: *Solus tu obis bis inclyte*. The reading of the manuscripts must be retained.

538. *Brabium* is the prize of victory. Modern writers prefer *braveium*, and Chamillardus says that *bravium* is a corrupt form; yet it is so read in the common text, and it is not as corrupt as Chamillardus thinks. Some write *brabium*, others *bravium*; but among the Greeks, from whom the word passed to ecclesiastical writers, it is written βραβεῖον, “prize.”

544. I understand “the robber” to mean Datianus rather than the devil, as some interpret it. In the hymn on the eighteen martyrs, verse 186: “Both, having confessed the Lord, stood boldly against the rage of robbers.”

548. Cellarius objects that this is fitting to Christ alone. But the doctrine of the intercession of saints is not to be sought from grammarians, nor from Cellarius and his followers, but from Prudentius and his contemporary holy Fathers, who all speak thus with one voice.

549. This form of prayer is very familiar to poets and orators.

552. Gifanius thinks that by the word *robur* Prudentius calls the prison stake an *eculeus*, or rack. But from the epithet “prison” and from the order in which the punishments are narrated, it is clear that the prison stake was a piece of timber or a block, as the gloss says, into which the feet were inserted. See above the commentary on verse 251.

555. Heinsius, with Ald., Oxon., and Sich., reads *per quem*, which, Heinsius declares, Weitz ought not to have changed. But Weitz followed the authority of the better manuscripts: Vatt. A, B, P, and Q, Alex., Mar., Rat., Prag., and others read *et quem*; nor does Heinsius cite any manuscript except Oxon. Yet *per quem* is more elegant and coheres better with what precedes.

[Col. 0410B] 556. The fact that the little bed on which St. Vincent lay was preserved for religious reasons is no slight evidence of the care of early Christians in obtaining and cautiously keeping the relics of martyrs. From this it is easy to answer those who ask how the relics of martyrs could have reached us in unbroken succession from so many and such ancient times.

561. A similar formula of prayer occurs often among Greeks and Latins. Terence, in the prologue to the *Hecyra*: “If I have never greedily set a price upon my art . . . permit me to obtain my request.”

562. The Mozarabic Breviary has *veneremur*; read *veneramur*, as later *sternimur*.

563. Vat. A, Mar., Rat., and Weitz. read *gaudia*. Most, including the old editions, read *gaudio*.

565. Fabr., Sich., and Gis. have *huc tu illabere*. Aldus and the manuscripts, more neatly, have *huc illabere*.

567. Vat. B, Rat., Mar. in the first hand, and some manuscripts cited by Weitz. have *sensu*.

568. Mar., as a divergent reading, has *solamen indulgentiae*.

569. Mar., Rat., and Weitz., with his manuscripts, have *restat*. Ald., Gis., and most manuscripts have *restet*, which is sound. For the particle *sic*, when placed after prayers, carries an optative force. Prudentius likewise, in the *Hippolytus*, after asking Bishop Valerian to celebrate Hippolytus’s feast-day in his diocese, says at verses 239 and following: “So may almighty Christ hear you praying for the people whose life has been entrusted to you.” Observe the poet’s most felicitous vein, and note what he wishes for Valerian and what for Vincent. For it is certain that complete human glory arises from the union of body and soul on the day of judgment, and that some accidental glory, as theologians call it, accrues even to the soul itself at the resurrection of the body. Mariettus, who read *restat* in his manuscript, inferred that Prudentius held the opinion, shared by many other Fathers, that the coming of the Lord and the last day of judgment were near.

570. The Mozarabic Breviary has *cum excitatam*.

571. The Prague manuscript transposes these verses, placing *Virtute* first and then *Carnem*.

572. Several common editions incorrectly have *perfuncta*.

573. On the resurrection of the body see the hymn *Exsequiarum*. After this hymn of St. Vincent, Vat. A has the hymn in honor of the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza; Vat. B has the *Passion of St. Laurence*.

The title is taken from Mar. and Rat., in which this hymn is placed after the hymn of St. Eulalia. Vat. A has: “Hymn in honor of the most blessed martyrs Fructuosus, bishop, Augurius, and Eulogius.” There it is placed after the hymn of the eighteen martyrs. Aldus: “Ode in praise of the most blessed martyrs Fructuosus, bishop of the Church of Tarragona, and Augurius and Eulogius, deacons.” Aldus writes *Terraconensis*, and shortly afterward, at verse 1, *Terraco*. Heinsius: “Hymn in honor of the most blessed martyrs Fructuosus, bishop of the Church of Tarragona, and Augurius and Eulogius, deacons”; he notes that Ambr. reads *Angorii* for *Augurii*, and Ox. *Aucorii*. Weitz. does almost the same as we do. In Alex., after the *Passion of Agnes*: “The Passion of Agnes ends. The hymn in honor, etc., begins,” as in Heinsius. Parrhasius: “Hymn in praise of the most blessed martyrs Fructuosus, bishop of Tarragona, and Eugorius and Eulogius, deacons.” He afterward also writes *Eugorius*, but in the corrected text says that some read *Augori*. Heinsius notes that the martyrologies celebrate, on 12 Kalends of September, the feast of Saints Julius, Julianus, Vincentius, Augurius, and Eulogius, according to a very ancient manuscript, as Holstenius testifies in his notes on that passage. These, however, seem different from St. Fructuosus and his companions, whose feast is kept on 21 January. Ruinart held the Acts copied by the Bollandists for that day to be authentic, and confirmed this judgment by the authority of St. Augustine and Prudentius. Ruinart published a somewhat fuller text from manuscript codices. No Acts of Spanish martyrs are older or more genuine. Their martyrdom is assigned to 21 January 259, which fell on a Friday. I have spoken of these saints and their relics in the *Hymnodia Hispanica* for 21 January. Nebrissa and Chamillardus affirm that they were Tarraconensians; but this is neither inferred from Prudentius’s hymn nor established by the genuine Acts. Flórez, *Hispania Sacra*, XXV, treatise 63, chapter 2, argues that they were Tarraconensians from certain words of the Gothic office, where this is expressed fairly clearly, and because Prudentius says in *Peristephanon* hymn 4: “Tarraco, mother of the pious, you will offer Christ a lovely diadem with three jewels,” etc. Certainly these saints are to be numbered among those whose homeland Prudentius did not state in their hymn; nor does he celebrate Tarragona for any reason other than their martyrdom, as is clear from the opening verses. In the Mozarabic Breviary for 21 January this entire hymn is read, with stanzas divided into groups of four verses. You will easily see how corrupt the first stanza is if you compare it with Prudentius; for the breviary prints: “Happy Tarragona, with your Fructuosus, raises her head with fires; a choir shines afar with the twin Levites. God looks kindly upon us through these pious men.” You see that the one word *coruscum* has been corrupted and divided into two verses, *chorus Cum*, and that from the three Spanish words *His piis nos* have been made, to say nothing of other errors.]

Now that peace has been restored to the just,

[515] the altar grants the blessed bones

their due rest.

For, placed beneath the sanctuary,

buried deep beneath the altar,

they draw in the breath of heavenly grace,

[520] steeped beneath in it.

Thus the body: but the very seat of God

contains what it has received.

It lies beside the brothers Maccabees

and near the sawn-apart Isaiah.

[525] [Col. 0408A] A simple crown of punishments

fell to those men;

death’s final end

brought their sufferings to an end.

What did the one who cut him apart dare?

[530] Did he cast the severed pieces

of the body, after the saw,

before wild beasts,

or give them to the waves?

Did the tyrant tear out

[535] the tongue of the Maccabean martyr,

or strip away the skin

from his head?

Did he offer it to bloodstained birds?

You alone, twice renowned,

alone did you bear away

the palm of a double prize:

[540] you won two crowns at once.

Victorious in death over suffering,

then afterward, after death,

you trample down the robber

with the same victorious triumph,

with your body alone.

[545] Be present now and receive

the suppliant voices of those who pray,

an effective advocate for our guilt

before the Father’s throne.

Through you, through that prison,

[550] an increase of your honor,

through fetters, flames, and claws,

through the prison stake,

through that fragment of pottery

by which your glory grew,

[555] [Col. 0410A] through which we, your trembling descendants,

kiss the little bed,

have mercy on our prayers,

so that Christ, appeased toward his own,

may incline his favorable ear

[560] and charge none of our offenses against us.

If with mouth and heart

we rightly venerate the solemn day,

if with joy we prostrate ourselves

before the traces of your footsteps,

[565] glide down here for a little while,

bringing Christ’s favor,

so that our burdened senses may feel

the relief of indulgence.

Thus may there now be no delay

[570] [Col. 0410B] but that he, noble in spirit,

may resume the resurrected flesh,

which has completed an equal service of courage,

so that, sharing in his labors

[575] and having borne the common ordeal,

it too may be co-heir of glory

for ever through all ages.

## VI. Hymn of the Most Blessed Martyrs Fructuosus, Bishop of the Church of Tarragona, and Augurius and Eulogius, Deacons

Happy Tarragona, Fructuosus, raises her head,

flashing with your fires

and shining from afar with the twin deacons.

God looks kindly upon the Spaniards,

[5] since the Trinity, almighty,

crowns the Iberian citadel

with a threefold martyrdom.

[Col. 0412A] Burning Augurius reaches heaven;

and bright Eulogius likewise proceeds

together to Christ’s heavenly seat.

[10] Fructuosus, illustrious in name,

leader, guide, and teacher of those men,

went forth from the episcopal dignity

to such great glory.

For, summoned suddenly

by the governor’s order,

the priest had come to the tribunal,

[15] accompanied by his two deacons.

From there the executioner,

fed on blood, dragged the men

to the prison’s chains;

Fructuosus gladly hastens forward.

And so that fear might strike neither of his companions,

[20] [Col. 0413A]

21. *Calore*: “love,” I.

24. *Palma*: “reward,” I.

30. *Purgamen*: “of sins,” I.

[Col. 0414B] 33. *Catastae*: “burning racks,” “the fiery execution frame,” “iron bed,” I.

35. *Insolens*: “proud,” I.

43. *Refert*: “answers,” Mar.

46. *Prosatum*: “born,” I.

24. Vat. A, Egm., Hailsbr., and Pal. have *nec mors*. Most have *ne mors*. The Mozarabic Breviary has *en* instead of *est*, not inelegantly.

25. The martyrs approached the prison with joyful and eager spirit. Damasus, concerning St. Agatha: “The prison was a delight to her.”

30. Ald., Hailsbr., Vat. Q, and apparently Alex. have *et purgamen aquae*, together with Noms., Ox., Alt., Thuan., Gis., Heins., the Mozarabic Breviary, and others. Vat. P incorrectly repeats *et purgamen aquae aquae*. Urb., Parrhasius, Vat. B, [Col. 0413C] Mar., Rat., and Weitz. have *et purgamina quae*. Egm., Pal., and Vat. A have *expurgamen aquae*. Chamillardus understands this of baptism and the sacrament of penance. The *Acts* report that Rogatianus was baptized in prison; concerning the other sacrament of penance, one can only conjecture. Prudentius had earlier spoken of the darkness of prisons, in *Vincentius* verses 237 and following, and in *Cyprianus* verses 51 and following. See Sagittarius, *De Cruciatibus*, chapter 2, where he shows that prisons were commonly called caves, caverns, and abysses because of their darkness.

33. Christians were formerly called brothers, as I said in the note on verse 73 of the hymn of St. Laurence. The other conjectures by which these three martyrs are made brothers are groundless. Here, too, *catasta* means the execution frame on which the martyrs were to be burned, as in hymn 1 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 56: “after the fiery racks.”

34. Vat. A in the first hand and Rat. write *Emelianus*. Others have *Emilianus*, others *Aemilianus*. This Aemilianus held the prefecture in Spain in the year 259 and is therefore distinct from the emperor Aemilianus, who was killed in 253 or 254.

36. The Mozarabic Breviary incorrectly has *daemoniacas*.

37. The pagans objected to and reproached the Christians for this: that they lured women and ignorant people into the Christian religion. Minucius: “They form a people of profane conspiracy from the lowest dregs, gathering the ignorant and credulous women who, through the weakness of their sex, are easily led astray.” See the notes of Heraldus, Elmenhorstius, and Wowerus on this passage.

39. Weitz., with Hailsbr., writes *distituant*. Pagans especially chose groves and mountains for the worship of their gods; this is suggested by Deuteronomy 12:2: “Destroy all the places in which the nations whom you are about to dispossess worshiped their gods, upon the high mountains and hills and beneath every leafy tree.”

40. Rat. in the first hand; Mar. above, as a divergent spelling; Parrhasius: *damna*, which Bigotius conjectured from *damnas* in Ambr., as also above in Rat. Most have *damnes*. The Mozarabic Breviary corruptly has *Augusti dogma*, “the dogma of Augustus,” instead of *anile dogma*, “the old-womanish dogma.” Lactantius, book I, chapter 13: “For if women fall through the weakness of their sex—for sometimes these people call that superstition womanish and old-womanish—men at least are wise.” And in chapter 20: “Soon, surely, the error and folly of those people will be mocked by old women, whom they despise, and by our own children.”

[Col. 0414C] 42. Vatt. A, P, Alex., Egm., Hailsbr., Pal., Widm. above, and Gis. have *ut colamus*, which Heinsius retained with Giselinus, noticing nothing contrary in his own manuscripts. Vatt. B, Q, Urb., Mar., Ald., Torn., Galland., and Weitz. have *hoc colamus*. Weitz. says that Aldus has *omne* instead of *omnes*. I find *omnes* in Aldus and the others. Fabricius is also cited by Weitz. for *ut*. Fabricius gives both *ut* and *hoc*, namely: “It was commanded by the mouth of Caesar Gallienus: ‘What the prince worships, let us all worship.’”

44. Nebrissensis thought nothing should be changed, but suspected *deorum*, “of the gods,” instead of *dierum*, “of the days,” which did not displease Chamillardus, as though the poet were saying “the god of gods.”

46. Prag. and Parrhasius have *satum*, contrary to the meter.]

48. From the Acts: The governor Aemilianus said to Bishop Fructuosus: “Are you a bishop?” Bishop Fructuosus said: “I am.” Aemilianus said: “You were.” The forceful word “you were,” as in Virgil: “We were Trojans; Ilium was,” and “the great glory of the Teucrians.” “I lived”; “we live.” Prudentius, in the preface to the poems: “For ten five-year periods now, / If I am not mistaken, we have been.” [Col. 0414D] Plutarch, in his *Alexander*, reports that when Alexander asked an ancient gymnosophist whether the living or the dead were more numerous, he replied: “The living, for the dead do not even exist.” Here the gymnosophist would have mocked the expression “he has gone to the greater number” for “he is dead.” By such ways of speaking—“you were,” “we have lived,” “we were”—the imminence of life’s end is signified. Hericus of Auxerre, book V: “We have lived, and have traversed the hours allotted to life.”

49. Rat., Parrhasius, against the meter, read *furorem* instead of *furor*. Prag. has *ut refrenet*, not improperly.

51. Rat. has *vulgus*. The Acts relate that Fructuosus was loved even by the pagans themselves: “Because he had such love not only from the brethren but also from the pagans.”

The energetic Teacher, as he goes, strengthens [them],

And kindles faith with the warmth of Christ.

“Stand with me, men,” the bloodstained serpent

Calls the ministers of God to punishment:

Let death not terrify you; the palm is ready.

[25] Prison is a step toward the crown for Christ’s people;

Prison advances one to the heights of heaven,

Prison reconciles the blessed to God.”

With these words, they approach the place of confinement.

There they undergo the mystical washing,

[30] And the darkness is astonished at the cleansing water.

1028 For six continuous days they lie hidden there.

At last the three brothers stand before the savage enemy’s tribunal;

The three scaffolds tremble for the brothers.

The judge Aemilianus stood over them,

[33] Savage, agitated, insolent, profane;

[Col. 0414A] He ordered the demonic altars to be worshiped.

“You, who are a teacher,” he said, “are sowing a novel kind

Of invention, so that foolish girls may abandon

The sacred groves and leave Jupiter behind,

[40] If you are wise, condemn an old-woman’s superstition.

By order issued from the mouth of Caesar Gallienus,

Let us all worship what the prince worships.”

1029 The priest calmly answered him as he spoke:

“I worship the eternal Prince, the Maker

Of days, and the lord of Gallienus;

And Christ, begotten from the everlasting Father,

Whose servant I am, and shepherd of his flock.”

Smiling, he said: “You have already been.”

Nor does the madness delay or restrain his anger;

He orders them to be burned in savage fires.

They exult, and prevent the crowd from weeping.

53. *Libandum*: “to be drunk,” “to be tasted,” I.

55. *Resignat*: “opens,” I.

56. *Jus dicatum*: “a prescribed fast,” I.

57. *Sacrum*: “a fast,” I., Mar.

58. *Crucis*: “of the passion,” I.

61. *Locum*: “the amphitheater,” Mar.

[Col. 0416A] 62. *Cavea*: “the amphitheater,” I.

64. *Perstrepunt*: “resound,” I.

66. *Fremit*: “rejoices.”—*Voluptas*: “the pleasure, in watching, of those who see such things,” I.

69. *Supremis*: “highest,” I. *Maximis*: Mar.]

53. Mar., Weitz. with some of their witnesses, read *poculum ferentes*, “bringing a cup.” Baronius, *Annals*, year 34, shows that the ancients customarily offered some drink to those condemned to death, so that, deprived of their senses, they might be free from the awareness of pain. He is discussing the myrrh-flavored wine offered to the Savior and cites these verses. John Tamayo de Salazar has more on this same subject in his *Hispanic Martyrology*.

54. Since these holy martyrs suffered on 21 January, no other fast can have been intended at that time except the one observed by the ancient Christians on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, as I explained in the notes on the hymn *Of Those Who Fast* and *After the Fast*. It was certainly a fast that could be broken at the ninth hour, as the following verse makes clear. It should also be noted that the ancient Christians, while fasting, abstained from drinking wine.

55. It is sufficiently clear that this passage concerns the partial fast observed on a station day, from the mention of the ninth hour as a suitable time for ending the fast. This was the Catholic custom, whereas the Montanists prolonged the station until evening. Tertullian, in *On Fasting*, or *Against the Psychics*—as he calls the Catholics—chapter 10, writes:

“Likewise they accuse our stations as unworthy, and some even as appointed until late, under the name of novelty; they also say that this observance is to be undertaken according to one’s own choice and not prolonged beyond the ninth hour, obviously following their own custom. . . . First, they should be asked why they prescribe the ninth hour as the limit for ending stations.”

Rigaltius thinks that *stationes nostras, ut indictas* should be read, “our stations, as appointed.” Priorius believes that Tertullian is attacking the Montanists here, not the Catholics; he offers no sound basis for this. Bingham, book XXI, chapter 3, §3, has more on the ninth hour, at which the station could be ended. Cassian, *Conferences* 2, chapter 26: “The ninth hour has been granted as a sufficiently convenient and useful time for taking food.” Alardus Gazaeus notes that this time for eating was granted, as it were, by grace and indulgence, because the first monks fasted until evening. Prudentius himself suggests this in *Cathemerinon* 8, verse 65: “A relaxed and unrestricted manner of abstaining / Is established for all.” Saints Basil and Benedict likewise prescribe the ninth hour for ending the fast.

56. Baronius, under the year 262, no. 65, thinks that by these words Fructuosus does not refer to the customary fast but to a stricter and longer one, namely from Wednesday to Friday. For, as is clear from Tertullian, bishops during times of persecution and in the face of some grave necessity used to prescribe stricter fasts. But Prudentius clearly describes the fast of a station, and it is shown that the holy martyrs observed the fast not so much from some vow as from the rule of ecclesiastical custom, by the names with which he calls the fast—“prescribed observance” and “sacred”—just as in the hymn *Of Those Who Fast* and *After the Fast* he called it a feast and a victim. The Acts confirm this:

“And when many, out of fraternal love, offered them [a cup] mixed with condiments so that they might drink, he said: ‘It is not yet the hour for ending the fast.’ For it was the fourth hour of the day. Indeed, they had solemnly celebrated Wednesday in prison. Therefore on Friday he hastened, joyful and secure, so that with the martyrs and prophets he might end the station in the paradise that the Lord has prepared for those who love him.”

57. Thus in hymn 8, *After the Fast*: “The ninth hour rolls the sun downward. . . . / We end the feast.”

58. Prag. has *crucis sub ara*, “beneath the altar of the cross.”

61. The amphitheater is being described, which consisted, as it were, of two theaters; for this reason the place is said to be enclosed by a rounded *cavea*. *Cavea* was the name for the area also commonly called the arena, because it was covered with sand so that gladiators would not easily slip. The prison where they were usually held was also called a *cavea*, as were the tiers in the circus from which the people watched. These tiers consisted of the highest, middle, and lowest *cavea*. The first, or lowest, was assigned to the senators and equestrians; the middle to the common people; the highest and last to women, as may be gathered from Seneca, book XI, *On Tranquility*. Earlier writers used *cavea* of a theater. Lipsius, *On the Amphitheater*, chapter 2, proves from the authorities of Tertullian, Prudentius, and similar writers that *cavea* could also be used of an amphitheater. The ruins of the Tarraconensian amphitheater still exist, but only ruins.

64. Chamillardus notes that gladiatorial spectacles were completely prohibited by King Theoderic. But it is clear that they had been prohibited much earlier by Honorius, as I said in the commentary at the end of book II of *Against Symmachus*.

65. Latinius reads *ense diro*, “with a dreadful sword.”

66. It has been noted in the commentary on book II of *Against Symmachus*, verse 1123, that *voluptas* is used in a special sense of spectacles. What now occurs to me is that Horace’s verse in the *Art of Poetry*, “Let fictions created for pleasure be close to truth,” can be understood of things invented for representation on the stage, for Horace is discussing theatrical poems at that point.

67. See another description of the pyre for burning martyrs in *Romanus*, verses 846 and following. Such pyres were constructed quickly. Eusebius, book IV, chapter 11, reports from the letter of the Smyrnaeans concerning the martyrdom of St. Polycarp:

“The people immediately brought together wood and branches, partly from workshops and partly from the baths, with incredible speed; above all, the Jews, as is their custom, eagerly contributing their labor to this task.”

69. In the Mozarabic Breviary, *fascibus* is found, but the law of the meter requires *facibus*. Nebrissensis understands *faces supremas* as “the last torches in the order of preparation.” Cellarius says that *supremis* may be taken as “funereal” or “mournful.” On a pyre, the torches nearest the body and burning last together with the body could be called “last”; and because the pyre was raised upward, they could also be called “highest” and “uppermost.” But Cellarius’s interpretation is more pleasing in this passage.]

The priest sees certain people from the crowd

Offering him a cup to drink:

“I am fasting,” he says; “I refuse the drink.”

[55] 1030 The ninth hour has not yet released the day;

I shall never violate the prescribed observance,

Nor will death itself dissolve my sacred fast.

Thus Christ, thirsting at the hour of the cross,

Refusing the cup offered to him,

[60] And unwilling to drink, completed his thirst.”

[Col. 0416A] Meanwhile they enter the place enclosed

1031 By a rounded cage, wet with the great

Blood of wild beasts, which frenzy often visits,

When bloody spectacles resound,

[63] And a worthless gladiator, struck by a hard sword,

Falls, while pleasure roars.

Here a black servant, amid the blazing pyre,

Ordered to prepare the burning punishment,

Built the pyre with the highest torches.

[70] [Col. 0417A]

70. *Qui*: “the pyre.”—*Solvit*: “destroyed, reduced to ashes by fire,” I.

71. *Lucis*: “of heaven,” I.

72. *Carceris*: “of the body.”—*Antro*: “the body,” I.

73. *Sodales*: “his companions,” that is, his own, I.

77. *Facessite*: “withdraw,” I.

78. *Gravet*: “hinder.”—*Obsequela*: this service is called *obsequium*, and *obsequela* is feminine, like *suasio* and *suadela*, with the same meaning, I.

[Col. 0418B] 79. *Atquin*: “certainly,” I.

85. *Ediderat*: “had uttered,” I.

88. *Cremationem*: “the pyre,” I.

90. *Pura*: “bare,” Vat. A.

91. *Calce mera*: “with a pure or bare foot.”

94. *Credite*: “all of you,” I.

95. *Citata*: “swift,” I.

98. *Contigit*: “it happened,” I.

99. *Olim*: “in the future,” I., Mar.]

70. Ald. mistakenly has *contremenda solvi*. Vat. B, Alex., Mar., and Parrhasius have *concremata solvit*. Heinsius also printed this, together with Oxon., Thuan., and Ambr. Later editors follow Heinsius, except Gallandius, who does not approve *concremata*. Vat. A, P, Q, Urb., the Mozarabic Breviary, Weitz. with his witnesses, Prag., and other old witnesses read *concremanda*. In Rat. *concremenda* has been corrected to *concremanda*. Prag. has *solum* for *solvit*, but there is no sense.

72. Vat. A, B, Alex. in the first hand, Mar., Prag. in the first hand, Rat., Widm., Hailsbr. and Bong. in the first hand, Thuan., and Heins. have *expediret*. Vat. P, Q, Urb., most of Heinsius’s witnesses, Ald., Parrhasius, the Mozarabic Breviary, Weitz., and others have *expedivit*, which Gallandius adopted, although he did not reject *expediret*.

73. Alex., Vat. Q, Mar., Prag., Rat., and *pii* with most editions. Aldus, the Mozarabic Breviary, Parrhasius, Vat. P, Urb., and others have *piis*.

74. Ald., Parrhasius, and the Mozarabic Breviary write *calciamenta*.

75. In the Acts he is called Augustalis, the lector of Fructuosus.

76. In Mar. there seems initially to have been *ora*, later changed to *ore*; in the margin, as a variant reading, *ora*, which alone is correct.

77. Ald. mistakenly has *premit*. Parrhasius corruptly has *sat est, si te*, “it is enough if you,” and affirmed that this was read in many copies; but in corrected editions he thought *facessite, inquit*, “withdraw, he said,” should be written.

78. Mar., Prag., and Vat. A have *ne nostram*.

79. The Mozarabic Breviary incorrectly separates the words as *at quin*. Jews customarily walked barefoot for worship. The same practice existed among other peoples. See Broverius, *On Worship*, chapter 16, where he attempts to prove that going barefoot was not a festival practice peculiar to the Hebrews; he also shows that some Christians were accustomed to walk barefoot in processions and in the adoration of the cross. Fructuosus appears to have done this freely, not under compulsion, perhaps moved by the example of Moses, which is related afterward.

83. Ald. has *ut siem*. In Alex. it seems to have been *ut fuam*. The true reading, and certainly the more common among the manuscripts, is *ut fiam*, with the first syllable of *fiam* shortened. Prudentius also shortened it elsewhere; Arator, Tertullian, and others did likewise. Gis. in the first edition printed *siem*, which in the second edition he changed to *fiam*, reproving the ignorant correctors who had corrupted the manuscript reading. Cellarius notes that “they ask him, while he is still alive and surviving, not when he is dead. . . . At that time the invocation of the dead had not yet become established.” Who would not laugh at this man’s leaden cleverness? It occurs once that they asked him while he was alive, and he foolishly concludes from this that at that time the invocation of the dead had not yet become established. Prudentius says a hundred times that martyrs who have died are invoked by entire provinces, yet Cellarius does not for that reason believe that invocation of the dead had become established in that age, and scarcely admits that it had then begun. In this very hymn, verse 145, these words are especially splendid: “It is a joy to exult in three patrons, / By whose protection all the peoples / Of the Pyrenean lands are cherished.” Had invocation of the dead not become established in that age? It was indeed then in use, as it is now, for Christians to commend themselves to the prayers of the living. But this invocation of the living, just as it is not opposed to invocation of the dead in our age, was likewise not opposed to it in the age of Prudentius or before it.

87. Egm. has *rubrum*: correct to *rubum*. See the commentary on hymn 5 of *Cathemerinon*.

91. Ald., Gis., Urb., Alex. above, Parrhasius, and the Mozarabic Breviary have *mero*. Most have *mera*. Juvenal, satire 6: “Where the kings observe the festivals with a bare foot.” Broverius, in the place cited, says that Juvenal is producing nonsense about the Jews, who, rather than walking barefoot, clothed themselves in all their Sabbath garments, thereby honoring the Sabbath through the splendor of their dress. On the word *merus*, see the commentary on verse 26 of *Apotheosis*.

94. La Thuan. has *credita poena*, “the punishment believed in.”

95. Mariettus advises considering whether *punctu* should be read, since in his manuscript it is clearly written thus without erasure; in Rat. it appears with a dot, but beneath an erasure, and it certainly seemed to have originally been *punctu*.

99. Of *olim* for future time, Virgil, book IV of the *Aeneid*: “Now, one day, whenever strength shall present itself.” And book I: “You shall one day receive him in heaven, laden with the spoils of the East.”

100. Prag. mistakenly has *nec inter*. Mar. has *cremantes*, and in the margin, by the same hand, *crepantes*, as a variant reading.

101. Mar., Gis., and Alex. have *ipsis*; most have *ipsi*. Just as above “the scaffolds tremble,” so here “they threaten the furnaces,” to demonstrate the courage of their spirit. Hilary describes this in oratorical rather than Prudentius’s poetic manner, in his commentary on Psalm 65, no. 21:

“For some glory in the chains of prisons; others rejoice when scourged; others submit their happy necks to be cut off by the power of the irreligious; many run toward pyres that have been built, and, while the ministers of punishment tremble, leap into the fire with a devoted eagerness; others, being plunged into the depths, fall not into murderous waters but into the refreshment of eternal blessedness.”

The Acts say that the stakes to which the martyrs had been bound remained; consequently Florezius thinks that Prudentius spoke poetically when he says that they leapt into the fire. But the Acts can be understood as referring to the fork that was often inserted around the neck, with the arms of those about to be thrown onto the pyre twisted behind their backs. See the commentary on verse 851 of *Romanus*.]

While it reduces the bodies destined for burning to ashes,

1032 The pyre frees the souls burning with love of the light

From the prison-cavern it has broken open.

The devout companions vie in service:

With their sandals loosened,

[75] One of them bent forward and tried to remove them;

But the holy Fructuosus forbids

Their faces to be pressed downward. “Withdraw,” he says,

“Lest your service burden our death.

But I myself will loosen my feet,

[80] So that my footsteps, hindered by fetters,

May not rush into the fire with slow strides.

Why do your tears wet your streaming cheeks?

Why do you ask me to remember you,

1033 That I may pray to Christ for all the peoples?”

[85] [Col. 0417B] Scarcely had he said this when he himself loosens

[Col. 0418A] The coverings of his feet, just as Moses

Once did when he approached the bush.

It was not permitted to tread upon the sacred burning,

Or to stand before God,

[90] Before pure footprints had been planted.

He stood with a bare foot; behold, his spirit leaps

To heaven and scatters speech,

Which made all who heard tremble.

“Believe me, it is not the punishment you see,

[95] Which passes swiftly in a moment:

It does not seize life, but transforms it.

Happy souls, for whom it has happened to climb

Through fire to the lofty heights of the Thunderer,

1034 Whom everlasting fire will one day flee!”

[100] Meanwhile they enter amid swiftly crackling fires

[Col. 0418B] And threaten the furnaces themselves

103. *Nexus*: “a fastening,” I.

106. *Cohibere*: “to bind,” I.

109. *Specimen*: “a likeness,” I.

111. *Stupuit*: “was struck with amazement,” I.

115. *Vaporus*: “hot,” I.

116. *Orant*: “the saints,” I.

[Col. 0420B] 120. *Missos*: for *dimissos*, I.

121. *Domo*: “household,” Mar.

123. *Insignesque*: “glorious,” I.

125. *Notam*: “sign,” Iso.

126. *Forum*: “assembly,” Iso.

128. *Sudum*: “serenity,” I.]

102. Hailsbr. and Bong. in the first hand, Gis. in the margin, have *crepitantibus*, “crackling”; *trepidantibus*, “trembling,” is better.

103. The Mozarabic Breviary and Teol. have *retrorsum*, “backward.” Martyrs about to be burned were bound to a stake or with ropes, or fastened with nails. Hence Christians were called *semaxis*, from *axis*, “axle” or “stake.” “Although now you call us brushwood-bundled and *semaxii*, who are burned fastened to half a stake and surrounded by bundles of brushwood,” as Tertullian says in *Apology*, chapter 50. See plate XVII. Here the arms are understood to have been twisted behind the back before they entered the pyre.

104. The Mozarabic Breviary reads *renovaverant* incorrectly.

106. Vat. B, Q, and Prag. have *poena cohibere*, but the law of the meter requires *cohibere poena palmas*, “to restrain the hands with punishment.”

107. When the ancient Christians prayed, they raised and extended their arms in the manner of a cross. This was also customary among the Hebrews, as Prudentius himself sang in hymn 12 of *Cathemerinon*, verse 170, concerning Moses: “With arms spread upward . . . / Which at that time was the likeness of a cross.” See also verse 32 of hymn 4 of *Cathemerinon*. Victorius, published at Rome in 1760, explained an ancient gem engraved for Christian use. He presents an image of the Mother of God, which Victorius thinks was carved by an unskilled artist of the ninth century in two-colored sardonyx, with her hands extended as I have described, in the form of a cross, in the appearance of one praying or entreating God. Several similarly ancient paintings and marble reliefs are illustrated by Bosio, Aringhus, Ciampinius, Buonarrotius, Boldettus, Blanchinius, Bottarius, Broverius, and others.

110. Parrhasius has *Babylonium*, less correctly.

Of the story of the three boys, see *Apotheosis*.

114. Ald. writes *incohante*, “beginning.”

115. The Mozarabic Breviary has *vaporeus*, against the meter. Gis. in the first edition has *vaporis*. Chamillardus declares *vaporus ardor*, “vaporous heat,” harsh and barbarous, and says that *vaporus* for “vapor-bearing” occurs nowhere else except in Prudentius. But before Prudentius, Arnobius used *vaporus* in book VI: “That one is cold in harshnesses, this one hot,” where some less correctly read *vaporeum*. Nemesianus clearly has it in *Eclogue* 4, verse 63: “Three times with ribbons, three times with sacred foliage, three times with smoking incense he purified.” I have already noted in the hymn *Of St. Lawrence*, at verse 345, that *vapor* can be used for heat by the best writers.

116. Vat. A and B have *orant sancti ut*, “the saints pray that”; the meter does not permit this. Vat. Q has *advocaret*; above it correctly has *advolaret*.

117. The Mozarabic Breviary has *periculis*, against the meter.

120. Prag. and Gis. have *erant*; Bong. and Fabr. have *missis*; others have *missos*. Nebrissensis explains it as “for themselves,” that is, for themselves alone. Better, however, is “for himself,” that is, for God himself. Compare the hymn *Of the Burial*.

[Col. 0420C] 121. Egm. writes *satellis*. This also shows that, according to Prudentius, the souls of the devout are carried up to heaven when nothing remains to be purified. Chamillardus says that Prudentius altered some things here because the Acts relate that Babylon and Mygdonius saw heaven opened, and also that the daughter of Aemilianus’s household showed her mother Fructuosus and his companions going into heaven. But Prudentius agrees perfectly with the Acts, which read as follows:

“And heaven was opened, while our brothers Babylon and Mygdonius, from the household of the governor Aemilianus, saw it; they also showed the daughter of that same Aemilianus, their carnal mistress, holy Bishop Fructuosus with his deacons ascending into heaven crowned, while the stakes to which they had been bound still remained. And when they called Aemilianus, saying, ‘Come and see . . .,’ Aemilianus came but could not see them.”

126. Ambr. has *quo foro*, “to what forum,” from which Heinsius conjectured *quos foro*. Here *forum* may be understood as the place where criminals were punished; this was usually done in the forum itself, in amphitheaters, or in circuses.

127. Mar. in the first hand and Prag. have *haec dum*, less correctly. *Virginitas* is used for “a virgin,” as in Claudian, poem 18, book I, *Against Eutropius*: “The Vestal virgin approaches.”

128. Ald., Vat. B, Q, Urb., Mar., Prag., Rat., and Hailsbr. in the second hand; Sich., Gis., Ald., and Widm. in the first hand; Weitz. have *patente coelo*. Ambr., Alt., Thuan., Vat. A in the first hand, Vat. P, and Hailsbr. in the first hand have *parente caeco*. Alex. and Widm. above have *parente coelo*. Vat. A above has *patendo coelo*. The Mozarabic Breviary corruptly has “He deserved an unfaithful blind parent.” The Acts read: “Aemilianus came but was not worthy to see them.” If these Acts preceded Prudentius, there would be no doubt that Prudentius had referred to this passage. Otherwise *patente coelo*, “with heaven open,” is not a reading to be dismissed. Virgilian *sudum* occurs in book VIII: “They see it gleam through the clear sky.”]

129. Tibullus, book III, elegy 7: “Happy is anyone who, through another’s grief, learns to be able to escape his own.”

131. I discussed this verse in the prologue, no. 159. In the Acts: “When night came on, they hastened to the amphitheater with wine, so that they might extinguish the half-burned bodies.” The ancients washed the remains of cremated bodies with wine. Virgil, book VI: “They washed the remains and the ashes soaked with wine.” The pyre itself was extinguished with wine, and then friends or relatives gathered the bones and ashes. Tibullus’s verses, book III, elegy 2, concerning his bones after death, show that some used old wine: “And first let them sprinkle what they have gathered with aged Lyaeus.” To gather bones is a phrase proper to funerals; hence *ossilegium*, “bone-gathering”; and Martial uses the expression ambiguously: “Your heirs will read my poems, you say—when? It was already time for you, Sosibianus, to be gathered.” Compare Tibullus, book III, elegy 2.

So that the ashes of the burned body would not be mixed with the other ashes of the pyre, the body was placed in a bier in such a way that, once the pyre had been extinguished, its remains would be separate from the other ashes. It is also established that in the funerals of nobles a kind of linen was used that was not consumed. Pliny, book XIX, chapter 1, says: “Funerary tunics of kings separate the body’s ash from the remaining ash.” Desiderius Heraldus, *Adversaria* 1, chapter 7; Kirchmannus, book III, chapter 6; la Cerda, in his commentary on Virgil; and others collect further information about this rite. There is also a dissertation by Giovanni Ciampini, *On Incombustible Linen, or on the Stone Asbestos, and on the Method of Spinning It*, Rome, 1691. Kirchmannus, book III, chapter 7, does not believe that this linen was actually used and considers what others report about asbestos more like fables. Yet it is certain that a shroud of asbestos of remarkable size is still preserved at Rome in an urn in the Vatican Library. Five years ago, moreover, an asbestos shroud containing human bones was found at Rome near the Porta Capena, opposite the tomb of the Scipios.

Parrhasius punctuates the passage: “Each one claimed the Brothers for himself: such was their love.” Agobard, in his poem on the death of Charles and Leidrad, imitates Prudentius: “They quickly lift the bones of Pantaleon, / All together, and bind them in cloths.” In martyrologies, the seizure of martyrs’ bodies often occurs; it expresses the diligence of the faithful who are hurrying. In our Acts: “Quickly,” and immediately afterward, “Each one claimed for himself, as he could, the ashes gathered from those same martyrs.”

Florezius thinks this was said by anticipation, because on the very day of the martyrdom it would scarcely have been possible for marble to be cut. But such sepulchral urns were made and prepared by craftsmen and were readily available for purchase. Hence it sometimes happened that the characteristic signs of pagans appeared on Christian tombs.

141. The Mozarabic Breviary corruptly has *Mixto marmori pulvere saranda*; Vat. B has *mixtum* for *mixtim*. Mixed ashes sometimes occur on funerary monuments. Florezius discusses the relics at length.

142. In Vat. A the *o* after *honor* is missing. Parrhasius has *lumen* for *culmen*; this variation in the manuscripts should be noted. At the beginning Prudentius says that the head of Tarraco is raised, gleaming with the fires of these martyrs; now he says that the same head is raised by this threefold light. Therefore, if the manuscripts support it, I would readily read *lumen*.

143. In the hymn on the eighteen martyrs, concerning any city that rejoices in a martyr as its patron, verse 13: “Its head raised from the great world.” Chamillardus understands “our city” as Caesaraugusta, because Caesaraugusta was in the province of Tarraconensis, whose capital was Tarraco. Bartholomaeus Leonardus Argensola intended the same in a letter to Mariana. This interpretation does not please me, nor did it please Nebrissensis, Cellarius, Peveratus, Teolius, and countless others, who say that Prudentius calls Tarraco “our city,” although they deny that Tarraco was Prudentius’s homeland. Prudentius does indeed return to the thought of the first stanza and understands that the head of Tarraco is raised.

Paulinus, letter 4 to Ausonius: “And Tarraco, with its distinguished head, looks down upon the sea.” Although Tarraco was the capital of the province of Tarraconensis, I doubt whether it can appropriately be called the head of any city contained within that province, such as Caesaraugusta or Calagurris. For “head” means the head of a body, not the head of a foot or arm. From those who think otherwise I would like examples in which Rome was called the head of Bologna or Ferrara, or Madrid the head of Caesaraugusta or Calagurris.

Mozzius, in his Italian translation of the book *Peristephanon*, grasped the true meaning and rendered it thus:

“O triple honor, O threefold summit,  
By which our city raises its brow,  
More sublime than every city of Iberia!”

I mentioned this translation in the prologue, no. 121. Later I obtained a manuscript prepared for publication, prefaced by a life of Mozzius, in which the following is said of the work:

“As an ecclesiastical person, he was pleased to translate into unrhymed verse, in the most polished Tuscan speech, the hymns entitled *The Crowns* by Prudentius, the distinguished Christian poet, which are now being printed. He had often had them performed in the academies of his homeland, to universal satisfaction; and if death had not intervened, he had intended to continue translating the other books.”
