I have supplied the inscription found in Alex. In Vat. A it is the same, but reads “in honor” and “of the Church of Sesclana.” [Col. 0424B] Mar.: “The hymn begins in honor of Saint Quirinus, martyr and bishop of the Church of Suscla.” Rat. has the same, but “of the Church of Susciana.” Aldus: “Ode in praise of Quirinus, martyr and bishop of the Church of Sisciana.” Weitzius: “In honor of Quirinus, martyr and bishop of the Church of Susciana.” Fabr.: “To Quirinus, martyr and bishop of Siscian Illyria.” Heinsius agrees with Alex.

In Egm., Rott., Ox., Torr. (in two copies), and Alt., Sescia is written for Siscia. In Vat. Q, Scitia. In Widm., Suscia. Prag. has Sesciae; Vatt. A and B and Rat., Susciae; Mar., Sisciae. The name Siscia or Syscia is confirmed by Ptolemy, Strabo, Velleius Paterculus, Pliny, the Itinerary of Antoninus, the Ambrosian codex, the Chronicle of Eusebius, and many passages in the martyrologies. Siscia was a city of Upper Pannonia, at the confluence of the Colapis and the Savus, about which Pliny writes in Book III, chapter 25. It is now a village called Sisek or Sisseg, near the episcopal see of Zagreb. See Cellarius, *Ancient Geography*.

Concerning Quirinus, the Roman Martyrology says on 4 June, following Prudentius’s hymn: “At Siscia in Illyria, Saint Quirinus, bishop, who, under the governor Galerius, for the faith of Christ, as Prudentius writes, was thrown into the river with a millstone tied to his neck; but when the stone floated, after exhorting the Christians standing around for a long time, so that they might not be frightened by his punishment or waver in the faith, he himself obtained from God in prayer that he might be submerged and attain the glory of martyrdom.”

Nearly the same account is given by Saint Jerome in his continuation of Eusebius’s Chronicle under the year 310: “Quirinus, bishop of Siscian, is gloriously put to death for Christ. For with a hand-mill tied to his neck, he was thrown from a bridge into the river; he floated for a very long time, and, speaking with the spectators lest they should be frightened by his example, scarcely obtained by prayer that he might be submerged.” See the notes of Vallarsi and others. Gregory of Tours, Bede, Usuard, and Ado report the same martyrdom, but rely in their narrative and authority on Prudentius.

The Bollandists, under 4 June, mention a summary of the Acts, taken almost entirely from Prudentius, serving in place of the three lessons on the feast of Saint Quirinus in the basilica of Saint Mary beyond the Tiber. The authors ask who Galerius was under whom, according to Prudentius, Quirinus obtained the palm of martyrdom, and they disagree among themselves.

Some Acts survive in Mombritius, in which it is related that Quirinus was beaten with clubs by the governor Maximus and sent to Amantius, governor of Pannonia, by whom he received sentence of capital punishment. Hence Baronius and Chamillard understand Prudentius’s Galerius to be Galerius Maximinus Caesar, who was called Maximinus Daza and had been appointed over the East by the emperor Galerius Maximianus.

Ruinart objects that the Maximus mentioned in the Acts was not a Caesar: for he sent the martyr to Amantius because he himself did not possess the right of the sword. Cellarius and Teolius add that Maximinus Daza had held no governorship when he was unexpectedly declared Caesar, and that afterward he ruled not Illyria but the East.

It should be noted, however, that Chamillard maintains that Quirinus suffered under Maximinus Daza when he was already Caesar, not before he became Caesar. I favor the opinion of Giselinus, who says that Prudentius means Galerius Maximianus, who, having been elevated to Diocletian’s rank, held Illyria, Asia, and the East and posted edicts on bronze tablets concerning the destruction of the Christians.

That Maximus and Amantius mentioned in the Acts were governors under Galerius Maximianus is clearly suggested by the Acts corrected by the Bollandists from a manuscript:

“Thus, while the laws of the emperor Maximianus pressed upon them, the Christian army was persecuted; throughout Illyria, Diocletian raged with sacrilegious commands against the people of Christ, adding to his tyranny another Maximianus, a partner in the kingdom, who displayed both his own fury and that of Diocletian throughout all Illyria. Yet sacrilegious decrees of the impious rulers were sent to nearly all the judges of the provinces, ordering them to compel Christians to sacrifice in the temples of demons. [lacuna] Blessed Quirinus, bishop of Siscia, was ordered to be arrested by the governor Maximus. . . . After three days Maximus ordered the bishop Quirinus to be led to the governor Amantius in First Pannonia.”

Previously the text read, “adding to his tyranny Maximianus”; the Bollandists restored “another Maximianus” from the Vatican manuscript, by which Maximianus Galerius is certainly meant. Ruinart and the Bollandists regard these Acts as genuine; but both he and they add Prudentius’s hymn.

In the Roman Martyrology, the words “under the governor Galerius” might perhaps more appropriately be changed to “under the emperor Galerius.” Prudentius called him *dux* (“leader”) in order to designate an emperor, just as he says of Honorius in Book II of *Against Symmachus*, verse 1114, “I beseech you, most august leader of the Ausonian realm,” and of the two imperial brothers Honorius and Arcadius in the same work, verse 14, “When the envoy had spoken, the brothers’ most peaceful words, the words of the two rulers, replied.” And in the *Romanus* concerning the same Galerius, verse 31: “Galerius, as leader, governed the condition of the Roman world.”

Ruinart, followed by others, thinks that the governor Maximus could have been called Galerius Maximus, and that therefore it coheres well that Quirinus suffered under Galerius as leader, as Prudentius says, and under Maximus as governor, as the Acts relate. That seems less probable to me.

In verse 1, Ald., Alex., Vatt. B and Q, Hailsbr., Thuan., Noms., Rat., Prag., Heins., and more recent editions read *meriti*, so that the adjective *insignis* is joined with the genitive. Others read *meritis*, and perhaps better, so that the meaning is “distinguished by piety or arms.”

5. Whether these words, by the expression “in the paternal embrace,” imply that Siscia was Quirinus’s native city may reasonably be doubted. Nothing is established by the Acts. His body, as the Acts report, was deposited in a basilica at the Scarabetian Gate. But since the Acts say that Quirinus suffered not at Siscia but in the city of Sabaria, this Scarabetian Gate seems to have belonged to Sabaria. Chamillard relates that later, when the barbarians were devastating the Pannonias, the body was transferred to Rome and from there to Milan by Angilbert, bishop of Milan. Ruinart, on the authority of Rudolph the Scholastic in the life of Blessed Rabanus, *Benedictine Centuries* IV, part II, p. 12, asserts that it was transferred from Rome to Germany and deposited in the celebrated monastery of Fulda. The Bollandists add further details.

11. Sagittarius, chapter 6 of *De Cruciat.* [title uncertain], carefully observes that the Fathers frequently join together, in listing martyrdoms, the sword, the cross, beasts, and fire, although sometimes one or another of these four is omitted, as the cross is omitted by many others and here by Prudentius. He gathers many authorities in support of this.]

[Col. 0426C] 15. Quirinus was washed as though in the bath of martyrdom, which is commonly called the baptism of blood. As Prudentius explains, it makes no difference whether someone is washed in an actual river of blood—that is, by shedding blood for Christ—or undergoes death in another way. In the Church’s office for martyrs, mention is often made of the shedding of blood even when blood was not actually shed, because the matter is equivalent, provided that the martyr gave his life for the faith.

25. In Ruinart’s Verona edition, from a German manuscript, the margin reads *ad oram ingenti lapidum mole* (“at the edge, with a huge mass of stones”), but this is corrupt. Lactantius discusses this martyrdom in chapter 15 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, concerning Diocletian: “Members of the household, with millstones tied to their necks, were submerged in the sea.”

Gallonius, chapter 1, discusses the weights with which martyrs were tortured. He notes that in Rome there are still preserved in the basilicas of the Holy Apostles, and of Apollinaris and Anastasius at Aquae Salvias, stones of enormous weight and black color, round or oblong, with an iron ring fixed into the stone, into which a cord was inserted for binding and suspending those hanging by their feet or hands. These stones are called *orbicularia* by Josephus in his book on the Maccabees to Polybius. Their form is shown in plate 3, letter D.

Gallonius also proves, following Baronius in his notes on the martyrology, that such stone globes were found for the purpose of inflicting torture, not for measuring loads, and that they were different from the weights which, under the Law of the Twelve Tables, were imposed on debtors.

Even if I grant that all these things are true, it remains to be asked whether these same weights now preserved in the basilicas of Rome and elsewhere were actually once instruments of martyrdom. I do not deny, however, that a substantial argument may be drawn from the fact alone that these weights are preserved together with an inscription indicating this purpose—especially if it can be shown that such inscriptions were attached on the authority of a reliable ancient testimony.]

37. Ald., Bong., Widm., Vatt. B, P, Q, Alex., Mar., Prag., Rat., Thuan. read *suos exemplo*. Cellarius and Teolius maintain that the manuscripts have *suo exemplo*, not *suos extemplo*; I agree with them concerning *exemplo* rather than *extemplo*. Heinsius merely says that the great Scaliger, in his edition of Eusebius’s Chronicle, read *suo exemplo*, for the Chronicle says *ne suo terrerentur exemplo* (“lest they be frightened by his example”); that Aldus and the Ambrosian manuscript have *tuos exemplo* (Aldus changed *tuos* to *suos*), and that the true reading appears in the margin of Giselinus’s edition.

Giselinus certainly printed *suos extemplo* and in the margin *suo exemplo*. I do not see why the manuscript reading *suos exemplo* should be abandoned, since it says more than *suo exemplo*: Quirinus’s example is understood even if it is not expressed, and *suos* energetically indicates the frightened crowds belonging to Quirinus. Gallandius therefore retained *suos exemplo trepidos* (“his frightened people by his example”).

Another reading, *suo*, occurs in Vat. A. Chamillard incorrectly printed *hos* for *os*, and Ruinart carelessly followed him.

42. The old editions and many manuscripts have *mirificis*. Heinsius restored *mitificis* from his own copies, including the Ambrosian, a word Prudentius also uses elsewhere. From the best parchment manuscripts Heinsius likewise read *mitificus* for *horrificus* in Silius Italicus, Book XII. In this hymn *mitificis* is confirmed by two manuscripts consulted by Ruinart and five consulted by Teolius.

[Col. 0428B] 44. Some editions have *ne constatis*.

53. In the martyrologies and in ecclesiastical writers generally, the palm is very frequently attributed to martyrs because among Greeks and Romans the palm was a sign of victory, and in chapter 7 of Revelation, verse 9, martyrs are described wearing white robes and holding palms in their hands. In 1668 the Sacred Congregation responsible for indulgences and sacred relics decreed that the palm and a vessel stained with the blood of martyrs were to be regarded as the surest signs of martyrdom. It was long debated whether the palm alone was a sufficient sign of martyrdom; now it is generally held that the palm alone does not constitute certain evidence of martyrdom.

57. Some editions incorrectly have *gloriae*.

59. Gis. has *calcare et fremitum*. Others, including Gis. in his first edition, omit *et*. The final syllable of *calcare* is lengthened by the caesura and because of the following *fr* sound.

67. Teolius explains: “Unstable because of its frequent whirlpools,” and thinks that Ammianus Marcellinus’s words concerning the river Druentia may be understood in this way, “twisted by wandering whirlpools,” Book XV, chapter 10, without the need to alter the reading with Valesius. I admit that this is ingeniously conceived. But I think Prudentius, imitating Horace, said *tortis vortices* of waves driven back from the place toward which they are carried, in order to describe the Jordan flowing back.

Horace, Book I, Ode 2, on the flooding of the Tiber: “We saw the yellow Tiber, with waves violently turned back from the Etruscan shore, rushing downstream, having overthrown the monuments of the king and the temples of Vesta.” *Yellow Tiber* is apt, for the Tiber is never more yellow with sand and muddy—although it is always muddy—than during floods of this kind. These occur when great quantities of water have accumulated from rain or melting snow and, in addition, the wind is so opposed to the river’s mouths that it drives its waves back and turns them around. Hence we understand *violently turned-back waves from the Etruscan shore* and, in Prudentius, *tortis vorticibus*.]

1. I have supplied the title from Mar. and Rat. Vat. A is the same, but adds *Calagorrae* (“at Calagurris”) after *est* (“is”). Aldus: “The place where the martyrs suffered, which is now called a baptistery.” Alex.: “The poem begins on the place,” and other readings as in Mar. Heinsius likewise follows Mariett., but after *est* (“is”) adds *Calagurri* (“at Calagurris”) from Oxon. Egm. adds *Calagorra*; Hailsbr., *Calagurra* (forms of Calagurris). Fabricius: “An imperfect hymn on the place of two martyrs, where there is now a baptistery.” This little poem seems complete to me: for the verses were made, as I think, to be affixed in some baptistery, as is suggested by the inscription in the Florentine codex mentioned in the prolegomena, no. 85 and following: “Verses in praise of a baptistery made illustrious by the blood of two martyrs,” or, as Urb. reads, “illustrious.”

The commentators inquire which baptistery this was. Giselinus, Weitzius, and Chamillard think it was the baptistery in the Mamertine Prison, where Saints Processus and Martinianus were baptized. This seems scarcely probable, however: Prudentius expressly says that two men suffered martyrdom in that very place, whereas neither the apostles Peter and Paul nor Processus and Martinianus were killed in the Mamertine Prison. Moreover, this poem concerns a baptistery open to everyone when Prudentius was writing. At Rome there was a public baptistery at Saint John Lateran; that there was one in the Mamertine Prison is not established. Weitzius did not know how far the Mamertine Prison is from the Vatican when he asserted that this baptistery was a place in the Vatican near the Mamertine Prison. Perhaps he meant to write “on the Capitol.”

Cancellieri, in the Italian dissertation on this prison which I have already cited, chapter 17, testifies that he found no mention of the Mamertine Prison, consecrated for ecclesiastical use, earlier than that made by Maffeo Vegio in his history of the ancient Vatican basilica dedicated to Eugenius IV, where he says: “Opposite the little shrine of Blessed Peter, in the prisons beneath the citadel of the Capitol.” C. Riscus maintains that, since Heinsius placed *Calagurri* in the lemma from Oxon., there is now no room for doubt that Calagurris is meant; he therefore thinks these verses should be placed immediately after the hymn on Saints Hemeterius and Celedonius. But before Heinsius Weitzius had noted a similar title in Egm. and Hailsbr.; and the argument drawn from inscriptions of this kind is not sufficiently firm, especially where ancient codices vary. For it is not clear what lemmata Prudentius himself wrote and of what kind they were. Add that in no codex are these verses joined with the hymn on Saints Hemeterius and Celedonius.

The inscriptions of the old codices therefore suggest, but do not prove, that the baptistery praised by Prudentius stood at Calagurris, since they seem to have been added not by the author’s hand but on the opinion of someone who thought so. Nor have I determined whether a baptistery was erected at Calagurris on the very spot where Saints Hemeterius and Celedonius suffered. Thus only this can be affirmed: these verses were made in praise of some baptistery, whether erected at Rome, Calagurris, or any other town, where two martyrs had earlier suffered for Christ. Epigrams of this sort used to be made to adorn baptisteries. In Ennodius, Book II, epigram 20: “In the baptistery at Agellus, where the martyrs whose relics are buried there are painted.” Saint Paulinus, Letter 12, sends Severus three epigrams that could be placed in a baptistery situated by Severus between two basilicas: two, that is, on the paintings of the baptistery, and the third on the baptistery itself; it may be compared with this poem of Prudentius, for it is very similar.

Already in verse 1 Egm. and Palat., Vat. P, and Weitz. have *locus hic, ubi* (“this place, where”). Weitzius added no glosses from his manuscripts to this hymn. The ancient glosses are also absent in most Vatican manuscripts. Mariett. noted from his codex at verse 2: *provehat* (“may carry forward”), that is, Christ [as its subject].]

3. This verse is absent from Aldus, who boasts that he restored it; but it already existed in many earlier editions. Gis. and Fabr. read *Christi* for *Domini*.

4. It is clear that the martyrs suffered at the site of the baptistery. Barthius took another interpretation, to which Cellarius seems to adhere. In Book XLIV, chapter 2, he reports that ancient Christians placed relics beneath baptisteries, and thinks this explains the Apostle’s words in 1 Corinthians 15:29: “Otherwise, what will those do who are baptized for the dead? If the dead are not raised at all, why are they baptized for them?” He cites these verses of Prudentius and the epigram of Ennodius mentioned above.

The verses of Ennodius clearly affirm that the bodies of martyrs were buried in baptisteries:

“Armenius, the founder, who is worthy of heaven’s honor, here brought forth a fountain of life-giving water. The painter animated bodies snatched from burial. Seeing living corpses, let death go into the tomb. This place contains their beginnings. Whatever face the wall displays, the faithful mind holds.”

Barthius adds: “Many other things could be piled up here; but we are content to illuminate the Apostle’s passage from poets alone, whom not a few theologian-sophists otherwise despise, first because they do not understand them, and then because they do not seek to know such things,” and he concludes that much about the customs of the ancient Church can be observed from this divine writer, Prudentius.

Two objections may nevertheless be made against Barthius. First, at the time when the Apostle spoke those words about baptism for the dead, there do not yet seem to have been baptisteries beneath which the relics or bodies of martyrs had been placed. Second, nothing at all is expressed in these verses of Prudentius from which it can be argued that the bodies of the two martyrs were certainly buried in that baptistery: Prudentius says only that they suffered martyrdom in that place. And, in my opinion, if their bodies had also been buried there, Prudentius would not have kept silent about it.

6. Fortunatus imitated Prudentius in his hymn on the Lord’s Resurrection: “The shining army comes forth from bright waters, and cleanses ancient sin in a new stream.” Giselinus noted this long ago, and others after him. The stream is called “new” in opposition to ancient stains and because baptism renews a person. Thus, concerning the grace of baptism, *Apotheosis*, verse 880: “And new grace cleanses the one who lacks Christ.” For ancient Christians sometimes used “the grace of Christ” by antonomasia for baptism; I briefly indicated this in the commentary on that verse, and it could be abundantly confirmed from ancient inscriptions and the Acts of the martyrs.

2. Heinsius, with Ambr., reads *vocitant*, which he says is more correct than *vocant*. Parrhasius follows him and likewise reads it. The ancient Acts can be compared with this hymn, but they were derived from this same hymn. Bede, in the prologue to the Life of Saint Felix apud the Bollandists, volume I of the January saints, under 14 January, says that he wished to compose the life of Saint Felix, priest of Nola, from the poems of Saint Paulinus and to imitate the diligence of the man who brought the martyrdom of Blessed Cassianus from Prudentius’s metrical work into common and accessible language.

Those Acts of Cassianus are found in Mombritius. All the ancient writers who wrote about Cassianus—Gregory of Tours, Book I of *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, Ado, Usuard, Notker, Peter Damian, and others—also rely on the authority and credibility of Prudentius.

9. Mar. *pro div. script.*, **obviam**. Retain **obvia**. It is clear that the image of Cassian had been placed upon the altar; nor do heretics have anything to set against so striking an example except quibbles and trifles. For even then Christians were offering prayers before that image:

> Hear, believe it, most gracious martyr, all prayers,  
> and confirm as effectual those which you see worthy.

This example of an image placed upon an altar, and another at Rome in the church of Saint Hippolytus, were such that they could neither have been unknown to many most holy bishops nor tolerated by them if there had been in them the idolatry which the heterodox imagine and wish to persuade others of.

10. **Fucus** was commonly used of pigment in painting. In the Theodosian Code, book 17, *On Penalties*, read: “We order all the images of Eutropius, whether of bronze or marble, or of pigments, or of any material suitable for forming likenesses . . . to be abolished.” See Gothofredus on this passage.

14. Thuanus has **concessa** instead of **confossa**, a reading which Chamillard preferred to adopt; Teolius says that it is perhaps correct on the authority of some manuscripts. Casaubon, in *Julius Caesar*, p. 42, discussing Suetonius’ words “He seized it and pierced him with a stylus,” treats of martyrs and others who died pierced by styli or pens.

15. Aldus has **praecurrere**. The Bollandists note what **unde sumi** is to be taken with, namely **stylis**. Chamillardus says that wax tablets were called *pugillares* because one wrote on them by pricking them with a stylus; Teolius derives the name from the fist or little fist, by which they were habitually carried around. Some think that *pugillare* means something belonging to the fist or filling the fist. In hymn 10 of the *Cathemerinon*, at verse 144, I said that *pugnus* and *pugillus* were units of measure among cooks and physicians. Among cooks, the term seems to mean what can be grasped in the fist; among physicians, a *pugillus* is what can be lifted or grasped with the five fingertips of the fist. The distinguished Franciscus Petraglia informed me of this—he is not only trained in the knowledge of his medical profession and known for his writings, but also adorned with more agreeable literary accomplishments.

19. Let those take note of this who think that Prudentius sometimes embellished the acts of the martyrs from paintings that he had not properly understood. I, rather, believe that, besides the account of more knowledgeable persons, he also consulted the genuine acts that then existed, but presented the events according to a certain poetic taste, as though reporting them from another person’s mouth—or because, after first hearing them from the sacristan, he later read them more carefully himself. This sacristan was not, as some think, an uneducated man; for he had to be an ordained cleric, as may be gathered from the letter of Pope Cornelius. See Thomassinus, vol. I, book II, chapter 30, *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*.

20. Although Prudentius calls the time ancient, the event could have occurred in the same fourth century. Thus, in the *Romanus*, verse 32, he says “as antiquity relates,” yet speaks of the emperor Galerius. But even if this antiquity or old age can suitably be referred to the beginning of the fourth century, it is inappropriate to explain it as the time of Julian the Apostate, who died in 363 after a brief reign. See verse 31.

22. Sitting generally indicates authority. Thus jurists are often said, in Cicero, to respond to those consulting them while seated or sitting on a tribunal. Judges also sat when they pronounced sentence. It is well known that Pilate sat on the tribunal. Jos. Ant. Gonsalus de Salas, commenting on Petronius’ words “and the knight who sits in the case,” p. 36, supplies other examples. Teachers of letters, whose business was with little children, sat on chairs that were not very high. Plautus, *Bacchides* III.3.28: “You would sit on a chair beside the teacher.” Christians also taught the children of pagans, as is clear from this hymn and may be inferred from the acts of Saints Montanus, Lucius, Flavianus, and others in Ruinartus. There Flavianus’ pupils urged him to sacrifice, saying that it was the height of madness to fear the evil of death more than to live; different readers report these words differently. But shortly before, in §12, “When Flavianus’ ‘assistant’ protested out of perverse affection,” the distinguished Giovenazzius correctly thinks that **auditorium** should be read instead of **adjutorium**, since the subject is the pupils.

23. This passage requires us to explain something about the *notarii*, whose art Cassianus taught. Dominicus Aulisius discusses the matter in *The Sacred Schools*, book I, chapters 17 and 18. From Cosmas, an Egyptian monk writing around the year 540, he reports that the scribes of the Jerusalem Temple wrote down the prophets’ sermons from dictation as they received them from the prophets themselves; hence a certain confusion appears in the prophets, which may be seen in Daniel Huetius, *Evangelical Preparation*, proposition 4, chapter 14, and Saint Jerome’s prologue to the prophecy of Jeremiah. Since the Roman court had scribes similar to those of the Jerusalem Temple, it may be inferred that some confusion in the acts of the holy martyrs arose from this. The ancients themselves, accustomed to observing the practice, greatly admired the speed with which the *notarii* wrote. Martial, book XIV, epigram 208:

> Though the words may race, the hand is faster than they;  
> before the tongue has finished, the right hand has done its work.

One may also read Ausonius’ epigram 137, addressed to a notary taking dictation with the greatest speed: “Boy of the flying signs,” and so forth. There seem to have been some *exceptores* who wrote with such speed that they reproduced every word. For in the homily on the martyrdom of Saint Genesius, among the works of Saint Paulinus, we read:

> “Thus Saint Genesius, in the first flower of youth, undertook the apprenticeship of provincial military service, embracing that part of the office with zeal and skill which, by the novel speed of his signs, made the movement of his right hand equal the advocates’ words.”

Concerning the shorthand signs, Isidore says in book I of the *Etymologies*, chapter 22:

> “The use of signs was this: whatever was said in a public address or in the courts, several scribes standing together would write down, dividing the portions among themselves, according to how many words each was to record and in what order. At Rome, Tullius Tiro, Cicero’s freedman, was the first to devise signs. . . . They are called signs because they mark words or syllables with prefixed characters and recall them to the knowledge of readers; those who have learned them are properly now called *notarii*.”

Peveratus claimed that Tiro’s manuscript signs existed in his possession, and he judged the signs that Gruterus attributed to Tiro to be spurious. From this you will gather that writing with letters and writing with signs were different things. The signs were points, marks, or individual small and brief figures containing the force of many letters—somewhat like the abbreviations of letters that we now call abbreviations and ciphers, but apparently simpler. Compare the epigram on the schoolmaster and the signs in Burmannus’ *Anthology*, vol. I, p. 453.

[Col. 0436C] 24. The points are signs, as we said. Ausonius, in the passage cited:

> “Completed by individual points,  
> so that a single voice is brought to an end.”

He joined the two expressions, “individual points.” Barthius, book XVII, chapter 9, observes that Prudentius elegantly uses the verb *sequi*, which indicates ease in moving flexibly over wax. Pliny the Younger, book VII, letter 9:

> “As wax is praised when it is soft and yielding, following learned fingers  
> and becoming the work commanded.”

Lucan, book IX: “The sun will follow the wax.”

25. Mar., Rat., Weitz., and Bong. from a second hand; Vatt. B, P, X; Gifanius in the *Index to Lucretius*, with **jussa** from an old book; Parrhasius and most of the Heinsian manuscripts, **jussa**. Ald., Bong. from the first hand, Fabr., Ambr., Noms., Heins., and Ruinartius from the manuscript of Saint Michael, **visa**, namely commands which seemed harsh and gloomy to the pupils. Giselinus printed **visa**, but found **jussa** in other copies; “This,” he says, “is so pleasing that I do not see what I ought to prefer.”

26. Mar. has **moverat**; above, **moverant**.

27. Saint Ambrose has similar remarks in book VI of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 6:

> “For what is generally an offense or terror to the lazy, the weak, or the impious is useful to others, just as these things are to little children from their tutors. They seem harsh, bitter, and troublesome; fearful because of the rod; they deny the freedom to behave wantonly; they impose the necessity of discipline; they restrain childish minds with terror lest they dissolve in luxury.”

Others make similar observations in various places.

31. Some infer from these verses that Cassianus suffered under Julian the Apostate, as though Prudentius were saying that he was arrested because he taught boys while refusing to sacrifice to idols, which was forbidden by Julian’s edict. But Prudentius seems to indicate an earlier time at verse 20, and clearly suggests that the cause of his martyrdom was his profession of the Christian name, not his teaching boys. Consult the Bollandists. Nor would Cassianus appear praiseworthy if he continued teaching boys against the emperor’s edict. Thus Augustine, book VIII of the *Confessions*, chapter 5, relates of Victorinus that he accepted Julian’s law and preferred to abandon his eloquent school rather than abandon the word of God. Eunapius reports the same of Musonius, and Jerome in the *Chronicle* of Proaeresius: “Proaeresius, an Athenian sophist, when a law was issued forbidding Christians to be teachers of the liberal arts, although Julian expressly permitted him to teach Christians, voluntarily abandoned his school.”]**

A similar martyrdom is related of Saint Felix in Pincis, who suffered at Rome on 19 February; the Bollandists, however, rightly reject it on 14 January in the preliminary commentary on the life of Felix of Nola, §6. Nicephorus, book XV, chapter 18, relates that Stephen, bishop of Antioch, was killed by boys with sharpened pens used as weapons. Theodoretus, book III of the *History*, Sozomenus, book V, and before them Saint Gregory of Nazianzus in his oration against Julian, mention that Marcus, bishop of Arethusa, was tormented by boys with penknives. On his orthodox faith and veneration among Catholics, see the Bollandists under 21 March.

A, Bong., and Weitzius have **ore** instead of **ora**. But **in ora** is more harmonious. Saint Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 43, seems to express nearly the same thing from Prudentius: “They strike wax tablets against his head.” Plautus, *Bacchides* III.3.36:

> “But now, before he is seven years old, if you touch him with your hand,  
> immediately the boy breaks the tablet over the pedagogue’s head.”

48. The ancients wrote on bark, papyrus, parchment or hide, tree leaves, but especially on wax tablets. *Pugillares*, or such wax tablets, were made of wood—beech, maple, citron, ivory, sometimes crystal and onyx, but usually boxwood. Saint Ambrose, book III of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 13:

> “Boxwood too, useful for expressing the characters of letters, forms the use of the child’s hand in its light material.”

Hence Scripture says: “Write on boxwood.” The passage occurs in Habakkuk 2:2, where the Vulgate has: “Write the vision and make it plain upon tablets, so that he who reads it may run.” Saint Ambrose renders the Septuagint as “in boxwood,” or “upon boxwood.” The words are *buxus, buxi*, and *buxum, buxi*. Propertius has a beautiful elegy in book III, *On the Lost Writing Tablets*, where, among other things, he says:

> “Gold had not made them fixed and costly;  
> the wax was common, soiled by boxwood.”

50. Vat. B, Mar., Rat., and Weitzius have **curva tumens**. Ald., Widman. above, most Heinsian manuscripts, Vatt. P and Q, and one Bollandist manuscript, **curta tumens**. Vat. X, **curvo tumens**. Hailsbr., **curve tumens**. Pal., **custe tumens**. Cauchius, **curva et humens**. Ambr., **chartae et humens**. Parrhasius, **rubentque ab ictu chartae, et humens pagina**. Gronovius, in chapter 5 of the *Ecclesiastical Observations*, conjectured **curta et humens pagina**. Namely, **curta** means mutilated, truncated, cut off; **humens**, wet with the martyr’s blood. Heinsius had likewise corrected the passage in Claudian and admitted it into the text with Thuanus. Giselinus recognized the variation of readings: in the common copies, **curva tumens**; in the Ghent manuscript, **curta tumens**; in the Deventer manuscript, **curve turgens**; in another, **curva tundens** (thus Fabricius printed it). But he asserts that his reading, **curva humens**, occurs in most ancient copies, and defends it by the authority of Bede, who teaches that it was formerly left to poets’ discretion whether the aspiration of *h*, like a strong consonant, prevented synaloepha, or whether, according to the weakness of the sound, it had no force. He also adduces an example from Fortunatus, whom he incorrectly calls almost Prudentius’ contemporary. Giselinus admits, however, that **curva et humens** is smoother. As for metre, Heinsius should not reject **curva humens**, since he so often recognizes that hiatus in Prudentius. Teolius says that **curta tumens** permits a convenient interpretation and occurs in all the Vatican manuscripts. But even if I grant that some convenient interpretation can be devised, the reading conflicts with the metre and is not truly found in all the Vatican manuscripts, as we have seen. Indeed, Alex. and Urb. explicitly have **curva et humens**, which therefore seems preferable. Heumannus, in *Poecile*, vol. II, book III, p. 364, thinks Prudentius wrote **nuda et humens**.

51. Althelmus, in his riddle on writing tablets:

> “Now the iron point furrows the lovely surface  
> with curves and makes it oblique with grooves, like a plough.”

In the stylus, the *stimulus* or point is the sharp part of the iron or bronze with which they wrote. Cicero, *On the Orator*: “Everything must submit to the point of the stylus.” The other part of the stylus was flat, by which writing was erased. Hence *stylum vertere* and *stylo depascere* mean “to correct” or “to alter.” Saint Jerome, letter 50 or 51 to Domnio:

> “I was foolish to have thought that I could not know these things without philosophers; I judged the better part of the stylus to be the one that erased rather than the one that wrote.”

Symposius, in his riddle on the *graphium* or stylus:

> “Flat at the top, but I am not flat at the bottom;  
> I turn in the hand both ways and perform different functions.  
> One part undoes whatever the other part has done.”

Yet none explains all this more clearly than our poet, as several have already noted. Pignorius, *On Slaves*, p. 112, gives the form of the ancient stylus and prefaces it by saying that Prudentius explained the ancient manner of writing with perfect precision. Hermannus Hugo gives a similar image of the stylus in chapter 9, where he asserts that the iron stylus is called *celtem* or *caeltem* in the Vulgate edition of Job 19. “This reading,” he says, “has been defended and explained most accurately by Ludovicus Molina in the first part of Saint Thomas, question 26, article 1, disputation 2. From the lexicons and Manutius’ orthography he proves that *caeltem* means sculptor’s iron, so called from *caelo* or the ancient verb *coello*, meaning ‘I cut.’ In Manutius’ *Orthography*, under the word *cloaca*, there is a funerary inscription of Servius or Sergius Polensis containing these words: ‘A literate flint with a little hammer and a *caeltes*.’ This monument deceived many, although it is known to have been fabricated in the fifteenth century.”]**

52. In some vulgate copies, incorrectly, **cerea**. In Torn. **cera** is absent. Latinius supplied **charta**. This verse describes the point of the stylus.

53. This is the flat surface or breadth of the stylus, by which the written characters were erased and the wax tablet renewed so that it could be written on again. Ausonius called the tablet’s surface *aequor* in the passage cited: “And with the right hand moved sparingly, it flies over the waxen surface.” The word *aequor* is discussed again in the hymn of Saint Hippolytus.

55. The point of the stylus pierces; the flat or broad part cuts. Hence we learn that the flat part of the stylus was made, either always or sometimes, so that it could serve this second purpose. Gregory of Tours, in the passage cited: “Cutting with the breadths of their styli and piercing his limbs with tiny points, they made the teacher a martyr worthy of God,” which he borrowed from Prudentius.

Ald., Gis. in the text, and the Buslidian manuscript cited by Giselinus have **pungere**, which Giselinus favors because of the elegant wordplay *pungere puncta*, “to prick points,” which continues in the following phrase, *sulcisque intexere sulcos*, “to weave grooves into grooves.” In the margin he added **pingere**, and acknowledged that others read **pangere**, but neither seemed to him as attractive as **pungere**. Most of our copies read **pingere**: Vatt. A and B, Alex., Mar., Rat., Prag. with Weitz., Widm. from the first hand, and others. Parrhasius, Ambros., three Heinsian manuscripts, Widm. above, and Pal. have **pangere**, as do Bong. and Fabr., followed by more recent editors. For in Festus *pangere* means “to fix,” as in *pangere clavum*, “to drive in a nail,” and *pangere plantam*, “to fix the foot in the ground.” I add that Columella often uses the same verb for the same matter and with the same metaphor, book X:

> “As the next letter is fixed beside the first  
> in wax by the learned teacher’s point.”

For **intexere**, Hailsbr. has the less suitable **intendere**. In Eulalia, it should be noted, wounds and blows are called *notae*, and writing is metaphorically expressed in verse 35: “Eulalia, counting the marks: ‘Behold, Lord, you are written for me.’” Plautus and others use the same metaphor, and now the boys are mocking their teacher Cassianus. Catullus, poem 25:

> “Lest the lashes, shamefully branded upon you,  
> should write all over your wool-soft sides and tender buttocks.”

I note in passing that Catullus shortens the first *i* in *conscribillent*. If Prudentius had committed that error, how many grammarians would have risen against him? This same metaphor remains common in Italian *graffiare*, “to scratch with the nails,” and is said to derive from *graphium*, as Vulpius observes on Catullus’ poem 25. See in the *Romanus*, verse 557: “He scratches both cheeks with writing claws.”]**

Chamillardus says that this may refer either to the signs mentioned above, or to the Runic script used by the Goths before Ulfilas invented letters for them, or to the peculiar method of writing used by the Gauls until the time of Clovis. Mabillonius provides specimens of these ancient scripts in his excellent work *On Diplomatics*, where one can observe curved strokes linked or entangled like chains. See book I, chapter 9, and book V, table II. In any case, Prudentius is speaking of the Roman signs that Cassianus taught, not of other barbarian letters.

96. The manuscripts consistently, with Aldus and Parrhasius, have **spes siqua tibi est**, which can be maintained with hiatus. Giselinus, perhaps to avoid it, has **tibi siqua spes est**. Fabricius, **spes si tibi est qua**. Weitzius conjectured **siqua tibi spes, siquid**.

97. Alex. has **audi**; above, correctly, **audit**. Vat. B has **credo**; **crede** should be retained. Cellarius, once again turning from grammarian into theologian, calls this kind of invocation a stain upon the faith, which existed—or began to exist—in Prudentius’ age. For, he says, it was not the opinion or error of everyone of that age. He cites Ambrose, commentary on Romans I, 21, and Jerome, letter 53 to Riparius. But the author of the commentary on the Epistle to the Romans—for Ambrose is not truly its author—says nothing in that passage opposed either to Prudentius, to Ambrose, or to Catholic doctrine concerning the invocation of the saints. Jerome, in his letter to Riparius, writes against Vigilantius, who dared to open his foul mouth and pour out the most disgusting stench against the relics of the holy martyrs and against us, who receive them, calling us “ash-worshipers” and idolaters because we venerate the bones of dead men. . . . “We honor the relics of the martyrs so that we may worship the one whose martyrs they are. We honor servants so that the honor of the servants may redound to the Lord.” What is this against the invocation of the saints? Jerome does indeed deny that the relics of the holy martyrs ought to be worshiped and adored. But Catholics also deny this, while allowing that such terms, used by many holy Fathers, may be employed if explained with a proper distinction between the worship or adoration of *latria* and that of *dulia*.

98. Prag. has **redde**, incorrectly. Mar., Rat., and Weitz. have **reddet**, less well. Hailsbr., **vidit**. The metre requires **videt**. Vat. X has, incorrectly, **ratasque Deo reddet**.

100. Latinius corrected the passage in Torn. to **altare**; **altar** is sound. Vat. X corruptly has “I ask the altar with my mouth.” Alex. has **tepessit**, corrected to **tepescit**. An example of this kind of piety had already occurred in Saint Gregory of Nyssa, *Oration 3 on the Forty Martyrs*: “I sprinkled the very reliquary of the sacred relics with bitter tears.” The tears of pagans at the altars of the gods, discussed by Broverius in chapter 23 of *On Adoration*, differ enormously from the pious tears shed by Christians for the sake of repentance.

102. Latinius corrected **timebam** for **timebo** in Torn. Parrhasius has the singular reading: “Then I murmur both what I sought and what I desired.” I discussed the meaning of the word **murmuro** at verse 36 of the first preface to the *Symmachus*. Add Broverius, *On Adoration*, chapter 8, who proves with many examples that those praying were accustomed to murmur, that is, to speak in a subdued voice.

103. Iso understands **domum** as “wife,” and afterward **futuri** as “children.” Perhaps these two glosses belong to **domum, uxorem, filios**, as though *domus* signified all of them. From this passage, I think, some have concluded that Prudentius was married, as is read in a note at no. 77 of the prologue in Vat. F. But even if he did not take a wife, he may nevertheless rightly be said to have had a household or family. For *domus* and *familia*, when applied to persons, denote the body of persons held under their own legal authority or by the common bond of kinship.]**
