This is the title found in the Marietti manuscript, where this hymn is placed after the verses *On the Place Where the Martyrs Suffered*. In Vat. A it is entitled *Book on the Blessed Martyr Romanus* and is placed after the hymn of Saint Eulalia. Aldus places it immediately after the *Hamartigenia*, with the title “Romanus the Martyr.” Alex.: “Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, of illustrious rank. Here ends Book II against Symmachus. Here begins the same author’s *Romanus against the Gentiles*.” Parrhasius: “Book of the Crowns,” and, without any other title, begins the first verse: “Romanus.” In the Ambrosian manuscript: “Sayings of Saint Romanus the Martyr against the Gentiles.” *The Minor Works of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, in iambic senarius metre.* At the end: “Here ends the Book of Saint Romanus, *Peristephanon*. Here begins Aurelius Prudentius Clemens’ hymn in praise of the holy martyrs Emeterius, etc.” In the Thuane manuscript, after the books against Symmachus, it is read with the title: “Here begins the same author’s *Romanus against the Gentiles*.” Perhaps this place in the Putean manuscript likewise belonged to the hymn. The Ambrosian manuscript contains this hymn almost complete and marks the first thirty verses as a preface. In the Oxford manuscript it is inserted under the title *The Passion of Romanus*, between the *Hamartigenia* and the *Psychomachia*. In the life of Prudentius contained in that manuscript, nine of his books are listed: *Cathemerinon*, *Apotheosis*, *Psychomachia*, *Hamartigenia*, *Against Symmachus*; likewise *Against Symmachus*, *Romanus*, and *Peristephanon*. In the Rotterdam manuscript this poem is the last among the hymns of the *Peristephanon*. In the Egmond manuscript: “Here begins *Romanus*.” Fabricius: “Hymn to Saint Romanus, the Antiochene martyr.” In Lotter’s edition of 1513: “The Book of Aurelius Prudentius, in which the passion of the blessed martyr Romanus is written, and in which an argument is made against all the gods, sects, and rites of the Gentiles.” Weitz, who places this poem after the verses on the place of the baptistery, entitles it: “Here begins Prudentius Clemens’ *Romanus against the Gentiles*.” Fabricius, in his special commentary on this hymn, reports that Nebrissensis titles it *The Contest of Romanus*; that Aldus Manutius calls it “a tragedy,” from verse 1113, “Arranging the sequence of so great a tragedy.” It may be added that the poem and its subject are tragic. Aldus, however, in my copy says only *Romanus*, while Nebrissensis has *The Punishment of the Martyr Romanus*. Perhaps Fabricius meant Murmellius.

1. Some have thought that this Romanus was the very man whom Saint Laurence converted to the faith. Nebrissensis relates that Romanus was an Antiochene monk. Chamillardus believes that two martyrs named Romanus suffered at Antioch in the year 303, on the same day, 18 November, and that Prudentius confused the two and thought them one and the same. Cellarius doubts this. Although Eusebius does not entirely agree with Prudentius—and this was the reason Chamillardus, following Baronius, maintained that there were two Romans—there could nevertheless have been one Roman, in whose passion either Eusebius or Prudentius was mistaken about certain circumstances. The Roman Martyrology plainly follows Prudentius. Bede, Usuard, and Ado speak of the same Roman, as do the Greeks in their menologion, almost in the same words, as Baronius admits under 18 November, although the Greeks distinguish this Roman from the Roman deacon of the church of Caesarea whom Eusebius praises.

Ruinart did not regard the Acts of Saint Romanus in Mombritius as genuine, and reports only what Eusebius relates in Book II *On the Resurrection and Ascension of the Lord*. From these accounts, and from other material Eusebius gives in Book *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, chapter 2, he concludes that Romanus was by birth a Palestinian, a deacon and exorcist of the Caesarean church, and that he suffered outside his homeland, at Antioch, in the year 303. From Prudentius he adopts the details concerning the martyrdom of the child, of which Eusebius makes no mention.

Eusebius’ silence is no reason to admit two martyrs named Romanus, suffering on the same day and in the same place. As for Eusebius’ implication that the martyrdom occurred under the emperor Diocletian, whereas Prudentius names Galerius, this makes no difference: Galerius was Caesar at the same time and was himself chiefly responsible for pressing the persecution against the Christians.

Fronto Ducaeus, in his note on Chrysostom’s first homily on Saint Romanus, judges very prudently that Eusebius, Prudentius, and Chrysostom celebrate one and the same Romanus: “I do not see, however,” he says, “what prevents us from saying that both events occurred . . . For it often happens that, when two historians relate the same battle, one touches on some of its parts while the other omits them.” Indeed, since Eusebius narrated Romanus’ martyrdom both in the book *On the Martyrs of Palestine* and in the book *On the Resurrection*, Eusebius seems more opposed to himself than Prudentius is opposed to Eusebius, as I shall explain later.

Baronius and other earlier writers had not seen Eusebius’ book *On the Resurrection*, first published by Sirmond, and therefore more readily distinguished two Romans, because Prudentius attributed to Romanus certain details that Eusebius omitted in the book *On the Martyrs of Palestine*. If Baronius had seen that book, and the many additional details Eusebius gives there concerning Romanus’ martyrdom—details entirely omitted in *On the Martyrs of Palestine*—he might perhaps have reached a different conclusion. Later writers, reading Baronius’ distinction between the Romans, have almost without further examination declared that Prudentius confused them.

Fabricius says that in this hymn most matters are presented so magnificently that one might say Christians alone possess wisdom and eloquence. For the same praise, see Barthius’ *Prolegomena*, no. 216. On Murmellius’ commentary, see the same work, no. 105. Fabricius says that nothing seems lacking in this hymn except that its invocation and conclusion are insufficiently devout. But how much more devout is this than invoking Phoebus or the Muses in the manner of other poets? I have often said how vainly heretics attempt to overthrow the invocation of the saints. I do not understand Ison’s gloss on this verse.

2. One commonly calls a person *elinguis* (“tongueless”) who is not eloquent; shortly afterward *lingua* (“tongue”) is used for eloquence and is contrasted with *infantia* (“inarticulateness”) and *facundia* (“eloquence”). Barthius assembled similar examples in Book X, chapter 14; Book XLI, chapter 20; and Book XLIII, chapter 16 of the *Adversaria*, in order to illustrate these passages of Prudentius.

And hope of some future good, perhaps wavering.

1062 “I am heard: I shall approach the City and enjoy favorable successes;  
I shall return home and proclaim Cassianus.”

## X. HYMN. HERE BEGINS THE PASSION OF SAINT ROMANUS THE MARTYR

[Col. 0444A]

Romanus, strong champion of Christ the God,

1063 Move, as the advocate, the instrument of an eloquent mouth:

3. *Comptum*: adorned. — *Infantissimo*: most ineloquent.

4. *Mira*: “miracles.”

5. *Nam*: because. — *Mutos*: speechless; Greek *alalos*, “mute.”

8. *Indixit*: imposed.

10. *Palpitet*: waver. — *Meatibus*: passages or ways.

11. *Haerens*: lingering.

12. *Absonis*: foul, shameful, dishonorable.

15. *Laxabit*: loosen, release.

17. *Messian*: Christ.

20. *Suggeram*: by supplying; I shall minister, I shall provide.

22. *Luculente*: clearly; he will speak openly.

23. *Explicabit*: he will release them, that is, explain them.

24. *Moverit*: he will have brought about, caused.

26. *Ictu*: by a blow, by striking.

3. In the Mozarabic Office Saint Romanus is celebrated on 18 November, and several stanzas are taken from this hymn. The verse is read in that breviary as: “Grant an adorned song, and one most auspicious.”

5. The Mozarabic Breviary has: “You yourself also know.” Parrhasius has *nam scis ipse* (“for you yourself know”), with *et* omitted. In his emendations Parrhasius says that, to preserve the verse properly, it might be better to write: “For you yourself know how the speechless can speak.” But even so the metre does not proceed correctly. Instead of *mutos*, Widmanstetter above, Vat. B, Marietti in the first hand, and Prag. have *mutum*, perhaps so that the meaning is not that the two martyrs celebrated here, but that one Saint Romanus, with his tongue cut out, spoke. In Rat. there was *mutos*, but traces of erasure were visible. Marietti conjectured *mutum os* (“a mute mouth”). It should be observed that *eloqui* means to speak elegantly, as Isidore explains in the *Differentiae*; and this is precisely what Prudentius intends: that the speechless, by God’s will, should not merely speak but speak eloquently.

6. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods*, chapter 59: “Our people commonly call a tongue like a plectrum the teeth of the strings.” Below, again, Prudentius, verse 988: “He would have spoken with a faltering plectrum, weak.” Many cite Suetonius as though he had written in *Claudius*, chapter 30, “the faltering plectrums of the tongue”; but the reading should be *praeterea*, not *plectra*.

7. *Revellit*, or *revulsit*, comes from *revello*.

10. Mar., Vat. A, and Rat. have *etsi recisis*; others have *nec si recisis*.

11. Teolius has this reading, perhaps deliberately, since the others have the same. “For the tongue to cling to the throat” is a phrase taken from the Psalms. Virgilian is “My voice stuck in my throat.” Instead of *lingua*, Aldus, Fabricius, Egmond, Bongarsius, Hailsbrunner, and several others have *linguae*.

12. Parrhasius, against the metre, has *balbutit modis et*. Heinsius would prefer *et laborat absonis modis* (“and labors with discordant modes”), if the manuscripts allowed it, because it is more harmonious. I do not think the manuscript reading should be disturbed.

13. Egmond has the erroneous *respersas*. Weitz preferred, with Hailsbrunner, *respargas*. “Heavenly dew” is used for heavenly grace, according to the style of Holy Scripture.

15. Parrhasius has *balabit*, less well, instead of *laxabit*. Heinsius likewise recorded this variant from the Ambrosian manuscript. In certain particular manuscripts Parrhasius agrees with the Ambrosian, and perhaps he consulted it; otherwise Parrhasius used a different manuscript, since elsewhere he differs from the Ambrosian.

16. Parrhasius, Ambrosian, Rotterdam, and three Torrentian manuscripts have *scribit*; others have *scripsit*. The passage is Matthew 10:19.

19. Vat. B, Mar., Rat., and Prag. have *providentes quaerere* (“taking thought to seek”).

21. Rat. has *facundia* (“eloquence”).

22. Vat. A erroneously has *me lingua*. The same manuscript has *luculente disserit*. Mar. and Rat. have *luculenter*; most have *luculente*. Vat. P, Q, and Alex. in the second hand have *disserit*; others have *disseret*. Nebrissensis says that one cannot read *Christus* but *Christo*, because *mea lingua* is in the nominative case. Murmellius wants *mea signa Christus*—that is, “Christ, the perceptions of my mind”—although he admits that some copies have *mea lingua*, which he wrongly asserts does not fit the metre. These authors do not seem to have grasped Prudentius’ meaning, or the elegant apposition: “Christ, who is my tongue.”

23. In these words, *supremo spiritu* (“with his final breath”) may mean that Romanus suffered in the final persecution, which was more savage than the others. Giselinus says it should simply be understood as in the passage about Laurence, verse 505: “While the demon assails God’s unconquered witness in battle, himself pierced, he falls.” He ridicules Murmellius for trying to twist the entire period into the story found in Matthew 17 and Luke 9, where the account of the lunatic boy is given.

24. Vat. A has *daemonum*, but *daemon* is the correct reading. Vat. B has *dederit*, rightly corrected to *moverit*, which appears in the margin as a variant reading.

26. In the margin of Vat. A, beside this verse, is written: “Aesop’s fable of the file and the serpent.” Perhaps this indicates Phaedrus, Book VII, fable 7:

> Let him who attacks one with a spiteful tooth  
> Recognize himself in this example.  
> A viper came into a smith’s workshop.  
> When it tested whether anything there was food,  
> It bit the file. The file, obstinate in return, said:  
> “Why, fool, do you try to injure me with your tooth,  
> When I am accustomed to corrode every kind of iron?”

Aesop and Camerarius composed a similar little fable about a weasel.

27. Florus, Book II, chapter 15: “The bites of dying beasts are usually as deadly as possible.” Seneca, *Controversiae*, Book IX, 6: “Rage is most violent in desperation, and at the approach of final death the mind is driven into frenzy. Some wild beasts bite the very weapons themselves and, through their wounds, rush upon the author of their death.”

28. The wild beast, shaking the iron and clinging to the spike with clenched teeth, thereby makes the wound more severe. He says *immoratur* (“lingers”), as later in verse 832: “Nor lingering over her young.”

Grant an adorned song to the most inarticulate:

1064 Enable me to sing the wonders of your praises:

[5] For you yourself know how the speechless can speak.

A savage torturer tore from you the plectrum of palate and throat, yet did not

Impose silence on the mouth by which you confessed God.

The voice that bears witness to truth cannot be extinguished,

[10] Not even if its passages are cut away.

Thus our lingering speech, with a feeble tongue,

Stammers and labors in discordant modes;

But if you sprinkle the heart with heavenly dew

And water the breast with spiritual milk,

[15] The hoarse voice will loosen its obstructed sounds.

1065 The Evangelist wrote that the Messiah himself gave

Such instructions to the apostles:

“When my sacrament must be proclaimed,

Do not anxiously seek your words:

[20] I shall supply the unprepared with what they are to say.

I myself am mute, but powerful in eloquence;

Christ, my tongue, will speak clearly:

He himself will explain those whom the demon’s tumult,

While it is being subdued, has stirred in its final breath,

[25] In a last fury worse than pestilence.”

Thus the serpent, wounded by the blow of the spike,

1066 Bites back at the iron, and, fiercer from pain,

Lingers upon it, shaking it with clenched teeth:

29. *Hastile*: sword.

30. *Cassa*: empty, vain.

32. *Refert*: relates, recounts.

36. *Legio*: thus called in Mar. — He now speaks of the legion of demons that had invaded two men, who lived not in houses but in tombs. Vat. A has another reading: “that demon which is called Legion.”

40. *Vel*: at least.

43. *Ecclesia tenus*: as far as the church, up to the church.

44. *Mancipandam*: to be bound, placed in custody.

45. *Nazarenam*: Christian.

46. *Ipse*: the prefect himself.

49. *Altaris*: of the sacrament. — *Pessumdare*: to hand over to destruction or destroy; it is one of the compounds like *circumdare*. *Pessumdo* means “I destroy” or “I scatter.”

29. Parrhasius has *manat*. The metre requires *manet* (“remains”).

30. Prag. has *haec cassa*; *nec* is better. Virgil, *Aeneid* XII: “He did not summon him to empty vows.” Elmenhorst, page 38, in his commentary on Arnobius, Book I, cites similar passages to illustrate Arnobius’ words: “There is no danger if what is said to threaten becomes empty and void.”

31. Prag. has *Valerius*; Egmond, *Calerius*. The reading should be *Galerius*, who was Caesar at that time. See the hymn of Saint Quirinus, verse 6. Aldus printed *Galerius urbis forte Romanae statum* (“Galerius perhaps ruled the condition of the city of Rome”); Teolius has the same without noting the variant readings. Most have *orbis Romani* (“of the Roman world”), and this is Prudentius’ meaning, confirmed by verse 34: “He had sent edicts throughout the whole world.” Gruter, page 280, preserves an inscription concerning Galerius, which I cited in the hymn of Saint Eulalia, verse 87. In Rat. at this verse: “Here ends the preface; here begins the passion.” This title also occurs before the same verse in the Ambrosian manuscript, and similarly in Parrhasius: “The Passion of Saint Romanus.”

34. Galerius’ edict is the very one about which Eusebius writes in Book VIII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 2: “It was commanded that all heads of the churches everywhere should first be thrown into chains and then compelled by every means to sacrifice to all the gods.” And in Book II of the *Life of Constantine*, chapter 51: “He wrote bloody edicts with bloodstained, so to speak, blades, and ordered the judges to apply the ingenuity naturally implanted in them to devising harsher punishments.”

36. Teolius has the erroneous *dicta* instead of *dictat*. Widmanstetter and Bongarsius in the first hand, Mar., Vat. B, Prag., and Rat. have *legio*. On this word see the glosses. The metre does not permit *legio*. “Royal mouth” means the mouth of the emperor or Caesar, and perhaps Prudentius also alludes to the word *basiliscus*, which means “little king.”

37. See Mark, chapter 5, and hymn 9 of the *Cathemerinon*.

38. Aldus has *clamabat*, against the metre. Vat. A and B have *advento*; read *adventu*.

41. *Imminere* indicates an attempt and efficacy.

42. Prag. has *judices* (“judges”); above, *milites* (“soldiers”).

43. Aldus and Tornacensis have *Ecclesiatenus quae de sacrariis*. Vat. A, Hailsbrunner, and two or three manuscripts cited by Heinsius have *Ecclesiatenus, ac de*. Rat. has *Ecclesiatenusque, ac de*. Vat. B, Weitz, and Mar. have *Ecclesiatenusque de*. Prag. has *Ecclesia tenus usque de*. Egmond and Pal. have *Ecclesiam tenus, ac de*. Ambrosian and Thuan. have *Ecclesias tenusque de*. Lotter’s edition of 1513, prepared by Hermann Tulichius, reads: *Ecclesia tenusque de sacrificiis*.

Heinsius, at his own risk, orders the text to be written: *Ecclesiasten usque de sacrarius raptare plebem*, because among the Greeks *ecclesiastes* denotes both one who hears sermons and one who preaches; he learned from Salmasius’ papers that this reading occurred in the Thuane manuscript. Perhaps this is another Thuane manuscript, since Heinsius had already indicated another reading from that manuscript. Later editors follow Heinsius, including Gallandius.

Parrhasius had read and punctuated it thus: *Ire mandat milites ecclesias per, usque de sacrariis raptare plebem* (“he orders the soldiers to go through the churches, even from the sanctuaries, to drag away the people”). Giselinus, with Murmellius, printed *Ecclesiatenusque de sacrariis*, but in his notes stated that he preferred *Ecclesia tenus, atque de sacrariis*, so that the meaning would be that the soldiers were ordered to break into the church itself and drag the people away from the sanctuaries.

This reading pleases me above all others, and it is found in Alt. and Vat. P. The phrase *ecclesia tenus* is characteristic of Prudentius, as in *crate tenus*, *Peristephanon* 3, verse 148; *aure tenus*, *Against Symmachus* 2, verse 729; *fundo tenus*, *Peristephanon* 13, verse 85; and *summo tenus extima tactu*, *Psychomachia*, verse 692. Perhaps, through some gloss, *usque ad* was later substituted for *tenus*, and the true reading was disturbed when the gloss entered the text.

In Alex. there seems to have been *Ecclesiasten usque de sacrariis*, which later became *Ecclesia tenusque de*; in Urb. it is joined together as *Ecclesiatenusque*. *Tenus* meaning “up to” is also used with verbs of motion by other writers. See the lexicons.

45. The Jews contemptuously called Christians “Nazarenes”; the Gentiles may perhaps have borrowed this term from them for use against Christians. See Vincentius, verse 25. Nevertheless Prudentius himself speaks in this way in *Against Symmachus* 1, verse 550: “To the pure inner chambers of the Nazarenes,” unless he too understands this name as one formerly given to Christians as an insult.

47. *Sancta sanctorum* (“holy of holies”) is used, after the Hebrew expression, for a sanctuary. *Psychomachia*, verse 815: “May she revisit the holy of holies.” Eusebius, in *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, says that Romanus was arrested because he rebuked certain Christians who were entering the temples of the gods; and in Book II *On the Resurrection* he relates that Romanus attacked the judge with reproaches. All these things could have been true.

48. Aldus has *profanis*, less correctly.

49. Thuan. has *arcam* (“ark”); read *aram* (“altar”). Prudentius distinguishes *ara* from *altare*, as in *Cathemerinon* hymn 7, verse 203: “The altar’s altar, which makes it propitious.” Murmellius calls the uppermost part of an altar an *ara*. Others teach that the *altare* is erected for the gods, while an *ara* is set up for God. Some think *altare* means, as it were, “high altar.” Giselinus simply considers any place dedicated to offerings—whether placed on the high altar or elsewhere—to be called an *ara*. He says that an *altare* is a structure raised from the earth and intended to receive people gathering at the tombs of martyrs.

Today, certainly, *ara* is distinguished from *altare* in such a way that the *ara* is the more sacred part of the altar, on which the sacrament of the Eucharist is accomplished and placed. This modern usage agrees with Prudentius’ words, as we shall say again in the hymn on Hippolytus.

Berthaldus, *On the Altar*, chapter 2, observes that Prudentius knew especially well the things belonging to the pagans, and that he declares here that the altar was placed upon the *ara*, while the *ara* itself was utterly scattered and destroyed, like some overturned foundation. In this sense the *ara* of the altar would be the foundation of the altar. But since Berthaldus himself concludes from the hymn of Saint Hippolytus that the *ara* is distinguished from the *altare* because the martyrs’ relics were placed beneath the altar and offerings were placed upon the *ara*, it is not sufficiently clear how the *ara* can be the foundation of the altar.

The fixed spear remains embedded more deeply,

[30] Nor does it feel the dangers of the empty bite.

Galerius, perhaps the ruler of the Roman world,

Governed its state, as antiquity relates:

Harsh, savage, cruel, implacable,

He had sent edicts throughout the whole world,

[35] That everyone should prefer to live by denying Christ.

This serpent dictates these words with his imperial mouth,

1067 Emerging from the tombs of the dead,

He cries: “Why do you dissolve my kingdoms

Before the appointed time, by coming so soon?

Spare me, Son of the Most High,

[40] Or command me at least to possess the hearts of swine.”

Asclepiades, the prefect in charge of these affairs,

Orders the soldiers to go as far as the church

And drag the people away from the sanctuaries,

To be bound in chains,

[45] Unless they immediately reject the Nazarene teaching.

Then he himself, intending to break into the temple,

And striving to disperse the holy of holies,

1068 Prepared impious weapons, profanely,

To destroy the altar’s altar from its foundations,

[50] And reduce the doors themselves to ruin.

When he suddenly learned these things, Romanus ran ahead as a scout,

A vigorous hero of outstanding courage,

Announces that the rebels are coming armed,

1069 Preparing the courage of the fearful with exhortations,

[55] So that they stand ready and do not yield to the storm.

The Christian flock, joined together in one spirit,

Forms a single company, an undaunted host

Of mothers, men, little children, and virgins.

One firm and settled resolve governs all:

[60] To preserve the faith, or willingly to die.

The repulsed soldier reports to the tribunal

That Romanus is leader of the rebellious people,

That all are burning with stubborn boldness,

Obstinately presenting their exposed throats,

[65] So that, strong in glory, they may meet death.

Romanus is then immediately ordered to be seized,

Alone, as the instigator and torch of all,

To plead the cause of the obstinate people.

He goes without resistance and asks to be bound,

[70] Even voluntarily twisting his hands behind his back.

1070 His love of the crown almost anticipates

The executioner’s savage art, as he willingly offers

His naked ribs to be cut with the two-pronged claws.

He bursts across the lofty threshold, and, while the heralds

[75] Stand mute with astonishment, he himself drags the torturer forward.

The tyrant begins thus, with Romanus standing before him:

“Infamous monster, vile, unworthy of testimony,

You, the agitator of the city and the light-minded

Storm of the people, disturb restless, mobile minds,

[80] So that the ignorant crowd does not submit to the laws.”

81. *Populare*: popular, venerable, or glorious.

82. *Illitterata*: uneducated, ignorant. — *Frequentia*: company, host, multitude.

83. *Autument*: let them judge, let them consider.

85. *Flammis*: fiery mountains. — *Montium*: of the leaders; for the gods, standing on mountains, used to hurl thunderbolts.

88. *Impiati*: corrupted, polluted.

91. *Aequum est*: it is just, right.

94. *Futurae*: namely, “which will be.” — *Exitium luas*: pay the penalty of destruction, suffer the danger.

96. *His*: with these words.

97. *Amplector*: I willingly accept and embrace your commands.

99. *Cuncta*: all the tortures. — *Consulis*: namely, “I shall answer.”

100. *Crudelitas*: namely, “I shall endure.”

106. *Gregem*: fellowship, company.

107. *Faxit*: may he do it; he speaks by way of wishing.

109. *Eculeo*: the torture-horse, rack. — *Eminus*: from a distance.

110. *Crescere*: swell, become larger.

111. *Apparitores*: executioners. — *Suggerunt*: indicate, report.

112. *Prosapia*: in his own lineage, by birth.

83. Aldus and Alex. have *autumans* above.

85. Iso interprets *montium* as “of the leaders.” The prefect alludes to the myth of the Giants, against whom Jupiter hurled mountains.

86. Prag. has *o perdite* (“O wretch”).

88. Pal., Egm., Vat. A, P, Q, and four manuscripts used by Heinsius have *impiali saeculi* without *sine*. In Vat. B it became *impiati*, with some letters erased. This too was an insult directed against Christians, namely, that they were profane, impious, and sacrilegious. Suetonius, in *Nero*: “The Christians, a class of people given to a new and harmful superstition.” The same is shown by Arnobius, Tertullian, Justin, and others. See the notes of Heraldus and Wowerus on Minucius’ words: “They organize the people into a profane conspiracy,” where you will find many passages resembling these of Prudentius.

92. In Prag., Vat. P, and Rott., *ut* is absent before *carnifex*; in Alex. it was deleted, and Heinsius followed this, as did later editors. Gallandius, with the older witnesses, printed *ut carnifex*. But it is better to omit *ut*.

94. Prag. in the first hand has the erroneous *primo* instead of *primus*. Aldus has *exitum*; *exitium* is better.

96. Egm. corruptly has *redduntur e libero*. *Reddere* for “to answer” is common among poets.

99. Prag., against the metre, has *dignus sum subire*. Mar. in the first hand, Rat., and some Vulgate copies have *si me consulas* (“if you ask me”).

101. A recent corrector in Rat., for *idolorum*, which seems to have been erased, inserted *pessimorum*, which cannot be accepted. “Servant of idols and demons” is an ecclesiastical expression for an enemy of God. In former times unbelievers were not permitted to enter the church; they stood in the inner narthex and proceeded no farther, as is clear from the Council of Carthage IV, Chrysostom, Augustine, and others. See Julius Laurentius Selvaggius, *Christian Antiquities*, volume III, Book II, part 1, section 3.

102. Among its other names, the church was also called an oratory, a house of prayer, and, as is clear from this verse, a house of salvation. Perhaps this was not a special designation of the church, but Prudentius describes the church in this way. At present I do not recall a similar designation commonly used by others.

104. Aldus, Mar., Widmanstetter, Pal., Urb., and most of the manuscripts cited by Heinsius have *confido in sancto Spiritu* (“I trust in the Holy Spirit”). Vat. B and Q have *confido in Spiritu sancto*. Ambrosian, Thuan., Alex., Lotter’s edition, and Parrhasius, for metrical reasons, have *confido sancto in Spiritu*. Giselinus has *confido in almo spiritu* (“I trust in the nourishing Spirit”) in the margin, with Aldus. Some Vulgate copies have *confido sancto Spiritu*.

106. Aldus and some old manuscripts have *nisi forte*. Virgil, Book II: “You shall be ours.”

107. Egm. corruptly has *merearis uni*. Rat. incorrectly has *merearis sumi*. Vat. B corruptly has *faxat Deus*.

110. Weitz, Fabricius, Hailsbrunner, and Bongarsius have *ungulisque crescere*, less well. Parrhasius has *pendere* and *uncis, ungulis decrescere*. The true reading is *vinculisque crescere*. The subject is the hooks to which the bonds were fastened, and the very bonds by which those being tortured on the rack were stretched, and therefore seemed to grow. Seneca, *Letter* 66, cited by Sagittarius: “Made longer than the rack.” Silius, Book I, verse 175: “By the art of cruelty, the limbs stretched as far as the tortures required grew longer.” I discussed the rack in Vincentius, verse 109.

Thomas Hurtado, *On True Martyrdom*, resolution 35, digression 2, section 3, thinks that the *eculeus* was the torture which the Spaniards call *potro*. That word means a rack, or a little horse, on which the limbs are stretched by cords until grooves are formed, and even until the bones break if the cords are twisted too tightly. He approves Calepinus’ explanation that *fidiculae* are called by the Spaniards *trato de cuerda*. But the Spaniards use this expression for the raising of the body by pulleys, which I discussed in Vincentius, verse 110, as Hurtado himself seems to have acknowledged in his *Anacephalaeosis*.

There he adopts Barthius’ opinion, *Adversaria*, Book XLII, chapter 27: that every kind of torture on which the accused were stretched was called an *eculeus* from its resemblance to mounting a horse, and that the term *cabalettum*, which Thomas Segetus wrote still survived at Mirandola, is not unrelated. The Italian word *cavalletti* indicates something of the same sort; in Latin it is *eculeus*.

112. Weitz, with Widmanstetter alone, printed *genitum prosapia*, against the metre. See Book VII, chapter *On Magic*: “Bodies endowed with honors are exempt from tortures,” except, of course, those crimes specified by the laws. The Theodosian Code, *On Interrogation*, Book IX, title 35, law 1, also discusses the exemption of nobles from examination or torture. Gothofredus explains more fully and observes that this law speaks only of exemption from the cords.

The crowd, under the appearance of glory,

Ignorant, believed some popular thing,

So that they might imagine themselves destined

To be consecrated forever if they waged war against the gods,

Like Giants,

[85] 1071 And, once defeated, were overwhelmed by the flames of mountains.

“You, wretch, prepared this spectacle

Of bloody slaughter, for citizens to be killed.

Since you regard them as profane, polluted, and guilty

Of this age, it is necessary that, under your leadership, they be put to death:

[90] You are the cause of death, you the standard-bearer of evils.

Unless I am mistaken, it is just that what the wicked author

Compelled many to endure, you, executioner,

Should endure in turn;

And for so many massacres, soon to come,

[95] You yourself should first pay the price of destruction

And suffer what you had advised others to suffer.”

He answers him with unconstrained voice:

[Col. 0452A] “I accept, prefect, and do not withdraw myself,

So that I alone may be sacrificed for the faithful people.

If you ask me, I am worthy to undergo

[100] Whatever your cruelty shall command.

1072 It is not permitted for servants of idols and demons

To enter our holy house of salvation,

Lest the pure place of prayer be polluted.

I trust in the Holy Spirit: it will never be granted to you

[105] To touch the blessed threshold with your foot,

Unless, perhaps, having become one of us,

You should deserve to be received into our flock—

May God the Father bring that about.”

Twice inflamed, Asclepiades ordered

That his body be stretched upon the rack,

To be torn apart at a distance by hooks,

[110] And grow larger through the bonds.

1073 But the attendants, speaking to the raging man, report

That he is of an ancient and noble lineage.

113. *Primum*: first, chief.

115. *Plebeia*: common, rustic, lowly. — *Clarum*: illustrious, noble.

116. *Tergum*: back; through the back, Iso.

117. *Extuberet*: let it swell or grow; let it become goitrous; it is inflated.

118. *Persona quaeque*: every person. — *Competenter*: according to its own nature. — *Plectitur*: is punished.

119. *Magnique*: of great price; of great difference.

120. *Gradu*: rank, nature. — *Datur*: suitably.

121. *Grandine*: persecution, or a hail of blows.

124. *Praestet*: let him make; let him make exalted.

125. *Secta*: doctrine.

126. *Incunabulis*: cradles; *incunabula*, cradles, trinkets, and rattles are the same.

127. *Textu*: order. — *Stemmatis*: lineage, nobility, descent.

128. *Parentis*: of the father. — *Ab ore*: when he first breathed the spirit of life into the first parent.

130. *Degener* is said of one who, through depraved deeds, does not correspond to the nobility of his parents.

131. *Stemmati*: nobility.

132. *Ut magistratus*: like a magistracy, like a dignity.

## Note: [Col. 0453B]

**116.** Ald., Mar., Rat., Vatt. B, Q, Urb., Weitz., Bong., Widm., and Gis. have *tundatur, inquit, tergum* in the text; Sich. has *tundatur, inquit, terga*. Alex., Vat. P, Alt., Rott., Thuan., Ald., and others correctly read *tundatur, inquit, terga*, so that it is a Graecism. Gifanius observed that the old books have *in vas*, and that the metrical structure requires this. For in this poem the outstanding Clemens consistently maintained that the fourth foot should contain an iamb. Prudentius occasionally admitted a tribrach in the fourth place, but not a spondee, as there would be if one read *tergum crebris*. Parrhasius and Lotterus, less elegantly, read: *Tundantur, inquit, terga crebris ictibus* (“Let their backs be beaten with repeated blows”). In Ambr. one finds *tendatur, inquit terga*, from which Heinsius conjectures: *Tendatur, inquit: terga crebris ictibus, / Plumboque cervix verberata extuberent* (“Let the backs be stretched out, he says, by repeated blows, and let the neck, beaten with lead, swell up”). Baronius, in his notes on the *Martyrologium* for 11 June, infers from the laws of the Theodosian Code that only persons of low status were tormented with leaded lashes. But those laws rather support Prudentius, since they show that blows from leaded lashes had been a punishment even for persons who were not of low status before those laws were enacted. Gothofredus, commenting on the second law at the cited place, shows that by this law the municipal officials were exempt from the *fidiculae* but not from the *plumbatae*.

**117.** Hailsbr. incorrectly has *exuberet* for *extuberet*. By synecdoche, Hilary, Ambrose, and Prudentius here use *plumbum* (“lead”) for *plumbatae* (“leaded scourges”). As many explain, these were whips made from cords or leather thongs, at whose ends leaden bullets were fastened; this description is not very convincing. Others say that the *plumbatae* were leaden balls sewn into leather. The very learned Lupius, in Dissertation 12, discusses the *plumbatae* that had been discovered in Rome, in the tomb of a certain martyr, under Pope Benedict XIII. They were, however, bullets of bronze, not lead, attached by small chains, not cords or leather thongs. Lupius suspects that the bullets were originally made of lead, from which the name *plumbatae* remained; for he had never heard of leaden *plumbatae* being preserved anywhere. Bronze *plumbatae* also exist, an impression of which we present on plate XXVI. They are preserved in the Vatican Sacred Museum, and, as it appeared to me when I examined them, the bullets are fastened with iron or bronze chains.

**121.** Parrhasius has *ille* (“that one”); *illa* (“that one,” feminine) is more correct. The *plumbatae* are often mentioned in the Theodosian Code in various expressions: blows of the *plumbatae*, torments, beatings, blows of lead, to be struck with lead, to be restrained with lead, to be crushed with lead, to be restrained with *plumbatae*. Prudentius includes all these expressions: “be beaten with blows,” “the neck beaten with lead,” “struck with hail,” “struck with leaden blows.” Libanius likewise, in *Oration* 7, *Against Aristophanes*, called the beating of the *plumbatae* “hail.”

**124.** I suspect that one should read *lex Curia* (“the Curian law”). A manuscript note in Lotterus’s edition explains it as *lex Portia*. But there were laws called *curiae* and *curiatae*, which Romulus enacted for the administration of the state after dividing the Roman people into thirty curiae. Other kings also enacted *curiate* laws. Saint Ambrose, in his commentary on Luke 3, has something similar concerning the curiae.

**125.** See Ouzelius on Minucius’s words: “Are you noble by birth? Do you praise your parents? Yet we are all born to the same lot; virtue alone distinguishes us.”

**126.** Parrhasius has: *Si prima nostri quae sit incunabulis*. Widm. has: *Si prima quae sit nostris in cunabulis*, contrary to the meter. Most have: *Si prima nostris quae sit*. But Urb., Vat. Q, and Alex. have *incunabulis*; others have *in cunabulis*. Heinsius, together with Ambr., preferred *nostri quae sit in cunabulis*, but conjectured *nostris quae sit incunabulis*, which Giselinus actually printed in his corrected edition.

**128.** Chrysostom admirably proves that those who call God “Father” in the Lord’s Prayer—“Our Father”—are equally noble as human beings, in his homily on Matthew 19, or 20: “For he granted one nobility to all, since he deigned to be called the Father of all alike.”

**129.** Parrhasius and Lotterus have *quisquis* (“whoever”); the meter requires *quisque*. I have already discussed elsewhere the use of *quisque* for *quisquis*, and more examples may be found in Burmann’s *Anthology*, p. 356. Someone wished *quique* to be written instead of *quisque*, or *quisquis*; I would change nothing, despite the manuscripts.

**131.** Parrhasius has *dein* (“then”); the meter requires *deinde*.

**132.** Fabricius thinks that *magistratus* here stands for *magisterium*, that is, the office or dignity of a master, just as, conversely, *potestas* is used for *praetor* in Cicero and Juvenal. He explains it as meaning: “when the magistracy comes,” that is, after the test of faith must be undergone. This seems obscure to me. Nor do I think Prudentius intended anything other than that immense splendor, such as comes from magistracies, accrues to Christians through martyrdom—as though he were saying that all Christians are noble, but martyrs enjoy something like the honors of magistrates. Thus, in the hymn of Saint Lawrence, he called him “this perpetual consul.”

And, by many merits, to be foremost among the citizens.

He orders the deadly stake to be removed,

[115] lest a noble man be condemned by a plebeian punishment.

“Let their backs be beaten,” he says, “with repeated blows,

and let the neck, beaten with lead, swell up:

1074 let every person be punished according to his rank,

and it makes a great difference whether a man is noble:

[120] according to the rank of the accused, the form of torture is assigned.”

Therefore, after the martyr had been struck by that hail,

after he had recited the hymn amid the blows of lead,

[Col. 0454A] he rose and began: “Far be it that

the blood of my ancestors, or the Curian law,

[125] should make me noble. The noble sect of Christ ennobles men.

If you review the origin of our first beginnings

in the order of our lineage,

we began by coming from the mouth of God the Father:

1075 whoever serves him is truly noble;

[130] whoever rebels against the Father is found degenerate.

A new honor then accrues to the lineage,

and immense splendor comes, like a magistracy.”

## Note: [Col. 0455A]

**133.** *Probum*: good.

**134.** *Inusta*: thoroughly burned.

**136.** Take care: *cave* should be joined directly to what follows. For *cave* is already negative and does not require any additional negation, just as we ought to say *Cave facias* (“Take care that you do it”), not *Cave ne facias* (“Take care that you do not do it”).

**137.** *Mi*: for *mihi* (“to me”). *Remissus*: softened toward mercy; made gentle.

**139.** *Ampliatus*: enlarged, extended, increased by prosperity.

**140.** *Flocci fecero*: “I shall consider worthless,” “I shall esteem lightly”; the expression derives from *floccus*, a tuft or shred which people pull from their clothing and throw away when it is utterly worthless, as though they considered it nothing.

**142.** *Cursim*: swiftly.

**143.** *Fasces*: honors, supreme dignities. *Sellae*: seats placed in the senate-house. *Praetextae togae*: a kind of clothing. The *praetexta* was worn by boys until their sixteenth year and was so called because a broad purple border was woven into its hem; afterward they wore the toga.

**144.** *Lictor*: bearer of the rods. *Trecenta*: a definite number used indefinitely. *Insignia*: ornaments or insignia.

**146.** *Initis*: you enter. *Vernae*: young men, slaves. As Isidore says, *vernaculus* is so called as though meaning “born as a good inheritance”; he is also called *domigena*, that is, “born in the household.”

**148.** From ivory: ivory eagles were carried on Roman standards because of the eagle, which is Jupiter’s standard-bearer.

## Note: [Col. 0455B]

**133.** The Christians of antiquity commonly used “the Christian name,” “the name of Christ,” and simply “the name” for the same thing. Mazochius, *Biblical Miscellany*, part 2, p. 90, thinks that the ancient Christians imitated the Jewish religion in the use of the tetragrammaton and therefore said simply “the name” when they meant the name of Christ. Certainly the name of Christ often seems to be intended, as in Cyprian, *On the Praise of Martyrdom*: “Through this, testimony is also rendered to the name, and the majesty of the name is renewed.” But sometimes it is clear that the reference is to the Christian name, for the confession or profession of which alone, without any other crime, Christians were punished, because that name was the mark of their religion.

**135.** Prag. incorrectly has *et inde dolorum* (“and hence of sufferings”). Rat., Vat. B, and Mar., from an old hand, have *finem dolorum* (“an end of sufferings”).

**136.** Vat. B, Mar., Rat., Sich., Weitz., Hailsbr., Bong., and Widm., from the first hand, have *perversibilis*, which does not fit the meter. Others have *perverse velis*. Fabricius has *perverse ut velis*.

**138.** Vat. B, from an old hand, has *tortor jam tum nobilis* (“executioner, now already noble”), contrary to both meter and sense. Prag. likewise incorrectly has *jam tamen*; above it has *jam tum*, or *jam sum*.

**139.** *Ampliari* refers to nobility, like *amplitudo*. See the examples in the dictionaries.

**143.** Mar., Rat., and Prag. incorrectly have *sellae* instead of *sella*: a spondee cannot stand in the fourth place, and therefore Weitzius was wrong when he printed *sellae*. Aldus and Vat. B have *praetexta, togae*. Ox. has *praetexta togae*. Fabr. has *praetextae, toga*. Hailsbr. has *praetextae toga*. Ambr. has *praetexta et togae*, as does Parrhasius. Heinsius wants *praetexta et toga*. Weitzius, Gifanius in *flere* from an old book, Vat. A, and Alex. have *praetextae togae*, which is sound. The ordinary garment was the toga; the *praetexta* was the toga proper to magistrates. Later editors agree with Heinsius; Gallandius, however, printed *praetexta et toga* and notes from other witnesses *sellae, praetextae, togae*. The fasces and axes were the insignia of consuls, the seats of aediles, and the *praetextae togae* of emperors. The lictor also belonged to the consuls, while the tribunal belonged to judges. Juvenal, *Satire* 10: “The bordered toga, the *trabeae*, the fasces, the litter, the tribunal.”

**144.** Egm. and Hailsbr. have *tribunal, haec trecenta* (“the tribunal—these three hundred”); Gis., in the margin, has *et cruenta* (“and bloodstained”).

**145.** *Detumescere* is also read in Petronius and Statius. Christian writers commonly use “swelling” to signify pride; Barthius thinks this was taken from Euripides’ *Hecuba* and Horace, *Adversaria*, book 30, chapter 19. I, however, believe it arises more naturally from the nature of the matter itself. Wipertus, a lover and imitator of Prudentius, book 1, chapter 11: “The excellence of intellect, by which worldly people ordinarily swell beyond measure and soon deflate.”

**146.** Vat. B has *ut vermes solent* (“as worms usually do”), which Colerus says appears in his manuscripts in his notes on Valerius Maximus, p. 548. The Codex Marietti, of which Colerus speaks, certainly has *vermes*, and above, as a variant, *verres*; in the margin, *vernae*. In the same Mar. there seems to be *dum* for *cum*. The usual interpretation of these verses is that, when Romans entered the consulship, they fed chickens with grain—a servant’s task—because it was considered ominous if the chickens abstained from grain, and Romans never undertook anything without auspices. Pignorius, *On Slaves*, p. 270, discusses the bird-keeper or poultry-man, whom Horace calls a *fartor*. His duty, he says, was to fatten and plump birds for sumptuous banquets. Prudentius therefore took the opportunity to have the Roman martyr ridicule the prefect Asclepiades. I consequently think that those who entered the consulship themselves fed the chickens in order to obtain auspices; hence Prudentius says: “you feed the chickens with grain, as household slaves do.” Giselinus says that this was done by the *pullarii*, because Romans, according to Halicarnassus, began neither magistracies nor anything important before consulting them. This explanation fits Prudentius poorly. Salvianus, book 6 *On the Government of God*, rightly censures this superstition among Christians: “For, surely, when consuls are designated, are chickens still fed in the manner of sacrilege, and are omens sought from the flight of birds, and are almost all the things done which those ancient pagans once considered frivolous and ridiculous? And although they themselves do all this, they who give names to the years, and so forth.”

**148.** Vat. B incorrectly has *sumpti* for *sumit*. Concerning this ivory eagle, see what was already said at verse 349 of book 1 *Against Symmachus*. Chamillardus says that Prudentius either made a mistake or that a different custom prevailed in Livy’s time, for Livy states that an ivory staff with an eagle projecting from its summit, made of the same material, was carried before those celebrating a triumph. But this is of no consequence: the staff was carried in the name of the triumphator and was a scepter, or consular emblem. Valerius Maximus, book 4, chapter 4, concerning Gaius Attilius Serranus: “Those hands, worn hard by rustic labor, established the public safety; they destroyed vast enemy forces; and those hands that had just guided the yoke of plowing oxen held the reins of the triumphal chariot. Nor did they blush, after laying aside the ivory staff, to return to the peasant’s plow-handle.” Fabricius reports that an ivory eagle distinguished by a red crest was found at Rome, and that one of this sort was carved on the arch of Vespasian, where Vespasian holds it in his hand. In the drawing of the arch and on the arch itself I find only Titus being carried into heaven seated upon an eagle, admitted among the gods according to the old superstition, on the vault of the arch. In the four corners, eagles with thunderbolts adorn the triumph.

If the upright witness in confessing the Name

is marked by wounds branded by iron and fire,

[135] and glorious death follows the force of sufferings,

take care that you do not perversely wish to be kind,

nor, by being gently lenient, spare me:

apply yourself to my limbs, executioner, so that I may be noble.

1076 If I enjoy these successes, thus enlarged,

[140] I shall consider my father’s and mother’s lineage worthless.

These very summits of your dignities—

what do you think they are? Do they not swiftly pass away:

the fasces, axes, seat, bordered togas,

the lictor, tribunal, and three hundred insignia,

[145] by which you swell and soon deflate?

When you enter the consulship, as household slaves do,

1077 I am ashamed to confess, you feed chickens with grain.

Its bearer takes pride,

[Col. 0457A] puffed up by an animal’s bone, which has the form of a bird.

## Note: [Col. 0457A]

**149.** *Ejus*: of the eagle. *Belluae*: of the elephant.

**150.** *Cui*: to the bone. *Alitis*: of the eagle.

**151.** *Sigillorum*: of images, statues, or signs; of idols.

**152.** *Siti*: placed.

**153.** *Projectius*: more contemptible.

**154.** *Carpentum*: vehicle, carriage.

**155.** *Proceres*: nobles. Properly, *proceres* are projecting ends of beams extending from walls; hence the more prominent persons among a people are called *proceres*.

**156.** *Lapis*: *gagathes*, on which it was painted, Vat. A. *Gagathes*. *Gemellus*: it may be called “twin” because, in the vehicle, she was accustomed to be sculpted or painted together with her son Cupid, Prag. *Essedo*: an *essedum*, a Gallic kind of vehicle, so called as though from *assidendo* (“sitting in”); a kind of vehicle.

**160.** *Almonis*: a river.

**162.** *Luperci*: naked men. Those who celebrated the Lupercalia were called *Luperci*, that is, those who celebrated the festival of the god Pan, at which every kind of impurity was practiced.

**165.** *Verbere*: by striking their buttocks.

## Note: [Col. 0457B]

**150.** Everyone knows that ivory is the elephant’s tooth. Prudentius calls it the animal’s bone.

**151.** Ald. incorrectly has *suberis* for *sub aris*. On *sigilla* meaning statues, see the commentary on verse 545 of book 2 *Against Symmachus*.

**152.** Vat. B, Mar., and Widm. have *intra*; others have *infra*. He calls a statue a cut oak; therefore *infra* (“beneath”) must be read.

**154.** Balduinus, *On the Ancient Shoe*, chapters 3 and 33, discusses the ancient custom of uncovering the soles during certain sacred rites. The knight Victorius published a dissertation in 1753 in which he illustrated a small statue of Cybele then preserved in the Vatican Victorius Museum, as Teolius noted.

**155.** Servius, commenting on *Aeneid* 1 and following Varro, also gives the etymology in the gloss: *proceres* are the heads or projecting ends of beams. Others derive *proceres* from *primus* (“first”).

**156.** Vat. B, Prag., and Mar., from the first hand, have *gemellus*; others have *nigellus*. Ald. and Alex., from a later hand, and Vatt. P, Q, and Urb. have *esseda*; most more correctly have *essedo*. Murmellius and Lotterus have *evehundus*. Arnobius, book 6: “You see the Arabs worship an unshaped stone, the Carians an unworked piece of wood instead of Diana, and the Pessinuntine stone, fallen from heaven, instead of the Mother of the gods.” Gisbertus Cuperus, in his notes on Lactantius, chapter 11 *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, says that either this stone had the features of a woman’s face, or that it was enclosed in a silver case shaped like a woman’s face; he leaves the matter for others to examine. I scarcely doubt that the stone itself had the features of a woman’s face, and this may be confirmed by the verb *sedet* (“sits”). Nevertheless, Bulengerus, book 1, chapter 18 *On Painting*, attempts to prove that columns were originally used as statues, as were trunks and stones. In the glosses, the black stone is called *gagathes*; *achates* might be understood, since *achates* is a blackish stone, as is clear from Pliny, Solinus, and Isidore, although *gagathes* is also celebrated by Pliny and Eugenius of Toledo. The more accurate spelling is *gagates*, from the Greek word. Johannes Fridericus Hervartius, *On the Admirable Mysteries of Ethnic Theology*, chapter 52, attempts to show that the first image brought from Pessinus to Rome was made of magnetite, and that the famous needle of the Great Mother of the gods, by which Servius says the Roman empire was sustained, was a magnetic needle whose use was already known. Johannes Winckelmann, in *On Unpublished Ancient Monuments*, volume 2, section 2, chapter 1, discusses statues of Cybele. In the Roman Maffaeian Calendar the Megalesian Games are indicated on April 4 as follows: “Games of the Great Mother.” In the Viennese calendar: “Megalesian Games.” In the Praenestine calendar: “The Games of the Great Mother of the Gods are called Megalensia because that goddess is called Megale. Exchanges of dinners among the nobles were customarily held frequently, because the Great Mother, summoned from the Sibylline Books, changed her place from Phrygia to Rome.” See the notes of Pietro Francesco Foggini.

**157.** Arnobius, book 7, speaks of the same stone as being tawny and black, irregular, with projecting corners. “Today we all see that very stone itself placed as an image of a face—perhaps a particularly important one—unworked and rough, while the likeness offers a less clearly formed face by imitation.”

**158.** The first syllable of *praeeundo* is lengthened here by a long interval and retains the force of a diphthong. Ammianus, book 23, concerning Julian the Apostate: “When the sixth day before the Kalends of April arrived, on which the annual processions of the Mother of the Gods are celebrated at Rome, and the carriage in which her image is borne is said to be washed in the waters of the Almo, after the solemnity of the sacred rites had been completed according to ancient custom, he spent the night in joyful celebration, having taken sleep during the period of leisure, and was glad.” Compare Saint Ambrose, book 3, letter 48; Augustine, book 2 *On the City of God*, chapter 4; Arnobius, Ovid, Valerius Flaccus, Lucan, and others.

**160.** Thuan. has *perventuri*, contrary to the meter. Hailsbr. has *praevenitis*. The Almo is a stream outside the Capena Gate, flowing along the Appian Way, or the road to Saint Sebastian. Its name is now *Acquataccio*, as though “corrupted water,” in my opinion. Its source is a spring of healing water, which many at Rome use to cure illnesses. In Italian it is called *acqua santa* (“holy water”), belongs to the chapter of the Basilica of Saint John Lateran, and exists near the Latin Way.

**161.** Enough has already been said about such pagan superstitions in the books *Against Symmachus* and in the hymn of Saint Lawrence; it is sufficient to have indicated this once.

**162.** Baronius, under the year 496, reports that Saint Gelasius prohibited the Lupercalia and refuted in writing the senator Andromachus, who defended them. Gelasius’s letter is preserved among the other papal letters. Andromachus argued that some image of the Lupercalia ought to be retained. Gelasius demonstrates that the Lupercalia could not be celebrated by Christians even in that form.

**164.** Running and hurrying were characteristic of slaves. In the prologue to Terence’s *Heautontimorumenos*: “Lest I should always have to deal with a running slave, an angry old man … constantly.”

**165.** Parrhasius has *pultet*, as he confirms in his notes, while arguing that Prudentius attempted to restore the ancient flavor: that is, that he used *volupe est* from Ennius and Plautus, *ninguidos* from Lucretius, and *pultet* for *pulset*. Ald., Torn., and some copies of the Vulgate have *actas* for *ictas*. The Luperci struck women who approached them with a whip or rod of goat-hide; the women willingly offered their hands, as though they would thereby become more fortunate in childbirth, as may be gathered from Ovid, Juvenal, and others. See book 2 *Against Symmachus*, verse 861. Iso explains that the buttocks were struck with a whip, a matter which Johannes Saubertus reports more fully from Choul, *On Ancient Sacred Rites*, chapter 6. But, for this ritual to be performed, the women themselves went to the Luperci.

The one who carries it, and the beast, boasts,

[150] swollen with the bone of the animal, whose form is that of a bird.

Now, if beneath the altars you lie at the feet

of images, placed beneath a cut oak,

what could I consider more contemptible than you?

I know that you uncover your soles before the carriage,

[155] 1078 while robed nobles perform the sacred Idaean meters.

A black stone, enclosed in silver in the form of a woman’s face,

is carried forth on a Gallic carriage.

As you lead it forward to the bath,

1079 you reach the stream of the Almo,

[160] rubbing your feet against the ground with your shoes removed.

What is the meaning of that shameful procession? Surely it shows

that you are ignoble, when you run as Luperci.

What slave would I not consider utterly despicable

if, naked, he ran through every street,

[165] striking girls with a playful whip?

## Note: [Col. 0459A]

**166.** *Sacrorum*: of idols.

**172.** *Vultuosus*: terrifying or gloomy.

**177.** *Mares*: males.

**178.** *Sexu duplici*: of the twofold sex, male and female.

**179.** *Abnepotes*: descendants born from grandsons. *Editos*: begotten, produced.

**181.** *Luduntur*: are deceived.

**182.** *Amasionum*: of lovers; *amasii* and *amasiones* are the same. *Comprimuntur*: are violated.

**183.** *Incesta*: violations, unchaste acts. There is a distinction between fornication, adultery, and incest: fornication is with girls and widows; adultery with other men’s wives; incest with sisters and consecrated women. It is called *incestum*, as though “not chaste.” “Of Jupiter and Juno,” Mar. “Of Mars and Venus,” Mar.

**184.** *Fallit*: deceives his wife. *Maritus*: Saturnus Opim, Mar.; Vulcan, I. *Pellicem*: a concubine; *pellex* is said to derive from *pellere* (“to lure away”), that is, “to deceive,” since men are captivated by beauty. A concubine.

**185.** *Deos*: Mars and Venus, whom Vulcan bound.

**187.** *Vervece*: *vervex* is said to derive from the worm it has on its forehead, which, by agitating it, incites it to battle.

## Note: [Col. 0459C]

**166.** Rat., Vat. B, and Mar., from the first hand, have *et pro me*, which is not very satisfactory.

**167.** Vat. B and Mar. have *secli*; the meter requires *seculi*. Rome is called “the supreme head of the world,” as “mistress of the empire” in *Apotheosis*, verse 507. *Saeculum* is understood as “the world” or “the globe,” as in Sedulius’s hymn: “Blessed author of the world,” and Saint Peter Chrysologus, sermon 160: “One whom the entire world could not contain in a tiny body.” See verse 584 in the hymn of Saint Lawrence.

**170.** Mar. has *velis, nolisne*; Rat. has *velis, nolisque*; both are contrary to the metrical rule. Parrhasius is no better with *nolis velis, nequid*. Gis. and Lotterus have *nolis velisve*. Most manuscripts have *nolis velisne*. He substituted *sordes* (“filth”) for *idola* (“idols”). In the hymn of Saint Lawrence, verse 263: “While you worship the filth of demons.” So Ennodius, in the *Nativity of the Epiphany*: “They fashioned filthy divinities with deceptive song.”

**171.** Vat. A has *ne terret* (“does not terrify”).

**172.** Apuleius, Donatus, Capella, Quintilian, and Sidonius use *vultuosus* and *vultuose*. An harsh, terrifying face is indicated. Juvenal uses *supinus* for “proud” in *Satire* 1: “and greatly resembling the proud Maecenas,” although here it is more likely to mean “soft” or “effeminate.” For “arrogant,” Persius, *Satire* 1: “Believing himself to be somebody because, proud of Italian honor, he has broken the unjust measures of the aedile of Aretium.”

**173.** Vat. B and Mar. incorrectly write *laeti* for *lethi* or *leti*.

**174.** Hailsbr. has *moveri*; Egm. has *ullus*.

**175.** The following saying of Minucius applies to this thought: “It is not the authority of the disputant but the truth of the argument itself that is required.” The commentators note several similar passages.

**177.** Aldus and Vat. Q have *feminas, ac mille mares*. Vat. B has this from a later hand; from the first hand it seems to have had, as Mar. does, *matres* for *mares*. Vat. A, Alex., and Giselinus in his corrected edition have the same. Heinsius and others have *feminas mille, ac mares*, which better suits both the meter and Prudentius’s usage. Besselius, p. 24 of his *Miscellanies*, conjectures that one should read: *Ut tecum adorem feminas, molles mares* (“that I may worship with you women and soft males”), so that Ganymede, Hebe, and other effeminate males may be understood. But the reading of the manuscripts proceeds correctly, and Hebe should not be counted among the males, since she is a goddess of youth, not a god. Lactantius, Arnobius, and many other Christian writers reproached the pagans for assigning different sexes to the gods. Arnobius, book 3: “For we cannot first be induced to believe that that immortal and most excellent nature has been divided according to sexes, with one part being males and the other females … For in prayers you are accustomed to say, ‘Whether you are god or goddess’; and this exception of uncertainty plainly shows that you assign sex to the gods by means of a distinction.” The prayers Arnobius mentions may be read in Macrobius, book 3 *Saturnalia*, chapter 9: “Whether it is a god or a goddess under whose protection the people and state of Carthage are placed,” and so forth. Aulus Gellius, book 1, chapter 28: “If anyone had profaned those days and an expiatory sacrifice were therefore necessary, he sacrificed a victim ‘TO A GOD, OR TO A GODDESS.’ Marcus Varro says that this was observed by decree of the pontiffs, because it was uncertain both by what force and through which god or goddess the earth might tremble.” The same formula occurs in ancient inscriptions: “Whether to a god or to a goddess”; “If it is a god, if it is a goddess.” This is relevant to what they sometimes said in prayers: “Whoever you are, god.” See Broverius, *On Worship*, chapter 7, besides Cato and others.

**180.** Ald., Weitz., and most manuscripts have *et tot*; Gis. has *ac tot*. Heinsius, with Thuan., has *ut tot*, which Alex. also has. Ald. and Oxon. have *prosapiem*.

**181.** Examples occur in Proserpina, who was married to Pluto; Hebe, who was married to Hercules; and Minerva, who was married to Vulcan. Europa, Aegina, Leda, Danae, and others were deceived by Jupiter.

**182.** Apuleius uses the word *amasionum* in book 7 of *The Golden Ass*.

**183.** Poets readily call illicit sexual acts “thefts.”

**184.** All these crimes are readily found in Jupiter. Ovid lists nine of his sexual violations in *Metamorphoses* 6; Hyginus, table 155, enumerates more than twenty illegitimate children.

**185.** Prag. has *duos* for *deos*, less correctly.

**186.** Vat. A has *adoras*; read *ad aras* (“to the altars”).

**187.** Weitzius, paying no attention to the meter, printed *verbecae*, together with Widm. and Bong. In Vat. B, *verbice* was changed by a later hand into *verbece*. Mar., from the first hand, has *verbice*. Rat. and Prag., apparently from the first hand, have *verbece*; others write *vervece*. *Verbex*, or *vervex*, is a male sheep, but castrated. Isidore, *Etymologies* 12.1, agrees with the gloss: “*Vervex* is said either from its strength, because it is stronger than the other sheep, or because it is a male, that is, masculine, or because it has worms in its head; when aroused by the itching of these, they strike one another and, fighting, hit with great force.” Varro thinks *vervecem* derives from *versa natura* (“a changed nature”). On the turf altar, see the hymn of Saint Eulalia.

I pity your sacred rites and your rulers,

and your customs, Rome, supreme head of the world.

1080 Come, let us explain, if you please, your mysteries,

Prefect; now you must hear,

[170] whether you like it or not, what sort of filth you worship.

Nor does that madness with which you swell terrify me—

because you are grim-faced, because you are haughty, because you are rigid,

and threaten harsh torments of death.

If you attempt to move me by any means,

[175] contend with me by reason, not by fury.

You order me, abandoning the rites of the Father and of Christ,

[Col. 0460A] to worship with you a thousand women and males,

1081 gods and goddesses, and those born of twofold sex,

children, grandchildren, and descendants of grandchildren,

[180] and the filthy lineage of so many sexual outrages.

Girls marry and are often deceived by tricks;

they are violated through the frauds of lovers.

Incest rages; the thefts of adulterers burn hot;

the husband deceives; the wife hates the concubine;

[185] chains bind the adulterous gods.

Show me, I beg, at which altars you command

that my turf altar should smoke after a ram has been slain.

## Note: [Col. 0461A]

**188.** *Palaestrici*: those who danced in the theater and sang obscene songs about the gods.

**189.** *Ephebi*: beardless youths.

**190.** *Effeminavit*: castrated. *Gymnadis*: of nakedness, or of the license of rustic exercise.

**191.** *Impuratus*: stained, defiled. *Impuratus* and *impurus* are distinguished in this way: an *impurus* person is unclean in himself, whereas one who is *impuratus* is said to have been contaminated by another.

**192.** *Disco*: a discus, a kind of game played with a discus; the youth was killed by the north wind while playing with it. *Florulentum*: “flowering,” in reference to the flower bearing his name, Mar. *Subcubam* or *succubam*: a woman who submits to another in lust; the word derives from *succumbere*, “to yield,” in submitting to shameful uses; she is also called an *amasio*. *Cucubam*: *cucuba* is an herb dedicated by Apollo to Hyacinthus, whose flower is the hyacinth, according to the boy’s name, Prag.

**194.** *Furem*: thief, robber. *Passus*: enduring, suffering.

**195.** *Tela*: bow and quiver.

**196.** *Cybebes*: Cybele, also called Cybele or Cybebe, who was said to be the Mother of the Gods and was also called Berecynthia.

**197.** *Puer*: Atys, Mar. *Gallus*: specifically, a castrated man. They called all those who had been emasculated *Galli*, after the Galli Senones captured Rome; afterward, whenever they captured a Gaul, they castrated him so that the stock would not increase, and they called all castrated men *Galli*. *Ob*: because of.

**199.** *Impudicae*: shameless.

**200.** *Matris*: of Cybele. *Spado*: eunuch.

**201.** *Credo*: ironically.

**202.** *Citetur*: be judged, or be summoned; be judged according to the statutes.

**203.** *Implicatus*: condemned. *Juliae*: the Roman law. The Julian law, named after its originator Julia, condemned adulteresses.

**204.** *Scantiniam*: named after its originator Scantinius; it judged adulterers. A Roman law, that is, an expression of anger; it is also the name of a goddess.

## Note: [Col. 0461C]

**188.** Vatt. A and Q have *vetant* (“they forbid”), which also seems to have stood in Alex. The story of Hyacinthus is indicated; see Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 10.

**189.** Mar., from the first hand, has *quam*, incorrectly.

**190.** They wrestled naked in the wrestling school; hence among the ancients the license of the gymnasium became proverbial.

**192.** In Vat. A a later corrector, erasing the earlier readings, wrote *florulentum* and *sucubam*. It seems to have been *cucubam*; in the margin one reads *cucubum* and *sucubum* as variant readings. Vat. B and Widm. have *florulentam cucubam*. Prag. and Mar. have *florulentum cucubam*; in Mar. a later hand changed it to *florulentam*. Alex., Ald., Weitz., Vat. Q, Urb., Lotterus, Heinsius, and others have *florulentum succubam* or *subcubam*. Bong. has *florulentum subcubum*; above it, *florulentam succubam*. *Florulentus* is a word used by the author of the *Pervigilium Veneris* and by Solinus.

**193.** The story concerns Apollo, who tended King Admetus’s herds, from whom Mercury stole cattle and weapons. The fourth foot seems to be a tribrach. This could perhaps be denied in some way, but in verse 978 the fourth foot is indisputably a tribrach.

**195.** Horace, book 1, ode 10: “Apollo, deprived of his quiver, laughed.”

**196.** Ald., Torn., and Gall. have *Cybellis*; Mar. has *Cibiles*; Vatt. A, Q, and Urb. have *Cybelis*; others *Cybaebis*; Hailsbr. *Cibelis*; Alex. *Cybeles*; Parrhasius *Cybelles*; Thuan., Egm., and Alt. *Cybebis*. Heinsius wrote *Cybebes* and persuaded others to adopt it from old copies of Virgil, Phaedrus, and Lucan, and from ancient inscriptions. In Greek she is called *Cybele* and *Cybebe*. Nevertheless, Chamillardus printed *Cybeles*. The rites of Cybele were usually celebrated in the mountains where there was a pine grove; the pine itself is sacred to Cybele, and her image was marked on coins with a crown made of two pine branches. Montfaucon, volume 1, presents several images of Cybele and discusses her deeds or myths extensively in chapter 1 and following.

**197.** On the Galli, see book 2 *Against Symmachus*, verse 522.

**200.** Vat. B, Mar., Prag., Weitz., Ambr., Thuan., and Oxon. have *matri*, which also appears in Alex. and in the text of Gis. and Heinsius. Others have *matris*. In Rott., above *sacra*, the variant reading was *aera*. From this Heinsius and Chamillardus suspect that Prudentius himself wrote: *Per multa matris aera plorandus spado* (“the eunuch to be mourned amid the many bronzes of the Mother”), referring to the cymbals of the Corybantes.

**201.** Juvenal, *Satire* 6, verse 47: “Worship the Tarpeian threshold.” From Arnobius, Ovid, Tibullus, and others it is clear that it was customary among pagans to kiss the thresholds of temples. Christians should not therefore be accused because they display the same signs of reverence toward their own temples. See the *Prolegomena*, chapter 14.

**202.** Widm. corruptly has *scitetur* for *citetur*. The same error occurs in Mar. and Prag. Vat. B has *qui siscitetur*. Latinius, in Torn., corrected *vestri* to *vestris*. Here is the reason why Prudentius, who embraced the tombs of the martyrs, denies that it is permissible to embrace the threshold of Jupiter.

**203.** Read *Julia*: adulterers were punished under that law. Juvenal, *Satire* 2, verse 37: “Where is the Julian law now? Are you asleep?” Cujacius discusses this law in *Observations* 20, chapters 18 and 19. The law was enacted by Augustus; nor should the gloss’s contrary explanation be considered. “The laws threaten” was discussed at verse 179 of book 2 *Against Symmachus*. Athanasius attacks the pagan gods with this argument: “Is it fitting that he—Jupiter—who appoints such things and is notorious for such crimes, which even the common laws of the Romans would not allow to go unpunished among human beings, should be regarded as a divinity? Who would not condemn him? Who would not judge him deserving of death?”

**204.** Ald., Fabr., and some others have *luet* for *luat*. Vat. B, Mar., Prag., and Rat. have *Luat severum victus, et Scantiniam*. Vat. A has *Luet severam vinctus et Scatiniam*. Thuan., Alt., Noms., and Rott. have *Luat severam vinctus et Scantiniam*, which is also the reading of Alex., Heinsius, and others. Latinius, in Torn., found *Cantiniam* and corrected it to *Scatiniam*. Parrhasius seems to distinguish two laws in this verse, for he has: *Luat severam victus, et Scantiniam*. There is, however, only one law called the Scantinian Law, concerning sexual offenses, enacted by Scantinius Aricinus against those who submitted to passive sexual practices, as the scholiast on Juvenal, *Satire* 2, verse 43, says. The Scantinian Law must be cited before all others. Some have thought that the law took its name from Gaius Scantinius, who accused Marcus Claudius Marcellus’s son of sexual misconduct and was condemned when the father brought a counter-charge, as Valerius Maximus reports in book 6, chapter 1. Although laws generally took their names from those who enacted them, they sometimes took them from condemned persons, as the Laian Law from Laius.

1082 Shall I go to Delphi? But the shameful reputation of the athletic youth forbids it—

your god, who unmanned him through the license of the gymnasium.

[190] Soon, after being defiled, he mourned the one killed by the heavy discus,

and dedicated the blossoming lover who submitted to him.

The same hired man tended another’s flock;

then, as a negligent herdsman, he endured the theft

[195] of the lost flock, and lost even the weapons.

[Col. 0462A] Or shall I go to Cybele’s pine grove?

1083 But the boy, the castrated man, stands in the way because of lust—
Through a grievous wound and a shameful mutilation,

safe from the embrace of the shameless goddess:

[200] a eunuch to be mourned amid the many rites of the Mother.

But, I suppose, I shall embrace great Jupiter’s threshold:

and if he is summoned as defendant under your laws,

entangled in the threatening snares of the Julian law,

let him, bound, pay the severe penalty and the Scantinian law,
