205. “As the one who knows,” that is, with you knowing or acting as judge; a *cognitor* is one who knows the cases of a trial, I.

206. “The founder,” that is, the establisher—namely Saturn, I.

[Col. 0463B] 207. “You judge,” you decide, I.

208. “He fears,” *reformido* and *formido* mean the same thing, I.

210. “Of concealing,” of hiding, I.

211. “Of those who disagree,” of those who are at odds, I.

213. “Lemnian”: Vulcan, from the island of Lemnos. Because Vulcan exposed the adultery of Venus and Mars, they are at odds with one another; and Vulcan is called “Lemnian,” as though “muddy,” from the Greek *linos*, that is, “mud.” For the defilement of lust arises from colour, which is Vulcan, because he was born from a concubine, I.

215. “By an image,” a likeness or seal, I.

219. “An abomination,” a crime. Iso. “Sin,” Mar.

[Col. 0464B] 221. “The swan,” in the form of Jupiter. Jupiter, transformed into a swan, violated Diana [as printed]. — “The violator,” referring either to Jupiter and Leda or to Jupiter and Pasiphae. — “The stage,” the gods’ couch or the steps of the theater stage, I.

222. “Dances,” sings. — “Tauricornem,” a proper name, apparently a certain mime-poet who sang of Jupiter, transformed into a bull, violating Europa. — “Lydian,” belonging to Jupiter, or the name of a musical mode: musical, I.]**

[Note: [Col. 0463C]

205. In the Ambrosian manuscript much is missing here up to verse 454. Heinsius adds a question mark after *carcerem*.

206. The Prague manuscript has *quod aureorum* incorrectly. The subject is Saturn, founder of the Golden Age, in whose temple the Romans therefore wished the treasury to be located.

208. The Thuanus manuscript has *furem*; *furtim* is better. Giselinus reports in the margin *dum pavesceret malum*, which Murmellius says occurs in other copies.

209. The Palatine manuscript has *audet*; correctly above, *audit*.

210. Mar. in the first hand has *colendi conscius*; above, *occulendi conscius*. The Prague manuscript has *oculendi conscius*. Read *occulendi conscios*.

211. Widm. has *dissidentium*; Alex., *discidentum*; Vat. Q, *dissidendum*. The true reading is *dissidentum*. The pagans’ opponents among our writers often brought against them the wars of gods fighting one another: Athanasius, Augustine, and others. Arnobius, Book IV: “They are said to be wounded, harassed, and to wage wars against one another with the frenzied heat of conflict.” Lactantius, Book I, chapter 3: “Homer portrayed the gods as fighting among themselves.”

214. Peveratus says that in many places Prudentius uses *quique* for *quicumque*, or *quisquis*, although today it has generally been changed, contrary to the authority of the old books and to Prudentius’ usage, into *quisque*. But he is mistaken: the old manuscripts have *quisque*, not *quique*, and the usage of Prudentius’ contemporaries was to use *quisque* for *quisquis*. See the commentary on verse 216 of Hymn 7 of the *Cathemerinon*. I would more readily alter that reading, if the manuscripts permitted, to *deum*: for I think we should read, “Everyone will feel Juno’s anger who has consecrated Hercules either by an image or in a shrine.” Hercules was the son of Jupiter and the stepson of Juno, born from the mistress Alcmene.

215. Latinius, in the Tornesian manuscript, corrected *aut* for *et*.

[Col. 0464B] 216. Ald., Urb., Gis., and Oxon. have *dices*; most have *dicis*. Augustine, Theodoretus, and others rejected this response by a similar line of argument. Arnobius, Book IV: “You wished it to be permitted only to poets to invent unworthy stories about the gods and shameful mockeries. What of your pantomimes, your actors, that multitude of mimes and effeminate performers? Do they not, for the sake of profit, abuse your gods and draw the procuring of pleasures from insults and divine indignities? The colleges of all the priests and magistrates sit in the public spectacles,” and so forth.

219. Vat. A has *tu turpia dum*; Vat. B, Mar., Lotterius’ edition, *tu cur piaculum*, incorrectly.

221. Some write *cycnus*, others *cygnus*. Martinus Roa, Book III of the *Singularia*, part 1, chapter 16, discussing the theatrical dance commonly called the *zarabanda*, quotes these verses to illustrate the matter: “The story of Jupiter was danced, who, transformed into a swan, embraced Leda.” In the theaters of our own age, similar crimes—or these very crimes—are represented by this dance. Juvenal, *Satire* 6, verse 63, “Leda danced by soft Bathyllus,” must likewise be understood of the dance of the swan-violator. Clement of Alexandria, Book II of the *Paedagogus*, chapter 10, and Cyprian, Letter 103, denounce the obscenity of the ancient pantomimes: “A man broken in every limb is brought on, and a man dissolved beyond feminine softness, whose art is to express words with his hands, so that the lusts of fabulous antiquity may be danced.” The learned Bulengerus gives further material in Book I of *On the Theater*, chapters 42 and 43, as does Meursius in *The Orchestra, or On the Dances of the Ancients*.

222. Vat. B, Rat., Prag., Mar. in the first hand, Widm., and Bong. have above *comantem* for *tonantem*, which is entirely correct. Ald., Urb., Gis., Heins., and others have *Lydius*. Murmellius preferred this spelling because this kind of dancing art was brought to Rome from Etruria, and the Etruscans traced their origin to the Lydians. Others write *ludius*, others *lidius*. Iso’s gloss attached to *tauricornem* better suits the word *Lydius*. Ovid and others used *Lydius* for a dancing actor. Velleius, Book II, describes the costume in which Planeus danced Glaucus: “After he had danced Glaucus, painted blue and naked, his head crowned with a reed, dragging a tail, and resting on his knees.”

223. Cuperus, in his commentary on Lactantius, chapter 36 of *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, thinks that *pontifex summus* here means the chief priest of the province. Cellarius says that Galerius is intended, either the one present, as Eusebius understands it, or the absent one addressed by apostrophe. The latter is quite probable, although elsewhere Romanus addresses Asclepiades.]**

1084 Worthy, with you as judge, of going to prison.

Do you think the founder of the Golden Age

deserves worship—the one whom you admit, while fleeing,

to have hidden secretly because he feared punishment?

If Jupiter hears that he lives happily,

[210] he must punish those who knew of his concealment.

What do you think should be done amid the altars

of quarreling divinities? The valor of offended Mars

will be indignant if the Lemnian is worshiped;

everyone who has consecrated Hercules as a god

[215] [Col. 0464A] 1085 by an image or shrine will feel Juno’s anger.

You say that poets freely invent such things;

but they themselves are also devoted to such mysteries with you:

whatever they describe, they worship.

[220] Why, while you look on, is it applauded in the theaters?

The swan-violator sins among the stage platforms,

and the Lydian dances the bull-horned Thunderer:

1086 while you, the chief priest, sit as spectator of these things,

224. “You wash away”: you cleanse such insults. *Diluere* means “to cleanse”; *diluere* also means “to mix together,” hence *diluvium*, because it mixes everything together, I.

227. “Of Alcmene, of Leda”: Alcmene is said to have been the wife of Amphitryon, whom Jupiter violated by taking Amphitryon’s appearance while the latter was besieging a certain city. — “The god,” Jupiter, I.

228. “The courtesan,” Venus. — “Adonis”: Ado, Venus’ lover, whom a boar killed; Venus therefore mourned him excessively. This is invented because Ado is the sun, the boar is winter, and the boar killed Adonis—that is, when winter arrives, the sun loses its heat and dies—and Venus, that is, the earth, weeps because at that time the earth produces nothing, clouded over by winter. “The eunuch Priapus.” — “The theatrical,” belonging to the theater, I.

230. “Of Cypris,” of Venus, from the island of Cyprus, where she is worshiped, I.

231. “What,” namely, “what is it?” I.

233. “The seal,” an idol or standard, I.

235. “The procurer,” the contriver of sexual violation, who arranges such violation. — “The worn-out favorite,” the young Ganymede: *exoletum*, because he has ceased to grow, that is, to mature. *Adultum*, obsolete and worn out; but *exoletus* sometimes means one who has completed growth, as when we call a fledged chick *adultum*, that is, mature. — “Who,” in what manner, I.

236. “Ceres,” seeking Proserpina, violently carried away, I.

237. “The maiden,” Proserpina, I.

239. “The Tirynthian,” Hercules, whom Omphale made spin wool. Omphale was his concubine; *omphalos* means “navel,” for lust is located at the navel. Hercules represents the strong and wise, because lust also deceives and mocks the wise, I.

240. “Why,” that is, “why did he do this?” Mar.

241. “The god,” of the gods, I.

242. “Priapi,” gods of gardens, I.

245. “A right,” namely, “a right to worship.” — “In seaweed,” in marine plants, I.

246. “Censor,” judge; he speaks ironically: judge, I.]**

[Note: [Col. 0465C]

224. Thuan. has *ridensque*. Ald., Heins., Cham., Gall., Alex. in the second hand, Urb., and Gis. have *deluis*; most have *diluis*, as does Teolius. See the remarks drawn from Arnobius on this applause at verse 1108 of Book II against Symmachus.

226. Vat. B incorrectly has *sacratae*. The story of Alcmene was written among the Latins by Accius, Caecilius, and Plautus, and among the Greeks by Aeschylus and Archippus, as Fabricius notes.

228. Rat. writes *meritrix*. Vat. A, Weitz., Heins., and Alex. have *Adonem*; others *Adonin*; instead of this, Vat. B, Mar., Prag., and Rat., without any erasure, and Parrhasius have *spadonem*. Arnobius, Book VII: “Venus will forget the offense if she sees Adonis, in costume, performing a pantomime in dancing movements.” Aratus the tragedian and Plato the comic poet are said to have written *Adonin*. Ovid, Book X of the *Metamorphoses*, and Lactantius, Book I of *On False Religion*, discuss Adonis wounded by the boar’s tooth. Theocritus also has an idyll on the same subject, which our friend Juan Francisco Sandoval has translated from Greek into Spanish in a thoroughly graceful and elegant verse together with other idylls by the same author, and has prepared for printing.

231. Ald. and apparently Alex. have *quidquid*. Others, in Gallandius, have *quia quod*; most have *quid quod*.

234. Pliny, Book X, chapter 3: “They deny that this bird alone—the eagle—was ever killed by lightning; therefore tradition has marked it as Jupiter’s armor-bearer.” In another sense *armiger* means an attendant and guardian of a king’s person, as I explained at verse 495 of the *Apotheosis*.

235. Mar. in the second hand has *quod tyranno*. Jupiter had, among his other titles, the name of king, and Prudentius rightly calls him a tyrant.

236. Egm. incorrectly has *praetendit*. Peveratus, with the Nebrissensis, preferred *praecincta* to *recincta*, because *recincta* means loosened, as in Virgil, Book IV of the *Aeneid*, “in a loosened garment,” and Ceres was seeking the daughter Proserpina, carried away by Pluto. But the meter does not permit *praecincta*, and Fabricius correctly explains *recincta* as “flowing,” as though she happened at that time to be wearing a loose garment; this indicates that the goddess was profoundly disturbed. In any case, many such words have two opposite meanings, as with *revincio*. This has already been noted at verse 37 of Book II against Symmachus. Ruaeus, commenting on the cited passage of Virgil, interprets *recincta* as “girded and gathered up,” because *re-* in many words does not negate but intensifies, while in others it has both forces, as in *recanto* and *recino*.

237. Parrhasius incorrectly has *quod si deorum*.

239. The story concerns Hercules when he served Iole.

240. Ald., Mar., Alex., and Lotterius have *cur sine aere*; but Alex.’s note has *Neaera*. Prag. has *cur si enereide*; Vat. Q, *cur sineore*; Rat., *cur si neere*; Parrhasius, *cur sibi nere*. Murmellius read *cur sine aere*, but says that one should read *quare*, or *cur hic sine aere*, that is, “why here without a bronze statue.” The true reading is *cur si Neaerae*. Neaera is a common name for beautiful prostitutes, as in Tibullus, Horace, Virgil, and many others. Athenaeus, Book XIII of the *Deipnosophistae*, discusses the courtesan Neaera, who had many lovers. Pausanias called the wife of Autolycus, whose proper name was Metra, Neaera because she prostituted herself to others. Licinius Imbrex wrote *Neaera*. See the commentary on verse 139 of Book I against Symmachus.

241. Vat. B, Bong., Fabr., and Gis. have *detestor*; most have *detester*.

242. Some think that the Fauns and Priapi too were called flute-masters. Others more correctly understand Pan, who was believed to have invented the pipes.

245. Parrhasius has *in ulvis*, incorrectly. Ald. and most manuscripts have *jus*. Fabr., Lotterius, and Gis. have *vis*, which Giselinus tries to persuade us is true against Murmellius. Nor would I deny that one could speak of “the power of divinity,” as Prudentius speaks of “the power of majesty,” and similarly elsewhere. But the authority of the manuscripts is preferable.]**

Why, if no god carried off the maiden,

does her mother wander sleepless through the night seeking her?

We see the Tirynthian turning the spindles—

[240] why, if he was not the plaything of Neaera?

1088 Why should I denounce the rustic monsters of the gods?

Fauns, Priapi, guardians of the pipes,

swimming nymphs and water-dwellers

lying beneath the deep lake, like frogs.

[245] Is the right to divinity in worthless seaweed?

Do you call me, good censor, to worship these things?

Can you, if you have sound judgment, regard anything of this kind as sacred?

[Col. 0467A] [Note: [Col. 0467A]

248. “The lung”: the lung takes in and expels air when a person laughs and speaks, I.

249. “Mockery,” derision. — “Follies,” vanities, I.

250. “Wine-filled,” full of wine. We call something *lentum* when it is full; hence *vinolentus* means full of wine, while *temulentus* means full of *temetum*, I.

251. “Mystical,” secret or figurative, I.

253. “Indiscriminately,” for metrical reasons, or *promiscue*, I.

255. “Canopus,” Egypt, named from a star, I.

256. “To pray likewise.” — “The monkey,” an Egyptian goddess, I.

257. “The asp,” the serpent worshiped by the physician Aesculapius, I.

258. “The crocodile,” an Egyptian god: an animal found both in water and climbing trees. — “The ibis,” an Egyptian stork, a species of bird, I. The southern region calls birds that inhabit the streams of the Nile *ibices*. The eastern and western regions, however, call small four-footed animals *ibices*, whose habit is to give birth on rocks and which know how to live nowhere except on rocks. Codex of the Bernese Library.

260. “The onion”: *cephal* is Greek for “head”; hence *cephe* received its name because only its head is useful, while the rest supports the body, I.

262. “Little vegetables”: this widespread idolatry, in which vegetables too were worshiped, began in Egypt on the following occasion. When Pharaoh went out with his chariots and horsemen to pursue the children of Israel and was drowned in the Red Sea with his entire army, the other Egyptians who had remained at home, occupied with various affairs, later fashioned images for themselves as though they had been delivered through them. For example, whoever had planted a leek at that time afterward worshiped the leek as his deliverer, and they did the same with other things, worshiping whatever they thought had brought about their deliverance. Prague manuscript.]**

[Note: [Col. 0467B]

248. Juvenal, *Satire* 10: “Democritus used to shake his lung with perpetual laughter.”

250. Ald. incorrectly has *vino lentae*. Mar. and Rat. write *vinulentae*.

251. Aldus has *aut siquid*; many have *aut siquod*. Gifanius shows at the word *QUOD* that the ancients sometimes used this expression for *siquid*. Heinsius writes *at siquid* with Giselinus. Most of our manuscripts have *aut siquod*.

252. Ald. and Urb. have *primum*; read *primus*, so that the meter is correct.

253. Alex., Vat. Q, Alt., Thuan., and Heinsius approve *promisce adora*. I think it should be punctuated *promisce, adora*. Weitzius, treating it as an adverb, printed *promisce adora*, together with Egm., Widm. above, Fabr., Hailsbr., Palatine, Bong., and Widm. Sich. and Gis. in the text, and Vat. B, Mar., Prag., and Rat. have *promiscue adora*. Ald. and Gis. in the margin have *pronusque adora*, which Heinsius printed in the text and later editors retained. Urb. has *permisce, adora*.

254. Roman comic and satiric writers mocked the Egyptian gods. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 7, relates that Serapis, Isis, and Harpocrates with his Cynocephalus were forbidden from the Capitol—that is, expelled from the council of the gods—and that their altars were overturned among the Romans, although their worship was later restored. On the Egyptian gods, see Book II against Symmachus, verses 864 and following, and the *Apotheosis*, verse 194.

256. See the commentators on Minucius concerning the Egyptian gods, where these and other passages of Prudentius are examined.

257. Mar. writes *Aescolapii*.

258. Weitz., with Widm. and Bong., writes *Ybis*. Ald. and Gis. have *canes*; most, and the more carefully corrected manuscripts of Heinsius and ours, have *canis*, correctly, since the subject is Anubis. Juvenal, *Satire* 15, verse 8, where he mocks these divinities: “Whole cities worship a dog.” I took the gloss on the ibis from a manuscript of the Bernese Library, which Sinner describes in his catalogue on pages 170 and following and assigns to the ninth century. The order of Prudentius’ works is nearly the same as in Weitzius: the hymns of the Nativity and Epiphany are placed after the Book of the *Peristephanon*. Its title is: “Here begins the preface of Aurelius Prudentius Clemens, a man most eloquent in liberal learning.” The first letter of the first verse, *Per quinquennium*, displays a portrait of Prudentius, whose head is surmounted by a blue-colored halo. The distinguished Fea, J. C., wished to share this catalogue with me, and I was certainly delighted to read these things in it. The same catalogue lists several hymns of Prudentius on page 160.

259. The Palatine manuscript incorrectly has *portis*. Juvenal: “It is a sacrilege to violate the leek and onion, or to break them with one’s bite.”

260. Mar. in the first hand has *acervum*; correctly above, *acerbum*. Giselinus is corrupt here: *cepe, et mordax halium*. For *allium*, some write *alium* with a single *l*.

261. Juvenal, *Satire* 9, verse 137: “O our little household gods, whom I am accustomed to adorn with a little incense, or meal, and a slender garland.” And *Satire* 12, verse 89: “I shall give incense to my ancestral household gods and scatter all the colors of violets.”

Prudentius is said to call the Lares “sooty” because sacrifices were made to them from things that exhaled smoke. I think the truer reason is that the Lares were located near the hearth. See the commentary on verse 511 of the *Passion of Saint Lawrence*.

262. Ald., Mar., Rat., and Cham. write *holuscula*.

263. Egm. has *at unde*. Giselinus printed *aut unde*, but preferred *at* in his notes. Most, and the better manuscripts, have *aut*.

264. Fabr. has *quam plantae*. The true reading is *nata*, and the passage derives from Juvenal, *Satire* 15: “O holy peoples, for whom such divinities are born in the gardens.”

265. Aldus printed: “If there is a fiery divinity in pots, there is a divinity in leeks also.” He corrected this, less successfully, to: “If there is a divinity in fires, in pots, and in leeks.” Murmellius, from copies printed in Germany, rightly preferred: “If there is a divinity in pots, there is a divinity in leeks also.” Many do not approve Rat.’s explanation of the gloss, *ollis* for *illis*. Here *ollae* may be understood as the pots to which divinity is attributed because, as Cellarius says, pots are on hearths and hearths were sacred; or rather, as I think, because certain small images were represented on the pots themselves, by which the Lares were worshiped, as I explained concerning other objects near the hearth in my commentary on the cited hymn of Saint Lawrence. Prudentius’ reasoning seems to me to be this: “If pots in which leeks are cooked enjoy divinity, why will you deny it to the leeks themselves?” From the response that follows one may infer that some image sculpted on bronze pots was regarded as a god. Nevertheless, the explanation of the gloss may perhaps be more correct. Cicero, speaking of the gods in Book II of *On the Laws*: “And those whom their merits have called into heaven, Hercules,” and shortly afterward, “those divinities,” using *olla* for *illos* and *illa*.]**

You ought not to consider anything of this kind sacred, should it not move the lung

of mockery when you look upon such follies,

[250] which wine-filled old women invent in their dreams?

Or, if anything anywhere of mystical vanity

must be worshiped by us, begin yourself:

worship indiscriminately whatever on earth is sacred:

1089 the Latin gods and the Egyptian gods,

[255] to whom Rome pours libations and Canopus prays.

You pray to Venus? Pray also to the monkey.

[Col. 0468A] Do you like the consecrated asp of Aesculapius?

Why do the crocodile, ibis, and dog displease you?

Place religious little altars beside leeks;

[260] venerate the bitter onion and biting garlic.

The sooty Lares are appeased with incense,

1090 while consecrated little vegetables are rejected?

Or whence is greater majesty believed to belong to hearths

than to what is born in cultivated gardens?

[265] If there is divinity in pots, there is divinity in leeks too.

[Col. 0469A] [Note: [Col. 0469B]

267. “What shall I invoke?” how far shall I curse. — “In the workshops,” or temples, I.

270. “Of yours,” of your own. — “Of the heavenly beings,” of the gods, I.

271. “Effective,” powerful, I.

272. “Encircles,” bends around, I.

274. “Clusters,” bunches, rings, circles, I.

275. “With serpents,” with snakes. — “Makes rough,” makes rough or rugged, I.

279. “The young man,” the youth, that is, Bacchus, the father Liber, I.

280. “With the thyrsus,” with the vine-stem, I.

[Col. 0470B] 281. “Softly,” an adverb meaning “softly” or “delicately,” I.

285. “The club,” Hercules’ spear or lance, Hercules’ staff, I.

287. “Elegantly,” ornately, I.

289. “Of the sacrificer,” of the one offering sacrifice, I.

290. “Pretends,” invents, I.

291. “Mentor,” the god’s silversmith, I.

292. “Phidias,” from *fidis*, “string,” hence *fidius*, one who plays the strings, I.]**

[Note: [Col. 0469B]

266. Mar. has *inaeris*; above, *inaere*; Prag., *in ere*. Read *in aere*.

267. Vat. A has *gratiae*; Vat. B, *Gretiae*. Correct to *Graeciae*.

268. Weitz. has *stultos*; *stultis* is better.

269. Giselinus criticizes Murmellius for changing the word order, *Polycleti malleus* for *malleus Polycleti*. But Aldus had already changed it before Murmellius, writing *Pollicleti*. The penultimate syllable of *Polycleti* is long, but Prudentius shortens it according to the rule of Greek accent, as in *Paraclitus*. Rat. and Heinsius with their manuscripts write *Polycliti*. Myron and Polyclitus were the most celebrated sculptors, contemporaries and fellow students.

270. Ald. incorrectly has *verorum est*. The manuscripts have *vestrum est*. Gifanius, in *Ecthlipsis*, concerning the elision of *-em*, page 437, otherwise 464, would remove the substantive verb *est* from the old books. But the manuscripts of Heinsius and ours oppose this.

272. Arnobius, Book VI: “Jupiter with curled and bearded hair,” and so forth. In *rigentem*, the stiffness of the beard where it clings to the chin is expressed; in *circumplicat*, the outer part of the beard that curls around; then, in *defluentem*, majesty and artistic skill gently descend, as Horace says in the *Art of Poetry*: “And he will imitate soft hair in bronze.”

[Col. 0469D] 273. The Palatine manuscript has *defluentes*, namely “hair.”

274. Poets commonly praise the hair of Bacchus, as also that of Apollo.

275. This refers to Minerva’s aegis, on which was the head of Medusa, or the Gorgon, with intertwined snakes, concerning which see Virgil, Book VIII, and Servius in his commentary. Cicero, *Against Verres* 6: “The Gorgon’s face, most beautiful, its hair composed of snakes.” Jupiter had given his aegis, his shield, to Pallas as a gift. The poets and mythographers say more about these matters. Prudentius uses *asperat* to express both the nature of snakes and the artist’s care.

277. It has been printed in some places as *aeris*; but the material of the fashioned thunderbolt is not *aer* (“air”), but *aes* (“bronze”).

278. Gis. in the margin has *Gorgonis*. This is the same Medusa who is called both *Gorgon* and *Gorgona*.

279. Some write *ephebum*, others *ephaebum*, others *ephibum*. Poets attribute unfailing youth to Bacchus.

280. Many say that the thyrsus was a weapon whose point was covered with ivy. Iso differs. The pagans thought that those struck by the thyrsus were driven into madness.

281. Some have *tum*, others *tunc*. Egm. writes *succintam*. [Col. 0470B] See the commentary on verse 366 of Book I against Symmachus concerning Diana “highly girded.”

282. Others have *virgines*; *virginis* is better.

283. Rat. in the first hand has *tristiores*, incorrectly.

284. Hercules appears on coins with flowing, curled hair.

[Col. 0470C] 285. Ald., Vat. Q, Egm., Hailsbr., Heins., Fabr., and Cham. have *clavam*. Others, and Nebrissensis, have *clava*. Latinius replaced *clavam* with *clava* in the Tornesian manuscript.

287. Thuan. has *iras*. Juno’s anger became proverbial among the Greeks and Romans. Virgil, Book V, verse 781: “Juno’s heavy anger and unsatisfied heart.”

288. Weitzius, with Hailsbr., preferred *velud*. Vat. B has *vel ut*. Mar. in the first hand and Prag. have *detort(s)* [reading uncertain]. The meter is against it. A twisted eye is a sideways eye, as *irretortus* means “straight” in Horace.

289. Vat. B and Mar. have *avertit*. Weitzius joined the words *delitantis* and, on the basis of Egm., indicates *dilitantis*. Correct to *de litantis*, as Aldus also corrected it, although he had printed *delitantis*.

290. In Cellarius’ second edition I regard *minus* instead of *minas* as an error, along with several others in that edition that I pass over without further comment.

291. Ald., Widm., Bong., and some others have *sacratis*. Weitz., Heins., and the rest have *sacrastis*. Mentor was famous for working in chased silver.

292. Vatican B, Mar., Rat., Prag., Hailsbr., and Widm. have *Fidius*. Read *Phidias*. Alex., Urb., and Vat. Q write *Fidias*, which Weitzius printed. Phidias was a most famous painter, statuary, and sculptor. Iso is far off the mark.

293. I shall discuss this verse at the following verse.

294. After this verse Vat. B, Urb., Mar., and Ald. insert: “When they founded gods for foolish peoples,” which Gallandius says is found in the Tornesian manuscript and the Paris edition of the Fathers, repeated from verse 268, though, as he himself thinks, incorrectly. Perhaps this verse was not repeated in this form by Prudentius’ own hand; otherwise it could be retained without difficulty. Fabricius says that this verse appears in some copies in which verse 293, “Makers of gods,” is absent; the latter is rightly preferred.

295. See Minucius and the commentators on his words: “For a god is fashioned, beaten with hammers and anvils, and given shape.”]**

But a statue sculpted in bronze is a beautiful thing.

What curses shall I call down upon the workshops of Greece,

which made gods for foolish peoples?

Myron’s forceps, Polyclitus’ hammer—

[270] 1091 these are your nature and origin, you heavenly beings.

Art, effective at sowing errors,

while it encircles Jupiter’s stiff beard,

while gently bending his flowing hair,

files the locks and the clusters of Liber,

[275] and while it makes Minerva’s breast rough with serpents:

it casts black terror before the terrified,

so that they shudder at bronze lightning as though it were the Thunderer’s,

and tremble at the poison of the hissing Gorgon;

they think that the young man, after his Indian triumphs,

[280] [Col. 0469B] can strike with the thyrsus when he is drunk.

[Col. 0470A] Then, when they see Diana softly girded,

they fear the bow of the hunting maiden:

1092 if the molten mass has fashioned, with curled liquid,

the face of the grim Hercules,

[285] it is believed to threaten with his club unless he is worshiped.

What terror now seizes the hearts of the frightened?

If it has elegantly represented Juno’s anger,

as she looks with twisted eyes,

even if the stone turns its face away from the sacrificer’s victim,

[290] it falsely feigns threats with stern brow.

I am amazed that you did not consecrate Mentor himself,

nor does Phidias himself have a temple and altars—

the makers of the gods, or the parents of the divinities.

If they had worked less diligently at their furnaces,

[295] there would be no cast-metal Jupiter.

[Col. 0471A] [Note: [Col. 0471A]

296. “To the village,” to the district or to paganism. As Isidore says, *pagi* are places suitable for buildings among fields, inhabited by rural people; hence “devoted to the village,” without the discipline of cities. *Villa*: *page* is Greek for “villa”; hence we call villagers *pagani*, as though removed from the city of God, I. Here *pagus* means stupidity, Vat. A.

297. “Provisions,” occupations or lowly things—that is, meats and similar things prepared for eating and set out for use; services, meals; *obsonor*, “I eat lunch”; hence *obsonium*, lunch, I.

299. “Basin,” a vessel for washing the feet. — “Cup,” a handled drinking vessel, a wine vessel, I.

303. “Juggler,” a deceiver, because he envelops and deceives others in a certain circle of error, I.

304. “Hoarse,” singing hoarsely; *raucidum* is a name derived from “angry,” because it makes people hoarse, I.

305. “Toothless women,” old women, as though without teeth, I.]**

[Note: [Col. 0471B]

296. The passage of Isidore indicated by Iso occurs in Book XV of the *Etymologies*, chapter 2. On the word *pagus*, and on why Prudentius says that idolaters are devoted and bound to the village, see the commentary on verse 449 of Book I against Symmachus. Weitzius observes that superstitious worship was common in villages and country estates, as is clear from Cicero, Book II of *On the Laws*; from this arose the rural festivals and holidays. Censorinus, Book I of *On the Birthday*, reports that the pagans had in their fields a portion consecrated to the gods where they worshiped them. As Christianity grew stronger, and idols could no longer be publicly worshiped in the cities, they withdrew to the villages so that they might freely display worship to their divinities. Saint Augustine, Sermon 62, formerly 6, *On the Words of the Lord*: “Many pagans have these abominations on their estates. Shall we approach and break them? First, we act so that we may break the idols in their hearts.” Mazochius, volume III of the *Biblical Miscellany*, page 295, labors to investigate the etymology of *Paganus*. Baronius may also be consulted in his notes on the *Roman Martyrology*, January 31. Some criticize Prudentius because here and at verse 1009 he has Romanus call the prefect *paganus*, although that word was supposedly used to mean an idolater only after Constantine’s time. But, to omit other considerations, these very verses show that before Constantine the word *paganus* could also be used for a person devoted to superstition, ridiculous rites, and gods such as were worshiped in villages.

297. The Nebrissensis understands *obsonia* as cakes offered to the Manes. But Prudentius is speaking of all offerings and banquets customarily made in honor of whatever gods. Cakes were indeed offered in other rites as well, sometimes raw and sometimes cooked. Properly speaking, *obsonium* is anything prepared and cooked as food apart from bread and wine.

298. Some write *dis*, others *diis*.

299. Mar. writes *cantarus*. Many writers address this same subject. Minucius: “For a wooden god is perhaps a piece of a funeral pyre or of an unhappy tree-trunk . . . and a bronze or silver god is made from an unclean vessel,” and so forth. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 12: “As for the images themselves, I discover nothing other than that they are made from the same materials as common vessels and instruments, or from those very vessels and instruments,” and so forth. Arnobius, Book VI: “Those images that terrify you . . . are bones, stones, bronze, gold, earthenware, wood taken from a tree, or glue mixed with gypsum; perhaps from the ornaments of prostitutes or from women’s adornments, from camel bones, from the tooth of an Indian animal, from pots, little jars, candelabra, lamps, or other more obscene vessels, gathered together.” See Juan Luis de la Cerda’s notes on the cited passage of Tertullian.

302. In Egm., Pal., Hailsbr., Alt., Noms., Vat. A, I, Q, and Alex., this verse reads: “Those who conceal the truth, who trust in a tree-trunk.” It also appears in Bong. in the margin and in Rat. between the two verses beginning *quos lana* and *quos saepe*, but in a different hand and not altogether ancient. Teolius testifies that this verse exists in three Vatican manuscripts and thinks it may be by Prudentius; however, he did not consult Heinsius’ *Addenda* at this point, although Heinsius explicitly said that it occurs in his three manuscripts. In any case, no one familiar with the rules of the iambic senarius and with Prudentius’ practice would attribute such an irregular verse to him. Ald., Urb., Thuan., Oxon., the three Tornesian manuscripts, Heins., and others have *discolora*, from the noun *discolorus*: *discolora*, *discolorum*, like *multicolorus* and *versicolorus*. See the commentary on verse 821. Hamartig., Weitz., Mar., Vat. B, Prag., Parrhasius, Torn., and Rat. have *discolor*, less well. Egm. and Gis. have *discolore*. Fabr. has *discolori*. Latinius has *discolore*. Alt. has *discolos*. This is not satisfactory. Gifanius, discussing words ending in *-r*, preferred *discolor* from an old book because he thinks that the ancients sometimes made such endings long; but he does not persuade me. The Nebrissensis thinks that the tricks of some juggler are meant, through the changing of colors. I do not greatly disagree with this interpretation, but I wish it could be strengthened by some ancient testimony concerning such tricks. Bulengerus, who carefully explained the arts and deceits of the ancient conjurers in his book *On the Theater*, reports nothing of the kind. Giselinus cites a verse of Virgil from the *Pharmaceutria*: “First I bind these three cords around you, differing in triple color.” For another explanation, concerning trees decorated with ribbons, see verse 1009 of Book II against Symmachus, which Arnobius, Book I, especially supports: “I worshiped the bones of elephants, the ribbons painted on ancient trees.” He calls ivory images “elephant bones.” Wool is said to terrify because of the fear and dread that in some manner belong to every religion. Weitzius adds that, according to the commentator on Sophocles’ *Oedipus Tyrannus*, a *stemma* was wool wrapped around a branch or trunk; from this it may be inferred that images were customarily crowned with such a wreath, as is gathered from Julius Obsequens. Weitzius likewise asserts, without producing a witness, that in former times jugglers carried wool on a painted staff to deceive children and fools. Therefore this passage is more appropriately understood of a tree decorated with ribbons, about which see more at the cited verse of Book II against Symmachus. Pliny, Book XII, chapter 1, speaking of trees: “These were the temples of the gods, and even now, according to the ancient rite, the simple countryside dedicates an outstanding tree to a god; no more brightly shining images of gold and ivory than the groves and the very silences in them do we worship.”

303. Weitz., with Egm., has *falsos*. Heinsius, with Thuan. and Alt., has *salsus*, as writers often use *homo salsus* for “a witty or ridiculous man.” Here *falsus* seems sound to me, although later editors follow Heinsius.

304. Ald., Urb., Hailsbr. in the first hand, and Bong. above have *vanulae*; older manuscripts have *rancidae*; Alex. has *rancide*. Heinsius strongly disapproves *vanulae*, since Martial speaks of “speaking with a rancid mouth” and Persius of “speaking with a rancid nostril.” Some old manuscripts have *raucide*, which Iso follows. Gis., first edition, has *vanulae*, with *rancidae* in the margin. Parrhasius has *quis omne*, namely *quis*.]**

1093 Do you not blush, fool devoted to the village,

that you have always wasted such provisions—

which, foolishly, you offered to gods of this kind,

whom a ladle, basin, cup, and frying pans,
[300] 1094  
Did they bring together broken and melted vessels?

[Col. 0472A] I forgive these things in the foolish common people,  
whom discolored wool on a stake terrifies,  
whom a false mountebank often deceives,  
and for whom everything is sacred that the song  
[305] of toothless, hoarse old women may have persuaded them to fear.

[Col. 0473A]  
**Note: [Col. 0473B]**

307. *Perpensa*: weighed, balanced; a thing *perpensa* is one weighed back with equal weight, restored as equal, I.

324. *Pollet*: properly, to exercise power; here, “excels,” I.

327. *Globos*: stars; he speaks of the moon and stars, I.

329. *Septentriones*: the Bears, I.

331. *Praerupta*: rough, precipitous places, I.

[Col. 0474B] 333. *Subjugales*: horses, oxen, and whatever is put beneath a yoke, I.

334. *Fruteta*: low shrubs, undergrowth, I.

335. *Vernant*: they flower, they grow green, I.

336. *Molitus*: attempted, endeavored, I.

339. *Verbo*: by the Word, the Son, I.

340. *In Verbo*: in the Word, in the Son, I.

[Col. 0473C]  
**Note: [Col. 0473C]**

306. Pagans called Christians inexperienced and ignorant; Christians, by way of mockery, called pagans experienced and learned. Thus Arnobius, book II: “You alone, endowed with wisdom and by the force of understanding, see I know not what else, and the deep . . . . . Tell us, O witty ones, steeped and satiated with an undiluted draught of wisdom.” Romanus responds appropriately to what the prefect had objected: “The unlettered crowd believed something popular under the guise of glory.” But concerning these matters see more in Heraldus, Wowerus, Elmenhorstius, Rigaltius, and especially Ouzelius on Minucius’ words, “unskilled in studies, profane toward letters, without knowledge,” etc. Add Elmenhorstius on Arnobius, p. 38. For we may not be more lengthy, and it will be enough for us to point a finger toward the sources.

308. Ald., *moralia*: read *mortalia*.

309. Egm., *quod*. Vat. A, *qui*. Others, *quo*. Ald., *edat*, incorrectly, for *regat*.

310. Ald., *creatum, quae*, without *est*. Vat. B, Alex., Mar., Rat., Prag., and others, *creatum est, quae*, as Heinsius printed it. Weitz., Sich., Egm., Hailsbr., Pal., [Col. 0473D] *creatum est, qui*.

311. Joannes Filesacus, chapter 1 of book I of the *Selecta*, illustrates this passage with similar passages from Ambrose, Clement of Alexandria, Paulinus, and others. Elmenhorstius, p. 17, likewise treats this subject in his discussion of Arnobius. With Livy and Valerius Maximus, *inaestimabilis* means “exceeding every value.” Cicero used *inaestimabile* for something that has no price.

312. Sich., *vivendo*. The meter requires *videndo*.

315. Gis., in the margin, *extraque*, and completes *intra*. Hilary, *On the Trinity* III: “He himself is outside all things and in all things.” Paschalius, *On the Holy Spirit*: “I do not doubt that he is present through all things,” that is, within and without. Petavius, vol. I, book III, chapter 9, confirms the same opinion with many testimonies.

316. *Intemporalis* is a word used by Caelius Aurelianus and Apuleius, although Aurelianus uses it for “untimely.”

317. God’s eternity is signified, as indicated in his name, “I am who I am.” Eternity is commonly circumscribed by this definition: “the complete and perfect possession, all at once, of interminable life”; this is Boethius’ definition in book V, prose 6 of *The Consolation*, approved by universal agreement. Hence God is always one in being and having been; and in him being, having been, and being future are the same.

318. He is the Son of God, and he is called “light from light.” See *Apotheosis*, verse 278.

320. Gis., *huic*; in the margin, *hic*. This should be retained in accordance with the manuscripts.

321. Noms., *una Filii*, without *est*.

323. Alex., Pal., Vat. B, *claritatis numine*. Others, *lumine*.

327. “The sphere of the moon” occurs in Virgil; “the sphere of the sun” shortly afterward, at verse 537. He refers to Genesis 1:16, “the greater light, to rule the day; and the lesser light, to rule the night.”

333. Vat. B, Widm. in a second hand, Mar., Rat., Prag., Gis. in the text of the second edition, *pecudes*. Parrhasius, Ald., Sich., and many others, *pecua*, a word used by Cicero, Livy, Pliny, and the earlier writers. See Nonius under *pecua*. Fabr. printed *pecora*.

[Col. 0474D] 334. Alex., Parrhasius, *fructeta*. Giselinus likewise printed this, but corrected it to *frutecta*; I am surprised that Heinsius did not notice this, since Giselinus’ typographical error was incorporated into Heinsius’ edition. Moreover, the verse does not scan with *fructeta*, and *frutetum*, or *frutectum*, as others write it, derives from *frutex*, not from *fructus*. Chamillardus did not guard against Heinsius’ error.

335. Parrhasius’ reading differs greatly from that of the others: “Which are fragrant, and whose tresses are blooming.” Aldus, contrary to the meter: “Which are fragrant, and which are blooming for food.”

336. Parrhasius has *molitur*. Theodoretus, *Greek Affections* IV: “By these words he plainly shows that God did not create all things from pre-existing matter . . . . But God, the maker of all things, needs neither instruments nor matter,” etc.

338. See *Hymn for the Catholic Hours* 9, “Every hour.”

339. On such words as *omniformis*, see *Hymn for the Catholic Hours* 3, verses 1–2.

Vos eruditos miror et doctos viros  
Perpensa vitae quos gubernat regula,  
Nescire vel divina, vel mortalia  
Quo jure constent: quanta majestas regat,  
[310] Quidquid creatum est, quae creavit omnia.

I marvel that you, learned and educated men,  
whom the rule of a measured life governs,  
do not know by what right either divine or mortal things exist,  
or what majesty governs  
whatever has been created—she who created all things.

Deus perennis, res inaestimabilis,  
Non cogitando, non videndo clauditur:  
Excedit omnem mentis humanae modum,  
Nec comprehendi visibus nostris valet,  
[315] Extraque et intus implet, ac superfluit,

1096 Intemporalis ante, quam primus dies:  
Esse et fuisse semper unus obtinet:  
Lux ipse vera, veri et auctor luminis  
Cum lumen esset, lumen effudit suum:  
[320] Ex luce fulgor natus hic est Filius.

The everlasting God, a thing beyond all estimation,  
is not confined by thought or sight.  
He surpasses every measure of the human mind,  
nor can he be grasped by our senses.  
He fills and overflows both outside and within,

timeless before the first day.  
He alone possesses being and having always been.  
He himself is true light and the author of true light;  
when he was light, he poured forth his own light.  
From light was born this radiance, the Son.

[Col. 0473B] Vis una Patris, vis et una est Filii,  
Unusque ab uno lumine splendor satus,  
Pleno refulsit claritatis lumine.

The power of the Father is one, and the power of the Son is also one;  
and one radiance, sprung from one light,  
shone forth in the full light of glory.

[Col. 0474A] Natura simplex pollet unius Dei,  
[325] Et quidquid usquam est, una virtus condidit,  
Coelum solumque, vim marini gurgitis,  
Globos, dierum noctiumque praesides,  
Ventos, procellas, fulgura, imbres, nubila,  
Septentriones, hesperos, aestus, nives,  
[330] Fontes, pruinas, et metalla, et flumina,  
Praerupta, plana, montium convallia,  
Feras, volucres, reptiles, natatiles,  
Jumenta, pecudes, subjugales belluas,

The simple nature of the one God is powerful,  
and one power created whatever exists anywhere:  
the heavens and earth, the force of the sea’s abyss,  
the spheres, guardians of days and nights,  
winds, storms, lightning, rains, clouds,  
the Bears, the evening star, heats, snows,  
springs, frosts, metals, and rivers,  
precipices, plains, and mountain valleys,  
wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and creatures that swim,  
beasts of burden, herds, and beasts under the yoke,

1097 Flores, fruteta, germina, herbas, arbores,  
[335] Quae sunt odori, quaeque vernant esui.

flowers, shrubs, shoots, grasses, and trees,  
which are for fragrance and which bloom for food.

Haec non labore et arte molitus Deus,  
Sed jussione, quam potestas protulit,  
[Col. 0474B] Mandavit esse, facta sunt quae non erant.  
Verbo creavit omniformem machinam:  
[340] Virtus paterna semper in Verbo fuit:

God did not fashion these things through labor and skill,  
but by a command uttered by his power.  
He ordered what did not exist to be, and they came to be.  
By the Word he created the universe in every form.  
The Father’s power was always in the Word.

[Col. 0475A]  
**Note: [Col. 0475B]**

341. *Cognostis*: you know, for *cognovistis*, I.

343. *Sanxerit*: has decreed, established. — *Donaria*: gifts, I.

346. *Ipse*: God himself, I.

348. *Incapacem*: incapable of being dissolved, I.

350. *Discriminatis*: distinguished, separated, divided, varied. — *Illitam*: smeared, painted. — *Coloribus*: namely, with virtues, I.

354. *Litari*: to be sacrificed, I.

355. *Placere*: namely, to please him, I.

359. *Parcitatem*: abstinence, I.

360. *Spem*: hope should not lie prostrate but raise itself, I.

[Col. 0476B] 361. *Amoenus*: delightful. — *Vapor*: smoke, I.

362. *Croci*: a kind of pigment, I.

363. *Persicorum*: Persia is a region where aromatics abound, I.

365. *Prosperatum*: made favorable, benevolent, I. *Propitiatum*, Vat. A.

366. *Infensus*: hostile, troublesome, I.

367. *Probatum*: probably a noun used adverbially, I.

369. *Ignis*: of the soul, which is of fiery nature, I.

374. *Cadaveri*: the body, which must be dissolved into a corpse, I.

375. *Supra*: heavenly things, Vat. A.

[Col. 0475C]  
**Note: [Col. 0475C]**

341. Hailsbr., *cognoscis*: *cognostis* is better.

342. Prag. wrongly has *tempus genus*.

343. Mar., *quae dicari*; Vat. A, *dedicari auxerit*. Egm., *quae dedicaris auxerit*. All these readings are corrupt.

345. Vat. B, Mar., Rat., *mandat*; *mandet* is better, so that he may ask or wish.

346. Giselinus found *sedem* in his manuscript instead of *aedem*. Murmellius prefers: “He himself established in the human mind a temple for himself,” so that the consonance is not lost. Giselinus likewise finds this acceptable and attests that the reading was drawn from ancient books. Lotterus certainly printed it this way. In general, Prudentius frequently developed this idea of the mystical temple in the human heart, but nowhere more elegantly than here. “This matter,” says Barthius, book LV, chapter 5, “no one ever expressed more pleasingly and sweetly than . . . . . that most charming augur and swan of Christ, Prudentius in *Romanus*: ‘He himself established a temple for himself,’ etc.” In the First Epistle of Peter 2:5: “You yourselves, as living stones, are being built into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, to offer spiritual sacrifices acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.” [Col. 0475D] The same idea is confirmed not only by the testimonies of Sacred Scripture and the holy Fathers, but also by statements of pagans. Pliny, *Panegyric to Trajan*: “For I observe that even the gods themselves take greater pleasure not in the carefully composed prayers of their worshipers than in innocence and chastity; and that the one who brings a pure and chaste mind into their shrines is considered more pleasing than one who brings a prepared hymn.” On the temple and altar in the heart, see also Berthaldus, *On the Altar*, chapter 29.

347. Parrhasius, Ald., *flebilem*; others, *flabilem*. Nebrissensis rightly explains *flabilem* as “spiritual.” But when he asks, “What if you read *stabilem*?” he does not attend to the rules of this poem. These verses explain the nature of our soul.

350. By “distinguished colors” I understand the virtues that are natural to souls, for he later refers to supernatural virtues. Lactantius, in *On the Anger of God*, near the end, also uses the word *destructilis*, although others there read *destructibilibus*, not *destructilibus*.

[Col. 0476C] 351. Parrhasius, Alex. in a second hand, *sacrata in limine*. Hailsbr., *sacrata limine*. Vat. A, Alex. in a first hand, *sacrata limine*. Others, *sacrato in limine*; but *in* is absent in Thuan.

352. Fabricius explains this by saying that faith alone brings acceptable and legitimate victims—heretically, as though faith alone pleased God. Faith therefore guards the first doors, because without faith it is impossible to please God, and because whoever approaches God must believe that he exists, etc. The same idea appears in book II *Against Symmachus*, verse 92: “Faith alone responds, most learned, first to open the vestibule truly into the inner sanctum of the sect.”

355. The victims designated as white are spotless, as Moses prescribes in Leviticus 3.

357. Fabricius and Giselinus, *oris quietem*. The Heinsian, Weitzian, and our manuscripts have *pacis quietem*. Fabricius attacks fasts, flagellations, and religious vows inappropriately. For if he merely means that these victims do not please God without faith, he agrees with us; but he openly seeks both to exalt the power of faith alone beyond what is proper and to diminish the usefulness of other good works—an error he repeatedly inculcates in his commentaries.

[Col. 0476D] 361. Vat. B wrongly has *hostigiis* for *hostiis*, as corrected there. Prag., *amaenis hostiis*.

363. Aromatics are customarily brought from Persia. Nebrissensis interprets *madentes* as “sprinkled,” namely, through which aromatics are scattered. But *madentes* is also rightly understood as “moistened,” for the breezes are moistened with aromatics.

367. In some copies, *probate*: this is a gloss explaining *probatum* in an adverbial sense.

369. He has spoken of fire from the vigor of the soul, just as Prudentius often spoke of God; we have explained this as well.

372. *Nationes* means peoples and pagans. Solinus used *carnulentus*.

375. Lotterus wrongly has *nunquam summa*. Fabricius says that *supra* is a transferred expression for *superna*, so that the order of the sentence may stand. One might conjecture *supera*, to which the gloss alludes. But *supra* is sound.

Cognostis ipsum, nunc colendi agnoscite  
Ritum modumque: quale sit templi genus,  
Quae dedicari sanxerit donaria,  
Quae vota poscat, quos sacerdotes velit,  
[345] Quod mandet illic nectar immolarier.

You know him himself; now recognize the rite  
and manner of worshiping him: what kind of temple it is,  
what gifts he has decreed should be dedicated,  
what vows he demands, what priests he wishes,  
and what nectar he commands to be sacrificed there.

Aedem sibi ipse mente in hominis condidit

1098 Vivam, serenam, sensualem, flabilem,  
Solvi incapacem posse, nec destructilem:  
Pulchram, venustam, praeminentem culmine,  
[350] Discriminatis illitam coloribus.

He himself established a temple for himself in the human mind,  
living, serene, endowed with sensation, spiritual,  
unable to be dissolved and not destructible:  
beautiful, lovely, rising to a lofty summit,  
painted with varied colors.

Illic sacerdos stat sacrato in limine,  
Foresque primas virgo custodit Fides,  
Innexa crines vinculis regalibus,  
Poscit litari victimas Christo, et Patri,  
[355] Quas scit placere, candidatas, simplices:

There the priest stands at the consecrated threshold,  
and the virgin Faith guards the first doors,  
her hair bound with royal bands.  
She asks that victims be sacrificed to Christ and the Father—  
victims she knows to be pleasing, white and pure:

[Col. 0475B] Frontis pudorem, cordis innocentiam,  
Pacis quietem, castitatem corporis,  
1099 Dei timorem, regulam scientiae,  
[Col. 0476A] Jejuniorum parcitatem sobriam,  
[360] Spem non jacentem, semper et largam manum.

modesty of brow, innocence of heart,  
the quiet of peace, chastity of body,  
fear of God, the rule of knowledge,  
sober moderation in fasting,  
hope that does not lie prostrate, and a hand that is always generous.

Ex his amoenus hostiis surgit vapor,  
Vincens odorem balsami, thuris, croci.  
Auras madentes Persicorum aromatum:  
Sublatus inde coelum adusque tollitur,  
[365] Et prosperatum dulce delectat Deum.

From these pleasing victims a fragrant vapor rises,  
surpassing the scent of balsam, frankincense, and saffron,  
and the breezes moistened with Persian aromatics.  
From there it is lifted and rises as far as heaven,  
and sweetly delights a propitious God.

Hanc disciplinam quisquis infensus vetat,  
Vetat probatum vivere, et sanctum sequi.  
Vetat vigorem mentis alte intendere,  
Nostrique acumen ignis ad terram vocat,  
[370] Nec excitari vim sinit prudentiae.

Whoever, in hostility, forbids this discipline  
forbids living rightly and pursuing what is holy.  
He forbids the mind to strain its strength toward the heights,  
calls the sharpness of our fiery spirit down to earth,  
and does not permit the power of wisdom to be awakened.

O mersa limo caecitas gentilium!  
O carnulenta nationum pectora!  
[Col. 0476B] O spissus error! o tenebrosum genus,  
Terris amicum, deditum cadaveri,  
[375] Subjecta semper intuens, nunquam supra!

O blindness of the pagans, sunk in mud!  
O fleshly hearts of the nations!  
O dense error! O dark race,  
friendly to earthly things, devoted to the corpse,  
always gazing upon what lies beneath, never above!

[Col. 0477A]  
**Note: [Col. 0477B]**

378. *Terrulenter*: in the earth, I.

381. *Deasciato*: cut with an axe; *ascia planato*, smoothed or formed with an axe. *Ascia* is a kind of tool by which things are shaped, I.

383. *Ofellis*: a diminutive of *offa*, which signifies a fruit, I. *Particulis praecisis*, Mar.

385. *Urnas*: tombs, Mar.

387. *Liberis*: from the devil’s servitude, I.

389. *Asserentibus*: affirming, I.

390. *Est*: namely, for them, I.

[Col. 0478B] 391. *Coquebat*: was preparing. — *Disserente*: while he was saying these things, I.

392. *Subdolam*: deceitful, I.

393. *Stomachatus*: angry; *stomachor*, I am angry, I.

394. *Bilemque*: bile, envy, or the anger of bile; the blackness of bile, from which anger proceeds, I.

396. *Pro!* an exclamation: “Ah, God!” I.

399. *Perorat*: speaks, I.

401. *Fas*: law, I.

[Col. 0477B]  
**Note: [Col. 0477B]**

378. Vat. A in a first hand, Gis., Parrhasius, Vat. Q, Alex., most of the Heinsian manuscripts, Bong, Widm. in a second hand, *terrulente*. Ald., Weitz., Mar., Rat., *terrulenter*. No earlier writer than Prudentius is found to have used *terrulentus* or *terrulenter*.

379. He also argued against the consecration of the elements in book I *Against Symmachus*, verses 297 and following.

381. Ald., Mar. in a first hand, Alex., Vat. Q, [Col. 0477C] write *deasceato*. Urb. has the erroneous *dissecato*. *Deascio* means “I smooth with an axe.” This word occurs in Plautus and in ancient inscriptions. An *ascia* is properly an iron tool used by carpenters to smooth wood; in Spanish, I think, *hacha*. For *runcina* seems to be *cepillo*, while *scobina* is a kind of file for scraping. See Mazochius’ letter *On Dedication under the Axe*. Tertullian, *Apology*, chapter 12: “Axes, planes, and files bear down upon your gods in all their limbs.” Minucius: “For a wooden god, perhaps a portion of a funeral pyre or of an unfortunate stump, is hung up, cut, hewn, shaped, and planed.” Barthius compares this verse of Prudentius, in book IV, chapter 12, with Tibullus, elegy IV of book II: “Whether a stump, cut down in the fields, stands.” Thus he read *desectus* instead of *desertus*, from one of the Palatine manuscripts. For however rough the stump may have been, it had nevertheless been cultivated in some manner, since it alone among the others was believed to possess some divinity. On this matter I spoke at verse 1005 of book II *Against Symmachus*, in connection with a similar verse of Ovid. But the reading I indicated there seems more correct: *desertus* from *desero*, from which come *desevi* and *deserui*, *desitus* and *desertus*, that is, “planted.” Others write *dissero, dissevi, disserui, dissertus, dissitus*, with the same meaning. Macrobius, book III of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 18, copies these verses of Suevius: “This kind of tree they planted in the cultivated borders of Greece, giving new fruits to mortals.”

382. Images were formerly accustomed to be inscribed on their bases; hence, “inscribed stones.” Pigs were sacrificed to Ceres, Cybele, the Bona Dea, Mars, and Terminus. Fabricius notes that these pigs were not properly boars, but castrated males—or, as Varro calls them, *nefrendes*. A *maialis* differs from a boar as a *vervex* differs from a ram, a *cantherius* from a horse, and a *caper* from a he-goat.

383. Ald., Widm., Bong., Vat. Q write *offellis*; but that *ofella* is formed from *offa* by removing one *f* is proved by the quantity of the first vowel, which is short. In the gloss, *frustum* should perhaps be read instead of *fructum*.

385. Nebrissensis reads *deorum*, not improperly. In these verses, as I think, the subject is emperors deified, whose urns the Romans kissed. *Morticinus* properly means one dead by himself, not killed by another. Thus *urnae morticinae* are tombs in which the bodies of the dead lay. Some punctuate: “to lick the dead urns of the accused,” that is, tombs and dead flesh. Fabricius attacks this superstition, as he calls it, among Italians, because they kiss urns in which the bodies of saints lie. But [Col. 0478C] these are signs of religion and true piety, not superstition, prevailing and always having prevailed among all Catholics, as is clear from Prudentius himself. What, then, does Prudentius reproach the pagans for? That they worshiped human beings, and indeed criminals, as gods. They did not show them such acts of reverence as holy men and friends of the true God, but as possessing divinity in their own right.

387. Weitz., with some of his manuscripts, *fortibus, et liberis*. The meter requires *fortibusque et*. *Jubeo tibi* is a Graecism of a later age, more familiar than it was to writers of the golden age. Scioppius defended it as thoroughly Latin on the basis of Cicero, Livy, and others.

388. Some have *nihil*. In Vat. B the verses are arranged as follows: 1. “Nothing is a cause of fear”; 2. “Nothing is stronger than love”; 3. “The everlasting God.”

389. Vat. A, B, Q, Weitz., Widm. above, and others in either a first or second hand, *numen*. Alex., Urb., Mar. in a first hand, Rat. from an old hand, Ald., Parrhasius, *nomen*.

[Col. 0478D] 390. Vat. B, Mar., Rat., *nil est pavori*. The verse does not scan. Fabr., Gis., Heins., *nihil est pavori*. Parrhasius, Ald., Hailsbr., Alex., and others, *nihil pavori est*. Aldus, contrary to the law of the meter, transposed *est*, and printed *mors* for *est*: *mors et*.

398. Ald. erroneously has *phoro* for *foro*.

399. Ald., Mar., Prag., Weitz., Rat., Parrhasius, Tornaes, and others, *hic perorat*. Gallandius followed this and thought there was an error in Chamillardus’ *ac perorat*. But Heinsius preferred *ac perorat*, with Egm., Pal., Thuan., Noms., Vat. A, Alex., and others. Instead of *perditus*, Prag. has *perditos*, with this gloss: “that is, by speaking he persuades the lost to believe him.” But that would be poor Latin.

401. Ald., Hailsbr., *O fas piorum*. *Priorum* is better. In some copies, *motis*, wrongly, for *moris*. Nebrissensis, who with Aldus reads *o fas piorum*, explains it: “Alas, piety, O law!” But *fas* is ordinarily said of what is permitted by religion.

Furorue summus, ultima et dementia est,  
1100 Deos putare qui creantur nuptiis?  
Rem spiritalem terrulenter quaerere:  
Elementa mundi consecrare altaribus:  
[380] Id, quod creatum est, conditorem credere?  
Deasciato supplicare stipiti:  
Verris cruore scripta saxa spargere:  
Aras ofellis obsecrare bubulis,  
Homines fuisse cum scias, quos consecras,  
[385] Urnas reorum morticinas lambere?

Or is it the height of madness and the final stage of insanity  
to think that gods are created by sexual unions?  
To seek a spiritual reality in the earth?  
To consecrate the elements of the world upon altars?  
To believe that what has been created is the creator?  
To pray to a stump smoothed with an axe?  
To sprinkle inscribed stones with the blood of a boar?  
To entreat altars with pieces of oxen,  
when you know that those whom you consecrate were human beings,  
and to lick the dead urns of criminals?

1101 Desiste, judex saeculi, tantum nefas  
Viris jubere fortibusque et liberis;  
Nil est amore veritatis celsius.  
[Col. 0478A] Dei perennis numen asserentibus  
[390] Nihil est pavori, mors et ipsi subjacet.

Cease, judge of the age, to command such wickedness  
upon brave and free men.  
Nothing is higher than love of truth.  
For those who affirm the divinity of the everlasting God,  
nothing is an object of fear; even death itself lies beneath them.

Dudum coquebat, disserente martyre,  
Asclepiades intus iram subdolam,  
Stomachatus alto felle, dum longum silet,  
Bilemque tectis concipit praecordiis,  
[395] Tandem latentis vim furoris evomit  
Pro Juppiter, quid est quod ex hoc audio!  
Stat inter aras, et deorum imagines,  
Et, quod fateri cogor, in medio foro,  
1102 Tacente memet, hic perorat perditus,  
[400] Quidquid sacrorum est, ore foedans impio?

For some time, while the martyr was speaking,  
Asclepiades was inwardly cooking up a deceitful anger;  
enraged with deep bile, while he remained silent for a long time,  
he gathered bile within his hidden entrails.  
At last he vomits forth the force of his concealed fury:  
“By Jupiter, what is this that I hear from him?”  
He stands among the altars and images of the gods,  
and—as I am compelled to admit—in the middle of the forum,  
while I myself remain silent, this wretched man speaks at length,  
defiling everything sacred with his impious mouth.

O fas priorum, moris o prisci status,

O law of our ancestors, O established custom of ancient times!

[Col. 0479A]  
**Note: [Col. 0479B]**

403. *Pompiliorum*: a patronymic. Pompilius first established the worship of the gods, in order to recall the people from the madness of war. Pompilius Numa, who turned the people’s ferocity toward religious rites. — *Carpunt*: they tear apart, break up; *carpere* means to pull something apart bit by bit; hence *carpunt*, “they break apart and disparage.” — *Saecula*: times, I.

404. *Sophistas*: that is, clever men; *sophos* means wise, *sophista* a clever and ingenious arguer; *falsos conclusores*, I.

407. *Consules*: those who worshiped these gods, I.

408. *Retexam*: lest I recount or bring forward. — *Nestoras*: ancient kings. Nestor was the most ancient king of the Greeks who worshiped the gods; from him that wicked custom grew, I.

410. *Pyrrham*: she was the wife of Deucalion, I.

412. *Divum favore*: in the honor of the gods. — *Mavortius*: warlike, or the son of Mars, I.

413. *Septicollem*: because Rome is surrounded by seven hills, I.

414. *Auspicato*: favorably, for *auspicio*, I.

415. *Statori*: Romulus, on one occasion when he was being pursued by enemies while his army fled, called upon Jupiter. Then the fleeing army stood firm; hence Jupiter is called Stator, I.

416. *Ab aevo*: from the beginning, I.

418. *Delubra*: temples. — *Faustus*: favorable, fortunate, blessed. — *Secundet*: may he prosper. — *Gloriam*: of the prince, I.

419. *Procinctus*: prepared, a military preparation, I.

420. *Frenet*: may he govern, I.

421. *Accingere*: prepare yourself, I.

422. *Rite*: rightly, I.

426. *Tunc ille*: namely, he said, I.

[Col. 0479C]  
**Note: [Col. 0479C]**

403. He means the superstitious trifles of Numa Pompilius.

404. Pagans called Christians *sophistae*; even our Savior is called a crucified sophist by Lucian, namely, using this word for someone who deceived others through deceptive arguments. He adds the reason: because they denied that the gods ought to be worshiped. Hence they were likewise called atheists, impious, profane, and sacrilegious.

407. A thousand consuls are a thousand years.

408. By *Nestoras* he means the heroic age. Prudentius often expresses the names of a single person in the plural, such as *Pompilios*, *Deucaliones*, and *Nestoras*; and among divine names, *Junones*, *Cythereas*, and *Priapos*.

409. On the objection made to Christians concerning the novelty of their religion, see book II *Against Symmachus*, Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 2, and Arnobius, books I and II.

410. Ald., Vat. Q, *Vis summam rerum nosse? Pyrrham consule*. The law of the meter does not permit this. In Mar. there appears originally to have been *summa*, later changed to *summam*, and then *consulem*; but the *m* had been deleted. Rat., Vat. B, *consulem*, with this meaning: “Do you wish to know the summit of things? Consult Pyrrha.” In Alex. the question mark is absent after *nosse*. Nevertheless, the reading I have presented is correct, and most manuscripts support it.

414. Vat. B wrongly has *pollet auspicio*.

415. Rat., contrary to the meter, *debetur*. Some write *dis* for *diis*. An image of Jupiter Stator appears in Montfaucon, *Explanation of Roman Antiquities*, vol. I, p. 39, with the inscription *IOVI STATORI*. Cicero, *Against Catiline*, addressing the Roman knights: “Jupiter Stator, whom our ancestors rightly named the Stayer of this empire, whose temple Romulus, after defeating the Sabines, established at the foot of the Palatine together with Victory.” They say he was so called because he made the Roman soldiers, fighting against the Sabines, stand firm. Seneca gives another reason: that through his favor everything stood. See book IV *On Benefits*, chapter 7. An ancient inscription reads: *I. J. M. STATORI*.

416. Ald., Parrhasius, and some copies, *ab avis*. Restore *ab atavis* for the sake of the meter. Minucius: “How much more reverently and properly should one receive the teaching of one’s ancestors, observe inherited religious practices, and fear the gods with whom one was imbued by one’s parents before knowing them more intimately and worshiping them?” Symmachus says similar things, as may be observed in the books written against him.

418. Fabricius notes that *delubra* are little shrines made of wood smoothed with an axe, in which several gods are worshiped beneath one roof. Others give a different meaning and say that a *delubrum* is a stripped or hewn trunk, which they venerated as a god. *Delubrum* is commonly used for every sacred building, without distinction.

419. Rat. wrongly has *utique* for *utque*. Barthius concludes from this, in book XLI of the *Adversaria*, chapter 12, that *procinctus* in the Christian age also signified an army. Properly, *procinctus* is military preparation for entering battle, or the army itself equipped and ready for war.

[Col. 0480D] 420. Virgil, *Aeneid* I.527: “To bridle proud nations.”

421. Virgil, book II: “Whoever you are, forget the Greeks already lost here.” Fabricius notes that it is arrogant and is said of people unknown to the common crowd: “Whoever you are.” Compare the commentary on verse 31 of the preface to the *Carmina*: “I must say: Whoever you are.”

422. Prag., *ritu*: correct to *rite*. He calls the emperor’s life “princely.”

425. Egm. wrongly has *principum* for *principem*. The Marietti manuscript reads this way and punctuates: “To have despised the temples, to have rejected the prince,” which seems better to Marietto, so that the meaning is: “Pay the penalty because you despised the temples and rejected the prince.” I like this less. In the same Mar. there seems to have originally been, in a different reading, *templum pro principem*; but the meter resists it.

Inventa regum pro salute publica  
Pompiliorum nostra carpunt saecula.  
Quis hos sophistas error invexit novus,  
[405] Qui non colendos esse divos disputent?  
Nunc dogma nobis Christianum nascitur  
Post evolutos mille demum consules  
Ab urbe Roma, ne retexam Nestoras.  
Quidquid novellum surgit, olim non fuit.  
[410] Vis summa rerum nosse? Pyrrham consule.

The inventions of kings for the public welfare,  
the institutions of the Pompilii, our ages tear apart.  
What new error has brought in these sophists,  
who argue that the gods should not be worshiped?  
Now a Christian doctrine is being born for us,  
only after a thousand consuls have passed  
from the city of Rome—not to recount the ancient kings.  
Whatever arises as something new did not exist long ago.  
Do you wish to know the summit of things? Consult Pyrrha.

1103 Ubi iste vester tunc erat summus Deus,  
Divum favore cum puer Mavortius  
Fundaret arcem septicollem Romulus?  
Quod Roma pollet auspicato condita,  
[415] [Col. 0480A] Jovi Statori debet, et diis caeteris.

Where, then, was this supreme God of yours,  
when, with the favor of the gods, the son of Mars,  
the boy Romulus, founded the seven-hilled citadel?  
That Rome, auspiciously founded, is powerful  
she owes to Jupiter Stator and the other gods.

Hoc sanctum ab aevo est, hoc ab atavis traditum  
Placanda nobis pro triumphis principis  
Delubra, faustus ut secundet gloriam  
Procinctus, utque subjugatis hostibus  
[420] 1104 Ductor quietum frenet orbem legibus

This has been sacred from the beginning; this was handed down by our forefathers:  
the temples that must be appeased for the prince’s triumphs,  
so that favorable military preparation may advance his glory,  
and so that, with the enemy subdued,  
the leader may govern the peaceful world by laws.

Accingere ergo, quisquis es, nequissime,  
Pro principali rite nobiscum deos  
Orare vita: vel, quod hostem publicum  
Pati necesse est, solve poenam sanguine.  
[425] Sprevisse templa, respuisse est principem.

Therefore prepare yourself, whoever you are, most wicked man,  
and rightly pray with us to the gods  
for the prince’s life; or, since you must endure  
the fate of a public enemy, pay the penalty with your blood.  
To have despised the temples is to have rejected the prince.

Tunc ille: Nunquam pro salute, et maximis.  
Fortissimisque principis cohortibus

Then he said: “Never, for the safety and the greatest,  
most valiant cohorts of the prince—

428. *Fidele*: faithfully, I.

433. *Succulentis*: moist with abundant tears, misty. — *Influens*: namely, that light, I.

436. *Crassum*: for *crasse*, I.

438. *Liquidis*: pure. — *Liquor*: purity, I.

439. *Natura fervens*: the soul. — *Ferventissimae*: most ardent, I.

442. *Si*: if indeed, I.

445. *Crede*: believe me, I.

[Col. 0482B] 447. *Vindices*: those who ought to avenge us from such things, I.

449. *Abditam rimamini*: search out what is hidden, I.

450. *In principem*: against, I.

452. *Hiulco*: split, fissured, gaping. — *Pensilis*: hanging, I.

453. *Tractim*: by drawing out, so that the torture might be greater; therefore they cut gradually, I. *Continuatim*, Vat. A.

456. *Nitendo*: exerting themselves, pressing or leaning upon him, I.

[Col. 0481B]  
**Note: [Col. 0481B]**

428. Parrhasius reads *quam fidei ut militent*, so that the second syllable in *fidei* is long. This is contrary to Prudentius’ usage, and the manuscript parchment resists it. See the commentary on verse 62 of the *Dittochaeon*. In addresses by emperors to the army, the soldiers’ loyalty was especially praised; and ancient coins contain expressions of this kind: “the loyalty of the soldiers,” “the loyalty of the army,” “the loyalty of the armies.” See Anselmus Bandurius, *On Coins*. Likewise in ancient inscriptions: “loyal legions.” This is the loyalty now under discussion; in the following verse, Christian faith. Justin, addressing Antoninus Pius, as Chamillardus notes: “We worship God alone, and in other matters render you willing obedience, acknowledging you to be emperors and leaders of men, and at the same time asking that you may be found to possess sound judgment along with imperial power.” Arnobius, book IV, near the end: “Why did our writings deserve to be consigned to the flames? Why were our meeting places savagely destroyed? In them the supreme God is worshiped, and peace and pardon are requested for magistrates, armies, kings, etc.” Athenagoras says similar things at the end of his *Apology*, where the notes of the Maurists may be consulted.

[Col. 0481D] 430. In Rat. some minor scholar, because of the words *Paraclitum* and *idolorum*, altered these verses after erasing the earlier ones: “Let them receive the sacred Spirit itself from heaven, and reject the darkness of evil spirits.” It is sufficiently clear that this inept corrector understood meter well enough to compose verses himself, but not to correct Prudentius’ verses. In Mar., *Paraclytum*, less correctly, instead of *Paraclitum*.

431. Aldus seems deliberately to have printed *uti dolorum*, so that the second syllable in *idolorum* would not be shortened. But no correction is needed, and the manuscripts require that it be read *ut idolorum*.

432. Ald., wrongly, *illum* for *illud*; Gis., Weitz., *cernant et*; most others, *cernant ut*.

433. He calls the eyes “succulent” because of the excessive moisture and fluid by which they become dull. With a similar meaning he says in the preface to *Hamartigenia*, “succulent rages,” and Paulinus, “succulent body,” in his poem to Cythera. Apuleius also uses this word.

[Col. 0482C] 438. In some copies, *liquidus*, incorrectly, instead of *liquidis*. On this word *liquidus* meaning “spiritual,” consult the prolegomena, chapter 15.

443. Ald., Urb., Cauch., Oxon., Rot., one Torrentian manuscript, and others, *resistat*. Most have *resistit*. Hailsbr., *resistis*.

445. Cauchius preferred *nunquam inserviam*. Why, when the manuscripts oppose him?

450. Thuan., Heins., *erupit* instead of *erumpit*.

451. Vat. B, Mar. above, two Torrentian manuscripts, Gis. in the margin, *utrinque* instead of *utrumque*. For *teterrimi*, Prag. and Mar. in a first hand have *deterrimi*. A vivid image of the horrible torture is expressed in these verses. Sagittarius, chapter 5, believes that these verses concern scorpions, a type of whip named from the scorpion’s tail because its curved wound was driven into the body. See Gallonius, chapter 4, and plate IX. Whether the martyr Romanus was beaten in this way on the rack, I shall discuss at verse 491.

454. Mar., *transversi*, and in a different reading, *transversis*.

455. Fabricius recognizes a transferred expression: “the bones whiten, the chest having been laid bare.”

457. In *heros* the *o* is shortened, although it is an omega; neither Chamillardus, Cellarius, nor Teolius noticed this in their indices, as I showed at verse 52.

458. Some copies, *audet sponte*.

460. Weitz., with Egm. and Hailsbr., wrote *lacinamur*. *Lancinamur* should be retained. Vat. A has *laniamur*; Vat. B, *lanzinamur*.

461. Ald., Gis., *insidet*. The better manuscripts, *insedit*. Gallandius, with Ald., Torn., and the Paris edition of the Fathers, *insidet*.

462. Ald., Torn., Galland., Widm., Bong., contrary to the meter: *Populos quod istos tecum trahis perditos*. Ambr., Thuan. in a second hand, Parrhasius, *perditus tecum trahis*. Thuan. in a first hand, *perditum*, which Heinsius considers correct. Thus in Terence: “Why do you lead him away ruined?” Teolius found the same reading in one Vat. manuscript; but he is wrong to say that the more important manuscripts in Heinsius have *perditum*. Fab., *Populos trahis tecum quod istos perditos*. Gis., *Populos quod istos perditus tecum trahis*. This reading is pleasing; nor is “the peoples whom, wretched man, you lead away with you” objectionable. Terence’s “Why do you lead him away ruined?” is not analogous: leading is one thing, going another.

Anter precabor, quam fidele ut militent,  
Christique lymphis ut renascantur Patri,  
[430] Capiant et ipsum coelitus Paraclitum:

I shall first pray that they may serve faithfully,  
and that through Christ’s waters they may be reborn to the Father,  
and receive the Paraclete himself from heaven:

1105 Ut idolorum respuant caliginem,  
Cernant ut illud lumen aeternae spei,  
Non succulentis influens obtutibus,  
Nec corporales per fenestras emicans,  
[435] Puris sed intus quod relucet mentibus.

so that they may reject the darkness of idols,  
and see that light of eternal hope,  
not flowing into moist eyes,  
nor flashing through bodily windows,  
but shining within pure minds.

Pupilla carnis crassa crassum perspicit,  
Et res caduca, quod resolvendum est, videt:  
Liquidis videndis aptus est animae liquor:  
Natura fervens sola ferventissimae  
[440] Divinitatis vim coruscantem capit.

The thick pupil of the flesh sees what is thick,  
and sees a perishable thing, what must be dissolved.  
The soul’s pure substance is suited to seeing pure things;

Hoc, opto, lumen imperator noverit  
[Col. 0481B] Tuus, meusque, si velit fieri meus  
Nam si resistit Christiano nomini,  
Meus ille talis imperator non erit:  
[445] Scelus jubenti, crede, nunquam serviam.

I hope that your emperor may know this light,  
and mine as well, if he wishes to become mine.  
For if he resists the Christian name,  
such an emperor will not be mine.  
Believe me, I shall never serve one who commands crime.”

[Col. 0482A] Statis, ministri, clamitans judex ait,  
Statis, manusque continetis vindices?  
Non rupta sulcis dissecatis viscera?  
Animam nec intus abditam rimamini,  
[450] Erumpit unde vox profana in principem?

“Are you standing there?” the judge cries out,  
shouting: “Are you standing there, and restraining your avenging hands?  
Do you not cut open entrails torn with furrows?  
Do you not search out the soul hidden within,  
from which the profane voice against the prince breaks forth?”

1106 Scindunt utrumque milites teterrimi  
Mucrone hiulco pensilis latus viri,  
Sulcant per artus longa tractim vulnera,  
Obliqua rectis, recta transversis secant,  
[455] Et jam retectis pectus albet ossibus.

The most savage soldiers split both sides  
of the man’s hanging body with a gaping blade.  
They furrow his limbs with long wounds, cutting slowly;  
they cut the oblique wounds with straight ones, and the straight with transverse ones,  
and now, with the bones laid bare, his chest grows white.

Nitendo anhelant, diffluunt sudoribus,  
Cum sit quietus heros in quem saeviunt.  
Haec inter addit sponte Romanus loqui,  
Si quaeris, o praefecte, verum noscere,  
[460] Hoc omne quidquid lancinamur non dolet:

Straining, they pant and stream with sweat,

Amid this Romanus voluntarily adds these words:

[Col. 0482B] Dolet quod error pectori insedit tuo,

It pains me that error has settled in your breast,
