465. *Crudum*: cruel, I.

470. *Perpetem*: lasting, enduring, I.

472. *Juge*: for *jugiter*, continually, I.

475. *Disjuncta*: separated. — *Mancipatur*: is seized, I.

477. *Olim*: in the future, I.

478. *Pacto*: by a law, I.

481. *Fidiculae*: cords for flogging. Although *fiducula* derives from *fides* (“string”), in this passage it signifies claws, or a kind of torture by which accused persons suspended on the rack are tormented, so that the truth may be discovered. *Fidicula* is a kind of torture or very thin iron by which martyrs were cut, I.

485. *Pleurisis*: an illness or pain of the sides, I.

486. *Inusta*: thoroughly burned, I.

465. Parrhasius, *crudum quae*: correct to *crudumque*. [Col. 0483C] Vat. B, Mar., Rat. in a first hand, Widm., Bong., transmit *exemplum trahunt*; the more correct manuscripts have *tremunt*.

### 467

The word *catasta* is discussed at verse 56 of Hymn 1, *Peristephanon*. In foreign writers, *catasta* is a wooden platform on which slaves for sale stood. Here it denotes a raised place where punishment was inflicted on the condemned. Saint Cyprian, in Letter 38, elsewhere numbered 33—or Letter 5 of Book II—speaking of Aurelius, who had confessed Christ upon the *catasta*, says that he came from the *catasta* to the pulpit, since he had been ordained lector by Cyprian himself. On the *catasta*, see Gallonius and Sagittarius, who correct the errors of others. In Homily 2 of Saint Chrysostom—or of another contemporary of Chrysostom—there is mention of the *eculeus* in connection with Saint Romanus: “They suspended him on the *eculeus* and tore him apart; but he embraced the *eculeus* as though it were the tree of life.” In Greek, however, there is only τὸ ξύλον, “the wood,” and I do not think it certain that Romanus was suspended on the *eculeus*, as I shall say later.

### 468

Parrhasius reads these verses as follows:

> Christ, the splendor of the Father’s glory,  
> God, creator of all things, and likewise a participant in us.

Christ is called “the splendor of the Father’s glory” in the Epistle to the Hebrews 1:3.

### 469

Prag., Lotterus: *nostri idem*, “the same as ours”; perhaps *nostri et idem*, “and likewise a participant in us,” as Parrhasius has it.

### 470

Hailsbr.: *perpetim*, “continually.”

### 474

Some of the vulgate editions read *intret*, “may enter.”

### 476

Mar., for the various reading, has *curandum*, “to be considered.” But meter and sense require *curanda*, “must be considered.” Cauchius emended the passage to *Curanda merces qualis, et quaenam mihi*; Heinsius adds that *qualis, ac quaenam mihi* comes closer to the vulgate.

### 478

Lucifer of Calaris, in his book *On the Necessity of Dying for the Son of God*, writes:

> As for the outcome, it makes no difference whether I die by a nail driven through me or by a spear, with my hands bound behind my back or extended and spread out, etc.

### 479

Weitz., with his manuscripts, reads *certa*, “certain.” Others more elegantly have *certe*, “certainly.”

### 480

Sich., and Bong. in his first hand, read *cadat*, “may fall,” instead of *ruat*, “may rush down.”

### 481

Vat. B, Urb., Prag., Mar. above, Weitz., and Gis. read *ignes*, “fires.” The better witnesses, with Ald., read *ignis*, “fire.” Instead of *et*, Fabr. has *an*. Ald., Weitz., Gis., Parrhasius, Alex., Vat. Q, Urb., Lotterus, and others read *fidiculae*. Prag. has *fidiclae*, which Heinsius printed, although he did not indicate the variant reading.

Many think that *fidiculae* means whips; others, instruments to which the condemned were fastened so that the truth might be extorted from them; others, iron claws, as stated in the note on verse 44 of *Peristephanon* 1. Magius’s view is less probable: that they were the same kind of instrument as the *eculeus*; still less probable is Laurentius Valla’s opinion that the instrument consisted of two slanting pieces of wood.

In place of “claws,” Isidore clearly understands *fidiculae* in Book V, chapter 27 of the *Etymologies*:

> They are called claws because they dig out. These are also called *fidiculae*, because with them the condemned are tortured on the *eculeus*, so that the truth may be discovered.

Prudentius also appears to use *fidiculae* in this sense at verse 550 of this hymn. Nevertheless, others take *fidiculae* to mean sinews or cords by which the condemned were bound and stretched, relying especially on Suetonius and Valerius Maximus. There is nothing to prevent the same word from having had two meanings, or a different meaning at different times.

### 482

Some write *langor*, “languor.”

### 483

Weitz., with Egm., reads *saevitas*, “ferocity.” Cauchius conjectured this, and Heinsius, with others, adopted it. Giselinus, already in his corrections, noted in the margin that *saevitas* should be written instead of the various reading. Most have *saevitia*, “cruelty.” Murmellius, however, observes that in the sixth section of the poem scarcely any foot other than the iamb occurs, and therefore prefers *saevitas*, a word found in Gellius. Others nevertheless read *scaevitas* in Gellius, as also in Apuleius. Firmicus certainly used this word.

Parrhasius reads:

> When often a greater illness and ferocity—

But the sense is defective and the meter stands in the way. Fabricius printed *saevitia* in the *Christian Poets*, but in his special commentary on this hymn he observes that *saevitas* is an ancient word used for *saevitia*.

### 484

Egm. has *fodet*, “will pierce,” incorrectly.

### 485

Weitz., Vatt. A, B, Q, Mar., and Alex. have *pleurisis*, which Heinsius asserts to be the true spelling. Many, including ancient witnesses, nevertheless have *pleuresis*. Some of the vulgate editions incorrectly have *male*, “badly,” and *quanta* instead of *quanto*; others no better distinguish the words as *fodit mucrone, quanto*. In connection with pleurisy, *mucro* is correctly used: in Italian this disease is called *puntura*.

### 486

On the sheets with which the bodies of martyrs were branded, see Gallonius, chapter 6.

### 488

Ald. incorrectly has *summam*, “the highest.”

### 489

Virgil, *Georgics* III, at the end:

> Burning pustules and foul-smelling sweat followed the limbs.

#### Notes

### 490

*Cauteribus*: here *cauterium*, “cauterizing iron,” uses both the second and third declensions; the word is said to derive from *caute tenendum*, “it must be held carefully, lest a person be burned.”

### 495

*Nodosa*: “that which is in the joints.” *Arthrisis*, *arthesis*, or *artisis*: pain of the teeth, or more generally of all the joints; it takes its name from the affliction of the joints.

### 498

*Laniena*: a medical instrument, or the place where animals are slaughtered, or the slaughterer of cattle and executioner of human beings, so called from *laniatura*, “tearing to pieces.” *Laniola* is the place where physicians prepare medicines and cut the flesh of the sick.

*Hippocratica*: Hippocrates was a physician; hence *Hippocratica medicina*, “Hippocratic medicine,” named after the foremost of physicians. *Hippocras* means the supreme physician; hence the adjective *Hippocraticus*.

### 499

*Viscus*: flesh.

### 500

*Scalpella*: that is, instruments with which decay is scraped away from bones.

### 501

*Chirurgos*: a physician who habitually cuts human beings; *chirurgus* is so called from the operation of the hands, for χείρ in Greek means “hand.” Surgeons are physicians who perform medicine with their hands; *cheir* in Greek means “hand.” Empiric physicians, however, recognize disease only through understanding and indicate bodily health by words alone, performing nothing with their hands.

### 504

*Isti*: these surgeons.

---

## Notes on the text

### 490

Widm. above has *cremari ut stridulis*. Ald. had printed *cauteribus* and corrected it to *cauteriis*. But *cauteribus* is correct, since Prudentius elsewhere also uses this word. The gloss is ridiculous. Although I did not intend to point out all such absurdities of the glosses, if I have not already said so, I say it now.

### 491

I have seen no one who does not understand these verses as referring to the punishment of the *eculeus*. Indeed, in Vincentius, verse 109 and following, the *eculeus* appears to be described in the same way. In Romanus, however, this is opposed by the fact that the judge had ordered Romanus to be tortured on the *eculeus*, but, after being reminded that he was a nobleman, ordered the penal stake to be removed:

> He orders the deadly stake removed,  
> So that he may not condemn a noble man  
> With a punishment fit for commoners.

See verse 108 and following. Moreover, it is certain that martyrs suspended outside the *eculeus* were sometimes torn by claws; for they were suspended so that the executioners could more conveniently rake their bodies with claws.

It is therefore probable that Romanus was suspended with his arms bound behind his back and that heavy weights were fastened to his feet. See Plate I, letter B, and Plate XIII, letter A. Fulvius Cardulus, in his notes on the history of Saints Abundius and his companions, reports that some define the *eculeus* as a kind of torture in which a man, suspended with his hands bound above him and with very heavy weights hung from each foot, is savagely tormented. But Cardulus himself seems to move toward another opinion, and Prudentius called the *eculeus* a “deadly stake.”

### 492

Prag. has *extensus ulnis*, “stretched out by the arms.”

### 493

Weitzius attributes *crepitantibus* to Aldus; Aldus did indeed print it, but in his corrections changed it to *crepantibus*. Fulvius Cardulus, in the passage cited, understands the words as referring to the sinewy cords by which the limbs were bound, which “cracked.” But Prudentius clearly speaks of the sinews of the body, which cracked while the limbs were stretched too far.

### 494

Vat. A writes *hejulantes*, “wailing.”

### 495

Heinsius calls *arthrisis* the true spelling, although it can scarcely be found in the manuscripts. Ald., Fabr., and Gis. have *arthresis*. Alex. and Prag. have *artesis*. Urb., Vat. B, Mar., and Rat. have *arthesis*. Vat. Q has *atresis*. Pal. has *artresis*. Parrhasius has *artisis*, and says that this is Prudentius’s own word for the joint disease which the Greeks call *chiragra*.

Someone, relying on the vulgate spelling of this passage, inserted *artesis* into Latin lexicons. Giselinus refutes him, because, although the Greeks call this joint disease ἀρθρίτις, in Prudentius’s time they called it *arthresis*. Thus from *pleuritides* they formed *pleuresis*, and from *phrenitides*, *phrenesis*.

Giselinus, however, labors in vain to persuade us that Prudentius used words formed in this way through ignorance of Greek and shortened the medial syllable. First, he already concedes that the third declension was sufficiently familiar to Latin speakers, but adds that Juvenal, Martial, and other Greek scholars lengthened its medial syllable, while Prudentius alone shortened it. Then, since Prudentius already saw these words in use in his own time and heard them commonly pronounced—as who could deny?—as he himself pronounces them, why, although highly learned in Greek, should he have acted contrary to ecclesiastical usage and the custom of his age?

Moreover, it is clear that before Prudentius the medial syllable in *phrenesis* had been shortened by Serenus. Finally, Ausonius’s knowledge of Greek cannot be doubted; nevertheless, these very forms criticized in Prudentius—or others altogether similar and more difficult to explain—are found throughout Ausonius.

We have discussed these matters more fully in the *Prolegomena*. Lucilius also joins *podagra* and *arthrisis* in Nonius, page 166:

> Since the ugly old man is arthritic and gouty.

Others read *paedidus*, others *perditus*, instead of *arthriticus*.

### 496

Parrhasius has *has*; read *hasce*.

### 498

Mar. in his first hand, Vat. B, and Prag. have *lammina* or *lamina*. Lotterus has *lamiena* for *laniena*, but corruptly. In Rat., a recent corrector, after erasing the earlier reading, wrote:

> But when the fire of Hippocrates rages.

The last word formerly stood differently. In *Hippocratica*, the antepenultimate syllable is lengthened by the same license by which it is shortened in *idolium*, because of the Greek accent in *Hippocrates*.

*Laniena Hippocratica* is the part of medicine called surgery; or the whole of medicine is called *laniena* from that branch.

### 499

Boher.’s earlier reading is *exsecatur*, “is cut out.” For the meaning of *viscus*, see the note on verse 56 of the hymn to Saint Cassianus. *Visceratio* means the distribution of meat individually. Livy, Book VIII, chapter 22:

> A distribution of meat was given to the people by Marcus Flavius at his mother’s funeral.

### 500

Ald. corruptly has *scalpellam*, “a scalpel.”

### 501

Some vulgate editions have *putatur*, “is thought,” incorrectly and contrary to the meter. Torn. has *chirugos*, incorrectly.

### 506

From the Epistle to the Galatians 5:17:

> The flesh desires against the spirit.

### 508

Gifanius, in *On the Rarer Intervals of Vowels* in the index to Lucretius, reads from an old manuscript *sorde tumescit*, “it swells with filth,” elegantly, as he thinks; he does not approve *sordet, tumescit*, “it is filthy, it swells.” He observes from Priscian, Book VII, that in certain Latin words ending in a lengthened nominative *-es* and having the same number of syllables as their genitives, the ablative in the third declension is lengthened, as in *mole*, *fame*, *tabe*, and *sorde*.

Weitzius followed this view, together with Egm. and Hailsbr. Our manuscripts and those of Heinsius have *sordet*, which should not be displeasing. Mar. in his first hand has *liquitur*, “is dissolved,” instead of *liquatur*, contrary to the meter. Parrhasius has *fetit*; retain *fetet*, “it stinks.” Nebrissensis thinks *sordet* may refer to avarice, since we find *sordes* used for avarice. Horace, Book II of the *Satires*, poem 5:

> Build the tomb entrusted to your discretion without sordidness.

>

>
> That my feet are torn apart,
>

>

>

>

### 511

*Regestum*: hidden away, drawn out from the earth.

*Luxus*: indulgence, sweetness, excess. *Arvina*: fatness.

## Notes on the text

### 509

The verbs *solvi* and *diffluere*, “to be dissolved” and “to flow away,” are properly used of lust. See the commentary on verse 87 of Hymn 7, *Cath.*

### 510

Weitzius and Ald. have *intincta*, “dyed,” instead of *tincta*. Parrhasius has *felle tacta*, “touched by gall,” less well. Mar. has *labores*, “labors”; above, correctly, *livores*.

### 512

Virgil, *Georgics* II:

> And garments embroidered with gold.

### 514

*Carnes* instead of *carnis* in Teolius is a metrical error.

### 517

Prag. has *rape*, “seize”; in the margin, correctly, *carpe*, “tear away.”

### 518

Parrhasius corrupts the meter by reading *carnis usu* instead of *carnis situ*.

### 520

Ald., Weitz., and others have *ne gestet*, “lest it carry.” Ald. has *tyrannos*, incorrectly.

### 522

Egm., Pal., and Becman’s manuscript, if it is distinct from Weitzius’s Palatine manuscript, have *hoc perdolosum*. Vat. A has *hoc per dolosum*. Read *hoc perdo solum*, “I destroy only this.” In Ald. and some vulgate editions, the error *praedo* has entered instead of *perdo*.

### 527

Egm. and Pal. have *quod carendum est*, “what must be avoided”; Gifanius, in his discussion of *utor* construed with the fourth case, insists that it should be read this way, although in the old books this passage is also damaged and partly erased. Instead of *extimescimus*, Vat. B, Rat., and Mar. in his first hand have *exgemiscimus*. Prag. has *pertimescimus*, less correctly.

### 529

In Rat. a recent hand incorrectly has *naturam*. Fabricius says that Prudentius speaks in a spirit of wonder, because nature cannot accomplish this: it is God’s gift if someone judges death to be glory. Otherwise, *natura* may mean the human being himself, or human nature, which by the gift of grace judges death for Christ glorious.

*Vertit* may also be taken for *vertitur*: why does nature, or the necessity of dying, not turn into a matter of glory? Justin Martyr, *To the Romans*:

> We would not be killed, nor would unjust men be stronger than we, unless it had been ordained that every human being born should also die. Therefore, paying that debt of death, we give thanks.

### 530

Cauch. and Rott. have *regale damnum*, “royal loss.” *Legale*, “lawful,” is more correct, since the subject is the law of dying.

### 532

Vat. A has *qui*; emend to *quae*.

### 533

Cauch. and Ambr. have *coelo refulsus*. Parrhasius printed *coelo revulsus*. I approve neither.

### 534

Prag. has *Dei perennis*, “of everlasting God.”

### 535

Ald. has *regente*; others *regnante*, “reigning.”

### 536

Weitzius chose to print *plecabitur*, because he found it in Egm. Isaiah 34:4 has:

> And all the host of heaven will waste away, and they will be folded up like a scroll of heaven.

Justin—or someone else—in the response to Question 94 writes:

> Just as the divine Scriptures sometimes compare the creation of heaven by analogy with the extension of a skin, saying, “He stretches out heaven like a skin”; sometimes with smoke that has been made firm, “Heaven,” it says, “has been made firm like smoke”; and sometimes with the rounded shape of a vaulted roof, “He stretches out heaven,” it says, “like a vaulted chamber”—so conversely they compare the dissolution of heaven with other things, such as a scroll being rolled up and folded together.

The same idea is expressed in similar language in Revelation 6:13–14:

> And the stars of heaven fell … and heaven withdrew like a scroll being rolled up.

See Ludovicus Alcazar on the cited passage of Revelation.

### 537

Parrhasius has *rotatus*, “rolled.”

### 538

Some write *spheram*, others *speram*, others *spaeram*, and others *sphaeram*. In this passage *sphaeram* can stand. Elsewhere, when the first syllable is shortened, it should be written *sphera*.

### 539

Egm. and Hailsbr. have *superstis*. Some vulgate editions incorrectly have *soles*, “suns,” instead of *solus*, “alone.” When God alone is said to remain, this means that God remains with the righteous and angels, while the condemned are excluded and cast into eternal fire. At the end of the *Hamartigenia*, Prudentius acknowledges that the condemned are to be punished eternally. But that is not the same as remaining together with God.

## Notes on the text

### 567

Mariettus had noted from his own manuscript *multis fusa*, “poured through many,” and conjectured *multis refusa*, “returned through many.”

### 570

Egm. and Hailsbr. have *quod*; read *quot*, “as many as.” In Homily 2 of Chrysostom—or Flavianus—on Saint Romanus:

> But he, as though he had received many more mouths, delivered a speech.

### 572

Fabricius observes that the old word *junis* signifies the punishment itself, or the executioners. Among poets, punishments are certainly called Furies because they avenge crimes.

### 573

Vat. B, Mar., Prag., Ald., and Weitz. have *ignes*, “fires.” Others more elegantly have *ignem*, “fire.” Juvenal, *Satires* 13:

> He swears by the sun’s rays and the Tarpeian thunderbolts.

Virgil, Book VI:

> I swear by the stars, I swear by the powers above.

### 574

Virgil, *Georgics* II:

> And the year rolls back upon its own tracks.

### 575

Prag. has *et annus reducitur*, “and the year is brought back.” The meter resists this.

### 576

Rat. damages the meter by transposing the words, *tibi jam*. Weitz., Gis., Urb., and Rat. have *ignis parandus*. Vat. A and B have *ignis parandos*. Most have *ignes parandos*, and in the following verse *devorent*.

### 577

Ald., Gis., Weitz., and others have *devoret*, “may devour”; the funeral pyre may be understood.

### 583

Suetonius, *Nero*, chapter 16:

> The Christians, a class of people given to a new and harmful superstition, were afflicted with punishments.

### 584

Mar. has *jam fuit*, “has already been”; above, correctly, *haud*, “not.”

### 586

Parrhasius incorrectly omits *est*, “is,” and in the following verse *haec*, “this.”

### 588

1 Corinthians 2:14:

> The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God, for they are foolishness to him, and he cannot understand them.

### 590

From 1 John 1:5 and following:

> The light shines in darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it.

### 591

Rat., Vat. Q, Torn., and Mar. omit *in*, which was added in the Mar. manuscript by another hand.

### 592

Some editions incorrectly have *lippos*, “blear-eyed,” instead of *lippus*, “the blear-eyed man.” Weitz., with Ald., has *oclos*, so that the fourth position contains an iamb; Nebrissensis notes that this is a syncope. Lotterus, Giselinus, Heinsius, and later editors, except Gallandius, have *oculos*, because, as Teolius says, two short syllables make one long one.

For the same reason, and on the basis of this example, at verses 481 and 550 above we must restore *fidiculae* and *fidiculas* from the manuscripts, rather than *fidiclae* and *fidiclas*. In the fourth position Prudentius and other writers of senarii sometimes admit a tribrach, a foot consisting of three short syllables.

Latinius, who found *lippos oclos* in Torn., corrected it to *lippus oculos*. Prag. has *obtegit*, “covers,” instead of *obteget*, “will cover.” Nebrissensis explains:

> Whoever believes will immediately understand,

in accordance with:

> Unless you believe, you will not understand.

Fabricius adds that Prosper of Aquitaine cites this passage in the same way; Prosper usually follows the Greek Septuagint version in his works.

### 593

Alex. in his first hand, Vat. Q, Prag., Egm., Pal., and Hailsbr. have *dicit*, “he says”; others have *dicet*, “he will say.” In Parrhasius there is a metrical error: *remove*, “remove,” instead of *removete*, “remove [plural]”; likewise in the following verse, *videntibus claritas*, “brightness for those seeing,” instead of *videnti*, “for the one seeing.”

### 594

Lotterus has:

> Brightness is hateful to one who sees nothing.

Restore *injuriosa*, “offensive,” rather than *invidiosa*, “envious.”

### 595

Parrhasius had correctly printed *gravatus*, “angered,” but corrected it, contrary to the meter, to *ingratus*, “ungrateful.”

### 599

Some vulgate editions incorrectly have *exordiorium*. Vat. B incorrectly omits *est*, “is.” Vat. Q in its first hand corruptly has *est et temporum, et dierum*, “is both of times and of days.”

### 600

This means that the Father is what the Son signifies: that they have the same nature. It would not correctly be said, “This is the Father who is the Son,” because that would imply that they are the same person.

Thus the Father and the Son are *alius et alius*, “one distinct from the other,” not *aliud et aliud*, “one thing distinct from another.” This is the rule of theologians: masculine nouns or pronouns are to be used distinctly of the individual persons, while neuter forms, not indicating plurality but one thing common to the three persons, are to be applied to them collectively. The masculine forms indicate persons; the neuter forms indicate essence.

### 602

Fabricius quotes the following verses of Prosper in the same sense:

> But my mortal nature is assumed, so that, because life cannot be held by death, death may perish for me; and I may no longer live in myself, but Christ, who has mingled himself with me, may live in me.

### 604

Ald., Vat. Q, and Heins. have *possit*, “may be able.”

### 605

Vat. B and Prag. have *surrexit*, “rose,” incorrectly.

### 606

*Congressa*: fought. *Congredior tibi* means “I fight against you.”

### 608

### 614

## Notes on the text

### 606

Ald. corruptly has *membra gestant ideo*, “therefore they bear limbs.”

### 607

In Rat. there was *fuit tentant*, incorrectly. Vat. B has *cessat*; above, *cessit*, correctly. Murmellius printed *cessat*, which is also found in Lotterus’s edition.

Nebrissensis conjectures *immortalitas* instead of *immortales*, so that the meaning would be that immortality yielded to death, since by the communication of properties we say that God suffered.

Heinsius writes *temptat* here and elsewhere instead of *tentat*. Teolius also printed *temptat*, but thought it a frequentative derived from *temno*, and explains it thus: “While death despises Christ clothed in our flesh, it afterward had to yield to divine power.” Most editions retain *tentat*, with a meaning not very different.

But whether one writes *temptat* or *tentat*, it is not a frequentative verb from *temno*. The meaning is sufficiently clear: while death tests, attacks, or destroys Christ’s mortal limbs, such as ours, it yielded to the God who rose again—or to the limbs endowed with immortality in the resurrection.

### 609

Ald., Fabr., Lotterus, and Torn. have *eligit*, “chooses”; *elegit*, “chose,” is better. The passage is from 1 Corinthians 1, which Paulinus similarly rendered in verse in his poem to Cytherius.

### 611

Peveratus thinks that Prudentius is implying that the true beast who nourished Romulus was a prostitute. This is not sufficiently clear to me. Prudentius also called prostitute women “she-wolves” in Book I of *Against Symmachus*, verse 107. See the commentary on that passage.

### 612

Ald. punctuates the passage as follows: “You recount the She-Wolf first, and the omen of the vultures.” On this omen, see the commentary on verse 396 of Book II of *Against Symmachus*.

### 613

Hailsbr. and Pal. have *respues*, “you will reject.” In Rat. there was *tamen*, correctly emended to *tam*, “so.”

### 614

The diminutive of *aetas* in the *Life of Urban III*, in Muratori, volume III, page 476, is *aetatuncula*. In Cicero, Suetonius, and Plautus it is *aetatula*. Asclepiades had said at verse 407, “After a thousand consuls had at last passed by.” That is, from the founding of the City approximately 1,050 years are reckoned to the beginning of the fourth century, when Romanus suffered martyrdom. Fabricius incorrectly counts approximately 1,200 years. Nor does that agree with the words of Asclepiades and Romanus. For although kings may have ruled at Rome for approximately 244 years before the consuls, nevertheless from that time to A.D. 303 there were not a thousand consulships; rather, Asclepiades and Romanus speak of a thousand consuls and a thousand *fasti*, so that an equal number of years is intended.

### 615

Aldus has it incorrectly: *condiore*, “from the augur.”

### 616

Egm., Widm. by a second hand, Mar. by a first hand, and Vat. B read *cognita*; *condita* is better. Prag. has *prius*, through metrical error, for *pridem*. This is an imitation of Plautus, *Aulularia* II.4.41: “There are six hundred things I could mention, if I had the leisure.”

### 618

Minucius: “And what things are sacred to Jupiter? The nurse is a she-goat,” etc. See what Elmenhorstius and Ouzelius comment on this passage. Mythological books are also readily available.

### 620

Parrhasius, not without elegance, has: “But are those things now?”—“These things did not exist even formerly.” For the question is negative. “But they will exist” is more correct than “they existed.” In his emendations Parrhasius says that some read: “But now those things exist; these things did not exist even formerly.”

### 622

Prag. has *primus*; correct to *primum*.

### 623

The cross was represented in the tree of life and in many other figures explained in the Old Testament, which Gretzerus enumerates in book I of *On the Cross*, chapters 42 and following. It was also foretold through the Sibyls. Cellarius punctuates the passage so as to understand “the signs of the cross” as the sacrifices of the old law, or rather the natural signs discussed by Minucius: “Certainly we have naturally seen the sign of the cross on a ship,” and so forth. The letters by which the cross is said to be “made clear,” Cellarius explains as the prophecies of Holy Scripture. On the natural signs of the cross, one may consult Tertullian, *Apologeticus*, and Heraldus in his notes, in addition to Justin and others.

### 625

Vat. B, Mar., and Alex. read: “It is foretold by the mouths of prophets.”

### 626

Fabr. reads, with most witnesses, “judges and rulers.” Aldus, with others, has “judges, and rulers.”

### 628

Ald., Weitz., Widm., Hailsbr., Egm., and Heinsius with his witnesses read: “They did not cease to depict the form of the cross”; most of our witnesses support this reading. Fabr. and Gis. in the second edition have: “They did not cease to depict this form of the cross,” which comes closer to the requirements of the poem. Latinius read this as well, although in an old manuscript he found: “They did not cease to depict the shadow of the cross.” Gis. in the first edition had, not badly: “They did not cease to depict the form of the cross.” Urb. and Bong. read *Non destiterunt formam pingere crucis*, “They did not cease to depict the form of the cross” (with *formam* before *pingere* and *crucis* after it), a reading which, since it is plainly corrupt and contrary to the meter, may perhaps have entered the Parma edition through a typographical error. Teolius indicates no variation of readings. I suspect that Giselinus and Fabricius were concerned not so much to follow the authority of the manuscripts as to accommodate the meter. Yet I do not see how the reading of nearly all the manuscripts, and of Heinsius, can be defended. A pyrrhic foot has no place in the fourth position, indeed not even in the whole senarius. I therefore adopt *pingere figuram crucis*, “to depict the figure of the cross,” which I find in Lotterus’s old edition; for Prudentius has more than once placed a tribrach in the fourth metrical position. The mystical figure of the cross and of the name of Jesus are called “the 318 household servants of Abraham” in the preface to the *Psychomachia*; more on this may be found there.

> 644. Bong. by a first hand and Sich. have *natura simplex*. Rat. incorrectly has *in natura duplex*. Heinsius punctuates thus: “And for us Christ, God, returned—the same who, dying, is human: a twofold nature dies and conquers death.” He professes that this punctuation is owed to the Ambrosian manuscript. But with Parrhasius one may punctuate quite well: “A twofold nature: one dies, and the other conquers death,” so that Christ is understood to have two natures, one of which dies and the other conquers death. Otherwise, through the communication of idioms, God too is said to have died.

Eucherius, or Eusebius of Emesa, or, as others maintain, the Gallican author, recounts the boy’s martyrdom in the homily on St. Romanus, but does not give his name. The name is likewise suppressed in the second homily of St. Chrysostom, or Flavian. In the prayers of the Mozarabic office this boy is called the little Theodulus. Perhaps, when his name was unknown, the Greek name Theodulus, because he was a servant of God, was assigned to him. For in the Mozarabic office of St. Romanus the history seems to be drawn from Prudentius’s hymn alone. In Egm. and Hailsbr. *luctuarier* is an error. > 673. Aldus and Tornaes omit *et*, although it is necessary to the meter. Cauchius conjectured *quod cuique est unicum*, perhaps without *et*, in this form: “There must be one who is unique to each.” The meaning is the same as that expressed in *Hamartigenia* verse 39: “To whom the only Son belongs.” Thus, although people commonly punctuate *et quod uni est unicum*, I think it should be punctuated *et quod uni est unicum*, as though he were saying that there is one God, who is Father, and the Son, who is unique to him; Lotterus clearly read it this way. Parrhasius printed: “There must be one: what is unique to one.” He emended it to: “There must be one, what is unique to one.” Neither is permitted by the metrical rule. Latinius found in an old manuscript: “There must be one who is unique in every respect.” But *undequaque* for *undecunaue* is scarcely Latin.

Latinius’s codex has *Nostros fatiget tantulos, at si dolor / Vexabit*. Thuan., Rott., Urb., and three Torr. have *quantulos autem dolor / Vexabit artus*, which Heinsius followed. Teolius, with Weitz., Ruinartius, and most Vatican manuscripts, has *quantulus autem dolor*. Heinsius noted that this is contrary to the meter. Teolius could reply that it is no more contrary to the meter than *Non destiterunt pingere formam crucis* at verse 628, as Heinsius printed it. I prefer Heinsius’s reading, because it agrees with the meter and does not depart from the sense—in fact, it coheres better with it: the pain was not small, but the limbs were small, and therefore were destined to be afflicted by a brief death. Fabricius seems to have printed *tantulos at si dolor* in a special commentary, for he explains *tantulos* as “so tender and still suckling.” Perhaps it will be better understood as referring to the mother’s limbs, as the following verses suggest.

> 697. *Sublime* is used for *in sublime*, “aloft.” Lucretius, Virgil, Nemesianus, and others use it thus. Boys used to be beaten with rods. Bede and Ado, concerning this child, say on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of December: “When the boy had said that only one God ought to be believed in, Asclepiades, enraged, ordered him to be suspended from the *catomus* and beaten.” The expressions *catomo suspendi*, “to be suspended from the catomus,” *catomis caedi*, “to be beaten with catomi,” and *in catomo levari*, “to be lifted onto the catomus,” frequently occur in martyrologies and the Acts of the Martyrs; hence the verb *catomidiare* in Spartianus’s *Hadrian*. But authors disagree about what these expressions mean. Some say that the *catomus* was a whip with which martyrs were beaten; others that *catomo caedi* means to be beaten with rods or leaden weights on the crown, or on the shoulders. Most plausibly maintain that it means to be suspended from someone’s shoulders and beaten in the manner used with boys, from the Greek κατά, “upon,” and ὦμος, “shoulder.” Gallonius, Sagittarius, and Ducange discuss this more fully in the *Dictionary*. See Plate IX, *Tortures*.

> 705. Egm., Hailsbr., and Pal. have *plaga fecerat*; Prag., *fecerat e roscidis*; Bong., Wid., and Rat., *feret*; Fabr., Murmellius, and Lotterus, *ferret*; Mar., Torn., and Vat. B, *ferat*. Parrhasius has *flebat*, which is the true reading, or comes closer to the true reading *flerat*, found in Ald., Gis., and Alex., and defended by Gifanius under *FLERE*, “to drip, to sprinkle with dew.” Lucretius I: “In rocks and caves the liquid moisture of the waters flows forth, and everything weeps with abundant drops.” See hymn 5 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 24. Giselinus calls this a very charming metaphor: for when the upper skin has been pierced, the blood does not pour forth in a mass but drips drop by drop.

> 713. Ald., Egm., Fabr., Hailsbr., Widm., Bong., and others have *stat impiorum*, explained in Lotterus’s edition by a manuscript note as referring to the torturers. But there is no doubt that the words must be separated as *stat in piorum*: the subject is the mother, in whose heart devotion stood stronger. Fabricius maintained precisely this in a special commentary. In the second edition of Giselinus, *impiorum* was written through a typographical error; in his emendations Giselinus corrected it. Heinsius did not notice this and consequently printed *impiorum*, which later editors carelessly followed—Cellarius, Teolius, and Chamillardus. Yet Chamillardus, although *impiorum* appears in the text, reads *in piorum* in the note and cites Cyprian’s words, which seem to confirm this very reading.

Ald., Weitz., Cauchius, Prag., Lotterus, and several others, with Gis., have *tristi*. Teolius [Col. 0500D] printed this very reading, but falsely says that everyone has it except one Vatican manuscript, in which *triste* occurs by a later hand—unless he means all the editions. Heinsius has *tristi* in the text, but in his notes, or rather in the additions and errata, or changes to be made in the text, he prefers *triste* and punctuates: “Gazing sadly, with face and stern words.” In this brief list of errata Heinsius changed *prematur* in book II against Symmachus, verses 148–149, to *prematur*—“Let there be struggle, let there be striving”—and at verse 151 he punctuated: “Let him love the condition; let him not pile up gold excessively.” I did not notice this at the time.

> 744. Teolius thinks *neminem diem*, “no day,” is a poetic license for “not any day.” Certainly one will scarcely find a similar example, and *nemo* is almost as though it meant “no human being.” Cicero said *nemo hominum*, “no one among men”; Virgil, *nemo divum*, “no one among the gods.”

> 760. Vat. A, Pal., Hailsbr. above, Bong. above, Gis. in the text of the second edition, Heinsius, and Teolius have *crepasset*, which Cellarius explains as “would have made a crackling sound.” Gallandius, with Aldus and the old editions, has *cremasset*, which Chamillardus thought *crepasset* a corruption. Cellarius defends *crepasset*, because verbs of the first conjugation that have a past tense in *-ui* often resume an ancient form, as Vossius proved with the examples *cubo*, *domo*, *frico*, *seco*, and *veto*. In any case, *cremasset* occurs in Vat. B, Mar., Prag., Parrhasius, and several others; it is acceptable and was printed by Murmellius.

> 761. Pagans also inflicted this kind of punishment on Christians, moved in particular by the belief that they could not otherwise erase the sign of the cross with which Christians’ foreheads were marked in baptism and in the sacrament of confirmation. When Julian the Apostate renounced the Christian faith, he tried to wash away with impure and wicked blood the sign of the cross inscribed on his forehead, as may be gathered from Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration* I against Julian.
>
> 762. Parrhasius has: “From the forehead the torturer, when he had stripped him of his covering.” The meter does not permit this. Aldus punctuates incorrectly: “From the forehead the torturer, with the bare skull, as a covering.” Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXIX.1 and XLIV.12, observes that *testa* elegantly denotes the sphere of the skull. For physicians and poets call *testa* the hollow, convex bone enclosing the brain. Hence *testa* means “head” among the French and Italians. So too *cara* means “head” among the Spaniards, in Corippus II.413: “After they came before the revered head of Caesar,” where the word is Greek. Indeed, *testa* for “head” is not unknown among the Spaniards.]

> 782. The Prague manuscript violates the metrical rule with *menses bis quinos*. Sacred Scripture mentions nine months; but ten months begun may be called both ten and nine. Thus Virgil, *Eclogue* 4: “Ten long months brought weariness to the mother.” Aulus Gellius III.16 sets out the opinions of physicians and philosophers: a human being is rarely born in the seventh month, never in the eighth, often in the ninth, and more often in the tenth; and ten months are the greatest limit for human birth—not ten months begun, but ten completed.

> 787. Nebrissensis says that the body does not come from nothing. Heumannus, in *Poecile* II, page 364, without hesitation substitutes *animusque*, “and the mind,” which pleased Gallandius. But the reading of the manuscripts is sound: the poet takes *nihilum*, “nothing,” to mean something very small, since this too was created from nothing at the beginning of creation.

799. Parrbasius, Vatt. A, B: *prosequebantur notas* (“they pursued the marks”).

802. Hailsbr.: *labentis*. Rat.: *labentem*, above in another hand *labentis*. *Labantis* (“tottering,” “falling”) must certainly be read.

803. Parrhasius: *potuisse*; likewise Alex., and Urb. has the related *potisse*. But Parrhasius, in his emendations, notes that *vos* is redundant. Vatt. A, B in a second hand, Q, Prag., Sich., Hailsbr., Palat., Bong., Gis. in the margin: *potestis* (“you are able”). Ald., Vat. B above Weitz., Gis., Heins. and others: *potesse*, which is sound as an old form for *posse* in Lucretius, Lucilius, and Arnobius.

807. Parrhasius: “the vulture’s bites”; *est* is redundant and harms the meter.

809. Vat. A: *in belli fame*. Prag., Rat.: *imbecilli famae*. Parrhasius, and some common editions, have *at* for *ac*. It should be read as printed here, or, with Widm., *Languetis imbelli fame fatiscitis* (“you grow weak and waste away through feeble hunger”); or, with Lotterus, *et fatiscitis*.

810. Torn.: *ferina socors*; Latinius corrected *ferina et socors*, but less well. The first syllable of *socors* is elsewhere also shortened by Prudentius.

814. Vat. B, Rat., Mar. in the first hand: *comburere*. Retain *vorabere* (“you will be devoured”).

815. Rat.: *ut* for *et*, but this seems to have been introduced by a recent corrector. Parrhasius corruptly reads *et favillae jam termes fies*. For *fies* Vat. A, Egm., Pal. in Weitzius and Becmanus, Hailsbr. above, Widm. in the margin, Alt., Rott., and Cauch. read *eris* (“you will be”), approved by Becmanus because an iamb should stand at the end of the line. But since Prudentius elsewhere shortens the first syllable of *fies*, this appears to be the true reading, found in most of the older manuscripts. In some the reading seems to be *sies*, as Lotterus printed it; this is not objectionable as a form for *sis*. In Vat. Q: *et favilla jam fumans* (“and now smoking ash”), with the final word missing. In other witnesses that have *eris*, one finds *fumans* instead of *tenuis*.

816. Vat. B, Sich.: *arriperent*.

817. Nebrissensis says that *pone* is superfluous, since *respecto* means “I look backward.” But there are many such pleonastic expressions, such as *quia nam* and *quia enim*.

818. In Vat. A, *ad* is absent, and indeed it can be absent: for the ancients said *Appello Caesarem* without a preposition, whereas later writers more often used one.

819. Vat. B, Mar., Widm.: *metum* (“fear”).

835. Fabr.: *ait* for *jam*. Raynaudus, in Book XVIII of his works, *On the Titles of the Special Cult of the Saints*, section 9, proves at length that communion of blood, nation, and homeland is a suitable title of special devotion by which we ought to venerate the saints.

838. Ald. writes *Davitici*. The psalm is numbered CXV in the order in which, at verse 15, it reads: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.”

840. Vat. A: *tuus ergo servus*. Pal. incorrectly: *tuus ego servus* for *tuus ergo servus*, which is also read in Alex. and Vat. Q. For *proles* Alex., Ambr., Thuan. and others write *prolis*. Nevertheless Heinsius printed *proles*, although its final syllable ought to be shortened. The thought seems drawn from Psalm CXXII, verses 2–3: “Behold, as the eyes of servants are on the hands of their masters, as the eyes of a maidservant are on the hands of her mistress.”

841. Vat. A, in the variant reading: *et plicabat*.

842. Gis. in the margin, Vat. A, Alex. in the margin: *sub ictum vulneris* (“beneath the blow of the wound”). Vat. Q incorrectly: *subictam vulneris*. Egm., no better: *tenebat sub ictum*. Pal.: *sanguine*; above it, *vulneris*. Latinius reads *manusque subtendebat ictu vulneris* (“and she held out her hands beneath the blow of the wound”), partly, it seems, by conjecture and partly from an old manuscript.

843. She uses *undam* (“wave”) for abundance and profusion, as elsewhere *unda meri* (“a wave of unmixed wine”).

844. Egm., Hailsbr. in the text: *orbis* for *oris*. Nebrissensis interprets it as “a congealed wave of blood”; the annotator of Lotterus’s edition and Teolius understand it as the severed head of the infant, which is more convincing; see the following line. Weitzius continued Ison’s gloss with the gloss on line 242. I have no doubt that there are two glosses, which must be separated from one another. Accordingly, I have separated them. The first is a different reading.

[Col. 0507D] 845. Parrhasius, against the meter, reads *excipit* (“receives”). Weitzius aptly conjectures that, according to a special custom, the mother applied the head to her son’s breast. Perhaps Prudentius had before his eyes the passage in Valerius Maximus, Book IV, chapter 7, concerning T. Volumnius, who lifted the severed head of Marcus Lucullus, killed by Antonius, and attached it to his own body. After this line, *Explicit*, “here ends,” was written in the margin of Vatt. A and I, evidently marking the end of the infant’s martyrdom.

846. On the manner in which such pyres were rapidly constructed, see the commentary on line 67 of *Peristephanon* 6 and Plate XVII.

847. Hailsbr.: *fimida*; I think *fumida* (“smoky”) should be read, agreeing with *fumidus*.

848. Urb., with the meter corrupted: *et struem feni* (“and a pile of hay”). You may note in Tertullian’s words on line 103 of *Peristephanon* 6 that Christians were called *sarmentitii* because of the branches with which they were burned alive.

849. Ald.: *liquata*; others, *liquato*. Parrhasius: *liquato rore* (“with liquefied dew”), referring to ears of grain.

[Col. 0508B] 850. Egm. incorrectly: *quos et ferocibus* for *quo et ferocius*.

851. Ald., Nebr., Torn.: *etiam* for *et jam*, which is preferable. In Mar., what seems to have been written *eminus* appears to have arisen from *minis*. Parrhasius: *furcae nimis Romanus aptus*, which also occurs in Mar., where *et nimis* is in the first hand and *eminus* in the second. Teolius interprets *furca* as a small fork. But Scaliger, in his commentary on Manilius, p. 462, on the line “and with the pyres kindled,” Book V, explains that persons were *patibulati*, as Plautus says—that is, carried through the city with their arms stretched out upon a fork, and finally thrown onto the pyre; or with their arms twisted behind their backs and a fork inserted into their necks. This is what Prudentius has in mind. For that reason, I think, he says *eminus*, as though the fork projected from the neck. In this way what Prudentius reports in the hymn of Saint Fructuosus—that the martyrs leapt into the pyre—can be reconciled with the Acts’ account that the stakes to which they had been fastened remained behind. Romanus himself, as Eusebius records, was thrown alive into an already kindled fire while carrying a cross on his shoulders; this can be explained in terms of the fork.

853. Thuan.: *ut nunc cremer* (“that I may now be burned”).

854. Ald., Oxon.: *dictum est mihi* (“it has been decreed for me”). *Passion* was a word commonly used by theologians for any kind of punishment; Fabricius observed that Saint Augustine’s expression is no less explicit in this sense. Tertullian used the word, as did Cornelius Gallus—or whoever else was the author of the elegies published under his name.

855. Vatt. A, Q, Parrhasius, Ambr., Thuan., two Torrentian manuscripts, Alex., Egm., Pal., and others: *et restat* (“and there remains”), the reading retained by the more recent editions except Gallandius, who, with Ald. and Torn., printed *sed* (“but”). Most editors and manuscripts have *sed restat*. In Rat.: *fiat ut*, but this is by a recent corrector, so that if *quod fiat* is read, the first syllable of *fiat* will be shortened. Lotterus also has *fiat ut*. Eusebius, in *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, tells the story as follows: “When the attendants who were about to light the pyre were awaiting the judgment of the emperor, who happened to be present at the time, he said, ‘Where is my fire?’ After these words he was summoned and brought before the emperor, to be punished by a new kind of torture, namely the cutting out of his tongue.” He says nothing about the miracle of the fire that could not be kindled. Yet Eusebius himself explains that miracle at length in *On the Resurrection*. Consider, then, how little reliance should be placed on an argument from silence.

856. Torn. incorrectly: *ossa sequitur* (“the bone follows”). Fabricius notes that some consider *cataracta* to describe the crash of a falling storm cloud. Properly speaking, however, a *cataracta* is a steep, narrow, precipitous place in a river, where water falls with great force and crashing noise. Fabricius may perhaps be referring to the “cataracts of heaven” mentioned in Genesis.

858. Vat. A: *fulmine ignes* (“fires with lightning”). Alex. corruptly: *flaminae ignes*. Parrhasius: *praeceps aquarum flumine* (“headlong in a river of waters”), and “fire overwhelms.”

“Remember your mother,” she said, now his patron through her son;

then, while the executioner struck his neck

1135 with a sword, the learned woman sang,

singing a hymn in the song of David:

“Precious is the death of the holy one in God’s sight;

[840] he is your servant, the offspring of your maidservant.”

Unweaving such words, she unfolded her cloak,

and held out her hands beneath the blow and blood,

so that she might receive the flowing wave

of blood issuing from the veins

and the ball of the quivering head.

[845] She received it, and applied the flesh to her breast.

But on the other side of the field the fire-setter

was constructing a monstrous pyre, smoky with dry pine,

[Col. 0508A] branches laid beneath in disorder, and a heap of hay,

1136 sprinkling it with melted drops of burning pitch,

[850] so that the flame might grow more fiercely from its nourishment.

And now Romanus, with his arms twisted back,

was being driven onto the pyre, with a fork projecting afar.

“I know,” he said, “that I shall not be burned,

nor has this kind of punishment been assigned to me:

[855] but a great miracle remains to occur.”

As he began these words, there followed an immense crash

1137 of a falling cloud; a rainstorm, black and wave-like,

headlong in a river of waters, overwhelmed the fires.

They feed the half-burned torches with olive oil,

[860] but the rain now conquers the soaked fuel.

[Col. 0509A] [Note: [Col. 0509B]

861. *Trepidare*, “to tremble”; *trepidabat*, “he was trembling,” I.

863. *Versare*, “to turn,” “to work”; *versabat*, “he was turning,” I.

865. *Semen*, “seed”; “a spark,” I.

869. *Thessalorum*. Thessaly abounds in poisons and herbs with which magicians practice magic; it also has many magicians and enchanters, among whom was Erichtho, as Lucan reports, I.

870. *Peritus*, “skilled,” “learned,” I.

874. *Coibit*, “it will come together,” “it will be joined,” I.

875. *Vertex*, “head,” I.

876. *Quampiam*, “some,” “any,” I.

879. *Oppetat*, “may die,” I.]

[Note: [Col. 0509B]

861. Vat. B: *trepidabat ether*, but this was formerly different. Rat.: *trepidabat aether*, but *aether* was introduced and *teter* written above it. Prag.: *trepidabat ater*. Mar.: *trepidat aether*; above it, however, a more recent hand wrote *trepidare teter*, which is the only correct reading—namely, “he began to tremble,” a familiar construction.

862. Egm., Hailsbr.: *possit*.

863. Mar.: *humidis*; above it, *aridis*.

865. The expression is Homeric: “the seed of fire,” σπέρματα πυρός (*spermata pyros*). Fabricius also notes that “to seek fire in the waters” is proverbial of an undertaking attempted in vain. The proverb applies especially well here.

866. Ambr., Thuan., Cauch., two Torr., Rat., Vat. B, Parrhasius, Mar.: *Quod cum tumenti nuntiatum judici / Movisset iram* (“When this was reported to the swelling judge, it would have stirred his anger”), a reading adopted by Heinsius and the more recent editors, though not by Gallandius, who follows the reading of Ald., Torn., and others and says that he does not know where Chamillardus obtained another. Prag.: *nuntiatum est judici, Movessat*, with a marginal gloss that *movesso* is a desiderative verb from *moveo*, like *capesso* from *capio*. Urb., Vatt. A, Q, Ald., Lotterus, and others: *nuntiatum est judici / Commovit iram* (“it was reported to the judge; he stirred up anger”). Alex.: *nuntiatum est judici, Movisset*, with *commovit* in the margin.

868. Since Christians were sometimes freed from torments in ancient times by divine aid, the insult directed against them was that they were magicians. Re-read Suetonius’s words on Christians under Nero at line 583.

869. Vat. A, Hailsbr., Pal., Alex., the two older Heinsian manuscripts, and Heinsius: *illudet*. Ald., with most others: *illudit*. Gis., first edition: *illudet*; second edition: *illudit*. Heinsius, with Ambr., reads *Thessalarum*, because the Thessalian women were infamous for magic. Thessalians were also infamous, and most witnesses have *Thessalorum*, including Parrhasius, who usually agrees with the Ambrosian manuscript. Cellarius foolishly cites Horace, *Odes* I.27—“What Thessalian magician could release you from her spells?”—for *Thessalis saga* (“Thessalian witch”). In that passage, however, the poisons themselves are called Thessalian. Others certainly call sorceresses *Thessalides* explicitly and frequently; nor is there reason for Gallandius to think *Thessalarum* in Chamillardus was a printer’s error. Erichtho, whom the gloss mentions, is a Thessalian witch in Lucan, Book VI. Ovidius gives the same name either to this very witch or to another.

872. Vat. A, Pal., Hailsbr.: *ense*; others, *ensem*. Alex. writes *hensem*.

873. In Vat. B, *amputatu*; but *amputatum* was written in the first hand.

874. Barthius, Book XIV of the *Adversaria*, chapter 1, shows from this and other passages that wounds are said *coire* (“to come together”) when they are joined by the surface skin. Barthius seems to imply that *coire* is always used of wounds that do not heal internally; I do not think this is correct unless one adds “the wounds come together badly,” or something similar.

876. As has often been said, the pagans tortured Christians for a long time so that they would die miserably and feel themselves dying.

877. Ald.: *truncate*, less correctly.

878. The pagans did not want Christians to die a single or simple death. See the notes on Laurence at lines 336–337. Plautus used the adjective *simplus*. Fabricius says that *simplum* refers to quantity and number, whereas *simplex* refers to quality and condition. Others do not recognize this distinction.

879. Ambr.: *cadat velat una*, from which Heinsius conjectures *cadatque et una*.

880. Chamillardus incorrectly has *quod membra*. Certain others in Gallandius have *quin*; read *quot* (“as many as”).

881. Parrhasius corruptly reads: *Libet experiri, Lernaea sicut traditur Hydra, an renatis pullulet hic artubus* (“I wish to test whether, as the Lernaean Hydra is said to do, it may sprout here with regenerated limbs”). Giselinus correctly observes that this passage had been corrupted and wrongly explained by others. Ald. and others, however, had already read it as Giselinus does. The explanation is neither difficult nor obscure. Asclepiades says that he wishes to test whether, after some part of Romanus has been cut off, others will grow again, as happened with the head of the Lernaean Hydra. If this occurs, he adds, some Hercules will not be lacking to kill this hydra.

882. Ald.: *pululescat* for *pullulescat*, as many have; but most have *pullulascat*, as Rat., Mar., Urb., Vatt. B, Q, Alex. in the first hand, and Lotterus.

883. Ald., Mar.: *imminutis*; read *imminuti*. Nebrissensis corrected it to *imminutus*. There is no need for this.

884. Rat.: *tunc erit*, printed by Gis. and Weitz. *Erit tunc* is better. Anselmus Bandurius, vol. II, p. 55, reproduces a coin of Maximianus Herculius whose reverse depicts Hercules attacking the Hydra with a club, bearing the inscription *HERCULI DEBELLATORI* (“To Hercules the Conqueror”). Learned men think this indicates that Maximianus claimed for himself the destruction of the Christian name, as is clear from an ancient inscription; see *Eulalia*, line 100.

885. Ald., Teol., Urb., Vat. Q, Weitz., and others: *ustum ire*, allowing hiatus. Pal., Egm., Hailsbr., Sich., Alex., Ambr., Thuan.: *ustuire*, like *hymnire* and *ignire*; Heinsius thinks it derives from *ustumire*, as *circuire* from *circumire*. Two Torrentian manuscripts, Alt., Fabr., and Parrhasius: *ustulare*, a conjecture favored by Cauch. Salmasius: *usturire* or *ustulare*. Hailsbr. above: *ustuare*. Lotterus, Latinius, Gis., first edition: *ire inustum*; second edition, with *ire inustum* in the margin: *ustulare*. Gifanius, in his index to Lucretius, where he discusses *ecthlipsis*, reads *ustum ire* for *urere* (“to burn”) from an old book, and from another old witness *ustuire*, more correctly, as in civil-law forms such as *credituiri* and *debituiri*, discussed by Antonius Augustinus, Book II of the *Emendationes*, chapter 2. Gifanius thinks *ustulare* arose from a gloss. Heumannus, in *Poecile*, vol. II, Book III, p. 364, corrected the passage to *Hydrina suetus is coire vulnera*. Gallandius prefers *ustuire*. The Hydra is said by the ancients to have been burned by Alcides. See Burmannus, *Anthologia*, p. 569. Albricus, in *On the Images of the Gods*, tells the story thus: “According to the myth, there was a Hydra in the marsh of Lerna; when one head was cut off, two grew out. Having placed fire around it, Hercules burned it.” Prudentius suggests that Hercules burned the wounds of the heads he cut off, so that others would not sprout from the wound; Apollodorus, Book III, relates that Hercules burned part of the nearby forest and, applying flaming logs to the Hydra’s regenerating heads, prevented the growth of new heads in that manner.]

The grim executioner began to tremble at these strange events,

confounded, and sought by whatever art he could to persist,

turning the logs with wet ashes,

stoking the embers with bundles of tow,

[865] and seeking the seed of fire amid the waters.

When this was reported to the swelling judge

and stirred the anger of his implacable fury,

“How long,” he said, “will this supreme magician

mock us with Thessalian witchcraft,

[870] 1138 skilled at turning punishment into ridicule?

Perhaps, if I order his neck to be cut,

it will not be exposed to the wound;

or, once severed, the neck divided by the wound

will come together again and be reattached,

[875] and a head, added to his shoulders, will rise.

Let us therefore first try to cut off with iron

some part of the body that remains,

so that the criminal may not fall by a single death,

or the traitor perish by one slaughter:

[880] I want him to die in as many ways as he has limbs.

I wish to test whether it, as Lerna is said to do,

1139 will sprout again with regenerated limbs,

and restore itself anew from the losses of its diminished body.

Then Hercules himself will be at hand,

[885] accustomed to cauterize the Hydra’s wounds.”

[Col. 0511A] [Note: [Col. 0511B]

888. *Disparare*, “to separate,” Vat. A.

889. *Hunc*, “such a one,” Vat. A.

894. *Fas*, “law,” Vat. A. — *Prophanavit*, “he corrupted,” I.

896. *Accitus*, “summoned,” “called for,” I.

902. *Scalpellum*, a type of iron instrument used by physicians. — *Insertans*, “inserting,” “thrusting in”: *insertare* means “to insert with some violence,” I.

903. *Sensim*, “gradually,” “little by little,” I.

906. *Rictu*, the opening of the mouth, I.

907. *Scaturiens*, “boiling up,” “bubbling forth,” I.

908. *Russo stemmate*, “with red blood,” I.

909. *Fert*, “endures,” “bears,” I.]

[Note: [Col. 0511C]

886. Giselinus aptly observes that this is an exceptionally elegant periphrasis for a true surgeon, drawn from the immediately accompanying circumstances—namely, knowledge of anatomy and the proper treatment of dislocations and wounds. He regrets that from that time onward the noblest parts of the art began, by this deplorable example, to be torn apart and mangled. Here Aristo seems to have been a surgeon only.

888. Widm., Bong., Vat. B, Mar., Prag., Rat.: *discrepare*. Sich., Bong. above: *dissipare*, to which Hailsbr. alludes in the text with *dissiparare*. Most have *disparare*.

890. Vat. B, Mar. in the variant reading: *novis*, against the meter, for *nodis*. Mar., Widm.: *compagina*; read *compaginat*. In Thuan. there was *sarcians*, from which Heinsius conjectured *sarcinans*, as Salmasius had also thought. But I would not readily change *sarciens* to *sarcinans*.

891. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VI: “He seized the tongue with the forceps and cut it out with the savage sword; the ultimate root of the tongue quivered.” Plautus, *Aulularia* II.3.72: “By Hercules, if I do not have you tongue-cut from the very roots.” Cicero, by contrast, vehemently denounced this monstrous punishment in *Pro A. Cluentio* 66: “For know, judges, that Strato was led to the cross with his tongue cut out—there is no one among the Larinates who does not know it. The mad woman feared neither her own conscience, nor the hatred of her fellow citizens, nor everyone’s reproach; but, as though all were not going to be witnesses of her crime, she feared that she would be condemned by the final voice of a dying slave. What portent is this, immortal gods? What such monstrous deed has existed anywhere? What crime so hostile and monstrous, and from what source are we to say it arose?”

892. Vat. B: *corpori*, less correctly. See what is said against the tongue—especially the evil tongue—in the Catholic Epistle of James, chapter III, and above in the commentary on line 768.

893. Ald., Mar. in the first hand, Vat. B: *illa procaci*, which appears to be Prudentian, so that the *a* in *illa* is lengthened because of the following *pr* in accordance with the probable spelling of several witnesses: *Dente frequenti exasperat*. Prag. corruptly: *illa pessima et procaci*.

894. Pal.: *motus*, incorrectly. Servius, in his commentary on *Georgics* I, observed that *fas* pertains to God and religion, while *jura* pertains to human beings: “Even *fas* and *jura* permit certain things to be done on festival days.”

896. Ambr.: *quondam medicus* (“formerly a physician”). Weitzius writes *ascitus*. Surgeons were called physicians of wounds, or surgical physicians.

898. Ald. punctuates: *Martyr retectam pandit, ima et faucium*. Fabr. and Gis.: *et pandit ima faucium*. Others: *pandit ima et faucium*. Teolius omitted *et* altogether, perhaps deliberately. In some common editions the reading is corrupt: *ima et pandit faucium*.

901. Alex.: *ab ore protrahat*; above it, *protrahet*. Read *protrahens* (“drawing out”). Prag. most corruptly: *trahens ab ore*.

902. *Inusque*, or divided as *in usque*, is used for *usque in* by Statius and Avienus. *Inante* is similar.

904. Arnobius, Book VI, uses a similar phrase: “compressing the evil tongue with his teeth.”

[Col. 0512D] 905. Hailsbr. in the first hand, Egm.: *ictis*. Weitzius writes *artis*. Sich., Gis. in the text, Fabr.: *aut cruorem*. Others: *nec*.

907. Weitz., Egm., Widm., Heins.: *scaturriens*. In Rott. and the Cauchian manuscript: *defluat* for *defluit*. Cauch. conjectured *defluens ebulliit*, rightly rejected by Heinsius.

908. Lotterus and Parrhasius: *ruffo*. Gis., first edition: *rufo*; Fabr.: *rubro*. Cellarius rejects Ison’s gloss and thinks it more correct to describe, from Seneca and Pliny, the marks of rank and nobility, attached by a line of succession to images, which are themselves small figurines. Yet there can scarcely be doubt that this passage concerns blood, which is called a “red lineage” because, when it is poured out, the martyrs are truly ennobled. Salmasius, in his notes on Lampridius’s life of Heliogabalus, asserts that *stammate* should be read for *stagmate*, as in Lampridius *simma* for *sigma*, and in Juvenal *stemma* for *stegma*. In Greek, *stagma* means a drop, a trickle, or liquid. This is an acute conjecture.]

Now let a skilled craftsman come for the cutting—

one who knows all the boundaries of the inner organs,

or how to separate bonds joined by sinews.

Bring this man who heals dislocated bones,

[890] 1140 or joins together broken structures by repairing their knots.

Let him drag out the foremost tongue by the roots,

which alone, throughout the whole body, lives more wickedly.

That tongue, the worst thing, with its shameless attack

upon our gods, has profaned ancient divine law,

[895] and in its boldness has not spared the ruler himself.”

A certain physician named Aristo, summoned, arrived.

He orders the tongue to be brought forth; at once it is brought forth.

The martyr exposes it and opens the depths of his mouth and throat.

[Col. 0512A] The physician examines the palate and, wandering with his finger

over the passage of the voice, searches out the place for the wound.

Then, drawing the tongue far out of the mouth,

1141 he drives the scalpel in as far as the throat.

As he cuts, severing the individual fibers little by little,

the martyr never bit or clenched his teeth

[905] tightly together, nor swallowed the blood.

Motionless, with his mouth held open, he stood,

while blood streamed outside, bubbling forth.

Beautiful, with his chin drenched in red blood,

he bears it and beholds the glory of his blood-stained breast,

[910] [Col. 0513A] [Note: [Col. 0513B]

913. *Oblatraret*, “he would bark,” I.

916. *Reponit*, “he replaces,” “he restores.” — *Ad*, “before,” I.

918. *Abdomina*, “fat,” from *folliculus suis*, “the pig’s belly,” I.

919. *Hos*, “such [things],” I.

922. *Inclementius*, “more harshly,” “more furiously,” I.

[Col. 0514B] 932. *Testudine*, “curvature”: *testudo* means “curvature.” He says *sub testudine* because *ouranos* in Greek, *palatum* in Latin, is so called because it is curved like the sky, which is also called *ouranos*. *Cavitate*, “hollow,” I.]

[Note: [Col. 0513B]

910. Vat. A, Rat. in the second hand: *fruitueque ostro*; *fruiturque et ostro* is better. Parrhasius: *fucatus ostro* (“dyed with purple”).

911. Manuscripts and old editions, such as Ald., Parrhasius, and others, consistently have *praefectus ergo ratus*, despite the meter; Alex. corruptly has *erga* for *ergo*. Giselinus dared to change the word order to *Ergo ratus praefectus*, citing other examples in which Prudentius shortens the first syllable of *ratus*. Heinsius and others followed him. Vosius, *On the Art of Grammar* II.22, declares that Prudentius lengthens the *a* in *ratus*, and that the word order should not be changed. See the prolegomena, no. 216.

[Col. 0513C] 912. Here and elsewhere *sacrare* means “to honor with sacrifices” and “to worship the gods.”

913. Alex., Vat. A, Thuan., Rott., three Torrentian manuscripts, Alt., Pal.: *blateraret*, which Heinsius approves because the first syllable of *blaterat* was also lengthened by the author of the *Philomela*. Ald., Fabr., Lotterus: *obblacteraret*. Most have *oblatraret*, which Gifanius defends in his index on *ecthlipsis* from three old books. Giselinus has *obblacteraret* in the text and, in the margin, *Nil oblataret in deorum dedecus*. It may be written *obblacteraret*, from *blatero*; for *deblacterare* is also written in Festus for *deblaterare*. Prudentius indeed favors such compounds with *ob-*. This is what Nebrissensis means when he notes from Festus that *blaterare* means to speak foolishly and excessively. I think *oblatraret* arose from *obblacteraret*, and it could be retained despite the hiatus. Fabricius explains *obblacterare* as barking in the manner of a sheep, in contrast with *blacterare*, as in the related expression *obgannire*.

914. Ald.: *et*; others: *ac*.

915. Parrhasius: *multi loquentis*; read *multo loquentis*.

[Col. 0513D] 919. Teolius places a full stop after *perspicit*, unless this is a printer’s error.

920. Aldus punctuates: *Insufflat ipsos, ceu videret daemonas* (“He blows upon them, as though he saw demons”). Barthius, Book IV, chapter 7, shows that *exsufflare*, a word common among Christian writers, means to abominate and detest by blowing in contempt, and consequently to mock. He cites Severus: “He saw behind him a demon of extraordinary size sitting there; at a distance, blowing at it contemptuously—or, to speak somewhat ungrammatically, since necessity requires it—and so on.” Barthius adds: “Tertullian uses the same word, *On Idolatry*, and, unless I am mistaken, Prudentius.” Saint Jerome, chapter 17 of the *Life of Pachomius*: “Fortifying his forehead with the sign of the cross, he blew upon him—the demon—and immediately he was put to flight.” He understood all the enemy’s tricks, and, endowed with divine fear, counted his illusions as nothing. See Rosweydius’s *Onomasticon*. Certainly Barthius had read no other word in Prudentius than *insufflat*, which has the same meaning. See the commentary on line 21 of the hymn of Saint Eulalia.

921. Sich., Bong.: *arridet hoc* (“this is pleasing”).

[Col. 0514B] 922. In some common editions: *nunquid insolentius* (“perhaps more insolently”), which fits the sense.

924. Pal., Vat. A, the Heinsian manuscripts, and others: *quidvis* (“whatever you wish”). Ald. and others: *quod vis* (“what you wish”). Ald., Weitz., Gis., first edition: *ac per ora edissere*. Parrhasius, Lotterus, Gis., second edition, the Heinsian manuscripts, and some Vatican manuscripts: *perora, et dissere* (“speak at length and explain”). Gallandius, with Torn.: *Effare quod vis, ac per ora edissere*.

925. Vat. A: *liber ut*, less correctly. Fabr. and Gis.: *libere exercere te* (“to exercise yourself freely”). The manuscripts read otherwise. There is a tribrach in the fourth foot, with hiatus admitted.

[Col. 0514C] 927. Vat. B, Rat.: *sic exorsus*. Widm., Mar.: *sic exorsus est*. The meter requires *et sic orsus est*.

928. The Mozarabic Breviary: *loquendi*, less well. Fabricius calls this an excellent statement, confirmed by miracles: for Gemblacensis reports that Christians whose tongues had been cut out by the Vandals spoke around the year 530. There is an unequivocal testimony to this in Justinian’s *Code* I.27.1: “We have seen venerable men who, after their tongues had been cut out by the roots, spoke their punishments miserably”—perhaps “miraculously.” Sagittarius collects many other examples in chapter 16. Chrysostom and Eusebius likewise confirm the same miracle concerning Romanus. Eusebius reports that Romanus, while he still possessed a fleshy tongue, was stammering, but after it had been cut out spoke perfectly. Eusebius greatly elaborates the matter in *On the Resurrection*; yet in *On the Martyrs of Palestine* he says nothing about so great a miracle. The argument from silence is therefore weak.

[Col. 0514D] 929. Some common editions: *quae*. More correctly, *quo*.

932. Isidore confirms the gloss, Book XI, chapter 1: “Our palate is positioned like the sky, and hence *palatum* is derived from *polus*; the Greeks likewise call the palate *ouranos* (οὐρανόν), because, owing to its concavity, it resembles the sky.” Here Grialius notes Cicero’s passage concerning Epicurus: “While he was judging what was best by the palate, he did not look up at the palace of heaven, as Ennius says.” The Spanish likewise call the palate *el cielo de la boca* (“the sky of the mouth”); I wish this feature of our tongue had been explained in the *Dictionary of the Spanish Academy*, with its origin from Greek and Latin indicated.

933. Ald., Ox.: *repercusso*. Nebrissensis likewise has *repercusso* and explains *palato repercusso* (“with the palate struck back”) as deriving from *testudo oris* (“the curvature of the mouth”). I do not accept his conjecture that one should read *nec ex palato* and, in the following line, *nec temperetur*, as though Romanus, with his tongue cut out, were speaking these words about himself.

934. Many letters are formed between the tongue and the teeth, as is well known.

935. Aldus incorrectly has *his augendis* (“for increasing these”). On the tongue as the plectrum [Col. 0515C] it was said at the beginning of this hymn. Chrysostom, *Homily 1 on Saint Romanus*: “For the mouth was a lyre, the tongue its plectrum; the craftsman was the soul, and the art was confession. Yet when the plectrum was removed, the tongue, I say, became neither useless craftsman, nor useless art, nor useless instrument.” And in *Homily 2*: “For, like a lyre deprived of its plectrum, it praises the Creator.”

And it enjoys purple cloth, so that it is already royal.

Thus the prefect, supposing that a man without a tongue could be compelled to sacrifice, since, deprived of speech, he could not bark any insult against the gods,

1142 orders the man, now silent and disabled, to be brought back,

[915] whom he had once greatly feared amid the tumult of his speech.

He again sets up the altars before the tribunal,

and incense, and a lively fire upon the coals,

and the entrails of bulls, or the bellies of swine.

When the man enters and sees these preparations,

[920] he blows upon them, as though he were looking at demons themselves.

Asclepiades, now more cheerful, mocks this.

Then he adds: “What, are you not prepared to speak more harshly,

[Col. 0514A] as you used to?

Speak out whatever you wish; plead your case and explain it.

[925] 1143 I freely permit you to exercise your voice.”

Romanus, sighing deeply from his heart,

drew forth a complaint in a groan and began thus:

“To the tongue that speaks of Christ nothing has ever been lacking.

Do not ask by what organ words are directed,

[930] when the very Giver of words is being proclaimed:

He who made the power of the voice, expressed from the innermost

lung, and twisted beneath the shell of the mouth,

now produce reflected sounds from the palate,

now modulate them from the comb of the teeth,

[935] and make the tongue a mobile plectrum for these operations.”

936. Parrhasius has *fauces sicut fistulas* (“the throat like pipes”), which is metrically erroneous. Nebrissensis interprets Romanus as saying that, if God wished, a pipe and a cymbal could speak, although these do not possess articulate voices. This is not the poet’s meaning: he is describing the organs of the voice and their formation in those who have a functioning tongue, in order to conclude that God, who made all these things, can likewise cause a voice to be formed without them. He calls the throat “pipes” because the throat is shaped like pipes, and the mouth “a cymbal” because the mouth resembles a cymbal.

[950] 1145 The sea is accustomed to bear swimmers; it bears footprints.”

Teolius indicates three Vatican manuscripts for the same reading, and notes that *ligula* is also called *legula* by Sidonius, and that in Joshua 7:21 *legula* should be read instead of *regula*, as Sidonius’s commentator Savaro observed: for the Hebrew word means not “rule” but “tongue.” Yet even if the Hebrew word means “tongue,” many still explain it as a rule, or a golden plate fashioned in the shape of a tongue; thus the word *regula* may be retained. Moreover, many appropriately read *lingua*, as Ald., Urb., Vat. B, Mar., Gis., and others do. A tribrach is admitted in the fourth foot of this verse. For this and similar examples, the common reading in verses 481 and 550, *fidiculae* and *fidiculas*, should be maintained.

996. Sichard., *nec: retine me* (“nor: restrain me”). The ancients used to swear by “the safety” or “the genius” of the emperor. See law 33, *Digest* 12, on oaths, and the commentators, as well as Tertullian, *To Scapula* and *Apology* chapters 28 and 32: “But we also swear, not by the genii of the Caesars, but by their safety, which is more august than all genii.” Also Josephus, chapter 42 of Genesis, verse 15: “By the life of Pharaoh, you shall not leave this place until your youngest brother comes.” See Cerda’s notes on the cited passage of Tertullian.

Joseph Scaliger, in Becmann’s *On the Origin of the Latin Language*, says that *suggillare* derives, according to Verrius’s opinion, from *gula* (“throat”). Teolius explains it as “by constricting the throat, force out words.” Prudentius uses this word for *suggerat*, and perhaps derives it from *suggero*. In Holy Scripture *suggillo* means “I strangle.”

B, Mar., Prag., Rat. in another hand, *quaerit an aliena* (“he asks whether another’s”). Ald., Hailsbr., Heinsius with Ambr., Thuan., Alt., Cauch., Rott., *ille* (“that man”). Weitz., Fabr., Vat. Likewise in *Laurentius*, verse 309: “Behold the talents; receive them.” Although *eccum* works well here in the sense “I am present,” namely, “behold me,” in *Laurentius* *eccum* is simply used for *ecce*, unless there too one understands “behold me: receive the talents.”
