1010. In Thuan., *promadescitis*. Heinsius thinks it should be written *pro madescitis*, for the ancients wrote *pro*, not *proh*.

1011. There is scarcely any longer doubt that Prudentius is speaking of the *taurobolium*. The older interpreters understood another sacrifice. Nebrissensis thought that the Terentine rites were being described—rites performed at Rome in the Campus Martius, in a place called Terentum, where an altar sacred to Father Dis was buried twenty feet underground and a black cow was sacrificed. Giselinus and Fabricius generally agree, the latter adding that these rites were performed once in each of September, October, and November, over three successive nights. Weitzius follows Nebrissensis and Fabricius; Chamillardus does not disagree, although he says that these same rites were called *Tauropolia*. Peveratus thinks that the sacrifice and profane, laughable rites are being described by which Julian the Apostate wished to be washed in bull’s blood—so that, according to the custom of the ancient emperors, he might receive the supreme pontificate together with the empire, erase the chrism of baptism, and wipe away the sign of Christ. But, as I said, the subject is the *taurobolium*. Antonius Van Dale discusses the origin and rites of this sacrifice in the first dissertation of his *On Antiquities*. He first states that the pagans adopted certain things from the Christians for their own rites, among them the *taurobolium*, by which they imitated the true expiation through Christ’s blood. The *taurobolium* began in the year 175 of Christ, or a little earlier; it was abolished under the consulship of Valentinian IV and Neoterius. Van Dale explains the rites from Prudentius, which Baronius, Bulengerus, and others had understood as referring to the consecration of the supreme pontiff. In this sacrifice, the bull’s powers were distinguished as “received,” “consecrated,” and “stored away.” The “received” power was the blood, the “consecrated” powers were the horns, and the “stored” powers were the testicles. Others explain them differently. And just as a corruption arose among Christians whereby some were baptized on behalf of others, so too the pagans were *tauroboliated* on behalf of others; for they introduced this word as well. Gisbertus Cuperus, in letter 4 to Van Dale, confirms that the pagans imitated Christian ceremonies and formulas of speech. Apuleius says that people are reborn through sacred rites, and there is an ancient inscription: “Reborn through the *taurobolium* forever.” On the *taurobolium*, see the distinguished Zacharias in his very useful *Lapidary Institution*, p. 42, drawing on Montfaucon, Gruter, Salmasius in his *Life of Heliogabalus*, p. 804, and the inscription of Ulpius Egnatius Faventinus: “Having received *taurobolia* again after twenty years, he established an altar”; this indicated that those who had undergone the *taurobolium* remained pure for twenty years and could not undergo it again until that period had elapsed. Julius Firmicus also discusses the *taurobolium*: “The *taurobolium*, or *criobolium*, drenches you with the accursed stain of blood. Let those impurities, then, be washed away which you gather. Seek noble springs; seek pure waters, so that there, after many stains, Christ’s blood may whiten you with the Holy Spirit.” Wowerius presents two ancient inscriptions, from one of which it seems possible to infer that *taurobolia* were instituted in honor of Cybele and Attis. Thus the supreme priest should be understood as the priest of Cybele, who perhaps used to undergo the *taurobolium* on behalf of others. The dissertation of Philippus a Turre, bishop of Adria, *On the Lyons Taurobolium*, appears in volume III of Sallengre’s *Thesaurus Antiquitatum*. In his preface to Anastasius’s *Lives of the Pontiffs*, Blanchinus presents several inscriptions concerning the *taurobolium* and *criobolium*, and adds some explanation from a commentary by Dominicus de Colonia, S.J., on this subject. Inscriptions of this sort are found in the Burghesian gardens on the Via Salaria. There appears Lucius Ragonius Venustus, *pontifex maximus*; and Quintus Clodius Flavianus, in the year 383, *pontifex maximus . . . pontifex of the Sun*; and in that same year, 383, “the most distinguished priestess . . . having undergone the *taurobolium* and *criobolium* again.” In the year 374, Clodius Hermogenianus Caesarius, a most distinguished man, proconsul of Africa and prefect of the City, appears “having received the *taurobolium* and *criobolium.” Consult Montfaucon, volume II of *Antiquities*, p. 171.

1013. Gis. in the margin, and three manuscripts, Torrent., Cauch., Rott., have *mitra infulatus* (“wearing a mitre and priestly fillet”), a reading accepted by Heinsius but rejected by Teolius, because the Romans did not use the mitre, much less the pontiffs. Gallandius thought *mire* in the old editions a corruption of *mitra*. Paschalius, *On Crowns* book IV, chapters 13 and 22, transcribes these verses and adds much about priests who were crowned, filleted, or wore the *infula*. In chapter 21 he shows that priests of the pagans wore the mitre; for the mitre was a kind of priestly cap, or *apex*, worn by the flamen. In more common usage, *mitra* means the episcopal and pontifical diadem of Christians.

Weitz., Egm., Hailsbr., Pal., Bong., Gilanius in *Plexus* from three manuscripts, and others, *replexus*. Vat. Q corruptly has *coronatum* for *corona tum*. Ambr., *coronatum repexus auream*, from which Heinsius in his notes orders that *coronam tum repexus auream* should be written, making it a Greek construction. 1015. “Gabinian.” Gabii is a city whose priests used to sacrifice with half-naked bodies. Therefore, when they were sacrificing, wolves appeared and carried off the flesh they themselves were sacrificing; so, being impeded as they were, they began to pursue the wolves and recover the prey. Hence the custom arose that people there performed sacrifices with naked bodies, Vat. A. A type of garment. The Gabinians were neighbors of the Romans, from whom they adopted a large part of their rites. — “Supported by,” having, I.

1016. “Above,” from above. — “Platforms,” the steps of a stage; “seats,” or the couches of the gods, I.

1017. “Of the framework,” of the joints. Here *pegma* means a joint; elsewhere it means a rounded iron implement with which theatrical performers play. It signifies the joining and fastening together. *Pegma* is a kind of machinery used for theatrical performances, I.

[Col. 0522B] 1018. “Then,” afterward. — “Floor,” the level surface of the boards, I.

1023. “Encumbered,” crowned, I.

1025. “Bracteal,” with gold plates. — “Stains,” mixes, I.

1027. “Breast,” namely, of the bull. — “With a hunting spear,” an iron instrument by which the animal is divided, suitable for hunters; that is, a small axe; a lance, I.

1035. “Putrefied,” filthy, I.

[Note: [Col. 0521C]]

1015. Vat. A writes *siricam*. Latinius’s manuscript and Gis. in the text have *russeam*; in the margin, more correctly, *sericam*. Some common editions corruptly have *seriam*. A Gabinian cincture is worn when the toga, with the right arm exposed, is thrown back over the shoulder in such a way that its lower flap, brought from behind toward the left breast, encircles the man. On Trajan’s Column the emperor and his soldiers can be seen dressed in this fashion. But Fabretti was not thereby entitled to infer in his explanation that this garment belonged exclusively to soldiers and magistrates and that Prudentius, by poetic license, attributed it to the supreme priest, as Lucan does elsewhere in book I of the *Pharsalia*: “The lesser crowd proceeds in the Gabinian girdle.” Either others also used this kind of garment, as many authorities teach, or Prudentius is describing a *taurobolium* performed by the emperor himself or by a leading man, to make the sacrifice appear all the more ridiculous. The more credible origin of the Gabinian cincture [Col. 0521D] is that, during a sudden attack by the enemy on Gabii, when there was no time to put on military cloaks, they tucked up their togas and threw them back, wrapping them around the body.

1017. Egm., Alex. in the first hand, *pigmatis*; write *pegmatis*.

1022. That oxen were customarily crowned in sacrifices is also clear from Acts of the Apostles 14:12: “The priest of Jupiter, whose temple was before the city, brought bulls and garlands before the gates and wished to sacrifice with the crowds.” Delrio, in his commentary on Seneca’s *Oedipus*, teaches that the horns of sacrificial victims were customarily yoked and bound with gold, and also crowned. Trebellius Pollio, *Life of the Thirty Tyrants*, p. 178: “On both sides there advanced a hundred white oxen, their horns yoked with gold and shining with variegated silk coverings.” On an ancient stone at Rome there is an inscription concerning the twentieth-year vow: “Faventinus twice ten years receives, that, renewing his sacrifice, he may slaughter the two-horned oxen with gilded forehead.” Delrio notes that both customs are confirmed by these verses of Prudentius. It should be observed that Faventinus’s vows are to be understood as referring to the *taurobolium*. Virgil called it a “golden forehead,” Tibullus a “gilded horn,” which many explain as horns smeared with gold. But verse 1025 of Prudentius indicates something further: “And the brightness of the gold plate stains the bristles.”

1023. Weitz., Iso, Gis., *impeditus*. Aldus, Parrhasius, and Heinsius’s manuscripts, *impeditis*. Among ours, Vat. B, Mar., Prag., Rat., *impeditus*. In Egm. the obvious error is *impenditis*.

1024. Parrhasius incorrectly has *nec non et tauro*. Concerning this custom, Pliny, book XXXIII, chapter 3: “For the honor of the gods, nothing else has been devised in sacrifices except that victims—only the larger ones—should be sacrificed with gilded horns.”

1025. Aldus writes *blattealis*; others *brattealis* or *bractealis*. In Mar., and apparently in Rat., there had first been *bratteolis*. Alex. likewise writes *brattealis*.

1026. Vat. B, *stimulando* (“goading”); above, in another and more recent hand, *est immolanda* (“is to be sacrificed”). Mar. likewise has *stimulando*; in the margin the true reading is written.

1027. Ald., Alex., Urb., Parrhasius, Mar. above, Gis., Weitz., and others, *sacrato dividunt venabulo* (“they divide it with a sacred spear”). Vatt. B and Q, Mar. in the first hand, Ratt., Prag., Thuan., Noms., Heins., *sacrata dividunt venabula* (“they divide the sacred weapons”). Heinsius found in two manuscripts *sacratum dividunt venabula*, namely “they divide the sacred breast.”

1029. Rat., *subdita*. The substantive *textum* is used in this way by Catullus, Lucretius, and others. See Gifanius.

1030. Mar. in the text, Widm. above, Hailsbr., *vaporem* (“vapor”); read *vaporum* (“of vapors”). Chamillardus notes in his index that it is a substantive. But it may also be an adjective from *vaporus*, as in hymn 7 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 115: “The vaporous heat.”

1031. Prag., *sequentes* (“following”); *frequentes* (“numerous”) is more correct. Indeed, this alone seems to be right.

1034. Vatt. A, Q, Hailsbr., Pal., Egm., *turpe objectans* (“presenting something shameful”). In Alex. it seems to be *turpes objectans* (“presenting shameful things”). *Turpe subjectans* (“submitting something shameful”) should be retained. Fabr. thinks *turpe* is an adverb and would prefer it to be read parenthetically as an expression of indignation.

1035. Aldus corruptly has *omne* for *omni*. Heinsius, with Thuan. alone, has *putefactus*, because, he says, in Prudentius the first syllable of *putrefactus* and *putris* is always short. The absurdity and falsity of this reasoning are clear from verse 9 of hymn 7 of the *Cathemerinon*: “The putrid gruel not sweating out.” Teolius and Cellarius follow Heinsius, but the manuscripts and old editions consistently and correctly have *putrefactus*. Chamillardus has *putefactus* in the text, but notes *putrefactus* only in the index.

Wearing a silken toga supported by the Gabinian cincture.

1151 Above, they construct platforms spread with boards,

cracked by the rare joints of the framework.

Then they split or bore through the floor,

and repeatedly pierce the wood with a sharp point,

[1020] so that it may open into frequent tiny gaps.

Here a huge bull, with a fierce and shaggy brow,

bound with garlands, or adorned with flowers around its shoulders,

or encumbered with them upon its horns, is led down.

And the forehead of the victim flashes with gold,

[1025] [Col. 0522A] 1152 and the brightness of the gold plate stains its bristles.

When the beast has been set apart for sacrifice,

they divide its breast with a sacred hunting spear.

The broad wound vomits a wave of boiling blood,

and pours a river of vapors over the woven boards of the bridge,

[1030] spreading widely and seething.

Then, through the thousand numerous passages of the cracks,

the rain slips down and pours a putrid drizzle.

The priest, buried within, receives it,

lowering his shameful head beneath every drop,

[1035] soaked in his clothing and throughout his putrefied body.

[Col. 0523A] **Note: [Col. 0523B]**

1041. “Having discharged,” having emitted, I.

1042. “Framework,” board, I.

1047. “Of expiation,” of purification, I.

1051. “Hecatomb,” a hundred; hence *hechatontam*, that is, “having a hundred powers,” and therefore a hundred victims were sacrificed to it, I.

1056. “Pulvinar.” He calls the *pulvinar* the rich slaughterhouse because the *pulvinar* was placed in the temple when they sought an omen through sacrifice, I.

1058. “Raw,” rustic, fat, I.

[Col. 0524B] 1059. “When,” since, I.

1060. “Votive,” that which comes through a vow, I. Vat. A, “voluntary.”

1061. “Fanatic,” a priest who dwells in a shrine, I.

1062. “Goddess,” Berecynthia, I.

1063. “To whirl,” namely, thrusting forward the head. — “Mystical,” figurative, I.

1064. “Sparing,” she who spares, not cutting herself. — “Is said,” is said to be, I.

[Note: [Col. 0523B]]

1036. Ald., Torn., *qui nos* (“who us”). Our better books, and Heinsius’s with Cauchius, Latinius, Parrhasius, Gis., *quin os* (“indeed the mouth”). Weitzius, *quinos*. Scaliger, book II, chapter 1 of his *Lessons on Ausonius*, finding *quinos* somewhere, corrected it to *cinnos* or *cinos*. The Glossary has *cinum*, Greek *ἐπισκύνιον*. *Cinnus*, Greek *νεῦμα*. Italian *in gua*, and old French use *cenno*, *accennare*, *accener*. Gattackerus, in his commentary on Antoninus’s *Life of Himself*, agrees with Scaliger. Yet Heinsius by no means approves this, nor should others.

1046. Egm., Palat., Hailsbr. in the text, *hinc* (“hence”) for *hunc* (“this”). Fabricius testifies that others read *contactibus* for *contagiis*. Salmasius, p. 180 in his commentary on Aelius Lampridius, calls this a vivid description of the *taurobolium*, and brings forward much about the *taurobolium* and those who underwent it, highly suitable for illuminating this pagan rite.

1047. In Prag. this verse is placed after verse 1050, “By foul things,” etc.

1050. Egm., Lat., Hailsbr., Vat. A, *laverit* (“has washed”), not incorrectly.

1051. Vat. A corruptly has *illam vis haec ad opem tuam* (“that one, if you wish, this for your aid”). Vat. B, Mar., Prag. write *echatontem tuam*. Egm., Widm., *eccatontem*. Most have *hecatombem* or *hecatomben*. Cauchius conjectured *si vis hecatombem* (“if you wish, a hecatomb”), to suit the meter. But Prudentius never places a dactyl in the fourth foot. He lengthens the second syllable of *hecatombem* by metrical necessity: there was no other easy way to use this word, and he ought not prudently to have avoided it. Ison’s gloss can be emended as follows: “*hecaton*, a hundred; hence *hecatombem*,” etc. A *hecatomb* is a sacrifice of a hundred oxen; it is said to have been instituted first by the Lacedaemonians, who, since they once ruled a hundred cities, sacrificed a hundred oxen each year for the hundred cities. Others say other things. See Eustathius on Homer’s *Iliad*.

1052. Vat. A, *fere* (“almost”); above, it seems to be *ferro* (“with iron”). Prag., *fere*. Rott., Prag., Hailsbr., Vat. B, Mar. above, Gis. in the margin, Sich., *cui cadunt* (“upon which they fall”). Others, *cum cadunt* (“when they fall”). Widm. and Parrhasius omit *cum* or *cui*, but the meter is corrupted.

1055. Ald., Vat. B in the text, Mar., Bong., Widm., [Col. 0524B] Sich., Gis. first edition, *profundum sanguinem* (“deep blood”). Alex., Urb., Vatt. A and B above, Q, Hailsbr., Pal., Fabr., Gis. second edition, Heins., *profundum sanguinis* (“the depth of blood”). Weitz., Egm., *profunda sanguinis* (“the deep places of blood”).

1056. In Vat. B there seems to have been *pluinarium*, or certainly *plumarium*, but incorrectly. He calls the *pulvinar* of the gods a rich slaughterhouse because the temples overflowed with the blood of victims.

[Col. 0524C] 1059. Vat. A, *vosmetipsos*. Prag., *cum vosmetipsos*, above *quando*. The law of the poem requires *quando vosmet ipsi*. The poet is now recounting the rites of the pagans in which they inflicted wounds upon themselves in honor of the gods.

1061. Prag., *cultros* (“knives”), against the meter. Mar., *lacertis* (“arms”), but *lacertos* is more correct. The priests of Bellona bloodied their arms and shoulders, and were called fanatics. Lactantius, book I, chapter 21: “The priests of Bellona sacrifice not with another’s blood but with their own. For, cutting their shoulders and brandishing drawn swords in both hands, they run, are carried away, and rage.” Horace, Lucan, Juvenal, and others speak of these fanatics. Under Commodus it became customary for fanatics to imitate the shedding of blood without actually cutting their arms. For Lampridius says in his life of him: “He ordered the servants of Bellona actually to cut off their arm, out of a desire for cruelty.” In Montfaucon, volume I of *Antiquities*, book IV, p. 262, a fanatic of Bellona, Isis, and Serapis is depicted holding two knives in his hands.

[Col. 0524D] 1062. Nebrissensis wishes *deum* (“god”) to be read instead of *deam* (“goddess”), so that Cybele, mother of the gods, may be understood, following Apuleius’s view, who thinks Bellona, Cybele, and Isis are the same deity. And indeed *deum* is read in Lotterus’s edition. In the *Acts of Saint Symphorianus*, Cybele is often called “mother goddess.” But perhaps both in those Acts and in Prudentius it will be better to read *mater deum* (“mother of the gods”), as occurs frequently in ancient inscriptions.

1063. Ald., *ac rotare* (“and to whirl”). *Ac rotari* (“and to be whirled”) is better. Rat., *et rotari*. Lotterus corruptly has *ejus* for *jus*. Minucius: “These are the frenzied men whom you see running together in public, prophets themselves without a temple; thus they rage, thus they revel, thus they whirl,” etc. Compare the notes of Heraldus and others on Minucius, and Elmenhorstius on book I of Arnobius, p. 1.

1064. Ald., Vat. B in the context, Torn., Mar., [Col. 0525B] Weitz., *parta* (“acquired”). The better Heinsius manuscripts, and ours with Parrhasius and Latinius, have *parca* (“sparing”). Giselinus likewise has *parca*: although he printed *parta*, in his corrected copies he changed it to *parca*, with the explanation: “The man who cuts sparingly is impious; he who cuts cruelly is pious.” Nebrissensis explains it as *parata* (“prepared”), because he reads *parta*; but that is contrary to the poet’s meaning, and *parta* cannot properly mean *parata*.

Indeed, he turns up his mouth and offers his cheeks to meet it,

1153 presents his ears and exposes his lips and nostrils,

and drenches even his eyes with the fluids.

He no longer spares his palate, but moistens his tongue,

[1040] until he has absorbed the black blood throughout his body.

After the priests have drawn back from that framework

the corpse, stiff with its blood discharged,

the pontiff comes forth from there, horrible to behold.

He displays his wet crown, his heavy beard,

[1045] his dripping ribbons, and his sodden garments.

All salute and worship from a distance this man,

stained by such contagions,

filthy with the gore of a recent expiatory rite,

because worthless blood and a dead ox

[1050] have washed him as he lay hidden beneath foul caverns.

[Col. 0524A] Shall we add that hecatomb of yours, if you wish?

When a hundred animals fall beneath the sword,

1154 And the blood, swollen with varied slaughter, forms a pool,

So that the augurs, swimming through blood,

[1055] Can scarcely make their way across its depth.

But why should I reproach the rich slaughterhouse,

The butchers of the greatest herds,

With flesh torn out and raw? There are sacrifices

When you yourselves cut yourselves open,

[1060] And pain, as an offering, mutilates the limbs.

The fanatic draws the knife across his upper arms,

And with arms cut apart appeases the mother goddess.

To rave and whirl is thought to be a mystical command:

1155 An impious right hand is said to be sparing in cutting:

[1065] [Col. 0525A] [Note: [Col. 0525A]

1066. “To be cut,” that is, “to be severed.”

1070. “Increased,” that is, “heaped up,” or “appeased.”

[Col. 0525B] 1071. “Each of the two,” he says ironically. “To holiness,” that is, “to that holiness.” “He dislikes”: the emasculated man despises both sexes, the male and the female.

1076. “Fragitidas”: *fragis* in Greek means a missile; hence *fragitidae* means darts, or larger needles, Vat. A. Others derive it from *frangere*, “to break,” Mar.

1078. “They will have marked with fire,” that is, “painted.”

[Col. 0526A] 1081. “Having completed”: “having died.” We say *fungi* of fulfilling an office; *defungi*, of ceasing from an office; *defunctus* is said of one who ceases from the office of life.

1083. “Sheets of metal”: plates of gold.]

[Note: [Col. 0525B]

1066. Parrhasius’ reading *dicat* is metrically erroneous; read *dedicat*. The priests of Cybele are now being criticized, as has already been done more than once.

1070. Prag. reads *vena defluenti*, contrary to the meter. Thuanus writes *efluenti* instead of *effluenti*, from which Heinsius conjectures *vena et fluenti*. Salmasius reads *vena fluenti*. Parrhasius printed these two verses in a thoroughly corrupt form:

“that torn vein of the male seed,
with Pasithea’s blood flowing.”

In his corrected edition he noted that some manuscripts read: “the vein, feeding on the flowing blood, increased.”

1075. Aldus, Parrhasius, and some common editions read *levibus*, or *laevibus*. Most manuscripts read *lenibus*. Heinsius printed *laevibus*.

1076. Vat. A reads *sacrandos*; read *sacrandus*. Parrhasius read the verse as follows: “What happens when the Phrygian Attis, who must be consecrated, dies?” I do not know in what sense. Aldus and Giselinus write *sphragitidas*, and Giselinus derives the word from Greek σφραγίζειν, “to mark” or “stamp.” Hence σφραγίς, “a seal,” and σφράγισμα, “an imprint.” Giselinus thinks the derivative *sphragitis*, meaning brands and punctures, is scarcely found elsewhere. In the manuscripts of Weitz, Heinsius, and our own copies, *fragitidas* is read. Nevertheless Heinsius printed *sphragitidas*. Nebrissensis explains *sphragitidas* as medicines made from *sphragitis* earth, or “sealed earth,” which is useful for healing wounds by forming scars. From Celsus, book V, chapters 20 and 26, a lozenge used for closing a wound is called *sphragis*.

Fabricius interprets the word better as signs or impressed marks, either for remembrance, as with a ring, or for religious purposes, as with a branding iron. Those who enlisted in the army were also accustomed to be pierced and branded with a hot iron; hence *sacramentum militare*, “military oath,” because the soldiers were, as it were, consecrated. Lipsius, *De Militia Romana*, book I, dialogue 9, discusses soldiers marked by punctures in the skin. Raynaudus, *De Stigmatismo sacro et profano*, section 2, chapter 7, treats this rite at length.

He does not, however, approve Primasius’ explanation of the Apostle’s passage in Romans 1, according to which pagans are understood to have dishonored their bodies by inflicting marks and burns upon themselves during the consecrations of idols; for the Apostle clearly speaks of dishonor through lust and sexual immorality.

1077. Prag. reads *ingegit*, perhaps for *ingerit*.

1078. Prag. erroneously reads *pergunt perurere, cum igniverint*. Egm. corruptly reads *verauntur aere*. Aldus, Parrhasius, the manuscripts of Heinsius and Gifanius, and our own read *pergunt urere, ut igniverint*, “they continue to burn, until they have branded.” Weitz, Heinsius, and others followed this reading. Heinsius acknowledges that a tribrach may be admitted in the fourth foot with hiatus. Giselinus and some common editions read *utque igniverint*; in this way the final syllable of *urere* is elided and the foot becomes an iamb. Gifanius indeed reads *urere, ut igniverint*, but recognizes an iamb, not a tribrach, in the fourth foot. He defends this on Mortianus’ view that words ending in *t* were treated as having an anceps interval; he therefore lengthens *ut*. Hermanus Hugo, chapter 19 of *De Prima scribendi Ratione*, where he proves that not only slaves and criminals but sometimes soldiers and sacred persons were branded with letters, also reads *urere, utque igniverint*.

Vossius, in *De Vitiis sermonis*, rejected *ignio* among barbarous words, attributing it to Hincmar. Paulinus, letter 4 to Ausonius, used *ignitus*, a word also employed by Gellius. Barthius, book IX, chapter 18, notes that Arnulfus took *ignire* from Prudentius. Arnulfus writes:

“His lofty eyes, and the burning excellence
of his keen light, the vigor of his understanding and mind.”

1079. Egm. reads: “Whatever part of the body the heated mark should brand.”

1080. In Vat. A, *stagnarit* appears to have been written by a different hand, with *stigmarit* in the margin; it is uncertain which reading originally stood in the text. Aldus and Rott. read *hanc si consecratam*. Egm. and Vat. A read *hanc sacratam*, with a defective meter. Hence Heinsius conjectured *hancce sic sacratam*, or *hancce consecratam*. Parrhasius reads *hanc consecratam*, but the verse is still not metrically sound. Most copies read *hanc sic consecratam*.

1081. Aldus and Bongarsius read *relinquit spiritus*.

[Col. 0526D] 1084. Prag. reads “a sheet remarkable for its gold.”

1085. Fabricius says that this part was enclosed in gold or silver and preserved as sacred after death. Prudentius merely suggests that the parts burned and marked by fire were covered with an impressed sheet of gold, and thus concealed. I do not recall anyone else mentioning this rite.

Raynaudus, in the passage cited, attacks Fabricius for believing that the custom of enclosing the fingers, arms, and joints of saints in vessels and presenting them for kissing arose in the Church from this pagan rite. Raynaudus says that Prudentius’ meaning is that, while the corpse was being carried out for burial, the limbs marked with the brand were honored in the manner described above, whether they were buried with the body or removed after the funeral procession, before the body was placed in the tomb, together with such ornaments.

I think, however, that the passage concerns not only the priests of Cybele, nor only the priests of Isis, but any priest who consecrated himself to some deity by burning marks into his body. Whether all priests were required to do this, or only the priests of some deity—and which deity—I do not yet understand clearly. Raynaudus, in the passage cited, lists the priests of Cybele, Bellona, Diana, the Syrian Goddess, and Mithras, and explains the different rites of each with a great display of learning.]

Credulity through wounds earns heaven.

But here this man dedicates what must be cut away:

He appeases the deity by severing the groin;

The half-man offers the goddess an obscene gift:

He feeds her, enlarged by the blood that flows,

[1070] From the vein of the male seed torn away.

Neither sex pleases her holiness.

He retains something between the two sexes:

He ceases to be a man, but does not become a woman.

The happy mother of the gods prepares for herself

[1075] Beardless attendants with gentle razors.

What happens when the one to be consecrated receives the *sphragitidas*?

[Col. 0526A] 1156 They thrust small needles into furnaces

With these they proceed to burn their limbs, once they have been heated:

Whatever part of the body the heated mark

[1080] Has branded, they proclaim to have been thus consecrated.

Then, when the spirit has departed from the body,

And the funeral procession is carried to the tomb,

Sheets of metal are impressed upon those very parts;

A distinguished sheet of gold covers the skin,

[1085] 1157 What has been burned by fire is covered with metal.

[Col. 0527A] [Note: [Col. 0527B]

1089. “Insults”: properly, insults are blows and injuries inflicted upon someone.

1103. “Those men”: the torturers and cutters.

1105. “Which”: Vat. A reads “unless.”

1114. “Fasces”: powers, Mar.

[Col. 0526B] 1115. “Long-lasting”: enduring for a long time.

1116. “Long duration”: lasting, age-old.

1117. “Decay”: old age.

1120. “Fades”: is erased. “Mark”: letter.]

[Note: [Col. 0527C]

1086. Minucius correctly says of the Cybele rite: “These are no longer sacred things; they are tortures.”

1087. Parrhasius corruptly reads *cohaerant lege*, although he himself insists that *cohaerant* is a word peculiar to Prudentius, meaning “they assign by bronze,” with an intervening aspiration to avoid hiatus. Read *coercere lege*: “to restrain by law” is far better than “to assign by law.”

1092. Prag. reads poorly *tyrannide cum impia*.

1096. Prag. reads less well *debitis*.

1100. Vat. A reads *desines*. Aldus punctuates badly: *desinas, Cessabit equidem tortor, et sector dehinc*. The words *cessabit equidem tortor* belong not to the Romanus but to the judge.

1101. Many have already taught that the adverb *equidem* can be used in very good Latin with the third or second person as well, although some object.

1103. Parrhasius, Egm., Rat., Hailsbr., and Ambr. read *succedit*. Ox., Rott., Urb., Vat. Q, and Pal. read *succedat*; Giselinus has *succedat illi* in the margin. Most editors and manuscripts read *succedet illis*. Eusebius, chapter 2 of *On the Martyrs of Palestine*, relates the event as follows: “When the emperor’s twentieth anniversary was approaching, and, according to customary practice, a public pardon had been announced by a herald to all who were held in custody, he alone, with his feet stretched out to four points and lying upon the rack, his throat broken by the cord, was adorned with martyrdom, as he had desired.” Thus Eusebius reports that Romanus survived for a long time in prison and, when the emperor’s twentieth anniversary arrived, was strangled in prison, evidently to avoid public outcry.

1105. Above he called the throat-tubes the mouth’s cymbal and the tongue’s plectrum; now he calls the voice’s instrument a trumpet.

1107. Vat. A and Egm. read corruptly *nox illis* instead of *noxialis*.

1108. Teolius thinks strangulation in prison an infamous form of death. I will not agree unless I see an ancient witness.

[Col. 0528B] 1111. *Intimare*, meaning “to announce,” is a word used by Cyprian, Vopiscus, Spartianus, and Symmachus, not by Livy, as Fabricius thought, having been misled by some corrupt edition. For in book IV, chapter 46, one should read not *intimasse filio* but *institisse filio*.

1112. Teolius observes that this was done according to ancient custom, citing Eusebius in the *Chronicle*, who says that it had formerly been the custom of provincial governors to report to the emperor whatever new event occurred among them, so that nothing might remain hidden from him.

1114. Prag. reads *tyrannus omne*, and in the following verse *suum laetatus*; but the latter does not fit the meter. Cauchius, by conjecture, and Latinius in the *Fasti*, read *suos tyrannus*, a reading retained by Giselinus and Heinsius; but both print *suum*, not *suos*, as Murmellius and Lotterus had formerly done. Most editions and manuscripts disagree.

Fabricius interprets *fasces* as the bundles and cases that were customarily rolled up or stored in the emperors’ palaces. Nebrissensis understands bundles of books, or rather annals, which took their names from the consuls and whose insignia were the *fasces*.

1116. Some common editions incorrectly read *illa sed aetas* instead of *illas*.

[Col. 0528D] 1117. Cauch., Thuan., Parrhasius, Sich., Vat. A and B, Mar., Rat., Weitz., and others read *uligo*. Most, with Aldus, read *fuligo*.

1119. Mar. reads *inscripto*; above, *inscripta*, correctly. Isaiah 49:16: “Behold, I have engraved you on my hands.” See verse 1 of hymn 1 of the *Peristephanon*, “The names of two martyrs are written in heaven,” and hymn 4, verse 171.

1120. Aldus reads *obsolescet*.

1121. From the Gospel of Matthew 18:10: “Their angels in heaven always see the face of my Father who is in heaven.” Fabricius, although heterodox, nevertheless admits that this was not poetically invented but is a true account by a man highly learned in divine matters. For sacred history testifies, and devout people experience, that God’s angels are present with us as guardians, companions, defenders, and observers.

1124. In Vat. A, a *u* had been added above *pingens*, making *pinguens*, ineptly.]

The pagan world is compelled to endure these penalties.

By this law the gods restrain their worshipers:

Thus the demon himself toys with those whom he has captured;

He teaches them to endure execrable insults,

[1090] And orders the wretched to be branded with tortures.

But this blood of ours flows from your

Cruelty: with impious tyranny

You ulcerate the bodies of the innocent.

If you allow us, we live without bloodshed;

[1095] But if we are punished with bloodshed, we conquer.

But now I shall be silent: the appointed end is near,

The end of evils, the glory of suffering.

Now, wicked man, you will no longer be permitted, as just now,

To torture or cut our entrails:

[1100] You must yield, defeated, and now desist.

[Col. 0527B] 1158 The torturer and the cutter will indeed cease thereafter;

The judge threatens: but the strangling hand

Of the executioner will succeed them,

For the restless voice of the babbling mouth

[1105] Knows no other way to be silent than if I break its trumpet.

[Col. 0528A] He spoke, and ordered the man to be dragged from the forum,

Thrust into the darkness of a death-dealing prison:

There the accursed lictor crushed the martyr’s neck

With a cord. Thus his passion was completed:

[1110] His soul, released from its bonds, sought heaven.

The prefect is said to have reported every deed

To the prince, adding the sequence of events,

And arranging the series of so great a tragedy:

The tyrant, delighted, records every crime

[1115] 1159 In his enduring little records.

But long duration consumes them,

Soot darkens them, dust covers them with decay,

Old age gnaws them, or buries them beneath ruins:

The page inscribed with Christ is immortal,

[1120] [Col. 0528B] And no letter in heaven ever fades.

The angel standing before God received

Both what the martyr said and what he endured:

He preserved not only the words of his speech;

But, painting the wounds themselves, he expressed them with his stylus—

[1125] The wounds of his sides, cheeks, breast, and throat.

[Col. 0529A] [Note: [Col. 0529A]

1131. “In the registers”: in hidden places. A *regestum* is called a book containing records of other books and letters collected into one; it is called *regestum*, as though “recorded again.” John Scotus used *registron*.

[Col. 0529B] 1132. “Monuments”: *monumentum*, *monimentum*, and *monimen* are always used in the same sense.

[Col. 0530A] 1133. “Formerly”: at a future time.

1134. “With the balance”: with the weight.

1138. “King”: Christ.

1140. “To clothe”: innocence.

[Col. 0530B] 1. *Romula*: he should have said *in Romulea*, but *Romula* is used for the meter.]

[Note: [Col. 0529B]

1131. Aldus printed incorrectly *hic intregestis*, and corrected it no better as *hic iter gestis*. The manuscripts read *hic in regestis*. He also used *regesta*. Vopiscus does so in his life of Probus. John Scotus, who, as the gloss says, used *registron*, appears to be John Scotus Eriugena, who flourished first in England and then in France under Charles the Bald, who reigned from 840 to 877. He was a contemporary of Iso, who died in 871, as is confirmed from Mabillon in the preliminary observations to the life of Saint Othmar. Iso wrote two books about the miracles of Saint Othmar; they also survive in volume I of the *Scriptores rerum Alamannicarum*, where volume II contains another work by the same Iso entitled *Formulae chartarum*.

1132. Most copies read *monimenta*; others write *monumenta*.

1133. Weitz, together with Egm. and Hailsbr., preferred to write *religendus*.

1135. Egm. and Hailsbr. incorrectly read *comparavit*.

1136. We explained this whole passage at length in chapter 19 of the *Prolegomena*. Dudo, Dean of Saint-Quentin, imitating Prudentius in book III of *On the Customs of the Normans*, played upon the passage according to the taste of his age:

“And when you see me bound among the stinking kids from afar,
for here, alas, my memorials promise me this.
Transfer me as soon as possible among the little white lambs;
as a right-hand fellow-lamb may I go in life-giving fleece.”

In a similar passage of Hericus of Auxerre, cited in the *Prolegomena*, the reading *vinctum* differs from *junctum*.

1137. Latinius, I think, reads by conjecture *si sum futurus*. Cellarius’ reading, *ut sum futurus*, is not bad: that is, “as I have altogether deserved by my sins to be placed among the kids.” Fabricius, in *Commentaries on Christian Poetry*, p. 118, asks: “What is this, Clement Prudentius, that you say you will be among the kids? Have you forgotten yourself, who earlier wrote: ‘Our cross is Christ’s; we ascend the gallows; Christ was put to death for us’?” He then attacks the invocation of Romanus.

Such are these men, proud in their heretical and perverse judgment: they not only freely scorn the opinions of the ancient Fathers, but also reproach those same Fathers as foolish writers and openly contradictory to themselves in the same work. The expurgatory index of Belgium ordered this passage of Fabricius, like many others that we have repeatedly noted, to be deleted. After the censure of the Christian poets of G. Fabricius Chemnicensis, printed at Basel by Johannes Oporinus in 1564, the index immediately adds:

“But those editions, whether German, such as those printed at Basel, Frankfurt, or elsewhere, or the Paris edition published by the same Jacob du Puys around 1560, which also contain prefaces or additions by Luther or Melanchthon, are much more suspect; they also contain highly suspect appendices. As for what remains, let all these editions, and the remaining editions, Latin as well as German, French, and Teutonic, be universally prohibited.”

I do not understand clearly whether these words refer to several other editions of the Christian Poets or signify something else. The heretics raised many storms concerning this index, and, as though it had been suppressed by its authors at the very beginning, they themselves reprinted it in 1599. Schelhornius, volume II of *Amoenitates litterariae*, p. 371, lists it among rare books.

A copy of the first edition, Antwerp, 1571, exists in the library of the Roman College, under this title: *Expurgatory Index of Books Published in This Century, Either Sprinkled with Errors of Unsound Doctrine or Mixed with the Gall of Useless and Offensive Slander, Compiled in the Netherlands in Accordance with the Decree of the Sacred Council of Trent, by Order and Authority of Philip II, Catholic King, and through the Counsel and Assistance of the Duke of Alba; Antwerp, from the workshop of Christopher Plantin, royal proto-typographer, 1571.* Arias Montanus wrote the preface.

1138. In Vat. B, *hoc* is missing. Vat. B, in the first hand, reads *precanti*, incorrectly.

1139. Teolius and Chamillardus followed Heinsius, who, together with Rott. alone, had printed *huc haedum*. But since Heinsius appears to have held a different opinion in his *Addenda*, and most manuscripts have *hunc haedum*, that reading should be retained. See *Prolegomena*, no. 186.

After this poem, Vat. A is followed by the hymn *The Nativity of the Lord*. In Vat. B and Mar. appears: “Romanus of Aurelius Prudentius Clement ends. Hymn VIII of the Kalends of January begins.” In Aldus: “Romanus ends. Of Aurelius Prudentius Clement, the *Peristephanon*.” Immediately afterward is placed the hymn of Saints Emeterius and Chelidonius.

In the Bongarsian manuscript, which I discussed in the commentary on the title of the hymn of Cassian, the following is read after the Passion of Romanus: “The *Cathemerinon* of Prudentius Aurelius Clement ends. This is the book of hymns in honor of the martyrs.” From this Sinnerus concludes that the hymns of the martyrs once circulated under the title *Peristephanon*. It would have been more correct to infer the copyist’s ignorance. The same Sinnerus notes that illustrations had been added to the martyrdom of Romanus in that manuscript. The codex formerly belonged to the church of Strasbourg, then to Frederick Casimir, Count Palatine of the Rhine and Duke of Zweibrücken, then, through his gift, to Jacques Bongars, and finally to the Bern library.

1. This hymn is so entitled in Vat. B, Mar., and Rat. In Heinsius: “On the Passion of Saint Hippolytus, the most blessed martyr. To Bishop Valerian.” In Aldus: “The Passion of the Martyr Hippolytus, to Bishop Valerian.” In Alex.: “To Bishop Valerian. On the Passion of Hippolytus, the most blessed martyr.” In Vat. A: “The Passion of Hippolytus, the most blessed martyr”; there *To Bishop Valerian* is omitted, because it was improperly attached to the title of the hymn of Saint Cassian.

Weitz follows Aldus, except that he writes *Yppoliti*, as it appears in some old manuscripts. Johann Albert Fabricius published, in two folio volumes, the works of Saint Hippolytus, bishop and martyr, with notes and dissertations by learned men. Hamburg, 1716. The present hymn of Prudentius and many testimonies concerning the various Hippolytuses appear there. The distinguished Simon de Magistris has long been preparing a new edition of the same works with a greater apparatus of learning; he will add new light to the controversy concerning the Hippolytuses. Already, in his preface to Daniel according to the Septuagint, no. 7, he has brought forward certain new observations about this Saint Hippolytus that others had not noticed.

Hospinianus, in *On Festivals*, under the feast of Saint Hippolytus, following the similarly heterodox Reinoldus in book I, chapter 1 of *On the Idol of the Roman Church*, judges that no such holy Hippolytus ever existed. Prudentius, he says, an ancient—and I do not know whether the first—author of this martyr seems to have indulged in poetic play … It appears, I say, that he adapted Ovid’s fiction in book XV of the *Metamorphoses* to the martyr Hippolytus from the etymology of the name.

I have reported these words so that, when the hymn is compared with them, they may expose the audacity of a most shameless man. For Prudentius not only testifies that the cult of Saint Hippolytus was extremely celebrated, but also asserts that he himself often prayed at his tomb, saw a painting in which his martyrdom was depicted, and learned the account of his martyrdom while tracing the details of past events through the monuments. What room, then, can there be for poetic fiction?

Another, well-known controversy is with Catholics, who say that Prudentius conflated three martyrs named Hippolytus into one: Hippolytus the soldier, who was torn apart by horses; Hippolytus the presbyter of Antioch, who embraced the schism of Novatus; and Hippolytus the bishop. I would be willing to argue the matter more fully against them, but there is no time.

Briefly, I will say that Prudentius’ account should be preferred to the accounts of those who are known to have written long after Prudentius and who did not apply as much diligence to investigating the acts of this martyr as Prudentius plainly applied in this hymn.

Constantinus Ruggerius, carried off by an untimely death, left an unfinished dissertation on the see of Saint Hippolytus, bishop and martyr of Porto; Achilles Ruschius published it, completed and enlarged with many annotations, at Rome in 1771. Ruggerius argues that Prudentius was speaking of Hippolytus, bishop of Porto and a distinguished writer, but that Prudentius simultaneously confuses the martyrdom of Hippolytus the soldier with the Novatian heresy of Hippolytus the presbyter.

Since the writers who defend Prudentius’ reliability add various conjectures about the single Hippolytus whom Prudentius celebrates, Ruggerius attacks such conjectures with many arguments, but he does not touch the heart of the matter. Prudentius stands supported by his own authority until a contrary monument of equal weight is produced.

It is clear from Prudentius that Hippolytus the presbyter, formerly a supporter of the Novatian sect, suffered martyrdom, was torn apart by horses, and had his relics transferred to a Roman cemetery. Whether he was also the bishop is not so clear; still less is it clear whether he was the author of the works that survive under the name of Hippolytus.

The martyrologies, in which many errors have already been corrected and, unless I am mistaken, will continue to be corrected, ought to be brought back into conformity with the testimony of Prudentius, who certainly wrote long before these martyrologies were compiled in the form in which they have reached us. They should be reconciled with Prudentius wherever possible; where that cannot be done, they should be rejected.

In the present matter, the authority of Prudentius concerning the martyrdom of Saint Hippolytus is defended by Ruinart, Tillemont, Ceillier, Basnage, Fronto Ducaeus, Pliny, Pietro Lazzeri in his *Theses on Ecclesiastical History*, Rome, 1747, and the recent interpreter of Prudentius, the distinguished Teolius, who nevertheless improperly cites Ruggerius as supporting the same opinion.]

Every measure of blood was marked,

So that each wound the furrow had carved—

Deep, gaping, near, long, or short—

Whatever the force of pain, whatever the extent of the cut,

[1130] He lost not a single drop of blood.

This book is in the heavenly registers,

1160 Preserving a record of imperishable praise,

To be read again one day by the eternal judge,

Who, with an impartial balance, will compare

[1135] The weights of evils and the abundance of rewards.

[Col. 0530A] I wish that, among the sinister flocks of kids,

I might be recognized from afar as I shall be;

1161 And that the excellent king might say, while he prayed this:

“Romanus is praying: transfer this kid to me.

[1140] Let him be a lamb on the right; let him be clothed in fleece.”

XI. HYMN. BEGINS: TO BISHOP VALERIAN, ON THE PASSION OF SAINT HIPPOLYTUS, THE MOST BLESSED MARTYR

Countless ashes of saints in the city of Romulus

3. “Cut into”: we have seen carved. “Each”: that is, if.

4. “To repeat”: to explain, to enumerate the origin.

5. “Drew up”: consumed, as though devoured.

[Col. 0532A] 6. “When”: whenever. “He worshiped”: he used to worship. “Troy”: built by the Trojans, Vat. A. “Because they derive their origin from the Trojans.”]

2. Giselinus and some common editions read *Christo*. Alex. has this from a second hand. Most manuscripts, together with Aldus and Torn., read *Christi*, more elegantly, as Heinsius proves by similar examples: Cicero, *Verrines* 3, “That island is thought sacred to those gods”; Pliny, book VIII, chapter 21, “the wild beast called the axim, sacred to Father Liber”; Ovid, “He went beneath the curved yoke of Mars’ sacred oxen.” Harduinus, in his notes on the cited passage of Pliny, does not approve of *sacer* with a genitive. But many refinements of Latin speech would perish if Harduinus’ judgment were accepted. Therefore *sacer* here does not mean so much “priest,” as Iso says, and as Parrhasius also thought, who declared it peculiar to Prudentius, but rather “consecrated to Christ.”

See the *Prolegomena*, nos. 31 and 32, concerning this Valerian, in whose diocese Prudentius was quite probably born. Fontaninus, *History of Aquileia*, p. 123, rightly charges the Magdeburg Centuriators with having wrongly conflated Valerian of Aquileia with the bishop of the same name praised by Prudentius in century 4, chapter 10, p. 974. Fontaninus calls our Valerian a native of Calahorra. Parrhasius writes *Valleriane*.

Castus Innocentius Ansaldus published an octavo pamphlet, *Dissertation on the Causes of the Scarcity of Ancient Monuments for Determining the Abundance of Martyrs, Against Dodwell*, Milan, 1747. Prudentius alone, whom Dodwell shamelessly cites in his own defense, would suffice to refute his rash opinion. For he is an eyewitness, committing to writing matters that were openly known; and, as is clear from his books against Symmachus, he charged the pagans with cruelty because they had killed countless martyrs—something he would hardly dare unless so great a crime were established.

In the first eight couplets of this hymn Prudentius proclaims this multitude of martyrs. From verse 43 to verse 77 he pursues the same subject at length. In the hymn of Saint Laurence we read, verse 541:

“Scarcely is the report known of how full
Rome is of hidden saints;
how richly the urban soil
blooms with sacred tombs.”

Book II against Symmachus, verse 671:

“After him Decius, raging with exposed throats,
fed his insane fury.
Soon this thirst burned, like that of many,
flaring through grievous wounds
to draw souls into the flames,
to toy with punishments,
and to pour deaths streaming into my bosom.”

And book I, verse 515, likewise concerning Rome:

“Then, remembering that the fields adjoining the city walls
had grown wet with the innocent blood of the righteous,
she sees around her thousands of tombs;
she grieves, and regrets the judgment all the more.”

Paulinus echoes Prudentius in *Natalia* 13:

“Here are Peter and Paul, the leaders; here all the martyrs,
whom the circuit of the great City holds together,
countless as they are.”

3. From this it is clear that the title, as I have often said, is used for a funerary inscription. I further infer that Prudentius also saw Hippolytus’ inscription, and therefore did not recount his acts from the painting alone. Giselinus, in his corrected edition, changed *tu* to *et singula*, which Heinsius did not notice. On tomb inscriptions, consult Kirckmannus, book III, chapters 19 and 20 of *On Roman Funerals*.

5. *Populus* signifies a multitude, although it is singular. Prudentius himself uses *populus* in the *Cathmerinon*, hymn V, verse 135: “a people of shadows”; in the *Psychomachia*, verse 798: “a people of virtues”; and Apuleius, book V of the *Metamorphoses*: “whether that people of nymphs.”

19. “Schism”: doctrine, dispute, heresy. “Of Novatus”: this Novatus was a schismatic; for there is a distinction between a schismatic and a heretic. *Schism* means a division; hence a schismatic is one who separates from the body of the Church through some novelty, such as this man, who said that a person once fallen into a grave sin could never rise again. A heretic is one who cultivates his own sect; for *heresy* means a sect, namely one who does not believe that there is one God, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, as Arius did.

This Novatus was a monk and bishop who said that if a baptized person sinned once, he could not afterward obtain forgiveness. Vat. A.

21. “Advanced”: that is, I found. “Distinction”: ornament. “To have borne”: to have received.

23. “You should not wonder”: you may wonder. “Old man”: Hippolytus.

24. “Enriched”: understood, “to be.”

25. “Victor”: he himself.]

7. Weitz, together with Widm., has *locuntur* written.

8. Parrhasius reads *aliquid*; read *aliquod*.

9. Giselinus in the text reads: “There are also many, nevertheless, closing silent crowds.” In the margin he has *muta* and *tumbas*. The more accurate manuscripts read *muta*; most have *tumbas*. Parrhasius, Vat. A from a second hand, B, Egm., Pal., and Widm. have *multa* above the line.

Valsecchius, who argues in book II, chapter 2 of *On the Foundation of Religion* from Prudentius’ authority for the multitude of martyrs, considers *turbas* the more genuine reading. Parrhasius, who reads *tumbas*, counts the word among the foreign terms used by Prudentius. It is Greek, τύμβος, “funeral pyre” or “burial mound”; from it, I think, *catacombs* was formed for the sake of euphony instead of *catatombs*, as it is actually found in some ancient writers. Others derive *catacombs*, with another meaning, from *cumbae* or *cymbae*, “boats,” and use it for burial places. Jerome, Alcuin, Rathbert, and many other Christian writers use *tumba* for a tomb. In Christian inscriptions *tumbus* occurs with the same meaning. See Ducange.

11. Mar. reads incorrectly *acerbis* instead of *acervis*. Torn. reads less well *conjectis* instead of *congestis*.

13. *Alicubi defossa* is erroneous. *Moles* is properly said of a tomb; thus *the mole of Hadrian*.

15. In the liturgical office one sings, “whose names are known in heaven.” See verse 1 of hymn 1 of the *Peristephanon*, and verse 1119 of hymn 10.

[Col. 0533D] 16. Giselinus has in the margin, “whom friendship specially joined.” That the righteous are called friends, and are friends of God, is known from sacred Scripture.

17. Prudentius’ diligence is noteworthy: he investigated the inscriptions so that he might become certain about the acts of the martyrs. What he adds—“I find Hippolytus”—clearly implies that he learned the history from definite inscribed monuments; for he could not have drawn so precise an account from the painting alone, which he mentions later. Nor is it believable that the true history of Saint Hippolytus was either unknown or falsely represented in so magnificent a church dedicated to him.

Those who claim that Prudentius, deceived by a popular account, made one person out of three Hippolytuses should consider that it is not plausible either that the history of Saint Hippolytus was unknown in Rome at that time in his own church, or that Prudentius was a man who readily lent his ears to popular tales, when he could easily have questioned more learned persons and examined ancient monuments. If the truth of the matter was not then evident to Prudentius, why should we believe that it became evident many centuries later to the authors of the martyrologies?

[Col. 0534B] 19. Mar. and Rat. read *inveni*; most read *invenio*. Prudentius seems to imply that in Hippolytus’ inscription, or epitaph, he read what he reports concerning the Novatian heresy. Certainly, as I have said, he could not have fashioned the account from the painting alone.

Novatus was a presbyter of Carthage who denied that the Church possessed the power to grant forgiveness for grave crimes, even when the fallen had performed penance. When Novatus came to Rome, he joined the antipope Novatian, who had raised a schism against Cornelius, the Roman pontiff, and drew Hippolytus into his heresy, either as a presbyter alone or also as a bishop, as is clear from Prudentius.

In the Roman Martyrology, after Baronius’ revision, under 30 January, Hippolytus the presbyter of Antioch is said first to have favored Novatus’ doctrine and afterward, having returned to the Catholic faith, to have offered his throat for Christ. But this Hippolytus seems to have been different: he truly favored Novatus, or else what Prudentius relates about his Hippolytus was attached to him. Sollerius, in the *Acta Sanctorum*, volume VI of June, in his note on Usuard’s Martyrology for 30 January, thinks that the matter was confused only by Ado, who appended that eulogy of Hippolytus of Antioch, from which the others copied it.

[Col. 0534D] “We hold our martyrologists,” he adds, “in the highest regard, but not so highly that I would everywhere prefer them to Prudentius, who lived so many centuries earlier.” In the gloss one should supply: “who departed from the body.”

20. Egm. and Hailsbr. have *sequere* above the line, incorrectly, instead of *sequenda*. Aldus and other printed editions read *presbyter*. Widman. corruptly reads *presbyter*. I consider *presbyteri* more correct, with Vat. B, Prag., and Mar., where another hand changed *presbyter* into *presbyteri*. Perhaps Prudentius calls Novatian the antipope Novatus. Novatian, however, was a Roman presbyter who was later schismatically consecrated bishop by three bishops; Novatus was a heretical presbyter of Carthage, whom Baronius and Chamillardus wrongly believe to have been an African bishop.]

23. Ald., *ne mirere*. What Prudentius says here about Hippolytus’s old age, and repeats in verses 78, 109, and 137, indicates that this Hippolytus was different from the soldier Hippolytus, as will become clearer below.]

[Col. 0536B] 45. *Janiculum*: that mountain. *Domum*: that is, the mountain. — *Fora*: places; *fora*, *fori*, and *forum*, as well as *fores*, are distinguished as follows: *fora* is the place for conducting lawsuits, derived from *fari*, “to speak”; *forum* is the place of merchants, because goods are displayed there; *fori* are the concave sides of ships, so called from carrying loads; or *fori* are places where grapes are trodden; *fores* are doors that swing outward, like *valvae*, which swing inward. — *Rostra*: the place where the bronze beaks of the ships of Antium were set up at Rome; they were so called because, after the Carthaginian ships had been captured in the Punic War, their beaks were removed and fixed in the Roman Forum as its distinguishing emblem. — *Suburram*: the name of a place in Rome where new hides are prepared; or the Subura, a district of Rome where public assemblies used to be held, I. Subura: the proper name of a place in Rome where hides are now prepared, Vat. S.]

[Note: [Col. 0535B]

27. Rat., in the first hand, *comitatibus*. Teolius, together with Ruinart, denies that Hippolytus can be inferred from these words to have been a bishop, but only a presbyter entrusted with some portion of the people, such as our parish priests or curates, whom Petavius and Mabillon also report—following Sozomen—to have existed formerly. It seems more likely to me that a bishop is described here, either of Portus or of Ostia; for either conclusion can be argued from Prudentius. Below, verse 80, [he says] that he “was himself the head of the Christian peoples.” Ruggerius attempts to demolish Ruinart’s opinion, but not with arguments as strong as he supposes. The Roman Martyrology records the following: “At Roman Port, Saint Hippolytus, bishop, distinguished for his learning, who under the emperor Alexander, on account of his illustrious confession of faith, was thrown, bound hand and foot, into a deep pit full of water and received the palm of martyrdom.” Prudentius relates a different kind of martyrdom; but either Prudentius should be trusted more, or we must hold that there were two martyred bishops named Hippolytus: one the author of the works circulated under Hippolytus’s name, the other the man about whom Prudentius writes in this hymn. The latter is easier to accept than the notion that Prudentius, while investigating the deeds of Saint Hippolytus in the church itself, was mistaken.

28. Many say that Hippolytus then first renounced the heresy, or schism, of Novatus. But this cannot be inferred from Prudentius. Hippolytus may already have withdrawn from the schism and, as martyrdom approached, have explained his position on the true faith to those consulting him.

30. On these verses, see the prologue, chapter 21.

33. Ruinart reads *piget et venerabile cerno*, against the meter. He explains it as: “I testify that these things are worthy of veneration,” or, “Now I, a martyr, …”

35. Ald., incorrectly, *his ubi detersit*.

37. In Vat. A, *e rectis* has correctly been changed to *recti*: namely, “the leader of the right way.”

39. Cellarius either supposes that the emperor Alexander was a mild ruler favorable to the Christian cause, so that Hippolytus could have suffered only through a popular disturbance, or he adds that Prudentius, confusing different Hippolytuses, invented another ruler here. Chamillard thinks that Prudentius is speaking of Ulpian, who was extremely hostile to Christians, whom Alexander appointed prefect of the praetorium and made master of the imperial archives. These authors take as true, or assume as established, what is false or ought to remain under inquiry. I say again: either there were two Hippolytuses, or the account of the Roman Martyrology is weakened and made unstable by Prudentius’s account, not the reverse. I consider it most probable that the Hippolytus whom Prudentius celebrates was crowned with martyrdom in the fiercest persecution of Decius, Gallus, or later Valerian. Since Prudentius speaks of Hippolytus as a supporter of the Novatian schism, it would be an intolerable anachronism to assign his martyrdom to the reign of Alexander Severus. Therefore the difficulty raised by Cellarius against the Roman Martyrology, where Alexander Severus is mentioned, may perhaps have force there, but it certainly does not affect Prudentius. In any case, it is clear from the martyrologies and ecclesiastical history that under Alexander several martyrs suffered, whether through Ulpian the jurist or through others who hated Christians.

40. There are two mouths through which the Tiber flows into the sea. Two cities once stood there, one on each side: one called Tiberine Ostia, on the eastern side, and the other Roman Port, or the Port of Augustus, on the western side. They were cities, and their distinguished names are still commemorated in the titles of two cardinals, of whom the cardinal-bishop of Ostia is dean of the Sacred College. From this verse it may be inferred that Prudentius’s Hippolytus was bishop of Ostia, since Tiberine Ostia was the proper name of the city simply called Ostia. Fabricius and Weitzius hold this opinion, which is confirmed by verse 151, “They leave Ostia,” a statement scarcely applicable to Roman Port. The feminine name *Ostia* is extremely ancient. Piazza, *Hier. Card.*, p. 16, discusses especially the martyrs of Ostia under Alexander Severus, at the instigation of Ulpian.

41. Cauchus conjectured *ipso* for *ipsos*: namely, “he had withdrawn on that very day.”

43. Ald., Rat. in the first hand, Hailsbr., Heins. with his more carefully corrected copies: *celsa*. Parrhasius, Vatt. A and B, Mar., Prag., Weitz., Gis., and others: *celsae*.

45. In the Gloss, at the word *rostra*, read [Col. 0537B] *Antiatium* for *Antoniarum*. Parrhasius writes *Suburam*, with Rat., Mar., and others.]

1166 His soul rejoicing as his flesh hastened toward destruction,

When asked which sect was the better, he replied:

“Flee, wretched men, the accursed schisms of Novatus;

[30] restore yourselves to the catholic peoples.

Let there be one faith, established in the ancient temple—

the faith which Paul preserves, and which is preserved by Peter’s chair.

I regret having taught what I taught:

As a martyr, I see as worthy of veneration what I had thought removed from God’s worship.”

[35] When by these words he had turned the people away from the left-hand path

[Col. 0536A] he likewise presented himself as the leader of the right way,

48. It is probable that Roman Port is indicated here. But since Tiberine Ostia was mentioned above, there is always room for doubt whether Hippolytus was crowned with martyrdom at Roman Port—which had earlier been called Tiberine Ostia less properly—or at Tiberine Ostia, which is now called Aequoreus Portus. Nevertheless, it seems more likely that Tiberine Ostia is intended here also, for below, in verse 151, the place of martyrdom is simply called “Ostia.”

50. Parrhasius, *structo*; Egm., incorrectly, *extratto*. Just as *ministeria* means ministers, so *officia* means those who perform an office; this usage is found in Suetonius, Pliny the Younger, and the ancient jurists, as in *pro praetore*, “in place of the governor,” *pro apparitore*, “in place of the attendant,” and *pro comitatu praetoris*, “in place of the governor’s retinue.”

51. Barthius marked *rebelles* with the genitive, just as in the following verse he opposes *perfidiam* to the vice contrary to faith. In the hymn of Saint Quirinus, verse 1, *insignis* occurs with the genitive; although the manuscripts vary, many find it more elegant to say *Quirinum insignem meriti* than *meritis*. Prudentius also uses *perfidos* elsewhere for unbelievers.

52. Parrhasius, less satisfactorily, *idoli*.

53. Ald., *crinata*: read *crinita*. In reference to verse 80 of the first hymn of the *Peristephanon*, it is said that Romans customarily allowed the accused to grow their hair; hence *crinita agmina*, “long-haired bands.”

54. Rott., *horrificis*. Parrhasius, *excruciata*, less correctly.

55. On the various instruments and methods by which the holy martyrs were killed, see plates of tortures X [Col. 0537D] and XI.

57. Ruinart numbers three instruments with which the martyrs’ bodies were torn: claws, hooks, and combs; he says that they are better explained in Gallonius’s illustrations. Compare plate XXVI, which we have added and which was drawn from the actual instruments. Number 1 shows an iron glove with fingers bent inward and sharpened at the ends—the kind of claw found in the cemetery of Callepodius. See Aringhus, vol. II of *Roma subterranea*, p. 687, and Mamachius, *De’ Costumi de’ primi Crist.*, vol. II, p. 306. Number 2 represents an iron hook found in the cemetery of Saint Agnes, driven into the head of a martyr; Mamachius discusses it in the work cited. Number 3 depicts an iron comb preserved among the sacred relics of the monastery of Dominican nuns of Saint Mary Magdalene on the Quirinal Hill; Boldettus, p. 319, and Mamachius in the cited work, p. 309, and vol. III of *Antiquities*, p. 205, discuss it. From the Vatican sacred museum I took numbers 4 and 8, two instruments with which martyrs’ bodies were torn; they should apparently be classified among claws or talons, for they resemble the claws of birds of prey. Number 5 shows forked claws preserved in the basilica of Saint Peter, discussed by Gallonius and previously by us. Number 6 shows leaden scourges from the Vatican sacred museum; see the commentary on verse 117 in the *Romanus*. Numbers 7 and 9 represent two cauldrons of the kind carved on the tombs of Victorina and Exuperantius and described by Mamachius among other instruments of martyrdom, vol. II of *De’ Costumi*, p. 306. See also vol. III of *Antiquitates Christianae*, p. 206. I thought it worthwhile to add all these instruments of martyrdom to Gallonius’s plates. Father Peregrinus Chiesa had prepared and completed them for the edition of Prudentius’s works that he was planning, and generously allowed them to be used for the purpose for which they were intended. They differ from the somewhat less accurately rendered images of the martyrdoms that Gallonius printed in his Italian work on the tortures of the holy martyrs. The paintings made at the command of Gregory XIII, at the urging and with the advice of Michael Lauretano, S.J., by Pomarantius and Matteo Senese in the church of Saint Stephen on the Coelian Hill—also called the Rotunda—and engraved in copper by Tempesta likewise differ from ours. I have seen a booklet entitled *The Triumph of the Martyrs Expressed in the Church of Saint Stephen on the Coelian Hill*, by Giulio Roscio Hortino, the work and craftsmanship of Giovanni Battista de’ Cavalieri. This booklet was, I think, published at Rome; some of its plates concern the martyrs of the *Peristephanon*: plate III, Saints Peter and Paul the Apostles; plate XVIII, Saint Laurence with Hippolytus being dragged by horses; plate XXII, Saint Agnes; and plate XXIV, Saint Vincent on the gridiron. Consult also Marcantonio Boldetti, book I, chapter 60, who discusses these paintings and depicts certain instruments of martyrdom that he himself saw, such as iron knives, a lance, and an iron forceps, in addition to the iron comb from the cemetery of Callixtus, which we exhibit, and the cauldrons carved on the tombs of Saint Victorina and Saint Exuperantius. He also gives reasons why these cauldrons should be thought to represent instruments of martyrdom. On instruments of this kind there is a notable passage of Saint Leo in his sermon for the feast of Saint Laurence: “You raged, persecutor, against the martyr; you raged, and increased the palm, while you piled up the punishment. For what did your ingenuity not devise for the victor’s glory, when even the instruments of martyrdom passed into the honor of triumph?” I think he is speaking chiefly of Saint Laurence’s gridiron, which is reverently preserved at Rome and has always been held in great honor, as I said in the hymn of Saint Laurence against Sagittarius.]

60. Sich., and in some copies of the Vulgate, *ad eram*, “with condition”: *cognitione* is better.

61. Ald. incorrectly omits *ex*.

62. Parrhasius, *vitiare animum*, “to corrupt the soul.”

63. Ald., Alex., Vatt. A and P, Q, Urb., Egm., *ab uno*. Others, *ab unco*. Heinsius took this from Giselinus but did not record the variation in readings. The martyrs were torn by iron hooks, and were also tortured on the rack and suspended on hooks. See the commentary on verse 173 of *Peristephanon* 5, Arnobius, book II, Gallonius, Sagittarius, and plates XIII and XXVI.

64. Noms., *morte agita*, less well. Torture by interrogation preceded the torments; but the word is also used for the torments themselves, because the questioning continued amid the torments. Saint Cyprian, letter 69 to Florentinus: “So many confessors, subjected to interrogation and tortured, glorious in the memory of their notable wounds and scars.” Rigaltius notes that after an inquiry had been conducted, the examination was first held and then the torments applied. But this was the madness of the pagans: they wished to force Christians by examination and torture to deny the Christian faith, not to disclose the truth.

65. Ald., Gis., *abscinde*. Heinsius with others, *abscide*. Parrhasius, Vat. B, Prag., Mar., Rat., *excide*. Peveratus thinks that in the words *crux istum tollat in auras*, “let the cross raise this man into the air,” Prudentius was referring to the etymology of the Greek word σταυρός, *stauros*, “cross,” about which Hesychius says: “*Stauroi* are stakes fixed in the ground, palisades, and all pieces of wood standing upright: from their standing they are called *stauroi*, or because they stand against the air.”

[Col. 0539D] 66. Vat. A, *viventisque*. Cathemerinon, hymn 6, verse 63: “But the other, fixed, the ravenous birds devour.” Horace, book I of the *Epistles*: “You will not feed crows on the cross.” Juvenal, satire 14: “The vulture hastens toward the young, leaving behind beast of burden, dogs, and crosses, and carries away a portion of the corpse.” Apuleius, book VI of *The Golden Ass*: “The torment of the gibbet, while dogs and vultures drag out the innermost entrails.” From this Lipsius notes, book II of *De Cruce*, chapter 13, that crosses were not always extremely high, since dogs could drag out the entrails of those fastened to the cross. See plates of tortures I and II. Some holy martyrs remained alive on the cross for several days, as is clear from Eusebius, book VIII of the *History*, chapter 8, and the Roman Martyrology. On martyrs whose bodies were left to the tearing of birds and beasts, see Sagittarius, chapter 8.

67. Ald. with some others, *hos cape*. On the custom of binding martyrs who were thrown onto the pyre, see verse 103 of *Peristephanon* 6 and plate XVII.

[Col. 0540B] 69. Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 6, reports that very many martyrs were killed in this way. Compare Gallonius, *On the Tortures of the Holy Martyrs*, chapter 9, and Sagittarius, chapter 11, who gives several examples. This punishment was not unknown among the ancient Romans, as may be inferred from Caesar’s words in Suetonius, chapter 66: “I shall order them, placed upon the oldest ship, to be carried by whatever wind to whatever lands.”

71. Ald., Pal., Thuan., Ox., Rott., Gis., Heins., *rapidum*; Vatt. A and B, Alex., Prag., Rat., Sich., Weitz., *rabidum*. Parrhasius, Mar. in the first hand, *gravidum*; in Mar., another hand changed it to *rabidum* from the various reading. Gifanius, under *VICTUS* and *VINCTUS*, read from an old book: “Whom, once received, the badly sewn boat will carry over the rabid sea, and, struck by the swollen waters, will float”; and he explains: “The metaphor is drawn from military affairs: a ship struck by swollen waves—since the sea is then rabid—*labrit*, as Virgil says, ‘The gate totters from repeated battering.’ Thus *labat* means ‘fails, comes apart, is loosened.’ He likewise used *caesa* of a roof, in almost the same way.” Barthius notes that Prudentius said *male sutam cymbam*, “a badly sewn boat,” as Virgil said *sutilem*, “stitched.”

72. Gis., *caesa lavarit*; at the margin, *celsa labarit*, or *levarit*. Parrhasius, incorrectly, *caesa libarit*. Vat. Q, *equis*; above, correctly, *aquis*. Cauchus’s manuscript, Hailsbr., first hand, *caesa levarit*. Fabr., *caesa lavarit*. Pal., *celsa lavarit*. Bong., Sich., *celsa lavarit*. The preferable reading is *caesa labarit*, with Aldo, to whom Weitzius nevertheless attributes *celsa labarit*. Barthius says that the boat is elegantly called *caesa*, “cut,” because gaps appear in it as though made by iron. An ancient poet has *Caesaque abra tument*, that is, “they swell as though cut.” See Nonius.

80. Ruggerius and others consider it very clear that Prudentius’s Hippolytus was a bishop, because the pagans said that he was the head of the Christians. This argument is indeed plausible, but not wholly conclusive. What prevented pagans from calling a presbyter whose authority among Christians was very great “the head of the Christians”? Compare Cajetanus Migliore’s commentary on the title “Neophyte presbyter.”]

B, Mar., first hand Rat., Prag., Weitz., Widm., and others. Vat. Q, incorrectly, *ferox* for *feros*. Gifanius, under *VITRICUS*, adopted *feros* from an old book, because *ferarum* is too general a term and because *Hi rapiant* follows. Parrhasius had already printed *feros*, but had divided the sentence differently, not without merit: “whips, bonds; *feros* they goad.” *Feros*, without another noun, can mean horses, as is confirmed by Catullus, Horace, and Virgil. Peveratus observes that for this reason the Hippocentaurs were called *semiferos*, that is, “half-horses,” since they are said to have the form of horses in one half of their bodies.

Gis. in the margin: *hic*; in the text he has *caeco et terrore*.
