123. Some think that Prudentius attributed the martyrdom of Hippolytus the soldier, which he saw represented in a Roman painting, to the other Hippolytus. But first I ask: who, unless many centuries after Prudentius, ever asserted that the soldier Hippolytus suffered such a martyrdom? Further, paintings in churches were customarily elucidated by accompanying verses and inscriptions, as may be inferred from the works of Damasus and Paulinus. Moreover, Prudentius was not so unsophisticated as to mistake one subject for another in a painting, nor so careless as not to inquire into the truth of the matter from learned men. Finally, his entire hymn shows that Prudentius relied not only on the painting but on other monuments as well.

124. In that age *fucus* designated pigment and color. Paulinus, Ausonius, and others attest this.

125. As Peveratus notes, under the Roman emperors painters represented natural colors, not by shadow and recession but in the brightest light; nevertheless, they sometimes added shadows, as may be inferred from this passage. Barthius, however, interprets *liquidas umbras* as clear likenesses and expressions of truth. See hymn 9 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 93.

[Col. 0544C] 126. Mer. in another hand, Parrhasius, Rat. first hand, *tractim*: *tracti* is more correct.

127. It is established from Cyprian, Jerome, Augustine, Rufinus, Sulpicius, and others that all bishops were once called *popes*. Later the name came to be assigned more particularly to the Roman pontiff; nevertheless, in Venantius Fortunatus and Eulogius of Córdoba, who flourished in the ninth century, other bishops are still called popes. In 1073 Gregory VII decreed at a Roman synod that no one might call himself or another by the name “pope,” because it belonged properly to the Roman pontiff. Baronius discusses this name at length in his note on the Roman Martyrology for 10 January.

129. Some think that Prudentius’s account here should not be trusted, because the painter could have represented the story as he preferred. But who will believe, or be able to persuade others, that the history of a martyrdom which occurred after the middle of the third century was distorted into fables shortly afterward through the license of some uneducated painter, while the others looked on and remained silent?

[Col. 0544D] 130. Parrhasius, incorrectly, *et nimio rufficolam saniem*. Thuan., *e nimio russeolam*. Vat. P, *ex minio roseolam*. Mar. in the old hand, Rat., Prag., Bong., Vat. Q, Urb., *et nimio roseolam*. Fabr., *rosseolam*. Alex., Ald., Mar. in the corrector’s hand, Ald., Weitz., Gis., and most printed editions, *russeolam*. *Russeolus* comes from *russus*; Gifanius calls it an old and excellent word for “red.” Barthius, book XXXV of the *Adversaria*, chapter 13, insists that *roseolam* should be read, because Christian poets often use *roseus* with its first syllable long. But Prudentius always shortens *rosa* and *roseus*, deriving them from *rosa*.

133. *Caros* is used substantivally for “friends.” Lactantius uses it for “children” in book VI, chapter 12: “since he knows that he is leaving his dear ones to God.”

134. Ald., Alex., Vat. P, Urb., Egm., Alt., two Torrent manuscripts, *quo*. Several others, *qua*.

135. Two Torrent manuscripts, together with Cauchus, read *lacrymantibus*, not *rimantibus*. The chief concern of the ancient Christians was to search diligently for the limbs of the holy martyrs and to assemble and fit them together carefully and skillfully, as is plainly seen in these verses of Prudentius. Even today at Rome the bodies of the holy martyrs, once their bones have been collected, are properly fitted together by similar art and care so that they may be displayed for public veneration. Blanchinus, in the preface to *Anastasius Bibliothecarius*, no. 26, reports from the account of the priest in charge of the church of Saint Paulinus of Nola that the intact bones of Saint Justa the virgin were found there, deposited with the hands crossed. At Rome, however, the martyrs’ bodies that are discovered are usually arranged so that the arms and hands extend downward along the sides. It is therefore uncertain whether that priest reported a matter clearly known to him. I am more certain that the inscriptions of that church which Blanchinus presents were not transcribed with sufficient fidelity.]

“Where sound and fear, where frenzy, drive them on.”

Fierceness inflames them, impetuosity carries them away, and the crashing din drives them on:

nor does their swift course feel its shifting burden.

[115] Through forests and over rocks they rush; no riverbank delays them,

nor does an opposing torrent hold them back.

They overthrow hedges and shatter every obstacle;

they seek the steep and rugged places, and leap over the heights.

The rough field, bristling with thorn-bearing stalks, snatches up fragments

[120] 1175 torn bit by bit from the mangled body.

Some hang from the highest cliffs; some cling to the brambles;

[Col. 0543B] in one part the foliage is red, in another the ground is wet.

[Col. 0544A] A wall coated with plaster bears the likeness of the crime,

in which multicolored pigment sets out the whole horror.

[125] Above the tomb, a painted scene lives through fluid shadows:

the bloody limbs of the man being dragged are represented.

I saw the tips of the rocks dripping, most excellent pope,

and purple marks placed upon the brambles.

The skilled hand, imitating the green thickets,

[130] 1176 had played at producing a reddish gore from vermilion.

One could see the limbs lying scattered in disorder,

their joints broken, strewn in uncertain positions.

He had added those dear ones who followed with their steps and tears,

wherever the broken path showed the way.

[135] Struck dumb with grief, and searching with their eyes, they went on,

[Col. 0544B] and filled their laps with the mangled entrails.

[Col. 0545A] Note: [Col. 0545A]

137. “That one,” namely, the lap. “Reverend, venerable,” I.

138. “Fosters, nourishes, or protects,” I.

139. “This one,” the other, I.

140. “Gathers, collects,” I.

141. “Moisture-absorbing,” from *bibere*, “to drink”—“sands,” from their dryness, I.

[Col. 0545B] 142. “Stained, corrupted, filthy, mixed, intermingled”—“dew,” blood, I.

143. “Whoever,” someone—“stakes,” thorns, stakes, posts, I.

144. “All,” the blood, I.

[Col. 0546A] 145. “Body,” of Hippolytus, I.

146. “Defrauds the funeral rites,” so that the body would not be buried, I.

147. “Having been counted over,” numbered, discovered, I.

151. “By measuring, searching out, assigning,” I.—“Ostia,” the city, Mar. Tiberina; “gates, doors,” I.

152. “Is pleasing, is chosen,” I.

[Col. 0546B] 153. “Not far away, not distant from Rome.”—“Near the boundary wall,” close to the wall: here *pomoerium* means a garden; elsewhere, a secluded place enclosed by a wall. It is called *pomoerium* because it is beyond the wall, I.

[Col. 0545C]

137. The painting displayed—and Prudentius saw—a snow-white head and venerable gray hair. Who would attribute this to the soldier Hippolytus, whose nurse Concordia was crowned with martyrdom together with him? It is well known that military age was reckoned from the seventeenth to the forty-fifth or forty-sixth year, and only in dangerous times to the fiftieth. In the epithalamium for Julian, Bishop Memorius, Paulinus ascribes apostolic gray hair to a younger man’s breast:

> Born later, yet older; because, as a priest seated,  
> he bears apostolic gray hair upon his breast;

as though venerable, or apostolic, gray hair were proper to an older bishop.

138. *Rat.* has *molle*; correct to *molli*.

139. *Ulnae* are the elbows.

[Col. 0545D] 141. Barthius understands *palliola* to mean thin strips, made, as he thinks, of delicate linen.

142. Ald., the two Torr., Ox., Cauch., Gall., *in intecto*. Vat. B, Mar. in the first hand, Prag., Parrh., Rat. in the text, *in intacto*. Most have *in infecto*. Alex. has *res maneat*; above, *ros*. In some editions the reading is *in intacto*.

144. Pal. has *insidit*; read *insidet*. Prudentius offers this splendid testimony concerning the Christians’ care and diligence in collecting the martyrs’ blood; Boldettus discusses it at greater length in his *Observations on the Cemeteries*, as do Aringhus, Marangonus, Muratorius, Lupius, Fabrettus, and others. Several vessels still exist in which congealed blood can be seen, and fragments of the sponge with which it was collected are visible. Boldettus presents several such vessels.

146. Vat. A has *haut* for *aut*, owing to a different orthography. Prudentius often shows with what diligence the ancient Christians cared for the burial of the dead, moved by the considerations that he explains more fully in the hymn *On Funerals*. Indeed, that widely repeated saying of Lucan, “He is covered by the sky who has no urn,” seems to me no wiser than if someone consoled a naked man by saying, “He is covered by the sky who has no clothing.”

147. Ald., Urb. Parrhasius, Gis., *recensitis*. Weitz., Heins., with most manuscripts, *recensetis*. Marietti notes that *recenseo* produces *recensetus*, or *recensus*; *recensitus* is nothing. Others disagree.

148. The number signifies a finished work, complete in all its parts.

149. Parrhasius has *retinerent invia*. Most have *deberent avia* with the same meaning. Rat., Weitz., *invia* for *avia*.

151. Weitz. with Egm. has *eligitur*.

153. Egm., Hailsbr., *cultu*; read *culta*. Rat. has *pomaria* in the first hand, which one of the glosses supports. Bingham, book XXIII, chapter 1, volume X, endeavors to prove that during the first three centuries of the Church, under Roman law, no burial places existed in towns, and that for several subsequent centuries Christian emperors’ laws did not permit burial within cities and churches. If *pomeria* is read, it may be understood as identical with *pomaria*, that is, a place planted with fruit trees. Otherwise, *pomoeria* is a place beyond the walls, which in antiquity were called *moenia*, and many interpret *pomoeria* as “beyond the walls.” Thus the cemeteries, or catacombs, of the martyrs were outside the cities; yet that altars existed within the catacombs, beneath which the martyrs’ bodies rested, is sufficiently clear from this hymn.

As for what some say—that the martyrs were not buried in cemeteries, because these were really churches, but rather that the faithful gathered in cemeteries because they had been consecrated by the martyrs’ relics and were removed from human traffic—this does not weaken the truth of the matter: namely, that martyrs, and indeed others, were buried in cemetery churches during the first three centuries of the Church. From ancient custom, I think the practice became so common that, conversely, wherever the bodies of martyrs were present, sacred rites were celebrated there, and wherever an altar was erected for sacrifice, the bodies or relics of martyrs were placed beneath it.

Therefore, the prohibition against burying the dead in churches after the first three centuries did not arise because such burial conflicted with ecclesiastical custom, but because Roman laws prohibited burial places within the City, while churches were then being erected within the City. In certain places there were exceptions to those laws, either because of municipal statutes or on account of particular persons, namely nobles and bishops.

As for this description [Col. 0547B] of the crypt, Barthius declares it extremely elegant and worthy of any great poet, with rhythms exceptionally well suited to it. Baronius, under the year 226, lists about forty cemeteries of this kind in the suburbs of Rome. Many report that the Neapolitan catacombs are more distinguished and more spacious than the Roman ones. In the learned Mamachi, volume III of *Christian Origins*, and volume III of *The Customs of the Early Christians*, one may see a ground plan of one of the Roman cemeteries.

Jerome, on Ezekiel, chapter LX:

> When I was a boy in Rome and was being trained in the liberal arts, I used, with others of the same age and inclination, to visit the tombs of the apostles and martyrs on Sundays. I often entered the crypts, which, dug deep into the earth, have on both sides, along the walls of those entering, the bodies of the buried. Everything is so dark that the prophetic saying is almost fulfilled: “They descend alive into hell.” Rarely does light admitted from above temper the horror of the darkness, so that you would think it not a window but a hole through which a little light is let down. Again one advances gradually, and, surrounded by blind night, that line of Virgil is brought to mind: “Horror everywhere terrifies the minds, and the very silences themselves terrify.”

Concerning the Roman cemeteries, besides Aringhus, Boldettus, and others, one may consult Marianus Parthenius—or, under his true name, Joseph Mazzolarius—in the pious little works he composed shortly before his death.

That one embraces the snow-white head and tenderly fosters the venerable

1177 gray hair in his lap.

This one gathers the shoulders, the severed hands, the arms and elbows,

[140] the knees, and the bare fragments of the legs.

With little cloths they also dry the moisture-absorbing sands,

so that no drop may remain in the stained dust.

If any blood, with its spray still warm, clings to the stakes,

the pressed sponge carries all of it away.

[145] [Col. 0546A] Now the dense thicket no longer holds anything of the sacred body,

nor does it defraud the full performance of the funeral rites.

And when, after the parts had been counted, it was clear

what number had belonged to the intact body,

and no part of the whole man remained in the unsearched places,

[150] 1178 once the leaves and rocks had been wiped clean,

the place for the tomb is chosen by measurement; they leave Ostia;

Rome is pleasing, the city that will hold the sacred ashes.

[Col. 0547A] Note: [Col. 0547A]

155. “Of this one,” the crypt, I.

156. “Winding passages,” spiral stairways, I.

157. “As far as the top,” from the top.—“Enters,” light.—“Opening,” aperture, I.

158. “Thresholds of the vestibule,” the entrance to the portico or crypt, I.

[Col. 0547B] 159. “Then, thereafter.”—“Where,” namely, where one proceeds, I.

160. “Dark night,” darkness, I.

[Col. 0548A] 163. “However many,” however numerous.—“Uncertain,” doubtful, I.

166. “Frequent,” numerous.—“The pierced vault,” the perforated crypt, I.

167. “Thus it is granted,” it is permitted in this way; and it is praise of the painting, I.

169. “Is entrusted, is commended”—“Covered, hidden,” enclosed, I.

170. “Beside,” next to that place, I.

[Col. 0547C]

154. Ald., Parrhasius, and most manuscripts have *patet*, which Heinsius rightly judges correct, since *luce latente* follows immediately. Below: *ampla, fauce licet pateat*. Rott. is not bad: *cavernosis crypta patet foveis*. Gis. has *latet*; in the margin, *patet*. Egm. has *pavet*. Bong. has *fovet*, less correctly.

Pinius, in the *Acts of the Saints* for 15 August, conjectures that the cemetery of St. Hippolytus existed in the region of the Tiber, not in the Veran field, as most believe. He bases this on verse 174, “It also feeds the Tiber-dwellers with sacred banquets.” The basis for the conjecture is certainly weak. Yet since he himself places the cemetery of the soldier Hippolytus near St. Lawrence in the Veran field, the falsity of the matter cannot be demonstrated. For although what Prudentius says—“Cultivated near the boundary walls” and “the hollow entrails of the excavated mountain beneath”—fits a cemetery in the Veran field more appropriately, it can nevertheless in some fashion also be applied to a cemetery on the Ostian Way, if the Hippolytus praised by Prudentius was buried there.

Aringhus, volume II, explains Prudentius as referring to the cemetery of Cyriaca in the Veran field. Baronius, volume II of the *Annals*, under the year 226, had held the same opinion. Fabricius, under the word *cryptae*, cites a letter of Pope Cornelius, who lived under Decius, to Lupicinus of Vienne, where he says: “Therefore Christians are permitted to celebrate Mass neither publicly nor in the more famous crypts.” This letter is spurious.

155. Mar. has *cujus*; a corrector changed it to *hujus*. Prag. has *hujus ad occultum*.

156. Iso explains *anfractus* as spiral passages, and Teolius elaborates this as winding stairways, so called because they curve like a snail shell. But *anfractus*, that is, bends, circuits, and windings, can also be understood without stairs.

157. Prag. has: “For it enters the first doors from the lowest point right up to the top, and illuminates…”—which I do not understand.

161. Ald., Vat. B, and Widm. in the first hand have *decurrunt* for *occurrunt*. Ald., Rat., Pal., Bong., Torn., the manuscript of St. Michael cited by Ruinart, and some editions have *celsis*; Mar. has *caecis*, above *caesis*, which appears in most copies. Heinsius had conjectured *caecis*, but admitted that *caesis* is correct. Ald., Pal., and Torn. in the text have *immensa*; others, *immissa*. Parrhasius: “The openings let down from the lofty roofs descend.”

162. Pal., Bong., Vat. A, Thuan., Alt., Noms., Cauch., and Ox. have *jactant*. Heinsius adopted *jaciant*, and later editors followed him; but Gallandius, with others and the old editions, retained *jaciunt*. In the crypts there were places illuminated by greater light admitted from above. The *Book of the Pontiffs* says: “The priest Marcellus collected by night the bodies [of Saints Marcellinus the pope and the others] … and buried them on the Salarian Way in the cemetery of Priscilla, in a bright chamber that remains open to this day … in the crypt beside the body of St. Crescention.”

163. Parrh. has *ancipitis*; read *ancipites*.

165. Mar. and Parrhasius have *cava subter viscera*. Virgil, *Aeneid* III: “At times rocks and the torn entrails of the mountain.”

167. Mar. has *subter terranea*; Rat. likewise, though something before *subter* has been erased. Most have *per subterranea*. The latter part of the gloss seems to have been transferred here from the preceding verses, where the painting is described.

169. *Operta* means dark places. *Psychomachia*, verse 745: “Let the inhabitant, snoring in the dark retreat, wither.” Paulinus, fragment of an uncertain *Natalicium*: “Where he was mortal, he lay hidden in the earth’s retreat.” *Operta* can also be understood as referring to mysteries. Gretzerus, book II, chapter 18 of *On the Sacraments of Pilgrimage*, confirms his argument with these verses: “Here,” he says, “the most learned poet Prudentius speaks most beautifully.”

170. On the ancient custom of constructing altars over the tombs of martyrs, see the hymn to St. Eulalia at the end. Some, distinguishing an altar from an *ara*, say that the saints’ bodies were deposited beneath the altar, but at or near the *ara*, not beneath the *ara* itself; and they praise this verse of Prudentius, where the *ara* is said to have been placed beside the body of Blessed Hippolytus, not imposed upon it.

Berthaldus, in chapter 2 of *On the Altar*, says that this matter has exercised and perplexed many minds. Some understand *ara* as the upper part of the altar, others as its lower part, almost the foundation and base of the entire structure, and others as the place dedicated to offerings, whether it was at the top of the building or elsewhere. This last opinion seems more probable to me than the others, especially because our way of speaking could easily have arisen from ancient custom.

Rosweydus, in the additions to his notes on St. Paulinus, nevertheless states from these verses that altars were customarily imposed upon or placed beside the bodies of holy martyrs. St. Paulinus, in Letter 12 to Severus, clearly teaches that the body of Clarus was placed beneath an altar:

> Worthily the chaste altars of Christ veil you,  
> so that the altar of God may cover the temple of Christ.

In volume XXXIV of *Hispania Sacra*, page 445, an instrument of Fruminus II, bishop of León, is transcribed; concerning St. Christopher it says: “Whose relics have been deposited in the city of León beside the bishop’s gate, beneath the altar of St. Cyprian and St. Mary, before the altars of the ancient see.”

Not far from the cultivated area by the boundary wall,

1179 the crypt, sunk deep among hidden hollows, lies open.

[155] Its downward path, turned back through winding steps,
teaches one to go by winding passages into its hidden interior, with the light concealed.

For daylight enters the first doorways from above through an opening,

and illuminates the thresholds of the vestibule.

Then, when the dark night of the place seems to grow blacker

[160] as one proceeds easily through the ambiguous cave,

openings cut into the roofs appear,

which cast bright rays over the chambers.

[Col. 0548A] Though narrow courts beneath shadowy partitions weave

however many perplexing recesses here and there,

[165] nevertheless abundant light penetrates the hollow entrails

of the excavated mountain through the pierced vault.

Thus, through the underground passages, one is permitted

to see the radiance of the absent sun and enjoy its light.

To such hidden places the body of Hippolytus is entrusted,

[170] beside which an altar dedicated to God has been placed.

[Col. 0549A] Note: [Col. 0549A]

171. “Of the sacrament,” of the Lord’s body or blood.—“Giver,” namely, it is, I.

[Col. 0549B] 174. “Tiber-dwellers,” Romans, I., Mar.

176. “Hopes,” expectations.—“Helps,” assists, I.

177. “Corruptions,” diseases, I.

178. “Aid,” assistance, I.

179. “Return,” reversal, I.

182. “Whoever,” someone.—“To assent,” to help, bestow, grant, I.

183. “Remains,” he speaks of the body, I.

[Col. 0550A] 184. “Flashes,” shines, I.

185. “Rich,” learned: “of the craftsman.”—“Surface,” level ground; every evenness is called a surface.—“Smooth,” level, I.

187. “Parian,” white. Paros is an island rich in white marble.—“Content,” sufficient.—“Entrance,” to cover the doors, I.

188. “For adorning,” for the purpose of adorning, I.

189. “To be greeted,” for greeting, that is, worshipping; for salvation.—“Worships,” the martyr himself, I.

191. “Latins,” Latins or Romans, I.

[Col. 0549C]

171. Oxon., in a variant reading, has *illa dicamenti*; likewise *mensa sub antro*. Egm. has *mens eademque*; *mensa* should be retained. Cauchius more aptly conjectured *mensa Petri* for *mensque Petri*, as in the same Paulinus shortly afterward: “the table and house of God.” Even pagans used *mensa* for an altar, as Ovid, Virgil, and many others did. Similarly, among Christian Greeks, τραπέζα (*trapeza*, “table”) means an altar.

172. The table is called the martyr’s guardian because it preserves his bones and so forth. In ancient monuments the guardians of martyrs are also called *martyrarii* or *cubicularii*. The martyrs’ tombs themselves were customarily called chambers; hence arose the name *cubicularii*, who guarded the chambers of the martyrs sleeping in the Lord. See the commentary on hymn 10, *Cathemerinon*, verse 56.

Juvenal speaks of the *cubicularii* in satire 5: “But who will guard the guards themselves?” Ovidius uses the verb “to guard” in book II of the *Amores*, elegy 2: “With whom lies the task of guarding the mistress, Bagoe”; and in elegy 3: “Alas for me, that neither man nor woman guards the mistress.”

173. Alex., Urb., Pal., Ald., Vat. P, Oxon., Cauch., and Alt. have *spem vindicis*. Others have *spem judicis*, as do most editions.

177. Vat. A has *corruptibilis*; above, *corruptelis* instead of the reading in the margin.

178. The custom of praying at the tombs of martyrs is again confirmed. See Dungal’s book against Claudius of Turin. Cellarius says most impudently: “The poet follows his own custom or error concerning invocation.” The poet describes both his own custom and that of the Catholic Church, which prevailed in his time.

184. Mar. and Prag. have *et* for *ex*. Martinus Roa, in *On Sacred and Profane Birthdays*, chapter 21, understands “the shrine flashes with solid silver” to refer to the disks or squares in which inscriptions or curtains decorated with images of saints are enclosed, together with the wreaths of branches and foliage displayed before church doors at the principal festivals in Rome, and called festoons; one can now see little plates of gilded brass flashing there.

I rather understand it as solid silver with which the altar was adorned, or from which even the burial chest was made. The tablets and talents that the poet goes on to mention suggest this. Likewise verse 193: “I see kisses impressed upon the metal.”

[Col. 0550C] 185. Barthius says that *tabulae*, in rustic writers, means level surfaces, as in this verse of Prudentius. I understand *tabulae*, or silver plates, polished with a smooth surface. Properly, a surface is where everything is even and flat, as Becmanus confirms with Cicero’s words in book II of the *Academic Questions*: “What is as flat as the sea, from which poets also call that surface an *aequor*?” Lucretius, book IV: “They return the image from the surface of mirrors.” Prudentius alludes to this. See verse 53 of the hymn to St. Cassian.

Teolius noted Muratorius’ error. In Paulinus, verse 557, “And thinking himself concealed, he stood out in the clear surface,” Muratorius said that the copyist’s error should be corrected to *aethere* or *aere claro*. Paulinus understood an open level space.

186. Macer, in his *Hierolexicon*, explains *recavum* here as embossed or engraved, and thinks that the Italian word *ricamo* is derived from it, meaning needlework raised above its background; this explanation is entirely absurd. Prudentius calls a mirror *recavum*, just as he calls the palate *recavum* in *Psychomachia*, verse 422. Covarruvias thinks that Spanish *recamo* comes from the Hebrew word *rāqam*.

[Col. 0550D] 188. *Talentum* is used for the silver material itself from which a talent is made.

189. The ancients customarily addressed the gods by greeting them, as is evident throughout many ancient writers. Martial, book XII, epigram 78: “While he greets Jupiter with many prayers.” Such a greeting was properly performed in the morning hours; the word derives from the Roman custom of greeting one’s patrons. Martial, book II, epigram 18: “I come to greet you in the morning.” So too Virgil, whom we shall soon cite. See Matthaeus Broverius, *On Ancient and Recent Forms of Adoration*, chapters 6 and 9, where he offers many testimonies from the ancients.

190. Parrhasius has *puppis*, erroneously, for *pubis* or *pubes*. Heinsius prefers *pubis*, with Thuan., Ald., Egm., and Pal., as *vulpis* and *gruis* are written in the oldest copies of Phaedrus. Many, including ancient witnesses, write *pubes*, as Mar., Prag., and Vat. B. In the two Torr. manuscripts, *plebis*. Widm. does not properly distinguish *omnis adorat*: “The youth go.”

That table, giver of the sacrament, and likewise

the faithful guardian placed beside its martyr,

preserves the bones in the tomb for the hope of the eternal judge,

and also feeds the Tiber-dwellers with sacred banquets.

[175] The marvelous sanctity of the place, and the altar readily available to those who pray,

helps the hopes of humankind with peaceful prosperity.

Here, sick with ailments of mind and body,

whenever I lay prostrate in prayer, I obtained help.

That I rejoice in my return, that it was permitted me
[180] to embrace you, venerable priest—these very things I write.

I know that I owe it to Hippolytus: Christ, God, has granted him
[Col. 0550A] the power to grant whatever anyone asks.

The shrine itself, which contains within it those bodily remains,

flashes with solid silver.

[185] 1182 A wealthy hand affixed polished tablets,

white, with a smooth surface like a gleaming hollow mirror.

Nor content merely to cover the entrances with Parian stone,

it added shining talents to adorn the work.

In the morning people gather to offer greeting; everyone worships,

[190] the youth; they go and return until the sun sets.

The love of religion gathers Romans and foreigners alike,
mixed together, into a wedge-shaped crowd.

[Col. 0551A] Note: [Col. 0551A]

193. “Clear,” bright, shining, I.

198. “Celebrating,” for celebrating, I.

199. “Augusta,” Rome, noble.—“Quirites,” Romans.—“Roman princes,” I.

200. “Ambition,” desire.—“Longing,” Mar.

201. “Plebeian,” rustic, common; the army, the plebeian soldiers.—“Bosses,” shoulders, I.

[Col. 0552A] 202. “Distinction,” discrimination.—“Rushing forward,” urging, driving, impelling toward this, I.

206. “Picenian,” a gentile name, like Roman, from the city of Picenum.—“Etruscan,” Italian, I.

207. “Samnite,” a citizen from the province of Samnium, I.

208. “Nolan,” from the city of Nola, I.

[Col. 0551B]

193. Barthius asks why Prudentius said “clear metal,” when above he said “solid silver,” since silver cannot be drawn into transparent plates, any more than ivory, as Macrobius records in *The Dream of Scipio*. The answer is easy and direct. The silver tablets were so highly polished that they shone with a smooth surface, like the gleam of a hollow mirror. This is what “clear metal” means: bright, and such that a person could see himself in it as in a mirror. For *perspicuus* is used not only of what is transparent, but also of what is bright and shining, as the glosses explain.

194. Alt. has *balsama desudant*. Heins., with others, writes *defundunt*. Likewise Alex. in the first hand has *diffundunt* above, a reading found in many copies. Weitzius has *difundunt*. It was then customary to bring perfumes to the tombs of martyrs. St. Gregory, writing to Secundinus in the second indiction, book VII, letter 54, says: “We have sent, through the bearer of this letter, aloe, incense, storax, and balsam to be offered to the bodies of the holy martyrs.” See the commentary on verse 519 of the hymn to St. Vincent.

195. Prag. has *nam cum se*. Parrhasius separates the words, and in corrected copies has *divisis* for *decursis*, less suitably.

196. It is a universally known fact that, in ecclesiastical usage, the day on which the holy martyrs were crowned with martyrdom is called their birthday. See Martinus Roa, *On Sacred and Profane Birthdays*. Emperors celebrated the beginning, or birthday, of their reign.

Many bishops used to gather to celebrate the birthday of the Roman pontiff’s cathedra, or episcopate, as is clear from a letter of Pope Sixtus to Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, during the consulship of Theodosius XIII and Maximus, as it is read in the acts of the Council of Ephesus; but Theodosius XIV, namely the year 433, should apparently be read, as is also clear from another letter of the same Sixtus to John, bishop of Antioch.

Pope Hilary, in a letter to the bishops of the province of Tarragona, says: “Having therefore read your letters in the assembly of the brethren whom the celebration of my birthday had gathered.”

Anastasius the Librarian, in the *Life of Hadrian I*, says: “Finally, his blessedness also made the great lamp in the same church of Blessed Peter, in the form of a cross, which hangs before the presbytery and has one thousand three hundred and seventy candles. And he decreed that this great lamp should be lit four times a year: namely, at the Nativity of the Lord, at Easter, on the birthday of the Apostles, and on the birthday of the Pontiff.”

Traces of such lamps in the form of a cross remain in the cross displayed in the Vatican basilica of St. Peter, adorned with numerous burning lamps on the night of the fifth day of Holy Week. Other private bishops also celebrated the birthday of their episcopate; on this subject Bingham may be consulted, book IV, chapter 6, volume II, page 188.

199. Parrhasius has *urbs angusta*; read *Augusta*. This title is given to Rome in the Theodosian Code, and likewise in Paulinus, Apollonius, Ammianus, and others. *Vomere* means “to pour out in great abundance.” Virgil, *Georgics* II, verse 462: “In the morning a flood of clients pours out from the entire house.”

[Col. 0552B] 201. You see Ison’s gloss; accept Barthius’ explanation: “with equal attire, with equal haste.” The nobles had clothing by which they could be distinguished, but all the clothing was then regarded as equal because of the excessive haste. Papinius says the same in *Violantilla*: “Every purple-bordered robe is worn amid plebeian tumult.” Cellarius adds: “In the zeal of piety and the haste of devotion, nobles and commoners went out without adornment.”

Chamillardus thinks that the equal bosses were clean, white shields, since nobles displayed on their shields the emblems of their families or their deeds. This seems to me to be Prudentius’ meaning. Just as the Quirites poured out of the City, and patricians hurried with equal eagerness, so the plebeians, equally armed with faith, rushed forward, and in this respect there was no distinction. The poet says “with equal bosses” for “with equal arms” allegorically, because he had spoken of armies and a plebeian phalanx, and soon afterward of a battle line.

[Col. 0552C] 203. Fabricius first explains this as the Alban Gate of Rome, now the Esquiline Gate, commonly called Taurina, which Procopius called Praenestina and the most ancient writers called Metia. Yet he prefers to understand it as the gates leading to Rome from the town of Alba. This is indeed how it should be understood.

Old Alba, or Alba Longa, was destroyed in the eighty-sixth year of the City. Toward the end of the fourth century, another town began to flourish under the old name of Alba, not far from the site, where Albanum now stands. The Appian Way, called the queen of roads, passed through this town; hence the Appian, or Alban, gates are mentioned first by Prudentius.

In Rome, in 1787, there appeared *Historical Memoirs of Alba Longa and Modern Albano*, by Giovanni Antonio Riccy. “White battle line” means those adorned with a fresh toga. See the commentary on verse 547 of book I against Symmachus, “In a whiter toga.” Just as we call unfortunate and mournful things black, so we call joyful, auspicious, and festive things white. Horace, *Odes* III.7, called the west winds white because, especially at Rome, this is the most joyful and gentle of winds. Virgil, *Eclogues* 5: “The shining Olympian threshold marvels at what is unfamiliar.”

204. Prag. has, incorrectly, *longis dulciter*. Egm. and Hailsbr. have *dicitur*, no better.

206. Parrhasius printed *Peligna* and *Picens*, not badly.

207. Most punctuate it thus: “The fierce Samnite inhabitant rushes forward, and the inhabitant of lofty…” Cellarius and Teolius say that *Samnitis* should be understood as a land or region in the possessive case. Parrhasius rightly punctuates: “The fierce Samnite rushes forward, and the inhabitant of lofty Campanian Capua.” *Samnitis* is in the nominative case, as in book II against Symmachus, verse 515, “the Samnite and the Marsian,” and in Cato, quoted by Priscian, book VII: “Gallic, Samnite, Apulian, Bruttian land.” Most pronounce it *Samnis*. They are called fierce because they were extremely warlike, or because they were so devoted to gladiatorial combat that their name came to be used for gladiators themselves. See Cicero’s speech for Sextius.

208. The first syllable in *Nolanus* is usually long; here it is shortened, something not noted in the indices of Chamillardus, Cellarius, and Teolius. Parrhasius reports that some, confusing the order of the places, write *janicolanus* for *jamque Nolanus*. Cauchius favored *jamque bolanus*.

1183 They imprint kisses upon the shining metal;

they pour out balsams and moisten their faces with tears.

[195] Now, when the year renews itself after the months have run their course,

and the festal day recalls the birthday of the martyr,

what great crowds, do you think, are gathered in emulous devotion,

and what vows assemble in celebrating God?

Rome, the Augusta, pours forth and disgorges her Quirites;

[200] 1184 the plebeian phalanx, with eagerness equal to that of the patricians,

effaces, with equal shields, the distinction of the nobles,

faith driving them onward.

No less from the Alban gates the white battle line unfolds

and stretches out in long ranks.

[205] The clamors of the various roads exult here and there;

the native, the Picenian, the plebeian, and the Etruscan come.

The fierce Samnite rushes forward, and the inhabitant

1185 of lofty Campanian Capua; now the Nolan is present.

210. “With pledges,” this is the distinction: pledges of things, pledges of children.—“Exults,” rejoices, desires, I.

[Col. 0553B] 216. “Noble,” royal, I.

217. “Proud,” noble, I.

218. “Rich,” wealthy, for *opulentum*, I.

220. “Gilded,” painted with gold, I.

221. “Shorter,” tighter, I.

[Col. 0554A] 224. “With a higher summit,” with greater height, I.

226. “Is raised,” is elevated, I.

[Col. 0554B] 227. “With difficulty,” scarcely.—“Waves,” crowds, throngs of peoples, I.

228. “Crowded,” full, I.

229. “Fosterlings,” children, I.

[Col. 0553B]

212. An excellent expression for signifying an immense multitude of people.

214. Prag. always writes *haut*.

215. Many confidently maintain that this church was consecrated to the same St. Hippolytus. But Ruggerius, in the place cited, number 18, thinks, with others, that in these verses Prudentius described the basilica of St. Lawrence in the Veran field, which truly stood beside the cemetery and shrine of St. Hippolytus and which Prudentius’ description suits very well. Anastasius the Librarian, concerning Hadrian I, says: “At the same time he restored the cemetery of Blessed Hippolytus the martyr beside St. Lawrence, which had fallen into decay from ancient times.” See Aringhus, book IV, chapter 16, where he discusses the church of St. Lawrence.

220. Parrhasius has, incorrectly, *suppositas*. The ancients gilded the beams of buildings. Concerning Christian churches, compare the following hymn and the hymn to St. Fructuosus.

221. This form of building can still be seen in very ancient churches.

222. Teolius found *extenuent* in one manuscript of Vat. and another manuscript, instead of *exsinuent*. Teolius thinks *extenuent* is a gloss on the verb *exsinuent*. Giselinus, however, explains *exsinuent* differently: “Let them spread out in the manner of folds or flaps, and extend more broadly.” Giselinus adds that our churches today are built in no other way.

In two manuscripts he also found the equally novel word *eximient*, leaving the choice to the reader. Fabricius reads *exinient*, and in his commentary says that *exinire* means to contract into a smaller space, as happens in rows of columns, when broad porticoes first become narrower. But the sound reading is *exsinuent*. Ausonius uses the verb in *Idyll* 14, verse 29: “And she spread out the gathered folds of her garment”; and Paulinus, Letter 36 to Macarius, elsewhere numbered 49: “When he saw the veil already spread out,” that is, expanded, or released and unfolded from its fold. This is what Prudentius means.

225. Barthius declares this description of the cathedra to be exceedingly elegant. In Book XXXII, chapter 2, he likewise infers from these verses that, in the center of sacred buildings, there were cathedrae from which priests proclaimed the mysteries. Dominicus Aulisius, in Book II, chapter 6 of *On the Sacred Schools*, argues from verses of Sidonius addressed to Bishop Faustus that a different practice prevailed in Gaul from that which Prudentius describes:

“Whether, upon the conspicuous steps of the venerable altar, you are about to preach, the attentive people gathers round.”

Sirmondus, in his note on Sidonius, page 151, recognizes no distinction: “For there,” he says, “they were accustomed to preach while seated in the tribunal-seat”; and he cites these very words of Prudentius. Sirmondus evidently distinguishes the tribunal, or cathedra, standing on the altar-steps within the chancel, from the ambo, to which Chrysostom ascended so that he might be heard by more people, as Socrates and others relate as a special practice.

Sozomen, Book VII, chapter 19, reports that in his own time no one in Rome addressed the people in church: “In that city neither the bishop nor anyone else teaches the people in church.” Valesius agrees with Sozomen in his notes, especially because Cassiodorus repeats Sozomen’s words. Yet Cassiodorus transcribed Sozomen at a time when it is universally acknowledged that the Roman pontiffs were accustomed to deliver homilies to the people. Cassiodorus’s testimony therefore gives Sozomen little or no support.

Whatever may be said about the time of Sozomen, complete credence must be given to Prudentius as an eyewitness. The lofty tribunal upon steps was not the steps of the altar themselves, as some maintain, but a pulpit, or even the episcopal cathedra itself. The Greeks likewise preached within the chancel, by which the sanctuary was separated from the nave, which they called the ναός (“temple”). The ambo, however, was situated not in the sanctuary but in the nave of the church; bishops sometimes mounted it so that they could be heard more easily by everyone. In the more sacred part of the bema, or sanctuary, or in the presbytery, a cathedra, or throne and episcopal seat, was erected within the chancel; beside it, the presbyters sat on lower benches on either side.

Although the entire sanctuary, since one ascended into it by steps, could be called—and sometimes was called—the bema or tribunal, nevertheless the “lofty tribunal upon steps” of which Prudentius speaks denotes the episcopal seat in virtue of its particular and expressly stated function of preaching about God.

The sanctuary of this church seems indeed to have been located not in this magnificent temple but in the small building described above, where, evidently, stood the table that dispensed the sacrament. Yet it must be observed that one must not immediately infer from the practice of one church or another that the same custom prevailed in all churches. Those who explain ecclesiastical antiquities are often deceived, or deceive others, in this matter: they simply assert that something was practiced in the Church in ancient times which perhaps existed in only one or a few churches, although it is not even established that such a custom prevailed throughout the whole period.

228. Vaticanus B has *consertis*; read *confertis*. Compare Lucretius, Book VI:

“All places and roofs they filled, and the more the heat,  
The more in crowded heaps death piled them together.”

Barthius, Book I, chapter 9, correctly observes that the manuscripts read *aestu*, from which Lambinus altered it to *aestus* against the Muses’ will. Others in the same passage of Lucretius read *confectos* instead of *confertos*.

229. Parrhasius: *condit*.

> Children, eagerly hastens to make the swift journey.
>

> Their joy, and a dense crowd clings to the great spaces.
>

> For such throngs, however widely its mouth may gape.

>

>

230. *Fetos*, “filled,” “stuffed,” I.

235. *Crede*, namely, “believe me,” I.

236. *Lucis*, “of the day,” I.—“Of the celebrated festive day,” Mar.

241. *Sic tibi*, “with this wish for you,” I.

244. *Sedulus*, “zealous,” “devoted,” I.

245. *Lacteolis*, “white as milk.”—*Compleveris*, instead of *compleas*, I.

[Col. 0556B] 1. *Coeunt*, namely, “what do they come together for?” I.

2. *Ovantque*, “they rejoice”; for the word derives from the triumphal celebrations in which a white sheep was sacrificed, I.

3. *Festus*, as though answering a question, I.

5. *Innovatus*, “renewed”: more truthful accounts hold that the two princes of the apostles suffered not after a year had elapsed between them, but absolutely on one and the same day, Prag.

[Note: [Col. 0555B]]

230. Gis. in the margin has *fetos accumulata suos*, together with Vaticanus A, in a second hand. In Mar., Urb., Prag., and Vaticanus B, in the first hand, there is *fetus*. Alex. has *fetas*; above, *fetos*.

231. When Prudentius says, “If I remember correctly,” he does not express doubt, but speaks deliberately and affirms cautiously. Thus, in verse 1 of the preface to the poems:

“Ten times five years, if I am not mistaken, we have passed.”

Cicero, in *Against Fonteius*, says:

“Whoever considers that first, most deliberate word of our customary speech, *I think*, which we use even when, under oath, we state what we have learned and what we ourselves have seen, has removed it from his entire testimony and claimed to know everything.”

Some think that the Hippolytus whom Prudentius says is celebrated on the Ides of August was only Hippolytus the soldier. But since Prudentius most certainly speaks of another Hippolytus elsewhere, it must be judged that the feast day of this Hippolytus, whom Prudentius praises, formerly fell on the Ides of August.

232. Rat. correctly has *ipsa* instead of *ipse*. Ald., incorrectly, places a full stop after *vocat*.

235. Gis. in the margin has *annos* instead of *ortus*.

236. “The rewards of the celebrated feast day” seem to be life-giving births, or years. Barthius adds “rewards from heaven”; I do not object.

237. Alex., Ald., Chelidoni. Vaticanus B, Mar., *Celedoni*. Parrhasius, corruptly, *Celeboni*. It should be noted that the feast day of Saint Cyprian was already being celebrated in Spain at that time.

239. Ald. has *tradita vita est*. Teolius attributes to one Vaticanus the gloss: “It belongs to the one who helps, that is, if you do this, Christ will then hear you.” I have no doubt that the reading should be *adjurantis est*, “it belongs to the one who adjures.”

[Col. 0555D] 242. Barthius thinks *rapta* should be written instead of *capta*. But the parchment manuscripts consistently have *capta*, and shortly afterward *raptus* occurs. Nor is *capta* inappropriate, as in “captured in war,” “captured by tricks,” or fish caught by spear or hook. Torn. has *captum*, incorrectly.

245. Compare *Psychomachia*, verse 792: “Pretending to be a milk-white sheep.” See the commentary on verse 165 of the hymn to Saint Eulalia. Sheepfolds are called *caulae*, from the Greek word with the *c* removed; for the Greeks say αὔλας (*aulas*). Perhaps Paulinus had this etymology in mind in *On the Return of Nicetas*:

> Now, made sheep under your leadership,  
> They flock into the court of Peace.

246. This seems to me a strong conjecture, supporting the belief that Hippolytus was a bishop: namely, that Valerianus, the priest of Christ, was destined to be the companion of holy Hippolytus in heaven by reason, as I think, of the priesthood or episcopate. *Raptus*, “snatched away,” is a term of sacred Scripture for one who is rescued from the dangers of this world and carried into heaven.

After this hymn, Vaticanus B and Mar. place the passion of Saint Cyprian. I have copied the title from Mar. and Rat. In Vaticanus A and Weitz., it is *The Passion of the Apostles Peter and Paul*. Ald. and Heins. add “of the blessed apostles.” In Mar. and Vaticanus B, this passion follows the passion of Saint Cyprian, as in Weitz.

1. Heinsius conjectured: “Why do they hurry throughout Rome, and rejoice?” Cellarius followed this conjecture, which I also find attractive, although the manuscript reading proceeds correctly and is not without elegance. In former times many people came from every direction to celebrate the feast of the apostles, including bishops. See Paulinus, Letter 13 to Severus, and Letter 16 to Delphinus.

2. The etymology of the verb *ovare*, indicated by the gloss, is confirmed by Servius and Plutarch. Others, with Festus, derive *ovare* from the shout uttered by victors, with the letter *o* doubled; others derive it from *evoe*, the cry of the Bacchants. See Beckmann, *On Origins*.

5. This was the opinion of Prudentius and others: that Saints Peter and Paul suffered martyrdom on the same day of the year, but not in the same year. Prudentius explains this opinion more clearly in verse 21, “When the rounded course of the world …” John M. of Brisighella, in the *Index of Forbidden Books*, which I cited at number 184 in the notes to the prolegomena, attacks this opinion with a censure because it is contrary to the more common view, although he admits that Augustine and Arator defended it. See pages 257 and 262 of his *Index*.

The most eminent Cardinal Stephen Borgia, in his celebrated work *The Vatican Confession of Blessed Peter*, supplies much material by which other ecclesiastical antiquities may be illuminated and almost the whole of this hymn of Prudentius more easily understood. He reopens this very question for examination and admits that Saint Augustine held the same view as Prudentius, in Sermon 295, “On the Birthday of the Apostles Peter and Paul,” and in Sermon 381, “On the Same Birthday,” where he says: “Therefore Paul suffered on Peter’s birthday.”

He found no other ancient Latin writer who asserted the same opinion, except the subdeacon Arator, who flourished in the sixth century and sang as follows in Book II of *The History of the Apostles*:

> The twins whom he brought forth to the stars,  
> Not on the same day, yet on one day,  
> The repeated light of martyrdom consecrated  
> After the year had completed its course.

Among the Greeks, Photius, in *Bibliotheca*, codex 276, cites a passage from Saint Nilus, a disciple of Saint John Chrysostom, in which it is affirmed that Peter died before Paul.

[Col. 0557A] Metaphrastes reports that Justin Martyr and Irenaeus recorded that Paul was crowned with martyrdom five years after Peter. Colomesius and Junius approve this in their notes on the First Letter of Saint Clement to the Corinthians.

Rupert of Deutz, who died in 1124 under Lothair III, writes as follows in Book VI, chapter 10 of *On the Works of the Holy Spirit*:

“It is believed that both—Saints Peter and Paul—glorified heaven by their illustrious martyrdom in one and the same year, on one and the same day; nevertheless, some maintain that they completed their martyrdom on the same day but not in the same year. Hence the same writer says above: ‘One day for both, and so forth.’”

[Col. 0557B] Great weight was added to the more common opinion that the holy apostles suffered martyrdom in the same year and on the same day by the famous decree of Gelasius I on apocryphal books, issued at the Roman council of 494. Chamillardus falsely said that this council was held under Damasus; I think he intended to say under Gelasius:

“To him was also joined the most blessed apostle Paul, the chosen vessel, who, contrary to what heretics—or heresy—babble, was not crowned with Peter at a different time but, struggling under Caesar Nero, received a glorious death at one time and on one and the same day with Peter in the city of Rome.”

Nevertheless, in 544 Arator, subdeacon of the Roman Church, expressed the same opinion, as we have seen. All the learned and most scholarly men urged Pope Vigilius to order that his poems be publicly recited, and in fact they were recited with the greatest applause in the church of Saint Peter at the Chains.

While Arator himself was reciting, the two books were heard on separate days seven times, since only half of a book was read at a time because of the frequent repetitions which the audience repeatedly requested with great enthusiasm. See Labbe, vol. I of *The Library of Manuscripts*, page 668.

[Col. 0557C] Thus Prudentius’s opinion was not as poorly regarded at Rome at that time as it might seem if Gelasius’s decree alone were considered. Saint Gregory of Tours also contributes the following in Book I, chapter 29 of *The Glory of the Martyrs*:

“But the apostle Paul, after the year had completed its circuit, was struck down by the sword and died at Rome on the very day on which the apostle Peter had suffered.”

Ruinart, in his notes, says that the words “after the year had completed its circuit” are absent from one manuscript. Although that reading seems more consistent with the truth, he is nevertheless uncertain whether it is more genuine.

## XII. HYMN. HERE BEGINS THE PASSION OF THE APOSTLES PETER AND PAUL

> More people than usual come together for joy. Tell me, friend, what is happening.
>
> [1189] They hurry throughout Rome and rejoice.
>
> This festive day of the apostles’ triumph returns for us,  
> Noble through the blood of Paul and Peter.
>
> [5] One day for both, though renewed after a full year,
>
> [Col. 0557A] [Note: [Col. 0557A]]

6. *Superba*, “noble.”—*Laureatum*, “crowned,” I.

9. *Crucis et gladii*, “of the cross and the sword,” namely, of Peter and Paul.—*Testis*, “witness,” Tiberis.—*Quibus*, “by which,” namely, by those trophies, I.

[Note: [Col. 0557C]]

6. Prag. has *mente*; read *morte*. Paschalius, in Book VIII, chapter 10 of *On Crowns*, proves that *laureatum* signifies “victorious” and is sometimes used for “triumphant,” as Prudentius uses it here.

7. In the Parma edition the meter has been corrupted by transposing the words to read *quae lambitur flumine*; in the note it correctly reads *quae flumine lambitur*. Teolius says that all the Vatican manuscripts have *lambitur*, not *labitur*. But there is no doubt that Vaticanus Q and others have *labitur*, which Mariettus read in Vaticanus A, B, Rat., and Prag.

In Vaticanus P, Oxon., Thuan. in the first hand, Egm., Pal., Fabr., and Parrh., the reading is *lambitur*. Heinsius printed *labitur*, but thought the passage should be emended to:

> The Tiber marsh knows, which is washed by the neighboring river,  
> The grassy plot dedicated to two trophies.

That is, it is the grassy plot, not the marsh, that is washed, as below concerning the same Tiber:

> Where the river grips the left-hand grassy plot.

A similar expression may be added from Ammianus, Book XXVII: “The Ister, where it washes Roman soil.” I do not dislike the conjecture, although Teolius considers the construction too harsh and forced. For the rest, I would change nothing, since the manuscripts resist the alteration.

Cellarius was remarkably mistaken: he not only printed *qui lambitur* but also appended the entirely false note, “Thus the manuscripts; commonly, *quae labitur*.” Giselinus says that one manuscript has *quae lambitur*, and the Daven­trian manuscript *quae lambit ex propinquo*. But he adds that both expressions may properly be said of the Rhône washing the Lake of Geneva and of similar rivers; not so, however, of marshes springing up at the foot of mountains and continually discharging themselves into neighboring rivers.

Nevertheless, I favor *quae lambitur*, understanding the Tiber marsh to be the plain beside the Tiber, which he calls a marsh because it was frequently covered by standing water, either from heavy rains or from the river’s floods, as the aforementioned eminent Cardinal Borgia explains admirably. From these words he correctly concludes that the place where Saint Peter suffered martyrdom was not the Janiculum, as the more recent opinion maintains, but the plain extending between the Tiber and the foot of the Vatican hill. He confirms this more fully by adducing other monuments of antiquity.

Teolius does not seem to have sufficiently understood this opinion as it has been explained, unless perhaps he devised some new theory of his own. For in his admonition to this hymn he says:

“As for the place, however, the argument is not the same. However attractive may be the conjectures of recent writers, who maintain that the holy apostles were executed in different places, they are nevertheless conjectures. No prudent judge of historical matters can fail to prefer to them an ancient witness, one everywhere commended for his sincerity and learning. Since, therefore, Prudentius plainly says in verse 9 that the same marsh, whatever it may have been, was stained with the blood of both apostles, we dare not call into question that the holy apostles completed their martyrdom in one and the same place; nor, in the absence of reliable monuments, dare we determine what that place was. For a careful and learned discussion of the whole matter, see the work of the most illustrious Cardinal Stephen Borgia.”

But the learned Cardinal Borgia plainly defends, on pages 84 and 85, the assertion of Peter Comestor: Paul was killed by the sword in the catacombs toward the west, while Peter was crucified in the Vatican, specifically in a district outside the city where wine jars were made. On page 89 he says:

“No one expressed more clearly the place where the teacher of the nations was struck down by the sword and died than Saint Gregory the Great, when he donated the estate of Saint Paul’s basilica at the Aquae Salviae. Concerning that estate or property at the Aquae Salviae, Saint Gregory says: ‘There, receiving the palm of martyrdom, he was beheaded.’”

This may be seen in the work of the distinguished bishop Galletti, an outstanding student of antiquity, *Roman Inscriptions of the Later Age*, vol. I, page 5.

8. By *cespes* understand grass or a field. Below, verse 46: “Where the river grips the left-hand grassy plot.” Weitzius, in his note on verse 50 of the hymn to Saint Vincent, had thought that *cespes* here meant an altar. The grassy plot of the Tiber is said to have been dedicated to two trophies.

Caius, or Gaius, a presbyter of the Roman Church under the Roman pontiff Zephyrinus in the second century, says in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book II, chapter 25:

“But I can point out the trophies of the apostles. For whether you choose to go to the Vatican or along the Ostian road, you will find the trophies of those who founded this Church.”

The trophies in Prudentius and Caius are the tombs of martyrs who obtained the palm of martyrdom. Saint Jerome, in his letter to Marcella, says:

“There is in Rome a holy church, there are the trophies of the apostles, and beside them the inscriptions.”

Perhaps the term *trophy* was applied more properly to the tombs of the apostles Peter and Paul; *inscriptions* were also used to designate other tombs and the churches built over them. Fortunatus called these trophies “bulwarks” in Book III, poem 7:

> Two bulwarks stand before the hostile front,  
> Which the capital of the world holds as towers of faith.

Above, in verse 2, “apostolic triumph” occurs. Saint Ambrose similarly says of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, in Letter 22:

> Noble relics are drawn from an ignoble tomb;  
> The trophies are displayed to heaven.

9. Egm. has *et crucis, et gladii testes*. Heinsius missed the point here, for he says that in Egm. the word is read in such a way that *testes* refers to the grass, not to the rain of blood. The true reading is *testis*, and it refers to the Tiber marsh, not to the rain of blood.

The meaning is: “The Tiber marsh knows, as witness of the cross and the sword, by which—that is, by the cross and the sword—the rain of blood flowed twice over the same grass.” Teolius infers from this verse that Peter and Paul suffered in the same place. But Prudentius means that both martyrdoms occurred in the same Tiberine fields, not absolutely in the same spot within the Tiber marsh. He designates the region of martyrdom, but not the precise location within that region, to speak like the jurists.

Thus he says that the Tiber marsh knows the grassy plot dedicated to two tombs; afterward he clearly distinguishes and separates those very tombs:

> The Tiber divides the bones of the two.

He likewise says “through the same grass,” although he maintains that the martyrdoms did not occur in the same year; and he says that the blood flowed twice, since he states that Peter was affixed to the cross. All these expressions convey and signify something different, although perhaps Peter’s blood also flowed. Jerome, in Letter 23 to Castrutius, says more strongly:

“What is higher than Peter, what than Paul? They stained Nero’s sword with blood.”

Sagittarius, chapter 6 of *On Tortures*, cites several Fathers who confirm this double form of death for Peter and Paul under Nero.

> [1190] He saw him crowned with laurel through a glorious death.
>
> The Tiber marsh knows, which is washed by the neighboring river,
>
> [Col. 0558A] [1191] The grassy plot dedicated to two trophies,
>
> And a witness of both the cross and the sword, by which, watering the same
>

[Col. 0560B] 21. *Ut teres*, “as round”; *circulus*, “a circle,” I.

11. Weitzius says that some doubt whether Peter was crucified at Rome or in Jerusalem. I know that some do doubt it, but they are heretics. What, however, do they answer to the whole of antiquity, in which there are so many who affirm that Peter suffered martyrdom at Rome and no one who denies it? The testimonies collected by the eminent Cardinal Borgia may be consulted.

13. Egm., Widm., above, Vaticanus P, have *aemulandae*; the meter requires *aemulando*. As for why Peter asked to be affixed to the cross with his feet reversed, Egesippus, Jerome, Chrysostom, Augustine, Eutychius the Egyptian, Maximus, and others give this same explanation. On Peter’s inverted crucifixion there is a polished encomium by Peter Labbe, which Sagittarius transcribed in chapter 8 of *On Tortures*.

14. Hailsbr. has *tantam*. Egm. has *tangi*, incorrectly, instead of *tanti*.

15. Gis. in the margin has *pedibus versum*. Ald. has *imprimat*; *imprimant* is better.

17. Parrhasius incorrectly has *solo* instead of *sola*. The word derives from *solum*, “sole,” with the *e* removed, not from *solea*, as the gloss says.

Seneca explains the various forms of crucifixion in *Consolation to Marcia*, chapter 20:

“I see crosses there, not of one single kind but made differently by different people. Some hang men head downward toward the ground; others drive a stake through their private parts; others stretch out their arms upon a crossbeam.”

Origen, as cited by Eusebius, Book III of *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 1, relates that Saint Peter was affixed to the cross with his head lowered downward:

“He came at last to Rome, where he was fastened to a cross with his head lowered downward; for he had prayed that he might be placed upon the cross in this way.”

Egesippus, *On the Destruction of Jerusalem*, Book III, chapter 2; Abdias—whoever he may be—the author of the *History of the Apostles*, although it is apocryphal; Palladius, in the *Dialogue on the Life of Chrysostom*; Augustine, Sermons 28 and 29 *On the Saints*; Eutychius the Egyptian, patriarch of Alexandria, in *The Origins of His Church*; Saint Maximus, Sermon 1 *On the Birthday of the Apostles Peter and Paul*; Jerome, chapter 1 of *On Illustrious Men*; Saint Ambrose, Book I of *On the Interpellations of Job and David*, chapter 1; Saint Gaudentius, bishop of Brescia, in his sermon *On the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul*; Saint John Chrysostom, in his homily *On the Chief Apostles*; Saint Gregory of Nyssa, in Oration 8 *On the Beatitudes*; and innumerable others agree with this account. Thus some people appear to have doubted the matter rashly.

In the Mozarabic Breviary there is a hymn attributed to Saint Ambrose in which this is clearly affirmed:

> With the cross’s position reversed …

And in the prayers for Matins:

> “While Paul, desiring to be released, died by the sword, Peter asked to be crucified with his feet reversed.”

Rupert of Deutz, Book VI, chapter 10 of *On the Works of the Holy Spirit*, cites these very verses of Prudentius:

“On this subject a certain faithful man, praiseworthy in his faith, sang these verses:

> “The hands therefore are fastened …”

20. In some Vulgate manuscripts, *defecit*; in others, *hora*. Correct to *dejecit ora*.

21. Vaticanus B, Q, Mar., Prag., Rat., and Weitz. with his copies, together with Thuan., Ox. in various readings, and Parrhasius, have *retro*; Ald., Vaticanus P, and others have *rota*. In Alex. this verse and the following one are missing.

23. Vaticanus A has *cruorem*; above, *furorem*.

24. Understand “to be struck by the sword,” as he indicated above. Saint Augustine often used *feriri* absolutely, as in Letter 260:

“If they were ordered not only to be struck suddenly but also to be struck in the neighboring place …”

See Sagittarius, chapter 7, on this expression “to be struck by the sword.” Since the sword was common to all peoples, whereas the ax was peculiar to the Romans, it was more disgraceful to be struck by a sword than by an ax. Victims to be sacrificed were cut down with an ax. See Baronius under the year 226, number 3.

Chamillardus did not notice this distinction when he repeatedly asserted that Paul was struck with an ax, claiming that this was known to everyone. Just as Prudentius willingly grants Peter the first place of authority, so he grants Paul the foremost praise for teaching the nations. The Mozarabic Breviary correctly expresses this distinction in the chapters for the *Benedictus* on this feast:

> “As they advance toward the heavenly kingdoms, the power of Peter admits them, but the devotion of Paul, who teaches, leads them there.”

25. Prag. has *Cato*, incorrectly, and the gloss above has *sapiens*. Read *cito*.

26. Parrhasius distinguishes the words: “It is already necessary to go to Christ; I am being released,” he says. Compare the Second Letter to Timothy 2:6:

> “For I am already being poured out, and the time of my release is at hand.”

Also compare the Letter to the Philippians 1:23:

> “Having the desire to depart …”

31. *Dextra regio*, “the northern region.”—*Aureis*, “noble,” I.

32. *Canens*, “growing white,” “shining white,” “bright”; derived from *canities*, “whiteness,” and related to *caneo*, “to be white.”—*Fluento*, “water flowing from a spring,” I.

[Col. 0562A] 34. *Fontem*, “baptistery.”—*Chrismatis*, “with the oil of anointing, with which the baptized are anointed,” Vaticanus A.—*Fontem*, “a permanent baptistery.”—*Feracem*, “fertile,” I.

[Note: [Col. 0561B]]

27. Parrhasius, corruptly, has: “This delay that is drawn out is given as punishment. He is sacrificed by the sword.” Ald. and some Vulgate manuscripts incorrectly punctuate the passage: *nec mora protrahitur*.

28. Vaticanus A has *autem*. Correct to *vatem*.

29. The more certain opinion is that Saint Peter was buried in the Vatican and Saint Paul on the Ostian Way. Some writers, relying on authorities that are not sufficiently trustworthy, assert that their bodies were transferred from the catacombs to the places where they now lie by Cornelius, the Roman pontiff. See Saint Isidore, *On the Life and Death of the Saints*, chapters 68 and 69. It cannot, however, be denied that the bodies of the blessed apostles were for some time hidden in the catacombs, as is demonstrated by the testimonies of Saint Damasus and Saint Gregory the Great.

31. Prag. has *perceptum*; it should be corrected to *receptum*. Here, too, the golden roofs of the Vatican temple are mentioned, as below those of the basilica of Saint Paul. Peveratus, in his note on this verse, transcribes the following words of Pompeo Ugonio from a manuscript sheet that he possessed:

“Augustus Constantine, at the request of Bishop Sylvester, constructed the basilica for the blessed apostle Peter in the temple of Apollo, and enclosed the body of Saint Peter in a small chamber. He enclosed that small chamber on every side with Cyprian bronze, which is immovable. Above, he adorned it with porphyry columns. These columns stood beneath the canopy until our own time; now they are in the altars of S. [lacuna], and other vine-like columns, which he had brought from Greece, still exist today. He made a golden cross weighing 150 pounds.”

It is easy to understand that these words are corrupted by errors; but they are not important enough to warrant emending them.

32. Mar. has *canans*; above, correctly, *canens*. Prag., Weitz., Vaticanus B, and Q have *olivo*; Rat. has *olivae*; Ald. has *oliva*, and *murmurans*. Most manuscripts have the reading as printed. Olive trees are still green in the Vatican.

Weitzius says that near the Vatican temple there was a spring from which Saint Peter baptized the guards of his prison, and that Prudentius speaks of this spring. I noticed and corrected this error in the hymn *On the Place Where the Martyrs Suffered*, and so forth. Weitzius derived the error from Giselinus.

[Col. 0561D] 33. Baronius, under the year 384, number 24, recognizes in these verses the baptismal font of the Vatican church. The old glosses refer to the same thing. I, however, think that Prudentius is describing a magnificently constructed fountain before the doors of the Vatican temple, where the faithful washed their faces and hands before entering the church.

Paulinus speaks of this fountain in Letter 33 to Alethius, or Letter 13 to Pammachius in the later edition. Pammachius had provided a banquet for all the poor of Rome in the basilica of the chief of the apostles:

“How great a joy you gave the apostle himself when you had filled his entire basilica with dense gatherings of the poor—whether in that part where, beneath the height of its roof, the broad central space lies open beneath the lofty coffers, and, shining from afar with apostolic majesty, catches the eyes of those entering and gladdens their hearts; or in that part where, beneath the same mass of roofs, the side aisles extend on either side through twin porticoes; or where, glittering before the atrium, it spreads out into the vestibule, where a domed roof of solid bronze adorns and shades the basin which serves water to our hands and mouths, pouring out its streams, not without mystical significance, while four columns encircle the leaping waters.

“For such an ornament is fitting at the entrance of a church, so that what is performed inside as a saving mystery may be marked outside by a work visible to the eyes.”

A similar fountain was later constructed by Leo the Great before the Ostian basilica of Saint Paul, and Ennodius celebrates it:

> The water washes the stains of the flesh, but faith,  
> Cleaner than the stream, purifies and cleanses souls.
>
> Whoever enters the venerable sanctuary of Paul,  
> Reverently wash your hands in the fountain according to your merits.
>
> Long neglect had destroyed the flow of the waters,  
> Which the basin now pours forth for you with full mouth.
>
> The provident care of the shepherd Leo  
> Has given these abundant streams to Christ’s sheep.

Eusebius, Book X, chapter 4, confirms this ancient Christian practice of washing the hands and face before the doors of the church or within the sanctuary; Tertullian indicates it in Book *On Prayer*, chapter 11:

“What reason is there for approaching prayer with hands washed but a spirit still soiled?”

The same custom existed among the pagans. In Christian churches, the vessel of holy water for the cleansing of venial sins, which is seen today, succeeded these fountains. Perhaps on the more sacred days of Holy Week the ancient Christians, when entering the church, did not wash their hands and faces, to signify through a sense of grief the Passion of the Lord. From this may have arisen the custom of not using holy water on Thursday and Friday of that week.

A short work appeared at Madrid in 1786 in which this custom was condemned. In 1782, an octavo volume had already been published at Perugia containing four works written in Italian. In the first, by an author identified as G. C., this practice is refuted; in the other three, written by entirely anonymous authors, it is defended.

If, then, the verses of Prudentius are compared with that ancient custom and with the words of Paulinus and Ennodius, it will become clear that he is not speaking of a baptismal font but of a fountain placed before the doors of the temple.

Prudentius therefore says that the region in which Saint Peter was buried was made conspicuous by golden roofs, olive trees, and flowing water. For the water springing from the mountain raises and nourishes the olive branch—I read *frondem*, “branch,” in this way—and from there it flows over marble and down the slope into a green pool or basin. Within the interior of the tomb or building, the waters flow from a basin and roll into a pool. The painting of the dome colors the waters, while the moss in turn reflects the gold, and the gold grows green from the moss. The blue water receives from the red color of the painting above a shadow or reflected image, and the coffered ceiling seems to move with the waves. The shepherd, or Roman pontiff, provides these streams for his sheep.

34. I said above that *frondem* should be read, and this is indeed how Vat. B, Alex., Mar., Prag., Rat., Weitz., together with most of their copies, Gis. in the margin, Sich., Thuan., the two Torrentian manuscripts, Heins., and Cham. read it. And just as Prudentius now says *frondem perennem* (“everlasting foliage”), so in verse 175 of the *Dittochaeon*, concerning the Mount of Olives, he says: “The rich sap flows down, abundantly laden with eternal foliage.” Janningus, volume VII of the June saints, also reads *frondem perennem* and interprets it as the olive tree. Nevertheless, Parrhasius, Aldus, and many manuscripts read *fontem* (“fountain”), as Cellarius and Teolius printed it; although the latter does not correctly assert that all the Vatican manuscripts except one have *fontem*. Although Chamillardus reads *frondem*, he nevertheless understands *liquore orto* (“the liquid that arose”), mentioned in the preceding verse, to mean that, according to Prudentius, a fountain burst forth at the death of Saint Peter, just as tradition records that three fountains burst forth at the death of Saint Paul. But Prudentius is speaking of a fountain that sprang up on the neighboring hill.

Peveratus, who, with Baronius, thinks that the passage concerns a baptismal fountain, reads *fontem* and supposes that it was completely destroyed together with the cemetery, so that no remains survive—unless perhaps the springs of water that are still visible around the rear pavement of the apse and beneath the porticoes of the Vatican courtyard are its remains. Urban VIII gathered several of these into a very clear fountain, adorned it with verses, and later the fountain of Pope Liberius and Damasus was brought into the courtyard of the Vatican palace and restored by Innocent X, who ordered the history of Pope Liberius washing the people in sacred baptism to be carved in marble.

Yet it is precisely this fountain of Liberius and Damasus, and no other baptismal fountain, that Prudentius describes. The verses of Damasus may be read in his works and in Baronius; for they contain nothing from which it can be argued that they were composed to describe a baptismal fountain. Baronius himself agrees that Paulinus of Nola described the fountain of the atrium of the Vatican basilica. Paulinus, moreover, agrees wonderfully with Prudentius. Baronius adds another inscription of Damasus, in which baptism is mentioned more explicitly; but it is by no means established that this inscription belonged to the Vatican basilica. Indeed, I think that in the time of Damasus there was no other public baptistery at Rome except that at Saint John Lateran, the only one Prudentius names, in *Against Symmachus*, book I, verses 586 and following.

>
> Neither the hour nor the day deceived the prophet.

>
> [Col. 0562A] On the right, the region holds Peter, received beneath golden roofs,
>
> with the olive singing and the stream murmuring.
>
> For the liquid, rising from the brow of the rock, caused
>
> **1195** everlasting foliage, productive of chrism,
>
