35. *Ruit*, “rushes”; *oleum*, “oil”; *lubricatque*, “and makes slippery”; *clivum*, “the slope,” the descent of the mountain, I.

36. *Colymbo*, “in the swimming-place.” Mar. and Prag. read *natatu* (“in swimming”); for in Greek *colymbin* means “to swim.” *Natatu*: “by the fruit of the olive.” *Corymbi*: clusters of ivy; *colymbi*: tubes through which water runs through hidden places, I. The *colymbi* are called tubes in Vat. A.

38. *Nivali*, “white,” I.

[Col. 0563B] 39. *Superne*, “from above,” an adverb. *Tingit*, “colors”; *pictura*, “painting,” I.

40. *Musci*, “green growths,” Vat. A. Those painted there. *Relucent*, “shine back from the gold,” I. *Aurum*, “from the moss.” Golden sheets fixed to the ceilings, Vat. A.

[Col. 0564A] 41. *Cyaneusque*, “green, glassy”; “green.” *Cyane* is a gleaming Scythian gem; sometimes it is pure in its brilliance and marked with dots, sometimes variegated with glittering golden specks. *Ostri*, “of red color”: *ostrum* is the purple dye obtained from the oyster, which in Greek is called *testa*. A kind of pleasantly scented murex, I. *Lazureus*, or “purple,” Vat. A. Mar. has *albus lapis* (“white stone”). [Col. 0564B] *Umbram*, “image,” Vat. A.

43. *Pastor*, “Peter,” I., Vat. A. *Rigore*, “cold,” I.

44. *Fluenta*, “teaching,” I.

45. *Ostiensis*, “of Ostia”; *Portuensis*, “of Portus,” from Ostia: a proper place-name, I.]

[Note: [Col. 0563C]

35. Ald. and Mar., in the first hand, read *murmura* (“murmurs”): read *marmora* (“marbles”). Ox. has *lubricatque clivo*, that is, “the liquid flows slippery over the slope.” Alternatively, *lubricat clivum* means that the slope is made slippery by the moisture.

[Col. 0563D] 36. Urb., incorrectly, has *fluctu et colymbo*. Alex. in the first hand, Thuan., and Gis. in the margin have *corymbo*. In his notes Giselinus says that he printed *corymbo* from the Deventer manuscript for the following reasons. First, *κολυμβός* should not be counted among the commonly used ecclesiastical words; second, *natatu* is ineptly applied to a stream; finally, shortly before this Prudentius had said that the region where Blessed Peter was buried was made musical by an olive tree. Repeating the same point here, he says that the stream, after rushing over precious marble and making the slope slippery, “undulates with green *corymbi*,” that is, with olive branches and leaves.

Heinsius does not approve *corymbo*, since it does not seem capable of referring to the olive; and *colymbades* olives occur in Pliny, Columella, and others. They were so called because they floated upon the brine in which they had been preserved. Many others understand *colymbades* olives in *colymbo*; but I do not see how *colymbus* could stand for olives, although olives are called *colymbades* from *colymbus*, or “swimming,” because they float.

Parrhasius writes *colymbo* and says that a *colymbus* is a basin into which descending water is received. Janningus explains *colymbus* as a channel or aqueduct. For Ugutio, *colymbus* is a plant growing in water, or a green thyrsus, or an aqueduct. It seems to me that *colymbus* means a swimming-place, or a place or pool suitable for swimming; and the glosses of Isidore agree: “*Colymbus*: a place where clothes are washed.” Lampridius, in the *Life of Heliogabalus*, says: “He provided swimming-pools of sea water in inland places”—that is, a pool and a swimming-place, as Salmasius explains.

Lupius, in his dissertation on Christian baptisteries, although he understands Prudentius’ words as referring to the Vatican baptistery, nevertheless adduces much evidence showing that *colymbi* and *colymbethrae*, or swimming-pools, were commonly used indiscriminately of sacred and secular baths. Instead of *colymbus*, some write *columbus*.

[Col. 0564C] 37. In the middle of that pool, or basin, and swimming-place, there stood a structure with a *cantharus*, from which water flowed down into the pool itself—unless perhaps the *cantharus* of which Paulinus speaks was set out in some corner for washing the hands. I conjectured that it is the inner part of a little pipe.

38. Mar. in the first hand, Hailsbr., Prag., Rat., and Parrhasius read *nivale*; *nivali* is better. Teolius interprets *nivali* as “white.” More truly, as I think, “cold,” as in the following phrase, “with the coldness of the fountain.”

39. Cauchus incorrectly has *pictura superba* (“proud painting”). In *superne*, the final syllable is properly shortened, as Gifanius demonstrates by the short *e*.

41. Paulinus said: “The vaulted roof, adorned and shaded by solid bronze, rises high.”

43. Some copies of the Vulgate have *adit* (“approaches”); read *alit* (“nourishes”). The glosses understand Peter as the shepherd in the words “the shepherd nourishes,” perhaps from the ancient designation by which Saint Peter was called “nourisher” in old monuments, as is clear from the *Liber Pontificalis*. Prudentius, *Against Symmachus*, book I, verse 585: “Where that ash lies, the beloved pledge of the father.” He calls Saint Peter this.

The most eminent Cardinal Garampi, everywhere renowned for his exceptional learning and erudition, while serving as apostolic nuncio to the emperor, appropriately called the prince of the apostles “our shepherd and nourisher,” in a diploma issued at Warsaw on 14 February 1774, imitating ancient usage.

Prudentius, however, here designates the Roman pontiff, probably Damasus himself, who constructed the fountain. Ennodius, in the verses quoted earlier, seems to have imitated Prudentius: “The provident care of the shepherd Leo throughout gave these abundant streams to the sheep of Christ.” In Prudentius, *rigore* (“coldness”) in *gelidi rigore fontis* means great cold.

44. Parrhasius, Vatt. B, Q, Mar., Prag., Rat., Weitz., Gis., and Heins. read *videt* (“sees”). Alex., Urb., Egm., Vat. Q, and Ald. read *vidit* (“saw”).

45. Ald. has *Pauli titulum*; read *titulum Pauli*. Prudentius always makes the third foot a spondee, the first two and the fourth dactyls. Cellarius explains *titulus* as the inscription of the tomb; most understand it as the Ostian basilica of Saint Paul itself. Properly, Prudentius here calls the tomb a *titulus*, and more particularly the bones contained in the tomb, for he uses a familiar word to signify that the bones are buried on the Ostian road. He preserves *servat* (“keeps”), which indicates that the bodies of the saints await the resurrection. In *Hippolytus*, verse 173: “The tomb keeps the bones for the hope of the eternal Judge”; he develops this more fully in the hymn *On Funerals*, verses 125 and following: “Now receive, earth, what is entrusted to your care,” and so on. See also the notes on verse 2 of hymn 18, *On the Martyrs*.]

47. *Princeps*, “Constantine,” I., Vat. A. *Arces*, “the temples of Peter and Paul,” Vat. A.

48. *Lusitque*, “he adorned,” as though he had made it in play. *Ambitum*, “circuit,” I.

49. *Bracteolas*, “beams with gold leaf,” or “sheets.” *Sublevit*, “surrounded, joined,” from *linire*. *Aurulenta*, “full of gold,” I.

[Col. 0566A] 51. *Parias*, “white, marble,” I. *Fulvis*, “red, gilded,” I.

53. *Camuros*, “curved,” Vat. A. *Recurvos*, “bent back,” Prag. *Curvos*, “curved, facing inward”; “curved.” *Camurum* is Greek for “curved”; hence a vaulted house whose shell is curved; hence also the camel, a crooked animal. *Hyalo*, “glass.” *Hyalum* is called glass in Latin. *Cucurrit*, “by adorning”; “he painted.” *Arcus*, “vaults,” I. *Hyalo*, “glass,” Vat. A., Rat. *Cucurrit*, “he painted,” Rat.]

47. Egm. incorrectly has *hac* for *has*. The Ostian basilica of Saint Paul is being described; for the temples of Peter and Paul are not “fortresses,” as the gloss says, but only the temple of Paul. The Ostian temple was consecrated solely to Saint Paul, and the Vatican temple solely to Saint Peter.

Some otherwise very learned men, who were writing at Rome, asserted that the Vatican temple had been erected in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul. They are sufficiently refuted by the inscription itself, which is displayed in enormous letters before the entrance of the Vatican temple. It is properly said that the emperor who constructed the temple “consecrated the fortress,” as in Saint Damasus concerning Constantina: “He consecrated the temple of the victorious virgin Agnes.”

But authors disagree about which emperor Prudentius has in mind. Most think it was Constantine; others, Valentinian. Yet an ancient inscription that still survives on the great arch of the basilica clearly proves that the matter must be understood of Theodosius:

> “Theodosius began it; Honorius completed the hall
>
> consecrated to the Teacher of the world by Paul’s body.
>
> Placidia’s pious mind, the glory of her father’s work,
>
> rejoices that it shines through the effort of the pontiff Leo.”

This inscription was formerly published in *Ancient Inscriptions of the Basilica of Saint Paul at Rome* (1654, folio), and has been repeated in many other works. Theodosius ordered Sallustius, prefect of the city, to undertake the magnificent construction of the basilica of the apostle Paul. Baronius, under the year 386, transcribed from the Vatican codex letters written in the names of Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius to Sallustius. From these it is clear that the old basilica erected by Constantine had to be demolished and a larger one built.

48. Vat. A incorrectly has *elusit*. Fabr. and Gis. have *clausitque*. But Giselinus says in a note that the reading is *lusitque*, and explains it as: “he raised it so liberally that he does not seem to have spared expense.” In his first edition Giselinus had indeed adopted *lusitque*, but his explanation is inept.

Prudentius uses *ludere* for “to paint” in *Against Symmachus*, book II, verse 44: “The increased painting dared to play with colored pigments.” In *Hippolytus*, verse 130: “He had painted a reddish gore with vermilion.” Perhaps *clusit* should be read for *clausit*, to which the gloss on *sublevit* seems to refer. The gloss appears to have been transposed, and it favors Vat. A, while the other manuscripts have *lusit*.

Teolius found *substravit* in two Vatican manuscripts, as though the ceiling had not merely been coated with gold but also covered beneath with solid sheets. In Egm., the gloss found in Burmannus’ *Anthology*, p. 317, is: “*Bracteolas*: very thin sheets of gold.”

For *aurulenta*, Aldus together with Urb. writes *aurolenta*. He says *aurulenta*, just as elsewhere *rorulenta* and *rosulenta*. For *aurulentus*, Forcellinus cites only Prudentius. On this custom of gilding roof beams, see Lipsius, *On the Greatness of Rome*, book III, chapter 14. Arnobius, book VI: “Let these things, then, be built either from massive marble blocks, or let them shine with golden ceilings; let gems glitter here and pour forth starry splendors with varied interlacing—or, according to another reading, interspersion. All these things are earthly.”

50. Browerus, in his notes on Fortunatus, p. 60, says that Fortunatus, who often praises temples because of the sunlight poured into them and their good illumination, did this following the example of Sidonius. But both had Prudentius as their author. Sidonius, book II, letter 10: “Within, light flashes, and the sun is so summoned to the coffered ceiling that it wanders, matching the golden metal in color.” Fortunatus, book III, poem 7: “You see the figures go and return as the quivering ray moves, and it stirs the ceiling as the wave of the sea does.”

51. A fourfold row of columns still exists in the basilica of Saint Paul. The learned Fea correctly observed, in his notes on Winkelmann, book I, chapter 2, that they are not *pariae*, as Prudentius calls them. He thinks that they had previously been placed in other older buildings, not in Hadrian’s structure, as popular opinion maintains.

Prudentius calls them *pariae* by metonymy, whereby one kind is put for another, or because *parium* is used in the sacred Scriptures for precious marble. 1 Chronicles 29:2: “And marble in great abundance,” where the Hebrew text has “stones of Sais.”

53. Ald., Mar. in the first hand, Alex., Widm., have *camyros*. Mar. in the second hand, Hailsbr., have *cameros*. Vat. A, Rat., Prag., and Parrhasius have *camiros*. Vat. Q and Urb. incorrectly have *carros*. Weitz., Gis., Heins., Vat. P, and others have [Col. 0566D] *camuros*. For *hyalo*, Prag. has *hiala*; for *varie*, Ald. has *variae*; for *cucurrit*, Mar. and Rat. have *percucurrit*. All these are written incorrectly.

Cauchius preferred *recurvat* for *cucurrit*, but *cucurrit* is correct. Salmasius, and at times Heinsius, thought that *camurus cucurrit arcus* meant that the arches themselves ran, and Fabricius accordingly printed it that way. But the correct reading is: “the good prince ran over the curved arches with splendid glass,” that is, he continuously adorned them with remarkable glass.

*Currere* for *percurrere* with an accusative occurs in Saint Damasus concerning Saint Agatha. The ancients often used simple verbs for compound ones, as *vertere* for *evertere*. The glosses show that *camuri* means “curved,” and Servius confirms this in his note on verse 53 of book III of the *Georgics*: “The ears bristling beneath the curved horns,” that is, “curved,” whence vaulted chambers are also called *camerae*.

What exactly is meant by saying that the emperor “ran over the curved arches with varied splendid glass” has not yet been adequately explained. Giselinus says: “Does he now mean the glass windows that are usually enclosed by vaulted arches? Or rather, were those curved arches, resting on marble columns, covered with the color or light of glass?”

Fea adopted the interpretation concerning glass windows enclosed by vaulted arches in his notes on Winkelmann, book XII, chapter 3, and again in volume III, pp. 208–209; there he rejects the explanation adopted by the eminent Cardinal Borgia from Janningus.

Janningus says that in the old manuscript notes of his codex there is a gloss reading *pinxit* (“he painted”) for *cucurrit*, and he explains the verse as follows: “The good prince Constantine, who adorned, mocked, or painted the circuit of both basilicas with great talents … likewise he ran over, traversed, distinguished, or painted the curved arches—that is, the curved or arched structures—with varied splendid glass, or remarkable glass.”

Peveratus merely notes that, on triumphal arches, various representations of objects were customarily carved, and that the procession of triumphal equipment and other things of this kind were represented in marble and distinguished with glass.

The true explanation should be drawn from what we still see in certain ancient churches, where vaults and arches appear adorned with mosaic work. Concerning mosaic painting, Pliny, book XXXVI, chapter 25, says: “Then floors, driven from the ground, passed into ceilings, made of glass; this too was a recent invention. Agrippa certainly painted encaustic work in the baths that he built at Rome, and adorned the remaining surfaces with white plaster. Without doubt he would have made glass ceilings if the invention had existed earlier, or if, as we have said, it had reached ceilings from the theatrical walls of Scaurus.”

Seneca, letter 86: “The ceiling is concealed by glass.” Statius, book I of the *Silvae*, poem 5, verse 42: “The ceilings gleam, their summits with varied glass; they shine in forms and colors.” Symmachus, book VIII, letter 41: “For you have discovered a new kind of mosaic, and one unattempted by earlier generations, which even our rusticity will try to attach for the adornment of ceilings, if we take from you, whether on panels or tiles, an example of the work you have planned.”

Consult Bulengerus, *On Painting*, book I, chapter 8, and the cited Fea, book I, chapter 2. *Hyalus*, or, as others write it, *hialus*, is glass or crystal. Here it means the glass tesserae from which ancient mosaic paintings were made.

Hadrian I, in a letter given in 787 to King Charles, in which he defends the veneration of sacred images, says in chapter 19: “Likewise, concerning the holy Fourth Council, the outstanding and wondrous preacher, Pope Saint Leo, himself also made churches, which he adorned by painting them in mosaic and with various histories or images. Moreover, when he made the great arch there in the basilica of Blessed Paul the Apostle and painted it in mosaic, he adorned the Savior, Our Lord Jesus Christ, and the twenty-four elders with verses bearing his name.”

Compare Ciampini, volume I of *Ancient Monuments*, chapter 24. Saint Paulinus, in letter 12 to Severus, concerning the basilica of Saint Felix which he founded: “The apse, marbled in floor and walls, shines with a ceiling adorned in mosaic.” Gregory of Tours, book V of the *History*, chapter 45: “He built a church, supported it with columns, varied it with marble, and painted it in mosaic.”

Hence the *musivarii*, mentioned in the Theodosian Code, title 2, *On Exemptions of Artisans*, and by Ciampini in the cited passage, where in chapter 10 he explains mosaic work as colored glass applied to the walls of the churches of the City.]

61. The bridge beside the structure, or tomb, of Hadrian is called the Aelian bridge by Dio, because the emperor Aelius Hadrian was so called. Cellarius says: “Where, they say, the apostle Paul was buried on the Ostian road.” He is completely mistaken. For the Ostian road does not lie on or beyond the Aelian bridge, nor was Paul buried in this place. Cellarius was perhaps misled by the gloss, which compresses many errors into a few words. Prudentius first recalls the Vatican feast, then the other feast on the Ostian road in the following verse.

64. Ald. has *hic*; others have *huc*. This is the oldest testimony to two Masses celebrated on one day by the same priest. In fact, in the Gelasian sacramentary two proper Masses are prescribed for the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul: one, “Properly at the feast of Saint Peter,” and the other, “Properly at the feast of Saint Paul.” There is a third, common Mass, to be celebrated outside the basilicas of the holy apostles.

These days, on which several Masses were said, were customarily called *polyturgical* days, as now on the day of the Nativity of the Lord. On these, see Walafrid Strabo, chapter 21 of *On Ecclesiastical Matters*. Formerly there were more such *polyturgical* days; now three Masses are celebrated only on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, and in Spain three on the day of the Commemoration of All the Faithful Departed.

Saint Ambrose, in the hymn of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, indicates that their feast was celebrated in three different places:

> “Throughout the circuit of the great city
>
> dense crowds press forward;
>
> along three roads is celebrated
>
> the feast of the holy martyrs.”

Perhaps the Mass prescribed in the Gelasian sacramentary for the night was performed in another church.

Cancellierius, in his work on the Tullian Prison, chapter 17, rejects Torrigius and Constantius, who thought that the place of the Tullian prison was indicated in the hymn cited. He thinks instead that the third church, or place to which the faithful gathered on the feast day of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, was the Vatican, or the tomb of Saint Peter. For he says that the other two churches were the Aquae Salviae, where Paul was struck down by the sword, and the Janiculum, where there was a tradition that Peter had been fastened to the cross.

Cancellierius denies, however, that he found this hymn among the works of Saint Ambrose. Yet there can be no doubt about the antiquity of the hymn, since it exists in the Mozarabic Breviary. Although the Maurists do not list a hymn on the apostle Peter and Paul among the Ambrosian hymns, just as they omitted many others that are certainly Ambrosian, this hymn is nevertheless read in the Paris edition of Ambrose’s works, 1661, volume V, column 358.

The reading of this stanza has been corrupted:

> “So great crowds, massed throughout the circuit of the world,
>
> hang suspended;
>
> along three roads are celebrated
>
> the feasts of the holy martyrs.”

It is read more correctly in the Hymnary of V. Thomasius, where this hymn is also attributed to Saint Ambrose.]

66. Ald. and Parrhasius have *bis festum*, contrary to the laws of the meter. In some Vulgate copies, *si colas*; read *sic colas*. In Vat. B and Mar., the hymn of the martyrs of Zaragoza follows this hymn.

1. This hymn is so entitled in Alex., Mar., and Vat. B. In Aldus: *The Passion of the Martyr Cyprian*. Heins.: *The Passion of Blessed Cyprian the Martyr*. Weitz.: *The Passion of Blessed Cyprian the Martyr and Bishop of Carthage*. In Vat. A the two verses are joined, as above. In Mar. the meter is described as follows: “An Archilochian meter consisting of a bucolic tetrameter and three trochees.”

Concerning Cyprian’s life before baptism, although Pontius is silent, let us believe Augustine, who says in sermon 311: “He himself writes, he himself bears witness to what his life was once like—how criminal, how impious, how blameworthy and detestable.”

Prudentius asserts that Saint Cyprian was devoted to magical arts before he gave his name to Christ. Most think that Prudentius, misled by the identity of the name, attributed to Cyprian, bishop of Carthage, what is related about another magician named Cyprian, who later also suffered martyrdom together with the virgin Justina. They offer as their reason the fact that both the writings and the acts of Cyprian the African, as well as Pontius the deacon, who committed his life to writing, are silent about such magic.

If you reply that Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, Metaphrastes, and others also testify to Cyprian’s magic, they respond just as readily that these writers too were deceived. I, to speak frankly about what I think, consider this negative argument to have no force against the authority of several very weighty writers, both in other matters and especially in this question itself.

The name of Cyprian the African was particularly famous in Spain, and Prudentius, who wished to compose his eulogy, could not have been ignorant of his genuine acts. It is especially important to note that in the hymns of Saint Vincent and of Saints Fructuosus and his companions, Prudentius agrees entirely with their acts, sometimes even so closely that the very same words are found in Prudentius and in the acts. Scarcely any other acts of the holy martyrs have come down to us more genuine, or equally genuine.

Therefore it is fair to form the same judgment concerning the hymns of the other martyrs: namely, that Prudentius composed them in accordance with the acts that were then read as genuine, even though the acts themselves have either perished or now been interpolated.

In the present hymn there is a particular reason for this view: for in the diocese of Valeria the feast day of Saint Cyprian was celebrated, as Prudentius himself testifies in the hymn of Saint Hippolytus, verse 237:

> “May this day also run among your solemn days
>
> of Cyprian, Celedonius, and Eulalia.”

It therefore seems most improbable that he described Cyprian’s deeds from false records.

Pontius the deacon arranged Cyprian’s life in such a way that he appears rather to have wished to pass over in silence than to narrate what Cyprian did before baptism. “Where, then,” he says, “shall I begin? Where shall I undertake the beginning of his good deeds, except from the beginning of faith and heavenly birth? For the deeds of a man of God ought not to be reckoned from anywhere else than from the moment when he was born to God.”

Pontius therefore writes Cyprian’s eulogy, not his life. I do not accept the doubts of some who question whether the Life of Cyprian now extant has Pontius the deacon as its author, on the ground that it is not as remarkable a volume as Jerome praised Pontius’ work.

In the acts now circulated concerning his martyrdom, only those matters pertaining to his glorious death are recalled. Cyprian himself, in letter 1 to Donatus, recalls many of his errors and sins before baptism. I willingly pass these over, because they may be understood as referring to paganism and to Cyprian’s Christian humility.

That this magical art once had great power even among men trained in other sciences may be gathered from Isidore, book VIII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 9, “On Magicians”; Lactantius, book II, chapter 17; and Tertullian, in the *Apologeticus* and in *On the Soul*, chapter 57: “There is already a public literature which promises that it will summon souls from the dwelling of the underworld—even souls lulled to sleep at the proper age, separated by an honorable death, and dispersed by prompt burial.”

Xiphilinus, drawing on Dio, reports that Caracalla was so accustomed to delight in magicians and wonder-workers that he honored Apollonius with honors and even with a monument of the kind consecrated to heroes.

Saint Gregory of Nazianzus, who above all praised Cyprian’s learning and nobility, considered it by no means absurd to believe that he had been devoted to magical arts. He was addressing the Constantinopolitans—or, as others think, the Nazianzenes—who celebrated Cyprian with annual honors and festivals. It is therefore not very likely that a false rumor about his magic had been spread among them.

The learned Aug. Ant. Georgius, in his approval of Bayer’s dissertation on the fatherland of Saints Laurence and Damasus, in which the rights of Spain were restored and declared immovable and secure, frankly confessed that Saint Gregory of Nazianzus was mistaken in making Cyprian, who suffered a distinguished martyrdom in the neighboring region of the East at the beginning of the same century, a Carthaginian by birth. He added that Saint Prudentius himself did not show himself free from the same error.

Georgius must therefore be counted among those whom I said had adorned our Prudentius with the title of saint, in note *a* of number 56 of the prolegomena.

The matter itself, however, requires explanation. Gregory of Nazianzus and Prudentius do not make the Cyprian who suffered martyrdom in the East a Carthaginian by birth. Rather, they say that the learned Cyprian, who was African by birth, was devoted to magical arts before his conversion—something which, as most now think, applies exclusively to the other Cyprian, the one from Antioch. Perhaps both Cyprians were magicians; but this is less certain of the Antiochene.

2. Some Vulgate copies have *inde domum*, incorrectly. Many assert that Saint Cyprian was born at Carthage; but the Maurists disagree in the Life prefixed to his works. Prudentius Maran, the author of his life, says that Prudentius and Suidas call Carthage Cyprian’s homeland, but that it is more probable that Cyprian was born elsewhere. The Bollandists, under 14 September, think that Cyprian was Carthaginian by nationality, but deny that this can be inferred from Prudentius’ hymn. The phrase *Inde domo* answers the more common question, “From what homeland?”

3. He calls Cyprian “ours by mouth and affection,” that is, a Spaniard, because Saint Cyprian is specially remembered in Spain on account of his celebrated letter to León, Astorga, and Mérida. The church and episcopal see of León had long been distinguished by the title of Saint Mary and Saint Cyprian. See the commentary on verse 170 of the hymn of Saint Hippolytus, and volume XXXIV of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 89.

The feast of Saint Cyprian is also celebrated in the Mozarabic rite; but a different hymn is recited, distinct from this hymn of Prudentius. The fast called that of the Kalends of November is observed for three days before the feast of Saint Cyprian. Compare the hymn of Saint Hippolytus, verse 237.]

Barthius, book XLI, chapter 20, explains certain matters in this hymn, and interprets *exsecutor* as “expositor.” The old glosses are not to be despised. In a certain Vatican manuscript Teolius found *praedicator* (“preacher”). *Opulentus exsecutor* means “a copious, eloquent advocate.” Lactantius, book V, chapter 1: “And if any of the learned happened to devote themselves to it [wisdom], they were not sufficient for its defense . . . Thus Cyprian alone emerged distinguished and renowned, since he had won great glory for himself through his profession of the art of rhetoric, and had written very many works remarkable in their kind.” Chamillard incorrectly interprets this verse: “Someone was lacking who would reduce the Gospel to practice.” For although among the ancient Latins, in Velleius and Suetonius, *exsecutor* means only “one who carries something out,” Prudentius’ meaning is plainly that a teacher was lacking who could instruct the world with rich and abundant eloquence—something Lactantius had said before Prudentius.

20. Teolius thinks that the Old Testament is called “the work of fear,” under which the Jews often carried out the law, moved by fear. Giselinus says that the phrase may be understood of those whose repentance for their sins is beginning, when fear of divine judgment and Gehenna recalls them to a better mind; or of steadfast self-abasement; or of the holy fear of God, worthy of his children, which is established as the beginning of wisdom. Chamillard’s interpretation seems to me not unsatisfactory: he suggests that works of salvation and knowledge of the mysteries are comprehended in this verse—namely, so that people might know how to work out their salvation with fear and trembling, and understand the mysteries of religion.

>
> There was one young man most learned in sinister arts,
>
> Skilled in violating chastity by fraud and regarding nothing as sacred;
>
> [Col. 0572B] Often also entering upon magical incantation among tombs,
>
> By which, while the bride burned with passion, he might dissolve the marriage-right of the bed.

[Col. 0573A] **Note: [Col. 0573B]**

28. *Oris*, “of the face.” — *Nitoris*, “of appearance” or “bearing,” I., Mar.

30. *Compescitur*, “is shorn,” I.

31. *Modesta*, “modestly.” — *Loqui*, “he was speaking.” — *Quaerere*, “he was seeking,” I.

32. *Vivere*, “he was living”; *penetrabat*, “he was penetrating,” I.

35. Gallienus, his son, I.

36. *Fatenti*, “to Cyprian,” I.

37. *Terrigenum*, “of the pagans,” or “of idols,” I.

[Col. 0574B] 39. *Quis*, “someone.” — *Ab egregiae*, “from the honor of,” or “from Christianity,” I.

40. *Neu*, “lest.” — *Pretium*, “death,” “martyrdom,” I.

41. *Modo*, “only,” “merely.” — *Conferat*, “let him reckon,” or “compare,” I.

44. *Cursim*, “swiftly,” I.

29. Vat. B, Mar., Rat., Gis., and Weitz. have *severum*. Alex., Urb., Vat. P, Q, Rott., and Noms. have *severam*, a reading preferred by Heinsius and others. Ox. alludes to this, having *severa*. Aldus writes *saeveram* incorrectly.

30. An ancient custom is indicated, traces of which still remain in the name and rite by which the first tonsure is conferred upon clerics. Canon 44 of the Fourth Council of Carthage prescribes: “Let a cleric neither grow his hair nor his beard”; some add “let him shave or cut it,” while others omit this, so that the meaning of the canon is that neither hair nor beard is to be grown. In the code of the canons of the Spanish Church published by Lopez, whose authority I do not assess, canon 66 says: “Clerics ought not to grow their hair and serve in that condition, but with the head shorn and the ears exposed; and, following Aaron, they should wear a long garment, so that they may be in an ordered habit.” I think this is relevant to what Marcellinus, book XXII, relates: a certain Christian named Diodorus was killed by the pagans of Alexandria under Julian the Apostate because, while supervising the construction of a church, he cut the boys’ curls too freely, believing this too to be connected with the worship of the gods. Consult Sirmond in his notes on Sidonius, page 52, on Sidonius’ words: “Short hair, a long beard.” There was various custom concerning whether the beard should be shaved or grown. At the Council of Barcelona, around the year 540, clerics were forbidden to shave their beards; at the Council of Coyac in Spain in 1050, priests and deacons were ordered always to have open crowns and to shave their beards.

32. Alex. has *Vivere justitiam Christi, penetrare dogma nostrum* (“to live Christ’s justice, to penetrate our doctrine”), the conjecture of Heinsius; Teolius adds that the more authoritative Vatican manuscripts confirm this very reading. But Urb. and Vat. P have *justitia*, and Mariettus did not record a variant reading from Vat. A, B, Prag., or his own manuscript. Vat. Q, Rat., Weitz., and Gis. in the margin have *vivere justitiae Christi*. Ald., Hailsbr., Ox., Alt., Rott., and three Torr. have *vivere justitia Christi*. Egm. has *ubere justitiam bibere Christi*. Thuan. has *bibere justitiam Christi*. Gis. printed *justitiam bibere Christi*. Heinsius suspected *justitiam imbibere Christi* (“to drink in Christ’s justice”); but Vertus thinks that *vivere justitiam Christi* means to express the divine law in one’s life and conduct, as in *Cath.* 2, verse 33, *vivere severum* (“to live austerely”). Tertullian has *vivere mortem* (“to live death”), Paulinus *vivere pabula mortis* (“to live the food of death”), Juvenal *vivere bacchanalia* (“to live the Bacchanalia”), and Solinus *vivere hominem* (“to live a human being”). Ald., Gis., and many manuscripts have *et* after *Christi*; Alex., Weitz., Mar., Rat., and others omit it. In Bong. *nostrorum* appears instead of *nostrum*, against the meter.

34. The bishop’s seat was higher than the other seats of the presbyters, in the more sacred part of the *bema*, or sanctuary. Gregory Nazianzen, in his poem *The Dream concerning Anastasia’s Church*, writes:

> I seemed to stand on a high seat, though not with a lofty mind;
>
> For even in sleep I was not proud in spirit.
>
> And grave presbyters sat on either side in lowered chairs,
>
> The chosen elders, leaders of the flock.
>
> In white garments a ministering crowd stood,
>
> Reflecting the splendor of the angelic host.

35. Ald. writes *Galienus*. Gallienus ruled for approximately seven years from A.D. 254 together with his father Valerian, and afterward alone. A similar phrase occurs in *Eulalia*, verse 81: “Maximian, lord of wealth.”

36. Ald. incorrectly has *poena capitis dominum fatenti*. Weitz., Vat. A, and also Prag. and Rat. have *capiti*, with the gloss *omni*, so that the punishment is imposed upon the head of one confessing God. But *poenam capitis* is the sound reading.

[Col. 0574D] 37. *Sacrari*, “to be worshiped,” as in *Romanus*, verse 912, *Cogi ad sacrandum* (“to be compelled to worship”). He calls idols “the foulest thousands of earth-born creatures,” as elsewhere he calls them “filth” and “filthy Jupiter.”

40. Ald. and others have *qui sumere*; read *quis*.

41. Ald., Alt., Oxon., Thuan., Heins., Sich., Vat. A, P, Alex., and Urb. have *conferas*; Vat. B, Q, Mar., Prag., Rat., Weitz., and Gis. have *conferat*. *Conferas* is more harmonious. The apostle’s thought is from Romans 8:18. Cyprian himself, *To Quirinus*, book III, chapter 17: “The things we suffer in this world are lesser than the reward that has been promised.”

44. Aldus printed *volucri tempore*; he corrected it to *volucri dat tempore*, but one should read *volucri cum tempore*. In some vulgates there is *nam tempore* for *cum*.

45. Widm., Bong., Vat. B, Q, Mar., Prag., and Rat. have *quietem*. The meter requires *quiete*.

46. Widm. in the first hand, Iso, Mar. in the margin, and Rat. above have *furoris* for *cruoris*, but the latter is unquestionably correct.

> Thus Christ suddenly restrains the frenzy of such lust,
>
> Shakes the darkness from his breast and drives away his madness:
>
> He fills him with love of himself, grants belief, grants shame for his deed,
>
> And now his face and appearance are different from what they had been:
>
> His countenance sheds its thin skin and passes into a stern one,
>
> [30] His flowing hair is restrained into short locks,
>
> He himself speaks modestly, seeks hope, keeps the rule,
>
> Lives Christ’s justice and penetrates our doctrine.
>
> By these merits, at last wholly worthy, he is advanced
>
> To the episcopal throne as a teacher and takes the highest seat.
>
> [35] [Col. 0573B] Valerian was the prince of wealth, and Gallienus;
>
> [Col. 0574A] [1207] Together they established the death penalty for one confessing God.
>
> They had ordered the foul thousands of earth-born creatures to be worshiped.
>
> Against the inclinations of the people the teacher Cyprian stirred them up,
>
> So that no one might depart from the honor of distinguished virtue,
>
> [40] Nor might any degenerate coward fear to accept the price of faith,
>
> Since suffering is light, if only you compare with it the future things
>
> Which God himself promised to brave men who persevere:
>

>

>

>

47. *Dicare*, “to offer,” I.

49. *His*, namely, “by these words.” — *Virum*, “of men.” — *Calefacta*, “kindled with the love of Christ,” I.

52. *Abdicata*, “separated” or “removed from the light.” — *Semota*, “removed.” — *Soli*, “to the light,” I.

53. *Specubus*, “caves,” I.

54. *Supremi*, “highest,” “most exalted.” *Supremus*, when derived from *supremus*, signifies “last”; when derived from the preposition or adverb *supra*, it signifies “first,” I.

58. *Tinctum*, “colored,” “stained,” I.

[Col. 0576B] 61. *Si luteum*, “if there is anything earthen.” — *Charismate*, “by the grace of the Holy Spirit,” “by grace or gift.” — *Expiasti*, “you cleansed,” I.

62. *Vise*, “visit,” “go to,” I.

[Col. 0576C] 64. *Liceat*, “let it be permitted,” I.

68. *Titubetve*, sc. “in his faith,” I.

47. Teolius, incorrectly and against the meter, has *seque gladio caput submittere*. Prag. has *sanguine*; retain *sanguinem*.

48. Ald., incorrectly, has *quis* for *qui*.

49. Pal. has *is ubi corda*. Others have *bis*.

51. Vat. A, Egm., Rott., Pal., Bong., Sich., and Gis. have *altius*. Weitz., Ald., and most manuscripts have *abditis*.

[Col. 0575D] 52. Vat. A and B incorrectly have *abdita soli* for *abdicata soli*.

54. Vat. B, Mar. in the ancient hand, Rat., Prag., Widm., Bong., and Teol. have *utraque manu*. Others more elegantly have *utramque manum*. Vat. B and Mar. in the text, Prag. and Rat. incorrectly have *invocabat summi*. Alex. has *invocat summi*; in the second hand, *supremi*, which is correct, since the other reading conflicts with the meter. Rott. has *invocat superni*.

55. Ald., Vat. P, Widm. above, Egm. in the first hand, and Gis. in the margin have *Christi decus*. Vat. Q corruptly has *Christi decet*. Vat. B, Mar., and Widm. have *Christe Deus*. Most have *genitor Christi, Deus, et*. Weitz. with Bong. has *Christus Deus*. Sichardus likewise.

56. Barthius, in the cited book XLI, chapter 20, would prefer *Christiparens hominis*, on account, he says, of the second generation. But since *quem diligis, et vetas perire* follows, *Christe, parens hominis* must be retained. 2 Peter 3:9: “Not wishing any to perish.”

57. Ald. incorrectly has *quae* for *quem*.

[Col. 0576C] 59. Teolius’ edition has the error *jamque tuus*; and Prag. has *fit* for *fio*.

60. Ald., Alex., and Vat. Q have *at novus*. Others have *et novus ex veteri*.

61. Vat. B incorrectly has *chrismate*, as do some vulgate editions. Rat. writes *carismate*. Widm. above, Pal., Alex., Vat. P, Ox., three Torr., and Rott. have *corpus*; most have *pectus*.

63. Prag. has *eripe carcereo de corpore*.

64. “This soul,” says Barthius in the cited passage, “speaks magnanimously as one offering itself willingly.” He proves this with many Virgilian examples, such as *Aeneid* I: “You could not have been able, and with your right hand to pour forth this soul”; *Aeneid* III: “Rather, destroy this soul by whatever death you please.”

66. In *invidia*, the final syllable is lengthened by the rule applicable to the incised phrase alone.

68. Vat. A, Mar. in the first hand, and Rat. have *titubetne*, incorrectly; Weitz. found the same in Egm., Pal., and Bong. One may instead prefer to read *titubet nequis tuorum*. From Ald. and Hailsbr. Weitz. cites *titubetque nequis*; but my Ald. has *titubetque quis*. Others have *titubetve*. Heinsius, with Oxon., Rott., and three Torr., has *neu cadat* for *ne cadat*.

69. Ald. incorrectly has *incolumen*. In Ado: “And when he was being led away, the people of the brethren, mourning, said: ‘Let us too be beheaded with him’”—a statement taken from the Acts.

73. Egm. and Hailsbr. have *at*; read *ad*.

> And would submit his head to the sword and dedicate his blood—
>
> he who wishes to join his soul to Christ, so as to follow as his companion.
>
> When by these words he had prepared the hearts of men, warmed with Christ,
>
> [50] He was led, bound, before the others, while the proconsul raged.
>
> [1208] The caves of Tyrian Carthage lie hidden, set farther back,
>
> Conscious of Tartarean darkness, cut off from the light.
>
> Shut in these caves, holy Cyprian, his hands bound
>
> With chains, invokes the name of the supreme Father:
>
> [55] [Col. 0575B] Almighty Father of Christ, God and creator of the world,
>
> Christ, parent of humankind, whom you love and forbid to perish:
>

>
> Though forgetful through viperous poisons and stained with various crimes;

>

>
> [Col. 0576B] Flowed into the people of Carthage, the source of keener
>
> Understanding, so that their hearts, urged on by goads, might burn

77. *Prope*, “near.” — *Margines*, “boundaries.” — *Refertam*, “filled,” I.

79. *Mortifer*: Emperor Hadrian died from the odor of lime, Vat. A.

87. *Candida massa*, that is, the three hundred martyrs are called Cyprian’s “white mass,” I.

[Col. 0578B] 88. *Thascius*: Cyprian is so called from a place, I. “Cyprian is so called from a place,” Vat. A, Mar.

89. *Indomiti furori*, “against unconquered fury.” — *Eminus*, “from afar,” I.

90. *Jussus*, “questioned,” Mar.

92. *Ille*, “the emperor then said,” I.]

[Col. 0577B] **Note: [Col. 0577B]**

76. Sagittarius, chapter 10, where he discusses the steadfastness of martyrs in fire, considered these verses—graphically describing the triumph of the three hundred martyrs—to be exceptionally fine.

78. Gis. in the margin, and an old manuscript in Weitz’s edition, have *exit* for *ardet*.

79. He calls the breath of the lime “deadly” because the vapor of lime can be lethal even in rooms coated with plaster, as happened to Jovinianus. Thus Barthius and the glosses, where Hadrianus is substituted for Jovinianus.

80. Egm. writes *stitisse*.

[Col. 0577C] 81. Rat. in the second hand has *salis ut micam*. Egm., Gis., and Heins. have *aut suis*. Weitz., Ald., and others have *et suis*. See *Eulalia*, verse 112: “If a little salt on the small vessels”; and there, verse 29: “To burn frankincense, the liver of a sheep.”

82. Ald. has *sponte ruerent*. Mar. has *corruerent*; above, with most, *sponte irruerent*. Ado relates the story as follows: “On the ninth day before the Kalends of September, at Carthage, is the feast of the holy martyrs of the white mass, who suffered in the time of Valerian and Gallienus. For, among other tortures, they say that the governor then heated a lime-kiln, placed embers with incense at its mouth, and said to the Christians: ‘Choose one of two things: either offer incense to Jupiter upon these coals, or be plunged into the lime.’ Then three hundred men, armed with faith, confessing Christ the Son of God to be God, threw themselves with a swift movement into the fire and were buried amid the powdery vapors of the lime.” These same martyrs are mentioned in the Roman Martyrology and those of Bede and Usuard. Ruinart, in the preface to the Acts of St. Cyprian, more correctly thinks that these martyrs suffered at Utica, although the martyrologies, apparently supported by Prudentius, relate that they completed their martyrdom near Carthage. The author of *Sermon* 317 in the Augustinian Appendix asserts that they were struck with the sword. But the authority of Prudentius and the others is much stronger.

83. Vat. A has *prosiliere*.

84. Barthius calls the expression “sharp,” because Prudentius calls lime, which suffocates like water, a “dry liquid.” In book LVI, chapter 12, he compares this with verse 78, where quicklime is elegantly called “snow-white powder.”

86. Vat. B, Mar., and Prag. have *candor venit ad superna mentis*. Rat. has *candor venit ad superna mentes*. In Prag. and Mar. *vehit* appears instead of the variant *venit*; in Rat. *vehit* was made from *venit*. Vat. Q has *vehit ad superna mentis*. Hailsbr. has *vehat*. In Egm., according to Weitz., *ardos vetat superna*; according to Heinsius, the same Egm. in a second hand has *ardor vehit*. In Alex. *ad* is absent; in Vat. A it was added by a later hand.

[Col. 0578B] 87. Barthius suspects that this verse was inserted by some monk. “And I would like,” he says, “to be told what it means, or what it is doing here.” Yet the place is suitable for it, and the designation “white mass,” known to the ancients, is aptly expressed here. St. Augustine preached a sermon in honor of these martyrs, *Sermon* 306, also numbered 112 *On Various Matters*, where he says: “It was called a mass because of the multitude of the number, white because of the splendor of the cause.” In *Sermon* 311 he also calls it the white mass of Utica. In his tract on Psalm 49 he says that there were more than one hundred fifty-three martyrs. Most count three hundred. The Acts of the innumerable martyrs of Zaragoza also mention a white mass, as I observed in the hymn concerning the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza.

88. Cauchus wanted *ob fidem suorum* (“on account of the faith of his people”); but *ob diem* (“on account of the day”) is sound. Valerius Flaccus: “The day, and his own [day], reminds all.” So too: “This is my day,” they said. Concerning the praenomen *Thascius*, see Pame­lius’ notes on letter 69: “Cyprian, also Thascius, to Florentius, also Papianus, his brother, greetings.” Some doubt whether *Tatius* or *Thascius* should be written. *Thascius* is supported by the fact that the first syllable of *Tatius* is short. The glosses assert that Cyprian was called Thascius from a place. The Mozarabic Breviary hymn agrees: “Master of the city of Tascia.” But I would more willingly read: “Master of the world, Thascius,” in the vocative, which is excellent.

90. Ald. has *Dogmatis, atque loci jussus genus edere: Christianus, inquit*. The verse is one foot too long. Therefore in Mar., Vat. B, Rat., Alt., Fabr., Gis., the first edition, Widm., and Bong., the word *edere* is absent; but the metrical structure is still not established. In Urb. *jussus* is absent, but the sense lacks this word or something similar. In Oxon. and three Torr.: *Dogmatis, atque loci jussus genus edere Cyprianus*, omitting *inquit*. In Rott.: *jussus genus Cyprianus, inquit*. Giselinus restored from a very old manuscript and the Daventriensis edition: “He had been ordered to declare what he lived by: ‘The One-Worshiper,’ he says.” Weitz., Heins., and others followed him; the reading appears in Egm., Pal., Alex., Vat. A, P, Q, and Alt., where this verse follows the other beginning *Dogmatis*; in Rat. it appears in the recent hand in the margin. Thuan. reflects it: “He had been ordered to declare what he lived by: ‘The One-Worshiper,’ he says.” Teolius attributes *Cyprianus, inquit* to Aldus, but my Ald. gives *Christianus, inquit*.

91. Ald., Alex., and Thuan. have *trado* for *servo*. Vat. P has the incorrect *tradere*.

92. An old manuscript in Weitz’s edition, in the copy belonging to the distinguished bishop Reggius, has not badly: *sat, ait, jam criminis* (“enough, he says, of crime already”).

> Fame relates that a pit was ordered to gape in the middle of a field,
>
> Filled almost to its upper edges with steaming lime.
>
> Reheated stones spew fire, and snow-white powder burns.
>
> It has the power to burn whatever it touches, and its breath is deadly by its odor.
>
> [80] They say that an altar had been set upon the top of the pit,
>
> Under this law: either they should offer a little salt, or the liver of a pig,
>
> [1210] Or the Christ-worshipers should plunge of their own accord into the depths of the pit.
>
> All three hundred leapt forth eagerly in rapid motion;
>
> [Col. 0578A] The dry liquid swallowed them, immersed in a whirlpool of powder,
>
> [85] And the headlong mass enclosed them down to the deepest bottom.
>
> Whiteness possesses their bodies; whiteness bears their minds upward.
>
> Thereafter the white mass deserved to be so called for all time.
>
> Meanwhile Thascius, now more joyful because of the day of his people,
>
> [1211] Is brought from afar before the fury of the unconquerable proconsul.
>
> [90] He had been ordered to declare what he lived by: “I am a worshiper of One,” he says,
>
> “I observe the mysteries consecrated to the saving Christ.”
>
> At this the other said: “Enough of crime now; he himself confesses it.”

[Col. 0579A] **Note: [Col. 0579B]**

93. *Fulmen*, “power.” — *Expedite*, “bring forth,” “draw out,” “unsheathe,” I.

[Col. 0580B] 97. *Cultior*, “more beautiful.”

103. *Imbuit*, “he instructs,” I.]

[Col. 0579B] **Note: [Col. 0579B]**

94. Egm., Pal., Fab., Vat. P, and Gis. have *carnificis gladio*. Ald., Weitz., Heins., and most manuscripts have *carnifices; gladio*. Sagittarius, chapter 7 *On Tortures*, cites several Fathers who report that Cyprian was killed by the sword; there he examines the formula used by judges when handing condemned persons over to the executioner: “It is decreed that he be punished by the sword,” or “Let him be struck with the sword.”

95. Ado, from the Acts: “And after saying these things, he read the decree from the tablet: ‘It is decreed that Thascius Cyprian be punished by the sword.’ St. Cyprian, hearing this, said: ‘Thanks be to God.’” The same formula appears in Augustine’s sermon on St. Cyprian; Sagittarius, chapter 7 *On Tortures*, confirms with many examples that martyrs, after hearing the capital sentence, customarily said: “Thanks be to God.” In Ruinart’s Acts of St. Crispina: “Crispina replied: ‘I give praise to Christ,’” and so forth.

96. The Parmensis edition has, incorrectly and against both meter and sense, *abire Christum* for *abire virum*. Ald., Egm., Pal., Urb., Vat. P, Q, Heins., and others have *abire virum*, not badly. Alex. has the corrupt *abirae*.

97. Vat. B, Mar., Prag., Rat., Weitz., and Widm. in the first hand have *dogma*. Alex., Urb., Vat. A, P, Q, and Heinsius’ manuscripts have *docta*, which seems more harmonious to Heinsius.

99. Heinsius would prefer *boni tantum*, if the manuscripts permitted it. See Baronius, volume II of the *Annals*, under the year 265; he uses this eulogy to commend Cyprian’s writings. Prudentius seems to have read Gregory Nazianzen’s words: “For he is placed not only over the Church of Carthage, nor merely over Africa, which is still renowned and celebrated through him and because of him, but also over all the western regions, and almost all the East, as well as the southern and northern coasts, wherever his fame and admiration have spread. Thus our Cyprian becomes [known].”

101. Barthius says that the verb *prophetare* is appropriate for expressing the gifts of the Holy Spirit mentioned by the apostle Paul, and that its use is not improper in Latin; Jerome, Adam of Scotland, Julian in book I *Against the Jews*, and others also use it. Before them Juvencus used it in book IV: “Christ, you will prophesy, whose palm has fallen to you.” Barthius adds that this verse of Prudentius deserves close reflection, for it contains much of ecclesiastical Latin. *Disserere* means “to persuade” or “to employ arguments.” *Eloqui* means “to speak elegantly.” *Tractare* is an episcopal term; the sermons of bishops are specially called *tractatus*. *Docet* refers to the nations; *instruit*, to disciples, as in Eucherius’ books of *Instructions*, and so forth.

102. Ald. has *exitusque*. Alex. has *exitque*; read *exit usque*.

103. Chamillard prints *Gallos fovet?* with a question mark. I believe this to be an error.

[Col. 0580B] 104. Most understand Hesperia here as Italy and the Iberians as the Spaniards. The author of the hymn to St. Cyprian in the Mozarabic Breviary, who, I think, had read this hymn of Prudentius, says: “Enriching Africa with blood, teaching Hesperia by the word,” where he certainly understands Spain. See verse 3 above.

106. Ald. and Urb. have *illic* for *illinc*. Vat. A incorrectly has *patronis*. In Vat. B and Mar. the Passion of the holy apostles Peter and Paul follows; Weitz. retained this order in his edition.

[Col. 0580C] In Vat. A and Weitz. there is the title I have given. In Aldus: “The Passion of the martyr Agnes.” In Heinsius: “The Passion of the virgin Agnes.” In Ambr.: “Here begins the Passion of Agnes.” In Thuan.: “The Passion of Agnes.” Parrh.: “The Passion of blessed Agnes.” Alex.: “The Passion of the eighteen saints ends; the Passion of Agnes begins.” In Vat. B it is placed after the Passion of the martyrs of Zaragoza, as in Mar. and Weitz. In Vat. A these verses are joined in pairs; in Mar., in groups of three. St. Agnes was celebrated with the highest praises by St. Ambrose, St. Augustine, St. Jerome, St. Damasus, St. Martin in Sulpicius Severus, St. Maximus, bishop of Turin, St. Gregory the Great, the Latin martyrologies, and the Greek *menaia*; concerning these, see the Bollandists and Ruinart. Prudentius’ hymn is read in the Mozarabic Breviary, though corrupted in many places. In the Hymnary of Ven. Thomasius there is a hymn in honor of St. Agnes composed by St. Ambrose. Hildebert described her martyrdom in elegiac verse. Barthius published an old poem about her in book XXXI, chapter 13 of the *Adversaria*. Some think that blessed Agnes suffered martyrdom around the year 310, when Symphronius, or Symphorianus, or Sempronius was prefect of the city; concerning him, see Corsini’s *On the Prefects of the City*. Ruinart rejects the commonly circulated Acts attributed to Ambrose, where it is said that the same virgin was thrown into the fire by order of the deputy Aspasius, under Valerian and Gallienus; he considers it more probable that the martyrdom occurred around the year 304.

1. Vat. A, the Mozarabic Breviary, Oxon., Cell., and Cham. have *Agnae*. Ald., Heins., and Weitz., with most manuscripts, have *Agnes*. Gis. has *Agnis*, as Stephanus Claverius preferred; this reading also appears in the manuscript of St. Michael cited by Ruinart. I have no doubt that she could be called *Agnae* from *Agna, -ae*, so that the name alludes both to her name and to its Greek origin, by which the virgin’s chastity is indicated. *Agnes* derives grammatically from *Agne, -es*; *Agnis*, from *Agnes, -is*; *Agnetis*, from *Agnes, -etis*. In ancient inscriptions *Hagnes* is found, with aspiration; some think it should be written thus if its Greek origin is considered. But usage commands otherwise: usage holds the authority, right, and norm of speaking, and no less of writing. Perhaps this usage began when aspiration was omitted in other words as well, such as *ymnus*, *Ippolytus*, and similar forms. In Vat. Q and Egm. *Agnen* is an error, as in Ald. *Romuli*. Barthius, book IV, chapter 13 of the *Adversaria*, observes that *Romulea in domo* is used for *Romae*, as in Horace, *domus Albuneae resonantis* (“the house of resonant Albunea”) for “the spring of the nymph Albunea,” and, by Barthius’ emendation, *Nec domus exsilii Plutonia* (“Nor the Plutonian house of exile”). Therefore, even if it must be granted from other monuments that St. Agnes was born at Rome, this cannot be inferred from Prudentius’ hymn; still less is Rome proclaimed in this hymn as her native city, since it is only asserted that Agnes’ tomb is at Rome. Barthius’ correction in Horace, *exilii* for *exilis*, however, will not easily be accepted by those who have carefully observed that Horace always lengthened such genitives of origin with a single *i*, as in *favoni*.

3. Peveratus says that the poet remembered towers whose name still survives, and that the Romans perhaps call them the “blood towers” from the blood of gladiators. He adds that St. Agnes’ tomb is now where the athletic circus once stood, and that Cicero mentioned these towers in his third oration against Catiline: “Surely you remember that, in the consulship of Cotta and Torquatus, several towers on the Capitol were struck by lightning.” But this explanation and correction require revision. Near the athletic circus at Rome there is a place called *Tor sanguigna*, now known as the Blood Tower. This place is far from the Capitol. Rome has other similar names derived from towers, such as *Tor di Specchio* and *Tor di Nona*, and in the Roman countryside Eschinardus lists forty-five places named from a tower. In the athletic circus, now Piazza Navona, there is the famous church of St. Agnes, which is believed to have been the site of the brothel where Agnes was prostituted. Her tomb is seen in another church bearing her name on the Via Nomentana, not far from the city. I understand Prudentius to refer to this church, which indeed stands within sight of Rome’s towers and palaces. Poets call lofty houses “towers”; hence expressions such as “tower-bearing cities” and “turreted walls.” Peveratus notes that St. Agnes was buried by her parents on the Via Nomentana, where the cemetery of Agnes was called by her name; that Roman girls frequented this basilica; and that two white lambs were customarily brought to the altar to be blessed. Their wool is believed to have been woven into the pallia of the new pontiff. Perhaps Christians introduced this custom in order to abolish another superstition mentioned by Festus under the word *ALBOGALERUS*: a cap made from a white victim sacrificed to Jupiter, to which the peak of an olive twig was attached. The *flamines Diales*, that is, Jupiter’s priests, wore this *albogalerus*. The true history, however, is that the archiepiscopal pallium is made from the wool of white lambs, which are given annually—two of them—by the regular canons called those of St. Saviour, on St. Agnes’ feast day, in her church on the Via Nomentana, as a canon-payment to the Lateran basilica. The supreme pontiff blesses them and sends them to a monastery of nuns, where they are to be raised at his discretion. For more about the pallium and this custom, see Macer’s *Hierolexicon* and the learned Zacharias’ *Selected Ritual Onomasticon*.

5. The name of St. Agnes was celebrated throughout the universal Church. Concerning her, see Jerome’s letter 8 to Demetrias, and from it the Roman Martyrology: “In the writings and languages of all nations, especially in the churches, Agnes was praised for her life; she conquered both her age and the tyrant, and consecrated the title of chastity by martyrdom.”

6. Gregory of Valencia, *Theological Commentary*, disputation 6, question 2, point 7, strongly confirms that the saints in heaven make God favorable to us when we pray, through the miracles and graces they obtain; he also brings forward these verses of Prudentius and similar verses of Paulinus.

7. Here “crown” seems to be understood not so much as the reward itself as martyrdom and virginity. Paschasius explains this distinction in book I *On Crowns*, chapter 6.

8. Some vulgate editions incorrectly have *virginali* for *virginal*. Barthius, book XXVI, chapter 12, says that the word is expressed with great elegance. “This word,” he says, “Iso interpreted very badly as the place where women are deflowered, and Georgius Fabricius as the place where virgins dwell.” Prudentius used it for the shameful part of the virgin body, as did Solinus and Apuleius, and as the glosses of Isidore read according to Barthius’ correction. In Macer’s *Hierolexicon*, *virginal* is explained as “virginity,” and, according to Carolus Widman, as “brothel,” both entirely incorrectly. Giselinus explains it as *ὑμήν* (*hymen*), that is, the virginal membrane, about which the physician Johannes Weyer writes. “Prudentius,” Giselinus adds, “dared to express in the singular what Augustine and others express in the plural,” just as earlier with the noun *altar*. Giselinus entirely rejects as spurious, and inconsistent with what follows, the reading *Intactum ab omni crimine corpus est* (“the body is untouched by every crime”), which he had found in some manuscripts but apparently written by another hand. As for Giselinus’ claim that *virginal* is Prudentius’ own singular form, it is easily refuted by the authority of Apuleius, Solinus, and others. Apuleius also used *feminal* in the *Metamorphoses*.

The custom alluded to is explained by the Pseudo-Ambrose: “Thereupon the insane judge ordered her to be stripped and led naked to the brothel, while the herald proclaimed: ‘Agnes, a sacrilegious virgin, insulting the gods with blasphemy, is being handed over as a prostitute to the brothels.’” See letter 1 among those separated by the Maurists.

39. Burmann the Younger, in the *Addenda to Claudian*, page 1012, read *fluxu in plateae*, “with a flow through the streets,” from two ancient Liège manuscripts and interpreted it as “the crowd’s flowing together through the streets.” See Gronovius on Livy, page 343. In Mar. and Rat. [Col. 0584B] *flexu*, “in a bend,” was made from *flexus*, “bent.” Prag. and Vat. Q incorrectly have *flexus in plateae*, “a bend in the street.” Aldus, from an old manuscript in Weitz’s edition, in the possession of the distinguished bishop Reggio, has *flexu in plateas*, “in a bend into the streets.” The Mozarabic Breviary has *flexam in plateas*, “bent into the streets.” The more correct reading is *flexu in plateae*, “in a bend of the street.” Iso interprets it as “at the crossroads,” where it was customary to build brothels. Peveratus wonders why the poet did not say *flexu in theatri*, “in a bend of the theater,” since those vaulted structures were in the agonalia circus. It is established [Col. 0584C] that public prostitutes were accustomed to remain in the vaulted structures of places of spectacle. St. Cyprian, or some other ancient writer, says in *On Spectacles*: “If I should again ask by what route he reached that spectacle, he will confess: through the brothel, through the naked bodies of prostitutes . . . . . He who, hurrying to the spectacle, had been dismissed and still carried with him, as was customary, the Eucharist, bore it among the obscene bodies of harlots.” Since *plateae*, “street,” also occurs below at verse 49, *flexu in plateae* must be retained; and, as I think, *flexus plateae* merely denotes an alley, or a narrow and winding street, which one entered from the main street. Petronius, concerning a brothel: “Then, through very dark winding passages, he led me out and brought me to this place.”

40. Vat. B and Mar. have *stantum*, “standing,” less well; Hailsbr. incorrectly has *statum*, “station.” The proper verb for female prostitutes is *stare*, “to stand,” since they stood before the vaulted structures for the sake of profit. Hence the brothel itself was called a *meritorium*, “a place of earning,” and Tertullian calls it, in book 2 *To His Wife*, a “meeting-place of public lust”: “the prostitutes themselves, who were prostituted, were also called *prostibula*.” Horace, *Satires* 1: “No woman except one standing in a stinking brothel.” In Seneca’s *Controversiae* 2: “You were called a prostitute; you stood in a public place.”

41. Vat. A, Egm., and Pal. have *adversa*, “turned toward”; the others *aversa*, “turned away,” which should be retained.

42. Peveratus explains this as “the temple.” Damasus does indeed say this in the verses that I shall present after the hymn, but another explanation is needed. Barthius notes, book 8, chapter 19, that “women’s places” in medical books designate the genital organs, as they also often do in Columella. But I do not think what he infers from this passage in chapter 5 of the same book is universally true: namely, that when naked women stood publicly as prostitutes—whether Christian women or others—those present turned their eyes away out of respect for the morals of earlier times. For this is narrated of Agnes as something arising from the special providence of God. What he says about “women’s places” could be confirmed by the more authoritative testimony of Lucretius. See Gifanius’s index under *LOCA* and *LOCI*.]

The Mozarabic Breviary corruptly has *gehennalis ignis flaminis in modum*, “hellish fire in the form of a flame.” Ruinart thinks that an angel appearing in the form of a winged creature may be understood. Certainly an angel was present to Agnes to defend her virginity; but nothing prevents our understanding this as a swift fire, blazing like a lightning bolt—not a bird—sent from heaven, which struck the impudent young man’s eyes. This is how I understand the passage; and the explanation is confirmed by verse 48, “Blind, he falls beneath the flashing light.” For the flashing light here is that very swift and burning fire by which the young man falls blind. I say “young man,” since the Acts show that he was the son of the prefect of the City, and at verse 29 the judge says: “Let every young man rush in,” etc.

63. Sich., Vatt. A and Q, Alex., Prag., Rat., Weitz. with his witnesses, Gall. with Torn., the Paris edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, and the manuscript of St. Michael preserved by Ruinart [Col. 0586B] soon give another reading: *Ascensus: iram nam furor incitat*, “A step: for fury provokes anger.” Heinsius noticed no variation in the reading, but following Giselinus printed *mox alius datur. Accensus iram nam furor incitat*, “soon another is granted. Inflamed, for fury provokes anger.” This is the reading retained by Aldus, Parrhasius, Vatt. B and P, Urb., and the more recent editions, although Teoli seems to prefer the other reading. Some report [Col. 0586C] that Symphorianus, so as not to incur the hatred of the Romans, substituted another judge named Aspasius, who ordered the virgin Agnes first to be handed over to the fire and then, when she was unharmed by the fire, struck with a sword. In my commentary on hymn 1 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 93, I examined why martyrs sometimes overcame other tortures but almost never yielded to the sword. Later I encountered Baruffaldi’s dissertation, “On the Blow of the Sword, or of Any Sharp Iron, Never Ineffective or Unreliable in Beheading or Killing the Martyrs of Christ,” volume 3 of the *New Calogeranian Collection*, Venice, 1757. Baruffaldi resolves the question by the same reasoning. For what he adds—that the sword was insuperable because God had decreed that this martyrdom should be completed by that manner of death and that the martyrs should be crowned by the blow of the sword—is precisely what is in question: why God decreed this rather than something else. Baruffaldi further denies that the sword ever failed against martyrs, and either calls into doubt the ancient stories that assert this or maintains that the event occurred without a miracle.

80. This may mean “higher than the ethereal heaven,” or he calls the darkness of heaven *poli*, “of the sky,” as at verse 95, “She beholds the lofty darknesses lying beneath,” because everything lying beneath the feet of the heavenly beings is darkness, even if it appears bright.

Aldus has *unum sub ictu*, “with one blow.” Most have *uno sub ictu*, “with a single blow.” In Bongarsius it occurs written together as *subictu*; Gifanius insists that this should be read from his old book, just as Prudentius elsewhere wrote *subtacitus* and Lucretius *subcavus*. He maintains that in the ordinary editions *uno sub ictu* is written incorrectly and barbarously; but he has not persuaded the learned men who have edited Prudentius.

Mar. and Vat. B have *vim rabidam siti*, “the force of ravenous thirst.” Urb. has the less satisfactory *et aurum: vim rabidam sitim*, “and gold: the force of ravenous thirst.”

105. From Virgil, *Georgics* 2, verse 464: “And garments embroidered with gold.” See the commentary on verse 48 of hymn 12 of the *Peristephanon*.

106. In the Mozarabic Breviary: *irati, mortem*, “angry, death”; correct to *iram, timorem*, “anger, fear.”

112. *Haec pede*, “these things with her foot,” is more harmonious, with Mar., Prag., and Rat., than *haec ac*, “these things and,” found in the other editions and manuscripts. In the Mozarabic Breviary there is the error *proculcat*, “tramples,” for *proterit*, “crushes.” In some editions *crepasset* is printed in the margin; I do not understand what it means or to what it belongs.

116. *Solum* is often understood as the sole of the foot. Compare Fronto Ducaeus on Paulinus, page 766, “to wipe with the holy sole,” *Letter 2 to Severus*, and Sirmond on Sidonius, page 113.
