Nor shall I hold back their burning desires:

I shall receive the sword entire into my breasts,

And draw the sword’s force down into my deepest chest.

Thus, married to Christ, I shall leap beyond all

[80] The darkness of heaven, higher than the ether.

Eternal ruler, open the gates

Of heaven, previously closed to earthly beings,

And call the soul that follows you, Christ,

both as a virginal sacrifice and as a sacrifice to the Father.

[85] Having spoken thus, with bowed head

She humbly worships Christ, so that her neck

May more readily endure the impending wound,

Bowed forward.

1221 But he fulfills that great hope with his hand:

With a single blow he cuts off her head.

[90] Swift death forestalls the sensation of pain.

[Col. 0587B] Then, freed from the body, the spirit leaps forth,

And flies out into the air; the angels

Surround her as she goes along a shining path.

She marvels at the world placed beneath her feet,

[95] She beholds the lofty darknesses lying below,

And laughs at what the sun’s wheel circles,

At what the whole world rolls and binds together,

At what is lived amid the black whirlwind of events,

[Col. 0588A] At what the vain instability of the age carries away:

[100] Kings, tyrants, empires, and ranks,

And the pomp of honors foolishly swollen.

The force of silver and gold, sought by all

With ravenous thirst through every kind of crime,

Dwellings built with lavish splendor,

[105] 1222 The empty finery of garments embroidered with gold,

Anger, fear, desires, dangers:

Now a long sadness, now a brief joy,

The smoking torches of black envy,

From which the hope and glory of humanity grow dark,

[110] And, what is worst of all evils,

The filthy clouds of paganism.

Agnes tramples these things; with her foot she crushes them,

Standing and pressing the dragon’s head beneath her heel—

[Col. 0588B] The savage creature that scatters all

The earthly things of the world with poisons

And plunges them into the underworld—

Now subdued beneath a virgin’s sole.

She presses down the crests of his fiery brain,

Nor, though conquered, does he dare raise his head.

Meanwhile God surrounds the brow

Of the unmarried martyr with two crowns:

[Col. 0589A]

[Note: [Col. 0589A]

121. *Unam*: one, a crown. — *Edita*: concerning martyrdom; *oblita*, “forgotten,” has been given for *edita* in one edition. — *Sexies*: six times ten makes sixty; the number sixty signifies the continence of widows. This was one crown for her, because of the labor that widows endure—for they endure the greatest labor, which is signified by the clasping of the fingers.

123. *In altera*: in the other, namely, concerning virginity.

126. *Colluvionibus*: stains, pollutions, impurities. [Col. 0590A] *Pollutionibus*: pollutions.

127. *Diademate*: crown.

128. *Cui*: namely, to you.

129. *Vel*: also. — *Fornicem*: a brothel; he refers to the place in the theater where virgins are deflowered.

130. *Purgabor*: I shall be cleansed. — *Oris*: of the face.

132. *Pia*: through a holy visitation. — *Visere*: to see, visit.]

[Note: [Col. 0589B]

121. Vat. A incorrectly has *una*, “one.” Others write *decimplex*, others *decemplex*, “tenfold.” He imitates Cyprian, letter 70: “Nor are virgins absent from their number, to whom the hundredfold fruit has been added to the sixtyfold, and whom doubled glory has raised to the heavenly crown.” Most maintain that the sixtieth fruit was promised to virginity and the hundredfold fruit to martyrdom in the parable of Matthew 13:8. Since in this passage Prudentius himself seems to assign the sixtieth fruit to virginity, one may read in book 2 *Against Symmachus*, verse 1059: “Hence ten times six,” where the reward of virginity is also discussed. The glosses offer differing opinions. In Iso you will understand the phrase “which is signified by the clasping of the fingers” from Jerome’s words at the beginning of book 1 *Against Jovinianus*: “The hundredfold, sixtyfold, and thirtyfold fruit, although it springs from one earth and one seed, nevertheless differs greatly in number. Thirty refers to marriage, for the joining of the fingers themselves, as though embracing one another with a gentle kiss and forming a bond, represents husband and wife. Sixty refers to widows, because they are placed in distress and tribulation. Hence they are pressed down by the upper finger, and the greater the difficulty of abstaining from the enticements of pleasures once experienced, the greater the reward. Moreover, the hundredfold number—pay attention carefully, reader—is transferred from the left hand to the right, and, with the same fingers but not the same hand by which married women and widows are represented on the left, it forms a circle and expresses the crown of virginity.” Bede explains this ancient practice of counting on the fingers more fully in his book *On Computation*, or *Speech through the Gestures of the Fingers*. See also Gazaeus in his note on Cassian, *Conferences* 24, final chapter, where he explains the matter in detail.

122. Egm. and Pal. have *mercis*, “of merchandise,” instead of *merces*, “fruit” or “reward.”

124. So also in the verses of St. Damasus about to be transcribed: “O happy virgin.”

128. Prag. alone has *solus Cunctiparens* (“the All-Father alone”) in place of *soli* (“to [you] alone”).

129. The Mozarabic Breviary incorrectly has *redde fornicem*, “restore the brothel.” Brothels were vaulted buildings where prostitutes stood: secluded and hidden places called *cubilia*, “bedrooms,” by the Apostle: “not in bedrooms,” etc. See the commentary on verse 108 of book 1 *Against Symmachus*.

130. Aldus, Vat. P, and some editions of the Vulgate corruptly have *purgabo roris*, “I shall cleanse the dew.” The Mozarabic Breviary, with no less serious an error, has *Purga jam corda propitiabili*, “cleanse now hearts with a propitiatory [power].” Parrhasius correctly printed long ago *purgabor oris*, “I shall be cleansed by the face.” Giselinus observes that most of the errors that have shamefully disfigured Prudentius arose through the ignorance of copyists, who sometimes fused entirely different words into one and sometimes separated words that belonged together. He gives these examples: *Secernere*, “to separate,” was written in verse 35 of the *Apotheosis* instead of *se cernere*, “to see oneself”; likewise verse 390 of book 2 *Against Symmachus*, *consulet*, “he will consult,” instead of *consultet*, “he may consult”; in the same work, verse 1024, *in acie*, “in the battle line,” instead of *in macie*, “in thinness”; and verse 193, *sed et*, “but also,” instead of *sedet*, “he sits.” In the hymn to St. Vincent, verse 146, *suam*, “his,” instead of *si jam*, “if now”; in the same hymn, verse537, *obis* (“you go/visit,” as written) instead of *orbis* (“world”); in the *Romanus*, verse 1036, *quinos*, “five each,” instead of *quin os*, “but the mouth”; and in the passion of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, verse 36, *fluctu et*, “and by a wave,” instead of *fluctuet*, “may it surge.” In the hymn to Cyprian, verse 102, *exitusque*, “and the exit,” instead of *exit usque*, “he goes forth continually.” Here, *purgabo roris*, “I shall cleanse the dew,” occurs instead of *purgabor oris*, “I shall be cleansed by the face.” Other similar examples could be added.

131. Cellarius objects that this refers to Christ and the divine Spirit. He ought to be ashamed so often to admit that Prudentius, so learned and pious a poet and so revered throughout antiquity, is so openly opposed to his heresy.

132. In the Mozarabic Breviary there is the error *quam pia viscera*, “how pious the entrails,” instead of *quod pia visere*, “because it is pious to see.” The same breviary adds certain verses which I can confidently affirm are not by Prudentius, at least as they now appear.

133. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book 36, chapter 4, says that the touch of the gods was considered effective, as in Horace concerning Venus: “Touch Chloe once, though arrogant.” “This,” he says, “the most learned poet Prudentius alluded to in ‘You deem it worthy to touch with a kindly foot.’” But, in my opinion, Prudentius means nothing more than that everything Agnes enters becomes chaste: she made the brothel itself pure. After this hymn, Vat. A is followed by the passion of the blessed Laurence. In the other manuscripts are verses of St. Damasus in praise of St. Agnes, in which the piety of this most holy pontiff shines no less than in his other poems. I think that an apology for Damasus and the other Roman pontiffs of the fourth century, against the manifest calumnies of Ammianus Marcellinus, would not be without value, if undertaken with care. Damasus’s poems themselves, as edited by Merenda, were printed in an extremely corrupt form through the printer’s negligence, quite apart from the editor’s blemishes. I shall now present corrected versions of the verses I mentioned in praise of St. Agnes.

Thus, after the hymn to St. Agnes, Vat. B, Mar., Prag., Rat., Widman’s manuscript in Weitz’s possession, and the Florentine manuscript discussed in the prolegomena, no. 86, which agrees with Urb., insert the following verses:

Verses of Constantina, daughter of Constantine, written in the apse of the basilica that she founded in honor of St. Agnes the virgin:

Constantina, reverencing God and dedicated to Christ,  
with every outlay prepared in devout purpose,  
greatly aided by divine power and by Christ,  
consecrated the temple of the victorious virgin Agnes.

A work that surpasses the temples and all earthly things,  
whose golden pinnacles of the highest temple gleam.  
For Christ’s name is celebrated in these seats—  
he alone was able to conquer Tartarean death,  
he alone, borne into heaven, to bear in triumph.  
Recalling Adam’s name, he summons back all limbs,  
raised from death’s darkness and blind night.

Therefore, O martyr devoted to Christ, you shall possess  
a worthy gift from our resources through long ages,  
O happy virgin Agnes of memorable name.

Most call her Constantine’s daughter Constantia, on the basis of inauthentic Acts. But she either had both names, or should rather be called Constantina, as the first verse makes clear: “Constantina, reverencing God.” The same name is also read in the first letters of the first eleven verses, for the poem is an acrostic. Perhaps one should read *Constantina Deo venerans, Christoque dicata* (“Constantina, reverencing God and dedicated to Christ”). For the first letters of the final three verses spell *Deo*. Concerning this church of St. Agnes on the Nomentan Way, see Ciampinius, *On Sacred Buildings*, chapter 9.

The manuscripts have various readings. In Widman’s title: “In honor of St. Agnes the virgin.” Verse 1: Vat. B has *Dei*, “of God,” instead of *Deum*, “God.” Verse 5: Widman has *opes*, “resources,” instead of *opus*, “work.” Merenda has *terrenaque juncta*, “and earthly things joined.” Verse 6: Merenda in the text has *aurea nam*, “for golden.” Verse 7: Merenda has *fastigia tecti*, “the pinnacles of the roof.” Verse 9: Widman, Prag., Mar. in a later hand, and Merenda have *solusque*, “and he alone,” instead of *solus*, “alone.” Urb. has *solus qui*, “he alone who.” Rat., incorrectly as a variant, has *vectus*, “carried,” while above it is *invectus*, “borne into.” Verse 10: Vat. B corruptly has *Nomen ferens retorquet et omnia membra*, “bearing the name, he turns back all limbs.” Rat. has *Numina vera ferens retro ciet omnia membra*, “bearing true divine powers, he summons back all limbs,” which seems to be written above in Vat. B. In the same Rat. manuscript, in smaller letters, is added: *Nomen Adae referens detorquet et omnia membra*, “recalling Adam’s name, he turns back all limbs”; Weitzius printed this from Widman. Prag. has *Numen ad aethra ferens post se ciet omnia membra*, “bearing the divine power toward the heavens, he summons all limbs behind him,” with the gloss “*Ciet*, that is, ‘he will call.’” In Mar., a corrector had written above: *Numen ad ethra ferens [Col. 0591B] retro ciet omnia membra*, “bearing the divine power toward the heavens, he summons back all limbs.” Merenda and Urb. have *Nomen adhuc referens, et corpus, et omnia membra*, “still recalling the name, and body, and all limbs.” The Florentine manuscript has the same. In some editions these two verses beginning *Nomen* and *A mortis* are omitted. Verse 11: Vat. B corruptly has *amo tenebris*, “I love the darkness,” instead of *a mortis tenebris*, “from the darkness of death.” Verse 12: Merenda in the text has *dignum Agnes munus*, “a worthy gift, Agnes.”

The following verses of St. Damasus are headed in Mar. and Rat.: “Likewise, verses of Pope Damasus concerning the same woman.” I shall nevertheless transcribe them from the copperplate engraving in Bayer’s dissertation on St. Damasus, taken from the original inscription in the church of St. Agnes on the Nomentan Way:

Tradition tells that her holy parents once brought Agnes  
When the trumpet had sounded mournful songs.  
The girl suddenly left her nurse’s lap,  
Of her own will trampled the savage threats and the tyrant’s fury,  
When he wished to burn her noble body with flames;  
With small strength she overcame immense fear,  
And, naked, let her flowing hair fall over her limbs,  
Lest her perishing face should see the temple of the Lord.  
O venerable one, sacred glory, nurturing honor of modesty,  
I beg you, illustrious martyr, to favor the prayers of Damasus.

Verse 1: Prag. and Widman have *flevisse*, “to have wept,” instead of *retulisse*, “to have related.” Urb. corruptly has *sanctos dudum regulis reparantes*, “the holy ones long restoring by rules.” Verse 2: Urb. incorrectly has *Agmen*, “a troop,” and *concrepavisset*, “had sounded.” Verse 4: Mar. has *rabiesque*, “and fury.” Mar. and others have *truces*, “savage.” Verse 7: Widman has *diffusum*, “spread,” instead of *profusum*, “flowing.” Merenda, in the works of St. Damasus, has *profusos crines*, “flowing hair.” Verse 9: Prag., contrary to the meter, has *Agnes tu decus*, “Agnes, you are the glory”; Rat. has *Agnes mihimet decus*, “Agnes, my glory,” with *tu*, “you,” written above. Mar. has *Agnes mihi decus*, “Agnes, my glory,” with *mihi tu decus*, “you, my glory,” written above and, in the margin, *columenque, et palma pudoris*, “and support and palm of modesty.” Others read: *O venerandum Agnes mihi tu decus alma pudoris*, “O Agnes, you are to me a venerable glory of chastity, gracious one.” In Urb. the verse is corrupt: “O veneranda m Deus alma pudoris,” “O venerable one, m God, nurturing [honor] of modesty.” Merenda and others have *inclyta virgo*, “illustrious virgin.” Moreover, there is scarcely any doubt that Damasus authored the preceding verses no less than these.

Concerning the word *lugubres*, “mournful,” with its first two syllables shortened, I spoke in the commentary on verse 79 of hymn 9 of the *Cathemerinon*. Among pagan writers *salubris*, “healthful,” also occurs with its second syllable shortened, as may be seen in Burmann’s *Anthology*. In Vat. B, Mar., and Weitz., these verses are followed by the hymn to St. Eulalia. In the others, by the Epilogue.]

One crown is completed by a tenfold reward produced six times,

1223 in everlasting light;

in the other appears the hundredfold fruit.

O happy virgin, O new glory,

[125] Noble inhabitant of the heavenly citadel,

Turn your face toward our stains,

With your twin diadem:

[Col. 0590A] To you alone the All-Father has granted power

To make even the brothel itself chaste.

1224 radiance of your face, if you fill our heart.

EPILOGUE.

[Col. 0591]

[Note: [Col. 0591D]

### Verse 1

In the Alexandrian manuscript the title is *Epilogue*, that is, “the conclusion” or “end of the book.” In Vatican B: “Here begins [the work] from the little works, dedicated to God the Father,” in trochaic trimeter hendecasyllables. It is placed before the *Dittochaeon*, but as the conclusion of the book *Peristephanon*, which had preceded it, since at the end one reads: “Here ends the *Peristephanon*. Here begin the titles of the stories.”

In the Marseilles manuscript: “Here begins [the work] from his little works. Trochaic trimeter hendecasyllables.” It is placed before the *Dittochaeon* and after the hymn on the Epiphany; but in this manuscript, as in others, the hymn on the Epiphany is the last in the book *Peristephanon*. Perhaps this led some people to place this ode—which in certain manuscripts follows the hymn on the Epiphany—as a preface to the book *Peristephanon*. It should, however, be noted that the distinction is this: in some manuscripts the hymn on the Epiphany closes the book *Cathemerinon*, while in others it closes the book *Peristephanon*.

Giselinus expressly states that in his own manuscript and in the Daventer manuscript these verses were prefixed to the book *Peristephanon*. He approves this arrangement because Prudentius says that he consecrates trochees and iambs to Christ, and because the book *Peristephanon* consists chiefly of trochees and iambs. But, as I shall say at verse 7, Prudentius names the verses of which this ode consists; he does not mean other verses of the book *Peristephanon*.

Giselinus adds that there is no other work to which he did not give its own prologue. Yet, apart from the fact that the *Dittochaeon* has no prologue, the book *Cathemerinon* has no other preface than the one common to the remaining works. And just as that first book begins with a common prologue, so this last book, which concerns the Crowns, is appropriately concluded by a common epilogue.

Heinsius admitted that none of his manuscripts placed this ode before the book dedicated to the martyrs—not the Putean manuscript, nor the Ambrosian, in which the beginning of the book *Peristephanon* was found; but this ode did not appear there. In the Oxford manuscript, as in Aldus, it closed the whole sequence of poems. In the Rottendorf manuscript it was read between the books *Against Symmachus* and the *Dittochaeon*; consequently, some editions, as well as the old Nomsian manuscript, make this ode the preface to the *Dittochaeon*.

In his *Addenda*, Heinsius confirmed that most old manuscripts make this very ode the epilogue of the volume, and that it ought, by right of restoration, to be recalled to its former place, from which it had unjustly been exiled.

The inscription in the Egmond manuscript was: “Here begins [the work] from his little works, Prudentius.” In the Thuan manuscript and the earlier Boher manuscript: “Prudentius, from his little works.” In the Rottendorf manuscript: “Here begins [the work] from his little works.” In the Thuan manuscript the poem is called “mixed iambic.” Aldus entitles it: “An ode in which the poet speaks about himself.”

In the Florentine manuscript, where these verses are placed after the book *Peristephanon*, the title is: “Prudentius dedicates his little works to God,” and the first verse is: “Pious, faithful.”

Scaliger discusses poets’ epilogues in book I, chapter 55 of the *Poetics*. He says that Horace separated his conclusions, as in “I have completed a monument more lasting than bronze,” and Ovid likewise, “And now I have completed my work”; Virgil, however, did not separate his epilogue in the *Georgics*, “That Virgil.” Yet scarcely any distinction can be recognized between Ovid and Virgil.

Our Juvencus offers another example of a pious epilogue, which I would gladly transcribe if I were not myself already hastening toward the end. Some Spanish writers of the fourteenth century, in works written in the vernacular, called an epilogue an *ultilogue*, explaining that a preface is called a *prologue*. Posterity rightly did not imitate this tasteless elegance.

In most manuscripts the first verse, “He dedicates [his works] to God the Father,” is absent, just as in others the last verse, “Under whose guidance we live,” is absent. Giselinus transcribed the first verse from a manuscript, believing that it was entirely required by the sense and that the iambic poem, always ending its sentence with a longer line, needed to be placed in the latter position, after the model of Horace:

> Neither ivory nor a gilded ceiling  
> gleams in my house.

He rejected the final verse, following Manutius, as spurious.

That first verse is found in the Rottendorf, Weitz, and most printed editions. Goldastus read: “He dedicates [them] to God the Father.” I believe that it is absent from many manuscripts because it has been incorporated into the title itself, as in Vatican B: “Here begins [the work] from his little works; he dedicates [them] to God the Father,” and so forth.

I think that Fortunatus had read these verses after the book *Peristephanon*, including the verse “He dedicates [them] to God the Father.” This is suggested by what he says in the preface to the *Life of Saint Martin*:

> Sending these sacred offerings to the pious martyrs,  
> prudent Prudentius wisely offers his deeds.

### 1225

He dedicates [his works] to God the Father,

Pious, faithful, innocent, chaste,

### 1226

The gifts of his conscience,

With which his blessed mind inwardly abounds.

[5]

#### Notes

11. *Approbat*: “he approves, praises.” I.

24. *Magno*: that is, at great cost. I.

25. *In atrio*: within the Church. I.

26. *Obsoletum*: through vices.—*Caducis*: worthless. I.

7. Aldus has *iambos* (“iambs”) against the meter, instead of *iambicos* (“iambic”). In some editions *iambicos* is written with *j* as a consonant, which the law of the poem rejects. In these two verses Prudentius explains the kind of meter in which he is now writing, as in *Cathemerinon* hymn 3, verse 28, “and mystical garlands in dactylic meter”; in the hymn to Saint Eulalia, verse 209, “I shall carry woven things in dactylic meter”; and at the end of the hymn to Saint Fructuosus, “revolving sweet hendecasyllables.”

He calls them “swift iambics,” as Horace does in the *Art of Poetry*: “A long syllable following a short is called an iamb, a swift foot.” In the same passage, as Barthius corrects it in book XVII, chapter 4: “Rage armed Archilochus with the hasty iamb.” Others read *proprio*, “with his own.”

Ausonius, letter 21:

> Iambus, swifter than the Parthians and Cydonian darts,  
> Iambus, swifter than the wings of birds,  
> more torrential than the force of the rushing Po,  
> denser than the great violence of resounding hail,  
> more flashing than the flames of a quivering thunderbolt.

8. Trochees are correctly called “rolling” (*rotatiles*), because their name derives from *trochus*, a wheel or disk. Cicero, *On the Orator* III: “Aristotle, your Catulus, excludes from the orator the frequent iamb and trochee; yet by nature they themselves rush into speech and our ordinary language. They are, however, conspicuous strokes of rhythm and short feet.”

10. From this verse some infer that Prudentius was not wealthy. It is sufficiently plausible that, when he devoted himself to a stricter life, he renounced wealth, if he possessed any, just as he renounced honors. In this ode, moreover, he seems to imitate Horace, book IV, ode 8: “I would give cups,” and “graciously favorable,” and so forth.

11. Vatican B has *approbet*, “may he approve,” which is less good.

13. From the Apostle’s Second Epistle to Timothy, chapter 2, verse 20:

> But in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver,  
> but also of wood and earthenware;  
> some indeed for honor, others for dishonor.

Many others have used the same comparison of the Apostle. Walafrid Strabo had certainly read Prudentius:

> The wealthy household of the rich master receives golden vessels,  
> counting up various forms of silverware.  
> It does not despise these vessels, though they are not molded from clay  
> or made of wood, but assigns them their proper uses.

16. In the Marseilles manuscript the earlier reading was: “Nor is a polished basin lacking, made of bronze,” which has correctly been emended above. Goldastus, for the variant reading, has: “Nor is a basin made ready for eating”; above, “polished.” Retain what we have printed. Prudentius also used *defit*, “is lacking,” instead of *deest*, in *Cathemerinon* 4, verse 85, and *Apotheosis*, verse 812.

17. The Marseilles manuscript has *aula*, “hall”; above, *olla*, “pot,” which is sound. Weitz printed *aula* incorrectly.

18. Vatican B has *paripsis*. Marseilles, Ratold, and Rottendorf have *parabsis*. Most have *parapsis*, as Oxford, Thuan, Bongars, Weitz, and Heinsius. Giselinus has *paropsis*. See the commentary on verse 532 of the *Psychomachia*: “and joins the right hand to a *parapsis*.”

23. In Vatican B, *ex inferunt* has correctly been changed to *instruunt*, “they furnish,” a very appropriate verb.

24. Vatican B incorrectly has *parato*, “prepared.”

25. Bivarius wished to conjecture *me materno*, absurdly and while devising some sort of nonsense about the church of Caesar Augusta, named for the Blessed Virgin of the Pillar, which he dreamed Prudentius was praising here. I discussed this matter in number 58 of the prolegomena.

26. Giselinus and several common editions incorrectly have *vasculis*, “little vessels.” We have spoken sufficiently in the prolegomena about Prudentius’ Christian humility from this and other passages. See there, number 46 in note a (in this edition, column 597, note a), the words of Barthius, who extols this ode with the highest praises.

27. Ratold has *abdat* instead of *aptat*; and in the following verse *sinatque* instead of *sinitque*. Mariettus approved and preferred both readings.

29. The faithful, illustrious in charity, are vessels of silver and gold; those fragile and weak in faith and righteousness are earthen vessels.

32. *Obsequela*, or, if one prefers, *obsequella*, is used in place of *obsequium*, “service.” Thus Lucretius called a prison *luelam sceleris*, “the expiation of crime,” instead of *luitio*, “expiation.” See Gifanius in his index, where he gives other examples under *CUSTODELA*, *CONFUGELA*, and so forth.

33. Heinsius, with the Thuan manuscript, preferred *Quidquid illud accidet*, “whatever it may be that happens,” instead of *accidit*, “whatever happens,” which is found in most manuscripts. Barthius, in the passage cited, does not understand what *Quidquid illud accidit* is intended to mean, and thinks that one should read *Quidquid illi ut accidat*, “whatever may happen to him,” since *quidquid* means “whatever.”

Nemesianus, *Eclogue* 1:

> Whatever song of yours Echo  
> answers from the woods.

He arranges the verses as follows:

> We enter within the palace of salvation;  
> whatever may happen to him,  
> it will be pleasing to have proclaimed Christ with our mouths,  
> under whose guidance we live.  
> Yet even to have rendered the lowest service to God is beneficial.

Whatever place the lowliness of our poems may occupy in the Church of God, it will nevertheless please us that we ourselves composed and sang them with our mouths. He doubts whether *ora*, “mouths,” or *ore*, “with the mouth,” should be read. But no adequate reason is offered for introducing so great a textual variation. The sense of this verse is: “Whatever that may be which will happen when I enter the palace of salvation.”

As for Nemesianus’ verse, which is obscure and perhaps corrupt, see the notes of Peter Burmann in his edition of the *Minor Latin Poets*, where he offers a different explanation.

34. Ratold has *personare*, “to proclaim,” whereas above *personasse*, “to have proclaimed,” is sound. Thus Horace said *sonaturum*, “about to sound,” and Pliny the Younger *juvaturi*, “about to help.” See the commentary on verse 760 of hymn 10 of the *Peristephanon*, where some read *crepasset*, “had cracked,” and others *cremasset*, “had burned.”

35. Aldus, Giselinus, Heinsius, Teolius, and others omit this verse. But since it is found in Vatican B, Marseilles, Ratold, Sichard, Alexandria, and other manuscripts, it is useful to print it. In one Vatican manuscript Teolius saw *Quo regnante vivimus*, “under whose reign we live”; but the meter requires *regente*, “under whose guidance.”

When Heinsius found this verse in the Rottendorf and Oxford manuscripts, he supposed that some part of the poem was missing. It is certainly true that Horace’s ode of this kind, book II, ode 8, is arranged so as to begin with a shorter verse and end with a longer one. But why could verses not be arranged otherwise if the poet preferred? Barthius affirms that this verse is entirely worthy of Prudentius.

Elsewhere, as a most polished poet ever consistent with himself, he says in verse 1 of hymn 8 of *Cathemerinon*: “Christ, the governance of your servants.” The meaning is that Christ is at once our king and our life.

Finally, it should be observed that Prudentius crowns his poems with nearly the same thought that he expressed in the preface:

> While I write or speak these things,  
> would that, freed from the chains of the body,  
> I might escape wherever my nimble tongue  
> shall carry its final sound.

Saint Jerome, in his letter to Demetrias, uses a similar thought at the end:

> Let the tongue know nothing else but Christ;  
> let it be able to sound nothing except what is holy.

### 1227

Another man cuts back his money,

From which the needy may live:

We dedicate our swift iambics

And rolling trochees,

Though lacking in holiness,

[10] And unable to relieve the poor.

Yet God approves

Poetry on foot, and kindly listens.

In the house of the rich

Furniture lies throughout every corner.

[15] A golden cup gleams,

Nor is a polished bronze basin lacking.

### 1228

There is also an earthen pot,

And a heavy, broad silver serving-dish.

Some vessels are ivory,

[20] Some are hollowed from oak and elm.

Every vessel becomes useful

That is suited to its master’s use;

For they furnish the house,

Whether purchased at great cost or prepared from wood.

[25] In my Father’s hall,

Like a little obsolete vessel, worn out and perishable,

Christ adapts me to humble uses,

And allows me to remain in a corner.

Behold, an earthen gift:

[30] We enter within the palace of salvation.

Yet even to have rendered

The lowest service to God is beneficial.

### 1229

Whatever that may be which happens,

It will please me to have proclaimed Christ with my mouth,

[35] Under whose guidance we live.

## In the Year of Our Lord 440. Dracontius

According to the edition of Arevalus.

### Dedication

To the most eminent and most reverend prince, the Lord Don Francisco Antonio de Lorenzano y Butrón, cardinal priest of the Holy Roman Church, archbishop of Toledo, primate of Spain, grand chancellor of Castile, distinguished with the grand cross of the illustrious Spanish royal Order of Charles III, and so forth:

Faustinus Arevalus.

#### I

I now gladly and deservedly return to you, most eminent prince, the ancient Christian poet Dracontius, whom in previous years I had received from you, reprinted in the most elegant typography among the works of the Fathers of Toledo, after carefully revising him against the manuscripts of the Vatican Library, so that I might satisfy your wishes.

It has proved especially convenient and pleasurable for me that at this very time Gregory Alfonso Villagómez y Lorenzana, your nephew on your sister’s side, archdeacon of Calatrava, has come to Rome. He is a most accomplished man, endowed with those virtues of character, those gifts of intellect, and those resources of learning that make him especially dear to you. Into his hands I transfer Dracontius from my own, so that this work of mine, however modest, upon a learned and gifted poet may also reach you acceptably. Otherwise you could rightly have demanded it back from me as your own.

And although I ought not to have owed you Dracontius revised by me as you see him here—and I owe you this in many respects—whom else could I more appropriately offer him to, now presented anew to the light of publication? Would that the labor I have devoted to illuminating this outstanding poet, as it is owed to you, might also be worthy of you and of your singular merit, learning, and integrity of character!

#### II

For you have joined to that ancient hereditary nobility of León, which first shook the Moorish yoke from the necks of the Spaniards, all the other virtues most fully suited to your exalted dignity. You are so diligent a cultivator and generous patron of divine letters that we may either compare you with, or even prefer you to, your predecessors Montanus, Helladius, Eugenius, Ildefonsus, Julian, and Cisneros; and we may set you before all prelates, present and future, for imitation or at least admiration.

It would be a lengthy undertaking, and unnecessary in a matter so evident, to recount your immortal services to students of ecclesiastical doctrine. Yet I consider it wrong to remain entirely silent about them when such an appropriate opportunity has been offered me.

#### III

For in the outstanding course of the higher disciplines, is there any branch in which you, most eminent prince, have not advanced gloriously—not merely through sharpness of intellect, gravity of judgment, and steadfast diligence, but also by publishing and ennobling, advancing and enlarging monuments both ancient and recent, your own and those of others?

To pass over the study of the sacred Scriptures—which includes not only the *Analogy of the Old and New Testament* by Martin Becanus, reprinted at your expense for the public good, but also many other works I shall mention—the first work that comes before my eyes is the *Science of Liturgical Matters*. In it the Catholic faith is contained for the greater part, established by the agreement of the ancient Fathers and by the unbroken succession of the centuries, or rather sung forth by the unanimous voice of all Christians.

#### IV

With great applause even among foreign peoples, that political—and still more Christian—hero, Cardinal Francisco Ximénez de Cisneros, is celebrated because he entrusted the Isidorian Liturgy, which some call Gothic and others Mozarabic, not merely to printing but to eternity.

When you wished to follow in his footsteps, you went still farther. This is evident whether we consider your *Explanation of the Mozarabic Mass*, prepared by you, together with the complete model of the Mass and the Hourly Prayers of this liturgy printed at Angelopolis; or whether we consider the polish, elegance, and magnificence of the Mozarabic Breviary, which you arranged to have reprinted at Madrid, along with the artistry of the engraved copper plates; or, most particularly, whether we examine the prolegomena to your new edition of this Breviary, in which you discuss the ancient divine office of the Church of Spain so learnedly that nothing could surpass it.

#### V

Here I would speak of the academic assemblies that you, most eminent prince, established or promoted for the elucidation of the liturgy, were I not, as I hasten, summoned onward by the costly and magnificent edition of the Fathers who in ancient times occupied your episcopal see.

You brought singular splendor and light to their writings, not only through learned and useful prefaces, but also through the accompanying notes, which proceed from profound theology, extensive knowledge of ecclesiastical antiquities, and refined understanding of the recondite arts.

In this field of study I must not pass over in silence the works of your fellow countryman, Saint Martin of León, a man taught by God. Learned men had long desired an edition of these works, and some had attempted one unsuccessfully; but you were the first to bring them into public light in four large volumes, according to a copy transcribed from the author’s own manuscript.

#### VI

Nor may one omit the most ancient councils of the New World. While you were adorned with the insignia of the archbishopric of Mexico, you collected them with the utmost diligence and zeal, illustrated them with catalogues of the bishops of the individual churches of the Mexican province and with other distinguished monuments, and committed them to print.

Nor may one omit those two excellent books for explaining Christian doctrine to the people, which we call catechisms. They were published at Mexico by order and authority of the Fourth Mexican Council, over which you yourself presided, chiefly with your assistance.

Everywhere the ancient councils of the Spanish Church are more renowned and of far greater weight. Sometimes reduced to a summary, sometimes arranged and distributed in the manner in which the body of canon law was digested, they have appeared for the common benefit under your distinguished auspices.

To this may also be added the timely opposition you offered to the many shameful books disseminated among the people against either the dignity or the foundations of religion: namely, the translation of the sacred Council of Trent into Spanish, adorned by your patronage.

#### VII

You have never ceased extending your generous hand to those who lead the minds of young people safely toward these more serious studies through the more agreeable principles of refined literature or through philosophical instruction.

In this matter, however, the highest praise is owed to the very works that you wisely delivered in the volume of your letters and other works printed at Toledo. There you commend a new edition of the incomparable man Luis of Granada’s *Sacred Rhetoric*, or speak about the proper method of study, which should, so far as possible, be adapted to the standard of our ancestors.

#### VIII

I would gladly add to all this, excellent prince, the singular generosity with which you have most liberally supported my own studies, however small or worthless they may be, if I were now acting to display a faithful remembrance and testimony of my gratitude—which certainly will never depart from my heart or lips—rather than merely to show, however partially, your outstanding services to sacred letters.

Yet this too is a mark of your goodness: in these divine sciences you judge that even the very efforts to make progress should be rewarded. You receive with the greatest kindness not only writers commended by achievement and maturity, but also those who display some promise and expectation.

#### IX

I must neither be silent about nor can I express adequately the fact that, in promoting ecclesiastical studies and publishing and generously disseminating throughout Europe so many monuments of ecclesiastical learning—not to mention the archiepiscopal library of Toledo, which you have conspicuously enlarged, and another private, select, and richly equipped library that you have acquired for yourself—you have proceeded with such expense and magnificence that anyone who merely cast his eyes upon these benefactions of yours could easily persuade himself that your generosity could not advance beyond these limits.

Yet it has shone forth much more greatly in supporting the poverty of many, relieving the calamities of peoples, strengthening public roads, building bridges, raising hospitals, establishing other buildings, or constructing them from their foundations—buildings in which the sick may be cared for and provision made for the insane—in a word, in greatly advancing the public happiness of mankind.

In the volume of your works, which I mentioned a little earlier, there are several letters in which the true method of providing for the welfare and needs of the poor is set forth. But one letter in particular deserves to be read and publicly celebrated: the letter in which you urge and most seriously exhort your own brother Thomas, bishop of Gerona, who, inflamed by the same studies as yourself toward acts of benevolence and who has deserved well and continues to deserve well of many, to complete a charitable hospital and other public works of piety.

You urge him, although he is already hastening forward, citing examples especially of the bishops of Spain who won everlasting renown for themselves—not by insane and envious constructions, still less by lavish expenditures accompanied by disgrace and dishonor, but by building structures for the public advantage and founding charitable houses in which provision could be made for poor people of both sexes, and in which boys and girls, men and women separately, could be trained in the arts and trades necessary to human life.

#### X

In these and similar instructions and exhortations of yours, most eminent prince, one may clearly see the image of your kindness.

For there stand throughout the extensive province of your diocese many enduring monuments of your pious generosity: some begun by others but completed by you, others carried by you yourself, through the most distinguished architects, from their foundations to their summits, and still others now being brought to completion.

With such expansive foresight, when the price of grain rises, you provide for the peoples entrusted to your pastoral care. Thus you advance the liberal arts, including their properly organized academic school. Thus you increase other crafts necessary for the uses of life.

By setting you alone before us as an example, it can easily be shown how much the discipline of Christian worship and the formation of the Catholic clergy surpass the empty theories of certain impious men in securing the welfare of the entire commonwealth.

#### XI

I understand, excellent prince, that such dignity and magnificence in the public works of piety that I have briefly outlined cannot exist without that private self-restraint and the other supports of virtue with which a bishop must be equipped—especially one who holds the highest rank of honor in the Spanish Church, and whom the most powerful Catholic king, Charles IV, the most equitable judge of merit, recommended to our Most Holy Lord Pius VI at the very beginning of his accession to the throne, so that you might be enrolled in the sacred college of the most eminent cardinals of the Holy Roman Church.

But Spain will not cease proclaiming these praises—which I do not intend to discuss briefly, so long as any sense of humanity remains alive—and throughout the entire Christian world, so long as the sacred Scriptures endure, your sweet and immortal name will resound.

#### XII

As I reverently approach to kiss the sacred purple, I not only expect one thing from you, most eminent prince, because of your humanity so well known to me; I also request it, and, if you permit, I earnestly press the matter: that, for the sake of your Dracontius, you may receive his editor into your protection and patronage.

The result will surely be that this very modest effort of mine, if I may hope so much, may one day obtain some place, however last, among the proofs of your singular love and goodwill toward cultivators of ecclesiastical disciplines.

## Prolegomena to the Poems of Dracontius

### Chapter One

#### Dracontius’ first mention among the ancients. Saint Isidore’s testimony concerning him. Saint Columbanus borrowed several verses from Dracontius.

#### 1

That the authors of outstanding works live principally in their writings, and that through those writings alone they sometimes come into the public knowledge of mankind, has been confirmed by many examples repeated across different ages.

This may be affirmed to a considerable extent of Dracontius. The ancients left us only a few things about him, and those things are not sufficiently clearly explained. More recent writers, proceeding by conjecture, have added certain details; but some of these can be corrected and others illuminated from the manuscript leaves of Dracontius’ poems that I recently discovered.

For while I was seeking everywhere the poems of the ancient Christian poets, examining them carefully, and diligently collating them with ancient manuscripts, I happened by good fortune upon a poem entitled *On God*, written on parchment under the name of Aurelius Augustine and divided into three books. The first of these contained the *Hexaemeron* of Dracontius, which had long since been published.

I now establish as certain that the beginning of this same first book, as well as the other two books, likewise has Dracontius as its author. Those who weigh the arguments I shall soon bring forward, or read the complete work, will not doubt this.

From this poem some light is shed on the life and circumstances of Dracontius. But much greater illumination comes from the letter to Guntharic, king of the Vandals, which Sirmond and others published in a greatly abridged form and as though it had been written to the emperor Theodosius the Younger.

#### 2

I therefore shall not allow, so far as lies within my power, the remarkable poems of Dracontius to remain longer in darkness. I shall, I think, please those who, as devout lovers of antiquity, prefer the works of ancient writers—especially ecclesiastical writers—to be renewed and illuminated rather than to have some new work composed and brought to light.

I have often reflected deeply with myself on what reason there might be for our preferring ancient writers so greatly to recent ones, although those same ancient writers were themselves new in their own age and loved earlier authors above all others.

That familiar saying about comedies is widely known. Muretus cites it in book XVII, chapter 11 of his *Various Readings* to commend the reading of ancient writers, from the prologue to Plautus’ *Casina*:

> I think those who use old wine are wise,  
> and those who gladly watch old plays.  
> For the new comedies now being made  
> are much worse than new coins.

Nevertheless, this complaint belonged to every age and every nation; Horace, Martial, and others have admirably refuted it.

#### 3

Yet no one can therefore rightly deny that nearly all the monuments transmitted to us through the long succession of centuries ought to be held in the highest honor and esteem.

Since in ancient times writings were disseminated only through the great labor of copyists, we must certainly judge that those manuscripts which were transcribed many years after the authors’ deaths possessed and displayed something capable of earning the praise of posterity.

I fear that many works which are now easily published in print and indeed printed with the greatest magnificence, and thus in a way commended to eternity, will scarcely be endured by anyone’s reading after twelve or fifteen centuries, when gratitude and favor have ceased and it is possible to judge freely.

To this prejudice—which favors all ancient writers whose works survive—there is added, in recommending Dracontius, the high opinion of him formed long ago from his incomplete poem.

#### 4

Since Dracontius flourished at the beginning of the fifth century, when good literature was still flourishing, when a certain particular taste for respectable Latin—especially among poets—remained, and when knowledge of ecclesiastical matters had reached its highest point, I do not doubt that students of both sacred and secular literature will receive my Dracontius with open arms.

I shall say no more about his praises, lest someone quote against me from Lucilius in Aulus Gellius, book III, chapter 14:

> Why not? Even the rag-dealer praises rags for sale,  
> and the dishonest man praises a broken scraper  
> and a half-made sandal.

This could be applied to Dracontius, who is still mutilated in many places and corrupt in many others.

If defense is needed on this matter, I shall summon the antiquarians, who compose lengthy dissertations and substantial volumes from the words of half a decayed ancient inscription. I shall summon the authors of conjectures, probabilities, variant readings, and adversarial notes, who like to discover obscure passages in writers and, for the most part, invent obscurity for themselves so that they may display the sharpness of their intellect.

All this body of men will be ready to assist me, and, as Horace said in *Satires* I.4:

> Just as we compel you,  
> Jew, to join this crowd.

#### 5

But, to carry out what I have undertaken to explain in these prolegomena, we must examine what the ancients once left written about Dracontius and what more recent writers have devised, so that from his writings I may finally determine and demonstrate what should be retained in these accounts and what rejected.

I have found no ancient writer before Isidore who called Dracontius by his proper name.

The name Dracontius does indeed occur in the Theodosian Code, where several laws appear to have been addressed to him in the years 364, 365, and 367, when he was vicar of Africa. On this matter one may consult Gothofredus’ commentary on law 16, *On Years and Tributes*.

But this man is too early to be the author to whom the poems published under the name of Dracontius could be attributed—unless perhaps he composed them in extreme old age. The reason that drives me to reject this possibility is that although Dracontius says much about the sufferings he endured, he says nothing about old age. That would have been especially important for him not to omit, so that he might more easily obtain pardon from the Vandal king and be released from prison.

Julian the archpriest, in the spurious work cited as *Advers.* 498, makes Dracontius the poet and the vicar of Africa the same man. But his authority is worthless and his opinion lacks every probable foundation, as I have said.

#### 6

A certain Dracontius, superintendent of the mint under the emperor Julian, is certainly different from our poet. Ammianus, book XXII, mentions him and relates that he was killed by pagans at Alexandria because he overturned an altar that had recently been set up in the mint over which he presided.

I also agree with Fabricius, who distinguishes this Dracontius from the poet, as well as Dracontius the bishop to whom Saint Athanasius’ letter was addressed, volume I, page 63 of Montfaucon’s edition; see below, number 32. He also distinguishes him from the bishop Dracontius who was deposed by the Acacians and Arians at the Council of Constantinople, discussed by Socrates, book II, chapter 42, and Sozomen, book IV, chapter 24.

In the synodical letter of the Council of Alexandria in the year 362, which Athanasius and the other bishops present at Alexandria from Italy, Arabia, Egypt, and Libya wrote to Eusebius, Lucifer, and others, Dracontius is named among those who wrote with Athanasius.

In the *Life of Saint Hilarion*, written by Saint Jerome, chapter 25, mention is made of Dracontius, a bishop and confessor, who by order of Constantius was exiled to the Thebaid fortress.

All these men—if indeed they are all distinct from one another—separate our Dracontius from them, both in time and in the circumstances of his life, insofar as these can be gathered clearly enough from the poem *On God* and from the *Elegy*.

A Dracontius closer to the age of our poet was the disciple of the abbot Pambo, who is called a remarkable man in Palladius’ *Lausiac History*, chapter 10, and in the *Paradise of Heraclides*, page 940, in Rosweyde’s *Lives of the Fathers*. But this monk also must not be confused with our Dracontius.

In the letters of Saint Nilus, translated by Leo Allatius, book I, letter 314, one letter is said to have been sent to Dracontius; book II, letter 327, to Dracontius Vindix; in the same book II, letter 94, to the monk Dracontius; and book III, letter 36, again to the monk Dracontius.

Montfaucon, in the catalogue of the Coislin Library, manuscript 363, entitles this last letter “To Dracontius the Deacon.” Nilus, the disciple of Saint John Chrysostom, lived under the emperor Theodosius the Younger; but his Dracontii are shown to be different from ours by his poems.

#### 7

Thus Saint Isidore was the first to mention Dracontius, listing him among ecclesiastical writers in chapter 37 in these words:

> Dracontius composed, in heroic verses, a *Hexaemeron* of the creation of the world; and he composed and wrote it brilliantly.

When Isidore wrote this, he seems to have recognized no other poem of Dracontius besides the first book of the poem *On God*, which by that time had been separated from the rest of the work and was entitled *Hexaemeron*. It was already very corrupt, as can be demonstrated from another passage of Isidore.

For in book XII, chapter 2 of the *Etymologies*, he writes:

> The ichneumon is so called in Greek because by its smell both wholesome foods and poisonous ones are revealed. Concerning it Dracontius says: “The pig-like one foretells the power of every poison.” The word *suillus*, “pig-like,” is derived from bristles.

Here the annotator Grialius observes that some read *praecidit*, “cuts off,” instead of *praedicit*, “foretells.” Gallandius, in his edition of Dracontius, infers from the context that *praecidit* is the true reading. But from the context itself I prefer *praedicit*, “foretells.”

In *suillus* there is an obvious error, which Isidore himself did not detect. For Dracontius is not speaking about the ichneumon, but about the Psylli, the peoples of Africa:

> Once the earth has been examined, with no breath of wind at all,  
> while the hisses remain silent and the serpent has not yet been seen,  
> the Psyllus foretells the power of every poison;  
> the physician sees the signs of death, and so forth.

He later concludes:

> Behold, a race of human beings is shown to know what is to come.

### 8.

Isidore, without mentioning Dracontius by name, quoted words from his elegy in Book VI, chapter 9, of the *Etymologies*:

> Wax, the material of letters, nurses of little children;  
> They themselves give boys the beginnings of understanding.

Grialius observes in his notes that this verse is from Book II of Dracontius’ *On the World-Engine* (*De machina mundi*): this is the title he gives to Dracontius’ elegy. From Dracontius’ manuscript codex, however, he read:

> Wax gives boys the beginnings of understanding;  
> From this it results that a letter either helps or harms.

And this is how the passage was subsequently printed in the Sirmondian edition and in the Madrid edition of the *Fathers of Toledo*. The reading *praestet* (“helps” or “excels”) is not objectionable, but I prefer *prosit* (“benefits”), in accordance with the oldest Vatican parchment manuscripts.

From the same elegy of Dracontius I find several other verses borrowed by Saint Columbanus—whom I must name before Saint Isidore—who, just as he borrowed other verses from Prudentius, Octavianus Romanus (as Goldastus believes), and others, also borrowed these from Dracontius in his letter to Hunaldus, which some entitle *Sethus*:

> Time drives all things onward; with time all things are dragged along.  
> The elements alternate their changes, and the seasons change.  
> Days receive their increase, and nights in turn receive theirs.  
> There are seasons of flowers; the harvest retains its own seasons.  
> There are seasons of rejoicing, and there are appointed seasons of sorrow.  
> Spring, summer, autumn, winter: the year returns into the year.  
> Though all things return, a person’s age does not return.

Some of these little verses have already been printed in the Madrid edition of Dracontius’ elegy; others will be found at the end of the same elegy, which I shall rescue from destruction from an old Vatican codex written in letters that have now almost faded away.

In his edition of Dracontius, Sirmond omitted all these verses. Indeed, when he reached the first verse, *Omnia tempus agit* (“Time drives all things onward”), he left the place completely blank and proceeded to print the pentameter, *Tempora sunt vitae* (“There are seasons of life”), etc.; and after adding five further couplets, he ended the letter. He did this either because he found the text so arranged in his own codex or, as I am more inclined to believe, because, when publishing the poems of Saint Columbanus together with those of Dracontius and Eugenius, he thought that verses which he noticed were present in Columbanus ought to be omitted from Dracontius.

That Columbanus took these verses from Dracontius, rather than Dracontius from Columbanus, is demonstrated not only by the chronology of their lives but also by Columbanus himself, who, in Goldastus’ edition, addresses the reader before that letter as follows:

> Since I cannot make them better, I use them as my own;  
> For to alter ancient sayings is sheer impiety.

Compare the note on verse 219 of the *Elegy*, *Omnia tempus agit*, and Book II, verse 44, and Book III, verses 526 and 545, where there are other verses that Columbanus took from Dracontius’ poem *On God*. Goldastus and Patrick Fleming, who published Columbanus’ poems, admit that many verses—and indeed complete verses—of ancient poets are found in him.

### 9.

Nevertheless, I do not number Columbanus among those who explicitly praised Dracontius; nor do I include Solomon II, bishop of Constance, the copyist of Papias and Isidore, according to Rivinus in his note on verse 57 of Dracontius’ letter in his edition. Solomon, he says, transcribed, under the entry *cera* (“wax”), Isidore’s passage in which Dracontius’ verses about wax occur.

I have not seen this Solomon. Papias the lexicographer, under the word *CERA*, quotes only these words from Isidore:

> Wax was the material of letters, which were nurses of little children.

Rivinus conjectured in Isidore that the reading should be *cerae litterarum matrices* (“wax, the matrices of letters”). I would change nothing.

I also now pass over others who at times imitated the same Dracontius; I shall identify them in their proper places. I shall merely point out that Saint Isidore himself appears not to have known whether Dracontius was a deacon, priest, bishop, or layman. For he specified none of these things, as he usually does with others. He was also silent about the man’s homeland, the place where he wrote, and the period in which he lived.

For when certain writers assign Dracontius to the sixth century, as I shall explain in section 30, because Isidore placed him between Avitus and Victor of Tunnuna, they are seriously mistaken. Isidore could not have preserved chronological order where he did not know the dates of the writers; nor, in reality, did he intend to preserve it where he did know when each writer lived—unless we are to say that the order of the chapters in the book *On Illustrious Men* was found reversed in manuscript copies through the negligence or audacity of scribes. Certainly, however, the ancient authors who compiled catalogues of writers were not concerned to maintain a precise chronological order.

## CHAPTER II. Saint Eugenius of Toledo corrected Dracontius’ *Hexaemeron*

### 10.

After Saint Isidore, Dracontius’ memory is preserved by Saint Eugenius of Toledo—whom most foreigners call the second of that name, but whom our writers prefer to call the third. He is indeed the third, for, in addition to the two Eugeniuses who governed the Church of Toledo in the time of the Goths, we must add a first Eugenius, sent from Saint Dionysius in Paris to Toledo. The Churches of Toledo and Paris celebrate his martyrdom, and Ildefonsus the abbot and the author of the *Life of Saint Gerard* mention him, although, while the Goths ruled in Spain, his memory and public observance seem to have been interrupted.

Eugenius, therefore, the third bishop of Toledo, attempted to correct Dracontius’ *Hexaemeron*, perhaps the very copy that Isidore had possessed, or a copy transcribed from it. The reason that moved him to do this will be better understood from his letter, which I append.

### LETTER OF EUGENIUS TO KING CHINDASUINTH

To the illustrious and glorious lord of affairs, Chindasuinth, supreme prince and greatest of kings, Eugenius, the little servant of your faithful subjects.

Most serene prince, while serving the commands of Your Clemency more through willingness than ability, I saw certain little books of a Dracontius entangled in many errors. With Christ the Lord granting strength to the weakness of my understanding, I made corrections in them. I preserved this method: I removed what was superfluous, supplied what was incomplete, strengthened what was broken, and altered what was frequently repeated.

The verses that I thought ought to be removed from this work were indeed tepid in meaning, inelegant in wording, and supported by no sound reasoning. Nor was anything found in them to animate the reader’s mind, to charm the learned reader, or to instruct the unlearned.

And since the author had said nothing at all about the seventh day, the little work seemed to me incomplete if nothing on that subject were included in this booklet. Therefore, at the end of the little book, although in prose, I marked out a recapitulatory account of the six days in individual verses that I had composed long ago; concerning the seventh day, I appended what seemed necessary to say. Thus I completed the royal command—as though not in the way I wished, at least in the way I was able—imploring the most lavish kindness of Your Throne to deign, by your glory, to make acceptable to itself the offering of your faithful little servant, and for wretched me to make the repayment of my labor fruitful through the peaceful contribution of your regard, grace, or favor.

### 11.

The copy of this letter in the Toledo codex, as published by Sirmond in his first Paris edition, agrees perfectly with it, except that the king’s name, at whose command Eugenius undertook Dracontius’ correction, is not given there.

Two other, minor discrepancies are noted. The Toledo codex reads *multis hactenus videns* (“seeing many things up to this point”), and shortly afterward *et crebrius repetita* (“and repeated more frequently”). In the 1677 Lyon edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, the final words read: *contribu . . . . vel favoris*. In the Paris edition of Sirmond’s complete works they read: *contributa gratia vel favoris* (“the grace or favor contributed”). In the copy of the first edition that I use, these words are not clearly visible because of typographical error.

Rivinus, who had seen only Sirmond’s edition, printed *contributio amoris vel favoris* (“the contribution of love or favor”).

Henricus Florez, the distinguished and first author of the *Sacred Spain*, possessed a handwritten copy made by Juan Vázquez del Mármol of excerpts from that Toledo codex. When he saw that the king’s name was absent at the beginning of the letter, he conjectured that the king had been Recceswinth, who took pleasure in the study of sacred literature.

The eminent Cardinal Lorenzana, whom I name here out of respect and whom I shall often have to name in this work, refuted this conjecture splendidly and forcefully in his learned notes on the Fathers of Toledo: first, because the study of sacred literature was shared by Chindasuinth and his son Recceswinth; and secondly, because Sirmond found the name Chindasuinth in a manuscript codex, and it ought therefore to be retained.

I myself believe that Florez either never saw Sirmond’s edition of Dracontius or failed to examine it. For he not only failed to notice that Chindasuinth’s name is expressly given there, but also asserts that the work of Dracontius published by Sirmond is not the *Hexaemeron* as corrected by Eugenius, but another work different from the poem existing in the Azagra codex. He appeals to the authority of Juan Bautista Pérez in his note on chapter 14 of Ildefonsus’ *On Illustrious Men*.

### 12.

First, then, I shall ask Florez how Pérez could have been speaking of the Sirmondian edition when he died in 1597, whereas Sirmond published Dracontius only in 1619.

Next, anyone who considers both editions—the Sirmondian edition and the one that the eminent Cardinal Lorenzana prepared from the Azagra codex—can clearly see that the Dracontius published by Sirmond was genuinely the work corrected by Eugenius.

Thus, when Pérez praised, in chapter 14 of Saint Ildefonsus’ *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 37, Isidore’s account of Dracontius, and added:

> Dracontius, moreover, the poet mentioned here, is said to have been printed long ago, though not as he had been corrected by Eugenius; but I saw this correction of Eugenius in that ancient codex of Ruiz of Azagra, which I mentioned above,

the eminent Cardinal Lorenzana added:

> And this Dracontius, as corrected by Eugenius, has been published several times: first by the most learned Sirmond, then in the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, and finally by us here among the other works of Saint Eugenius, reprinted above.

Florez may perhaps have been misled by the fact that Nicolás Antonio, in *Bibliotheca vetus*, volume I, book V, chapter 5, did not explain clearly enough that the editions preceding the Sirmondian edition lacked the letter, the metrical prologue, and Eugenius’ recapitulatory passage appended to Dracontius’ work. In book III, chapter 3, after recounting from Ildefonsus that Dracontius’ *Hexaemeron* had been corrected by Eugenius and enlarged with a recapitulation and an appendix on the seventh day, he added:

> This revised work first appeared at Paris from the library of Saint Victor.

Cardinal Aguirre himself, who prepared the edition of the *Bibliotheca vetus*, added a marginal note to book V, chapter 5, saying that he possessed from a Toledo manuscript codex Eugenius’ letter to the king—“perhaps Recceswinth,” he says, “or Chindasuinth”—a preface to the same work written in verse, and a recapitulation appended to the end of Dracontius’ book. By this he sufficiently indicates that he had not seen Sirmond’s edition, in which all these materials occur and the name of King Chindasuinth is placed before the letter.

As far as chronology is concerned, the letter could have been addressed to either king. But regarding the name Chindasuinth, which is derived from Sirmond’s ancient codex, there should be no doubt—unless some doubt should arise as to whether that name is truly found written in ancient letters in any codex.

### 13.

Here I shall say what I think about Sirmond and about many other critics of the preceding and earlier centuries. But I shall first say that I esteem Sirmond as highly as I do very few others. In the maturity of his exact judgment and in this more sacred and more agreeable learning, I place no one above him.

I am also greatly delighted by his calm and even style of expression, even in controversies; from it I would infer, even if I knew nothing else, that he possessed a gentle and tranquil spirit.

But for that reason one should not immediately accept without examination everything he presents in such a way that it might seem to have been taken from an ancient manuscript. I shall pass over certain tolerable lapses of attention, which human nature cannot entirely avoid.

What I do not approve is that Sirmond and others often brought ancient writings to light without explaining more fully what appeared in the parchment manuscripts and what had been added by themselves—whether to correct, supplement, or clarify them—and sometimes without even indicating where the codices were preserved.

They acted in good faith and without concern for posterity; but we often encounter difficulties from which we cannot extricate ourselves because, although they could have done so, they did not make the way clear.

For this reason Ruinart’s diligence deserves praise. When he obtained the manuscript codex that Sirmond had used in publishing the *Notice of the Provinces and Cities of Africa*, he not only restored the ancient title but also employed the wording of the codex in places, omitting Sirmond’s interpretation or restoration, although it appeared probable to him.

### 14.

Some assert that Sirmond published those writers from a manuscript codex of the Parisian library of Saint Victor. Nicolás Antonio seems to suggest this in the passage cited from the *Bibliotheca vetus*, or at least to provide an opportunity for error.

Andreas Rivinus remained uncertain in his edition of Dracontius:

> Sirmond, he says, published Dracontius . . . undoubtedly from that Spanish copy of Azagra, unless perhaps from the Vatican copy itself . . . .

As I understand it, Rivinus thought that Dracontius had been printed from the work of Michael Ruiz of Azagra.

Nothing of this sort can be inferred from Sirmond himself. In the list of works he was publishing together in 1619, after the names of Eugenius, Dracontius, Martin of Braga, and Columbanus—without clearly stating where he obtained them—he adds only:

> The doctrine of Bishop Severinus, from the royal library and the monastery of Theologia. The confession of Prosper of Aquitaine, from the Vatican.

The same wording is repeated in the 1697 Paris edition of Sirmond’s complete works, prepared by Jacques de la Baune, volume II. The editor merely notes beside the word *Theologiensis*:

> Now Tholey, a monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict on the River Saar, in the territory of Lorraine and the diocese of Trier.

I have been able to discover nothing else either from the Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum* of 1677, where Dracontius’ works were reprinted from Sirmond’s edition, or from the Venetian edition of Sirmond’s complete works published in 1728.

### 15.

In the Parisian library of Saint Victor, Montfaucon lists a *Draconicium*, which is our Dracontius. But since a mutilated Dracontius emerged from that library in 1560, without the letter, the metrical prologue, or Eugenius’ recapitulatory passage, we must believe that this imperfect codex is still preserved in that library, and not another codex to which Sirmond conformed his edition.

I have nothing to bring forward concerning the library of the monastery of Theologia. I am more certain that Sirmond prepared his edition of Eugenius and Dracontius from a codex in the royal library of Paris, which I shall describe in section 46. The author of the catalogue of the manuscript codices of that library either suggests this or expressly asserts it.

It remains to be investigated, however, whether Eugenius’ letter to King Chindasuinth was written in the ancient script of that codex, or whether it was added in this form by some more recent person on the basis of conjecture, or appended by Sirmond for purposes of explanation.

It must be observed that nowhere in the entire work is there a note by Sirmond from which one could know whether he altered or corrected any obscure or corrupt word. Who, then, could persuade himself that the codex was written exactly as Sirmond published it?

I readily believe that Sirmond ventured nothing except for a just reason or on the basis of a probable conjecture. But it is important for us to know what must be held with certainty from the authority of the manuscripts and what may reasonably be accepted from the conjectures of editors.

How many words of some ancient writer do we commonly present as established when perhaps they are not his at all, but belong to the first editor, who supplied, explained, or corrected a mutilated, difficult, or corrupted passage on his own authority? Yet most editors of this kind cannot be compared with Sirmond.

What I have argued here is not intended to reject the name Chindasuinth, but to conclude that it should be retained cautiously, until something else is established. I also intend to encourage Spanish scholars to seek out and collate more diligently any other codices of Dracontius that may still exist.

### 16.

Eugenius’ letter makes clear what he accomplished in correcting Dracontius. Some think that Eugenius did nothing more than correct a codex corrupted by age and by the negligence of scribes.

But his words imply something else:

> I removed what was superfluous, supplied what was incomplete, strengthened what was broken, and altered what was frequently repeated.

This is also shown by what he adds concerning the verses he removed, because they were “tepid in meaning, inelegant in wording, and supported by no sound reasoning,” and because nothing was found in them “to animate the reader, to charm the learned, or to instruct the unlearned.”

We shall shortly see whether everyone approved Eugenius’ judgment.

He himself was not unaware that this method of proceeding could expose him to criticism; consequently, in a second preface, he takes pains to excuse himself. Ancient writers sometimes used to place two prefaces before their books, especially before poems.

This can be seen in Martial; for this reason I noted on page 232, in connection with Prudentius, that such a preface was simply called a letter. Statius confirms this in the preface to Book II of the *Silvae*.

Among Christian poets, Prudentius adorned the *Apotheosis* with two poetic prologues. Juvencus is published with only one prologue; but in a very ancient Vatican manuscript, the Royal Swedish codex no. 333, I found two clearly distinguished prefaces composed in hexameters. Before the first appears *Here begins the preface*, and after it has been completed, likewise *Preface*.

I shall follow this codex in the edition of Juvencus that I am preparing, revised against ancient codices and editions and illustrated with continuous notes.

Arator prefixed two elegies to the *Acts of the Apostles*. But since one was addressed to Florianus the abbot and the other to Vigilius the bishop, and since both serve as dedicatory letters, I think that Arator gave one copy to Vigilius with the letter addressed to him and another to Florianus with the letter addressed to him.

Even now, some people fortify their works with two dedicatory letters, either following the custom of the ancients or moved by some other consideration.

Some attribute three prefaces to Sedulius: the first, in prose, addressed to Boniface; the second, in elegiac verse, in which he speaks about his *Paschal Work*; and the third, called the *Dedication to Theodosius Augustus*.

But I have found this *Dedication* in none of the Vatican codices—of which there are many belonging to Sedulius or concerning him—and Sedulius followed the laws of meter in a different way.

### 17.

Led by these examples of ancient poets, Eugenius appended a second preface to the first, in which he excuses himself for having corrected Dracontius’ poem. It reads as follows in both the Sirmondian and Madrid editions, without any discrepancy, and is reproduced here by us:

> Little book, when you go to behold the illustrious face of the prince,  
> At whose command you have deserved to be cleansed of filth  
> And, after a long time, to receive a shining robe,  
> When you begin to approach the threshold of the royal palace  
> And behold the seat radiant with gleaming gold,  
> Begin at once to pay abundant thanks  
> That you are held corrected, free from the cloud of errors.  
> Then, prostrate on the ground, ask pardon with entreaty,  
> And stand as the skillful advocate of your bearer.  
> May he pardon—may he pardon with a kindly mind—  
> That, while I strive to wash you properly, somewhat soiled,  
> My hand, thinning you out, has polished you by pressing too harshly.  
>   
> But if some commoner, scorched by envy, should say:  
> “And who is this who alters the poems of the ancients?  
> He who writes empty epigrams in slight little books?”  
> Let him know this for himself: no fault is imputed  
> That is nowhere judged a fault which one sees to be not voluntary, but compelled by a greater command.  
> Finally, when good commands are being proclaimed for execution,  
> The wise man fulfills them; the madman wishes to despise them.  
>   
> If Virgil and Homer, greatest of poets,  
> Deserved after death to undergo a new censorship,  
> Imposed by Aristarchus, Tucca, Varius, and Probus,  
> Why should he disdain that, ordered by a great prince,  
> I, little Eugenius, have prepared the slight poems of Dracontius’ little book  
> And cleansed them of their mass of trifles?

### 18.

In verse 17, the phrase *quam non velle videt* (“which he sees not to be willing”) is obscure. Perhaps Eugenius wrote *velle meum* (“my willingness”), *velle suum* (“his willingness”), or *velle jubet* (“he orders willingness”). Christian poets use *velle* for “will” or “volition,” and *posse* for “power” or “ability.” See Dracontius, Book I, verse 367: *Velle pares, et nolle pares* (“equal in willing and equal in refusing”).

The rest proceeds reasonably well, except that he frequently lengthens a short syllable merely for the sake of the caesura.

Rivinus, in his emendations, I do not know why, corrected verse 3 from *Et capere nitidam longo* (“and to receive a shining robe after a long time”) to *Et nitidum capere longo* (“and to receive the shining one after a long time”). In the same place, verse 14, he replaced *et quis est* (“and who is he?”) with *et quisnam est* (“and who, then, is he?”). But it should not seem surprising in Eugenius that he lengthened *quis*, and *quisnam est* is a cold expression in this passage.

In Rivinus, *nitidum* appears to be an error for *nitidam*. The first syllable of *Draconti* ought to be shortened if the etymology of the name is considered; but Christian poets claimed great license for themselves in proper names.

The phrase *summus vatum* (“greatest of poets”) should also be noted, as in Prudentius, *Psychomachia*, verse 530, *magnus discipulorum* (“great among the disciples”), or, as many read it, *summus discipulorum* (“greatest among the disciples”).

It is handed down in the *Life of Virgil* circulated under Donatus’ name that Tucca and Varius, at Augustus’ command, lightly corrected Virgil’s *Aeneid*, and did so without adding anything or completing imperfect verses. Marcus Valerius Probus wrote notes on Virgil’s *Bucolics* and *Georgics*.

In his emendations, Rivinus changed *Tucca, Variusque, Probusque* to *Variusque et Tucca probusque*. He seems to wish *probus* to be taken as an adjective agreeing with *Tucca*. But in that case, what would the two conjunctions mean in *et Tucca probusque*?

Aristarchus corrected Homer’s verses in such a way that he denied that those he did not approve were Homer’s. Others exercised censorship over Homer more openly; and some even think that so many corrections by others were made in his works that they should be regarded as the product of many authors rather than of one.

In the celebrated controversy concerning the corruption of ancient books, a considerable difficulty may arise from this circumstance: many thought they were permitted to reshape the works of others into a better form—that is, if we speak plainly, to corrupt them.

Nor should we believe that all who corrected the writings of the ancients possessed Eugenius’ candid intention, or were moved by so plausible a reason that they did not blush to confess their boldness.

From this very preface, however, it may rightly be inferred that even then it was considered blameworthy to interpolate the codices of ancient writers without just cause:

> And who is this who alters the poems of the ancients?

It would certainly be intolerable if the writings of the ancients were altered in such a way that a codex were published under the name of a particular author without any indication that another person had corrected it.

### 19.

Eugenius not only corrected Dracontius’ poem but also added a recapitulation and a supplement concerning the seventh day, because without some mention of the seventh day the work seemed to him, as he himself says, *semum* (“incomplete”), or, as Ildefonsus says in Eugenius’ eulogy, *semiplenum* (“half-complete”).

In fact, in Dracontius’ complete poem, as I publish it, there was no reason why the seventh day should be included.
