Since Dracontius’ aim was to proclaim God’s goodness toward human beings and his justice—above all his goodness—he carefully described in Book I the creation of humanity and everything God did for human beings during those first six days, because he could greatly illuminate his argument through the work of the six days. Then, in the remaining two books, he pursued other works of God from the Old and New Testaments in the same sense.

In Book I itself, and in the very portion of that book which Eugenius revised, Dracontius went far beyond the sixth day. For he describes the first parents already placed in paradise, their sin, and God’s sentence tempered by mercy and justice, by which they were expelled from paradise; but at the same time nature was commanded, for their benefit, to carry out its works through marvelous and varied changes of things. On this occasion he expounds the resurrection of the human body by examples drawn from nature.

### 20.

Eugenius had composed Dracontius’ recapitulation on his own initiative before the king assigned him the task of correcting Dracontius. Many such recapitulations of ancient poems exist, namely, brief summaries of their contents expressed in a few verses.

The Greeks call them *periochae*. Examples include those written by Ausonius for Homer’s *Iliad*, by Sulpicius Apollinaris for Terence’s comedies, and several for Virgil’s *Georgics* and *Aeneid*, as may be seen in the *Collectio Pisana veterum poetarum*, volume IV, pages 472 and following, and in Burmann’s *Anthology*.

In Christian poets, *periochae* are not so common. In the Vatican Library, Palatine codex no. 1717 contains Arator’s works. I collated it with other manuscripts, and in it are found two rhythmic verses at the beginning of each chapter, presenting its subject.

Peter of Riga’s *Aurora* also contains recapitulations of both Testaments, which Leyser published from manuscripts in *Historia Poetarum Medii Aevi*, page 703. This is the Peter of Riga who was called *Aurorarius* from his work *Aurora*, which remains for the most part unpublished, although many have promised a complete edition.

In Rome it could be brought to completion very successfully, for many manuscript codices of his work are found not only in the Vatican Library but also in the archive of the Vatican Basilica of Saint Peter and in other libraries of the city.

While looking for something else, I came upon a codex in the Vatican Library that I found much fuller than the codices cited by Fabricius in the *Bibliotheca Latina mediae et infimae aetatis*. From it it is clearly established that the poems on the New Testament are the work of this same Peter, a point that many had called into question.

### 21.

I shall therefore now append Eugenius’ recapitulation, together with his supplement to Dracontius. I have decided to reproduce in these prolegomena everything Eugenius wrote about Dracontius, and this seems an appropriate place for it; perhaps another more suitable opportunity will not arise.

The variant readings observed in Dracontius’ work as corrected by Eugenius and in the Vatican parchment manuscripts will be presented more appropriately beneath the individual verses themselves.

> The first day in the world took up the beginnings of light;  
> The second fixed the heaven in its resplendent regions;  
> The third gave the wave-covered sea together with earth’s offspring;  
> The fourth has Phoebus, the moon, and the stars of heaven;  
> The fifth, feather-bearing birds and swimming fish;  
> The sixth, four-footed creatures, creeping things, and intelligent human beings;  
> The seventh is rest for the Lord, these things having been duly completed.  
>   
> Not because the Almighty labors at his tasks in human fashion,  
> Or, wearied, seeks at last to rest,  
> He who is always at rest in his activity and rests while creating;  
> But because sacred rest, covered with symbolic figures,  
> Performs many things through signs and reveals mysteries to us.  
>   
> God’s rest was so called because, for things rightly to be created,  
> It itself was the measure and the greatest end of all:  
> For whatever new things are made are then shown to have been begun.  
>   
> God’s rest was so called because Christ, our redemption,  
> Coming in the flesh and releasing the bonds of the flesh,  
> Rested on this returning day through a blessed death.  
>   
> God’s rest was so called because, after a thousand labors,  
> He alone, fostering us everywhere, compels us to rest in him;  
> Nor is any rest granted to the wretched unless he himself receives them.  
>   
> It was also called rest because, after six ages,  
> During which the world proceeds in order,  
> The present activity of the world rests, receiving eternal leisure in peace.  
>   
> It was also called rest because it is our final lot.  
> For the course of life is like the mass of the world.  
> There are six ages for a human being, but the seventh is death.  
>   
> The first contains the origin of the race: simple infancy;  
> The second, following, is called tender childhood;  
> The third that follows is itself called adulthood;  
> The fourth bears the splendid support of virtue: youth;  
> The fifth is burdensome old age, declining toward its final times;  
> The sixth is decrepitude, which ends the span of life.  
>   
> This, supreme king, compelled by your lordly command,  
> Your little servant Eugenius has dedicated to you with devoted mind.

### 22.

Sirmond placed these verses after Dracontius’ letter and prefixed them with this title:

> Monostichs of the recapitulation of the seventh day, to be appended by Blessed Eugenius at the end of Dracontius’ book.

The opening words, *Monosticha recapitulationis septimi diei*, seem to have been taken from the codex, as may be inferred from the catalogue of the royal library of Paris.

In the Azagra codex, *septem dierum* (“of the seven days”) is more correctly read in place of *septimi diei* (“of the seventh day”), unless the title should instead be read:

> Monostichs of the recapitulation of the six days, and supplement of the seventh day.

Most such inscriptions belong to scribes, not authors. Eugenius himself says in his letter to the king:

> I marked out a recapitulation of the six days in individual verses that I had composed long ago, and concerning the seventh day I appended what seemed necessary to say.

From this, the following title could have been extracted:

> Recapitulation of the six days, and appendix of the seventh.

Although Sirmond, perhaps following his own codex, placed the recapitulation after Dracontius’ letter, the place designated by Eugenius seems to me to have been after the end of the *Hexaemeron*, that is, after Book I of Dracontius’ poem *On God*. For one cannot say that he confused Dracontius’ letter with the poem on the work of the six days, unless he happened to encounter a very corrupt and depraved codex.

In the codex of the Parisian library that I shall catalogue in section 47, only the *Hexaemeron*, or Book I in heroic verse, is indicated; Eugenius’ supplement is added to it, without any mention of the letter.

The letter itself, as published by Sirmond and in the *Collection of the Fathers of Toledo*, plainly demonstrates, if one examines it carefully, that it has nothing to do with the poem about the six days.

It is certain that Eugenius’ recapitulation was appended at the end of the little book in which Dracontius had treated the *Hexaemeron*. This is why it is called a recapitulation.

In sacred Scripture, *recapitulation* is the term used when Scripture returns to something whose narration has already passed, as Isidore explains after Tichonius and Augustine in Book I, chapter 109, of the *Sentences*. Tertullian uses the verb *recapitulate* in approximately this sense in Book V, chapter 17, *Against Marcion*, and Commodianus does so in poem 41.

But since Eugenius says that he corrected Dracontius’ little books, and Ildefonsus confirms this, it seems certain that not only the *Hexaemeron* but also Dracontius’ letter was corrected, while the appropriate distinction between the *Hexaemeron* and the *Elegy* was preserved.

Indeed, what Eugenius says about certain verses having been removed applies more to the letter than to the *Hexaemeron*, as will be clear to anyone who compares them.

### 23.

Eugenius asserts that he composed long ago the verses comprising the recapitulation. But it is not established whether he wrote them to indicate the subject of Dracontius’ work or merely to summarize the creation of the world from Genesis in a few verses.

The latter view appeals to me more. Among Eugenius’ other poems, Book I, no. 19, contains a *Heptameter on the Beginning of the World*, namely, the first seven verses of the recapitulation.

In Vatican Alexandrian codex no. 2078, of the ninth century, several poems of Eugenius are copied after other works under this title:

> Here begins the little work of Blessed Eugenius, bishop.

The sixth poem is this very *Heptameter on the Beginning of the World*.

In the catalogue of the manuscript codices of the Florentine Laurentian Library, volume II, column 752, Bandini records, among miscellaneous works written in the tenth or eleventh century:

> Seven verses on the days, or monostichs on the seven days of the week.

These differ from Eugenius’ verses, as is clear from their first verse:

> The first day, sacred to Phoebus by divine power, shines.

The difference is even more clearly observed in Vatican Urbinate codex 584, formerly 828, where, after many other verses, poems by various authors concerning the year, months, weeks, and so forth are inserted.

The first is *On the Seven Days of the Week*, and its first verse is more correctly written than in the Florentine codex:

> The first day shines, sacred by the name of Phoebus.

For the subject is the days of the week, which retain their names from the gods of the pagans.

### 24.

The following points should be noted in Eugenius’ verses.

In verse 6, Sirmond printed *hominesque fugaces* (“and fleeting human beings”). But he himself had printed *hominesque sagaces* (“and intelligent human beings”) among Eugenius’ poems in the *Heptameter on the Seven Days*, and *hominesque sagaces* is also found in the Toledo codex, in the Vatican codex, and in the work of Bridefert of Ramsey on Bede, volume II, page 70, where the first seven verses are quoted. This is the correct reading, for *sagax* is used of a participant in reason and of one who possesses insight.

Helpidius, in his poem *On the Beneficence of Jesus Christ*:

> Content, and our race with discerning reason, …

And to have fortified [it] with a strong hand. Cicero, *De finibus* II, chapter 14: “Human beings differ very greatly from beasts in this respect: they possess reason given by nature, and a mind both keen and vigorous, swiftly considering many things and, so to speak, discerning.” In verses 8 and 9, I think *laboret / Actibus aut fessus* should be punctuated distinctly. After verse 12, *Multa gerat*, the three verses that follow are absent from Sirmond, but were added from the Toledo manuscript in the Madrid edition. In verse 24, the Toledo manuscript reads *otia praecipiens* (“prescribing leisure”). In verse 26, Rivinus conjecturally read:

> For, in the course of life, after the pattern of the worldly mass,  
> There are six ages.

and so forth. But the manuscript reading should be retained. In verse 27, the Toledo manuscript has *aetates hominum* (“the ages of human beings”). In verse 29, Sirmond printed: “Then a second, tender childhood is held.” Rivinus read: “Then a second, tender childhood of a human being is held,” but in the errata corrected it to: “Then a second age, childhood, is held,” because, as he says, some such little word was missing. The Toledo manuscript has *loco* (“in place”). In verse 31, instead of *opem* (“help”), I would read *opus* (“work”). Dracontius, book II, verse 114: “That he might perform the work of virtue”; and book III, verse 211: “He completed the work of virtue.” In verse 32, Sirmond has *gravis ad ultima* (“grave toward the final [age]”); the Toledo manuscript is better, *gravis et in ultima* (“grave and in the final [age]”); one might also read *gravis et ad ultima* (“grave and toward the final [age]”). In verse 33, Eugenius correctly distinguishes *senium* (“extreme old age”) from *senectus* (“old age”). Isidore, book I of the *Differentiae*: “Old age is the more burdensome period that follows youth. Extreme old age, however, is the final period that comes after the burdensome one.” Nevertheless, Isidore, book XI of the *Origines*, chapter 2, counts the six ages of human life differently: he makes the sixth *senectus*, of which *senium* is the final part. Compare the note on verse 223 of the elegy. In any case, the comparison of the six days with the six ages of the world is taken from Saint Augustine, book I of *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*. In the final verse I would prefer *dicavi* (“I have dedicated”).

## CHAPTER III. Saint Ildefonsus’s judgment concerning Dracontius, whose work was corrected by Saint Eugenius. Dracontius’s work recorded in a tenth-century catalogue of books

25. I now proceed to Saint Ildefonsus, who, in his eulogy of Saint Eugenius, praised the correction of Dracontius carried out by him. It will not be unpleasant to hear the entire eulogy. Thus he writes in chapter 14 of *On Illustrious Men*:

> Likewise Eugenius, another [man] after Eugenius the bishop, was appointed as his successor. When he was an outstanding cleric of the royal church, he took pleasure in the life of a monk. Fleeing with discerning purpose, he sought the city of Zaragoza; there he clung to the tombs of the martyrs, and there he fittingly maintained both his studies of wisdom and his monastic vocation. Hence, recalled by the ruler’s force and summoned to the episcopate, he led a life marked more by the merits of his virtues than by bodily strength. For he was thin in body and small in physical power, but his spirit burned intensely with the strength of virtue, pursuing the force of good studies. He corrected chants corrupted by the worst practices through his knowledge of melody, and arranged the neglected orders and oversight of the offices.
>
> He wrote a little book on the Holy Trinity, polished in expression and clear in the truth of its subject; it could have been sent without delay to the regions of Libya and the East, had not storm-tossed seas delayed the uncertain journey of frightened travelers. He also wrote two little books, one composed in various poetic meters, the other in prose composed of diverse material; by these he was able to commend his holy memory enduringly to the industry of many.
>
> He also took the little books of Dracontius on the Creation of the World, which antiquity had handed down corrupted, and, by removing, altering, or conjecturally improving whatever he found unsuitable, forced them into such a form of beauty that they seem to have proceeded more beautifully from the craft of the corrector than from the author’s hand. And because that same Dracontius, by remaining entirely silent about the seventh day, seemed to have left his work incomplete, Eugenius also noted in individual little verses a recapitulation of the six days and added, concerning the seventh day, what seemed to him elegantly expressed.
>
> He was prominent in the times of the kings Chindaswinth and Recceswinth, holding for nearly twelve years both the dignity and the glory of the priesthood; and thus, after the setting of the world’s light, he holds a burial place in the basilica of Saint Leocadia.

26. Much can also be added to this eulogy for illuminating the life of Eugenius from his *Life*, which the most eminent Lorenzana placed before his minor works. I discussed the tombs of the martyrs of Zaragoza in my note on Prudentius’s *Peristephanon* 4, which concerns the eighteen martyrs of Zaragoza. By Ildefonsus’s phrase *principali violentia* (“the ruler’s force”), he means the command of the prince or king. Eugenius called it a royal decree, and in the Eighth Council of Toledo the words of the law promulgated by Recceswinth are: “We promulgate the decree of royal observance.” Velleius, Tacitus, Pliny, Prudentius, and others likewise use *principalis* in this sense.

Some minor discrepancies may be noted in Sirmond’s edition, such as the phrase at the end, *tenet habitationem sepulcri* (“he holds a burial place”). Nicolás Antonio suspects that *meliora conficiendo* (“by producing better things”) should be read instead of *meliora conjiciendo* (“by conjecturally improving things”). Ildefonsus’s judgment, however—that Dracontius’s little books seem to have proceeded “more beautifully from the craft of the corrector than from the author’s hand”—did not please Nicolás Antonio. Speaking of Ildefonsus in volume I, book V, chapter 5 of the *Bibliotheca vetus*, he says:

> The very direct observation (*αὐτοψία*, “personal inspection”) of this most holy man’s judgment concerning both poets detracts no little from it, for it shows abundantly how much each of them possessed in the ability to compose poetry, when one also considers the barbarous age under which Eugenius was born.

He had said the same thing, in exactly the same words, in book III, chapter 3, but added certain expressions, namely “and of the age, and of the society of the barbarian people amid which he was born,” and so forth. Dracontius, however, had come into the world in more fortunate times, under Roman rule. Someone might call this criticism overly free; no one could call it false.

Barthius, indeed, in *Adversaria* book LV, chapter 11, writes concerning Eugenius’s correction:

> Would that Eugenius had also published Dracontius’s little books in their entirety, so that the method of his alterations might be known to posterity. For what he now reproachfully calls tepid, inelegant, unsupported by any reasoning, might perhaps seem beautiful, pleasing, and learned to us, even though it was not tightly constructed, faulty, bloodless, anxious, and altogether nothing—except insofar as an unfair judge of everything plain and easy wanted and forced it to be so, to our irreparable loss.

Saint Isidore’s testimony also works against Ildefonsus’s judgment, for Isidore testifies that Dracontius composed and wrote the *Hexaemeron* elegantly. Who would not prefer Isidore’s authority to Ildefonsus’s criticism? I have no doubt that Dracontius is far preferable to Eugenius, whether we examine the *Hexaemeron* interpolated by Eugenius, or Dracontius’s poem as it is read in the Vatican manuscripts, and still more when we carefully consider the letter, which has suffered less corruption from scribal negligence.

27. After Saint Ildefonsus, no ancient writer comes to mind who mentions Dracontius, except one: Honorius of Autun, who, as is his custom, copied this from Isidore in book II, chapter 28:

> Dracontius composed the *Hexaemeron of the Creation of the World* in heroic verses.

What is relevant here, however, is the catalogue of manuscript codices preserved in the monastery of Bobbio, which appears to have been copied in the tenth century and is found in Muratori, volume III of the *Italian Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, page 818. This catalogue lists the books that Dungal and others had given to the most blessed Columbanus—that is, to the monastery of Bobbio itself, founded by Saint Columbanus. But before these, other codices are mentioned which seem to have belonged to the monastery’s older library, and perhaps most of them to have been there from the time when it was founded.

Among these older books the catalogue records:

> One book of Lucretius; one book of Dracontius; one book of Ennodius, containing other little works as well; three books of Donatus; etc.

“One book” of Dracontius, like “one book” of Lucretius, means one codex, whether the poems were divided into several books or contained in a single one. Similarly, the three books of Donatus are three codices of Donatus’s work.

I already observed in section 8 that Saint Columbanus had borrowed several verses from Dracontius; shortly afterward, in the following section, I shall report that at the end of the fifteenth century Dracontius’s work was found in the monastery of Bobbio. These facts agree remarkably with the ancient codex of that monastery’s library. It is not appropriate here to recount what is written about Dracontius in the chronicles of Dexter, Maximus, and Haubert, and in the *Adversaria* of Julian the archpriest. For although the names are ancient, the authors who fabricated these works are recent, and therefore they belong to the following chapter.

## CHAPTER IV. Dracontius’s memory revived among recent writers, and differing opinions concerning him

28. In the fifteenth century, when literature had begun to be restored, ancient books were being sought everywhere. The matter concerning Dracontius that I recently mentioned belongs to the end of that century, and is reported by Raphael Volaterranus in book IV of his *Commentaries*. Concerning the monastery of Bobbio, situated on the ridges of the Apennines and built by Theodelinda, queen of the Lombards, he says:

> In the year 1494 books of this kind were found here: Rutilius … various works of Dracontius, the hymns of Prudentius, and so forth. A good part of them has recently been brought to Rome by my fellow citizen Thomas Phaedrus (Inghirami), a professor of the liberal arts.

It would be most desirable if this various work of Dracontius, should it still lie hidden somewhere, whether in Milan or Rome, were brought into public light. For this appears to be that very ancient codex mentioned in the tenth-century catalogue of the library of the monastery of Bobbio, and perhaps it is the very one used by Saint Columbanus. Its title suggests that it contains not only the *Hexaemeron* interpolated by Eugenius. Moreover, among the verses that Columbanus took from Dracontius are some that are missing from the Toledo manuscript and that we shall publish from the Vatican parchment manuscripts.

29. Guilielmus Morelius, who first published Dracontius’s *Hexaemeron*, says only this in his dedicatory letter:

> The works of Hilary, Cyprian, and Dracontius that follow were supplied to us by the library of Saint Victor in Paris … The exemplar that we used was disturbed and confused in many of its parts, so that it should not seem surprising if some passages are not free from corruption. To remove such corruption, I applied all the diligence I could; nevertheless, I preferred to present complete passages, in the form in which the book contained them, for others to judge, rather than to exhibit them contaminated by any emendation of mine.

Morelius entitled the work: “Dracontius, *On the Work of the Six Days*.” Some folio seems to have been missing from this codex, for altogether 58 verses are absent, in which the sin of the first parents is described. That these verses existed before Saint Eugenius is demonstrated by Saint Isidore, who, in book XII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 2, quotes one of them, omitted in Morelius’s Paris edition.

The question is whether the poem *On the Work of the Six Days*, published at Paris by Morelius, is the very work interpolated by Eugenius, or rather the original work as it proceeded from Dracontius, with only those errors that arose through scribal carelessness. In a letter to Weitzius, Goldastus thinks that this *Hexaemeron* of Morelius, which Weitzius himself intended to publish, is Dracontius’s very *Ἀρχέτυπον* (“archetype,” or original text). He is moved to this conclusion because in that *Hexaemeron* there is neither the slightest trace nor any vestige of the recapitulation of the six days or of the supplement concerning the seventh day.

He believes that these sections are missing before verse 449, *Vomere non tellus* (“Not the earth with the ploughshare”), where the description of the garden of Eden begins. For the other poets of the *Hexaemeron*—Cyprian, whom some now hold to be Juvencus; Hilary; Victor; Alcimus; Gregory the Great; Ambrose the Younger; Pisides; Theodulf of Orléans; Nicephorus Callistus; Peter of Riga; and others—treat the seventh day in the same manner. Compare the note on verse 116 of book I.

Barthius disagrees in *Adversaria* book VII, chapter 20, arguing from the style of the entire little work that it has two authors. “Certainly,” he says,

> this repetitive (*ταυτόλογον*, “tautological”) little work, by no means consistent with itself in developing its narrative, already extends almost to its end, inserting one abrupt section after another in places that do not belong to them.

But Barthius said this because he knew that Dracontius’s little books had once been reworked by Eugenius. I should like to know what someone entirely free from this preconceived opinion, and unaware of what had happened, would think. Nicolás Antonio in *Bibliotheca vetus*, book V, chapter 5, and Gallandius in volume IX of his *Bibliotheca* also adopted Barthius’s opinion.

To settle this controversy, the variant readings of Morelius’s edition, Sirmond’s edition, and our edition from the Vatican codex must be compared with one another. As for me, after considering the Vatican codex and all Dracontius’s works, I approve Goldastus’s opinion. At the same time, however, it is remarkable that so few and slight alterations appear between Dracontius’s archetypal *Hexaemeron* and the same work interpolated by Eugenius.

I therefore think that not only the *Hexaemeron* but also Dracontius’s *Elegy* was revised by Eugenius. In the latter, some verses were added by Eugenius and more were removed, as will become clear from our edition. Goldastus, who had not seen Eugenius’s preface, said that the supplement concerning the seventh day was missing before the description of paradise. But since Eugenius wished to add a recapitulation and supplement at the end of the little work, Goldastus’s reasoning must be reformulated as follows: at the end of Morelius’s exemplar there is no recapitulation and no supplement by Eugenius; therefore this exemplar must be regarded as Dracontius’s original work.

30. Fabricius followed Morelius’s edition in his *Collection of Christian Poets*. Although he was accustomed to compare other poets with ancient books, he did not do so in the case of Dracontius, since he lacked manuscript codices. In his *Commentary*, page 45, he says:

> Dracontius was a Christian poet, but it is unknown from what people or country he came. His poem *Hexaemeron*, that is, *On the Work of the Creation of the Six Days*, is learned and distinguished. We have added to this work the edition published at Paris from the library of Saint Victor, correcting three or four errors made by the printer.

In fact, among the ancients there is profound silence concerning Dracontius’s country and people. Johannes Vasaeus, in his *Chronicle* under the year 651, where he begins to speak of Saint Eugenius, says that Dracontius appears to have been a Spaniard, insofar as this can be inferred from Saint Isidore, and to have flourished in the time of the emperor Justinian and Athanagild, king of the Goths.

But from Isidore’s words, which are given in section 7, I do not know how anyone could infer that Dracontius was a Spaniard or flourished in the sixth century. Since Vasaeus himself confirms that Eugenius restored Dracontius’s *Hexaemeron*, already corrupted by age, to its original purity, he ought to have considered Dracontius somewhat earlier. For Eugenius corrected Dracontius in the seventh century, around the year 645.

Many others embraced Vasaeus’s opinion, including Johannes Grialius, in his 1599 Madrid edition of Isidore, *Etymologies* book XII, chapter 2, where he expressly says:

> Dracontius composed the *Work of the Six Days* in verse during the reign of Athanagild. Eugenius III, archbishop of Toledo, under Chindaswinth and Recceswinth, both corrected this poem and enlarged it with verses concerning the seventh day.

As for the period in which Dracontius lived, there is a notable error in Gerardus Johannes Vossius, chapter 9 of his book *On Latin Poets*. He lists Dracontius among poets of uncertain date and places him after Charlemagne, around the year 800. This is plainly refuted not only by Dracontius’s works but also by the testimonies of Isidore and Ildefonsus.

Funccius, *On the Decline of the Latin Language*, chapter 3, section 97, rightly rejects Matthias Koenig, who says in his *Bibliotheca vetus et nova* that Dracontius flourished under Justinian; but Funccius himself, without any foundation, assigns the definite year 450 as the date when Dracontius departed from human affairs.

31. Dracontius’s homeland was uncertain not only to G. Fabricius but also to Nicolás Antonio, who declares in volume I, book V, chapter 5 of his *Bibliotheca vetus*:

> Some rashly say that Dracontius was Spanish by nation, believing fabricated authors.

He reached this judgment partly because of the silence of the ancients and partly because of a certain hostility of his own toward the authors of false chronicles, which perhaps sometimes allowed him to be carried too far in the opposite direction. We have seen what Vasaeus thought—he died around 1562, and many followed him—long before the fabrication of the chronicles, which is dated to 1594, with the first edition completed in 1619.

The same opinion remained influential among almost everyone even after Nicolás Antonio’s *Bibliotheca* had been published, although no one any longer placed confidence in the fictitious chronicles. Some strengthened Vasaeus’s reasoning by arguing that Saint Eugenius had undertaken the correction of Dracontius at the king’s command, which might indicate that the author was Spanish. Or, as I am more inclined to think, the opinion may have arisen from some tradition or manuscript codex and then passed to the others.

Gallandius, who included Dracontius in volume IX of his *Bibliotheca* from Sirmond’s edition, adds this explanation for the probability of the opinion: the Spanish nation had previously been fertile in illustrious men who sang sacred matters in verse—Juvencus, Prudentius, Merobaudes, and others—so that Dracontius too, imitating them, composed his *Hexaemeron*.

[Col. 0618A] 32. Let us now examine what Nicolás Antonio says: that some, relying on fabricated authors, believed Dracontius to have been Spanish by nation. The *Chronicle of Dexter* is especially famous. In the notes to the most recent Madrid edition of Nicolás Antonio’s *Bibliotheca Hispana vetus*, book III, chapter 3, the learned editor says that it is remarkable that nothing about Dracontius is found in the pseudo-Dexter—not only in the fragment of the chronicle that Nicolás Antonio published after the *Bibliotheca vetus*, but also not in the fuller copy of the Royal Library.

Yet it is beyond doubt that some mention of Dracontius occurs in the *Chronicle of Dexter* printed with Bivarius’s commentaries. From this, however, it cannot at all be inferred that Dracontius was Spanish; indeed, Bivarius inferred the opposite. For when the chronicle relates under the year 382 that the bishops Dracontius and Adelphus were exiled in Spain, Bivarius asserts that this was the poet Dracontius and does not consider him different from Dracuntius or Dracontius, to whom a letter of Athanasius is extant.

Nor was he the first person to whom this very opinion had occurred, as one will understand from these words of Goldastus in his letter to Weitzius:

> What has been suggested concerning this Dracontius from Baronius has no bearing here. That one was Eastern, this one Western; that one Asiatic, this one European; that one Greek, this one Spanish; that one a bishop, this one a court official; that one lived under the emperor Constantine the Great, this one under the emperor Justinian the Great; that one flourished from the year 330 after Christ’s birth, this one from 540.

Goldastus, like Vasaeus, is mistaken concerning Dracontius’s date. But one may wonder where he got the idea that Dracontius was a court official, since most others call him a presbyter. I shall demonstrate from the Vatican parchments, section 122, that Goldastus’s opinion is the more accurate.

I think these details had been suggested to Weitzius by Baronius because, under the year 328, section 23, Baronius mentions the monk Dracontius, whom Athanasius urged by letter not to refuse the episcopate; and again, under the year 356, sections 47, 48, and 52, he mentions from Saint Athanasius’s *On His Flight* and *To the Solitaries*, and from the *Life of Saint Hilarion* written by Saint Jerome, the bishop Dracontius exiled in Egypt. Baronius considers him one and the same as the monk Dracontius to whom Athanasius wrote letters.

We discussed the different Dracontiuses earlier, in sections 5 and 6. Goldastus’s words should not be omitted, by which, rejecting the opinions of others, he assigned Dracontius to Spain:

> It is certain that he belonged to a people nourished by letters, nurtured by studies, a colonist of the Muses, and a rival of Parnassus and Helicon themselves; and that among his countrymen from the ancient pagans were Sextilius Hemina, Seneca, Lucan, Victorinus Statorius, Columella, Silius Italicus, Decianus, Licinianus, Caninius Rufus, Martial, the emperor Hadrian, Festus Avienus, and Aquilius Severus; and among the Christian company, Metronianus, Tiberianus, Juvencus, your Prudentius, Damasus, Leander, Fulgentius, Isidore, and Orontius, whom Laurentius Ramiresius, a noble young man of elegant talent, recently published first.

33. Nicolás Antonio cites the words of the fictitious Haubertus of Seville from his chronicle under the year 433, section 24:

> The holy man Dracontius died at Huesca of the Celtiberians, where he was a presbyter.

But apart from the fact that this Haubertus was fabricated toward the end of the seventeenth century, you will find no one who makes Dracontius a presbyter of Huesca, at least among those who have any standing among critical scholars.

Long before this Haubertus, however, I find someone who called the poet Dracontius “saint.” In the *Index of Prohibited Books* prepared by Johannes M. of Brisighella in 1607, page 85, the title “Saint Dracontius” in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* by Margarinus de la Bigne, 1589 edition, is ordered to be deleted. Likewise, on page 256, the titles “Saint Belisarius the poet,” “Saint Liberius the poet,” “Saint Venantius,” “Saint Dracontius,” “Saint Theodulf,” and elsewhere “Saint Prudentius” are ordered deleted. See section 55.

Itigius, chapter 3 *On Libraries*, asserts that copies of this Index are extremely rare. He himself had not seen it, because, as he says, the Roman edition had been suppressed and the new edition being prepared in Belgium had been stifled. I consider his statement concerning the suppression of the Roman edition false, unless he means that a second volume, which was being prepared, was not published.

It should be observed that in this Index the word *divus* (“saint” or “divine”) is denied even to those regarded as saints, according to the opinion of those who think that this word signifies divinity. Not everyone holds this view, nor do all think that the contrary usage of devout and learned men should be resisted.

Dracontius’s memory, moreover, appears in no martyrology. Indeed, among the first six months of the year I have found in the Bollandists no other saint who was called by this name.

34. Nevertheless, although Nicolás Antonio, in the place cited from the *Bibliotheca vetus*, while discussing Saint Eugenius, said that Dracontius was rashly called Spanish by some, he nevertheless assigned him a place among Spanish writers in volume I, book III, chapter 3, where he speaks more cautiously. For he says that he does not know what moved Miraeus in his notes on Isidore, Labbeus in his dissertation on Bellarmine’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and Bigneus in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* to call Dracontius openly Spanish.

The reason that moved them can be seen above, in section 31. Bigneus himself, however, does not call Dracontius Spanish. Rather, in a later edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, namely the Lyon edition of 1677, modeled on the edition produced by Sirmond, the editor called Dracontius a Spanish presbyter.

Nicolás Antonio adds that he knows to which side Bivarius was drawn: namely, by the pseudo-Maximus under the year 430, “Dracontius the presbyter died at Huesca,” and under the year 412, “another Dracontius, a remarkable Spanish poet, is considered.” Bivarius does not dare conjecture whether the two are one or two.

I discussed Bivarius’s opinion in the commentary on pseudo-Dexter in section 32. I now add that in the chronicle of pseudo-Maximus, which Nicolás Antonio appended at the end of the *Bibliotheca vetus*, another Dracontius is recorded under the year 600: “Dracontius, poet of Complutum, flourishes”; and under the year 603: “Dracontius, poet of Zaragoza, dies.”

The fabricator of this chronicle may have had before his eyes the opinion of those who had transmitted that Dracontius lived under the reign of Athanagild; for from Athanagild’s time his lifespan could easily have been extended to the year 603. Those who later enlarged Maximus’s chronicle according to their own invention, as did the author of pseudo-Haubertus, after they understood from Dracontius’s works as published by Sirmond that the elegy refers to Theodosius the Younger, wrote that Dracontius flourished in 412 and 430 and died in 433.

From Sirmond also, who edited Bellarmine’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* in 1617, arose, as I believe, the chapter of that book on Dracontius. It is absent from the first edition, and in it Dracontius’s lifetime is assigned to the year 440.

### 35. From these facts it can be gathered that, in assigning Dracontius’s homeland and date, the false chronicles did not lead others, but their authors adhered to the opinions of earlier writers, and therefore often varied among themselves. The defenders of those opinions could not reconcile these variations unless they invented several Dracontiuses.

Nor have I so far been able to discover who calls Dracontius a presbyter of Huesca, Complutum, or Zaragoza, or a vicarius of Africa, as pseudo-Julian wished, while many call him a presbyter of Toledo—a designation not found in the false chronicles. Thus Dracontius is called by Johannes Gottfried Olearius in his *Bibliotheca ecclesiastica*, by the author of the catalogue of the manuscripts of the Royal Library of Paris, and by others.

Some call Dracontius a Toledan without explicitly naming him a presbyter, such as Weitzius in his edition, Rivinus likewise in his edition, and Fabricius in the *Bibliotheca Latina medii aevi*. Many call him the same Spanish presbyter Dracontius without specifying his native town or where he lived: Sixtus of Siena in the *Bibliotheca sancta*, published in 1575; Possevinus in volume I of the *Apparatus sacer*, who wrote at the beginning of the seventeenth century; Miraeus in his notes on Saint Isidore; Labbeus in his dissertation on Bellarmine’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; the editor of the 1677 Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum*; Remigius Ceillier in volume XV of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 29; Johannes Nicolaus Funccius, *On the Decline of the Latin Language*, chapter 3, section 97; the author of the catalogue of the Casanatense Library; and Natalis Alexander in the fifth-century section of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

But where Dracontius was born, where he lived, or what office he held is in no way established by the ancients. From them alone it can be argued with some probability that he was Spanish, as I said in section 31.

36. After Sirmond published Dracontius, something more certain was established concerning the period in which he lived. After the poem *On the Work of the Six Days*, Sirmond added an elegy by the same Dracontius addressed to Theodosius the Younger Augustus. Thus it is entitled, and Theodosius the Younger Augustus is mentioned again in its summary.

The summary of the elegy is explained as follows:

> This following little work contains the author’s apology, in which he asks Almighty God for pardon, lest he should have inadvertently made some mistake in the preceding poem. Then he offers a prayer to Theodosius the Younger Augustus, explaining why he had remained silent in the same work about that emperor’s triumphs.

These words are reproduced verbatim in the Madrid edition of the Toledo Fathers and are mentioned in Bellarmine’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. But, as I think—and as I said in section 34—they derive from Sirmond’s manuscript codex.

The title does indeed appear to have been taken from the codex itself, since its wording has an ancient flavor. But I should like to know whether the title was written in the same ancient hand as the verses themselves. For I shall subsequently show, from the ancient Vatican parchments and from the elegy itself, that it is false and does not fit the elegy.

In the meantime, I shall point out that it is strange that Grialius did not notice this title, if it exists in the Azagra codex. For in his note on Isidore’s *Etymologies* book VI, chapter 9, Grialius quotes two verses of Dracontius found in the Azagra codex; and in his note on book XII, chapter 2, he mentions the same codex and at the same time asserts that Dracontius composed the *Work of the Six Days* during the reign of Athanagild.

Therefore either the title of the *Elegy to Theodosius* was not then in that codex, or Grialius, when he wrote these things, did not attend to it. I do not intend to deny that Dracontius became known under the emperor Theodosius the Younger. Rather, I maintain that this must be proved by other arguments, and I shall finally prove it after I have discussed Dracontius’s manuscript codices and the editions produced thus far.

## CHAPTER V. The manuscript codices of Dracontius

37. I discussed in sections 27 and 28 the codex of Dracontius that was preserved around the tenth century in the library of the monastery of Bobbio, and another codex—or perhaps the same one—that was found in the celebrated monastery at the end of the fifteenth century.

38. I also explained in section 29 which codex Morelius used in preparing the first Paris edition of Dracontius. Montfaucon, in *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum manuscriptorum*, page 1370, reports the following among the books of the library of Saint Victor in Paris, column 2:

> Draconicius, *On the Work of the Six Days*.

This is Dracontius, and, in my opinion, this is the codex from which Dracontius first emerged.

39. On page 133, the same Montfaucon publishes a catalogue found among the manuscripts of D. Claudius Etiennot, or Stephanotius, in which 33 different works are listed as existing in the Vatican Library. Dracontius’s *Hexaemeron* is mentioned in this catalogue.

Some works have a number added by which they are to be sought; others do not. Perhaps Stephanotius had marked them in his catalogue so that he might search for them. No certain number is assigned to Dracontius in that catalogue, and his *Hexaemeron* is not found in the old Vatican Library.

In the manuscript papers of Laurentius Zaccagnius, formerly prefect of the Vatican Library, Dracontius’s name likewise appears among the unpublished works that Zaccagnius was considering publishing, but no codex number is given. This increasingly confirms my suspicion that some codex of Dracontius lies hidden in the Vatican Library, one that Thomas Phaedrus Inghirami brought from the monastery of Bobbio and that is not different from the very one used by Saint Columbanus.

In Montfaucon’s index this Dracontius is called “Stratonicaean.” But this surname properly belongs to Draco Stratonicaeus, whose Greek codex *On Poetic Meters* is in the Royal Library of Paris, listed by the same Montfaucon on page 946; and also to the work entitled in Greek *On the Measurement of Poems*, written on papyrus among the books of the president of Mesne, in the same work, page 1326, column 2.

40. In the cathedral library of Laon, Montfaucon, page 1297, records the following codex as number 276:

> The metrical work of Saint Hilary of Poitiers. Alcimus Avitus, *On Original Sin*, *On the Divine Judgment*. The Letter of Dracontius. A Book of Questions on Genesis from Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, Hilary, Isidore, and Eucherius.

This codex is said to be extremely ancient. I think Dracontius’s letter is the *Elegy to King Guntharius*, which I shall discuss later. I find nothing else in Montfaucon that could relate to our Dracontius.

41. We must now discuss the celebrated codex of Michael Ruiz Azagra. I first find mention of it in Ambrosius Morales, book XI, chapter 34; thereafter in Azagra himself, in the edition of Corippus, which, because it is rare, will be described here:

> Four books of the African grammarian Corippus, *On the Praises of the Younger Justin Augustus*, in heroic verse, now first brought from darkness into the light; also illuminated with scholia and observations by Michael Ruiz Azagra, a Celtiberian, for Albert, cardinal archduke of Austria. Antwerp, from the workshop of Christopher Plantin, 1581, in octavo.

The dedicatory letter was dated Madrid, 1579. In it Azagra recalls that he had formerly been attached to the service of the emperor Ferdinand and Caesar Maximilian, and at that time to Caesar Rudolf.

After Corippus’s poems there is added a votive congratulation in heroic verse by the same Azagra, sung at Frankfurt on the Main in 1562 to Maximilian II, the designated emperor.

In his observations on Corippus, shortly after the beginning of page 74, Azagra writes:

> In our exemplar—which, as we have stated at length elsewhere concerning the work of the poet Dracontius *On the Making of the World* and also concerning the poems of Saint Eugenius, bishop of Toledo, was certainly copied more than seven hundred years ago, not on the basis of conjecture but with wholly reliable certainty—the words *TOTIENS* and *QUOTIENS* are always read …

The codex, therefore, had been copied in the ninth century or earlier.

This codex contained, together with Dracontius and Eugenius, Corippus’s poems, mutilated and corrupted in many places. Many critical scholars after Azagra contributed their efforts to restore them to their original purity. For no other codex of Corippus’s poems has yet been found, except that Azagra notes on page 89 that several variant readings, added in the margin near the end of book III, had been collected from an ancient volume of the Church of Oviedo. In that volume two speeches—those of the envoy of the king of the Avars and of the emperor Justin—taken from Corippus were read together with various other works. To these may be added the eighteen verses of the speech of the Avars, which were published among the poems of Sidonius and others as Sidonian poems by Elias Vinetus in 1552 from a codex of Saintes.

The greater thanks are therefore owed to Azagra, who rescued this writer from darkness. It was certainly not appropriate for Petrus Franciscus Fogginius, who twice published Corippus with Azagra’s notes, those of others, and his own, to make this sharp and inaccurate criticism of Azagra in his note on the panegyric poem in praise of Athanasius:

> May his departed spirit pardon me: it is sufficiently clear from this how much ability he possessed in reading and correcting manuscripts. No great acuteness of intellect was needed to read *TROPICIS* [instead of *trepicis*] or to supply *VERSIBUS* (“in verses”).

But Azagra recognized the error in *trepicis* and did not attempt to correct the word, which is not Corippus’s either. Nor do I think Fogginius’s conjecture will please everyone. If I had the time, I would show that Fogginius often yields in judgment and ingenuity to the first editor of Corippus—for example, when, in book IV, verse 266, he restored:

> “And, vowing his prayers to Christ, he dedicated his empire,”

he did so, as he says, both for the sake of the meter and because the poet intended to express that the emperor deliberately wished Christ to be understood under the name of Sophia. But although the second reason is invalid, the first is plainly false. Compare Barthius’s words in the following section.

42. The codex of Azagra was also praised by the most learned Juan Bautista Pérez, whose notes are attached to the works of St. Isidore and St. Ildefonsus *On Illustrious Men*. He died as bishop of Segorbe in 1597. In his note on chapter 14 of St. Ildefonsus, Pérez says:

“I saw this emendation by Eugenius in that ancient codex of Ruiz Azagra, which I mentioned above.”

He is referring to the note on chapter 7 of Isidore’s *On Illustrious Men*, concerning Verecundus:

“I also saw Verecundus’s own little book *On Penance*, written in hexameters, whose beginning is:

> Who will give my sorrowful face tears in mournful showers?

That book, written in Gothic letters, once belonged to the Church of Oviedo and later came into the possession of my friend Michael Ruiz Azagra.” [Col. 0623B]

He also mentions it in his note on chapter 47 of St. Isidore’s *On Illustrious Men*, where the prefatory notice to St. Isidore’s books, written by Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, is recorded. There Pérez says concerning the word *DESTINA*:

“Corippus, the African poet, uses that word in his book *On the Praises of Justin the Younger*, recently published by the most learned Ruiz Azagra.”

When these statements are compared, it is clear that Azagra’s words concerning Corippus—“As we stated elsewhere concerning the work of Dracontius …”—must not be understood to mean that he published Dracontius in print, but only that he had prepared an edition. [Col. 0623C]

Barthius, in *Adversaria*, Book 55, chapter 11, very much wished to see this edition:

“We also wish to inform learned men that, even before Jacobus Sirmondus—whom we shall always rightly praise for restoring this and many other authors—Michael Ruiz Assagrius published in Spain this Dracontius, abridged and interpolated by Eugenius, through whose generosity we possess Corippus. Yet despite every effort we have been unable to obtain the edition, which we have sought with the greatest eagerness. If anyone can place it at our disposal, he will earn our deepest gratitude.”

Barthius therefore did not disparage Azagra’s labor and zeal. In Book 21, chapter 2, he speaks even more explicitly of Azagra’s notes on Corippus:

“We cannot fail to bear witness to Assagrius’s sound judgment, which certainly appears on every page.” [Col. 0623D]

Would that this Dracontius, as well as Eugenius—who made an epitome of Dracontius—had also come into our hands! What would Foggini reply to this?

43. Yet no edition of Dracontius and Eugenius had been printed by Azagra, as Barthius supposed. Deceived by Azagra’s words, which I have just cited, Barthius asserted this, and others later confirmed it on Barthius’s authority. The opinion became widely accepted and was adopted by Fabricius in his *Bibliotheca Latina vetus*. In the *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, however, he spoke more cautiously, saying that Michael Ruiz de Azagra had undertaken to publish Dracontius, interpolated by Eugenius of Toledo, but that neither Barthius nor Nicolás Antonio had seen this edition.

Nicolás Antonio discussed Dracontius twice, and not superficially, in his *Bibliotheca vetus*. Since the work was posthumous and had not been revised, he sometimes repeats the same words and arguments, and at times contradicts himself. He says in Book 3, chapter 3:

“Sirmondus published Dracontius together with Eugenius’s collected verses—namely, both books of Dracontius—although the second, or later, book was first published by Michael Azagra, as he himself says in his notes on Corippus.”

The same Nicolás Antonio wrote more accurately in Book 5, chapter 5:

“Michael Ruiz Azagra was preparing to publish the poems of Eugenius and Dracontius from a Gothic codex written, as he believed, seven hundred years earlier.”

Nicolás Antonio himself saw these poems prepared for publication, together with Azagra’s letter to the dean and chapter of the Church of Toledo, dated the first day of April 1577, in the manuscripts of the Villumbrosana Library, volume 7 of the *Miscellanies*. [Col. 0624A]

José Rodríguez de Castro began to review Spanish writers in Spanish, but death prevented him from completing his work. Perhaps he read Nicolás Antonio’s first passage rather than the second, for he wrote:

“Dracontius’s *Hexaemeron*, corrected by Eugenius, exists in volume 9 of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, Lyon 1677, from the codex of Pedro Ruiz de Azagra, who claims in his notes on Corippus to have been the first to publish Dracontius. This edition,” he adds, “must be considered older than the editions of Weitzius and Sirmondus, both produced in the same year, 1619.” [Col. 0624B]

44. I now pass over the fact that Sirmondus’s and Weitzius’s editions were not produced in the same year, as will soon become clear. In the Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum* of 1677, volume 9, it is expressly stated that Dracontius’s poems were taken from Sirmondus’s edition. Since Rodríguez cites only Azagra’s words in his notes on Corippus—words that must be understood as referring to an edition prepared but not brought to completion—his testimony should not move us. [Col. 0624C]

As for his calling our Michael “Pedro,” this is not his individual error but one shared with others. In the *Index of Books to Be Expurgated* compiled by Juan M. of Brisighella in 1607, page 269, certain material concerning Dracontius is set out for addition to the *Bibliotheca Patrum*. Concerning the emendation made by St. Eugenius, it says:

“The commentator on St. Ildefonsus affirms that he saw this emendation in a very ancient manuscript codex of Pedro Ruiz Azagra.”

This refers to Pérez, who added notes to St. Ildefonsus’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Yet Pérez, in his note on chapter 14 of St. Ildefonsus, omitted the name Ruiz Azagra; in his note on chapter 7 of Isidore’s *On Illustrious Men*, he clearly names Michael.

The author of the note on Dracontius to be added to the *Bibliotheca Patrum* was the highly learned Thomas Malvenda, as may be gathered from what I said about that *Index* in the prolegomena to Prudentius, page 159. Those words of the *Index* were reproduced in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* of Cologne, 1618, volume 6, and of Lyon, 1677. From this source the name Pedro became attached to our Michael in other writers, such as Rivinus in his edition of Dracontius and Leyserus in his *History of Medieval Poetry*. [Col. 0624D]

Nicolás Antonio had also given Michael the name Juan in the *Bibliotheca nova*. But in his corrected work he acknowledged that Michael was the proper name, after having listed the same man twice: first under the name Juan, being misled by Jerónimo Román de la Higuera, and then under his true name, Michael.

In the most recent Madrid edition, Azagra is praised under the name Michael alone; but in the index both names remain, as though they belonged to two different writers. In the *Censura of Fictitious Histories*, published in this century by Mayansius, Nicolás Antonio had not removed the error by which Azagra was called Juan Ruiz. Mayansius pointed it out in the *Life of Nicolás Antonio* prefixed to the *Censura*. [Col. 0625A]

I find another name and surname for Azagra in Grialius’s notes on chapter 2 of Book 12 of Isidore’s *Etymologies*. Speaking of the Azagra codex, he says:

“This book, written in Gothic characters, is now preserved in the library of Martín Rodríguez Azagra.”

In these words Rivinus, in his notes on Dracontius, recognizes the same Azagra whom some called Pedro Ruiz and others Michael Ruiz. But perhaps Grialius is indicating a different man, to whom Michael Ruiz Azagra’s library had passed by inheritance or through some other arrangement. [Col. 0625B]

45. Whether Grialius means Michael or someone distinct from Michael, he nevertheless seems to be mistaken about the matter itself. He published St. Isidore’s works in 1599. Before that date, the distinguished Bayerius testifies, the Azagra codex had been preserved in the library of the Church of Toledo. In his notes on chapter 3 of Book 3 of Nicolás Antonio’s *Bibliotheca vetus*, Bayerius says that the Azagra codex existed in the Toledo library, shelf 15, no. 15, through the generosity of the distinguished Juan Bautista Pérez, bishop of Segorbe.

Since Pérez died in 1597, either the Toledo library did not possess the book through his generosity, or the Azagra library did not preserve it in 1599. [Col. 0625C]

The codex certainly now exists in the Toledo library, and it is described in the Madrid edition of the Toledan Fathers, after the preface to the first volume, as follows:

“The Gothic codex called Azagra, containing, besides various short works by other authors, not only the previously published epigrams of St. Eugenius III, together with his emendation of Dracontius and his letter to King Ervig, but also many other poems by the same author, which we now publish for the first time. It is a very ancient codex, and from the character of its script it can be inferred that it is no later than the tenth century. It is preserved in the Toledo library, shelf 31, no. 18.”

I could readily persuade myself that this codex was copied before the Moors’ invasion of Spain and, having been rescued along with a few others from that common Spanish calamity, was preserved in the Church of Oviedo. But since I have not seen the codex, I dare determine nothing with certainty, especially since Bayerius disagrees and assigns it to the eleventh century—unless there is an error in the numbers. [Col. 0625D]

It is certainly precious not only because of its antiquity, but also because it alone still contains certain materials deserving public light, such as Verecundus’s little book *On Penance*, mentioned in section 42. Corippus’s poems ought also to have been compared more carefully with this unique codex. For Azagra sometimes arrogated to himself the freedom to restore corrupt verses by his own ingenuity, without showing others the words of the codex.

Barthius nevertheless says, in chapter 1 of Book 8 of his *Adversaria*:

“It must be noted that that Michael Assagrius acted rather shamelessly in imposing upon us his correction of seven complete verses, concealing the old reading of the codex, which he knew to be the one and only surviving copy, although he admits that he found the verses extremely corrupt.” [Col. 0626A]

See section 13.

46. It might be questioned which codex Sirmondus used for his edition, and in fact some disagree among themselves about identifying it, as I said in section 14. But the editor of the catalogue of manuscripts in the Royal Library of Paris completely removes every doubt. He describes codex 2832, a parchment manuscript formerly belonging to Bigot, written approximately in the ninth century, as follows:

1. Thirty-one poems of Eugenius of Toledo, the same as those published by Sirmondus.

2. Dracontius the priest’s poem *On the Making of the World*, or *Hexaemeron*. Eugenius’s letter to King Chindaswinth is prefixed; in it Eugenius declares that he suppressed some passages in Dracontius’s work and enlarged and polished others.

3. A poem in elegiacs by the same author to Theodosius the Younger Augustus, bearing this title: *Satisfaction*, in which he asks Almighty God’s pardon in case he had inadvertently erred in the preceding poem; he then offers a prayer to Theodosius the Younger Augustus, explaining why he had been silent about that emperor’s triumphs in the same work. [Col. 0626B]

4. The monostichs of Eugenius of Toledo summarizing the seventh day.

5. Verses of St. Cyprian to a certain senator, and so forth.

I do not believe that Dracontius is called “the priest” in the codex itself; I think the editor added this description as an explanation, on the basis of a preconceived opinion. The heading of Dracontius’s elegy *Satisfaction* seems to have been taken from the codex itself. See section 36 and what will be said below, section 92 and following.

It should not be omitted that among the other works in this codex, at item 22, there is placed a hymn of Bishop Eugenius on St. Dionysius. Sirmondus either did not see this hymn or judged that it did not belong to St. Eugenius of Toledo. [Col. 0626C]

Other Gallic writers vigorously defend this hymn and contend that it should be assigned to Eugenius of Toledo. On this controversy one may consult Menardus, *Dissertation on the One Dionysius*; Natalis Alexander, dissertation 16 of the first century; and, in opposition to them, Franciscus Pagius, *Dissertation on St. Dionysius, Bishop of Paris*.

I am certain that the verses which are demonstrably by Eugenius of Toledo are entirely unlike the iambic dimeters of this hymn, which are wholly irregular and unmetrical. Eugenius is especially commended for his skill and elegance in iambic and trochaic verse. [Col. 0626D]

47. In the same catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris, codex 8093 is listed. It is a parchment manuscript written partly in the ninth, partly in the tenth, and partly in the fourteenth century; it formerly belonged to Colbert. Among other works, it contains:

3. Poems of Eugenius of Toledo.

6. The first book of Dracontius of Toledo’s *Hexaemeron*, in heroic verse. There is added a supplement by Eugenius III, bishop of Toledo, to Dracontius’s *Hexaemeron*.

7. Poems of Martin of Braga.

This codex lacks Dracontius’s *Elegy*, which certainly has no connection with the *Hexaemeron*. Eugenius’s supplement, although not necessary, is placed in a less unsuitable position. For after the *Elegy*, in which nothing is discussed about the making of the world, what place could there be for a supplement concerning the seventh day? See section 22. [Col. 0627A]

Sirmondus, who published the poems of Martin of Braga together with Eugenius and Dracontius, appears to have used this same codex.

48. Another codex is recorded in the same catalogue under no. 8321. It is partly parchment and partly paper, formerly belonged to Colbert, and was written in the fifteenth century. At item 6 it contains Dracontius of Toledo’s poem *On the Work of the Six Days*.

Perhaps it is a copy of, or similar to, the codex of St. Victor in Paris. For the heading *On the Work of the Six Days* is the same in both, and since no mention of Eugenius occurs, it must be believed that this copy was not emended by Eugenius. See section 29.

49. From Philip Labbe’s *New Library of Manuscript Books*, or *Specimen of Ancient Readings*, in the *Poetic Appendix*, where he mentions several ancient poems not yet published in his day, I cite the following from page 58:

“We shall add some poems of Dracontius—unless the heading is deceptive—to those that Jacobus Sirmondus long ago brought into public circulation together with several others by Eugenius of Toledo.” [Col. 0627B]

As I believe, the codex existed with Labbe himself, since elsewhere he usually indicates the library in which codices are preserved. Since the codex attributes the poems to Dracontius, Dracontius should be regarded as the author unless some adequate reason for doubt exists.

This could perhaps be inferred from the style. But where in the world should I imagine that codex to be hiding now? If, indeed, it is hiding anywhere, rather than having been lost through some misfortune.

50. To the same most learned Labbe, in the work cited, page 59, I owe the following reference to Dracontius:

“Verses of Gilbert, abbot of Golden Valley and of the Cistercian order, on the most holy Eucharist could be added from the Petavian catalogue, together with centos on penance from Dracontius, a prayer to Christ in Adonic verses, a poem in elegiacs on the meanings of the Mass, a work in heroic verse containing moral precepts, and several others.” [Col. 0627C]

The manuscript read *Diacontio*, but it is clear from the catalogue—which identifies the passage under the word *DRACONTIUS*—that it should be read *Dracontio*.

Dracontius’s poem contains much about God, especially in the elegy to King Guntharic; from these passages centos on penance could be composed. Thus the poem of St. Columbanus, discussed in section 8, consists largely of verses taken from Dracontius and others.

Centos on sacred subjects collected from secular poets by Faltonia Proba and Sedulius are extant. Among secular subjects, the poems *Hippodamia* and *Alcesta* in volume 4 of the *Pisaurian Collection*, without the authors’ names, are centos from Virgil, as it seemed to me when I read them. [Col. 0627D]

Apart from Dracontius, no other sacred poet now comes to mind from whose verses centos were composed. The Petavian catalogue cited by Labbe is the catalogue of the library of Alexander Petavius, which passed to Queen Christina of Sweden and from there to the Vatican Library.

Montfaucon, on page 64 of the *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum manuscriptorum*, reports from the library of Alexander Petavius a poem on the Eucharist by Gilbert, abbot of Golden Valley, among the Vatican manuscripts. But it is not now found in the Vatican Library, just as several other Petavian codices are missing.

51. Although I diligently searched many catalogues of manuscripts, I was unable to find any other codices of Dracontius. A few things remain to be said about manuscript notes on Dracontius. [Col. 0628A]

I have already said more about Azagra’s brief notes in section 41 and following. Nicolás Antonio, Book 5 of the *Bibliotheca vetus*, chapter 5, thinks that Sirmondus’s edition of Dracontius was more correct than the edition promised and prepared by Azagra, and that it was of little importance whether the poems of Eugenius and Dracontius were published from Azagra’s manuscripts after Sirmondus’s edition.

Flórez disagrees in volume 5 of *Hispania sacra*, treatise 5, chapter 3, because he thinks that Dracontius’s *Hexaemeron*, as emended by Eugenius, exists in Azagra’s manuscripts and not in Sirmondus’s edition. This argument is false, as I proved in section 12. [Col. 0628B]

In any case, even after Sirmondus’s edition it would have been of benefit to the republic of letters for Azagra’s notes and conjectures to be brought into the public light, since Barthius very much wished to see them. Sirmondus published the poems without notes, and Rodríguez de Castro should not be believed when, in his *Bibliotheca Hispana*, he wrongly attributes new and learned notes on Dracontius to Sirmondus.

I pass over the fact that the Azagra codex is somewhat fuller than Sirmondus’s codex. Certainly Dracontius’s *Elegy* was published from that codex in the Madrid edition of the Toledan Fathers, and a book of Eugenius’s poems that had not previously been published was added.

Mayansius informs me that Nicolás Antonio himself wrote very brief notes, or variant readings, in his work on Eugenius and Dracontius. Mayansius had these manuscripts in his possession and at one time intended to publish them, as he states in the *Life of Nicolás Antonio* prefixed to the *Censura of Fictitious Histories*. But perhaps these are the brief notes and variant readings that Azagra left in manuscript and that Nicolás Antonio testifies he saw. Nicolás Antonio was exceptionally curious and diligent in seeking out and acquiring such monuments of antiquity. [Col. 0628C]

I have no knowledge at all of whether Mayansius committed these brief notes to print.

52. I learned from Bayerius that Andrés Marcos Burriel compared Sirmondus’s edition with the Azagra codex and recorded the differences in reading. Although Burriel is celebrated with the common applause of all, it will nevertheless not be unwelcome to hear his praises from the most learned Bayerius, in his note on Book 3, chapter 3, of Nicolás Antonio’s *Bibliotheca vetus*:

“Andrés Marcos Burriel, a priest of the Society of Jesus, compared Sirmondus’s Dracontius with the eleventh-century Toledan codex of Michael Ruiz Azagra and recorded the variant readings. He was taken from scholarship by a premature death several years ago, to the great loss of letters. I now have in my hands these materials, together with many other products of that astonishing labor and industry of his, later transferred to the Royal Library of Madrid in his own handwriting.” [Col. 0628D]

For the age of the codex, compare what was said in section 45.

I must expect everything from Burriel’s diligence. But if he merely recorded differences between the Azagra codex and Sirmondus’s edition, without adding his own particular conjectures, his variant readings are now less necessary, since Dracontius has been published in the Madrid edition after the most careful comparison with both the Azagra codex and Sirmondus’s edition.

I further observe that Ceponius is different from Dracontius. Barthius possessed a manuscript of Ceponius’s *Hexaemeron* and intended to publish it in Book 109 of his *Adversaria*, had he lived. [Col. 0629A]

Barthius calls Ceponius a monk, but Nicolás Antonio, Book 3 of the *Bibliotheca vetus*, volume 1, chapter 4, thinks that he was a fifth-century Spanish bishop, to whom, and to Idacius, a letter of Turibius, bishop of Astorga, is extant.

Barthius, in his note on Statius, *Silvae* Book 2, poem 4, verse 24, says:

“See Ceponius in the *Hexaemeron*, whom we shall establish in his proper place as the author of the *Life*, hitherto perceived by no one, even by hearsay.”

Bayerius replies to these words of Barthius in his notes on Nicolás Antonio’s *Bibliotheca vetus*:

“But who the author of the *Life* is, or what the addition ‘of the *Life*’ means, I entirely fail to understand.”

The learned man was thrown into these difficulties simply because the first letter of *vitae* in Barthius was capitalized. Barthius means only that, when he undertook to establish or restore Ceponius, he was restoring him to life, since he had been lying in darkness. [Col. 0629B]

Concerning Ceponius, consult Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca Latina medii et infimi aevi*.

## CHAPTER VI. Editions of Dracontius

53. The first edition of Dracontius appeared in 1560, with the following title:

“Three books of *Truth* [*ΑΛΗΘΕΙΑΣ*], or Commentaries on Genesis, by the illustrious Marius Victor; various epigrams by a certain ancient author, among which are several psalms rendered in verse; *Genesis* by Hilary, bishop of Poitiers; *Genesis* and *Sodoma* by Cyprian; Dracontius’s *On the Work of the Six Days*. All now printed from ancient codices for the first time. Paris, 1560. At the press of Guillaume Morel. Octavo.” [Col. 0629C]

For the codex from which Dracontius’s work was extracted, see sections 29 and 38.

At the end there are some brief notes on Victor, who is called Victorius at the beginning and end of Book 3.

The *Genesis* attributed to Cyprian is a fragment of a poem on Genesis that some assign to Tertullian and others to Juvencus. I think it was composed after the fifth century, despite the Muses and Apollo. I discussed it more fully in the prolegomena to Prudentius, page 196, and will add further remarks when I revise Juvencus and commit him to public circulation.

54. The second edition appeared in 1564. It is a collection of Christian poets prepared by Georg Fabricius and published at Basel that year in large quarto, although some, misled by this, describe it as folio. I discussed this edition in the prolegomena to Prudentius, page 88 and following. [Col. 0629D]

As for Dracontius, Fabricius followed the copy published by Morel, correcting three or four errors, as I explained in section 30.

Johann Albert Fabricius, in chapter 4 of Book 2 of his *Bibliotheca Latina vetus*, says that in this collection of Georg Fabricius only the first book of Dracontius is extant, and that it is mutilated at the end. It should be noted, however, that this book of Dracontius is indeed mutilated in the Morel and Fabricius editions, but not at the end. The fifty-eight missing verses belong to the account of the first parents’ sin, after the verse “Nor the boundary-setter.” [Col. 0630A]

In his commentaries—which are in a later volume, rarer than the first—Fabricius discusses Dracontius’s poems. The title of this second part is:

“Commentary on the Christian works, remains, and fragments of the ancient ecclesiastical poets by Georg Fabricius of Chemnitz. In it not only are obscure matters and words explained, but also certain uncommon historical materials, the lives of the authors themselves, and matters relating to various poetic genres, all elaborated with exceptional care and inserted. Basel, by Johann Oporinus.”

This work of Fabricius is arranged alphabetically. It would certainly be useful if, after a new and fuller collection of the Christian poets, it were published in an enlarged and corrected form, especially with the matters censured in the *Expurgatory Index of Philip II*, promulgated at Antwerp in 1571 by order and authority under the decree of the Council of Trent, duly marked.

55. The third edition appeared in 1589, in volume 8 of the second edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, printed in Paris by Margarin de la Bigne. This edition, together with the other works of the same *Bibliotheca*, was reviewed in the *Expurgatory Index* of 1607 by Johann M. of Brisighella. The censors, however, noted nothing in Dracontius’s poem *On the Work of the Six Days* that was judged worthy of censure or that was said to require cautious reading, as happened with many other works. [Col. 0630B]

They ordered only that the letter *D*, or *divi*, be deleted in the words “D. Dracontius’s *Hexaemeron*.” This was not carried out in the Paris edition of 1644, in which volume 8 still contains these same words at the beginning in the catalogue of writers.

Thomas Itigius, in his book *On Libraries*, published in the *Bibliotheca Patrum and Doctors* at Leipzig in 1602 under the care of M. Joachim Zehner, lists Dracontius among the ancient ecclesiastical writers published there. But that library appears to contain not the complete works of the Fathers, but certain fragments. [Col. 0630C]

56. The fourth edition appeared in 1610:

“*Hexaemeron of Dracontius of Toledo, a Spaniard*, or *On the Work of the Six Days and the Creation of the World*, a single book, with the index, glossary, and notes of M. Johann Weitzius, which may take the place of a full commentary; the opinions of ancient writers, especially the holy Fathers, concerning the creation of the universe having been compared with one another. Frankfurt, printed by Wolfgang, at the expense of Peter Kopff, 1610. Octavo.” [Col. 0630D]

Fabricius, in Book 4, chapter 2, of his *Bibliotheca Latina vetus*, assigns Weitzius’s edition to 1619. Rodríguez de Castro may have been misled by this when he asserted in his *Bibliotheca Hispana* that Sirmondus’s and Weitzius’s editions were both produced in 1619. Fabricius, however, correctly assigns Weitzius’s edition to 1610 in his *Bibliotheca medii aevi*.

Weitzius prefixed Goldast’s letter on Dracontius, which I have cited in several places. This edition is rare in Rome; I know of only one copy preserved in the Angelica Library.

The index, glossary, and notes are useful. After the notes there are several corrections of verses devised by Weitzius and others, which will be of some use to me.

57. The fifth edition appeared in 1616, in the second part of the *Choir of Poets*, quarto, Lyon, prepared by Alexander Fichettus. I saw this information handwritten in a copy, since the editor’s name is not printed.

58. The sixth edition appeared in 1618, in volume 4 of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* of Cologne, page 500.

59. The seventh edition appeared in 1619, in Sirmondus’s works, under the following title:

“Little works of Blessed Eugenius, bishop of Toledo, in which are inserted two little books of Dracontius, once revised by that same Eugenius. Various works of several other ancient writers are likewise added. Paris, from the Nivellian press, at the shop of Sebastian Cramoisy, 1619. Octavo.” [Col. 0631A]

Jacobus Sirmondus dedicated these little works to Henri de Bourbon, son of the king and bishop of Metz.

Besides Eugenius and Dracontius, there are several works by Martin, bishop of Braga; a paraenetic letter of the abbot Columbanus to Hunald; *The Teaching* of Severinus, bishop; and *The Confession* of Tiro Prosper of Aquitaine.

Michael of St. Joseph, in his *Bibliography*, assigns Sirmondus’s edition to 1617. This may be a typographical error, unless he copied the year from Moreri’s *Dictionary*, where the same year is given.

For this edition, see section 46 and following. [Col. 0631B]

Before Sirmondus, all editions followed Morel’s, with a few corrections. Sirmondus published the *Hexaemeron* from manuscripts in a fuller and more correct form, and was the first to publish Dracontius’s *Elegy*.

Barthius praises him magnificently for editions of ancient writers of this kind. He says in Book 29, chapter 2, of his *Adversaria*:

“Many writers of the later age have been brought into the light and restored to life in this century by Jacobus Sirmondus, a man of outstanding judgment and reliable learning, who deserves to be counted only among those who have served antiquity well.”

He says at length in Book 51, chapter 4:

“How great are the merits of Jacobus Sirmondus’s patience and most generous scholarship, I have already proclaimed more than once; yet I shall never be able to praise them sufficiently or match them in words, even if I were to proclaim them very often thereafter. He has rescued so many worthy writers from darkness; with such penetrating intelligence, refined judgment, reliable reading, and faithful industry he has restored monuments, rescued from the moths, to the deserved praise of posterity, that whenever I see the catalogues of booksellers bearing the name of this man—catalogues that come to us twice each year—I cannot help rejoicing and promising myself a new pleasure in the reading of some writer previously unknown. [Col. 0631C]

“Let us not be disturbed in praising and commending this man by malicious talents, which once attempted to distort our youth—when they ought to have encouraged praise—into attacks upon learned men who, although learned, did not share their view of what ought to be defended in the circumstances of our religion. We shall not fail our own candor; we shall pursue this most distinguished virtue with the highest applause. Thus it will happen that some fruit of our own goodness will return to us as well, when those eminent men are encouraged to persevere in their undertaking by seeing that their merits are not deprived of praise.” [Col. 0631D]

I have willingly included these words, although they are rather long, either out of regard for Sirmondus or to commend our own labor to some extent.

60. The eighth edition appeared in 1624, in the appendix to the *Bibliotheca Patrum* of Margarin de la Bigne, Paris, page 837. Although produced after Sirmondus, it still reproduces Dracontius mutilated, from Morel’s edition.

Dracontius was reprinted in the same way in the Paris *Bibliotheca Patrum* of 1644, volume 8, and again there in 1654, volume 8—if these are indeed distinct editions and not merely editions differing in their title pages. I myself saw the first copy; Itigius saw the second in his book *On Libraries*.

61. The ninth edition appeared in 1651, prepared by Andreas Rivinus, who added this very long title:
