“*The Pair of Little Books of Dracontius the Spaniard*: the first of which, *On the Work of the Six Days and the Creation of the World*, under the title *Hexaemeron*, was formerly published in heroic meter but mutilated by 111 verses; the second, a later work in elegiacs, is a kind of postface and apology, both for the preceding work and for itself, addressed to God and to King Theodosius the Younger Augustus. It first appeared twenty [correct: thirty] years ago in Paris and has nowhere else been printed. Now both works, and especially that *Hexaemeron*, or *On the Structure of the World*, after Eugenius, bishop of Toledo—whose summary of the seven-day creation is also included here, together with the remaining epigrams and other poems placed below—then after Georg Fabricius, Johann Weitzius, Jacob Sirmondus, Caspar Barthius, Simon Toelmannus, Wolfgang Seberus, and others, have been completely restored and corrected. In them he has separated what was confused, reduced obscure passages to a more convenient and accessible meaning, and, selecting the earlier notes of others, enlarged and illuminated them with new ones: Andreas Rivinus, Doctor of Divinity and Professor at Leipzig. In the Dionysian era, 1651. Octavo.” [Col. 0632A]

There appears to be an error in the number of verses said to be missing in the earliest editions. Only fifty-eight verses are missing in the account of Adam’s sin, together with one verse in the account of Eve’s creation.

In Morel’s edition there are 575 verses; in Sirmondus’s, 634, apart from Eugenius’s preface. Leyserus corrected this error in his *History of Medieval Poetry*. He also notes that the statement on the same title page—that Dracontius first appeared twenty years before 1651, enlarged by Sirmondus’s later book—cannot be accepted. [Col. 0632B]

Rivinus himself noticed this and corrected “twentieth” to “thirtieth” at the end of the book; he would have corrected it more accurately to “thirty-second.”

Many such typographical errors, neither few nor insignificant, crept into this small book, a circumstance sufficiently common in books published in Germany. Editors usually shift the blame to the approaching fair and the pressure of booksellers; yet they accommodate the sellers at great cost to purchasers. As Dracontius rightly says in Book 1, verse 613:

> The losses of some commonly become the profits of others.

Rivinus nevertheless corrected many of these errors at the end of the book. But in the very sequence of errors that he corrects, several new ones appear. I even carefully investigated whether there might be another index warning about these errors. [Col. 0632C]

I shall indicate Rivinus’s conjectures on Dracontius in their proper places. Anyone will readily notice that they are sometimes probable, but generally unnecessary.

Leyserus, who was preparing a collection of medieval poets, states in his history that he had decided to reprint Dracontius fourth from Rivinus’s edition. But that plan never came to fruition. [Col. 0632D]

62. The tenth edition appeared in 1677, in volume 9 of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* at Lyon, based on the edition prepared by Sirmondus.

63. The eleventh edition appeared in 1696, among Sirmondus’s other works, folio, volume 2, under the care of Jacobus de la Baune, who added several notes in the preface and in the margin of Dracontius. [Col. 0633A]

This edition was reprinted at Venice in 1728, with several notes on Dracontius taken from Barthius’s *Adversaria*, by the press of Bartholomeus Gavarina; and again there in 1778, as I have read recorded somewhere.

64. The twelfth edition appeared in 1773, in Gallandius’s *Bibliotheca Patrum*, published at Venice from 1765 onward, volume 9, printed in that year. Gallandius added brief notes to Dracontius from Barthius, Baunius, the editor of Sirmondus’s works, and Heumannus.

65. The thirteenth edition appeared in 1782, among the works of the Toledan Fathers, revised against manuscript codices and illustrated with several notes. It was published by the authority and at the expense of His Eminence Cardinal Francisco de Lorenzana, archbishop of Toledo and primate of Spain, at Madrid, by Joaquín Ibarra, folio.

In volume 1, page 34, Dracontius’s little books appear revised against the Azagra codex, with variant readings written in the margin. Volume 2 appeared there in 1785.

This edition of the Toledan Fathers is exceedingly elegant. From it one can readily recognize the extraordinary learning of its distinguished editor and his truly exceptional services to ecclesiastical scholarship. By his example, assistance, and books—which he published, many of them his own and others belonging to other men, for the public benefit, and gave as gifts to learned people—he also encouraged us to illuminate these monuments of the ancient Fathers.

Dracontius’s poems were published together with the poems and other works of Blessed Eugenius. Both authors’ works are fuller here than in Sirmondus, especially those of Eugenius.

[Col. 0633C] 66. Bayer, in his notes to Niccolò Antonio’s *Bibliotheca vetus*, points out certain matters by which the edition of Eugenius’ works might still be enlarged. Among these he mentions a Psalter of David, copied more than a thousand years ago, listed in the *History of the Cottonian Library*, p. 35, col. 2. Sewn to it is a fairly ancient gathering bearing the heading “Prayer of Eugenius of Toledo in verse,” which begins:

> Immense King and God, by whom the structure of the world stands,  
> What in my misery I implore, do you, Christ, mercifully accomplish.

Bayer adds that this does not disagree with the character of Eugenius of Toledo. His judgment is sound, except that Eugenius would more likely have said, “Christ, mercifully accomplish it,” or arranged the words in another way, so that the final syllable in *Christe* would not be lengthened without justification. Bayer could, however, have observed that this very prayer is read among Eugenius’ poems both in this Madrid edition and in the Sirmondian edition; indeed, it is the first poem of Eugenius after the preface.

There is nevertheless this difference: in these editions the first verse reads, “King God, by whom the structure of the immense world stands”; the second verse reads, “What in my misery I, Eugenius, ask, mercifully accomplish.” I think this was altered for the use of the churches in which the prayer was sung; it was not appropriate for Eugenius to be named when someone else was praying on his behalf. Browerus altered it differently at the end of his notes to Venantius Fortunatus: “What in my misery I implore, accomplish through Christ, gentle one.” Browerus also notes several other variants in the rest of the prayer. In the first verse I think the more accurate reading is, “Immense King and God, by whom …”

Dracontius’ letter, as it is read in the Vatican manuscripts, begins, “Immense King and God”; in the printed editions it now reads, “Eternal King and God.” That same prayer of Eugenius, bishop of Toledo, is listed in the catalogue of manuscripts of the Royal Library of Paris under cod. 528, cod. 2085, and cod. 5371. In Vatican Alexandrinus cod. 1360, or 2078, there are several poems of Eugenius, including “The Prayer of that same Eugenius,” which differs in some words from the Madrid edition but agrees with it in the first two verses. The venerable Cardinal Thomasius published the same prayer in his *Hymnary* under the name of Eugenius of Toledo; he observed that Alcuin assigned it in the offices for weekdays. Thomasius reads:

> King God, by whom the structure of the immense world stands,  
> What in my misery I implore, do you, Christ, mercifully accomplish.

## CHAPTER VII. [Col. 0634B] The two manuscript codices of Dracontius in the Vatican Library, fuller than the others, of which no one else has made mention

67. Thus far I have explained what others have taught about Dracontius. It remains for me now to describe two Vatican codices, previously collated by no one. The first belongs to the Urbino Library, no. 352. It is a parchment codex in the largest folio format, written most elegantly in many-colored letters. It contains various works, all of which are indicated around the circumference of a beautiful circle prefixed at the beginning of the book. At the end, the age of the codex and the name of the copyist are recorded in these words: “Federicus Veteranus of Urbino transcribed this in the year of salvation 1481, on the Ides of August.” Veteranus formed his letters most beautifully; nevertheless, I do not find his name among the copyists of the codices of the Laurentian Library diligently listed by Bandini. I shall report not only the order of the works contained in the codex, but also provide some information about them.

68. First comes the *Anticlaudianus concerning the Blessed Boy*, with no author’s name given in the codex. It is nevertheless established that the author is Alanus Magnus, discussed by Baillet in his book on *Writers* and by Fabricius in his *Bibliotheca Latina medieval and later*. I have seen nine books under this title, concerning the Blessed Boy, cited by no one. Although others think differently, I agree with those who maintain that the poem was entitled *Anticlaudianus* by its author because he attempted to imitate Claudian—that is, to reproduce his style—as can be inferred even from the opening verses:

> I beg the style of the author and the poet’s ornaments,  
> lest, through my sluggishness, Clio, cast down, grow old.

For *anti* does not always signify “against” in compounds. Thus *antibasileus* (ἀντιβασιλεύς) does not mean “against the king,” but “viceroy,” or one who occupies the king’s place.

69. *Arator* follows the *Anticlaudianus*. Since I have compared this poet’s works with this and other codices, I hope that a more suitable opportunity to discuss him will not be lacking. For now I will merely point out that the division into two books, expressed in other codices, does not appear in this one.

70. After *Arator* there are Aesop’s apologues, under this title: “The fables of Aesop the Phrygian, called apologues and translated into the Latin language, begin.” Laurentius Zaccagnius added this note in his own hand in the margin: “A translation by an ancient author different from Phaedrus, which also exists in Vatican codex no. 2868, fol. 33.” There could indeed be no serious doubt about this: the verses of this work are elegiac, whereas the verses of Phaedrus are freer iambics. The more appropriate question would have been whether the author of these fables was Avienus. But when I compared the two, the difference immediately became clear. I infer from the verses of the prologue that the author was a Christian:

> So that the value of the harvest may rise from a humble little field,  
> water the dry little words, God, with new dew.

For pagan poets did not usually speak in this manner. In passing, I will correct one word in the following verse:

> The gentleness of words carries the honorable weight of character.

For *lenitas* I would read *levitas*, in order to satisfy the meter.

When Philip Labbe, in his *New Library of Manuscripts*, or *Specimen of Ancient Readings*, was listing poets whose poems he was attempting to bring into publication, he mentions on p. 66 Aesop’s Fables in elegiac verse from Royal codex 893, whose opening was:

> So that it may help and benefit, the present page strives;  
> serious matters painted with jokes smile more sweetly.

These are certainly the fables found in this Vatican codex, for the opening is the same in both. Labbe had not yet investigated whether the fables of the Royal Codex were the same as those of a certain Vignerian codex entitled *The Book of Hisop*, which contained a fairly long fable about a wolf and a shepherd. In the Vatican codex the final fable is about a wolf and a shepherd, but it is not very long. Among the poems of Marbod, col. 1169, there is a fable about the deception practiced by a wolf against a shepherd, and it is sufficiently long that it could in this respect be the very one cited by Labbe. Leyser, in his *History of Medieval Poetry*, under the year 1314, p. 2007, presents fables by a certain Adolphus against women, which are entirely distinct and very different from the fables of the Vatican codex.

71. After the fables, the codex contains the *Epigrams of Prosper derived from St. Augustine*. They have often been published, but this version ought to be compared with the printed editions, and I shall compare it if I have the opportunity. An epigram absent from the printed editions is placed first; Mansius had nevertheless published it in his *Additions to Fabricius’ Bibliotheca medieval and later*, from a codex of Francesco Maria Florentini. The final verse is corrupt in Mansius:

> If at last those who desire to climb the kingdom of heaven …

Our codex has, “The starry [kingdom] of heaven,” and so forth.

72. Next comes a poem entitled *Evax, King of the Arabs, On the Properties of Stones*, which begins:

> Evax, king of the Arabs, is said to have written to Nero,  
> who, after Augustus, ruled second in the world.

The author is not named in the codex, but he is Marbod, who says that he condensed the books of Evax. Consult Fabricius’ *Bibliotheca Latina medieval and later* and the works of Hildebert and Marbod published at Paris in 1708.

73. A poem on the Last Judgment follows, of which I have encountered no mention elsewhere. Its title is *Crisias*. It consists of three books. The following title is prefixed to the first: “The first book of the *Crisiad* concerning the signs preceding the Judgment begins.” Its opening is:

> Come here, Calliope, accompanied by your company of sisters;  
> hasten here, and hold the plectrum and the sounding lyre.

The second book concerns the coming of Antichrist, whom the poet calls *Antitheon* (“Anti-God”). The third book concerns the death of Antichrist, the resurrection of the dead, and the form of the Judgment.

Some catalogues of manuscript codices mention poems on the Judgment, but it is easy to establish that they are different from this poem. Montfaucon, while listing the codices of Queen Christina of Sweden, mentions under no. 1360 the anonymous poems on the signs of the Judgment, together with works by Theodulf, Avitus, and others. I have seen this codex, now Alexandrinus no. 2078. Those verses on the Judgment comprise only twenty-five hexameters, mentioned by John of Salisbury in *The Frivolities of Courtiers*, book II, chapter 5; but in this codex they are mutilated and incomplete. The first reads:

> The sign of the Judgment: the earth grows wet with sweat.

The same Montfaucon, p. 1136, lists from the Germanic Library the Sibylline verses on the Day of Judgment, cod. 675. These appear to be the verses on the Judgment in the Vatican codex just mentioned. For Antonius Beaugendre of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, in the previously mentioned edition of the works of Hildebert and Marbod, col. 1630, published those verses among Marbod’s miscellaneous poems as though they were unpublished, under the title “The Sibyl’s Verses on the Day of Judgment.”

The first verse correctly has *madescet*, “will grow wet.” In the last verse, “The fire and sulfurous stream will fall from heaven,” I would prefer “fire from the heavens and a stream of sulfur.” These verses occur among the works of Bede, vol. II, Basel, 1563, p. 353, and with different wording in the Sibylline Books. Ancient Christians brought forward such Sibylline verses to establish the reality of the Last Judgment. From this they passed into the prose, or sequence, of the Dead:

> Day of wrath, that day  
> will dissolve the age into ashes,  
> as David and the Sibyl bear witness.

Certain unmetrical verses entitled *On the Last Judgment*, cited by Leyser in his *History of Medieval Poetry*, p. 2091, or, according to the correction, p. 1191, differ still more from this poem. Their opening is:

> From the four parts of the world angels have been sent.

Among the works of Tertullian there is also a single book *On the Judgment of the Lord*, but it is likewise different from the poem in this Vatican codex. The author seems ancient to me for many reasons, the explanation of which I postpone to another time. It may nevertheless be conjectured that the author was Verecundus, an African bishop, whom Isidore, chapter 7 of *On Illustrious Men*, testifies to have published two modest and brief works in dactylic verse: the first on the resurrection and the Judgment, the second on penance. Verecundus’ book on penance exists at Toledo in that famous Azagra codex of which I spoke in no. 41. If I obtain a copy of it, I shall be able to give a safer judgment on the whole matter. Some maintain that Verecundus’ poem on the Judgment is precisely the work attributed to Tertullian.

74. Another unknown poet follows in the same codex. Certain special details about him are recorded, which we must not omit; perhaps from them others will discover the true author.

“By a certain Calabrian, *On the Abduction of Proserpina*. The book of a certain nobleman, soldier, and most distinguished poet begins, addressed to Vespasian of Sorrento, his companion and friend.” After this inscription, an elegy to Vespasian begins:

> O guardian of the soul, now another Pylades for Orestes,  
> Vespasian, known often to me, farewell.

The manuscript writes *Pilades* and *Horesti*. After the elegy, which serves in place of a prologue, the poem begins:

> I am that man who once composed songs on a slender reed;  
> I sang of Eurydice’s grievous wound and of anger;  
> leaving the infernal lakes, with a greater cothurnus  
> I sang at once of the Punic wars and the mutual wounds  
> of the Ausonian people and the Punic commander,  
> when dread Tisiphone prepared the worst seeds of war.  
> But now the immense heats of Ceres and the long labors …

Thus he continues, setting out the subject. At the end this epitaph is read:

> Sicilian soil gave me birth; a friendly land  
> nourished me among its Calabrians; Rome holds my corpse.  
> My body is exiled from its homeland; may the spirit itself, reader, not be exiled from its author—pray.  
> While the spirit leaps into the various shadows of the air,  
> it has left behind your sorrows, hospitable land.  
> But, reader, it returns for what it hid beneath the earth  
> at the close time when, I ask, you should pray that I be safe.

I have written these verses in this form, correcting certain words. For the third verse, the manuscript had “the body is not exiled, O shore”; for the fourth, *ab actore*, “from the author,” which could nevertheless be retained; for the fifth, “While the spirit prevailed over various shadows in the airs”; and for the seventh, *arto* instead of *arcto*.

75. This anonymous poet, whether Sicilian or Calabrian, is followed in the codex by Bonino Mombrizio’s *First Book on the Passion of the Lord*, addressed to the most holy lord Sixtus IV, supreme pontiff. An elegy to the pontiff serves as the prologue; a heroic poem of six books follows. For information about it and about the author himself, see Sassi, *History of Printing in Milan*, p. 146. The poem on the Passion of the Lord, published for Sixtus IV, was printed at Milan in 1481. Mombrizio’s principal work is the *Lives of the Saints*. Its edition, published by him in two folio volumes, is magnificent, rare, and now sought at great expense.

76. Dracontius occupies the final place in this codex, but under another name. His poem is entitled as follows on fol. 260: “Augustine’s *On God*. The book of Aurelius Augustine *On God* begins auspiciously.” At the end: “The end. A. Augustine’s *On God*.” Immediately afterward the copyist’s name is recorded, as I stated in no. 67, and nothing else occurs in this codex.

Since Dracontius is certainly the author of this entire poem *On God*, as I shall soon demonstrate, it is unnecessary to ask why it bears the name of Augustine rather than Dracontius. It frequently happens in manuscript codices that the work of one person is attributed to another. The reason is often that ancient copyists bound and mixed many works together in a single volume. Consequently, the author who appeared first was often thought to have composed all the works that followed, especially since the author’s name had sometimes been omitted or had been erased by the passage of time or by some other accident.

Perhaps Dracontius’ name was also Aurelius, and this name, prefixed by some copyist only to the work, gave others the opportunity to suppose that he was Aurelius Augustine. That Dracontius had still other names may be inferred from the custom of his age, when it is known that noble men were called by four or five names. It may also have happened that Dracontius’ poem, brought from Spain into Africa, was found among Augustine’s papers and thereby gave someone occasion to inscribe Augustine’s name on it. Because of similar accidents, many works have often been attributed to Fathers to whom they did not truly belong.

77. It is much more surprising that Dracontius’ poem, described under the name of Aurelius Augustine, escaped the diligence of Augustine’s editors, especially the Maurists, so completely that they said nothing about it. Readers ought to have been informed that a poem of this kind existed under that title, but that Augustine was not its author.

Nor in Montfaucon’s *Library of Libraries* of manuscripts, or in similar catalogues, do I find any trace of this poem attributed either to Dracontius or to Aurelius Augustine. In the Vatican Library of Queen Christina of Sweden, Montfaucon mentions under cod. 1336 “Verses of Augustine and Jerome,” and again under cod. 1587 “Several poems of Augustine, Plato, Avitus, Juvencus, and Fortunatus.” These seem, however, to be a few short verses that are also listed under Augustine’s name in other catalogues.

The book of St. Augustine *On Praying to God*, addressed to Proba, his *Hexaemeron*, and excerpts from this work have no connection whatsoever with Dracontius’ poem. In the Library of Saint-Germain, Montfaucon, p. 1125, lists codex 125, containing St. Ambrose’s work *On the Sacraments*, certain works of St. Augustine, and verses on God by Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans. Nor should Dracontius’ poem be understood by these verses: among Hildebert’s published poems there are many verses that could bear such a title.

You will find such titles, “On God,” among several Christian poets—for example, the verses of Victorinus of Pettau, or of Fabius Marius Victorinus the African, to whom they are more correctly attributed, *On Jesus Christ, God and Man*. John Baptist Mantuanus also published a poem entitled *On God-Man*. Under a similar title, a poem by the Mexican Didacus Josephus Abadius appeared at Cesena in 1780: *Heroics on God and God-Man*. This was the third edition of a work praised by many.

78. Dracontius’ poem *On God* is divided into three parts. Although the codex does not explicitly mark three books or parts—for, as I said in no. 69, the two books of *Arator* are likewise nowhere distinguished in the same codex—the division and separation of Dracontius’ parts is nevertheless employed. The beginning of each book is marked by very large letters, elaborately designed, so that it seemed appropriate to enumerate the three books distinctly. The sequence of the subject matter itself and the beginning of each part support this division.

In the first book, after verse 116, the narrative of the work of the six days is connected in the same stream of discourse: “For the first day was that of light,” and so forth. This section had previously been published under the title *Dracontius’ Hexaemeron*, or *On the Work of the Six Days*, beginning: “The first day is light for the lands,” and so forth. The book then proceeds to verse 755, “You who promise yourself,” and a hemistich is added to it, “Almighty eternal God,” as though it were the final verse of the first book.

After this hemistich, with the interval and division I have mentioned, the second book begins: “Inventor, begetter,” and so forth. But it is sufficiently clear in itself that the hemistich “Almighty eternal God” is the beginning of the second book, not the end of the first. Perhaps an ignorant copyist joined it to the end of the first book so that he would not begin the second book with a verse that he had found mutilated and incomplete, thereby making the opening of the book less attractive and elegant.

The second book, including this hemistich, continues through verse 808, “They condemn the hosts,” and so forth. Then, after another division, the third book begins: “Of eternal light,” and continues to the final verse, “Added to the innocent people,” which is verse 682. It should be observed that both the second and third books begin with an invocation of God.

79. Although the codex is recent in age, there are strong indications that it was copied from a very ancient volume. The lacunae, especially those occurring shortly after the beginning, suggest this, as do verses that begin only with their first letter. This appears to have happened because the other letters had already vanished through the passage of time.

Perhaps the frequent errors noted in the codex also arose because the copyist did not sufficiently understand the form and force of the characters. He left a blank space wherever a verse or words were missing, so that they could be supplied from another codex if one should appear somewhere. If all the defects now visible in the codex had already existed in the older volume, it must be judged that the name of Augustine, which the title bore, induced some learned man not to allow this poem to perish entirely. Perhaps we would now lack even this imperfect work of Dracontius if it had not at some point been adorned with a false title.

The spelling in this codex is generally as follows: *herebus*, *hyatus*, *cohercens*, *cathena*, *catherva*, *temptator*, *totiens*. The rest differs little or not at all from common orthography. There is no punctuation, except that two points are occasionally added, arbitrarily, where they were unnecessary or even where the sense entirely rejects them.

80. The second codex of Dracontius that we used is of much greater value, if we consider its antiquity and the care with which it was written, without errors or at least with few. Otherwise, it contains nothing else by Dracontius except the *Elegy*, or *Satisfaction to the King of the Vandals*.

[Col. 0639D] This Vatican codex belongs to the Library of Queen Christina of Sweden, no. 508 or 1267. It is a parchment codex containing various works: six books of Euclid’s *Elements*; thirty-seven chapters of Boethius’ *On Arithmetic*; an *Algebra* by an unknown author; a treatise *On the Sphere* by an unknown author; a *Practice of the Quadrant* by an unknown author; an *Explanation of the Calendar*; and verses by the poet Marcus on St. Benedict, which should be compared with those published by Mabillon in the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of St. Benedict*, vol. I.

81. After these verses of Marcus, Dracontius’ *Elegy* is read; it is the final work in this codex. No title is prefixed, but a blank space was left where one could have been written. The *Elegy* is complete in this codex except for a few missing words; it consists of 158 distichs.

In Sirmond’s edition there are only ninety-nine, after which Rivinus noted, “The rest is missing.” In the Madrid edition, eleven distichs were added from the Azagra codex. When the elegy ends in our codex, the same ancient hand adds: “The *Satisfaction of Dracontius to G&nbsp;uthamund, king of the Vandals, while he was in chains, ends.” This is written in larger letters.

The other works in this codex are written by a different hand and belong to a different period. The verses of Marcus on St. Benedict and Dracontius’ *Satisfaction* are written in the same script, which is distinctive and very different from the scripts commonly known. Trombellius, in his little work *On the Art of Recognizing the Age of Codices*, chapter 14, gives several letters of this script. He had seen only a few codices of this kind in Italy, but had heard that more were preserved in the Vallicellian Library in Rome; Joseph Blanchini had assured him that they had been brought there from Spain.

Later Trombellius also learned that this was the same script called in Italian *gotico cordellato*, which is still used in certain papal bulls. Trombellius concluded that this script was characteristic of codices from approximately the eleventh century. I myself have seen in the Vallicellian Library several lectionaries for ecclesiastical use written in this script. They seem to belong to the tenth or eleventh century, and perhaps they are the very codices that Blanchini claimed had been brought here from Spain.

The Vatican parchment on which Dracontius’ *Satisfaction* was written certainly does not seem to me later than the eleventh century. A similar example of this script is reproduced in the preface of the highly esteemed Cardinal Francisco Lorenzana to the *Isidorian Breviary*, p. 26, from the Gothic codices of his *Breviary* preserved in the Toledo Library.

The system of punctuation in this Dracontius codex is highly distinctive. One point is placed at the end of every hexameter, and one point followed by another with a comma at the end of every pentameter. More noteworthy still is the fact that a particular interrogation mark is always attached to the word where the question begins.

The Spaniards are now attempting to introduce this practice: they retain the customary interrogation mark after the final word of the question but place the same mark, inverted, before the word with which the question begins, in order to assist readers. From the cited Vatican codex we provide an engraved specimen of the script.

## CHAPTER VIII. [Col. 0640D] Dracontius, author of the poem *On God* and of the *Satisfaction*

82. Since the poem *On God* is attributed to Aurelius Augustine in the Vatican codex, while Dracontius’ name does not appear, someone may first ask why we deny it to St. Augustine and then why we confidently assert that Dracontius is its author.

There is less reason for doubt concerning the *Satisfaction*. Although the Vatican codex differs from the other codices in presenting the subject, it agrees completely with them in assigning the authorship to Dracontius. One scruple must nevertheless be removed: Rivinus says that Barthius, in his notes to Claudian, p. 507, doubts whether the letter should be attributed to Dracontius’ corrector rather than to Dracontius himself. Barthius does not doubt that Dracontius wrote this elegy; he doubts whether the verses he cites at verse 87 of Book III of Claudian’s *Third Consulship of Honorius*, “When enemies perish,” and so forth, belong to Dracontius’ elegy or rather to Eugenius, who corrected Dracontius’ letter.

We shall therefore establish by the same procedure that Dracontius, and no one else, is the author of both the poem *On God* and the *Satisfaction*: namely, from the connection of the parts of the poem with one another; the agreement of its subject matter, ideas, phrases, and words with the *Elegy*; and the agreement of the verses now published for the first time with others already published and known to be Dracontius’.

83. No one doubts that the verses entitled *Hexaemeron*, or *On the Work of the Six Days*, which have often been printed under Dracontius’ name, are his. If anyone were now to doubt this because they are inserted in the Vatican codex into the poem attributed to Aurelius Augustine, the doubt could easily be refuted by the authority of Isidore. Isidore not only attributes the *Hexaemeron* to Dracontius but also cites a verse from this work, naming Dracontius as its author. Eugenius and Ildefonsus likewise bear witness: the former revised this *Hexaemeron* of Dracontius that is extant, while the latter recorded in Eugenius’ eulogy the correction of Dracontius made by Eugenius, as we explained at length above in chapters 1, 2, and 3.

I omit the fact that Augustine taught in many places that the world was created in a single moment of time and that the division into six days was allegorical, whereas Dracontius holds and explains the contrary and more widely accepted view that the work of creation was actually completed over a period of six days.

That the author of the letter is Dracontius, not Eugenius, is inferred from Isidore, who long before Eugenius cited a verse from that letter, though without naming its author, as I said in no. 8. To tell the truth, this argument is not as compelling as it may seem to many. If some poet older than Isidore—whether Dracontius or someone else—had composed such a verse among his other works, Isidore could have cited it, and Eugenius could subsequently have inserted it into the letter. Ancient Christian poets commonly borrowed certain hemistichs and complete verses from earlier writers; we shall observe this also in Dracontius.

Nevertheless, until something else is established, this argument is in itself probable: it prevents us from calling Eugenius the author of the letter. It becomes much more probable when compared with the manuscript codices, which agree remarkably in designating Dracontius as the author of the letter. This also explains why Eugenius’ supplement on the seventh day is placed not immediately after the *Hexaemeron* but after the letter: the intention was to prevent Dracontius’ Book II—for that is what the letter is called in these codices—from being separated from Book I by Eugenius’ supplement.

84. But what need is there for conjectures? In our Vatican codex the letter is said to have been written to the king of the Vandals; I shall later confirm from the verses themselves that this is true. Eugenius, therefore, could not have composed it, since he flourished after the destruction of the Vandal kingdom. There are also many other features in the letter that cannot at all suit Eugenius, as will later become clear. Dracontius must therefore be regarded as its certain author.

Once this has been established, we must now examine the connection between the two works. In the Vatican codex the poem *On God* is so closely connected with the already published verses of the *Hexaemeron* that it is completely evident that these verses are part of the same work.

Indeed, if you carefully consider these verses on the work of the six days, you will easily perceive that they have been torn from a longer poem. The first verse in the printed editions is:

> The first day is light for the lands, death alone for the darkness.

Who cannot see that this is not the opening of someone who intended to write about the work of the six days? It is inept, since the subject has not been stated, to begin, “The first day is light for the lands.” Rivinus, although he did not notice this, nevertheless detected an error in the first verse. For it is not correct to mention the earth on the first day, since it appeared or was created on the third day, as Dracontius himself explains shortly afterward, in the third day, verse 150 of Book I:

> That day itself earned the earth, drawn forth from the waves;  
> the earth was extracted, submerged in the vast depths.

Rivinus wished to correct the error as follows:

> The first day is light for the dread lands, death alone for the darkness.

But the true reading is obtained from joining this verse to the preceding verses in the poem *On God*, Book I, verse 115:

> Through so many works God created what he made in the sixth light,  
> for the first day was that of light, death alone for the darkness.

85. The ending of the verses on the work of the six days likewise shows that the poem was not yet finished. Thus Dracontius says in Book I, verse 747:

> Look upon the despised one; raise up the fallen for a little while;  
> help the confused one, because he repents of being guilty,  
> so that I may be able to recount your praises in this poem,  
> as much as I am able.

Dracontius therefore still intends to linger in this poem on proclaiming the praises of the Lord, which he accomplished splendidly in the following two books. Compare now the verses near the end of Book III, verse 663 and following:

> Command that what has been preserved be restored by your accustomed mercy,  
> so that I may deserve to sing your praises through poems.

The same author is recognized in both books. In the first book he had determined to proceed further in celebrating God’s praises in the same poem; in the final book he asked God’s grace for other poems and another time. Therefore he adds in Book III, verse 670:

> But who will be able to recount your work in speech?  
> It is enough to have looked upon God with a trembling heart  
> and reverently approached him with tears and devout prayers.

86. Although the title *Hexaemeron*, or *On the Work of the Six Days*, is old and earlier than St. Isidore, it is nevertheless less suitably applied to the collection of verses published under that title. Most of them proceed beyond the six days.

Even if we grant that Eve was created on the sixth day, only 299 verses—from verse 116, “For the first day,” through verse 416, “God had said these things”—are concerned with recounting the work of the six days. The remaining 338 verses, through the end of Book I, explain the sin of the first parents and God’s judgment. Since the author’s stated subject is to pursue God’s praises through created things, and especially to extol his kindness toward human beings, he gathers much material relevant to his purpose: the merciful judgment in which God’s piety shone no less than his justice; the good things he allowed human beings, expelled from paradise, to enjoy; and the resurrection of the dead, which he proves by many arguments in order to make us increasingly certain of God’s mercy. For God punished humanity with death in such a way as to provide for its immortality through the resurrection of the bodies.

Indeed, even in the verses in which Dracontius recounts the work of the six days, he has only one aim—which Sirmond also recognized: to commend God’s wisdom and goodness toward humanity, always adhering to his stated subject. He begins this narrative as follows:

> Who does not know the Creator and Lord God,  
> wishing to preserve the human race, to whom he gave the world,  
> through all those works that God created in the sixth light?  
> For the first day was that of light.

He concludes the narrative at verse 427 in this way:

> God never forgets so many good works,  
> which he made for humanity and ordained to remain.

Earlier, at verse 339, he had said of living creatures:

> To provide food for the earth-born creatures destined to be created after all things.

To St. Eugenius, Dracontius’ work seemed incomplete, as he himself says, or half-complete, as Ildefonsus explains, because Dracontius had been silent about the seventh day. The true reason, however, is that Dracontius was not composing a poem on the work of the six days, but another poem with a broader subject: God, or God’s praises as revealed through his works. It was therefore not appropriate for him to speak of the rest of the seventh day, as I established more fully in no. 19.

87. In addition, many other features in the verses I am now publishing for the first time and in those formerly published are partly very similar and partly connected with one another. I shall indicate some of them now and discuss others in the notes to the poems.

Book I, verse 2:

> They will recognize that the temples of heaven and the walls of the sky,  
> confessing their creator, will reverently adore him.

These and the following verses are repeated in similar words in the previously published *Elegy*, verse 3:

> The stars, flame, day, sun, night, and moon confess him  
> as their creator; all the ages acknowledge him as lord.

Book II, verse 256:

> What the viper accomplishes when its tail and neck have been cut off,  
> what benefit the spotted serpent provides, medicine declares—  
> the asp, and so forth.

The following published verses of Book I correspond to this, at verse 288:

> And the spotted serpent, scaled, creeps through the entrails,  
> sending forth deadly black poisons from the breath of its mouth,  
> suddenly scattering grievous deaths through its hissing,  
> and itself imparting remedies to the limbs.

The *Elegy*, verse 65, also agrees:

> The asp possesses deaths, and the serpent possesses medicines;  
> the viper often helps, the viper often harms.

In Book III, verses 610 and following, the dry bones restored to life are described; these concern Ezekiel, chapter XXXVII, where the same phrases occur as in the account of the creation of the first human being in Book I, verse 336.

God’s mercy is commended in almost the same words and ideas in Book I, verses 81, 100, 429, 544, 556, 690, 726, and 754; Book II, verses 96, 670, 684, 693 and following, and 800; Book III, verses 185, 210, 533, 658, and 663; and the *Elegy*, verse 288 and following.

From Book II, verse 216, namely,

> Spring, summer, autumn, winter, as the years return,

a nearly complete repetition occurs in the *Elegy*, verse 253:

> Spring, summer, autumn, winter—the year returns upon the year.

This verse is absent from the editions published thus far, but it exists in the most ancient Vatican codex, from which we shall bring the complete elegy to light. It was also used by St. Columbanus.

88. To pass over the many other ideas repeated by Dracontius in his books, as well as certain characteristic expressions of his, such as “panting fire,” “modest in virtue and piety,” and *placidus* for “merciful,” it is especially important to observe that, just as he pleases God, so he prays to him in Book III, verse 597:

> Look, I beg, favorably; do not close your ears to our prayers,  
> holy one, you who kindly give commandments;  
> may human anger fall together with the sun from the heart of the raging man,  
> and may the night itself bring pardon. You who command that it be so,  
> make it happen as you yourself command; have mercy on the one who prays.

Shortly afterward, at verse 646, he presents this example:

> The lord of the Persians feared a herdsman after his kingdoms,  
> among the pastures and cattle, he who afterward ruled in the citadel;  
> restore me now, I beg, released into freedom.

In the *Elegy* he first compares himself to King Nebuchadnezzar, at verse 31:

> The king of the Persians, holding the kingdoms of Babylon …

After the glory of empire, who would deny that he was an ox?

And they disfigured the diademed forehead with a crown;

the words of the leader were the lowings of cattle.

After his Parthian reigns, he feared the ploughman and herdsman,

and, trembling, submitted his royal neck to the yoke.

He wandered through the meadows, grazing on poor grass, [Col. 0644C] and he who had been a man was an ox; from an ox he became a man. Then, to obtain pardon from the king whom he had offended, he sets forth Christ’s command, verse 155:

> Do not God’s commands enjoin that the sun should not set,

> while another is angry, but that a man should remain devout?

From this another argument arises for demonstrating that Dracontius composed the entire poem *On God*, no less than the *Elegy*—as I shall now show more fully.

## CHAPTER IX. Dracontius composed the poem *On God* and the *Satisfaction* to the Vandal king while he was in chains.

89. The fact that Dracontius had been thrown into chains and, while detained in prison, had written the *Elegy* in order to make his king [Col. 0644D] well disposed toward him—something no one had hitherto suspected—is hinted at none too obscurely in the *Elegy* itself, as it was previously published by others, and is now established with complete clarity from both Vatican manuscripts. At Sirmond’s time, this title of the *Elegy* is everywhere reported in print:

> In the following little book is contained the author’s *Satisfaction*, in which he asks pardon from almighty God lest he may have inadvertently erred in anything in the preceding poem.

Then he presents a plea to Augustus Theodosius the Younger for having been silent about that ruler’s triumphs in the same work.

Yet it is astonishing to me that no one has raised even the slightest doubt about the falsity of this title. In Sirmond’s epistle itself, however, there are many indications that Dracontius is not speaking about the preceding poem—that is, about the verses published under the title *Hexaemeron*. For he would have asked pardon from God in a different manner, almost as Marius Victor does in the prologue to his poem on Genesis:

> Do not condemn so harshly the gift which I, now accused, dare to offer;

> look indulgently upon my crimes, and mercifully spare me.

> But if, by the law of metre, the arrangement has sinned in any respect,

> if unsuitable language has gone astray, and the meaning falters,

> let no danger to the measure of faith arise from this.

But Dracontius admits that he had actually committed some serious crime. He does not place that crime in having remained silent in some poem about the triumphs of his sovereign; rather, he says that, although he could have celebrated the sovereign’s praises and had received rewards from him, he had celebrated another person unknown to him and, as I think, an enemy of his sovereign.

90. Thus Dracontius speaks in Sirmond’s text:

[Col. 0645B]

> Thus my tongue, O God, by committing the crime,

> binding me in guilty fault, dragged me toward forbidden things.

In the Madrid edition, from the Azagra manuscript, it reads: “Thus my heart, O God.” Dracontius continues:

> Since I was able to recount the deeds of your leaders,

> from which gifts could at the same time come to me.

The Azagra manuscript reads better: “to recount my own.”

Dracontius immediately adds:

> I despised rewards, with so many gracious kings kept silent,

> and suddenly sought certain dangers, wretched man that I was.

The Azagra manuscript has the less satisfactory reading *tactis* (“touched”) instead of *tacitis* (“silent”).

Again Dracontius casts his guilt upon his tongue:

> Alas for me! For indeed my tongue inflicted wounds upon me.

A little later he adds: “He himself will spare my errors,” that is, God; and: “The fault is indeed serious.” More clearly still, below:

> It had been my fault to keep silent about my gracious lords,

> and to write about one unknown to me, and not about my lord.

[Col. 0645C]

In the Azagra manuscript, *molestos* (“troublesome”) is wrongly given instead of *modestos* (“gracious” or “moderate”).

Dracontius then explains his guilt by means of an apt example:

> Such guilt also follows the ungrateful, who, with profane minds,

> although they know the Lord, worship empty idols,

> so guilt held the people of Israel,

> when the people, forgetting God, worshiped the calf.

I ask: how can these words be applied to the sacred poem on the work of the six days? Why was it a fault not to speak about the sovereign? Or why should he have become angry over this silence? Or why is the man who sings the praises of God and remains silent about his sovereign compared with one who, although he knows the Lord, worships empty idols?

Therefore the following verses are not to be understood as referring to the poem by Dracontius that we possess, but to another poem, which angered his king because it had been composed in praise of one of that king’s enemies:

[Col. 0645D]

> First, before you, I repent—I confess it—of the beginnings of that poem

> which I composed badly.

> After you, most high God, I stand accused before my king and lord,

> from whose authority I groaning seek pardon.

All these statements, and many others that follow, establish what I have said: in this epistle Dracontius is not asking God’s pardon in case he had inadvertently erred in some passage of his poem on the work of the six days, nor is he asking the Younger Theodosius to pardon him for having remained silent about that ruler’s triumphs in the same work.

91. Indeed, when I had examined the Vatican manuscript in which the poem *On God* is preserved, and had read in Book III of this poem through what hardships Dracontius composed the work, I concluded without any doubt that he was seeking pardon from his king, whom he had so gravely offended that he had been thrown into chains and even feared that he might be deprived of his life. For Dracontius says in that book, verses 576ff.:

> Alas for me! For a deed committed not at one time,

> the appointed time has brought together, so that I might pay for my actions.

> [lacuna] Oppressed and burdened on every side,

> chains bind me, tortures subdue me, poverty consumes me.

> A laughingstock to my kind, a source of grief to all, and made

> an enemy, and stripped of a large part of my possessions,

> with uncut hair and wearing filthy rags.

> Acquaintances and strangers are absent; my parents have gone away;

> my kinsmen soon forgot me, though I had spent myself for them;

> whoever had been my friend suddenly went away.

> Bands of servants flee; clients have turned away,

> nor did they grieve at my downfall in so great a calamity.

> While God is angry, all comforts are denied.

> This alone remains: that life should fall, unless you, merciful,

> command that mercy be shown to the afflicted man whom such sufferings have broken.

Dracontius mentions these things and others there, and especially chains at verse 648:

[Col. 0646B]

> Restore me now, I beg, released into freedom,

> crushed beneath the iron weight of the disaster of chains.

Perhaps he is also referring to this at verse 602ff.:

> And turn your attention to my tears, which I pour out by day,

> grieving, and with my body stretched out I lament;

unless in this passage he is hinting at the piece of wood or the stocks in which the feet of defendants were customarily enclosed and their legs stretched out, or, as Prudentius says in the poem *On Vincentius*, spread apart.

92. These indications are clear, but those that I found in another Vatican manuscript are clearer still. There Dracontius’ *Elegy* is preserved before it was interpolated by Eugenius or others. In the genuine *Elegy*, the very passages that I quoted from Sirmond are explained more distinctly, and other passages are added that make the whole matter completely plain. Thus at verse 17 Dracontius says:

> Your words, spoken by the prophet Moses, prove this,

> that you were going to harden Pharaoh’s heart.

[Col. 0646C]

> Thus, O God, my heart, while our guilt of excessive delay sins,

> drives me toward forbidden things.

> Since I was able to recount the deeds of my leaders,

> the war-bearing triumphs of the Asdingian name,

> from which, together with the reward of saving praise,

> great gifts from the reigning lord could come to me,

> I despised rewards, etc.

Then at verse 49 it reads:

> God himself commands and will command my lord

> to restore me and mercifully look upon me.

He calls the king his lord, and continues about him:

> May he preserve me, so that I may speak the praises of his grandfather, his ancestral line, and his own,

> and through his offspring sing the royal vows.

Later, at verse 283:

> If I myself have sinned, what, I beg, is the fault of my people,

> whom cold and needy hunger afflict together?

And again at verse 311:

> Grant pardon, have mercy, I beg; come to the aid of one who pleads;

> let the former blows, chains, and hunger suffice.

[Col. 0646D]

To all this is added a note written by the same ancient hand at the end of the *Elegy*:

> Here ends Dracontius’ *Satisfaction* to Guthamndus, king of the Guandals, while he was in chains.

93. It is therefore also established that Dracontius’ *Satisfaction* was addressed not to Augustus Theodosius the Younger, as Sirmond’s manuscript has it, but to the king of the Vandals—or, as others write, the Wandalans. As for the fact that the Vatican manuscript calls him the king of the “Guandals,” it makes no difference. Even if this were an error, it would nevertheless be a minor one.

I find, however, that the Vandals were once also called Guandals. Certainly they are called this in the glosses on Arator in Vatican Regina manuscript no. 300, of the first century, at verse 2 of preface 2, where the glossator says:

> “Then”—that is, when Rome was besieged, and at the time when the Guandals had besieged Rome and devastated the entire region—a dispute arose over the election of the apostolic [bishop]. But afterward, once Pope Vigilius had been elected, the enemies withdrew, and this is what he is now discussing.

It is indeed false that Rome was then besieged by the Vandals, whose power in Africa had shortly before been utterly destroyed by Belisarius. But I have no doubt that the glossator understood “Vandals” by “Guandals,” or at least that a copyist wrote “Guandals” for “Vandals.”

Nor is there any lack of reason why the Vandals could be called Guandals: *w* has the same force as *gu* in many names, such as Wlphilas and Gulphilas, Wilielmus and Guilielmus. Hugo Grotius notes in his index of Gothic, Vandalic, and other names, published after the historians edited by him and others, that *w* is frequently changed into *gu* by Italians [Col. 0647B] and Gauls.

He could have added the Spaniards. If they paid attention to this and similar observations, they would more easily discover the origin of many words in their own language. In the Dictionary of the Spanish Academy, nothing is established about the origin of *guante*, meaning “glove,” except that the opinion of Brocensis is reported: he thought that the word had been named from the city of Ghent, from which gloves used to be brought.

Stephanus Terreros, who died at Forlì a few years ago, had left in Spain a laborious and learned manuscript *Spanish Dictionary of the Names of Arts and Sciences*, which appeared publicly at Madrid after his death. But it sheds no light on the word *guante*. The true origin of the word is *Wanto*, with *w* changed into *gu*: *guanto*.

Bede, in *The Life of Saint Columbanus*, chapter 14:

> Coverings for the hands, which the Gauls call *wantos*, that is, gloves.

Papias, in his vocabulary:

> *Chirotheca*, *vanti*, that is, a covering for the hand. Sleeves, which we commonly call *wantos*.

In *The Life of Saint Philibert the Abbot*, Book I, chapter 12:

> The robber, with unlawful presumption, stole his gloves there.

See Ducange under the word *WANTUS*.

94. There is another name in the verses of the *Elegy* that we have cited, from which it is proved beyond all doubt that Dracontius had dealings with the king of the Vandals. After naming his leaders, he clearly declares to what people those leaders belonged:

> Since I was able to recount the deeds of my leaders,

> the war-bearing battles of the Asdingian name.

They were therefore leaders of the people of the Asdingi. Who else are the Asdingi but the Vandals?

In other writers, manuscripts and printed copies vary somewhat in representing this name; but the people are the same, whether they are called Astingi, Astringi, Asdingi, or Asdingui. I find the first mention of this nation in Dio Cassius, Book LXXI, where he discusses the Marcomannic War under Antoninus the Philosopher:

> The Astingi, who had Rhaum and Rhatum as leaders, also came, wishing to inhabit Dacia.

He later relates that they obtained peace from Antoninus on the condition that they inflict defeat upon the nations then waging war against him. They did in fact fulfill some of what they had promised.

In Volume I of the *Byzantine History*, page 24 of the Paris edition, in the *Excerpts on Embassies* of Peter the Patrician and the Master, the same event is briefly related:

> The Astingi and the Lacoragi also came to Marcus’ aid.

For this same name, Asdingi, Grotius cites Priscus the Patrician, but perhaps he meant to say Peter the Patrician.

Jordanes, *On the Gothic Affairs*, chapter 16, speaking of Ostrogotha, king of the Goths under the emperor Philip, says:

> He led thirty thousand armed men into battle, having summoned the Thaphili and Astringi to his aid.

Bonaventura Vulcanius, in his notes, writes as a variant reading: “Thaifali and Asdingi.”

The same Jordanes, *On the Gothic Affairs*, chapter 22, speaking of Geberich, king of the Goths under Constantine:

> He equaled the glory of his race through illustrious deeds, soon wishing to extend the beginnings of his reign against the Vandal people, against Visumar, their king, who was of the stock of the Asdingi, the most distinguished among them, and whose lineage, according to the historian Dexippus, showed itself to be the most warlike.

Thus in his preface to Jordanes and the other historians, Grotius lists the first kings of the Vandals: Rhaumus, Rhaetus, Wisimar, Crocus, and Frididala.

In the index of Gothic, Vandalic, and other words, Grotius says that the word *Asdingi* comes from *Haist-dingen*, meaning “swift in public judgment.” Jordanes explains it differently.

## CHAPTER X. Dracontius was writing in Spain under Guntharius, king of the Vandals.

95. The name of the king to whom Dracontius’ *Satisfaction* was written is given in the Vatican manuscript as Guthamndus. We must therefore ask why we confidently hold that this king was Guntharius, since the corrupted name could be twisted to refer to another Vandal king.

This question opens the way for us to explain the history of the Vandal kingdom in Spain, which has been rendered astonishingly complicated and confused by the contradictory accounts of mutually disagreeing writers. This history will receive some illumination from Dracontius; conversely, when it is itself illuminated by Dracontius and other records, it will greatly help us to define Dracontius’ precise age within its proper limits.

The Alans, Suebi, Vandals, and other peoples, stirred up by Stilicho—who himself was a Vandal—crossed the Rhine and disturbed the Roman Empire. After raging through Gaul, they reached the Pyrenees. Temporarily repelled by the barrier there through the efforts of Didymus and Verinianus, they soon entered Spain in the year 409, as Orosius relates in Book VII, chapter 40, Hydatius in the *Chronicle*, Olympiad 297, and Isidore in his *History of the Vandals*. Isidore says that Didymus and Verinianus, as he calls them, were most noble Romans and extremely powerful brothers.

It is not sufficiently certain which leader the Vandals then followed. Grotius, in his preface to the *Vandal Histories*, relates that Godigisel was king of the Vandals when they invaded Spain, and that Guntharius succeeded him in Gallaecia. Ruinart, in *History of the Vandal Persecution*, chapter 1, reports that the Franks were the first of all to resist the efforts of the Vandals, killing their king Godigisel; afterward the Vandals, joined with the Alans and with Guntharius substituted in Godigisel’s place, crossed the Rhine.

96. Grotius’ account seems more accurate, since it rests upon the words of Procopius, Book I, chapter 3:

> From there the Vandals settled in Spain under the leadership of Godigisel, Spain being the first Roman province from the Ocean. Honorius made an agreement with Godigisel that they should hold that dwelling without harming the peoples.

When Ruinart quoted these words in chapter 2, he judged that one should write “under the leadership of Gunderic” instead of “under the leadership of Godigisel,” since Guntharius is called Gunderic by many, while others name him differently.

But Procopius clearly contradicts Ruinart. Shortly afterward he repeats that the Vandals established their settlement in Spain near Africa, where, he says, after Godigisel’s death, his two sons had assumed power: Gontharis, born from his legitimate wife [this is Guntharius or Gunderic], and Gizericus, his illegitimate son [this is commonly called Genseric]. The former was still a boy, and so on.

Isidore says the following about Guntharius in his *Chronicle*:

> The first king of the Vandals in Spain, Gunderic, succeeded and reigned for eighteen years in the regions of Gallaecia.

These words are obscure, but because of the word “succeeded,” they seem to indicate Procopius’ view rather than the contrary one.

Hydatius, in his *Chronicle*, does not explain under whose leadership the Vandals invaded Spain. But after recounting the four scourges by which Spain was devastated—war, famine, pestilence, and wild beasts—he continues:

> After the provinces of Spain had been overthrown by the ravaging of the aforesaid scourges, the barbarians, moved to make peace by the mercy of the Lord, divide among themselves by lot the regions of the provinces for settlement. The Vandals and Suebi occupy Gallaecia, situated at the western extremity of the Ocean Sea; the Alans receive Lusitania and the province of Carthage; and the Vandals called Silingi receive Baetica.

Isidore, in his *History of the Goths*, calls these people the Vandals Selingui. Speaking of Wallia, king of the Goths, he says:

> He destroyed all the Vandals Selingui in Baetica by war.

The punctuation should not be placed as some do, “the Vandals, Selingui.”

In his *History of the Vandals*, Isidore calls them the Vandals, Silingi. Although he derives most of his account from Hydatius, he presents this matter in a very different way:

> The Vandals and Suebi occupy Gallaecia; the Alans, Lusitania and the province of Carthage; but the Vandals called Silingi, having abandoned Gallaecia and devastated the islands of the province of Tarraconensis, receive Baetica by lot.

But greater confidence must be placed in Hydatius, who was present. He says, under Olympiad 299:

> The Vandals Silingi in Baetica were all destroyed by King Wallia.

The Alans, who ruled over the Vandals and Suebi, were so thoroughly slaughtered by the Goths that [lacuna] they submitted themselves to the protection of Gunderic, king of the Vandals, who had settled in Gallaecia.

Later he reports that the Suebi had been besieged by the Vandals; that, abandoning the siege when Asterius, the count of the Spains, was approaching, they left Gallaecia and crossed into Baetica; and that Castinus, master of the soldiers, who had undertaken war in Baetica with the assistance of the Goths, was deceived by the treachery of his auxiliaries, defeated, and forced to flee to Tarragona.

Then, in Olympiad 301, he relates that the Vandals plundered the Balearic Islands and destroyed Carthage Spartaria.

97. The nation of the Vandals therefore seems to have been divided into two tribes when they entered Spain, but in such a way that both those simply called Vandals and the Vandals Silingui were designated by the same Vandal name. For no distinction of the name “Silingui” appears before the division of the provinces.

The word “Asdingi” is certainly different from “Silingui.” For Dracontius, after the Silingui had been destroyed, commends Guntharius—who was king of the Vandals, not of the Silingui—through the glory of the name Asdingui.

Nor do I see on what grounds Ambrosius Morales, Book XI, chapter 22, asserts that after the Vandals had crossed into Africa the Silingui remained in Baetica.

Wolfgang Lazius, in Book XI of *On the Migrations of Certain Peoples*, relates that Godogesitus led the Vandals into Spain and that Modogisel governed them there; that Guntharius and Genseric were Modogisel’s sons. Perhaps, beneath those two corrupted names, two different leaders are concealed, one of whom ruled the Silingui and the other the remaining Vandals. But Lazius neither explains from which author he derived his account, nor can I discover it.

The sequence of events may therefore be arranged, especially from Hydatius and Procopius, as follows. The Vandals invaded Spain under the leadership of Godigisel. Those who were called the Vandals Silingui inhabited Baetica. The other Vandals, who were not Silingui, established their settlements in Gallaecia, where Guntharius—or Gunderic, as others call him—succeeded his father Godigisel and reigned for many years. He also took his brother Genseric as his associate, so that Genseric might have primary responsibility for military affairs.

After several wars among the barbarians, after Wallia had destroyed the Vandals Silingui, Guntharius with his people crossed into Baetica. From there the Vandals waged wars against the Romans and other barbarians, by land and sea.

This was the state of affairs around the year 425, when Dracontius lived in Baetica under Vandal rule and composed the poems that we now possess while he was being held in chains. Everything that Dracontius reports in his epistle corresponds remarkably to this period and to this king, and can scarcely be applied to any other Vandal king.

98. The king’s name, expressed at the end of the epistle as Guthamndus, is either one of the many names by which Guntharius was customarily called in different forms, or it was corruptly written by the copyist in place of Guntharius.

Although Gontharis, Guntharis, Guntharius, and Gundericus are not genuinely distinct names for the same man, they are one and the same name used in different forms by writers, as commonly happens with barbarian names. Thus his brother Genseric is called by some Gizericus, by others Gisericus, by others Gaizericus, and by others Gantzrichus.

Of the Vandal kings who reigned after Guntharius—Genseric, Huneric, [Col. 0650D] Guntabundus, or, as others write, Guntamundus, Trasamundus, Hilderic, and Gelimer—the name Guthamndus could, because of some resemblance, refer only to Guntabundus. But other considerations are available for saying that the epistle was written to Guntharius, not to Guntabundus.

For Dracontius, in order to praise the clemency of his king, sings at verse 211:

> God, seeing that you did not wish to shed blood,

> bestowed upon you, while absent, triumphs by land and sea,

> so that he might give them without sin, yet not without praise:

> Ansila bears witness; the Moor lies everywhere.

It is clear from this that the king whom Dracontius praises waged wars and obtained triumphs through others, without having been personally present.

[Col. 0651A] 99. That this fits Guatharius especially well can clearly be gathered from Procopius, Book I of the *Vandal History*:

> When Boniface saw that he could neither resist the emperor nor have any hope of safety if he went to Rome, he decided to exert every effort to form an alliance with the Vandals, whom I have mentioned above as having established settlements in Spain near Africa. After Godigisel’s death, his two sons had assumed power there: Gontharis, born from his legitimate wife, and Gizericus, his illegitimate son. The former was still a boy and by nature not very energetic; the latter was highly practiced in arms and the most capable of all mortals.

Since Guntharius was younger than Genseric and naturally not very energetic, whereas Genseric was capable and practiced in arms, Dracontius’ verses can scarcely fit anyone other than Guntharius.

And indeed Dracontius twice calls them his lords and leaders, whom he himself could have praised, as at verse 21:

> Since I was able to recount the deeds of my leaders,

and again at verse 93:

> It had been my fault to keep silent about my gracious lords.

By this he indicates Guntharius himself, by whom he had been thrown into chains, and Genseric, who, because he directed the war, was regarded as a kind of second king.

100. A more certain argument could be drawn from the triumphs won by land and sea if it were clearly established what kind and whose triumphs these were. But Dracontius says only:

> Ansila bears witness; the Moor lies everywhere.

In the Paris edition of Sirmond’s complete works, the following note appears in the margin beside this verse:

> A learned man suspects that *ATTILA* should be read—the man whom Theodosius diverted with money when he was threatening Thrace.

Theophanes, *Chronography*, under the final year of the Younger Theodosius.

But now that it is clear to us that this *Elegy* was not written to the Younger Theodosius but to one of the Vandal kings, there is no reason to think of Attila threatening Thrace.

If there were an error in *Ansila*, one might conjecture *Amsagha*, which is a river on the coast of Numidia, as Mela and Pliny show. Others write *Ampsaga*, others *Ausaga*; it is now called Suffegmar by some and Rumel by others. With part of Numidia lying between, it separates Africa proper from Mauretania.

This river is also mentioned by Victor of Vita, Book II of *The History of the Vandal Persecution*, chapter 5. Relating the cruelty of Huneric, king of the Vandals, toward his own people, he says:

[Col. 0651D]

> He imitated Geiseric, his father, who, after binding his brother’s [Guntharius’] wife to a weight of stones, threw her into the famous river Ampsaga of Cirta and drowned her, and after killing the mother also murdered her sons.

One might also conjecture *Antala*, whom others call *Antallas*. Of him Procopius says in Book II of the *Vandal History*:

> Antalas alone of the Moors inhabited Byzacena; alone during this period he was loyal to the Romans,

that is, under Gelimer.

And in Book I, chapter 9, he relates that the Vandals were routed in battle by the Moors of Byzacena, who obeyed Antalas, while Hilderic was king.

But even if we wished to read “Ampsaga bears witness” or “Antalas bears witness,” the precise date of the battle indicated by Dracontius could not be derived from it. Before Genseric transferred all his Vandals to Africa after his brother Guntharius’ death, he waged war in Mauretania, as I shall soon say. He could therefore have won some victory at Ampsaga and fought against and defeated some Moor named Antalas.

101. But since the Azagra and Vatican manuscripts agree completely with Sirmond’s manuscript in giving this name as *Ansila*, it should be retained—especially because Grotius, in his index of proper Gothic, Vandalic, and other names, also lists *ANSILA*, from *ans ile*, that is, “hastening toward favor.” He refers to *festinatio* (“hastening”) under *ilunge* in the dictionary, and notes that *festinare* (“to hasten”) remains in use there.

It is therefore most probable that Ansila was some leader among the Goths or Suebi with whom the Vandals were accustomed to wage war in Spain.

For when Orosius, Book VII, chapter 43, had related that the Goths fought on behalf of the Romans against the other peoples who had settled throughout Spain, he added:

[Col. 0652B]

> Although the other kings of the Alans, Vandals, and Suebi had also entered into an agreement with us on the same terms, sending a message to the emperor Honorius: “You make peace with all and accept hostages from all; we will fight among ourselves and perish among ourselves.”

Nor would it be absurd to assert that the Ansila mentioned by Dracontius was the one whom the Goths count among their *anses*. For they called certain of their nobles *anses*, as though demigods; Grotius suspects that the origin of the cities called Hanseatic may be sought in this word.

Among the other *anses*, or Gothic nobles, Jordanes lists the following in *On the Gothic Affairs*, chapter 14:

> Ostrogotha begot Unilt. Unilt begot Athal. Athal begot Achiulf. Achiulf begot ANSILA and Ediulf, Vuldulf, and Hermeric.

Since Ostrogotha flourished under the emperor Philip, the chronology permits us to believe that Ansila lived during Guntharius’ lifetime.

Hydatius, Olympiad 306, mentions Aiulf, who killed Censorius at Seville. The name Aiulf seems to be the same as Achiulf, who fathered Ansila.

It may be inferred from this that the battle in which Ansila was defeated was naval, because in the preceding verse Dracontius joins together triumphs by sea and land and gives as examples in this verse Ansila and the Moors, who lay defeated everywhere. The victory over the Moors seems to have been on land; the first victory, therefore, was naval—that over Ansila.

This also fits very well the period of which I am speaking and Guntharius. For it is established from Orosius and others that the Goths acquired a number of ships at this time, and it is no less certain that the Vandals used ships.

After Hydatius has reported in his *Chronicle* that the Vandals, already dwelling in Baetica under King Guntharius, had won a victory over Castinus, master of the soldiers, he adds that in Olympiad 301 they plundered the Balearic Islands. On that occasion it may be inferred that they fought the Goths at sea, even from these verses of Dracontius alone.

102. Wolfgang Lazius speaks of the naval strength of the Vandals while they were established in Baetica in Book XI of *On the Migrations of Certain Peoples*. He adduces several verses from Sidonius’ panegyric to Augustus Anthemius and from another panegyric to Sidonius’ father-in-law in support of his view.

But Sidonius clearly describes the maritime power of Genseric in Africa:

[Col. 0653A]

> From there the Vandal enemy

> presses upon me, and each year with a numerous fleet

> wages war for our destruction; and, with the order of fate reversed,

> the parched Byrsa brings the Caucasian furies upon me.

Here he uses “Byrsa” for Carthage.

Prosper may be cited more accurately in his *Chronicle*, where he rightly complains under the year 427:

> From that time the sea was made accessible to peoples who did not know how to use ships, when they were summoned by the combatants to provide aid; and responsibility for the war begun against Boniface was transferred to Count Sigisvult. The nation of the Vandals crossed from Spain into Africa.

That the Vandals under Guntharius won a triumph over the Moors may perhaps seem difficult for some to accept. The common opinion of writers is that the Vandals did not cross into Africa until after Guntharius’ death. This is true if it is understood of the entire nation crossing at once, with Spain completely abandoned; but it is not true if it is taken to mean that there had been no earlier incursions by Vandals from Spain into Africa.

There are two ways in which the Moors may be explained as having been defeated by the Vandals before the entire Vandal nation invaded Africa: either before their alliance with Count Boniface was initiated, or after it had been initiated.

103. Boniface, well known for his friendship with Saint Augustine, incurred the emperor’s displeasure through the treachery and betrayal of Aetius and was declared a public enemy. Finding himself unequal to the emperor’s power, he joined the Vandals to himself as allies, as Procopius relates at length in Book I of the *Vandal History*.

After sending, he says, some of his most powerful friends to Spain, Boniface entered into an equal treaty with both sons of Godigisel, so that a third of Africa would be assigned to each of them; and if either were attacked by war, the danger would be shared.

After this Vandal treaty had been concluded, they crossed the Strait of Gades into Africa.

Others relate that Boniface himself went to Spain in order to establish friendship with Guntharius and Genseric.

Guntharius was therefore alive when Boniface summoned the Vandals to his aid, and it is hardly likely that the Vandals delayed providing assistance. This is why different writers disagree about the year [p. 79] of the Vandals’ crossing into Africa: some failed to distinguish one of their incursions from the crossing of the entire nation.

Ruinart, in chapter 3 of *History of the Vandal Persecution*, considers the consular dating in Prosper’s *Chronicle* more certain. It says that Genseric crossed from Spain into Africa during the consulship of Hierius and Ardabur, that is, in the year 427.

Cassiodorus likewise writes in his *Chronicle* that the Vandals, driven out of Spain by the Goths, crossed into Africa during the consulship of Hierius and Ardabur.

But since Hydatius lived in Spain at precisely this time, and reports the migration of the entire Vandal nation into Africa more distinctly, dating it to the year 429, his account should rather be followed.

For he says, under Olympiad 302, year 1—that is, 429, according to Pagius’ calculation:

> King Gaiseric crossed from the coast of the province of Baetica with all the Vandals and their families in the month of May, leaving Spain for Mauretania and Africa. Before he crossed, he was informed that Hermigarius the Suebe was plundering the neighboring provinces along his route. He turned back with some of his men and caught up with the plunderer in Lusitania. Not far from Emerita, which Hermigarius had contemptuously treated despite the injury done to the holy martyr Eulalia, many of those whom he had with him were killed by Gaiseric. Seizing, as he thought, a swifter Eurus [perhaps: having seized a faster horse, as he supposed], he was driven headlong by divine power into the river Ana and perished. With him thus destroyed, Gaiseric soon sailed on from where he had begun.

The Vandals therefore did not cross into Africa because they had been driven out by the Goths, as Cassiodorus confidently writes. They crossed voluntarily and, as we have said, at Boniface’s invitation.

Nor does Hydatius allow us to doubt the year 429: he specifies even the month of May and relates the particular circumstances of the return journey against the Suebi.

104. If, then, we wish to interpret Dracontius as speaking of the triumphs that the Vandals won over the Moors after they had been summoned into alliance by Boniface, we must hold that Dracontius composed the *Elegy* while Guntharius was still alive and the Vandal nation had not yet abandoned Spain, although war had already been undertaken against the Moors and on Boniface’s behalf.

For Hydatius traces the beginning of Boniface’s revolt back to the year 423, where he says:

> Boniface, abandoning the palace, invades Africa.

The revolt became more openly manifest in the following years, however, and the alliance established between Boniface and the Vandals should perhaps be dated to around the year 426.

But there is no need to defer the battle between the Vandals and the Moors until the time of Boniface’s open revolt and the alliance formed between him and the Vandals. Hydatius, than whom we have no more authoritative witness for these matters and periods, reports under the year 425:

> The Vandals plunder the Balearic Islands.

Then, after Carthage Spartaria and Seville had been destroyed and Spain plundered, they invade Mauretania.

Why should we deny that all these events occurred in the same year 425 to which Hydatius assigns them? How well does Hydatius agree with Dracontius?

> He granted the absent man triumphs over land and sea;

> Ansila bears witness; the Moor lies everywhere.

Wolfgang Lazius attempts to prove from Sidonius, in Book XI of *On the Migrations of Certain Peoples*, that the Vandals, once they had entered Spain, already coveted Africa and practiced piracy in the Atlantic and Mediterranean seas. But Sidonius is plainly speaking of the time when Genseric held the Vandal kingdom in Africa, as I observed shortly above in section 102.

Hydatius clearly supports us, and his testimony is sufficient.

## CHAPTER XI. Several arguments are proposed and examined by which Dracontius is said to have written in Africa.

105. In his *Elegy*, Dracontius indicates another event from which an argument may be drawn for determining his age. Thus he addresses the king of the Vandals at verse 299:

> Illustrious, mighty in arms, source of your piety,

> learned, inclined by nature toward pardon,

> “I do not forgive the man,” he said, “but his tongue deserves it.”
