This guilty and learned man had been Vincomalus. If only we could discover who this guilty and learned Vincomalus was, we could easily identify the king to whom Dracontius is writing. But first, in the manuscript codex the name Vincomalus itself is corruptly written as *vinco malos* [“I conquer the wicked”]. Someone might therefore suspect that *Victovalus* or *Victovales* should be read, as though the reference were to earlier times, when the Vandals entered into an alliance with the Victovales under Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus. Others might perhaps conjecture *Winodamus*, who, as the fifth century advanced, enjoyed great favor and friendship with Childeric, king of the Franks; Petavius discusses him in *Rationarium temporum*, part 1, book VI, chapter 13.

But the true reading is the one I have given, *Vincomatus*, or, if you prefer, in Greek fashion, *Vincomalos*. Since it is established that persons of this name lived around this period, *Vincomalus* is correctly inferred from *vinco malos*. In the year 453 the consuls were Vincomalus and Opilio; and Marcellinus, in his *Chronicle*, reports that the head of Saint John the Baptist was discovered under the consulship of Vincomalus and Opilio, in the month of February. In the *Notice of the Provinces and Cities of Africa during the Vandal Persecution*, among the bishops of Mauretania Caesariensis, number 98 lists Vincemalus of Baparas; Ruinart notes that the Laon manuscript reads *Vincemalos Baparensis*. At the Thirteenth Council of Toledo, in the year 683, Vnicomalus, a deacon acting as representative of Atilanus, bishop of Pamplona, subscribed the acts; in this name, with a slight transposition of two letters, *Vincomalus* may perhaps be read. But this person—whether Vnicomalus or Vincomalus—belongs to a later period.

### 106

Although no other Vincomalus or Vincemalus now occurs to me, there may nevertheless have been several persons so called, and probably there were. If, among these two, we wish to understand Dracontius as referring to the consul Vincomalus, the event could have occurred under Godigisel, father of Guntharius, while he was opening a route for himself through the Pyrenees against the Romans who resisted him, or after he had settled in Gallaecia with his Vandals—namely, if Godigisel forgave Vincomalus while he was still young, and that same Vincomalus later attained the consulship as an old man, since only forty-four years elapsed between the Vandals’ entry into Spain and Vincomalus’s consulship.

If someone attempts to explain Dracontius by reference to the bishop Vincomalus or Vincemalus in Africa, this can scarcely be understood unless we maintain that Dracontius lived and wrote in Africa. From this someone might draw the conjecture that Dracontius’s *Satisfaction* was addressed to Guntabundus, king of the Vandals in Africa. For the king’s name, written in the Vatican codex as *Guthamndus*, can be altered with equal ease into *Guntabundus* or *Guntamundus* as into *Guntharius*. Moreover, when Dracontius says:

> Illustrious, mighty in arms, source of your graciousness,  
> And learned, by nature more inclined to pardon,

he alludes to Genseric, founder of the Vandal kingdom in Africa and grandfather of Guntabundus; for Genzo, Guntabundus’s father, did not reign. Genseric is rightly called mighty in arms and learned: he acquired a great name for himself by his weapons, possessed considerable intelligence, and aspired to the reputation of learning.

### 107

The other distich of Dracontius, which he immediately adds:

> “I do not forgive the man,” he said, “but his speech deserves it”—

> This guilty and learned man had been Vincomalus,

fits admirably the bishop Vincemalus of Bapara in Mauretania Caesariensis. He was one of the Catholic bishops who came to Carthage to give an account of the faith in the eighth year of King Huneric. Huneric succeeded Genseric, and Guntabundus succeeded Huneric. It therefore fits perfectly that Vincemalus was regarded as guilty by Genseric, but was released through pardon on account of his learning, which he ought not to have lacked as a bishop; and that Dracontius, asking pardon from Guntabundus, recalled the example of his grandfather.

Some who believe that they can distinguish the styles of different nations and periods, even when those periods are not far removed from one another, will add that a certain African quality appears in Dracontius, and that phrases and words are found which seem more characteristic of the late fifth century than of its beginning. On this difference of style I shall say briefly that it is extremely difficult to find, in diction alone, a distinction between two writers who lived in the same fifth century, one a Spaniard and the other an African. Furthermore, Dracontius composed these poems after being thrown into prison and overwhelmed by hardships. It is therefore not surprising if his language sometimes flows turbidly, although many features of this kind that might cause displeasure must be attributed altogether to the scribes and interpolators by whom Dracontius was badly treated.

### 108

As for the other conjecture concerning the bishop Vincemalus, I would not deny that the order of the narrative proceeds suitably. But since Dracontius can be explained by reference either to the consul Vincomalus or to another person of the same name under Guntharius, the argument drawn from this is weak, and is plainly refuted by the triumphs on land and sea that Dracontius mentions.

For concerning Guntabundus Procopius relates the following in book I of his *Vandal History*:

> This Gundemundus, after fighting many battles against the Moors and treating the Christians most harshly, died of illness.

There is nothing from which one can infer that he fought these battles while absent; still less can one infer that naval battles were fought in his time, or that the Vandals fought against the Goths, whose leader was Ansila. Add to this that Guntabundus obtained the Vandal kingdom in Africa toward the end of the year 484 and died in the year 496 or the following year, as some maintain.

Eugenius, however, who corrected Dracontius’s booklets before the year 650, seems to attribute greater antiquity to them when he says that they “take on a shining robe after a long passage of time”; and he again raises the objection to himself: “And who among the ancients alters poems?” Ildefonsus confirms this in his eulogy of Eugenius, where he reports that Eugenius corrected Dracontius’s booklets, which antiquity had handed down in a corrupted state.

These considerations certainly favor assigning Dracontius’s date to the beginning of the fifth century rather than its end. Columbanus too, who flourished at the end of the fifth and beginning of the sixth century, referred to Dracontius’s poems among ancient writings, as I said in number 8.

### 109

A further conjecture may be drawn from the praises with which Dracontius addresses the king, making it unlikely that this king was Guntabundus. Although Guntabundus was more lenient toward the Catholics than Genseric and Huneric had been, he was nevertheless an Arian and a persecutor of Catholics, as Procopius and others state; or at least he did not restrain the Arians when they raged against the Catholics.

Dracontius, however, held the Catholic doctrine concerning the Holy Trinity and professes it throughout his poem. It is not superfluous to demonstrate this here. In book I, verse 562, he writes:

> God alone is eternally ruler and creator,  
> God is triple in power, God threefold and yet one,  
> From whom every gracious thing hoped for is granted.

Sirmondus reads: “God is one in power, God is triune.” But the unity of nature is sufficiently expressed by the words “God alone” and “God, all and one”; while the expressions “God is triple in power” and “triune God” are customarily employed by ancient Christian poets to explain the three persons.

Claudius Marius Victor, or Victorinus, used the same words at the beginning of book I of his work on Genesis: “God is triple in power.” Nor does the Brasichella Index of Expurgated Books note anything against him when his work is reviewed. Elsewhere one finds *triple majesty*, *triple piety*, *triple power*, *triple manifestation*, *triple divinity*, and *triple name*. More serious still, *triple deity* is sung in the Church. I have discussed these expressions more fully in my commentary on Prudentius, pages 259, 396, and 587 (*Patrologia Latina*, vol. LIX, col. 797, commentary on verse 20; the same volume, col. 915, commentary on verse 1; this volume, col. 19, commentary on verse 3 of the *Psychomachia*).

In S. Eugenius’s poem 4, *On the Good of Peace*, Sirmondus printed:

> Holy supreme Peace, God, grants rewards for sins;  
> Holy supreme Peace, God, destroys those who quarrel.

In the Madrid edition no variant is noted from the Azagra codex. In the Vatican Alexandrian codex, which I have cited elsewhere, both verses read: “Triple supreme Peace, God.” This seems to be the correct reading, and it is expressed in the same way as “God is triple in power,” unless one prefers to accommodate the meter in this fashion: “Threefold supreme Peace, God,” as Prudentius has in verse 1 of the *Apotheosis*: “The supreme God is threefold.”

### 110

Dracontius has other statements about the Trinity that agree perfectly with Catholic doctrine. Thus in book II, concerning Christ, whom he had called God, he continues in verse 68:

> Remaining consort with the Father, and one Spirit,  
> God in a threefold mind, God the creator, beyond time.

With the same meaning with which he said in book I, “God is triple in power,” he now says, “one God in a threefold mind.” A little earlier, in verse 65, he had spoken of the Father’s divine mind:

> Living, all-producing, immeasurable, one mind.

Then, in verse 80, concerning the Son:

> And God becomes, after the temples of heaven, a figure under flesh,  
> A passible, mortal man, everlasting without end.

And again, in verse 89:

> How, O God, by your mouth—[the wording is uncertain]—  
> You deigned to enter a virgin’s breasts and womb.

He continues in verse 50:

> For whoever has understanding knows that thus he bore the limbs,  
> And was on earth, so that the Almighty might not leave  
> The heavenly tribunal; the Son was never acknowledged without the Father,  
> Nor the Father ever named without the pledge;  
> The Spirit, immeasurable, holy, good, arbiter and judge,  
> Third yet one and the same, eternal first and middle.

In the same book, concerning the Son of God:

> God alone everywhere, source, creator, and hope of all things,  
> You will always be what you are, what you were, and what you were before . . .  
> Although the heavens, the earth, and the sea could not contain you,  
> You place yourself within the small heart  
> Of the human breast, conceived by a faithful mind . . .  
> For Christ has been given to us as the one hope of salvation.

He has many other similar passages concerning Christ as God, eternal and one with the Father. These plainly contradict the heresy of the Arians, and specifically of the Goths, from whom the Vandals are said to have learned that heresy. For, as Isidore reports in his *History of the Goths*, the Goths maintained that the Son was inferior to the Father in majesty and later than him in eternity. They held that the Holy Spirit was neither God nor a substance of the Father, but had been created through the Son and was devoted to the service of both, subject to the obedience of both.

### 111

It is therefore not credible that Dracontius, who professes himself anti-Arian and, with great humility of spirit, asks God’s pardon for his sins both in the poem *On God* and in the *Elegy*, should have lavished such extensive praises on Guntabundus, an Arian king and the grandson of Genseric, the most savage persecutor of the Catholics—or even have asked that his life be prolonged so that he might celebrate Genseric and other heretics in his poems.

For in the *Elegy*, verse 49, he prays:

> My God himself commands and will command my lord  
> To restore me and look upon me with compassion.  
> May he preserve me, that I may sing the praises of his grandfather,  
> his father's, and his own,  
> and, through his offspring, sing the royal vows.

Someone may perhaps reply that Dracontius cannot be excused at all, whether he wrote in Africa or in Spain; for Guntharius was an Arian, and therefore a Catholic man ought not to have heaped so many and such great praises upon him.

The question deserves examination: whether, and when, the Vandals in Spain embraced the Arian heresy. As I consider the chronology and the writings of contemporary authors, the Vandals in Spain seem to me to have been Catholics. Perhaps they were deceived only toward the end by the fraud of the Arian Goths—if indeed they were deceived in Spain, and not rather in Africa, where the Arian Goths whom Boniface had brought with him began widely to spread their heresy while Saint Augustine was still alive.

Orosius, although living in Africa, was himself a Spaniard; and, writing around the year 416 about events in Spain, he gives the following testimony concerning the barbarians’ clemency and religion, excepting the Goths, whom he does not name:

> Yet even after this, the barbarians immediately abhorred their swords and turned to the plough; and they cherish the Romans who remain as allies and friends, so that some Romans are now found among them who would rather endure poor freedom among barbarians than tributary anxiety among Romans.  
>   
> Indeed, if the barbarians had been admitted within Roman territory for no other reason than that throughout the East and West the churches of Christ are commonly filled with Huns, Sueves, Vandals, Burgundians, and various innumerable peoples of believers, the mercy of God would seem worthy of praise and exaltation; for although such great nations received the knowledge of the truth at the cost of our own ruin, they could not have found it except on this occasion.

This account by Orosius clearly indicates, at least for the most part, the Catholic faith of the Vandals.

### 112

At the same time Idacius was living in Spain, specifically in Gallaecia, where the Vandals remained for a long period under King Guntharius. After narrating Guntharius’s unfortunate death, he then reports that Genseric succeeded him in these words, under Olympiad 301:

> His brother Gaiseric succeeds him in the kingdom. According to the report of some, having become an apostate from the Catholic faith, he is said to have passed over into the treachery of Arianism.

The fact that Idacius says that Genseric, an apostate from the Catholic faith, passed into the treachery of Arianism; that he reports this after Guntharius’s death without reproaching Guntharius with the Arian sect; and that he attributes Genseric’s apostasy only on the report of some—these points clearly indicate that the Vandals in Spain either never adhered to Arianism or did so only shortly before crossing into Africa.

Isidore stated the same thing more clearly in his *Vandal History*:

> Giseric, the brother of Gunderic, succeeds to the kingdom for forty years; having become an apostate from the Catholic faith, he is said to have been the first to pass into the treachery of Arianism.

Albert Krantzius, in book I, chapter 27 of his *Vandalia*, relates that Genseric, frightened by the unfortunate death of his brother Guntharius, initially appeared more restrained but was later found to be different. Let him bear responsibility for this statement; he does not support it with any authority.

### 113

Someone may object that Boniface had married a Vandal woman who had previously been an Arian, but that he married her only after she had renounced the Arian heresy, as we learn from Saint Augustine’s letter to Boniface, number 220, or 70 in another numbering. Writers generally report the matter this way, and Ruinart states it explicitly in chapter 3 of his *History of the Vandal Persecution*.

But in Saint Augustine I find only the following:

> You sailed, you took a wife . . . I heard that you refused to marry her unless she had first become Catholic; and yet the heresy of those who deny the true Son of God prevailed so greatly in your household that your daughter was baptized by them.

Augustine does not explain where Boniface sailed, still less from what people he took a wife. If she had been infected with Arian heresy, as Augustine’s words suggest, and had been brought from Spain, she might have belonged to the Gothic people. For Boniface had gone to Spain to fight against the Vandals alongside Castinus and the Goths; unable to endure Castinus’s arrogance, he returned to Africa.

Later, the Goths serving under Boniface in Africa brought with them the Arian bishop Maximinus, who dared to challenge Saint Augustine to a public disputation. The Arians had already become so influential in Africa that even the comes Pascentius, formerly a disciple of Auxentius, the Arian bishop of Milan, wished to enter into a debate about the faith with Saint Augustine, as is demonstrated by Augustine’s works and by the Life written by Possidius.

What if Boniface’s marriage, censured by Augustine in that letter—which is believed to have been sent toward the end of the year 427—took place at the time when we do not deny that Arian errors had begun to spread among the Vandals? Nor can one infer that King Guntharius, or the greater part of the Vandal nation, had already adhered to the Arian heresy, even if some Vandal woman given in marriage to Boniface is said to have been imbued with Arian errors.

### 114

Ruinart, in chapter 2 of his *History of the Vandals*, records that at this time the Vandals launched a very severe persecution against the Catholics in Spain, citing Gregory of Tours, book II of the *History of the Franks*, chapter 2.

Although Gregory of Tours names King Trasamund as the author of this persecution, Ruinart nevertheless concludes that Gregory uses this name to designate Genseric. Some Spanish writers assign this persecution to approximately the year 424. But, apart from the fact that they rely on spurious chronicles, Ruinart rightly refutes them by the chronology itself: Genseric reigned after Guntharius, who died in the year 427 or 428. Therefore, if Genseric ever harassed the Catholics in Spain on religious grounds, this occurred shortly before he migrated with the Vandals into Africa.

It seems more likely to me, however, that Genseric did not begin to rage against the orthodox until after his entry into Africa. Prosper, in his *Chronicle* under the year 437, relates that in Africa he wished to overthrow the Catholic faith through Arian impiety, and adds:

> At the same time four Spanish men—Arcadius, Probus, Paschasius, and Eutychianus—who had formerly been held in high honor and affection by Genseric because of their wisdom and faithful service, were ordered by the king, who wanted to make them more acceptable to himself, to pass over into the treachery of Arianism . . . They met their end with glorious martyrdom.

Genseric began to reign at Carthage in the year 439, and it was chiefly in that city that the Vandal persecution exerted its force. If, however, some people in Spain suffered martyrdom at King Genseric’s command, this could have happened while the Vandals were already living in Africa and, having been transported by ships into Spain, made some incursion there, as Idacius reports under the year 449:

> The Vandals suddenly arrived by ship at Turonium on the shore of Gallaecia and captured the households of many people.

### Chapter XII

## The deliberate interpolation of Dracontius’s poems by the ancients. A conjecture concerning a statue erected to Dracontius at Rome.

### 115

At the time when Guntharius was praised by Dracontius, he may have deserved those praises, or at least may not have been considered unworthy of them. Certainly no record survives from which we should believe that he was hated by Catholics. After that time occurred what Idacius records under the year 428:

> Gunderic, king of the Vandals, having captured Seville, when, in impious exaltation, he had stretched out his hands against the church of that city, was soon seized by a demon and died by the judgment of God.

Isidore follows this account in his *History of the Vandals*. Speaking of Gunderic, or Guntharius, he says:

> He destroys Seville and, after a massacre, gives it over to plunder. When, with the authority of royal power, he had irreverently stretched out his hands against the basilica of Vincent the martyr in that city, he was soon seized by a demon at the doors of the temple and died by the judgment of God.

This passage would have been especially suitable for both Idacius and Isidore to mention Guntharius’s Arian heresy, which they immediately charge against his brother Genseric. Thus Guntharius’s name became odious not because of Arianism, but because of the impiety by which he laid hands upon the basilica of Saint Vincent and the fatal death which followed.

Procopius indeed says, in book I of his *Vandal History*, that there was a report that Genseric caused the death of his brother Guntharius; but he himself had learned from the Vandals that Guntharius had been captured by the Germans in battle in Spain and fastened to a cross. Yet Idacius’s authority in this matter is far greater, especially since Isidore adds something to Idacius, drawn either from other records or from the tradition of Seville, where he himself was bishop while it still flourished.

### 116

To the disgrace of Guntharius, seized by a demon and dying unhappily, was added Genseric’s cruelty in persecuting Catholics in Africa and plundering many other provinces, including Spain and Rome itself. For these reasons the Spaniards must have abominated and hated the Vandals. It is therefore surprising how the most noble Spanish province of Baetica could retain from the Vandals the name Vandalusia—albeit with some difference between its ancient and modern boundaries—if indeed it ever bore that name.

The opinion is widespread, even among very learned men, that Baetica is now called Andalusia because it formerly received the name Vandalusia from the Vandals; though some call it *Vandalia*, others *Vandalitia*, and others *Vandalosia*. On this matter one may consult Rodrigo, archbishop of Toledo, *History of the Vandals*, chapter 12, and those who seem to have followed him: Rodrigo Sánchez de Arévalo, *History of Spain*, part I, chapter 7; Nebrija, in the prolegomena to the *Decades of the Deeds of Ferdinand and Isabella*; Vasaeus, *Chronicle*, chapter 8; Mariana, book I of the *History of Spain*, chapter 4; and Ambrosius Morales, book XI of the *History*, chapter 13, to omit Wolfgang Lazius, Grotius, and others.

For my part, when I survey ancient writers who lived from the time of the Vandals through many following centuries, I always find that they call this province Baetica, never Vandalusia or any other name derived from the Vandals. They wrote in Latin, certainly; but since they adopted many other words from the vernacular, it is difficult to believe that they would never have called it Vandalusia if that designation had been accepted in use.

Rodrigo, archbishop of Toledo, in the passage cited, derives the origin of the name from the Siling Vandals:

> This region, he says, is still called Vandalia from the Siling Vandals, though in common speech we call it Andalusia, with the word corrupted.

The word *Andalusia* was therefore already vernacular in the thirteenth century, when Rodrigo wrote. As Flórez rightly conjectures, *España Sagrada*, vol. IX, treatise 28, chapter 4, it was taken from the Arabic word *Andalos*, signifying the western region. And, apparently, Andalusia first denoted all Spain, or all the provinces held by the Moors; afterward the name adhered to the province which was formerly almost Baetica and in which the Moors remained longer.

There is an extant, rare work, difficult to find, by Abunazarius, *On the Studies of the People of Andalusia*, that is, of Arabic Spain. Consult Nicolás Antonio in the preface to the *Bibliotheca*, and in the *Bibliotheca Arabico-Hispana*, under the entry **ABU CHATIM ANDALUSIUS**, where he discusses this name at greater length and rejects the common opinion that Andalusia was named from the Vandals.

### 117

However this may be, the Spaniards and Goths, who had been enemies of the Vandals, especially after they had renounced Arian impiety, could by no means have approved the praises with which Dracontius had heaped honor upon Guntharius. Unless I am greatly mistaken, this was the reason why some persons corrected and interpolated Dracontius’s poems, especially the *Satisfaction*, rather freely.

I would not venture to determine whether this was done in any part by others before Eugenius of Toledo. Certainly, already in Saint Isidore’s time, the portion of the first book entitled *On the Work of the Six Days* was separated from the rest of the work, and a certain verse of that first book was read very corruptly by Isidore, as I noted in number 7. At the command of King Chindaswinth, Eugenius undertook to correct Dracontius’s booklets composed *On the Creation of the World*, as Saint Ildefonsus puts it.

Some changes were made in the verses belonging to the first book *On God*, but they are neither very frequent nor of such great importance, as will be clear to anyone comparing our codex with Sirmondus’s. Especially in the letter, Eugenius seems to have done what he recounts in his preface to King Chindaswinth: he removed superfluities, as he thought them; supplied half-completed passages; repaired broken ones; altered frequent repetitions; and deleted little verses which were feeble in sense, inelegant in expression, and supported by no argument—verses in which nothing was found to delight the learned reader or instruct the unlearned.

But Eugenius, or another—for perhaps there was another interpolator before or after Eugenius—had no prior concern other than to erase completely every memory of the Vandal king and to omit the verses from which the occasion on which the *Satisfaction* was written might be understood. Hence these verses were entirely omitted:

> The triumph-bearing wars of the Hasding name . . .
>
> May he preserve me, that I may sing the praises of his grandfather, his father’s, and his own,
> and, through his offspring, sing the royal vows.

### 118

The final verses of the *Satisfaction* also seem to have been deliberately omitted; they describe Dracontius’s distress more clearly and recount the deed from which the ancients could recognize the king being praised:

> Illustrious, mighty in arms, source of your graciousness,
> and learned, by nature more inclined to pardon:
>
> “I do not forgive the man,” he said, “but his speech deserves it.”
> This guilty and learned man had been Vincomalus.

Yet I would not attribute to Eugenius the supposition of the title *Satisfaction*, as though it had been written to Theodosius the Younger, after an earlier inscription naming the Vandal king had been erased. I cannot believe that a man upright and devoted to truth would have taken so much upon himself.

Either he did not know to whom the praises in the letter were addressed and, from chronological considerations, conjectured that the *Satisfaction* referred to the emperor Theodosius the Younger; or, what I think truer, he left the elegy without an inscription, and others later added the title which we now read in Sirmondus, on conjecture. I shall offer one or two examples of other alterations made in order to explain passages differently from their author’s intention.

### 119

Dracontius comprised God’s providence concerning the good things which he gives and the evil things which he permits in this single distich, verse 15:

> Whatever men do—good things, sad things, prosperous things, wrong things—
> the wrath and favor of God permit these things to happen.

Similarly, in book I, verse 18, of the poem *On God*, he had said:

> All things that come—good things, joys, sad things, bitter things—
> descend from the height of God, from the seat of the Thunderer.

The interpolator found the thought of the elegy harsh; he therefore inserted these two distichs:

> Whatever men do—good, prosperous, holy, modest things—
> comes about through your action, through whom all good things come about;
>
> but, on the contrary, adverse, shameful, malign, dishonorable things
> you permit to happen, you who do no evil.

And, that you may see more clearly what displeased the interpolator in Dracontius’s distich, observe, I ask, his alteration of the following distich, which Dracontius had published thus:

> Your words spoken to the prophet Moses prove this:
> that you were to harden Pharaoh’s heart.

The corrector did not wish it said that the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart. He therefore wrote:

> Your law, set down by Moses the recorder, taught this,
> when it says that Pharaoh’s heart was hardened.

But Dracontius reproduced the words of Exodus, chapter VII, verse 3. This is not the place to defend Dracontius; at present we merely show the difference between Dracontius and his corrector. It occurs again, in nearly the same thought, shortly afterward, in verse 27:

> Who, unless driven mad by heavenly wrath,
> would seek every hardship and reject every prosperity?

In Sirmondus’s codex this distich is presented thus:

> By what means, unless the sight of the heavenly Lord in the heights,
> do all hardships oppress, and no prosperities help?

The Azagra codex in the Madrid edition reads:

> By what means, unless the conception of the heavenly Lord from heaven,
> does every hardship oppress, and no prosperities help?

Rivinus had earlier troubled himself over Sirmondus’s reading and read:

> Whom, unless the sight of the Lord from heaven had saved,
> all hardships oppress, and no prosperities help.

He saw that there was an error, but did not see the true reading, which is found in the uninterpolated elegy. The corrector considered it absurd that someone driven by heavenly wrath should seek every hardship and reject every prosperity. But this was Dracontius’s meaning; he affirmed it of himself, as is clear from the whole course of the discourse.

In a slight alteration of a single word one may observe the corrector’s studious care. Dracontius, speaking in the person of the emperor Commodus, placed this precept in verse 189:

> Noble precept, rulers, learn from me:
> let him who wishes to be a god be good in life.

The interpolator considered the final word either an error or intolerable. He therefore amended it:

> Let him who wishes to belong to God be good in life.

But Commodus, who utters these words, means the pagan apotheosis by which emperors after death were enrolled among the gods.

### 120

I now omit many other matters which will be clearer when the *Elegy* published from the Vatican codex is compared with the variant readings of the Sirmondian and Azagra codices. But since such effort was made to ensure that Dracontius’s poems reached posterity in interpolated form, someone may ask by what means those same poems could have been preserved complete outside Spain and in Italy. For the copies in Gaul seem to have proceeded from Eugenius’s revision, except for the Paris codex of Saint Victor, which I think was copied from some older manuscript containing only the verses *On the Work of the Six Days*, such as Isidore also saw before Eugenius.

Yet it would not have been difficult for some codex to have been carried from Spain to Italy before Saint Isidore’s time, containing the complete poem *On God* and the *Satisfaction* addressed to King Guntharius—unless we also choose to conjecture that Dracontius himself, at last released from prison, came to Italy. This is the conjecture which I hold and now propose.

### 121

In the *Excusatio to Felix*, poem 9, Sidonius praises three poets who had been companions of his own father and Felix’s father. He does not name the third, but says that he was born in Baetica and tells other things of him in these verses:

> Lest those who were, in their earliest years, the greatest companions of our fathers . . .
>
> But neither will that third man now be read,
> who, once leaving his native Baetis,
> sought the thirst of wave-washed Ravenna;
> for him the applauding Roman citizens
> and a prince beloved for his popularity
> set up a shining statue in Trajan’s forum.

In his notes on Sidonius, Sirmondus conjectures that this Spanish poet was Merobaudes, of whom Idacius says under the year 443:

> Asturius, master of both services, is sent to Spain, and his own son-in-law Merobaudes succeeds him; he was noble by birth and, by merit of eloquence, especially in the pursuit of poetry, comparable with the ancients, and was honored also by the testimony of statues. In the short period of his authority he broke the insolence of the Bacaudae of Araceli. Soon afterward, pressed by the envy of some persons, he was recalled to the city of Rome by a sacred command.

Sirmondus adds that this is the Merobaudes whose poem *On God* survives. These are ingenious thoughts. Yet Sirmondus himself observes that at that time many statues had been set up in Trajan’s forum, a point which he proves also from ancient inscriptions. There therefore remains room to doubt whether Sidonius may be understood more suitably of another Spanish poet.

It should therefore be noted that Sidonius was born about the year 428 and says that this Baetican poet was a companion of his father in his father’s earliest years, which I interpret as his father’s very youth. Sidonius further says that the poet once left his native Baetis and came to Ravenna; by this he indicates that he formed his friendship with Sidonius’s father at Ravenna. I understand also that Sidonius’s Spanish poet left Baetis permanently; for that is what the adverb *semel* (“once and for all”) signifies here.

These points being established, it follows that Sidonius is less suitably explained as referring to Merobaudes, who in the year 443 was sent to Spain as general, or master of both services, and was soon recalled to Rome by a sacred command. On the other hand, all Sidonius’s words suit Dracontius: he was Baetican, and could already have been living at Ravenna about the year 427, after leaving his native Baetis once and for all.

This conjecture is supported by the fact that Saint Columbanus had read Dracontius’s *Elegy* complete, as is argued from the verses of his cited in number 8, and by the fact that a codex of Dracontius is listed in the most ancient catalogue of the monastery of Bobbio, founded by Saint Columbanus himself. This, together with Sidonius’s verses, provides some reason to suspect that Dracontius lived in Italy.

### 122

For, if Dracontius gained his freedom, he ought, in order to provide for himself and remove himself from the calamities with which Spain was afflicted, to have loved honorable leisure and retirement. Indeed, he prayed for this from God in book III *On God*, verse 647:

> I pray, now restore me, released into freedom,
> though crushed by the iron weight of the disaster of chains.
> Let there be rest for my life and leisure for my weary soul;
> let there be secure repose, let there be night with night’s gift.

For when he continues, “Let fortune return,” and so forth, he seems to ask only for those goods of fortune which are in no way opposed to leisure for his weary soul and secure repose. He had been a court official, as may be conjectured from his verses; and Goldast above, in number 32, positively affirmed it, though I do not know on what authority. At the least, he was rich and noble, as may be gathered from book III, verse 589:

> The troops of slaves flee; clients despise [me].

For he lists this among the other troubles by which he was afflicted.

## Chapter XIII. Dracontius’s confession and penitence

### 123

This is the difference between the poem *On God* and the *Elegy*: in the *Elegy*, addressing the king and wishing to win his favor, Dracontius asks for his life to be prolonged so that he may sing the praises of the Vandals; in the poem, after a most humble confession of his sins, he prays to God as follows in book III, verse 663:

> Command, in your accustomed mercy, that one who has been saved be restored,
> that I may deserve to sing your praises in song.

[Col. 0665C] **124.** Moreover, it should be noted that in the *Elegy* Dracontius implies that his crime was nothing other than having celebrated in verse some enemy of the Vandal king. And, if we indulge in conjecture, perhaps that man was Castinus, whom Dracontius had praised. For thus Idatius records under the year 422:

> Castinus, master of the soldiers, with a large force and Gothic auxiliaries, brought war against the Vandals in Baetica. When he had pressed them so hard by the force of the siege that they were already preparing to surrender, he rashly engaged them in open battle; deceived by the treachery of the auxiliaries, he was defeated and fled to Tarraco.

While the Vandals had been reduced to want by the force of the siege, the time might have seemed opportune for someone who had not yet expelled the alliance of the Romans from his heart to exalt the commander Castinus in verse. Although no trace of the poem that Dracontius then composed has reached us, his own testimony nevertheless makes it certain that he had published a poem by which the king was offended. Nor is it surprising that this poem has not survived: the Vandals, who at that time controlled affairs in Baetica, must have suppressed it.

**125.** In the poem *On God*, where he confesses his sins before God according to the conviction of his heart, Dracontius says nothing at all about this poem, perhaps because he thought that he had other, more serious crimes, and that God had allowed him to fall into the calamities he suffered in order to punish him for them. In the *Elegy*, verse 105, he says:

> Before you first, I repent and confess  
> the audacity of that poem, which I wrongly composed.

But in Book III of the poem, verse 576, after many other things:

> Alas for me! For deeds committed at more than one time,  
> the time has converged into one, that I may pay for my actions.

How numerous and of what kind these crimes were, for which Dracontius accuses himself as guilty, he does not explain distinctly. But some will infer from the preceding verses that they were innumerable and horrifying. For thus he says:

> I am the first of them, and must be regarded as more than a sinner.  
> For when shall I declare the number of my crimes, and the guilt  
> of my heart and flesh? Not even if I had an iron voice,  
> and mouths arose as numerous as the teeth that shine white in bones,  
> or if I had as many tongues as the entire head  
> combs hairs, could I honestly complete the number.  
> But it is enough to have said that I am guilty under every charge.  
> Whatever your commands forbid, I confess that I alone have done;  
> I will not deny having done anything that horrifies you . . .  
>
> Therefore I confess, with a pitiable mind, a guilt  
> full and great—a great evil produced not by one crime.  
> For all my wickedness will surpass the number of the sands  
> of the shore, and the waters of the sea will be outdone by our evils.  
> I do not think that the Flood punished as many guilty acts  
> as I myself bear, pressed down by the weight of my faults.  
> Rivers of crimes carry me away, and storms shake me,  
> and at once the torrent of sins overwhelms me with its flood.  
> Streams have submerged me in waves of wrongdoing;  
> the wave has reached my very soul—the heavy terror of the waters.

Unless we judge all this to have been exaggerated by Dracontius, we shall believe that no one was more wicked than he.

**126.** In the prolegomena to Prudentius, chapter 2, sections 44 and following, I attempted to prove that the words with which Prudentius accuses himself of his crimes in the preface can be understood as proceeding from the modesty and humility customary among upright Christians, and do not imply a notably criminal and abandoned man, as others commonly interpreted them. Nor do I now think otherwise. Indeed, I interpret these very words of Dracontius, which will seem more serious to most people, in the same sense.

But although I then indicated this clearly enough concerning Prudentius, I now openly declare that I am not arguing this case as though either Prudentius’s or Dracontius’s innocence were established. I assert only that no argument should be drawn from their humble confession for affirming the gravest crimes concerning them.

I shall now offer a striking example from the verses of Saint Eugenius of Toledo, in the *Lament on the Approach of His Own Old Age*, Book I, poem 12:

> I oppressed, seized, stripped, and fabricated crimes;  
> my mind was deaf to the voice of the poor.  
> I corrupted my own body with a wanton wound;  
> hence miserable, hence fearful, hence drunken, I proceed.  
> No pardon ever restrained my angers;  
> never was I raging without gall, nor without bloodshed.

And lest anyone doubt the author, he gives his name in the final pentameter:

> For wretched Eugenius, I beg, let the punishment be light.

No one will deny that it is more difficult to interpret these words kindly than those spoken by Dracontius only in general terms; for Eugenius seems to descend to the very particulars of some dreadful wickedness.

**127.** Indeed, Barthius, who interprets this poem of Eugenius in *Adversaria*, Book LV, chapter 11, says explicitly:

> He says that he corrupted his own body through fornication . . .

That Eugenius was more inclined to such offenses can also be learned from a third epigram, where he says:

> Now we follow what is right; now in our hearts we hold what is wrong;  
> now we are holy and chaste; now we cherish prostitutes.

Although in that passage he speaks generally about the inconstancy and fickleness of the human mind among all people, he nevertheless reviews and detests all these things from his own conscience and experience of his former life. In the same poem 12 he also confesses that he was not pure with respect to bloodshed. For these words must be understood simply, in no other way than they sound . . . He confessed that he had passed through every kind of lust in his youth.

So says Barthius. If he had seen the other poems of Eugenius published from the Azagra manuscript at Madrid, he would have confirmed his opinion more fully from poem 1 of Book II, which begins:

> Heavily burdened by the weight of my faults,  
> supreme in crime, abounding in vices.

**128.** I would not dare agree with Barthius on the basis of Eugenius’s confession alone, even if there were no other records that repelled such crimes from Eugenius. But since such evidence exists, I plainly disagree. Hear the most authoritative witness, Ildefonsus, in the *Life of Eugenius*:

> Since he was an eminent cleric of the royal church, he delighted in the life of a monk. Fleeing with prudence, he sought the city of Zaragoza; there he clung to the tombs of the martyrs, and there fittingly cultivated the studies of wisdom and the monastic purpose. Hence, when he was brought back by royal compulsion and called to the episcopate, he lived a life marked more by the merits of virtue than by bodily strength. For he was slight in body and small in physical power, but his spirit burned fiercely with the strength of virtue.

Does this praise fit the man whom Barthius describes for us? Nor should one object that Eugenius was accusing the crimes of his youth. For Ildefonsus’s testimony confirms that his life in adolescence was conducted uprightly and piously; and Eugenius himself, in his epitaph, encompasses the whole period of his life, as though he had been entangled in crimes up to the very point of death.

What, then, remains except to say that Eugenius speaks in a somewhat less literal, but genuine and humble, sense, so that truth is joined with humility in his words, and that his words should not be understood simply as they sound or appear to sound?

**129.** Eugenius, moreover, described not only himself in words proceeding from Christian humility but also—strange as it may seem—King Chindaswinth in a similar manner, as though he were a wicked and abominable man. In Book II of Eugenius’s poems from the Azagra manuscript, in the Madrid edition, poem 75 is an epitaph written for King Chindaswinth. Among other things Eugenius says:

[Col. 0667D] **100**

> I am Chindaswinth, always a friend of crimes,  
> I am Chindaswinth, perpetrator of wicked deeds.  
> Impious, obscene, disgraceful, shameful, unjust,  
> desiring nothing good, capable of every evil.  
> Whatever one does who desires what is wrong and seeks what is harmful,  
> I have committed it all, and thereby became worse.  
> There was no fault I would not have wished to commit;  
> greatest in vices, I myself was the first.

I have restored *pejor* in place of *pejus*, which is what is read in the Madrid edition. In these verses I first recognize a humble exaggeration of Chindaswinth’s vices. Secondly, I argue that the epitaph was composed not by Eugenius but by Chindaswinth himself. For how could Eugenius, either while Chindaswinth was alive or after his death, attribute so many and such serious crimes to him?

**130.** Eugenius himself celebrates Chindaswinth’s exceedingly generous piety in the letter by which he sends Dracontius, corrected by his own hand. It is well established that this same Chindaswinth flourished in religious devotion and piety: he even sent Taio as an envoy to Rome to bring back various works of Saint Gregory that were lacking in Spain, and he commissioned Eugenius to correct Dracontius’s little books.

Mariana, in Book VI of his *History of Spain*, chapter 8, notes one vice in him, which is not distinctly mentioned in the epitaph, and praises the rest of his life:

> He governed well the kingdom he had seized through tyranny, striving to compensate for the fault of his inauguration by the integrity and steadfastness of his entire life.

This epitaph, therefore, must be attributed not to Eugenius but to Chindaswinth himself. Nor was it without good reason that the highly diligent editor, Cardinal Lorenzana, warned before Book II that not all the verses presented there should be represented as genuine offspring of Eugenius, although in the Azagra manuscript they are all found written continuously under Eugenius’s single name and intermingled with those that Sirmond had previously published.

It would be easy to show that among the very poems published by Sirmond there are several whose author is not Eugenius, such as poem 21, *On the Inventors of Letters*, which is found in the *Latin Anthology*. And since we have attributed Chindaswinth’s epitaph to him, nothing prevents us from assigning to the same king poem 31 of Book I, *On the Death of the Wife of King Chindaswinth*, in which the king addresses the queen.

If, then, Chindaswinth is believed to be the author of his own epitaph, the one example of Eugenius that I proposed must now be divided into two. This will further confirm that Dracontius’s humble confession of sins can stand without the disgrace of an immoral life. And since these examples of Christian humility have been drawn from Spaniards, a new conjecture will arise—if a matter that is not obscure needs confirmation by conjectures—that Spain, the homeland of Dracontius, may be confirmed from a similar modesty especially customary among Spaniards.

## CHAPTER XIV. Dracontius’s Style, Latinity, and Prosody

**131.** As with all other writers, learned men have formed differing judgments concerning Dracontius. Du Pin, *Bibliotheca Nova*, volume IV, page 210, censures Dracontius for a barbarous and unpolished manner of expression. Ceillier, volume XV of *Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 29, considers nothing in Dracontius’s poem worthy of attention.

Goldastus says in a letter to Weitzius:

> Dracontius is a sound author, polished, and commendable for his very brevity, though belonging to a later age. Yet, as in Prudentius, little flowers of elegance, like certain embedded purple ornaments, shine and sparkle through him.

Fabricius, in his commentary on *Christian Poets*, under the entry DRACONTIUS, says:

> His poem is learned and distinguished.

Cunradus Rittershusius, in an ode to Weitzius:

> Now Dracontius goes with him,  
> and in lofty verse sings the beginnings of things.  
> Long unknown to many—  
> not well hidden, until your care  
> brought him himself back from darkness  
> into the regions of light, clearly showing  
> how much discovered material he compresses  
> within a brief grasp.

*Quot via* seems to be an error; perhaps Rittershusius wrote *quot dia reperta*.

Barthius often points out Dracontius’s little flowers of elegance, but praises his talent in *Adversaria*, Book VII, chapter 20:

> There was very great talent among the ancient Christian poets, and often talent so excellent that, while they wished to illuminate certain things, they confused everything. Indeed, the Spaniard Dracontius speaks of most incidental matters with such acuteness and force that he scarcely seems to have understood himself adequately—far less could his meaning be grasped by those who in our age have studied the matter.

To some, this mode of praise may seem obscure and ambiguous; but what Barthius meant is sufficiently clear: there is a certain sharpness of talent which, while dealing with matters too subtly, produces some obscurity, especially among those who possess little natural ability. Shortly afterward Barthius says that Dracontius was a craftsman in speaking acutely and concisely, and that both his nature and his age inclined him in this direction.

**132.** Barthius rightly observes in the passage cited that Dracontius still teems everywhere with numerous errors which, unless removed, make it useless to labor at interpreting spurious readings as legitimate and interpolations as genuine. He adds:

> In these acute and concise writers, later copyists presumed to stuff in many additions, since everyone with even a little literary education delighted in this kind of writing—indeed, so improperly that eventually all eloquence was cut through with these quibbles.

When the same Barthius, in Book LIV, chapter 9, calls Dracontius a poet much better and more accomplished in sense and learning than in eloquence, and elsewhere says that his phrasing is more intricate, this amounts to saying that Dracontius, partly by nature, partly through the custom of his age, and partly through the fault of copyists, is excessively acute and ingenious, and in this respect has departed from true eloquence.

I have no doubt that Barthius would have judged differently if he had seen Dracontius as we present him. First, Barthius thought that the *Hexaemeron* then extant was an epitome of Dracontius’s poem *On the Work of the Six Days*, and from the style he inferred that there were two authors, as I said in section 29.

But since it is now clear that Dracontius did not set before himself the subject of a work on the six days, but rather the praise of divine majesty from created things, the poem must be judged according to this purpose. In this respect, everything proceeds correctly.

**133.** Moreover, although Dracontius does not yet appear as corrected as one might wish, many signs of uncommon eloquence are already evident in him, especially in the *Elegy*, where we have obtained a more accurate manuscript. In the poem *On God*, the flow of the discourse is often so even that it is most evident that, in the places where the language is more intricate, the fault lies not with the author but with copyists or interpolators.

I would not, however, deny that some blemish from contact with barbarians has adhered to Dracontius’s style; that the same ideas, and often the same words, are frequently repeated; or that the order of the subject may perhaps have been arranged with insufficient care.

But Ovid rightly said, though oppressed by a lighter misfortune, in Book I of the *Tristia*, elegy 1:

> Even these things that I do, a fair judge will admire,  
> and with indulgence will read them, whatever their quality.

[Col. 0670A]

> Give me Maeonides, and look around at all these disasters:  
> every talent would fall away beneath such evils.

Dracontius was writing in chains and bonds. What wonder, then, if he everywhere implores God’s goodness and mercy, even where circumstances might not seem to require it? Or if he neglects variety of phrasing and vocabulary? Or if he sometimes proceeds with the order of his subject confused?

Meanwhile, it cannot be denied that the gravest ideas, and those most fully shaped by Christian piety, shine forth in his poems—ideas drawn from Holy Scripture and the holy Fathers. Thus Sirmond, who had seen only a small part of them, rightly said in his dedicatory letter to Henry of Bourbon, son of the king and bishop of Metz:

> Dracontius will lift the mind to the praises of God through contemplation of his wondrous works.

I pass over for now Dracontius’s exceptional learning, both sacred and secular, which reveals itself without any index to those who read his verses.

**134.** As for the polish of his Latin expression, many passages in Dracontius are pure and graceful, and many others arise from his imitation of the best poets, whom, as is clear, he had diligently read and whom he in a certain way compels to speak as Christians.

There are, however, other expressions that should not indeed be considered barbarous, but should by no means be proposed for imitation by those who wish to shape their language according to the taste of the Golden Age. One must also take account of the subject, which admits certain words untouched by the ancient secular poets—especially words bearing a certain ecclesiastical flavor, because they arose from Holy Scripture and the usage of the Church.

Certainly, those who wish to know the full range of the Latin language should not be unfamiliar with poets contemporary with Dracontius, since they have preserved for us many words of pure Latinity and added others that were in use in their own time and are not unworthy of being used in ours as well.

Although in the notes we shall point out which words and phrases are peculiar to Dracontius, or shared by only a few writers with him, it will nevertheless be useful to observe a few things here.

**135.** In Book I *On God*, verse 4, he used the adverb *veneranter* (“reverently”), and again in Book III, verse 672. Tertullian—or whoever else was the author of the poems published under his name—and Sedulius also used it.

Dracontius formed other similar adverbs: in Book I, verse 94, *moderanter* (“moderately”); in the same book, verse 331, *dominanter* (“lordly” or “as a lord”); and in the same book, verse 609, *incessanter* (“unceasingly”). In Book III, verse 223, *tonanter* (“thunderously”); and in the same book, verse 671, *trementer* (“tremblingly”).

**136.** Dracontius took extraordinary delight in the adjective *modestus* (“modest”). In Book I, verse 29, God’s piety is *virtute modesta* (“modest in virtue”). In the same book, verse 435, God is *virtute modestus* (“modest in virtue”). In Book II, verse 70, God is *pietate modestus* (“modest in piety”); in the same book, verse 308, *non jure modesto* (“not with modest justice”); and in the same book, verse 758, Tabitha is *modesta* (“modest”). In Book III, verse 379, *vultus modestos* (“modest faces”); in the *Elegy*, verse 93, *dominos reticere modestos* (“to keep modest masters silent”). See section 148 concerning the word *placidus* (“peaceful,” “gentle”).

**137.** Dracontius also often applies the adjective *anhelus* (“breathing heavily,” “panting,” or “fiery”) to fire or the sun: in Book I, verse 26, *solis anheli* (“of the panting sun”); in the same book, verse 187, again *solis anheli*; in the same book, verse 659, *ignis anheli* (“of panting fire”); in Book II, verse 91, *ignis anheli*; in Book III, verse 70, *anhelantes flammus* (“panting flames”); verse 169, *non fervor anhelat* (“the heat does not pant”); and verse 308, *anhelantis vaporis* (“of panting vapor”).

**138.** Weitzius, at the beginning of his index to Dracontius, notes that Dracontius joins two epithets or adjectives to a single noun, as in Book I, verse 180, *odoriferis nunquam marcentibus herbis* (“fragrant herbs that never wither”), and elsewhere.

He gives as an example of *complosio*—the bringing together of such expressions—Book I, verse 396:

> *Omnia pulchra gerens, oculos, os*  
> “Bearing everything beautiful—eyes, mouth.”

He classifies the cited verse 180 under the hyphen, *nunquam-marcentibus* (“never-withering”), and similar forms such as *male viventi* (“living badly”) and *semper-vestita* (“always-clothed”).

He refers *funera viva* (“living funerals”) and *vivax cadaver* (“living corpse”) in Book I, verse 648, to the category of ὀξύμωρα, *oxymora*. Dracontius is full of such *oxymora*—that is, expressions that are, as it were, “sharply foolish,” because they appear foolish at first sight but are in fact pointed.

**139.** Finally, to say something about Dracontius’s prosody: he rarely departs from the rules of meter by which the stricter and better poets bound themselves. He pronounces *idolum* (“idol”) with the second syllable short. This is a common fault of his, if it is a fault at all, shared with Prudentius and many other Christian poets. I explained the reason for shortening this syllable in the prolegomena to Prudentius, chapter 24 and following.

It is peculiar to Dracontius that he lengthens the first syllable of *thronus* (“throne”); but this too can be defended from what I discussed in the cited passage, unless perhaps the manuscript is corrupt in the two places where this word is used.

In the verb *fiant* (“let them be made”), Dracontius varies: sometimes he lengthens it with the ancient poets, sometimes he shortens it with Prudentius and others. Yet one may suspect an error wherever Dracontius shortens it. See the note on Book I, verse 82, and Book II, verse 191.

I shall note in their proper places a few other words that Dracontius pronounces with a different quantity from other writers. It is also customary for Dracontius, as for other poets of the later age, to lengthen a short vowel solely because of the caesura, as in Book I, verse 430:

> *Projicere nec plasma suum*  
> “Nor to cast away his own creation.”

In some places Dracontius also lengthens a short syllable merely because of aspiration, something that can be defended both by grammatical reasoning and by the example of the ancients.

**140.** Christian poets, and even the secular poets who wrote at the same time, allowed themselves great license with proper names. Dracontius, using a similar freedom, fits proper names into the meter as he pleases, pronouncing the same name now with a short quantity, now with a long one.

Thus in Book II, verse 572, he correctly shortens the first syllable of *Stephanus*:

> *Martyrium Stephano qui fecerat, inde recepit*  
> “He who had brought about martyrdom for Stephen received it in return.”

But in the *Elegy*, verse 171, he lengthens the same syllable:

> *Stephanus ante alios lapidum sub grandine martyr*  
> “Stephen, a martyr before the others, beneath a hail of stones,”

unless, against the authority of the manuscripts, one prefers to transpose the words:

> *Ante alios Stephanus lapidum*, etc.  
> “Before the others, Stephen of the stones,” etc.

The same Dracontius shortens the first syllable of *Isac* in Book III, verse 139:

> *Quid pater Abraham, quid Isac meruisse leguntur?*  
> “What are Abraham the father and Isaac read to have deserved?”

But shortly afterward, in verse 155, he lengthens it:

> *Omnia perpetuo generi manifestius Isac*  
> “Isaac made all things more clearly known to the everlasting race.”

Barthius, in *Adversaria*, Book IX, chapter 7, introduces his restoration of one of Dracontius’s verses as follows:

> It is the custom—or certainly the established practice—of Christian poets to use in verse the names that grammarians call proper as they please, sometimes shortening their syllables, sometimes lengthening them. Hence I detect an obvious error in Dracontius himself, etc.

Whether Barthius was correct in his judgment concerning this error I shall say in its proper place.

**141.** Yet it should not be passed over in silence that Christian poets themselves recognized that proper names possess a fixed syllabic quantity, which ought to be preserved. There are many examples of ancient Christian poets who did not dare to use such proper names against the meter, or who prefaced an appeal for indulgence whenever this could not be avoided.

But I shall give an example from the barbarous centuries. Galfridus de Vino Salvo, who was alive in the year 1216, addresses Pope Innocent in his *Poetria* as follows:

> Pope, wonder of the world, if I say, “Pope NOCENTI,”  
> I shall give you a headless name; if I add the head [IN],  
> you will be an enemy of the meter. Your name wishes to resemble you.  
> Neither does your name fit the meter, nor does your great virtue  
> wish to be confined within a measure. I have nothing with which to measure it.  
> It surpasses human measures. But divide the name.  
>
> . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .  
> Put IN before it and add NOCENT,  
> and it becomes a companion of the meter. Thus your virtue too,  
> divided among many, is equaled by many, but whole is equaled by none.

Thus Galfridus plays with the name *Innocent*, which cannot be contained in a hexameter verse. Nevertheless, shortly afterward he disregarded the laws of meter in the name of Gregory:

> Stop, Gregory; pause. What shall I say of all . . . !

Yet he could have arranged the verse in another way so as not to lengthen the second syllable.

I conclude, therefore, that Christian poets used proper names freely in verse, especially names originating in another language, partly because they followed popular pronunciation and partly because they thought poetic license could more easily be allowed in such names than in others.

But I have treated at length and deliberately in the prolegomena to Prudentius all matters relating to the distinctive prosody of ancient Christian poetry; it is not necessary to repeat them here. Nor does it seem appropriate to add many other matters, even though this could be done without difficulty.

## CHAPTER XV. The Method Observed in the Edition of Dracontius

**142.** Weitzius, in the preface to his edition of Dracontius, reports the judgment of a certain highly distinguished man:

> In a polished writer such as our author is, everything ought rightly and deservedly to be complete, and even the slightest error ought to cause him distress.

Accordingly, nothing required more effort from me than to present Dracontius complete and, insofar as possible, free from every error. For Muretus truly said in Book VIII of the *Various Readings*, chapter 4:

> Every day I understand more clearly that no error is so small that it does not greatly matter to remove and correct it in the monuments of antiquity; nor is there any class of people more beneficial to scholarship than those who devote themselves accurately and faithfully to cleansing and correcting them. For an error in a single little letter sometimes casts such darkness over even the most learned men that, wandering as though in a profound night, they arrive anywhere rather than where they wish.

The same learned and elegant writer also asserts in Book I, chapter 16, that scarcely any manuscript is written so incompetently that a learned person cannot derive benefit from it.

**143.** Relying on these arguments and testimonies, I present Dracontius’s verses chiefly from manuscript codices. But since one of the two Vatican manuscripts is riddled with numerous errors, I corrected those that seemed to me certainly or very probably erroneous, and restored the reading that I judged true or closest to the truth.

Nevertheless, I left others free to judge and correct differently, supplying beneath the corrupt words the readings found in the manuscript. In this matter I used a certain excessive diligence—one that may seem obscure—by regularly recording copyists’ errors even where they were by no means doubtful.

This labor should not, however, be considered useless. First, because it often happens that one and the same word appears clearly corrupt to some people but genuine to others. Then, because the true reading can sometimes be extracted from a corruptly written word, and perhaps others will not approve what I have restored but will discover something else from the manuscript’s error. Moreover, it is useful to know the copyist’s hand in a certain sense and, from the errors he habitually makes, to conjecture the true writing in other obscure passages.

**144.** In Book I of the poem *On God*, up to verse 116, *Prima dies* (“The first day”), only the Vatican manuscript is used. From verse 116 up to the final verse of the book, verse 754, *Quo te promittis* (“Where you promise yourself”), variant readings are given from four manuscripts:

first, from the manuscript of Saint Victor in Paris, or from the first edition of Dracontius published at Paris in conformity with that manuscript;

second, from the manuscript of the Royal Library in Paris, or from the edition of Dracontius that Sirmond prepared using that manuscript;

third, from the Azagra manuscript, or from the Madrid edition of the Fathers of Toledo, in which the variant readings of the Azagra manuscript are recorded in the margins of Dracontius’s poems or at the bottom of the page;

fourth and finally, from our Vatican manuscript.

The abbreviations by which we designate these manuscripts are easy to understand: *Vict.* signifies the first manuscript, that of Saint Victor; *Sirm.* the second manuscript, used by Sirmond; *Azagr.* the third manuscript, which belonged to Azagra; and *Vat.* the fourth manuscript, which is the Vatican one.

In Books II and III of the poem *On God*, no manuscript other than the Vatican is available for citation. In the *Elegy*, or *Satisfaction*, three manuscripts are cited: the Sirmondian, the Azagran, and the Vatican.

Since our purpose is to publish Dracontius’s original poems, we prefer the Vatican manuscripts to all the others, since they have been preserved entirely free from Eugenius’s correction or interpolation. But the stains that entered the Vatican manuscripts through the negligence of copyists and the ravages of time have been wiped away with the help of other manuscripts whenever this could conveniently be done.

**145.** Three other editions could also be counted among the variant readings—namely, those prepared by Georgius Fabricius, Weitzius, and Rivinus. But I thought it preferable to relegate the conjectures of these editors to the notes appended to the variant readings. I call them conjectures because, since they had no handwritten manuscript before their eyes, whenever they differ from the earlier editions they do so only by conjecture.

Our annotations on Dracontius therefore include not only matters relating to sacred and secular history, philosophy, Holy Scripture, and theology, but also critical observations on the propriety and meaning of words, as well as the conjectures of others and our own concerning which variant readings of verses should be accepted or rejected.

For it sometimes happens that a reading retained on the authority of a manuscript is not particularly satisfactory, and is therefore disturbed by some conjecture. At other times a word has been restored because of an obvious error in the manuscript, but another word might perhaps be substituted more suitably or just as suitably; this could not be understood without some explanation. The reason why the conjectures of others are sometimes unacceptable must also be given, and this will be done at the appropriate places in the notes.

**146.** It could be debated whether the gaps occurring in the poem *On God* ought better to be left as they are or supplied in some manner. Following the practice and example of others, I preferred to add supplements of this kind.

A reader can be greatly assisted if he reads the sentence without interruption in the same continuous thread of discourse and thus joins what precedes with what follows. For if, through the absence of a verse or half-verse, the sense is left wholly incomplete, he will have to pause and consider with himself what the author said and why he added the words that follow.

Provision has nevertheless been made so that these supplements are clearly distinguished from Dracontius’s words; thus no one can complain that he has been deceived.

I am aware that certain grammarians have a bad reputation because they attempted to supplement verses that Virgil had left unfinished. But apart from the great difference between Dracontius’s verses, which are incomplete through the fault of manuscripts, and Virgil’s verses, which he himself had not yet completed and had not wished Varius and Tucca to complete, those grammarians were criticized chiefly because they mixed their own worthless rag recklessly and foolishly into Virgil’s purple.

Thus, where Virgil had begun a verse:

> *Quem tibi jam Troja*  
> “Which Troy already for you . . .”

they completed it:

> *Quem tibi jam Troja peperit fumante Creusa*  
> “Which Troy, with Creusa smoking, has already borne for you.”

I do not know whether it is more deserving of laughter that some people believed these incomplete verses of Virgil contained some secret of poetic art, which they too proposed to imitate.

Aonius Palearius, whose works would perhaps be less sought after had he not died such an infamous death, indulged in this same fault in his poem *On the Immortality of the Soul*, publishing certain verses merely begun, as though nothing could occur to his mind that would equal the majesty of what preceded and followed.

This chapter was omitted by Johann Burchard Menckenius in his little book *On the Charlatanry of Scholars*.

**147.** The industry of many others who removed blemishes from the writings of the ancients has been praised by most people. Cicero, if the Eusebian Chronicle is to be trusted, corrected Lucretius’s poem. Isidore, in Book I of the *Etymologies*, chapter 21, mentions Aristarchus, Leagoras of Syracuse, and Zenodotus of Ephesus, who devoted their efforts to correcting the verses of Homer.

Among more recent scholars, Franciscus Nansius is commended by Lipsius, *Century* 2, letter 60, because he cleansed Nonnus of Panopolis of errors. More closely relevant to our subject is the fact that Azagra restored by conjecture certain wholly corrupt passages in Corippus; Demsterus supplied lacunae and defended this method of procedure; finally, Fogginius added new conjectures and corrections.

The supplements of Johannes Freinshemius to Tacitus, Curtius, and Livy are well known. In the *Leipzig Miscellanies*, volume I, for the year 1716, there is a supplement to the fables of Phaedrus, by M. Christoph Hauptius.

Conjectures and corrections of this sort are generally more necessary in writers whose works survive in only one manuscript, or in several manuscripts all copied from a single exemplar. Such is the case with Velleius Paterculus, whom Beatus Rhenanus first published from one mutilated, prodigiously corrupt, and shamefully degraded exemplar; and with Catullus, who has many manuscript copies, but all descended from a certain exemplar discovered in Gaul.

But everyone must exercise his own judgment in such matters. It is enough for me to repeat that the supplements will be arranged in such a way that no one can justly complain of having been deceived.

## CHAPTER XVI. Subject and Synopsis of the Three Books *On God*

**148.** Sirmond rightly declared that Dracontius raises the mind to the praises of God through contemplation of his wondrous works. This could indeed be established as the subject of the poem *On God*, not unlike the title of Cardinal Bellarmine’s excellent little book, *The Ascent of the Mind to God*.

The inscription of the poem in the Vatican manuscript, *On God*, suggests this very subject. More explicitly, the subject of Dracontius’s poem encompasses knowledge and praise of God from his works of mercy and justice, but especially from his mercy, clemency, and piety toward human beings, which shine most brightly throughout the entire poem.

Dracontius begins from the first verse:

> Those who wish to know the gentle Thunderer in their minds  
> should read this poem with attentive thought, etc.

The word *placidus* (“gentle,” “mild,” “merciful,” “pious”) is exceedingly familiar to him. Indeed, in the *Elegy*, verses 287 and following, he himself taught us, in a certain way, the definition of this word:

> If there had been no sins of the human race,  
> from where could God have obtained the name “pious”?  
> But because he grants pardon and releases peoples from their sins,  
> through the work of piety he bears the name “gentle.”

That Dracontius also wishes to commemorate works of divine justice can be gathered from the preface to Book I, verses 10 and following:

> This the poem does, and amid varied circumstances follows divine anger,  
> and God’s merciful purposes, here toward the wretched and there toward the blessed,  
> according to the merits of their character and the fixed course of their life.

Dracontius explains God’s justice and anger in such a way that he always has before his eyes what he himself said of God in Book I, verse 691:

> Inferior in no virtue, except in the anger of punishment.

And more clearly in Book II, verse 693:

> You are more pious than just,

where he argues many other things to the same effect.

Indeed, he takes occasion from God’s very anger to praise his piety, as in Book I, verse 556:

> Great is God’s piety, for he always restrains his anger.

And at the end of Book III, verse 658:

> Because I am alive, I am preserved from death by your piety,  
> not by anger; for if the Lord’s anger had been severe,  
> you would not have delayed, but would have killed me by sudden death,  
> so that I could not ask the pardon which, holy one, you have never denied,  
> or so that I would not exist at all as one whom you could spare.  
>
> Command that the one preserved be restored by your accustomed piety,  
> so that I may deserve to sing your praises in my poems.

I now come to explain each book briefly.

## SYNOPSIS OF BOOK I
149. All created things acknowledge, praise, and proclaim God. Everything that happens—prosperity [Col. 0676B] and adversity—comes from God; yet he does not punish sinners suddenly, but warns them beforehand through portents, so that they may ask forgiveness. Several prognostics are described by which a human being foreknows joyful and sorrowful events. When God terrifies, he loves; and he does not deny forgiveness to one who asks it, nor does he inflict punishment unless they persist in crimes. For God wishes all human beings to attain eternal salvation; this is shown by so many things created for human beings. On the first day, light was created, from which very many benefits come to humanity. On the second day, heaven, fire, and water were created; on the third day, the sea, earth, grass, trees, flowers, and spices. The earthly paradise is described. On the fourth 113 day, heaven was adorned with the sun, moon, and stars; all these lights obey God and serve human beings. On the fifth day, fish were produced in the waters, destined to become food [Col. 0676C] for human beings, and birds emerged from those same waters. On the sixth day, terrestrial animals were created, and different animals were assigned to different lands, just as various gifts were distributed throughout the world. To rule over all these things, humanity was created in the image of God; and, so that the human being would not be alone, a partner of the same race was given to him—a wife formed from his rib—so that their mutual love might be perfect. God therefore entrusted all created things to their free choice and gave them the task of devoting themselves to the propagation of their race. While they were enjoying the delights of paradise, the serpent deceived the woman into eating fruit from the one tree that had been forbidden. The deceived woman deceived the man; and only then, overcome with shame, did they begin to flee, as though they could hide from God reproving them. But since human beings possess so many signs by which they can know hidden [Col. 0676D] things, how could the first parents have hidden their crime—and themselves—from God? After their confession, therefore, God pronounced a sentence tempered by mercy: death itself was inflicted upon them as punishment, but also as a certain alleviation of punishment, so that human beings would not live perpetually amid the hardships of this life. Yet, mindful of his own work, God expelled the first parents from paradise in such a way that he granted them dominion over the world and over the things in the world. He decreed that everything should proceed in its proper order and under a constant law, and that some things should succeed others, so that all things might be subject and render service to the first human being and to those who were to be propagated from the first human being through continuous succession. Nor did merciful God provide only that, when human beings died, others [Col. 0677A] should be born in their place; he also provided that those who had died should be restored to life after many ages. Nature itself makes this resurrection of bodies plausible through many examples of things that in some manner die and come to life again. Much more, then, will human bodies rise through the power of God, by which all created things were made and endure, since his clemency toward human beings is as great as befits the Almighty. The praises of God arise from his infinite majesty, power, knowledge, and above all his goodness. Dracontius invokes God’s aid in celebrating God’s praises in verse.

## SYNOPSIS OF BOOK II

150. God is the author and ruler of all things; the stars, moon, sun, and all the elements obey him. God’s immensity. Everything depends upon his will, by whose [Col. 0677B] word all things were created. Confession of the divine Trinity. The Word became flesh in order to save humanity. The Son is consubstantial with the Father; the Holy Spirit is the same as the Father and the Son. God assumed a true body. Christ’s miracles, so that human beings might believe in him. His disciples were endowed with the grace of miracles. God’s dominion over created things. The Israelites’ passage through the Red Sea. Food and drink are supplied to the Israelites in the wilderness through divine assistance. Again, God’s praises are drawn from created things and the harmony of the elements. All things confess and praise God, even animals that are sometimes harmful. Why God created these things. Adam’s first sin. How grave the crimes of his descendants are. Even harmful animals sometimes do good. Human beings are worse than wild beasts. Their boldness and perversity. All other [Col. 0677C] things obey the divine laws. Human beings are restrained neither by God’s anger nor by his mercy. The universal Flood to punish humanity; after the Flood, people resume their crimes.
