The punishment of the Sodomites, who perished in a conflagration. God’s mercy in both punishments. Lot is rescued from the fire, just as Noah is rescued from the Flood. Human beings incur punishments because, though warned by God, they do not amend. Human happiness, had they not sinned. The angels’ sin cannot serve as an excuse for human beings; their punishment ought to inspire terror. God’s mercy toward humanity, whom Christ redeemed. The Jews’ faithlessness. Christ’s passion, death, resurrection, ascension into heaven, and future judgment. The fruit of Christ’s passion, which would also have benefited Judas had he not despaired. Paul’s conversion. Faith obtains many things from God. God’s grace is offered to all. [Col. 0677D] Examples of faith in Abraham, Tobit, David, Ezekiel, and Anna, the mother of Samuel. The power and efficacy of prayers before God. Zechariah, the father of Saint John the Baptist, was punished because he delayed believing. God’s mercy is greater 115 than his justice. Why God does not allow wicked people to reach old age, so that they might be converted to him. A contrite heart as a sacrifice to God. Almsgiving commended. The prayers of the poor have great power before God. The example of Tabitha, restored to life. The greedy are rebuked. God’s justice and mercy in the Israelites’ passage through the Red Sea, when the Egyptians were drowned.

## SYNOPSIS OF BOOK III

The praises of God: his infinite knowledge, justice, mercy, [Col. 0678A] goodness, generosity, and liberality in supplying grain. Grain-hoarders and the greedy are rebuked. The example of the condemned rich man who requested refreshment from the poor Lazarus in the underworld. Those who seize what belongs to others deserve condemnation even more. Neither riches nor any other good things should be preferred to God, the giver of them all. Perishable things must be despised so that eternal things may be acquired. Abraham taught us this by his own example when, commanded to do so, he led his son to sacrifice. God wished a ram to be substituted for Isaac. But Saturn, a false deity, did not act in this way: children were sacrificed to him every year. God wished Abraham to be an example to others, so that nothing, however dear, might be placed before the Lord. The reward of Abraham’s obedience: his descendants were extended through all times and regions. Another example: the three boys who remained unharmed in the burning [Col. 0678B] furnace. Daniel among the lions. A description of the amphitheatrical hunting of wild beasts. Hercules’ legendary strength yields to Daniel. The cruelty of Taurian Diana. The primacy of Peter, chief of the apostles. Through his prayers, Simon Magus was hurled down at Rome. These and other things of this kind came about through faith, hope, and prayers to God. The pagans, however, undertook many daring deeds not moved by hope of eternal life, but solely by love of praise or of their country. Menoeceus, son of Creon, killed himself so that his father would not lose the kingdom. The tragic history of the Theban kingdom. Codrus willingly allowed himself to be killed by the enemy for his country. Leonidas, with a few Lacedaemonians, fought boldly at Thermopylae. The Carthaginian brothers Philaeni allowed themselves to be burned alive so that the boundaries of their country might be extended farther. [Col. 0678C] Brutus, avenger of violated chastity and defender of liberty, 116 ordered his sons to be struck with the axe. Virginius, so that he would not see his daughter Virginia’s liberty and chastity taken from her, stabbed her with a knife. Torquatus condemned his victorious son to death because he had fought against orders, while everyone groaned. Curtius threw himself headlong into the lake. Regulus, so as not to break the faith he had given, returned voluntarily to Carthage to savage tortures and a most cruel death. The faith and steadfastness of the Saguntines. Women too, just as they are bold in crimes, often undertake outstanding deeds. Judith, after killing Holofernes, freed her country. Thomyris defeated Cyrus. Evadne climbed upon the pyre on which her husband’s body was burning. Dido built a pyre for herself. Lucretia took her own life. Many other women performed crimes or difficult [Col. 0678D] deeds out of love of praise or for a vain divinity of the gods. Nothing good can arise from these, since there is only one true God, immense and eternal, who is our father and whose children we are. Since all created things serve him, a human being is bold and wicked if he neglects to obey his commands. Dracontius’s confession and repentance. He enumerates the hardships into which he had fallen because of his crimes. He asks forgiveness from God. He presents the example of Job and the resurrection of the dry bones in Ezekiel, which he depicts vividly. The repentance of Nebuchadnezzar. Dracontius’s prayers to God for release from his bonds and for the attainment of the goods of this life and of eternal life.

[Col. 0679]

# DRACONTIUS’S POEM ON GOD (C, S)

## BOOK ONE

Verse 1. Vatican manuscript: “The peaceful Thunderer not to know.”

2. Vatican manuscript: “Let them read the poem while he recites it under pressure of voice.”

3. Vatican manuscript: “Perhaps ‘whom the temples of heaven, whom the walls…’”

4. Vatican manuscript: “Having turned, they venerate and adore their own.”

Verse 1. In place of *nescire*, which is clearly erroneous, I restored *rescire* (“to learn” or “to recognize”). One might also read *praescire* (“to foreknow”), and perhaps *sentire* (“to perceive”) would be better, for this verb is appropriately and frequently used to indicate divine majesty. Thus Martial, addressing Domitian, who called himself a god, *Spectacula*, epigram 16, elsewhere 17: “Believe me, even he perceives your divinity.” Marius Victor, in the preface, verse 100: “In whom, gracious God, I pray to you, who by your favorable divine power grant minds to perceive [you].” Dracontius below, Book I, verse 225: “Established by the power of God, whom the sphere of the heavens sustains and through all things perceives as the thunderous Lord.” Arator, Book II, verse 232: “Which deserved to perceive God,” where a gloss in a certain Vatican manuscript has: “To perceive, through faith.” Concerning the word *placidus*, meaning mild or merciful, I spoke in the prolegomena, no. 148. Prosper uses it in the same sense, epigram 12: “Nor does anger, avenger of crimes, move the peaceful one”; and 103: “When angry, he would allow what, when peaceful, he forbids”—both statements referring to God. Dracontius and other Christian poets, imitating the ancients, simply call God “the Thunderer.” Arator, Book I, verse 103: “Nor do the elements cease to serve their Thunderer.” But in this passage Dracontius perhaps intends something more: namely, that the clemency of God even when angry, and while he thunders, should be recognized, as in Book II, verse 696: “And whenever you are moved to anger, you appear most peaceful.”

2. In *prae mente legant* I recognize the tmesis *praelegant mente* (“let them read with their minds beforehand”). This figure was familiar to many Christian poets, and in some indeed was used to the point of nausea or ridicule. Thus Barthius notes in Abbo, *Adversaria*, Book XXXVI, chapter 7: “And they enter into islands”; “and they cut faces into throats”; “and, as the sun was setting, they approached Burgundy”; in Agobard: “February migrated on the fifth day before the Kalends.” There are also certain similar examples among the ancients, such as Ennius’s *Cere comminuit brum* (“he crushed Ceres’ grain”), and Sempronius Gracchus’s *Medi spernere cinam* (“to despise the middle of cinnamon”). Eugenius of Toledo composed an epigram, poem 23 of Book I, addressed to John and filled with words divided across boundaries: “O John, because you despise connected little verses…” and so forth. He did this to mock the excessive use of the figure, as Rivinus observed in his notes. In fact, Eugenius concludes the epigram: “Like Lucilius, I am forced to break apart the verses,” which he took from Ausonius, *Epistle* 5 to Theon: “Soon you will possess Lucan’s villa; learn, once the name has been cut apart, to compose a verse; thus you will imitate the poet Lucilius.” In any case, a sparing use of this figure, especially when the two parts composing a single word are divided, has elegance. There is also an elegant alteration between the verbs “to read beforehand” and “to recite”; for *recensere* (“to recite” or “review”) would more properly suit the mind. The meaning, then, is that the poem must be read with attentive concentration, in such a way that the mind somehow anticipates the words.

[Col. 0680B] 3. In the sequence of the phrase, either *quem* (“whom”) or *quod* (“that” or “which”) may be read; the meaning will not differ greatly whichever one is chosen. Tertullian, *On Judgment*: “It is good to know all the miracles of things, so that throughout all things we may acknowledge the true Lord, who prepared the light, the seas, heaven, and earth.” Dracontius carries out both ideas in this poem, so that we may acknowledge whom created things adore, and that these things adore God and serve him. Temples, walls, atria, palaces, roofs of heaven, and similar expressions occur frequently in Dracontius and other Christian poets. Others commonly illustrate these with similar examples from pagan poets; it is enough for us to point out these stylistic beauties. As for Dracontius’s amplification of the same matter through many names that may appear synonymous, he imitates sacred Scripture, in which created things are similarly enumerated one by one when God’s praises are drawn from them.

4. There is no doubt that *confessa* (“having confessed”) should be read in place of *conversa* (“having turned”). Although *conversa* yields some meaning, *confessa* agrees much better both with the sense and with the poet’s style. Thus in Book II, the same Dracontius, verses 205–206: “The signs and stars praise you, having confessed you as their author; the lightning adores you.” *Elegy*, verse 3: “The stars, flame, and day—whom the sun, night, and moon acknowledge as author—the ages all acknowledge as lord.” Prosper, epigram 4: “And all created things sing their ruler.” One might read *venerantur, adorant* (“they venerate, they adore”), or *venerentur, adorent* (“let them venerate, let them adore”); but *veneranter adorent* (“let them adore reverently”) seems better. The adverb *veneranter* is pleasing; Dracontius also uses it in Book III, verse 672: “To approach reverently with tears and pious prayers.” See the prolegomena, no. 135. Tertullian, *On Judgment*: “And all, kneeling, adore reverently.” Sedulius, at the end of Book V: “They adore reverently.” The fact that things without reason adore God is a phrase consecrated by ecclesiastical usage. In the Office of Blessed Mary the Virgin, at Saturday Matins: “Whom earth, sea, and stars cultivate, adore, and proclaim.” Fortunatus, the author of that hymn, had written: “Whom earth, sea, and ether…”—that is, *aethera* in place of *aetherae*—from which *aethra* has become more common. Some have also used *aether* in the neuter gender.

5. If you read *quem* in verse 3, you can retain *quemque plagae* here as well, namely, “whom the zones adore.” But *quinque plagae* (“five zones”) is much more attractive than simply *plagae*, for *septemque poli* (“and seven heavens”) follows, and mention of five zones is common among poets; they also call them belts. Virgil, Book VII, verse 226: “And if the middle of the extended zones divides anyone into four zones under the unequal sun”; and in the *Georgics*, Book I, verses 233 and following, he describes them beautifully: “Five zones hold the heaven,” and so on, as does Ovid, Book I of the *Metamorphoses*, verses 45 and following. Dracontius, *Elegy*, verses 89 and following: “The temperate region does not possess the middle sphere of heaven, for of the five zones it scarcely holds two.” The ancients distinguished seven heavens or celestial poles; some distinguished more, others fewer. Paulinus, final poem: “This heaven also, which we see raised high, has six others beneath it, rising at equal intervals, and after the seven thrones…” I have cited other examples in my commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* 7 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 36: “Before the prince of the sevenfold heaven.” In the manuscript’s corrupt reading *lunaque et omnis* or *omnes*, one might conjecture *lunaque, et aether* (“the moon, and ether”), or *et ignis* (“and fire”), since celestial fire is often mentioned by Dracontius; or *et orbis* (“and the sphere”); or *et omnia sidera* (“and all the stars”), with *omnia* contracted by synaeresis, as at the beginning of Virgil’s Book VI: “Then they would read all things through with their eyes”; or *lunaque, coeli sidera* (“the moon and stars of heaven”), or something similar. I prefer *lunaque, et astra* (“the moon and stars”), for Dracontius uses a similar enumeration in Book II, verse 205: “The hosts of stars praise you, the signs and stars praise you.” Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book III, chapter 60: “Stars, constellations, and heavenly bodies differ among themselves. A star is any single star. Constellations are formed from many stars, such as the Hyades and Pleiades. Heavenly bodies are great stars, such as Orion and Boötes.” And in Book I of the *Differences* he adds that a *signum* is the figure by which the image of a living creature is formed, such as Taurus or Scorpio. Here he says that stars are numerous groups, such as the Hyades; constellations are those by which navigators take their bearings, since they guide their course—where perhaps *quae navigantes* should be read.]

117. Those who wish to recognize the peaceful Thunderer in their minds  
should read this poem with attention, while reciting it aloud.

118. They will recognize that the temples of heaven and the walls of the sky,  
[Col. 0680A] having confessed their own Author, adore him reverently;

[5] the five zones, the seven heavens, the sun, the moon, and the stars.

8. Above, in verse 3, he says “the walls of heaven,” while enumerating its individual parts; now he means heaven as a whole. Repetition of the same word is frequent in Dracontius, as in other Christian poets. Thomas Wopkensius observed this in Paulinus of Petricordia, *Critical Adversaria* on Book III, verse 27. Among the created things that praise God, chaos is also listed, as in verse 3 of the *Elegy*: “Night and moon confess,” and in the *Song of the Three Boys*, “nights and darkness.” In place of *axis* (“axis”), it may perhaps be preferable to read *aer* or *aura* (“air” or “breeze”), although *noti* (“winds”) has already occurred above.

9. I suspect that this verse is corrupt. If you read it as it stands in the manuscript, you will understand *praecepta creare* (“to create commands”) as equivalent to *jussa creare* (“to create orders”): Book I, verse 402, “All the earth and whatever his commands created are given to them”; Book II, verse 76, “Whatever nature created”; and the same book, verse 260, “And whatever evil avenging nature created.” Avitus, Book I, verse 26: “They received the race commanded to be created without seed.” Marius Victor, *On Genesis*, Book I, verse 118: “Nature formed [them] in various ways, commanded to bring forth parts from the whole and forms from an unformed body”; and after verse 339: “Every animal that the earth, commanded, will have created to this point.” These authors use the verb “to create” in a less proper sense, meaning to bring forth or produce from already existing matter. For producing from nothing—which is properly creation—belongs to God alone. This should nevertheless be understood according to scholastic usage, as I shall explain at verse 2 of the *Elegy*. The verse might be restored as *dedit per cuncta creatrix* (“the creative [nature] gave throughout all things”); shortly afterward, at verse 27, *natura creatrix* (“creative nature”) occurs, and *per cuncta* (“throughout all things”) occurs in the Tertullian quoted at verse 3, as well as in Dracontius, Book I, verse 226, “the Lord thundering through all things,” and verse 292, “would have been through all things.” This verse could also be connected with the following one: “Or whatever nature gave.” [The phrase] “commands to create” could then mean: “It accomplishes this and follows…”]

10. I understand the poem to be making human beings recognize God in created things, and in addition to be following—or recounting—the works of God’s anger and mercy. Thus Juvenal, *Satire* I, verse 86, proposes his subject: “Whatever human beings do—desire, fear, anger, pleasure, joys, and our wanderings—is the medley of my little book.” *Sequor* (“I follow”) is not improperly used for “I recount.” Thus Seneca, *Troades*, verse 236: “It is pleasing to follow the famous praises and illustrious deeds of the great father.” I would not object, however, to restoring the passage as *haec etenim exsequitur* (“for this accomplishes”), or *haec namque*, or something similar, so that nature is understood as carrying out God’s angers and pious wishes. In this sense Prosper, epigram 5: “God is the beginning of the world, by whom all things are moved; and what the author permits or commands, they do. Hence the immutable order of mutable things serves the laws of the eternal craftsman. Each will advances toward its own ends, nor is the just judge absent from differing merits: he rules hearts, grants strength, remits sins, is gentle toward the submissive and implacable toward the proud. Thus neither punishment receives anyone as evil nor glory as righteous except with the praise and honor of God.” Dracontius, *Elegy*, verse 15: “Whatever human beings do—good, sorrowful, prosperous, wicked—anger and favor of God permit to happen.”

11. “Pious wishes of God” indicates God’s mercy and favor. Book II, verse 609, again of God: “They hate delays to pious wishes.” Among the earlier Latins, *pietas* generally denoted the virtue of justice proper to honoring one’s ancestors, or religion, by which one venerates God. Christian writers commonly use *pietas* for clemency, gentleness, goodness, and mercy; the word is extremely frequent in this sense in ecclesiastical prayers. Some pagans likewise give *pius* and *pietas* this meaning, including Suetonius, Claudian, Statius, and Justin; nor do I understand Virgil otherwise, Book V, verse 687: “Almighty Jupiter, if you are not yet wholly hostile to the Trojans, if ancient piety regards human sufferings, grant the fleet escape from the flames.” The meaning of *miseris* (“wretched”) should also be noted; it is certainly opposed to *beatis* (“blessed”). Concerning this word, see the note on verse 150 of Book II. Cicero, *Partitiones oratoriae*, chapter 17: “For nothing is so pitiable as a person who has fallen from blessedness into misery.” But Christian writers commonly call holy people blessed and wicked people wretched. Wopkensius noted this in his commentary on Paulinus of Petricordia, Book II, verse 195: “May they deem worthy, the flames of the wretched…” The same Paulinus, Book III, verse 239: “This is not the judgment of Christ the Lord concerning the wretched.” Thus devout men, out of humility of spirit, used to describe themselves as wretched and sinful. See the epitaph of Eugenius of Toledo, Book I, poem 14, in which the first letters of the verses form *Eugenius* and the final letters *misellus* (“little wretched one”).

12. Later, Book II, verse 418: “The Almighty separates merits according to the ways of the world.” And Book III, verse 241: “Those whom it pleased to live according to such a path of life.”

13. I restored *salus* (“salvation”) in place of *scelus* (“crime”). Although crime is committed by human beings with God’s permission, and virtue and prudence are also listed here, it would nevertheless seem excessively harsh to say that crime descends from God’s citadel; and after *vita* (“life”), *salus* (“salvation”) follows appropriately. Thus in Saint Damasus’s epigram on the Names of the Savior, poem 6 in the latest Roman edition: “Hope, way, life, salvation, reason, wisdom, light.” In that verse *via* (“way”) has been incorrectly omitted in this edition, though it is clearly read in earlier ones. These verses of Damasus occur under another name in certain manuscripts.]

14. One might conjecture *taedia, tristitia, splendor* (“weariness, sorrow, splendor”), or distinguish *taedia tristitiae*, so that *tristitiae* would be the singular genitive. But *tristitiae* in the plural seems better. Rivinus punctuated the later poem of Ratbert of Corbie in the same way: “Wearinesses, sorrows, cares, torments, disasters,” where Ratbert seems to imitate Dracontius. Properly, *compendium* means profit gained through frugality and is opposed to *dispendium* (“loss” or “expense”); but here and elsewhere Dracontius and other excellent writers use it for any profit or gain.

15. Properly, *laudes* means public praise or commendation of virtue; but sometimes, by metonymy, the word denotes right actions, whose reward is praise. This meaning is extremely common in sacred Scripture, as Martinus Roa observes in Book I of the *Singularia*, chapter 13; he also provides examples from Virgil. Lexicographers add many more from Cicero and other authoritative writers. Dracontius appears to use *laudes* metonymically in this sense.

16. *Affectus* means any movement of the mind, whether bad or good. But here it may perhaps refer to some bodily illness or impaired health, as in Celsus, Book III, chapter 18: “Other bodily disorders remain, which supervene upon this fever” (some read “these fevers”); and Book II, chapter 15: “In such disorders those kinds of exercise are also necessary.” *Successus* is used simply for a favorable outcome; the lexicons are full of examples. Ratbert, in the passage cited, used *casus* in a negative sense: “anguish, poverty, sorrow, death, misfortune, need.” Since Dracontius seems to oppose this verse to the preceding verse’s *gaudia* (“joys”), *affectus* will more correctly be understood as mental distress. But doubt remains concerning *successus*, which I have never seen used for an adverse event. I suspect *succussus* (“shaking” or “disruption”).

17. Someone might conjecture: “The dread cross of the powers, the indignation of kings.” But in this manuscript *trux* (“fierce”) has elsewhere also been changed to *crux* (“cross”), as in Book II, verse 422: “He is taken from the death of the cross, seen without crime”; and Book III, verse 106: “Exile without the death of the cross.” In both places I would read *morte truci* (“by a fierce death”). See also whether the passage can be punctuated: “The anger of the powers, the cross; the indignation of kings.”

18. Despite the manuscript’s obvious corruption, the sense is clear whether one reads *tristia, amara* (“sorrowful, bitter”), *tristia, acerba* (“sorrowful, harsh”), *tristia, prava* (“sorrowful, wicked”), or *tristia, saeva* (“sorrowful, savage”). In the *Elegy*, verse 15: “Good, sorrowful, prosperous, wicked”; and verse 55: “For Almighty God could have given only joys, when he created the world, removing sorrows.” And Book II, verse 456: “Character removes sweet things and supplies bitter ones.”

19. One might punctuate: “They descend from the citadel, from the seat of the thundering God.” Thus Book II, verse 894: “From the citadel he sent gracious Christ through the stars of heaven,” where *arx* (“citadel”) is used absolutely for heaven, since *coeli* (“of heaven”) refers to the stars, and *arx* properly means a lofty place. In the punctuation I follow, however, *ex arce Dei, de sede Tonantis* may mean that works of divine mercy descend from God’s citadel, while works of justice descend from the seat of the Thunderer. Prosper expresses this thought in epigram 10: “In all things there is a twofold work of the Almighty; whatever he does is either justice or mercy. Both descend upon earth from the citadel of light, so that neither part may lack the other good.” In the Pisaurian edition of the *Collection of Poets*, the word *opus* (“work”) is missing from the first verse, and the fourth verse is entirely absent from Prosper’s first epigram. That edition is full of errors; this should be noted so that others may use it cautiously and not be surprised by the many blemishes found in manuscript copies.

20. Someone else may correct the passage to *qua pietas* (“by which there is mercy”), and the following verse to *atque ubi dicuntur* (“and where they are said”). I prefer *cui pietas* (“to whom mercy belongs”). Ardor is attributed to God, just as fire is throughout sacred Scripture. See the commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* 10 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 1: “God, fiery source of souls.”

21. It would not be bad to read: “And to whom praises are owed”; but *dicuntur* (“are spoken”) is sound. Avitus, Book IV, verse 191: “The angelic choir without end, which proclaims and celebrates God with everlasting praise.” Dracontius, Book II, verse 73: “Singing prayers without end in angelic fashion.” This phrase, *sine fine* (“without end”), is very familiar to Christian writers and occurs frequently in Dracontius, as in Book II, verse 81, *sine fine perennis* (“everlasting without end”); others say *nullo fine* (“with no end”) or *dempto fine* (“without end”). Martial, Book III, epigram 46: “Endless service in the toga.” Ovid, *Heroides* 3, Briseis, verse 15: “But I shed endless tears and tore my hair.”

22. Likewise verse 501: “And rightly so, because he makes all things.” In a few words he encompasses eternity: “Lacking an end, he knows no beginnings.”

23. Perhaps *terrae chaos* (“the chaos of earth”) would be better than *tetrum chaos* (“dread chaos”). One verse seems to be missing here, or this verse and the following five may belong elsewhere. Their position after Book I, verse 146, “Neither separated nor mixed do they remain,” would not be unsuitable. It may also be said that the creation of the world is joined here to God’s eternity as part of the subject of divine praise. Dracontius attributes to fire the fact that God dissolved the dreadful chaos by its power. In my view, he means that, on the second day of the world’s creation, God made the firmament and divided the waters beneath the firmament from those above it. The proper power of fire is to loosen and dissolve. This may also be explained of the darkness of night, which is dissolved by the fire of the rising sun; the following verses support this interpretation.

24. Book I, verse 224: “Who cherishes heaven, sea, stars, and lands with pious fire.” *Elegy*, verse 2: “Who rules the heavens with fire”; and verse 82, concerning the sun: “Preparing all things to be created, cherishing all things created.” Horace, Book I of the *Epistles*, verse 16: “When he comes, let the sun look upon the right side; as he departs in his fleeing chariot, let him warm the left.” Concerning fire, Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XX, chapter 10: “*Focus*, because in Greek *phōs* (φῶς) means ‘light,’ in Latin is *ignis*, ‘fire’; hence, according to certain philosophers, all things are produced from it.” Indeed, nothing is born without heat, so that the poet says of the North: “Nothing is generated by sterile cold.”

25. Perhaps read *at flammae* (“but the flames”). The following passage in Book I, verse 675, belongs to this interpretation: “From whose immense flames the stars grow weak, unless they are nourished by cold waters through the blue sea.” Saint Ambrose, in his hymn for the second day: “Establishing the place among the heavenly bodies, and likewise among the streams of earth, so that water may temper the flames, lest it dissolve the soil of the earth.” Perhaps *dissipent* (“lest they dissolve”) should be read; but the printed editions, including Thomasius’s *Hymnary*, have *dissipet* (“lest it dissolve”). And in Book II, chapter 3 of the *Hexaemeron*: “Thus we frequently see the sun wet and dripping with dew; in this it gives clear evidence that it has taken nourishment from the waters to temper its own heat.” This was taken from Aratus’s *Phenomena*: “Although the sun is fiery, it grows hotter through the excessive motion of its revolution; philosophers say that its fire is nourished by water and receives from the contrary element the power of its light and heat. Hence we see it frequently wet and dripping with dew.” The same point is made by Glycas of Sicily, who holds that waters were placed in heaven because of the sun’s extremely ardent motion and heat (*Annals*, Part I, Day 2). Marius Victor leaves the matter unresolved in *On Genesis*, Book I, verses 71 and following: “Perhaps someone may discuss the matter in this way, with learned error: lest nourishment be lacking for the heavenly flames, and lest excessive heat, descending to the depths in pursuit of nourishment, burn up the mortal race, and the gleaming heaven be unable to endure earthly things, the firm structure of the sky has been set beneath it. While its shadow protects us, the heaven above, meanwhile, grows cool from the waters placed upon it. But may our mind flee far from seeking the causes of divine power.” Fabricius printed it thus, but the Paris edition of 1560 reads: “While its shadow protects us, but it is veiled by waters; yet may our mind flee far from seeking such causes,” and so forth. When Dracontius says, “by which all things are sustained,” he means water and fire. Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book XIII, chapter 12, on water: “The element of water rules over all the others. For waters temper heaven and fertilize the earth… They become the cause of everything born on earth. They produce crops, trees, shrubs, and grasses.” On both elements, in the same place: “There are two especially powerful elements of human life, fire and water; hence those are gravely condemned from whom fire and water are withheld” (perhaps “to whom fire and water are forbidden).]

26. It would be more elegant to read *et radiis pascentia solis anheli* (“and nourished by the rays of the panting sun”). Concerning this epithet of fire, by which it is called *anhelus* (“panting”), see the prolegomena, no. 137. Virgil, Book VIII, verse 420: “The steel rings in the caverns, and fire pants in the furnaces.” In *pascentia* (“nourished”) the accusative *se* (“itself”) is understood; the verb *pasco* (“to feed”) is used in this way, especially in the present participle.

27. Ovid, Book XV of the *Metamorphoses*, verse 252: “No form remains for anything; nature, renewer of things, restores one shape from another.”

28. Perhaps read *per saecla refudit* (“has poured forth again through the ages”). Just as *fundo* (“pour forth”) is used for “to produce” and signifies abundance, so *refundo* means “to produce again,” or almost “to return through generation what was received.” Cicero, Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*, chapter 46: “From these vapors the stars are renewed, and the whole ether pours forth the same things again and draws them back from the same source.” Some manuscripts have *refundunt eodem* (“pour forth again into the same place”).

29. Concerning the word *modestus* (“moderate” or “merciful”), see the prolegomena, no. 136. In Plautus, *Trinummus* IV.1.12, *modestus esse alicui* means to behave moderately toward someone by sparing or helping him: “This is worthy of the gods: they are always moderate toward beggars”; or, as others read, “may they be,” with *ut* understood, namely, “so that they may always be favorable to the needy.”

30. This same thought occurs in many places, such as Book II, verse 689: “You restrain one ignorant of anger by warnings, not by disaster,” and so forth; Book III, verse 121: “He does not desire the deaths of the innocent, nor quickly consume the lives of the guilty, while he reserves everything for forgiveness”; and in the same book, verses 655 and following.]

31. Perhaps *assumens* or *assurgens* should be read for *assumat*. Book II, verse 486: “But because heavenly mercy threatens forgiveness,” etc. Salvianus, *On the Government of God*, Book V: “Such is the mercy of God that, although he wishes us to suffer something for our offenses, he nevertheless does not wish us to endure everything: for he chastises the wicked but does not inflict evil, and prefers that we acknowledge our sins rather than endure them; that is, by pious and salutary scourges he wishes to show us what we deserve to bear, yet he does not inflict what we deserve.” Prudentius, *Cath.* 7, verse 103: “But he would know that it is better for that threatening judge to preserve than to strike and punish.”

32. This verse may be emended in either of these ways: *Conscia quo Dominum*, “so that our mind, conscious [of sin], may pray to the Lord,” or *Quo contrita Deum*, “by which, crushed, [it approaches] God”; the latter is preferable. For the threats of the Lord are directed toward the crushing of hearts. Saint Gregory, at the beginning of Homily 1 on the Gospels: “If we are unwilling to fear God in tranquility, at least let us fear his approaching judgment, worn down by blows.” Nevertheless, the former reading should be retained because it comes closer to the manuscript’s writing and has a sound meaning.

34. So too concerning King David in Book II, verse 655: “But acknowledging his crime, he openly confesses his offenses without penalty”; and again concerning the same person, *Eleg.* verse 159: “Having confessed his crime, the guilty man earns pardon for his ruin, though guilty without penalty or death.” Paulinus, final poem: “He grants this still more, he gave this greater gift also: that the sinner who repents, though previously fallen, is not counted among the multitude of sinners. For the punishment is sufficient when his own guilt is a source of grief; fear is the proper punishment, guilt the torment. Then he suffers, as it were, when he confesses that he deserved it.”

36. I have supplied this lacuna from the meaning, as I judge it. Dracontius suggests that the anger of God had been foretold in the ancient law by the words of the prophets, but that after Christ’s coming it was made manifest through prodigies and portents. In explaining these monsters, Dracontius perhaps imitated Juvenal, whose verses he reproduces elsewhere and whose *Satire* 13, verses 65ff., contains these lines: “If I behold an excellent and holy man, I anxiously compare him to this two-bodied monster of a boy, to fish discovered by a plowman now wondering beneath his plow, and to a pregnant mule, as though a shower had poured down stones,” etc. Claudian likewise, Book I *Against Eutropius*: “Half-bestial offspring and dreadful pledges to the mother,” etc.

“Feeding on clouds and the rays of the panting sun.

But because divine mercy is restrained by God’s power,

### 124

It restrains punishment and threatens punishment,

But after Christ descended from heaven, dissolving our guilt,

### 125

Nature teaches whatever draws near,

[40] Forewarns in advance, and makes the elements labor,

So that by prodigies and signs they may create monsters to inspire fear.

For often even quadrupeds have been terrified at offspring unlike themselves,

And heat inflames the womb of the barren mule, now more fertile and about to give birth.”

50. Beasts are also *pecudes* (“cattle” or “domestic animals”), but the terms are often distinguished from one another, as in Lucretius, Book IV, verse 1190: “Nor in any other way do birds, herds, wild beasts, cattle, and mares [differ].” Dracontius, Book I, verse 284: “Every kind of cattle is born, every kind of wild beast.” See Gifanius, *Index to Lucretius*.

52. Book I, verse 666: “Cold light, the image of the sun.” Book II, verse 10: “The sun’s heat, by which the cold moon shines.” Just as the sun is called burning because it is fiery or hot and shines with its own light, so the moon is called cold because it gleams with light received from the sun, and the light reflected from it to us heats nothing or very little. By a similar reasoning Virgil calls Saturn’s star cold in Book I of the *Georgics*, verse 336, and Claudian agrees with him in Book I of *The Praise of Stilicho*, verse 178.

53. Genesis, chapter I, verse 14: “Let them be for signs and seasons.” See Book II, verse 11.

54. For *somnus* (“sleep”), which this passage does not permit, since the subject is signs derived from living creatures, I have written *corvus* (“raven”). Later, verse 527: “The heifer, frog, cranes, ants, raven, and swallow foretell the rains, nor do the omens now deceive.” Virgil likewise, Book I of the *Georgics*, verse 381: “And, departing from the pasture in a great column, the army of ravens resounded with dense wings,” which he says is a sign of rain.

55. *Proditor* (“betrayer” or “revealer”) means an informer or indicator in Horace, Ovid, and others. It would not be wrong to read *quid sit* for *sit quid*, or *siquid*.

56. Perhaps read *Cornices fantur* (“the crows speak”). Concerning the crow, Isidore, Book XII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 7: “Among many other omens, they also attribute to it the prediction of rain by its cries; hence the saying: ‘Then the wicked crow calls for rain with its full-throated voice.’” The verse is Virgil’s, from the *Georgics* cited above. Other poets often have similar statements. Cicero, *Letters to Atticus*, Book XV, letter 16: “Indeed, I fear the rains too, if our prognostics are true: for the frogs *rhetoreuousin* [ῥητορεύουσιν], ‘speak rhetorically,’ declaiming in the manner of rhetors, or rather cry out.”

57. I read *Quod hominis* (“that which belongs to man”), since the conjunction *-que* seems to have been inserted by someone wishing to accommodate the meter. Yet *quod* is correctly lengthened because of the aspiration of the following word. The evil tongue of man is called a wild beast; for I do not think *tacet fera bellua* should be punctuated separately: “the wild beast is silent.” Rather, the evil human tongue is a wild beast that is silent about the fish. Shortly afterward, in this same Book V, verse 487: “Among all the limbs, that part itself is considered the purer, which alone was more harmful in the entire body,” etc. See other passages against the evil human tongue in Book III, verses 629ff., and *Eleg.* verse 44, as well as Prudentius, *Hymn* 10 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 892: “Which alone, throughout the whole body, lives more wickedly.” The same Prudentius had said in the passage cited, verse 768, that the good tongue is the body’s best part.

58. Marcellus Victor, Book I of *Genesis*, verse 141: “Each offspring having received the forms of its own kind.” What Dracontius intends here is not easy to conjecture. It may be understood that the fish despise their own kind, or that they seek to preserve their life, while shameful or their own limbs rebel against nature—such things as happen when a comet flashes, creating deaths and monsters and staining the water with blood, etc. For this entire narrative may be concluded by verse 79: “With the fish of the Ocean thirsting for their own waters.” Yet I find nothing in ancient writers to confirm these portents.

Oppian, indeed, in Book I of the *Halieutica*, says: “For, more than other creatures, the fish-bearing kinds fear the raging sea.” I do not know whether this can be applied to Dracontius. What Isidore reports in *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 38, comes closer to his words: “A change of wind toward the south occurs when squids or swallows fly, or when dolphins display themselves in full leaps and strike the water with their tails. For the wind always arises from the direction in which they are borne. Nor is it surprising that mute animals divine beneath the waves. For the waters always incline at the movement of the first-rising breeze; the earliest inhabitants of the sea sense this change. Therefore they struggle against the force, either from fear that they may be carried onto the shores, or by nature, lest the wave drive forward the necks of those turning away. What then? Do only the dolphins fear this injury? No, the other fish do as well. But these alone appear because they leap.”

If one wishes the meaning and sense to be concluded at verse 59, “Against nature,” etc., the suspicion may arise that the passage concerns the chastity of fish, about which Ambrose says in Book V of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 3: “Then, finally, how pure and inviolate is their succession! None mingles with another, but each with its own kind: grayling with grayling, wolf-fish with wolf-fish. The scorpion-fish also preserves the chastity of an unstained union with its own kind; thus it possesses the modesty of its kind, though not its poison—for the scorpion-fish does not strike but restores. Thus fish of alien kinds know nothing of adulterous contagion, as do those that mate with asses, etc.; these are true adulteries of nature . . . And you, man, arrange these things, interpreter of bestial adultery . . . You make a eunuch, so that what nature denied among human beings, audacity might accomplish.”

From these passages a suitable interpretation of Dracontius’ verses may be extracted, provided that *prospiciunt* (“look ahead” or “take forethought”) is read for *despiciunt* (“despise”). It must be observed, however, that the chastity of fish described by Ambrose is neither universal nor common, as Basil notes in Homily 7 on the *Hexaemeron*, where he calls the coupling of the moray eel and the viper a kind of adultery of nature.

From the same Basil a more certain explanation of Dracontius may be drawn. He says in the passage cited: “If creatures without reason habitually devise and preserve their safety, and a fish knows what it should seek and what it should avoid, what shall we say of ourselves, who . . . arrange matters concerning us much more crudely and irrationally than the fish themselves? If they foresee and anticipate the future, while we, deprived of hope for future things, bring our life to an end by devoting and surrendering it to pleasure fit for beasts?”

Glycas follows Basil in Book I of the *Annals*, day 5. Add Pliny, Book IX, chapter 19, section 35: “For most fish have an evident reason for passing into ponds and rivers, so that they may produce their offspring safely, since there are none there to devour the young and the waves are less violent.”

I shall therefore read *prospiciunt*, and after verse 60, *Jam micat* or *Tum micat* for *Nam micat*. Here *prospicio* means “I take forethought” or “provide for,” as in Livy, Book IV, chapter 49: “Who, after granting you city and fields, send you to colonies and provide a settlement for your old age.” The infinitive *servare* is used in place of an accusative.]

59. Consider whether *propria* should be read for *turpia*. The sense may be that human beings rebel against nature while fish strive to preserve their kind; or that fish take forethought for themselves while the sea is disturbed; or that fish neglect—if *despiciunt* is read—to preserve their kind while nature is shaken by the prodigies reported in the following verses.

60. I have just said that it is preferable to read *Jam micat* for *Nam micat*. In manuscripts *tam* and *jam*, as well as *tam* and *tum*, are often confused; nor is *tum* unsuitable to this passage.

61. For *creant* or *creat*, as I corrected it, *ruunt* may perhaps be better. This was the opinion of the ancients concerning comets. Seneca, *Natural Questions*, Book VII, chapter 17: “Some comets are bloody and threatening, carrying behind them an omen of future bloodshed.” They thought that a comet presaged wars, pestilences, and other evils, which Manilius lists at the end of Book I: “Whether the god, pitying the fate that threatens the world, sends signs through their effects and fires of heaven. Never has the ether blazed with empty flames,” etc. Dracontius explains particular kinds of monsters. Virgil, at the end of Book I of the *Georgics*: “Nor at the same time . . . did the flow of blood from the wells cease . . . nor did dreadful comets burn so often.”

[Col. 0689D] 63. Virgil, Book V, verse 695: “A turbulent rain rushes from the entire heaven, water”; others read *aqua* (“water”). But *pluo* with an accusative is good Latin. Concerning prodigious rains, Cicero, Book I *On Divination*, chapter 43: “What of the birth of an androgyne? Was it not a certain fatal monster? What of the fact that a river flowed blackened with blood? What of the frequent showers of stones, sometimes of blood, at times of earth, and once even of milk?” Livy frequently records these prodigies. Pliny, Book II, chapter 56, reports rain even of flesh, iron, wool, and baked bricks. Dracontius seems to mean warm water as a rain of blood, for he adds: “The dewy earth with blood,” that is, drenched with bloody moisture. Virgil, Book VII, verse 683: “The cold Anio and the dew-covered Hernician rocks are cultivated by their streams.”

65. Not all violets are pale, or, as Virgil says, pallid; some are purple and some white. Dracontius therefore says that the violet, which by nature was yellow, put on the color of a rose after driving away its pallor. Yellow violets do indeed seem to have been more common among the Romans; Horace too, Book III, Ode 10, attributes pallor to the violet: “Nor the pallor of lovers dyed with violet.”

66. From the rain of blood by which the earth was irrigated, all flowers of different colors were tinged with that unhappy redness.

67. Book III, verse 404: “The third lot, deprived of light.” Erebus is called the third lot because, as the myths relate, the rule of heaven fell to Jupiter, of the sea to Neptune, and of the underworld to Pluto, the younger brother. Seneca, *Hercules Furens*, Act III, scene 1: “And if the places of the third lot had pleased me, I could have ruled”; and later, verse 831: “This alone was lacking from the number of my labors: to strip the king of the third lot.” Tibullus, Book III, elegy 5: “The third kingdom of the god.” Claudian, *The Rape of Proserpina*, Book II, verse 167: “The third heir of Saturn.” Manilius, Book I, verse 155, concerning the sea: “The third lot spread out the waters and swimming waves.”

[Col. 0690C] 68. *Serenum* is used substantivally; see the note on verse 586.

69. Avitus, *On the Darkness of Egypt*, Book V, verse 203: “You might think that the foul multitudes of living creatures had likewise entered the infernal dwellings, or perhaps, when the earth’s barrier had been torn away, had migrated from the squalid homeland of the abyss to the upper world, and, with the light driven away, had brought the universe beneath their laws.”

70. In Claudian, Book II *On the Rape of Proserpina*, verse 220, Pallas addresses Pluto as he carries off Proserpina: “Leave your brother’s dwelling, abandon another’s lot; depart, content with your own night. Why do you mingle the living with the buried?”

71. Hercules brought Alcestis back from the underworld (Hyginus, fable 51). Apollodorus, Book II, relates that Theseus was raised from the underworld by Hercules, and that Cerberus himself was captured and brought to Eurystheus. Ovid, Book VII of the *Metamorphoses*, verse 410: “The Tirynthian hero dragged Cerberus, who resisted and turned his eyes askance from the daylight and its gleaming rays, bound in adamantine chains.”

73. Book II, verse 11: “Having divided the turns with his brother, traversing his own periods.” In the plural, *tempora* sometimes means “countenance” or “face”; in that sense one might explain Dracontius as referring to the moon’s face, unless the passage cited from Book II indicates the period through which the moon completes its course. But why is the moon called “not moist”? Since the moon is especially associated with night, or is called moist, while here the darkness of day is being described, as though bursting forth from the underworld, it follows that the moon in these darknesses is not moist. One may also read *non lucida* (“not bright”), since afterward the moon’s sphere is said to be covered by a darkened lamp.

74. Virgil, Book VI, verse 256: “The ground began to roar beneath their feet, and the ridges of the woods to move.” Lucan, Book III, verse 418: “Often the hollow caverns roar with an earthquake.”

76. Perhaps read *roseove colore* (“with a rosy color”), so that the day is blue with pallor or with a rosy color; for a rosy color is not opposed to the darkness of night, since it commonly appears in the sky at night, and the blue color may be formed from rose and yellow.]

77. Book II, verse 49: “Having embraced the lunar spheres.” Claudian, Book II *On the Rape of Proserpina*, verse 298: “Placed beneath the lunar sphere.” Many others speak of the lunar sphere, the sphere of the moon, and the sphere of the sun.

78. He describes the sea as not entirely dry—which never happens—but only partly so, which often occurs. If one asks why he calls the sea purple, one may answer that it also became purple from the rosy color mentioned shortly before. In any case, many have already noted that poets use *purpureus* for any beautiful color; thus swans are called purple and snow purple. Roa, Book IV of the *Miscellanies*, chapter 8, maintains that the sea is called purple as though shining with fiery blackness, although, if we attend to the force and meaning of the Greek word, it may also signify something disturbed and tossing, violently agitated by winds. Dracontius favors this latter interpretation, having borrowed the epithet from the Greeks. Aulus Gellius, Book XVIII, chapter 11, approves the old poet Furius for saying *spiritus purpurat undas* (“the breeze makes the waves purple”), but explains that the wind brightens the blue sea by ruffling it.

[Col. 0691C] Cicero, in fragments preserved by Nonius, chapter 2, number 717: “What of the sea—is it not blue? Or, when its wave is struck by oars, does it not become purple?” Indeed, the water is somehow dyed and colored. Propertius, Book II, elegy 20, verse 5: “Helen driven by purple waves.” Ambrose spoke of the sea’s becoming purple; his words may be read at verse 149.

80. *Eleg.* verse 61: “A letter eloquent in learning, akin to bees,” that is, suitable to them; perhaps one should read *rebus cognata* (“akin to things”).

81. Claudian, Book I of *The Rape of Proserpina*, verse 42: “The elements, almost resisting, would again have broken faith, fighting against one another.” Dracontius further suggests that nature does not deceive in some of its prognostics. The phrase *pietate parentis* (“with a parent’s devotion”) should be noted; likewise below, verse 726: “Who nourishes whatever he creates with a parent’s devotion.” Marcellus Victor, Book I of *Genesis*, verse 462: “But the holy devotion of a parent forbids despair”; and Hilary, Book I of *Genesis*, verse 52: “What you, Father, were preparing to create with paternal devotion”; and again, verse 142: “Caring for the pledge of a father’s devotion.” Dracontius, Book III, verse 529: “Although he is lord, he nevertheless wishes to be a father.” Hence the pagans sometimes called those who excelled in generosity and deserved well of others “parents” and “gods,” as Cicero says in *After His Return to the Quirites*, chapter 5: “The consul Publius Lentulus, parent, god, and salvation—or savior—of our life,” etc. Christians, however, taught by Jesus Christ to pray, call God above all our Father.

82. In *forem*, one may read *forent* for *erunt* by enallage. In some manuscript copies, *furent* is written for *forent* in *in venio*. Nor would it be wrong to read *quaecunque sient* for *erunt*, since formerly they said *sies* for *sis*. Lucretius, Book II, verse 1078: “Of whatever age they may be.” The proper tense here would be future, as in *quaecunque fient* (“whatever will happen”), which can be defended from what was said in the Prolegomena, number 139. Here *participare* means “to make certain people participate,” as in Plautus, *Stichus* I.1.21: “While they themselves meanwhile live and prosper, where they are and what they do, they neither share it with us nor return.” Otherwise *participo* means “I become a participant,” and sometimes “I grant a share” or “I make someone a participant.”

85. I do not know whether *portendant* can be tolerated, as though it meant “they threaten”; certainly *portendant ipsa ostenta* (“the portents themselves threaten”) is better. *Placare* (“to appease”) also suits this passage much better than *pacare* (“to pacify”). Events that occur contrary to expectation usually affect people far more gravely, as Josephus says in Book V of the *Antiquities*, at the end. By contrast, Seneca, Letter 76: “A premeditated evil comes with a softened blow.” On this sentiment see Saint Gregory the Great, Homilies 1 and 35 on the Gospels, and Alcuin, poem 179. A Spanish proverb likewise says: “No harm is done when it is foreseen, for foreknowledge helps one moderate oneself.” Alfonso Barros, *Moral Proverbs*, 26.

Nevertheless, *post saecla* (“after the ages”) should be retained, indicating that God’s rule will remain after the ages of the world; in Book II, verse 31, God is called “the prince of all things and survivor of the world.”

Do you wish to live? [Col. 0692D] 89. Book II, verse 598: “Ready indulgence forestalls guilt, and pardon precedes the wrongful crime.” There is some sense in the manuscript reading, namely that God, who sends torments, wishes to find no guilt. Someone may conjecture *et nulli capiunt tormenta reatus*, “and the torments of guilt seize no one,” that is, no guilty persons are punished, or no one falls into the torments of guilt. It is probable that *reatus* is in the genitive, as in Paulinus, final poem: “The torments of guilt; then he suffers, as it were, who confesses that he deserved it.” The sense, therefore, would be that the torments of guilt seize or overtake no one because repentance precedes punishment. Yet the first explanation is more pleasing in the old manuscript reading, with a metonymical meaning: God, who threatens torments, wishes there to be no guilt for him to punish.

116. From this verse onward, the editions published to date begin under the title *Hexaemeron*, or *On the Work of the Six Days*, and continue to the final verse of this book; I now append their variant readings. When Rivinus recognized that the first verse was corrupt, he emended it: “The first day is light, one death to the gloomy darknesses,” or *mors ima*, that is, “the lowest” or “first” death; or “living death,” or “sound death.” Barthius, in the same Rivinus, has: “The first day is light for the earth, death whence darkness.” Thus Moretus’s author: “And now, once light has been conceived, the darknesses withdraw.” It is clear that there is no place here for the word *terris* (“for the earth”). For although the opening words of Genesis, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” can be understood to mean that on the first day heaven together with the elemental earth was produced, Dracontius nevertheless seems to follow another opinion—namely, that Moses, in these words, comprehended the creation of the world as having occurred in time, and afterward explained it in its parts and days. On this opinion see Petavius, *On the Work of the Six Days*, book I, chapter 2; he adheres to this view and confirms it with testimonies of the holy Fathers, rejecting other explanations. Thus, just as Dracontius says in the following verse, “Light is given before the poles,” so he could have said, “Light is given before the ground,” or “before the earth.” It remains open to conjecture, however, whether instead of *mors una tenebris* (“one death to the darknesses”) one ought to read *nox unde tenebrae* (“night, whence darknesses”): for in the Vatican manuscript there is *mox*, which I find used elsewhere in place of *nox*; and other poets who narrate the work of the six days mention night, so that they may complete one day and express Moses’ meaning. In any case, calling the light of the darknesses “death” is a metaphor used by others as well. Plautus, *The Menaechmi*, I.2.45: “The day indeed is already half-spent and dead.” Statius, book IV of the *Silvae*, 6.3: “When the day was already dying, dinner carried me off.” In this book Dracontius, verse 663: “Dead night falls beneath the light”—for so the printed editions read; but in the Vatican manuscript, “dead light,” as I shall soon say. More clearly, verse 672: “Everywhere it brings the day, destined to perish beneath the shadows of night.” All these matters which Dracontius recalls in expounding the work of the six days are discussed at length by theologians and interpreters, especially those who deliberately wrote on the work of the six days. See some poets collected by Goldastus at number 29 of the prolegomena, where Gregory the Great and Ambrose the Younger are mentioned; perhaps, however, Goldastus is referring only to the *Hexaemeron* hymns composed by Ambrose of Milan, which some attributed to Gregory and others to Ambrose the Younger. The *Hexaemeron* of Hippolytus of Africa and of our Prudentius has perished. Leyser, *History of Medieval Poetry*, p. 391, under the year 1136, published the *Hexaemeron* of Hildebert of Tours, or Le Mans, which is found in the Paris edition of his works. Barthius preserved in manuscript the *Hexaemeron* of Ceponius, a fifth-century Spanish bishop, in hexameter verse, as I said at number 52 of the prolegomena. Calmet lists other writers or interpreters of the *Hexaemeron* in the *Sacred Bibliotheca* before the *Biblical Dictionary*.

117. Mar. Victor, at the beginning of book I: “Before the poles and the day of heaven”; this supports the Vatican manuscript’s reading *ante polos*. You will find no fuller praise of light elsewhere: Dracontius gathers together everything that others have said in praise of light. Augustine, book I of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 17, judged that the spiritual, not bodily, light was created by God on the first day. Abbot Rupert, book I on Genesis, chapter 10, confirms this opinion, because this one day would be the poorest of all days if only bodily light had been created on it. Rupert therefore did not attend to the true praises and exalted nature of light. Saint Ambrose, book I of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 9: “God himself was indeed in the light,” and so forth; “but he willed that light to be made which could be grasped by bodily eyes. Whoever desires to build some structure worthy of the head of a household first investigates, before laying the foundations, from where he may pour light into it; and this is the first grace, which, if absent, causes the whole house to bristle with an ugly neglect. It is light that commends the remaining adornments of the house.”

118. “It would not be inappropriate to say ‘a boundary for night and shadows’; but Dracontius, book II, verse 707, also used the genitive construction: ‘a boundary of crime and punishment.’ Ambrose, book I, chapter 9 of the *Hexaemeron*: “We observe, therefore, that the rising of light appears to open the day before the sun: for the beginnings of day close the exit of night, and the end and fixed boundary of time appears to have been prescribed for night and day.” But one should also note from Basil, homily 2 on the *Hexaemeron*, that the former state of the world—that is, before the first light arose—was not called night but darkness. For night is the portion of time which is distinctly and oppositely related to day; having succeeded day, it acquired this new name. Dracontius therefore says that light is the boundary of the darknesses which were not night, and of those which afterward were called night.

119. The Vatican manuscript is corrupt; but I suspect that even in the commonly received reading there is a corruption.

120. Rivinus conjectures *factisque color* (“and color for created things”) and cites Drepanus Florus: “And distinguishing varied colors by the light.” I change nothing: light is also warmth for created things, just as it is the sun’s grace; and in the preceding verse it has already been said, “light, the face of all things,” which is more than “light, color for created things.”

122. Again, at verse 127: “the origins of the world.” Ambrose, in his hymn for the first day: “Preparing the origin of the world from the beginnings of new light.” Tertullian, Mar. Victor, and others use the same word for the same subject. Paulinus, poem 19: “Do you stir me to know the causes of things and the origins of the world?” Rivinus considers this verse spurious, or at least superfluous, if it is compared with verse 118, “the ethereal radiance,” and verse 127, “the origins of the world shine.” Yet Dracontius and other Christian poets delight in repetitions of this kind, although there is some distinction between “ethereal radiance” and “the splendor of heaven”; and it is one thing for light to be the origins of the world, another for all the remaining origins of the world to receive splendor from light. Weitzius reads *lux est primordia mundi* (“light is the origins of the world”), which may be a corruption, since the others have *lux et* (“light, and”).

**Editorial notes**

124. Rivinus conjectures: “the radiance of the former age; light also gives times to the middle harvests. Light is honor for farmers.”

127. This is almost what Paulinus says in his final poem: “He called the cosmos from adornment, the world from light,” drawing on Pliny, book II, chapter 4: “What the Greeks called *kosmos* by the name of adornment, we call ‘world’ from its perfect and complete elegance.” The Greek term *κόσμον* means “adornment”; hence the association with “world” as an ordered whole.

128. The reading of the Vatican manuscript, *maculabilis*, is altogether preferable, as the sense requires, although this word is absent from the lexicons of Forcellini and others.

129. Perhaps the Vatican manuscript’s reading, in which two verses become one, is also from Dracontius’ own hand. One might also read: “Whom whatever obscure things are done do not darken, nor are darknesses hidden from him in any respect.” But the received reading stands soundly. Many explain this very idea: Basil, homily 2 on the *Hexaemeron*; Macarius, homily 16; Cyprian; Clement of Alexandria; Isidore of Pelusium; Minucius Felix; Justin Martyr; and others. See the commentary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 2, verse 105: “the watcher stands above.”

130. Rivinus suspects that one should read “nor are they hidden from him.” I change nothing: for *celo* with a dative of the person is found in good authors—Nepos, Ovid, Hirtius, and Paulinus—although some restore the accusative in Ovid and Hirtius.

131. I retain *initium*, with the first syllable long, because three short syllables come together; this regularly occurs among sound poets in similar words. Dracontius again, book II, verse 516: “Nor was it the beginning of being born.” God is called “the origin of light” by the same Dracontius in book III, verse 1. See the notes there.

132. Rivinus thinks “by which life was promised to the world” is better. Weitzius, with the Paris manuscript of Saint Victor, reads “which life was set before the world.” I retain the reading of the Vatican manuscript. The final syllable in *quanta* is lengthened before the *sp* of the following word; ignorance of this may perhaps have caused the alteration.

135. Prudentius, *Cathemerinon*, hymn 5, verse 151: “The light than which you grant nothing more precious, the light by which we see the remaining gifts.”

136. Rivinus conjectures *convexa tuetur* (“he beholds the vaulted spaces”), which could be supported by the Vatican manuscript’s reading at verse 232, “the fifth day saw.” Here *convexa coeli* (“the vaults of heaven”) means the whole heaven. *Meretur* has the same meaning as “obtains” or “receives,” just as *meruit* does at verses 140 and 150. Mar. Victor, book I of *Genesis*, verse 50: “The vaults of the lofty pole and the earth lying below: the first part of the work.” Isidore, book III of the *Etymologies*, chapter 39, explains what the vaults of heaven properly are; lexicographers should be consulted alongside him, for writers have differing opinions about this term.

137. Rivinus reads *hac* (“on this day”) instead of *ac*. The force of the verb *dantur* (“are given”) should be noted: it can mean “come into existence,” but here it should properly be understood as “are placed by God.” Moses expressly affirms that there are waters above the heavens, and sacred Scripture confirms this in many other passages. Some deny that these are real waters and interpret them either as angels or as the crystalline heaven, or understand them as rainwaters. Such opinions openly contradict sacred Scripture and are unanimously refuted by the holy Fathers and Catholic interpreters. See the note on verse 25.

138. Rivinus confidently reads: “On this day the life-giving waters are given dominion over the gathered springs,” namely, “on this day.” But this does not persuade me, and I would scarcely accept “On this day the waters hold dominion,” or “On this day the water holds dominion,” for *dominatur* seems to imply the reason already given at verse 25: that water moderates the flames of heaven.

139. The subject is elemental fire. Rivinus rightly criticizes Weitzius for explaining these “ethereal fires” in his index as the stars, since the stars were created on the third day, as is narrated later.

140. Fabricius, following Dracontius’ first edition, has *unde* (“whence”); Weitzius restored *unda* (“wave”).

141. Weitzius, with M. Wolff and Seberus, corrected the line to: “The lofty waters, suspended at the command of God the thundering maker,” so that *suspensa* refers to *unda* and there should be a full stop after *tonantis*, not a comma. Rivinus finds this correction acceptable. Barthius, book XXIII of the *Adversaria*, chapter 19, does not doubt that one should read *Dei fabre jussu*, that is, “by God’s skillful command.” But the only unquestionably correct reading is what is found in the manuscripts: “The lofty things, by God’s favor, by command,” and so forth. *Favor* is often changed to *fabor*, and generally *v* to *b* in ancient monuments.

143. Rivinus wants these words enclosed in parentheses: “Nor does water extinguish the flames, nor does fiery fire warm the ice.” I retain them. Rivinus observes that *teporat* is unusually used for “warms”; nevertheless Pliny uses the related word *teporatus* in book XXXVI, chapter 26. Forcellinus included Pliny’s word *teporatus*, but omitted the verb *teporo* entirely. In the Vatican manuscript, *reponit* (“restores,” “puts back”) is not negligible as a substitute for “removes,” “sets down,” or “causes the water to set down the ice.” Again, in the same Vatican manuscript at verse 148: *reponunt* (“they restore”).

146. The Vatican manuscript: *nec discreta* (“nor separated”); the printed editions: *non discreta* (“not separated”).

148. The Vatican manuscript: “they restore the green waters”; in the margin: “they melt.”
