**Editorial notes**

144. Weitzius, following the old editions, wrongly punctuates *ignis: aquae*, or *ignis. Aquae*. For *aquae* refers to *glaciem* (“ice”). Virgil uses *tenor* in the same sense, *Georgics* II.336: “I would not believe that, at the first growth of the world, other days had shone forth, or that the world had possessed another order.” Arnobius said *tenor rerum* (“the order of things”), Petronius *tenor sensuum* (“the order of perceptions”), Gunther *tenor veli, belli, legum* (“the order of the sail, war, and laws”). Commodianus, poem 80: “Meanwhile the heaven changes, its order altered.” Lexicographers will provide other examples.

145. Rivinus reads *licet* (“although”) instead of *non* (“not”). Either reading gives a sound sense: for the elements partly attack one another in turn, and partly do not attack one another.

146. Paulinus, final poem: “Although he joined these different things and united what was separated, and separated what was joined, which now, divided, cling together.” Mar. Victor, in the preface to *Genesis*: “Contrary things, which the skillful laziness of the human mind thinks, while they contend, possess more peace.” Fabricius has the same. Others give only: “Certain contrary things, if they contend, possess more peace.” So greatly do the editions of Christian poets vary. On this discord and concord of the elements Dracontius again writes, *Elegies*, verse 59: “Thus the powerful Creator mingled contrary elements, moist with dry, fiery with cold.” See Isidore, *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 11, to omit countless other pagan and ecclesiastical writers.

147. *Aequor ponti* (“the level of the sea”) is not a tautology: properly speaking, *aequor* is not *pontus* (“sea”), but “evenness” or “level surface.” *Caeruleum* (“blue”) is derived from color, whence *caerula* is used for the sea. See Wopkens on Sedulius, book I, verse 122, where he observes that poets often join *mare*, *pelagus*, *aequor*, *marmor*, and so forth because of their abundance of expressions.

148. From the Vatican manuscript one might conjecture *freta glauca reponit* (“it restores the green straits”), namely, the third day. Valerius Flaccus, book I, verse 652: “He spoke, and the father restores the sea and its troubled shores, and drives away the south winds.” Horace also uses *ponere freta* (“to settle the straits”) in book I, ode 3. But *liquescunt* (“dissolve”) is sound: thus the sea is called “the liquid plains.”

149. *Mare navigerum* (“the sea bearing ships”) is Lucretius, book I, verse 3. Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* III.5: “Although the appearance of this element is beautiful, whether when it whitens with rising heaps and whirlpools of waves, and the cliffs drip with snowy spray; or when, with the level surface rippling under gentler breezes, it displays a purple color beneath the gentle serenity of calm,” and so forth.

150. Rivinus reads: “The day itself sees the earth brought forth from the waves,” as at verse 136, “he beholds the vaulted spaces.” Retain *meruit* (“obtained”), as there *meretur* (“obtains”). *Actam* (“brought forth”) is better than *auctam* (“increased”): for immediately afterward the earth is said to be submerged and brought out. The waters covered the earth; when they were gathered into their proper place, the earth appeared. Ambrose, for the third day: “Great Founder of the earth, who, uncovering the world’s soil, after driving away the troubles of the water, gave the earth immovable.”

151. Rivinus reshapes the line: “The earth submerged in the poured-out deep is washed clean.” Our reading is correct.

152. Tertullian, *On the Judgment*: “By his word he was able to suspend the solid earth.” Rivinus explains *solidante globo* as “the globe having been made solid,” as one says “with the moon diminishing,” “with the year turning,” and similarly. There is nothing to prevent understanding *globo solidante* as the globe itself making the earth solid, or reading, if one prefers, “And made solid by the globe.” *Inane* for “empty space” is an elegant expression adopted by Christians from the ancients. Mar. Victor, book I of *Genesis*, verse 86: “When God, driving away the remaining waters of the abyss, opened the great void in aerial spaces.” See Barthius, book XXXV of the *Adversaria*, chapter 16, who praises Dracontius along with several others.

153. I embrace the reading of the Vatican manuscript, which is elegant: as though the earth were held by its own axis. Or read “supported by the sea”; *stant* (“stand”) takes the place of *radicibus* (“roots”) for the waters. Hilary, *Genesis*, verse 42: “And, fixed in place, founded upon the sea, it settled.” Pisides, in the *Hexaemeron*, as Weitzius notes: “You rounded the waves as the foundation of the earth, and sustain it, weighed upon a shifting support.” Others say that the sea is higher than the earth; Pererius, in his commentary on Genesis, chapter 1, verse 9, teaches that this should be rejected, together with the philosophers and astrologers.

154. Psalm 135:6: “Who established the earth upon the waters.”

155. Barthius, book XXI of the *Adversaria*, explains *materies* (“substance” or “material”) as the element of earth. Mar. Victor, book I of *Genesis*, verse 88: “Then the dry, lowest part of the world first revealed its face.” Isidore, book XIV of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1: “Properly speaking, earth is called dry in distinction from water, just as Scripture says, ‘which God called dry land.’ For dryness is the natural property of earth.” The sea is called “the flowing heart,” or is understood as “the heart of what flows,” that is, of the waters; just as the earth is the inward parts, and the sun, according to the physicists, is the heart of heaven in Macrobius, book I of the *Dream of Scipio*, chapter 20. Rivinus suspects *Arida mater iis* (“dry mother to them”), that is, to the fluids; this can scarcely yield any satisfactory sense.

156. Earth is commonly called mother, but it was not yet mother when it was seized or drawn out from the flowing heart. Pliny, book II, chapter 63: “Next comes earth, the only one among the parts of nature to which, because of its outstanding merits, we have given the title of maternal veneration… What else generates under compulsion? What else pours forth spontaneously? What perfumes and flavors, what juices? What returns what has been entrusted to it with such good faith? What nourishes us for our sake?” See Balthasar Corderius’ notes on Job 1:21, “Naked I came from my mother’s womb.” The Vatican manuscript reads *arenas* (“sands”), as Dracontius also says elsewhere. Some have denied that *arenas* occurs in the plural, but examples exist in Virgil, Ovid, Horace, Valerius Flaccus, Suetonius, and others.

> One part binds its members into clods; another swells into rock;
>
> And the mountain’s peak stands as crags; another part plunges into rivers;
>
> One part lies stretched out in a plain; another bends the shores;
>
> One part rises into hills; another bristles with rough rocks;
>
> One part stiffens into crags; another is enclosed by a deep valley,
>
> And swollen hills raise lofty ridges upon their mounds,
>
> And fit the low plains into spaces of equal extent.
>
> Some land is allotted to fields rich in sweet-flowing, abundant springs.
>
> Green grass is brought forth; every shoot rises into the air,
>
> And the ever leaf-clad olive grows green with foliage.
>
> The flourishing tree produces every kind of fruit and does not travail in birth;
>
> The laurel, the tongue’s honor, releases gifts to be bestowed on poets [reading uncertain].
>
> The vine winds in twisting clusters through oblique circles,
>
> And the vine-branch lashes the branches with its flowing tendril.

[Col. 0701A] **Textual notes**

157. The Vatican manuscript: “Into a clod, one part binds its limbs; another swells into rocks.” Victorinus: “another part touches rocky ground.”

158. Thus the Vatican manuscript in Sirmond: “The peak of the mountain rises from cliffs,” and so forth. In Victorinus: “The peak of the mountain rises from cliffs; another part joins the rivers.”

159. The Vatican manuscript: “another part bends the shores.”

160. The Vatican manuscript: “it clings to the rocks.”

161–162. The Vatican manuscript has this form. Sirmond and Victorinus: “One part grows stiff and uncultivated; another settles in a deep valley, and swollen hills raise lofty ridges upon their mounds.” Victorinus punctuates: “One part grows stiff; uncultivated, it settles.” After verse 162, “It is girded,” the Vatican manuscript places verse 149, “And the sea that bears ships.”

163. The Vatican manuscript: “it fits with equal spaces.”

164. The Vatican manuscript: “overflowing from springs.”

165. Thus Sirmond. In Victorinus, *et* (“and”) instead of *it* (“goes”). The Vatican manuscript: “Every green herb brings forth its whole offering into the air.”

167. The Vatican manuscript: “nor does it labor in birth.” The printed editions: “it does not labor in birth.”

168. The Vatican manuscript: “let the laurel leave [or bestow].”

169. Victorinus: “through the dark.” The Vatican manuscript: “let the vine go through oblique…”

170. The Vatican manuscript has this form. Sirmond: “And the vine-branch lashes the reeds of the palm with a flowing whip.” Victorinus likewise, but not *ante* (“before”) instead of *fluitante* (“flowing”).

**Editorial notes**

157. Compare Ovid, book I of the *Metamorphoses*, verse 43 and following. Rivinus observes that the earlier reading *saxea tangit* (“touches rocky things”), or *tinget* (“will touch”), was wrong, and suspects *saxea jungit* (“joins rocky things”), with *pars flumina tangit* (“another part touches rivers”) in the following verse.

158. From the Vatican manuscript one should correctly write: “And the mountain peak stands as cliff.” Rivinus preferred “the peak of the mountain rises from cliffs” to “the mountain peak rises from cliffs.” Prudentius also used “peak of the mountain” in *Cathemerinon*, hymn 7, verse 136.

161. Rivinus restored: “One part grows stiff in an uncultivated state; another settles.” So it appears in the *Errata*. The reading of the Saint Victor manuscript, with the punctuation “One part grows stiff; uncultivated, it settles,” makes the valley uncultivated and is less probable than Sirmond’s wording. But both are better than the Vatican manuscript’s reading. “To grow stiff upon crags,” as Tibullus says in book IV, poem 1, verse 156: “But hardened, it grows stiff into dense ice and snow,” namely, water.

162. After this verse the Vatican manuscript has verse 148, “And the sea that bears ships.” This placement is not entirely inappropriate, provided that one later reads *aptat* (“fits”) rather than *aptant* (“they fit”); the sense will be that the sea strikes against the mountains and is fitted into the equal spaces of the plains.

163. Later, at verse 218: “He fitted [them] to their courses,” namely, the stars.

164. *Undantis* (“overflowing”) signifies abundance and multitude, as Weitzius proves with many examples in his index. Forcellini relegated *dulcifluus* (“sweet-flowing”) to the barbarisms, but unjustly, since he acknowledges that Dracontius uses it, while he admits the verb *auroresco* (“to become golden”) among Latin words solely on Adelhelm’s authority.

165. From the reading of the Vatican manuscript one might conjecture *et flosculus* (“and a little flower”). I read *prodit* (“comes forth”) for *prodest* (“is beneficial”), but Sirmond’s reading is not objectionable. Again, at verse 169, *it vitis* (“the vine goes”), as here in Sirmond, *it surculus* (“the shoot goes”).

166. Book II, verse 221: “And the olive, which will never lack foliage, grows green with leaves.” Pliny, book XVI, chapter 19: “For some trees the leaves fall; others remain green with everlasting foliage”; and chapter 20: “The leaves of these kinds do not fall: the olive, laurel, palm, myrtle, cypress, and so forth.” Glycas, book I of the *Annals*, day 3: “Among those which always flower, some trees cast off their leaves, while others retain them perpetually. The olive and pine, for example, cast them off; for their leaves silently and almost imperceptibly succeed one another, so that they never seem to be stripped of their foliage.”

167. Barthius explained *profert* (“it produces”) as follows: “That is, without labor”; *non parturit* (“it does not labor in birth”) for the same reason, because it produces without labor, whereas *parturit* implies labor and effort. Rivinus thinks *virens* (“green”) should be corrected, on the grounds that “the tree labors in birth for seed,” from Genesis 1:11–12, and because Dracontius himself says at verse 574: “What the harvest bears in ears, what the tree bears in labor upon its branches.” But that verse already speaks of the fruit of trees after Adam was expelled from paradise, and Dracontius seems to hold that fruit came forth more easily in paradise than outside it after Adam’s sin. Mar. Victor, book II, *On Adam and Eve Expelled from Paradise*, verse 8: “Wondrous, with what a mouth the uncultivated farmers gape at such barbarous fields, which flourish neither with fruit-bearing crops nor with a varied tree.” Fabricius has this form. In the Paris edition of 1560: “Pitiable, with what a mouth… which flourish neither with a fruit-bearing trunk made diverse,” a reading based on the manuscripts. Or Dracontius may be speaking of the first day, on which fruits immediately came forth, according to Genesis 2:4 and following: “In the day when the Lord God made heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field before it arose in the earth, and every herb of the region before it germinated.” If you wish to retain *parturit*, you could, with a slight alteration, read either *profert* (“produces”) or *parturit arbor* (“the tree labors in birth”). Moses says: “A fruit-bearing tree making fruit according to its kind, whose seed is in itself upon the earth.” Saint Augustine, book V, chapter 4 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, explains this thus: “Therefore it was said causally that the earth then produced grass and a tree—that is, it received the power of producing.” Dracontius, with most of the Fathers and interpreters, asserts that grasses, trees, and ripe fruits were actually produced on the third day. *Pomum* (“fruit”) is used of every kind of fruit that comes from trees. It would be preferable to transpose these verses and read first “all fruits,” and then “and ever clothed,” or even to move this verse to after “the laurel, the tongue’s honor.”

168. A probable conjecture is that one should read: “The laurel, the tongue’s honor, rises to be given to poets,” because the meaning is clearer and Dracontius uses similar words in narrating the production of other things. In the old book’s reading, *solvit donanda* (“loosens what is to be given”) is understood with *donanda* as an accusative. Poets were crowned with laurel. Horace, book IV, ode 2, speaking of Pindar: “He must be given the Apollonian laurel.” But when Cicero said and approved in book I of *On Duties*, chapter 22, “Let arms yield to the toga, let the laurel yield to the tongue,” he meant the laurel carried by triumphants. Pliny alluded to this when speaking of Cicero in book VII, chapter 30: “Hail, first to have earned a triumph in the toga and the laurel of the tongue”; others explain this as “to have earned primacy in eloquence.”

169. Rivinus corrected *tetra* (“dark, dreadful”) to *laeta* (“joyful”), but acknowledged that *torta* (“twisted”) is better.

170. Christian Daumius wrote *motante* (“moving”) instead of *non ante* (“not before”) in the old editions; Rivinus had *nutante* (“swaying”); the manuscript codices have *fluitante* (“flowing”). But no one has yet noticed the error in *et palmae calamos* (“and the reeds of the palm”): without any doubt one should read *et palmes* (“and the vine-branch”), as it appears in the Vatican manuscript at book II, verse 220: “Again, with a budding vine-branch,” and so forth. Isidore, book XVII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 5: “The upper parts of vines and the lashes of shrubs are called *flagella* because they are shaken by the wind. The vine-branch is the soft material of the vine, which, sent out through young arms, bears fruit… The clusters are rings which bind and grasp each neighboring part, lest, stretched too far, the vine-branches be scattered by the blasts of the winds.” *Ramos* (“branches”) is even better than *calamos* (“reeds”), for the vine-branch itself is a branch of the vine, and the reference may be to the branches of trees around which the vine twines. It would not be absurd to rewrite *auras* (“breezes”) instead of *ramos* or *calamos*.

[Col. 0703A] **Textual notes**

171. The Vatican manuscript: “The vine, leafy beneath the reed, darkens the fields.”

172. The Vatican manuscript: “promising gifts of joy.” In the margin, *numera* (“count”) instead of *munera* (“gifts”).

173. The Azagrensis manuscript: “from varied fruits.”

174. The Vatican manuscript: “The one [earth] poured forth one fragrance.”

175. The Vatican manuscript: “If there are herbs, so many fragrances are mingled.”

176. The Vatican manuscript: “India was then a world, doubling spices among the herbs.”

177. The Vatican manuscript: “they brought forth beneath…”

178. The printed editions: *interea* (“meanwhile”); the Vatican manuscript: *in terra* (“on earth”).

179. The printed editions: *ambrosus geminato cespite* (“ambrosial, with doubled turf”); Victorinus: *ambrosiīs geminato cespite* (“ambrosial flowers, with doubled turf”).

181. The Vatican manuscript: “happily in all regions.”

**Editorial notes**

171. Forcellini placed *subarundinare* (“to support with a reed”) among the barbarisms and explains it as “to prop with a reed,” citing Dracontius. This passage is corrupt in the Vatican manuscript, and the readings of the others do not fully satisfy me. I conjectured: “The leafy vine stretches out shadows beneath the reed.” Virgil, *Eclogues* 7.58: “The vine begrudged the hills their leafy shadows”; and *Georgics* II.410: “Twice the shadow falls upon the vines,” namely, from the leaves. Weitzius elegantly calls the vine *ebria* (“drunk”) to mean “full,” but it could also be called drunk from its effect.

172. He calls wine “gifts of joy,” just as Bacchus is called by Virgil “the giver of joy.” Juvencus, book I, verse 133: “Do you see that the liquid of joy has now failed?” I omit the many obvious things that Weitzius assembles concerning joy derived from drinking wine.

174. *Fundere* (“to pour forth”) often occurs in the sense of producing abundantly and profusely. Here *odor* (“fragrance”) means a kind or species, or the thing itself from which a pleasant smell emanates. Horace, book II of the *Epistles*, at the end: “I shall be carried to a street selling incense and fragrances.” Tertullian, *On the Judgment*: “Sweet things, various drinks, rich and fragrant things.” I omit others. Here the earth is already called mother, whereas at verse 156 it was not yet called mother.

175. Mar. Victor, book I of *Genesis*, verse 246: “He mingles one nectar from different fragrances.”

176. What the spices are can be gathered from verses attributed to Isidore as though inscribed in his library. Under the heading “The Spice-Seller,” the author lists cinnamon, myrrh, fragrant leaf, shining cassia, balsams, frankincense, calamus, and Corycian saffron. These verses were published long ago under Saint Isidore’s name by Muratori, and for the most part, long before Muratori, by Juan Tamayo de Salazar in the *Spanish Martyrology*. They were later reprinted in an expanded form by Flórez in *Sacred Spain*, and after Flórez in the Madrid edition of Saint Isidore’s works of 1778, volume II, p. 67, appendix. In the prolegomena to Prudentius, number 242, I expressed some doubt as to whether Isidore was truly the author of these verses. Recently Eugenius de Levis published the first six verses as previously unpublished in volume I of the *Anecdota*, p. 18, attributing them to Saint Damasus as composed for the Epistles of Paul. But they were not written solely for Paul’s letters; they were written for some library, as is perfectly clear to the reader, and they are very far removed from Damasus’ age, like two other poems that Levisius falsely attributes to the same Damasus. Leyser, in his *History of Medieval Poetry*, under the fifth century, observes that Dracontius sought paradise in India, which, he says, can be set against those who regard this opinion as excessively paradoxical. Yet Malvenda himself embraced this opinion and wrote about paradise with the greatest care; Jerome, Alcimus Avitus, Anastasius of Nicaea, and Moses Bar-Cepha favor it. The author of the *Questions to Antiochus*, published under the name of Saint Athanasius, adds this reason in question 47: “For this reason all spices of the sweetest fragrance grow around the more easterly regions, or the borders of India, since they are near paradise.”

177. Rivinus suspects that *sub sole novo* (“beneath the new sun”) is corrupt and should be read *Eduxit fulgore novo* (“it brought forth with new radiance”), since the sun had not yet been created. But I think Dracontius used *sub sole novo* by anticipation, to describe the east. Thus Avitus, book I of *On the Beginning of the World*, verse 196: “There is a place reserved in the eastern axis of the world, in the hidden regions of nature, where the rising dawn, born at the sun’s rising, strikes back upon the neighboring Indians.” If any correction is needed, I would prefer *sub vere novo* (“beneath the new spring”). See verses 197 and 230: “It displays beneath the new spring.” I had conjectured that *sub flore novo* (“beneath the new flower”) was better. The “immature clusters” are the new fruits of any tree, resembling clusters of grapes; perhaps Dracontius uses *racemi* (“clusters”) for the grains and fruit of any herb from which perfumes and spices are obtained. Some aromatic trees bear a clustered fruit or seed, such as amomum, concerning which see Pliny, book XII, chapter 13; Dioscorides, book I, chapter 14; and Isidore, book XVII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 8, where it is called “clustered seed.” Although Hardouin reads *frutice myrtuoso* (“myrtle-like shrub”) in Pliny rather than *botruoso* (“clustered”), the same meaning can nevertheless be gathered from Pliny, who says: “The cluster of amomum is used; it is the fruit of the Indian wild vine.”

178. Rivinus’ conjecture is to read *in terra* (“on earth”) instead of *interea* (“meanwhile”); our manuscript confirms this.

179. Rivinus says that some have read *gemmato vertice pictus* (“painted with a gemmed crown”). Mar. Victor, book I of *Genesis*, verse 235: “Here the cinnamon-plants, animated by the power of an ambrosial gift, release their fragile stalks, breathing fragrances.” Fabricius has this form; others: “And whatever dry things, with a dry covering, now release their fragile stalks, animated by the power of an ambrosial gift, pour forth fragrant cinnamon.” To “paint the earth with flowers,” meaning to adorn, vary, or distinguish it, is found in Lucretius, Virgil, and the best authors. See Gifanius’ index to Lucretius. Turf is called “gem-studded” because the flowers themselves are like gems. Lucretius, book II, verse 319: “The herbs, gemmed with fresh dew, invite”; Manilius, book V, verse 256: “He cultivates a garden gemmed with shining flowers.”

180. Rivinus thinks Dracontius alluded to Genesis 27:27: “Behold, the smell of my son is like the smell of a field which the Lord has blessed.”

181. Rivinus reads “A garden from the mouth of God.” Someone might conjecture “a garden given in the world,” since it was not planted; or “a garden at the edge of Eden”; or “the garden of Eden, of the whole world.” The reading of the manuscripts is supported by Isaiah 51:3: “He will make her wilderness like delights, and her solitude like the garden of the Lord,” that is, paradise.

143 The vine, drunk with grapes, spreads its leafy shoots over the fields,

promising gifts of joy in its hanging clusters,

and the flowering countryside breathes the fragrance of various fruits.

The earth, one parent, does not pour forth one fragrance alone,

[175] but as many as the herbs are, so many fragrances are mingled.

Then India, first producing spices among the herbs,

[Col. 0704A] 144 brought them forth beneath the new sun and among the unripe clusters.

There is a place on earth dispersing four rivers,

painted with ambrosial flowers upon a jewel-like turf,

[180] full of fragrant herbs that never wither,

a garden in God’s world, happier than all gardens.

[Col. 0705A] [Note: [Col. 0705A]

182. In Victorius, *f. in annos*; [another reading] *est, cum*.

184. Vatican manuscript: *Arboreus hinc inde chorus vestitur amoene* (“here and there the arboreal chorus is clothed pleasantly”); printed editions: *Arboreis hinc inde comis vestitur amoenis* (“here and there it is clothed with pleasant foliage”).

185. Victorius: *f. intortis r.* (“read *intortis ramis*”). In the Vatican manuscript this verse is absent: *Frondibus*.

186. Victorius: *arbore poma* (“fruit on the tree”).

187. Victorius: *non fructus anhelis*; Sirmondus: *non solis anhelis*; Vatican manuscript: *non solis anheli*.

188. Vatican manuscript: *flatibus illic*.

190. Printed editions: *domat, non*; Vatican manuscript: *nec*.

192. Azagrius and Victorius: *sed placidi fructus*; Sirmondus: *sed placiti fructus*; Vatican manuscript: *sed placidi flatus*.

193. Victorius adds *exsurgens* (“rising”).

[Col. 0706B] 194. Sirmondus punctuates: *comas de flamine molli, / Frondibus impulsis immobilis u. v.*

196. Sirmondus so reads. In the Vatican manuscript: *F. omnis honos*, and *mutat p. p.* In Victorius: *F. hic onus omne*, and *nutant p. p.*

198. Vatican manuscript: *n. l. frondes et*.

202. Vatican manuscript: *pendet exoptatae v.*

203. Victorius: *v. pictura f.* Vatican manuscript: *Litora dependent solers pictura figuras*.]

[Note: [Col. 0705B]

184. Rivinus conjectured *amoene* instead of *amoenis*, which our manuscript also exhibits. “To be clothed with foliage” is a customary metaphor for trees; thus, at verse 166: “and the olive, always clothed with foliage, grows leafy.” In the same way the earth is said to be clothed with grass, and birds with feathers.

186. Rivinus thinks *fructus* better than *poma*, because the former is more general. At verses 167, 196, and 198 Dracontius seems to use *pomum* for any fruit of a tree; and indeed it will scarcely be possible to find a firm and clear distinction.

189. Claudian, *On the Third Consulship of Honorius*, verse 98: “and the conspiring winds come to the trumpet-call”; and *On the Gothic War*, verse 49: “or complain that the conspiring calm shines.”

190. Fabricius incorrectly printed *grandinis ictu* (“by the blow of hail”), a reading Weitzius also reproduced. In the first edition *ictus* (“blows”) was already printed, and Sirmondus restored it. *Districta* properly means “very tightly drawn,” but something else lies behind it: ice is called *districta*, like a drawn sword—or rather *destricta*, since ice also cuts. Virgil, *Eclogue* 10, verse 49: “Ah! may harsh ice not cut your tender feet.”

191. “To scourge the hail” is a very common metaphor. See Broukhusius’s note on Tibullus I.2.7, “May rain scourge you.” Weitzius calls *canescunt prata pruinis* (“the meadows grow white with frost”) a most elegant metaphor. Avitus I, verse 223: “or the fields grow white with frost as the cold thickens.” Conversely, Horace and Prudentius express grayness by speaking of the snow of the head. Rivinus observes that some have wrongly read *calescunt* or *calvescunt* (“grow hot” or “grow bald”) instead of *canescunt* (“grow white”). I do not know who these persons are, for *calescunt* is an error in Weitzius, while in his index he clearly reads *canescunt*.

192. The correct reading is *placidi flatus* (“gentle breezes”). The preceding passage has already spoken of fruits, whereas here the subject is a soft breeze and gentle winds, in contrast with storms, ice, hail, and frost. Although at verse 188 he said that the garden is shaken by no winds, this must be understood of violent winds, as the verb *quatitur* (“is shaken”) indicates, and as follows from the next verse. The phrase *nec conjuratis* (“nor by conspiring [winds]”) makes this clear.

194. *De* is superfluous, as many have already noted. In the *Vigil of Venus* we find *De favoni spiritu* (“of the spirit of Favonius”). Sirmondus’s punctuation, and that of the older editions, is not satisfactory. *De flamine molli / Frondibus impulsis* gives, as it were, the reason why the motionless shade wanders, as I shall explain in the following note.

195. The shade is motionless because there is always shade in the grove; yet it wanders because the trees’ leaves move. Perhaps Dracontius wrote *impulsis, et mobilis umbra vagatur* (“the leaves being driven, and the mobile shade wanders”).

[Col. 0706C] 196. The reading of the Saint-Victor manuscript, *Fluctuat hic onus omne* (“this whole burden fluctuates”), leads me to suspect that the Vatican manuscript’s reading, *Fluctuat omnis honos* (“all honor fluctuates”), is original. For fruit is the honor of a tree.

197. Boethius, poem 2 of book I: “Who tempers the calm hours of spring, so that he may adorn the lands with rosy flowers?” Dracontius perhaps hints that the world was created in the first spring, which he asserts more clearly at verse 230. Others teach that the world was created in autumn, and support this with many arguments.

198. The Vatican manuscript’s *frondes* (“leaves”) is not displeasing. Nevertheless, *flores* (“flowers”), evidently the flowers of the trees, seems better. Rivinus corrects the text to *Ne laedant* (“lest they harm”), that is, “lest the breezes harm [them]”; Weitzius seems to have recognized this in his index. The manuscript reading can be defended, namely, *Ver temperat, ne laedat* (“spring tempers [the air], lest it harm”), which amounts to “so that it may preserve the flowers unharmed.” Fruits are said to “cook” as they ripen. See Pliny XV.24, Seneca’s tragedies, Varro, Virgil, and Martial.

199. Weitzius explains *cicutas* as the cells of bees, or reeds like pipes in which honey is contained. I do not object strongly. But one should consider whether another interpretation can be drawn from Isidore, *Etymologies* XVII.7.61: “*Cicuta* is what is between the joints of reeds, so called because it lies hidden.” Reeds and canes are said to grow in the pools of India, from whose roots people drink the sweetest juice when it has been pressed out; hence Varro says:

“An Indian reed grows on a tree not overly large;  
its moisture is pressed from its pliant roots,  
to whose sweetness even sweet honey cannot yield.”

The first of these three verses is corrupt in the editions of Isidore that I have seen. Read: “An Indian reed grows on a tree not overly large.” In the second, it is also better to read: “Its moisture from pliant roots.”

202. He is speaking, I think, of the tree of life in the middle of paradise, from Genesis 2:9, although it can also be explained of other leaves from which medicine is prepared.

203. In the old editions Rivinus joined these verses and read them as follows: “The rest nature depicts with various figures, when the fourth day had emerged from the waves of Dawn,” so that the third day would end at verse 202 and the fourth begin at verse 203. *Depingere* (“to depict”) means “to adorn” or “to vary,” as stated above at verse 179.]

145 There is fruit throughout the year, although it knows no seasons of the year.

There the earth is always in flower beneath perpetual spring;

here and there it is clothed with arboreal foliage,

[185] a dark wall of branches is bound with interwoven leaves;

and fruit hangs from every tree,

and lies scattered throughout the meadows: it is not scorched by the rays

of the panting sun,

nor shaken by any winds,

nor does a whirlwind rage there in storms conspiring together.

[190] No drawn ice overcomes it, nor does the blow of hail

scourge it, nor do the meadows grow white with icy frost.

[Col. 0706A] There are gentle breezes there, which the softer air

146 brings forth as it rises from the garden’s shining springs.

That air moves the trees’ foliage; because of the soft breeze,

[195] the leaves being driven, the motionless shade wanders;

the whole grove fluctuates, and the hanging fruits nod.

Perpetual spring tempers the common airs,

lest it harm the flowers, and so that all the fruits may ripen.

The bees have no labor of forming cells from wax:

[200] 147 heavenly nectar-honey sweats from the tree,

and gentle cups hang from the leaves, soon to become so;

there hangs also the living medicine of desired salvation;

nature depicts the rest with various figures.

204. It follows from the next verse that the ancient manuscripts had a different reading from the one now extant. For the Vatican manuscript has *compresserat ora* (“had compressed the horizons”), which seems more correct than *compresserat astra* (“had compressed the stars”). From Victorius one may conjecture that the reading was: “The fourth day had already sent Dawn forth from the waves, and with the reddening sky—or, ‘with the ruddy day’—had compressed the horizons with its redness.” For the stars are mentioned afterward. The phrase “the fourth day of Dawn” is used just as “the first day of light.” One might also read: “The fourth day of Dawn had already sent forth its rising, and the shining sky had compressed the horizons with redness.” But since a clearer light does not emerge, let us retain Sirmondus’s reading.

205. Ambrose, hymn for the fourth day: “Who paints the shining center of the heavens with fiery brightness.”

206. The globe of the sun and moon is frequently mentioned by poets, and more than once by Dracontius. Marcellus Victor, book I of *Genesis*, verse 97: “It was commanded to gather itself into flames, and into a globe of fire—the first day of the sun.” On the sun’s life-giving fire, by which all things are warmed, see verse 24 and following, and the *Elegy*, verses 81 and following.

207. Rivinus thinks this verse belongs to Eugenius of Toledo, or to someone else, and, to make the sense work, reads *perfundit* (“pours over”) instead of *perfundi* (“to be poured over”), following Sirmondus and Weitzius in the index. Yet Weitzius had also printed *perfundit* in the text. Fabricius, following the first edition, has *perfundi*. That this verse is earlier than Eugenius is sufficiently clear from the Saint-Victor and Vatican manuscripts. Nor are repetitions of this kind alien to Dracontius’s style, as must often be said: “fire of salvation,” “saving flame,” “life-giving vapor.” To flood the world with light is a beautiful metaphor; see Gifanius’s index to Lucretius under *fundo*. Victorius’s *salutari* (“saving”) is not bad.

208. Ovid, Statius, and Martial use *salutifer* (“life-giving”); Ausonius and Prudentius use *salutiger*. The metaphor “the elements smile” is also graceful; see the same Gifanius under *rideo*. Rivinus suspects *elementa tepore* (“the elements with warmth”), but approves *vapore* (“with vapor”) in place of *calore* (“with heat”). Dracontius, as often do others, frequently uses *vapor* for heat.

209. Rivinus conjectures *Cujus ab igne suam* (“from whose fire its own”), but *suam* scarcely fits here. Either another reading must be sought, or *suo* (“its own”) retained as an uncommon pleonasm. Perhaps *pio* (“benevolent”) should be read instead of *suo*, as at verse 224: “who with benevolent fire warms heaven, sea, stars, and lands.”

210. Rivinus would prefer: *Nigra tenebrosae corrumpere tempora noctis* (“to corrupt the black hours of the dark night”).

211. Rivinus rejects *minitante quiete* (“with rest threatening”) in Weitzius, and *comitante quiete* (“with rest accompanying”) in Sirmondus. He reads and punctuates: “And to bring forth the warm day, with bright rest inviting,” and so forth. Fabricius printed—and Weitzius with Fabricius—“and to bring forth the warm day, with rest threatening.” Sirmondus and the Vatican manuscript agree, differing only between *trepidum* and *trepidam*. But what is a “trembling day”? I think it means doubtful and uncertain, since it is not a true day, when the moon itself is only an image of the sun. *Trepidum* is known to have this meaning, as in “in troubled circumstances” and other familiar expressions.

212. The ancients generally said *somnifer* (“sleep-bringing”), not *somniger* (“sleep-bearing”), as Ovid, Pliny, and Lucan do. Although an example is not found among the older writers, *somniger* should not be rejected in Dracontius, unless one prefers to follow the Saint-Victor manuscript. The Vatican manuscript’s error *somnigeris* indicates this reading.

[Col. 0708C] 213. Weitzius, as usual, praises several authors who discuss the moon, but does not explain what Dracontius means here, as Rivinus observes. Rivinus says that “the greater and lesser number” perhaps means a greater and lesser number of days. With the Vatican manuscript we read *crescente* (“increasing”) instead of *majore* (“greater”). Pliny XXXVII.9.63: “Selenitis … containing an image of the moon, reproduces it day by day in increasing and decreasing numbers.” Certainly on the first day the moon is small and beginning, while on the fifteenth day it is full; but it then decreases again in the same order until the final day. Yet this does not sufficiently, or properly, explain Dracontius’s verse, for the moon is larger on the fifteenth day than on the first. The moon is therefore called “brief with increasing number,” considered in the final days and compared with the fifteenth day, or approximately so.

214. Prudentius, *Hymns* 5, verse 145: “You might believe that above, the star-bearing expanse stands adorned with twin Bears.”

215. Virgil, *Georgics* I.137: “Then the sailor assigned numbers and names to the stars.” Rivinus corrects *jussit* (“commanded”) to *cessit* (“yielded”). *Jussit* is better. Statius, *Thebaid* VII.32: “It will be my right; I shall look upon the lands and command peace for all.” Tacitus, *Annals* IV.72: “Drusus had ordered tribute to be paid to them.”

217. Rivinus prefers *jubare induit* (“clothed with radiance”). But *induere* is more customary with an accusative; just as *in loca contulit* is understood with *stellis*, so here *in jubar induit* is to be understood.

218. Book III, verse 5: “giving names to the stars and fitting the star to its courses.” Rivinus conjectures *auxit* (“increased”) instead of *addit* (“adds”).

219. Book III, verse 4: “the number of the countless stars, which no one fails to know.” Fabricius followed the punctuation of the first edition and Victorius, which Seberus and Weitzius had corrected before Sirmondus.

220. Fabricius printed: “They abandon whatever day and light oppress them.” Weitzius: “They abandon on whatever day, but are pressed by light.” I retain the Vatican manuscript’s reading, so that *quaecunque* refers to the stars—namely, “any stars.” See verse 667.]

The fourth day had already sent Dawn forth from the waves,

[205] and, with the sky glowing red, had compressed the stars in its redness.

Soon he commands the sun’s globe to radiate with saving fire:

the saving flame floods the world with light,

148 and all the elements smile with life-giving vapor,

by his own fire he commands the moon to follow as second,

[210] to corrupt the black hours of the dark night,

and to bring forth the trembling day with rest accompanying it.

She illuminates the heavens with her white, sleep-bringing horns,

[Col. 0708A] being small as her number increases, but full as it decreases.

The fiery adornment of heaven shone through the stars:

[215] 149 he assigned duties, numbers, and names even to the stars,

distributed their times, assigned their places, drove them by fires,

fixed them within boundaries, clothed them with radiance, and revolved them upon the axis,

fitted them to their courses, and added them to the regions of heaven.

The fiery stars of the countless host do not abandon heaven

[220] on any day, although they are pressed by light.

223. Vatican manuscript: *s. quae mundum*.

229. Vatican manuscript: *cum lunae et sidera cuncto / Ostentans s.*

221. *Fusi* (“poured forth”) is preferable to *phoebi*. The radiant crown is understood here as the sun. Ennius, quoted by Cicero, *On the Orator* III.40: “Seize with your eyes the final radiated light.” The ancients commonly imagined the sun’s crown, or head, adorned with rays. I would read more clearly: *fusa*, that is, “light poured forth from the radiant crown of immense light.” Book III, verse 1: “of eternal light, the moon’s light, the source of light.”

223. He seems to be assigning a reason why the stars are hidden beneath the sun. But what is this reason? Or, if no reason is offered here apart from the sun’s immense light, what does he mean by “by which a measure shows the world to be smaller”? [Col. 0709C] The Vatican manuscript has *quae* (“which”) instead of *quo* (“by which”), but the same difficulty remains. I would therefore read: “The stars, which he shows to be smaller than the world.” Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* I.314, of the sun: “and what no one denies to be smaller than the world and sky.” For the expanse is larger than the one who traverses it.

If you prefer to read it this way, write *Non mirum* (“it is not surprising”) above, or understand *nec* as *non*, as in Sedulius’s preface to the *Paschal Poem*: “whose manifold riches are not counted.” On this meaning of the adverb *nec* for *non*, see Wopkens there. If the common reading is retained, understand *mundum* as referring only to the earth, not to the totality of things; for pagan writers too used *mundus* for the earth and its mortal inhabitants, as does Dracontius at verse 705 of this book. If this is intended as the explanation, it is not surprising that the stars should be hidden beneath the sun, since the sun is larger than the earth. Another explanation, drawn from astronomy, is that the stars are hidden beneath the blazing sun all the more because the sun appears smaller to our sight: namely, the nearer the sun’s diameter approaches the zenith, the more it seems to diminish to us.

224. Compare verse 24 and following. It is uncertain whether Dracontius believes that even the stars called fixed receive their light from the sun, which this verse suggests, or whether he means only the planets. This matter was once very obscure and is not altogether clear even now; we can scarcely assert that no argument has been presented by which it might be maintained that the fixed stars borrow their own light from the sun.

225. The Vatican manuscript’s reading may perhaps be better: *Concepta virtute Dei, quem* (“conceived by the power of God, whom”), or one might read *Conceptus virtute Dei, quem* (“conceived by the power of God, whom”). Sirmondus understands not merely the sun itself to be conceived, but recognizes it as the one sustained by the sphere, not God. But how can the sun be called “the lord thundering through all things”? One might conjecture: “Conceived by the power of God, whom the sphere of the poles sustains, and it feels the lord moving through the signs.” It is preferable, however, to retain the Vatican manuscript’s reading.

227. *Cujus* refers to God. Hence *ministrant* (“serve”) is more correct than *ministrat* (“serves”), following the Vatican manuscript and Sirmondus. Nor is Sirmondus’s punctuation satisfactory: “it serves; everything acts at command, the whole labors under the law.” The meaning is that all things which serve or minister come from God’s command. Propertius II.18: “See how now the sun, now the moon, serves in heaven.”

228. I would prefer *agit cursum* (“pursues its course”), a phrase found in Pliny V.24. Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* I.334, of the sun: “subject under one prescribed law to its duties.”

229. Book II, verse 25: “to serve faithfully, with its own soldiery serving”; see the note there.

230. Dracontius hints at the opinion of certain ancient writers who asserted that the stars shine with light received from the sun; on this, see Isidore, chapter 24 of *On the Nature of Things*. See also verse 224. One may also explain it thus: “when God displays the moon and all the stars,” since at verses 216 and 217 fires and radiance of their own are granted to the stars.

231. *Tiro* (“new recruit”) is also used adjectivally, as in *tiro exercitus* (“a newly enlisted soldier of the army”) and *tiro miles* (“a novice soldier”). *Tiro* is opposed to *veteranus* (“veteran”), which is appropriate to soldiers but is also applied to other old or long-established things.

232. Victorius’s punctuation is inept. Whether one reads *vidit* (“he saw”) or *addit* (“he adds”) makes no difference. See verse 136.

233. Perhaps read *nervisque ligantur* (“and are bound with sinews”). Book III, verse 614: “now the limbs are bound with sinews.”

235. *Gemmantur* (“are jeweled”) should probably be written instead of *geminantur* (“are doubled”), although the latter is not wholly to be dismissed, since the eyes are twin. At verse 315 both ideas are expressed: “the eyes’ lights, jeweled in a twin orb, shine.” See book III, verse 618. The eyes *gemmant* (“jewel”) because they shine like gems; they are *gemmantur* (“are jeweled”) when they become gem-like. Although the verb is generally used actively, the participle *gemmatus* shows that it can also be used passively as *gemmari*. Rivinus conjectures *palatum* (“palate”) instead of *gelato* (“frozen”), but I cannot agree. The eyes are jeweled with waters when the moisture freezes or contracts like frost. Marcellus Victor, book III of *Genesis*: “the green plant, when it had hardened its golden ears, into grain through the sun’s heat, with milk frozen.” Other editions give verse 66 differently: “the plant for itself, and the stalks into grain, with milk frozen.”

236. The older editions punctuate: *pisces / Incedunt*, and so forth. Sirmondus punctuates: *pisces. / Luserunt*, and so forth, perhaps so that *luserunt* refers to the animals of verse 232 and *factura* at verse 239 to those same animals. Verse 239 could be placed immediately after verse 232, and the difficulty would disappear. But even if there is no comma or period after *pisces*, so that the fish themselves are the ones that “played,” *factura* must nevertheless refer to the animals, or to the fish, which are animals of the deep.

237. *Luserunt* (“played”) is more harmonious than *incedunt* (“move”). Book II, verse 158: “let the fish play upon the waters.” Terence, *Adelphoe* III.3.23: “let that enormous conger play in the water.” Virgil, Statius, and others call the sea *caerula* (“the blue sea”).]

Poured forth from the radiant crown of immense light.

Nor is it surprising if the stars lie hidden beneath the bright sun,

by which a measure shows the world to be smaller,

150 who warms heaven, sea, stars, and lands with benevolent fire—

sustains and perceives as lord thundering through all things,

from whose command come all things that serve;

[Col. 0710A] everything acts at command, the whole labors under the law,

itself a soldier of God, when it displays the moon and all the stars

[230] beneath the new spring, beneath the first season,

prepared as a new recruit for enduring ages.

The fifth day saw all the animals of the deep.

151 The waters are solidified into a body, and sinews are bound together.

The fluid became muscle, the wave hardens into bones,

[235] and the eyes are jeweled with waters, their moisture frozen;

and as many as the waves are, so many perhaps in the sea

the fish played through the vast blue waters by swimming,

239. Victorius: *per cuncta*.

[Col. 0711B] 242. This verse appears thus in the Vatican and Saint-Victor manuscripts. It is entirely absent from Sirmondus.

247. Vatican manuscript: *pectora fulgor*.

238. Verse 578: “with the murmur by which the blowing winds wrinkle the wandering waters.” Valerius Flaccus I.311: “Tithonia, wrinkling the sea for the new Phoebus.” Here *crispante* is used absolutely, like *luna minuente* (“as the moon wanes”), and *se* may be understood. Persius, *Satires* 3.87: “he redoubles his trembling laughter with wrinkling nostrils.” Pliny the Elder uses the expression more than once. Rivinus would prefer *proflabant naribus* (“they blew forth from their nostrils”), which I find even more attractive.

[Col. 0711C] 239. *Terrigenae* (“earth-born”) are human beings made from the mud of the earth. Lucretius calls the first humans *terrigenae*, book V, verse 1425: “For cold tormented the earth-born naked, without skins.” Others use the term in the same way. See the note on verses 115 and 236.

240. Marcellus Victor I.126: “Hence the birds too drew their gentle strength,” which concludes the description of birds: “Therefore one substance belongs to birds and fish alike.” But this verse, cited by Fabricius, is absent from other editions. I pass over Basil, Ambrose, and others.

242. Since this verse appears in the Saint-Victor and Vatican manuscripts but is absent from Sirmondus and apparently from Azagrius, one may conclude that it was omitted by Eugenius of Toledo.

243. Note the Grecism in *collaudant meruisse creari* (“they praise [God] for having deserved to be created”), instead of *quod meruerint creari* (“because they deserved to be created”). Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* V.12 and following, treats at length the creation and kinds of birds. Rivinus reports the opinion of some that *alaudae* (“larks”) derives from praise of the Lord. Others more plausibly say that the word is Gallic.

245. Saffron-colored and golden differ little from one another, but they do differ to some extent.

246. Rivinus conjectures *stellantur* (“are starred”) instead of *solidantur* (“are made firm”), and notes that Barthius reads *hyalis* (“glassy [stones]”) instead of *aliis* (“others”). I reject both conjectures. *Solidantur* also occurs at verse 233; since *his* and *has* precede, *aliis* (“others”) is not bad, although I would more willingly read *alis* (“wings”). It remains only to explain what the *ocelli* (“little eyes”) are, which some interpret as the various colors of the feathers. But, in my view, *ocelli* here are the roots of the feathers, or the shafts into which the feathers are inserted. Thus in trees “eyes” are knots from which leaves emerge, as Isidore explains, *Etymologies* XVII.6.15. Likewise, in the roots of reeds there is an eye, also called a bulb and called an *ocellus* by Pliny, XXI.4. The Vatican manuscript’s reading raises the question whether one should read: *has aureus ornat Galbanus, ast aliis pennae solidantur ocellis* (“golden Galbanus adorns these, while on others the feathers are made firm with little eyes”). *Galbanum* and *galbanus* denoted a more refined garment of green, blue-gray, yellow, and golden-yellow color, and sometimes golden, as in Vopiscus, *Aurelian* 34, where the emperor’s tunic is called *galbana*. See Salmasius on this passage and on Lampridius, *Alexander Severus* 41, although he insists that *galbinum* should be read. He also notes that *galbea*, *galbina*, and *galbula* designate a kind of green bird. If one reads *has aureus ornat Galbanus*, Rivinus’s conjecture becomes more suitable: *ast aliis pennae stellantur ocellis* (“while on others the feathers are starred with little eyes”), or *variantur ocellis* (“are varied with little eyes”).

248. *Decorat* with a lengthened medial syllable is rare. Silius XII.743: “they cry out to Tarpeian Jupiter and adorn his shrines,” where many read *coronant* (“crown”), perhaps because *decorant* ordinarily has a short medial syllable. There is also an inscription of uncertain date, volume I of Muratorius’s *Inscriptions*, page 54, no. 4, where the syllable is lengthened: “and with his spoils I adorn you yourself and the temple.” Dracontius’s authority is certain, and his reading is confirmed no less by Silius than by the Muratorian inscription. The reason also supports it: from *decus, decoris* comes *decoro, decoras* with the penultimate syllable shortened, whereas from *decor, decoris* the same syllable is lengthened. Martial, book XIV, final epigram, calls cocks “crested axes of light”; Ovid, *Fasti* I.455, calls the bird *cristatus* (“crested”); and Pliny XI.37 speaks of the crests on birds’ heads as points.

250. Tertullian, *On the Pallium* I.3, says of the peacock: “Although the peacock too is a garment of feathers … multicolored, various-colored, changing-colored,” and so forth. See Cerda’s notes on this passage. Pliny and others call birds of different colors *discolores* (“variegated”). In another sense *discolor* means “of a different color,” or “differing in color,” as in Ovid, *Tristia* V.16.8: “let the white one, differing in color, be assigned to my fates.”

252. He repeats this at verse 264, as is his custom, using *rudibus pennis* (“with new feathers”) for “new” or “recent.” *Subtexere* means “to cover,” and Statius and others speak of birds as “covering the air with feathers.”

253. On the third day the trees and herbs had been brought forth with their branches, leaves, and flowers. But since birds are mentioned here, that account is repeated, as though on the day when the birds were created leaves and flowers had emerged in greater abundance for their use.

254. *Evomit* (“vomits forth”), like *undare* (“to overflow”) and similar expressions, signifies abundance. The Vatican manuscript’s reading is plausible, or from it one might read: *et spicas acuit seges omnis aristis* (“and every crop sharpens its ears with awns”). Compare book III, verse 25: “Thus the crop, nourished, standing, arms its stalks with awns.” On the verb *spicare* (“to produce ears”), see elsewhere.

255. Such metaphors are frequent in Dracontius: “clothed with foliage,” “with feathers,” and so forth. Book III, verse 24: “Thus the bird is clothed with feathers, thus the herbs with leaves.” See verse 166 of book I: “and the olive, always clothed with foliage.” Virgil XII.475: “gathering small fodder and food for the chattering nests,” which Dracontius imitates.

256. Just as nests are “chattering,” so the forest is called “garrulous” when it sings. *Decanto* means “to recite” and “to repeat what has been dictated by another.” Here, however, it may simply mean “to sing.” Although with a slight change one could write *et varia decantat garrula voce* (“and the garrulous [forest] sings variously with its voice”), the more elegant reading is *et varias decantat garrula voces* (“and the garrulous [forest] sings various voices”), like *vivo vitam infelicem* (“I live an unhappy life”) and similar expressions.]

And, with the sea rippling, they blew through the waters with their nostrils,

a creation destined, after all else, to provide food for the earth-born creatures yet to be created.

shaking the air with wings in a rattling flight.

They pour forth varied voices in gentle melody,

and, I think, praise the Lord for having deserved to be created.

These shine with snowy whiteness; purple clothes those;

[245] for these the saffron color of the feather exists; golden adorns those;

on others the feathers are made firm with whitish little eyes,

and hyacinth appears, gleaming around necks and breasts.

with a pattern running through countless birds;

and with new feathers they cover the delicate air.

The day itself vomits forth leaves on the branches and herbs with flowers,

and every crop sharpens its ears with awns.

154 and the garrulous forest sings various voices,
