257. Rivinus, following the older editions, defends *Cum vacuanda volat* (“when it flies through the empty [air]”), and says that Sirmondus substituted the obvious error *vagabunda* (“wandering”) for *vacuanda*, since in *vagabunda*, derived from *vagari* (“to wander”), the second syllable is long. He explains *vacuanda volat* as “it flies through the void.” This is obscure, and Dracontius would more likely have said *Cum per inane volat* (“when it flies through the void”). Nor can examples easily be produced to establish that the second syllable of *vagabunda* must necessarily be shortened. The Vatican manuscript’s *natabunda* (“swimming”) is not to be dismissed. Although *natabunda* is a new word, it can be defended by analogy and would be elegantly applied to birds, which also share something with the waters from which they originated, cutting the air with their wings like swimming fish. If one wishes to alter the reading, one might write *Cum vagat, atque volat* (“when it wanders and flies”), from *vago, vagas*, a verb used by many. It is unnecessary to say anything about birds’ applause while they fly. Above, verse 241: “shaking the air with wings in a rattling flight.”

258. *Insidens* with a lengthened medial syllable comes from *insido*, a verb widely used, especially by poets, in place of *insideo* (“to sit upon”). Perhaps one should read: “It sits upon the flowers, moving in the wind with the foliage.”

259. It is fixed to the branches, as in book II, verse 261: “it hung upon the necks.”

260. Rivinus says that *nemus* (“grove”) is an extremely bad reading for *genus* (“race”). But since all the manuscripts have *nemus*, I would not easily change it to *genus*: first, because the passage seems properly to concern the grove, which flourishes for the use of the birds’ offspring; and second, because even if one understands the birds to be in a “feathered race,” one can certainly explain this through metonymy, in which the container is used for the contained. Much the same occurs at verse 256, where the forest sings various garrulous voices.

261. Notice the oxymoron *molli durescunt* (“they grow hard through softness”), of the sort frequently found in Dracontius. Eggs are warmed so that the young may be formed. Ovid, *Fasti* I.443: “you who make nests, you who warm eggs with feathers.” The reference is to this warmth, which is called “soft” because it occurs in a soft egg and produces a soft egg.

262. There is no doubt that the Vatican manuscript’s reading is correct and the others false. The eggs themselves, which grow hard, are feathered in their limbs, animated, breathe, burst, and, once broken, make a sound. Columella VIII.5: “Let the moon increase during the days in which the eggs are animated and formed into the likeness of birds.” The verb *membrare* (“to form into limbs”) will be mentioned again at verse 336: “it is formed into limbs.” *Penno, pennas* (“to provide with feathers”) is a new verb, but *pennatus* (“feathered”) is in common use. Cassiodorus uses *pennesco* in book I, letter 38: “until, gradually withdrawing from soft down, they become feathered in mature age.” *Pennantur* means what Columella calls “being formed into the likeness of birds,” or “being clothed with feathers.”

263. *Confracta sonant* (“once broken, they sound”) means “they are broken with a sound.”

264. Poets and other writers commonly say that birds are *librari in aere* or *in aera* (“balanced in the air” or “into the air”).

[Col. 0714C] 265. *Elementa coacta* means “elements joined together” and “elements compelled,” so that the verb *coacta* has two meanings.

266. *Vel* (“or”) is used for *et* (“and”), as in Virgil, “by piety or by arms”; I omit Livy and other early writers, since authors of the later age overused this manner of speaking. Water and fire agree in producing the offspring of birds, both because birds derive their origin from the waters and their young are produced in warm eggs, and because everything consists chiefly of water and fire, as was said at verses 24 and 25; birds are animated from the egg’s moisture and heat. Weitzius, following the first edition, reads *faecibus eductis* (“drawn forth from dregs”) and explains it in his index as “to draw forth the dregs of the elements.” Rivinus rightly rejects this.

269. He who reads *intactis* (“untouched”) will not err, since the manuscripts vary. Pliny XVIII.25: “the meadows grow old.” Ovid and others likewise speak of the old age of fields and herbs.

270. *Jumenta* (“beasts of burden”) is a species used for the genus.

273. The weapons of wild beasts are horns, claws, teeth. Marcellus Victor, book I of *Genesis*, verse 353: “and armed them with hand, horn, foot, tooth, poison, and other things.” I would read *alis* (“with wings”), although the various editions report *aliis* (“with other things”).]

### Variant-register glosses: Col. 0705A–0713A

- **Col. 0705A, 182–203.** Vict.’s *f. in annos est, cum*, *f. intortis r.*, and Vat.’s *F. omnis honos, et mutat p. p.*, *n. l. frondes et*, *pendet exoptatae v.* are inherited abbreviated readings: their abbreviations are not expanded beyond the recoverable surrounding sense. Vat. reads *Arboreus hinc inde chorus vestitur amoene* (“a tree-like chorus is clothed beautifully on every side”), while printed texts have *Arboreis hinc inde comis vestitur amoenis* (“it is clothed on every side with pleasant tree foliage”). Vict. has *arbore poma* (“fruits of the tree”). At 187 Vict. has *non fructus anhelis* (“not fruits with parching [heat]”), Sirm. *non solis anhelis* (“not by the sun’s scorching breaths”), and Vat. *non solis anheli* (“not by the scorching sun”). Vat. has *flatibus illic* (“there by winds”). At 190 printed texts have *domat, non* while Vat. has *nec* (“nor”). At 192 Azagr./Vict. read *sed placidi fructus* (“but gentle fruits”), Sirm. *sed placiti fructus* (“but pleasing fruits”), and Vat. *sed placidi flatus* (“but gentle breezes”), preferred by the commentary. Vict. has *addidit exsurgens* (“rising, he added”).
- **Col. 0707A, 204–220.** Vict. has the abbreviated *Aurorae i. q. d. permanserat u.*; Vat. omits the verse. Vat. gives *Et r. die c. ora r.* and *c. salutifera*, preserved as inherited abbreviations. Vict./Sirm. read *trepidam* (“trembling,” feminine) against Vat.’s *trepidum* (“trembling,” neuter), and Vict. *minante q.* remains abbreviated. Vict. has *c. somniferis* (“with sleep-bringing [rays]”); Vat. *c. somnigerunt collustrans c.* remains damaged/abbreviated. At 213 Vat.’s reading is retained against *Quae numero est majore brevis, et plena minore*: “small as her number increases, full as it decreases.” At 215 Sirm. reads *officia stellis* (“duties/services to the stars”), while Vict./Vat. have *officia et stellis* (“duties and to the stars”). Vat. has *curribus aptavit* (“fitted to chariots”); Vict.’s punctuation is retained. At 220 Vat./Sirm. read *destituunt quocunque die, sed* (“they fail/leave off on whatever day, but…”); Vict. has *destituunt, quocunque dies et l.* with the final abbreviation unexpanded.
- **Col. 0709A, 221–237.** Vat. has *vertice fusi* (“poured from the summit/crown”), others *v. phoebi* (“of Phoebus”); *fusi* is preferred. Other Vat. forms include *nec murum si*, *s. quae mundum*, *concepta v.* (“conceived power”), *cum lunae et sidera cuncto Ostentans s.*, *solidantur que n.*, *masculus humor* (“male moisture”), *f. tot forsitan aequore*, and *notato* with marginal *natatu* (“by swimming”); abbreviations remain marked as inherited. Vict. gives *quaecunque ministrant, Omnia: jussus agit totum, sub lege laborant* (“whatever things minister—all do what is commanded; they labour under law”), while Vat./Sirm. have the singular *ministrat*.
- **Col. 0711A, 238–254.** Vict. reads *f. perlabant n.* and *per cuncta* (“through all things”); Vat./Vict. preserve line 242 while Sirm. omits it. Vat. has *Est croceos…has aureus ornat…* (a damaged colour-description), *pectora fulgor* (“a breast’s brilliance”), *E studiis his pluma color*, *pluma per* against others’ *multa per*, *sexta dies f.*, and *et spicans a.*; these incomplete forms are retained without invented expansion. At 246 Barthius’s *hyalis* means “glassy [stones/ocelli]” against *aliis* (“others”).
- **Col. 0713A, 257–274.** Vat. has *Cum natabunda volat nec mox q'plausibus ales* (“when the swimming-like bird flies…”; damaged abbreviation retained); Vict. *Cum vacuanda v. c. p. a.*. Vat. has *tenacibus erret*, *P. venerare n. v. unget i. u.*, *molli curescunt o.*, *aera plumis* (“air with feathers”), *faecibus eductis* (“with dregs drawn out”), *parvula mundus erat, sed*, *Affuit intactus*, and abbreviated *n. parit, gignitque a.*. Vat.’s preferred 262 reads *Pennantur tunc membra globis, animantur, anhelant* (“then limbs are feathered with globes; they are animated and breathe”); Vict. differs. At 274 Vat. has *buccula*; Azagr. *vaccula* (“little cow”) for *bucula*; Vict.’s damaged *vagus…vincula taurus* is retained as such.

274. A little after verse 285: “Wandering among the meadows.” *Elegies*, verse 37: “He wandered aimlessly through the meadows.” Weitzius follows the first edition: “the wandering bull follows its own bonds,” and interprets this as referring to erotic bonds. Rivinus says that Sirmond’s reading, “the heifer follows wandering bulls,” appears reversed: it is not the heifer that follows the bulls, but the bull that follows the heifers. Nevertheless, he does not dislike Sirmond’s wording, since in the preceding line Dracontius had mentioned young bulls. The Vatican reading seems somewhat more elegant. It may be understood that the heifer follows the bull as leader and father of the herd, or even for the sake of love. For the heifer is a symbol of sexual immorality; accordingly, when the prophet Hosea had compared Israel to a prostitute, he says at chapter 2, verse 5: “For she said, ‘I shall go after my lovers, who give me my bread,’ etc.”; and again, at chapter 10, verse 11, he compares Ephraim to a heifer: “Ephraim is a heifer trained to love threshing,” as Roa Singius explains, book 3, chapter 13, where he adduces further material on the same subject. The word Dracontius uses supports this explanation; for the ancients called women who followed men for love’s sake *secutuleiae*, from the verb *sequi* (“to follow”), which they frequently used in this sense, as did Virgil, Propertius, Valerius Flaccus, Sabinus, and others. Ovid, *Heroides*, epistle 16, “Paris,” verse 323: “If you are ashamed and fear that you may seem to have followed me,” etc. Dracontius perhaps had Horace before his eyes, who, after comparing Lalage to a heifer in book 2, ode 5, adds: “Soon she will follow you . . . soon Lalage will assail her husband with bold brow.” Add Cato, *Dirae*: “Heifer,” etc.]

As the wandering bird flies, beating its wings,

sitting among the leaves, it moves with the leaf in the wind,

fixed to the branches with its tenacious claws,

clinging fast.

[260] The heat urges the feathered grove to bring forth springtime

for the uses of its offspring, and the eggs harden

in gentle warmth:

the members are feathered, enclosed in globes, are quickened,

and breathe;

155 they burst open, sound when broken,

nourished, they attempt flight,

and are balanced in the air on untried wings.

[265] But although the elements, being joined together,

[Col. 0714A] are at variance among themselves,

water or fire agrees in bringing forth the offspring.

Water creates birds; flame produces birds.

The mountain’s meadows were their food,

but there was no one to graze upon the grasses.

The untouched grasses would have grown old among their flowers,

[270] unless the earth had provided cattle to be pastured

through the fields.

The sixth day of Phoebus had advanced with radiant sunrise,

when parent Nature brings forth living creatures for the earth.

Young bulls burst forth, armed upon their horned brows,

156 and through the meadows the heifer follows her wandering bull.

[275] [Col. 0715A]

[Note: [Col. 0715A]

276. Vatican manuscript E: “bursts forth from the horses, a source of war.”

278. Victorinus: “about to suffer the treachery of hardships.”

280. Vatican manuscript: “death with a sharpened tooth.” Vatican manuscript: “threatening”; other copies: “threatens.”

281. Vatican manuscript: “through the crowds.”

282. Thus the Vatican manuscript, but it writes *marsyla*. Sirmond and Victorinus: “And fierce with its jaw rages against the hard shoulders.” Thus the Azagrensis manuscript, but it has *destituit* in place of *desaevit*.

[Col. 0716A] 283. Thus the Vatican manuscript; in the others: “Boldly contending, seeking battles.”

284. Vatican manuscript: “the serpent is brought forth, so that it may be.”

285. This line is absent from the Vatican manuscript.

286. Vatican manuscript: “the beast presses forward, having the appearance of a mountain; the mass of the beast is extended.” Victorinus punctuates: “Having the appearance of a mountain, the beast advances; with its bulk the serpent is brought forth.”

[Col. 0716B] 287. Vatican manuscript: “the venom is shaken beneath its tooth.”

288. Victorinus: “it drags its scales.”]

[Note: [Col. 0715B]

275. Ovid, book 3 of the *Tristia*, elegy 11, verse 11: “As the fleeing stag, caught by hungry bears.” Weitzius explains *palmata cornua* (“palm-shaped horns”) in his index as the conspicuous, upright horns with which stags are adorned, “like victors with a palm.” The true interpretation is sought in Pliny, book 11, chapter 37, section 45: “Nowhere else is Nature’s playfulness greater. She has played with the weapons of animals. She spread these into branches, as in stags . . . She formed those of others into palms and sent out fingers from them; hence they are called *platycerotes*.” Capitolinus mentions palmated stags near the end of chapter 3 of his *Gordianus*. Dracontius again speaks of *palmata cornua* at verse 640. Aldrovandus depicts the palmated horns of a stag in book 1, chapter 28, of *On Cloven-Hoofed Quadrupeds*.

276. Just as at verse 273 *erumpunt* (“burst forth”) is used of young bulls, so here *prorumpunt* (“break forth”) is used of horses; in both places the creation of animals that move and rush forward with force and impetus is signified. Because of its use in war, the horse was dedicated to Mars and is called warlike by Virgil, Valerius Flaccus, and others.

277. *Impia* (“impious”) is used for “savage,” just as *pius* is used for “gentle.” The earth is called impious because the lions it produces are impious.

278. Dracontius often uses *simplex* and *simplicitas* for “harmless” and “harmlessness.” Weitzius, following the first edition—or rather Fabricius—correctly printed *fraudem passura laborum* (“about to suffer the treachery of hardships”), but in his index he correctly printed *passura luporum* (“about to suffer the wolves’ attack”). Rivinus neither corrected the error nor noticed in Sirmond the true reading *luporum*. Just as sheep are gentle and constitute a guileless kind, so wolves are commonly said to lie in wait for the sheepfold.

279. Ovid: “Thus does the doe flee; the lions fight by their courage.” Virgil, *Eclogue* 8, verse 28: “When timid does will come with the dogs to the drinking bowls”; and *Georgics* 3, verse 539: “Timid does and fleeing stags.” Thus does are usually called unwarlike and fearful, for they derive their name from a Greek word signifying fear. Note also the epithet *raucos* (“hoarse”) applied to the Molossian hounds, which Martial calls barkers in book 12, epigram 1, and the word *discurrens* (“running about,” running here and there), which suits creatures in a state of panic extremely well. The construction itself is figurative, standing for “the doe runs about in fear.”

280. Rivinus, along with the older editions, prefers *mortem limato dente* (“death with a sharpened tooth”). Sirmond and the Vatican manuscript have *mortes lunato dente* (“deaths with a crescent-shaped tooth”). “Sharpened” is rightly said, because boars sharpen their teeth, as Virgil, Horace, Seneca, and others say. Yet *lunato* (“crescent-shaped”) is also good, meaning “like the moon,” whose shape the boar’s teeth resemble. The author of the poem *On the Praises of Hercules*, included among Claudian’s works, writes: “The untamed boar reigned, terrible in its solitary body, and with crescent-shaped teeth it scattered the ash trees.” Statius likewise says of the boar, book 11, verse 532: “Its eyes tremble with fire, and its crescent-shaped jaws resound with hooked teeth.” Shortly afterward, at verse 283, Dracontius speaks of the boar’s “foaming battles”; *to foam* is appropriately said of it, as in Claudian, book 2 of *The Rape of Proserpine*, verses 242–43: “Let the boar foam everywhere without fear, and let the savage lions roar with impunity.”

281. *To rush obliquely* is also appropriate to the boar. Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, book 8, section 4, verse 344: “And with an oblique blow he scatters the barking hounds.”

282. The reading of the Vatican manuscript is far superior to the common reading. *Massyla fames* refers to the wild beasts of Mauretania, which hunger goads on. Statius, *Achilleid* 2, verse 188, speaking of a tamed lion gathering its rage: “Faith renounced, and the hostile tamer; against him hunger is first, and it is ashamed to have served a timid master.” Dracontius likewise writes in the *Elegies*, verse 269: “When the hunger of a rabid lion, though fasting.” The shoulders of boars are hard, unless one prefers to read *duris descendat in armis* (“descend upon the hard shoulders”). Ovid, in the passage cited, verse 419, speaking of the boar: “And he buries his shining hunting spears in the opposing shoulders.” On the word *Massyla*, see book 3, verse 189.

283. The meaning is that no other wild beast, nor another boar, should oppose a boar contemplating battle.

284. Perhaps *promitur* (“is brought forth”) is better with the Vatican manuscript than *gignitur* (“is generated”) with the others, although *promitur* occurs again at verse 287.

286. Weitzius printed *bestia* (“beast”), but in his index he placed *bellua* (“monster”), which Rivinus seems to prefer. From the Vatican manuscript one might suspect the reading: “The beast, having the appearance of a mountain, extends its bulk as it advances.” Isidore, *Etymologies* 12.2.9: “The Greeks think that the elephant was named from the magnitude of its body, because it presents the form of a mountain. For in Greek a mountain is called λόφος (*lophos*).” Johannes Ludovicus de la Cerda, *Sacred Adversaria*, chapter 117, section 21, illuminates this passage of Isidore.

287. At verse 638: “The gaping serpent crawls.” Oppian, *Halieutica* 1, says of the serpent: “In it he pours forth deadly venom, and spits from his teeth all the mournful, violent bile—the treasure of destruction.” Apuleius, *Apology*: “To breathe black poison after the manner of a viper, with its white little tooth.” Lucan, book 9, verse 628: “They have venom in their bite and threaten death with their tooth”; others read: “They threaten fate in their tooth.” *Quatera* means “to throw out” with violence. Terence, *Eunuch* 2.3.66: “The man will certainly be shaken out of doors with the gift.”

288. Book 2, verse 257: “What benefit does the spotted serpent provide? Medicine knows.” In the first edition, based on the Victorinus manuscript, *rapit squamas* (“it drags its scales”) was adopted for metrical reasons, since the first syllable of *repit* (“it crawls”) is lengthened. Barthius preferred *redit* (“returns”), which Rivinus calls extremely acute. But the genuine reading seems to be *repit*. Isidore, *Etymologies* 12.4: “The serpent received its name because it creeps by hidden approaches; for it does not advance with open steps, but crawls through the tiniest movements of its scales . . . Serpents are reptiles because they crawl with belly and breast.” One might read *per gramina* (“through the grasses”), but Dracontius says that crawling with belly and breast occurs *per viscera* (“through the entrails”). That he shortens the first syllable in *repit* should not seem surprising, since in his period certain words were not pronounced with the same quantities as among the ancients, and some even possessed common quantity. Moreover, if the origin of *repo* (“I crawl”) is examined, its first syllable is short: it derives by metathesis from the Greek verb ἕρπω (*herpō*), whose first syllable is naturally short.]

The fleeing stag wanders into the fields with palm-shaped antlers,

and the swift horse breaks forth, a beast useful in war.

The impious earth produces terrifying lions.

The guilelessness of sheep, destined to suffer the wolves’ treachery,

157 feared the hoarse Molossians while the doe ran about.

[280] The boar foams, threatening deaths with its crescent-shaped tooth,

and, turning its flank obliquely, grimly contemplates battle.

May neither Massylian hunger descend upon its hard shoulders,

[Col. 0716A] nor another boar go forth to stir up foaming battles.

Every kind of domestic animal and every kind of wild beast

[285] wanders among the meadows and grasses without a keeper.

158 A beast advances, having the bulk and appearance of a mountain.

The gaping serpent is brought forth, shaking venom beneath its tooth,

and the spotted serpent crawls through its entrails upon its scales.

[Col. 0717A]

[Note: [Col. 0717A]

289. Vatican manuscript: “about to send forth with its blasts.” Victorinus: “about to send forth with its breath.”

290. Vatican manuscript: “about to endure sudden, heavy deaths.”

[Col. 0717B] 291. Vatican manuscript: “And the same, destined to perish in the marrow of its limbs.”

292. Vatican manuscript: “so that the unequal part should not be all.” Azagrensis manuscript: “so that, everywhere through the meadows, they should not be all.” Victorinus: “so that springtime should not bring forth all things everywhere.”

294. Vatican manuscript: “They come at a time when.”

[Col. 0718A] 295. Vatican and Victorinus manuscripts: *ictus* (“a blow”). Sirmond: *ictum* (“the blow”).

296. Vatican manuscript: “the viper has deaths.”

298. Sirmond: “does not always burn.” Likewise Victorinus in the Vatican manuscript; the Azagrensis manuscript: “nor does it always burn.”

300. Printed editions: “According to the region of the zone the water moderates the heat.” Vatican manuscript: “According to the region of the zone, according to . . . it moderates the waters.” By conjecture: “according to the season.”

303. Azagrensis and Victorinus: “and pure.”]

[Note: [Col. 0717C]

289. Book 3, verse 303: “Or if the earth were not harmed by viperous blasts and the hisses did not consign any deaths.” Compare also book 2, verses 223ff., and the *Elegies*, verses 65ff. Perhaps one should read *missura flatibus*, with the *a* lengthened before the *fl* of the following word.

291. Understand “of the limbs” as “from its own part,” as he says in book 2, verse 255. Isidore, *Etymologies* 12.4: “From the viper are made tablets called *theriaci* [θηριακοί, ‘theriac’] by the Greeks.” On this medicine extracted from serpents, see again book 2, verse 257, and the passage cited from the *Elegies*. Isidore should be compared with John of Salisbury, who in book 7, chapter 10, reads: “which are called *theriacē* [θηριακή, ‘theriac medicine’] by the Greeks.” Pliny, book 29, chapter 4, section 21, has: “From the viper are made tablets called *THERIACI* by the Greeks, with three finger-lengths cut off on either side,” and so forth—that is, three finger-lengths are cut off from the head and from the tail. In that chapter Pliny reports other remedies from serpents against the poisons themselves.

292. Thus the first edition, based on the Victorinus manuscript, which the Vatican manuscript supports, for *pars impar* (“the unequal part”) is corrupt from *passim per*. Fabricius thought *Sed ne cuncta simul* (“But lest all things together”) was corrupt. Since *passim per cuncta* (“everywhere through all things”) follows, he corrected it to: “But lest, all mixed together, they should be everywhere through all things.” Weitzius copied Fabricius; Sirmond retained *Sed ne cuncta simul*, but, as one should believe, changed the following words according to his own manuscript to *passim permixta fuissent* (“should have been mixed everywhere”). The Azagrensis manuscript has: “But lest all things together should have been everywhere through the meadows.” The original reading is extremely elegant, and the sense is: “so that everything should not be in everything at once.” For *fuissent* (“had been”) to be used in place of *essent* (“were”), one tense for another, is customary in the fifth century, as Barthius observed in his notes on Rigortus. Dracontius uses *per cuncta* at verse 226, and Tertullian likewise, as I noted on verse 9. See below, verse 348.

293. Consult the note on verse 315.

294. Things that are savage either do not come at every time or do not always cause harm. Dracontius treats this same subject in the *Elegies*, from verse 55 to verse 92.

295. Virgil, book 12, verse 6: “Then at last the lion moves his weapons.” A scorpion certainly does not always strike, but it is always prepared to strike. Pliny, book 11, chapter 25, section 30: “Its tail is always ready to strike, and at no moment does it cease to be on the lookout, lest it ever lack an opportunity.” It should nevertheless be observed that scorpions outside Africa are not venomous; this is said to have been established by many experiments of modern investigators.

296. In another sense, *habere ictum* means “to have been struck.” But *habere* is also used for “to do” or “to bring about,” as in *habere dialogum* (“to hold a dialogue”), *sermonem* (“to hold a conversation”), and *iter* (“to make a journey”). Cicero, *On the Provincial Consulship*, chapter 4: “The cavalry suffered destruction”—that is, “brought about,” as some interpret it. But it seems that the punctuation should be: “Then, upon his arrival in Syria, the first cavalry suffered destruction,” so that *equitatus* is in the genitive case.

298. See Lucan, *Panegyric to Piso*: “Nature itself undergoes changes,” etc.; Ovid, book 4, elegy 4 of the *Epistles from Pontus*, verse 1: “No day is so drenched with southern rain clouds,” etc.; and Alcuin, poem 178: “Nothing remains eternal beneath the lofty vault of heaven; everything is changed by varying times,” etc.

300. From the Vatican manuscript I read it thus, because the meaning seems to be that the sun moderates fires and waters according to the varying season and the different regions. *Epistles*, verse 81: “The sun gives the seasons, the world’s most pleasing forms.”

301. Rivinus says that one should write *bellantis fluctus* (“waves that battle”), or *bullantis* (“boiling”), that is, “seething.” Pliny, book 9, chapter 7: “The blowing of boiling waters.” But here the subject is the sea being made calm. Thus Horace, book 4, ode 12, verse 1: “Now the companions of spring, which calm the sea.” Dracontius therefore says that waves, which had just been restless and as though battling, are made calm and somehow lie down. See Prudentius, preface 1 against Symmachus, verse 10: “But when the battles of the blue whirlpool.” Weitzius cites from Statius, *Thebaid* 3: “Where the shores reclined in unwarlike sleep,” and “The rivers, drained by the sun, lie still.” The former passage is more relevant to Dracontius.

302. Statius uses *grande* as an adverb in book 12, verse 683: “But he rouses battles and threatens war, roaring loudly.” Ovid, book 2 of the *Tristia*, verse 35: “Now that it has thundered itself out and terrified the world with its din, it restores the clear air after the waters have been scattered.”

305. *Vipereos angues* (“viperous snakes”) means vipers, a species standing for the genus. Rivinus thinks one should correct the text to *Africa vipereos*, followed in the next verse by *Numida sortitur tellus* (“the Numidian land receives”). But, apart from the fact that the first syllable of *Numida* ought to be short, Africa itself abounds in lions. Solinus, chapter 40, speaking of Lesser Africa, says: “Its interior contains many wild beasts, but chiefly lions.” Moreover, “The dry sand received snakes; the moist earth, lions” is much more elegant. In truth, wild beasts are chiefly produced in forests, where the earth is certainly moist. Solinus, chapter 39, or 26, says of Numidia: “Where it is wooded, it produces wild beasts; where it is lofty with ridges, it nourishes horses.” Lucan, book 9, after relating that Cato’s army had traversed the sands of Africa, full of serpents, adds at verse 945: “And now the dust began to grow harder and harder for them, and Libya, thickened, began to return to earth; now from afar the sparse foliage of the forests began to rise, and the uncultivated huts began to stand forth, their thatch heaped up. What joy did the better land give the wretched men, when they first saw savage lions opposite them!”]

Sending harmful black poisons from the blasts of its mouth,

[290] and suddenly scattering heavy deaths through its hisses,

and the same creature imparting remedies to its limbs.

159 But lest all things should be everywhere together,

God distributed them among fixed places and appointed their seasons.

Those things called savage do not come at one time.

[295] The lion does not always move its weapons, nor does the scorpion

always have its sting; nor does the fierce viper always make its bite;

nor do the horned serpents always raise their necks for wounds;

[Col. 0718A] nor does the sea’s wave always rage, nor does the sun’s heat

always burn everywhere; according to the season it moderates its fires,

[300] according to the region of the earth’s zone it moderates the waters,

and now the battling waves will lie still in sluggish seas.

The very sky, which thunders loudly, serene without a cloud,

now keeps silent, and its lights return to the clear heaven.

Many things have been scattered through the world and assigned to various places.

[305] The dry sand received viperous snakes,

[Col. 0719A]

307. Vatican manuscript: “ivory, shining with gems.”

309. Vatican manuscript: “and, burning badly, the fragrant beast seizes ambrosial harvests.” Victorinus and Sirmond, as printed; but Sirmond has *sapit* (“tastes”) for *rapit* (“seizes”); Victorinus has *mensas* (“tables”) for *messes* (“harvests”).

310. Vatican manuscript: “and its color has begun.”

311. Azagrensis: “it came and . . .” Vatican manuscript: “Hyrcanian mountains . . .” (or “I see”) “with its husband.” Victorinus: “it comes from secret mountains.”

[Col. 0720A] 314. Victorinus: “through the mountain.”

315. Vatican manuscript: “God distributed, distributed among different places.”

316. Vatican manuscript: “so that the unequal part should . . .”

317. Vatican manuscript: “of the rich field.”

306. Note *fera colla leonum* (“the wild necks of lions”) for “lions,” just as in the preceding verse *vipereos angues* (“viperous snakes”) means “vipers.”

307. Verse 286: “Having the appearance of a mountain,” referring to the elephant. Tertullian, *On the Judgment of the Lord*: “Both the creatures of the sea and the deformed monsters of swimmers.” Alcimus Avitus, book 1, verse 40: “And the monsters which the rare sea is accustomed to produce,” referring to whales and other marine beasts. Virgil, book 1 of the *Georgics*, verse 56: “Do you not see how Tmolus sends saffron fragrances, how India sends ivory?”

308. Rivinus thinks Dracontius is speaking of venomous animals produced from corrupt odors. But there is scarcely any doubt that he is speaking of the elephant, which is frequently called a *bellua* (“monster”), as in “Getulian monster” and “Indian monster,” a point Weitzius notes in his index. The sentence itself demands this. For after Dracontius had said that India produces elephants along with gems, he immediately added that elephants are generated among divine fragrances. Dracontius attributes fragrances to India at verses 176ff., just as he attributes gems above and at verse 318. They are called divine fragrances because they are destined for the worship of God.

309. Perhaps the reading should be *sapit male fragrans bestia messes* (“the ill-smelling beast tastes the harvests”). The Vatican manuscript provides a basis for conjecturing whether one should read *frangens balsama* (“breaking the balsams”), since *balsamum* is a tree from which a juice, also called balsam, flows. Ambrosia is also a kind of herb, but here “ambrosial harvests” means fragrant, sweet, pleasant herbs, as in “ambrosial juices” in Columella and Silius, and shortly afterward at verse 325 in the same matter: “And the tears give an exceedingly ambrosial gift of fragrance.”

310. The construction is figurative, standing for “the tiger of uncertain and varied color,” and therefore one that is varied and spotted. I suspected the reading: “And the tiger of uncertain color.”

311. Fabricius reproduced the error of the first edition based on Victorinus: “from secret mountains,” which Weitzius correctly emended to “from the Hyrcanian mountains.” Virgil, book 4 of the *Aeneid*: “And the Hyrcanian tigers offered their breasts.” Barthius gathered much concerning Hyrcanian tigers from this passage of Dracontius and others in his notes on Statius, *Thebaid* 4, verse 678. I suspect there is an error in *effeta marito* (“having given birth, with its husband”), for an *effeta* tiger is one that has produced offspring; but what does the added word *marito* mean? “Sent by her husband”? I do not think so. Yet the Vatican manuscript clearly has *marito*, while the preceding words are corrupt. Perhaps something else should be written in place of *effeta*, such as: “it came, with its husband pursuing,” etc.

312. The tiger is described as deprived of its cubs and therefore *effeta*, or *feta*, since *feta* is sometimes used for *effeta*. Lucan, book 5, verse 405: “Swifter than the fires of heaven and than a pregnant tigress, she runs across.” Ovid, book 13 of the *Metamorphoses*, verse 677: “More savage than a pregnant bear.” But speed is characteristic of the tiger, which is said to receive its name from the Persian word for “arrow.” Solinus, chapter 27: “Their power is especially demonstrated when they are driven on by maternal concern, when they pursue the robbers of their cubs. Let horsemen follow one another, and let them wish to remove the prey by whatever cunning they can; unless they have the sea as protection, every effort is vain.” I attempted to restore the whole passage as follows: “And the tiger of uncertain color, through a thousand colors, pursued by a husband of varied appearance in the Hyrcanian mountains, is sent forth to overcome storms in its running.” *Sectata* is taken passively, as Varro uses it in book 2 of *On Agriculture*, chapter 9: “who would wish himself to be pursued by a dog”; or, if preferred, “with a powerful husband pursuing.” *To overcome storms* is correct. Horace, book 2, ode 16: “Swifter than stags, swifter than the east wind driving the rain clouds.”

314. Rivinus thinks something is concealed in the words *per montes* (“through the mountains”), as they are read in the Vatican manuscript, or *per montem* (“through the mountain”), as the older editions have—perhaps “the rocks of the Garamantes receive.” But Dracontius is more likely speaking of a mountain in Ethiopia, where dragons are born. Solinus, chapter 43, on Ethiopia: “On the southern side a lofty mountain overhangs the sea, perpetually hot with its native fire; and amid its blazing ridges, where the heat burns restlessly, there is a great abundance of dragons.” He later speaks of the dragons’ lairs. Compare Isidore, who also mentions the dragons’ caves in book 12 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 4, and adds: “It is born in Ethiopia and India amid the very burning of perpetual heat.” Perhaps one should read: “in Ethiopia, and amid the very fires of perpetual heat,” since Isidore is copying Solinus. Yet in book 14, chapter 3, speaking of India, he says: “There are also golden mountains there, which it is impossible to approach because of dragons, griffins, and monsters of immense human size”—a statement that has the flavor of a fable, or is certainly fabulous.

315. “God distributed” refers back to verse 293. Virgil, book 1 of the *Georgics*, after explaining “what each region bears and what each region refuses,” adds at verse 60: “Immediately Nature imposed these laws and eternal covenants upon fixed places.”

316. Rivinus explains *cespite multa diremit* (“he separated many things by a sod”) from Avienus and Barthius as “he placed broad stretches of earth between them.” Avienus uses *cespes* (“sod,” “piece of ground”) for “region” in the *Periegesis*, verse 227: “Rocky Charambis rises from Paphean ground”; and verse 388: “Countless peoples furrow everywhere the fields of that extended land.” Others read *sala cespitis*. Nevertheless, I would prefer: “He joined very many things together, but separated many seeds,” or “and separated many seeds”; for Dracontius enjoys such repetitions, which are not without elegance.

317. “Of the rich field” might perhaps seem better than “of rich gold,” so that all the riches mentioned afterward may be included. But since gold is nowhere else mentioned, I retain “of rich gold.” Broukhusius, in his notes on Tibullus, book 1, elegy 10, verse 31, says that “of rich gold” is a beautiful epithet, also customary in Tibullus elsewhere, and used here by Dracontius.

318. Verse 307: “India with gems.” See Isidore, book 14 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 3.

319. Pliny, Solinus, and countless others write about the gems of the Red Sea. The snow-white pebbles are pearls; the green ones are emeralds. Seneca, *Phaedra*, verse 388, act 2, scene 1: “Nor should a snow-white stone lead down to the ears, a gift of the Indian sea.”]

The moist land receives the wild necks of lions.

India, together with gems, brings forth ivory monsters.

161 A monster is generated among divine fragrances,

and the beast violently ravages the ambrosial harvests,

[310] the tiger of uncertain color through a thousand colors

comes from the Hyrcanian mountains and, having borne young, is sent forth by her mate [the sense of *marito* is uncertain], deprived of her cubs, to overcome storms in her running.

[Col. 0720A] 162 Africa, allotted its does with erect horns,

the hollow rocks among the mountains receive dragons.

[315] He distributed the remaining seeds among different lands;

he joined very many things together, but separated many by the soil.

Moreover, gifts of rich gold are poured forth;

richer India produced excellent gems;

the shores of the Red Sea produce snow-white pebbles.

[320] [Col. 0721A]

[Note: [Col. 0721A]

321. Printed editions: *Persida*. Vatican manuscript: *Persica*. Sirmond, Victorinus, and the Vatican manuscript: *nobilitat* (“ennobles”).

323. Vatican manuscript: “The Seres draw threads, not pulled beneath the thumb.”

324–25. Thus the Azagrensis, Vatican, and Sirmond manuscripts; but Sirmond has “a gift of fragrances.” Victorinus: “And the exceedingly ambrosial balsam-shrubs weep through the fields; their tears offer Caesarean fragrances as a gift.”

326. Thus the Azagrensis manuscript; in the Vatican manuscript: “the land under Phoenice presents.” Sirmond and Victorinus: “the Phoenician land produces.”

327. This verse and the following one, “These are the flowers of nard,” are absent from the Vatican manuscript, in place of “not now, Victorinus.”]

[Note: [Col. 0721B]

320. Babylonia can mean the part of Mesopotamia whose capital was Babylon, or the city of Babylon itself. Barthius understands “flaming and green crusts” as marble slabs applied to buildings and other large structures. But the subject is still gems; one might suspect that *baccas* (“berries”) or *conchas* (“shells”) should be read instead of *crustas*, unless gems too could be called *crustae*, as in Sidonius, cited by Barthius himself from letter 7 of book 9: “crystalline or onyx crusts.” Barthius, *Adversaria* 9.7, explains this as crusts made from precious stones. Add Pliny, book 37, chapter 4: “The diamond is broken into such small crusts that they can scarcely be seen.” Concerning the Chaldaeans, whose royal city was Babylon, Solinus, chapter 50, writes: “Whatever peoples drink from the Euphrates shine with different stones . . . Sagda flowed from the Chaldaeans all the way to us . . . delightfully green.” Pliny, book 37, chapter 10, section 67: “The Chaldaeans find sagda clinging to ships, of a leek-green color.”

321. Fabricius corrected *nobilitant* (“ennoble”) to *nobilitat* (“ennobles”) in Victorinus. Sirmond printed *nobilitat*, but scarcely any suitable meaning can be extracted. If the manuscripts allowed it, I would read: “Persian shores are ennobled by precious gems,” which the Vatican manuscript suggests. But *Persida* must be retained. Claudian, *On the Third Consulship of Honorius*, verse 204: “And to scatter a gem-studded Persia beneath humble ornaments,” etc.

322. Mar. Victor, book 1 of *Genesis*, verse 282: “Here, where the carbuncle shines red with lightning-like fire”; others: “The carbuncle, shining red with lightning-like fire, sparkles.” Tertullian, *On the Judgment of the Lord*: “Here the green stone shines; there the carbuncle burns.” Cyprian, *On Genesis*: “The name of this one is green stone; that one is burning carbuncle.” Drepanius, final poem: “Thus the red carbuncle vomits red fire,” where others read “the carbuncle vomits forth.” Why, then, does Dracontius call it “cold”? Because, although it appears to burn, it does not burn and remains cold. What if, instead of *frigidus*, one read “and Phrygian, rosy,” or “and Libyan, red”? Isidore, book 16, chapter 14: “The carbuncle holds first place among all fiery gems . . . It is generated in Libya.”

323. In place of *nullo sub pollice* (“under no thumb”), Rivinus conjectures *molli de stipite* (“from a soft stem”), as in Claudian, *On the Consulship of Probinus and Olybrius*, verse 179: “With thread which the Seres shear from a soft stem.” But *nullo sub pollice ducta* (“drawn under no thumb”) is much more pointed, indicating that the threads are drawn not in the way they are among us, but “under no thumb.” Dracontius is evidently speaking of his own time, when the silk craft was peculiar to the Seres or shared by only a few peoples. Properly speaking, a thread was something drawn beneath the thumb from linen, wool, or a similar material. On the Seres, see Pliny, Solinus, Isidore, and others.

324. Barthius, book 34, chapter 10, following Victorinus, reads this verse and the next, but in the next verse he reads *caesa sacros* (“sacred cuttings”) instead of *Caesareos*, because the bark of the balsam tree is cut in order to draw forth that most precious liquid. “For why,” he says, “did he say ‘Caesar’s fragrances’ rather than royal or other fragrances?” But he had forgotten his own correction in book 9, chapter 7: “The ambrosial shrubs of Idumaea weep through the fields; balsams, Caesar’s tears, give a gift of fragrances.” Idumaea is Judaea, the chief—or even the sole—region producing balsam. The fields of Caesar are near the city of Caesarea in Palestine; that city is mentioned in many places by Josephus, Stephanus, Pliny, and others. “Of Idumaean Caesarea” distinguishes it from several cities of the same name. This is essentially Barthius’s account; he adds that Dracontius habitually says many things in a few words, as compactly as possible. From this the interpretation of *Caesareos* as “through the fields” is derived.

325. From Barthius’s conjecture one might write: “through the fields of Idumaea, ambrosial,” etc.; or: “through the fields—Idumaea’s ambrosial,” etc. Other conjectures are possible, such as *Eminus ambrosium* (“ambrosial from afar”) or *Nec minus ambrosium* (“no less ambrosial”). The moisture released by plants is called “tears,” so that the plants themselves are said to weep and shed tears as they pour forth moisture. Poets speak this way, but so also do Pliny, Columella in prose, and many others.

326. Rivinus, following the common reading, says that “Phoenician land” is used in the same way as “Gallic snow.” The Vatican manuscript agrees fairly clearly with the Azagrensis under *Phoenice*. Someone apparently inverted this reading to satisfy the meter, since the middle syllable of *Phoenice* should be long. But Christian poets paid little attention to syllable quantity even in the extensions of proper names; and again at verse 653 there is *Phoenicis* with its second syllable shortened, *Phoenicis exactam* (“Phoenice exhausted” or “drained”), as Sirmond also reads it, although others printed *Phoenici exactam*. The proper name of the region is *Phoenice, Phoenices*, with ablative *Phoenice*. The same region is also called *Phoenicia*, but more rarely. *Phoenicius* is an adjective belonging to *Phoenice*. There was therefore no reason for Rivinus to devise the expression “Phoenician land” on the model of “Gallic snow,” since *Phoenicia* may be an adjective agreeing with *tellus* (“land”). Solinus, Ovid, Statius, and Claudian relate that the Phoenix builds its funeral pyre from cinnamon branches. It can be inferred from Isidore’s description of cinnamon, book 17, chapter 8, that the cinnamon of the ancients is the same cinnamon that we now call *cannella* or *canela*. “The inner land beneath Phoenice” suggests the part of Phoenice nearest Arabia, or even Arabia itself, since poets commonly name neighboring regions for one another. Solinus, chapter 33, or 46, on Arabia: “The cinnamon-bird, likewise an Arabian bird, builds its nests in the finest groves from cinnamon shrubs. Since no one can reach them because of the height and fragility of the branches, the inhabitants attack the piles with lead-weighted arrows; they sell what has been knocked down at a high price, because merchants value this cinnamon more than any other.” On some of the Philippine islands, such as Mindanao, Jolo, and others, which are extremely rich in cinnamon, nests are woven by a certain bird; when brought to Europe, they are rare and costly delicacies for princes. It is not yet clear from what shrubs they are woven, but they do not seem very different from those Solinus describes.

327. The meaning is that the interior part of Phoenice, more exposed to the sun’s heat, produces cinnamon, while other parts, more remote from the sun’s heat, produce nard and amomum. I understand it this way if the reading is sound; for these two verses are absent from the Vatican manuscript, and they are certainly not very necessary. Other manuscripts vary; consequently I would more willingly read: “Much too friendly to the sun, and not yet scorched by the sun—these are the flowers of nard,” etc., so that either Phoenice itself, or any other region scorched by the sun, may be understood to produce nard and amomum. Rivinus, in his list of errors, reads: “Much too friendly to the sun, not yet scorched by the sun.”]

163 Babylon produced flaming and green crusts;

Persian shores are ennobled by precious gems;

the cold carbuncle burns with rosy splendor;

the Seres draw threads under no thumb,

[Col. 0722A] the balsam shrubs weep through the Caesarean fields,

[325] 164 and the tears give an exceedingly ambrosial gift of fragrance.

The inner land beneath Phoenice produces cinnamon,

much too friendly to the sun; for it is not scorched by the sun.

330. Vatican manuscript: “The form of God, by God’s power, is shaped into limbs.”

331. Victorinus: “So that the ruler may go, more moderate than all these.” Sirmond, Vatican, and Azagrensis: “So that one, proceeding as ruler, may be more perfect than all [the rest]”; but Sirmond has *dominator*, Azagrensis *dominanter*, and the Vatican manuscript *dominantur*.

332. Sirmond: “What Nature ordered.” Azagrensis: “What Nature commanded.” Vatican manuscript: “What was born and commanded.”

333. Vatican manuscript: “the nature that brings forth.”

334. Vatican manuscript: “purer spring.”

335. Printed editions: “But the highest ruler of rulers and creator.” Vatican manuscript as printed here.

336. Vatican manuscript: “is shaped through”; the others: “he polished through”; from the Vatican manuscript’s error, by conjecture: “he shaped through.”

[Col. 0724B] 338. Thus the Vatican and Victorinus manuscripts; Sirmond: “corporeal form.”

339. Vatican manuscript: “The water sees, for a little while, the man’s shapeless mind.”

340. This verse is absent from the Vatican manuscript.

343. Victorinus: “the marrow.”

344. Victorinus: “a vast body.” Vatican manuscript: “an immersed body.” Sirmond: “a body in the harvest.”]

[Note: [Col. 0723B]

328. On amomum, see Pliny, book 12, chapter 13. Virgil calls amomum “Assyrian” in *Eclogue* 4 because it either grows in Assyria alone or especially there.

329. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 1, verse 76: “Something holier than these animals, and more capable of a lofty mind, was still lacking—something able to rule over the rest.”

330. “He is polished” denotes a human being perfectly formed, as though smoothed by a file.

331. I choose *dominanter* (“as ruler”), because Dracontius delights in similar adverbs. See the prolegomena, section 135. *Moderatior* (“more moderate”) here means “more perfect,” formed in a better manner.

332. Rivinus punctuates differently and reads: “more moderate than all these, Nature’s first ruler, by whose command everything was brought forth,” that is, God. Barthius, book 33, chapter 21, follows Victorinus but explains *princeps* as “first,” without any intelligible sense. The variation among the manuscripts suggests that a corruption lies beneath the text. See whether one should read: “Nature, at the command of the first ruler, brought forth everything.” But concerning the human being, etc. In Sirmond’s reading one might understand: “The first ruler of Nature brought forth by command,” etc. Book 2, verse 31: “The hope of human beings, the ruler of things.”

333. Book 2, verses 250ff., pursues the same thought at greater length. Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 1032: “At the command of the ruling One, all things brought forth drew new forms. Man alone deserved to receive the Lord’s fearsome face.”

336. *Limavit* (“he polished”) could be retained, as above at verse 330: “He is polished into limbs.” Rivinus observes that *limavit* might be derived from *limus* (“mud”), but it is better derived from *lima* (“file”). I much prefer this origin from *lima*. The verb *plasmare* (“to shape,” “to form”) is frequently used by the holy Fathers when recounting the creation of humanity. Dracontius, book 2, verse 87, where he describes the formation of Christ’s body: “And the flesh is shaped.” Compare also book 3, verses 620ff.; everywhere you will find Dracontius resembling himself.]

337. Censorinus, On the Birthday, chapter 11, no. 7: “The infant is articulated in thirty-five days.” Above, verse 262: “The articulated limbs are feathered with rounded forms”; and Book II, verse 78: “The man who deigned to be born is articulated in the womb”—or, as I would rather read it, “in the limbs.” Jacob Mosantus Briosius listed *membrari* among the words used exclusively by Censorinus.

338. Book II, verse 98: “Therefore, when the ruler and creator puts on bodily limbs”;” and verse 236, concerning man: “Ungrateful, because he had been made the heavenly image”; and Book III, verse 532: “The image of the Maker.”

339. Rivinus says that this expresses an error: since man was already the heavenly image, he could not lack a mind. He emends it to “of the man, when the Spirit had been infused with the supreme mind”—namely, God—etc. I change nothing, nor do I recognize any error. For although man, according to his soul and not according to his body, was made in the image of God, nevertheless the whole man is said in Holy Scripture to have been made in God’s image; and Dracontius, in the preceding verse, relates that man, who is the heavenly image, was formed in bodily limbs. Man, however, consists not of body alone but also of soul, whose creation he now describes. The image of God also shines forth in some manner in the body, since the body itself is called the image of the soul. Thus Tertullian, who did not confine the image of God to the human body, nevertheless says in chapter 6 of *On the Resurrection*: “Thus that clay, already then assuming the image of the Christ who was to come in the flesh, was not merely God’s work but also a pledge.”

342. Verse 395, concerning Eve: “A cheek beautiful with blush.” Book III, verse 624: “And the twin cheeks blushed.”

344. The older editions, with Victor, read: “The immense hairs rise”; and Weitzius, in his index, notes that *immensa* is an adverb, like *transversa*, *sera*, and similar forms, which are used adverbially. Rivinus takes *immensa* to mean “in an immense number of hairs”; I would rather understand it of hairs which, unlike the other parts of the body, grow without a fixed measure. Nor would I object if someone read *immense*, with the final syllable short, as in *inferne* and *superne*. In Fabricius’s edition of the Christian Poets, in the copy belonging to the distinguished Bishop Reggius, I find the manuscript reading *in summa* in the margin instead of *immensa*. The Sirmondian text is plausible but somewhat obscure. In place of “the harvest of hairs rises,” one might conjecture “the locks rise upon the crown,” or “the hairs rise upon the forehead,” or “from the forehead.” Thus in Book III, verse 620, where the resurrection of the body is described: “The stage of hair, pouring a crown from the forehead”; or “the hairs rise in the garment.” Ambrose, *On Noah and the Ark*, chapter 7, no. 21: “How pleasantly the hairs of the head clothe the head as a garment”; and Book VI of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 9, no. 73, concerning the bones of the head: “They are clothed with denser hairs”; and Dracontius, at the cited passage, verse 621: “And time clothes the whole head with the adornment of hair.” I add another conjecture: “the hairs rise in merchandise,” that is, “for sale.” Pliny, Book XII, chapter 25: “The branches too are *in merce* [for sale].” Ovid, Book III of *The Art of Love*, verse 165: “The woman comes forth thickly covered with purchased locks, and with money makes others her own in place of her own. Nor is there shame in having openly bought them.”

165. These are flowers of nard; this portion pours forth amomum.

so that, as the sole ruler, it might proceed as the more moderate of all things,

But man is not born from earth, nor does the sea create him from its waves,

nor heaven, nor the stars, nor the purer air:

[335] rather, the ruler and creator who was to rule all things

formed from dust the man fashioned through his limbs.

within the bones; the hairs rise in a harvest,

345. The printed editions read *visu*; the Vatican manuscript has *visus*.

348. The Vatican manuscript has *atque oculos*.

350. Thus the Vatican manuscript; the others have: “and, grasping the banks with a water-flowing whirlpool.”

352. The Vatican manuscript reads *miratur: sed quid*; the printed editions, *miratur se: quid*.

353. Victor has *simplex est, non*; Sirmond distinguishes the text as *cupit, simplex et*.

354. The Vatican manuscript has *qui meritos s.*; Sirmond, *pars mundi*; Victor, Azagrensis, and the Vatican manuscript have *pars mundus*.

355. Thus the Vatican manuscript; in the Azagrensis manuscript: “And the alternating home, a grove through flowering fields”; Sirmond and Victor: “And the eternal home of the grove through flowering fields.”

356. Thus the Vatican manuscript; the others have: “From afar a little vineyard looks upon the yoked beasts”; but Victor has *vineta* rather than *jumenta*.

357. Thus the Vatican manuscript; the others have: “Silent about this matter, he turns it over and seeks it in his heart.” The Azagrensis manuscript has *angit* and Victor *cogitatque* instead of *volvitque*.

358. Sirmond has *vel quare*. The Vatican manuscript reads: “And why does he not ask himself what all these things are?” Victor has the reading printed here.

361. Sirmond and Victor have *demus solatia facto*; the Vatican manuscript, *demus adjutoria facto*; the Azagrensis manuscript, *demus adjutorio facto*.]

[Note: [Col. 0725B]

345. Compare verse 235, Book II, verse 652, and Book III, verse 618: “From there the eyes, with jewel-like radiance, flash forth.” Rivinus notes from Pliny that the eyes are formed last; but in the latter passage Dracontius mentions the tongue afterward.

346. Rivinus thinks the better reading is: “And he gave voice to the new structure of the machine, rising to praise its Maker.” Book II, verse 84, supports this conjecture: “God is clothed in structure, the framework is bound together.” Compare Book III, verse 644. After *surgens* the printed editions incorrectly place a comma; it is understood as “rising to praise.”

347. Verse 243, concerning the birds: “And, I think, they deserved to be created to praise the Lord together.”

348. Marcellus Victor, Book I of *Genesis*, verse 155: “Nor is there a spectator present whom the greatness of so vast a work might fill, and lead with eager eyes through each detail.” Fabricius printed this passage, as many others from Victor, quite differently. Dracontius usually says *per cuncta* rather than *per omnia*. See verse 292 with its note. Virgil, Book II of the *Aeneid*, verse 570: “And everywhere, as he carried his eyes through all things.” Others say “to cast” or “to direct” the eyes. Rivinus conjectures *miratur amomis*, a plural form used by Persius. But *amoenum* is so good that nothing better is needed.

350. Of rivers, *stringere ripas*—“to bite” or “lick the banks”—is a mark of elegance. *Undisonus* is a word used by Propertius, Valerius Flaccus, and Statius.

351. *Ire* of water is poetic; poets also attribute feet to water. See Broukhusius’s note on Tibullus, Book I, elegy 10, verse 36: “And to have traversed the pure paths of the river.”

352. The Vatican reading is graceful and seems more correct.

354. Sirmond’s reading can be defended; but *mundus* seems better, as in the following verse: “And the nourishing home, the grove.”

355. Cyprian, *On Genesis*: “In the midst of the houses, from paradise.” *Domus* and *aedes* mean a dwelling and any sort of abode, as “the home of birds” or “of cattle.”

356. Verse 270: “The yoked beasts through the fields.” Instead of *exspectat*, one could substitute *aspectat*; but *exspecto* is used by Plautus, *Aulularia* IV.8.7, Petronius, *Satyricon* 17, and Paulus in the *Digest*, Book XLI, title 1, law 26, with the simple meaning “I look at.” Although some people emend the reading in these passages, it is sound; for they change it because they think *exspecto* cannot mean “to look at,” an inadequate reason. In good editions I find *exspecto*, not *specto*. Moreover, Statius, Book V of the *Silvae*, 2.22: “The horse is awaited”; and Ovid, Book XIV of the *Metamorphoses*, verse 418: “He had been awaited.” Both use the compound *exspecto* for *specto*. The common reading is not tolerable. For what does “the little yoked beasts” mean? Nor does Victor’s reading, “the little vineyards,” fit this passage.

357. Perhaps: “what they are.” Victor’s reading is *cogitatque*, which conflicts with the meter. Fabricius emended it by conjecture to *voluitque*. Sirmond printed this same reading; but since the Azagrensis manuscript differs, one may reasonably doubt whether Sirmond wrote it from his own manuscript or from Fabricius’s correction. *Requirit de se* means “asks from himself,” rather than “from himself” in the sense of “on his own” or “from within himself.” Nor would I strongly object if one wished to restore *Et a se*, since I have often seen such monosyllables lengthened, especially at the beginning of a verse, as in *It eques*. Elsewhere I shall show that this syllable too may be common.

358. Weitzius reads *non sint haec, ipse volutat*, which Rivinus approves less. Here too I suspect that Sirmond printed *Vel quare* from Fabricius rather than from his own manuscript. For since Victor’s first edition has *Et quare*, to which the Vatican agrees, Fabricius printed *Vel quare* either by accident or deliberately. The other animals were not in paradise with Adam, according to verse 356, “And from afar he sees the yoked beasts,” and verse 454, “Moreover, that place was given to the two alone.” Some, including John of Damascus, Book II of *The Orthodox Faith*, chapter 11, think so; nor is it plainly affirmed in Holy Scripture that animals were in paradise, since only trees and rivers are mentioned. Pererius, in his commentary on Genesis 2:9, considers it more likely that animals were in paradise, and adduces arguments and writers who hold this view.

359. Perhaps: “Nor, lacking a companion with whom he might converse, did he have one.” Here *conferre* means “to converse” or “to share plans.”

361. Thus the Vatican manuscript, supported by the Azagrensis. The other editors perhaps inserted *solatia* by conjecture to satisfy the meter instead of *adjutoria*. Genesis 2:18: “It is not good for man to be alone; let us make for him a helper like himself.” Ecclesiasticus 17:5: “He created from him a helper like himself.” Columella, Book XII, chapter 1, preface, quoting Cicero’s *Economics*: “So that from this same fellowship, aids for mortals in old age, and no less defenses, might be prepared.” The fact that the first syllable of *demus* is shortened here is no obstacle; it is also shortened in Book III, verse 678: “From your judgment, gracious God, let triumph be granted thereafter.” Either that syllable was common, or its quantity had changed in Dracontius’s time. Tertullian, Book I against Marcion: “While time is granted, and enduring patience through piety”—unless here too he reads *datur*.

From the Vatican manuscript one may extract the reading: “But lest the removed rib should give the young man pain”; or “And lest it should give…”; or, as I printed it, “Lest, forcibly removed, it should…,” supported by verse 377: “The Maker wishes to be her own thief.” Marcellus Victor, Book I of *Genesis*, verse 361: “Therefore God undertakes the familiar work, and quickly loosens the man’s heart, languid with so great a sleep, so that, while he was without consciousness, he might remove one rib”; or, as others have it, “while he, powerful, removed the rib … he might take it from limbs unharmed.” Alcimus, Book I of *Genesis*: “The almighty Father sent heavy sleep through his heart and delayed his senses with immense weight, so that no force could loosen his sleeping limbs—not even if a crash struck his untroubled ears, nor if heaven then thundered along its shaken axis; indeed, not even a hand pressed upon the limbs could have broken their rest.” Others read these verses differently. The opinion of Cajetan, who twists the formation of Eve from Adam’s rib into a metaphorical and parabolic sense, is rightly and deservedly rejected by theologians. The reason Dracontius gives for God’s sending Adam to sleep does not please Saint Augustine, who thinks that Adam’s sleep was a kind of inward contemplation of the soul, almost a rapture or ecstasy, in Book IX of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 29, and in his *Expositions on Psalm 56*, no. 11. Saint John Chrysostom, *Homily 15 on Genesis*, recognizes not only bodily sleep in Adam but also gives the reason that the removed rib might not cause pain. Suárez notes in *On the Work of the Six Days*, Book III, chapter 2, that Chrysostom does not deny that a revelation was made to Adam, but postpones it until the time when he had already awakened from sleep. Dracontius, in verse 392, plainly indicates that spiritual contemplation occurred during the sleep itself.

Marcellus Victor embraces this very reasoning in Book I of *Genesis*: “Now at this point cease at last, most foolish crowd, to torment your minds with vain questions, nor ask there why woman was fashioned from the man’s limbs, when from the beginning she could have been formed from soft dust and from nothing. 383. Fabricius and Weitzius, with Victor’s first edition, incorrectly punctuate *formatur adulta*. Cicero and others use *adulta virgo* of a maiden in the flower of age, so that she is fit to marry. In this sense, 1 Corinthians 7:36 has: “But if anyone thinks that he is behaving improperly toward his virgin, because she is past the age of puberty, and it ought to be so, let him do what he wishes: he does not sin if she marries.” The Greek for “past the age of puberty” is *ὑπέρακμος*, “surpassing the suitable time.”

384. There is an opposition between *rudis* (“new”) and *matura* (“mature”): she was newly born and at the same time mature. “Swelling years” are the age at which maidens swell and become fit for marriage. Cyprian, *On Sodom*: “Within are born for me two yoked maidens; marriageable age, virginity swelling in flower, already given to the harvest.” Perhaps: “already destined for the harvest.” Virgil, Book VII, verse 53: “Now mature for a husband, now marriageable in her full years.” Statius, Book I of the *Achilleid*, verse 292: “Mature virginity for marriage beds, and swelling years”; and Book II of the *Thebaid*, verse 202: “Deiphile, now to be joined in marriage with her virginity swelling.” Claudian, *Epithalamium of Palladius and Celerina*, verse 125: “He took her from her mother’s lap; mature virginity swells.”

386. Rivinus correctly says that, with Weitzius, the reading should be *infantia pubis*, rather than Fabricius’s *infantia pubes*. Victor’s first edition reads *infantia, pubes*. Weitzius printed *pubis* in the text, *pubes* in the index, and conjectured *pubis* in his emendations. Whether *pubes* may also be written *pubis* is an orthographical question. Barthius, Book XXIII of the *Adversaria*, chapter 19, thinks nothing should be changed, because “infancy already strives toward the sharpness of puberty,” since, though newly born, she was already mature. He reads *crevit*, not *crescit*, because she had not actually grown in body but had been formed at her proper stature as though she had already grown. The passage is better restored from the Vatican manuscript as *fit mox infantia pubes*, that is, “infancy immediately becomes puberty,” or “the first age of Eve immediately becomes mature.” The sense is the same if one reads *fecit infantia pubem*. It should also be noted that *lacte pio* occurs as in verse 224: “which cherishes with pious fire.”

Barthius, at the cited passage, explains: “Sleep was like childbirth, the conception of no seed.” But he thinks it should be read: “conception was from no seed”; and he adds: “This he repeats shortly afterward, wonderfully pleased with himself in the condensation of the pointed expressions,” namely in the following verse. Rivinus printed *erat parcus* and in his *Errata* corrected it to *erat parvus*, unless this itself is an error for *partus*. See Book II, verse 316.

Weitzius, with Victor, reads: “together, like a snowy nymph of the deep,” and understands Venus, who arose from the sea. *Profundum* means “the sea,” as Lucretius says in Book V: “He established heaven, earth, and the deep waters of the sea.” The sea is called snowy, like white-haired, foaming, or frothy; Weitzius supports this with many examples. The Vatican reading could be retained: “together, almost a nymph in the snowy deep.” The word *simul* seems redundant unless it means “entirely”; with that meaning I would better read *semel*. Cicero, *For Deiotarus*, chapter 3: “Although you are easily entreated, Caesar, you are accustomed to be entreated only once,” that is, “completely.” Raderus, in his commentary on Martial’s *Spectacles*, page 62, epigram 24 [or 26], says that Dracontius compares Eve’s beauty to a Nereid, and that one should read: “Naked in body, like a nymph of the snowy deep,” not “naked bodies,” a reading whose source I do not know.

Servius on *Aeneid* I.594 takes a different view.

Perhaps he intended to say “only of Eve”; for there is no reason to say that Adam alone is discussed here, since from verse 393 onward the preceding verses express only Eve’s beauty.

405. Perhaps the better reading is “And fill the earth, all-parent, with your seed,” with the Vatican manuscript, where *omnipotens* occurs instead of *omniparens*. Virgil, Book VI, verse 595: “Nursling of all-parent earth.” Lucretius, Book II, verse 705: “Through all-parent earths.” Apuleius, *On the World*: “the beauty of the all-parent world.” Nor is the word *Omnipotens* necessary: God and creator, who joined the two into one, said to them, “Increase and fill the earth,” etc.

Weitzius explains *ingeniti* as “not generated but created by God.” Rivinus writes *Sanguinis ingeniti natos* and explains it as “offspring of consanguineous posterity.” The common reading, “nourish born descendants,” scarcely yields a satisfactory sense. In the Vatican manuscript the sentence proceeds correctly: “Nourish descendants born from the same blood, and then restore new generations.” For this explains Moses’ word, “Multiply.”

407. Here too Sirmond seems to have followed Fabricius rather than his own manuscript, for Fabricius abandoned Victor’s edition, where *copulate* occurs, and inserted *reparate* to accommodate the meter. The Vatican and Azagrensis have *copulate* as well. Sirmond printed *reparate*. *Copula* has a long first syllable in the ancient poets, but Licentius, a contemporary of Saint Augustine, shortened it: “Love restrains and holds the bond of shared honor.” His poem survives among Augustine’s works in Augustine’s letter 26, elsewhere numbered 39. Licentius was a pagan; therefore we should not think such faults peculiar to Christian poets, but rather characteristic of the age—or even call the practice a fault in writers of otherwise approved usage.

From the Vatican manuscript I conjecture: “And while earth holds the sea, while air flies beneath the earth.” Meanwhile, one may say that the earth is partly supported by the sea and partly supports the sea itself. Lucan, Book I, verse 89: “While earth shall raise the sea, and air shall raise earth, and long labors shall roll the Sun,” which is explained so that the lower earth raises the waters, while the air contains and restrains the earth on every side like a center. Tertullian, Book III against Marcion: “This God restores before the eyes what had been reformed for man, for whom, being rich, he first made all things abundantly.” Read *primum*. See the note on verse 115.

429. Rivinus, with Weitzius and others, printed *pietatis opem*; but in the note he wrote *opus* instead of *opem*, perhaps by mistake.

430. In the printed editions, “The creator of eternity does not wish his creature to be nothing at all” makes no sense. From the Vatican and Azagrensis manuscripts I adopt *scit* instead of *vult*.

434. “God the judge,” as I said at verse 114.

435. In Book II, verse 695, God is called “good beneath piety”; here too one could read, with the Vatican manuscript, “good in continual piety,” as in the prayer for the twenty-first Sunday after Pentecost: “Guard us with continual piety.” But since the following verse has “good in simplicity,” I do not change this passage: “pious in goodness.”

436. Book III, verse 17: “Higher than the lofty.”

437. Perhaps: “and joyful pairs of roses.” *Ibant bini* (“they went in pairs”) is elegant, meaning two joined together.

440. Rivinus wishes to write: “With naked bodies, with hearts unaware of shame. What part…”—that is, how would they know which part of the limbs ought to be regarded as private, or what was honorable according to custom? One could also conjecture: “but their hearts, unaware of blush, did not know which part of the limbs ought to be regarded as private.” Whether one reads *ruboris* or *pudoris*, the same idea is suggested. Whiteness, as Rivinus notes, suggests divinity; shame and blush follow the works of darkness.

441. The Vatican reading, “What part,” can have this sense: why should some part of the body be regarded as more private?

444. The Vatican reading, *arrectibus*, may support Weitzius’s explanation of the following verse. But above, in verse 392, we read: “And gentle sleeps brought forth new affections.” Avitus, Book II, verse 238: “Adam, joyful, spread through the grasses of the field, sought the embraces and chaste kisses of his wife.”]

445. Rivinus suspects: “And there was no blush, when the source of shame ceased.” It would be easier to read *erat* (“was”), since “the source of shame was lacking.” Weitzius, explaining “when the source of shame stood,” understands bodily movements, which are indecent after the transgression but were not so beforehand. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book VII, chapter 20, explains it thus: “He used *staret origo* by a metaphor from springs, whose source, while standing still, sends forth no stream”; but unless something else is added, this explanation is obscure. Dracontius seems merely to have intended to convey Moses’ statement in Genesis 2:25: “Now both were naked, Adam namely and his wife, and they were not ashamed.” Thus you may rightly interpret “when the source of shame stood” as meaning “when they were naked”: that nakedness is now the source of shame. Or rather, I would say that honesty itself is called the source of shame; for shame, insofar as it is opposed to shamelessness, is good and proceeds from honesty, though honesty would not have produced shame had guilt not preceded it. Alcimus, book II, verse 21:

> They are not ashamed to see their naked bodies  
> And behold each other’s limbs; nor does unformed honesty  
> Sense anything disgraceful. Not human nature,  
> But guilt is the cause of shame.

And later, verse 274:

> For rebellious guilt shone forth, and bodies sensed  
> Indecent movements. Then for the first time, whether I should say  
> That shame, extinguished or born, surveyed their naked limbs, is doubtful.  
> The mind, now conscious of its own guilt, blushed.

Concerning the manner in which human beings would have propagated in the state of original integrity, theologians disagree among themselves. Some of the Fathers indeed taught that, in the state of innocence, human propagation would have occurred through creation rather than through natural generation. But the Scholastics, with Saint Thomas, hold as certain that marriage and the union of male and female would also have existed in that state. They add that bodily movements would have lacked disorder, though not pleasure and delight. Shame, however, arises from disorder. This is more or less the view of most of the Fathers.

447. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book VII, chapter 20, asserts that Dracontius unquestionably wrote *quibus omnia jussit Adonai* (“to whom Adonai commanded all things”), because in the Vulgate there is no “one who commanded.” In the margin, however, Barthius had noted *jus dat ad unum* (“he gives the right to one”). Neither reading pleases Rivinus, even if one reads *jusserit unus* or *unum* (“one [God] may have commanded” or “commanded one”). He prefers, with Sirmondus, *jussit ad usum* (“he commanded for use”), but thinks *cessit* (“yielded” or “granted”) better than *jussit*. Certainly, if a change must be introduced, I would prefer *quibus omnia cessa fuerunt* (“to whom all things were granted”), or *quibus omnia cessera auctor* (“to whom the author had granted all things”); for in truth, from verse 437, “They went through the flowers,” no mention of God occurs. Many Christian poets used *cedere* in the sense of “to grant,” a usage also found in Cicero and other ancient writers. On this meaning of the verb *cedo*, see Schroderus, *Observationes iuris civilis* 3.4, and Arntzenius, *Miscellanea*, chapter 5. But since the manuscripts consistently give *jussit*, one may try *quibus omnia jus erat uti* (“to whom it was lawful to use all things”), with *uti* taking an accusative, as in Cicero, Lucretius, and Cato; or *jus erat esse* (“to whom it was lawful to be”), that is, “to eat”; or *quibus omnia jus erat unum*; or *jussa subesse* (“to whom commanded things were subject”); or *jure licebant* (“to whom they were lawfully permitted”). For thus this verse answers the preceding one, “And they thought nothing unlawful for themselves.”

> What he had made and ordained to remain because of man,  
> The Lord does not wish to withdraw the aid of his mercy from him,  
> Nor to cast away his own creature. The maker of the ages knows  
> That absolutely no one but himself must everywhere be entreated, and that, unless he comes to help,  
> There will be no one to succor him.  
> Therefore God is good to man in his distress, author of all things:  
> Hope, craftsman, lord, ruler, leader, arbiter, judge,  
> [435] Pious in continual goodness, restrained in virtue,  
> Good in simplicity, and higher than every summit.  
> They went in pairs through the flowers and the whole rose-gardens,  
> Among fragrant harvests and green groves,  
> [Col. 0734A] Simply, in the manner of cattle or the custom of wild beasts,  
> [440] With naked bodies, but with hearts ignorant of what part of their limbs  
> [177] Ought to be regarded as more private.  
> How would the untutored know what was honorable according to custom?  
> What they thought of their fingers and eyes, they thought of every shameful part.  
> They joined public kisses everywhere with their affections,  
> [445] And there was no blush, when the source of shame stood,  
> And they thought absolutely nothing unlawful for themselves.  
> And rightly they believed this, since he had commanded all things for their use,  
> [Col. 0735A] [Col. 0735B]  
> [Note:]
