448. Above, verse 415: “Learn not the taste of one tree only.”

449. The Vatican reading is confirmed by a similar verse of Ovid, *Metamorphoses* 1.101:

> The earth itself, untouched and exempt,  
> Wounded by no hoe or plow, freely gave all things.

Virgil, however, book IX, verse 608, said that the earth was subdued by hoes.

452. In his emendations Weitzius reports that Hoeschelius communicated to him Simon Toelmann’s conjecture, who read and punctuated as follows: “Always in the absence of rain-bearing showers: the turf was the rain, and by the husband’s will the yield grew.” That is, in Paradise no rains had fallen; in place of rain, the turf itself was rain to itself through its own sap, and its fertility grew, as it were, at the husband’s discretion—that is, *feronia*, in Varro’s expression, or the fertility of the earth, whence the Fortunate Islands were called such because they are fertile and naturally productive. But Sirmondus’ text is sound, and it had already commended itself to Barthius before Sirmondus’ edition. “Rain-bearing rains” is expressed by hendiadys—one thing through two expressions—as in book III, verse 21. The thought is taken from Genesis 2:5: “For the Lord God had not caused it to rain upon the earth.” Alcimus, book I, verse 227:

> The nature of the place does not demand rains which it does not possess,  
> But the plants, content with their own dew, are endowed.

453. Rivinus conjectures *uber cespes* (“the fertile turf”) and *a genio crescit natura marito* (“nature grows through the husband’s generative power”). But *et arbitrio crescit fetura marito* (“and the offspring grows at the husband’s will”) is good; Barthius, book VII, chapter 20, explains *arbitrio marito* as “by natural inclination, innate pleasure.” To do something *arbitrio* is to do it willingly, not by command or compulsion. *Fetura* is used for *fetus*, which means not only the offspring of animals but also the fruit of trees and plants. Pliny, book XVII, chapter 22:

> Even if a vine in poor soil has strength, once cut back within the frame it remains there, and all its fruit comes forth below it.

Again, *fetura* occurs at verse 616: “Nor does the fleshly race diminish by producing offspring.” Dracontius says *arbitrio marito* because others commonly say that the earth produces shoots through “husband rains,” or through “the husband rain.” See *Pervigilium Veneris*, “concerning husband rains.” Marcus Victor, book II of *Genesis*, verse 166:

> Then the richest earth, its clods broken down,  
> Moved into diverse fruits, which, bringing them forth  
> Through husband rain, it dissolved through a putrid flow.

Others read *putrido* (“through rotting” or “fertile decay”).

454. That Paradise was given only to Adam and Eve, excluding the other living creatures, was shown above at verse 358, according to the opinion of certain authorities; for most hold otherwise.

456. In his list of errors Rivinus substituted *rapidas* (“swift”) for *placidas* (“gentle”), foolishly: both gentle birds and birds with bloodied mouths are excluded. Book II, verse 735: “Who may help both the gentle and the fierce.”

458. Above, verse 284: “Every kind of cattle is born, every kind of wild beast.”

460. Marcus Victor, book II: “That head of crimes, the world’s most hostile enemy.” Prudentius repeats the verse in book III of *Hamartigenia*, verse 203:

> Hence the native head of vices; from that prince  
> The origin of evil flowed.

Prudentius had earlier called God “the head of virtues.”

461. Tertullian, book I *Against Marcion*: “He carries about poison mixed with honey for the wretched.” Rivinus rejects *mollitum* (“softened”), which Weitzius printed in place of *mellitum* (“honeyed”), and adds that Barthius, on page 353 of the *Adversaria*, preferred *exire* (“to go out”) to *ex ore* (“from the mouth”), though Rivinus does not approve this. I do not find it in Barthius. Perhaps Rivinus saw a note in his manuscript containing that conjecture.

[Col. 0736D]

462. Barthius, in the passage cited, says that one must unquestionably read *Funera jam sub dente parans* (“already preparing death beneath the tooth”), which pleases Rivinus. *Munera* (“gifts”) in the old editions is plainly erroneous. From Azagrinus one may extract the plausible reading *Fundere de sub dente parans* (“preparing to pour forth from beneath the tooth”). It is not especially unusual for Latin writers to join two prepositions. Cangius gives examples of *de sub* in his dictionary from ancient *Acts of the Martyrs*, Gregory the Great, and others. Similar forms occur with *depost* or *de post*. Nor is *in ante* and *ex ante* dissimilar. Consult Holstenius on the acts of Saint Perpetua. Concerning poison beneath the tooth, see verse 287: “The gaping serpent foams in its palate,” because it vomits poison and gore.

463. For the sense to be coherent, one must read *Ergo ibi livor* (“there, therefore, was the devouring envy”), or in the following verse *habet* (“has”) must be taken for *habens* (“having”), or the period must continue through verse 469, “He foresaw,” and so forth. In place of *contusum* (“crushed”), *concussum* (“shaken”) may perhaps be better, as at verse 287: “The gaping serpent is brought forth, shaking the poison beneath its tooth.”

469. Book III, verse 404: “The third lot, which is without light.” Hilary, *On Genesis*, concerning God: “Who is without origin.” Marcus Victor, book I of *Genesis*: “The mind’s fall, bereft.” Thus also *inops rationis*, *consilii*, *humanitatis*—“bereft of reason, counsel, humanity.”

178. With the fruit of one tree forbidden under the law.

> The earth was not ordered to be subdued by the plow,  
> Nor by the hoe; nor was it compelled by any toil  
> To seek fruits, or to irrigate the fields from any spring.  
> With rain-bearing showers always absent, the fertile turf,  
> And by the husband’s will the produce, grew.  
> [Col. 0735C]

> [455] Constructed only for the shaded delights of human beings.  
> It does not support gentle birds, nor does it know how  
> To endure birds armed with bloodied mouths and claws.  
> It knows no kind of cattle, no kind of wild beast.  
> Only the serpent crept in there with its scaly body,  
> [460] [Col. 0736A] Steeped in the deceits of death, the source of every evil,  
> Preparing honeyed poison from its viperous mouth  
> Beneath its deadly tooth, with foaming palate.  
> 180. Therefore there ravenous envy, having beneath its modest brow  
> The poison of gnawing envy, crushed by its tooth,  
> [465] Seeks aid for crime, by which honesty may be deceived,  
> And simplicity fall, or trusting hearts incur guilt  
> Not through their own deceit, but through an everlasting disaster.  
> The serpent foresaw that the man’s strong heart could not be overcome,  
> Bereft of piety, and [foresaw] the wife’s ears—  
> [470] [Col. 0737A]

[Col. 0737B]

471. Victorius punctuates *corda*: *puellae ingerit o* (“he puts into the girl’s heart…”).

473. Vatican and Victorius: *semel* (“once”). Sirmondus: *simul* (“at once”).

475. Victorius: *p. rescisse d.*

[Col. 0737B]

476. Thus Sirmondus; in the Vatican manuscript: *e. spa . . . . procedere pejus Ausum quippe nefas tentat s. m.*

477. Vatican manuscript: *aut suum quippe.*

478. Vatican manuscript: *f. vinctum*. Victorius distinguishes: *insontem jam n. f. victum Circumventa perit*.

480. Vatican manuscript: *sic*; Victorius: *circumscriptum s.*; Sirmondus: *circumscripta [Col. 0738A] s.*

481. This verse and the following ones through verse 539, “To crime,” are absent from Victorius; they are, however, fifty-eight verses found in Sirmondus, the Vatican manuscript, and Azagrinus.

482. Vatican manuscript: *m. futuros.*

484. Sirmondus: *s. et m.*; Vatican manuscript: *sed m.*

485. Vatican manuscript: *putant patremque et prolis o.*

486. Thus the Vatican manuscript, where *digesti* occurs for *digestio*. Sirmondus: “And that which had previously been the shameful digestion of the belly.”

[Col. 0737B]

470. With Silius, book VII, verse 260, one might say: “And he attacks their minds with the poison of deceit.”

471. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book VII, chapter 20, takes *adit* as “he receives,” as in *adire manum* in Plautus. But here *adire* is rightly used for “to approach” or “to attack.” Barthius reads and punctuates: “The treacherous one approaches—alas!—the tender heart; he puts food into the girl’s mouth.”

475. Weitzius, following Victorius, reads: “She regretted having tasted the food”—that is, having learned it by tasting—“and the losses of the completed period of time are thought to proceed toward something worse. For, having been seduced, she attempts a daring crime against her husband.” Here *quippe* is trisyllabic according to Barthius, who asserts that in this and several other places verses have been transposed; their restoration requires particular notation. Rivinus prefers our reading and explains it: “The crime attempted has advanced toward something worse.” But he does not explain what is meant by “the losses of the completed periods of time.” Perhaps Dracontius’ meaning is that Eve considered it a loss that she had previously abstained, and therefore advanced voluntarily toward something worse.

477. Marcus Victor, book I, verse 413 of *Genesis*:

> Having now learned through experience the associations of guilt,  
> She seeks her husband, unwary and ignorant of deceit,  
> And attacks him by the same art through which she previously perished.

478. Prudentius, *Dittochaeon*, verse 3: “And he stained innocent Adam with sordid marks.” Barthius reads *victum*: “Circumvented, she presses him; deceived by hope, she tricks him.” For Eve thought that, if she invited her husband into sin, she would lighten her own burden. Rivinus saw in the margin a manuscript note in which Barthius had conjectured *femina rictum* (“the woman opens her mouth”). Rivinus himself punctuates and reads: “And she takes the innocent. Now the guilty woman, having surrounded her victim, attacks him; but having been outwitted, she deceives him.” But *petit victum* (“she attacks the conquered man”) is less satisfactory, since the conquered man does not ask when she attacked him.

479. In place of *sed* (“but”), *et* (“and”) would be better. I would also gladly read either “The deceived woman perishes, and the deceiver tricks him,” or “The surrounded woman perishes, and, while deceiving, she tricked him.” Orentius, verse 340, concerning Eve:

> You, quickly deceived; you, quickly deceiving.

The *Commonitorium* of this poet Orentius—or Orientius, or Orontius—likewise a Spaniard, is learned and graceful, though corrupted and depraved in many places. Emmanuel Joseph Fernandez Vinjoy rendered it into Spanish verse, Madrid, quarto, 1790; on the title page he calls Orentius a saint, though I do not know on what authority. Orentius’ and Dracontius’ statement that Eve deceived Adam, captured the innocent man, and tricked him does not conflict with the Apostle’s words in 1 Timothy 2:14: “And Adam was not deceived, but the woman, having been deceived, was in transgression.” For most Fathers and interpreters admit that Adam was in some sense deceived by Eve, although they interpret the Apostle’s words in different ways so that they do not appear contrary to Adam’s deception. It seems probable to me that Saint Paul is showing that Adam was less exposed to deception than Eve, because she was first deceived by the serpent, whereas he was deceived by a woman who had already been deceived. Ambrose, book IV *On Paradise*: “The woman was deceived first, and she herself deceived the man.”

480. Tertullian, book II *Against Marcion*, chapter 7: “Finally, suppose that God intervened; suppose that he revoked the freedom of choice while calling him back from the tree, while keeping the very deceiver, the serpent, from contact with the woman.” Rivinus was dissatisfied with the common reading because these verses connect poorly both with one another and with what follows. He therefore wrote: “Now the guilty woman has conquered the victim, and the deceiving serpent triumphs with impunity,” taking *triumpho* passively and entirely omitting the preceding verse’s *circumventa* (“having been surrounded”). But the text restored by us is clear and easy. The only possible objection is that the following verse gives the reason why the serpent will not triumph with impunity, although nothing more is subsequently said about the serpent. This difficulty affects both readings; therefore this verse, in which the serpent is discussed, ought rather to be moved elsewhere than the preceding verse, *circumventa perit* (“the surrounded woman perishes”). In any case, the following verse, “For after,” begins the account of the punishment inflicted on Adam and Eve. The serpent did not triumph with impunity because God tempered anger with forgiveness and also decreed their resurrection after death.

483. *Sapit* is used for *scit* (“knows”); the passage explains what the tree of the knowledge of good and evil effected in Adam. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book LVI, chapter 5, notes that *sapere* in the sense of “to feel,” “to know,” or “to judge” is characteristic of writers of declining Rome, and cites Augustine in support. Yet the same verb *sapere* is sometimes used by ancient writers in such a way that, even if it does not mean “to know,” it is certainly not far from that meaning. Some modern languages now derive their word for “to know” from *sapere*, such as Spanish *saber* and Italian *sapere*.

484. *Simplicitas* (“simplicity”) occurs for “innocence” in book II, verse 804. At the moment when Adam recognized simplicity, or what was good and honorable, he fell from grace and lost the good. But what of this? Did he previously not know what was honorable? Certainly he did not fail to know it. Rather, through sin he came to know by experience the good he had lost and the evil into which he had fallen, as most Fathers and theologians explain. There is also a considerable question concerning the knowledge Adam possessed of supernatural mysteries; it is more probable that this was true supernatural faith.

486. Rivinus acknowledged that Sirmondus’ text was false and restored it by conjecture: “And the part that was the shameful discharge of the belly.” In truth, *egestio* (“discharge”) would properly suit this passage. Caelius Aurelianus, book V *On Chronic Diseases*, chapter 10, section 8, used *egestio per ventrem* for the expulsion of matter through the belly. But *digestio ventris* (“digestion of the belly”) is not improperly used for the expulsion itself, which is its effect. Macrobius, book VII of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 4:

> Thus the first digestion occurs in the stomach, the power of the digestive organ turning whatever has been taken in into juice; its dregs are the refuse, which flows through the intestines through the lower opening, and evacuation is brought about by the function of the fourth power, whose name is ἀποκριτική (*apokritikē*, “separative” or “excretory”).

> He attacks beneath a pious voice, with a malicious speech.  
> The treacherous one approaches—alas!—the tender heart of the girl,  
> And places in her mouth foods filled with deadly destruction.  
> Once these have been taken in, the eyes of the heart are opened,  
> And, mingled with good things, the doctrine of evils became clear.  
> [475] She regretted not having known the food, and the losses are thought  
> Of the completed span of time to proceed toward something worse:  
> [181] For, seduced, she attempts a daring crime against her husband.  
> And now the guilty woman captures the innocent man as her victim.  
> Surrounded, she perishes, but having been outwitted, she deceives him,  
> [480] [Col. 0738A] Nor does the deceiving serpent triumph with impunity,  
> For after the young man, his mind violated, had eaten  
> The deadly food unlawfully, destined for death,  
> [182] Soon the unhappy man knows what is wrong and what is honorable:  
> Simplicity is recognized, but soon it is driven from his heart.  
> [485] He thinks the shameful limbs are the part that gives rise to offspring,  
> And that which had been the digestion of the belly is considered shameful.  
> [Col. 0739A] [Col. 0739B]

487. Sirmondus: *ipsa* (“itself”); Vatican manuscript: *illa* (“that”).

489. Thus the Vatican manuscript, but *lumina* (“eyes”) for *limina* (“thresholds”). Sirmondus: “The mouth, the entrance of death, then brought forth and received [it].” In Azagrinus: *aditus* (“entrance”). The rest agrees with Sirmondus, apparently.

490. Thus the Vatican manuscript, but *lumina* (“eyes”) for *limina* (“thresholds”). Sirmondus: *Lingua malisuada, s. e. a. limina mortis.* (“The evil-persuading tongue … the thresholds of death.”)

491. Sirmondus: *omnem* (“every”); Azagrinus: *hominem* (“man”); likewise the Vatican manuscript. Conjecturally: *homines* (“human beings”).

492. Azagrinus: *perdiderat* (“had lost,” singular). Sirmondus and Vatican manuscript: *perdiderant* (“had lost,” plural). Vatican manuscript: *comessit* (“ate”).

494. Sirmondus: *jam foedos artus* (“already foul limbs”). Vatican and Azagrinus: *fecundos artus* (“fertile limbs”).

495. Thus the Vatican manuscript; in Azagrinus: “They regard the unlawful as lawful”; Sirmondus: “They regard the unlawful as lawful.”

497. Vatican manuscript: *s. quos j.*

499. Vatican manuscript: *Tunc m. o., cum quaerunt p. l.* Sirmondus: *Hinc m. o., quod credunt p. l.*

500. Thus the Vatican manuscript, but *tuum quocunque* (“your whatever”) for *suum quodcunque* (“his whatever”). Sirmondus: “Then whatever belongs to God, to whom all created things are open.”

501. Vatican manuscript: “And deservedly, because he makes all things…” The remainder is missing.

502. Sirmondus: *a. calidos q. m.*; Vatican manuscript: *a. calybs quem m.* Hence: *chalybis quae* (“which rust of steel…”).

503. Sirmondus thus; Azagrinus: *r. labens quae*; Vatican manuscript: *r. latens quod v.*

504. Vatican manuscript: *excedat quod missa*.

505. Azagrinus: *hinc non.*

506. Sirmondus: *promittens* (“promising”); Vatican manuscript: *promittit* (“he promises”).

488. On the evil tongue, see the note at verse 57: “What the evil tongue of man keeps silent.”

489. Rivinus suspected in Sirmondus’ text: “The mouth, the entrance of death, then brought forth and received.” The Vatican reading is more accurate. I understand the harmful part to be the mouth, the entrance of death, which the mouth both brought forth and received, as well as the tongue and ears; or else the harmful part is the tongue, which the mouth—for the mouth itself is the entrance of death—both brought forth and received. For the first sin was committed more by the mouth than by the tongue. The ears were the thresholds of death because Eve listened to the serpent’s voice, while Adam was deceived by Eve’s persuasion.

490. The meter is better served, with the Vatican manuscript, by *Lingua suada mali* (“the tongue persuading evil”) than by Sirmondus’ *Lingua malisuada*. Perhaps Sirmondus intended to divide it as *mali suada* (“the persuader of evil”). Just as Dracontius more than once made *suetus* trisyllabic, so here he uses *suada* as trisyllabic. Apuleius, at the end of book VI of the *Metamorphoses*: “the majesty that persuades the divine dream.”

492. Adam’s sin is said to have generated shame in one sense and extinguished it in another. See the note at verse 445. They had therefore lost the virtue that produces shame, yet they were still affected by natural shame, which is not good unless it proceeds from the virtue of modesty. They had lost it through cruel deceit, because verse 467 said: “Let them incur it, not through their own deceit.”

[Col. 0740B]

494. Sirmondus’ reading is not displeasing. But *fecundos artus* (“fertile limbs”), in place of *fecundantes* (“fertilizing”), is the more accurate text, since he earlier said *prolis origo* (“the source of offspring”). “The recognized limbs give guilt” means “it is guilt to recognize or see the naked limbs.”

495. What had previously been lawful they think unlawful; and what would truly have been lawful, had guilt not preceded it, they believe to be wicked—for example, nakedness. The Adamites were insane, since they cited Adam’s example in support of nakedness.

497. Compare book III, verse 561: “As though with sacrilegious mind I should think that we do not know all things.”

499. The meaning is the same in both readings. But from the Vatican reading I derive another text that pleases me much more: “Then they are more exposed, when they believe that God, who sees everything, can be hidden by any concealment.” On *obtentus* (“concealment”), see Virgil, book XI, verse 66: “They shade the built-up couches with the concealment of foliage.” On *ostensus* (“exposed”), Lucan, book II, verse 192: “So that this crime of Sulla, and the exposed slaughter, might please.” Marcus Victor, book I of *Genesis*:

> Then, fleeing the Lord, can you escape?  
> Then did you hope to lie hidden from him who sees all?  
> Though you lie in vast darkness, you will never be concealed.

See Alcimus, book III of *Genesis*.

501. Sirmondus punctuates *jubendo* (“by commanding”): “He does not escape.” Rivinus notes that *in jubendo* has an entirely absolute sense. The same argument concerning divine infinite knowledge is given in book III, verse 10.

504. From the Vatican manuscript I conjecture either *Exedat, et quae massa semel* (“what mass may consume [it] once”), or *quae missa semel fornace liquescant* (“what things, once sent into the furnace, may melt”).

505. The passage concerns those who know where metals lie before the earth has been dug up, and who seek gems in the rocks.

507. Statius, book III of the *Silvae*, verse 84: “Wandering sailors and explorers of the deep.” He calls fishermen “explorers of the deep.”

509. *Sperare* (“to hope”) is also used of fearing the evils we imagine, or even of believing that what we do not want will occur. *Spondet* (“he promises”), which Sirmondus has, is also used of prophets and oracles; but I find no examples of it in connection with future evils that are foretold.

> Yet the one that was more harmful in the whole body  
> Was the mouth, the entrance of death, which it brought forth and received,

> The Omnipotent had seen that human beings had learned shame,

512. Since both Azagrinus and the Vatican manuscript have *ante*, I retain it. Perhaps the preceding verse should read *undas* (“waters”), for the word is obscure in the sequence of letters in the Vatican manuscript. The sense would be: “The water-wise man promises waters, pointing out springs before the taste,” or, with the common reading *undae*: “The water-wise man promises springs, indicating beforehand the taste of water.” The printed editions punctuate *saporem*: “Having observed the earth once, without any breath…” But it seems better to punctuate: “Indicating beforehand the taste, having observed the earth once.” “Without any breath” should then be connected with *inspecta tellure semel*, so that a new period begins with “Without any breath”; this punctuation also pleased Rivinus in his list of errors. A *providus undae*, that is, someone skilled at examining water veins, was called an *aquilex*. Pliny, book XXVI, chapter 6: “Where wild coltsfoot grows, they believe water lies beneath it; this is a sign used by water-finders.”

515. On this verse, see prolegomenon 7, where Isidore’s passage concerning it is examined. From the entire context it is clear that one must read *praedicit* (“foretells”), not *praecidit* (“cuts off”), as Galladius wished. Examples are given of people powerful in the art of prediction, both in the preceding and following verses. Lucan, book IX, from verse 893 onward, says much about the Psylli; concerning this art of prediction he says only:

> Then, bending over the pallid wounds,  
> He licks them, drawing out the poison with his mouth,  
> And dries the limbs with his teeth. Holding the death  
> Extracted from the frozen body, he spits it out;  
> And the Psylli can already identify even by taste the venom of any serpent  
> Whose bite one has survived.

Others read “know the venom.” Pliny, book VII, chapter 2, reports that besides the Psylli there was also in the Hellespont, near Parium, a people who were accustomed to relieve snakebites by touch and to draw poisons from the body by laying on their hands. Some think that the Psylli possessed not a special power or knowledge but merely boldness, since snake venom harms through the wound, not by taste. Celsus taught this long ago in book V, chapter 27, and modern physicians confirm it in detail. The Marsi are compared with the Psylli; Alcimus, book II:

> Hence the Marsi are praised for what they can do through song,  
> When by silent art they bring forth fierce serpents  
> From hiding.

Add Pliny at the passage cited.

520. See Matthew 16:2 and following.

521. “Viperous nation” is taken from Matthew 12:34, “brood of vipers.”

[Col. 0742B]

524. With the Vatican manuscript one might read *probatum*, that is, “it is proved that human beings know future things.” But *probatur* seems more characteristic of Dracontius, as at verse 385: “By which it is shown to be suitable.” See the note at book II, verse 26.

525. Rivinus more correctly thinks that, if one reads “Nor is it strange, if the image of Christ perceives a future cloud, when many animals warn us of what will come,” nothing here concerns Christ’s coming. In the common text, however, the sense is coherent even without thinking of Christ’s coming. Dracontius says that a human being foretells future things; nor is it strange that a human being, who is the image of Christ, foresees what will happen, since many animals warn us of what is to come. Man is the image of Christ, as at verse 338: “the heavenly image.”

527. It is preferable to read *bucula, rana* (“heifer, frog”) with the Vatican manuscript rather than *ardea, rana* (“heron, frog”) with Sirmondus and the others. Virgil, book I of the *Georgics*, verse 363, teaches that signs of rising winds are taken from the heron:

> And the heron leaves the familiar marshes  
> And flies high above the cloud.

But shortly afterward, concerning signs of rain—the subject also treated by Dracontius—Virgil writes:

> Never has rain harmed the unsuspecting;  
> Nor did cranes flee it as it rose from the lowest valleys,  
> Nor did the heifer, gazing toward the sky, draw in the air  
> Through her wide nostrils, nor did the chattering swallow  
> Fly around the pools, nor did frogs sing their ancient complaint  
> In the mud, nor did the ant, wearing a narrow path  
> Through hidden chambers, carry her eggs out more often,  
> Nor did the great rainbow drink, nor did the army  
> Of crows, leaving their feeding, resound with dense wings.

Dracontius has compressed all these signs into this single verse. Therefore I confidently changed *sues* (“swine”), which appears in all printed editions and manuscripts, to *grues* (“cranes”), which Virgil mentions first. Dracontius had the whole of Virgil’s teaching on weather signs before his eyes, as is plainly evident from the preceding and following verses. Even when he expresses the earlier signs in Christ’s name, he nevertheless borrows certain things from Virgil, such as what Virgil says at verse 424:

> But if you observe the swift sun and the following moons  
> In order, tomorrow’s hour will never deceive you.

Dracontius has: “Winter does not deceive.” Cicero also agrees about the heifer in book I of *On Divination*, in the section on weather signs:

> And the soft-footed cattle, gazing at the light of heaven,  
> Drew humid fluid from the air through their nostrils.

Compare the notes at verse 54 and following of this book I.

529. Someone cited by Rivinus attempted: “Why do I call lifeless things as witnesses? Do you see fire sparkle in a burning lamp, with mushrooms growing?” The sense seemed clearer to Rivinus, who nevertheless restored it as follows: “Indeed lifeless things”—that is, they foretell rains—“when oil sparkles in a burning lamp, with mushrooms growing in the rain.” Dracontius imitates Virgil, book I of the *Georgics*, verse 390:

> Nor did the girls, carding their nighttime wool,  
> Fail to know winter when they saw the oil  
> Sparkling in a burning shell and rotten mushrooms growing together.

From these verses, compared with the manuscripts, I derived the reading that I published. When the air begins to become humid, the ash that usually exits with the smoke is held back by the thickness of the air and settles on the lamp, producing the appearance of mushrooms, as Virgil’s commentators explain. See also Apuleius, book II of the *Metamorphoses*, before the middle.

> If rainy winter or rocky rain presses down,  
> It is not hidden from the farmer. The water-wise man beneath the earth

> While the hisses are silent and no serpent has yet been noticed,

532. The passage returns to what he had said at verse 498. Rivinus conjectures: “Of rock; or, woven from fallen leaves, a garment—does the sight obstruct God?” *An* (“or”) would be correct, but the sense is the same; the meaning is “or from the leaves,” and so forth.

533. Sirmondus published “To obstruct the sight of God,” but that would be scarcely Latin. Rivinus conjectured “To restrain God’s sight.” From the Vatican manuscript I conjecture “To obstruct the One who looks, God.” One might also read “The sights obstruct God,” for formerly *aspectus, aspecti* was declined in this manner, according to Nonius, chapter 8, no. 15, who cites two examples from Accius.

Rivinus reads the remainder as follows:

> Then, the thing created by a voice [reading uncertain], he confesses that he nevertheless sinned through a woman's crime;  
> The unhappy husband casts the deeds back upon his wife,  
> And, though guilty, makes excuse, but is not held to be acquitted.

But in that form the participle … [Col. 0743D] etc.

Sirmondus reads and punctuates:

> Then he acknowledges guilt aloud, confessing that he himself sinned through a woman's crime.  
> The unhappy husband casts the deeds back upon his wife,  
> And, though guilty, excuses himself, but proceeds though not to be acquitted.

And thus the participle, etc.

These lines become much clearer as we restore them:

> Then, recalled by his voice, Adam, the unhappy husband, recalled by the voice of God—

This is elegantly said of one who is forcibly brought back to the place from which he had fled. Adam confesses that he himself sinned, induced by the woman; and therefore the fault “overflows into his wife,” that is, he partly shifts the sin onto his wife. *Redundo* with the accusative, as Statius says in *Silvae* IV.3.71 of a river: “It overflows from its broad jaws.” “Into his wife” would be more elegant, but “in his wife” is not poetically objectionable. Lucretius, *De rerum natura* VI.712: “The Nile rises in summer and overflows into the fields.” See Gifanius in the *Index*.

The Vatican reading is graceful:

> And, though guilty, he accuses; but he acted as one not to be acquitted,

which the copyists, not understanding it, corrupted. Adam not only excused himself but also accused his wife, although he himself was guilty. The words “but he acted as one not to be purged” are added; “but he acted as one not purged” would be better. The verb *agere* properly applies to those who legally pursue their own affairs and bring an action against others; in this sense an “actor” is opposed to a defendant. Thus Adam, who was guilty and could not be acquitted, arrogated to himself the role of plaintiff.

[Col. 0744C] 537. Perhaps one should read “Conscious of the ruin, he took a companion,” or “Conscious of the ruin, he took a female companion.” But *cordis* is not bad.

538. *Conscius* used absolutely for “the guilty party” occurs in Plautus, Seneca in the tragedies, and other authors. Rivinus reads *ceu femina posset* (“as though a woman could”); other editions and manuscripts have *possit* (“could”).

539. Book II, verse 401: “For savage expiations.” Book III, verse 263: “Such savage expiations.”

540. In Fabricius there is an error, *revelare* (“to reveal”), which Weitzius had already corrected to *relevare* (“to lighten”). The first edition of Victorius also has *relevare*. It means “to lessen, to make light.” Pliny, *Panegyricus* 19: “So that you might intensify the zeal and labor of all, as an exactor, and lighten them, as a participant and associate.”

541. Book II, verse 467:

> Every completed crime looks back to its author,  
> Involves all his associates and accomplices.

Compare also Book II, verse 419:

> Punishments do not unite those whom guilt has not joined.

Lucan, Book V, verse 289:

> Caesar was my leader on the waters of the Rhine; here he was my companion.  
> Crime makes equal those whom it stains.

Arator, Book I, verse 472, concerning Sapphira:

> The impious wife falls, struck by an equal punishment,  
> Because from a single crime a shared wickedness arises  
> Whenever agreement makes an earlier crime one’s own.

543. Weitzius asserts that he restored *nam* in place of *non*. In the first edition of Victorius and in Fabricius’s second edition I find *nam*. Perhaps Fabricius’s copies differ.

545. Book II, verse 697: “The judgment of heaven is light.”

546. I think one should read *Supplicium felix* (“a fortunate punishment”), for in all these verses there is a pointed contrast:

> A judgment severe in piety,  
> A sentence alike of life and death,  
> A fortunate punishment by which death is both given and denied,  
> Vital vengeance restrained at the threshold of death.

547. One may also read *limite mortis* (“at the boundary of death”). The meaning is vengeance against human life; for a person burdened with so many miseries, it is a kind of happiness to die, as the following verse explains, and verse 555 explains more fully:

> And death is given as the limit of life, together with the end of evils.

The same result follows if one says that “living vengeance” is restrained by the boundary of death; this seems preferable to me.

548. Perhaps: *vivere pejor* (“living is worse”), namely, punishment.

Could almighty God be unable to know the hiding places

of the rock, and the garment woven from fallen leaves

obstruct the One who looks, God? Then, recalled by his voice,

he confesses that he himself sinned through the woman’s crime,

[535] the unhappy husband; the deed rebounds upon his wife,

188 and, though guilty, he accuses, but acted as one not to be acquitted.

And so, conscious of the ruin, he enlisted an associate as a companion for solace in the calamity; as though a woman could,

by joining two in the horrendous crime, or in the savage

[540] expiations of death, lighten the guilt through punishment.

The unhappy man believed; but an equal sentence condemns

[Col. 0744A] those whom equal guilt holds: the interval between them

is only one of time, for a common cause binds both.

God’s judgment rises with severe compassion,

[545] and a sentence alike of life and death is pronounced.

An unhappy punishment, by which death is both granted and denied;

189 vital vengeance is restrained at death’s threshold.

The punishment of dying was cruel, but living was worse.

They lose leisure and pleasures, and learn toil,

[550] those who, with God as cultivator, had possessed the fruit of the earth,

[Col. 0745A]

551. Sirmondus has this form; the Vatican manuscript has “the Lord who had never divided the farmer”; perhaps the reading is *quae non* (“which had never”).

552. The Vatican has “another sower and reaper”; others read “another author, reaper.”

553. The Vatican has “they offend this pious one”; Sirmondus, “they offend now”; the Azagruntine manuscript, “they offend then”; Victorius, “they offend this one.” In the Vatican, *ortu* (“rising”) appears instead of *horto* (“garden”).

554. The Azagruntine manuscript has this form; Sirmondus, “the perpetual flower has no …”; Victorius, “the perpetual flower neither has …”; the Vatican, “the perpetual flower, nor is there under the law of the guilty.”

556. Thus the Vatican; in the others, “who always …”

558. Thus the Vatican; the others have “the vigorous heart revives.”

559. The Vatican has “rest or certainty.”

[Col. 0745B]

551. Victorius agrees with Sirmondus, but Fabricius printed *cum* instead of *quam* through an error into which Weitzius also fell. Rivinus suspects *Agricolae vomis cum nondum verteret agrum* (“with the farmer’s plow, while he had not yet turned the field”). Barthius, *Adversaria* VII.20, considers this verse spurious; once removed, the statement is perfectly clear. From the Vatican one may conjecture: “The Lord farmer, whom he had never yet seen.” The words of Genesis 2:5 are: “And there was no man to work the ground.”

552. From the Vatican’s error *alter*, I prefer to read *altor* (“nourisher”) rather than *auctor* (“author”), despite the printed editions. See Book III, verse 315, with its note. Cicero, *De natura deorum* II.34: “The universe is, so to speak, the sower, planter, parent, educator, and nourisher of all things governed by nature.”

553. Rivinus conjectures: “Both these offend the pious one,” or “God,” taking *haec* for *hi*. The Vatican reading proceeds correctly in meaning.

554. The Vatican reading may be emended as follows:

> They are driven from the garden  
> Of perpetual flowers, nor is there any shelter under the law of the guilty.

For *est*, writers of a later age, such as Commodianus, Sedulius, and others, use *adest*.

[Col. 0745C] 555. Prudentius, *Hymn V, Peristephanon*, verse 527:

> The supreme outcome of death has provided an end to evils.

558. Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXV.10, explains *recidivus* as “restored to life,” like a shoot sprouting again from a severed root. He confirms this meaning with another passage of Dracontius and with Paulinus, *To Nicetas*, concerning Christ:

> Abel, restored to life, feeds the lambs redeemed  
> At the price of his shed blood.

Rivinus objects that in this passage of Dracontius *recidivus* comes from *recido*, not from *caedo*. Yet there is no doubt that *recidivus* means “renewed,” whether it derives from *caedo*, as many think, or from *recido*, meaning “to return”; for things that return or come back are called *recidere*. Virgil, Book X, verse 58:

> While the Teucrians seek Latium and walls restored to life;

where Servius explains the word as “renewed” and seems to derive *recidivus* from *caedo*. Others less suitably explain it as walls that have fallen twice.

Strictly speaking, the second syllable of *recidivus* should be long if the word derives from *caedo*, but quantity often varies in derivatives. Charisius recognizes this distinction between *recidivus* and *redivivus*: we call things *rediviva* when they return after destruction, and *recidiva* when they are restored after their own fall. If this distinction were always observed, the reading here should rather be:

> Which is more truly restored to life.

The printed editions have “revives with a vigorous heart,” which may be understood of the soul surviving the body’s death. In the Vatican I understand “with renewed hearts” as referring also to the resurrection of bodies, which will be granted to righteous people for eternal happiness. Dracontius later discusses this resurrection at length, beginning at verse 621.

559. Rivinus thinks this verse belongs to Eugenius of Toledo, who says in Epigram 4, “Peace is rest for the weary, peace finally the sure [end] of labor.” I would prefer “the goal of labor.” Since Dracontius’ verse in the Vatican has *requies vel certa* (“rest or certainty”), it would not be unreasonable to read *requies vel meta* (“rest or goal”), taking *vel* for *et* (“and”); the meaning would be “it is,” even though the verb is not expressed. Thus in verse 555:

> And death is given as the limit of life, together with the end of evils.

I do not agree with Rivinus that this verse belongs to Eugenius: it exists in both Victorius and the Vatican, where I think there is no correction by Eugenius. [Col. 0746B] Eugenius therefore imitated Dracontius in that epigram.

As for the interpretation of this verse and the next two, Barthius should be heard, *Adversaria* LIV.9. Michael Glycas, Book I of the *Annals*, agrees with other ancient Fathers that, without the aid of death, the first parent after the Fall would have continued forever in the miseries of this life that he deserved; but that God, taking pity on his infinite sufferings, introduced death both as punishment and as consolation. Glycas produces Basil, Chrysostom, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Anastasius of Sinai as witnesses and foundations for this assertion … But, even if these authorities are accepted, we must know that after we have died following a dissolute life we do not in the least put an end to our evils; rather, we continue our crimes and their punishment together in another death, which will never die. On this matter John of Salisbury writes very well in Book XI, chapter 27, of *The Frivolities of Courtiers*, quoting an older ecclesiastical writer:

> There is one thing that must be avoided with all the strength of mind and body. What is it, you ask? Shamefulness and every form of dishonor. For these make death not the end of evils but the link between what precedes and what follows.

Dracontius also set this same doctrine before us … “The death of worldly people,” etc.

Barthius, *Adversaria* VII.20, explaining the verse “And a saving end is granted to one who lives badly,” says: “To grant is to affect someone with a benefit.” Death is given to mortals as a kind of benefit, so that at last they may become participants in salvation. Elsewhere, however, as Rivinus observes—or perhaps Barthius wrote this by hand in relation to this passage—one should read:

> And to one who lives badly, it grants an end for salvation,

which Rivinus rejects, explaining *fine salutis* as “for the sake of salvation.” I think the meaning still remains obscure. For if death is rest from labors only for those who live well, how is an end granted to one who lives badly “for the sake of salvation,” or so that he may become a participant in salvation? And what, I ask, does it mean that death continues whatever harms, whether evil or good? For whom does the good harm? And if death continues whatever harms, why is it given to one who lives badly, either for the sake of salvation or as an end?

Rivinus would prefer:

> Continuing whatever kills, whether evil or good.

But the difficulty is the same whether one reads *necat* (“kills”) or *nocet* (“harms”). I therefore think Dracontius means that death is rest from the labors of this life and is granted to a person living badly—that is, living amid misery and suffering—as a benefit and favor, because death brings these troubles of life to an end.

The verse “Continuing whatever harms” could be joined with the following verse, so that God is the one who continues human lives and whatever harms them, whether adversity or prosperity. Unless one prefers to read:

> Whatever harms, whether evil or good, is continuous,

or *continuans* in the neuter sense, that is, “whatever is continuous,” whether evil or good, harms. This latter interpretation pleases me most: the meaning would be that even the good things of this life, if they were perpetual, would bring satiety, since they are not truly good. Then in the following verse one could read:

> Alone is the eternal ruler good, and the author,  
> The triune God, is virtue.

Matthew 19:17: “Why do you ask me about the good? There is one who is good, God.”

[Col. 0746A] The grievous life of human beings is withdrawn by death’s assault,

190 which is more truly renewed when hearts are converted.

The death of worldly people is a sure rest from labors,

Continuing whatever harms, whether evil or good.

[Col. 0747A]

563. Thus the Vatican; others have: “God is one virtue, a triune God, altogether both three and one.”

[Col. 0747B] 565. The Azagruntine manuscript has “no presumption deceived”; the Vatican: “Nor did the pure mind deceive anyone whom it had presumed upon”; Sirmondus: “No presumption refuted.”

566. The Vatican has: “The effect of what was to live would not be absent at that same time.”

567. The Azagruntine manuscript and Victorius have: “With whom many beginnings speak through the senses.” Sirmondus: “With whom both the senses and many beginnings speak.” The Vatican: “With whom, through the sense, mute beginnings speak from the heart.”

568. Sirmondus: “And, while the voice is silent, speech sounds above the upper air.” Victorius: “And speech sounds above the upper air while the voice is restrained.” The Vatican: “And, while the tongue is silent, speech sounds beneath the earth in serenity”; in the margin, *sermo* (“speech”) is given in place of *sereno* (“serenity”).

569. Victorius: “This mind.”

[Col. 0748A] 570. Sirmondus and Victorius: “He himself then, the author of himself.” The Azagruntine manuscript: “God himself then.” The Vatican: “He himself, God, then.”

[Col. 0748B] 571. The Vatican: “Let them rule in the world.”

572. Victorius: “Is held under the law.”

573. The Vatican: “But whatever the fertile earth bears, whatever the green grass produces, whatever the garden brings forth.”

574. The Vatican: “Whatever the harvests produce as ears, whatever the tree bears on its branches.”

575. The Vatican: “Whatever the vines produce as buds.”

576. Sirmondus: “Whatever the rivers send forth, whatever the springs pour out, whatever the sea billows.” The Azagruntine manuscript has the same, but *aequor* (“sea”) in place of *amnis* (“river”); Victorius likewise, but “the sea pours forth” in place of “the sea billows.”

577. Sirmondus and Victorius punctuate “the wave of the sea, which …”; the Vatican has *tundat* (“strikes”) in place of *tundunt* (“strike”). All have *freti* (“of the sea”).

[Col. 0747B]

563. This verse was discussed in the preface, no. 109 and following, where I spoke of Dracontius’ orthodox doctrine against Arian impiety. See the note on Book II, verse 69.

564. Epistle of James 1:17: “Every good gift and every perfect gift is descending from above, from the Father of lights.”

565. *Praesumptio* (“presumption”) is used by Tertullian, Sulpicius Severus, Apuleius, and similar writers for boldness, excessive confidence, or stubborn preparation of mind. Sometimes, however, it is taken in a favorable sense for trust.

566. From the Vatican conjecture arises: “The one who was to live was not deceived; effects are not lacking at the same time,” or “the victor,” etc.

567. Rivinus thinks the reading was: “Whom the mind and the mute beginnings of the senses speak.” Barthius, Book VII, chapter 20, reads: “With whom both the senses and the mute beginnings speak,” and explains it of the elements of all things created by God. Rivinus, on the contrary, thinks that silent prayers proceeding from the mind are here contrasted with the tongue and clear speech; our text supports this interpretation fairly clearly.

568. Weitzius reads with Victorius “and with the voice restrained,” explaining it as “with the voice held back.” Rivinus approves neither Weitzius nor Sirmondus: for how, he asks, can speech sound with the voice silent? He rejects what Weitzius says, namely that *retinente* means *retenta* (“restrained”). He himself conjectures: “And speech, resounding, sounds above the upper air through the voice.”

Rivinus is easily refuted if he also attacks our reading. Dracontius’ point is that he says the inward prayers of the mind sound while the tongue is silent, just as in the preceding verse “the mute heart speaks” is a similar oxymoron, and in the following verse the mind rather than the tongue prays; this explains what precedes.

Paulinus of Petricordia often mentions such cries of the heart while the tongue is silent, apparently imitating Dracontius. Book I, verse 380:

> Again toward the Lord, tears and sighs rise upward,  
> And groans, the cry of the heart, the great voice of one who is silent.

Book III, verse 334:

> The heart cries out, though the tongue is silent.

Book V, verse 423:

> Humble in heart, exalted in merit, crying out without a murmur.

Book VI, verse 9:

> The crying hearts plead their own causes  
> Without voice or murmur.

Dracontius again, Book II, verse 592:

> You hear what the tongue is silent about beneath the eloquent heart;

and verse 605:

> He grants sins to the guilty when asked without a voice,  
> Through the heart’s affection, secret mind, faith, and hope.

See also Book I, verse 751.

[Col. 0748C] 571. I think one should read: “Having departed from their peaceful seats, let them rule the world,” and in the following verse, “hold all things under the law”; or “to depart from their peaceful seats, so that they may rule the world,” etc. I prefer the former.

572. Barthius, Book VII, chapter 20, reads *sub jure tenetor* (“let him be held under the law”). Rivinus: “If the meaning is that everything is held under the law.”

574. *Spicare* means “to send out ears of grain,” and figuratively “to sharpen,” as in *inspico*. On this verb see Barthius, *Adversaria* XXIX.11, and Turnebus XXI.25. Dracontius uses it again in verse 587: “The wind ears the grain.”

575. *Geminare* (“to bud”) is used of vines by Columella, Varro, and others, meaning “to put forth a bud or eye.” Dracontius speaks similarly elsewhere, as in Book II, verse 220:

> After the vine-shoot has budded, it brings grapes beneath the leaves.

Compare Book I, verse 719.

Weitzius explains *amoena comantia* as “pleasantly leafy,” taking *amoena* adverbially; alternatively, he says that the two adjectives mean “pleasant, leafy.” Sirmondus punctuates—and Weitzius seems also to intend this—“pleasant leafy rivers grow green,” as though the pleasant rivers became leafy because the trees around them commonly put forth foliage, a point Weitzius clearly affirms in his index.

But *amoena comantia* means “pleasant places that themselves become leafy”; the earth, trees, and forests are called *comantes* (“leafy”). *Amoena* is used absolutely for pleasant places. Tacitus, *Annals* III.7: “Through the pleasant regions of Asia and Achaea.”

576. Barthius, in the passage cited, reads:

> Whatever the rivers send forth, whatever the springs pour out, and whatever the sea produces.

Rivinus understands rivers as being sent forth from springs and being poured out by the sea, but suspects:

> Whatever the rivers send forth, whatever the springs, and whatever the sea pours out.

In our reading, the meaning is that rivers are sent forth from springs and that the sea has waves; all these things were given for human use, as were the harvest that bears ears, the vines that bud, the earth that flowers, and so forth.

577. Rivinus rightly rejects Sirmondus’ and the old editions’ punctuation. He reads, with Barthius and Weitzius, “the sea, which beats the shores,” taking *freti* as a plural nominative, following Lucretius, who used *fretus* for the sea.

But Lucretius, like many other ancient writers, did not use *fretus, freti* in that way, but *fretus, fretus*, as could easily be demonstrated. From the Vatican, therefore, I read:

> The strait that beats the shores.

One might also read *freta quod littora tundunt* (“the seas that beat the shores”), lengthening the *a* of *freta* because of the caesura. Catullus, poem 11, addressed to Furius and Aurelius, verse 4:

> The shore … is beaten by the wave.

Horace, *Epodes* XVII.55:

> The rocks … Neptune beats with his wintry sea.

---

God alone is ruler and creator for eternity,

the triune God, the threefold God, altogether both three and one,

from whom every hoped-for good is graciously granted,

[565] and no expectation fails in anything that he commands;

nor is the effect of doing lacking at the same time,

192 in whose presence mute hearts also speak inwardly,

and, while the tongue is silent, speech sounds above the heavens,

and the pure mind prays to God rather than the tongue.

[0570] Therefore God himself, mindful of his work, commands both

[Col. 0748A] to depart from their peaceful seats so that they may rule the world,

and to hold under their authority everything that the world possesses;

whatever the earth flowers with, whatever the green grass produces,

whatever the harvest bears as ears, whatever the tree bears on its branches,

[0575] 193 whatever the vines produce as buds, whatever the pleasant leafy places put forth,

whatever the rivers send forth from springs, whatever the sea billows,

whatever the wave of the sea carries, whatever the strait beats against the shores,

[Col. 0749A]

579. The Vatican has “whatever the earth produces, whatever the flame”; Victorius has “the wind and the upper air.”

581. Victorius: “like that by which …”

582. Victorius: “he should rule.”

585. The Vatican: “nor is the air denser.”

586. The Azagruntine manuscript has *hoc* (“this”) in place of *hinc* (“hence”). Victorius: “and the calm, clear sky.” The Vatican: “From here the rains come, and the calm, clear sky.” Sirmondus: “Hence the rains come, and the serene wind nourishes the fruits.” The Azagruntine manuscript has the same.

587. The Vatican, Victorius, and the Azagruntine manuscript have *fluctus* (“waves”); Sirmondus has *fructus* (“fruits”).

588. Victorius has *quae* (“which”) in place of *quas* (“which,” feminine plural). The Vatican has: “Come … which …”; the apparent reading seems corrected to *aura* (“breeze”).

589. Victorius: “the fruit and shakes the tree.”

[Col. 0750A]

591. The Vatican: “The breath of another’s alternating life”; the printed editions: “the breath accompanying alternating life.”

592. The Vatican: “the southern breath.”

593. Sirmondus: “and driven by the wind”; the others: “and restored by the wind.”

594. The Vatican: “running out and now …”; others: “running out into the nostrils.”

595. Thus Victorius and Sirmondus: “the breeze refreshes.” The Azagruntine manuscript: “a joyful life animates.” The Vatican: “vital souls through the sudden …”

596. The Vatican: “and now whatever …”

[Col. 0749C]

578. Barthius, Book VII, chapter 20, thinks one should read “they wrinkle the wandering breezes as they blow into the upper air,” or “the wandering things into the air,” so that *aer* is neuter. In Book XXXII, chapter 19, he more suitably retains the common reading and proves with many examples that *marmor* (“marble”) can sometimes mean the sea. Dracontius’ point lies in joining *vaga* (“wandering things”) with *marmora* (“seas”). Ambrose also said *aequore crispanti* (“the rippling sea”). I cited his words at verse 149. See also the note on verse 238, “with the sea rippling.”

581. Rivinus, while explaining verse 571, “Having departed from their peaceful seats, let them rule the world,” incidentally emends this verse and reads:

> And let the one who was made from dust, like Christ,  
> Rule over all.

Now he says that Sirmondus has excellently read:

> So that the one who was made from dust, like Christ,  
> Might rule over all,

namely, like the Word; but that the person who should rule is missing—namely, man, who was created like his Savior according to the flesh, except for sin. Since Rivinus’ edition is full of typographical errors, we can scarcely grasp his true meaning in many places. I think he approves Sirmondus’ reading [Col. 0749D] and changes only the following verse, “Let these rule” into “Let him rule,” so that the man who was destined to rule is understood.

But when it is said that the one who was made from dust was like Christ, it is sufficiently clear that this very person is the man who should rule. On the similarity of man to Christ, see the note on verse 339.

582. Perhaps: “created in the flesh.”

584. After saying that all bodies serve man, he adds that the wind also serves him, even though it has no body. He uses “body” for what can be clearly seen and perceived by the eyes. Hence air is also called *spiritus* (“spirit”), and *spiritus* is transferred to signify the mind.

585. Virgil, *Georgics* I.462: “Let the wind drive the clouds.” Cicero, *De natura deorum* II.39: “The condensed air is forced into clouds.” Virgil, *Georgics* V.20: “The air is forced into a cloud.” The same phrase occurs in the Vulgate, Job 37:21: “Suddenly the air will be condensed into clouds, and the passing wind will drive them away.”

[Col. 0750B] 586. Sirmondus reads:

> Hence rains come, and the serene wind nourishes peaceful fruits.

“Calm and clear” seems better, meaning tranquil and bright. Book II, verse 801: “With the clear sky shining,” and Book I, verse 68: “To violate the clear sky.” For from the wind come not only rains but also clear weather, since the wind drives away the clouds, as is clear from the cited passage in Job, which Dracontius seems to express. *Serenum* (“the clear sky”) is used absolutely for “clear weather” not only by poets but also by Cato, Livy, Pliny, and Suetonius.

587. In this verse and verse 589, Fabricius and Weitzius, following Victorius, read *fluctus* (“waves”); Sirmondus has *fructus* (“fruits”), which is preferable.

588. Rivinus, with the old editions, has *quae*; Sirmondus has *quos*, referring it to *fructus* in the following verse. In the Vatican, *quas* refers to *aristas* (“ears of grain”).

589. *Deflorare* and *defloratus* occur in Livy, Quintilian, and Gellius. Although the readings vary, this passage of Dracontius confirms the use of *defloro* for “to remove the flower” or “to shake flowers from a tree.” Weitzius says that in Symmachus *deflorare* means “to select.” Tertullian uses *defloratio* (“defloration”). In Dracontius one might also try “the wind gives flowers” or “the fruit gives to the flower.”

591. The Vatican reading *commercia vitae* (“the exchanges of life”) is easily preferable to the other common reading *comitantia vitae* (“the companions of life”). The word *commercium* has a remarkable use among writers. Alcimus, Book I, verse 99:

> A rigid thorn, with frequent knots between its exchanges,  
> Spreads a double framework of ribs in ordered rows.

These verses are absent from some editions. The same Alcimus describes the function of the lung in Book I, verse 105:

> The lung is added, nourished by thin air;  
> Drawing in the breaths it has gathered,  
> It receives and gives back the airs it has taken,  
> And in turn the breathing is repeatedly driven  
> By frequent inhalation.

Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXII.8, reads with Fabricius “so that it may receive what has been gathered” and “through repeated turns,” and notes that the phrase “it receives while giving back” is beautifully expressed by Dracontius through the word *reduci* (“restored”) in “and by the returning [wind],” verse 593.

593. In Sirmondus, *duci* (“driven”) seems to be a typographical error. See the note on verse 591.

596. Prudentius, *Apotheosis* 837:

> Observe how many kinds of vapor we pour from the mouth,  
> Whenever we breathe out the airy breaths of the soul.  
> Now the exhaled heat breathes forth warm air,  
> Blowing moistening mists from wet throats;  
> When it wishes, the subtle spirit issues forth  
> Into a cold wind chilled by frost, and the air whistles.

---

With their murmur the blowing winds ruffle the wandering seas,
whatever the earths, rivers, sea, and air produce,
[580] all these things have been given for human use.

So that he who was made from dust, like Christ,
might rule all these things created in the flesh;
all bodies, subdued, might serve bodies.

Meanwhile the wind, a spirit, serves without a body;
the wind drives the clouds; the denser air
is gathered into clouds: hence rains come, and calm clear weather.
The wind nourishes fruits, and the wind makes ears on the grain,
[588] which a gentler breeze winnows with its summer breath;
it strips the fruits of bloom and shakes flowers from the tree;
with blasts it kindles flames and moderates heat;
by alternating breaths the exchanges of life return.

It goes and returns, repeating its draughts of breath.
With the returning wind the fibres of the lungs pant,
as the air in turn runs out through throat and nostrils;
[595] it gives life to the vital senses through the warming limbs,
and now with cold, now with warm breaths the mouths
are made bright and flourish, while breezes touch the palate.

196 These breaths were not given only to human limbs,

but air returns to all living creatures.

[600] That Spirit of God, by which all bodies are moved,

embracing everything, stirs, cherishes, inserts, and drives it onward.

From him different kinds and the seeds of things derive their origin,

and the immense mass, to be sent forth from an everlasting source.

Formed by the craftsman’s hand and arranged,

[605] 197 everything is poured forth according to its own order: the irrevocable gift remains,

yet perishing things do not perish according to the law of each day.

Who could deny that rivers flowing in waves proceed from springs,

[Col. 0752A] whose source never expects their return?

Although it may pour forth waters ceaselessly in full force,

[610] the wave nevertheless denies that the flowing stream suffers loss.

It is the custom of all things to take flames from flames,

nor does the fire diminish when something is removed from the fires.

The losses of one commonly produce the gains of another.

Whose losses do these gains cause? When flames are taken from the fuel,

[615] 198 from what fire, pray, is its radiance cut off?

Nor does the fleshly race diminish through the creation of offspring.

Behold, the author and king God gave more to man than to himself.

By God’s power one male and one female are formed,

and one man creates many, an offspring destined to remain,

[620] [Col. 0753A]

620. Victorius has “with whom …”; the Vatican has *fudit* (“poured out”); others have *fundit* (“pours out”).

621. Victorius: “The small concern of the divine parent was to succeed.” Sirmondus: “It was a small concern for God that the dead should succeed.” [Col. 0753B] The Vatican has the reading printed here, but writes *perentis*.

622. Victorius: “lest, when consumed …”

623. The Vatican: “But … fixed … lest it be …”; the words *ne sit* are absent.

625. Sirmondus: “they behold.” The Vatican and Victorius: “they may behold.”

627. Victorius: “from the trunk’s …”

629. The Azagruntine manuscript: “the vine-bearing foliage.” The Vatican: “the vine-bearing leaf …,” from which *uviferae* (“grape-bearing”) seems to have arisen. The same Vatican manuscript has *armenta* (“herds”) instead of *sarmenta* (“vine-shoots”). Sirmondus and Victorius: “the grape-bearing leaf of the vine-shoot.”

630. Thus the Vatican; Sirmondus: “and the doubled rose of itself.” The Azagruntine manuscript: “and the attempted rose.” Victorius: “and the doubled rose.”

[Col. 0754A] 631. The Vatican: “they burst from the bark.”

632. The Vatican: “What is life, fleeing away, and old age equal to the flower?” Sirmondus and Victorius: “And for whom is life fleeting, and old age equal to the flower?”

[Col. 0754B] 633. The Vatican: “It becomes renewed, flowering, and …”

634. The Vatican: “under the covering of …”

635. The Vatican: “which no grass …”

636. The Vatican: “having stripped off …”

[Col. 0753B]

620. Barthius conjectured from his own ingenuity: “what little origin poured forth.”

621. In Victorius this line is one foot longer. To avoid this defect, Fabricius printed: “It would have been a small concern of the divine [parent] to make what had perished succeed again, lest, once consumed, it should perish.” Barthius had proposed in the margin: “It would have been a small concern of the divine [parent] to make what had perished succeed again, lest, once consumed, it should lie idle.” Rivinus explains: “It would have been a lesser concern to make new things grow again than to make things reduced to nothing rise again.” This explanation is sound, but it is especially evident in our manuscript reading. *Parva Deo fuerant* should be understood for *parvum* or *parum Deo fuerat*, as in Book II, line 286: “People think it a small thing to cross the perilous waves.” For the rest, I think Dracontius wrote: “A small concern for God was to make what was born for the dead succeed again,” or “A small concern of God was to make it succeed,” and so forth. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I.47: “The care of God distinguished [them] by the same number.” Since this is much more elegant, with *erat* or *fuisset* understood, it more easily escaped the copyists’ grasp; consequently, having omitted *cura*, they inserted *fuerant*.

622. After the ages—after the ages of the world. See the note on line 86.

624. *Legis sancta* for *legem sanctam*, like *vana rumorum* and similar expressions. Psalm 86: “If they profane my ordinances.” Fabricius incorrectly punctuates: “There is no return for the buried hearts of those who profane the holy things of the law.”

625. Tertullian, *On Judgment*:

> Thus the dry seeds are restored to empty fields,  
> And the dead, fixed deep in the furrows, rot.  
> Is the stalk not also enlivened from these, its ears restored?  
> And do the strong crops not again grow yellow with living grain,  
> And new harvests rise with varied increase?

And in Book II *Against Marcion*:

> In the grain the tree lies hidden; and unless, buried in the earth,  
> It first rots, it does not yield fruits adorned by the tree.

See, if desired, what I noted on Prudentius, Book II *Against Symmachus*, line 194.

627. *Truncis* is better—namely, “with roots cut off”—than *trunci*, which Victorius, Fabricius, and the other older editions present.

629. *Uviferae* is drawn from the Vatican manuscript, as Barthius had already conjectured. *Uvifer* is used by Silius and Statius; *revestio* by Tertullian.

630. Rivinus finds it strange that neither Fabricius, Weitzius, nor Sirmond corrected *Et geminata* to *Et gemmata*. He also rejects Barthius’s conjecture, which reads *rubetis* for *ruboris*. Certainly *gemmata* is found in the Vatican manuscript, and this reading is supported by line 179: “His sustenance was amid ambrosial flowers on a gem-encrusted turf.” But the syntax of this line still needs investigation. For what is *virgulta sui ruboris*, or *gemmata rosis virgulta ruboris*? I would prefer:

> And, gemmed with roses, the shrubs return in rosy bloom,

so that *roseo* is disyllabic and means “beautiful” or “flowering.” *Roseus* is understood in this sense, as I shall explain at line 717. One might also conjecture:

> And the shrubs return, gemmed with the rosy bloom of their redness,

or:

> Gemmed with rosy bloom, the shrubs return.

For the conjunction *et* is superfluous, since in *gemmata*, at the caesura, the final syllable can be lengthened.

632. Rivinus read *Est cui vita fugax*, and testifies that Barthius praised these two verses extravagantly. The Vatican reading is good, and perhaps better if one reads:

> For whom life is fleeting, and old age equal to the flower.

The substantive verb is often elegantly omitted.

633. The Madrid edition has *Sit rediviva*. Since no different reading is indicated, I believe *sit* was a typographical error for *fit*. The poets frequently celebrate the hairs and locks of plants, as I have already noted elsewhere.

634. Rivinus thinks *grana* should be read for *ligna*, and *granum* in the following line for *lignum*. Tertullian likewise said, “In the grain the tree lies hidden”; see his words in the note on line 625.

635. Barthius conjecturally supplies *lignum jacit*, that is, “lays down the wood”; *lignum facit* would be clearer. But I think Dracontius was understood neither by Rivinus nor by Barthius. In this line he takes *lignum*, and in the preceding line *ligna*, for the material of trees or shrubs separated from the root and suitable for fire or some work—hence the Italian and Spanish *legna* and *leña*. Dracontius therefore says that all such dead wood is restored and reborn beneath a renewing shoot; and that what was previously grass and a sprout later lies as wood upon the earth. From that wood, turned into manure, the field is fertilized, and through reciprocal succession the grass is reborn.

636. Pliny, Book X, chapter 67, section 86: “The salamander, an animal shaped like a lizard and marked with stars.” Ovid, concerning the *stellio*, Book V of the *Metamorphoses*, line 460: “And it has a name suited to its color, its body starred with various spots.” On the creature itself, see Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 27, section 41; and, leaving aside Tertullian, Isidore, Lucretius, Ovid, and countless others.

639. Hildebert, in his physiological poem concerning the stag:

> It makes itself young again when it casts its antlers.

Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 32, section 50: “The males [of deer] have antlers, and alone among animals they shed them every year at the fixed season of spring,” and so forth. Virgil, *Aeneid* I.193:

> Carrying their lofty heads, he strikes them down with their tree-like horns.

638. The Vatican manuscript: “hanging by each g.”; in the margin, “by hisses.”

639. Thus Sirmond and Victorius; in the Azagrensis, “with leafy branches a.” The Vatican has “from the fountains a. a. c. of the raven,” but perhaps it originally read “of the stag.”

> The greatest of its kind comes to be, which a very small origin brought forth.  
> It would have been a small concern for God to make what had perished succeed again,  
> Had he not granted life to rise again after the ages, once consumed.  
> But lest it be fixed that return is not granted to the buried—  
> To the hearts of those who profane the holy things of the law—  
> Let them behold yearly grain being reborn in the fields,  
> Dead beneath the furrows split by the earth-cleaving plough.  
> And a tree rises greater from truncated roots,  
> Green, clothed with returning leaves as the years come back.  
> The vine’s shoots are clothed again by the leaf of the grape-bearing vine,  
> And the shrubs return, gemmed with roses, in their rosy bloom.  
> Restored fruits burst from ambrosial bark,  
> For whom life is fleeting, and old age equal to the flower.  
> The green grass is made alive again, with its newly restored locks.  
> All the wood is reborn beneath a renewing shoot:  
> What was grass now lies as wood, destined to become grass again.  
> The scaly serpent casts off its star-studded covering,  
> Its skin renewed, its youth returning once more;  
> The gaping snake crawls on, opening its hissing throat.  
> The stags lose their antlers from their tree-like foreheads.

[Col. 0755B]

640. Victorius: *assumptis s.*; Vatican manuscript: *unguibus absumptis s.*

641. Vatican manuscript as printed; Sirmond, Victorius: “The birds of the air are stripped, when their old feather …”; thus the Azagrensis, but “when the old feather is.”

645. Azagrensis: *v. redire s.*

646. Vatican manuscript: *d. occultatur i.*

647. Thus Vatican manuscript and Azagrensis; in Sirmond and Victorius: “one part lay.”

648. Vatican manuscript: *gemens*; the others: *gerens*.

649. Vatican manuscript: *v. in morte*; the others: *v. m.*

650. Vatican manuscript: *redivina*, but it seems corrected to *rediviva*.

651. Vatican manuscript: *intalia* for *vitalia*.

652. Thus Vatican manuscript; in Sirmond and Victorius: *c. sudansque medullas*. Azagrensis: *c. gignensque m.*

653. Victorius: *Phoenici exactam*. Sirmond: *Phoenicis exhaustam*. Azagrensis: *Phoenicis exactam r.* Vatican manuscript: *Fenicis exacta me renovat*.

654. The Vatican manuscript begins “Ex [lacuna]” and contains nothing else of this line.

657. Vatican manuscript: *e divino l.*

658. Victorius: *vorax*; the others: *volans*.

661. This line is absent from the printed editions; it survives in the Vatican manuscript, where *civis* is read for *cinis*.

662. Thus Vatican manuscript; in the others: “And, returning to heaven, it wanders with erect crest.”

640. See Dracontius, *Elegies*, line 67. Isidore, drawing on the passage of Pliny cited above, Origen in Homily 2 on the *Song of Songs*, and Servius on Virgil’s Eclogue 8, says in Book XII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1, that stags are enemies of serpents. When they feel themselves weighed down by illness, they draw them from their caves by the breath of their nostrils; once the danger of their poison has been overcome, they restore themselves by feeding on them. Perhaps it would be preferable to read, with the Vatican manuscript, *absumptis*. For why the antlers of stags are called “palm-shaped,” see the note on line 275.

641. Pliny, Book X, chapter 24, lists certain kinds of birds that lose and change their feathers. In the other reading, *cum penna vetusta* is understood as *cum penna vetusta est*: *penna* cannot be in the ablative of separation.

642. Forcellini omitted the verb *subvestio*, to which he granted no place even among barbarous words.

643. Miracles are related from evangelical history. Their more suitable place, however, would be after the other marvelous works of nature that are subsequently enumerated, namely after line 682, “Rising in the morning.”

646. An oxymoron: “days of night.” *Oculare* is Tertullian’s word.

647. Book II, line 124: “One part of the man lay dead, another alive.”

648. Oxymora: “living funerals,” “a corpse alive in death.” Book III, line 398: “When the earth swallowed a living corpse”; and line 503, “with a living funeral.”

649. Again oxymora: “destroyed without death” (namely, one part of the man), “alive in death.” The meaning is the same.

652. Rivinus explains the reading of the older editions, *sudansque medullas*, as “watering” or “drenching the marrow,” but seems to prefer *sudansque medullis*, “sweating through the marrow,” as in Gallienus’s riddle, “Sweat through all your marrow.” The Vatican reading is sound, but *udansque medullas* seems preferable, meaning “making the marrow moist.” Macrobius and Augustine use this verb; and *udansque* could easily have become *sudansque* through the addition of *s*. Dracontius also attributes moisture to the marrow in Book III, line 613: “When moisture had first entered the exhausted marrow.”

653. On the middle syllable of *Phoenicis*, see the note on line 326. The history or myth of the phoenix is recalled by so many writers, especially poets, that compiling their catalogue would be endless. One may consult especially Claudian’s poem on the phoenix and the elegy on the same subject attributed to Lactantius. The Sirmond reading *exhaustam* has the correct sense, but *exactam*, with the Vatican manuscript, seems better, as in Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I.39: “The fortune of those who die after completing their lifespan is praised.”

654. Barthius, in his second edition of Claudian, page 985, and in the notes on the poem concerning the phoenix, praises these verses of Dracontius. They say that not the phoenix itself but its old age—or the old phoenix—is burned, “without the lot of a tomb,” as Claudian says, “and with false tombs.”

656. The dead flame that rises again is the phoenix itself, described here in imitation of Claudian:

> A secret radiance shines from its eyes; a fiery glory  
> Encircles its face; a star akin to flame  
> Rises from its gleaming crest, and the crested summit  
> Cuts through the darkness with serene light.

Dracontius, however, seems rather to assert that after the fire in which the phoenix was burned has been extinguished, new flames burst forth again, from which a new phoenix emerges.

657. The phoenix that is reborn is first a worm of milky color. Lactantius, *On the Phoenix*:

> From this the animal is said first to arise without limbs,  
> And is said to be a milky-colored worm.

658. Rivinus also preferred *Et scintilla volans* (“And a flying spark”); but *vorax* (“devouring”) is not a bad reading.

660. *Rutilatur* is used passively by Pliny, Martianus Capella, and others. Barthius conjectures *fax cerea lambit* (“the waxen torch licks”). But *fax caetera lambit* (“the flame lightly touches the rest”) is clearer. The meaning is that the crown of the head burns as if with fire, while the flame lightly touches the other parts of the body, since they do not shine with so fiery a brilliance. Virgil uses *lambere* of a flame touching lightly without burning, *Aeneid* II.683:

> And the harmless flame, with gentle touch,  
> Licked his hair and played around his temples.

> Having swallowed the snakes, they soon rise again with palm-shaped antlers.  
> It strips the winged birds of their old feather,  
> And clothes the restored birds in new plumage.  
> Moreover, the long-dead eyes of the blind,  
> Once the cloud of darkness has been dispersed and light restored,  
> Return to their sight, and the image that had suffered buried  
> Days of night looks again upon the face.  
> How often one part of a man lay dead while another lay alive,  
> Bearing living funerals, a corpse alive in death,  
> Yet destroyed without death, alive in death?  
> And restored health is born again through the limbs with renewed warmth,  
> And the hot sensation returns to the vital organs,  
> Holding the bones, stirring the veins, and moistening the marrow.  
> God renews the phoenix’s fully completed youth by fire,  
> And the burned old one emerges from the tomb grown mature.  
> The consuming pyre gives back the limbs without the lot of a tomb;  
> Once the fires are extinguished, the now-dead flame rises again,  
> The devouring fire is restored, glowing with renewed light,  
> And a flying spark brings back vast conflagrations;  
> What had been smoke hisses as the radiance of panting fire.  
> The crown is made ruddy by wandering fire; the flame lightly touches the rest,  
> And the extinguished ash, as the cold ember dies,  
> Is lifted high, seeking the heights, wandering with upright hair.

[Col. 0757B]

663. Thus Vatican manuscript; the others: “dead night beneath the light.”

664. Vatican manuscript: *per assensus et*.

665. Victorius: *latent*. Vatican manuscript: *dum coelo latet r.*

670. Sirmond and Victorius: *exhinc nocturnis i.* Azagrensis likewise, but *nocturnus*. Vatican manuscript: *Et nocet unus eques i. e. i. c.*

673. Vatican manuscript: *Sole premit commissa rubebat*; in the margin, obscurely, *perit*. Victorius: *petit*.

674. Vatican manuscript: *sola cujus coeli*.

675. Victorius: *ab aspectu l. s. coeli*.

676. Victorius: *ne g. animetur a.* Sirmond: *ni g. animetur a.* Vatican manuscript: *ni g. animantur a.*; above it, *animentur*.

663. Until now everyone has read: “The dead night falls beneath the light,” supported by the similar sense in line 116: “For the first day was of light, one death of darkness.” But the Vatican reading suits this passage especially well: examples are being given of lights that die beneath a greater light and afterward appear again. Virgil, *Georgics* I.431, and Ovid, *Metamorphoses* X.448, call the moon “golden.”

664. Virgil, *Georgics* I.427: “When the moon first gathers its returning fires.” In Pliny, Book XXIX, chapter 4, the rising of the stars signifies their elevation above the horizon, as some explain it. Dracontius takes the moon’s rising to mean its increase and the period during which it grows. But I scarcely doubt that *accessus* (“approach”) should be read. Macrobius, *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio* I.11: “Nor is there any doubt that the moon herself is both the author and the creator of mortal bodies, so that some bodies undergo increase through the approach of her light, and diminish as she wanes.” Perhaps Pliny too should read *accessu siderum*, for he is speaking of the moon’s increase in the cited passage.
