666. Drepanius, in the hymn of the three boys: “Let the moon, shining with icy light, praise this.” Above, line 52: “What is the cold orb of the moon?” where I explained why the moon is called cold.

668. Above, line 557: “He is withdrawn from the onset of death,” and Book III, line 114: “That he might withdraw the boys from death.” Daytime death is the death that day brings with its light.

669. Lucifer, among the stars—namely, during the night—restores his flames, or shines brightly. See the note on line 682.

670. Barthius read: “The radiance emerges from the nightly darkness and flashes with coruscating fire.” The common reading is indeed obscure: “From here the radiance flashes with coruscating fire through the night.” It could more easily be corrected to: “From here the nightly radiance.” From the Vatican manuscript we obtain a word by which this passage can be restored: “And the nocturnal horseman flashes forth radiance with coruscating fire.” The Azagrensis also supports this: “From here the nocturnal [horseman’s] radiance.” Thus, from this manuscript and the corrupt Vatican reading “And one horseman harms,” we obtain “And the nocturnal horseman.” There is no writing so corrupt that it cannot sometimes yield some benefit.

It should also be noted that Dracontius’s recondite learning gave ignorant copyists an opportunity to corrupt his poems. Poets assigned a two-horse chariot to the moon, a four-horse chariot to the sun, and a horse to Lucifer. Statius, *Thebaid* VI.237:

> Nine times now Lucifer had sent the dewy stars from heaven,  
> And as many times had preceded the moon’s fires,  
> Nocturnal upon his changed horse.

Claudian, *The Rape of Proserpina* II.121:

> While my Lucifer, carried upon a dewy horse,  
> Moistens the golden fields.

Ovid, *Fasti* II.314:

> Hesperus went dewy upon his dark horse,

and *Metamorphoses* XV.189:

> And when Lucifer emerges, bright upon his white horse.

“Nighttime horseman” may be understood by apposition with *jubar*, unless one prefers to read: “And the radiance flashes forth at night upon the horse.” Severus, in his poem on Etna, and Ennius apud Priscian, Book V, used *jubar* in the masculine gender: “Meanwhile white Hyperion flees the course of his radiance,” which I take as referring to Lucifer, who flees when the sun rises. Others read “the course of Hyperion.”

671. Ovid, Seneca in his tragedies, and Corippus call the dawn “dewy.” Virgil, *Aeneid* XII.77:

> When tomorrow’s dawn, carried across the sky on crimson wheels,  
> First grows red.

673. Barthius read *quoi missa*. *Quo missa* means “sent from that source,” because the radiance of dawn announces the sun and arises from the sun. Fabricius and Weitzius, with Victorius, printed *de sole petit* (“it seeks from the sun”), and failed to notice what appears to be an obvious error: the sense is that the dawn, overwhelmed by the sun’s radiance, perishes.

674. Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* IV.1: “The sun is the eye of the world, the delight of the day,” and in *On the Ark and Noah*, chapter 7: “They [the sun and moon] are, in a certain sense, the eyes of the world.” Dracontius, *Elegies*, line 243: “The sun, eye of heaven.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* IV.227:

> You who see all things, through whom the earth sees all things,  
> Eye of the world.

Others read *Mundi oculis* (“with the eyes of the world”); I prefer it in the same sense, so that the sun is called the eye of the world. Capella, in his hymn to the sun, Book II: “The world’s eye, the radiance of shining Olympus.” The Egyptians carved a scepter and represented an eye upon it; by this sign they indicated Osiris, signifying that he was the sun, because, Macrobius says, antiquity calls the sun the eye of Jupiter, *Saturnalia* I.21. See Barthius, *Adversaria* XI.3, and Roam, *Singularia* I.15. Prudentius also called the sun God’s servant, *Against Symmachus* I.343.

675. Perhaps *languescant* (“may grow faint”) should be read, so that it agrees with the following line: “Unless they are enlivened by icy waters.”

676. Rivinus seems to approve Sirmond’s reading, *Ni gelidis animentur aquis* (“unless they are enlivened by icy waters”), because the stars in the other hemisphere seem to revive through the cooling of the sea. In Sirmond, *animetur* may perhaps seem to Rivinus a typographical error; but the same word appears in the Madrid edition, and no discrepancy is noted in the Azagrensis manuscript. Believing something else to be concealed here, Barthius substituted either *vannentur* or *pascantur* for *animentur*. *Vannere* means to move, winnow, or sift grain with a *vannus*, a winnowing basket or sieve. But I do not understand what it would mean for the stars to be “winnowed.” *Pascuntur* (“are fed”) has no other sense than *animentur*.

In Sirmond and the Azagrensis, *animetur* can be understood of the sun. In my notes on lines 24–25 I supported the ancient opinion that celestial flames and fires are nourished by the contrary element, namely water. Experience provides the basis for this: we see that stars sparkle most strongly when they are nearer the horizon or when the air is cold and icy. Dracontius’s meaning may therefore be: “The stars will fail because of the sun’s immense heat unless they are nourished by the waters of the sea.” But since Dracontius seems to teach in line 224 that the stars shine by the sun’s light no less than the moon does, Sirmond’s reading is preferable: “unless the sun is nourished by icy waters”—that is, unless it were fed by waters, its heat would be so great that the stars would fail and be obscured by the sun’s immense brilliance. Unless we say that Dracontius is speaking sometimes according to one opinion and sometimes according to another.

> Dead light falls beneath light; the golden moon perishes,  
> And, through its rising, gathers its horns of fire.  
> While it lies hidden in darkness, it shines with restored light,  
> The cold light, image of the sun, pretending to be day.  
> When Lucifer returns to the sky, the stars also die.  
> The herald of dawn, withdrawn by daytime death,  
> Lucifer restores his extinguished flames among the stars,  
> And the nocturnal horseman flashes radiance with coruscating fire.  
> The dewy dawn, scattering crimson redness,  
> Leads day everywhere, destined to perish beneath the shadows of night.  
> Yet it perishes because of the sun, from which it was sent and by which it glowed.  
> The sun, eye of heaven, servant above the stars of the Thunderer,  
> By whose immense flames the stars grow faint,  
> Unless they are enlivened by icy waters across the sea.

[Col. 0759B]

677. Vatican manuscript: *occidet ipse*.

678. Thus Azagrensis and Vatican manuscript, though the Vatican manuscript has *abit* for *obit*. Sirmond: *et quo demersus n.* Victorius: *et quo conversus n.*

679. Sirmond: *nocturno hunc radiata*. Victorius: *hac* for *hunc*. Vatican manuscript: *nocturno radiat ulixe rubentem*.

680. Vatican manuscript: *P. attollit aquis*. Victorius and Vatican manuscript: *diurnae*.

681. Victorius: *dispositum n.*

682. Thus Vatican manuscript; in Azagrensis: *f. ore recepto*. Sirmond and Victorius: *f. orbe recepto*.

684. Victorius: *qua*. Sirmond: *quae*. This line is absent from the Vatican manuscript.

685. Azagrensis: *tonanti*. Vatican manuscript: *tonantem*, corrected to *tonante*.

686. Azagrensis: *teneat stillantis et*. Victorius: *s. et aptum Aera c.*

689. Victorius: *dum jussu r. ima*. Vatican manuscript: *Unus ubique [lacuna] dum jussio r. una*. *Deus* is absent.

692. The printed editions: “But by vows, and good voluntarily, by devotion and love.” Vatican manuscript: “But by vow, for voluntarily good by the love of devotion.” Hence *Et voto*, etc., as printed.

677. Tertullian explains this similarly in *On the Resurrection of the Flesh*: “All the stars fall and shine again, reborn; day dies in dense night together with its light; night too perishes, while things soon are revealed by light; and now one day after another rises from the stars; and the sun falls, bright with light-bearing radiance; the light perishes while evening casts the world into shadow.” He adduces all this to prove the resurrection of bodies. Barthius thought that two half-verses had been transposed here, but in our reading everything is in proper order.

679. From the Vatican manuscript, *hunc* or *hac* after *nocturno* is rightly omitted. It could, however, be added after *radiata*: “radiant with this light.”

680. Weitzius understands “purple waters” because of the brilliance of the sun’s rays. The sea is called purple at line 78, where I discussed this epithet more fully. Barthius, *Adversaria* XXXIII.16, reads *redditque diurnae* and understands it as referring to the light. Rivinus thinks a parenthesis should be inserted: “in the waters (and by day restores the deposit of nature, buried beneath the night) rising in the morning,” and so forth. Sirmond’s *diurne*, the adverb from *diurnus*, pleases me, even though no example is found. It is used for “by day” or “on each day.” Book III, line 602: “And direct my tears, which I pour forth daily.”

681. Barthius, in the cited passage, elegantly says that Dracontius calls the sun “nature’s deposit,” supporting this with similar examples. But it should be observed that a deposit is said of something as if dead; Lactantius alludes to this in his poem on the phoenix: “Nor does she fear the pledge of so great a deposit.” Hence Christians called a tomb a *depositum*; and *depositus*, meaning “dead,” or rather “committed to the earth,” occurs frequently in ancient Christian inscriptions.

682. Rivinus thinks *orbe reducit* should be written so that the sense may be clear. But the meaning is excellent if, with the Vatican manuscript, one writes *orbe refecto*—namely, “with the sun’s sphere restored by the waves.” See the notes on lines 25 and 676, and above, line 669, “restores the flames.”

684. Perhaps: “by which all things created and generated thrive.”

686. Weitzius read *et aptum Aera* (“and the fitting air”), and explains it in his index as “contiguous” or “connected.”

688. Lactantius, Fortunatus, or some other author of the poem *On the Resurrection of the Lord*: “He encloses all things in his fist.” Venantius Fortunatus, in his hymn to the Blessed Virgin: “Holding the world in his little hand, he was enclosed beneath the arch of the womb.” Dracontius beautifully says that all things created by God’s speech or voice are held in his one hand.

689. Since the word *Deus* is absent from the Vatican manuscript, one may conjecture that the reading should be: “What the Word created—one God everywhere, while one command burst forth”; or: “What the Word created—one, while everywhere chaos was broken apart by one command.” The same construction occurs in line 685, “Who, when…” and in line 693, “Whom a mind…,” where God is understood.

The phrase “God, while one command broke apart…” is obscure, as is “while he broke the depths by command.” Barthius explains *rumperet* as “while he could break.” But the obscurity of the matter remains. It would be clear if one read *dum vox erumperet una* (“while one voice burst forth”), or if *rumperet* were taken for *erumperet* (“burst forth”), just as *verto* is used for *everto*, and there are similar examples. But it seems more likely to me that Dracontius wrote *dum jussum rumperet unum* (“while one command broke forth”). Dracontius readily imitates certain distinctive phrases of the ancient poets. Virgil, Ovid, Silius, and others use *rumpere vocem* for “to open a way for the voice.” Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.553: “She burst such groans from her breast.” Claudian, *The Rape of Proserpina* II.249: “And burst empty laments toward the clouds.” This is better than the reading of others, *fundit inanes*. Silius IV.458: “And burst a groan toward the stars.” Hence *rumpere jussum* means “to command.” The line should therefore be read, as I think:

> What the Word created—one God everywhere, while one command broke forth,

or:

> What the Word created—one; everywhere God, while one command broke forth.

There is elegance in *una manus*, *unus sermo*, *unum jussum*: one hand, one word, one command.

> The day itself sets, as the sun falls over the waters;  
> Sunk in the sea it dies, and newly rises from the sea in the morning.  
> At nightfall nature hides in purple waters that which is red with radiant light,  
> And daily restores its own deposit, buried beneath the night,  
> Rising in the morning from the waves, its orb renewed.  
> Warned by so many examples together, let us believe that the dead are reborn  
> By the power of God, by which he created all things,  
> And that created things thrive beneath the sustaining Thunderer:  
> He who holds the realms of the starry and lofty heaven,  
> Encloses the air, raises the earth, and looses the waters;  
> And one hand contains all that the Word created.  
> One God is everywhere, while one command broke forth,  
> Who is as merciful as befits the Almighty,  
> And inferior in no virtue, save in wrath of punishment,  
> And by intention—for of his own will he is good through love of mercy.

690. See the note on line 30 and following, and on line 88.

692. Book III, line 16: “A monitor of justice, but more a lover of mercy.” I read *Et voto*, namely, “and by the desire to punish.” Marcellus Victorinus pursues the same thought in Book I of *On Genesis*, line 462:

> But the holy piety of the father forbids despair,  
> His mercy, if I may say so and may rightly approve what I have said,  
> Exceeds justice.

In Rivinus, someone attempted *Sed totus est sponte bonus* (“But he is wholly good of his own will”), which Rivinus did not favor.

693. See the commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* 10 *Peristephanon*, line 346. Understand that a sacrifice offered without a pure mind does not please God.

[Col. 0761A]

695. Sirmond and Victorius: *succedant*. Vatican manuscript: *succendant*. Azagrensis: *succendent*.

696. Vatican manuscript: *I. enim d. q. n. retraxit o.*

697. Sirmond and Victorius: *fluiscunt*. Azagrensis: *fluescunt*. Vatican manuscript: *fluuntur*; in the margin, *fluescunt*.

698. Thus Vatican manuscript; Sirmond: *erit; quem dura ligabant*. Victorius: *quod*.

699. Vatican manuscript: *semel*; the others: *simul mox*.

700. Printed editions: *subito*. Vatican manuscript: *subitum*.

701. Vatican manuscript: *ac formidatus*.

702. Thus Vatican manuscript; Azagrensis: *violento v. turgens*. Sirmond and Victorius: *violato v. turgens*.

703. Vatican manuscript: *s. amnes*.

706. Vatican manuscript: *l. aestus*.

707. Victorius: *flamina*. Sirmond: *flumina*. Vatican manuscript: *Et jud [lacuna] aurus ventorum flammea mittit*.

694. Rivinus finds it strange—and it is indeed strange—that *poeniteant se sceleris* is used actively. He conjectures *Aut si poeniteat sceleris*, that is, unless a pure mind is present (as he said in the preceding line), let at least a contrite heart be added. With a slighter alteration it may be restored as *Ut si poeniteant sceleris mala vota reorum*, or *Ut sic poeniteant*, or *Ausi poeniteant*, and so forth. In the *Elegy*, line 100: “If a guilty mind should repent of a crime committed,” and line 304: “Unless, grieving its sins, it should repent of its crime.” *Poeniteo* with a similar nominative is rare, but it is nevertheless used by Pacuvius, Justin, and Livy, though Livy’s reading varies.

695. I see no reason why Rivinus should prefer, with Weitzius, *voce piorum* to the reading of the others, *corda piorum*. Indeed I consider *voce piorum* in Weitzius a typographical error. For Weitzius follows Fabricius as his guide and never departs from him without giving a reason for the emendation; here, however, he is wholly silent.

696. The meaning of the words is plain: the true God is he who is without a beginning. Yet from the following verses one may infer that “whom no origin delays” can signify God’s power to create things immediately. The Vatican manuscript likewise points to this with *retraxit*.

697. Isaiah 64:1: “At your presence the mountains would melt”; verse 3: “At your presence the mountains melted.” Augustine too used the verb *fluesco*. Gunther seems to imitate Dracontius in Preface I.x, “The city melts into ashes,” and Book X, line 470, “Towns, collapsed into ashes by the fires of the camp, melt away.” Rivinus writes *fluiscunt* among the errata. See the note on Book III, line 443.

698. Fabricius and Weitzius, with Victorius, have *quod dura ligabant*. Rivinus conjectures *pulvis erit, quem gleba ligabat*, or *quem rura ligabant*. But the discourse is still about rocks reduced to ashes and dust. The Vatican reading *pulvis erit, quae dura rigebat* must therefore be retained: that is, what had previously been rock. *Pulvis* in the feminine gender, which is less usual, led scribes to corrupt the passage.

699. Psalms 17:8, 76:19, and 103:32: “Who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble.” This is greater than what the pagans say of Jupiter: “With a nod he made Olympus tremble.” See the note on line 704. The Vatican reading could be defended, for *semel* is sometimes used for *simul*.

701. Understand that the mountains themselves seem, as it were, to hang suspended. The words are from Job 9:5–6: “Who removes mountains, and they know it not, whom he overturns in his wrath; who moves the earth from its place, and its pillars are shaken.” Dracontius explains them, as do most interpreters, of a violent movement of the earth. But Didacus Stunica (Zúñiga), a polished Augustinian writer of the sixteenth century, in his commentary on Job, thinks this passage can be explained according to the opinion of the Pythagoreans, who held that the earth moves by its own nature. Finally, he says, no passage of sacred Scripture will be given that says so plainly that the earth does not move as this one says that it moves. Pineda sharply refutes this opinion in his commentary on the cited passage of Job.

702. In Sirmond’s reading, *alveus violato vertice turgens* is a channel swollen with waters turned back to their source. In our reading it is a channel boiling up, overflowing, and flowing violently, which, while flowing thus, was afraid because it sensed the waters returning. The miracle is related of the Jordan’s waters, which stood still so that the people of Israel might cross there. Joshua 3:15: “But the Jordan had filled the banks of its channel at harvest time.” This is indicated by our reading; what follows in verse 16 confirms Sirmond’s text: “The descending waters stood in one place and appeared swollen from afar like a mountain.”

703. Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* Hymn 12.178: “in the channel of the returning river.”

704. Thus at line 697, “at whose sight,” and line 699, “who, having seen the earth.” Psalm 76:17: “The waters saw you, God, the waters saw you and were afraid.” Elsewhere in sacred Scripture occur “at the presence of God” and “at your presence.” *Facies* is used for “presence”; hence ecclesiastical writers frequently use *in facie mundi*, *in facie Ecclesiae*, *in facie publica*, and simply *in facie* for “openly.” Ludovicus Legionensis, in *On the Names of Christ*, says that “face of God,” or “face” (Spanish *fazes*), is a proper name of Christ, because in sacred Scripture the face of God is often understood to be Christ. The final words of this verse concern the miracle of the Red Sea, which offered the people of Israel a passage when it was divided, as is narrated more fully in Book II, line 160 and following. The meaning would be plainer if one read: “The face of God was seen; it drove away this greenish marble.” But the other is more poetic. See Exodus 14.

705. Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* I, preface, line 10: “the battles of the blue sea.” Virgil, Ovid, Statius, and others similarly use *gurges* for “sea.” Again in Book II, line 485, “of the sea’s deep.” *Mundus* is used for “earth.” Mela, at the beginning of his work: “The land, raised aloft, is surrounded on every side by sea.” Some called the whole earth an island.

706. This verse is obscure and, unless I am mistaken, corrupt. Consider whether it should be restored as *Et pelago spatiante fretis fit littus in aestu*. *Spatiari* means to spread or increase, as in Pliny’s words, Book V, chapter 9, section 10: “The Nile, on fixed days, having spread with great increase through all Egypt.” Thus the shore, land adjacent to the sea, comes to be amid the very surge of the agitated sea and its gathering waves, while it spreads into other straits. Of the same prodigy Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* Hymn 5.65: “The broken waters offer a place to travellers, passable in the form of shores.”

707. Job 28:25–26; Psalm 134:7: “Bringing clouds from the end of the earth; he made a way for lightning; who brings forth winds from his treasuries.” See the note on line 711 and Corderius on the cited passage of Job. Sirmond’s reading *flumina mittit* cannot be tolerated.

> So that the guilty may repent of the evil vows of their crime,  
> And new hearts of the pious may succeed in their souls.  
> For he is God, whom no origin delays,  
> At whose presence mountains and rocks melt  
> Into ashes, and the dust will be what was once hard and rigid;  
> Who, as soon as he sees the earth, immediately shakes  
> The weight of the world and displays the earth’s sudden wandering tremor,  
> And shows its feared, swaying movements.  
> The torrent in its channel was terrified, its crest violently swollen,  
> When it sensed the waters returning and made the river stand still.  
> The face of God appeared, and drove away the greenish marble  
> Of the sea’s deep, by which the whole world is encircled,  
> And, as the sea spread through the straits and the shore heaved,  
> He who sends the winds’ blasts from the treasuries of the winds.

[Col. 0763A]

708. Vatican manuscript and Victorius: *rapidas*. Sirmond: *rabidas*.

709. Vatican manuscript: *nivis venientis quae*.

710. This verse is absent from the Vatican manuscript.

711. Vatican manuscript: “Who hides waters in rocks and conceals fires.” Sirmond and Victorius: “Who hides broad waters and contains rains”; thus Azagrensis, except that it has *latas* for *laxas*.

712. Azagrensis: *creatus*; the others: *creatur*.

713. Vatican manuscript: *mutatur*; the others: *imitatur*. Victorius: *hiberna* for *aquarum*.

716. Printed editions: “Who established the courses of Phoebus and the labours of the moon.” Vatican manuscript: “By which he established the courses of the moon and the labours of the sun.”

717. Vatican manuscript: *rosis*. Victorius: *roseis*. Sirmond: *rosulis*. Vatican manuscript has *stillare* for *stellare*.

708. *Rapidas* seems better than *rabidas*. See the note on line 312: “It is sent, that, running, it may overcome the bereft storms.” Book II, line 154: “You command that swift storms disturb all things.”

709. Job 38:22: “Have you entered the treasuries of snow, or have you seen the treasuries of hail?” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XV, 69: “What god [there is], whence the snows come, what the source of lightning is.”

710. Job 37:2 and following, with the commentary of the aforementioned Corderius. It should nevertheless be observed that God is there said to thunder wondrously and that his light is over the ends of the earth, but it is not expressly stated that lightning is sent by him—which interpreters nevertheless understand in these words.

711. In the Vatican reading one might conjecture that the subject is hail, which is in a certain sense water hidden in stone; for this reason the Spaniards call it *piedra* (“stone”). Claudian, *On the Consulship of Mallius Theodorus*, v. 108: “Who draws on the rain-bearing clouds, whence the rocks of hail are formed, whence comes the cold for the snows.” The Vatican’s words *condidit ignes* (“he concealed fires”) could also be understood of fire hidden in rocks and flashing forth when they are struck together. But the common reading is preferable: for Dracontius chiefly draws upon the Book of Job to praise the divine majesty. Job 38:28: “Who is the father of rain? Or who begot the drops of dew?” And 28:25–26: “He who made a weight for the winds and weighed the waters by measure, when he established a law for the rains and a path for resounding storms.” And 26:8: “He binds up the waters in his clouds.” The Hebrews attributed four keys to God, which he would not have given even to any seraph; the first of these they called the key of rain.

712. *Crystallus* is rarely masculine. Job 38:29–30: “From whose womb came the ice? And who begot the frost from heaven? Waters are hardened into the likeness of a stone, and the surface of the deep is congealed.” In the first verse it is asked from whose womb ice comes forth; in the second the freezing of water, from which crystal is formed, is recalled, as Corderius explains, although most explain it only of frost. Gaspar Sanctius, in his commentary on Job, somewhat favors Corderius’s opinion. Dracontius appears to understand the question as referring to crystal, to which the following verse responds by asserting that waters are hardened into the likeness of a stone. Dracontius explains this very point in the following verse.

713. Weitzius says that the white substance is a pearl or a large pearl (*unio*). Rivinus conjectured *glacies imitata nivales* (“ice imitating snowy things”), since Cinna is said to call crystal an imitator of snow. Barthius had written in the margin *glacies imitatur Iberas* (“ice imitates Iberian things”), that is, Iberian [snow], but on p. 1031, in his notes on Claudian, he read *glacies meditatur hibernas* (“ice meditates winter things”). Weitzius, together with the Victorinus manuscript, has *glacies imitatur hibernas* (“ice imitates winter things”). The first syllable in *hibernus* is lengthened from *hiems* (“winter”), but shortened when the word derives from *Hibernia* (“Ireland”). All these readings can readily be rejected because Dracontius wished to encompass the meaning of the Book of Job and to explain it of crystal. From the Vatican’s *mutatur* I infer the reading *glacies duratur aquarum* (“the ice of waters is hardened”). The words of Job are “waters are hardened.” But I will not omit other conjectures which, even if they are not approved, will certainly not be displeasing. The Book of Job says: “The surface of the deep is congealed.” This may correctly be expressed by *facies duratur aquarum* (“the surface of the waters is hardened”). I also suspect that one might read *Candida mater ei glacie durata per annos* (“a white mother, hardened for him by ice through the years”), or *Candida mater, nix glacie d[urata] p[er] a[nnos]* (“a white mother, snow hardened by ice through the years”), or *C[andida] mater ei glacies d[urata] p[er] a[nnos]* (“a white mother, ice hardened for him through the years”). Although this may seem remote, it can nevertheless be confirmed from Isidore, who may perhaps have wished to quote this verse. Thus Isidore, Book XVI, chapter 13: “Crystal is handed down as shining and watery in color, because it is snow hardened into ice through the years.” The white mother, or white substance, is snow. Now, the possibility of reading *Candida mater ei* (“a white mother for him”) is supported by the fact that in Job the father of rain is treated first, and then the mother of ice or crystal; and Dracontius says in the preceding verse: “From what womb bright crystal is born.” To this *Candida mater ei glacie durata per annos* (“a white mother for him, hardened by ice through the years”) corresponds aptly. Two epigrams by Claudian (three according to others) survive concerning crystal, in the middle of which dissolved water could be seen: “Nor could it falsely pretend to be a gem throughout its whole body, but the liquid remained as an informer in the middle of its orb.” Marbod, in the *Book of Evax on Gems*, refers to Isidore and perhaps to Dracontius in chapter 41: “Crystal is ice hardened through many years, as it seemed to learned men who wrote thus: in some it retains the cold and color of ancient hail. One part denies,” and so forth. He means Solinus, who denies it. Hardouin, in his notes on Pliny, Book XXXVII, section 9, says that the ice from which crystal is made is sap in the bowels of the earth, glued and compressed among the crags by the force of cold.

714. Just as *soles longi* (“long suns”) is said of long days, so *soles minores* (“smaller suns”) refers to short days. See Barthius on Statius, *Thebaid* V, 460.

715. Dracontius uses the verb *flammo* (“I flame,” “I set aflame”) more than once, as do Statius and others. Barthius, in his usual manner, has collected examples in his note on the argument of Book III of the *Thebaid*, v. 5.

716. “I understand,” says Weitzius, “the sun’s decline from the southern regions toward the northern, and its return from those regions to the former ones; no one should apply this to the childish tale according to which the sun is said to leap at the feast of the Lord’s Resurrection.” Others, however, foolishly tell the story that the sun leaps on the feast of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist—although by now, as I think, not even children believe it. The moon is said by poets to labor when it is eclipsed, and its eclipse is called a labor. The common reading is based on this explanation. But the Vatican reading is preferable. Dracontius is imitating Virgil, *Aeneid* I, at the end: “Here he sings of the wandering moon and the labors of the sun.” Dracontius calls the moon’s movements its “leaps.” The same Virgil, *Georgics* II, 478: “The varying eclipses of the sun and the labors of the moon”; there he speaks of the eclipse of the sun and moon, but here of the course of both.

717. The original reading seems to have been *roseis* (“with rosy [flowers]”). Sirmondus perhaps restored *rosulis* (“with little roses”) by conjecture, although in Book II, v. 441, we find: “And winter might bring forth little roses.” Rose-colored flowers, that is, beautiful flowers, are mentioned by many writers, as by Claudian in his poem on the magnet, v. 29; yet shortly afterward he says *stellata rosis* (“starred with roses”). Boethius, Book I, poem 2, perhaps imitating Dracontius: “Who tempers the calm hours of spring, so as to adorn the earth with rosy flowers?” Tertullian, *On the Judgment of the Lord*, middle of the poem: “The snowy fields are crisped with rosy flowers.” Incidentally, from this I would correct the second verse of this poem, which I find written thus in several editions: “And he will mark the spring breezes with rosy flowers.” I read: “And he will mark the springlike breezes with rosy flowers.” A field is elegantly said to be “starred” with flowers, as the sky flowers with stars. See Gifanius, *Index to Lucretius*, under *floreo*. Claudian, *The Rape of Proserpine* II, 130: “She walks, starred with roses.” Marius Victorinus, *Genesis* I: “Here the earth, distinguished, scatters starry heats”; read *colores* (“colors”). Earlier he had said: “And the stars, painting the sky with distinct zones, scatter various colors with ethereal flowers.”

He restrains the swift storms amid the tempest,

Of hail and snow, who knows what their origin is,

[710] Who gives the lightning fires from colliding clouds,

Who hides the flowing waters and contains the rains,

Who knows in what womb bright crystal is formed—

[Col. 0764A] 210 A white substance, ice hardened from the waters.

Who lengthens the nights of winter with the lesser sun,

[715] And extends the sun’s course through flaming hours;

Who establishes the moon’s leaps and the sun’s labors;

211 Who makes the grove starry with roses, or the fields with flowers.

718. Vatican manuscript: *poma saporant* (“the fruits are flavorful”).

719. Victorinus: a fragment of *hiemis* (“winter”) is placed beneath the verse. Vatican manuscript, together with Sirmondus, has *uvae* (“grapes”) rather than *uvas*.

721. This verse is absent from the Vatican manuscript.

722. Vatican manuscript: *noverat et vultur* (“and the vulture knew”).

723. Sirmondus: *Dux odor usque sagax quem mox invitat ad escam* (“a guide, an ever-sagacious scent, which soon invites it to food”). Vatican manuscript: *dux odor atque sagax quem mox invitat ad escam*. Victorinus: *dux, rectorque sagax quem* (“a guide and sagacious leader whom…”).

724. So Sirmondus and the Vatican manuscript; Victorinus has *praecipit aut*, Azagrus *a[quilae] senium renovare juvent[a]* (“to renew the old age of the eagle”).

725. Vatican manuscript: a fragment of *tolerabit* (“will endure”) beneath *ab unco* (“from the hook”).

726. Sirmondus: *quaecunque*; Azagrus, Victorinus, and the Vatican manuscript: *quodcunque*.

727. Vatican manuscript: *vita certa* (“certain life”).

728. Vatican manuscript: *vita opulenta major* (“a richer life is greater”).

718. Sirmondus distinguishes the passage as: *Imperat autumni, qui* (“He commands autumn, which…”). I do not approve this. Fruits, not flowers, are attributed to autumn; its symbol is the horn of plenty filled with grapes and fruits. Forcellinus relegated *saporo*, *saporas* to barbarisms, indicating that Dracontius and Peter Chrysologus used them. He does admit the adjective *saporatus*, which is certainly more customary.

719. Rivinus had conjectured *plenis* (“full”), but acknowledged that Sirmondus’s *gemmis* (“gems”) was better. The phrase “gems of the vine” was discussed above at v. 575. Propertius, Book IV, elegy 2, v. 13: “The first grape varies on darkening clusters.” Grapes are called fragile either because the vines themselves are fragile, or because they are glasslike, and *vitreus* (“glassy”) and *fragilis* (“fragile”) are often used in the same sense. Publius Syrus, *Maxims*: “Fortune is glassy when it shines; then it breaks.” Or, finally, because grapes are in a certain sense broken and easily burst.

720. Just as the breasts of mothers provide food and drink to their children, so grapes, which are like the breasts of the vine, supply food and drink to human beings. Columella also uses this beautiful metaphor, Book III [or IV], chapter 21: “To these vines the nourishing earth, happy as though in an eternal childbirth, every year lowers breasts swollen with must for mortals.” These words were once read most corruptly in the older editions, but were later happily restored; the manuscript in the Altieri Library likewise presents them. Otherwise *uber* also signifies fertility and abundance, as in *uber agri* (“the fertility of a field”), *uber glebae* (“the richness of the soil”); and of vines Virgil, *Georgics* II, 275: “Bacchus is no less vigorous in the dense richness”; likewise Claudian, Columella, and others.

721. Psalm 146:9: “Who gives their food to the beasts, and to the young ravens that call upon him.” Job 38:41; Luke 12:24. Many writers say that young ravens are abandoned by their parents. Consult Pineda and Corderius on the cited passage in Job, among others.

722. Job 39:30; Proverbs 30:17; Matthew 24:28; Luke 17:37. In these passages the eagle is said to feed on corpses. Dracontius, with the Septuagint, Jerome, and others, names the vulture, because eagles that pursue dead bodies resemble vultures; for other eagles do not touch corpses. Most writers classify the vulture and kite under the common genus of eagles.

723. Isidore, *Etymologies* XII, chapter 7: “Vultures, like eagles, perceive corpses even beyond the seas: for, flying high, they see from above many things concealed by the obscurity of mountains.” Here an extraordinary power of smell is not being commended, as Forcellinus thinks under *vultur*, but sharpness of sight. As for the wording of this verse, when it was formerly read *Dux rectorque sagax quem mox* (“a guide and sagacious leader whom soon…”), Sirmondus restored it to *Dux odor usque sagax quem mox invitat ad escam* (“a guide, an ever-sagacious scent, which soon invites it to food”). “Sirmondus could do nothing better, nor Dracontius,” says Rivinus. Nevertheless I prefer the reading which I draw from the Vatican manuscript, restoring *mos* (“custom,” “instinct”) in place of *mox* (“soon”), namely, the vulture’s own nature and instinct.

724. Rivinus thinks *Praecipit aut aquilae* (“or the eagle commands”) more suitable to the sense. I would prefer something else in place of *praecipit aut*: perhaps *Praesciat aut aquila* (“or the eagle foreknows”), or rather *Perpetis aut aquilae* (“or of the enduring eagle”), which might be called *perpes* because, when it reaches old age, it grows young again. The Azagrus reading is plausible. Arator, Book II, vv. 528 and following, narrates at length how the eagle lays aside old age. When Barthius, Book XXXIII, chapter 3, had quoted those verses, he added that, as far as he remembered, he had not read that history or fable of the eagle elsewhere except in Aldhelm’s *Book of Riddles*, who may perhaps have imitated Arator. But this story is much older than Arator; and Barthius, in his preface to Claudian’s third consulship of Honorius, citing Jerome’s letter to Praesidius—which they commonly deny to Jerome—thinks that Arator and Aldhelm took the narrative from it, and he shows from Paulinus that the eagle’s youth is renewed in another manner. The words of Psalm 102:5 provided the occasion for such narratives: “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s.” It is certain from this that the eagle’s youth is renewed in some manner, although different writers describe that renewal differently. Dracontius followed Augustine on the cited psalm and Epiphanius in the *Physiologus*, who relate that an aging eagle strikes its beak, which has become too hooked for eating, against a stone; when the beak is broken, it takes food and grows young again, and, Augustine says, “a kind of resurrection occurs in it.” Consult Petavius, *Annotations on Epiphanius’s Physiologus*, chapter 4. Add Hildebert of Le Mans, *Physiological Poem on the Eagle*. Some explain the psalm’s words of the change of feathers by which birds in a certain sense grow young again.

725. In the Vatican manuscript, *tolerabit* (“it will endure”) may perhaps stand for *toleravit* (“it endured”). A beak is called *aduncus* and *obuncus* (“hooked”), and there are good examples of both words. In the Vatican manuscript *ab unco* (“from the hook”) stands for *obunco* (“from the hooked beak”), unless one prefers to retain *ab unco*: namely, “it endured hunger from the growing hooked beak,” or, “with the beak growing, it endured hunger from the hook of the beak.”

He commands autumn, which makes the sweet fruits flavorful,

And varies the fragile grapes on the vines with gems,

[720] So that the breasts of the must may be food and drink;

212 Who gives nourishment to the young ravens and makes the vulture know

In what region the corpse lies,

A guide, a scent, and a keen instinct that soon invites it to food,

[Col. 0766A] Or to renew, in old age, the youth of the swift eagle,

[725] 213 Which, as its hooked beak grew, endured hunger:

Who feeds whatever he creates with a parent’s compassion,

Certain salvation of life through a thousand dangers of death,

Strength to the weak, a greater wealth to the needy,

[Col. 0767A]

731. Vatican manuscript: *qui facit aeterna mortalia* (“who makes mortal things eternal”). Other copies: *qui facit aeternam ut mortalia* (“who makes the eternal as mortal things”).

732. Vatican manuscript: *animum* (“soul,” “mind”).

733. Victorinus: *jubet, ut mare crescat* (“commands the sea to grow”).

734. Vatican manuscript and Sirmondus: *abjectis* (“cast down”). Azagrus and Victorinus: *adjectis* (“added”).

735. Victorinus: *in capiti g[enere]* (“in the head’s [kind]”). Vatican manuscript: *in capitur g[enere]*.

736. So the Vatican manuscript, although it seems to read *muniente* (“assisting”) instead of *minuente* (“diminishing”). Sirmondus: *liquores* (“fluids”). Victorinus: “And as the water diminishes, with the moon diminishing, the lesser and waning [fluids] diminish according to an eternal law.”

737. Vatican manuscript: “As things diminish when the moon diminishes according to an eternal law.” Sirmondus: “And as it diminishes, may they diminish according to an eternal law.”

741. Vatican manuscript: *consolatur abactos* (“he comforts those driven away”); the printed editions: *consolatur adactos* (“he comforts those compelled”).

742. Victorinus: “with blows and pains.”

743. Sirmondus and Victorinus: “You, unconquered God, [bring] healing to us”; Azagrus likewise, but has *tunc* (“then”) instead of *tu* (“you”). Vatican manuscript: “And for us, salvation troubled by pains,” from which I restored the passage.

744. Sirmondus: “You bestow [it], to whom all salvation exists without any medicine”; Victorinus likewise, but has *tu* (“you”) for *cui* (“to whom”) and *quod sine est* (“which is without”) for *nullo*. The Vatican manuscript has the reading printed here, but *cui* for *tu*.

729. Book II, v. 685: “A greater defense for the oppressed.” There are several other similar passages at the place cited.

730. A little earlier, at v. 728, he said: “Strength to the weak”; that is, he willingly repeats the same words. Otherwise one might read *Fessorum vires* or *Fessorum robur* (“the strength of the weary”). Rivinus conjectures *dans nutrimenta solutis* (“giving nourishment to those released”), namely, those released from illness or old age. The manuscript reading is better.

731. *Ut* (“so that”) is elegantly omitted after *facio* (“I make”), as in the Vatican manuscript and at v. 733: “He commands that the waters rise.” It is nevertheless often added, and may be added here. Mortal limbs cover an eternal soul because flesh is like the soul’s garment, prison, and bond. This union of soul and body occurs by a hidden law; for the recent philosophers have achieved nothing by composing lengthy commentaries on a matter necessarily obscure to mortals.

733. Rivinus attributes to Sirmondus the reading *jubet, aethera crescant* (“he commands the heavens to rise”), or perhaps this is one of Rivinus’s many typographical errors; for in Sirmondus I find *jubet, aequora crescant* (“he commands the waters to rise”). The ebb and flow of the sea has so certain a connection with the moon’s motion that many philosophers reasonably suppose the former depends upon the latter. But Dracontius speaks of the motion by which, as the moon grows, the sea grows, and, as it wanes, the sea wanes. Isidore, *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 18, seems to describe Dracontius: “As the moon grows, all waves grow, and as it diminishes, they diminish.” Thus it should be read, not—as I see in the more recent Madrid edition—“all fruits grow.” In fact, Dracontius says not only that the sea grows, but also the rivers together with their springs. Basil, *Hexaemeron*, homily 6, agrees concerning the motion of the tides. Seneca, *Natural Questions* III, chapter 26, discusses why certain rivers increase in summer and observes that one explanation is sought in the stars. That all fluids increase and decrease with the waxing and waning moon will be established in the note on v. 735.

734. *Adjectis fluctibus* (“with the waves added”) is preferable, because the sea grows when the waves increase and are, as it were, added. Isidore, at the cited passage: “All waves grow.”

735. Either form can be used: *inclusum capite*, with the final syllable lengthened because of the caesura, or *inclusum capiti*. Dracontius illustrates this entire thought again in the elegy, vv. 235 and following; at v. 241: “The hidden marrow itself observes the moon’s horns; the covered brains observe the moon’s spheres.” Hence the lunatics. See Macrobius in the note on v. 664. Isidore, *Etymologies* XII, chapter 6, §48, from Palladius, his final book, chapter 6: “For all enclosed animals of the sea and shellfish swell in their bodies as the moon grows and are emptied as it wanes. For when the moon is increasing, it increases moisture; but when it declines, the fluids decrease.” Pliny, *Natural History* II, chapter 99: “As the moon approaches, it fills bodies; as it withdraws, it empties them.” See Palladius, Book XIII, title 1, on marrows. Alcimus, Book I, *On Brains*; Fulgentius Placiades, *Mythologies* II, near the end. Compare Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* XI, at the beginning; Manilius, *Astronomica* II, preface, v. 93; Oppian, *Halieutica* V, vv. 589 and following; Aulus Gellius XX, chapter 8, *On Things That Seem to Have Sympathy*—Greek *sympatheian*—with the moon as it waxes and wanes; Nonnus, *Dionysiaca* 5, v. 162; Basil, *Hexaemeron*, homily 6, near the end; Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* IV, chapter 7, §29; and Rivinus’s dissertations on Venilia and Salacia, which he himself cites.

736. Rivinus attributes to Sirmondus the reading: “And may the waters diminish, as the moon diminishes the fluids”; he himself prefers by conjecture: “And may the waters diminish, the moon diminishing the fluids.” But in Sirmondus I plainly read: “And may the waters diminish, the moon diminishing the fluids”; only the punctuation differs in Rivinus, through which the sense is made clearer. Isidore, cited at v. 733, likewise says *luna minuente* (“with the moon diminishing”) instead of *imminuta* (“when it has diminished”); Dracontius in the *Elegy*, v. 238, uses *minuo* in the manner of a neuter verb at v. 240: “These same things diminish, while Cynthia diminishes.” Aulus Gellius I, chapter 3, has *famae minuentis* (“of diminishing fame”), although others read *famae imminentis* (“of threatening fame”). Corippus, preface, v. 31: “Looking up at the moon’s diminishing horns.” Palladius, Book III, title 24: “If one sows when the moon is diminishing.” Caesar, *Gallic War* III, chapter 12: “As the tide again diminished.” Thus *augere* (“to increase”) is used for “to be increased” by Sallust, Cato, and Lucretius.

738. From the song of the Blessed Virgin in Luke 1.

740. Perhaps also *et pius ultro* (“and voluntarily merciful”). Otherwise *pius ultor* (“the merciful avenger”) is good. Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 6, v. 93: “Yet the same benign Avenger blunts his anger.”

741. Book II, v. 741, has *poenis adactos* (“driven by punishments”). *Abactos* (“driven away”) or *adactos* appears to mean “subdued.” One might also say *consolaturque subactos* (“and comforts the subdued”). Statius likewise used *adactum* for *subactum* in *Thebaid* I, v. 19: “And twice the Rhine under the yoke, twice the Danube compelled by laws.”

744. In place of *Impendis* (“you bestow”), Rivinus conjectures *Impertis* (“you grant”). But *impendere* in the sense of “to confer” is also in use, and occurs in Book III, v. 248: “May he bestow,” and so forth. Rivinus explains Sirmondus’s reading, “to whom all salvation exists without any medicine,” as follows: “Although salvation itself could not save him, even if it wished to” (as the Comic poet says), “you, God, grant healing.” I prefer the Vatican reading. Christian poets willingly use this expression in a sacred manner when addressing God. Book II, v. 597: “Foreseeing the medicine first, holy one, you prepared it before you made man”; and Book III, v. 598: “Your [healing], holy one, for our…”

Auxiliary help for the wretched, hope, and defense for the oppressed,

[730] Strength for the weary, giving nourishment for salvation.

He who makes mortal limbs cover an eternal soul

By a hidden law, with the loquacious wind breathing.

Who commands the waters to rise with the moon’s growing sphere,

214 With waves added; may the rivers rise with their springs,

[735] And may the whole race of the brain enclosed in the head grow,

And may the liquid waters diminish as the moon diminishes,

[Col. 0768A] And, as it wanes, may they wane according to an eternal law.

215 Who subdues kings and kingdoms and lays the powerful low;

He casts down the haughty and sinks the proud from their citadel,

[740] And God oppresses oppressors, the merciful avenger;

He raises the crushed and comforts those subdued

By griefs and losses, those suffering severe wounds.

Is our salvation afflicted? In your mercy you bestow healing,

You, holy one, with no medicine at all,

[745]

745. Victorinus: *languoris adepti* (“having incurred illness”). Sirmondus: *l[anguoris] ad aestus* (“to the heats of illness”). Vatican manuscript: *p[?], sermonis l[anguoris] ad aestu[m]*.

746. Printed editions: *cernens* (“seeing”); Vatican manuscript: *intendens* (“directing [your attention]”).

747. Vatican manuscript: “Look upon the rejected one, raise up the despised one for a little while”; Victorinus likewise, but has *tolle* (“raise”) instead of *attolle*. Sirmondus: “Look upon the despised, cast-down one; raise him for a little while.”

748. So the Vatican manuscript; others: “and help the confessed one, whom…”

749. Vatican manuscript: *memorare* (“to recall”); others: *narrare* (“to tell”).

751. Vatican manuscript: “Or the small work of the maker, which my mind proclaims.” Sirmondus: “Or the small work of the maker, which my guilty mind cries out.” Victorinus likewise, but has “which my mind may proclaim.”

753. Vatican manuscript: *Obsess[us] … tuus* (“besieged … your”); “our speech” is lacking.

754. This is the final verse in Sirmondus, Victorinus, and Azagrus. In the Vatican manuscript *Omnipotens aeterne Deus* (“Almighty eternal God”) is immediately added, by which half-verse the first book is concluded. But this is plainly the beginning of the second book.

Which earthly remedies provide for the attacks of illness.

Directing your attention to the hopes of human beings, and fulfilling their prayerful vows,

Look upon the despised one; raise up the cast-down for a little while,

216 And help the confused one, because he repents of being guilty,

So that I may recall your praises in this poem,

[750] [Col. 0770A] As I shall be able; for no creature can recount

Even the smallest work of the Maker, which my mind proclaims

With a beaten breast, weeping and with faithful voice.

For your word is held as a pledge in our heart,

By which, in your great mercy, you promise yourself to be a father.

## BOOK TWO

[Col. 0769]

1. This half-verse, as I have just said, closes the mutilated end of Book I in the Vatican manuscript.

3. *Cunctarum quae* (“of all the things which”).

5. *Astra rotatum* (“the stars’ revolving”).

6. *Vibrat* (“shines,” “flashes”). Fragmentary.

1. I supplied the final words from Sedulius, in whom this verse is complete shortly after the beginning of Book I: “Almighty eternal God, the only hope of the world.” Dracontius often indeed calls God “hope,” in the phraseology of Sacred Scripture; for example, shortly afterward at v. 31, “Hope of human beings”; at v. 584, “Creator and hope”; and in Book I, v. 434, “Hope, maker, lord, ruler, leader, arbiter, judge”; and in the *Elegy*, v. 1, “Immense God, King, creator and hope of all things.”

2. “God the nourisher,” as in Book I, v. 685, “under the thundering Nourisher,” and v. 552, “He himself was irrigator, sower, sustainer, reaper, and plowman.” God is also the lover of all that he created. Wisdom 11:25: “For you love all things that exist, and hate nothing that you have made.”

3. “The lofty regions of the heavens,” like “the sweet things of the world” and similar expressions, unless you prefer *tecta polorum* or *templa polorum* (“the roofs” or “temples of the heavens”). But in Book III, v. 542, we likewise find *Celsa poli* (“the heights of heaven”).

4. Shortly afterward, at v. 47: “Nor are the secrets of heaven empty.” Claudian, at the beginning of Book I of *The Rape of Proserpine*: “And the secrets of your heaven,” where he is speaking of the underworld. An uncertain author, *On the Praises of the Lord*, under Constantine: “To the secrets of the highest heaven, where the bright ether forbids the sluggish clouds to kindle in their own sky.” I would read *succedere* (“to follow”) for *succendere* (“to kindle”). *Parumper* means “meanwhile,” “for a little while,” “for a short time,” “at some point,” “gradually,” according to Servius; or “quickly, speedily,” according to Nonius, chapter 4, who interprets Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, 382: “And the pain, driven for a little while from his heart.” Servius observes that, according to the opinion of others, *parumper* means “very little.” Here it appears to mean “to some extent” or “in part.” For the secrets of heaven are so hidden that they nevertheless make themselves manifest to human beings to some extent, insofar as is sufficient to recognize and proclaim God’s power.

6. The stars are “hanging,” because fixed in the sky they seem to hang. I considered whether it might be necessary to read *Splendida quod tremula* (“because they shine, trembling”). *Vibrare* (“to flash”) can be used for “to shine” or “to sparkle” without an accusative, but one is always understood, as in *vibrare flammas* or *vibrare lumen* (“to flash flames” or “to flash light”); for *vibrare* means “to throw” or “to shake.”

217 Almighty eternal God, the only hope of the world,

Creator, begetter, nourisher, ruler, lover

Of all things that the world contains, of all that the heights of heaven contain,

Which cover the secrets of heaven and reveal them for a little while,

[5] 218 Because the starry sphere revolves above the stars from its axis,

Because the hanging, trembling stars flash with their flaming light,

[Col. 0771A]

7. And beautifully: “The light beneath which the hidden light shines…”

9. “So that it puts the stars to flight…”

11. *Partica cum parte v[ices]* (“sharing turns with his counterpart”).

13. Corrected: “two through chaos”; afterward *noctis* (“of night”) is absent.

14. “When by your power, not by craft, you made the world.”

17. “But he who is perfect.”

7. See Book I, v. 220: “But they are oppressed by light,” and v. 675: “By whose immense flames the stars grow faint,” and so forth.

8. Book I, v. 668: “Messenger of dawn,” and so forth.

9. Perhaps: “And it puts the stars to flight.” Horace, Book III, ode 21, at the end: “While returning Phoebus puts the stars to flight.” Ovid, *Heroides* 2, v. 47: “And I gave the oarage by which you would depart in flight from me.” Thus *fugiturus* was also used by Pliny, Petronius, and Statius. The “reins of light” are those of dawn or the sun; for poets also imagined dawn riding in a four-horse chariot, or at least a two-horse chariot.

10. The reason is given why the moon is called “cold,” as in Book I, vv. 52 and 666: namely, because it receives its light from the sun. The moon is also called cold because it is dewy, as it is often said to be, and because it presides over the cold night. One might conjecture: “Because the sun’s heat is what shines in the cold moon, sharing turns with her brother.”

11. *Partita* derives from *partior, partiris*, with the final syllable lengthened because of the caesura. Sedulius, Book I, v. 253, says of the sun: “He shares his turns with night and is not always everywhere.” One might try *Partita cum fratre vice* (“sharing turns with her brother”). The manuscript has *parte*, and perhaps *patre* (“father”) should be written, as though the sun were the moon’s father because he imparts his light to her. But poets very frequently call the moon the sun’s sister and the sun the moon’s brother, and therefore I think Dracontius intended this instead. *Tempora lunae* (“the moon’s seasons”) is also read in Book I, v. 73. Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, v. 585, says *tempora Phoebi* (“the seasons of Phoebus”): “For this reason the night is sadder than the seasons of Phoebus.” In fact, the seasons are nothing other than the motion of the sun, moon, and stars: Genesis 1:14, “Let there be lights … and let them be for signs, and for seasons, and for days and years.” See Book I, v. 52 and following. *Lustrare* means “to go around” or “to traverse.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, chapter 20: “The star of Mercury, in about a year, traverses the star-bearing sphere.”

14. Thus I restored a very corrupt verse. The meaning is clear: if the darkness of night were to invade the world without any light from the moon and stars, that chaos which God destroyed when he created the world would seem to be present. Book I, v. 116: “For the first day belonged to light, and death alone to darkness.” See the note on v. 197 of this Book II. *Necare* means “to drive out” or “destroy.” Seneca, *Hippolytus*, v. 454: “Why do you restrain and destroy your noble nature?”

15. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II, v. 327: “Here lies Phaethon, the driver of his father’s chariot.” *Inspirare*, “to breathe into” or “to impart an inner light,” is frequent in ecclesiastical usage, but is supported by the best Latin writers. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, v. 11: “To whom the Delian prophet inspires great intelligence and spirit.” Quintilian, Book II, chapter 5: “With what powers he inspires, with what pleasure he charms.” Justin, Book V, chapter 1: “Those who are accustomed to be inspired are called mad.”

17. Martianus Capella, Book II, in the hymn to the sun: “They say that four winged horses bend you by the reins, since you alone control the chariot which the elements provide.” Dracontius investigates and explains the origin of the story of the sun’s chariot. Aratus, *Phaenomena*: “For this reason too they assign that [chariot] to him, either because he completes the circle of the year through the fourfold changes of the seasons—spring, summer, autumn, and winter—or because he measures the extent of the day along a fourfold boundary.” Fulgentius, *Mythologies* I, supplements the passage: “For this reason too they assign him a four-horse chariot, either because he completes the circle of the year through the fourfold changes of the seasons, or because he measures the extent of the day along a four-part boundary.” Empedocles, Hippocrates, and other philosophers established the four elements as the principles of all things perceived by the senses; they maintained that all elements are present in all things, but that each received its name from the element it contains in greater abundance, as Isidore explains this opinion, *Etymologies* XIII, chapter 3. Dracontius implies in Book I, v. 25, that the sun consists chiefly of fire and water. But all the elements have a mutual connection among themselves; and, as Ambrose explains, *Hexaemeron* III, chapter 4, water, as though with two arms—one of cold and the other of moisture—seems to embrace earth with one and air with the other: earth with cold, air with moisture. Fire, hot and dry, is joined to air by heat and to earth by dryness. Others explain it similarly.

18. It would be easy to read *calores* (“heats”) for *colores* (“colors”), for shortly afterward four heats of the sun are distinguished—those of summer, autumn, winter, and spring—which may also be observed at the different hours of any day. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II, v. 134: “So that they may bear equal heats for heaven and earth, neither press the chariot down nor drive it at the summit through the ether.” But the old reading should be retained, for four colors of the sun, differing in the four parts of the day, are noted. Aratus, *Phaenomena*: “Hence they also gave the horses suitable names: Erythraeus, Actaeon, Lampros, and Philogaeus.” *Erythraeus* means “red” in Greek, because he rises red with the morning light. *Actaeon* means “bright,” because he shines more brightly as the third hour approaches. *Lampros* means “shining” or “burning,” because this is what he becomes when he has climbed toward the Arctic Circle at the midpoint of the day. *Philogaeus* means “loving the earth” in Greek, because, inclining downward at the ninth hour, he leans toward sunset. Fulgentius uses almost the same words in Book I of the *Mythologies*, but has *centratum* (“centered”) for *contra arcticum* (“toward the Arctic”). Others call the sun’s horses by other names. See Hyginus, fable 183, and Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II, v. 153: “Meanwhile the winged ones, Pyroeis, Eous, and Aethon, the horses of the Sun, and the fourth, Phlegon.”

20. Book I, v. 737, similarly: “May they diminish according to an eternal law.”

21. *Ditione* means “by command” or “by dominion.” Cicero, *Laws* II, chapter 7: “Let this therefore be accepted from the beginning by the citizens: that the gods are the lords and governors of all things, and that what happens is brought about by their power, dominion, and divine will.” *Vapores* (“vapors”) is used for *calores* (“heats”).

23. The sun’s radiance is called “cold” in winter because it warms less and does not prevent frost. One might write *prae duce jussu* (“by the command of a guide”). But *praedux*, supported only by Dracontius, is acceptable to me; thus others have also used *praeduco*. *Perpete jussu* (“by perpetual command”) would not be bad.

And the stars lie hidden beneath the light, beneath night they shine,

Because the herald of dawn, the fiery morning star, flashes,

So that it puts the stars of heaven to flight, itself about to flee the reins of light,

[10] Because it is the sun’s heat by which the cold moon shines,

Sharing turns with her brother, traversing her appointed seasons,

So that darkness may not invade the world together, without light,

And chaos may be thought to be present within the extent of night,

Which you destroyed by your power when you made the world.

[15] [Col. 0772A] 219 You, God, breathe into us that the sun is called a charioteer,

Not because it is carried by four horses on a revolving axle,

But because the perfect sun, a skillful charioteer, alternates

Four colors derived from the four elements,

220 The sun, commanded, changes the four seasons of the year,

[20] Not daring to pass beyond the appointed turns under an eternal law

Of its own accord, nor temper its central fires,

24. Book I, verse 86, “God remaining after the ages.” Here too, *post saecla* (“after the ages”) would be suitable.

25. Book [I], verse 333, “The glorious soldiery of heaven.” Zephaniah, chapter I, verse 5: “And those who worship upon the roofs the host of heaven,” namely the sun, moon, and stars. Concerning the soldiery of the sun, Dracontius, Book I, verse 229: “He too is a soldier of God.” Since the Lord is called God *Sabaoth*, that is, “of hosts,” some interpret this as referring to the stars, which are presented as though standing under arms in battle formation at God’s command. See Calmet, *Biblical Dictionary*, under the word *Sabaoth*.

26. *Mundus* (“world”) is used for “earth,” as in Book I, verse 705: “Of the watery gulf by which the whole world is encircled.” A similar usage is found in Book I, verse 385, “By which it is shown to be suitable,” and in verse 524, and Book II, verses 190, 265, 583, and 716, and in the *Elegy*, verses 187 and 295, although the manuscripts vary in some passages. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* II, verse 92: “And through paternal fear I am proved to be a father.”

27. The metrical pattern is not satisfactory if one reads *tuum visibile non latet* (“your visible [work] is not hidden”). I thought it should be restored as *visum est*, namely, “it was seen” through the sun. Concerning light, Book I, verse 135: “By whose command he ordered all created things to shine.”

30. Perhaps, “Preparing without end,” or “You who give beginnings to things and [their] end; who, being without an end, do not know beginnings.” Book I, verse 22: “And deservedly, because, being without an end, he knows no beginnings.”

31. “God, hope,” as stated in verse 1 of this book. *Princeps* (“first,” “chief”) is used for “inventor” and “author” by Cicero and others. Of God, Dracontius uses it in Book I, verses 332 and 399, and Book III, verse 154. *Superstes* (“surviving,” “present”) with a genitive occurs in Cicero and other highly authoritative writers. Here the word may have its first and proper meaning, namely, “one who stands above” and is present to the world.

32. Genesis, chapter I, verse 2: “And the spirit of God was borne over the waters.” Many interpret this as the Holy Spirit. Dracontius speaks of this spirit of God in Book I, verses 600 and following: “That spirit of God by which all bodies are moved, embracing all things,” and so forth. It may be understood as divine nature and power itself, for God is the Holy Spirit, insofar as “spirit” signifies an incorporeal substance.

33. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, verse 726: “The spirit within nourishes, and the mind infused through the limbs moves the whole mass.” Dracontius, Book I, verse 603, concerning the world: “The mass, immense.”

34. I do not think that Dracontius shortened the first syllable of *aer* (“air”), although some say that this can occur. “As diffused air” seems more characteristic of Dracontius.

[Col. 0774B] 35. The manuscript reading can scarcely have the correct meaning, and I have no doubt that Dracontius wrote *per partes* (“in parts”): just as the noun *omnia* (“all things”) is opposed to *singula* (“individual things”), so the adverb *generaliter* (“generally”) is opposed to the words *per partes*, which function adverbially, as though meaning “one by one.” Columella, Book I, chapter 4: “Although this is sometimes costly in parts, it nevertheless proves economical as a whole”; and Book IV, chapter 24, shortly after the beginning: “These things must be guarded in general, those in parts.” See below, verse 183 of this book. After I had made this conjecture and explanation, I came upon these words of Saint Isidore, *Sentences* I, chapter 2: “God does not fill all things piecemeal, but although he is one and the same, he is wholly everywhere.” In this sense the old reading may be explained and retained.

36. “Ministering,” as explained at verse 227 of Book I, is used in the sense of “serving.”

37. “Vibrating nature,” as at verse 64, concerning the mind of God: “Simple, lofty, gentle, vibrating, immense, serene.” Vibrating nature is nature stirred with the utmost rapidity, or even flashing.

39. Book I, verse 337: “Into bodily limbs,” and verse 601: “He moves, cherishes, inserts, and drives.” The order will be better if *continuanda* (“things to be continued”) is read first, followed by *corporeos* (“bodily”).

40. The reading *succidenda manent, et continuanda labascunt* (“things to be cut off remain, and things to be continued grow weak”) seems more characteristic of Dracontius’s wit and style. He also uses *succido* in Book I, verse 615. The first syllable of *labuntur* is long; for that reason I substituted *labascunt*. In the later period the verb *labor* seems commonly to have had a long first syllable. Victorinus, *On the Maccabees*: “Now the place is better than the falling kingdoms of the king,” and shortly before: “And the kingdoms that are given while they endure for a brief time.” Fabricius gives these examples in his *Index of Christian Poets*. But in the first passage one may read *labantia*; in the second, *labitantia* is a frequentative from *labor, labas*.

41. Book I, verse 258: “Sitting upon the foliage,” from *insido*. The metre argues against *insidet*.

43. *Illustrare* (“to illuminate”) can sometimes mean *lustrare*, “to traverse” or “survey,” in which sense the same verb occurs in Book I, verse 597. Cicero, *Dream of Scipio*, chapter 4: “The sun … is of such magnitude that it illuminates and fills all things with its light”; although this is commonly explained as “brings brightness to all things,” the following verb *compleat* (“fills”) requires another meaning. Some unnecessarily restore *sua luce lustret* (“surveys with its light”); there is no reason to deny *illustro* the meaning “to survey” or “to illuminate throughout.”

45. I was attempting *quo cuncta reguntur tempora* (“by which all times are governed”), or *spatia* (“spaces”), instead of *quem*. I nevertheless change nothing: the phrase may be understood as “the spirit of all time and space.”

*Is shown to serve the Ocean, the world, or heaven as witness.*

[30] *And prepare an end without end, who know no beginnings:*

222 *It settles in minds, penetrates the head, bones, and marrow,*

56. “But you by law.”

47. Compare verse 4, “Which cover the secrets of heaven.” *Vacant* means “are empty,” or also “are free and exempt.”

48. See whether *Non adeat virtute sua vel tua* (“May it not approach by its own or your power”) is better. *Habeat* (“may it have”) is also good, as in verse 44: “Whom all things carry, by whom all things are governed.”

49. Book I, verse 77: “And the lunar sphere.”

50. Shortly afterward, verse 114: “To perform the work of power”; and in the *Elegy*, verses 290 and 298, “the work of piety.” Here *the work of piety* is the beneficent influence of the sun, moon, and stars upon the earth. Book I, verse 224: “Who with pious fire cherishes heaven, sea, stars, and lands.”

51. This passage seems corrupt. Perhaps the verses should be transposed: first, *Circulus haerebit* (“The sphere will remain fixed”), then *Qui nihil est* (“Which is nothing”).

53. Perhaps *haereat* is a disyllable by synaeresis; or in the following verse one should read *mutant* (“they change”), followed afterward by *cadit* (“it falls”). The meaning is: “The sphere will remain fixed unless you command it to go on its course; it is nothing unless it is preserved by your law forever. For unless it is preserved, immediately the revolving sphere and the starry splendor will remain fixed, the elements will change their alternations, and the machinery of the universe will fall before its appointed day.”

54. In the *Elegy*, verse 247: “The elements alternate their turns.” The opposite is *mutant* (“they change”). Rusticus Helpidius, *On the Benefits of Jesus Christ*: “Even discord preserves faithful alternations among the elements.” Below, verse 335: “They remain for a thousand ages,” from which one might conjecture *per saecla morantes* (“remaining throughout the ages”). But Dracontius seems to have intended *circla* from *circulum*, neuter, for which I have no example. The syncope in *circla* is supported by Virgil, *Georgics* III, verse 166: “Loose circles of slender willow.” Many words were contracted by syncope by the ancients and altered by copyists because they thought them corrupt. In the elegy called *Paracteria*, or *Repercussoria*, as it is named in manuscript copies, in which Sedulius describes the deeds of our Savior, the final verse is: “With the Holy Spirit, great glory to the Father.” Some changed this to “Glory to the Spirit and to the Son, great glory to the Father”; but already in Bede’s time it was read, “With the Holy Spirit.” In his book *On the Art of Meter*, Bede says that Sedulius neglected the rule of grammatical arrangement so that he might sing aloud the glory of the holy and undivided Trinity. Yet Sedulius could have written “With the holy Breath” or “With the holy Pneuma.” I therefore think that Sedulius wrote *Cum sancto Spritu* or *Spirtu*. I read the same in Victorinus, *On Jesus Christ God and Man*: “It was time for the Thunderer to release his spirit to the Father.” In the second book of the poems of Eugenius of Toledo, poem 75, the last verse is: “And may he likewise turn adulterers into peace and embraces.” The most diligent editor, Cardinal Lorenzana, noted: “*ADULTEROS* cannot stand; but whether we read *ADULTOS*, no meaning can be extracted.” I therefore read *adultros*, by syncope from *adulteros*; thus both metre and meaning are preserved.

55. *Ante diem* (“before the day”) is contrary to the order of nature, before the time established by nature, before one’s appointed day, because, as Virgil says, *Aeneid* X, verse 467: “Each has his appointed day.” Thus *obire diem* (“to meet the day”) means to meet one’s own day, or to die. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, verse 148: “The son seeks his father’s years before his day.” Cicero and others commonly say *ante tempus* (“before the appointed time”).

58. Perhaps, “If you should command the world to be destroyed.” *Reputare* is used for “to charge” or “impute,” as though by making a reckoning. Papinian, *Digest* XI, title 7, law 17: “But if the father has not yet recovered the dowry, the husband alone will be sued, with the intention of crediting to the father whatever he has paid on that account.” Dracontius is interpreting Job 11:10: “If he overturns all things, or confines them together, who will oppose him?” That is, who will demand an account from God if he overturns the world? The same thought occurs in Wisdom 12:12: “For who shall say to you, What have you done? Or who shall stand against your judgment? … Or who shall charge you if the nations perish which you made?”

60. With some hiatus, *Deum ante omnia Christum* (“Christ God before all things”) could be retained. See Broukhusius on Propertius, elegy 12, verse 1. Rusticus Helpidius, *On the Benefits of Christ Jesus*: “By this word, by which the Sower prepared such kingdoms for himself, he proved you also a companion of his kingdoms and one born [of him].” Dracontius maintains the same manner of speaking in explaining the generation of the Son as Prudentius in *Cathemerinon* hymn 3, verse 2, and hymn 11, verse 17, where he says: “Although you were born from the Father’s mouth and brought forth by his word, nevertheless in the Father’s heart you were called Wisdom beforehand. She who readily founded heaven, heaven, the day, and all else. All these things were effected by the power of the Word, for the Word is God. But when the ages had been ordered and the arrangement of things set in order, the Founder and Artificer himself remained in the Father’s bosom.” And in the *Apotheosis*, verse 524: “But made by the Lord’s Word, not by a resounding voice, but by the Word that always was, the Word was made flesh.” Thus God made all things by the Word, or speech, and by the Word also generated his Son, that is, the Word, which, although it was made flesh, was nevertheless begotten, not made. Since Dracontius says *Quo libuit* (“by which it pleased him”) and “God Christ,” it is certain that he is speaking of a second and temporal generation, but in such a way that in the following verse he immediately explains the eternal generation, in which he also acknowledges the Word conceived and begotten by the Word. Christ, however, was begotten before all things because he was foreordained and predestined before all things. Psalm 109:3: “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot you.” See the notes on the cited passage of Prudentius.

62. It must certainly be read *non unquam* (“never”), since *nonnunquam* (“sometimes”) is opposed to the doctrine of the Catholic faith and to the meaning of the whole passage. See the prolegomena, no. 109 and following.

63. *Multa* means “great.” Cicero, *Letters to Friends* II, letter 10: “Our name has great influence in these regions.”

64. *Levis* means gentle, mild, pleasing; by contrast, *gravis* (“heavy”) is said of something unpleasant and troublesome. *Levis* may also be understood spiritually, that is, “without weight.” See the note on verse 37 concerning *vibrans*. A serene mind is joyful, happy, and prosperous; for this reason the pagans called Jupiter by the special titles *Serenus* (“Serene”) and *Serenator* (“the one who makes serene”); hence emperors were called *serenissimi* (“most serene”).

65. Perhaps *cunctiparens* (“parent of all”) is better, a word used by Prudentius, as also *cunctipater* (“father of all”) by Theodulf of Orléans. Prudentius also used *cunctipotens* (“all-powerful”). But since Virgil used *Omnipatens* (“all-pervading”), *cunctipatens* (“all-pervading”) should not readily be rejected. A mind may be called innumerable on account of its effects, though it is one in its own nature. I suspect that one should read *cunctipatens, immensurabilis, una* (“all-sustaining, immeasurable, one”). Salvian and other Christian writers used the word *immensurabilis* (“immeasurable”), and above the holy mind of the Father has already been mentioned.

67. Here the adverb *mox* signifies eternity itself, as today in Psalm 2:7: “You are my son; today I have begotten you.” Hebrews, chapter I, verse 5.

68. The Son is shown to be the Father’s companion or consubstantial one. See verse 103 and following.

69. Concerning the triune mind of God, see what was said in the prolegomena, no. 109 and following. Dracontius, Book I, verse 563, wrote: “God, a threefold power,” as Paulinus, poem 26, natal poem 11: “For the one God is a threefold power.” So also, “a triune mind.”

70. See Book I, verse 29. I think the punctuation should be: *pietate modestus, inn umera, coelis* (“modest in piety, immeasurable, [present] in the heavens”), as a form of multiple power.

73. *Canentes* (“singing”) is grammatically connected with *coelis* (“heavens”) and *fluctibus* (“waves”).

80. *Post templa poli* (“after the temples of heaven”) is the same as what is said in the creed: “He descended from heaven.” Augustine, sermon 187, formerly 27, *On Time*: “How much more could this Word, so great and such, having assumed a body, make fruitful the womb of his mother, and yet not depart from the bosom of the Father? From here emerge before human eyes, and from there illuminate angelic minds? From here proceed to the earth, and from there extend the heavens?” Add Saint Leo’s passage cited at verse 99.

Book I, verse 346, concerning the creation of Adam: “And the new structure rising gave him a voice,” or, by conjecture, “And it gave a voice through the structure.” Avitus, Book II, verse 96: “Heaven holds the earth, and earth, raised by a poor structure, rules.” Concerning the structure of the body and the bones of the hand, Celsus, Book VIII, chapter 1: “All the elongated and triangular parts are joined together by a certain structure.” Dracontius, Book III, verse 643: “The fragments of a long ruin build the human being, but before the limbs existed they were joined by a structure,” and so forth.

85. Book III, where the restoration of life to dry bones is discussed, verse 614: “Now the limbs are joined by sinews.” Perhaps one should read, “They grow fat within the marrow; from here blood, from here fluid.” In the cited passage, verse 612: “When the fluid of blood had entered the marrow previously drained.” Marrow is a more refined fat.

87. Concerning the verb *plasmo* (“to form”), Book I, verse 336: “He formed the man through his limbs.”

89. The Virgin conceived because she believed. “Faith comes from hearing.” Compare verse 591. Augustine, sermon 13 *On Time*, formerly 128, in the appendix: “The word of God marries a woman who does not know a man.” Sedulius, in the alphabetic hymn: “Knowing no man, she conceived the Son through the Word.” Ennodius of Pavia, Book II, hymn 10: “She conceived a son through the ear … What the tongue uttered is seed.” Sedulius perhaps also wrote, “She conceived a son through the ear.” See the note on verse 60. Dracontius uses *fetare* (“to make fruitful”) at verse 217 and in the *Elegy*, verse 83. Here it means “to fertilize,” as in Saint Augustine and others. In Columella, *feto* means “to give birth to offspring.”

91. “Panting fire,” as in Book I, verse 26, “the panting sun.” See the prolegomena, no. 137.
