99. This verse is corrupt, but without any doubt its meaning is: the Son assumed bodily limbs in such a way that he nevertheless did not leave heaven. The following words are clear and are expressed in the manuscript without any error. One might also correct it to: “He did not leave the lofty heaven of the Father.” Helpidius, *On the Benefits of Jesus Christ*: “Never inferior in the Father’s power, never absent from the ether.” Saint Leo, sermon 2 *On the Nativity of the Lord*: “Jesus Christ our Lord enters these lower realms, descending from his heavenly seat and not departing from the Father’s glory.”

103. Thus by conjecture, unless one prefers, “Never proved without the Father, and the Father never named without his pledge,” and so forth.

104. The same divine nature, with all its attributes, is acknowledged in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. Book I, verse 434: “Hope, maker, lord, ruler, leader, arbiter, judge.” I explained how God is called “judge” at verse 114 of Book I.

105. The same word is neuter, for in the masculine the first syllable is long. This results from theological usage. One should not correctly say that the Holy Spirit is *eumdem* (“the same one”) as the Father and the Son, for that implies that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are the same person. Yet one may truly assert that the Holy Spirit is *idem* (“the same thing”) as the Father and the Son, which signifies that the same nature exists in the three persons. Paulinus, poem 26, natal poem 11: “The one nature of God is God; what the Son is, and what the Spirit is, the Father is.” Arator, Book I, verse 972, explains the contrary heresies of Arius and Sabellius thus: “Against this faith the contentious Arius falls, denying that the three persons are one.” “Sabellius confessed one, but said that it was the Father, who thereafter in turn is called Son and Holy Spirit—the same one—but that the whole is the Father himself.” In one manuscript: “But that the whole person is the Father himself.” Masculine nouns indicate persons; neuter nouns, essence. See the commentary on Prudentius, verse 600 of hymn 10 *Peristephanon*: “Christ is from the Father: the Father is that which the Son is.” Perhaps it would be preferable to read: “The third, one and the same; the first, middle, and everlasting.”

108. The harsh mortal things that Jesus Christ endured could refer only to, or belong only to, the true form of his body. *Spectare* (“to concern”) generally takes an accusative with the preposition *ad*, but it is also found without it. Papinian, *Digest* II, title 14, law 42: “The necessity of payment would concern the debtor.”

109. The meaning is this: if certain miracles had appeared in the Savior’s body by which he seemed exempt from the labors of this life, people would not have believed that his suffering was real.

114. Above, verse 50, “the work of piety.” Book III, verse 211: “He performed the work of power, the greatest miracles.” Virgil, Book X, verse 468: “To extend fame by deeds—this is the work of power.” Paulinus of Périgueux, Book IV: “And may presumption of heart stain the work of power.” Tertullian, Book V *Against Marcion*: “So that the work of power may remain with everlasting praise.” Miracles are called “the work of power.” Matthew, chapter XIII, verse 58: “And he did not perform many works of power there because of their unbelief.” Hence the power of miracles is so called. Sedulius, Book IV—or, according to others, Book V—verse 1: “Among these works of power, the day of Easter had already begun to draw near.” *Catervas* (“crowds”) could be conjectured in place of *catenas* (“chains”), namely: “To perform the work of power through a thousand crowds.” But chains are mentioned because of Mark, chapter V, verse 3, concerning the demoniac: “He had his dwelling among the tombs, and no one could bind him even with chains.” For he had often been bound with fetters and chains, but had broken the chains.

115. Christ’s miracles are indicated, such as the healing of the lunatic and the demoniac.

117. These are lepers, whose flesh is usually sprinkled with reddish spots and flows with corruption. Perhaps one should read [Col. 0781B] *tumefacta rubebat* (“swollen, it was red”), since swellings are also an indication of leprosy.

118. The disease of paralysis is described, for *paralysis* in Greek means “loosening.” Juvencus, Book II, verse 76: “Limping limbs, whose function a harsh illness had dissolved.”

119. From *clade* (“affliction”) I understand “the affliction having been expelled.” The use of the preposition *de* should be noted: when it refers to time, it is used for *in* or *post*, as in *media de nocte* (“in the middle of the night”), *de die* (“by day”), and similar expressions.

122. He calls the eyes that had previously been blind “darkness.” “To know an unknown day” is an oxymoron.

[Col. 0781C] 123. *Simul* (“at once”) is redundant, as in Plautus, *Amphitryon* II.1.12: “Nor can it happen that one person is in two places at the same time.” Or *simul* means “immediately” or “entirely.”

124. Book I, verse 647: “Whenever one part of a human being was dead, another living part lay there.”

125. Perhaps it is better to read: “And, by God’s command, afterward healthy.”

128. I restored this passage from extremely corrupt words and from the matter itself. I do not change *praestitit* (“he provided”), for it may be retained in the sense of “was useful” or “obtained a benefit.” Luke, chapter VII, verse 12: “When he drew near the gate of the city, behold, a dead man was being carried out, the only son of his mother; and she was a widow, and a great crowd of the city was with her. When the Lord saw her, he was moved with compassion for her and said to her: ‘Do not weep.’” But I think the following belongs to Dracontius’s hand: “He did this with the whole body, so that the bereaved parent of a premature son might weep over the funeral,” or “so that the bereaved parent might [weep] with lamentations,” and so forth. *Praecox* (“premature”) is something ripening before its time, which applies very well to a son who dies before his mother. Book III, verse 392: “The bereaved parent did not lament the funeral of her son.”

[Col. 0781D] 129. The daughter of Jairus, ruler of the synagogue, who was twelve years old, was restored to life, Matthew chapter IX, Luke chapter VIII, Mark chapter V.

130. *Vel* (“or”) may stand for *et* (“and”), unless one prefers to take it as meaning “also.”

132. There is an opposition, or oxymoron, in *sanguinis insoliti solitus fluxus* (“the customary flow of unusual blood”); for the manuscript reading *sanguis sanguinis* (“blood of blood”) is corrupt. One might write *decurrere rivus* (“the stream runs down”), but the following verse again has *recurrit amne cruoris* (“it returns in a river of blood”). *Decurrere* seems better than *discurrere*. Juvencus, Book II, verse 389, concerning this hemorrhage: “The flow of blood continued, tearing without end.” Matthew, chapter IX, verse 20: “And behold, a woman who suffered from a flow of blood.”

133. The third syllable in *muliere* is short, but is lengthened because four short syllables come together, as in many similar words. The same occurs below, verse 660: “From the same woman, a man,” as in the epistle, verse 161: “Created from the same woman.” See also Book III, verse 111: “He substitutes a ram for the altars.”

[Col. 0782B] 135. Matthew, chapter XIV. Perhaps there is a transposition, namely: “When he wondered, nature compressed the water, over which Christ accomplished his journey when Peter came.” But with a suitable parenthesis, no other correction is necessary. Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 670: “The servant of the Lord’s step endured the water, and, deprived of its mobility, it tightened itself beneath his solid feet.” The thought is also pointed: nature compressed the water out of wonder. The nature of water is such that when its parts are compressed or squeezed too tightly, they become stationary and in a certain way solid, as happens with ice. Thus Gellius, Book XVII, chapter 8, says that the whole sea called Scythian was compressed and solidified by ice.

137. The waves were conquered because they lost their natural force. The conjecture *vinctis* (“bound”) in place of *victis* (“conquered”) is not to be despised, on the basis of verse 135, “nature compresses the water.”

138. John, chapter II. Here *vertere* (“to turn”) means “to change.” Propertius, elegy 7, Book II, verse 31: “All things are changed; certainly loves are changed.” Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III, chapter 12: “Earth changes itself into water.”

139. *Latex* properly means “water,” although it is also commonly said of wine and every other liquid. Here *latices* is therefore used in its proper sense. In contrast, *poculum* (“cup”) applies to any vessel from which one drinks, but the word is sometimes used in a special sense to indicate drinking wine. Cicero, *Philippics* II, chapter 25: “If this had happened to you during dinner in those enormous cups of yours.” Florus, Book II, chapter 10: “Feasting and playing, and, wherever they were, not knowing anything because of the cups.” Dracontius imitates Virgil, *Georgics* III, verse 528: “They feed on leaves and the nourishment of simple grass; their cups are liquid springs, and rivers worn smooth by their course.” Virgil’s meaning is that liquid springs served for drinking wine; Dracontius’s, however, is that true wine was made from water, which the following words explain more clearly: “And the river’s wave makes [him] drunk.” Macrobius also uses the verb *ebriare* (“to intoxicate”).

140. Matthew, chapter XV; John, chapter VI.

141. *Virtutes* (“powers”) means “miracles,” as stated in the note on verse 114.

142. Perhaps, *miramur* (“we marvel”).

143. *Suus* is not always reflexive, but is sometimes used for “his” or “that person’s,” as is confirmed by countless examples, including those of the best authors.

144. Book III, verse 218. The apostle Peter is called “appointed as leader to innumerable nations under faithful law.” Paulinus, poem 26, natal poem 11, concerning the martyrs: “They were heavenly seed for innumerable nations.”

145. Perhaps *Hos simul* (“these together”), or *quos simul* (“whom together”). In place of *moneret*, *moveret* would not be unsuitable. From the manuscript reading, this meaning may be extracted: the apostles were understood as all the Jews of different nations who were present in Jerusalem. Acts of the Apostles, chapter II, verses 6 and following: “When this sound occurred, the multitude came together, and was confounded in mind, because each one heard them speaking in his own language … And how have we each heard our own language? … We have heard them speaking in our own languages the mighty works of God.”

146. This may be understood as “after Christ’s return, who is heavenly light, to the ethereal regions,” or “after the return of heavenly light to the ethereal regions.”

147. Anyone who wishes to preserve the metre can easily correct *tractus* to *soliumque parentis* (“and the throne of the Father”). See the prolegomena, no. 139, and verse 204 of this book.

150. Perhaps “Although dissimilar.” Certainly the reading is corrupt: “With a dissimilar sun.” The apostles are those called blessed. From the earliest centuries it was customary to call men endowed with holy morals blessed, in contrast to wretched and unhappy sinners and the condemned. See the note on verse 11 of Book I: “And the pious prayers of God are hence for the wretched, there for the blessed.” The title “Blessed” is now ordinarily applied to the heavenly beings whose worship is permitted; in Rome, however, the appellations “His Beatitude” and “His Holiness” are used interchangeably for the supreme pontiff.

151. *Elegies*, verse 2: “Whom every land fears,” or “trembles,” as others read it. That created things adore God is expressed in many places, for example Book I, verse 4, and Book II, verses 72 and 206.

152. Book I, verse 710: “Who gives lightning fires to the clouds when they collide.”

154. “The swift storm,” as explained in Book I, verse 708.

155. Book I, verse 147: “The blue surface of the sea.”

156. Book I, verse 105: “When the ruin subsides.” Wind is often said to fall, and *recidere* is used in the same sense. But here perhaps one should read “when the east winds have subsided.” Virgil, Book VII, verse 27: “When the winds have ceased, and suddenly every blast has fallen silent, and the oars struggle upon the sluggish marble.” He also joins winds and blasts.

157. Book I, verse 78: “And the purple sea.” See the note. “To stretch upon tranquil marble” means to level out, to spread the waves of the sea into a flat surface.

158. “Let the fish play,” as in Book I, verse 237, “They played,” with the note. The following verse is similar: “And let the huge beast rejoice.” If the manuscript reading is retained, the *a* in the adverb *una* must be shortened, as sometimes happens in *frustra*, *contra*, and *ultra*. Yet I would more willingly read: “That the sea, laid low,” or “That after the sea’s surface had been spread out.” Virgil, Book V, verse 763: “The gentle winds spread the waters flat”; and *Eclogue* 9, verse 57: “And now the whole sea lies silent before you, and all the breezes have fallen from their windy murmuring.”

159. Ambrose, chapter 10 of Book V of the *Hexaemeron*, after Basil: “Whales, those immense kinds of fish, bodies equal to mountains.” Tertullian, *On the Judgment of the Lord*: “Misshapen monsters of the swimmers.” Horace, Book I, Ode 3, verse 18: “Who, with dry eyes, [can behold] swimming monsters,” etc. Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, verse 729: “And the sea carries monsters beneath the marble surface.” By “the huge beast” the whale is understood, or any other enormous whale-like creature, as Virgil calls them. See the commentators on Job, chapter XL, verses 20 and following, and Isaiah, chapter XVII, verse 1, where they explain what kind of fish Leviathan is.

160. This miracle was indicated in Book I, verse 704. See the note, and below, verses 787 and following of this book.

162. Moses’ name is pronounced in the same way in the *Elegies*, verse 17: “Spoken by the prophet Moses.” Understand *sub*.

163. Book I, verse 703: “While he perceived the returning waters.” There *returning waters* are waters flowing backward; here they are waters returning to their former place, for *redux* has both meanings. “Again the returning waters reclaim” is a pleonasm, as was stated and confirmed by examples in Book I, verse 111.

165. Latin writers generally say *demersus*. *Dimersus* is attributed to Tertullian, unless this is an error.

167. The manuscript error can also be corrected in this way: “By such a shipwreck as avenger she protects herself from disaster.” The clause could be understood as “She who earlier feared, but afterward…”; or “She who had been fearful”; or “She who became a survivor.” Alternatively: “By such an avenging shipwreck he is blotted out beneath the disaster,” namely the people who were preparing savage deeds. In *deletur* the first syllable is long, and I do not think Dracontius shortened it.

170. “To preserve the limbs for the tomb,” like “to preserve the bones for the tomb,” and similar expressions occur in Prudentius, as I said in my commentary on *Peristephanon* hymn 12, verse 45. By the route through which the Israelites found salvation, the Egyptians found death. The ancients considered it a kind of disgrace if the bodies of the dead were deprived of burial. See the commentary on Prudentius, *Peristephanon* hymn 5, Saint Vincent, verse 390. The Gentiles believed that the souls of the unburied could not even be received into Charon’s boat; the Hebrews imagined that these souls were not granted rest until the body had been committed to the tomb.

171. God himself, who commands the winds, gives them strength so that they may rise. Numbers, chapter XI, verse 31: “And a wind going forth from the Lord carried quail from across the sea.” Psalm LXXVII, verses 26–27: “He brought the south wind from heaven, and by his strength he led in the southwest wind. And he rained flesh upon them like dust,” etc. See verse 153, “You command the winds to rise,” and Book I, verse 707.

172. I was attempting to read *Illusurus adest*: for a gentle wind can be said to play. But *Illaesurus* should be retained, from *illaedo*, from which comes *illaesus*. Tertullian and Lactantius also used *illaesibilis*.

174. I restored “birds” from the passage of Scripture cited above and from Exodus, chapter XVI, verses 4 and following: “Behold, I will rain bread for you from heaven… Behold, the glory of the Lord appeared in the cloud… And it came to pass in the evening that quail came up and covered the camp, and in the morning dew lay around the camp.”

175. Psalm LXXVII, verses 24–25: “And he rained manna upon them for food, and gave them the bread of heaven. Man ate the bread of angels.” John, chapter VI, verse 31; First Corinthians, chapter X, verse 3. “Angelic food” means food from the portion allotted to angels. Suetonius, chapter 18 of the *Life of Caligula*: “He sent a Roman knight who was eating more cheerfully and greedily than Caligula himself his own portion.” Petronius, *Satyricon*, chapter 33: “I myself almost threw away my portion, for it seemed to me that it had already turned into a chick.”

179. This phrase was discussed earlier in the note on verse 26.

180. Mar. Victor, preface, verse 57: “That you might become a reward for the just and for the merits of the pious, you would also confer this by granting that you were a debtor.” Alternatively: “That the work of virtue might come to be, and for the merits of the pious,” etc. The same author, Book I of *Genesis*, verse 329: “While he desires that what he lavishly grants to his servants, not because of their merits but solely from his kindness, should be considered our labor, and prefers to appear indebted for what he gives.” So Fabricius. Others read: “That it should become the work of our praise, which he freely grants,” etc.

Although eternal life is given to the good for their good works as though it were a reward, it is nevertheless the grace of God: because of election, which precedes good works; because of prevenient and assisting grace; because of justifying grace, with which a person must be endowed so that his works may merit eternal life; and finally because of final perseverance, which no one can merit. But if the subject is the natural order of things, which Dracontius here principally, or even exclusively, has in view, God so repays all things to all people as though he were under obligation, because he observes the laws of nature that he prescribed.

Above, verse 55: “And let the lofty structure of things fall before its time.” I would readily allow the reading “If they should be separated,” whether *fuant*, *sient*, or *forent*; and I would say the same concerning Book III, verse 135. If a change is made, for in Book II, verse 505, the first syllable of *fiunt* is lengthened. Lucretius, Virgil, and other older writers used *fuam* for *sim* or *fuerim*, from the ancient *fuo*, whose past tense is still *fui*. In *fiunt* and *fiant*, Christian poets vary: some lengthen the vowel in accordance with the older writers, others shorten it. See the *Prolegomena*, number 139, and the note on Book I, verse 82.

234 The unharming wind comes, with no storm accompanying it,

196. “About to return again” is a pleonasm, concerning which see Book I, verse 111: “But not about to return a second time.”

197. Above, verse 13: “And chaos may be believed,” etc. *Chaos* is customarily taken to mean raw, undigested matter from which things were afterward produced. But Dracontius understands *chaos* as the destruction itself of all things and the darkness that preceded the creation of the world, and that would follow if those same things were reduced to nothing. “You alone surviving, destined to remain,” as in verse 31, “surviving the world.”

198. The verse is seriously corrupt. *Adorande* does not fit the meter. *Venerande* does not offend against it. Seneca, *Hercules Furens*, verse 1218: “And through venerable white hairs for the pious.” I corrected the text from a similar passage in Prudentius, *Peristephanon* hymn 10, verses 536 and following: “One day the heavens will be folded up like a book… God alone will survive, and at the same time the just will remain with the everlasting angels.” See what I noted in my commentary on Prudentius, where I explained in what sense God is said to remain alone as survivor, and at the same time with the just and the angels.

200. It would be clearer to read: “And there will be no labor, when you command that the many ages should already know their end.” In the manuscript the order is: “when you have already commanded that the many ages should know their end.” The construction is involved, but not impossible.

201. Just as *not to know an end* is used for “not to bring something to an end,” so *to know an end* means “to bring something to an end,” or “to reach an end and finish.”

204. Above, verse 147, *thronus* occurs with its first syllable lengthened. The correction would also be easy here: “And the lofty throne entreats you in a humble voice.” But “The throne in the heights” seems more genuine. *Excelsa* means “heaven.” Book III, verse 17: “Higher than the heights”; Book I, verse 101: “Until from the heights.” Arator, Book I, verse 91: “When the ruler of Olympus raises to the heights whatever he has taken up from below,” where Arntzenius needlessly attempts *excelsi*, against the printed books, the manuscripts, and the sense itself. *In excelsis* is an ecclesiastical phrase originating with good Latin authors, among whom *ab excelso* and *in excelso* are often found for “from a high place” and “in a high and eminent place.” Pliny said *excelsa urbis*, “the high parts of the city.”

Dracontius lists five orders of angels: cherubim, seraphim, angels, virtues, and thrones; for in Hebrew, *virtues* are called *Sabaoth*, and *Sabaoth* means “host.” Most writers distinguish nine orders or choirs of angels, and perhaps Dracontius intended to include virtues and powers under the name “hosts,” and angels and archangels under “the angelic choir.”

213. *Coruscare* is active when it means “to shake” or “to vibrate”; but here it means “to flash,” as in verse 152: “At your command the clouds rain, and flash with fire.” It takes the accusative *te* because of this particular meaning. The sense is: “The clouds praise you while they flash,” as in verse 208: “Every spirit resounds with you,” and more clearly in verses 223 and following: “Every kind of poison hisses your name with savage mouth.” Thick clouds are dense and compact, as are thick water, a thick sky, and thick mist or marshes.

218. “The flower breathes,” that is, “gives off fragrance.” Claudian, Book II of *The Rape of Proserpina*, verse 81: “Whatever Panchia breathes forth in its incense-bearing woods.” An accusative is usually joined to the verb, as in “to breathe fragrance,” or an adverb, as in “to breathe heavily” or “sweetly.” Juvenal, however, *Satire* 7, verse 208, used it absolutely: “And the saffrons breathing fragrance.” In the verses of the Library of Saint Isidore, under the title *The Perfumer*: “Here cinnamon and incense breathe their fragrance.”

The statement that harmful animals were given because of our crimes must be understood in this sense: animals would not have harmed humans in the state of innocence but would instead have been subject to human authority. It is also disputed among commentators and theologians whether those animals that are now wild and harmful to others would have acted savagely toward one another in the state of innocence. See Pererius in his commentary on Genesis, chapter I, verse 29.

[220] After the vine has budded, the tendril brings forth grapes.

258. *Obliquus* is a common epithet for other snakes, meaning “twisting” or “crooked.” He perhaps calls the asp’s limbs “fat” because, as Lucan says in Book IX, verse 714: “The blood is fuller in this one, and a drop of thick poison falls.” According to Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 23, section 35, it is commonly said that asps’ necks swell when they threaten to strike; Nicander likewise says in the *Theriaca*: “When anger has flared, and, threatening with its stone, it rages against those approaching, its scaly neck swells, and it hisses with broad mouth.” The asp’s usefulness in medicine is also asserted in the *Elegies*, verse 65: “The asp has deaths, and the snake also has medicines.” Pliny, Book XXIX, chapter 4: “Furthermore, it is established that against the bites of all snakes, however incurable, the entrails of the snakes themselves, applied externally, provide assistance.” And in Book XXX, chapter 4, he says that, for curing glandular swellings, a remedy is made from the ashes of asps applied with bull’s fat.

[Col. 0791D] 259. The bear, lion, and wolf are also useful in some respects. Pliny, Book VIII, chapter 36, section 54, says of bears: “Their fat is suitable for medicines.” He lists these medicines individually in many places. For remedies made from the wolf, consult the same Pliny, Book XXVIII, section 49, and elsewhere. What remedies can be made from the lion is explained by Conrad Gesner, *History of Quadrupeds*, volume I, page 589; in the same volume he discusses the wolf and bear and explains the medicines customarily made from them.

I was considering “The snake, unaware, performs its work,” or “performs an unknown evil,” or “performs the work of resentment.” But it is preferable to read “The snake makes its bite in anger.” Book I, verse 269: “Nor does the fierce viper always make its bite.” *Bite* is frequently said of snakes, by which they inject poison. He compares snakes, which bite only when provoked, with human beings, who often do harm without any cause and, though knowing justice, despise it. See above, verse 232, and Book III, verse 549: “We are a criminal race, deserving nothing of piety.”

268. Perhaps “What we, knowing justice,” or “What, or even justice, we…”

[Col. 0792D] 269. Below, verse 455: “Punishable conduct.” This word occurs often in the Theodosian Code and in Mamertus and other writers of the same period. Perhaps one should read “Punishable, yet ignorance deserves pardon,” etc. Avitus, Book II, verse 53: “For the author heaps up the crime; in the ignorant person the guilt is less than in the sinner.” Some printed editions have *in ignoto*, “in the unknown,” less appropriately. Ignorance rightly merits pardon, because the law provides that the ignorant are excused in certain cases. Ulpian, Book III of the *Digest*, title 2, law 11: “The woman who married him is also marked with infamy, but only if she knew; for ignorance excuses, not ignorance of the law, but ignorance of fact.” See Barbosa, *On Legal Maxims*, maxim 113. Among theologians there is a long controversy, irrelevant here, concerning what kind of ignorance, and when, excuses. This much should be considered certain: even ignorance of the law, if it is truly invincible, excuses a person from formal sin.

The snake makes its bite in anger; but we, a wicked throng,

276. *Elegies*, verse 67: “The hind, having fed on a snake, prepares healing marrow.” Solinus, chapter 31, on deer: “It has been established that they never suffer fever; for this reason ointments made from their marrow calm the heat of sick human beings.” Lucan, Book VI, verse 673: “The deer’s marrow, after it has fed upon a snake,” which was also used in magic, as Lucan himself relates. See further material in Gesner, *History of Quadrupeds*, and, among more recent writers, Bomarius in the *Dictionary*.

277. It could be corrected to “What harm did the hare do through the fields?” For *lepus*, even when a female is meant, is ordinarily expressed in the masculine gender. But *passura*, “about to suffer,” is suitable, or, if preferred, *peritura*, “about to perish”; for Priscian, Book V, establishes that *lepus* may be used in either gender. Hares, moreover, sometimes do cause harm. Dracontius, however, is criticizing human boldness and lust, because people pursue and torment even animals that cause little or no harm and are of no use, or only slight use, in medicine, for other reasons.

278. The hare, fallow deer, and goat are also useful in medicine, as Gesner confirms on the authority of the ancient physicians in his *History of Quadrupeds*. Dracontius therefore reproaches human beings only because they hunt these animals chiefly for pleasure and luxury.

[Col. 0793D] 280. Perhaps “What have the fish of the sea deserved?”

281. It should be noted that the verb *pervaditur* is passive. Although *pervado* is sometimes used with an accusative without a preposition, as in “Our people crossed the strait,” the preposition is omitted because it is already contained in the verb itself.

284. “The route is frequented,” that is, “is traveled often,” as Cicero and others use *celebrare viam*. The reading *sed jussus* is plainly corrupt, and no more certain correction occurs to me than *sejunctus*, namely, “man, separated by nature from the water,” etc.

285. “To shake the oars” is perhaps novel, but elegantly expressed.

286. Book I, verse 621: “Small things had been for God,” meaning “too little.”

287. “Moreover” is elegant after *parva* or *parum*. Plautus, *Mercator* IV.2.1: “Is it not enough of misfortune that this Demipho is in love, unless he is also extravagant besides?” Livy, Book III, chapter 67: “If the fault is ours, take authority away from the unworthy; and if that is not enough, exact punishments besides.” *Grassari in undas*, “to advance into the waves,” is also attractive, like *grassari in senatum*, “to attack the Senate,” or *in homines*, “to attack men.”

288. It could be changed to “And troubles the blue strait”; but this kind of construction is not unusual, and when used sparingly it is graceful. The hand, evidently, is what troubles the strait. If one reads *sollicitant*, “they trouble,” this verse will be connected with the preceding one.

290. Perhaps “What the earth had borne…”

291. Perhaps “And what is neighboring,” “nearby,” or “rival.”

293. *Implicitant* is a frequentative form from *implico*, used by Pliny the Younger in Letter 33 of Book IX, although some read *implicat* instead of *implicitat*.]

294. Perhaps by imitation of Lucan, who sang, “Wars more than civil across the Emathian plains.” Some indeed criticize him for saying “more than civil” of those wars, but unjustly. For a civil war is one in which citizens wage war against one another; but if such a war has been stirred up and kindled by related commanders—such as kinsmen, fathers-in-law, fathers, sons, or brothers who are at odds with one another—one may rightly call it “more than civil.” This interpretation can also be applied to Ovid, who, in Book XII of the *Metamorphoses*, line 582, says of Neptune: “Hating savage Achilles, he exercises his remembered anger in a manner more than civil.” For Thetis, Achilles’ mother, was Neptune’s granddaughter through Nereus.

295. Catullus likewise, at the end of the epithalamium of Peleus and Thetis, describes the multitude and enormity of crimes in a similar manner: “Brothers stained their hands with a brother’s blood,” etc.

296. *Noviter* for *nove*, “in a new manner,” as at the first occasion. This adverb occurs in Plautus and Fulgentius the Mythographer, and in an inscription in Gruter, p. 171, no. 7, which is thought to belong to the fourth century and the Constantinian period. Perhaps one should read: “Nor is novelty now attempted—the beginnings of the world.”

297. Lucan, Book I, line 95: “The first walls were wet with a brother’s blood,” namely those of Rome.

Medicine seeks the stag’s marrow, that it may fall.

243 What harm did the hare deserve, destined to suffer? What harm the doe, or the goat?

Whom does this medicine command to be seized for such purposes?

So that they may fall through the deceit of hunters, or beneath an iron spear?

[280] What harm have the fish of the sea done? What harm the multitude of birds?

Our race has traversed the sea; the air is traversed,

so that birds innocent on every side may be captured.

What nature forbids, through us the elements are sought:

[Col. 0793B] Across the sea the journey is made: separated from the waters,

[285] he sails, striking the daring oars upon the waves.

[Col. 0794A] People think it a small thing to cross the harmful waves;

moreover, armed, they advance into the midst of the waters;

244 He wounds the blue-green sea with a bloodstained blade,

and a foreign hand transfers war to unfamiliar lands.

[290] Was it not enough that the earth endures bloody wars,

unless even a neighboring people should produce enemies?

The armed hand, unable to restrain itself, why does it fasten weapons

upon those nearby and carry on—horror!—civil wars?

Nor is civil war alone enough: [295] brothers attack fathers-in-law, fathers, and brothers in savage conflict.

[Col. 0794B] Nor is it attempted anew only now; the beginnings of the world

lamented the appalling crime and saw the righteous man,

the second human being, drenched in his brother’s blood.

299. G.: “*hoc i.*,” and afterwards “*conditor o.*”

301. “With the throat blocked, the traveler falls—*alugrisne*?”

299. Since the passage concerns Cain killing Abel, I corrected the error from the sense itself, although the wording is very different.

301. I restored *oblisis*. Prudentius, *Psychomachia*, line 535, has *obliso collo*, “with his neck crushed,” and line 590, *obliso gutture*, “with his throat crushed.” “To fall by a robber” means by the hand of a robber. Ovid, Book V of the *Metamorphoses*, line 191: “You will bear great consolations to the silent shades of death—to have fallen by such a man.” Suetonius, *Otho*, chapter 5, and others. Robbers were so called because they beset the roads. Juvenal, Satire 10, line 22: “The traveler without baggage will sing before the robber.” Cicero, *For Milo*, chapter 21: “A traveler is not always killed by a robber; sometimes a robber is killed by a traveler.” Hence the true reading is: “The traveler falls by a robber.”

302. Perhaps “covered with a small cloak,” so that he may be more unencumbered. Cicero, *For Milo*, chapter 3: “The Twelve Tables decreed that a nocturnal thief might be killed in any way, but a daytime thief only if he defended himself with a weapon—that is, because we can guard against a nocturnal thief with greater difficulty.”

304. Book III, line 50: “The examples of the condemned rich man teach us.”

305. A little earlier, in a similar manner: “Thus the wretched thing comes into use.”

308. For this word *modestus*, see the preface, no. 136. Marius Victor, Book II, line 506 of *Genesis*: “Sent with a modest judge,” etc. In the Visigothic legal code, Book II, title 1, chapter 2, in Lindenbrog: “We give modest laws both to ourselves and to our subjects.” Elsewhere in the same code *modeste* is used with the same meaning. [Col. 0795D] Juvenal likewise attacks such abuses in Satire 14, lines 141ff.: “And I would like to set forth the limits,” etc. “But what respect for the laws? What fear or shame has the greedy man who is always in haste?” The ancients had a notable example of joining house to house in Nero’s Golden House, concerning which this distich is found in Suetonius, chapter 3: “Rome will become one house; migrate to Veii, citizens—unless that house also occupies Veii.”

310. Perhaps “Nobility deceived many.” Tertullian, *On the Judgment of the Lord*: “If he had gone on as a robber, if by fraud he had delayed his clients, if in his mind he had been insufficiently attentive to a friendly relationship.” Virgil, Book VI, line 609: “Or a father struck, or fraud entwined with a client.” The ancients especially praised devotion and loyalty toward clients, while they considered it disgraceful to deceive, betray, or abandon them. Suetonius, *Caesar*, chapter 71: “Devotion and loyalty toward clients were not lacking even in his youth.”

[Col. 0796B] 312. I transposed these verses because the sense seemed to require it. Juvenal, Satire 6, line 596: “She who makes women barren and hires men to kill human beings in the womb.”

313. *Parvi* and *parvuli* are used simply for “children” and “infants” by Cicero, Statius, Suetonius, and others.

315. Or should one read “those outside, and likewise his own”? Alternatively, understand “those born outside,” since sons also belong to their father; or it may be indicated that they were conceived by an illegitimate father. *Furit* with the infinitive is good usage. Perhaps a new sentence should begin more suitably with *furit*.

316. *Conceptus* means “fetus,” as in Book I, line 390: “Conceived by no seed.” Pliny, Book XXVIII, chapter 19: “The conception of a hare removed from the womb.” Suetonius, *Domitian*, chapter 22: “So that it even became the cause of death”—of his brother’s daughter—“when he forced her to abort the fetus conceived by him.” *Damnare* means “to inflict harm upon the fetus,” as in Spanish *dañar*, “to injure.” See Prudentius, *Hamartigenia*, line 650: “Harm my ears, merciful Father.” Sedulius, Book III, line 125: “And bold confidence harmed the open veins with dry streams.”

317. He calls the potion by which the fetus is expelled and deprived of life “poison.” Jerome, *To Eustochium on the Preservation of Virginity*: “Some women, when they realize that they have conceived, prepare poisons for the crime of abortion.” At the Council of Lerida in 546, canon 2, those who prepare such potions are called poisoners. Read Augustine’s words on line 322.

[Col. 0796D] 318. The order and sense are: “Whatever woman drinks this poison drinks in death, but not for herself,” because such a medicine is death for the fetus, not for the mother. Yet because the mother’s life is sometimes endangered in this crime, he said above: “Nor does she care for her own danger.” The ironic praises with which Horace addresses Canidia in *Epode* 17, at the end, belong here: “You have a hospitable breast and pure hands; and your womb—*partumeius* [uncertain reading]—and the midwife washed her red cloths in your blood—however strong and slender the woman in childbirth.” Others explain this passage differently. Minucius, in the *Octavius*, says of pagan women: “There are women who, by drinking potions while the child is still in their own wombs, extinguish the origin of the future human being and commit parricide before they give birth.” Compare the notes of Elmenhorst, Ouzel, and others.

319. He says that the crime committed by stepmothers, when they kill the children of a former wife with poison or by some other means, is less serious than the crime of mothers who compel their own children to die before they are born. Stepmothers suffer from the disgrace of pursuing the children of a former wife with hatred, especially after they themselves have borne children and have them surviving. Ovid, Book I of the *Metamorphoses*, line 147: “The terrifying stepmothers mix pale aconites”; and *Heroides*, Letter 12, line 187, Medea: “If I am worthless to you, look upon our common children. The savage stepmother will rage against my offspring.”]

Impiety did this when the world was first founded,

[300] 245 and, as though it were a law, the wretched practice thus came into use.

The traveler falls with his throat crushed by a robber.

What does the nocturnal thief, covered for his wicked deed,

do, with iron accompanying him through the shadows, so that he may not be caught?

Many savage examples of those who came before us teach us this.

[305] What of the fact that sweet adultery has perversely come into use?

And does lust deserving punishment pursue the crime of incest?

Many invade the fields of another’s territory,

and join houses to houses without lawful restraint,

[Col. 0796A] while the promised fidelity is not kept toward a friend.

[310] Many clients of the nobles, deceived by fraud;

the gray hair of old men is despised, and parents are injured.

246 Would that the savage right hand had struck only those already born,

and that guilt had made only the little ones guilty.

But they hasten to strike even those not yet born in the womb;

[315] the impious mother rages to condemn both others and her own unborn children.

She condemns the fetus, and has no concern for her own danger.

What savage impiety drinks this poison with impunity?

Who discovered this great crime, that whoever drinks it

does not drink death for herself? Behold, how much less a stepmother—

320. *Quam*—uncertain.

322. “Death, rather than what…” is written with *quam* joined as one sequence of letters.

323. “Nor evil.”

326. C.: “you have favored, h…”

[Col. 0798B] 328–329. “And he sang, bringing forth the prophet’s soul, *aqi nocti*; ‘the bundles and crimes…’”

337. “They refuse to keep the law.”

339. I.: “*quintia n.*”; previously, “*quintia montes*.”]

[Note: [Col. 0797C]

321. “A stepmother’s right hand,” as in other authors *novercalia odia* (“stepmotherly hatreds”), *novercales oculi* (“stepmotherly eyes”), and *novercalis animus* (“a stepmother’s disposition”).

322. Augustine, *On Marriage and Concupiscence*, Book I, chapter 15, addressed to Valerius: “Sometimes this lustful cruelty, or cruel lust, proceeds so far that it even procures poisons for sterility; and, if that achieves nothing, it destroys and expels the conceived fetus in some way within the womb, wishing its offspring to perish before living—or, if it was already alive in the womb, to be killed before being born.”

323. “Lest the evils be sufficient”: that is, lest the evils they committed be the only ones, or lest other evils follow. I prefer the former interpretation, for the canons of the councils often mention the adultery from which these fetuses were conceived, since abortions are generally procured from illicit intercourse. At the Council of Elvira, canon 63: “If a woman has conceived through adultery while her husband is absent, and afterward kills the child after the deed, it has been decided that communion is not to be given to her even at the end of life, because she has doubled the crime.”

[Col. 0797D] 324. Perhaps *membra quieta*, “quiet limbs”; the same sense is expressed by *linquit membra quieti*, “she leaves the limbs to rest,” and it is not uncommon for *linquo* to be used with a similar dative.

325. Perhaps “now freed by the law.” In the Council of Elvira there is a canon 34: “It has been decided that candles are not to be burned in cemeteries during the day, for the spirits of the saints must not be disturbed.” Mendoza proves very well that these words are to be understood of the kind of magic that I shall explain shortly.

326. The use of herbs was extensive in magical incantations. Horace, against Canidia, *Epode* 5, line 21: “And the herbs that Iolcos and Iberia, rich in poisons, send.” Valerius Flaccus, Book VII, line 352, on Medea: “She prays for greater spells, for Hecate to send her greater powers, and is no longer content with familiar poisons. Then she girds her robe and, where no power is more trustworthy to her, brings forth the Caucasian flower from the fibre of Prometheus’ blood and plants nourished by thunder. That sacred blood endures amid snow and bitter frosts, and flows when, its entrails devoured, the vulture rises from the crags and sprinkles it with open beak. The same blood, ever green and immortal, does not languish through the bounds of a long age; it withstands lightning, and the plants flower amid the flames.” Add Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, lines 261–263.

327. Perhaps “the buried seek them with a dark voice,” or “the buried seek them from a dark voice.”

[Col. 0798C] 328. A passage almost incurable, though I have brought some remedy to it from the story of Saul, who summoned Samuel’s soul from the dead, as Dracontius indicates. First Book of Kings, chapter 28, verses 7ff.: “And Saul said to his servants, ‘Seek for me a woman who has a python-spirit’ … and they came to the woman by night, and he said to her, ‘Divine for me by the python, and raise up for me the one whom I shall name’ … But Samuel said to Saul, ‘Why have you disturbed me, that I should be raised up?’” It could also be emended in another way: “And he sang while bringing forth the prophet’s soul beneath the night.” *Cantavit* is taken as “he enchanted with magical songs,” as in line 326, “with baleful incantations,” unless one prefers to read *incantavit agens*, “he enchanted while bringing forth.” Concerning this infamous art of calling souls out of tombs, Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, line 253: “Under my guidance, no ghost will be ordered to emerge from a tomb, nor will an old woman break open the earth with an infamous incantation.”

329. Compare line 253.

331. One may also punctuate: “The sun, clear light, the day.”

333. Perhaps Dracontius intended *perclara*, “very clear,” like *percarus*, “very dear,” and *percautus*, “very cautious.” But *praeclarus* is more common. Concerning the stars, “the soldiery of heaven,” see the note on line 25, “Serving faithfully with its attendant soldiery.”

334. He uses *reservant*, a compound, for the simple *servant*, “they preserve.”

335. See lines 54 and 348, and Book I, line 142, concerning the verb *morari*.

336. See lines 94 and 388.

339. Apollo was called *Cynthius* from Mount Cynthus on Delos, and Diana *Cynthia*. Lucan, Seneca in his tragedies, and others use *Cynthia* for the moon; Dracontius does so again in the *Elegies*, line 239.

340. Solinus, in a fragment preserved by Pithoeus, p. 267: “The bright ether set with jewels the star-bearing face of Olympus.”

341. *Undosum aequor*, “wave-filled sea,” is used by Virgil, Book IV of the *Aeneid*, line 313.

343. Perhaps *pontum* should be read for *punctum*. Yet *punctum* may be retained for the smallest and indivisible part of a line. Claudian, Book I against Rufinus, line 5, presents the boundaries prescribed for the sea as one of the arguments for divine providence, by which created things are governed. Sedulius, Book I, line 62: “You prevent the roaring storms of the sea, rising in waves, from engulfing the neighboring borders of the land.” Aldhelm, in the preface to his book *On Virginity*: “Thus also you restrain the blind waves of the wandering sea, lest they be able to submerge the shores of the lands in their waters, but that the barriers of the rocks may break the swollen waves.” Barthius, *Adversaria*, Book LVI, chapter 1, rightly observes that Aldhelm has corrupted this argument: it is no longer a miracle for the sea not to engulf the lands when rocks stand in its way; but it is more than a miracle when, although the shores lie level with the plain—or even thrust forward against the waves—such enormous waves do not follow one another farther inland, but all return together upon themselves with the single wave. Hence some philosophers considered the ocean a breathing creature. This is approximately what he says; from it one can perceive how aptly Dracontius treats this argument. In a similar manner the author of the poem *On the Praise of the Lord* under Constantine: “At his command the sea stood within fixed shores; nor is it permitted to run across the lands with its boundless expanse, and level shores enclose the mountainous waves.”]

247 He dares against children born to others the deed that a mother commits.

The stepmother’s right hand now sends children already born to the shades;

the mother compels her offspring to die before being born.

Lest the evils be sufficient, the guilty make them worse.

Even after death they do not leave the limbs to rest,

[325] but disturb souls already quiet under the law of death,

with baleful incantations, herbs, and forbidden art;

248 and they seek answers from the darkness, from the voice of a tomb,

as unhappy Saul incanted while summoning the prophet’s soul through the python-spirit.

Why should we not have deserved more severe things,

[330] [Col. 0797B] all of us who sin so wickedly?

[Col. 0798A] The sun, clear light, bright day, the moon, and the shining stars,

and whatever heavenly bodies serve the great God,

the splendid soldiery of heaven, or the sea and air,

and the earth, preserve the commands received from God,

[335] and obediently remain through a thousand ages.

Nor does so long an age of differing time move them

to refuse to keep the law or to alter the seasons

against the laws of God, against the commands of the Thunderer.

The day shines with the sun; Cynthia illuminates the nights,

[340] and the stars, as though set with jewels, adorn the sky.

249 The wave-filled sea boils, as though it attacked the stars with waves and threatened to cover the earth with foam.

Yet it does not pass beyond the boundary by a single point:

351. “Nor does it fear, and nothing invades it from the waves.”

354. “The leader of the boundaries of time.”

355. “And, forgetting himself, committing”; one witness.

344. Job, chapter 38, verse 11: “And I said: Thus far you shall come, and you shall go no farther, and here you shall break your swelling waves.” See Proverbs, chapter 8, verse 29. Basil of Seleucia, Oration 1: “The sea is indeed said to be raised high by its waves, but when it reaches its boundaries, it turns back and recoils; and when it sees the Lord’s voice inscribed upon the shores, it worships the setter of the boundaries with bowed waves; and when it violently strikes the earth, it is driven back, and, mindful of the divine command, is carried into retreat.” Tertullian—or rather Novatian—in *On the Trinity*, chapter 1: “When the roaring wave and the foaming water from the deep bosom had come, it returned again into itself and did not exceed the boundaries granted to it, preserving the prescribed laws; so that man might guard the divine laws all the more carefully, since even the elements had preserved them.” Corderius, on Job chapter 38, verses 8ff.: “The sea’s obedience to the divine command is shown more clearly when it is stirred by winds and its waves swell. For sometimes it raises its waves so high that they seem to reach heaven, and with such force and violence rushes upon the land that it appears ready to bury it completely. Yet, precisely when it touches the weak and light grains of sand, it restrains itself so that it does not cross them in any way.”

346. Perhaps *feriant sua littora*, “let them strike their own shores,” and thus the sentence would begin more suitably: “Although the force is strong,” etc. Virgil, *Eclogue* 9, line 43: “Come here; let the raging waves strike the shores—allow them.”

347. *Scindere fretum*, “to cleave the sea”: thus a ship cleaves the waters, and the sea is cleft by the blows of oars; rivers are cleft by swimming. But the earth does not cleave the sea, because it does not prevent the sea from reaching its own boundaries, nor does it itself burst into the sea. The earth is called “hanging” because Dracontius and others represent it as resting upon the sea as upon a foundation. See Book I, line 152: “And when the globe solidified, it hung more heavily through the void.”

348. *Moratur* means “remains, stands firm, is restrained.” Book I, line 142: “The elements remain contained within their own boundaries.” Dracontius frequently uses this verb *morari* with the same meaning, as here in Book II, lines 54 and 335.

[Col. 0800C] 351. Perhaps *invaditve*, “or does it invade.”

352. Compare the notes on line 344 from Tertullian and others.

354. Perhaps *terminus aevi*, “the boundary of life”; but I do not understand what this would mean here. Someone conjectured *mortis dux, terminis aevi*, “the leader of death, the boundaries of life,” so that Adam would have been the leader of death, which is the boundary of human life. It is established from Varro, Book IV of *On the Latin Language*, chapter 4, that *termen* was used for *terminus*.

355. “Of the father”—Adam or God—for nothing better occurs to me for *patrans*. Dracontius, moreover, very often calls God “father” and “parent.”

356. Adam was the first and only one who, although all the elements served God, transgressed God’s command shortly after he had been created. On his sin, see line 235. His descendants imitate Adam.

358. Perhaps *nascimur*, “we are born.” On original sin, above at line 240. Here the Catholic doctrine is explained more clearly.

362. *Nota* could also be substituted for *nova*. But Dracontius wrote “savage expiations” in Book I, line 539: “For horrendous crime, or the savage expiations of death”; and in this Book II, line 401: “Their ways return to savage expiations.”

[Col. 0800D] 365. I find no example of *gigantorum* in the second declension; and someone could easily have changed *gigantaea* to *gigantorum*, not knowing that the final syllable is long by the rule of the caesura. *Praesumpta* means “bold,” from which *praesumptuosus* was also formed in a later age. The verse could be restored as: “From there the bold mass of the giants rebelled.” This is taken from Genesis, chapter 6, verses 4ff.: “There were giants upon the earth in those days … these were the mighty men of old, men of renown. And God, seeing that the wickedness of men was great upon the earth, and that every thought of their heart was intent upon evil at all times, repented that he had made man, and was touched with inward grief: ‘I will destroy,’ he said, ‘the man whom I created,’” etc. Many Greek poets, and Catullus in the *Epithalamium of Peleus and Thetis*, embroidered this narrative with myths, as Grotius observed in Book I of *On the Truth of the Christian Religion*, followed by others.

368. Line 225: “And confessing that whatever it possesses owes its existence to you,” which was said of the serpent.]

[345] the swell and wave of the sea, although a strong wind

stirs up the surface and raging waves strike against the shores;

the suspended earth does not dare to cleave the blue sea,

250 though it is about to invade it, but remains content,

joined to its own course, while the shores marvel at the sea,

inventor of crime, discoverer and author of wickedness,

forgetful of his creator, leader of death, seed of Eve,

[355] [Col. 0799B] forgetful of his own father, an enemy and adversary

[Col. 0800A] of all, and of himself, alone after but a brief time.

He transgresses God’s commands; a criminal offspring

[360] Neither piety nor any anger of God restrains us.

When the ages had passed down to the time of Noah,

and the world added continual crime or savage expiations,

370. The ancients invented giants born from the earth in their myths; hence the Greek name, meaning approximately “earth-born.” In Book I, line 239, Dracontius calls all human beings *terrigenas*, “earth-born,” which is another meaning of the word.

372. Perhaps *cum* should be read for *quod*; but the copyist seems to have intended *quod*, since he always writes *cum*, not *quum*.

375. Horace describes the Flood in a similar way in Book I, Ode 2: “When Proteus drove all his herd to see the high mountains. The race of fish clung to the summit of the elm, a dwelling once known to doves, and frightened does swam over the submerged plain.” I think Horace would have mocked Seneca’s criticism of Ovid, which I shall discuss now at line 378.

376. *Gestiret in auras*, “would rage into the air,” for I think *in undas*, “into the waves,” is an error—namely, that the waters attacked the air as though they were invading it.

377. The fish and the sea raged when they attacked the air; but the birds were killed by the water, although they had originated from it. See Book I, line 240.

378. Ovid, Book I of the *Metamorphoses*, line 304: “The wolf is born among the sheep; the wave carries tawny lions, the wave carries tigers,” etc. Seneca, *Natural Questions*, Book III, chapter 27, criticizing Ovid here, says: “It is not sufficiently sober to indulge in extravagance after the whole earth has been devoured.” Muretus and Lipsius agree with Seneca. But poets’ imaginations should not be judged by the standard of philosophers. See the note on line 375.

379. Virgil, *Eclogue* 4: “The herds do not fear the great lions.”

380. Marius Victor, Book II on Genesis: “When the fury of a single rain and a single death had lasted forty days.”

[Col. 0801D] 383. Alcuin, poem 199, probably taken from Dracontius: “Behold, the ark swims upon the waters with the inhabitants of the world.” Perhaps read *enatat in*, “swims upon.”

384. Perhaps *conceptos paritura*, “about to give birth to those conceived.” Genesis, chapter 7, verse 7: “And Noah entered, and his sons, his wife, and the wives of his sons with him, into the ark, because of the waters of the Flood.”

385. The boys are Noah’s sons, Shem, Ham, and Japheth; the tender girls are their wives. They may also be called pious mothers, since the human race was to be propagated from them after the Flood.

386. There is no difficulty in saying that the same day produced those newly born and their fathers, as the following verse says; but that it produced grandfathers and grandsons is unintelligible unless we believe that the wives of Noah’s sons were his granddaughters. Even then, however, one should have said “late granddaughters” or “late grandsons,” since *nepos* is sometimes applied to a female as well. In Valerius Flaccus, Book VIII, line 394, *seri nepotes* means those who will be born much later, as *sera posteritas* means “late posterity” in other authors. But in what sense could one day have produced a grandfather and those who were to be born much later? I believe that Dracontius thought that some sons of Noah’s sons emerged from the ark—namely, that they were born inside the ark. For it is expressly stated that only eight people entered the ark, in the First Epistle of St. Peter, chapter 3, verse 20: “In which ark a few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water.” I am equally certain that only eight people emerged from the ark, and I do not recall that anyone else shared Dracontius’ opinion. Muhammad invented in the Qur’an that Noah’s family, except for Canaan, and others—altogether seventy-eight or eighty people—were brought into the ark. The stories told by certain Jews that Og, king of Bashan, escaped the Flood by sitting upon the roof of the ark; that the Babylonian Sibyl was in the ark with Noah, as she herself relates; and that Philemon, an Egyptian priest, entered the ark with his family, as some rabbis once taught—these are nonsense and fables. Pererius, in his discussion of Genesis chapter 6, Book X, disputation 1, affirms that the common opinion of Jewish and Christian teachers is that Noah and his sons, for as long as they were in the ark, did not engage in procreation. This makes Dracontius’ opinion just explained still more difficult. Perhaps Dracontius followed the account of the Babylonian Sibyl, for the Sibyls’ poems were held in esteem by some of the ancients. Since this Sibyl reported that she had been preserved in the ark with her husband, some suppose that she was none other than Noah’s wife.

388. Earlier, line 336: “An age of differing time”; and line 67: “The origin of differing blood.”

389. Perhaps read: “Nor human beings, and he poured forth again.”

390. Amid such darkness I do not see what better reading I can retain.

391. I supplied this from Hilary on Genesis: “After the swelling of dawn had fallen, the water subsided.”

392. Since *abyssus* is feminine, *alta* can and should be read, with the final syllable lengthened because of the caesura. Avitus, Book IV, line 535: “And the abyss, having been confined by its own barriers, absorbs again the streams that it had previously vomited from its deadly mouth.” For according to Genesis, chapter 7, verse 11, at the Flood all the springs of the great abyss were broken open.]

Earth-born offspring—and the unspeakable race deserved

to suffer a terrestrial shipwreck, while the earth, however far extended,

gave shores nowhere, so that the sea might overwhelm the rivers,

and the harmful rain conceal the sea,

while all woodland creatures, dying, swam upon the waters;

[375] and the aquatic race fed upon the high mountains,

while the sea likewise strove up into the vast air,

252 when the wave killed the flocks of birds it had brought forth.

The wolf swims through the countryside with the herd; the hunter and the bear

are submerged, and herds fear no lions.

[380] For there was one terror; the lot of death held everything,

and there was none who might survive: one death held them all.

[Col. 0802A] And the ark, alone emerging, built by divine command,

swims among the waters with the inhabitants of the world,

pregnant, about to give birth together to young men and old men,

[385] and to boys, pious mothers, and tender girls.

One day produced a grandfather and late grandchildren.

253 The earth received together sons and fathers,

and makes origins of differing times contemporaries.

The more fertile ark pours forth not human beings alone.

[390] The earth was enriched by peace for a short time indeed;

for after the swelling of the sea had fallen, the water subsided,

and the deep abyss received the harmful Flood,

the shores, mountains, sea, rivers, and forests are laid bare;

the springs appear, and little by little the dry earth

[395] is restored, and anger and fear return to all,

now that the earth is covered with wild beasts, herds, and birds.

397. “The vows of crimes,” as at line 405, “the worst vows,” and Book I, line 694, “the evil vows of the guilty.” Cyprian, *On Sodom*: “But the recurring impiety of humanity, together with the second race, and again a new age of evil springs forth”—that is, after the Flood. “To resume vows of crime,” as in Claudian, Book II against Rufinus, line 141: “But he returns to his former appearance and monstrously resumes the disposition for crimes.”

The sense seems to be: “God permitted human beings to wander unpunished, so that, joined together in much crime, they might be recalled.” *Princeps* means “God,” as noted at line 31. *Vagari stadium* with the accusative, as at line 185: “Thus the merchant sailor wanders across the sea with its flying sails.” Eugenius of Toledo, in an address to God, says: “And to run through the course of life with gentle steps.” See whether it would be better to read: “And the Lord endured for a long time as he watched them wander”; or, “And the Lord endured for a long time”; or, “And the Lord endured the zeal”; or, “And the Lord endured the reckless zeal,” so that God may be understood from line 405.

[Col. 0803D] 409. Genesis, chapter 9, verse 11.

410. “These,” namely those whom he saw committing greater sins. As you see, he is speaking of the Sodomites. Genesis, chapter 19.

411. Perhaps “the rain rushed down with avenging flames,” or “the rain burns.” *Compluo* is a word used by Varro.

412. Pentapolis, as its name indicates, is a region consisting of five cities. But not all five cities were consumed by fire, for Zoar was saved from the conflagration by Lot’s prayers; the remaining cities—Sodom, Gomorrah, Admah, and Zeboiim—perished in heavenly fire. Dracontius therefore expressed the name of the region in Latin words, as in Wisdom, chapter 10, verse 6: “She delivered the righteous man from the ungodly who were perishing, when fire descended upon Pentapolis.” It is also reported that certain small towns subject to those cities perished in the fire with them. Besides this Pentapolis of Palestine, several other regions in different parts of the world were called Pentapoles.

413. Marius Victor, Book III, line 778 of *Genesis*, concerning the same fire: “And when the turf had been consumed, the sunken fields reveal their hollow expanses.”

414. *Putrescit* comes from *putris* in the sense in which *putris* means “soluble, dissolved, slack.” Statius, Book VI of the *Thebaid*, line 234, says *putres cineres*, “dissolved ashes.” See the *Elegies*, line 84, *putris arena*, “dissolved sand.” Marius Victor, in the cited book, line 776: “Until the rocks and the resounding earth pass into ashes, and the buried sands are dissolved completely.” It may also be understood of fruits, concerning which Cyprian writes in the *Song of Sodom*: “The fruit is dissolved into ash and becomes empty dust.”

415. Albinovanus, *Consolation to Livia*, line 12: “So that you may be stronger than your misfortunes.”

417. Dracontius taught in Book I, lines 13ff., that all these things descend from the citadel of God. Yet even there he attributes to human sins the fact that God exercises his anger against them. Human beings deserve such punishments not only because of original sin, but also because of the other sins that each person commits privately, from which no one in this life is free. Moreover, certain more severe punishments with which God sometimes afflicts cities and kingdoms generally punish the openly corrupted morals and public crimes of human beings.

418. See Book I, lines 12 and 541ff., and Book II, lines 467ff. and 808, where the same thought is repeated. Here Dracontius expresses Abraham’s words to God, Genesis, chapter 18, verse 25: “Far be it from you to do this thing and to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should be as the wicked: this is not like you.” Yet although after human beings’ death God will most certainly separate their merits according to the conduct of each person, and sometimes even in this life delivers innocent people so that they are not swallowed up in some punishment together with the wicked, nevertheless he sometimes allows them to be involved in the same temporal punishment or calamity. In former times, the course of divine providence was generally such that temporal evils befell the wicked and good things the righteous; from this Job’s friends mistakenly concluded in general that no innocent person is chastised in this life. See Job, chapter 4.

421. “Multitudes of crimes,” meaning metonymically “multitudes of criminals,” as in Terence; and in Plautus *scelus*, “crime,” is often used for “a criminal.”

422. I read *de morte truci*, “from savage death,” as at line 703: “And recalling him from savage death.”]

The impious human race soon resumes its criminal vows,

and wishes to restore its wrongdoing, lest it lose the practice

254 of crime and suffer, as it were, a loss;

[400] thus sins cling to the wicked while guilt spreads,

thus everywhere their ways return to savage expiations.

And the Lord endured the course of their wandering unpunished,

so that they might be recalled, joined together in much crime.

But after God saw that the worst vows of human beings

[405] were advancing toward worse things, lest he lose the world again,

or release all the guilty everywhere with impunity,

he chose from all those whom he saw committing greater sins,
God’s judgment driven above the stars by punishment.

[Col. 0803B] And because the floodwater will no longer bring a second deluge,

[410] he pours sulfurous waters over them, rains black bitumen,

[Col. 0804A] and a shower scorches them with avenging flames,

burning five cities, condemning their peoples and walls,

255 with the heavenly fires, the turf cut away and baked.

The rich soil, loosened, rots into ashes,

[415] We are all the authors, alas, of our own disasters;

poverty, groans, death, tortures, and pains

we ourselves bring upon ourselves by our deliberate wicked sinning.

The Almighty separates the world’s merits according to its character;

punishments do not unite those whom guilt has not joined.

[420] Lot, righteous and a servant of God, without deceit, faithful,

the one pious and innocent amid so many crowds of criminals,

[Col. 0804B] is seen to be rescued from cruel death without guilt,

256 and departs, preserved, as a lover of a better life,

just as Noah, rescued, is preserved in the ark.

425. I read *specialior hospes* (“a more particular guest”); for although *hostis* formerly meant “stranger” or “foreigner,” I nevertheless think that Dracontius wrote *hospes* according to the usage of his own time. Lot was indeed a guest, both because he was an immigrant and because he had received the angels as guests. *Specialis* means “particular,” opposed to *generalis* (“general”).

427. Perhaps *laxare jugum* (“to loosen the yoke”), as in Silius, Book XI, verse 17. Others have *laxare frenos* (“to loosen the reins”) or *laxare habenas* (“to loosen the reins”); but *frenos* does not suit the meter. Pliny, Book XXXII, chapter 2, section 5, wrote *laxare fores* (“to open doors”), which can be extended metaphorically. One may also conjecture *nondum correpta* (“not yet seized”), or *audax criminibus laxat frenos* (“the bold man loosens the reins to crimes”).

428. Perhaps *supplicia et scelera* (“punishments and crimes”). Punishments for crimes increase when the crimes themselves increase. Hence “obscene hunger,” diseases, and so forth.

429. *Obscena fames* means “inauspicious hunger,” as in Virgil and others.

431. The punctuation may be: “For thus man had been made, our first beginnings, so that, like the birds, he was to be fed,” and so forth.

432. Lucretius, Book V, verse 370, *cladem importare pericli* (“to bring the disaster of danger”). On God’s providence toward the birds, see Matthew, chapter VI, verse 26, and chapter X, verse 29. Prudentius, *Psychomachia*, verses 617 and following, develops the same argument.

433. Compare Book I, verses 449 and following.

435. *Committere* means “to entrust” in a situation of uncertain outcome, as in “to entrust oneself to navigation, a road, or danger,” and in Justin, Book II, chapter 12, *committere salutem navibus* (“to entrust one’s safety to ships”). Dracontius imitates Juvenal, *Satire* 12, verse 157: “Go now, and entrust your life to the winds, trusting in your hewn timber.” Claudian, preface to Book I of *The Rape of Proserpina*: “Who dared to entrust the alder-tree to doubtful blasts.” Horace, Book I, Ode 3, verses 9 and following: “That man had oak and triple bronze around his breast who first entrusted a frail boat to the savage sea.” The ancient pagans strongly condemned the use of navigation in their writings and asserted that it had been devised against the will of the gods. Columella, in the preface: “Whether, for those who hate war, the risks of the sea and of commerce are more desirable, so that man, a land animal, having broken nature’s covenant and exposed to the anger of the winds and sea, dares to entrust himself to the waves.” See Barth, *Adversaria*, Book XVII, chapter 9, and Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, verses 94 and following.

438. Book I, verse 166: “And the olive, always clothed with foliage, grows green.” The meaning is that the olive would produce fruit at every season of the year.

439. Book I, verse 199: “The bees have no labor,” and so forth. Virgil, *Eclogue* 4, verse 30: “And the hard oaks will sweat dewy honey.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, verse 112: “And yellow honey dripped from the green holm-oak.”

[Col. 0806B] 440. Book I, verse 176: “Producing perfumes among the herbs.”

441. Book I, verse 717: Some read *qui rosulis stellare nemus* (“who would star the grove with little roses”); others read differently. Here too one might read *atque rosas proferret* (“and would bring forth roses”).

442. *Staret* means “would stand,” “remain,” “always flourish,” and “be sustained and established by its fragrance.” Virgil, *Aeneid* VI, verse 300: “The lights stand in flame.”

443. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, verse 107: “It was eternal spring, and the west winds, with their gentle warm breezes, caressed the flowers born without seed.”

445. Virgil, *Eclogue* 4, verse 45: “Of its own accord the purple plant will clothe the grazing lambs.” From this verse some conclude that *sandix* was a plant with which lambs, after feeding, were dyed the color of *sandix*. Servius understood Virgil in this way, as did Pliny, Book XXXV, section 23, chapter 6; Pliny himself, however, says that *sandix* was an artificial red color and explains how it was made. Dracontius suggests that *sandix* was not a plant, but that the lambs would acquire the color of *sandix*—although Virgil too may be explained in the same sense: while the lambs grazed in the usual way, they would clothe themselves in wool of the *sandix* color, just as he says nearly the same of purple dye (*murex*). Since Pliny lists *sandix* among the cheaper colors, one may ask why Dracontius calls it precious. I think the only reason is that fleeces dyed that color are precious, or that the color itself is precious in wool.

446. Virgil, *Eclogue* 4, verse 43: “The ram himself in the meadows will now change his fleeces to soft red purple, now to saffron-colored yellow.”

[Col. 0806D] 447. *Phrixei* is correctly given by the manuscript; others less correctly write *Phryxeus*. Ovid, *Heroides* 6, verse 104: “He tears away the golden fleece from the Phrixean ram,” and *Heroides* 18, verse 103: “I envy Phrixus, whom the golden-fleeced ram carried safely across the gloomy seas.” Phrixus reached Colchis on a gilded ram, where he sacrificed the ram and placed its gilded fleece in the temple of Mars; Jason removed it with Medea’s help. See Hyginus, *Fabula* 3, Ovid, and other mythographers.

448. I have restored it thus, conjecturing. I think the passage concerns Medea’s tragedy, which was repeatedly performed on the stages of antiquity. Horace, *Ars Poetica*, verse 185: “Nor should Medea slaughter her boys before the people.” I therefore understand *famam scenarum*, or, if preferred, *scenai* in the Lucretian manner, as referring to the fame of the Golden Fleece, which Medea betrayed. Then people would see the golden fleeces without Medea’s crime and would lend credence to the story about them. The word *scena* (“stage”) is often used when crimes displayed in tragedies are being indicated. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* III, chapter 27: “Nor is the stage alone filled with these crimes, but ordinary life is almost fuller of worse ones.” Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, verse 471: “Orestes, driven mad by the stage.”]

Nor did the special guest suffer the common evil.

Our race, not yet checked by so many evils, even dares

to open the doors to crimes, without a show of shame,

and does not condemn wicked punishments and crimes, but increases them.

Hence obscene hunger, diseases, death, grief, want,

[430] weariness, wars, pestilence, disasters, loss, and toil.

For thus man had been made, our first beginnings,

so that, like the birds, he was to be fed without the disaster of labor;

he would not cleave the earth with a plow or mattock,

nor, wandering, demand foreign things from the rushing waters,

[435] boldly entrusting his life to winds and waves,

257 freely producing fruit, and wine from the fountains of the grape

[Col. 0806A] like flowing river water; the long-lived olive,

always green, would bear its liquids without a fixed season;

the brambles would give honey, the thorn would sweat *amomum*,

[440] every field would yield perfumes from flowering herbs,

and winter would bring forth little roses, while summer preserved

purple lilies; every flower would remain with its fragrance,

and the honor of the violet would not wither in its becoming pallor;

the lambs’ color would not be merely black or white,

[445] but precious *sandix* would give them ruddy fleeces,

and would clothe the wool-bearing sheep in purple from the *murex*;

258 the gold of Phrixus’s fleece would be a true story,

a truthful account would bear the fame of the stages

among the peoples, and would establish certain belief without so great a crime.

450. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* I, verse 138: “They went into the earth’s entrails; the riches which it had concealed and brought near to the Stygian shades were dug out.”

451. See Book I, verses 505 and following.

452. The *face of the earth* is the uppermost and outermost part of the earth; hence the word “surface.” Virgil, *Eclogue* 4, verse 39: “Every land will bear everything.”

453. Virgil, at the cited passage, verse 38: “The traveler himself will yield to the sea, nor will the nautical pine change its merchandise.” Perhaps: “No region will lack merchandise.”
