455. *Plectibiles mores* (“punishable ways”), as at verse 269, *plectibilis actus* (“a punishable act”). All the calamities of this life derive their origin from original sin alone, but in such a way that they are greatly increased by people’s particular sins.

458. “Purer air,” as in Book I, verse 334, and *Elegy*, verse 89. The argument is taken from Job, chapter IV, verse 18: “Behold, those who serve him are not steadfast, and he finds perversity in his angels. How much more will those who dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is earthly, be consumed like a moth?”

460. In verse 101 the throne of God is called “the heavenly tribunal.”

461. Consider whether it would be better to read *corporis expertes, terreni et ponderis omnes* (“all without body and earthly weight”). Prudentius, *Hymn* 5 *Peristephanon*, verse 163, likewise says of the body: “A vessel loosened and made of clay, to be broken in whatever way,” from the Apostle, 2 Corinthians, chapter IV, verse 7. Dracontius takes from the Book of Job and explains the words “earthly foundation.” The Apostle likewise says, 2 Corinthians, chapter V, verse 1: “If our earthly house of this dwelling is dissolved.” Wisdom, chapter IX, verse 15: “For the corruptible body weighs down the soul, and the earthly dwelling presses down the mind that thinks upon many things.” In short, the body is the soul’s prison.

465. It is evident that no one’s guilt is excused by another’s guilt; Epiphanius also teaches this in his letter to Jerome, among Jerome’s letters 91, formerly 73: “As though the multitude of sinners diminished the crime, and as though the flame of Gehenna did not grow greater through the number of the logs.” Jerome says the same at the beginning of Book I against Rufinus: “As though the number of sinners diminished the guilt.”

469. From Lucan, Book V, verse 290: “The crime which stains them makes them equal.” Arator, Book I, verse 501: “Nor does punishment separate those whom equal guilt binds.” See the note to Book I, verse 541, and Book II, verse 418, and Law 22 of the Code, *On Punishments*, by which those are removed from punishment whom association in crime does not make guilty . . . . Sins, therefore, should hold their own authors, and fear should go no farther than guilt is found.

470. Cicero, *On the Response of the Haruspices*, chapter 18: “So that anyone might know the punishment that would follow that crime.” Likewise Horace, Book III, Ode 2: “Rarely has punishment, with its halting foot, abandoned the guilty man who went before.”

472. Concerning the number of angels, the author of *The Celestial Hierarchy*, under the name of Dionysius the Areopagite, says in chapter 14 that the scriptural tradition concerning angels speaks of “thousands of thousands,” multiplying and heaping together the greatest numbers we use, thereby openly declaring that the orders of the heavenly essences cannot be numbered by us. Isaiah, chapter XIV, verse 12: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer,” and so forth, which most explain of the Devil. Revelation, chapter XII, verses 4 and following: “And its tail”—that of the dragon—“dragged a third of the stars of heaven and cast them to the earth. And there was a great battle in heaven: Michael and his angels fought with the dragon . . . . and that great dragon was cast down . . . . and his angels were cast down with him.” Allegorically, those words in Job, chapter XXV, verse 5, are also understood of the angels: “Behold, even the moon does not shine, and the stars are not clean in his sight. How much more man, who is rottenness, and the son of man, a worm?”

473. *Superum* means “of those above,” namely Michael and his angels. Or read: “the vengeance of the Most High restrains,” or “the overcoming vengeance restrains the ranks of the heavenly beings.”

474. *Clade perenni* (“with everlasting ruin”), as in Book I, verse 467: “May they fall, not through their own deceit, but through everlasting ruin,” and in Tertullian, Book I against Marcion: “Destined to perish by everlasting death.”

475. The stars are also called the “army of heaven” at verse 333. Of the angels, see Job, chapter XXV, verse 3: “Is there a number to his armies?” Genesis, chapter XXXII, verse 1: “Jacob also went on his way, and the angels of God met him. When he saw them, he said: ‘These are God’s camps.’” 1 Kings, chapter XXII, verse 19: “I saw the Lord sitting on his throne, and the entire army of heaven standing beside him on his right and on his left.” In ecclesiastical usage angels are often called the heavenly army. Sacred Scripture makes clear in many places that angels often appeared in military form: at times splendid on horses, at times holding a drawn sword, at times clothed in fiery and hyacinth-colored breastplates—that is, prepared for the defense of the good and as rescuers in battle. Instead of *districta*, meaning “punished,” or “constrained and bound,” perhaps *disjecta* (“scattered”) should be read. *Sine usu* (“without purpose”) also seems corrupt. The meaning, however, is that so great a part of the heavenly army had been cast down from the honor in which it rejoiced, and, as it were, from military purpose and service; or, if preferred, that no place of either defense or repentance had been left to the sinning angels.]

The earth’s entrails would preserve not only precious metal,

hidden too deeply, nor would any gem lie concealed;

but the surface of the earth would possess everything everywhere,

no region in any land would lack merchandise,

and that land would be of little value to peoples, with the east winds carrying it.

[455] But now everywhere the punishable ways of the human mind

withdraw what is sweet and provide what is bitter.

Perhaps people might object, confessing their sins,

that the angelic race sinned, which held the purer air

259 and the region above the stars, or the realms of heaven.

[460] They were before the tribunal, where all without earthly bodily weight

could see what was pure and holy;

and thus error held them, and an unspeakable crime.

[Col. 0808A] What of wretched human beings, captive beneath the fragile covering

of flesh, whom their limbs and bodily functions hold fast?

[465] Thus I shall answer you: Why is another’s guilt

brought forward? Can what the wicked person has done,

whatever crime another has committed, be purged?

Every crime that has been carried out concerns its author,

involves his accomplices and all his servants,

and presses upon only those whom the deed stains.

[470] Hence our mind is all the more guilty because punishment followed;

the heavenly servants were struck, and severe anger did not spare them.

478. *Allatro* (“to bark”) is used by other poets and writers. I find *inlatro* nowhere else, and therefore consider *inlatret* a corruption for *allatret*. Since the first and second syllables of *vibices* are long, I thought it should be corrected to *vibices si ora* (“the scars, if the face”), and in fact *ora* seems more suitable than *terga* (“backs”).

480. A description of night. The day produced by the sun perishes in night. Book I, verse 672: “Everywhere it leads the day, destined to perish beneath the shadows of night,” and verse 677: “The day itself falls when the sun sinks over the waters.” The shadows of night are produced when the earth is placed in the sun’s way. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* II, chapter 19: “For the shadow of the earth itself, obstructing the sun, produces night.”

483. I have restored this nearly incurable passage in the following way. The meaning is: “Can a little stream boast that it can drive away the ocean’s thirst, which not even great rivers can assuage, even if they all flow into the sea?” Perhaps *siccante* (“drying”) should be read instead of *siccato* (“dried”), just as *minuente* for *minuto*, *crispante* for *crispato*, and *solidante* for *solidato*.

Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 615: “We saw this boy, they say, carried through the stars.” In my commentary on Prudentius at that passage I have shown that this expression does not mean that the boy was carried by a star or seen by magi, but that Christ’s birth was announced through a star.

495. The Devil is frequently indicated by the Fathers under the name of the serpent, to whom arts and cunning are attributed, just as power is attributed to Christ.

498. *Perpete culpa* (“everlasting guilt”), because no place or time for repentance was left to the angels, and a wicked will always persists in them. 499. *Expaveo* (“I tremble in fear”) occurs in the past tense and frequently with an accusative among poets and other writers.

505. The first syllable in *fiunt* (“are made”) is lengthened, which perhaps indicates that the following passage in this book, verse 191, *si disjuncta fiant* (“if they should become separated”), and Book III, verse 135, *si jactura fiat* (“if loss should occur”), are corrupt. For I would more readily believe that an error entered such corrupt manuscripts than that Dracontius varied the quantity of the same syllable. On this crime of Judas, Sedulius, Book IV, also called 5, says: “When wicked Judas saw him bound in chains, he stiffened, and, returning the price of his crime in vain, he left behind the price of the deed, not the deed itself.”

508. It would seem more in keeping with Dracontius’ style to read: “One party loses the price, the other party loses the merchandise,” since it is unsurprising that in a purchase and sale the buyer loses the price and the seller the merchandise. It would also be true if one said: “Each party loses the price; each party loses the merchandise.” But perhaps Dracontius is indicating precisely this: “One party loses the price,” namely Judas the buyer; “the other party loses the merchandise,” namely the Jewish sellers.]

yet there was never any fear in us.

What dog would bark if weals marked a lion’s face,

261 neck, and head, and tawny weals reddened with blood?

[480] Or, when the day of the sun perishes and the earth is placed between,

would the stars look down upon the shadow by which everything is covered,

Or would a stream, when the sea is thirsty, boast that it can drive away

a thirst which not even great rivers can assuage,

510. *Distracti* means “sold,” “alienated.” *Distrahere* (“to sell,” “to alienate”) is a word familiar to jurists and also to other writers, such as Lucilius, Gellius, Suetonius, Justin, and Tacitus.

511. Perhaps *mundabitur amne cruoris* (“will be cleansed by the stream of blood”), as below at verse 601. Hebrews, chapter IX, verse 14: “How much more will the blood of Christ . . . cleanse our conscience?” 1 John, chapter I, verse 7: “And the blood of Jesus Christ, his Son, cleanses us from every sin.” Revelation, chapter I, verse 5; 1 Peter, chapter I, verse 19.

515. *Ingerere supplicia* (“to inflict punishments”) is correctly said; likewise *ingerere vias lethi* (“to inflict the ways of death”), since tortures are the ways of death. Perhaps the corruption lies in *cui lex ab origine mundi*. The following meaning can be extracted: “For whom there was a law from eternity, that he should have neither a beginning by being born nor an end by dying.” Or understand *ab origine mundi* (“from the origin of the world”) to mean that Christ was predestined before the foundation of the world in such a way that he would have neither a beginning by being born nor an end by dying. See whether one should read: *cui lex ab origine mundo / Nec fuit initium nasci*, that is, “whose law from the world’s origin was to have neither a beginning in being born into the world nor an end in dying.”

516. The first syllable of *initium* is lengthened, as stated in Book I, verse 131.

518. Above, at verse 480, the day is called the sun’s day; but here it seems better to punctuate so that the sun’s hours are understood to have remained, as in the following verse: “And he gave night beneath the light.” See Matthew, chapter XXVII, verse 45, where this darkness is reported.

520. *Sine more suo* (“without its usual custom”), because they returned before the proper time, while the sun was still above the earth.

521. *Palla* (“robe”) is a woman’s garment, which, like *pallium* (“cloak”), is elegantly attributed to night. See examples in the commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* 5 of the *Cathemerinon*, verses 27–28.

523. *Cardine sub gemino* (“beneath the double hinge”), because the sun was absent from one side and obscured on the other. Night “hung” because it remained suspended and uncertain. Victorinus, *On Jesus Christ, God and Man*: “That night was day: a confused cloud pressed upon the fields and homes; chaos; the steadfast axis stood unmoving.”

525. Matthew, chapter XXVII, verse 52 and following.

528. I dealt at greater length in the prolegomena to Prudentius, chapter 18, with the opinion according to which some Fathers affirmed that the punishments of hell were mitigated on the day of the Lord’s resurrection. I now add Arator, who in Book I, verse 232, introduces the Apostle Peter speaking thus: “Seeking the pale realms, he shone upon the frightened shades; chaos could not darken him, radiant in his own light. Pains fled; then hell feared that it existed, and, restraining no punishment within itself, the torturer grew weak into new inactivity. The gloomy Tartarus groans, because all bonds are at rest. What could death do there, where the bearer of life was going?” Arator’s authority ought to carry considerable weight, because his poem, dedicated to Pope Vigilius and received by him, was recited in the church of Saint Peter ad Vincula in Rome with great acclaim. The history of this event is reported by Labbe, and after Labbe by others, in such a way that Arator’s two books are said to have been heard on seven separate days. I myself indicated this in *Hymnodia Hispanica*, page 105 and following, number 131, and explicitly affirmed it in the commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* 12 *Peristephanon*, verse 5, page 1190. But after later examining the Vatican manuscript cited by the writers, I discovered that the matter stands thus in that manuscript, while it is narrated differently in the older manuscript of the Queen of Sweden, number 598: “While Arator was reciting, both books were heard on four separate days, since on one day only half of a book was read because of the frequent repetitions which they requested with great enthusiasm.” The same recitation took place on these days: first, the Ides of April; second, the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May; third, the eighth day before the Ides of May; but on the fourth day, the third day before the Kalends of June. There is therefore an error in Vatican manuscript no. 1665, which reads “seven times” instead of “four times.” For Arator’s entire work was not recited more often, but was read through on four separate days, in such a way that on each day only half of one book was read—a matter which, I hope, I shall confirm more fully at another time.

To return to the opinion of certain ancient writers that the punishments of the damned were at times mitigated: Saint Ildefonsus—or whoever else may be the author—also supports this same view in sermon 5, *On the Assumption of the Mother of God*, page 364, volume I of the Madrid edition of the Fathers of Toledo: “The whole world today rejoices and delights with fitting exultation; only Tartarus howls, rages, and mutters beneath its breath, because the joy and gladness of this day provide some remedy and refreshment to those enclosed in the infernal prisons. Today, I think, the Tartarean ministers do not dare to touch their captives, whom they remember to have been redeemed by the blood of him who deigned to be born from a virgin for the salvation of the world.” In the *Index of Expurgated Books* of Brasichella this is noted on page 285 and following: “Saint Ildefonsus seems to have spoken hyperbolically in sermon 5, *On the Assumption of the Mother of God*, unless perhaps he wished to imitate the opinion of Aurelius Prudentius, who granted the inhabitants of hell a holiday from punishments on the night of Christ’s resurrection.”

Since so many ancient writers support this opinion, and Dracontius may now be added to them from the manuscripts, I am pleased to repeat the judgment of Petavius, volume III, Book III, *On Angels*, chapter 7: “Therefore this opinion of the most holy Fathers should not rashly be rejected as absurd, although at the present time it is foreign to the common understanding of Catholics.” The judgment of the highly esteemed editor of the Fathers of Toledo, the eminent Cardinal de Lorenzana, is similar in his note to the cited sermon of Saint Ildefonsus: “What? Is it really so alien and unheard-of that some relief from their punishments could happen even to these—the damned—although those punishments would not therefore eventually come to an end?” He discusses much excellently in support of this view. See Giovanni Battista Gener, volume IV of *Theology*, part 2, treatise 3, Book III, chapter 2, who observes that it was transcribed from Prudentius by Abbot Odilo in his sermon *On the Assumption of the Mother of God*. But this sermon of Odilo is not different from the sermon which Gener himself cites under the name of Ildefonsus; it is from this sermon, of course, that we quoted the words. Compare the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, volume I, column 401.]

530. Arator, verse 61 of Book I: “When day entered among the dead, the fleeing stars abandoned the sky, accompanying God.” Perhaps he wished to imitate Dracontius; but Dracontius’ description of the light is much better: “The descent of God accompanied it, driven from the world at the same time,” since darkness had fallen over the whole earth. There is no reason why the stars should be said to have abandoned the sky and be joined with the day when it entered among the dead.

531. *Satiabilis* (“satiable”) was rejected as barbarous by Forcellini. But since *insatiabilis* (“insatiable”) is frequently used, *satiabilis* should be admitted into Latin on the authority even of Dracontius alone. Poets commonly call Tartarus greedy, insatiable, and incapable of being filled. Fortunatus, in his elegy *On the Resurrection of the Lord*: “The underworld, opening its hollow throat insatiably, which has always seized its prey, becomes your spoils, O God.”

532. *Neci* is an ablative in the customary manner, used by Lucretius and others. I would not object if one read *nece*, with the final syllable lengthened according to the caesura.

535. The name “the underworld” refers to the place where the souls of the righteous were held before Christ’s resurrection; the same name also includes the place where the condemned are tortured by eternal punishments. The bosom of Abraham, however, was separated from the place of punishments, so that no passage from one to the other was possible, as is clear from the story, or parable, of Lazarus and the rich man in Luke, chapter XVI. In imitation of this, the pagans placed the Elysian Fields in the underworld, separated from the dwelling of the wicked by an impenetrable wall and a river of fire. Virgil, Book VI, verses 336 and following: “To the right is the road which extends beneath the walls of mighty Dis; by this road we reach Elysium, but on the left he inflicts punishments upon the wicked and sends them to impious Tartarus . . . . Aeneas suddenly looks back and sees, beneath the left-hand cliff, broad walls surrounded by a triple wall, which the swift Tartarean Phlegethon encircles with rushing flames and torments the sounding rocks. Opposite stands a huge gate, its columns of solid adamant, which no force of men, nor even the heavenly inhabitants themselves, could cut down with iron; an iron tower rises into the air.” Virgil also suggests that the groans of the wicked reach the dwelling places of the blessed: “From here I heard groans and the savage sound of blows; then the clank of iron and dragging chains.”

Of the bosom of Abraham, Tertullian, Book III against Marcion: “Beneath the earth’s body, in an unknown part, there exists an open place, relying upon its own light. This is called Abraham’s bosom, higher than the darkness, far removed from the fire, yet beneath the earth,” and so forth. Dracontius seems to call Abraham’s bosom itself an eternal prison, because even those souls would not have been freed from there unless Christ, descending there, had triumphed over death and over the law of death, which is soon called the law of Avernus.

[Col. 0814B] 536. Prudentius, *Hymn* 9 *Cathemerinon*, verse 75, of those who rose with Christ: “With the law reversed, the dark threshold, now to be trampled, lies open.” Fortunatus, in his elegy *On the Resurrection*: “With the laws of hell crushed,” and so forth. *Defleo* (“I lament”) takes an infinitive, as *fleo* does in Valerius Flaccus, Book I, verse 633.

537. Fortunatus, at the cited passage: “And chaos trembled to be pressed by the face of light.” In the Isidorian Missal, Wednesday after Easter: “Even punishment itself trembled at its judge, because the nature of the dreadful darkness, already checked—or dulled—by the presence of his radiance, feared to be judged.”

538. Although *opto* can be understood as “I seek,” “I wish,” or “I ask,” in this passage, with an accusative, *orat* (“he prays”) is clearer.

539. Hecate is called the Moon in heaven, Lucina and Diana on earth, and Proserpina in the underworld. The name is used here for the underworld. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XIV, verse 405: “He prays to Hecate with magical howlings.” Perhaps one should read *ne gravet ora Hecates jubar* (“may Hecate’s faces not burden the radiance”), since three faces were attributed to her. Virgil, *Aeneid* IV, verse 511: “And triple Hecate, the three faces of the virgin Diana.” Ovid, *Fasti* I, verse 141: “You see Hecate’s faces turning toward three directions.”

It should nevertheless be observed that ancient Christians freely used mythological names in their poems and often alluded to the myths themselves, even when speaking of the most sacred mysteries of our religion—not because they assented to the myths, but either to mock them or at least to show that true things had been shadowed forth by myths. Dracontius has much to say about Curtius, who was plunged by a precipitous leap into the vast chasm of the earth, in Book III, verses 399 and following; these passages carry the flavor of ancient myths. He can, however, be excused more readily there because he is treating a profane subject. I have noted some relevant matters at verse 405.

When Nonnus explains Lazarus’s being called back from the dead in chapter XI of John, he alludes in several verses to the pagan myths of the underworld, as though Pluto had anxiously sought Lazarus’s soul around the river Lethe and had not found it. Heinsius, in his *Exercises on Nonnus*, criticizes this freedom of recalling myths, chiefly because Nonnus is acting as an interpreter of John’s Gospel, in which certainly no trace of myths appears. It is less objectionable in other Christian poets.]

540. Christ, to be sure, was not going to extract the souls of the damned from the underworld; but the terror of the demons is poetically described, as though they feared this. In an old poem without an author’s name, entitled *The Triumph of Christ*, published after Juvencus by Theodorus Poelmannus at Basel, there are similar lines:

> When Christ, the King of heaven, entered the realms of Phlegethon,  
> the royal prince Pluto looked out from his palace,  
> as soon as he perceived Christ approaching his own regions.  
> “O companions,” he cries, “now is the time to take up arms,  
> since this man, his limbs drenched in gore, is drawing near  
> to plunder our riches, our shades, and our souls,” etc.

This author too must be numbered among those who thought that the torments ceased while Christ descended to the underworld:

> And what more need be said? Groans, torments, and sufferings fall silent.

542. That Christ rose while it was still dark is established by the Gospel; that he rose at midnight was the opinion of many. Dracontius indicates that the resurrection occurred when the morning star had risen and the light of day had begun to brighten the ocean. Victorinus likewise writes concerning Christ, God and man:

> Perhaps the royal light of heaven was then first beginning to shine,  
> bearing witness to the eternal day; and bright throughout the universe,  
> with its lightning-bearing point, it had divided the darkness of night,  
> spreading its radiance by a starry yoke. Behold, God the avenger  
> returns from the shades.

This same opinion belongs to many ancient and modern writers and rests upon the sacred Scriptures, as Maldonatus and Calmet prove. For this reason Christians formerly in Rome prolonged the fast of the Paschal vigil until dawn; and in the blessing of the Paschal candle the Church sings:

> May the morning star find its flames—

that morning star, I say, which knows no setting; he who, returning from the underworld, shone serenely upon the human race.

[Col. 0815C]

266. and, suppliant, laments the increase; for these increases brought

[535] the prison of eternity, to return to the uses of the light,

547. *Arx* simply means “heaven,” as at verse 494. *In arce* can also mean “on high,” “in the heights.” Above, at verse 68: “And remaining consort with the Father.” When the Son is called the Father’s consort, the same nature of the Son and the Father is indicated. Drepanius, *On the Paschal Candle*:

> We worship you and your offspring, whom, watching over all things,  
> you created as your consort through the Word who proceeds from the Father.

548. *Post saecla* (“after the ages”) is a phrase peculiar to Dracontius, meaning “after the lifetime of the world.” See the note on verse 86 of Book I.

551. Perhaps read: “He will require what is owed for a life either wicked or good.”

552. Perhaps: “to have despised the Father.”

556. *Donatque reatum* (“and grants pardon for guilt”) is used in place of “remits” or “forgives”; it is an elegant expression. Ovid, *Letters from Pontus* II.7.51:

> A grave fault is often forgiven at the prayers of one’s relatives.

Prudentius, *Psychomachia* 781:

> He forgives every offense.

Tertullian, *Against Marcion* I: “God forgives everything done through error to the wretched.” Dracontius below, verse 605, uses a similar expression: “He grants sins to the guilty without being asked in words.”

557. Clearly, even the wretched Judas would have received pardon from God if he had hoped for it. Prudentius likewise pronounces the name *Judas* in the *Dittochaeon*, verse 155; against Gifanius I have shown in my commentary that this follows Latin usage and that the final syllable is shortened.

558. The name *Deicide*, or *Christicide*, now exists; but certainly it did not exist before Judas. See Book III, verse 262, where Dracontius, speaking of suicide, says: “This crime has no name.”

559. *Nihil* becomes a monosyllable through synaeresis; alternatively, write *nil*. *Veniale* is found in Macrobius, Ammianus, and Sidonius.

560. I prefer the manuscript reading *judicioque suo* (“and by his own judgment”). But since in manuscripts *judicium* and *indicium* are often confused, someone may suspect that *indicioque suo* (“and by his own information”) should be read. Arntzenius, in *Miscellanies*, chapter 5, on Arator, prefers, with the editions of Aldus and Basel, *indicio tali* (“by such information”), because, he says, Judas was an informer. But in Arator too the sense requires *judicio*: thus he says in Book I, verses 141–142:

> And, reviewing his crime, by such judgment he surrendered his limbs  
> to madness, so that in the midst of the air he might assign  
> the place of the punishment owed to the common enemy.

Judas did this by his own judgment, not by information, through which he betrayed the Savior. Sedulius, Book IV, poem 5:

> He seeks death for himself, as though he were then more sane,  
> when he hastened to avenge his crime …  
> His anger was milder, indeed, for so great a crime of guilt,  
> for which no punishment of all evils could be equal.

Dracontius speaks similarly in Book III, verse 42: “By her own judgment the ever-greedy mind, punished, pays the penalty.” Thus Dracontius says that Judas believed no place of pardon remained for him and, having deprived himself of pardon by his own judgment, laid hands upon himself. He uses the wording of Matthew 27:5: “And departing, he hanged himself”; and of Luke, *Acts* 1:25: “From which Judas by transgression fell, that he might go to his own place.”

561. *Ad colla pependit* means “he hung by the neck,” in place of *e collo* or *collo pependit*. Book I, verse 259: “Fixed to the branches.” In place of *redditur* (“is returned”), I would prefer *reddidit* (“he returned”).

562. *Vix tandem justus* (“scarcely at last just”) means that he scarcely at last displayed some appearance of justice—not that he was truly just, but that he ceased to be greedy. *Vix tandem* refers to time. Cicero, *Letters to Friends* III, opening of letter 9: “I have scarcely at last read letters worthy of Appius.”

563. I will not object if you read *obiit semet ultore*, with the final syllable of *semet* lengthened by the pause.

564. As is clear from Matthew 27:5, Judas “hanged himself with a noose.” Luke, *Acts* 1:18, adds: “And being hanged, he burst open in the middle, and all his entrails poured out.” The Fathers and commentators adopted various explanations of how this happened. Some say that the weight of his body bent the branch to which he was clinging and that, after he had been released from it by someone’s assistance, he burst open not long afterward, having contracted dropsy. Others report that he was opportunely taken down from the tree on which he was hanging and then threw himself headlong from a high place, whereupon his entrails were poured out. Others think that, already dead, he burst open after being thrown into a sewer. Others suppose that Judas, driven by despair and as though strangled, fell face downward, or threw himself down and was torn apart. Oecumenius, in his commentary on Acts, holds that Judas, after the noose by which he was hanging broke, burst open in the middle; this is precisely Dracontius’ opinion. Papias, cited by Oecumenius, wrote that Judas remained in this world as an example of impiety: his body became so swollen that he could not move forward, and finally he was crushed by a wagon and burst open. See Gronovius, *Academic Exercise on the Destruction and Death of Judas*; Calmet, *Biblical Dictionary*, under “Judas”; Andrea Austen, *Dissertation on the Manner of Judas’s Death*; and John Warneccius, *Discussion of the Hanging of Judas*.]

567. It seems certain that many of the Jews who had brought about Christ’s death, as well as others among the Gentiles who inflicted it, obtained pardon from God, since the Lord, hanging on the cross, prayed for them and was heard because of his reverence, as the Apostle says in Hebrews 5:7. See Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, *Treatise on the Seven Words of the Lord on the Cross*, in the *Library of the Fathers*.

569. Book III, verse 455: “The gifts of eternal life that we hope for.” *Sumpsisse munera* (“to have accepted gifts”) does not fit the meter; hence one might read *sumpsisse haec munera* (“to have accepted these gifts”), or *venisse ad munera* (“to have come to the gifts”), or:

> Or the ministers of death accepted the best gifts  
> of everlasting life,

or *sumpsisse praemia vitae* (“to have accepted the rewards of life”), with the final syllable of *sumpsisse* lengthened because of the following *pr-* sound. Sedulius, Book I, verse 340: “You will receive the golden rewards of everlasting life.”

570. *Exstans* may be pleonastic, or may mean “standing above,” “preeminent.” Paul is called their leader, those who attempted to destroy and extinguish the Church and Jesus Christ in his members. See 1 Timothy 1:13 and *Acts* 8 and 22.

572. The first syllable of *Stephano* is correctly shortened, although it is improperly lengthened in the *Elegy*, verse 171, unless, as I think, one should read: “Before the others, Stephen.” The verb *facere* has an extremely broad meaning and is used with a dative in the sense of “to bring,” as in “to bring medicine, a remedy, destruction, or death to someone.” Paul received martyrdom from Stephen’s martyrdom, because he was converted to faith in Jesus Christ through Stephen’s prayers, and was crowned with martyrdom for that faith.

573. Perhaps there is an allusion to the name *Stephen*, which in Greek means “crown.”

I understand Matthew 7:2: “For with what judgment you judge, you shall be judged; and with what measure you measure, it shall be measured to you.” The same saying is repeated in many other places in sacred Scripture. Nor is the Apostle’s statement in Ephesians 6:8 dissimilar: “Knowing that whatever good each person does, he will receive the same from the Lord.”

The middle syllable of *idola* is shortened, as in the *Elegy*, verse 96: “Although they know the Lord, they worship empty idols.” Prudentius, Arator, and countless other Christian poets always pronounce *idola* in this way. I gave the reason for this usage in the prologue to Prudentius, no. 208.

580. Arcas was the son of Jupiter and Callisto, whom the poets later made the Great Bear in the heavens, as *Arcada Arctophilaca*, or Bootes. Here the adjective *Arcas* seems to be used so that Jupiter is called “Arcadian,” because he was born in Arcadia, as many maintain; others prefer Crete. *Arcas* may also be taken for Mercury, who was born on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia and therefore was called by many *Arcas* and *Arcadius*. Statius uses *Arcada* absolutely for Mercury in Book V of the *Silvae*, poem 1, verse 107.

581. *Titania* is Diana, sister of the Sun, who is called Titan. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* III.173: “While Titania was bathing there in her accustomed water”; and *Fasti* IV.943: “When Titania had left behind her brother, Phrygian Assaracus.” Some read *Tithonia* there.

585. Book III, verse 523:

> He who changes the ages,  
> yet the ages do not change him; for what was, that he is,

*Elegy*, verse 8: “You will always be the same, who are now or who have been.”

590. This is precisely what the Church sings of the Mother of God: “Him whom the heavens could not contain, you received in your womb,” as I observed at verse 92, where there is a similar statement: “Yet not to be contained by those same things.” Among the poems of Damasus, poem 2, and after the poems of Claudian:

> Mortal hearts enclosed the Maker of heaven,  
> beneath the earth’s deepest breast—  
> he who embraces the whole world far and wide,  
> and whom neither the spaces of earth, nor the waves of the sea,  
> nor heaven itself can contain,  
> gathered himself into tiny limbs.

See also Fortunatus’ hymn, “Whom earth, sea, and sky …” When Dracontius says, “You place yourself in the small heart of the human breast,” he speaks figuratively, along with many Fathers, to suggest that the Blessed Virgin conceived him first in her mind and then in her womb. It should be noted that many such figurative expressions, especially taken from Christian poets, have been retained in the Church’s liturgy, as in the fifth Responsory for the Feast of the Circumcision:

> The Virgin’s heart was strengthened,  
> in which, when the angel announced it,  
> she conceived the divine mysteries;

and there, from Sedulius’ alphabetical hymn:

> The house of her chaste breast  
> suddenly becomes God’s temple;  
> untouched, knowing no man,  
> she conceived the Son through the Word.

Against the error of those who assert that the Mother of God conceived in her heart rather than in her womb, consult what I noted on Prudentius’ *Apotheosis*, verse 583:

> Virginity and ready faith drank Christ  
> in the deep place of the heart’s womb,

where, by conjecture, one should now read *bibit alto Cordis* (“drank in the heart’s depth”), although *alvo* (“womb”) is also good; for what follows is: “and, destined to give birth, she enclosed him in untouched hiding places.”]

Saint Leo, *Sermon 1 on the Nativity of the Lord*, chapter 1: “The royal Virgin of David’s lineage is chosen, who, destined to be made pregnant with the sacred offspring, would first conceive the divine and human child in her mind before conceiving him in her body.” See the note on verse 89 of this book, where in the following verses Dracontius declares the true conception of Christ in the Virgin Mother’s womb: “He deigns to enter the virgin recesses and the womb capable of containing earth and heaven.”

593. Perhaps: “Before future faith,” or rather: “Even if there are no future things for you, O Omnipotent One.”

594. Perhaps read: “Clearly, O Omnipotent One.” To God all things are present, even those that are future or already past for us. Eternity is commonly compared to a point or center that exists simultaneously with the many lines drawn to the circumference. Nevertheless, in accordance with the capacity of the human mind, the words “past” and “future” can properly be used of God. Augustine, *Tractate on John* 99.5: “Although that immutable nature does not admit ‘was’ and ‘will be,’ but only ‘is’ … nevertheless, because of the mutability of the times in which our mortality and mutability exist, we do not falsely say both ‘was,’ ‘will be,’ and ‘is,’” etc. See Raynaud, *Natural Theology*, distinction 7, question 1, article 7, where he explains eternity at length.

595. Below, verse 732:

> To whom all things are open, through whom are all things that exist,  
> both things already past and things that will one day be future.

The sense seems to be that to God all things are present—or rather, things that are future to us appear to him as already past. Alternatively, read: “Both things already past and things that are created to come.” *Ventura creantur* (“things future are created”) is used for *creabuntur* (“will be created”); or *creantur* may refer to the eternal predetermination of things and divine providence.

597. Book I, verse 743: “You apply healing through your own piety, holy one, without any medicine.”

600. Thus the Church sings at the Nativity of the Lord: “Christ is born for us.” 1 Thessalonians 5:9–10: “For God has not appointed us to wrath, but to the acquisition of salvation through our Lord Jesus Christ, who died for us.” Some theologians teach that Christ was predestined as the end of all things God was going to create, before the original sin was foreseen; others say that he was predestined after the original sin was foreseen, but before the actual sins of other human beings were foreseen. Dracontius seems to teach that Christ was predestined first—namely, in the order and manner of our conception—before the creation of humanity had been decreed. But I think it more likely that Dracontius did not treat this subject with such subtle reasoning, but merely asserted that Christ was predestined from eternity before humanity was created; and therefore mercy and pardon, in this predestination of Christ, precede guilt and crime.

601. Perhaps: “Who may wash away our sins,” with the final syllable of *nostra* lengthened by the pause; for here *hic*, *haec*, or *huic* is superfluous. See verse 511: “By which our mind will be cleansed with the sacred rain of blood.”

602. John 1:29: “John saw Jesus coming toward him and said: ‘Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sin of the world.’” Dracontius rightly says *ferat maculas* (“may bear the stains”); for this is the meaning of *tollit*: he carries and bears. 1 Peter 2:24: “Who himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree.” Isaiah 53:4: “Surely he himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows … and the Lord laid upon him the iniquity of us all … and as a lamb before its shearer he will be silent … and he himself will bear their iniquities … and he bore the sins of many.” Saint John the Evangelist also uses that same verb in 1 John 3:5: “And you know that he appeared to take away our sins, and there is no sin in him.” Christ therefore in a certain sense took the sins of the world away from human beings and carried them upon himself, or bore them in his body.

603. Jesus Christ is often called a lamb in sacred Scripture; this is also expressed by the ancient Christians in many monuments and images that still survive. Ludovicus de Leon, a theologian of the Augustinian order, a particularly weighty and elegant writer, discusses this title of the Savior with remarkable learning and elevated theology in his splendid Spanish work *On the Names of Christ*. I was deeply distressed when I once saw this work in certain manuscripts in the worst condition, as though it taught monstrous doctrines, by a theologian—so-called, as our times permit—of very little worth, except that he himself valued his private theological judgments, filled with melodious trifles, at a high price. Christ is also called the Father’s only heir, from Psalm 2:8. Prudentius, *Hymn* 12 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 81: “He is made the only heir of the highest Father.”

604. God is called “the living God” in the language of sacred Scripture, to distinguish him from the false gods of the Gentiles, who are truly dead. Jerome, *Commentary on Matthew* III, chapter 16: “Peter, speaking in the person of all the Apostles, professes: ‘You are Christ, the Son of the living God.’ He calls him the living God to distinguish him from those gods who are thought to be gods but are dead.” The Son’s eternity is declared by the fact that he himself will always live—indeed, that he is life itself.

624. On the verb *recido*, see Book I, verse 105, and Book II, verse 156. I was considering *vis materna perempta* (“the maternal power destroyed”), corresponding to *membra praemortua* (“limbs dead beforehand”). But *peracta* (“exhausted”) appears sound, as in Statius, Book XI, verse 746: “His strength exhausted,” that is, consumed and drained.

625. I supply *praesumptio simplex* (“simple confidence”), since in Book III, verse 248, faith is called simple confidence: “What pure faith and simple confidence can accomplish.” *Praesumptio* is used for confidence, and in both passages Abraham’s faith is being discussed. Judith 9:17: “Hear me, wretched woman, praying and trusting in your mercy.” Spartianus, *Hadrian* 2: “He had an expectation from a shrine of the empire that was soon to come,” etc. Pliny, Book IX, letter 3: “I consider one person happier than another: the one who enjoys the expectation of a good and lasting reputation and lives with certainty of posterity and future glory.” One could read: “Hope alone increased faith, simple confidence”; yet faith, hope, and confidence can all properly be called *praesumptio*.

627. Barrenness was a disgrace among the Hebrews, as is well known. Paulinus, poem on Saint John the Baptist:

> What earlier generations placed as a reproach upon mothers,  
> she, lacking offspring, sadly led a barren old age.

*Flebile inane* (“a mournful emptiness”) consists of two adjectives attached to one noun; other commentators on the poets have discussed this at length.

629. Genesis 17:1ff.: “The Lord appeared to him and said to him … And from her [Sarah] I will give you a son,” etc.

633. *Redivivo* (“reviving”) seems more correct than *recidivo* (“returning”). See the note on verse 558 of Book I. Although the ancient grammarians recognized *recidivus* and *redivivus* as having nearly the same meaning, it is nevertheless probable that earlier writers always said *redivivus*, from which *recidivus* was corruptly produced in the sense of “reborn,” “returning,” or “revived.”

655. *Elegies*, verse 159, on the same David: “Having confessed his crime, the guilty man deserves pardon for his ruin, unpunished,” etc. See Book I, verse 34. David, acknowledging and confessing his crime, did so because it is scarcely possible for a person seriously to weigh the gravity of crimes without detesting them.

656. Perhaps, “pardon for the crime.” The expression *sub voce* (“with a spoken word”) is used because, immediately after he said, “I have sinned against the Lord,” Nathan replied, “The Lord also has taken away your sin,” as is related in 2 Kings, chapter XII, verse 13.

657. It may be punctuated: “he deserves, Credulus.” David was often called the servant of God after the crime of adultery had been forgiven, just as in the Old Testament priests and prophets are commonly called servants of God; from this the same expression passed to Christians, who are specially devoted to the service of God. But I do not find the word “faithful” spoken of David after that time in Holy Scripture; nevertheless, the praises attributed to him convey this very idea.

659. On the phrase “to such an extent,” see the commentary on Prudentius, verse 153 of the *Hamartigenia*. It is indeed found in the Vulgate, 1 Samuel, chapter I, verse 6: “To such an extent that she reproached him”; but for that reason it is no less employed with propriety by good Latin writers.

660. “The third syllable of *muliere* is lengthened,” as in the epistle, verse 161: “Moreover Solomon was begotten by the same woman.” So also in Book III, verse 111, in *arietem*, and in this Book II, verse 133, in *muliere*. *Eadem* is a two-syllable word, with its first two syllables contracted through synaeresis, as *una eademque via* in the ablative in Virgil.

661. I think that *merito genitoris amato* should be written, namely, “to Solomon, loved because of his father’s merits.” 2 Kings, chapter XII, verses 24 and following: “She bore a son and called his name Solomon. And the Lord loved him. And he sent by the hand of Nathan the prophet, and called his name Beloved of the Lord (*Jedidiah*), because the Lord loved him.”

662. 2 Kings, chapter XX, verse 4: “And before Isaiah had gone out from the middle part of the court,” etc. “Thus says the Lord . . . I have heard your prayer, and I have seen your tears, and behold, I have healed you . . . . And I will add fifteen years to your days.” From this I have restored the corrupt verse. It could also be read: “And by prayer he deserves that life be extended to three lustral periods.” But “and by the first prayer” is better, as in verse 665, “through former vows,” and verse 673, “for whom one voice, once uttered, or no prayer at all.” The meaning is the same.

664. *Murmur* is often used of a prayer made in a subdued voice. In the Isidorian rite, on Holy Saturday, in the prayer for blessing the deacons: “So that, perceiving the blessing of all your benefits, they may murmur over the lamp and the candle.” Here a clearer voice, or even singing, is expressed. See the commentary on Prudentius, Preface to Book I *Against Symmachus*, verse 36. Of this Anna, the mother of Samuel, 1 Samuel, chapter I, verse 13: “Now Anna was speaking in her heart, and only her lips moved, but her voice was not heard at all.”

665. Is it not better to read “Anna had mourned her barren womb (*matricem*)”? 1 Samuel, chapter I, verse 5: “But the Lord had closed her womb.” *Matrix* is used for the receptacle of the fetus in women by Vegetius, Book I of *On Military Matters*, chapter 5, and by Pliny, Book XXVII, chapter 10, although Harduinus there reads *arteriam* rather than *matricem*.

668. Here *vota* means prayers; *piarent* means, as it were, “they might make satisfaction.” Propertius, Book III, elegy 17, also numbered 18, verse 17: “For why should I recall Medea, when the love of her children atoned for her mother’s anger by their slaughter?”

669. *Cum*, meaning “since” or “inasmuch as,” with the indicative occurs in Cicero and other good authors.

670. *Votum* is also taken for the thing that is desired, as here. *Meruere* means “they obtained,” as often elsewhere.

671. Dracontius plays the poet described by Claudian Mamertus, who wished for such a poet in the poem *Against Vain Poets*, addressed to a colleague:

“For these things I pray; rather for these things I vow my zeal and labor, in reading and in writing. Sing of the great beginnings of the Thunderer; write the origins of created things by the Word, and chaos before day, and the first twilight of light. Then learn, from the sacred books, whatever elements were spoken or done by God through the various ages; what Moses taught, inscribed on the legal tablets, or what the New Law of the Gospel marks out, revealing Christ, the mysteries formerly hidden. Then I shall truly call you a divine poet.”

You see the poem of Dracontius described here.

674. Perhaps: “He demanded what complete faith [demanded].” But *quid* is better, as in the following verse.

Aulus Gellius, Book III, chapter 16, reports, on the authority of ancient physicians and philosophers, that a human being is rarely born in the seventh month, never in the eighth, often in the ninth, and more often in the tenth month; and that ten completed months, not merely begun, constitute the maximum period for human gestation. Nevertheless, he reports from Varro that a human being was sometimes born in the eighth month and even in the eleventh.

690. Above, verse 555: “He hears with greater clemency.” Paulinus, poem 6 on Saint John the Baptist: “How great is God’s mercy, and how ready to be entreated is the divine power! It is enough to have repented.” The author of the poem *On the Praises of the Lord*: “You, steadfast in chastity and righteousness, are easily moved to bend your laws after crime.” This author wrote under Constantine, and, from the period in which he flourished and the similarity of his style, one is led to suspect that he was none other than our Juvencus. Both close their poems with praises of Constantine. The former writes:

“But now make Constantine for me a lord worthy of his merits, a father through his piety, lenient in authority, a teacher in the law of life, equal to the edicts that your established law sanctions; make him victorious and joyful. You have given nothing better than this offspring to the world before, nor will you give it; may his children equal their father.”

Juvencus writes:

“This peace of Christ has granted me, this peace of the age, which Constantine, the ruler who kindly protects the open earth, fosters; he is present, deserving a grace worthy of his merits. He alone among kings fears that the burden of the sacred name should be imposed upon him, so that, more deserving through righteous deeds, he may receive eternal life throughout the divine ages through the Lord of light, Christ, who reigns forever.”

So the Vatican manuscripts read; others differ slightly.

708. *Usque* is often joined with the preposition *ad*, although the latter is sometimes omitted, as again in Book III, verse 607: “May virtue endure to old age,” and elsewhere. It is gathered from Holy Scripture that the impious generally do not reach old age. Psalm 54, verse 24: “Men of blood and deceit shall not live out half their days.” Psalm 57, verse 10: “Before your thorns understand the bramble, as though alive, so anger shall swallow them.” Job, chapter XV, verse 32: “Before his days are fulfilled, he shall perish.”

712. *Si fuerat* could be retained, with one tense used for another, as in the *Elegies*, verse 294: “What piety had there been?” But *si fuerit*, “if it has been,” is more correct.

713. No other conjecture for healing this corrupt passage occurs to me that is more suitable than *mox poenitet esse modestum*, “soon it repents of being restrained.” I have observed in the prolegomena, number 136, that Dracontius often uses the word *modestus* with various meanings. The question may be raised why God deprives some wicked people of life before they are converted, while allowing others to live longer in their crimes, so that at last they are converted before they depart from life. The only answer to this question is that God’s judgments are just and inscrutable.

But Dracontius is not comparing the wicked with the wicked; rather, concerning the wicked who die before old age, he asks why God removes them before that time, when he could preserve them until old age so that they might return to a better way of life. Certainly there are some criminal people who, even when they reach old age, do not thereby become better, but are overwhelmed by even graver crimes. Yet there are others who, if they lived longer, would be converted.

Concerning these, then, Dracontius replies first that the wicked ought not to be allowed to sin with impunity for long, lest they become a bad example to the good; and second, that sinners are not granted only a brief delay, so that they may obtain pardon if they wish. Ecclesiastes, chapter VIII, verse 11: “Because sentence against evil deeds is not quickly carried out, the hearts of the children of men are filled with fearlessness to perpetrate evil.” Read Lorinus’s commentary on this passage.

The same point is relevant to what is said in Psalm 9, verse 2: “While the wicked man exalts himself, the poor man is set on fire”; and Job, chapter XVII, verse 8: “The righteous shall be astonished at this, and the innocent shall rise up against the hypocrites.” Although, as the following verse adds, “the righteous shall hold to his way, and he whose hands are clean shall add strength,” nevertheless it cannot be denied that some are moved by the prosperity and happiness of the wicked to abandon the way of virtue.

Euripides, in the *Dictys*:

“I have often seen, and often endured with indignation, the good following the example of the wicked in their conduct.”

Sophocles, in the *Aletes*:

“It is grievous to see the wicked, sprung from impious fathers, flourishing in prosperity; and the stock of the good, again, though sound in character, subdued by evil disasters, sunk and oppressed. God ought to have ordered the affairs of mortals otherwise: for it was fitting that the pious should openly obtain the good things of heaven through generous bounty, while the wicked should openly suffer punishments equal to their crimes from the avenging gods. Thus no wicked man would boast of his prosperity.”

Claudian, however, in this agitation of mind, concluded in favor of divine providence in Book I *Against Rufinus*, at the beginning:

“At last the punishment of Rufinus removed this tumult from my mind and acquitted the gods. I no longer complain that the unjust have grown to the heights of power; they are raised up high so that they may fall with a heavier crash.”

[Col. 0830C] 718. That the erring person is preserved for a long time for pardon is proved by the fact that whoever is converted gives joy to heaven. Luke, chapter XV, verse 10: “So I tell you, there is joy before the angels of God over one sinner who repents.”

719. The first *quisque* may be taken as *unusquisque*, “each person,” but the second *quisque* should be understood as *quisquis* or *quicumque*, “whoever.” I established this meaning of the word in the commentary on Prudentius, hymn 7 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 216. This is another reason why the delay granted to the erring should not be considered brief: repentance is easy and can be accomplished in a short space of time, namely with the help of supernatural grace.

720. *Arbitretur* means “let him seek for himself by judging,” “let him assign,” or “let him weigh.” In place of *requirit*, I think *relinquit*, “leaves,” is more correct; for we seek things whose absence we find difficult to endure. The meaning is the same as in verse 656: “Thus the guilty man, by confessing aloud, deserves pardon for his crime.” See also Book III, verses 240 and following. Isaiah, chapter XXX, verse 19: “Weeping, you shall not weep; he will surely have pity on you. At the voice of your cry, as soon as he hears it, he will answer you.” Fabricius, in his commentary on Christian poets, observes that Alcimus lengthened the second syllable of *arbitris*; but since a mute and liquid follow, Alcimus used his privilege, and Dracontius uses the same in *arbitretur*.

752. *Tristis* may be referred to *cujusque*, namely, “the prayer of some unfortunate or sorrowful person.” Here *precatio* means a curse, although it is more often used for a simple entreaty, unless one prefers to understand “a sorrowful prayer,” so that it may more clearly signify a curse. It is in no way permissible to invoke evil upon others as vengeance for harm inflicted by them. See Suárez, Volume II, *On Religion*, Book I, chapter 19.

That God sometimes hears such curses may be inferred from the history related by Saint Augustine, sermon 322, formerly numbered 31, *On Various Subjects*, and Book XXII of *The City of God*, chapter 8. We also hear Salvian in Book VII *On Providence*: “Now, what sort of thing is that, or how grave? Different in kind, perhaps, but not different in injustice—unless the difference is that it is greater? I speak of the proscription of orphans, the afflictions of widows, the crosses of the poor, who, groaning daily to God and calling down an end to their miseries, and, what is most grievous, sometimes through the force of excessive bitterness even asking for the arrival of enemies, have occasionally obtained from God that they should finally endure at the hands of barbarians in common the overthrow which they had previously endured alone at the hands of the Romans.”

764. The power of prayer and supplication is expressed with great force. Similar statements occur in Holy Scripture. Thus in Exodus, chapter XXXII, verse 10, the Lord said to Moses while he was praying: “Let me alone, so that my anger may burn against them.” Saint Jerome infers from Ezekiel, chapter XIII, verse 5, that God’s judgment is broken by the prayers of the saints; he strongly confirms this in his commentary on that passage.

[Col. 0833D] 765. Salvian, in his customary manner, declaims these matters gravely in Book IV *On Providence*: “For how many poor people, living beside a rich man, are either unharmed or safe? Indeed, through the persuasions of the powerful, the weak lose themselves, or even lose themselves and their families together, so that the sacred word has not unjustly testified concerning both classes of persons” (Ecclesiasticus, chapter XIII, verse 23). “The wild ass in the desert is the lion’s prey; so the poor are the pasture of the rich.” Although nearly the whole human race, not only the poor, suffers this tyranny. For what else is the dignity of the lofty than the proscription of cities? Or what else is the authority of certain men—whom I pass over—than plunder? No devastation of the poor—or perhaps of peoples—is greater than power. Other editions vary greatly.

768. This verse and the following appear incurable; I have supplied the emendation that occurred to me as suitable. *Xenia* are any gifts customarily sent by friends, clients, or others, as can be seen in Martial’s book entitled *Xenia*. The first syllable is short, but it is also lengthened by Greek poets and, in a later age—namely, around the year 1314—by a certain Adolphus in poems against women preserved by Leyser, *History of Medieval Poetry*: “Paris gives many gifts to the chaste woman.” One might conjecture *pauper det serica nobis*, “let the poor man give us silk,” since *sericum* and *serica* in the plural are used for silk clothing.

769. Dracontius says that we ask the poor not only for gifts but also for plunder, because the rich in a certain sense plunder the goods of the poor from whom they demand gifts. Cicero, *Against Verres* V, elsewhere Book III, chapter 50: “He made the greatest profits and plunder.” Dracontius, Book III, verse 75:

“Or who is the rash and bold plunderer who seizes what belongs to another, whose deeds the despoiled poor man laments and mourns? For these are the people whom banquets alone, won by plunder, delight.”

Isaiah, chapter I, verse 23: “Your princes are faithless, companions of thieves; they all love gifts and rewards.” Concerning gifts, civil law provides in Digest, Book I, title 16, law 6: “The proconsul ought not entirely to abstain from gifts, but should impose a limit; he should neither abstain from them altogether with excessive strictness nor greedily exceed the proper measure of gifts.”

770. Book III, verse 39: “The rich man is rightly poor; always greedy, needy, poor beneath a wealthy coin.”

771. Beautifully and truly said, as though the poor were begging not for themselves but for the rich, who scrape everything together from every side. Even on account of these two verses alone, this poem of Dracontius was especially worthy of not remaining hidden any longer.

[Col. 0834D] 772. Some learned men disapprove of *ad haec*, or *adhaec*, and in Cicero, Sallust, Tacitus, and other ancient writers where it occurs, restore *adhuc*. But since the best manuscripts present *ad haec*, it would be rash to change it to *adhuc*. Consult Vossius, *On Analogy*, Book IV, chapter 21.

774. Perhaps: “And if he repents.” God calls human beings to repentance because he does not desire the sinner’s death, but rather that he should be converted and live.

775. God’s goodness toward human beings seems to be commended in that he invites and awaits their repentance, whereas he cast the wicked angels into eternal fire. See verses 170 and following: “Therefore our mind is more guilty, because punishment overtook the heavenly servants.” *Crepitare flamma* means “to burn with a certain crackling sound.” Tibullus, Book II, elegy 5, verse 81: “So that the laurel, kindled for sacred rites, may crackle brightly in the flames.” Pliny, Book XXXI, chapter 7, concerning Tragasaean and Acanthian salt: “In fire it neither crackles nor leaps.” Thus one finds “crackling flame” and similar expressions.

But how can the angels crackle with flame, since, as Dracontius says in verse 461, they are all “free from bodily weight and earthly matter”? This difficulty can be answered from the following verses: the fire by which even spirits might be punished is subject to God’s power, and God himself appeared in crackling fire in the bush, because he can use fire both for punishment and for doing good. A different and more accurate explanation emerges from the following verse, as I shall now say.]

776. “All” (*omnis*) seems unquestionably to be read instead of “all” (*omnes*): for *igneus* requires *omnis*, and “spirit” is singular for metrical reasons. From this verse it is plainly gathered that the subject is the good angels, who are God’s pious host and are compared with fire. Psalm 103:4: “Who makes your angels spirits, and your ministers a burning fire.” These words are repeated in the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 1, verse 7, but instead of “a burning fire” it has “a flame of fire,” and verse 14 adds: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent out for service on behalf of those who are to inherit salvation?”

777. Perhaps: “What of the fact that God himself…” That fire is a symbol of divinity is shown by many passages of Sacred Scripture. “With speaking fire,” because God was speaking in the fire. See the commentary on Prudentius’ *Dittochaeum*, verse 29. For this is how I entitled the work, following earlier printed editions and manuscripts, which others call the *Enchiridion* or *Diptychon*. Although I have said more about the title *Dittochaeum*, it should nevertheless be added that some think *Dittochaeum* derives from διττὸς and χάϊος, because it contains examples of virtue from the two Testaments. My authority is Nicolaus du Nortier, *Etymologiae sacrae*.

Here too the sun may be understood in the words “eternal light.” Tertullian, *On God*, Book IV: “Origin of profound light, fountain of life,” etc. Marius Victorinus, in the preface to *Genesis*: “You, life and begetter of life and of profound light, you true light, God, cause and strength of all things.” Dracontius, Book I, verse 131: “The origin of light gives light as the beginning of creation.” The Isidorian Missal, Holy Saturday, in the prayer for blessing the lamp: “Lord our God, light of the one light, fountain of light, light, author of lights.” Merobaudes, concerning Christ: “Now begotten, though you always were, and discoverer of light.”

2. “Radiance of the ether,” as in Book I, verse 615, where *jubar* is attributed to fire, and Book II, verse 778, “fiery radiance.”

3. Concerning the harmony of the elements, see Book I, verse 142 and following.

4. Book II, verse 472: “of countless stars,” which there is said of the angels. Book I, verse 219, concerning the stars: “of a countless host.”

5. Book I, verse 218: “He fitted them to their courses,” namely, the stars. Perhaps one should read *das, aptas, jubes*—“you give, fit, command.” Sedulius, at the beginning of Book I: “You who count the stars, whose names, signs, powers, courses, places, and times you alone know.”

6. Virgil, *Aeneid* III, verse 518: “After he sees all things standing beneath a clear sky.” The seven Triones are called motionless because they always seem to stand still. Other poets call them slow and never-setting; the reason for this is understood from the following verse. *Immoto* or *immobilesque* conflicts with the meter.

9. It is not sufficiently clear what Dracontius intends to say; but he does not seem to have been far from the meaning that I supplied.

14. Perhaps: “the empty space of the unknown.”

[Col. 0838D] 16. Repeat what was said in Book I, verse 60; Book II, verse 689; and elsewhere.

17. “Lofty things”: Book II, verse 204; Book I, verse 436: “higher than every summit.” Perhaps one should read *specie*—“in appearance”—or *pulchrior*—“more beautiful”; or *sed* is used instead of *et*. At the cited place in Book I, the Vatican manuscript likewise reads: “Good in simplicity, but higher than every summit.” Compared with other passages of Dracontius, this reading seems preferable.

[Note: [Col. 0839A]

24. See the note on verse 255 of Book I.

25. See the note on verse 254 of Book I. Perhaps one should read: “Thus the standing crop, nourished by its stalks, arms the ears of grain.” But the manuscript reading is supported by the *Elegies*, verse 231: “The green growth of the crops arms itself with ears.”

26. *Ceres* seems to be used for the grain itself. *Pubesco*—“to grow”—is elegantly transferred to grasses and plants. Cicero, *On the Nature of the Gods* I, chapter 2: “And the changes of the sky, by which everything that the earth produces grows ripe and reaches maturity”; and Book II, chapter 19: “The things that arise from the earth grow and attain maturity.”

27. One might conjecture: “Thus the green field blossoms.” But Dracontius still seems to be speaking of the crop, by which the field first becomes green and later turns yellow, imitating Virgil, *Eclogue* 4, verse 28: “The field will gradually yellow with soft grain.” Thus: “yellow Ceres,” “yellow field,” “yellowing crops,” “yellow ears.” Columella, Book X, verse 311: “But when the harvest shall yellow with ripened ears,” where some read *flammebit*, “will blaze”; but I would more willingly read *flavescet*, “will yellow,” after Virgil. “Without seed having been sown,” because, when God brought forth the crop, no seed had been sown. One might also read: “Thus the green field turns yellow: without seed having been sown, the creditor beneath the plow extorts interest,” etc. This coheres better with the following verses. In the manuscript reading, which I retain, the meaning may perhaps be similar to that explained by the unknown author of *On the Praises of the Lord* under Constantine: “And so that human salvation might pass a secure life, spontaneously, O health-giving grasses, you rise from the turf: the Father himself sows you by a nod, rich without a plow.”

28. The farmer is compared with a creditor who exacts interest from the field. Ambrose, *Hexaemeron* III, chapter 8, no. 35: “The earth returns with interest what it received, multiplied by a heap of profits”; and *On Duties* III, chapter 6: “The fertile earth returns multiplied what it had received; the faithful field is accustomed to repay its interest-bearing produce.” Cicero, *On Old Age*, chapter 15: “The earth never refuses obedience, nor ever returns without interest what it received, but sometimes with lesser, generally with greater, interest.” See Gronovius’ note.

29. I have restored the corrupt reading so that the sense is that the field desires to return the greatest interest. Lucan, *Pharsalia* I, verse 181: “Hence voracious interest and greedy interest over time”; others read “interest in due time.” Thus *usura edax*, “devouring interest.” The *centesima* is interest at which one unit is paid for every hundred each month—that is, twelve for every hundred each year. This was the heaviest rate; other rates were lower. Seneca, *On Benefits* VII, chapter 10, calls the *centesimae* “bloodstained.” Observations on *centesima* interest were written by Johann Friedrich Gronovius.

[Col. 0839D] 30. Perhaps from Virgil, opening of the *Aeneid*: “Although the fields obeyed the greedy farmer.”

31. Since the field is the debtor here, a difficulty arises as to why it is said to desire to return “thousandfold profits.” For *millesima* interest is that in which one unit is paid for every thousand each month—clearly a very small rate, namely twelve per thousand each year. But that the field desires to return great interest is gathered from verse 33: “The contrary desires of the two coincide.” I therefore think that these “thousandfold profits” are in excess of *centesima* interest. For among the Romans there were people who were not satisfied with *centesima* interest and sought greater profits. Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* V, final letter: “Everyone present shouted that nothing was more shameless than Scaptius, who was not satisfied with *centesima* interest with compound interest—that is, interest on interest; others said that nothing was more foolish. To me he seemed more shameless than foolish. For either he was satisfied with *centesima* interest on a sound investment, or, on an unsound one, he hoped for four *centesimae*.”

32. “Shame stains,” as in Book I, verse 342: “Blush stains all his limbs”; unless one prefers to read “shame hinders.”

33. *Exactus*, “the one from whom money is exacted,” may seem to be an unusual expression; and perhaps there would now be no example of an ancient writer, unless Aulus Gellius had preserved one for us in Book XV, chapter 14, where he records the words of Quintus Metellus Numidicus: “Associates came weeping to the senate to complain that enormous sums of money had been exacted from them”; and those of Caecilius: “I am exacted for that harbor tax less than nothing.” This seems to have been expressed by Aulus Gellius in a Greek construction. The farmer’s and the field’s desires are contrary because receiving and returning are contrary to one another, and usually the creditor desires to exact while the debtor refuses to repay. Their desires nevertheless coincide because the field wishes to repay and the farmer to receive.

34. He appropriately attacks those who suppress the grain supply so that it becomes more expensive and its price rises at their discretion. Italians call such a person an *incettatore*, a grain hoarder or market manipulator. Unless I am mistaken, it is strange that the ancient Latins lacked a proper name for these pestilential men. I find that Ulpian and Paulus call them *dardanarii*, a word of unknown origin, in the *Digest*. Monopoly is a related vice. Suetonius, *Tiberius*, chapter 71, reports that Tiberius especially avoided Greek speech in the senate, to such a degree that, when he was about to use the word *monopolium*, he first asked permission because he would have to use a foreign word. Monopolies are not all of the same kind. Moral theologians discuss them. See Molina, *On Justice and Law*, treatise 2, disputation 345, where he discusses those who conceal and store merchandise for a time of scarcity. Throughout this discussion Dracontius draws out the opinions and words of Saint Ambrose against grain speculators. Thus Ambrose, *On Duties* III, chapter 6:

“And another says: ‘Cursed among the people is he who seeks to raise the price of grain’ (Proverbs, chapter 11). … Why do you turn nature’s industry and generosity toward fraud? Why do you begrudge people the public fruits? Why do you diminish abundance for the people? Why do you strive to create scarcity? Why do you make the poor wish for sterility? For when they do not experience the benefits of fertility, while you raise the price and store away the grain, they would rather wish that nothing were born than that you should trade upon the public hunger. You court scarcity of grain and shortage of food; you lament the produce of the fertile soil; you weep over public fertility; you deplore storehouses full of crops … Shall I call this robbery or interest? … Your profit is the public loss … Have you read how the Lord Jesus portrays this speculator in the price of grain in the Gospel? … He did not know what to do, as though he lacked provisions; he was trapped in uncertainty. The storehouses could not contain the grain supply, yet he believed himself needy.”

The passage cited by Ambrose, Proverbs, chapter 11, verse 26, reads in the Vulgate: “He who hides away grain will be cursed among the peoples, but blessing is upon the head of those who sell.”

35. “Devouring,” as in verse 29, “devouring interest”; and it should be noted that *vorax pretii*—“devouring of price”—is formed with the genitive, or that the price-speculator is “devouring,” according to the distinction in “the unjust speculator and devourer of the grain supply and price.”]

39. Book II, verse 770: “Now the rich man is needy,” etc.

40. “Beneath wealthy money,” as in Book I, verse 317, “of wealthy gold”; I discussed this epithet at that passage.

41. One may punctuate: “beneath wealthy money he burns, and the guardian…” Juvenal, *Satire* 14, verse 302: “Things acquired through such great evils are guarded with still greater care and fear; the guardianship of a great fortune is wretched.” Ecclesiastes, chapter 6, verse 2, concerning the miser: “God does not grant him power to eat from it, but a stranger will consume it.” Sacred Scripture is full of such sayings against misers, and the books of pagan and Christian writers are equally full of them.

43. He calls the body the “seat of the spirit,” which the miser does not know how to love, since he preserves his goods for an heir while living sordidly himself.

44. The miser, who does not love his own body, loves his heir. Columbanus, in his letter to Hunaldus, took these lines from Dracontius: “While he heaps up riches, not knowing how to love himself, he loves the heir more, and faithfully preserves everything for him.” In the *Mimes* of Publilius Syrus, verse 60: “The miser does nothing rightly except when he dies.”

48. “Impious,” that is, cruel, not pious or not compassionate. Book I, verse 277: “An impious earth brings forth terrors.” See the *Elegies*, verse 70.

50. Book II, verse 304: “The savage examples of many earlier men teach us.” Here, Book III, verse 96: “May the examples of our father Abraham now teach us.” Perhaps one should read “of the rich man condemned to fire.”

51. The expression “after his limbs” should be noted: after his death, after his limbs have been left behind.

52. He seems to take “bosom” for Abraham’s lap, as many explain that Lazarus was carried into Abraham’s bosom, like a beloved son into his father’s arms and lap. Paulinus, poem 17 to Nicetas, near the end: “Then, I pray, remember us greatly, and, reclining in the lap of the holy Father, with your dewy finger drive away the raging flame for us.” Luke’s words are in chapter 16, verse 22: “And he was carried by the angels into Abraham’s bosom.” Maldonado observes that at banquets the person seated nearest to another reclined in that person’s bosom; from this custom he explains the passage. It has become common usage to call Abraham’s bosom the subterranean place in which Abraham and the other holy Fathers rested before Christ’s resurrection; and Dracontius’ words also admit this interpretation. Julian of Toledo, *Prognostics* II, chapter 3: “I do not doubt that, according to the judgments of many teachers, Abraham’s bosom has been defined to signify the rest of the Father, or a secluded place of repose, or even paradise.”

The passage is read somewhat differently in the Madrid edition, which the eminent Cardinal Lorenzana—often praised by me, though never praised enough according to his merits—prepared on the model of the Douai and Leipzig editions. I followed the old parchment manuscripts that I have at hand, which, as I judge, are not later than the twelfth century, and compared the Madrid edition with them. It is certainly unfortunate that the manuscript of this work which Spain apparently possessed as its only copy, in the Cistercian monastery called La Espina, was destroyed by fire in 1731. Ambrosius Morales had seen that manuscript.

53. I think *tormenta*—“torments”—was written by Dracontius’ hand, with the *a* lengthened in *tormenta* because of the following word’s initial consonant. But the manuscript reading may be retained: for *exspecto*, or *expecto*, is sometimes used for *specto*, as I proved with examples in the note on Book I, verse 356: “And from afar he awaits the green fields and the beasts of burden.” Some think that *exspecto* should be written with this meaning.

54. In imitation of Virgil, Book VI, verse 121: “He redeemed him by an exchange of death.”

55. Perhaps: “Whom the thin silk garment burdened”; or *in serica tenuis* should be understood as “a thin garment in silk.”

56. An imitation and explanation of Juvenal, *Satire* 1, verses 28 and following: “Crispinus, drawing Tyrian lamps back over his shoulder, fans the summer gold with sweating fingers and cannot bear the weight of a larger gem.”

57. “Broken” indicates the rich man’s softness. Having put off his thick and heavier purple garment, he demanded another, thin and lighter, for summer. *Ostrum* and *murex* are somewhat distinct, but writers commonly use them interchangeably for the same thing.

58. The subject is still summer, when the rich are unable to bear either a heavier gold ring or the weight of even a small gem.

60. “Panting” and “panting” as an epithet of fire are often used by Dracontius. See the prolegomena, no. 137.

61. Ovid, Book II of the *Metamorphoses*, verse 612, called it “cruel punishment.” Here “cruel penalty” means harsh, severe, and never-ending. Book I, verse 548: “It was cruel punishment to die.”

62. Perhaps: “Nor does he endure,” since *tolerare* means to bear patiently. But because he previously said that he could not bear the weight of the gem, it is correct now to say *tolerat*, “he endures,” that is, he suffers and bears it.]
