[Col. 0844C] 88. I supplied the verse from the following verse 79. If others offer something better, I will gladly accept it. Synesius wished to extract this advantage from corrupt manuscripts of ancient writers, namely, that minds might be trained to attempt something similar. For when, near the end of his *Dio*, or *On the Manner of His Life*, he had stated that the copies of Dio that he possessed were corrupt, he added:

“Thus, when understanding is compelled to supply and attach what is missing from the sequence of the narrative, and when it does not have everything placed before its eyes, it becomes more practiced by itself in daring something similar, and grows accustomed not to depend on others but to contain within itself. For these corrupt books seem to require a mind that presides over the eyes. This was also what the teaching of Pythagoras prescribed to adolescents, partly to test each person’s natural disposition, partly so that it might serve as an exercise.”

As for how great Synesius himself was in talent of this kind of exercise, read, if you please, the note on verse 409. Meanwhile I would have you observe how ancient it is to find corrupt manuscripts and to devise supplements for them. If only in works that have reached us it were possible to distinguish those supplements!

93. *Spectat* for *exspectat*—“awaits”—is a word of Plautus and is attributed to Cicero, just as, conversely, *exspecto* for *specto* was explained above in the note on verse 53. In this passage, however, *spectat* can stand for “looks at” or “regards.”

94. Someone might conjecture: “How foolish it is,” so as to accommodate the meter better. But apart from the fact that such monosyllables seem to me to have had a common quantity among the ancients, there is a special reason why *sit* can be lengthened: for *sit* was formed from *siet*. Cicero, *On the Orator*, chapter 47: “*SIET* is full, *SIT* is shortened; use either, if you wish.” Lucretius, Terence, and Plautus frequently use *siem* and *sies*. See Gifanius’ index to Lucretius. Arator, Book I, verse 976, has in printed editions: “But may the Father himself be wholly as he is”; yet in two manuscripts of the Vatican Library, one Palatine, no. 1716, and the other Vatican, no. 1665, I find written by the first hand: “But may the Father himself be wholly,” while above it reads as in the printed editions. The first reading is more correct. When Capella observed that the ancients regularly shortened *it* and *et*, and other words ending in *t*, he judged all these syllables to have common quantity. See Riccioli, part 4 of the *Prosody*, rule 6.]

98. *Contempsit*, “he despised,” that is, rejected or abandoned. Below, verse 414: “He despised his children and the City.” Thus Virgil, *Georgics* IV, verse 104, concerning the bees: “And they despise the honeycombs and leave the chilly dwellings.” Likewise *sperno*, “to reject,” after Ennius, is used by Prudentius, *Psychomachia*, verse 149: “He rejects the faithless standards and spurns the mournful monuments far away.” In Dracontius one may distinguish: “He quickly despised, ordered by Hope, and led [him] to the altar.”

99. Dracontius often uses *pietas* for compassion; here, however, it means religion and obedience toward God, which is rightly called excessive—that is, great. *Nimius*, “excessive,” meaning “many” or “very many,” is a hyperbole not unknown even to pagan writers, as is *nimis* for “very.” In these and the following verses Dracontius creates oppositions familiar to him: compassionate yet bloodstained, a father with the sword unsheathed, a savage priest, one about to strike the beloved, a merciful yet ruthless man.

101. *Stabat* denotes steadfastness and is said of soldiers who show themselves ready for battle in the line. The grammarians’ rule is that *ferio*, “I strike,” lacks a perfect tense and supine. Servius, however, in his note on *Aeneid* VII, verse 498, used *feriturus*, “about to strike,” and Charisius, Book III, among defective verbs, assigns the perfect *ferii* and supine *feritum* to *ferio*. Examples do not appear in the older writers.]

### 103

“*Undando*” is used with the accusative in place of *inundando* (“by flooding”). Statius and others use the word in this way.

### 104

“Blows,” as in the preceding verse: “tearing his face with his nails.” The strokes made in lamentation and mourning are often called *verbera* (“blows”). See the notes on verses 377 and following.

### 105

I read: “Piety, unafraid of sin, threatens the son with destruction.” No more certain conjecture presents itself. “Piety secure of sin,” that is, without fear of sin. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* XII, verse 199: “Let your prayers be, he said, secure of refusal: choose what you should pray for.” See the notes on verses 164 and 438.

### 106

I read “without savage death,” as in Book II, verse 703: “and recalling him from savage death.”

### 108

A *victima* is the larger sacrificial animal, such as a calf; a smaller sacrificial animal, such as a lamb, is a *hostia*. Nevertheless, one word is often used for the other. Even the pagans observed that sacrificial victims which resisted more violently were displeasing to the gods; but an animal that stood still when offered was thought to be given to the willing deity. Hence our poet [Virgil]: “and the sacred he-goat, led by the horn, will stand at the altars.” This is what Macrobius says in Book III, chapter 5 of the *Saturnalia*, which it will be useful to consult.

### 109

“Was displeasing to God, and pleased him”—namely, God did not wish an innocent victim to be sacrificed, and he approved the will of both father and son. As I have said, Dracontius is full of such oppositions. “With faithful heart,” as Alcimus writes in Book I, shortly after the beginning: “That with faithful mind he may devote a life serving him through long years.”

### 111

The third syllable in *arietem* is short, but it is lengthened because three short syllables come together, as Dracontius often does in *muliere*. See the note on verse 133 and Book II, verse 660. Statius likewise lengthens the third syllable in *arietibus*, Book II of the *Thebaid*, verse 492, or 490 in some editions: “The lofty city appears, struck repeatedly by battering-rams.” Some say that the third syllable is joined to the second by synaeresis, so that the first may be lengthened. But the first syllable should not be lengthened merely because of synaeresis; the situation is different when the second is pronounced like a consonant. Then the first is lengthened, the second has the force of a consonant, and the third is shortened, so that in *ariete* a dactylic foot is ordinarily formed.

### 113

Commodianus, *Instructions* 4:

> “And Saturn, the old man—if he is a god, when does a god grow old?  
> Or if he was a god, why did he devour his children,  
> Driven by terrors? But since he was not a god,  
> He consumed the entrails of his children in monstrous rage.”

See what I noted in my commentary on Prudentius, Book II *Against Symmachus*, verse 296: “The Saturnian rites smoke with the slaughter of infants.” Commodianus speaks of the sons of Saturn, whom Saturn devoured; Prudentius and Dracontius speak of other infants who were sacrificed during the festival days of the Saturnalia, before Hercules’ arrival in Italy—a custom that continued for a long time in Africa. *Falcifer* (“sickle-bearing”) is a proper epithet of Saturn; see Macrobius, Book I, chapters 7 and 8 of the *Saturnalia*. Some call him *falciger*. The sickle is attributed to Saturn because he taught human beings agriculture, or because it signifies time, in which everything is harvested.

“Should rescue from death,” as in Book I, verse 668: “rescued from death,” and in verse 557 of the same book: “is rescued from the assault of death.” I therefore think that *neci* is used for *nece*, as in verse 532: “and accustomed to rejoice in death.”

> 121. God’s mercy is praised in similar words in Book I, verses 30 and following, and frequently elsewhere. See Book III, verses 657 and following.

> 123. He also shortened the first syllable of *Isac* in verse 139, but lengthened it in verse 155.

> 124. *Auferre* means “to take away,” or “in order that he might take away,” as in *facilis cedere* and similar expressions. God had not determined to take Isaac away from his father by means of the murder that the father was to commit; nor did he wish to test and examine the will of both as though he were ignorant of the human mind. God commands whatever he commands for a reason. For what reason, then, did he command Isaac to be sacrificed? So that through Abraham’s example he might show us in what manner he wishes to be loved: so that nothing may ever be placed before him.

> 126. In Genesis, chapter XXII, verse 1, it is said: “God tested Abraham”; the same statement is found in Judith, chapter VIII, verse 22, and Hebrews, chapter XI, verse 17. Dracontius therefore explains these words according to the sense of the Catholic Epistle of James, chapter I, verse 13: “Let no one, when he is tempted, say that he is tempted by God; for God is not a tempter of evil, and he himself tempts no one.” A twofold temptation is distinguished: one that deceives or leads into fraud, and another that tests. The first in no way belongs to God; the second belongs to God in such a way that he does not test as though ignorant of the human will, but gives a person an opportunity to earn merit, exercises him in virtues, and strengthens others through a good example.

> Saint Julian, bishop of Toledo, in Book I of the *Antikeimena* (“Contradictions”), no. 37, proposes and resolves the question as follows:

> “How can Moses say in Deuteronomy, chapter XIII, verse 3, ‘The Lord your God tests you,’ while the apostle James, on the contrary, declares, ‘God tempts no one’?

> “Answer. In the Holy Scriptures two temptations are commonly understood: one that deceives, and another that tests. In accordance with the temptation that tests, it is said: ‘The Lord your God tests you.’ In accordance with the temptation that deceives, the apostle James declares: ‘God tempts no one.’”

> I have seen an edition of this work that is little known, printed at Cologne in the workshop of Eucharius Cervicornus in 1540 and divided into three books, based on a very ancient manuscript of the Fulda library, as Henricus Sachsius testifies in the preface. The work has sometimes been falsely attributed to him because it appeared anonymously. Andreas Schottus was the first to identify the true author; in the Madrid edition, the most eminent Cardinal Lorenzana confirmed this with new evidence. Most people divide this work of Julian’s into only two books.

> But is it true that the Romans derive their origin from Esau? This is indeed Dracontius’ view, but it is difficult to confirm it through reliable authorities. An Eastern tradition says that, under Abdon, judge of the Hebrews, the Idumaeans—who are Esau’s descendants—led a colony into Italy, from which the Latins and Romulus are said to derive their origin.

> Others invent the story that the Romans descended from Tzepho, Esau’s grandson through his son, who was supposedly a companion of Aeneas. Fazellus, Book VIII of the first *Decade on Sicilian Affairs*, chapter 1, cites two Chaldaean inscriptions once read at Palermo.

> One of them was carved on marble and, while William II was ruling, was translated from the Damascus-born Abraham into Latin as follows:

> The other inscription, carved on ancient square stones from which the gate of the old city called Patitelli was constructed, was translated into Latin by a Syrian in the year 1470 as follows:

> 147. Genesis, chapter XXVII, verse 40, Isaac to Esau: “Your blessing shall be: you shall live by the sword.” Although the Israelites too became renowned for the glory of war, they were much more distinguished by commerce and the arts of peace. Esau, insofar as he sold and lost the rights of the firstborn, represents the Israelites, in whose place the gentiles converted to faith in Jesus Christ succeeded to the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. The same Esau, because he was bloodthirsty, is a type of the gentiles, who were pitiless and bloody in their savagery and rejoiced in the shedding of blood.

> 167. The name of the Lord often signifies God himself in the Holy Scriptures and denotes his majesty. Here *tepuere* means “grew less hot” or “lost their heat.” Lucan, Book IV, verse 284: “Little by little the fierce anger falls, and their minds grow warm no longer.” Martial, Book II, epigram 1: “You will drink as a guest from a mixed cup, but first let the cup set before you begin to grow lukewarm.” Several oppositions familiar to Dracontius are heaped together: “the heats grew cool,” “cold fire,” “flames icy,” “the torrid heat does not breathe.”

> 170. Perhaps *ast aditum* should be read instead of *aut*: the point seems to be that, while the three boys were unharmed in the middle of the furnace’s blazing fire, the flame killed the men who had thrown them into the furnace, as related in Daniel, chapter III, verses 23 and 47: “And the flame was poured over the furnace to a height of forty-nine cubits, and it burst forth and burned those Chaldaeans whom it found near the furnace.”

> There is also room for the conjecture that one should read: “They marvel that he fell, within the hollow, while the torrid heat does not breathe, but the flame licked the entrance,” and so forth. For Daniel says “in the middle of the furnace of blazing fire,” “in the midst of the burning furnace,” “in the middle of the flame,” and “in the middle of the fire,” which is properly expressed by *sinu* (“hollow,” “interior”). I will not conceal, however, that *lambo* is sometimes used of the flame’s light and harmless touch; hence the reading becomes uncertain and a conjecture may be required. Alternatively, another word must be sought in place of *lambebat*.]

> 171. Hair is attributed not only to comets and stars but also to fire. Valerius Flaccus, Book I, verse 205: “When the fire, struggling amid the dense entrails, brought forth a mane.” Thus *coma ignis* (“the mane of fire”) occurs in Seneca’s *Oedipus*, verse 311, in Albinovanus’ *To Livia*, verse 256, and in Catullus, poem 60, nuptial verse 77 and following, with Vulpius’ note. It could also be understood of the hair of the three boys, not burned by the fire but shining in the manner of fire. The first explanation is more likely, for below the discussion concerns the boys’ hair. On the verb *ignio* and *ignitus*, see the commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* 10 *Peristephanon*, verse 1078.

> 172. Someone might conjecture *fastiditque famem* (“and hunger rejects it”), as though the fasting flame refused food and disdained hunger. The manuscript reading means that the hunger of the fire, fasting, rejected despised nourishment. What Saint Basil says in Homily 1, *On the Praise of Fasting*, fits this passage: he compares these three boys, unharmed in the furnace, to asbestos.

> 183. The first syllable in *Danielem* is shortened, while the following two are lengthened; this is not unusual in such foreign proper names. Most people shorten the first two, or form synaeresis from the second and third.

> 185. Thus in Book I, verse 556: “The great mercy of God.” But what does *jejuno utroque leone* (“with both lions fasting”) mean? I suspect *utrinque leone* (“with a lion on either side”), or *jejuno ventre leonum* (“with the lions’ bellies fasting”). I do not think a satisfactory explanation can be drawn from Daniel, chapter XIV, verse 31: “There were seven lions in the pit, and two bodies and two sheep were given to them daily; but at that time they were not given to them, so that they might devour Daniel.” Dracontius does not seem to imply that the lions were fasting from both kinds of food. Perhaps he is referring to ancient pictures in which Daniel is shown between two lions.

> 186. The sense is: what unarmed hunter has wrestled with wild beasts and not been killed? A similar expression occurs in Exodus, chapter XXXIII, verse 20: “For no human being shall see me and live.” Just as *venatio* (“the hunt”) refers not only to the pursuit of wild beasts through woods and fields but also to a hunting spectacle, so *venator* (“hunter”) may mean a *bestiarius*, one who fights wild beasts in the amphitheater. Some *bestiarii*, hired for pay or volunteering themselves, entered the arena armed; others, condemned to the beasts for their crimes, were thrown to them unarmed.

> 187. Claudian, *On the Consulship of Mallius*, verse 298: “And the lions, pierced through, fall, while the people grow pale.”

> [Col. 0852D] 188. “The extended hunter,” that is, the *bestiarius*. Lucan, Book IV, verse 708: “The deadly arena compels those brought forth for its spectacles to engage in combat, driven not by ancient anger.” Actors too are said to be brought forth onto the stage. *Productor* may nevertheless be retained in the sense of the trainer who brings out the wild beast and provokes it to combat with a rattling sound or a whip. Martial, *On the Spectacles*, epigram 21: “While the frightened trainers provoke the rhinoceros,” and so forth.

> 189. *Massylum*, namely “the lion,” or, better, a contraction of *Massylorum* (“of the Massylians”) through poetic usage. Virgil, Book VI, verse 59: “and the Massylian peoples hidden deep within.” Statius, Book II of the *Silvae*, poem 5: “You perish, skilled destroyer of lofty beasts, neither enclosed in a Massylian herd nor surrounded by a curved hunting net.” The Massylian herd is a band of hunters from the people of Massylia, whether in Numidia or in Libya near the Gaetuli; the name is often used for the Mauritanians.

> If in the preceding verse one reads *productor*, an interrogative clause may be attached to it: “and by his art provokes the Massylian.” In that case this verse begins a new period: “Standing farther away,” namely the hunter whom he mentioned earlier. Hunters standing at a distance provoked the beasts to charge, so that they could more easily evade them.]

> 199. In *fera*, the *a* is lengthened because of the *st* of the following word. I conjectured *stant unus ad unum*, or *stat unus ad unum*, with *stat* lengthened for the reasons given at verse 94.

> 200. *Ferro, hinc* has a hiatus, especially because aspiration among the ancients sometimes had the force of a consonant. A hiatus of this kind in the penthemimeral position is attractive. Martial, *On the Spectacles*, epigram 27, on Carpophorus fighting beasts: “This armed hand would have been a single death for the Hydra.”

> 201. Several hunters entered the arena in order to bring one another mutual assistance. Martial, in the same work, epigram 23: “When a lion fled him, it ran headlong upon the spears.” As Martial says, Carpophorus directed his hunting-spears with such certain aim that the beasts fled him and rushed headlong onto the weapons of other hunters, as though they feared being killed by others less than by Carpophorus.

Dracontius returns to Daniel, who alone emerged victorious among seven lions tormented by ravenous hunger, although unarmed. *Saevās rabies* refers to savage lions exhausted by hunger. Virgil, Book IX, verse 63: “The gathered rage of eating, exhausted by long hunger,” and Book II of the *Aeneid*, verse 356: “whom the wicked rage of the belly drove blind.”

210. But it is lengthened because of the aspiration of the following word. See verse 200 and the note on verse 94 concerning such monosyllables, which appear to have ordinary quantity. This miracle is attributed to faith [Col. 0855D], Daniel, chapter 6, verse 23: “And Daniel was brought out of the pit, and no injury was found in him, because he had believed in his God.”

211. Virtue is spoken of miracles in the sacred Scriptures, as I noted on book II, verse 114, “That he might perform a work of virtue.” Here, however, the word *virtue* is also rightly used because *virtus* was assigned to athletes in a particular sense. Prudentius, *Hymn* 4 of the *Peristephanon*, verse 101: “Our boy, and ours in the wrestling-ground, by the skill of virtue and the olive of faith,” etc. Although the contests of athletes, gladiators, and hunters were distinct, nevertheless *virtus* is also attributed to gladiators and hunters in the same sense.

212. “By Diana’s lot”: I understand this as “by Diana’s service,” a phrase drawn from the sacred Scriptures and from Israelite usage; for priests and Levites received by lot, in rotation, the duty of serving the temple. Juvencus, book I, verse 45: “But when Zacharias brought incense to the shrines and altars by lot” [Col. 0856B]. Some have printed *forte* (“by chance”), but *sorte* is the true reading, confirmed by two very ancient Vatican manuscripts. A little earlier Juvencus says, verse 38: “Zacharias, to whom the care of guarding the temple belongs in turns,” which concerns the same matter. Compare Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XI, chapter 12. Daniel, therefore, was a servant of the living God, as Darius called him, not devoted to the service or protection of Diana. Nor is Diana mentioned without good reason: not only rustic hunting but also the theatrical hunt was under Diana’s protection. Martial, *On the Spectacles*, epigram 12: “Amid the savage dangers of imperial Diana”; thus he calls the theatrical hunt. Claudian, *On the Consulship of Mallius*, verse 291: “May Latonia favor the amphitheatrical procession.” Cassiodorus, book V, letter 42: “A spectacle distinguished only by its structures, but most dreadful in its action, discovered in honor of Scythian Diana, who rejoiced in the shedding of blood.” See Mazochius, *Commentary on the Inscription of the Campanian Amphitheater*, chapter 5, and Petrus Taffinus, *On the Secular Year*, and Lud[ovicus], *The Secular Year*, part 1, chapter 8 [Col. 0856C].

214. I punctuate it this way. *Satiata* takes a genitive. Silius, book IV, verse 437: “The spear glutted with the blood of the Titans in war.” Ovid, book VII of the *Metamorphoses*, verse 808: “I was safe from the spear; but when my right hand had been glutted with the slaughter of the wild beast, I returned to the coolness and shade.” Later: “after the host of guests had been slaughtered,” as in Lucan, book V, verse 11: “The senate heard the guest in foreign dwellings.” Many others use *hospes* adjectivally. Nor would I unwillingly read *catervis hospitium caesis* in the plural genitive, in place of *hospitum*, like *haereditatium* and *civitatium*. Severus, in *Aetna*, verse 127: “But if the earth sends out different channels, a fellowship of rivers”; although some say that *hospitium* there is accusative, so that the channels are “a fellowship of rivers.”

216. “Taurican,” because Diana was worshiped in the Tauric Chersonese (now Crimea), where the Tauri, a people of European Scythia, sacrificed their guests. Ovid, book IV of the *Tristia*, elegy 4, verse 63: “Nor is the place far from us where, in Taurica, the altar of the quiver-bearing goddess is fed by dreadful slaughter.” Juvenal, satire 15, verse 114: “More savage than the Maeotian altar is Egypt; for that Tauric altar, inventor of the unspeakable rite, sacrifices human beings”—if one believes the poems that report such things as worthy of trust. The mention of the virgin is also skillfully made. Athanasius, *Against the Gentiles*, section 25: “For the Scythians who are called Taurians slaughter shipwrecked persons and all whom they capture from among the Greeks as victims for their virgin”—that is, Diana.

“Among the Colchians,” wherever the land of the Colchians extends. Colchis, now called Mingrelia, lay between the Black Sea to the west and Iberia to the east. Formerly all who inhabited the shores of the Black Sea sacrificed strangers, and for that reason the ancients first called the sea *Pontus Axenus*, “inhospitable”; afterward it was called *Euxinus*, “hospitable.” The cruelty of Diana’s altar in the Tauric Chersonese also extended to the Colchians. For Thoas was king of the Tauric Chersonese, and the Colchians were subject to him. Ovid, book III of the *Ex Ponto*, elegy 2, verse 59: “Thoas held a kingdom, famous on the Maeotian shore; nor was another better known upon the waters of the Euxine.” Hyginus, *Fabula* 261, relates that Orestes went with Pylades to Colchis and, after being captured for sacrifice to Tauric Diana, killed Thoas and carried away the goddess’s image. [Col. 0857A–B]

217. Peter is preferred to the other apostles, and his primacy is clearly asserted: “standard-bearer of the saving cross, appointed leader of innumerable nations under the law of faith, diligent herald of God, interpreter of the true doctrine, heavenly doorkeeper, first priest in the world, acting in the place of the Lord.”

219. The power of governing the whole Church, granted to Peter and his successors, is clearly expressed in these words. Since some leader on earth must necessarily be acknowledged, appointed over innumerable nations—that is, over the universal Church—to guard the deposit of faith, who else can this leader be but Peter and his Roman successor, the Roman pontiff? We gladly add this testimony of antiquity, brought forth again from darkness, as an argument for the chair of Peter and for the perpetual devotion of the Spaniards toward the Roman apostolic see, to the countless other testimonies: a small drop added to the Ocean, yet an addition of some value, and not wholly unworthy to be consecrated to the honor, merits, incomparable virtue, and immortal name of our most holy lord Pius VI, acting in the place of the Lord [Col. 0857C].

220. “After the most worthless nets of the watery sea’s fish.” Virgil, book IV of the *Georgics*, verse 233, concerning the Pleiad: “Or when, fleeing the same star, the sadder fish of the watery heaven descends into the winter waves.” Dracontius calls it a “watery fish” because it cannot live outside the water.

221. Tertullian, *On the Judgment of the Lord*: “And you have often driven away the heralds of God” (a dreadful thing). Noah is called a herald of righteousness by Saint Peter, Second Epistle, chapter 2, verse 5. “Interpreter of the true doctrine” is a more distinctive epithet of Peter, as in verse 159, “Interpreter of the light-bearing sun.” See the note on book I, verse 114.

222. Hilary, commentary on Matthew 16, section 7: “O blessed doorkeeper of heaven, at whose discretion the keys of the eternal entrance are entrusted.” In the hymn of Saints Peter and Paul at Vespers, attributed to Elpidius, the wife of Boethius: “Teacher of the world and doorkeeper of heaven.” Alcuin, poem 81: “Once a fisherman, now the gracious doorkeeper of heaven.” Victorinus, *On Jesus Christ, God and Man*: “He spoke sublimely to Peter: ‘Take the keys of heaven, and be its doorkeeper.’” Strabo, poem on Saint Peter: “The doorkeeper of heavenly life, opening its double [entrance].” The editor notes that *gemina* is corrupt. I would correct it to *limina* (“thresholds”). For the same reason Peter is called the key-bearer in the hymn of the praises of all the saints: “The key-bearer of highest heaven.” Among the pagans, Janus was the doorkeeper of heaven.

223. Someone ineptly corrected the manuscript to *Temporibus placidis* (“in peaceful times”). The proper reading is *Temporibus nostris* (“in our times”), namely, in the times of our Christian religion. Thus far Dracontius has presented examples of believers from the Old Testament; now from ecclesiastical history he presents Peter, chief of the apostles, working miracles through trust in God. In the Mozarabic Missal a Mass is celebrated for Saint Martin, in whose prayer, after the names, we read: “Grant also that this man, whom the times of our age have brought forth, joined to the martyrs as an object of wonder to the heavenly ones, may bring help to our times.” Lesleus, in his elegant and learned notes, says: “From this it is clear how ancient the cult of Saint Martin was in Spain, and how ancient this Mass is.” But although I readily believe that the cult of Saint Martin in Spain is ancient, and that the Mass is ancient, I by no means believe that this prayer was written in the age or century in which Martin died. “Our age” and “our times” are opposed to the earlier times in which the Church was ennobled by the blood of many martyrs. In this sense the prayer could appropriately have been written and recited one or two centuries later, when the times of peace in the Church were called “our times”—unless in this prayer too “our times” is understood of the troubled times of the Christian religion. In Dracontius the explanation is clear from the following words, “with Christ reigning thunderously”: *tonanter* can be retained, since Dracontius uses similar adverbs elsewhere, as I said in the prolegomena, section 135. I will not, however, object if one reads *tonante*.

226. The use of *simul* for *similiter* is not unprecedented. Cicero, *Against Verres* 2, former act I, chapter 4: “His urban praetorship was the plundering of sacred buildings and public works; at the same time, in administering justice, he assigned and bestowed goods and possessions contrary to all precedent.” Peter, relying on the virtue of his master, according to Acts of the Apostles, chapter 3, verses 12 and following: “Why do you look at us as though by our virtue or power we had made this man walk?” etc.

228. “With Paul accompanying him”: not because Peter and Paul arrived in Rome at the same time, but because they lived together in that city, since Peter had come there long before Paul.

229. Earlier editors shortened the first syllable of *Magus*. Nevertheless I restore *Magum*, which Dracontius freely uses as a proper name assigned to Simon, and whose first syllable he lengthens according to his customary practice. There is also the example of Sedulius, in the dedication to the Emperor Theodosius: “The king’s ambushes, the rewards of the Magi, for his learned disciples.” These verses certainly belong to an ancient author, but many deny that they are Sedulius’s.

As for the history of Simon Magus described by Dracontius, it is widely known and was handed down long ago by reliable authors: Arnobius, book II *Against the Gentiles*; the author of the *Apostolic Constitutions*; Lucifer of Cagliari and other legates of Pope Liberius writing to Eusebius of Vercelli; Cyril of Jerusalem, *Catechesis* 6 of the Enlightened; Eusebius, book II of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 12; Epiphanius, heresy 21; Augustine, *On Heresies*; Theodoret, book I of the *Heretical Fables*; Maximus of Turin, sermon 5, formerly attributed to Saint Ambrose; Dungalus, at the end of his *Response*; Isidore of Seville and Isidore of Pelusium; Sulpicius Severus; Basil of Seleucia; Philastrius; Pacian; Peter Chrysologus; and countless other Christians—to say nothing of the pagans Suetonius and Dio, who, though not openly, nevertheless hint at the same event in some fashion.

I will not omit the common testimony of the entire Gothic Church, which commemorated this story on the feast of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, as it is read in the Isidorian Missal after the *Sanctus*: “Christ, Son of God, who destroyed the magical prodigies of nebulous art, exposed by the truth of apostolic contest in Simon’s presumption; him, as he vainly sought ascent into the heavens by the movements of the air, deceived by demonic illusion, boastfulness raised higher so that he might be dashed down more grievously,” etc. Dracontius now joins this testimony in confirming the same opinion.

Yet, as is sufficiently clear in itself, certain historical opinions have their own stars and their own times. A refined kind of scholarship now flourishes that denies much once firmly established and calls many things into question. I often ask myself what the reason may be that certain histories are now rejected as plainly false, although our ancestors formerly regarded them as certain. Have some new arguments been discovered that escaped them? In most such matters, none at all. Do we see more sharply? I wish that were so, unless the audacity of certain impious men had already advanced so far that they attempt freely to tear down all the most sacred doctrines of the Christian religion.

But, to return to Simon Magus: Cajetan Golt recently defended his flight and fall against the observations of certain modern critics in a brief but learned dissertation, which was wholly and deservedly inserted in the *Roman Ecclesiastical Journal* of 1787, numbers 4 and 48. Lesleus also treated this subject learnedly and refuted Cotelerius forcefully in his notes on the *Mixed, or Isidorian, Missal*, page 578 and following. See also Fogginius, *On the Roman Journey of Saint Peter*, and Philippus Laurentius Dionysius, *Monuments of the Sacred Vatican Basilica*, page 198 [Col. 0859C].

230. Sedulius, book III, or book IV, verse 113, gave the name *Simonis* the same quantity: “He seeks the ponds and sits in Simon’s little alder boat.” Some shorten both the first and second syllables; others lengthen both. Petrus Aurorarius agrees with Dracontius and Sedulius in his books on the Maccabees: “He labors to destroy Simon’s children along with their father.” I report this from the Vatican manuscript. In Dracontius’s codex it is written *Symona*, as in the Isidorian Missal.

231. Simon Magus had so deceived the people of Samaria by magical arts and tricks that he was regarded as the power of God. Acts of the Apostles, chapter 8, verse 10: “They all listened to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, ‘This man is the power of God, which is called Great.’ They attended to him because for a long time he had driven them mad with his magic.” After receiving holy baptism, he wished to buy with money the power of conferring the Holy Spirit, and, when he was rejected by the apostle Peter, he traveled through many eastern provinces and came to Rome. There he pretended to be Christ and openly declared that he would fly up to the God whom he boasted was his father. There still survive, in Saint Jerome’s commentary on Matthew 24, words from one of his books in which he said of himself: “I am the word of God, I am the beautiful one, I am the Paraclete, I am all things of God.” For these reasons Dracontius calls him the “fabricated offspring of God.”

Whether he was ever regarded as a god by the Romans is not yet clear. Many report from Saint Justin that, by order of the senate, a statue of Simon Magus was erected on the Tiber Island, with the inscription: *SIMONI DEO SANCTO*, or *SIMONI SANCTO ET DEO* (“To Simon, holy god,” or “To Simon, holy and divine”). That Justin was deceived by some statue and inscription dedicated to *Semo Sancus Deus Fidius* does not seem unlikely; nevertheless many critical scholars regard the report as entirely true [Col. 0860A].

The chief cause of this controversy was a stone excavated on the bank of the Tiber in the sixteenth century bearing the following inscription, which I reproduce from a letter sent by Julius Jacobonius to Muretus in 1574:

**SEMONI SANCO DEO FIDIO SACRUM SEXTVS POMPIVS S. P. F. COL. MVSSIANVS QVINQVENNALIS DECVR BIDENTALIS DONVM DEDIT.**

“Sacred to Semo Sancus, the god Fidius. Sextus Pompius Mussianus, son of Sextus, of the Publician tribe, quinquennal and *decurio bidentalis*, gave this gift.”

The stone had been found shortly before Jacobonius sent his letter to Muretus. Everyone now agrees that this inscription was set up not to Simon Magus but to Semo Sancus, or Sango, the Sabine god; yet when the stone was excavated many thought otherwise.

“I scarcely withdrew honorably yesterday evening,” Jacobonius says, “from a gathering of certain men who obstinately maintained that the stone recently excavated on the bank of the Tiber, inscribed to Semo Sancus, the god Fidius, designated that Simon Magus. Since I wholly opposed them, I began to be mocked and despised by everyone. When I asserted that I had once read about a certain Fidius Sango or Sancus, and that earthly gods had formerly been called *Semones*, I was mocked even more by certain men who preferred to say that *Sancus* in the Sabine language meant ‘Magus,’ and *Semo* ‘Simon’ in Hebrew” [Col. 0860C].

Muretus confirmed Jacobonius’s opinion with many arguments. Indeed, besides the ancient writers in whom frequent mention of Semo Sancus occurs, there are several stones inscribed to him in Gruter and others. Yet one sometimes finds *Sancto* for *Sanco*, and *Semopatri* or *Semipatri* for *Semoni*. Nevertheless, although Justin testifies that he saw in Rome a statue dedicated to Simon Magus, I cannot dare to assert that no such statue ever existed. Justin’s authority is defended by Calmet in his dissertation on Simon Magus, Fogginius in *On the Roman Journey of Saint Peter*, Travasa, Grotius, Mazochius, and others.

240. This is conjectural. *Simplex spes* (“simple hope”), as in verse 248, *praesumptio simplex* (“simple presumption”). See the note on book II, verse 625. Nevertheless, someone may prefer the manuscript reading, *Exigit hoc semper spes* (“Hope always demands this”). In place of *vota fidelis* someone rightly conjectured *vita fidelis* (“faithful life”), that is, life ordered according to Christian faith. Not badly. *Sors pia* (“pious lot”) could be retained, according to the note on verse 212. In place of *vota fidelis*, *sermo fidelis* (“faithful speech”) would also not be unsuitable, as in verse 236. I suspected *bucca fidelis* (“faithful mouth”). *Exigit* means “completes,” as in verse 211, *Exegit virtutis opus* (“he completed a work of virtue”). Horace, book III, final ode, verse 1: “I have completed a monument more lasting than bronze.” Although in this verse *exigit* is more likely used for “obtains” by demanding and exacting, as in verse 235, “Behold what saving faith demanded from the citadel of the Thunderer.”

252. *Quirinus*, an unmistakable name of Romulus. It is doubtful whether it can be used adjectivally for “Roman”; for although it occurs adjectivally in Horace, Propertius, and Ovid, some alter the text and read *Quirini* in the genitive. This passage of Dracontius confirms that *Quirinus* can be used adjectivally. If you object, you can just as easily correct this passage as others and read *gentisque Quirini* (“and of the Quirinian people”). The conjecture *currat* (“let the profane person run through”) is not bad. But *currant* (“let them run through”) can be defended, as though the speech turns from one person to all profane people [Col. 0862B].

253. The second part is obscure in the connection of the letters. I thought of *Quid pro laude sua, vel quid pro regno alieno, mentibus infectis animosae cladis amore*: “What did they do, with minds corrupted by a love of fierce destruction, some for their own glory, others for a foreign kingdom?” Or the period may continue up to *ausi*, with a question answered by what follows, *Omnes scelerare*, namely, “What did they dare?” or “What did they all dare?”—“to defile their hands,” etc.

I prefer the reading I published conjecturally. *Qua, qua*, repeated, signifies “partly … partly,” or “both … and.” Examples are countless. Plautus, *Trinummus* IV.3.35: “Laws serve morality, but morals hasten to seize both sacred and public things.” Livy, book II, chapter 35: “And they used both their individual strength and the strength of the entire order.”

I would also gladly read *Qui pro laude sua, vel qui pro regno alieno*: “some for their own glory, others for a foreign kingdom.” A similar idiom exists in Italian and Spanish: *chi, chi; quien, y quien*—“one, another.” This idiom appears to have arisen from the Latin phrase *qui et qui*, which became current in a later age.

That Dracontius wrote *qui, vel qui* is also suggested by his imitation of Virgil, book VI, where, listing the crimes of the condemned, Virgil says, verse 621: “This man sold his country for gold … this man violated his daughter’s marriage chamber,” and then adds, “All dared monstrous wickedness,” as Dracontius says in verse 255, “All dared to defile their hands,” etc.

254. *Mentibus infectis amore*: “with minds corrupted, defiled, and, as it were, imbued with poison.”

255. *Suorum*, without another noun. Cicero, *Letters to Atticus*, book XIV, letter 12: “Octavius, whom his own people called Caesar, but not Philippus.” Dracontius chiefly means blood relatives, as can be inferred from the examples cited. Below, verse 327: *Orbatricesque suorum* (“and bereaved of their own”). Livy uses it in this sense, book I, chapter 58: “They find Lucretia sitting sadly in her chamber; at the arrival of her own people, tears arose.”

256. It certainly seems to be used for “also,” or rather “even,” as verse 262 shows. Statius and others pronounce *Menoecaeus* with the first syllable short, the second long, and the third and fourth short, book X, verse 611: “And he feels that Menoecus is demanded.” Dracontius uses the license customary to him in such proper names. Menoecus, son of Creon, king of Thebes, after an oracle had declared, “Let the last surviving descendant of the Serpent-born fall: victory is granted only on this condition,” struck himself with a sword and threw himself headlong from the city walls. Statius tells the story in book X.

259. Statius, in the passage cited: “Then he sprinkles the towers with blood and purifies the walls.”

262. Book II, verse 558, concerning Judas: “Yet mindful of an unspeakable and nameless guilt.” Martial called this crime madness, book II, epigram 80: “When fleeing his enemy, Fannius himself killed himself. I ask, is this not madness—to die lest you die?” Seneca, letter 58: “To die in this way is to be defeated.” Some find Seneca lacking in firmness because he nevertheless praised Cato, who killed himself so as not to fall into Caesar’s hands. But perhaps Seneca would have placed some distinction in the different circumstances of suicide.

Dracontius denotes the gravity of the crime by saying that it has no name, as though it were unspeakable and because it is rarely committed. In our age, however, this deed has both the name “suicide” and great frequency; nor have there been lacking impious and deranged people who have pursued so monstrous a crime with praise.

263. “Savage expiations,” as in book I, verse 539, and book II, verse 401. *Hominum* should be referred to *nemo* rather than to *gentis*: “Let no one among humankind marvel at such savage expiations of that people.”

265. Oedipus, son of Laius, king of the Thebans, and of Jocasta. Unaware of the truth, he killed his father and married his mother; thereafter he tore out his own eyes and went voluntarily into exile at Athens.

266. *Iocastae* has four syllables. Because of the crime, and because Eteocles and Polynices, her sons by Oedipus, destroyed one another with mutual wounds, she laid hands on herself. Creon had seized the kingdom after the death of Laius; it had been given to Oedipus because he solved the riddle of the Sphinx and at the same time married Jocasta. After Jocasta’s death, Creon succeeded as her heir. Hyginus, *Fables* 66 and 67, should be compared with this, for the whole story or myth is confused in the ancient writers.

Having learned the oracle of the god and the enemy’s instructions, he changed his royal clothing, entered the enemy camp dressed in rags and carrying brushwood around his neck, and there was killed amid the crowd by a soldier whom he had cunningly wounded with a sickle. When the king’s body was recognized, the Dorians withdrew without a battle.” Add Valerius Maximus, book V, chapter 6. Some write “Thracians,” others “Lacedaemonians,” instead of “Dorians.”

274. The battle of Leonidas at Thermopylae against the army of Xerxes is narrated differently by different authors. Dracontius appears to have followed Diodorus Siculus, book XI of his *History*, who reports that all the Lacedaemonians who fought and fell at Thermopylae under Leonidas numbered no more than five hundred. He then adds:

“Obeying orders, they break into the Persian camp in close formation toward nightfall. The barbarians, surprised and unprepared, rush from their tents amid great tumult and without order. Believing that the Trachinian forces joined to them had perished and that all the Greek armies were pressing upon them, they panic in terror. Thus the men of Leonidas inflicted great slaughter upon the Persians, and the Persians inflicted even greater slaughter upon one another, since they could not distinguish enemy from friend. For because there was no recognition of the truth during the night, and fear was growing throughout the camp, it is not surprising that a disgraceful slaughter of the enemy was then committed. They attack one another with mutual killings, and the condition of affairs permits nothing certain to be determined, because there was neither the commander’s authority, nor the challenge for the password, nor any settled state of mind.”

Herodotus says that the battle was fought by day. Justin, book II, relates that the battle lasted from the beginning of night through much of the day [Col. 0864D].

It may likewise be read as *quae*—“which cohort, with the light driven back,” etc.

“Once, here, four thousand men from the land of Pelops drove back two hundred myriads in battle.”

### 288

I do not understand what was written in Dracontius’ manuscript, and yet I read: “For by the covenant the guilty man”—namely, the father, who was involved in the same case as his son, and so guilty by this covenant, just as the son is guilty of parricide—“is punished by a holy crime,” that is, by a crime joined with excessive filial devotion. See Book II, verse 409: “The deed by which they are stained presses upon them.” Prudentius, in *Hamartigenia*, speaking of the viper killed by its young as they burst through its sides inside the womb, says at verse 597: “The mother seethes with the inward crime of filial devotion,” because it is filial devotion that the offspring avenge the father, who was killed by the mother during intercourse, but it is a crime because it kills the mother. In the same sense Dracontius says, “He is punished by a holy crime.”

### 289

This is taken from the history of the Persians. Herodotus, Book I, chapter 137:

> They say that no one has ever killed his own father or mother; but whenever such things have happened by some chance, they say that, once every necessity had been removed, those persons were finally discovered to be either supposititious or illegitimate. For they say that it is in no way plausible that one who is a true parent should be killed by his own child.

See Barnabas Brissonius, Book II, *On the Kingdom of the Persians*, p. 197, where he treats the matter carefully.

### 290

Brissonius, in the place cited, p. 213, proves that among the Persians it was lawful for men to take their mothers in marriage, on the evidence of Philo in *On the Special Laws*, Tertullian in the *Apology*, Minucius, Catullus, Diogenes Laertius, and Strabo. Wowerus and Elmenhorstius add further evidence in their notes on Minucius: “Among the Persians it is lawful to have intercourse with mothers.” Plutarch, in *On Alexander’s Fortune*, says that Alexander, after defeating Darius, prohibited such incestuous marriages.

But Theodoret, in *Against the Greeks*, Oration 9, on the laws, asserts that the marriages of mothers, sisters, and daughters, which had been permitted among the Persians according to the institution of Zarathustra, were abolished after they had heard and accepted the Christian religion:

> “The Persian nations, which had long been following the laws of Zarathustra, thoroughly mingling in marriages with mothers, sisters, and daughters, and considering as most just what was in fact most unjust, heard the law of the fishermen and accepted it; they trampled Zarathustra’s laws underfoot as the greatest iniquity and immediately embraced evangelical self-restraint.”

Perhaps Alexander prohibited such incestuous marriages, and after Alexander the Persians renewed their ancient custom. Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 8 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*, adds that even when they had left Persia they retained this custom of incestuous unions.

### 291

Some write *Phyleni*, others *Philaeni*; others, as in the Vatican manuscript, *Phileni*. The story has been recorded by many writers. Valerius Maximus, Book V, chapter 6:

> When there was an extremely obstinate dispute between Carthage and Cyrene concerning the boundary of their territory, at last it was agreed that young men should be sent from both sides at the same time, and that the place where they met should be regarded as the boundary for both peoples. But this agreement was forestalled by two Carthaginian brothers named Philaeni, who, by fraud, hastened their steps before the appointed hour and advanced the boundary farther. When the young men of Cyrene realized this, they complained for a long time about their deceit; finally they tried to settle the injustice by imposing a harsh condition. They said that the boundary would be considered valid only if the Philaeni allowed themselves to be buried alive there. The outcome did not correspond to their design: nevertheless, without delay, they handed over their bodies to be covered by that earth. 

Sallust gives almost the same account in *The Jugurthine War*, adding that the Carthaginians dedicated altars at that place to the brothers Philaeni. The name remained attached to the place: “the Altars of the Philaeni.” On this, see Mela, Book I, chapter 3, on Lesser Africa.

It is therefore clear what Dracontius means. The brothers Philaeni, by the deed that earned them altars named after them, secured the Libyan sands for the Carthaginians to possess.

### 293

Sallust, in the place cited:

> There was a sandy plain between them, uniform in appearance; there was neither river nor mountain to distinguish their boundaries.

They fought over this territory.

### 294

He sets the heavenly fires against the cold horned serpents; he repeats the thought in the following verse. Isidore, Book XII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 4:

> Every poison is cold, and therefore the soul, which is fiery, flees cold poison.

Hence “the cold snake,” “the icy poison,” and similar expressions. Lucan, Book IX, verse 716, speaking of the asp:

> Itself lacking heat, it does not pass into the sphere of warmth;

and at verse 864, speaking of serpents generally:

> By their hot vapor  
> They attract the cold pests of the nighttime chill.

### 296

Lucan, Book IX on Libya, verse 435:

> The change of seasons is absent from life … and amid unmoving sands it does not feel the year.

Changing in turn is counted among the blessings of human life. Alcimus, at the beginning of Book I:

> Having received their changes in turn.

The author of the poem *On the Praises of the Lord*, under Constantine:

> And by pleasant change to add fruit to mortal beings.

Compare the *Elegiacs*, verse 247:

> The elements alternate their changes, and the seasons change.

Book II, verse 54, uses the phrase with another meaning:

> And may they change the elements in turn,

that is, may they reverse them.

### 297

Perhaps he alludes to the names *Punicus*, *Phoeniceus*, and *Phoenicius*: *Punicus* is found in the sense of “Phoenician” or “red,” and the color *Phoenicius* is not far removed from *puniceus*. The names of the Carthaginians are *Phoenices*, *Poeni*, and *Punici*.

“Under a huge sun,” as Lucan says in Book IX, verse 432:

> Cast out beneath an overpowering day,  
> It scorches the harvests beside the seared heaven.

Others read: “Stretched out beneath an overpowering day.”

namely, the basilisk. Dracontius understands any snakes whatsoever. Book I, verse 289, speaking of a serpent:

The phrase “they might consign deaths to hisses” is also noteworthy. A similar example occurs in Juvenal, Satire 10, verse 52:

and in Apuleius, Book IX of the *Metamorphoses*, near the end: “to consign someone to hanging.”

305. Here too the greatly corrupted wording invites many conjectures. The meaning is that, if a dispute had arisen over acquiring more fertile land, the Philaeni would gladly have traversed any regions of the world, whether those beneath the torrid zone that endure the sun’s heat, or those beneath both poles that stiffen under perpetual ice.

Someone may read, “Would they not have gone through the Euxine?” But how would that make sense? “Would they not have gone through the extremities?” or “Would they not have gone as travelers?” would seem better. I prefer to read *pererrantes* (“wandering through”), because it is clearer, although it is more remote from the manuscript reading.

“Where the fiery axis extends” indicates the torrid zone, as in verse 160, speaking of the sun:

> Where it does not know how to traverse the poles,  
> Where the fiery [sun] burns.

306. The torrid zone is explained more distinctly. Someone might conjecture, “It shows the zone by which the poles are [marked],” namely, on a right sphere. But Dracontius perhaps has Virgil in view, Book VII, verse 226:

> And if some extended region of the four zones  
> Divides in the middle the zone of the unequal sun.

The “zone of the unequal sun” extended in the middle of the four zones is the torrid zone. *Extenta* in Virgil means *extensa* (“extended”), and in Dracontius “the zone extends the poles” has the same meaning as “the zone is extended through the sky.” One may therefore read: “Where the zone extends the poles.”

307. The perpetual cold beneath which the earth or water lies pressed under the poles is beautifully described. Ovid, Book II of the *Letters from Pontus*, letter 7, verse 63:

> No earth beneath both poles lies anywhere more sorrowful than this.

308. The phrase “of panting vapor” is familiar to Dracontius, as I said in the *Prolegomena*, no. 137.

309. Dracontius asks what the brothers would have done if they had sought flowery fields. They would even have gone toward the region lying beneath the north, if necessary. But, he says, that region would have left them a free course, so that without a rival they could have extended their measured kingdom from the frosts of the north all the way to the Scythian marshes. So gloomy is that region, and so worthy of no one’s envy!

310. Virgil, Book XII, verse 898:

> A boundary was placed in the field  
> To separate the dispute over the lands.

311. One might read *tuta* (“safe”), but *tracta* (“drawn out”) is better as a form of *protracta*, just as one says *tractum bellum* (“a drawn-out war”) and *tracta comitia* (“elections prolonged”). The Maeotian marsh is a gulf of the sea above the Euxine Pontus; the Maeotae, peoples of European Scythia, gave it its name. Columella, Book VIII, chapter 8:

> The Scythian pools of Maeotis wash away …

*Retineret* means “would occupy.” Lucretius, Book IV, verse 413:

> Many thousands of lands  
> Which diverse peoples and generations of wild animals retain.

313. Two methods of punctuation are possible: “If I am able to speak, I shall prove it in truthful speech”—that is, I shall demonstrate it—or: “To speak, if I am able, I shall prove in truthful speech”—that is, I shall attempt to say it, if I can.

314. *Exempla* is used for the singular *exemplum*, as in Sedulius, Book V, verse 22:

Wopkensius illustrated this manner of speaking in his note on Minucius’ words: “Considering earthly empires, for which examples certainly come from heaven.”

318. I suspect the reading is *quod castae ingessit*, as in verse 374, “Filial devotion, hostile to itself, inflicted sorrow.” Livy calls it “royal outrage” and “royal crime” in Book I. After the crime committed by Tarquinius, son of Tarquinius Superbus, king of the Romans, he was “the adulterer of the chaste woman,” namely Lucretia. Tacitus, Book III of the *Annals*, chapter 24, says: “And he punished their adulterers,” speaking of the daughter and granddaughter.

The phrase may also mean “what the adulterer inflicted upon the chaste woman,” that is, what he inflicted upon the chaste Lucretia. Valerius Maximus, Book VI, chapter 1, calls Lucretia “the leader of Roman chastity.”

319. In “Now a marital, nuptial violator” I read “the invader of the nuptial chamber, the violator of chastity.” Below, verse 484: “He invaded the bridal chambers”; and concerning the same violent sexual assault, verse 506: “After the stain of the bridal chamber.” Virgil, Book VI, verse 623:

> Here he invaded the bridal chamber of the daughter.

*Invasor* is a word used by Aurelius Victor, Constantine the emperor, and their contemporaries.

The *thalamus genialis* is the marriage bed spread in honor of the Genius. Cicero, *For Cluentius*, chapter 5:

> He orders that the nuptial bed, which two years earlier he had spread for his daughter when she married, be prepared and spread for himself in the same house, after his daughter had been driven out and expelled.

See the commentary on verse 256 of Book I of Prudentius’ *Against Symmachus*: “Now the nuptial couch is prepared for the pregnant woman.” Arnobius, Book IV, uses the phrase absolutely: “to insult another’s nuptial beds,” though others read “another’s genital organs.” Shortly before this Arnobius had said “the assault of the nuptial bed.”

In Dracontius, consider whether it is better to read: “By marital right, the violator of the nuptial chastity,” that is, as though by marital right; or “and the marital violator of nuptial chastity,” that is, the violator of marital nuptial chastity; or “now the matronly violator of nuptial chastity.” Ovid, speaking of the same Lucretia, Book II of the *Fasti*, verse 828:

> And the matron’s cheeks blushed.

Macrobius, in another context, Book V, chapter 17:

> The queen is brought out not only from the inner chambers of matronly reverence, but is also forced to run through the middle of the city.

320. Orosius, Book II, chapter 5:

> In the year 241 after the founding of the City, Brutus, the first consul among the Romans, strove not only to equal the first founder and king of Rome in parricide but even to surpass him. For he dragged into the assembly two adolescent sons of his own and two young brothers of his wife, the Vitellii, accused of favoring the plan to recall the kings to Rome; he beat them with rods and struck them with the axe.

Salisberiensis, Book V, chapter 11 of *The Trifles of Courtiers*, gives reasons by which Brutus may be excused from the crime, but concludes: “I readily agree that Brutus sinned, because he exceeded the proper measure of the remedy.”

321. He “struck severely,” because, as Livy reports in Book II, chapter 1, he compelled them by oath to allow no one to reign at Rome. The same point is made by Livy in the same place:

> The origin of liberty should be reckoned from the fact that consular power was made annual, rather than from any reduction of royal authority.

322. Kings at Rome had also used the bundles of rods with axes bound into them. The same honor passed to the consuls and other magistrates, but especially to the consuls, so that the fasces are often used for the consulship itself; in this sense they may be called “festive.” The *acta* were commentaries in which events were written down, with the name of the consuls under whose authority they had occurred.

323. “Wars of nature,” because he killed his sons against nature’s impulse and law.

324. “Returning from the enemy”: I understand this to mean after he had expelled the Tarquins. Livy reports the conspiracy of Brutus’ sons and other noble youths formed in favor of King Tarquin before the war threatened by the Tarquins.

326. Among jurists, *fraus legis* is what occurs when something is done that the law did not wish to be done but did not forbid. Here, however, *fraus* is better understood as “harm,” as in Horace’s *Carmen Saeculare*, or as “crime.” Cicero, *For Rabirius*, chapter 9: “For if Gaius Rabirius committed a capital fraud …” Elsewhere he likewise speaks of “impious and inexpiable fraud.”

327. “Bereaving,” as in Ovid, Book XIII of the *Metamorphoses*, verse 500:

> The destruction of Troy, and Achilles, bereaved of his own.

328. “A detestable old age,” figuratively, “a detestable old man.” The phrase “he went to the funeral” has emphasis, for to go against someone is to attack someone as an enemy. Virgil, Book IX, verse 423:

> At the same time, with his sword drawn,  
> He went against Euryalus.

It is a peculiar poetic expression to say “to go to the funeral” for “to go to the funeral rites” or “to accompany the funeral.” Terence, *Phormio* V.8.37:

> Those who wish may go to Chremes’ funeral; come, it is time.

Alternatively, “now is the time.” Ovid, Book II of the *Amores*, elegy 6, verse 2:

> He has died; go often to the funeral, birds;  
> Go, dutiful birds.

Silius, Book XV, verse 394:

> Go, proud ones, to the funeral  
> Of the soul, and offer the ashes  
> The service of the final gift.

331. Virgil, Book VI, verse 822, speaking of the same Brutus:

> Unhappy, however his descendants may interpret those fates:  
> Love of country and an immense desire for praise will prevail.

333. What has been said thus far—“This crime committed with so savage a guilt is not …”—seems to be an excuse for Brutus proposed by someone to whom Dracontius replies: “For whom did he bear arms, who deprived himself of this pledge?” Or: “This man bore arms for whom, who deprived himself of this pledge?” Or: “For whom did he bear arms? Which enemies did he deprive of their pledge?”

When Brutus killed his sons, for whom did he bear arms? Why not rather for his own sons than for others? If you say that he bore arms for his fatherland, what enemies did he deprive of their sons? For he deprived himself—who certainly was not an enemy—of his children.

This seems to be Dracontius’ reasoning, by which he concludes that Brutus cannot be freed from the crime. Yet it must not for that reason be denied that we ought to value our fatherland more dearly than ourselves. Brutus therefore sinned, but, as Salisberiensis said, because he exceeded the proper measure of the remedy.

334. Livy treats at length, in Book III, chapter 44 and following, the story of Virginius, who killed his daughter Virginia; Orosius treats it briefly in Book II, chapter 13:

> The enormous lust of Appius Claudius increased the resentment. In order to violate the virgin Virginia, he first brought forward a claim that she was a slave. On this occasion the plebs occupied the Aventine Hill and compelled Appius Claudius and the other decemvirs to resign their magistracy.]

### Notes [Col. 0871B]

335. Livy, in the place cited, chapter 50, relates the lamentations of Virginius and his complaints about the crime of Appius Claudius to the soldiers.

336. Perhaps “affection destroys.” But “affection forestalls” seems to follow from the context. For when Virginius saw his daughter being carried into the slavery of Marcus Claudius and toward the sexual violence of Appius Claudius the decemvir, he asked permission to question her nurse in the girl’s presence as to whether he himself was truly her father. After permission had been granted, he seized a butcher’s knife and said: “By the one means that is available to me, daughter, I claim you for liberty.”

Thus paternal affection forestalled the event, so that the lust of Appius Claudius would not take away his daughter’s chastity together with her liberty.

338. Above, verse 323: “He waged wars against nature.” *Diremit* could be understood as “broke apart,” but “divided” is better, since Dracontius regards Virginia’s liberty and her father’s love as laws of nature, as is clear from the following verse.

340. I read “forgetful of the City.” Livy, Book VIII, chapter 7, says the same of Manlius Torquatus when he decreed the death of his son:

> You have brought me into such a necessity that I must forget either the state or myself and my own people.

341. The infamy with which stepmothers are burdened was discussed in the note on verse 321 of Book II.

343. Since Appius Claudius had unjustly decreed that Virginia should be claimed into the slavery of his client Marcus Claudius, Virginia’s sons would also have been treated as slaves. Virginius’ honor therefore feared the weight of slavery.

346. This may be reconstructed by another conjecture:

> He shuddered; enraged, he groaned, and poured out  
> The blood of his daughter Virginia,  
> A savage heir of the maiden’s funeral.  
> He made liberty’s honor a consolation for his lamentations.

347. I suspect *virginiae*, but *virginei* is not bad, because it was a consolation to the father that his daughter had not been corrupted. Valerius Maximus, Book VI, chapter 1:

> Virginius … killed the girl when she had been brought into the forum; he preferred to be the father of a chaste daughter whom he had killed than of one who had been corrupted.

348. The meaning is that Virginius drew consolation for his lamentations from the liberty that had been secured when the decemvirate was abolished; or that it consoled Virginius that he had repelled the injury of slavery from his son.

The passage may be punctuated another way:

> He poured forth, the savage heir of the maiden’s funeral,  
> The work of liberty; he made consolation  
> For his lamentations,

so that *solatia* is an accusative in apposition. See Book II, verse 114, and Book II of this work, verse 214: “He accomplished the work of virtue.” Below, verse 415, occurs “the aid of liberty”; but here *opus* (“work”) is more suitable.

350. Perhaps “who was captivated.”

351. “Twice an enemy” is unsatisfactory. I therefore read “a drinker of blood,” namely, of his own blood in his daughter. Virgil, Book VI, verse 835:

Lucan used *haustor* (“drinker”) from *haurio* (“to drink up”). “To drink up gore” or “blood” is common.

352. The consul Titus Manlius Torquatus ordered his son to be struck with the axe because, contrary to his order, although successfully, he had fought against Metius, who had challenged him. Livy, Book VIII, chapter 7; Orosius, Book III, chapter 9; and many others.

353. Shortly afterward, verse 431: “He brought danger upon himself for the sake of praise.” In both places *periculum* means death. Arnobius, Book I, shortly after the beginning:

355. “By his own wounds,” which he himself had inflicted. Virgil, Book II of the *Aeneid*, verse 436:

356. “As though youth had been overcome,” as if this young son of Torquatus had been overcome. *Juventus* is used in a similar figure to “detestable old age” in verse 328. Livy, in the place cited:

357. Perhaps: “No one his own …”

358. “He killed.” Who? The father Torquatus, or no one? I prefer the second interpretation. When Titus Manlius, the consul’s son, had defeated Geminius Metius, who commanded the Tusculan cavalry, in single combat, nevertheless no one after that duel routed the Latin cohorts or killed the remnants of the disaster; thus the consuls’ order was observed for the most part. Nevertheless Manlius the father condemned his son to death.

Dracontius may, however, mean that Manlius’ son had been wounded by Metius, for verse 355 says: “He gave himself over to his own wounds.” On this assumption, we can understand “the remnants of the disaster” to mean Manlius’ son himself, whom his father killed. Livy does not indicate that Manlius was wounded. See the note on verse 360.

### Notes [Col. 0873B]

361. Perhaps it is written “Has any leader ever dared this against the victors?” But no sense emerges unless one corrects it to: “What commander, I ask, has ever dared such a thing against the victors?” *Audere talia* (“to dare such things”) is found in Virgil, Ovid, and others. Tacitus used *audere* with a dative in Book XII of the *Annals*, chapter 55: “They dared violence against the inhabitants and townsmen.” The same author, Book II, chapter 40: “Tiberius, not daring to inflict his punishment openly, ordered him to be killed in a secluded part of the palace.”

One may therefore restore: “What commander, I ask, has ever dared to punish the victors?” That is: “What commander has ever punished a soldier because he had won?”

367. *Votivus* signifies what pertains to a vow; accordingly, things made from a vow as a testimony to a benefit received are called *votiva*. That meaning is not foreign to this passage. In a later period, however, *votivum* also came to mean pleasant, agreeable, or successful. Prudentius, *Peristephanon* hymn 2, verse 330:

> Death is a desired gift for the martyr.

Add Trebellius Pollio, Apuleius, and their contemporaries.

368. Livy, in the place cited:

> Then voices arose in unrestricted lamentation, so that no restraint was placed upon either mourning or curses; the young man’s body, covered with spoils, was burned on a pyre erected outside the rampart, with all the honors that military devotion could bestow upon any funeral.

370. Prudentius, *Psychomachia*, verse 695, says *prospera nostra* (“our successes”). Lucan, Book V, verse 781, *prospera belli* (“the successes of war”), and Book VII, verse 107, *prospera rerum* (“successes in affairs”).

372. I read *justitium*, which was a suspension of judicial proceedings and a cessation of other official duties on account of public mourning. See the commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* 5 *Against Symmachus*, verse 80: “The sad suspension of the tyrannical citadel.”

For illustrating this entire passage of Dracontius, the description of the *justitium* in Albinovanus’ *Consolation to Livia* is especially relevant:

> The mournful house resounds with lamentation; the master  
> Had vowed to fix there the weapons won in his hand.  
> The city groans and assumes a single, pitiable face;  
> May that appearance, I pray, be shown to hostile nations.  
> The anxious close their houses and throughout the city  
> Grieve here and there, secretly and openly.  
> The laws are silent, and the mute statutes are quiet without an avenger;  
> No purple is seen anywhere.  
> The gods hide in their temples, and so forth.

373. The enemies groaned because Metius had been killed; but the father of the killer avenged those groans, taking revenge by destroying his son.

374. Filial devotion hostile to its own blood inflicted upon the Romans a grief that barbarous fury would have inflicted by a hostile spear. Manlius’ filial devotion toward his father was hostile to his own blood in his son. See the note on verse 351.

375. Livy also mentions the spear: “When they had charged with hostile spears …”

376. Juvenal, Satire 3, verse 213:

> The nobles in mourning dress; the praetor postpones the court appearances.

Prudentius, *Hymn* 7 *On Fasting*, verse 151:

> The fathers in mourning, their robes loosened, are squalid.

In public mourning the nobles assumed mournful black clothing. *Vadimonium* was a pledge to appear before a court on a fixed day; during a *justitium* and public mourning it was postponed.

*Fuissent* is a change of tense for *fuerunt*, just as in the following verse *lacerasset* is used for *laceravit*, and in verse 379 *scinderet* for *scidit*. The passage could easily be restored as:

> No court appearances took place;  
> With hair disheveled, she tore her breast with her palms;  
> The dutiful crowd, cutting their modest faces with their nails,  
> Clawed them apart.

Christian poets, however, variously transpose tense and mood, as Barthius demonstrates in Book XLI of the *Adversaria*, chapter 24, with an example from Prudentius, and in Book XXII, chapter 6, with examples from Christian writers of the later age. In Book XXIX, chapter 16, he proves that this was a manner and habit of speech used by good ancient writers.

377. These are signs of grief among mourning women. Petronius, *Satyricon*, chapter 3:

> To accompany a funeral with hair loosened, or to beat one’s bared breast in the sight of the crowd.

Compare Book I, verse 752.

378. It was also common during weeping to strike the arms and upper arms. Ovid, Book IX of the *Metamorphoses*, verse 635:

> She tore the garment from her breast  
> And, distraught, beat her own arms.

Lucan, Book II, verse 37:

> Her cheeks torn, her dark arms livid from beating.

Claudian, Book II of *The Rape of Proserpina*, verse 248:

> And beats her arms with lamentation.

At this point Barthius collects many similar examples and believes that earlier writers had not noticed this ancient custom.

379. Above, verse 103:

> Not tearing her face with her nails.

Ovid, Book III of the *Tristia*, elegy 3, verse 51:

> Yet spare your cheeks from being torn, and do not tear your hair.

Elsewhere: “She wounds her cheeks with her nail.” Dracontius seems to distinguish these practices so that tearing the breast belonged particularly to noble matrons, the arms to common women, and the face to women of more modest status. Others commonly attribute all these practices to every class of person.

380. Homer, at the end of the *Iliad*. Albinovanus, in the *Consolation to Livia*, gives other examples in a similar form:

> Thus Clymene wept, and thus the lofty daughters of Clymene, and so forth.

381. I think he means the nymphs, the virgin daughters of King Lycomedes, among whom Achilles was hiding in women’s clothing. Ulysses discovered him and took him to the Trojan War. Statius, in the *Achilleid*, mentions the lamentation of Deidamia alone. Perhaps the lamentation intended is that of Thetis, Achilles’ mother, and of the other Nereids, to whom the name “nymphs” truly applies.]

What commander, I ask, has ever dared to punish victors?

Or who, while the people praised him throughout the cities,

Among victorious cohorts, bold after the wars,

[334] And after dreadful battles, before triumphal chariots,

[365] Would strike a lofty head, join lamentations

To triumphs, and mingle sadness with joyful affairs?

Grief overwhelmed the festive offering; the celebrations withdrew;

Public joys were thrown into confusion by funeral mourning.

The commander regretted having won, for whom glory

[370] Brought death, and the soldier mourned the successes of war.

While the victor paid the penalty for honorable virtue,

[Col. 0874A] His greatest victory prepared a great suspension of public business.

The savage right hand of the father avenges the groans of the enemies;

Filial devotion hostile to its own blood inflicted grief,

[375] [335] Which barbarous rage, sent by a hostile spear, would have inflicted.

The nobles in mourning dress—there were no court appearances—

With hair disheveled, a grieving noblewoman would have torn her breast

With her palms; the common woman her arms;

The dutiful, modest crowd would have cut their faces with their nails.

[380] As once the mothers of Ilium wept for Hector,

So then the crowd of nymphs mourned their Achilles,

[Col. 0875A] [Note: [Col. 0875B]
