### 382

I understand Brutus, concerning whom it was said above at verses 314 and following. I do not know, however, whether the reference is to the funeral of the sons whom he ordered to be struck down with the axe. Livy indeed says, *History* II.5:

> The noblest young men stood bound to the stake; but, unlike the others, as though they were unknown heads, the consul’s sons turned every eye upon themselves, and the people pitied them—not so much for the punishment as for the crime by which they had deserved punishment. For in that very year they had formed the resolve to betray to the former king Tarquinius Superbus—then a hostile exile—the liberated fatherland, their father the liberator, the consulship that had arisen from the Junian house, the senators, the plebs, and everything belonging to Roman gods and men.

### 385

Livy, *History* VIII.12:

> When the war had been conducted and rewards and punishments had been paid to each according to his deserts, Titus Manlius returned to Rome. It is recorded that only the older men went out to meet him; the young men, both then and throughout the rest of his life, shunned and cursed him.

Orosius states the matter more clearly, *History* III.9:

> Although Manlius was victorious, he did not deserve the customary greeting of the noble Roman youths, since, as a parricide celebrating a triumph, he was not worthy of it.

Valerius Maximus adds, *Memorable Deeds and Sayings* IX.3:

> They pitied a man of their own age who had been punished with excessive severity.

### 386

Arnobius, *Against the Nations* III, near the middle:

> Let fire-bearing Vulcan forge swords for these men.

For Dracontius, *flammipotens* means “able to withstand flame.” Poets freely use similar compounds, such as *ignipotens* (“fire-powerful”) and *bellipotens* (“war-powerful”). It has nevertheless been observed that Ovid scarcely ever used such compounded names.

*Dignus* is often joined with an infinitive. Here *dignus contemnere* means “worthy to despise,” or “worthy to have despised,” since he was bold and reckless. Alternatively, it may carry the sense expressed by Valerius Maximus, *Memorable Deeds and Sayings* III.3:

> For, I believe, hating his right hand because he had been unable to use its service in the killing of the king, he allowed it, when thrust into the brazier, to be burned.

### 387

Someone might suppose that the reading is *licet ense fefellit* (“although he failed with the sword”); but it is preferable to read *licet ipse fefellit, non manus* (“although he himself, not his hand, failed”). Mucius punished his hand because it had erred in the killing of the king.

Martial, *Epigrams* I.22:

> When his right hand, deceived by the guards, sought the king,  
> He thrust it into the sacred fires, destined to perish …  
> Greater is the fame and glory of the deceived right hand:  
> Had it not erred, it would have done less.

Dracontius restores the point: it was not the right hand that erred, since it truly struck the man whom it had sought; rather, Mucius himself erred, because he mistakenly thought that the king’s secretary was the king—or at least, uncertain of the target, he struck.

Livy, *History* II.12:

> When a military payment happened to be distributed there and the secretary, sitting beside the king and dressed almost alike, was conducting much business, the soldiers commonly approached him. Mucius, fearing to ask which of them was Porsena—lest, by not knowing the king, he reveal who he was—allowed Fortune to bring about the deed recklessly, and killed the secretary instead of the king.

### 389

Valerius Maximus, at the passage cited:

> He returned himself to the city under the name of “Scaevola,” destined for everlasting glory;

so called from his left hand, which alone he used thereafter.

### 390

Porsena, moved by Mucius’s boldness and endurance, and no less by the danger to himself, voluntarily offered the Romans terms of peace. *Nurus* is sufficiently common for any woman, especially a married woman. *Per bella* means “because of the wars,” or “through the wars”; here it refers to one killed in war or placed in danger. *Per* in the sense of *propter* (“because of”) is used by Plautus, Pliny, and others.

### 396

One may also punctuate the passage as: “What? A Roman horseman? Into the vast …,” without another question.

### 397

Compare Book II, verse 497: “By the precipitous throw, whom …” Tertullian uses the verb *dimersus*, but *demersus* is more frequent. In a similar context Horace, *Odes* III.16.11:

> The house of Argive Amphiaraus fell,  
> overwhelmed in ruin for the sake of gain.

The Argive prophet is Amphiaraus, who was swallowed by a chasm in the earth, as I shall soon explain.

### 398

Perhaps Curtius leapt in, if these words are spoken without a question. But *ingemuit* (“he groaned”) appears to have been taken from Statius, *Thebaid* VII, at the end, concerning Amphiaraus:

> As he fell, he looked back at the sky and groaned  
> that the plain was closing together.

Dracontius denies that Curtius groaned, when he asks, “What? … Did he groan?” *Vivum cadaver* (“a living corpse”) is an oxymoron, discussed in Book I, verse 648.

### 399

By conjecture one may read *deterret* (“he frightens”), so that a new sentence begins with *Armato*. If *deterrens* (“frightening”) is retained, it refers to the corpse. This is an imitation of Statius at the beginning of Book VIII, concerning the submerged Amphiaraus:

> He disturbed the shades with an armed funeral.

### 401

Livy, *History* VII.6, relates this event—or story, for he himself is uncertain about it. When an oracle had replied that the chasm opened in the middle of the Forum could be filled only by that in which the people possessed their greatest strength, Curtius interpreted this as meaning arms and courage. Mounted on a horse adorned as splendidly as possible and armed, he threw himself into the pit.

### 403

“An allotment of punishments,” as though an inheritance; hence, in the following verse, “a lot.” The adjective *tristis* (“sad,” “gloomy”) properly belongs to the underworld, from which *Acheron* is understood as “without joy.”

Thus in Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis* XII.34, no. 66, one should read that the origin of the Greek name for the underworld signifies that it possesses nothing pleasant, not that it possesses nothing within itself. Julian of Toledo, *Prognostics* II.5, quotes Augustine’s words, and in the manuscript which I collated it reads *nihil suave* (“nothing pleasant”); the Leipzig edition likewise prints this. The sense itself requires it, for the preceding words are:

> All lower things are sadder.

Hence, it is said that in the Greek language the origin of the name by which the underworld is called resounds from the fact that it possesses nothing pleasant. The same is almost expressed by ᾄδης (*Hades*).

### 404

See the note to Book I, verse 67, “The third lot of Erebus,” and to verse 469, “He foresaw, bereft of piety.” Lucretius, *On the Nature of Things* III.1026:

> Tartarus, lacking light.

---

### 336

As the Senate, together with the grieving people, lamented Brutus,

there was no age or sex that did not groan over the bitter funeral,

considering it its own: thus the Torquate line,

long bewailed, lay prostrate beneath the crime of its father.

Scaevola, powerful over flame and worthy to despise his right hand,

resolved to punish his hand, although he himself had failed,

not the hand; his bold spirit gained more from the error,

so that, without the death of the leader, a man alone might possess so much glory.

### 337

No Roman bride mourned her husband through the wars,

no father lamented his son, no daughter her father,

no bereaved mother bewailed the funeral of her son,

no German sisters mourned the dead.

Nor did any peace bind the war, nor did any price redeem it:

one unarmed hand alone suppressed so great a war.

“What? Did the Roman horseman Curtius groan,

voluntarily plunged by a precipitous leap through the vast

chasm of the earth into the shadows,

when the earth swallowed the living corpse,

frightening the shades with an armed funeral?

Brave and unhurt, buried while the people marvelled,

he was still seen, helmeted, with his body clad in iron,

### 338

to have descended thus among the Tartarean darkness.

The pale people of Erebus, a sad portion of punishments,

the third lot, which, deprived of light, labours in condemnation,

---

### Notes

#### 405

Hercules’ descent to the underworld was discussed in Book I, verse 71. Seneca describes it in *Hercules Furens*. Compare also the note to Book II, verse 539.

Antonius de Escobar y Mendoza, in the preface to *On the Style of Sacred Scripture*, observes that Scripture imitates the practice of citing pagan stories—such as the Titans, Centaurs, Cocytus, the daughters of Night, Orcus, Arthur, and Orion—not because the sacred text approves these stories, but in order to adapt itself to the common manner of speaking. Re-read the note to Book II, verse 539.

#### 407

Since it was fated that, if the prophet Amphiaraus went to the Theban war, he would not return from it, he was betrayed after his wife had been bribed with a gift of a golden necklace. He was led to the war, where, while fighting bravely, he was swallowed with his chariot by a chasm in the earth. See Hyginus, *Fables* 73, and Statius at the end of Book VII and beginning of Book VIII of the *Thebaid*.

#### 409

I would now need some Synesius in order to restore this place. For Synesius, in *Dio*, or *On His Way of Life*, explains the usefulness that can be gained from supplementing corrupt books, and speaks frankly of himself as follows:

> With no other person, but with you, I shall nevertheless boast truthfully. I often think that one need not wait for a book’s misfortune in order for something good to happen to me. Instead, I raise my eyes and apply myself to the work itself, never interrupting even for a moment, but, as circumstances require, supplying what is needed; and, just as though I were reading, I attach to what has been written whatever seems to follow from it, devised by myself. Then I compare what is said with what has been written, and I remember that I have often attained not merely the same meaning but even the same wording. At other times I have so skilfully conjectured the very thought that, even if some words differed, the result was nevertheless wonderfully devised for the joining together of the work. If the meaning were different, it still suited the author of that book, and was something which he would certainly not have despised had it occurred to him … Thus God has implanted in me a certain pliable receptacle for what is expressed in words and conduct. If I had tried to exercise the attention of my mind upon corrupt books, nature would have brought the habit of the attempt to that degree of perfection. I too have attempted something similar and, as best I could, supplied the passage by conjecture.

One might also punctuate the passage as: “The Punic embassy, the consul having been sent, bears witness? On his return …” This is the famous deed of Marcus Atilius Regulus.

Florus, *Epitome* II.2:

> The bravest general came alive into the hands of the enemy. Yet he was equal to so great a calamity. For he was broken neither by the Punic prison nor by the embassy entrusted to him. Indeed, he gave an opinion contrary to what the enemy had ordered: that peace should not be made and that an exchange of prisoners should not be accepted. Nor was his majesty disfigured either by his voluntary return to his enemies or by the final punishment, whether of prison or of the cross.

He had sworn to the Carthaginians that, if their prisoners were not returned, he would return to them. See Valerius Maximus I.1.14.

#### 411

Regulus had advised that peace should not be made and that the prisoners should not be exchanged. He therefore despised his own leisure and that of his fatherland. “Leisure” indicates peace and is opposed to war.

*Elegies* 258:

> Leisure has its season, and so does the labour of military service.

Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.813:

> He who will break the leisure of his fatherland.

#### 413

Thus I restore the text from the words of Florus.

#### 414

Above, verse 340: “Mindless here of his lineage.” *Contemnere* means “to cast away” or “to abandon,” as in verse 98 concerning Abraham, who quickly abandoned his son in hope.

#### 415

Someone may suspect that one should read *libertatis opus* (“the work of liberty”), as elsewhere *virtutis opus* (“the work of virtue”), *pietatis opus* (“the work of piety”), and in this book, verse 348, *libertatis opus*. But here *opem* (“aid”) is correct, meaning assistance, strength, power, or the capacity to help.

In the *Elegies*, verse 167:

> Even Solomon, himself the enemy of enemies, did not demand their necks,  
> when he sought the Lord, but the aid of the wise.

#### 416

I suspect that the reading is *captivum tum sorte ducem* (“then, by fortune, the captive leader”). If Regulus had judged that the prisoners should be returned, or if he had refused to go back, he was acting as a captive leader—he was conducting himself on behalf of the captive leader. Alternatively, the meaning is this: the leader who had been a captive was now enjoying freedom at Rome, but he wished to be killed so that the Carthaginian prisoners would not be returned.

#### 419

*Insisto* (“I persist”) is used with an infinitive on the model of the best writers, Cicero, Nepos, and Livy.

#### 420

*Elisaeus*, or rather *Elissaeus*, is often used by Silius for “Carthaginian.” Below, verse 500: “of the Elissaean city.”

#### 421

*Par cum duce* means “equal to the leader,” rather than “equal and the leader.” *Par* with the ablative and the preposition *cum* is good Latin.

*Trojugenae Romani* means “the Romans descended from the Trojans.” Juvenal, *Satires* I.100, calls the Roman nobles themselves *Trojugenae*. Livy, *History* XXV.12, from an ancient poem:

> Roman, Trojan-born, flee the river Cannae.

#### 422

“He brought his limbs into torments”: he gave himself over to torture.

#### 423

Aulus Gellius, *Attic Nights* VI.4, relates Regulus’s death from the histories of Tubero:

> They shut him in darkness, deep and black; and long afterward, when he had been exposed to a blazing sun, they suddenly brought him out and held him facing the sun’s rays, forcing him to direct his eyes toward the sky. They even stitched his eyelids apart, pulling them upward and downward, so that he could not close his eyes.

#### 424

*De* is superfluous, as in other authors. See the note to verse 409.

Florus adds at the passage cited:

> Indeed, more admirable than all these things: what else was he but a man conquered by conquerors, since, because Carthage had not yielded, he triumphed over Fortune?

#### 425

“To give wars” means “to inflict” or “to wage,” as one says “to give slaughter,” “destruction,” or “pain.”

#### 426

“An honorably accomplished corpse”: one that had completely fulfilled its duty.

He believed that Alcides had returned to reclaim a second prize,

or that some other prophet had recalled the disasters of Amphiaraus,

you, Amphiaraus, whom your treacherous wife sold.

“What of Roman fidelity?” A Punic embassy,

with the consul sent, bears witness. Regulus fulfilled

his promise faithfully upon his return,

### 339

a lover of horrible death, despising peace,

and compelled the great Senate, together with the people,

unhappy as it was, to an inexorable agreement,

so that, under the law given concerning the captives, they would bear the bonds of punishment.

Mindless of his wife and children, he despised Rome,

nor did iron chains hold back the aid of liberty.

Then the leader, captive by fortune, acted as one already free

among patricians, praetors, and tribunes

### 340

of the plebs, worthy of reverence, which had subdued the world by its strength.

He persisted in being killed, so that after the wars

the Elissaean enemy would not survive,

whom equal fortune held together with the leader

of the Trojan-born Romans. He returned on the appointed day,

and, raging against his own limbs, thrust his body into torments,

rejoicing to be extinguished, wide awake, by the bare light,

so that he might frighten the Tyrians more by the threat of death

than by swords, when he gave battle and stirred up the fight.

Soon they feared the old man’s honorably accomplished corpse.

Unviolated fidelity—to what savage wars did it compel Saguntum,

### 341

and yet to the cruel fires of death?

Hannibal, while they were shut in, with no charge having arisen against them

except that they had been friends of the human race,

counting friendship a crime, brought danger instead of praise

and exacted punishment from the faithful city,

punishment which the treacherous crowd would suffer under a just judge.

What was wholly intolerable it endured for eight months,

though it violated its faith neither willingly nor when forced by disaster.

Yet the conquered troop, so that the enemy might conquer it

### 342

with swords, set fire to the people of their fatherland together with the city walls,

and gave itself torches along with death, unconcerned about a tomb;

it demanded deaths from the fire, withdrawing its own marvel from the enemy’s triumph

and its necks from the yoke.

One funeral pyre for all:

the walls are their fatherland, the mound is the same ashes for all;

the great power of the standards, the monuments of the leaders,

lay scattered in its own ashes together with the walls of the city.

Nor were the yokes of the Roman Senate to be feared:

the victor loves to spare, but he presses on to subdue the proud

and urges them to beg for pardon, accustomed

to bear similar triumphs of peace and arms.

They preferred to find those to whom they might grant safety after the wars

rather than punish them in war. Yet that city

burned all that was its own in its own civil flames,

fearing not the anger of the illustrious Senate after the wars,

but pardon: whoever is free refuses to serve,

and it is a terror to bow one’s neck to the African ruler.

### 343

Nor at that time were the promises revealed

which we hope will be the gifts of eternal life.

### Notes

#### 428

See verse 65: “The savage fires of death.”

#### 429

Again, verse 508: “When she fell as guilty, with no guilt rising against her.”

#### 430

These words could easily be brought back to the more common Latin usage: *praeter quam quod erant* (“except that they were”). But in writers of this period certain phrases should be retained even without examples from earlier authors, since they bear the mark of good Latin. They are shown to be all the more genuine because the vernacular languages derived from Latin preserve a similar manner of speaking.

*Praeter quod* is equivalent to *praeter id quod* (“except for the fact that”). With a similar meaning, Plautus, *Persa* III.1.87:

> There will be no virgin or woman who is not bad,  
> who thinks beyond what pleases her parents;

and Terence, *Heautontimorumenos* I.1.7:

> What I see you doing beyond your age  
> and beyond what your circumstances encourage you to do.

In Dracontius one could similarly write *praeter quam fuerant* (“except that they had been”). But Vossius, *On the Construction of Speech* 26, shows that *praeter quod* is correctly used for *praeter illud quod*, citing Caesar, *Gallic War* I:

> They burn all the grain except what they intended to carry with them;

and Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* V.3:

> For I had not yet received any letters, except the two that were once delivered at Trebulanum.

#### 432

Compare verse 352: “He brought danger upon his son for the sake of praise.” Therefore the reading here is *intulit*.

#### 433

I prefer *sub justo vindice* (“under a just avenger”). In manuscripts *judex* (“judge”) and *vindex* (“avenger”) are often confused.

#### 434

*Semel* (“once”) means “entirely”: what was wholly intolerable, the faithful nation endured for eight months.

Cicero, *Letters to Atticus* XIV.13:

> For he—Antony—since he had once brought himself to believe that he might do whatever he wished, would nevertheless have done it against my will.

It may also be understood as “on one occasion,” indicating that what Saguntum endured for eight months was not tolerable merely for a short time.

#### 436

Consider whether *victa caterva tamen* (“though the troop was conquered”) is preferable: “so that the enemy might conquer disaster.” For these two words are elsewhere also interchanged in the manuscript.

#### 437

A little later, verse 443, again: “with the walls of the city.”

#### 438

I had thought the reading was *cum morte fugam* (“flight with death”), but *faces* (“torches”) seems more appropriate, since these would serve the funeral pyre. *Secura sepulcri* means “unconcerned about the tomb,” caring nothing for burial.

Ovid, *Tristia* I.1.49:

> Finally, remember to go secure in your reputation and free,  
> and let it not shame you that you displeased your reader.

Statius uses the phrase with another meaning, *Thebaid* XII.780:

> Go, destined to give black punishments,  
> yet secure concerning the final tomb—

that is, having set aside concern for the tomb, which you will certainly possess. Consult the note to verse 105 of this book.

#### 439

*Sua mira* (“her own wonders”), as Plautus says *nimia mira* (“excessive wonders”) and *tanta mira* (“such wonders”).

#### 440

> The whole region is a funeral pyre.

> And the rocks melt into ashes.

Horace, *Odes* IV.13, final verse:

> The torch dissolved into ashes.

Alcuin, poem 178 of the old edition:

> Melting the walls into ashes.

If the people of Saguntum had submitted to Hannibal, they would not for that reason have needed to fear the yoke—or Roman cruelty—when they later recovered Saguntum, as is explained more fully at verse 451.

#### 445

From Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.853:

#### 446

*Urget debellare* means “he presses on to subdue.” Horace, *Odes* II.18.20:

> of the sea that roars at Baiae.

*Suetus* is trisyllabic, as at verse 663, *sueta*. Perhaps one should read *et hortatus veniam implorare suevit* (“and he was accustomed, after urging them, to beg pardon”), from *sueo* (“to be accustomed”).

#### 448

Change of number is not uncommon among writers, especially when a progression is made from the singular of a noun that includes a multitude to the plural: “to whom the Senate,” “the senators,” “the Romans,” should give.

### 456–476

But lest it perhaps be thought that words have been addressed only to men,

and lest woman, like an inactive sex, soft beneath a fragile body,

fearing the work of praise lest her reputation survive the torments

which eternal life follows, should reject the many gifts of God,

### 460

a wicked woman can retain material

for the highest praise.

Nothing is more daring than women

caught in the act; they derive courage from their crime,

### 344

and anger gives women an excessively great fury.

From where, then, can they assume a frenzied crime?

From that same source let them seize holy impulses beneath the breast,

and let them do what honour requires, what the reputation of modesty

demands, and what benefits the life destined for praise.

Judith, most chaste, pretended to love Holofernes,

a heroine who entered the commander’s camp, feared by men.

Amid the warlike tumult and bloody weapons,

amid sword-bearing troops beneath savage Mars,

she entered clothed in faith, clothed in modesty,

and what so many men had not undertaken,

a woman alone accomplished beneath the dark night,

and, with the leader’s head cut off, widowed the tyrant’s camp.

### 345

She carried the severed head to the city and presented it to the nobles;

with it she gave the citizens triumph together with liberty.

##### 524

“*Saecula nec tamen* … other material is missing; but immediately the complete verse is given, ‘*Nec mutant hunc* …’; accordingly, *Saecula nec tamen* is a corrupt beginning of this verse, *Nec mutant*.”

#### 479

“The promised pleasure” was what Holofernes himself had promised himself, deceived by Judith’s ambiguous answer.

Judith XII.13:

> Who am I, that I should contradict my lord?

Judith was openly invited to a banquet but secretly to an outrage. Following the open sense of the words, she showed herself ready to obey Holofernes; Holofernes was looking toward another, hidden meaning of her words.

Some think that Judith promised Holofernes a lawful marriage, but this interpretation appears less compatible with Dracontius’s words and intention.

#### 481

“Of the appointed night,” that is, the night fixed by him for himself, which he had certainly promised himself. *Nox* (“night”) is often used for the forbidden intercourse itself.

In the *Latin Anthology* IV, Pisaurian edition, p. 502:

> While I seek the price of your night;

the epigram is found among those attributed to Martial. Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* I.143:

> Liber paid the price of the night with this honour.

Cicero, Horace, Ovid, Statius, Plautus, Terence, and others speak similarly. In the plural, Juvenal, *Satires* I.37:

> Those who earn wills by their nights.

#### 482

*Impollutus* (“undefiled”) is a word of Tacitus and of the later period.

#### 483

In the corrupt manuscript reading I think one must certainly read “Semiramis and Ninus,” both of whom are clearly mentioned. It makes no difference that some shorten the first syllable of *Semiramis* and lengthen the second, and make the first syllable of *Ninus* short: Dracontius and other writers of his period were freer with proper names.

Prudentius likewise lengthens the first syllable in *Ninivitae*, from *Ninus*, *Hymn* VII.131:

> He was compelled to hasten against the Ninevites.

Similarly Theodulf of Orléans, in the verses placed at the front of the Bible, writes:

> The world possesses both Nineveh and life in its name.

Others shorten the first syllable of *Ninive* and lengthen the second.

#### 484

“Inhabited the chambers,” etc.; see the note to verse 319.

Justin, *Epitome* I.1, concerning Semiramis:

> She pretended to be the son of Ninus in place of his wife, and a boy in place of a woman … She then accomplished great deeds, whose magnitude, when she thought that envy had been overcome, she revealed … Finally, when she sought intercourse with her son, she was killed by him.

#### 486

A mother is the mother-in-law of her son’s wife. Semiramis, therefore, who desired marriage with her son, was her own son’s mother-in-law.

#### 488

Perhaps the reading is *quis neget orbatae Tomyris* (“who would deny the bereaved Tomyris”). Others write *Thamiris*. Valerius Maximus, *Memorable Deeds and Sayings* X.9, concerning her:

> She ordered Cyrus’s severed head to be thrown into a sack filled with human blood, reproaching him for his insatiable thirst for blood and at the same time exacting punishment for the killing of her son.

Herodotus I.214 relates the same story, although he admits that many other accounts are given of Cyrus’s end.

#### 489

Some lengthen the first syllable of *Cyrus*.

#### 491

I had thought the reading was *demersum* (“submerged”), but Valerius Maximus uses *dimitti* (“to be sent away”) in the same matter.

#### 492

“Blood enclosed in a wineskin”: the blood was so abundant that it covered and, as it were, enclosed the head.

#### 494

Hyginus, *Fables* 256, counts Evadne, the wife of Capaneus, among the most chaste women. I read *Capaneia conjux* (“Capaneia, the wife”), rather than *in Capanea*. Statius, *Thebaid* XII.545:

> Capaneia, the wife, daring before all others.

#### 495

Capaneus is said to have perished at Thebes, struck by lightning. See Statius at the end of Book X. *Jaculatus* (“having been hurled”) occurs passively in Lucan.

#### 497

Hyginus, *Fables* 243; Statius at the end of the *Thebaid*: “He climbed,” as at verse 502.

#### 499

Dido, also called Elissa or Elisa, fled secretly from Tyre after her brother Pygmalion had murdered her husband Sychaeus, coveting his treasures; she dug them up and carried them away with her. Therefore all the words of this verse convey significant meanings: rich, fugitive, avenger of her murdered husband.

#### 501

The manuscript reading *pyram construxit* (“built a pyramid”) can in some way be defended as “built an altar,” but it does not seem correct. *Contruxit* for *construxit* is clearly an error.

#### 502

Above, verse 497: “Soon she climbed the funeral pyres alive.” Virgil, *Aeneid* IV.646, concerning Dido:

> She climbed the pyre in a frenzy.

#### 503

“Alive in the funeral,” as at verse 398, “a living corpse”; Book I, verse 648, “living funerals”; and the following verse, “in living death.” A similar oxymoron occurs in Victorinus, *On Jesus Christ*:

> Enduring the violence of men, buried in living death.

Dido killed herself with a sword, but on the pyre on which her body was to be burned.

#### 504

Macrobius, *Saturnalia* V.17, recalls that Virgil arranged Dido’s love so elegantly that the story of the lustful Dido—which everyone knows to be false—has nevertheless retained the appearance of truth through so many centuries and flies as truth from everyone’s lips.

Justin, Book XVIII, reports that Hiarbas, king of Mauretania, demanded Dido’s marriage under threat of war. The queen, however, constructed a pyre in the furthest part of the city, supposedly to appease her husband’s spirit and offer funeral rites before the marriage. She sacrificed many victims, took up a sword, climbed the pyre, and, looking back toward the people, said that she was going to her husband as he had ordered; then she ended her life with the sword.

There are nevertheless some who wish to confirm Virgil’s account with testimonies of ancient writers. Ruaeus refutes this opinion at the beginning of his commentary on Book IV of the *Aeneid*.

---

By a woman’s blade the brave and bold leader perishes,

whom wars did not subdue, but promised pleasure subdued.

Although this anticipated desire was not fulfilled,

the adulterer, still undefiled by any completed crime,

paid the penalty of the appointed night.

Semiramis, bereaved of her husband Ninus,

### 346

invaded the marriage chamber and the kingdom of her beloved son.

Unhappy, she displays a mother in an incestuous heart,

and, most shameful of wives, was her own son’s mother-in-law.

For a long time she waged wars, pretending to be a young man beneath arms.

Who would deny the cruel wars of the enraged Tomyris,

successfully waged with Cyrus, leader of the Persians?

### 490

Having become the avenger of her son after his grievous death,

while she enclosed the royal head, severed and dripping with much blood,

in a wineskin, the blood which her mind, frenzied with grief,

had shed from the innumerable necks of young men.

What the chaste wife Capaneia did, Evadne did,

### 495

when, after the sulphurous blows of the hurled lightning,

her husband’s bones were burning amid the fires prepared,

she soon climbed the funeral pyre alive. Or should we call her a widow,

who at the same time went with her husband to the infernal shades?

### 347

Rich Dido, fugitive and avenger of her murdered husband,

after fully completing the walls of the Elissaean city,

built the pyre and altar with her own hands,

then, in her frenzy, climbed it with her feet and burned.

Either love for Aeneas or fear of approaching Hiarbas

drove her to hurry into the flames, alive in her funeral.

---

### Notes

#### 505

Livy, *History* I.57, concerning Lucretia:

> Then both her beauty and her proven chastity aroused him. Lucretia had sent word to her father and her husband that they should come to her, each with a trustworthy friend. When they were present, she recounted Tarquinius’s crime and stabbed herself with a knife.

507. “Carried away,” “took away.” Virgil, *Eclogue* 9.51: “Time carries all things away, and the mind as well.” Or “carried away above herself,” that is, so that she might undergo death in place of him, in ecclesiastical phrasing, as in the note on Book II, verse 602: “Although he himself bears our stains and crimes.” *ALIENI POENA PUDORIS* (“the punishment of another’s shame”) is a genitive of apposition, as in verse 270: “She receives it, unhappy, as the cause of another’s triumph.” Lucretia therefore became for herself the punishment of another’s disgrace. “Shame” is used metonymically for disgrace, especially disgrace remaining from illicit intercourse. Ovid, *Heroides* 11.79: “He rushes in and proclaims our shame with a shout.” Justin, Book III, chapter 4: “Those born from them, on account of the mark of their mother’s shame, were called Parthenii.”

508. See above, verse 429.

510. “As the reward of shame,” as in verse 507, “the punishment of shame.” *Merces* means a penalty or punishment. Livy, Book XXXIX, chapter 55: “A heavy penalty for recklessness ought to be imposed.”

511. “Among female bands,” that is, “in female bands.” Perhaps one should read *femineae catervae* (“female bands”). Frederick Furius Caeriolanus pursued the character and disposition of women in a similar encomium in his work entitled *Bononia*, Book II, pp. 281 ff.: “For what if they are found to be superior to men and more worthy of praise? [lacuna] Read the annals and histories of every age and you will learn of chaste, modest women, etc., who have excelled in every kind of virtue, etc. I do not wish to list Semiramis, Lucretia, etc. Why should I mention to you many thousands of maidens, wives, and widows?”

This, however, is the distinction between Caeriolanus and Dracontius: the latter exhorts women to the praise of true virtue, whereas the former reasons in such a way as to conclude that the reading of the vernacular version of the sacred books ought, without distinction, to be permitted to everyone. From this you will understand how ineptly, in the *Catalogue of the Hulsian Library*, vol. IV, p. 337, this book of Caeriolanus was placed among those dealing with Rome and the ecclesiastical state, or the dominion of the Roman pontiff—as though it contained a description of the city of Bologna—when it was entitled *Bononia* because it explains a dialogue between Caeriolanus and Bononia, a Sicilian theologian and rector of Louvain.

Here is the title of this rare work: *The Two Books of Frederick Furius Caeriolanus of Valencia, entitled Bononia, or On Translating the Sacred Books into the Vernacular, addressed to Francisco Bovadilla Mendoza, Cardinal of Burgos*. Basel, by Johann Oporinus, from the workshop of Michael Martin Stella, 1556, March, octavo.

I do not know whether the hallucination of the hypercritical Bayle is more ridiculous. In the *Dictionary*, under “Furius,” he asserts that Frederick Furius was called Caeriolanus because he had been born at Valencia; and he cites Nicolás Antonio, whom he claims to have written that the inhabitants of the kingdom of Valencia were commonly called *Seriols*, and that for this reason Furius was surnamed *Seriolanus*. Hear the words of Nicolás Antonio, which Bayle also copied:

“Frederick Furius Seriolanus—called *Seriol* in the vernacular usage of the Valencian people, from whose kingdom’s principal city he originated—cannot be commended by any more fitting encomium,” etc.

As you see, Nicolás Antonio merely implies that Frederick, from his common surname *Seriol*, made for himself the name *Seriolanus*. In any case, his two surnames were Furio Ceriol. I would add some information about his lineage and family from the acts of the beatification and canonization of Blessed Nicholas Factor, and other information about the office of royal historian which he held and his historical writings from the preface of John Matallius to Jerome Osorius’s books on the deeds of Emmanuel, king of Portugal, if this were not an inappropriate place.

526. In the manuscript’s text, *minuitque volatile tempus* (“and fleeting time lessens”) appears, as in verse 523, “He changes the ages.” Ovid, *Metamorphoses* X.519: “The fleeting age slips away secretly and deceives.” I suspect the reading: “Since fleeting time takes away and lessens everything, God [gives] increase,” etc. I am certain that Columbanus, in his letter to Hunaldus, reproduced this verse: “Fleeting time gives, takes away, and lessens everything”; he reports this verse mixed together with others by Dracontius. I therefore wish to follow my conjecture.

528. *Elegy*, verse 7: “Changing everything, yet unchangeable through no age; you will always be the same.”

529. On the name “Father,” by which God wishes to be called, consult the note on Book I, verse 81.

530. On the verb *impendo* (“I bestow”) used for “I confer,” see the note on verse 248. *Adoptare* (“to adopt”) has the particular meaning of taking someone into the place of a son, with one’s own name bestowed upon him. Hence the addition, “We, though begotten, he calls his own.” For God adopts us into his family and, by grace, gives us the name of his sons. Perhaps *adoptat* is also used for *optat* (“desires”).

531. *Genitus* (“begotten”) is used substantively for “son.” See the commentary on Prudentius, *Hymn* 5 of the *Cathemerinon*, verse 157. First Epistle of John, chapter III, verse 1: “See what sort of love the Father has given us, that we should be called children of God, and that we should be so.” Chrysostom, Homily 14 on Matthew: “He wished to be called Father rather than God, in order to give us great confidence in asking.” Dracontius, at the end of Book III: “Your word is held as a pledge in our heart, by which in great devotion you promise yourself to be our father.”

532. See Book I, verse 338: “The form of a human being, a heavenly image.”

533. *Factura* (“making”) is often used by Christian writers for a work that has been made and for a creature. Compare the commentary on Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 304. Here it more likely denotes the action itself, or the process of making; Pliny and Gellius use the word in this sense. “With piety as guide,” like “with light as guide” and “with custom as guide”; many such expressions can be found in poets.

534. Book II, verse 698, similarly: “Pious king.” The sentence is obscure, and the text may be corrupt. I attempted: “Pious king, to whom the whole power of warriors becomes submissive: whatever you command comes to pass.” Or: “Pious king, accompanied by the power of warriors, whatever you command always comes to pass.”

539. *Ministrat* (“serves”) has the sense it bears in Book I, verse 227: “Whatever things serve.” Perhaps: “It rejoices at having been commanded; glad in service, it completes [the command].” Sedulius, Book I, verse 222, elsewhere 237: “To the Creator, whose works, whether seen or hidden, and whose fabric of things is a servant, all its work performs service and follows the command of him who orders it, wherever the intention of his nod draws it.” Cellarius printed *et rerum machina sermo est* (“and the machinery of things is speech”). But Wopkens, in *Critical Miscellanies*, restored *serva est* (“is a servant”) from other books, and then conjectured *sequiturque jubentis imperii, quocunque trahit sententia, nutum* (“and it follows the command of the ruler, wherever his intention draws his nod”).

541. Virgil and others use *tremisco* (“I tremble”) with the accusative. Many old books write *tremesco*, and this is also found in the Vatican manuscript, but the more common spelling is *tremisco*.

542. “The heights of heaven,” as in Book II, verse 3, “the heights of the heavens.”

543. Thus I restore the text. “Nature eagerly desires to serve, trembling”; for the same nature “rejoices in serving” and “trembles after serving.” Dracontius often uses such oppositions of words. I had considered: “To which the beast eagerly desires to serve.” *QUOTA PORTIO* means “how small a portion.” Lucretius, Book VI, verse 650: “And you may see how small a part one heaven is of the whole sum, and of how many parts it consists, and what a fraction one human being is of the whole earth.”

545. This passage is corrupt. I find the half-line of the following verse in Alcuin, a frequent imitator of Dracontius, poem 179, which consists of single verses and contains, among other things: “Let him who wishes his own vows to come to pass himself fulfill God’s vows”—that is, let him fulfill God’s vows who wishes his own wishes to succeed for him.” Nevertheless, I prefer the opinion of Canisius, who, in the appendix to volume I of *Various Readings*, attributes this poem to Saint Columbanus from a certain manuscript; several verses from his letter to Hunaldus have been quoted here. In the recent edition of Alcuin, this poem is included among the doubtful works. I corrected the passage as I was able, not as I wished. I wish our Petrus Chacon had applied his remedy; of him Nicasius Erythraeus says in the *Pinacotheca*: “He possessed this quality above all: in healing the wounds of ancient books, no one could apply a better remedy than he, to such an extent that the minds of those same authors seemed—as Pythagoras dreamed—to have migrated into him and, in a certain way, to have disclosed to him their opinion concerning the matters under dispute.”

547. There will be no metrical fault if you read *facere contemnimus* (“we disdain to do”).

548. Book II, verse 267: “We, the wicked crowd, although knowing justice, disdain it in a punishable act.”

550. An imitation of the Apostle, First Epistle to Timothy, chapter I, verse 15: “Of whom [sinners] I am the first.” The entire question of what this confession of Dracontius refers to was discussed at length in the prolegomena, chapter 13.

552. An uncertain author, *On the Praises of the Lord*, under Constantine: “Even if I were covered with an iron wall, even if I had an iron voice and a thousand tongues with which to sing,” etc. Virgil, Book VI, verse 625: “Not even if I had a hundred tongues and a hundred mouths, and an iron voice,” etc. Thus pagan and Christian poets commonly express the difficulty of explaining something point by point. As for Dracontius ending this verse, and not infrequently others, with a monosyllabic word, whether this is correct has been disputed by some. Labbe, in the *New Catalogue of Manuscripts*, p. 68, cites from the library of Gabriel Naudé an anonymous dialogue, “Whether a verse may correctly be closed with monosyllabic words, and with which ones,” written against Thomas Correa, who had written books at Bologna on eloquence, elegy, and epigram. Examples from the finest poets are open to everyone.

553. Virgil, Book XII, verse 36: “And the plains grow white with great bones.”

554. *Quantos* (“how many”) for *quot* (“how many”) is customary in good Latin authors: Seneca, Propertius, Statius, Claudian, and others.

555. *Pectinare* (“to comb”) is a verb used by Pliny and Apuleius. In Psalm 39.13 David compared his sins to the hairs of his head: “My iniquities have overtaken me, and I was unable to see; they have multiplied beyond the hairs of my head.” Dracontius carries the hyperbole further.

556. “Guilty,” namely, “me.” *Cunctus* in the singular occurs in Virgil, Cicero, and many others, as in *cunctus orbis* (“the whole world”), from *a cuncto populo* (“from the whole people”).

558. Virgil, Statius, and Valerius Flaccus use *horresco* (“I shudder”) with the accusative.

560. Jeremiah, chapter XXIX, verse 23.

561. See Book I, verses 497 ff., “the sacrilegious,” etc., and verses 531 ff. of the same book.

562. I read *sibi* (“to himself”) instead of *cui* (“to whom”); for even with the question “To whom will my mind, which keeps silent, do harm by deceit?” the meaning is not sufficiently clear. First Epistle of John, chapter I, verses 8 ff.: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves [lacuna]. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins.” First Book of Kings, chapter VIII, verses 46 ff.

563. Perhaps *quod si* (“but if”). The manuscript has *cum si*. *Cum* may be taken as “when,” with adversative force. Martial, Book VII, epigram 83: “My face will be more secure in my poem; untouched by any misfortune, indestructible through the years, it will live when the Apellean work dies.” That is, the painted image of Caecilius Secundus will die, but his face, represented in my poem, will not.

564. *Admissum* (“an offense committed”) is used for “crime” by Livy, Tacitus, and others. It would not be bad to read *venia sperata sequatur* (“let hoped-for pardon follow”). But *sequetur* (“will follow”) can be defended with *cum*, as I just explained.

565. “He who denies”—namely, the crimes, the offense committed.

568. The manuscript has *superabit* (“will surpass”), not *superavit* (“surpassed”), in keeping with the following verse, *vincent* (“will surpass”): if I should count my crimes, they will surpass the sand of the shore and exceed the waves of the sea. In the sacred Scriptures, a great multitude is often compared with the sand of the sea. Theodulf of Orléans, Book IV, poem 4, verse 296: “I confess that I have committed many sins against God, which in number surpass you, the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, the wave of the sea, the stars of heaven, the grasses and shrubs, and all the earth’s growth. This is why I have been sent into these troubles, since such great evils are not what I deserve.”

570. Dracontius exaggerates his crimes with words drawn from sacred Scripture. Hermann Hugo, in *Pious Desires*, Book I, poem 11, explains in this sense the words of Psalm 68.16: “May the tempest of water not overwhelm me, nor the deep swallow me,” etc.

573. Psalm 17.5: “The torrents of iniquity troubled me”; and Psalm 37.5: “For my iniquities have risen above my head.”

575. From the cited Psalm 68.2: “The waters have entered even to my soul.” Ovid, *Tristia* II.101: “No small part of the whirlpool harmed me, but all the waves pressed upon this head, and the ocean did so as well.”

581. Among the sayings of Publilius Syrus, maxim 825: “It is best not to uproot the wicked, but their wickedness.” Prosper, epigram 8: “In the end, human beings always commit evil crimes; he gives time for crimes to perish, not human beings.” And epigram 44: “The lover of the law hates those who despise the law—not the human beings, but what they do he condemns.”

584. Perhaps “broken and stripped.” Verse 593: “Whom griefs have broken in this way.”

bonds bind me, torments subdue me, want consumes me;

I have become the mockery of my kind, a grief to everyone, and an enemy,

stripped and deprived of a large share of my possessions,

585. The appearance of defendants among the Romans is commonly known: uncut hair and worn, dirty clothing.

586. Similar things occur in Psalm 37. I take *parentes* (“parents”) to mean blood relatives, a sense already current at that time and later passed into the vernacular languages. Jerome, Book II against Rufinus, near the beginning: “Unless perhaps he calls relatives and in-laws *parentes* in the military and common language.” Certainly Capitolinus, Lampridius, Curtius, and Julius Firmicus spoke in this way, to omit later writers and some earlier ones whose meaning is nevertheless not certain.

587. “And to whom I have rendered service” can be defended; for Dracontius uses *impendo* in the sense of “confer” or “provide” in verse 530. Nevertheless, I think “those to whom I have rendered service” more likely.

589. Euripides, *Alcestis*, verse 208: “For not all servants wish their masters well, so as to approach them benevolently in misfortune.” Dracontius must have possessed a considerable number of servants. Alcimus reasons beautifully about the origin of servants in Book IV, where, speaking of the time of the Flood, he says: “For nature had not yet given servants to be called servants, nor had order learned to distinguish masters from attendants. His middle son was the first among these children to perceive the stain of the servile name; perhaps he perished in a miserable spectacle, laughing when his father was exposed, and, more shamefully deformed, mocked the source of his own disgrace. After holy Noah was able to recognize this, he gave the son to his brothers as a servant; from that time such a yoke was discovered, for we are all born from one seed. It is clear that guilt created the cause of servitude, and that a free person, by sinning, becomes a slave through his crime. If again a servant is bound by the bond of honorable birth, making noble offspring for himself, he is now noble.”

Thus in the old edition of Molther, where *distectum* is read instead of *detectum*. Roman wealth consisted, among other things, in the great number of slaves. C. Caecilius Claudius Isidorus is said to have left 4,016 slaves in his will, although he had lost much property in the civil war. Crassus had as many as five hundred architects and craftsmen among his slaves. Seneca, *On Tranquillity of Mind*, chapter 8: “You call Demetrius Pompeianus happier—the man who was not ashamed to be richer than Pompey? The number of his slaves was reported to him every day, like an army to a general.” See Lipsius in his notes and Book II, chapter 15, *On the Greatness of Rome*. Since Dracontius therefore recalls not only slaves but whole ranks of slaves, he sufficiently suggests that he abounded in the goods of fortune, or was even one of the foremost men. The word *clientes* (“clients”) in this passage indicates the same thing. Book II, verse 310: “Many clients of the nobles, deceived by fraud.”

590. Above, verse 583, he says “a grief to everyone”; why then does he now say, “Nor did they grieve”? The distinction is that in this verse “nor did they grieve” accuses servants, clients, friends, and relatives of ingratitude because they did not grieve over Dracontius’s misfortune in such a way as to offer some remedy, at least through consoling words, insofar as it lay within their power. But in verse 583 he says that he had become a mockery of his kind, a grief to everyone, and an enemy, because from his misfortune grief, like mockery, ought to have spread to his relatives. They therefore grieved not for Dracontius’s misfortune but for their own loss—or, if they did grieve for Dracontius’s misfortune, they pretended not to, behaving as enemies.

591. *Elegy*, verse 29: “When God is angry, minds and limbs are changed.”

593. Ovid, Book III of the *Tristia*, final elegy, verse 33: “Misfortunes have broken my spirit.” Thus one says that someone is broken by grief, distress, care, and similar things.

594. I think the reading is *miserere fatentis* (“have mercy on the one confessing”), as in verse 601, *miserere rogantis* (“have mercy on the one asking”), and also elsewhere with the genitive. Nevertheless, *miserere fatenti* (“have mercy on the one confessing”) can be defended. Corippus, Book II, verse 402: “The Lord, having had mercy on needy servants.” Diomedes, Book I, Putsch edition, column 294, recognizes the Latin form *misereor tibi* (“I have mercy on you”), and there are examples in Hyginus, Quintilian’s *Declamations*, and others.

595. “Spare the lash”: refrain from the lash, as in “spare me fear.”

598. “Holy one,” referring to God, as in verse 661. See the note on Book I, verse 744. Juvencus, Prudentius, and others speak in this way.

599. *Elegy*, verse 155: “Let not the sun set as it enters,” etc. From the Apostle, Ephesians, chapter IV, verse 26: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger.”

600. Perhaps *qui praecipis hoc sic* (“you who command this”).

602. “And direct my tears,” as in Book I, verse 746, “the hope of human beings directing.” *Diurne* is used for “for a long time,” or “on every day,” or “continually.” Properly, *diurnum* is what pertains to the day, as *nocturnum* pertains to the night. But that *diurnum* can be used for “long-lasting” is shown by certain passages in Cicero, although some prefer to read *diuturnum*.

603. The posture of suppliants and those praying. Cicero, *For Ligarius*, chapter 5: “What we ask at home, prostrate at your feet with prayers and tears.” The conjecture also occurs to me that the passage refers to a punishment by means of cords, by which bodies were stretched out and prostrated; that interpretation, however, is less satisfactory.

607. *Tulerunt* (“bore away”) for *abstulerunt* (“took away”). See the note on verse 507; or read “Whatever bitter day, whatever time has taken away.”

> With uncut hair, wearing filthy rags;

known and unknown alike are gone; my relatives have departed,

those to whom I rendered service, and soon my kin forgot me;

and whoever was once a friend suddenly withdrew.

Bands of servants flee; clients have shown contempt,

[590] 355 nor did they grieve my downfall in so great a disaster.

When God is angry, all consolation is denied.

What remains is that life should fall, unless you, merciful,

command that you spare the afflicted man whom griefs have broken in this way.

You punished the one who went astray; now have mercy on the one confessing.

[595] 356 Alas, I regret having sinned so greatly; now spare the lash,

[Col. 0892A] for in my misery I cannot endure being driven by so many calamities.

Look upon me, I beg you; do not close your ears to our prayers,

holy one, you who kindly give commands.

Let the anger of the raging man fall from his heart with the setting sun,

[600] and let the night itself bring pardon. You who command that it be so,

make it happen, as you yourself command; have mercy on the one who asks,

and direct my tears, which I pour out continually.

Sad and with my body stretched out, I lie prostrate and lament.

Wretched me! I who endure so much, for whom you have prepared such great

[605] punishments for crimes. Although I may deserve to be burned more severely,

may I receive the Lord’s gifts when his favor returns,

whatever bitter day and harsh times have carried away.

[Note: [Col. 0893B]

608. “Restore the light; far off, you who take away Job’s times …”; in the margin, *precor* (“I beg”) for *procul* (“far off”).

608. These verses appear confused and transposed in the manuscript. I arranged them as I judged suitable to the speech and sense. Perhaps one should read *Lucida redde, precor* (“Restore the light, I beg”). By using the example of Job, Dracontius implies that he has lost many things.

610. See Ezekiel, chapter XXXVII: “And he led me out in the midst of the plain, which was full of bones [lacuna]. There were very many upon the face of the plain, and they were exceedingly dry [lacuna]. Prophesy concerning these bones and say to them: Dry bones, hear the word of the Lord.”

[Col. 0893C] 612. Perhaps “And you command the human beings whom your creation assists, as blood creeps onward,” or “And you command your creation to fill human beings with blood.”

613. He attributes moisture to the marrow, as in Book I, verse 652: “Stirring the veins and moistening the marrow.” Isidore, Book XI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1: “They are called marrow because they moisten the bones; for they irrigate and strengthen them.” Thus the dry bones from which human beings were to be made are first supplied inwardly with marrow.

614. The cited chapter of Ezekiel: “And behold, the sinews and flesh came upon them, and skin was stretched over them from above.” Cicero, Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*, chapter 55: “What shall I say of the bones? They lie beneath the body and have marvelous joints [lacuna]. Add to this the sinews, by which the limbs are held together [lacuna], which, like the veins and arteries drawn from the heart and distributed throughout the whole body, are conducted everywhere.” Celsus, Book II, chapter 10: “The vein is joined to the arteries, and the sinews to these.”

616. The cited chapter of Ezekiel: “And there was a sound as I prophesied, and behold, a movement; and the bones came together, each one to its joint.” The anterior part of the neck is the throat; the posterior part is the nape.

[Col. 0893D] 617. The crown of the head is the part where the hair of the head is gathered and in which the locks turn. Isidore, Book XI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1.

618. Cicero, Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*: “The eyes, like watchmen, occupy the highest place.” The manuscript has *geminato* (“doubled”) incorrectly. See Book I, verses 235 and 345. *Vibrant* (“they flash”) is used for *micant* (“they sparkle”).

619. Cicero, Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*, chapter 57: “And the eyelids, which are coverings of the eyes [lacuna], most suitably made both for closing the pupils—so that nothing might enter—and for opening them [lacuna]. The eyelids are fortified as if by a rampart of eyelashes [lacuna]. Moreover, they usefully lie hidden and are enclosed on every side by elevated parts.” Compare Ambrose, Book VI of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 9, and Isidore, Book XI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1, with the notes of Grial.

I conjectured that Dracontius read: “And the eyelid covers the lights and fortifies the windows.” Celsus used *palpebra* in the singular, Book V, chapter 26, section 23. Nonius, chapter 3, testifies that *palpebrum* is used in the neuter gender: “Usage requires *palpebrum* in the neuter, *palpebra* in the feminine.” From this one may retain “And the eyelids cover the lights”; then, instead of *mandantque*, one should preferably read *mundantque* (“and cleanse”) the windows. He uses “lights” for eyes, as do Ovid, Statius, Rutilius, and others. Nor is Cicero far from this meaning in the *Aratea*, verse 96: “Those lights which shine from the radiant face,” although he is speaking literally of stars. Prudentius likewise used “windows” for eyes in *Hamartigenia*, verse 870: “And with obstructing moisture they impede the wandering windows.” See the commentary on that passage of Prudentius.

Some interpret mystically, with reference to the eyes, the words of Jeremiah, chapter IX, verse 21: “For death has climbed through our windows,” and of Isaiah, chapter LX, verse 8: “Who are these who fly like clouds and like doves to their windows?” If one reads *mundantque fenestras* (“and cleanse the windows”), this can be explained from Isidore, Book XI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1: “At the upper edge of the eyelids, in the places where the two closed lids meet, hairs grow out in orderly fashion, providing protection for the eyes, so that they may not easily receive injuries when things rush upon them—or, as some read, when filth rushes upon them—and suffer harm from them; they ward off contact with dust or any denser material, and, by breaking the force of the air itself, soften it, so that they make the sight delicate and clear.”

620. Properly, *scena* means a tent, tabernacle, or leafy shade; hence, by transference, “the stage of the hair.” Ovid, Book XIII of the *Metamorphoses*, verse 718: “His abundant hair projects over his fierce face and shades his shoulders like a grove.”

621. *Tempora* (“temples”) is more often said in the plural, and here one could also read “the temples and the whole head.” But *tempus* in the singular also signifies both temples. “The whole head” means “the entire head,” as above, verse 554: “As many hairs as the whole head has.” The hair is the clothing of the head, as is clear from the note on Book I, verse 344: “Made both to provide adornment and to protect the brain against cold and defend it from the sun,” as Isidore reports in Book XI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1.

622. Book I, verse 345: “They sparkle with a double orb from the eyes,” and Book II, verse 652: “And with a double orb he receives the day.” See the note.

623. I read *naribus abductis* (“with the nostrils drawn apart”), as though separated and receding, so that a double passage might open.

624. See Book I, verses 342 and 395, where redness is attributed to the cheeks. Pliny, Book XI, chapter 37, section 58, on the cheeks: “These are the seat of modesty; blush is displayed there most clearly.”

627. I read *muratum*, a word used by Vegetius. *Moratum* (“delayed” or “characterized”) means nothing here; *muratum* (“walled”) aptly presents the teeth as walls by which the palate is enclosed.]

357 Restore the light, I beg, you who take away Job’s

harsh times, restoring whatever the evil enemy took away;

[610] you who restore dry bones from ancient deaths,

bones which returned to their limbs when the prophet cried aloud,

and command men, your creation, to move forth,

Veins are born; now the limbs are joined by sinews;

and the twin cheeks grow red; the jaws are downy,

[625] 359 their down curling, still green after the old age of bones,

[Col. 0895B] 629. “R. tongue.”

630. “And the creation lies as a bridge for the words of the mouth.”

628. *Elegy*, verse 47: “The melodies of a silent tongue.” Cicero, Book II of *On the Nature of the Gods*, chapter 59: “Then the tongue is situated in the mouth, enclosed by the teeth. It shapes and limits the voice when it pours forth without restraint; it produces distinct and controlled sounds by directing them against the teeth and other parts of the mouth. Thus our writers commonly call the tongue like a plectrum, and the teeth the strings; the nostrils are like the horns against which the strings resound in songs.”

629. Aulus Gellius, Book I, chapter 15: “Homer, on the other hand, says that Ulysses, a man endowed with wise eloquence, sent forth his voice not from his mouth but from his breast [lacuna]; and he aptly said that the barrier of the teeth was set against verbal recklessness, so that the rashness of speech might be guarded not only by the watchfulness and custody of the heart [lacuna], but also enclosed by something like sentries stationed in the mouth.”

The Homeric words of which I spoke above are:

> Ἀλλ᾽ ὅτε δὴ ῥ᾽ ὄπα τε μεγάλην ἐκ στήθεος ἵει,  
> Τέκνον ἐμόν, ποῖόν σε ἔπος φύγεν ἕρκος ὀδόντων.

“But when he had poured forth a great voice from his breast:

‘My child, what kind of word has escaped the enclosure of your teeth?’”

630. Perhaps: “And the creation conceals the guilty thing in the recesses of the mouth.” See the note on Book I, verse 57, where the subject is the evil tongue.

632. Ambrose, Book VI of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 9: “What, then, is the mouth of a human being except a kind of sanctuary of speech, a fountain of discussion, a hall of words, and a storehouse of the will?” Ambrose says much more there about the marvelous structure of the human body.

633. Avitus, Book I, verse 87: “Thus the flexible tongue is compressed into the hollow palate, so that, struck in the chamber by the blow of a plectrum, speech resounds in measured form through the air.”

635. Propertius, Book II, elegy 18, verse 59, first lengthened *flabellum* (“fan”). And fans [are] like the tail-feathers of a proud peacock; but Ovid corrected this in *Amores* III, elegy 2: “Which fans, moved by our hand, may make.” Yet elsewhere some read, “Which a tablet (*tabella*), moved by our hand, may make”; likewise *flagello* (“whip”) or *tabella* (“tablet”) instead of *flabello* (“fan”), lest the first syllable of *flabello* be shortened. But corrections of this sort are generally made less on the authority of ancient manuscripts than according to editors’ preconceived opinions. Lips, like the tongue, may not improperly be compared with a fan, by which wind is stirred. Cicero, *For Flaccus*, chapter 23: “His tongue, as though it were the fan of sedition, then stirred up that assembly of the needy.” Eugenius of Toledo, in the preface to his poems: “Nor should you fear fans rivaling your books,” which verse is read in the Vatican Codex Alexandrinus, no. 1360, as follows: “Nor should you dread fans rivaling your books.”

636. From Celsus, Book VIII, chapters 1 and 10: the arm is the part of the human body extending from the elbow to the hand. The remaining portion, from the elbow to the shoulder, Celsus calls the *os humeri* (“bone of the shoulder”), or *humerus*; others call it the *lacerti* (“upper arms”), since *humerus* more commonly denotes that part from which the upper arms and forearms depend.

637. Prudentius, *Apotheosis*, verse 859: “Is God’s hand arranged joint by joint? Is it a palm? Or are there flexible nails for closing?”

639. The spine is the series of vertebrae in the back, whence the Spanish *espinazo*. Ovidius, *Metamorphoses* VIII, verse 804: “Dry bones projected beneath the curved loins; there was a hollow instead of a belly; you would have thought the breast hung down and was held only by the cage of the spine.”

640. On the cage or ribs of the chest, see the commentary on Prudentius, *Apotheosis* V, verse 891, and *Peristephanon* hymn 3, verse 148. The *juguli* are two bones called the clavicles, situated above the upper ribs, where the neck begins; it would not be wrong to read *jugulisque ligantur* (“and they are fastened by the clavicles”). See Heister, *Compendium of Anatomy*, no. 144. For a fuller understanding of this entire description of the human body, a work published a few years ago is especially useful: *Anatomical Tables drawn from the original works of the excellent painter Pietro Berrettini of Cortona and engraved on copper*. In this second edition, Francesco Petraglia, professor of philosophy and medicine, revised the work, removed the inaccurate illustrations, and added continuous explanations. Rome, 1788.

641. *Propago* (“offspring”) is translated as *progenies* (“descendants”), in which sense its first syllable is ordinarily shortened; properly, it is a shoot of a vine or another tree that is bent down into the earth so that it may be renewed by roots formed there, in which sense its first syllable is lengthened. Dracontius transfers this meaning to the renewed bones of the human being.

642. Perhaps read *cuncta ministrant* (“all serve”), *aedificant* (“they build”). Otherwise, *ministra* as an adjective is well attested in Cicero, Lucretius, Ovid, and others.

644. *Compage ligata* (“bound by a structure”) is better than *compago ligata*. See Book I, note on verse 346, and Book II, verse 84: “God is clothed in a structure; the structure is bound by bones.” *Compages* and *compage* frequently occur among Christian poets.

645. Beautifully expressed: for the movement of the bones occurred before the individual limbs had been formed, but they could not be moved so as to obey the Lord’s voice unless they heard it. This amounts to saying that God can also be heard without the ministry of the ears. John, chapter V, verse 25: “The hour is coming, and now is, when the dead will hear the voice of the Son of God, and those who hear will live.” … “Those who are in the tombs will hear the voice of the Son of God.”

646. I supplied *dominus* (“Lord”), so that the verse and sense might be complete. The same story is retold in similar words in the *Elegy*, verses 31 ff., from Daniel, chapter IV, verses 30 ff.

647. *Pecus* means “cattle,” specifically an ox; for in the preceding verse he says, “After his kingdom he feared the herdsman,” and in the *Elegy* he expressly says that he became an ox: “He wandered aimlessly through the meadows … and he who had been a man was an ox.” After seven years, or “times,” Nebuchadnezzar was restored to his right mind and reigned in the citadel—that is, in the palace of Babylon. Book I, verse 739: “He casts down the proud and plunges the arrogant from the citadel.” See the commentary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 5, verse 80: “The sad suspension of the tyrannical citadel.”]

654. Or *amissa dolent* (“they grieve over what has been lost”), T.

659. *Non iram nam* (“not anger, for”).

650. I suspect that these five verses should be transferred to after verse 672, “And with tears.”

[Col. 0897C] 651. *Munere noctis* (“the gift of night”), that is, sleep. In mythology, night is the mother or nurse of sleep. Euripides, *Orestes*, verse 174: “O venerable, venerable night, giving sleep to weary human beings.”

652. A temple of Fortuna Redux (“Fortune who brings back”) had been erected at Rome; many stones and coins inscribed to her still survive. Dracontius sought and hoped from God for the return of his former condition; pagans attributed this power to the divinity Fortuna, a practice which Juvenal also censures at the end of Satire 10. “Until old age,” as I said at Book II, verse 708.

653. Perhaps read: “And also whatever prayers ask for, / or what they grieve as lost.”

654. One might read *amissumve dolet* (“or grieves for what has been lost”), so that *amissum* would be more closely connected with *quidquid*. Yet *quidquid* has the force of a plural. Propertius, Book IV, elegy 5, at the end: “Whoever you are who love, cut this tomb with rough stones.” Dracontius, in the *Elegy*, verse 15: “Whatever human beings do—good, sad, prosperous, or wicked.”

[Col. 0897D] 656. *Formido* (“dread”) is a more intense fear, one that lasts for a long time and is accompanied by horror. In this sense, dread of losing salvation is removed by hope of pardon.

658. Here *inops* (“lacking”) is applied to things of which we are deprived. In this passage, *inops mortis* (“lacking death”) means someone removed from death, not yet dead. You may also punctuate it appropriately as: “Because I am alive, lacking death, I am preserved by mercy.”

660. See Book I, verses 29 ff. Dracontius repeatedly returns to the same point in order to commend God’s clemency.

661. “Holy,” as I said at verse 598.

662. See whether the better reading is *prorsus, qui poscere possem* (“entirely, so that I might be able to ask”).

663. *Sueta* is trisyllabic, as at verse 446.

664. Compare Book I, verse 749: “That I may be able to recall your praises in this poem.” What Dracontius now asks—that God, having preserved him, restore him so that he may sing divine praises in poems—does not refer so much to this present poem as to others. *Per* denotes the means; alternatively, it is equivalent to “to sing in poems.”

[Col. 0898B] 665. *Nemo tibi praeconia congrua* (“no one [has given] fitting praises to you”) would not be a bad reading. I discussed the word *congruus* (“fitting”) in the commentary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 11, verse 110. *Congruens* is more strictly Latin.

666. I explained the three times of praying to God—morning, evening, and midday—in the commentary on Prudentius, *Cathemerinon* hymn 3, verse 86.

667. *Elegy*, verse 5: “And free from time.”

668. *Ante* (“before”) and *post* (“after”) are used as substantives. See Book II, verse 732 ff., on this subject. Prosper, epigram 41: “He feels neither late nor early in the order of things, for all things accomplished and to be accomplished stand before him together.” This epigram concerns God’s providence and is placed seventh in other editions.

669. *Plenus at esset* (“but he would be full”) seemed to me preferable by conjecture to *plenus adesset* (“he would be fully present”).

671. *Trementer* (“tremblingly”) could be changed to *trementi* (“with trembling”), but it should be retained even without an example. Likewise, in the following verse, *veneranter* (“reverently”) should be retained. See the preface, no. 135.

672. On *veneranter*, see what was said about this adverb in Book I, verse 4. Add Theodulf of Orléans, Book I, poem 13: “Thus let us also sing the annual feasts reverently.”

673. The error in the manuscript has provided an opening for other conjectures, such as *sint reditus tenues* (“may there be slender returns”) or *sic victus tenuis* (“thus may sustenance be meager”). I prefer *sint reduces vires* (“may my strength return”), because Dracontius’ strength really had been broken, as is clear from verse 593. Eugenius of Toledo, in his prayer to God, poem 1, Book I: “May kindly health and sufficient sustenance be my companions; may riches be absent,” and so forth. [Col. 0898D] Paulinus, in his prayer, poem 5: “May I live on meager food … May I not suffer in mind or body.” Other words of Dracontius are taken from Juvenal, Satire 10, verse 356: “We should pray for a sound mind in a sound body.”

674. Paulinus, in his morning prayer to God, poem 4: “Hear me, if I ask what is just: let no day be sad for me, and let no night break peaceful rest.”

675. I will indicate elsewhere other conjectures for restoring this verse: “May my household and wife be happy, and my offspring numerous.” “May my household be without blemish and happy.” “May a joyful household be present”—the last half-line is Paulinus’ in his morning prayer, where he continues: “May a servant born in the household delight in the unbought feast, a faithful companion and shining attendant, an obedient wife, and dear children born of that wife.” From the same Paulinus, in a second prayer, one might conjecture for Dracontius: “May I always be a father, happy.” Paulinus has: “And always a father without the wound of this name.” The ancients regarded having many children as a kind of happiness. Ovid, *Metamorphoses* VI, verse 153, on Niobe: “Neither the lineage of both nor the power of a great kingdom pleased her so much, although all these things pleased her, as her offspring; and Niobe would have been called the happiest of mothers, had she not seemed so to herself.” For she despised Latona because, as she said: “Add here seven daughters born to me, / and as many sons, and soon sons-in-law and daughters-in-law. / Ask now what cause our pride may have … She became the mother of two; this is the seventh part of my womb. / I am happy—who could deny it?” This pride, however, was the reason why, as the mythographers relate, she was turned into stone together with her children. Juvenal does not approve of people making such prayers—that a wife be fertile—in Satire 10, verse 350: “Driven by impulse, blind and mighty desire, we seek marriage and the birth of children from a wife; but the gods know what sort of children they will be and what sort of wife she will become.” Nevertheless, numerous offspring are represented especially in the Old Testament as a reward for virtue, as in Psalm 127, verses 3 ff.: “Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine at the sides of your house. Your children shall be like olive shoots around your table. Behold, thus shall the man be blessed who fears the Lord.” Moreover, Dracontius does not seem so much to ask God to grant him a multitude of children as to make happy the numerous offspring he already had. For I understand him to be speaking of his children when he says in the *Elegy*, verse 283: “If I myself have sinned, what fault, I ask, belongs to my children, whom cold and needy hunger torment together?”]
