[Note: [Col. 0899B]

677. Purgatorial fire is clearly implied. Julian of Toledo, Book II, chapter 10 of the *Prognosticon*, cites excellent passages on this subject from Julianus Pomerius: “Those spirits who do not depart from here with such perfect holiness that they can go immediately to paradise after laying aside their bodies, nor live so criminally and damnably, or persist so in their crimes, that they deserve to be condemned with the devil and his angels—while the Church effectively intercedes for them here, and they have been cleansed by medicinal punishments—will receive their bodies again with blessed immortality and, made participants in the heavenly kingdom, will remain there without any diminution of their blessedness.” I follow the old parchment manuscripts praised elsewhere.

678. I understand the final judgment, as at Book II, verse 548: “He will come at the future judgment after the ages.” In *detur* (“may it be given”), the first syllable is shortened, as in *demus* at Book I, verse 361. See the note, and add Ademar’s acrostic in Mabillon, *Analecta*, volume I, page 418: “I, Ademar, shall have given you such gifts; why? Soon it is right to know your own, whence I demand that it be returned.”

679. The heavenly paradise is described by imitation of things perceived by the senses. Paulinus, poem 35, *On the Death of Celsus*, at the end, calls it “eternal green places.” Tertullian, *On the Judgment of the Lord*: “To go through ancient kingdoms that are always blooming, through promised riches, through ever-pleasant green places.” Helpidius, *History of the Old and New Testament*: “Through the pleasant green places of the sacred grove, under the Lord’s guidance, the fortunate thief earns a living dwelling.” In Appendix 9 to the poems of Damasus, page 244: “Thence he reigns amid the distinguished fragrances of paradise, where every meadow continually blooms.” An uncertain author, *On Bebianus’ Baptism*: “The secrets of the ethereal sky and blessed dwellings … He tells of the heavenly grove of the ethereal paradise.” Virgil, Book VI, verse 638, on the Elysian fields: “They came to joyful places, the pleasant green spaces of the Fortunate Groves, and blessed dwellings”—a passage which, as you see, Dracontius imitates.

680. Perhaps read *ad nemus aeternum* (“to the eternal grove”). Paulinus, poem 37 from a letter to Severus, on a painting of the martyrs: “The heavenly grove of the flower-bearing paradise.” Hence *ad nemus aetherium* (“to the ethereal grove”) seems better. Book II, verse 147: “To the ethereal regions of light.” Tertullian, *On the Judgment of the Lord*: “And the heavens hold high groves in the flowering season.”

681. Eugenius concludes his prayer in a similar way: “And when the final day of death has opened the urn, grant pardon to him whose guilt removes his crown.” I gathered more prayers of this kind in the preface to Prudentius, chapter 19. I add verses by Bishop Engelmodus to Abbot Rathbert in volume IX, part 2, of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, page 897, Cologne, 1618: “When the high-throned King has separated the world by the urn of judgment … But you, holy one, I beg, place yourself amid the dangers, and defend the wretched one with your merciful dew; calmly restrain the smoking vapors of punishment.” Perhaps read *auxiliique pio* (“and with merciful help”). The “bundle of evildoers” consists of demons and the impious condemned to eternal fire. Isaiah, chapter XXIV, verse 22: “And they shall be gathered together in the gathering of one bundle into the pit, and there they shall be shut up in prison.” Matthew, chapter XIII, verse 30: “Gather the weeds first and bind them into bundles to be burned”; and verse 40: “Therefore, just as the weeds are gathered and burned with fire, so shall it be at the consummation of the age.” Jerome, on the cited passage of Isaiah: “These princes, therefore, who did not preserve their rank, the Lord will gather on the day of judgment, as though bound together in one bundle, and will cast them into the pit of hell … according to what the Lord says”—Matthew, chapter XXV—“Go into eternal fire,” and so forth. Some think that the condemned will be gathered into various bundles according to the variety of their crimes: the greedy with the greedy, the lustful with the lustful, and so on.

I will say here something that I could have said in many other places, and which should by no means be omitted. Dracontius and the other early Christian poets often treat their subject in such a way that, although they use pure Latin speech, they skillfully insert and accumulate the very phrases and sentences of Holy Scripture. This is exceedingly pleasing to those endowed with a taste for ecclesiastical literature; but it greatly displeases others who have little knowledge of sacred doctrine, or do not even care to know it, because they want our poets to pursue learned fables and subjects such as they themselves read in mythological writers. Yet when Gellius, Macrobius, and others found something skillfully drawn from the ancient discipline of the augurs or from pontifical law in Virgil, they praised it to the skies. Why, then, should we not admire in Christian poets the sublime theology and hidden learning of Sacred Scripture?

I will use the example offered by this passage. Dracontius represents the final day of judgment in such a way that, on one side—namely, the left—he views the wicked as bound together in a single bundle, because they are both mixed together and prepared for the fire. He asks to be received or removed from this bundle and added to the innocent people. The saints are God’s chosen people. Psalm 148, verse 14: “A hymn for all his saints, for the children of Israel, the people who draw near to him.” God frequently calls Israel his people, and the chosen in Israel are destined for eternal life, which is also called the lot of the righteous. Psalm 124, verse 3: “For the Lord will not leave the rod of sinners upon the lot of the righteous.” Dracontius likewise has, Book II, verse 682: “Under the blessed lot.” Among the Hebrews, a lot was the portion of inheritance assigned to each person. See the note on verse 212. God himself is the inheritance of the righteous. Psalm 15, verse 5: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance and my cup; you are the one who will restore my inheritance to me.” This restoration takes place for the righteous when, after death, they enjoy God; but it will be complete only when, after the resurrection, they are blessed in soul and body.

The lot of the impious is the opposite. Ecclesiasticus, chapter VI, verse 4: “For a wicked soul will destroy its possessor, and will make him a joy to his enemies, and will lead him into the lot of the impious”—that is, into the eternal punishments prepared for the wicked. Job speaks of the same portion or lot of the impious, chapter XXIV, verse 18: “May his portion be cursed upon the earth, and may he not walk by the way of the vineyards. May he pass from snow waters into excessive heat, and may his sin reach even to hell.” Corderius discusses this passage extensively in that sense.]

682. The mention of the people in the explanation of the final judgment is skillfully made, and arises from that full knowledge of Sacred Scripture of which I was speaking just above. Julian of Toledo, *Prognosticon* III, chapter 34: “Behold,” says the Psalmist, “he will summon heaven above and earth, to distinguish his people.” What does he mean by “to distinguish his people,” unless it is to separate the good and the wicked by judgment, as sheep from goats? For then he will place the sheep on his right, but the goats on his left. The passage cited by Julian is Psalm 49, verse 4.

Many other matters come to the point of the pen, but they must be omitted; for what I have already presented is perhaps excessive, and the readers’ satiety must be remedied, if possible, since most people today are such that one may properly apply to them Martial’s verse at the beginning of Book XI: “He does not read books, but little books.”]

1. Sirm.: “Eternal King, God, author, and serene ruler.” The Azagrensis Codex agrees with the Sirmondian Codex; where they differ, I do not indicate the discrepancy. The text represents the wording of the Vatican Codex.

2. Sirm.: “whom every land trembles before.”

5. This verse and the following one are absent from Sirmondus.

[Note: [Col. 0901C]

1. Eugenius of Toledo expressed this opening in his prayer to God: “God, immense King, by whom the structure of the world stands.” This should probably be read rather than “King God, of the immense [one] upon whom the structure of the world depends.” See the preface, no. 66. Dracontius often transfers phrases and sentences from the *Poem on God* into this *Elegy*. I will point out some of them. Book II, verse 584: “God alone everywhere, source, creator, and hope of all things.” Compare the note on Book II, verse 1.

2. *Quem tremit omne solum* (“whom every land trembles before”) may perhaps seem better with Sirmondus. Thus Book II, verse 151: “You are God, before whom the earth trembles,” and Book III, verse 541: “And nature, the parent of things, serves and trembles.” But since *timet* (“fears”) is read in the Vatican Codex, this should rather be believed to have been written by the author’s own hand. “You who rule the heavens with fire,” as in Book I, verse 224: “Who cherishes heaven with kindly fire,” and so forth. See the note on Book I, verse 25.

3. Rivinus says that it should be punctuated as printed. Sirmondus had punctuated it: “Stars, fire, day, the sun, night, the moon.” This subject is treated frequently in the books *On God*. See Book I, verses 3 ff., with the notes.

5. Book III, verse 667: “You, free from time.” Dudo, Dean of Saint-Quentin, in the preface to Book I of the *Deeds of the Dukes of Normandy*: “Without beginning and remaining without end.” Perhaps it should be read: “You are without beginning and remain without end.” Certainly there is an error in the first verse of that poem, which I will correct in passing: “O threefold exemplar, three highest things, one virgin God”; read instead, “O three highest things, one powerful God.” The words are taken from the first verse of the preface to Prudentius’ *Apotheosis*: “God is three highest things, a threefold exemplar, one power.” The same Dudo, Book III, page 102: “He who remains three highest things, a threefold exemplar, one power.” Dracontius uses *seu* for *et* (“and”). See the *Digest*, Book XXXIV, title 2, law 31.

6. *Alterni* (“alternating”) and *vice* (“in turn”) denote variation and succession. Below, verse 247: “The elements alternate their changes, and the seasons change.”

7. Book III, verse 523: “Who changes the ages,” and verse 528: “He will always be the same, unchanging through every age.”

8. Rivinus conjecturally read *fueras* (“you had been”) instead of *fueris* (“you may have been”), which is in fact found in our codex. Book II, verse 585: “You will always be the same as you are and as you were before.”

9. Book II, verse 586: “Adding nothing or taking anything from you.”

10. *Nam* sometimes means “for” or “but,” as if one said, “Everything has its time, but you have no time.” For this use of the particle *nam*, see Forcellini, to whom Tursellinus’ discussion of particles comes very close, when he says that it serves to anticipate an objection.

11. In Sirmondus, *quamvis* (“although”) is nonsensical. The Vatican reading is correct: *qua vis* (“by whatever force”).

12. I do not see why an interpolator, omitting Dracontius’ excellent verse, fashioned another in its place. *Dirigere ingenia* means “to direct, guide, or shape human character and disposition.” It amplifies what he said in the preceding verse. Dracontius’ meaning is that everything that happens to a human being—prosperity and adversity alike—comes from God; human beings are good with God’s help and bad by his permission. Nor is the word *jubes* (“you command”) an obstacle: even if one wishes to understand it as God’s command concerning good and illicit actions, it can be used in the same sense as in the Second Book of Kings, chapter XVI, verse 10, where it is said of Shimei: “For the Lord commanded him to curse David.” Dracontius very often borrows not only ideas but the actual words of Sacred Scripture.]

16. In the Vatican Codex it is written *ammittunt* (“they admit”) and *fabor* (“I shall speak”).

17. Sirm.: “This law of yours, prescribed and recorded by Moses.” Azagrensis: *Mose* (“Moses”).

20. Sirm.: “A harmful guilt, binding me, dragged me to illicit things.”]

[Note: [Col. 0903B]

13. Sirmondus’ wording, whether it is the interpolator’s correction or not, is far removed from Dracontius’ subtlety. Dracontius says that when God is angry with a human being and wishes to punish him, he makes that person desire what is contrary and harmful to him. Such a desire in a person who seeks what will harm him often has no crime mixed into it. If an action or desire of this kind is tainted by wrongdoing, even then it occurs through God not willing but permitting the sin; nevertheless, he uses its effects to punish the person with whom he is angry.

14. In Sirmondus, *gerat* (“may he carry out”) refers to the human being in the preceding verse. But since the preceding verse in the Vatican Codex has *homines* (“human beings”), *gerant* (“may they carry out”) is necessary. God commands those human beings toward whom he is favorable to perform good works that will benefit them. Perhaps the reading should be *propitiusque juvas* (“and in your favor you help them”). I showed in the preface to Prudentius, no. 205, that the first syllable of *propitius* may be lengthened.

15. Juvenal, Satire 1, verse 86: “Whatever human beings do—desire, fear, anger, pleasure.” In this distich it is clear how much Dracontius has been altered for us by his interpolator. Dracontius affirms that all things are governed by divine providence—good, sad, prosperous, wicked—which arise either from God’s favor or from his anger: good and prosperous things from favor, sad and wicked things from anger. Consistent with himself everywhere, he says in Book I, verse 18: “Everything that comes—good things, joys, sadness, bitterness—descends from God’s citadel, from the seat of the Thunderer.”

What he now calls *prava* (“wicked” or “crooked”) he understands as adverse or distorted things. See Book I, verse 561. Even if you wish to explain *prava* as things done wickedly, Dracontius carefully uses the verb *admittunt* (“they admit”), which suits God’s favor when he wills something and his anger when he permits it. The interpolator wished to distinguish more clearly between what God does as author and what he merely permits, and he expressly mentioned virtues and vices, which Dracontius omitted.

Rivinus, in Sirmondus’ verses, read *tu facis, ut fiant, qui bona cuncta facis* (“you make them happen, you who make all good things”) instead of *te faciente, fiunt quo bona cuncta fiunt* (“when you act, they happen, by which all good things happen”). It would certainly not be absurd if Dracontius had shortened the first syllable of *fiunt*, as Prudentius and others did; indeed, it can be inferred from the *Books on God* that he sometimes shortened it. See the notes on Book III, verse 135. But this verse of the *Elegy* only proves that Dracontius’ interpolator made the first syllable of *fiunt* short; Rivinus’ correction is not necessary.

16. Book I, verse 10, also mentions anger under various circumstances and “God’s loving prayers,” through which he grants both adverse and prosperous things. *Admitto* has the sense of granting, approving, or permitting, and here applies commonly to both kinds of event.

17. Book II, verse 162, similarly: “With Moses as leader of the people.”

18. Here the interpolator wished to correct Dracontius, who reports the Lord’s words to Moses in this way: “For you were about to harden Pharaoh’s heart.” The interpolator did not approve this and therefore substituted: “When he says that Pharaoh’s heart had been hardened.” Certainly Exodus, chapter VII, verse 13, says: “Pharaoh’s heart was hardened.” But since earlier the Lord had said to Moses, chapter IV, verse 21: “I will harden his heart, and he will not let the people go,” Dracontius was referring to these very words, which fit his argument better. He shows that God hardens the human heart and confirms this by his example.

Such expressions often occur in Sacred Scripture. The Apostle, Romans, chapter IX, verses 17 ff.: “For Scripture says to Pharaoh: ‘For this very purpose I raised you up, that I may show my power in you, and that my name may be proclaimed throughout all the earth.’ Therefore he has mercy on whom he wills, and whom he wills he hardens.” Isaiah, chapter LXIII, verse 17: “Why have you made us wander, Lord, from your ways; you have hardened our heart so that we would not fear you.” I omit countless other examples, which must nevertheless be understood in such a way that God is in no respect believed to be the author of sin, as Calvin impiously asserted.

Jerome, on the cited passage of Isaiah, column 757, says: “Not that God is the cause of error and hardness, but that his patience, as he awaits our salvation and does not punish those who sin, may appear to be the cause of error and hardness.” Augustine, Letter 194, formerly 105, no. 14, column 719: “God does not harden by imparting wickedness, but by not imparting mercy”; and *Tractate 53 on John*, chapter XII, no. 6, column 646: “Thus God blinds and hardens by abandoning and not helping.” Saint Thomas, in his commentary on Romans, chapter IX, lecture 3, states distinctly and precisely: “It must be said that God is not said to harden some directly, as though he caused wickedness in them, but indirectly, insofar as, from what he does within or outside a person, that person takes an occasion for sin, and God himself permits this. Thus he is not said to harden by infusing wickedness, but by not adding grace.”

19. Rivinus emended Sirmondus’ wording as follows: “Thus, holy God, my tongue, committing the offense, / harmful guilt, binding me, dragged me to illicit things.” The genuine reading of the Vatican Codex is much more consistent with what precedes and follows; the interpolator deliberately altered it, deterred by the difficulty of explaining the following verse.

One should now note the change of number in *mea corda* (“my hearts”) and *nostro reatu* (“our guilt”), a usage familiar among ancient Christian writers. Victor of Vita, Book I, *On the Vandal Persecution*: “For us, to whom the custody belonged.” Barthius collects many further examples in Book XLII of the *Adversaria*, chapter 13, and testifies that this change of number was not unusual among the best writers.]

20. Dracontius accuses his own fault of excessive delay. In Book III, verse 576:

> Alas for me! What crime, committed not at one time,  
> has brought time together into one, that I may atone for my deeds?

He says that he was driven by God toward unlawful things as punishment for his long-standing crimes. But can it be said that God drives someone toward unlawful things? It can, in the same sense in which God is said to blind, harden, or hand people over to dishonorable passions. Augustine, *On Grace and Free Will*, chapter 21, no. 43, col. 742:

> It is sufficiently clear, as I think, that God works in human hearts to incline their wills wherever he wishes—either toward good, through his mercy, or toward evil, in accordance with their merits—by his judgment, sometimes manifest and sometimes hidden, but always just.

When, however, some people inferred from Augustine’s statements, as though it were absurd, that God by his power compels human beings to sin, Prosper of Aquitaine answered on Augustine’s behalf in *Response to the Gallican Chapters of Accusation*, XI:

> No Catholic has said or says that God by his power compels people living piously and rightly into sins . . . . But when we read that some have been handed over by God to their own desires, or hardened, or abandoned by him, we confess that they have deserved this through their great sins.

But, to use the distinction of Saint Thomas recently explained, God drives people toward unlawful things as punishment for preceding sins, not directly but indirectly. Indeed, the example that Dracontius presents in his own case corresponds excellently to Saint Thomas’s explanation. Dracontius had published a poem in praise of someone—I do not know whom—which deeply offended the mind of the Vandal king; through that poem he also confesses that he sinned before God. He therefore says: God, who wished to punish my old crimes, led me to despise the rewards that I might have hoped to obtain from praising the king and to seek certain dangers by praising another man.

Saint Thomas, in the passage cited, explains the matter beautifully:

> God inclines human wills toward good directly and of himself, as the agent—or author—of good; but toward evil he is said to incline or rouse people only occasionally, insofar as God places something before a person, inwardly or outwardly, which in itself tends to lead toward good, but which the person, because of his own wickedness, perversely uses for evil. This is what happened in the case of Pharaoh: when he was roused by God to protect his kingdom, he abused that arousal for cruelty.

The Fathers and teachers of the Church have always explained God’s inclining human wills toward good or evil in such a way that the freedom of indifference remains wholly intact in human beings. Dracontius, who in this passage says that God inclines hearts wherever he wishes, drives people toward unlawful things, and hardens them, openly declared what he thought about free will in Book II, verse 611:

> In our gracious God has placed everything within our own choice:  
> the human mind is free either to sin or to live holily.

369. You make human beings, when angry, desire what is contrary,

and, when propitious, command them to accomplish every good thing.

[15] Whatever human beings do—good, grievous, fortunate, or wicked—

anger and favor of God permit this to happen.

Your words, spoken through Moses the prophet, prove this:

that you were going to harden Pharaoh’s heart.

Thus God drives my heart toward unlawful things because of the guilt of our excessive delay in sinning.

The original wording of this verse had created a difficulty for the interpolator because it repeats the teaching expressed in the preceding verses: namely, that God indirectly hardens, blinds, hands a person over to his desires, and drives him toward unlawful things as punishment for sins. Rivinus, dissatisfied with Sirmond’s reading, attempted:

> Unless the Lord’s gaze from heaven had saved him,  
> harsh things would press upon him, and fortunate things would help him none.

Conjectures are often so deceptive and depart so far from the true meaning of the writings.

28. “May he deny,” “may he refuse,” “may he deny it for himself.”

30. *Species* means appearance or form. Book I, verse 338: “The appearance of a human being.” Thus *actus* (“actions”) would seem preferable in the preceding verse to *artus* (“joints”): for if he had said “the joints too are changed,” it would be unnecessary to add, “the senses are turned, and the appearance too is turned.” Yet *artus* is not wrong, because what follows explains the same thought, so that the senses correspond to the minds and the appearance to the limbs. Alcuin, imitating Dracontius in poem 178, likewise has:

> Thus the coming day will change minds and limbs.

31. It is easy to read *Babylonica*, *Babylonum*, or *Babylonis*. But I do not alter the reading of Vaticanus. Book I, verse 320: “Babylonia bore flaming and green stones.” Likewise, one could say *Babylona* or *Babylonae*. The story of Nebuchadnezzar is indicated in Book I, III, verse 646.

33. Rivinus reads *Tum diademalem* in the text and *Tum diadematam* in his notes, but he did not notice the discrepancy; hence one may doubt whether *diadematam* in the notes is an error. Certainly *diadematus* is more Latin, since Pliny used it; yet *diademalem* is more genuinely Dracontian, and Theodulf also used that word. Rivinus objects, too sharply, that Daniel does not report that horns grew from Nebuchadnezzar. The controversy is usually framed in other words: whether Nebuchadnezzar actually assumed the form of an ox, or whether, having merely become mentally deranged, he believed himself to be an ox. Daniel’s words are in chapter IV, verse 30:

> The statement concerning Nebuchadnezzar was fulfilled: he was driven away from human beings, he ate grass like an ox, and his body was wetted with the dew of heaven, until his hair grew like the feathers of eagles and his nails like those of birds.

Calmet, in the dissertation prefixed to Daniel on Nebuchadnezzar’s metamorphosis, reports and refutes various opinions collected from different sources. Bodin held that Nebuchadnezzar changed into a real bull in bodily form and mind. Others commonly think that he assumed not the soul of a bull but only its outward appearance. The more common and better-supported opinion is that Nebuchadnezzar fell into madness, through which his disturbed imagination persuaded the king that he was a bull.

35. Book III, verse 646: “After royal power he feared the ox-driver.” Dracontius seems to believe that Nebuchadnezzar was even subjected to the plow.

39. Rivinus conjectured:

> What? And the bishop too, that same father of John,  
> speaks again, although he had previously been silent.

But the old reading should be retained, since it is preserved unchanged even in the interpolated copies. Book II, verse 676: “That holy father of John incurred guilt.” In place of *deliquit* (“he sinned”) stands *liquit*, that is, “he sinned,” “he incurred guilt,” or “he failed.” Simple forms are often used for compounds, as *verto* for *everto*, and *fero* for *aufero*. A person is said to be *linqui* when his strength fails him, and Curtius used the verb actively in the present participle, Book VI, chapter 1:

> With spirit and blood alike failing him, the dying man fell upon his weapons.

40. Rivinus points out the tautology of *elinguis*, *tacente*, and *silens* (“tongue-tied,” “silent,” and “speechless”). Yet repetitions of this sort frequently occur in Dracontius.

41. Sirmond punctuates the passage so that God is called “lord”; but in that case the conjunction *que* in *dominoque* (“and lord”) would be superfluous. Dracontius calls the king “lord,” as in verse 107: “After you, supreme God, I am guilty before the king and lord,” and in verse 110: “My king and lord, always and everywhere merciful.”

42. “Worse than a dog” is a proverb. See the commentary on Prudentius, *Peristephanon*, hymn 5, verse 147, and *Apotheosis*, verse 216, “worse than a dog-soldier,” for *miles* is a Molossian dog. Rivinus rightly proves against Barthius that this passage should not be understood as referring to the lust of Eugenius. But I understand Dracontius to be the true author of the *Elegy* in place of Eugenius: for the elegy, as it appears in the Vatican manuscript, is entirely free from Eugenius’s correction.

43. The tongue of the tormented Molossian cares for its own wounds. The reading of Azagr cannot be retained.

44. Dracontius’s tongue gave the wounds because he had recited a poem that displeased the king. The tongue often stands for eloquence and sometimes for a poem. Book I, verse 168: “The laurel of the tongue pays honor, to be bestowed upon poets.” Paulinus, poem 15, birthday poem 4:

> My yearly vows return, together with the yearly  
> obligations owed by my tongue;

and poem 16, birthday poem 5:

> Joys, to which I owe the appointed gifts  
> of my servant tongue.

Therefore, even if Dracontius did not recite that poem, he rightly assigns the blame to his tongue—that is, to the poem.

45. Sirmond’s reading *tyrannum* (“the tyrant”) is clearer than *tyranni* (“of the tyrant”) in Vaticanus. Yet it can be explained as referring to the one who restored or transformed the limbs of the beast, so that the tyrant’s hand was made from the split hoof; alternatively, *post* may be an adverb.

[Col. 0907B] 46. A hoof is the horny shoe of animals that do not have toes.

48. Rivinus confidently reads:

> So that, when the tongue was changed, it might produce sounds while bound.

Sirmond’s reading means that the tongue, previously bound and mutilated, uttered sounds. The sense of our reading is that God reshaped the tongue so that it would not produce words bound and mutilated—that is, so that he would speak clearly. Pliny, Book VII, chapter 16:

> Teeth, by their arrangement, structure, and size, mutilate, soften, or blunt words.

*Mutilante sono* (“with a mutilating sound”) is used for *mutilato sono* (“with a mutilated sound”), for participles of this kind commonly have passive force. One might also read *Ne mutilata sono* (“so that they may not be mutilated in sound”).

[Col. 0908C] Perhaps Dracontius is representing the old age of Zachariah, in which words are commonly uttered broken and mutilated because the organs serving the modulation of the tongue have been largely damaged. In Book III, verse 628, he says that teeth enclosed the palate “so that the mouth might sound words well, with the organs themselves modulating them.” God therefore so reshaped the modulations of Zachariah’s tongue that, although he was an old man, he nevertheless spoke distinctly and clearly. Dracontius likewise uses *dare verba* (“to give words”) for “to speak” in Book III, verse 456.

49. Rivinus corrects Sirmond’s reading as follows:

> He himself will spare my errors, and, when he has felt shame,  
> then, in his mercy, he will look upon me and restore me.

The true reading is found in our manuscript: God himself, who caused these changes, commands and will command my king and lord to restore me to freedom.

50. Sirmond’s transposition of the words is not displeasing: “So that he may look upon me and restore me, merciful.” In sacred and secular writings, *respicere* (“to look upon”) means “to look upon in order to help,” as is well known. There seems to have been in Rome a shrine of *Fortuna Respiciens*, with many inscribed stones still surviving.

[Col. 0908D] 51. Who this grandfather and father of the king were, whose praises Dracontius wished to sing, has been discussed in the preface, nos. 106 and 111.

52. Dracontius often uses *suas* (“his own”) for *ejus* (“his”). Perhaps one should read *Postque suas proles* (“and afterward his own offspring”), or *Proque suo prole* (“and on behalf of his own offspring”). *Per* may be retained, so that the royal vows are “through his offspring.” The preposition *per* serves in oaths and can therefore also be extended to vows and wishes.

55. He gives the reason why God permits human sins, although he could prevent them: namely, so that God’s mercy may shine forth in the forgiveness of sin. Just as, in the physical order of things, God created not only good and pleasant things but also adverse and sorrowful things for the greater beauty of the world, so in the moral order he commands and enjoins good things but permits evil, so that he may produce good from evil—good that could not come about without evil. Augustine, *Enchiridion*, chapter 11:

> That which is called evil, when rightly ordered and placed in its proper position, commends good more notably, so that good may please more and be more praiseworthy when compared with evil.

See also Book II of *On Order*, chapter 4.

Apuleius, Book I of *On the World*, after the middle:

> Nature mingled dry things with wet, and fiery things with icy ones.

Air is wet, earth dry, fire hot, and water cold.

61. Ennius, Martianus Capella, and others used *doctiloquus* (“learnedly speaking”). *Doctiloquax* (“learned-speaking”) is not found in Dracontius among the older writers. Sirmond’s reading, *cognata* (“related”), may be confirmed by a similar expression frequently used by Dracontius, as I said in my note on Book II, verse 26: “It is related.” It also suits Dracontius’s style, as in verse 69, “it is said to bear harm.”

Letters have a kinship with bees because in former times they were learned on wax-covered tablets; and just as bees inflict harm with their sting but provide benefit through honey and honeycombs, so letters also possess a capacity both to help and to harm. Dracontius himself learned at times that letters can do harm. They harm not only those who are instructed in them but also others.

62. *Ut* is lengthened because of the aspiration of the following word. Sirmond’s reading is plausible, but *vulnera*, *castra*, and *favos* (“wounds,” “forts,” and “honeycombs”) seem more correct; for just as bees have their own wars, so do learned people.

In Book I, verse 567, some read *sensus primordia* (“the beginnings of sense”), for which I wrote *sensu praecordia* (“the heart of understanding”). Lucretius, Book IV, verse 534, used *primordia vocum* (“the beginnings of voices”).

Yet since *prosit* is found in the original, uninterpolated elegy, it should be retained.

Poets often use *cerva* (“hind”) without regard to gender to signify either a male or a female animal. Virgil, Book IV of the *Aeneid*, verse 69:

> Like a hind struck by an arrow.

Brouckhusius collected several similar examples in his notes on Tibullus, Book IV, poem 3, verse 13.

76. A corrupted temperateness takes days and souls away from human beings; that is, it makes human life shorter. Statius, Book II of the *Thebaid*, verse 657, uses *dies* (“day”) for “life”:

> Now throw away arms and life.

[Col. 0911C] 80. The interpolator completely reversed the meaning of this verse. *Vicibus* means “by turns,” or “alternately.” Columella, Book II, chapter 2, at the beginning:

> Qualities which, mixed with one another by turns and alternated, produce very many varieties of fields.

Dracontius therefore says that rain, snow, hail, and frost are generated by fire, vapor, and ice—or cold—alternately, or in such a way that these things are mixed and alternate in turn. Isidore, *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 33:

> The exceedingly bitter waters of the sea are lifted up by subtle vapor and aerial heat. There, boiled by the fire of the sun, they are changed into the sweet taste of rains.

And chapter 34:

> Often waters stiffened by the icy blasts of winds solidify into snow.

And chapter 35:

> The waters of the clouds are constricted by the coldness of the winds into ice and become hard.

See Ambrose, Book II of the *Hexaemeron*, chapters 3 and 4, whom Dracontius and Isidore often follow, just as he himself followed Basil.

81. Capella, Book II, in the hymn to the sun:

> For you alone traverse the middle path, giving friendly temperateness to the heavens.

By *temperies* in the plural I understand the various seasons of the year. Isidore, *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 17:

> For this reason God appointed for the sun different places and times in its course, so that, if it always remained in the same places, it would consume them by its daily heat.

But as Clement says, Book VIII of the *Recognitions*, chapter 22, the sun takes different courses so that the temperateness of the air may be distributed according to the seasons and the order of alternations and changes maintained. Ausonius, *Eclogues* 2:

> All things that we measure amid the varied activity of the world  
> are governed by the dominion of the stars; only earthly  
> limbs belong to human beings, while fortune and spirit from above  
> are governed by the sevenfold choir. But golden sun presides over them,  
> having received the governance of the shining ether.  
> Nor does he alone regulate the seasons of our life,  
> while we extend the brief span of our anxious age.  
> He is believed, by looking, to shape hidden seeds  
> and the periods of life to be spent in the mother’s womb.

This should be handled cautiously.

82. See Book I, verses 24 and following, and verse 224: “Who cherishes heaven with kindling fire,” and so forth. In Book I, verse 9, I noted that Dracontius, together with other ancient writers, takes the verb “to create” to mean “to bring forth” or “to form”; many modern writers use it to signify production from nothing. Mariana, commenting on Genesis I, verse 1, observes that the question whether creation is production from nothing should be left to theologians:

> I shall contend, he adds, that this is not signified by the force of the word and the proper meaning of the language.

The particular meaning by which philosophers and theologians define creation as the making of a thing from nothing is therefore indeed ancient, but was established for the use of the schools.

83. Book II, verse 217: “The earth gives birth,” and so forth. Compare the note on Book II, verse 89.

84. Isidore, *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 17:

> Although this good servant—the sun—was born to regulate the alternation of the seasons, nevertheless, when correction is imposed upon mortals according to God’s will, it burns more fiercely, scorches the world with more powerful flames, disturbs the air, inflicts a plague upon human beings, brings corruption upon the earth, disease upon living things, and introduces a pestilential year for mortals everywhere.

When Dracontius says “rotten sand,” he means dry and arid sand, following the ancient authorities. Propertius, Book IV, elegy 3, verse 39:

> What land is made sluggish by frost, what land is rotten from heat?

Statius, Book IV of the *Thebaid*, verse 728:

> Then the earth, rotten from the sun and dust,  
> exhales a hot cloud.

And Book III, Book IV, verse 126:

> The foul grove and rotten sands.

Lucan uses the expression in a similar sense in Book VIII, verse 83:

> And the whole of the rotten sands of the Ethiopians would dissolve.

86. *It* stands for *abit* (“goes away”). Lucretius, Book III, verse 527:

88. Rivinus, who reads with Sirmond *sidus et hoc docuit* (“the star taught this”), interprets the star as the Star of Jacob and Lucifer as Satan. Dracontius was thinking of something entirely different: he is speaking of Sirius, the star in the mouth of the Dog, and contrasting it with Lucifer. The excessive heats occur when Sirius is joined with the sun, at which time bodies commonly become afflicted with disease; for this reason some say that the constellation was called the Dog or Dog-Star.

89. The temperateness of the sky is its temperate zone or region. Ovid, Book I of the *Metamorphoses*, verse 50, concerning the zones:

> Deep snow covers two; between the two he placed as many more  
> and gave them a temperateness mixed with cold and flame.

91. Book I, verse 334: “No purer air.”

92. Rivinus conjectures: “They did not deserve together; in this way the fourth possesses it.” For air is temperate through a mixture of wet and hot, heaven—that is, fire—is dry and hot, earth is dry and cold, and water is wet and cold. That is his view, in his own words. Sirmond’s reading, “in this way when he has,” plainly appears corrupt. But Rivinus’s conjecture scarcely admits any meaning. The Vatican reading is confirmed by the Azagr manuscript, although it has the error *habet* for *habeat*. Dracontius’ meaning is: since good things are mixed with evils in all created things, when will there be a human being who is always good and stained by no crime? See the note on Book II, verse 458, and Saint Isidore’s *Synonyms*, Book I.

a gentle bird is the dove, a harsh bird is the vulture.

98. I am certain that *flans* (“casting”) comes from Dracontius’ own hand, but that others, not understanding it, corrupted the verse. Exodus XXXII, verse 4:

> When he had received them, he shaped them by casting and made from them a molten calf.

Instead of *conflare*—to soften and melt metals with fire—*flans* is used. Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 19:

> Phrygian stone, first soaked with wine, is burned and blown with bellows until it glows red.

Thus one says “cast money,” “blown bronze,” from blowing and striking bronze.

110. Octavian Augustus, as Suetonius reports in chapter 53, always detested the title “lord” as a curse and insult. As time went on, this honor was extended to priests and nobles, and later to all other people without distinction.

115. Prosper, epigram 95:

An anonymous writer in an apologetic poem for the Roman curia, Volume IV of Mabillon’s *Analecta*, verse 923:

> Here is our hand for you; who could see the secret hearts  
> of people from afar? No work of art will reveal them.  
> God alone possesses the knowledge of the mind’s secrets.

This poem is learned and elegant, beyond what one would expect from the thirteenth century in which it was written, except that it is corrupt in many places. Thus, when Aprilis Hispanus, one of the interlocutors, speaks about the effectiveness of gifts, he says:

> Moreover, I see that, if the axle is not joined,  
> the journey begun continues more slowly.

Read “if the axle is not greased,” for that is how the familiar Spanish proverb runs.

Cicero, preface to the *Paradoxa*: “But Cato, in my judgment a perfect Stoic, holds opinions which are certainly not approved by the populace.” I thought of *soli moriuntur in armis*, or *in ense*. Lucan II.263: “Who would not wish to die by that sword?” But others read *ab isto*. To you now, prince, I turn back my sails as a suppliant,

Petitioning with heart and mind, entreating with voice and hand.

Give your right hand to the wretched; grant pardon to one who begs:

[120] After so long a time, anger does not become the merciful.

For you threaten the faults of enemies with pardon,

And feast your captives with delights.

You spare the guilty, so that Christ may have something to punish,

While you reign under his vengeance and flourish under his watch.

[125] Those who perish in war die only as enemies;

The survivor of the battle, you command to live, as you yourself do.

The captive lives secure, while the rebel alone

[Col. 0915B] fears death; the quiet prey sits at rest.

You preserve lives and yourself provide food for the vanquished,

[130] So that life may not be burdensome as hunger gradually consumes it.

No one will fall under your authority, under a bloody death;

He who wishes to be yours knows that he will live.

However often the crowd of rebels persisted in arms,

It would conquer, or certainly become inactive prey.

[135] Secure and without death, an enemy gives his hands to enemies,

For you rightly preserve necks subdued beneath the yoke.

Thus the lion roars terribly, bristling, with bloody mouth,

Its claws shaken and its tooth threatening death;

More fiercely enraged, with the gleam of steel brandished,

[140] And, if there is delay, rages more fiercely still.

But if the trembling hunter lays down his spears,

And, terrified, lies prostrate, his anger soon falls away and perishes.

The predator scorns food that he himself has not made—the corpse—

And, savage though he is, forgives, as though he had received enough.

[145] He grants pardon to the prostrate man, conquered without a wound,

[Col. 0916B] lowering his eyes with a modest expression.

So your anger, O ruler—not cruel—is broken,

When the accused has confessed the crimes he committed.

By forgiving, merciful one, imitate the Thunderer,

[150] Who forgives sins and grants pardon.

The rule of a prince is like the kingdoms of heaven,

As the holy page of God sings to the peoples:

Yet in the Vatican manuscript *Non* is correctly present: “if, not having been entreated by suppliants, he had given no benefits or gifts.” Although there are two negatives, they properly belong to two different verbs. *Praestita* is used substantively. Eutropius, book VII: “He was of such gentleness and generosity [Titus] that he refused nothing to anyone … Moreover, one day at dinner, remembering that he had provided nothing for anyone that day, he said: ‘Friends, today I have lost a day.’”

188. L. Antoninus Commodus, generally meant when the name Commodus is used, was regarded as an enemy of the human race. His father was M. Aurelius Antoninus, called “the Philosopher,” whose mercy and goodness were celebrated with the highest praise by pagans. See his life by George Stanhope, prefixed to the twelve books of his *Meditations*, and book II of that same Antoninus, section 17, with Thomas Gataker’s commentary. It is the saying of this emperor that Dracontius praises.

189. “Rulers, learn from me”—you who will reign after me.

[Col. 0920C] 190. Sirmond’s interpolator changed *esse Deus* (“to be God”) into *esse Dei* (“to be God’s”). Rivinus recognized the error and corrected it to *esse Deum* (“to be God”): that is, to be such after death. The Vatican has the same meaning: “who wishes to be God.” Dracontius clearly says this in the person of a pagan emperor. After their death, emperors who had deserved well were awarded divine honors by the Senate. Above, concerning Caesar, verse 178: “From there he departs, called worthy of God’s honor.”

The precept, then, is that one must be good in life, so that at death heavenly honors may justly be accorded him; and that such honors, if they are awarded, do not suit those who were not good during life. In another sense Ausonius says in *Eclogue* 15: “It is established that some do not wish to become gods,” as the following words show: “Juturna protests: ‘Why did he grant eternal life? Why was the condition of death taken away?’”

Christian emperors abolished such vain and ridiculous apotheoses. Nevertheless, some traces remained in certain expressions, as when imperial constitutions were called *divales*. In the Carolingian books of the eighth century, Constantine and Irene are mocked because they called their rescripts *divalia*. But the same usage had earlier prevailed in Spain, as I observed in the prolegomena, section 26. A king’s decree was called a *decretum divale*, and a decree of *divalis observantia*. Justinian, speaking of the correction of the Code and its second edition, says: “We ordered that it [the Code], resting on the authority of our divinity, should be used in all judgments, only insofar as imperial constitutions are concerned.”

It is remarkable that pagan emperors, even if they believed that no god existed, nevertheless sought divine honors. Similar is the madness of certain people today who, while wishing to overthrow all temples together with religion from their foundations, nevertheless take offense if their associates or teachers—those from whom they learned impiety—are deprived after death of burial honor in temples. The solemn translation of Voltaire’s bones to the Parisian church of Saint Genevieve has just been carried out; someone mocked this ridiculous apotheosis in the following quatrain:

“Voltaire occupies royal temples—he who sought  
To drive kings from their throne and God from heaven’s height.  
Thus the dregs of mankind extort honors for themselves,  
Which they would grant neither to princes nor to heaven.”]

192. The wording in Sirmond’s text is not suitable to this passage. The Vatican’s reading is obscure, but it can be explained as follows: people who are good and gentle while they live are, after death, worthy—according even to the judgment of a pagan emperor—to be adorned with honors. Clemency therefore supplies and bestows good things upon the soul. *Praestat bona dans* means the same as “it provides and gives good things.”

[Col. 0921C] 195. “So that the peoples may call you lord with genuine feeling of heart”: make it possible for them truly to call you merciful.

196. By *merx procerum* I understand “the reputation of princes.” *Merx* is something bought and sold. But the term *mala merx* is used of any bad thing and even of a bad person; in that sense any good thing may be called *bona merx*. Accordingly, *merx* by itself here seems to mean a good or bad reputation—one that flies through the world’s speech or depends upon it. This interpretation becomes clearer from the following verses.

197. In Sirmond’s text *mors*, and in the Vatican *mos*, have no suitable meaning. I therefore read *merx*, so that the same word is repeated from the preceding verse.

199. I retain the Vatican’s wording. The glory of wars concerns both the commanders and the army. One might punctuate: “The glory of wars for commanders and peoples, the triumphs given in common, the mighty in arms divides,” so that the mighty in arms distributes triumphs among commanders and peoples. The former explanation is more pleasing.

The thought is expressed from Cicero’s speech *To Caesar for Marcellus*. At chapter 2 he says: “For some people customarily diminish military praises in words and take them away from commanders, sharing them with many [or ‘with the soldiers’], so that they may not belong exclusively to generals. Certainly, in war the courage of soldiers, the advantages of places, the assistance of allies, fleets, and supplies contribute greatly; but Fortune claims for herself, as though by her own right, the greatest part of whatever has gone well, and counts almost everything successfully accomplished as her own. But of this glory, Gaius Caesar, which you have just acquired, you have no partner,” and so forth. At chapter 4 he says: “For this achievement belongs exclusively to Caesar; the others, although accomplished under your leadership, were great indeed, but with a large and mighty retinue. In this achievement, however, you are both leader and companion.” He is speaking, as is well known, of the clemency by which Caesar spared Marcellus.

As I have read noted somewhere, Ovidius expressed the same thought in this distich: “The glory of conquering, Caesar, is shared with the soldier; Caesar, the entire glory of sparing is yours.” Dracontius imitates Cicero’s amplification, as comparison makes clear.

[Col. 0922B] 200. *In commune* is good Latin usage. Cicero, *On Invention* II.3: “We too have contributed something from our own resources for the common benefit.” Add Livy, Tacitus, Phaedrus, and others. Sirmond has *omnipotens* (“the almighty”); but *armipotens* (“the mighty in arms”) suits this passage better. The word occurs again at verse 299, *Inclytus armipotens* (“the renowned mighty one in arms”), though there it is an epithet of a certain Vandal king, whereas here it refers to God.

202. “Denies,” that is, “refuses.” Above, verse 28: “Let him refuse all prosperous things.”

203. *In arma pares* means “equal for fighting,” or “equal in battle.” *Fuimus in arma*, “we were in arms” or “at arms,” is also Latin. Varro, quoted by Nonius, section 2, no. 499: “Then there came to me those who knew that he was a little book.” Cicero, *To Atticus* X.4, near the middle: “Curio was with me for quite a long time”; and letter 18: “I had just sent you a letter about several matters when Dionysius was with me early in the morning.” The Spanish language, which preserves Latin especially faithfully, uses *fui, fue, fuimos*, etc., for “I went,” “he went,” “we went.”

204. It seems that the punctuation should be: “While I fought, companion, you return victorious from the enemy,” and perhaps *comes* (“companion”) implies a rank or dignity. But *comes* more probably alludes to Cicero’s phrase, “with a large retinue … you are both leader and companion.”

205. I would gladly read *intrat* (“enters”) instead of *instat* (“presses upon”), and I think I see here a Hispanic usage in which one who conducts his business in some matter or approaches when summoned is said to “enter.” In Latin too, *intrare* can sometimes mean “to insinuate oneself.” Cicero, *For Flaccus* 10: “I shall enter still further.” The one who conducted the affair is not present.

208. Perhaps the punctuation should be: “The horrible one, raging as he rushes into the arms of Mars, conquers amid the weapons,” that is, “rushing into dreadful arms, he conquers while roaring.”

210. Perhaps the meaning is “he accomplishes this when he subdues his own heart.” Proverbs 16:32: “The patient man is better than the strong, and he who rules his spirit than he who captures cities.” From this I conjectured: “More than a troop accomplishes he who subdues his own heart.”

212. Even in a just war the killing of a man leaves some stain upon the killer, which Dracontius calls *peccatum* (“sin”), not in the sense in which sin is a crime, but insofar as any blemish or disgrace is a sin—or, as theologians say, a failure of gentleness, from which irregularity is incurred. The Church has always abhorred the shedding of blood, as Gonzalez proves at length in his commentary on chapter *Petitio de Homicidio*, title V of the *Decretals*. The pagans held the same opinion. Aeneas says in Virgil, *Aeneid* II.717: “You, father, take the sacred objects in your hands, and the household gods. I, returning from so great a war and fresh from slaughter, must not touch them until I have washed in running water.” See Macrobius, *Saturnalia* III.1.]

214. The identity of this Ansila and the battles with the Moors indicated here are discussed in the prolegomena, sections 100 and following.

215. See the words of Cicero quoted at verse 199. Continuing to praise Caesar’s clemency, he says at chapter 2: “Indeed, Fortune herself, that mistress of human affairs, does not offer herself as a partner in this association of glory.” Victory in wars was customarily attributed to the generals’ Fortune. Barthius, in his commentary on Statius, *Thebaid* II.197, gives several examples and among them praises this passage of Dracontius, as he also does in his notes on Claudian, page 507. From Otbert’s *Life of Henry IV* he quotes: “Yet the king’s Fortune conquered,” which he considers an imitation of the ancients. Plutarch wrote one treatise on the Fortune of the Romans and another on the Fortune and Virtue of Alexander the Great.

216. He attributes the changes of peoples and the transformations of kingdoms to the order of time, evidently established in advance by God. Ecclesiastes 1:4: “One generation passes away, and another generation comes.” Franciscus Vallesio, *Sacred Philosophy*, chapter 62, thought that this passage signified the perpetuity of generations through cyclical recurrence; Cornelius à Lapide refutes him in his commentary.

217. I think *discurrere* means “to go away elsewhere,” unless one prefers to read *discedere*. The sense seems to be: if death spared the weak, neither children nor women would die. In other words, it is not the strength of powerful kings, which overthrows peoples resisting them, but the order of the ages established by God that produces or requires such changes. For even weak children and the inactive female sex perish, although wars do not—or should not—harm them.

This interpretation can be extracted from a difficult and perhaps corrupt passage, but I would prefer another.

218. Book III, verse 457: “And, as though an inactive sex, concerning women.”

219. Ecclesiastes 3:1: “For everything there is a season … a time to be born and a time to die.” Columbanus, in his letter to Hunaldus, inserts this verse of Dracontius along with others by the same author, prefacing them as follows:

“Beautifully the voice of the truthful poet sang such things,  
Counting the seasons of fleeting life and passing time:  
Time governs all things; with time all things are drawn along.”

I think that in these words Dracontius is probably called “the truthful poet,” since Columbanus immediately cites other verses of his expressing the same thought. In Patrick Fleming’s *Sacred Collectanea*, the note on Columbanus’s verses says: “POET: it is unclear who this poet is, unless perhaps by that name he intended Solomon, who transmitted the division of time that this holy man is explaining.”

Yet since Columbanus immediately presents seven or more verses of Dracontius, including some matters omitted by Solomon, there can scarcely be doubt that he called Dracontius “the truthful poet.” Nor would Columbanus’s annotator have hesitated had he understood where those verses had been taken from. A little earlier Columbanus had said:

“Let divine doctrines of the law be your riches,  
And the chaste disciplines of life taught by the holy fathers,  
All that obedient poets have written in verse.”

Here he clearly distinguishes Sacred Scripture, the holy Fathers, and Christian poets, whom he calls *vates* (“poets” or “prophets”) and from whom he draws much material.

221. *Usque senectam sine* (“even into old age without”) also occurs in book II, verse 708, and book III, verse 652. Eugenius of Toledo, however, enumerates the ages of human beings in the verses summarizing the *Hexaemeron*, quoted in the prolegomena, section 21: “There are six ages for a human being,” etc.

223. Eugenius in the passage cited also said *infantia simplex* (“simple infancy”). In Sirmond’s text, *adulterii* (“of adultery”) is an error or the correction of an interpolator. Dracontius certainly wrote *adultorum* (“of adults”), for he contrasts infancy and old age with youth. Isidore distinguishes the six ages of man in *Etymologies* XI.2 as follows: infancy, childhood, adolescence, youth, maturity, and old age. Infancy extends to the seventh year, childhood to the fourteenth, adolescence to the twenty-eighth, youth to the fiftieth, maturity—which is the decline from youth into old age—to the seventieth year, and old age thereafter until death.

Eugenius of Toledo calls the fifth age *senecta gravis* (“burdensome old age”) and the sixth *senium* (“extreme old age”). He likewise calls the third age *adulta* (“mature adulthood”); but the noise and uproar of adults mentioned by Dracontius suit youth better. See the prolegomena, section 24.

224. *Senectus*, with its final syllable shortened, as *palus* in Horace and *servitus* in Paulinus. In the elegies published under the name of Cornelius Gallus or Gallus Maximianus, elegy 1: “Ailing old age has continual groans.”

225. “He does not bear childish things as a *catulastra*.” In the Vatican manuscript the earlier form is *catuiaster*, not clearly written, from which *catulaster* seems to have arisen.]

225. In the Sirmond manuscript, *catulastra gerit* is an error that has exercised the ingenuity of several scholars. Rivinus says that Barthius wrote in the margin (I think in his notes on Claudian, p. 507) that *catulastra* means “rattle,” but regarded the passage as abandoned. Baunius, in the edition of all Sirmond’s works which he prepared at Paris, had interpreted *catu astra* as little dogs made of paper or wood, such little figures as boys are accustomed to amuse themselves with; [Col. 0924D] but in the preface to vol. II he says that later, in the Latin–Greek glossaries of Philoxenus and other ancient writers collected by Charles Labbe, he found *catulaster* Βούπαις, “a large boy,” and *catulester* πάλληξ, “a young man,” leaving the matter to the reader’s judgment. Forcellinus, under the word *catlaster* in his *Lexicon*, observes that this word was restored to Vitruvius by Turnebus, *Adversaria*, book XXIV, chapter 7, in place of what was read as *catastos* in book VIII, chapter 4; and that the form *catlastri*, found in Charisius, book I, is contracted from *catulaster*, which Priscian, book III, lists among diminutives formed from *catulus*. Forcellinus explains *catulaster* as “a larger boy, a young adolescent,” and says that from it *catulastra, -ae* was formed, meaning “a girl already grown and capable of intercourse with a man”; thus he understands this passage of Dracontius:

> “A *catulastra* does not produce childish things.”

But Rivinus had corrected it long before as:

> “The *catulaster* does not perform childish acts,”

having observed that Desiderius Heraldus, *Adversaria*, book I, [Col. 0925B] had correctly restored Βούπαις, *catulaster*, in the Greek–Latin glosses of Stephanus, where *carulaster* had been read. Βούπαις means a large and stout young man, almost a young bull or “son of an ox”: this is what the Latins express by *catulaster*. In this verse of Dracontius, childhood and adolescence are compared with one another.]

A mature age is *gravitas*, or the decline from youth into old age; trembling old age is extreme and decrepit old age, [Col. 0925D] or senility. Understand *tractat* as “he manages affairs, cases, matters, and the state,” whose administration belongs chiefly to men already mature.

233. Solomon speaks similarly of the sun in Ecclesiastes, chapter I, verse 5:

What he says, “to lose their courses,” means either that no trace of the course remains after the sun has withdrawn, or that the sun completes its course in such a way that, as though it had not completed it, it again traverses the paths already passed. The thought is similar in verse 250:

235. Or “fails,” that is, “diminishes”; the subject is not an eclipse, which is ordinarily called a failure, as is clear from the examples that follow.

See Dracontius, book II, verses 10 and 54, and book III, verse 296, with the notes. Barthius, *Adversaria*, book LVI, chapter 1, explaining Claudian, book I *Against Rufinus*, at the beginning:

> “And the turns of light and night,”

declares with great elegance and learning that this is so expressed because the alternations have been assigned, as it were, and have never failed to be observed. He confirms this with many similar examples and cites this verse from Columbanus, whom he calls an ancient and reliable author among the poets, unless such verses are attributed to so great an author spuriously or genuine passages are badly corrupted. [Col. 0927C] He notes that the published books incorrectly print *alimenta vices*, “the nourishment of alternations,” instead of *elementa vices*, “the elements’ alternations.” Moreover, it has been proved in the prologue, no. 8, that Columbanus took this very verse, together with many others, from Dracontius. Dracontius, for his part, often uses the word *vices* to indicate the succession of things and times. Arnulf of Luxeuil, *On the Renewal of Spring*, writing from Dracontius or Columbanus—for the monastery of Luxeuil was founded by Columbanus—writes:

> “The elements alternately change both their work and their powers.”

See also the author of the *Panegyric to Piso*, verse 132:

> “Nature herself undergoes alternations  
> And orders her varying courses,” etc.

252. One might read: “Time and autumn; times have winters.” Up to this point we have made use of the Azagr manuscript; and the passage itself requires us to offer special thanks to the most eminent Cardinal Lorenzana, who not only arranged the magnificent edition of the Toledan Fathers, but also was the first to publish, for the great benefit of ecclesiastical scholarship, ancient monuments of this kind from the innermost recesses of the libraries of Spain. What reason, then, should I suppose—or rather say, since several reasons come to mind—caused the author of the *Paris Ecclesiastical News* in 1788 to attack this distinguished prelate and even dare to prescribe to him the manner and method by which he might better spend his time? He took the opportunity for abuse from an address published in 1778—not 1787, as the Paris *News* reports—to the Catholic king Charles III by the archbishop, in the name of the Royal Assembly of Theologians of Madrid, established to promote the mystery of the Immaculate Conception of the Virgin Mary. In this assembly the author of the *News* foolishly thought and declared that the University of Alcalá must be intended, because, supposedly, there is no university at Madrid. I could readily persuade myself that this pious and learned address, everywhere received with the greatest applause, *On the Present Cult of This Holy Mystery—the Immaculate Conception—and on the Pious Opinion Concerning It, Deservedly to Be Advanced to a Further Degree of Certainty*, had offended the writer of the *News*. But I suspect that other causes of this kind lay behind his offense, and I have no desire even to investigate them. I would nevertheless ask him whether he also thinks it worthy of reproach that the most eminent cardinal, disregarding his advice, ordered printed for the common benefit of the people, in this very year 1791, the pastoral instruction of his predecessor, the archbishop of Toledo, Valero; and in the preceding year, the *Practice of Providing Spiritual Assistance to Those Afflicted in Their Final Agony*, by Luis de la Puente.

265. Thus I restore the corrupt passage. Up to this point Dracontius has proved by enumerating events that the changes of kingdoms must be attributed to the order of time, which drives everything and with which all things are drawn along. He now returns to his argument: he says that he deserves pardon not only because it is fitting for a merciful king to spare a prostrate defendant, but also because Dracontius himself must not be judged worthy of the anger of so great a king.

272. I read *nebrida membra*. *Nebros* (νεβρός) is a young deer, and also a doe. Hence *nebris, nebridos*, a garment made from the skin of a fawn or doe, worn by Bacchus, the Bacchantes, and hunters. Dracontius forms the adjective *nebridus* from *nebros*. I had conjectured *grandia membra*, “large limbs.”

273. I do not know who has written that the leopard does not bite again after its first wounds. Nevertheless, in Gesner and Jonston’s *History of Quadrupeds* one may read of certain examples of gentleness among leopards.

274. “With pious savagery” is an opposition of terms, such as Dracontius often employs.

[Col. 0930B] 275. I had thought that *balantibus* should be restored in place of *pastoribus*, for substantivally *balantes* means “sheep” in Virgil, Lucretius, and others. But I retain *pastoribus*, in the sense in which Claudian, describing a lion that vents its rage upon the shoulders of a heifer, adds in book II of *The Rape of Proserpine*, verse 213:

> “And he scorns the feeble anger of shepherds.”

[Col. 0930C] 276. *Flammeus*: thus “flaming eyes.” Dragons have extremely sharp vision, and are therefore called *dracones* from δέρκω, “I see.” It would be sound, and perhaps correct, to read *despicit et talpis*, “and he despises moles,” with *irasci*, “to be angry,” understood.

279. Book II, verse 488:

> “Or if it has lightning, it touches mountains and summits,  
> And with its head the trees, cedars and lofty cypresses.”

See the note. Ovid, *Remedies for Love*, verse 369:

> “The winds blow through the highest places;  
> The lightning sent from Jupiter’s right hand seeks the summits.”

280. Seneca, *Hercules on Oeta*, verse 493:

> “Where lofty Pindus inserts its head among the stars.”

Silius Italicus, book VI, verse 2:

> “Cloud-bearing mountains and rocks threatening heaven.”

281. See book II, verses 419 and following.

283. By *liberos* I understand Dracontius’ children, on the basis of book III, verse 675:

> “Happy in numerous offspring,”

as I explained in the note.

290. “The work of piety” occurs again at verse 298. Book II, verse 50:

> “Whatever the work of piety possesses.”

“The gentle name” and “the pious name” at verse 288 mean the same thing, namely, the name of one who is merciful or mild.

[Col. 0930D] 291. Matthew, chapter V, verses 43 and following; chapter XVIII, verses 15 and following; Luke, chapter XVII, verses 3 and following.

293. From Matthew, chapter V, verses 44 and following:

> “Do good to those who hate you … so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven, who makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil and sends rain upon the just and the unjust. For if you love those who love you, what reward will you have? Do not even the tax collectors do this?”

295. For confirmation of this phrase, see the note on verse 26 of book II.

296. The sick implore the help of physicians. Matthew, chapter IX, verse 12:

> “Those who are well have no need of a physician, but those who are sick.”

297. Ovid, *Tristia*, book II, verse 31:

> “But if I had not sinned, what could you grant?  
> My fate supplied you with the material for pardon.”

299. Some father or grandfather of Guntharius is praised here. Re-read chapter 11 of the prologue. Although the speech is directed only to the king, the name *vestrae* is used, [Col. 0931B] a usage that had already begun at that time and later passed into the vernacular languages. In vernacular sacred translations the old custom lingered longer, though it too gradually disappeared. Vernetus published nine letters concerning the formula to be used in translations, especially sacred ones, *Tu* or *Vos*. He chooses the former because it is older and more dignified.]

He has ordered the seasons to be observed, and God himself has done so.

Christ, working miracles, sought the hour;

The holy suffering of the cross awaited its hour.

[265] Why should you be angry with me? Why should I, in such a way,

Be judged more worthy of the anger of so great a king?

When, with an eagle flying through the ether in pursuit of prey,

Was a sparrow, swallow, or woodpecker its prey and food?

When did the hunger of a ravenous lion, however famished,

[270] Choose the hare as food for its jaws?

It devours magnificent bulls of enormous body,

399 And eagles seize the doe’s limbs with their talons.

Once angered, the leopard grants pardon after its wounds,

And in its kindly savagery does not inflict repeated bites.

[275] The excellent tigress scorns becoming angry with shepherds,

[Col. 0929B] And the dragon, flaming in its face, scorns moles.

Lightning does not strike creeping grasses upon the earth,

Nor does forked flame burn modest willows.

But it strikes lofty cedars that beat against the clouds,

[280] And vast mountains, rocks close to the pole.

Only their own guilt troubles guilty sinners;

[Col. 0930A] Behold, harmful punishment also assails the innocent.

If I myself have sinned, what fault, I ask, belongs to my people,

Whom cold and want of food assail together?

The guilty perished in the flood, while the pious suffered no harm;

400 Good Lot, and the just man, was taken away from Sodom.

If there had been no sins of the human race,

From where could God have obtained the name “pious”?

But because he grants pardon to peoples, releasing sins,

[290] He bears the gentle name through the work of piety.

If a brother is commanded to grant pardon to his brother,

What of a king toward his subjects, and a master toward his servants?

If the Lord had given the sun and rains to the just,

But not given them to the unjust, what piety would there have been?

[295] [Col. 0930B] He does not seek pardon who is proved to have sinned in nothing;

Do not the hands of a physician seek weakened limbs?

The guilt of the accused supplies you with material for praise,

And the work of piety gives titles to fame.

Renowned and mighty in arms, the source of your piety,

[300] [Col. 0931A] [Note: [Col. 0931A]

302. Vatican manuscript: “Here the guilty and learned Vincomalus had overcome the wicked.”

313. Vatican manuscript: “if, touching the horn.”

316. In the Vatican manuscript it seems to read *abscisi* instead of *abscissi*, [Col. 0932A] or perhaps *abscissa*. This is the final verse of this elegy in the Vatican manuscript, to which are added the words: “The Satisfaction of Dracontius ends,” etc.]

[Note: [Col. 0931B]

300. Ovid, book I of the *Letters from Pontus*, elegy 6, verse 5:

> “Unlovely savagery does not enter into such character,  
> Nor is it less at odds with your studies.  
> Through the liberal arts, for which you have the greatest concern,  
> Hearts grow gentle and harshness flees.”

And book III of the *Art of Love*, verse 545:

> “Clearly we are softened in spirit by peaceful art,  
> And character proceeds in harmony with study.”

The same thought occurs in book II of the *Letters from Pontus*, elegy 9, verses 47 and following. Bacon of Verulam, book I of *The Advancement of Learning*, observes that superficial knowledge tends rather to bend things in the opposite direction.

302. Vincomalus, who later became consul with Opilio, or another man somewhat older than he. Compare the cited chapter 11 of the prologue.

303. Sins do not injure God, who can never be injured, as Jerome says in his commentary on Jeremiah, book II, chapter 7. In a certain sense, however, sin is an offense against God through the sinner’s intention, though not in its effect, as theologians distinguish it. See also the interpreters on Job, chapter XXXV, verse 6:

> “If you sin, what harm do you do to him?”

304. The same syntax occurs above at verse 100:

> “If the guilty mind of the deed should repent of the crime.”

305. “Releasing sins,” as at verse 289, *peccata relaxans*, meaning “forgiving sins.” So one says *relaxare claustra*, “to loosen bolts,” and *fores*, “doors.” The ecclesiastical power of binding and loosing is expressed by the symbol of the keys.

306. Taken from the Lord’s Prayer.

307. From Matthew, chapter XVIII, verses 21 and 22, and Luke, chapter XVII, verse 4. For the sacred interpreters explain the Savior’s words so that a finite number is used for an infinite one, and pardon is granted as many times as there has been fault.

310. Perhaps from Wisdom, chapter XV, verse 2:

> “For even if we sin, we are yours.”

The same thought may be drawn from several other passages of Scripture, such as Psalm 119, verse 94, and Psalm 138, verses 8 and following, and Isaiah, chapter XLIV, verse 5.

313. I read *cornea pulsans*, “striking with its horn”; *palpans*, “touching,” can scarcely be explained in any useful sense. Silius Italicus, book XVII, verse 136:

> “Striking the air with raised hooves.”

Ovid, book VI of the *Metamorphoses*, verse 218:

> “The field beaten by unremitting horses.”

Lucan, book VI, verse 83, concerning horses:

> “The horny hoof has struck apart the leafy field.”

314. Ennius, in Macrobius, book VI of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 1:

> “The hoof shakes the whole earth,”

and elsewhere:

> “With loud resounding the hoof shakes the earth,”

and elsewhere:

> “With a beat the hollow hoof tramples the earth.”

Virgil, book VIII, verse 596:

> “With pounding sound the hoof shakes the crumbling field.”

Both are speaking of horses. Pliny, book VIII, chapter 45:

> “With the horse pounding beside it.”

316. In the manuscript, the letters having faded—as commonly happens on the final pages of ancient manuscripts—it can scarcely be read whether the word is *abscisi* or *abscisa*. The meaning is clear: the rider corrects the horse’s fault with a whip, and does not cut off its legs and feet. It is also clearly read after this verse:

> “The *Satisfaction of Dracontius* ends,”

etc., in the form of lettering that I reproduced engraved in copper at p. 59. Since it is therefore completely certain that Dracontius is the author of this elegy, there can be no doubt that he is likewise the author of the three books of the poem *On God*. Of both poems we may affirm what Terence says in the prologue to the *Andria* concerning Menander’s comedies, the *Andria* and the *Perinthia*:

> “Whoever knows either one correctly will know both.”

Their subject matter is not very different. I would add that their diction and style are also similar.]

And learned, with a disposition inclined toward pardon,

401 He said, “I do not pardon the man, but his language deserves it:

This guilty and learned man was Vincomalus.

Sins do not injure God, but the sinner is injured,

Unless, grieving over his sins, he repents of his crime.

[305] He who asks God according to this law to release sins

Must himself also everywhere spare his own guilty subject.

The holy law did not say that guilt should be pardoned once only,

[Col. 0932A] But that as often as there is guilt, so often there should be pardon.

I shall speak the pious words of the prophet to my ruling lord:

[310] ‘Though I have sinned, I am nevertheless your own.’

Grant pardon, have mercy, I beg; come to the one who begs:

Let the former blows, chains, and hunger be enough.

If, while the rider is making his way, a horny hoof

402 Of a galloping horse should shake him,

The fault is corrected by the blow, the whip administering punishment,

[316] But the legs and feet do not at the same time lie severed.”

# INDEXES OF PRUDENTIUS

[Note: These indexes refer to the works of Prudentius in PL 59 and 60.]

[Col. 0931]

## INDEX OF WORDS AND PHRASES

A. designates the *Apotheosis*; C., the *Cathemerinon*; D., the *Dittochaeon*; H., the *Hamartigenia*; P., the *Peristephanon*; Ps., the *Psychomachia*; S. I., *Against Symmachus*, book I; S. II., *Against Symmachus*, book II; Pr., the Preface; Prol., the Prologue of the Poems; Ep., the Epilogue. A Roman numeral after C. gives the number of the hymn in the *Cathemerinon*; after P., the number of the hymn in the *Peristephanon*; an Arabic numeral gives the verse.

# INDEX OF SUBJECTS AND NAMES OCCURRING IN THE POEMS OF PRUDENTIUS, THE ANCIENT GLOSSES, THE PROLEGOMENA, AND THE COMMENTARIES

## A

A in Greek compounds, as in *atomus*, is shortened, 484. Aaron, with the second syllable long, 662. Aaron’s rod, ibid. Abacuc, Habacuc, 279. Annibal Abbot Olivieri Giordani, 1050. Abbo, 197. Abdias, 1192. Abdicatus soli — “withdrawn from the sun,” 1208. Abel, 495, 1134. Whether he was killed with a hoe, 496. Abel and Cain, soul and body, 667. Paintings of Abel in cemeteries, 496. *Abire ad plures* — “to go to the greater number,” 1029. *Abjunctus* — separated, 835, 922 ff. *Abluiturus*, *abluturus* — about to wash, 462. From where *aboleo* is derived, 230. To abolish death, 352. *Abolla palmata* — a palm-banded cloak, 746 ff. Aborigines, 787. Abraham, 405, 577 ff. Abraham’s bosom, 565. What Abraham’s 318 home-born servants signify, 3, 163. Abraham received the Lord, 668. Abraxaean, 704. Absalon, Abessalon, 542. *Abscidere* — to cut off, 483. *Abscisus*, *abscissus* — cut off, 976. *Absis*, *absida* — apse, 270, 633. Abstinence from meat, 145 ff., 261. In Spain, 277. ## D

Dactylic poem, 198. Dactylic Archilochian verse, 202, 1230. *Daemonium* with a short first syllable, 176, 181, 188, 840ff. The head of vices, 515. Sent into the swine, 682. Under the name of Trivia, 730.

Whether they roam in the air at night and are frightened by cockcrow, 238. Whether they enjoy frequenting unclean places, 349.

Demon-possessed persons, 885. Why they inhabited tombs, 341. Demonic, 948. Daha, Daa, 834. Saint John Damascene, 90, 348. Saint Damasus, 142, 859, 946, 1003, 1027, 1194ff. His verses, 57, 60, 71. To condemn, 548. Whether the number of the damned is small, 148, 150. Their seat, 566; see *Punishments of the damned*. Those condemned to death drank myrrh-flavored wine, 1029.

He strikes the asp, 692. *Defit*, *deest* (“is lacking”), 281, 1228. *Defuga*, 204, 877. *Defundo*, *diffundo*, 681.

According to what custom the bodies of the dead were formerly buried, 133. *Dehonesto* with a long first syllable, 1130. The unmarried Virgin Mother of God, 453. *Deitas* used for divinity, 404. *Delibuta* with a long second syllable, 176, 182, 185, 610. *Delicia*, *deliciae*, 722f. *Delitare*, 514. Delos, 1238. Delphi, 804, 1238. Bishop Delphinus, 747. Deuteronomy, chapter II, 1028; XIX, 553. There is one God, not the only being, 588. His nature, 1095f. Fiery, 349, 920. Boundless and present everywhere, 102, 256, 727. God used for the ark of the covenant, 654. The unknown God of the Athenians, 690. God’s hand and fingers: in what sense, 489. God called “mind,” 1231. ## DRACONTIUS

Dedication letter, 595.

Prolegomena to the poems of Dracontius, 599.

Chapter I: Dracontius’ first mention among ancient writers. Saint Isidore’s testimony concerning him. Saint Columbinus borrowed several verses from Dracontius, ibid.

Chapter II: Saint Eugenius of Toledo corrected Dracontius’ *Hexaemeron*, 604.

Chapter III: Saint Ildefonsus’ judgment concerning Dracontius as corrected by Saint Eugenius. Dracontius’ work listed among the books of the tenth century, 613.
